# TO THE REVEREND IN
## CHRIST FATHERS AND
## LORDS, LORD FREDERICK OF SCHUT-
### TERN; LORD LAWRENCE OF ETTENHEIM,
### *Münster and Altorff; and Lord LOUIS of Gengen-*
### *bach, Abbots, my lords to be honored with all*
### *reverence.*

---

The **CABALISTIC** <term>Kabbalah (Cabala): A traditional system of Jewish mysticism and scriptural interpretation that seeks to uncover hidden meanings within the Hebrew Bible.</term> discipline—which once held the highest admiration among the Hebrews, and in which they believed a perfect and hidden understanding of all things and arts was contained—now lies almost entirely in oblivion, Reverend Fathers in Christ and respected Lords, neglected and abandoned by everyone. I believe this has happened for two reasons: First, because those who applied their efforts to this excellent art either handed down many things foolishly or disfigured it with superstitions and trifles; and second, because others, seeing the corrupted art set before them, and having achieved no understanding of the art themselves, failed to exercise judgment. They did not distinguish the correctly preserved truths from the errors; indeed, even some things written without fault were perverted through slander by overly clever and malicious interpretations. 

And so it happened that, while many slandered this excellent subject and no one defended it, the art itself gradually grew obsolete. Oppressed by the injustices of men, it lived as an exile from the public light—all the more so because it had gained troublesome and ridiculous patrons, while those who attacked it flourished in the highest reputation and dignity. 

But in my judgment, there was certainly a great deal of fault on both sides: both from those who taught and sprinkled this divine study with their own errors, obscuring the splendor of a praiseworthy science; and from the rest, who never spent any labor in learning this unknown matter, but preferred to mock and slander rather than moderate the ignorance of the interpreters so that it would not harm the art itself. 

I have always been of this opinion, even when I first approached the study of the **KABBALAH** almost as a boy: that the vices of the practitioners or the insults of men should not be held as a strike or prejudice against an honorable discipline. Later, however, when I perceived what was contained within the veils of this study, and what great power it held for perceiving the most hidden and greatest...

<summary>In this dedication, the author addresses several prominent Abbots, lamenting that the study of Kabbalah has fallen into disrepute due to both the poor quality of its practitioners and the unfair prejudices of its critics.</summary>
<keywords>Kabbalah, Jewish mysticism, dedication, Frederick of Schuttern, Lawrence of Ettenheim, Louis of Gengenbach, scholarly defense, religious philosophy</keywords>

# P R E F A C E.

...to perceive things which nature wished to be separated and removed from the common understanding of men: I began to be of a more certain and confirmed mind. I no longer considered what was being disputed against this art by its adversaries—even though they were holy and most serious men—nor what had been inserted into the books by foolish teachers. Instead, I looked toward this: that I might draw out the art, free from all mixture and plainly pure, from these impure books; nor in that undertaking would I allow any hindrance to intervene. Since I could not do this without the aid of commentaries, I collected as many books as possible written in Hebrew and Latin concerning the **KABBALAH** <term>Kabbalah (Cabala): A mystical Jewish tradition of interpreting the Bible through secret or symbolic meanings.</term>. I will not say here how far I have progressed in that discipline, or whether I have achieved through my diligence and industry that which I had intended. This I will say: that I have persisted in the opinion once embraced, and that friends, who were not ignorant of the number of books in my possession, have demanded in daily conversations and letters that I should bring either all or some of them into the public eye, and illuminate this now obscure art with new lights. But the authority of my friends and their persistent demands could not move me—for I foresaw the deep-seated hatred already conceived in the minds of all, the envy, and the great offense to the common customs of men—until at last a certain supreme and foremost **Prince of Germany** <note>This likely refers to a patron of the work, possibly the Holy Roman Emperor or a high-ranking Duke who supported Renaissance humanism.</note>, by his own right which he holds over me, specifically demanded that I turn my thought and care toward publishing those books, and that I should no longer allow myself to be deterred by the ill-will of men.

For then, that which until then I was not only not doing, but not even thinking of entertaining in my mind without the mandate of a Prince—and especially *that* Prince—I began no longer to fear but to despise the common judgments which very many are accustomed to make about the **KABBALAH**, whether from the fault of writers or the thoughtlessness of others. Rather, I began to consider how I might not disappoint the expectation of so great a Prince, rather than what might be insultingly objected by the malevolent against my authority or the authority of the **ART**. However, lest I should sail out into the tumultuous sea with all sails set at the first attempt, I wished, upon leaving the harbor, only to row a little and make a trial of how great the tide of the sea and the agitation of the waves would be.

Therefore, I have now collected into the first **VOLUME** <note>original: TOMVM</note> those writers who, having professed the Christian religion, lived religiously and honorably; and whose books, for that reason, no one can easily detest as "Jewish ravings." I have added a few Hebrew authors, but only those who have recorded nothing foreign to Christian piety in their writings and books, and who have not entangled their works with excessive trifles. And so that I might...

# PREFACE.

# ):( 3

...so that our undertaking and purpose might be established and protected from detraction, we have added all the works of **PAULUS RICIUS** <note>Paulus Ricius (Paolo Riccio) was a 16th-century Jewish convert to Christianity, physician to Emperor Maximilian I, and a central figure in the Christian Kabbalah movement.</note> and certain other things. These do not in themselves encompass the tradition of the **KABBALAH** <term>Kabbalah (Cabala): A mystical Jewish tradition of interpreting the Bible through secret or symbolic meanings.</term>, but nevertheless they have flowed from the **KABBALAH** as if from a most fertile fountain of many arts and the best subjects. They are either drawn from the mysteries of our faith, or taken from the pagan philosophers, serving as examples to illustrate the truth of the art and to demonstrate the agreement between different disciplines. These and similar writers, with this purpose and by that command, I have gathered into one book. Obeying the will of my Prince, I have ordered them to be published by public types <note>original: "publicis Typis", meaning printed by a press</note> so that they might be seen together. I did this so that they might mark the beginning of our voyage <note>original: "remigationis," literally "rowing," a common nautical metaphor for an intellectual project</note>; and then, if this first sailing succeeded according to our intention, the **KABBALISTS** of the primary traditions from Hebrew literature would follow in a second **VOLUME**.

From this effort, Reverend Fathers and Lords, this **Volume** emerged. I wished it to appear in public under your most illustrious names, and perhaps not without good reason. For to whom should I consecrate a **THEOLOGICAL** book so full of mysteries rather than to you? Although I deliberated long and hard, and looked around attentively with my mind at every possibility, I could not find a better choice. You are not only **THEOLOGIANS**, but are placed among **THEOLOGIANS** in a sublime and most ample rank of dignity. You are the overseers of **THEOLOGIANS** and of the mysteries handed down in our Christian religion. The knowledge of such matters is yours, and most proper to your high office. Because these things are quite hidden and enfolded, and not subject to the common understanding of men, they pertain to you all the more: so that you, who surpass others in the excellence of your honor, might also surpass them in skill and in the perception of obscure yet praiseworthy things.

Furthermore, recently I encountered you—venerable **FATHERS**—by chance, Father **FREDERICK**, in your most ancient and religious monastery. You all bestowed upon me the greatest kindness, and in our first meeting and conversation, you gave many illustrious signs of singular goodwill. I judged that the duty of my office required me to be a grateful and pious man in the memory of those merits. Because I seemed able to testify to this in no other way now than by sending this book, I felt I must do so. I wished to address all three of you, my **FATHERS** and **LORDS**, into whose goodwill I had entered in a single banquet and a single conversation, with one Preface. Thus, I give this **VOLUME** into the sight of men under your names, especially since I hoped that you, receiving it from me with the best and most clear...

# PREFACE.

...it was done with such a favorable mind toward you, that you might bear it kindly and conveniently.

Receive therefore, Reverend FATHERS, this **MYSTICAL BOOK** inscribed to you, a treasure of hidden and profound knowledge. Do not only store it in your libraries—which, having been received from your ancestors, are being greatly expanded by you—but when you find time free from your duties, read it. Seek out what this doctrine is that they call **KABBALISTIC** <term>Kabbalistic (Cabalasticam): Relating to the Kabbalah, a Jewish mystical system that Pistorius and other Renaissance scholars sought to integrate into Christian thought.</term>. Impart some of your leisure and study to the investigation of our cause. Judge whether the **KABBALAH** has been condemned and proscribed rightly or through some error; and when it appears to have been treated with injury, come to the aid of this innocent doctrine. Grant your patronage—which cannot be anything but very great—to this most excellent matter. As for me, do not hesitate to treat me with that benevolence with which you once received me, and to enroll me among those who love you reverently; expect from me and my study everything that can be hoped for from a man most devoted to you.

As for the rest, I desire that you live for a very long time, placed by the grace of **GOD** in a course of excellent and flourishing fortune, and overflowing with all things to be desired. From Karlsburg <note>original: "Carolicastro". This refers to the residence of the Margrave of Baden-Durlach.</note>, on the Kalends of March <note>March 1st</note>, in the year 1591 <note>original: "CIO IO XCI", a Roman numeral variation for 1591.</note>.

->Your Reverend Lordships,<-

->*Zealously honoring and*<-
->*loving you,*<-

->*Johannes Pistorius of Nidda,*<-
->*Doctor of Medicine and Counselor to the*<-
->*Marquises of Baden.*<-

The opinion of **Averroes**, who thought that the immense beauty of God is imprinted immediately upon any parts of both the corporeal and angelic world, without the work of any intermediary being required: and that such an impression exists as more illustrious or obscure,

according as created things either approach closer to the Creator himself or recede further from him: and that from a clearer or thinner impression of the divine form in created things, there proceeds a more vehement or sluggish love, as well as an observed desire for divine beauty, whether more intense or relaxed, in them 528.
The opinion of **Avicenna, Algazel, Rabbi Moses** <note>Maimonides</note>, and several others, who all unanimously wished that love and that supreme beauty run down and flow from God through all the intermediate intelligences, and through all the celestial spheres step by step and in a certain succession, all the way to doctrine; and from there, in the manner of a certain circle, it ascends again through all the intervening forms step by step, and with the same succession retained, until it finally returns to God himself 526.

### P R E F A C E.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' containing two putti figures amidst foliage and floral patterns.</image-desc>GOD, the highest sower of all things, the craftsman of the world, and the celestial husbandman, who—from the sublime and inaccessible throne of His glory—looks upon the fleeting, decaying, and wretched race of mortals with eternal and inscrutable providence and compassion, and into them He pours the seeds of every kind of gift and virtue from the inexhaustible storehouse of His bounty. He Himself nourishes and cherishes those same seeds, and grants them growth. This is done under this law: that a diligent and watchful tiller of the earth be present to plant, to water, and to prepare the field of his Master for bearing, cultivating it with anxious labor and diligence. Otherwise, no assurance of fruitful growth, nor any hope, could be given or occur. For we are His helpers <margin>1 Corinthians 3.</margin> <note>referring to 1 Cor. 3:9: "For we are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s field, God’s building."</note> and His field of agriculture (as the herald of faith and truth speaks), who obtain fruit and reward according to our labor and the zeal of our diligence. Therefore, since this celestial field and estate—which the Celestial Husbandman, God Himself, had once entrusted to His faithful workers when it was cultivated and flourishing with faith, religion, and moral integrity—now (alas!) lies almost entirely uncultivated, squalid, and nearly deserted, the seed already cast into it either puts forth no sprout at all, or produces a thin and defective one, or bears a degenerate crop of weeds and tares. Or, if it produces anything noble, it is very meager due to the sloth and inactivity of the tiller. And since the burden falls upon the faithful and skillful worker to watch wakefully and look around, so that if he sees anything rough, dry, thorny, or poorly cultivated in the field committed to him which does not sufficiently answer his Master's wish, he may providently prepare, support, clear, and fertilize it. Therefore, it seemed... <note>The text breaks here at the end of the page.</note>

Ricius dedicates the work to Emperor Charles V and King Ferdinand I, lamenting the current neglected state of spiritual and moral life.</summary>

it is also required of me, having been called into this most sacred company of farmers, to expend some measure of owed labor and study, so that I may avoid the mark of the lazy and wicked servant (who hides the talent <note>original: "minam"; referring to the 'mina' or talent of money in the biblical parable of the faithful servant.</note> committed to him in the earth) and flee the penalty; and so that from that highest celestial God, the husbandman of the land of the living (who, to restore the cultivation of His field, did not spare even the innocent blood of His only-begotten Son), I may bring back some wage and celestial reward. Furthermore, since many of those things which pertain to the work undertaken suggest great and hidden mysteries of truth, which the dull and boastful ignorance of some, and the venomous
<margin>Ecclesiastes 10.</margin>
envy of the malignant, strive to defile and—like dying flies (according to the proverb of the Wise Man <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 10:1: "Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savor."</note>)—strive to destroy the sweetness of the ointment. Therefore to you, Charles, Greatest Emperor, and to you, noble Ferdinand, King of the Romans, as if to an uncorrupted asylum of faith and piety, and a strong force and foundation, I flee, I appeal, and I call upon Caesar and Caesar: <note>Ricius addresses both brothers, Charles V and Ferdinand I, who shared the leadership of the Holy Roman Empire and the Habsburg lands.</note> whom the supernal providence of God has placed in this sublime watchtower and high tribunal as ever-watchful, sacrosanct moderators of the Christian world and just judges. May you exhibit yourselves as pious and strenuous protectors, tutors, and defenders of what is honorable for all those who diligently exert themselves toward virtue and the strengthening of true piety and faith (as befits the foremost leaders of the most holy cross). Wherefore, I humbly offer these very volumes on **CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE**, built upon the foundations of the Gospels, the saints, and also sound reason, to the clemency of your Majesty, and I offer them prostrate on my knees. When these works have been sprinkled and protected by the just, honorable, and constant favor of your Highnesses, there will be nothing for me to fear or dread regarding what "human day" <note>original: "humana dies"; a Latinism likely referring to human judgment or the transitory nature of time.</note> might feel or judge. For Truth itself shall surround me with a shield, and the sacred protection of Your Highnesses shall cover me; under these I shall live and hope until I have trodden upon this soil and so long as breath and the spark of life remain in me, with the help of Christ.

However, since in four ways (according to Gospel teachings and the natural order of things) the lot of the field to be cultivated varies and is defiled by the laziness and inertia of the tiller, I have thought it worthwhile to attend to this **CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE** with a four-part consideration. Indeed, some part of this field to be cultivated is the path, worn down by the footprint of those walking, rough, harsh, and left incapable of any fruitful seed. This is the spiritual field and the mind of those who boast of worldly wisdom and the technicalities of vain philosophy. Because these people are intent only on the images of sensory things and are driven by the impulses of the stars, they are less fit or suitable to grasp the divine seed and the sacrament of revealed faith; instead, because of the perpetual entanglements of their imagination and the turning cycle of the heavens, that seed is immediately crushed, snatched away, and vanishes. Another portion of this field is rocky, not filled enough with the clods of the earth; although it may bring forth some sprout, yet because it lacks a root (due to the poverty of the soil), as soon as the sun shines...

### P R E F A C E.

[ra]diating sun, it is consumed by rot and dryness: Such is the rigid and hardened spirit of the Jews, who, although they receive the super-celestial seed of secret truth, poured out through the mouth of the prophets, with a firm and stubborn faith; yet because they do not believe all the foundations that belong to faith, nor do they conceive them; or, if conceiving them, they lack the solid root of truth, at any easy onset, or by a thin and light breeze, they soon despise the pre-conceived sacraments of truth, and renounce them as if they were trifling and vain fictions. Another portion of the soil is given over to thorns and briars, which, although it sprouts a stalk or an ear from the received seed, being overwhelmed by thorns, is finally choked and perishes: by which likeness, in these turbulent times, the soul of certain people professing faith in Christ, although it grasps the foundations of truth and preserves its root, yet contaminated by depraved and distorted understanding and worldly allurements, it overshadows, kills, and corrupts almost all external works of virtue and faith, and their fruits. Finally, another cultivation and fertile field is given, which brings good and desired fruit to its peak, yet less abundantly, because of the sloth and laziness of the farmer: like certain devoted faithful, who embrace and cherish the revealed mysteries of faith with a sincere mind and sound understanding; yet because they are less suited, or know how to spend less industry and study than the true method of exercising faith requires, they therefore do not know how to produce and propagate an abundance of rich fruit from it.

In short (to touch on the matter briefly), as many of wandering mortals as exist must necessarily fall under one or another of four conditions: for they either believe nothing at all of the secrets of faith, such as the arrogant sort of certain philosophers; or they hold a truncated and defective faith, like the younger and stubborn synagogue of the Jews; or they believe falsely and wrongly, like the leaders of heresies <note>original: "hæresiarchę"; the foundational authors of heretical movements.</note> and their followers; or they exercise the act of believing too remissly and coldly, like many sluggish and yawning faithful, who wake up and burn with spirit less than is necessary to obtain perfect salvation and a blessed life. Therefore, according to this fourfold and fallen lot of men to be instructed, I have compiled (by the nod of the heavens) four volumes on **C E L E S T I A L  A G R I C U L T U R E**: The first of which adapts the rough and unfit mind of certain philosophizers to the celestial seed by the plowshare of the senses and reason, and by the furrows of the Peripatetics <note>original: "Peripatheticorum"; the school of philosophy following Aristotle, known for walking while discussing.</note>, as the Prince of the Apostles <note>St. Peter.</note> commands that the Wise among the faithful be ready to give a reason for their faith to everyone who asks, just as the Apostle <note>St. Paul, in his Epistle to the Romans.</note> admonished the Romans that the invisible things of God must be understood through the visible.

The second Volume of this work heaps up and fills in the stony and hard ground of the Jews—who, through a lack of things to be believed and of the land of the living, lack a root—with the rich soil of the prophets and also with the help of the Talmudists <note>original: "Thalmadeorum"; referring to the authors of the Talmud, the body of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note>.

The third Volume, with the hoes and weeding-hooks of the New and Old Testament, clears the thorny spirit overwhelmed by the briars of error, and restores it to the purity of fruitful faith and understanding.

# PREFACE.

Finally, the **Fourth Volume** fertilizes the faithful soul—which might otherwise bear fruit only thinly and sparingly—through secret meditation. It lifts that soul up from these sordid and failing streams of water to the heavenly flows and the perennial spring of living waters, so that it may be able to draw forth and propagate the fruit of faith and truth more abundantly. With all these things thus set forth and examined with precision, even if I have not accomplished everything I might wish or everything the nature of the matter requires, I shall nevertheless strive to perform diligently (as becomes a servant of Christ and a faithful tiller of His field) what I can and ought to do according to my smallness, with the help and grace of that same heavenly farmer, God, to whom be praise, glory, and honor.

## A PIOUS EXHORTATION TO THE READER.

For the progress of many pious faithful and the strengthening of the orthodox faith, I urge, ask, and entreat every provident and sincere worshiper of faith and truth, by the most sacred cross of Christ, to read carefully and revolve with attentive meditation and a pure mind these noble volumes on **CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE**. These works have been approved through accurate examination and with the highest praise and commendations by many of the most celebrated heads of theological schools (as is evident from their open letters added at the end of this book). From these volumes, anyone will be able to be instructed and directed, with exquisite care and little effort, onto the true path of life and the narrow way of eternal salvation.

## Preface to the FIRST VOLUME of CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE.

<margin>
Those who philosophize prove nothing except what the senses or reason grasp; they reject all faith.
The **Mycrologists** <note>original: "Mycrologi"—a term likely used here to describe narrow-minded or pedantic people who obsess over small details while ignoring the bigger picture of reason.</note> accept only faith and immediately despise those things that belong to reason.
</margin>

<note>Decorative initial 'Q' inside a square woodcut border featuring floral scrolls and a central portrait medallion.</note> **SINCE** we are here undertaking the task of cultivating and preparing the squalid and rough mind of certain people who philosophize, who wander so far from the true path of philosophy that they now—just like many of the more dull-witted and arrogant among the faithful—firmly believe that the entire faith of orthodox piety is in direct conflict with the teachings of the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, whose work formed the basis of medieval science and logic.</note> and the light of nature. Consequently, in this wretched time of ours, many who boast of worldly philosophy think they may claim the name of "philosopher" more excellently the further and more stubbornly they reject the foundations of revealed faith and mock them as if they were some kind of fanatical ravings. On the other hand, those **Mycrologists**, though they are devoid of all prudence and the discipline of truth, nevertheless wish to seem solid and more devoted in the faith; they immediately despise and curse everything established by the light of nature and sound reason as if it were rebelling against the orthodox faith. Since, therefore, this class of "philosophers" thinks nothing should be deeply agreed to or embraced except what they can prove by the art of logic and debate, we have decided to deal with them in the manner of a **dialogue**. To soften the bitterness of their minds and correct their follies, we shall use some of their own debating instruments—the hoes, plowshares, and plows of **celestial agriculture**—so that they may see and learn clearly by the light of reason that the teachings of legitimate philosophers not only do not disagree or fight with faith in any way, but rather support it and, with certain and solid proofs, build up and stabilize its foundations. [As for the dull-witted class of **Mycrologists**, they fail so badly at the very "threshold" (as the saying goes) that their refutation requires little effort or study, as we have shown more extensively in the third volume of this work.]

Nor was a boastful and lazy slanderer ashamed to assert in certain "censures" (as he calls them) of his, that everything written and contained in the **Apostles' Creed** <note>original: "symbolo Apostolorum"</note> is believed contrary to sense and reason. If this position were granted and admitted, no one is so ignorant or so devoid of Christian piety that they would not see and understand that faith and religion are subverted, and all orthodox piety falls to ruin. For we know from the decrees of the sacred laws and the opinion of all theologians that divine law, or divine right, consists in nature; and whatever things have been received by custom or contained in writings, if they are adverse to natural law, they are to be considered vain and void.

<margin>The light of grace and nature offer mutual help.</margin>

Since, therefore, the law of nature consists solely in the implanted light of reason, it is in no way fitting to doubt that everything believed against sound and manifest reason must be held as vain and void. Therefore, truth and reason (according to the teachings of the saints) must be placed before any customs or constitutions. If, then, everything contained in the Apostles' Creed is believed (as that man’s babbling theme suggests) against reason and sense, one would have to confess—oh, the shame!—that the entire faith of truth is vain and void.

<margin>
Distinction 8. "By what law."
Distinction 9. "Sound."
Distinction 1. "Natural law."
Distinction 1. "Custom."

</margin>

Furthermore, if those things which belong to faith were opposed to the light of nature and were to be embraced as contraries, how could the Prince of the Apostles <note>St. Peter</note> admonish the wise among the faithful to "always be ready to give a reason to everyone who asks for the reason for the faith and hope that is in them" <note>1 Peter 3:15</note>? How could the wise Architect of faith <note>St. Paul</note> dare to debate with the philosophers in the **Areopagus** <note>The high court in Athens where Paul famously preached to Greek philosophers.</note> about the things of faith and persuade them to embrace the faith in Athens? Those philosophers feel nothing and accept nothing whatsoever that is adverse to the innate light of reason. And by what law does the same Apostle teach that the Gentiles, who rely on reason alone, have known God—if, according to this impious hypothesis, it is believed against reason based on the Apostles' Creed? And why does the Apostle teach that the invisible things of God are seen from the creation of the world, being understood through the things that have been made, and for that reason he says the Gentiles are without excuse? Finally, I would consider it superfluous to bring forward the various testimonies of other ancient and more recent theologians here, who seek and urge nothing more anxiously against the attackers of the faith than to show the coherence of the things of faith with the experience of sense and reason. As **Augustine** says in *On the Trinity*, chapter 14: "Faith," he says, "is sired, nourished, defended, and strengthened in us through knowledge." This is what we shall strive to show and explain at great length in the present volume to the best of our ability, with divine grace breathing upon us and the breeze of the super-celestial Spirit favoring our beginnings and making the vows of piety bear fruit.

**Philalethes** <note>The name "Philalethes" is Greek for "Lover of Truth."</note>: The day is already passing and the shadows are lengthening; the hour of my departure is pressing. <margin>A follower of Epicurus.</margin>
**PHILALETHES**: Seriously, by the immortals! **PHILOSOMATUS**: Ha ha he! You are certainly raving, brother, and "black bile" <note>The Latin *atra bilis* refers to melancholy or a state of madness according to ancient medicine.</note> agitates you, since you leave behind reality to follow empty dreams and shadows. Surely nothing sweeter, nothing more excellent, nor more happy could be given or even imagined? **PHILALETHES**: Indeed, I judge that what is commonly said is not at all false: namely, that speech itself is the indicator of character and life, and exists as its shadow. I have known for a run of many years now—not just recently—that you "have hay on your horn" <note>original: "in cornu fœnum." This is a Latin idiom from the poet Horace referring to a dangerous bull; it indicates a person who is volatile or ill-tempered.</note> (as they say). For this reason, I have frequently warned our brother **Philadelphus** <note>The name "Philadelphus" is Greek for "Lover of Brothers."</note> here to beware of your unrestrained and poisonous habits, you who always strive to twist us toward the empty allurements of the senses and the filthy delights of the flesh. But now, O Philadelphus, why do we linger longer and allow our ears to be defiled by the most shameful speeches of a man of pleasure? I judge we must flee from here as if from the song of the Sirens, and leave this insane Philosomatus behind. **PHILADELPHUS**: Please, do not be so difficult and austere, brother, but linger a little while and let me contend with him. For although he indulges too much in the care of the body, he is nevertheless sometimes accustomed to lend his ears calmly to the discourses of reason. **PHILOSOMATUS**: By Hercules, I desire nothing more right now than that you should be willing to deal with me—and more gently, too. For this Philalethes seems to be incensed and to heap insults upon me more harshly and rigidly than is fitting for a brother joined by blood. **PHILADELPHUS**: Believe me, he broke out into such bitterness against you not out of contempt or hatred, but out of spiritual zeal. **PHILOSOMATUS**: I do not deny it; nevertheless, you showed that you would deal with me, and I ask that it please you to pursue that now. **PHILADELPHUS**:

Especially since human society is preserved by this indulgence and by the necessity of the soul’s connection with the body. must be bound. **PHILADELPHUS**: The multiple ways a name can be understood prevents you from understanding the matter correctly. For we do not call someone a "Body-lover" <note>original: "Philosomatum"</note> simply because they take any kind of care for the body, just as we do not call someone a "Money-lover" <note>original: "philochrimatũ"</note> simply because they seek profit in some way. Rather, I call someone a lover of any thing who desires the thing itself, not for the sake of something else, but for the sake of the thing itself. For thus we call a man a lover of wealth not if he seeks profit for his needs or the comforts of life, but if he gapes for profit only for the sake of profit. Nor do we call a man a philosopher <note>meaning "Lover of Wisdom"</note> if he applies himself to the study of wisdom out of a desire for ambition and empty glory; we call him a "lover of honor" <note>original: "philotimũ"</note> instead. A true philosopher is one who pursues the knowledge of things solely out of a desire for knowing.

<margin>Who may be called a Body-lover.</margin>
Finally, we call a man a "Body-lover" not if he strives to fulfill the necessary duties of nature, but if he (observing no higher end) thinks himself born for pleasure and embraces it as the highest good. **PHILOSOMATUS**: What you say is worth hearing and sounds like the truth. However, as the proverb goes, I am still "rolling the same stone" <note>A reference to Sisyphus, suggesting he is stuck on the same difficult point.</note>. For I do not yet see clearly why you judge a man who indulges more carefully in the pleasures of the body to be so contemptible. **PHILADELPHUS**: Such a man is to be despised because, while he follows the lures of the senses in the manner of brute beasts, and pampers and fattens this little earthly body, he ignominiously defiles the divine and immortal thing that lies hidden within him, and plunges it into the pit of eternal death. **PHILOSOMATUS**: You give arduous and sublime answers, but while you remove one doubt, you seem to throw a new obstacle in my path. **PHILADELPHUS**: For what reason do you say that? **PHILOSOMATUS**: Because you try to explain a doubt by using something about which I hesitate far more. Who can satisfy a doubter that something more noble than the body—something divine and immortal—lies hidden within the human frame?

<margin>Something divine and immortal lies hidden in the human body.</margin>
For our entire disagreement and struggle turns upon this point, as if on a hinge. **PHILADELPHUS**: It is not a laborious task for someone who considers it—provided they possess even a small spark of natural wit—to grasp the certainty of this inquiry through various and solid arguments. But, lest I overwhelm you with a multitude of proofs, I will try to reveal it to you with a single line of reasoning. **PHILOSOMATUS**: Go on then, best of brothers, and untie this "untyable knot" <note>original: "inenodabilem hunc mihi nodum"</note> for me. **PHILADELPHUS**: Pay attention, then, and listen diligently. Do you think the craftsman who prepares the raw materials is different from, and superior to, the one who cleans the stables? **PHILOSOMATUS**: Why wouldn't he be? **PHILADELPHUS**: And is the goldsmith not different and more worthy than the supplier of raw materials? **PHILOSOMATUS**: More worthy, certainly. **PHILADELPHUS**: And the physician more than the goldsmith? **PHILOSOMATUS**: Exactly so. **PHILADELPHUS**: And is he who holds the magistracy and the rudder of the State superior to the physician? **PHILOSOMATUS**: Nothing is more certain. **PHILADELPHUS**: Tell me then, my brother, by what rule or firm thought do you judge their differences, and why is one more excellent than the other? **PHILOSOMATUS**: I judge that person to be different and more excellent who is occupied with a different and more worthy matter, and who handles something more noble. **PHILADELPHUS**: You answer wisely indeed, and you solve your own problem. For it will be clear and proven: if there is any power in the human body that is occupied with something more excellent than that which the physical powers work upon, then such a power is entirely foreign to the powers of the body. It must be placed above all of them, just as the matter and subject it handles surpasses the material objects of the physical powers. **PHILOSOMATUS**: You discuss the matter skillfully and appropriately, as I see. However, I do not quite understand what you call "corporeal power."

<margin>What corporeal power is.</margin>
**PHILADELPHUS**: I call "corporeal power" that power which can neither exist nor operate without the benefit of a body. Just as elemental heat neither exists nor acts except in fire, or in a body where fire prevails; likewise, cold can neither exist nor produce cold things except in the element of earth or water, or in things where their power dominates. Thus, the power of sight does not know how to exercise vision if it lacks an eye; nor does the power of hearing operate if the ear is missing. In short (to settle the matter in a few words), every corporeal power is held in the body just as an image is in wax or bronze. For when the wax melts...

<margin>How the conception of the universal itself is born in us.</margin>
**PHILADELPHUS**: If the nature of a soldier is to repel the enemy, tell me please: when there is no enemy present for you to drive away, do you still wish to be called a soldier? **PHILOSOMATUS**: Certainly. For although I am by no means repelling an enemy right now, what prevents me from being a soldier? **PHILADELPHUS**: How can that be consistent? For if a man is called wealthy who abounds in riches, a man who lacks them should not be considered wealthy. By the same law, if the nature of a soldier is to repel the enemy, he who does not repel one cannot be called a soldier. **PHILOSOMATUS**: You would call me truly unrefined and devoid of reason if I thought the nature of a soldier was merely the *act* and *work* of repelling an enemy. For I assert that a soldier is one who, from frequently repeated encounters in battle, possesses the skill and power to strike or put to flight any enemy equal to himself, whenever that enemy appears and joins him on the battlefield. **PHILADELPHUS**: You judge rightly, and I do not think you unrefined, for I have always known you to be strong in mind as well as in body. And now, since you respond in a Philosophical rather than a military manner, let us proceed. Answer again: do you attribute this nature of a soldier only to yourself, or do you have it in common with others? **PHILOSOMATUS**: Undoubtedly, this nature of a soldier (which is to repel the enemy) belongs to many others. For no one is ignorant that this nature also applies to these companions, Philochrimatus <note>meaning "Lover of Money"</note> and Philotimus <note>meaning "Lover of Honor"</note>, as well as to other soldiers of our company. **PHILADELPHUS**: Does it also apply to those who live a long distance from us and inhabit Thule <note>original: "Tylen" — the mythical far northern land, used here to mean the ends of the earth.</note>? **PHILOSOMATUS**: To those same men, indeed. **PHILADELPHUS**: And to those who were and who will be soldiers? **PHILOSOMATUS**: It must be attributed to all of them. **PHILADELPHUS**: You clearly recognize, then, that this name and its nature apply to all soldiers everywhere—those who are, those who were, and those who will be. **PHILOSOMATUS**: Nothing is more certain to me. **PHILADELPHUS**: Tell me then, sweetest brother: did you come to know the certainty of this matter by sight, or smell, or any other sense? **PHILOSOMATUS**: By Hercules, I am not so dull or so "ignorant of the lyre" <note>original: "lyrae expers" — a proverb meaning uncultured or lacking understanding.</note> (as they say) that I cannot easily guess that what is not present in a physical thing cannot be grasped by any sense. **PHILADELPHUS**: Yet you affirm that not only those who are soldiers here, but all who wander through the world, and those who were or will be, share in the same nature of a soldier. **PHILOSOMATUS**: I have no doubt of it.

Here, he uses a logical argument to prove that the human mind must possess a non-physical (incorporeal) power to understand these eternal concepts, leading toward a proof of the soul's immortality.</meta>

# PAULUS RICIUS,

<margin>What this thing called the *universal* signifies.</margin> **PHILADELPHUS**: Do you then recognize something that is enclosed by neither place nor time? **PHILOSOMATUS**: I do. **PHILADELPHUS**: That which is prescribed by neither time nor any specific place is the very thing that the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, named for his habit of walking—*peripatein*—while teaching</note> are accustomed to call the *universal*. For just as a military law is called "universal" because it maintains its force everywhere and always among soldiers, so too this *universal*—which is the concept of a "soldier" and its definition—designates not only you or these companions of yours, but anyone else at any time or place as a "soldier." **PHILOSOMATUS**: I judge it to be so. **PHILADELPHUS**: Do you then think that this thing we call a *universal* is comprehensible to us? **PHILOSOMATUS**: I approve of that idea. **PHILADELPHUS**: But did you not admit just a moment ago that this can be perceived by no physical sense? **PHILOSOMATUS**: I admitted it. **PHILADELPHUS**: Through what power, then, do you think this *universal* is perceived? **PHILOSOMATUS**: Through some other virtue that lies hidden in the citadel <note>original: *arce*; a common philosophical metaphor for the head or the highest part of the soul</note> of our body. **PHILADELPHUS**: Is it a corporeal or an incorporeal power? **PHILOSOMATUS**: Perhaps it is corporeal. **PHILADELPHUS**: This cannot be. For the very same reason that prevents the outward-working senses from knowing the *universal* also prevents any other corporeal power hidden within from grasping it. **PHILOSOMATUS**: But what is the reason that prevents this? **PHILADELPHUS**: I would like you to tell me first: what is the reason that a man whose head and neck are bound to the trunk of a tree with an unbreakable bond—so that his face is fixed toward the ground and he can see nothing except what crawls on the earth and meets him on the soil—perceives nothing of those things that are above, to the right, or to the left, let alone those things situated behind him? **PHILOSOMATUS**: I think no one is of such dull wit that they do not see that the hard and tight bond is the cause, preventing him from being able to lift his eyes on high or look around. **PHILADELPHUS**: In a similar way, then, since every sense and every corporeal power is joined to the body by an inextricable knot, it cannot grasp anything except what is present before it. That which is not present—either because of a gap in space or time—it cannot grasp at all. Therefore, since the *universal* itself is not destined for or fixed to this or that specific body, nor respects any certain places or times, it follows most evidently that no corporeal power at all—neither those outside nor those within—can reach the *universal* itself. **PHILOSOMATUS**: By these little persuasions of yours, you have now led me step-by-step to the point where I am forced to confess that something is known to us through a virtue that cannot be corporeal, and that what is known is that which is usually called the *universal*. However, I most greatly desire to hear by what argument you might prove that this *universal* is more excellent than that which is perceived by corporeal power. **PHILADELPHUS**: This can be established for you with little effort (as I suppose), since I see you have now been led to the true path of reason and intelligence. That the *universal* is more excellent than that which corporeal power perceives is apparent from this: the *universal* is subject to no change, succession, or corruption. For (according to the order of nature) the human race is eternal, and there will always be some soldier; but such an individual man, or such a specific soldier, must necessarily undergo corruption and death. Since, therefore, the eternal is immeasurably more excellent than the corruptible, it will be plain that the *universal* is, without limit, more excellent than the singular. For this reason, the intellectual virtue—whose proper object of knowledge is the *universal*—is far more excellent than the sensitive virtue, whose object of apprehension is the singular.

<margin>The power by which the universal is conceived must be divine and immortal.</margin>
**PHILOSOMATUS**: Although you demonstrate by your clear reasonings that the intellectual power is another, more noble thing than the sensitive faculty, you have not yet taught by what path the intellectual power is to be considered entirely immortal and divine. **PHILADELPHUS**: It will be very easy for you to grasp exactly what you seek if you rightly consider what has been said. For you have learned from our discussion that the power which apprehends the *universal*—which we call the "intellect"—exists as something incorporeal. Moreover, every incorporeal virtue must be simple <note>In medieval philosophy, "simple" means not composed of parts. Only things with parts can be broken or "dissolved"</note>; that which is simple can by no fate be dissolved or corrupted; and that which does not suffer corruption is immortal...

<summary>Philadelphus argues that because the human mind can understand abstract "universals" (concepts that are eternal and not tied to a specific place), the mind must possess an incorporeal power called the intellect. He concludes that since this power is non-physical and "simple," it must be immortal and divine.</summary>

# ON CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE, BOOK I.

is such and so divine: this is moreover clearly proclaimed by the prophecies, the works of miracles, and finally the doctrines of both philosophers and theologians, as well as the purity of their lives and the uprightness of their character. For I remain silent for now concerning the fame and holiness of those Prophets, Apostles, and Martyrs who were filled with divine inspiration and heavenly power, the splendor of whose lives has already made the entire circle of the earth illustrious. Truly, I bring forward the memorable acts and laudable deeds of the Philosophers, who (with the light of nature <note>original: *naturali lumine*; referring to human reason unaided by divine revelation</note> as their guide) held scepters, magistracies, wealth, and other things that the human race is accustomed to admire in contempt, so that they might preserve the integrity of their souls. They avoided these things as if they were the bait and fuel for evils. Pursuing the virtues themselves through solitudes, travels, and poverty—along with the total lack of resources common to all the poor—the voluntary abdication of Pythagoras <note>A Greek philosopher who required his followers to give up private property</note> demonstrates this, as does the chosen poverty of Bias and Anaxagoras, the studious solitude of Orpheus and Epimenides, the constant chastity of Xenocrates, the abstinence of Heraclitus upon a diet of herbs, the total penury of Diogenes, and finally the voluntary death of Socrates. And there are (so to speak) the innumerable oracles of wisdom from these men, who certainly would not have chosen such bitterness of life, but would rather have devoted themselves to glory, riches, and the lusts of the belly (like the ignoble crowd), unless they had recognized something more noble than physical power—something immortal and divine—joined to the human body. There are also many other testimonies of this kind which declare the inviolable certainty of our inquiry and proposal, but as the present method of discussion requires, I have judged these to be sufficient. Ponder these things with yourself and revolve them in a busy mind. **PHILOSOMATUS.** You bring forward quite excellent and sublime sacraments <note>original: *sacramenta*; here used in the sense of "sacred mysteries" or "deep truths"</note> of truth, in which (I call the gods to witness) my mind and reason now immediately rest, no longer wavering nor with any fear, but with certain and firm understanding. Nevertheless, I greatly desire to hear some evident likeness <note>original: *similitudinem*; an analogy or metaphor used for teaching</note> drawn from those things that stir the senses, so that I might be able to penetrate with a clearer intelligence this eminent knowledge of universal things which you have shown, and their relationship to these vain shadows of earthly things, and by what law we may climb from these decaying and momentary little bodies to the sublime and everlasting shrines. **PHILADELPHUS.** 

<margin>A remarkable analogy suggesting the way by which the human mind climbs from these shadows of decaying things to the heavenly lights, and clings to the origin of eternal life.</margin> You think and ask rightly and very providently, my brother—you who demand that an analogy be given for perceiving those super-celestial things (which surpass all sense), since examples are accustomed to bring a great deal of light to the understanding of things. Therefore, though I may perhaps make a longer speech here than the method of a summary allows, let no weariness take hold of you, nor let the reading distress you. For if you weigh each thing included in this analogy (soon to be explained) on the scale of right reason, you will clearly understand that not even a single little word is brought forward that does not contain some mystery and hidden truth within itself. Apply your ears, therefore, to these things, and stretch the sharpness of your mind. Imagine a man of supreme beauty and grace standing on the summit of a towering and very bright mountain, whose remarkable image reflects in that shining and mirror-like mountain; then, let this very image be cast into a rapid torrent (which glides past the base of the mountain). Moreover, near the bank of the torrent, let a certain beautiful girl, a shepherdess of sheep, wander about. When she approaches the torrent, let her soon see and notice the form of the man flashing there. From the sight of this, let the likeness and specimen of that mountain-dwelling and graceful man steal into the mind of the girl, from which she may gradually lift and raise her gaze higher, until she reaches and beholds the image reflecting splendidly on the mountain. From this she infers the beauty of the marvelous form of the heavenly man and his grace; immediately she gapes at the sight and the approach to him, whose company and embrace she finally longs for with a burning love. When she realizes that she cannot become the possessor of such a wish unless she first swims across the torrent and overcomes the steep summits of the mountain by climbing, she immediately girds herself with all her strength and, with an unshaken spirit (having left her flock behind), she crosses the torrent and seeks the ridges of the mountain. When she has arrived there, she continually strives with anxious care for the condition of soul and body...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical dialogue between Philadelphus and Philosomatus. Following the previous discussion on the immortality of the soul and the example of virtuous philosophers, Philadelphus now employs an allegory of a shepherdess, a mountain, and a stream to explain the Platonic hierarchy of reality—moving from fleeting material reflections to the eternal divine Archetype.</meta>

# BY PAULUS RICIUS,

...to adapt her habit, and to make herself conformed and pleasing to the wishes and pleasures of the beloved; and she continues without intermission to worship and soothe him with the sweetness of songs and praise, and with suppliant prayers, until that beloved and **Archetypal man** <note>original: *Architypus homo*; the divine, original blueprint of humanity in the mind of God</note>, enticed by the form and beauty of the girl, turns a peaceful gaze upon her, nods, extends his right hand, deems her worthy of a kiss, and embraces her, and finally joins her to himself in modest and conjugal love. Do you grasp, O brother, the image <note>original: *typum*; a symbolic figure or type</note>, and does it glide into your mind?

**PHILOSOMATUS.** I grasp it indeed, and as if seized by a divine spirit, I listen in amazement.

**PHILADELPHUS.** Now therefore (if you notice), the condition of the form of the heavenly man is allotted in a threefold way. <margin>The threefold kind of forms is shown by a clear similarity.</margin> First, this very form exists in the Archetypal man. Second, it shines back upon the **specular mountain** <note>A mountain acting like a mirror (speculum)</note>. Third, it gleams forth in the torrent. However, these three kinds of forms are distant from one another by a long interval. For that form of the heavenly man exists unproduced and invariable, uniform, and always remaining the same in number, nor does it depend on anything else. But the form and image which is in the mountain retains one quality in itself but loses the other: it preserves the gift of invariability, because it remains perpetually the same in number; yet it loses the gift of independence, because it flows from that very super-eminent and exemplary form at every moment. But the wretched form in the torrent has earned neither of these gifts. Indeed, it is not independent, since like a thin phantom <note>original: *simulachrum*</note> it never ceases to flow from the Archetypal and specular form without any gap in time. Nor can it be invariable, for it does not remain the same in number for even the smallest moment of time, since no little portion of the water of the torrent is given which does not flow away in some moment, and which does not glide down in an irrevocable course. Whence it is necessary that even that thin phantom, which is carried through that very portion of water, is continually destroyed and vanishes. Do you accept, brother, these three distinctions of forms and of being, which are worthy of all attention?

**PHILOSOMATUS.** I am so persuaded.

**PHILADELPHUS.** Since these things have been perceived, tell me, I pray, would you not call the girl sluggish and astonished if, while she is occupied with the duty of watering the sheep, she should notice the phantom of such great beauty in the torrent, yet not be moved by any admiration? Or even if a powerful admiration should seize her, and nevertheless, if she fixes her gaze on that phantom and does not lift her eyes higher, but places her whole solace and delight in the mere shadowy image of the torrent, would you not call her insane and dull?

**PHILOSOMATUS.** I certainly would.

**PHILADELPHUS.** By a similar argument, therefore, do not doubt that he who indulges only in bodily allurements and the lust of the senses, and does not admire the beauty of things and the grace of nature, is a stupid and senseless man, to be placed rather among the genus of cattle. Again, even he who examines these flowing and falling bodies and their natures—if he stops his feet there and does not proceed from that place to sublime things, and does not raise his gaze to the **super-celestial spectacles**—he is undoubtedly to be judged a foolish and empty little man.

**PHILOSOMATUS.** By what similarity you compare this foolish man to the insane and sluggish shepherdess, I do not sufficiently guess.

**PHILADELPHUS.** You will easily understand this if you pay attention to the individual things expressed by this image, and refer them to the individual parts of the **triple machine** <note>original: *trinæ machinæ*; a common Renaissance term for the threefold structure of the universe: the elemental, celestial, and intellectual worlds</note> and to the human mind. For the **Mountain** (which the ancients call **Olympus**) designates the celestial body. The **Torrent**, with the thin phantom that is in it, proclaims **prime matter**, **Chaos**, or **hyle** <note>original: *hylen*; the Greek term for the fundamental, unformed matter of the universe</note>, together with the forms of generated bodies. The **specular brightness** on the mountain, with the true and splendid image of the heavenly man, shows exactly the choir of souls which inhabits the heavens and the **Empyrean** <note>The highest, fiery heaven</note> globe, along with the **reasons** or **Ideas** <note>original: *Idæis*; the eternal patterns of all things</note> of sensible things. Finally, that **Heavenly Man**, with his beautiful form and his organs, shadows forth the **angelic mind** (with the exemplary and paradigmatic forms existing within it). But the **intellectual power** of the heavenly man, lurking further within, suggests **God**, the best and greatest founder of all things. The **shepherdess of the sheep** represents the **mortal mind**, the contemplator of falling and eternal things; but the **sheep**, which she pastures...

<summary>Philadelphus presents a Neoplatonic allegory using a shepherdess, a mountain, and a stream to illustrate the hierarchy of reality: from the fleeting "shadows" of the material world to the eternal "Ideas" in the divine mind. He argues that humans who only focus on physical pleasures or material science without seeking the divine source are like a girl staring at a reflection in a moving stream while ignoring the real person above.</summary>

<keywords>Neoplatonism, allegory, Archetypal Man, Hyle, Prime Matter, Ideas, Empyrean, celestial hierarchy, human soul, divine reflection, Olympus, triple machine of the world</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical dialogue where Philadelphus uses the allegory of a shepherdess to describe the soul's journey. Having established the three levels of reality (Archetype, Mountain/Reflection, and Torrent/Matter), the conversation now turns toward the practical pursuit of divine union and the transition from philosophy to theology.</meta>

### ON CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE, BOOK I.

...the girl represents the bodily powers of the human frame (which are governed by the guidance of reason and mind). Accept these things, sweetest brother, according to your just and pious requests, and as much as the method of this summary permits; revolve them with repeated thought and investigation.

*PHILOSOMATUS.* By Hercules! Skillfully and very gracefully do you reveal these hidden oracles of wisdom. By hearing them, I know not what force and latent energy stirs my spirit, so that now, having despised and trampled upon the shadows of earthly things, it strives toward the heavens and the summits of the celestial mountains, seeking the very source of all goods and the origin of the supernal life.

*PHILADELPHUS.* I have always had such expectation and hope for you; nor does divine mercy and the invariable order of things allow a man, who walks according to the law of reason and nature, to fall headlong into the eternal darkness of death. Come then, my brother, and hasten to betroth and join your "girl" <note>The human soul, personified as the shepherdess in the previous page's allegory</note>—now touched by the spiritual lightning-bolt of love—to the man of supreme beauty and excellence himself.

*PHILOSOMATUS.* There will be no delay on my part, if only I might know the certain path more clearly. For although I have learned from what was said before how one must leave the sheep (that is, the senses and the powers and allurements of the body), cross the torrent (that is, the understanding of material things), and climb the mountain (that is, to acquire the knowledge of the heavens and the spiritual forms that lie hidden in the heavens), nevertheless, even after long and tireless labor, when I have traversed all these and seen the beauty and grace of the supernal mind from afar and through a cloud, I do not know with what familiarity and care this little shepherdess—this weak mind of mortals—may presume to sustain the presence of such high and awesome majesty, to win his love, and to seek a conjugal partnership. For the whole difficulty and labor seems to consist in this.

<margin>We attain the heavenly betrothal not by the law of logic, but by the light of grace.</margin>

*PHILADELPHUS.* <note>Though the speaker label says PHILAD. here, the text shifts to Philalethes (the "Lover of Truth") joining the dialogue</note> I confess that I too do not sufficiently grasp the certain rule of this betrothal. For thus far I have drunk the dogma of the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, who relied on observation and logic</note>, which was never able to carry anyone higher than the point where the nature of the heavens remains far off, under a certain dense darkness, reached only by the thin and shifting discourse of reason. But no one could discover or devise the method of prophetic and beatific contemplation, except one who has consulted the divine and Theological oracles. For this reason, if you desire to achieve and fulfill that vow, search out and embrace the dogma and tradition of the Theologians, who handle divine gifts. Therefore, you would act more wisely if you immediately go with us to Gometius, a man distinguished in Theological wisdom; for a glowing plate of iron must be worked with the hammer and frequent blows before it cools.

*PHILOSOMATUS.* And I indeed would ask for that very thing, but a suspicion arises in me, lest your brother Philalethes <note>original: *Philalethes*; "Lover of Truth"</note> should still look at me with stern eyes and hold my company in contempt.

*PHILALETHES.* No (by the gods above!), rather I shall receive you now with a more intimate and spiritual kiss and embrace. I do not doubt that the notion of orthodox truth will be more sincere and solid in you hereafter, precisely because the lust of the flesh and the senses has flourished in you until now; for he who has previously seen the crooked judges what is straight more exactly. Therefore, let there be no fear in you, my brother, but having left behind this vain spectacle of a dance, walk now fearlessly with us. Behold, even now we are departing to seek the house of the theologian Gometius.

*PHILOSOMATUS.* See, I am here, and wherever you proceed, I will not desert you as long as life is my companion.

*PHILALETHES.* May the heavenly powers save you, venerable Gometius.

*GOMETIUS.* And may the individual and eternal Trinity preserve and enlighten you, my Philalethes. Why do you come so late? I have been expecting you at home for a long time.

*PHILALETHES.* A certain not-unfruitful controversy of my brothers detained me.

*GOMETIUS.* Concerning what? 

<margin>Epilogue.</margin>

Over what matter was the contention?

*PHILALETHES.* Concerning the immortality of the soul, and the right path of eternal salvation.

*GOMETIUS.* They have certainly undertaken arduous and sublime examinations; but what, at last, seems to have been discussed and decided between the two?

*PHILALETHES.* The immortality of the soul was indeed proved by the most exquisite and manifest discourses.

<summary>Philosomatus expresses his desire for divine union but fears his mortal mind is too weak for such majesty; Philalethes then leads him to the theologian Gometius to move beyond Aristotelian logic toward divine grace.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Gometius and Philadelphus. Having previously discussed the allegory of the soul as a shepherdess, the characters now debate whether human salvation can be achieved through natural ability alone or if it requires the divine "light of grace." Philadelphus argues from the perspective of natural law (using examples of animals and elements), while Gometius prepares to explain why human nature requires a higher, supernatural perfection.</meta>

# PAUL RICCI

...is proven. Regarding the right path of true salvation, my thoughts doubt just as I do; for which reason we flee to you as a just judge and fair arbiter, so that you may resolve this dispute—as you recently offered to do—and that you may instruct us and direct us to the right track of eternal salvation.

**GOMETIUS.** I have promised, and I will endeavor to fulfill that very thing (with the Holy Spirit as my guide).

**PHILADELPHUS.** Come then, my father <note>original: *parens*, used here as a title of respect for a teacher</note>, and rescue us from this filthy and most foul prison of ignorance.

**GOMETIUS.** But since the varied intention of names often dulls the understanding of a thing, it is necessary that you declare what this name, "Salvation," indicates to you. 

<margin>What the name "Salvation" signifies.</margin>

**PHILADELPHUS.** I call "true salvation" that state in which one possesses the highest of all goods and enjoys it; for he who possesses the Highest itself certainly enjoys (and indeed far more perfectly) all the goods that are subject to that Highest. Just as one who gazes upon the exemplary beauty <note>The "exemplary" here refers to the original Divine Idea or "Blueprint" from which all physical things are copied</note>, though he does not look at the physical image itself, nevertheless is ignorant of nothing that is within that image. Since, therefore, the highest good (as is taught by the doctrine of the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: followers of the Greek philosopher Aristotle, known for walking while they discussed philosophy</term>) is God, the very spring and creator of all things and goods. It is proved that the possession of all goods can be had in no other than in God, the best and greatest. Therefore, to cling to Him and to enjoy Him is what we call true salvation, the right path of which we now seek from you.

**GOMETIUS.** Now you agree with me regarding the meaning of "true salvation," and you have produced a most apt example regarding exemplary, reflective, and shadowy beauty—an example which shows, by a clear likeness, the manner of Divine Providence and knowledge itself. But since human intelligence, in this dark and slippery soil, stands toward the most manifest things of reality (as the Stagirite <term>The Stagirite: a common name for Aristotle, who was born in the city of Stagira</term> taught in his second book of *Divine Wisdom* <note>original: *Metaphysics*</note>) just as the eyes of an owl toward the light of day. Therefore, just as a dim-sighted eye cannot be capable of perceiving solar light unless some help is supplied from the outside, in the same way, no mortal is able to track down and grasp the path of eternal salvation revealed to us by God, unless the light of God is poured over it from above. Wherefore, you especially must implore His divine mercy and inexhaustible bounty, so that He may impart to you the gift of His grace and shake off the darkness of your mind with the splendor of His countenance. For even though He inhabits a high and inaccessible throne, He does not reject those humble in spirit; for He is mild and can be won over by all who call upon His name with a pure heart.

**PHILADELPHUS.** Although you advise justly and piously (O man of celestial mind), I nevertheless have an argument that fights to the contrary. It suggests that the path of human salvation—and indeed salvation itself—requires no gift of super-celestial grace at all, but that we are able to achieve it from the nature implanted within us.

<margin>He argues that the light of grace is not entirely required for salvation.</margin>

**GOMETIUS.** And what subtle reasoning (I ask) suggests this fallacy to you, by which you are led toward the precipice?

**PHILADELPHUS.** It is experience and induction, the mistress of things herself. For if I look around and consider individual sensible things, I see all things, by their own nature and with no outside protection, attaining the perfection destined for them. For example, it belongs to the completion of fire that it dwells upward with the ether. Therefore, as soon as it is produced, it is raised to the heights with no external help joined to it. So too a clod of earth gapes for and seeks the abyss; a plant and a lowly vegetable takes up its own growth from the earth; with nature alone as a guide, the ant gathers food at harvest time; bees skillfully glue their dwellings together; the spider weaves a web; the swallow builds a nest; the same must be judged regarding every single thing in nature. If, therefore, all things, even the lowliest, attain their end by their own nature, it cannot be that the noble and divine race of mankind requires an external and adventitious <note>original: *adventitium*, meaning something coming from the outside rather than being innate to the person</note> help for its ultimate progress and the eternal salvation destined for it.

**GOMETIUS.** 

<margin>The order of nature demonstrates that the light of grace is required for salvation.</margin>

On the contrary, from the very same foundation upon which you doubt, we draw an unbreakable argument for our proposition—one which you will easily understand if you consider the variety of perfections. For the order of nature has established a twofold perfection for any sensible thing. The first is that which the thing attains from itself and by its own nature...

<summary>Philadelphus defines salvation as the enjoyment of God, the "Highest Good," but argues that humans should be able to reach this end naturally, just as animals and elements follow their instincts. Gometius counters that human intelligence is like an "owl's eye" in daylight, requiring divine grace to see spiritual truths.</summary>
<keywords>salvation, divine grace, natural law, Aristotle, Peripatetics, Pelagianism, theology, human nature</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Gometius and Philadelphus. Having established that "Salvation" involves the possession of the Highest Good, Gometius now moves to distinguish between "natural" perfection (what a being can do on its own) and "supernatural" perfection (which requires external or divine help). This distinction is central to the author's argument that human reason alone is insufficient for eternal life.</meta>

### ON CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE, BOOK I.
<sig>b</sig>

But there is a second perfection which a thing acquires from elsewhere. The first of these perfections is acquired by man, no less than by all other beings, through the instinct of nature alone. However, to attain the second perfection, both other beings and man himself alike require external assistance.

**PHILADELPHUS.** I pray you, please explain these things more broadly.

**GOMETIUS.** I will therefore question you to satisfy your request; and you, if you know the answer, respond: What is most sought after by brute animals—say, a donkey, an ox, or a horse?

**PHILADELPHUS.** Food, surely, and bedding, and to fatten and keep their bodies healthy and safe.

**GOMETIUS.** But for what purpose did provident nature produce the donkey, the ox, and the horse? For just as with all the limbs of the human body, so too with the parts of the universe—as it pleased the Prince of the Peripatetics <note>Aristotle</note>—the very order of things requires that some exist for the sake of others.

**PHILADELPHUS.** Nature produced these brute animals so that they might serve human use: the donkey for carrying small packs, the horse as a vehicle, and the ox for the plow. Indeed, all these perishable bodies (as is taught in the first book of the *Politics* <note>Aristotle’s *Politics*, where he discusses the hierarchy of nature</note>) were devised for the benefit of the human race. And man himself, like the entire machine of the world, is ordered toward a single goal, just as an army is ordered toward its leader.

**GOMETIUS.** You answer correctly, but tell me again: Is it not true that a thing which holds a lower degree of dignity in the scope of things is rendered more worthy the more it serves and closely adheres to a higher thing?

**PHILADELPHUS.** It certainly seems so. For that which is closer to the "First" is prior, and that which is closer to the noblest is more noble; just as he who serves a great and powerful king is more honored than he who serves a humble head of a household or only himself. For those who are slaves by nature, it is—as Aristotle says—profitable and just for them to serve.

**GOMETIUS.** Therefore, you now establish a double perfection for the horse, the donkey, and the ox. One is that by which they respect nothing but themselves—namely, to keep their bodies alive and safe. The other is that by which they serve and adhere to a higher thing; though a foolish and dull animal may not desire this at all, Mother Nature nevertheless intends it for the animal's completion and desires it greatly. It is just as a youth might value the study of literature very little, yet the Pedagogue <note>original: *Paedagogus*, a tutor or teacher</note> values it highly and directs the youth toward it for the convenience of this life and the eternal salvation of the soul.

**PHILADELPHUS.** No one of sound mind is ignorant of that.

**GOMETIUS.** You have found, therefore, that the donkey, horse, and ox attain their first perfection without external assistance; for they seek what is suitable and flee what is harmful, they take their food, digest, walk, and rest by the sole power that nature implanted in them. But they by no means attain the second perfection unless certain aids and added instruments are provided to them from the outside. For the little donkey does not know how to carry packs unless a goad is applied and a halter to pull him. Nor will a horse be fit for riding without a spur and a bridle; nor will the ox be fit for plowing without the yoke and the plow. 

So, finally, man by the instinct of nature acquires for himself all things that his first perfection and natural virtue require (with no light of grace infused from above). But the second perfection—by which he is advanced toward a nobler thing, indeed toward the noblest of all things—he attains from nowhere else than from the added gift and patronage of that Noblest One. Having inspected all these things, we easily prove that the very arguments which led you to believe the opposite of our proposal actually support our opinion and provide it with a strong foundation.

<margin>
Aristotle clearly asserts that true salvation <note>original: *salutem*, meaning both safety/health and spiritual salvation</note> is not given unless the light of grace is present.
</margin>

**PHILADELPHUS.** Now I too acknowledge that very thing, and you bring to my mind a passage from the tenth book of the *Ethics* <note>Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics*</note> by which your assertion is clearly proven. "A life of happiness," he says, "surpasses human nature; for it is not by the fact that he is human that he will live so, but by that which is divine within him." And in the first book of the *Ethics* it is read: "If, therefore, there is any other gift of the gods to men, it is consistent with reason that happiness is given by the gods themselves." These are the words of the Stagirite <term>Stagirite: a common nickname for Aristotle, referring to his birthplace, Stagira</term>, by which we may clearly hear that the right path of human blessedness becomes known to us mortals from nowhere else than the gift of the celestial beings. Therefore, I myself [now seek] to implore these gifts of grace and the path of life...

<summary>Gometius uses the analogy of domestic animals to explain that while humans can manage physical survival through nature, achieving a higher spiritual "perfection" or salvation requires divine assistance (grace). Philadelphus concedes, noting that even the pagan philosopher Aristotle admitted that true happiness is a gift from the divine.</summary>
<keywords>natural vs supernatural perfection, Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Grace, human nature, teleology, salvation, light of grace</keywords>
