<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous section. Gometius, having discussed the nature of human and animal purpose, now offers a profound prayer that synthesizes Christian theology with Kabbalistic thought. He maps the traditional nine choirs of angels and the different spheres of the heavens to specific Hebrew names of God. This reflects the author’s (Paulus Ricius) background as a scholar who sought to bridge Jewish mystical tradition with Christian doctrine.</meta>

# THE WRITINGS OF PAULUS RICIUS

<margin>
A humble prayer, full of celestial mysteries, for obtaining the light of grace.
</margin>

...to be implored, I turn myself (following the warnings of your <term>Syntheresis</term> <note>A scholastic term referring to the innate spark of conscience or the natural knowledge of moral principles</note>) toward the heavens and the lights of the Empyrean sky, and I adore the immortal King of all ages in this manner: O Thundering One <note>original: "Altitonans," a classical epithet for Jupiter, here applied to the Christian God</note> and founder of the highest world, who from the high and inaccessible throne of Your glory governs all things with eternal and ineffable providence and wisdom, and grants to each thing its being and its benefits: You forge the Archetypal machine of the world: You establish the entire firmament of heaven, nor do You desert this falling world: You, God **Eheie** <note>original: "Eheie" (Ehyeh), the Hebrew name meaning "I AM"</note>, procreate the seraphim: You steady the Empyrean globe, nor do You leave the void of things empty: You, God **Yah** <note>original: "Ioh"</note>, produce the cherubim: You roll the highest movable heaven <note>The Primum Mobile</note>, and You do not cease to shape the formless Chaos of nature: You, God **Tetragrammaton** <note>The four-letter name of God, YHWH</note> (pronounced as **Elohim**), establish the thrones: You turn the star-bearing sphere, and provide the form for shifting nature: You, God **EL**, set the dominations in charge: You revolve the high star of Saturn, and shape the raw mass of the perishable body: You, God **Eloha**, bring forth the virtues: You rotate the sacred star of Jupiter, and establish the elements of slippery nature: You, God **Elohim**, substitute the powers: You wheel the fearsome star of Mars, and the temperament for the varieties of metals: You, God **Tetragrammaton of hosts**, substitute the principalities: You direct the steps of the life-giving Sun, and grant growth to the vegetative body: You, God **Elohim of hosts**, arrange the army of archangels: You lead the graceful orbit of Venus, and care for the offspring of brute animals: You, God **Shaddai** <note>original: "Sadaij"</note>, distribute the assembly of angels: You carry around the sphere of prophetic Mercury and form the rational race of men: You, God **Adonai** <note>original: "Aedonai"</note>, produce the choir of celestial souls: You provide the swift course of the Moon, and You illuminate and adorn the minds of the saints in this mortal life with the brightness of Your countenance: O magnitude of immense and tremendous power! O height of incomprehensible wisdom and providence, how sublime and hidden are Your ways. Every tongue is exhausted in You, thought is deceived, reason goes blind, the mind grows dark, and is consumed as if by a bolt of lightning from heaven. Therefore, let the voice be silent, let thought restrain itself, let reason be struck with wonder, let the mind of mortals hide itself—for silence is Your greater praise. To You, eternal and formidable majesty, I lift up my soul: To You, immense piety, I pour out my anxious spirit, I adore You as the only hope of salvation, I implore You with a humble and weeping heart, that from the spring of Your inexhaustible mercy and bounty You might deign to abolish all wickedness and the guilt of impiety within me, to blunt and extinguish the fuel of sin and lust, to direct my soul which wanders out of its orbit and is covered in the thick darkness of ignorance, and to illuminate it with the ray of Your clarity, so that I may deserve to know You as the Father of lights: to love You as the giver of all good things, to possess You as the pinnacle of riches, and finally to enjoy You, the highest of all goods, through infinite and eternal ages. AMEN. <note>original: "GOMET." indicating Gometius has finished his prayer</note>

**GOMETIUS.** Now that you have heard this most pious prayer, full of divine instruction—in which, with such skill and super-celestial artistry, you compose and weave the threefold machine (according to the order of things) with the ten paradigmatic names of God—I shall now, by a divine nod, proceed to explain the very path of true salvation which you seek. You, therefore, strain all the powers of your mind, and diligently give ear to these following clauses.

However, a man reflects very little on the fact that such a power exists within him, unless he thinks of some "whole" object present before him, and thereafter refers that whole to its part. If either of these is missing—so that either the imagination <note>original: "phantasia"</note> does not hold the "whole" as present, or even if it does hold it, the intellectual power is distracted by some other thought and does not compare that same whole to the part—that man reflects very little on being endowed with such a power, even though he has it by his very nature and in reality. **PHILAL.** Nothing is more certain. **GOMET.** Consider the light of grace in the same way: namely, that the cause by which one who is sound in mind may be ignorant of his own light is either inadvertence or the lack of any (or proper) presence of a believable thing. Inadvertence occurs when the thinking faculty (which is the mediatress and messenger of those things which the intellect comprehends) is turned toward these vain, earthly shadows. However, absence or improper presence occurs when those things which are to be believed or seen in the light of grace are not proposed, or are explained incorrectly. In your case, therefore, I would say the cause by which you hesitate and are rolled in doubt concerning the certainty of things to be believed is not indeed inadvertence—since I have always known you to seek spiritual doctrines and search them out with the greatest zeal since your tender years. This has brought me no small comfort and has always offered hope of finding the path of eternal salvation. **GOMET.** Let there be no fear in you, my son, nor shall you be frustrated in your hope. **PHILAL.** A happy omen <note>original: "praesagium"</note>, O man of signs, and worthy of all applause. **GOMET.** Finally, remember to gather from all these things said here that it is not absurd for someone to be a participant in the light of grace, yet for that same person to be uncertain of the presence of that light. **PHILAL.** Truly, the opinion of Aristotle supports these warnings of yours; for while he considers celestial bodies (in the second volume of *On the Heavens and the World*) and inquires into the cause of their variety of motions, he says: "Regarding difficult things, small and sufficient reasons are to be cherished." If, therefore, small reasons suffice for moving things whose operation and motion are subject to the senses, it will be far more reasonable that small reasons be accepted regarding things whose knowledge transcends not only the senses, but also the natural limit of human reason. You syllogize <note>To syllogize is to use formal logic to reach a conclusion from two premises.</note> rightly and most learnedly so far, my Philalethes; proceed then, my son, proceed, and bring forth whatever is ambiguous and hidden to you. For I will explain each thing to you and (with the Holy Spirit’s protection) I will try to render them both believed and understood.

<margin>One must ask about each part of the Creed's content: what, by what means, and why.</margin>

**PHILAL.** Therefore, a three-part question is required here: First, what the word "I believe" <note>original: "credo"; the opening word of the Apostles' Creed</note> designates; next, by what law that which the word indicates is proven to be true. Third, one must ask why it is necessary to believe at all for salvation that which is recognized as true, since the belief in every truth is not necessarily required for a blessed life. First, therefore, the word and expression "I believe" occurs in the Creed proposed to us, whose meaning you ought to declare beforehand.

<margin>I believe.</margin>

**GOMET.** We say that to "believe" is to think in the mind with the assent of the will. I say "with the assent of the will" because we also think through the innate discourse of reason, but such thinking is called "to know" <note>original: "scire"; referring to scientific or logical certainty</note>. To "believe," however, is not that at all, because thinking through the discourse of reason does not come from the assent of the will; this is because this very thinking precedes every act of the will, and nothing that comes before results from or depends on what comes after. To think (for example) that God is incorporeal <note>without a physical body</note>: this could be said to be both "believing" and "knowing." It will be "knowing" when a legitimate demonstration has been held about this, namely by syllogizing:

> Every substance of infinite power is incorporeal, 
> God is a substance of infinite power: 
> Therefore, God is incorporeal.

For once this argument is perceived, the intellect immediately assents to the conclusion without any command or work of the will. But "to believe" will be when no reason has been brought forward for the proposition; for then the intellect will not accept the proposed conclusion at all unless it is inclined from elsewhere to assent. No power exists in man that can command and incline the intellect except the will itself. Therefore, to think that God is incorporeal—with no discourse of reason compelling it—can happen from nowhere else than the assent of the will, which is what we call "to believe."

**PHILAL.** But from where (tell me, I pray) can the will be induced to make the intellect acquiesce to the proposition? For the will itself (just like every apprehensive desire) is not carried or moved except toward that which has been foreknown and understood. If, therefore, the intellect does not foreknow the certainty of the believable thing, in what way can the will be excited and induced to assent?

**GOMET.** Know, Philalethes, that the pure will of reason has the spirit as a sort of teacher <note>original: "Paedagogum"; a tutor or guide</note> and leader, just as pack animals have nature, which frequent experience demonstrates in us. For those who use logical discourse less, but are carried by a certain hidden impulse, are more fortunate and foresee future things; this is because they are not led by the doubtful and deceptive motion of reason, but are driven by the unerring influences of celestial and super-heavenly things.

**PHILAL.** I find that those things you have just reviewed agree exactly with the tradition of the Peripatetics; for in the treatise *On Memory and Reminiscence*, Aristotle says: "The silent foresee future things, because their own motions do not disturb them." Again in the treatise

### PAUL RICCI,

->on good fortune, it is read thus: Driven by God <note>original: "A' Deo uecti"</note>, they have an impulse without reason toward doing something; and if anyone asks one having such an impulse, "for what reason does it please you to work this way," they will say "I do not know, but it pleases me to work so." Thus it is said there.<-

To these words it seems consistent that a certain stable concept of the mind is given, which the will commands without reasoning or the law of argumentation—which one might choose to call "believing." From this, it must be asked why the path of eternal salvation requires this very act of believing at all. 

<margin>Why it is necessary to believe for salvation.</margin>It seems that the mortal soul, decorated with the light of grace, could by its own nature—and without any act of belief—seek again that Supreme Good from which it flowed. This is shown by the experience and induction of individual things: by an implanted instinct of nature, they return to their own origin (once any hindrance is removed). 

**GOMET.** And we certainly assert right along with you that every single thing, by the instinct of its own nature, returns to that place from which it had its beginning, provided that the impeding occasion has been taken away. No wise man is ignorant that this is also true of the human soul, when the gift of grace goes before it and the impediment is removed. However, what hinders and stands in the way is the wicked and corrupted choice of the will, by which the mind is bent toward earthly and filthy pleasures of the flesh, and indulges in them with unbridled lust. 

Consider fire: like a small body, as long as it clings to oil, wax, or any airy moisture by which it is nourished, it suffers a kind of exile and stays far from the ether <note>In ancient and medieval science, "ether" was the pure, fiery upper atmosphere where the stars resided; fire naturally sought to rise to this region.</note>. But the less that fire is baited by fatness, the more it flames upward and is raised to the heavens. Since, therefore, believing is nothing other than the turning and approach of the soul toward that which the soul itself tends through the act of believing, and a turning away from all things providing an obstacle, it follows that everyone who desires to transfer his soul to his heavenly Parent can fulfill his vow in no other way than through the act of believing. Therefore, it must be concluded that the true path of eternal salvation absolutely requires believing in God. 

**PHILAL.** If it is to be judged that we are transferred to the Father of Lights <note>A biblical title for God, from James 1:17.</note> through the act of believing, we must admit that the path of salvation would be common to all people, because this act of believing (as you handed down just a moment ago) is committed to the assent of the will. Now, there is no human being so cowardly and senseless that they would not want to walk the path of life and attain eternal salvation; and thus, easily and without any study of sciences or disciplines, every person could be capable of the blessed life. 

**GOMET.** It should be judged exactly so. For it is the very nature of the Supreme Good to pour itself out into the universe according to the fitness and capacity of the receiver. Indeed, the acquisition of sciences—although it provides beauty and no small amount of advantage to happiness—is nevertheless not necessarily required for the blessed life. 

**PHILAL.** If we obtain salvation with such little trouble, what then prevents either all or most mortals from reaching it and attaining eternal life? (A thing which is approved neither by the authority of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note> nor of wise theologians), who contend with one voice that very few become participants in true salvation, and that very few "elect" are given. 

**GOMET.** Although eternal salvation is easy and common to all who wish for it, there are nonetheless three things that often make it difficult and do not permit it to be common to everyone: the deviance of nature, wicked habit, and earthly concupiscence <note>Concupiscence refers to strong worldly desires or lusts that pull the soul away from spiritual matters.</note>. 

<margin>Three things provide an obstacle so that salvation is not common to all.</margin>The deviance of nature happens to those whose minds are dulled from the womb or by disease, or who are completely delirious. These people relate to the secrets of truth just as an owl, or a completely blinded animal, relates to the light and brightness of the Sun; such people are called "men" only by an equivocal name <note>Meaning they are human in name only, lacking the functional use of reason.</note>. 

Wicked habit, however, which provides a barrier to true salvation in the second place, is that by which a man is imbued with erroneous and false traditions. Such a man (except with the greatest study and labor) can hardly be instructed and educated in the solid faith of truth. He is like one who, having been kept in a dark and long-lasting prison, when he goes out free into the air, is then unable to look upon or perceive the splendor of the Sun (except after a long time and gradually). 

The third thing, and that which more vehemently fights against the path of salvation, is empty luxury and earthly...

From the sound of these words, one may understand that the Philosopher established that happiness would be common to all, without a heap of other speculative sciences, but through another kind of diligence and discipline. Moreover, no discipline or diligence can be given or even devised that is common to all for attaining human happiness, except that which provides an easy and common way and path for all to contemplate the object—the very highest of all goods. Aristotle demonstrates in a long examination in the tenth book of the *Ethics* that all human happiness consists in this contemplation. Therefore, since 
<margin>Salvation is obtained far more easily through faith than through knowledge.</margin>
this kind of contemplation cannot be common to all through the investigation of the sciences, it remains that it is achieved through belief and faith alone. For he who practices the contemplation of the highest good through the study of the sciences and the law of <term>syllogizing</term> <note>The process of formal logical reasoning used by scholars to reach conclusions.</note>, as the wise men of the Peripatetics do, is indeed like one who builds a dwelling with long and relentless labor so that he may inhabit it. But he who, by faith alone, clings to the certainty of the matter, and from there raises his mind to the contemplation of the highest good believed in, is to be compared to one who inhabits a house already built by another, with no labor of his own applied. Now, it is clear that it is far easier and more common for men to inhabit a dwelling built by another than for the inhabitants themselves to want to build it first for the sake of living there. If, therefore, the happiness which can be given in this slippery life does not entirely require the discipline of argumentation, but is admitted as easy and very common through belief and faith alone, it follows that the salvation of the future world (which follows the true happiness of this life) is made easy and common through faith and the act of believing alone. Therefore, I have clearly recognized that the dogmas of the philosophers not only do not oppose all these teachings of yours, but even support them everywhere. <meta>This page continues the dialogue between Gometius and Philalethes. Previously, they discussed how faith provides a "shortcut" to divine contemplation. Now, Gometius begins to reconcile Aristotelian philosophy with the Christian concept of "Creation from nothing" (ex nihilo), arguing that God’s omnipotence is limited only by the capacity of the recipient, not by His own power.</meta>

-># PAUL RICIUS,<-

there is no student of whom it is true to say they can learn everything exactly; otherwise, that student could himself turn into a man of supreme wisdom, and thus two supreme beings would exist in the same category, which clearly (as you will hear in what follows) contradicts the inviolable order of things. By the same law, it must be judged that God can do all things by His immense power, but the nature of a created being is not at all suited to become all things. Just as the inability to be taught does not prove laziness or ignorance in the teacher, so the inability for something to be produced or happen in no way indicates a lack of power in the actor, but rather the weakness and unsuitability of the recipient. *PHILAL.* If I am not mistaken, you have described a two-fold condition of power that Aristotle seems to have taught in the ninth book of his *Divine Wisdom* <note>original: "Diuinæ sapientiæ," referring to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*.</note>, calling one "active" and the other "passive." But whether an active power exists that can act where no passive power is able to endure or receive it remains undiscussed there. However, based on the reason you assigned and the experience of reality, I acknowledge that it is not inappropriate to attribute effective omnipotence to God, the supreme founder of things, even if no passive virtue corresponds to the omnipotence of the agent. Yet, I do not yet fully grasp whether it is altogether necessary to believe in God’s omnipotence.

<margin>The Creator.</margin>
<margin>Creation demands omnipotence.</margin>
*GOMET.* This can easily be seen from the statement that immediately follows in the same clause of the <term>Creed</term> <note>original: "symboli," referring to the Apostles' Creed.</note>, which says: "Creator of heaven and earth." For since creation is nothing other than the production of a thing from nothing, and such production can only be done by a power of infinite strength, and since infinite strength can effect all things, it is proven that one must profess and believe that God, the creator of the universe, is omnipotent.

*PHILAL.* But regarding this very point you have assumed—namely, that something is produced from nothing—I doubt even more whether it is permissible to believe it, since the entire school of modern <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>The followers of Aristotle, who famously taught while walking about the "peripatos" or covered walkway of the Lyceum.</note> considers the creation of things to be something unimaginable and fantastical, and they claim that the world and motion are and always have been perpetual.

<margin>The explanation of true creation is production from nothing and in nothing.</margin>
*GOMET.* Those who think that the <term>Stagirite</term> <note>Aristotle, named after his birthplace, Stagira.</note> and his followers reject creation do not judge rightly. They fail to consider that the term "creation" signifies two things: one by its very nature, the other by association. By its nature, creation indicates production *from nothing* and *in nothing*. I say "from nothing" because the power of the earth produces grass and crops, yet not from nothing, but from pre-existing seed. I say again "in nothing" because the sun also produces brightness from nothing—that is, from no pre-existing tiny portion of brightness—yet it does not produce brightness "in nothing," but in the air or whatever transparent medium receives it. But if it were possible for the light, which the sun perpetually transmits, to exist without any recipient, then the production of light would be called a true creation. The other thing we attribute to creation by association is that this kind of production happened *recently*, whereas before it was nothing—as if the sun were only now emitting brightness which it had not poured out before. This is entirely accidental to the definition of creation. Therefore, one who denies that creation occurred at the beginning of time should not be thought to deny creation itself. Just as the nature of illumination is not taken away by the fact that illumination accompanies the sun perpetually. Therefore, the prince of the Peripatetics himself, since he admits a simple emanation of things from God, the maker of all, undoubtedly professes a true creation of things, even if (due to the absence of the light of grace) he perhaps rejects that other point which follows creation by association.

*PHILAL.* Although this explanation of creation holds together, there are two things that must be investigated and known: first, where exactly Aristotle taught that this creation is possible, and what logical argument can be assigned to demonstrate it. Second, once the truth of creation is known, we must see by what argument that other point stands—the one you claim is merely "accidental" to creation.

*GOMET.* It will not be difficult to prove the truth of this proposition using the foundations laid by the Peripatetics. For he who proves that there is one single principle of all things, yet denies this kind of creation, involves himself in a contradiction and refutes himself—which you yourself will admit if you answer my questions correctly, as you usually do. Tell me, then, I pray...

<summary>In this passage, Gometius defines creation as production "from nothing" and "in nothing," arguing that Aristotle's belief in an eternal world does not necessarily contradict the concept of divine creation. He maintains that the temporal beginning of the world is an "accidental" quality of creation, whereas the essential quality is the total dependence of all things on God's infinite power.</summary>

### ON CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE, BOOK I.

I ask you, does not the dogma of the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, known for walking while they taught.</note> demonstrate that a first cause of all things must be granted? **PHILAL.** It is certain, otherwise the series of causes would progress to infinity. **GOMET.** That which is the first of causes, will it not also be the highest and greatest in the universal scope of things? **PHILAL.** That is clearly evident; for (as taught in the tenth book of *Divine Wisdom* <note>original: "diuinæ sapientiæ," referring to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*.</note>), just as in any category of things there is one that is greatest, so in the entire breadth of beings there is one which is the principle and the greatest of all. **GOMET.** Since there are four types of causes <note>The Aristotelian four causes: efficient, formal, material, and final.</note>, in which of these do you think that first cause of all things should be placed? In the category of the efficient cause, or rather the formal, or material, or final cause? **PHILAL.** Since the final cause <note>The "end" or purpose for which something exists.</note> is prior to these four causes (for the end induces the efficient cause to act), in view of which the actor prepares the matter, and introduces the form according to the requirement of the end. Therefore, I judge the final cause to be the first of all other causes. **GOMET.** But not the efficient and producing cause? **PHILAL.** Not at all. **GOMET.** Do you admit then, that some beings exist which are not produced by a first cause? **PHILAL.** So it seems it must be judged. **GOMET.** Either then those beings are completely unproduced, or they are produced from somewhere other than the first cause. **PHILAL.** I think some beings are entirely unproduced, such as the celestial bodies; others I assert are produced, such as the sub-celestial things <note>Things below the heavens, i.e., the earthly realm.</note>. **GOMET.** So you affirm the celestial things are completely unproduced? **PHILAL.** I think it must be so affirmed. **GOMET.** But what is unproduced, does it not have existence from itself? **PHILAL.** Why not? **GOMET.** That which has its being from itself, is it not as much as it desires to be? **PHILAL.** So it should be thought, unless there is a hindrance. **GOMET.** A thing that does not depend on another cannot be prohibited or hindered. For (as your **Stagirite** <note>Aristotle, who was born in the city of Stagira.</note> taught you in the seventh book of *Physics* <note>original: "de auditu," a common title for Aristotle's *Physica*.</note>), that which is prohibited from motion from the outside is not moved by itself, but by another; therefore, what has being from itself cannot be hindered from the outside from having all that it desires. **PHILAL.** Even if I affirm it cannot be prohibited from the outside, nothing prevents it from being unable to reach all it desires because of the weakness it has by its own nature. Like a person with failing vision <note>original: "hallucinator," here referring to someone with weak or dim eyesight.</note> who wants to look at the sun's brightness, but the weakness of nature and the circumstances do not permit it. **GOMET.** The reason the person with failing vision is not capable of seeing the solar rays is because he depends on other things—for instance, an imbalance of humors, the air, food, drink, and the influence of the stars. If that person had been the craftsman and maker of himself, do you think any of the desired perfection would be lacking to him? **PHILAL.** I think not at all. **GOMET.** Therefore, that which has being from itself obtains as much capacity and fitness as it wants, and consequently will have as much of the perfection of being as it desires. **PHILAL.** I see no escape; I feel the same as you. **GOMET.** And is not the highest possible thing desired in every desirable thing? **PHILAL.** No one doubts it. **GOMET.** Therefore, having being from itself, it must necessarily obtain the highest of both capacity and perfection? **PHILAL.** I cannot deny this either. **GOMET.** So, according to your hypothesis, will there be something supreme and greatest in the scope of things, besides the first cause of all? **PHILAL.** It seems so. **GOMET.** Therefore the first cause will not be the supreme, which—as in individual categories (as you admitted a little earlier from Aristotle's opinion)—so in the universal breadth of beings, one measure and supreme of all others is given. And thus only one supreme is given in the scope of things and not more. But you admitted that both the first cause and that which is unproduced by the first cause are equally supreme. Either you will grant two supremes, or you will confess the first cause is not supreme, by which you openly contradict and deceive yourself. It remains therefore that nothing exists from itself and unproduced except the first cause. **PHILAL.** I must affirm the same. **GOMET.** Therefore you confess that whatever the universe contains is produced, and indeed not by another than the first cause, otherwise

it would have proceeded to infinity. Since, however, the same is said to be the producing and efficient cause, it is proven that God exists not only as the final cause (as you believe) but also as the efficient cause of all things. **PHILAL.** This must likewise be admitted. **GOMET.** Therefore, those things for which you affirm God is the efficient cause—do you think they are produced from something, or in something, or directly out of nothing and in nothing? **PHILAL.** What prevents them from being produced from something or in something? **GOMET.** Tell me, I pray, does that "something" from which or in which you think those beings are produced have its existence from itself or from another? **PHILAL.** Certainly not from itself; for it would then hold (as you taught a little while ago) the highest place in the scope of things. that God is the Creator of the entire heaven and earth. Suppose there are two small portions of fire: let one of them produce a four-foot fire from a one-foot volume of air; but let the other produce a four-foot fire from only a half-foot volume of air. <meta>This page continues the dialogue between Gometius and Philalethes regarding the nature of God as the Creator. Gometius has just argued that God is the "efficient cause" (the active maker) of the universe, not just its ultimate purpose. He is now using a geometric and logical analogy to prove that creating something out of nothing requires infinite power.</meta>

-># ON CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE, BOOK I.<-

...you judge. **PHILAL.** I judge it by this: that the further the starting point from which an agent begins to work is from the end point toward which the agent proceeds in working, the stronger the power of the agent must be. For example, if two people reach Rome in the same amount of time, but one started the journey from Augsburg <note>original: "Augustæ Vindelicorum," a major Roman-founded city in Bavaria</note> and the other started from Bologna <note>original: "Bononiæ," a city in northern Italy much closer to Rome than Augsburg</note>, it is clear that the one who began at Augsburg possesses much more strength than the one who started at Bologna. Thus, it is certainly manifest that a half-foot size is further away than a foot-long size—and a half-palm size even further than a half-foot—from a four-foot magnitude of fire.

**GOMET.** You judge correctly. If, therefore, the starting point from which the action of the agent began was separated from the goal by no limit at all, would it not require an immense transition across a boundless width, and a power without limit?

**PHILAL.** No one doubts that.

**GOMET.** Since, therefore, "non-being" (or pure and simple nothingness) is infinitely distant from "being"—because even if you were to multiply "nothing" an infinite number of times, it would never reach the boundary of "being"—it is thereby proven that the power which transfers and produces something from pure nothingness into existence must possess infinite vigor.

**PHILAL.** I see indeed that I have been led by these arguments of yours into such a narrow corner that there is no room for escape. That which I rejected a moment ago as a great absurdity, I now accept with firm and clear understanding: namely, that the power of creating demands an infinite vigor that cannot be shared with any created being. From this, it is concluded that the one and only omnipotent God exists as the creator of heaven and earth. Nevertheless, so that my mind and reason may be fully at rest, I would like you to bring forward some testimonies from Aristotle that might prove such a creation of the world.

**GOMET.** If you leaf through the writings of Aristotle, you will find several places where the philosopher proves that God exists as the producing and efficient cause <note>The "efficient cause" is the person or thing that actively makes something happen, like a carpenter making a chair.</note> of things. Since we have already shown that the production of things can only happen out of pure nothingness, to say "God produced the universe" is the same as saying "God created the universe."

**PHILAL.** No one would doubt that he who asserts God is the efficient cause of things also affirms Him to be the creator of things. But I do not yet see that Aristotle judged God to be the efficient cause.

<margin>
*Aristotle and his commentator Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were essential to Renaissance thought.</note> pronounce in various places that God is the efficient cause of things.*
</margin>

**GOMET.** For we read in the second book of *Metaphysics* <note>original: "diuinæ sapientiæ," literally "Divine Wisdom," a common title for Aristotle's Metaphysics in this period.</note>: that a First Principle is given, which is the cause of all other things being "beings," just as the first truth is the cause of other things being "true." It is established, moreover, that the first truth (that is, a self-evident proposition which they call a "maxim") is an efficient cause for a conclusion to be true. Therefore, the First Efficient [God] is the cause of others being "beings." 

Again, in the twelfth book of *Metaphysics*, it is taught that heaven and nature depend upon the First Being. It is clear to anyone looking closely that the discussion there concerns the "dependency" by which motion depends on a mover—that is, on the one who produces and effects the motion. Therefore, heaven and nature depend on the first principle, God, as on an efficient and producing cause. Finally, if Aristotle proves in various places that a First Mover is given, from whom flows and is produced "eternal motion"—which (in the opinion of all the Peripatetics <note>The "Peripatetics" were the followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy.</note>) is the proper operation and action of the heavens—then since that action depends on the efficient Mover himself, it is necessary that the very substance and existence of the heaven also depends on that efficient cause. For if the heaven had its existence from itself, it would surely have its operation from itself, which contradicts Aristotle's doctrine and sound reason in many ways. 

I will say nothing for now of Averroes, the great interpreter of the Peripatetic dogma, who in the twelfth book of *Metaphysics* calls God the "Agent," who carries the concern and care for all things, who alone grants eternity to things, and who provides not only motion, but also being and permanence. The same man, in his treatise *On the Substance of the Celestial Sphere* <note>original: "de substantia orbis"</note>, says: "We see that heaven has one power, not only moving all things, but acting upon and preserving all things." A little later he adds: "Some have said that Aristotle does not speak of an 'acting cause' but only a 'moving cause,' and that is truly absurd." So says he. Finally, if you examine the matter with right reason, and if you consider the words of Aristotle and his interpreter Averroes...

He then cites Aristotle and Averroes to prove that God is the active "efficient cause" of the universe's existence, not just its movement.</summary>

# PAUL RICIUS,

...if you weigh the traditions of the most eminent philosophers, and do not permit yourself to be captured and fascinated by the illusions of certain men, you will understand more clearly than light that God (who is blessed above all things) is the acting and producing cause of all things, and therefore exists as the true creator of heaven and earth. **PHILAL.** Indeed, you compel me to come at once to your opinion, and I now hold nothing more certain than that the best and greatest God is the creator of all things. Nevertheless, I have not yet been able to gather from these arguments that which you attribute to creation as an external quality—namely, that it was allotted a beginning in time <note>original: "temporis sortitam esse primordium"</note>. Therefore, there is still a need for another and indeed more fruitful investigation into these matters.

<margin>How creation was allotted a beginning in time.</margin> **GOMET.** Although the assertion of this question seems opposed to the traditions of the <term>Stagirite</term> <note>A common nickname for the Greek philosopher Aristotle, who was born in the city of Stagira.</note> and his followers, we shall nevertheless overcome and conquer them with their own weapons, with heavenly grace cooperating. Therefore, focus your strength and respond diligently to my questions. Have we not, up until now, found it proven according to the <term>Peripatetic</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy, so named because they often walked while discussing.</note> dogma that God exists as the producing and creating cause of things? **PHILAL.** I certainly admit it. **GOMET.** Moreover, that which is produced does not have the power of being from itself, but whatever it has, it received from elsewhere. **PHILAL.** That is well known. **GOMET.** If, therefore, you were to take away from it the whole of what it had from another, would it not be left participating in no entity at all? **PHILAL.** Without a doubt. **GOMET.** Thus, a produced being has "non-being" from itself. **PHILAL.** That is clear.

<margin>What a thing has from itself is prior to what it has from elsewhere.</margin> **GOMET.** Now, that which a thing has from itself—is that not more fundamentally applicable to the thing than what it has from elsewhere? For instance, wax has softness from itself, but it has the image of Caesar from elsewhere. Therefore, softness is in the wax first, and the image is there later. Likewise, a human has ignorance of things from himself, but wisdom from elsewhere; therefore, in time, he participates in ignorance before wisdom. Thus, since a produced being has non-being from itself, but has its existence from elsewhere, it follows that the produced and created universe previously had non-being. Your Stagirite <note>Aristotle</note> seems not to have clearly taught this part of divine wisdom when he proves that in the same individual thing, <term>act</term> <note>original: "actus"; the state of being fully realized or actually existing.</note> is posterior to <term>potency</term> <note>original: "potentia"; the capacity or potential to become something else.</note>. For "act" is nothing other than to exist in being, while "potency" is the opposite.

**PHILAL.** It does not seem that what you are striving for can be gathered from these points—namely, that the universe underwent a beginning of time. And although I do not deny that those things which are brought forth out of some pre-existing matter through the change of transformation exist in "potency" before they exist in "act" (as the authority of the Stagirite proves), this is by no means admitted in those things which are produced out of nothing. For in wax, non-being is prior to the being of images, and in a man, ignorance is prior to knowledge; but both of these were "something" in which there was the potential for the thing to be introduced. However, where the production is made out of nothing, potency cannot precede act. For if you contend that potency preceded it, it would surely have preceded either in the producible thing itself or in the producer; but it could be neither. For nothing pre-existed of a thing producible from nothing which could be subject to potency. As for the producer, since He is the purest act, it is not right to attribute any receptive potency to Him; moreover, it would then follow that the producer and the produced, the creator and the creature, were the same thing. For the "act" which is led in or led out exists in the same place where the "potency" resides. It remains, therefore, that in a thing produced from nothing, no potency preceded the act.

**GOMET.** Although it has been demonstrated and made manifest that God exists as pure act in every way, and that no potency preceded the act of things produced from nothing, nothing nevertheless prevents Him from having created and produced them at some point, and not before then, so that it was arranged by His eternal will that a new action should come forth at such a time. And thus, the non-being of things produced from nothing entirely preceded their being.

<margin>A new action does not come from an eternal and uniform will.</margin> **PHILAL.** In wishing to avoid Scylla (my good man), you seem to have fallen into Charybdis <note>A classical idiom meaning to run into one danger while trying to avoid another.</note>. For reason especially recoils from the idea that a new action could proceed from an eternal and uniform will. I ask you: when that new production of things (as you propose) was made, did the will of the producer behave in the same way as before, or not? If not, then the will of God the creator was not uniform. If so, then the effect should have behaved in the same way as before; for the cause...

<meta>This page continues a philosophical dialogue between Gometius and Philalethes. They are debating whether the universe has existed eternally or was created at a specific point in time. Philalethes has been presenting the Aristotelian (Peripatetic) view that because God is eternally good, His creation must also be eternal. Gometius has just countered that we see things being born and dying all the time, suggesting that "non-existence" is a natural part of the created order.</meta>

...for [cause] and effect—as is taught in the second book of *The Physics* <note>original: "de auditu," a literal translation of the Greek title of Aristotle's *Physics*, *Physica Auscultatio*</note>—always preserve the same proportion. If the effect was previously under "non-being," it would therefore remain so afterward, and thus no new production of things could ever have happened from any side. Added to this is the fact that the object of the will is the "good." Now, "good" and "being"—as is taught in the fourth book of *The Metaphysics* <note>original: "divinæ sapientiæ," literally "of divine wisdom," a common name for Aristotle's *Metaphysics*</note>—accompany one another. Therefore, He who from eternity and perpetually wills "being" itself, at no moment permitted it to "not be." **GOMET.** Although you reason <note>original: "syllogizes"</note> in the manner of the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note> and with a sharp and skillful wit, nonetheless, the senses themselves demonstrate the contrary of this view. For we see many—indeed, all <term>sublunary</term> <note>Things on Earth, literally "beneath the moon," which in ancient science were subject to change and decay.</note> things—being generated anew, which after a brief period of time are turned into rot and corruption. Therefore, just as the divine goodness permits some existing things at times not to be, so by a like law He permitted the universe at some time not to be, which He thereafter, in its own time, produced out of nothing. **PHILAL.** The sensory evidence that you bring forward seems to offer no testimony to this proposal, nor take any away. For the privation or lack of the universe as a whole is one thing; the lack of this or that specific thing—say, of Socrates or Plato—is quite another. **GOMET.** If any individual thing among beings is "good," then the lack of any individual will also be an "evil." Since, however, the will of the Highest Good wills nothing of evil, and nonetheless permits and sustains the alternation and corruption of these things, in a like way He could also have permitted that lack of the universe. **PHILAL.** This argument of yours based on similarity—if you will pardon my saying so—seems to have no bearing on the matter.

<margin>The order of things permits a small evil so that a worse evil is avoided, or a great good may result from it.</margin>
For the inviolable order of things mostly permits a small amount of evil so that it may guard against a worse evil, or so that a great good may emerge from it. Since that unformed <term>chaos</term> <note>The "prime matter" or raw material of the universe before it takes on specific shapes.</note>—as is taught in the first book of the *Physics*—is naturally fit to receive all the forms of sensible things, and because in it (as it pleased <term>the Corduban</term> <note>A reference to Averroes, the famous 12th-century Islamic philosopher from Córdoba, Spain, who wrote influential commentaries on Aristotle.</note> in the tenth book of *The Metaphysics*) are all perfections and forms in potentiality, which in actuality exist in the <term>First Mover</term> <note>God, as the ultimate source of all motion and change in the universe.</note>; and since any little portion of that unformed matter is equally fit to receive all sensible forms into itself, and because that cannot be done or fulfilled all at once (for contrary things drive each other out), therefore parent Nature took pity. What could not be done all at once, she accomplished through the succession of generation. Therefore, although it is an evil to lose the form of a previous individual, it is a lesser evil than to lack the multitude of all other possible forms.

In the same way, although it is a good thing to preserve the form of a single individual, it is better and more divine to become a participant in all sensible forms than to hold only one form—for example, the matter of a bare earthly clod <note>original: "terrestis giebulæ"</note> or a mass is born no less fit to receive the form and perfection of water, air, fire, metal, a plant, a beast, or a man, than the form and perfection of earth. But since one and the same little portion of matter cannot be associated with all these forms at the same time, it therefore loses the earthly form with which it is already sated and claims for itself the form of water. When that same particle of matter has again obtained the form of water, deserting that also, it adapts itself to the form of air; and so it proceeds gradually until it has filled the whole "latitude" of sensible things (as Averroes speaks in the second book of *On the Heavens*).

By this same path, the individual parts of the celestial bodies—endowed with agility and spiritual power and emulating the First Mover—demand to be present everywhere. Because they cannot accomplish this all at once at the same moment, they strive to fulfill that wish by a successive and most rapid motion in a circle. By the same law, the rational intellect (which they call the "possible" and "material" intellect), since it is capable of grasping all intelligible things but is not able to conceive them all at once, does not cease to run and wander from one thought to another until it has traversed the whole circuit of understandable things. **GOMET.** You have brought forward things worthy of hearing, but more than the proposed question required. But such is the way the flow of speech and the nature of things sometimes demands. Finally, from all these things you have said, you seem to conclude that the Founder of the world and the universe permits the corruption and non-being of these sensible things, insofar as in any little portion of matter—just as its innate fitness and potential requires—the whole *Epilogue.*

<summary>Philalethes explains that the physical world is characterized by constant change because matter "desires" to experience every possible form (water, air, life) rather than being stuck in one state. This constant cycle of birth and decay allows the finite world to reflect the infinite perfection of God through succession over time.</summary>

the breadth of forms may be filled; and thus the order of nature permitted a small evil so that a worse evil might be avoided, and it neglects a meager good so that a greater and more divine good may follow. *PHILAL.* Our entire previous speech aimed at this goal, from which I finally conclude that the example of these corruptible things can by no means be compared to the whole scope of things, such that you would want to argue by saying: "In all these things capable of generation, their non-being precedes their being; therefore, non-being also once preceded the being of the universe itself." Wherefore, the same stone is still being rolled between us <note>A reference to the myth of Sisyphus, implying a repetitive or unending argument.</note>—namely, since the will of the Founder of all things is uniform and in no part changeable, and He always and perpetually wills the good, it seems impossible that the entire breadth of beings was produced anew after having not existed at all, and that the potentiality of the universe (like that of individual things capable of generation) preceded the act. Therefore, you must prove by some other and more solid argument that creation is something <term>adventitious</term> <note>original: "aduentitium"; in this context, it refers to something that is not an eternal necessity but was added or brought into being at a specific point.</note>. *GOMET.* I suspect, Philalethes, if I wished to unravel every single point regarding this question here, our discourse would be made longer than the intent of this compendium allows. <margin>He shows that all beings of the sublunary machine were produced with the beginning of time by a three-part argument, and first from the mutual order of things.</margin>

*GOMET.* If you pay attention, the very order of things, the indwelling nature and power of the heavens, and finally the end toward which celestial bodies yearn, all declare this. <margin>Action in rest is more perfect than that which is based on motion.</margin>

*GOMET.* And the more perfect any of the beings is, does it not have a more perfect operation and act? *PHILAL.* That is certain. 

<margin>Rest is more suitable to the celestial and every corporeal nature than motion.</margin>

*GOMET.* The most perfect of bodies, however, is the heaven. *PHILAL.* No one doubts it. *GOMET.* Therefore, its operation is more excellent—namely, of the kind that is exercised in a state of rest. *PHILAL.* It must be so. *GOMET.* Since, therefore, motion is suitable to a corporeal thing, and likewise a stable state, or rather rest is more suitable to it than motion—since all things are moved only by an adventitious and secondary intention, and that only for the sake of rest, as the experience of the thing demonstrates—for a thing is moved only when, by chance, it is found outside its own proper place. But when they reach their own places, they immediately rest; wherefore we clearly perceive that a stable state of rest is more suitable to a celestial body than motion. *PHILAL.* Truly, I know not what to think or say: for your arguments persuade me to agree, but the senses and the authority of the <term>Peripatetic</term> <note>A follower of Aristotle.</note> warn me to refuse. For we see the heaven rotated with constant rolling, yet reason convinces us that rest is more suitable to it. *GOMET.* I wonder greatly, my Philalethes, how, beyond the usual clarity of your wit, you do not see that here the senses fight against reason in nothing. For nothing prevents something by its own nature from being inclined toward some disposition, yet by event or secondary will, existing under the opposite of that same disposition—just as a portion of fire, which by its own nature tends upward, nevertheless remains downward as long as it is nourished by some air in wood or any fatty moisture. When the moisture fails, however, it immediately flies out and seeks the upper air. Whence your <term>Stagirite</term> <note>Aristotle, who was born in the city of Stageira.</note> says in the 1st book of *On the Heavens*, Commentary 5: "We say all physical bodies and magnitudes are mobile according to place." For he did not teach that all physical bodies *are moved*, but that they are mobile and fit by nature [to be moved], when [they are] outside...

By the same law, therefore, even if our senses judge the heaven to be revolving, it is not contradictory—indeed, the very order of things requires—that it once rested, and that it will rest in the future, as you will be able to understand more broadly from what follows. **PHILAL.** Though what you say is plausible and not difficult to grasp, because Aristotle and his interpreter Averroes <note>Averroes (1126–1198) was a medieval Andalusian philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational for Western scholasticism.</note> establish that the motion of the heaven is perpetual and will never have an end, I often find myself in doubt, and I cling to the recognized truth with a certain fear. **GOMET.** I believe it has not escaped you that from the very beginning of our conversation, I reminded you that Aristotle and his faithful interpreter taught a true creation; however, they failed in this: they did not see that the beginning of time was added to the creation from the outside, as an <term>adventitious</term> <note>original: "aduentitio"; meaning something added or coming from without, rather than being an essential, eternal part of the thing itself.</note> quality. Not, of course, by the kind of discourse where the unknown is revealed through the better known, as happens to us mortals, but because it turns from one intelligible paradigm to another. **PHILAL.** Since the Mover of the heaven is the immortal God, we would then have to admit that God understands through discourse, and is therefore changeable. **GOMET.** You are mistaken, my Philalethes, and you have not sufficiently observed the teachings of your man of Córdoba <note>Referring to Averroes, who was born in Córdoba.</note>, who affirms that there are twin movers of the heaven:

<margin>A twofold mover of the heaven is given, according to the Peripatetic <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy.</note> dogma.</margin>
One which makes use of no partnership or familiarity with a body; and another which exists within the moving heaven and perpetually performs its contact with it. Therefore, the first of these movers is touched by no change, neither physical nor spiritual. But the other mover, which is inherent in the body, must undergo a spiritual change through discourse. **PHILAL.** I have no doubt that according to Averroes, Avicenna, Al-Farabi, Avempace, Al-Ghazali, and also Themistius and Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus was Aristotle's successor; the others were major Islamic and Greek commentators who shaped medieval science.</note> (the principal student of Aristotelian doctrine), as well as the entire Platonic Academy and the school of the ancient Allegorizers (whom they call the Kabbalists), the movers of the celestial bodies are divided into two parts. One of these, which exists as a pure and naked intellect, moves the heaven as "the beloved moves the lover" <note>original: "amabile amantem"; a famous Aristotelian metaphor meaning the heavens move out of a desire to emulate the perfection of the Unmoved Mover.</note>. The other, however, moves it as an efficient cause of motion, just as the power that informs the lover moves the lover himself. And such a mover of the heaven is the innermost and ultimate form of the heaven. In view of this, in the second book of *On the Heavens*, commentaries 8 and 61, Aristotle calls the heaven "animated and alive, having animal action." So too in the seventh book of *Divine Wisdom* <note>Likely referring to the *Metaphysics*.</note>, commentary 31, Averroes judged that a soul is enclosed within the celestial body. He explains the very same thing in a clear series of words in the twelfth book of that same work, and in the second book of *On the Heavens*, commentaries 3, 7, and 61, and even more frequently in his treatise *On the Substance of the Orb*. Furthermore, reason and the inviolable order of things demonstrate this quite clearly: for if these earthly and opaque little bodies of the falling world are naturally fit to receive within themselves this noble spiritual form (which we call the soul), how much more fit and suitable to receive it are the sublime, bright, and everlasting bodies of the heaven? Finally, I accept and approve all these things reviewed here with a firm understanding. **GOMET.** That state of rest which accompanies the heaven will become plainly known to you a little later (when we conclude the state of the heaven with our third argument). But now—lest our speech wander too far afield—I proceed to the second argument, by which I promised to show the state of the heaven. However, I should like you first to summarize the things we have discussed in our long examination,

the very production and emanation of things from the first cause <note>The "First Cause" is a philosophical term for God, the primary origin of all existence.</note> out of nothing and into nothing—an idea proven by the authority of Aristotle and his follower Averroes. The other part is from what is adventitious—namely, that this kind of emanation occurred at the beginning of time and was "new," a point which the dogma of the Peripatetics <note>The "Peripatetics" were the followers of Aristotle, named after the covered walkways (peripatoi) of the Lyceum where they studied.</note> seems by no means to approve. <margin>
The future state of the heaven is shown from its innate nature.

For instance, the mover of the daily sphere cannot complete the circuit of its sphere faster than in a period of twenty-four hours. Thus the sphere of the Moon completes its course in the period of a month, the Sun in the circle of a year, and so one must judge for each individual mover of the spheres. **PHILAL.** Aristotle taught exactly that in the same place. **GOMET.** But does not the mover, as we gather from the sixth book of the *Physics*, <note>original: "sexto de auditu"; referring to Aristotle's *Physica*.</note> relate to time in the same way it relates to magnitude and motion? **PHILAL.** That is well established. **GOMET.** Now, the mover relates to these things in such a way that it can neither move with infinite velocity nor revolve an infinite magnitude. **PHILAL.** That is manifest. **GOMET.** Therefore, can it move for an infinite time? **PHILAL.** Reason dictates it cannot, and Averroes <note>original: "Cordubensis" (The Cordoban), referring to Averroes.</note> openly maintained this in his book *On the Substance of the Orb*, chapter 2, saying: "Everything that is of finite dimensions and bounded by a containing surface, when the intellect considers it as existing by itself, without anything bestowing permanence and eternity upon it, must necessarily have a finitude of permanence just as it has a finitude of action." By this series of words, Averroes clearly taught that a thing relates to the infinity of time or duration in the same way it relates to the infinity of action—that is, to an infinite velocity of motion. Wherefore you correctly conclude that a finite power cannot perform a motion for an infinite time, just as it cannot move with a motion of infinite velocity, nor move an infinite magnitude.

<margin>
A body of finite power and magnitude cannot perform an infinite motion.
</margin>

**GOMET.** Therefore, the heaven could not have been moved from eternity by its own vigor and its own nature. **PHILAL.** Thus the argument stands. **GOMET.** Therefore, it is necessary to admit that its motion once began. **PHILAL.** As I see it, we are not forced by what has been said to admit that consequence. ### ON CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE, BOOK I.

...to maintain motion perpetually, which many of the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> also seem to feel, and **Averroes** <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to Western science and philosophy.</note> clearly testifies to this very thing (in that same booklet on the *Substance of the Orb*), saying: <note>Original Latin: "Cùm Aristoteles considerauit... destrueretur motus coeli."</note> "When **Aristotle** considered these celestial appetitive powers <note>The 'desires' or 'souls' that ancient and medieval philosophers believed drove the planets.</note>, he found they are moved toward an object of desire more noble than themselves, and that they possess finite powers. The cause of the continuation of motion is not that power by which the heaven is moved; rather, that which grants them continuation is something desirable—an abstract intelligence—which the celestial body itself understands and desires. Unless there were such a moving intelligence, the motion of the heaven would be destroyed." These are the words of **Averroes**. By which it is clearly understood, not without reason but rather by necessity, that the heaven, by virtue of its own nature and that of its immediate mover, is at rest; but being supported from without by a more sublime power, it exercises its motion eternally.

**GOMET.** Whatever external patronage and adventitious <note>Coming from the outside; not innate.</note> strength there may be, you still prove that the heaven, according to its own nature and that of its immediate mover, at some point demands rest and stability. **PHILAL.** For the arguments brought forward by you persuade me so, and the authority of the **Corduban** <note>Averroes, who lived in Córdoba.</note> supports them. **GOMET.** This is exactly where our entire speech was tending, from which we gather the second mode of arguing: from the very nature of the heaven, by which we most firmly prove that the rest and stability of the heavens is granted.

**PHILAL.** But according to the assertions of **Aristotle** and **Averroes**, this seems by no means to be concluded from the aforesaid: for motion will be preserved perpetually, not indeed by the merit of the nature of the heaven, but by that intelligence of infinite vigor which moves it, as a thing beloved.

<margin>If the motion of the heaven were perpetual, it would ultimately become violent.</margin>
**GOMET.** If we were to admit such a perpetuity of motion, we would be forced to call the motion of the heavens **violent** <term>Violent motion (motus violentus) is an Aristotelian term for movement that is forced upon an object against its natural inclination, like a stone thrown upward.</term> in the end, because it is violent for anything to perpetually exercise that which is repugnant to its innate aptitude and nature. Because, therefore, the nature and aptitude of the heaven (as shown before) requires rest and stability, it would surely be violent for the celestial body to be agitated by perpetual motion and never reach its longed-for rest.

**PHILAL.** That which is committed by choice is not violent. Since, therefore, the heaven is a voluntary agent, perhaps it chooses perpetual motion for itself, by which it provides permanence to lower things through its own cycles. For **Aristotle** judged (in the eighth book of *Physics* <note>Literally "on hearing," a common title for Aristotle's Physics in the Renaissance.</note>, Commentary 1) that the motion of the heaven is the life of all **sublunary** <term>The "sublunary" world refers to the Earth and everything below the Moon, characterized by change and decay.</term> things.

<margin>The heaven is revolved by its primary intention for its own sake.</margin>
**GOMET.** Your response would not be out of tune if the motion of the heaven occurred with a stronger and primary intention for the sake of this earthly, unstable, and falling world. But the **Peripatetics** (as **Averroes** testifies in *Divine Wisdom* <note>Referring to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*.</note>, Book 2, Commentaries 3 and 6) by no means approve of this, establishing that the heaven is revolved most especially for its own sake—and only as a consequence for those things which are here. Given this, it would surely be absurd and ridiculous to think that these sublime and sempiternal celestial bodies would neglect their own perfection to assist muddy and transitory things and impart momentary benefits to them.

**PHILAL.** These evident and solid arguments finally lead and draw me to your opinion—that the prince of the **Peripatetics** <note>Aristotle.</note> with his followers is largely blind and hallucinates in these matters which exceed the limits of sensory things. Indeed, **Aristotle** himself seems to acknowledge this ingenuously and with the greatest modesty of mind (in *Divine Wisdom* Book 2, Commentary 1, and likewise in *On the Heavens* Book 2, Commentary 60), asserting that no one (at least by the light of nature) can worthily and exactly attain the Theory of Truth. Proceed then, O excellent man, and complete the third reasoning you proposed, by which the future state of the heaven is concluded.

<margin>From the end toward which the heaven tends, the state of the heaven is concluded.</margin>
**GOMET.** In the third place, you will discover their future state from the very **end** <note>The "final cause" or ultimate purpose.</note> for which the celestial bodies yearn. But first, consider the manner and cause for which the heaven is revolved in constant motion; if you know it, bring it forth.

**PHILAL.** The reason, manner, and mode of the celestial motion seems to be a spiritual movement, and a mode of understanding belonging to the soul of the heavens itself. For the **Stagirite** <note>Aristotle, born in Stagira.</note> taught (in the first book *On the Soul*) that the operation of a rational soul exists similar to a circle; hence, in the second book *On the Heavens*, and the second book *On the Substance of the Orb*, **Averroes** [says] that circular motion is the proper [motion] of the rational soul...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Gomet and Philalethes concerning the nature of the heavens and the soul. Philalethes is explaining why the physical motion of the stars and planets corresponds to the internal, intellectual activity of the soul that governs them, drawing heavily on Aristotelian (Peripatetic) thought and the commentaries of Averroes.</meta>

# PAULUS RICIUS, #

...willed it to be moved; therefore, we say the cause by which the heaven is carried in a circle is that the proper operation of the rational soul mirrors a sphere. **GOMET.** Since this position of yours contains two points: First, that the operation of the rational soul is similar to motion; Second, that it is similar to circular motion: I ask you, by what reasoning can the operation of the soul, which consists solely of intelligence, be compared to bodily motion, when the nature of the body is separated from the nature of the soul by such a vast distance?

<margin>
Why the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> liken the operation of the rational soul to circular motion.
</margin>

**PHILAL.** We compare the operation of the rational soul to motion because the soul, unable to grasp all intelligible things in a single glance, is forced to seek them one after another in a kind of spiritual discourse <note>The process of reasoning from one premise to another.</note>. For this reason, the understanding of the rational soul is said to be like motion. Moreover, it is compared to circular motion because, just as a circular motion is a continuous movement that always seeks the same destination from which it began, so the rational soul, in the very act of understanding, extends from itself toward the object of thought. From there (as is taught in the first book of *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle's *De Anima*.</note>), it reflects back upon itself. Because that which has now been made intelligible in act is nothing other than the act of the "possible intellect" <note>The capacity of the mind to receive and become the things it understands.</note>, by understanding the object, the soul understands itself. Therefore, by considering these things, the entire **Peripatetic** school judged the operation of the rational soul to be similar to motion and to a circle.

**GOMET.** You answer skillfully, as becomes a student of Peripatetic doctrine. Nevertheless, you have not yet indicated by what law this physical rotation of the heaven follows that spiritual motion of the soul, as I was hoping to hear from you.

**PHILAL.** The physical rotation of the heaven follows the spiritual discourse both because of the natural bond between the celestial body and the soul, and also by the work and command of the will. For just as in this mortal frame of ours, whenever the soul exults in something delightful and pleasant, the bodily spirits (in which the soul dwells) immediately rejoice and are stirred by certain "ticklings," as it were. These are spread far and wide through the entire mass of the body along with the blood, making the limbs of the whole body ready and agile for movement. It is like when a vigorous young man hears a pleasant and sweet melody for a dance; he soon moves with his feet and hands and, by natural instinct, strives to imitate the harmony of the melody. In the same way, when the soul of the celestial bodies runs through those **Ideal forms** <note>The perfect, eternal archetypes or blueprints of things.</note> and supreme beauties, and is carried from one paradigm to another, it is affected by an ineffable exultation and joy. Consequently, that affection soon overflows into the agile celestial body associated with it, and it continually breaks out by natural instinct into this most rapid motion that our senses perceive. Added to this is the command of the will. The will, desiring to produce those Ideal forms (which the soul contemplates and conceives) within this material of generable things <note>Things that are born and die on Earth.</note> and this bodily mass, and foreseeing that this can only be done through motion, willed to exercise this constant circular movement. By doing so, it imitates the image of its Creator, whose immense goodness pours itself out through the universe, bestowing the gift of being even upon the lowliest things and providing for the needs of their natures.

**GOMET.** Therefore, the spiritual discourse of the soul produces the rotation of the heaven through its bond with the celestial body, and additionally through the will’s desire to print the Ideal forms into the substance and matter of fleeting things.

**PHILAL.** So the reasoning of the Peripatetics suggests, and the authority of **Averroes** in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics* testifies.

# PAUL RICIUS, #

**PHILAL.** Aristotle clearly demonstrates this through a long sequence of arguments in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics* <note>Original: *Diuinæ sapientiæ 12*—literally "Divine Wisdom," a common Renaissance way to refer to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*.</note>. **GOMET.** Is God, therefore, an intelligent being? **PHILAL.** There is no doubt of it. **GOMET.** No being is intelligent except by the fact that it produces within itself and receives an image of the thing it understands. **PHILAL.** Indeed, in his book *On Memory and Reminiscence*, Aristotle calls the concept of the mind the "image" of the thing that can be conceived. **GOMET.** Is the thing itself, which God understands and of which He generates an image in Himself, not that very same divine essence?

<margin>12. Com. 31.</margin>
**PHILAL.** It is established that He understands Himself first, and from the understanding of Himself (as Averroes <note>Averroes was a 12th-century Muslim philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were essential to medieval and Renaissance scholarship.</note> says in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*) He understands every mode of being. **GOMET.** Is it therefore God Himself who understands, and is He also the same thing that is understood? **PHILAL.** Certainly. **GOMET.** Since, therefore, the one who understands produces within himself an image of the thing understood, you must admit that God produces an image of Himself. **PHILAL.** That is exactly how it must be judged. **GOMET.** Come then, and answer again: do you think the image is one thing, and the one who produces the image is another? **PHILAL.** Are you not asking whether the nature or essence of the image is one thing, and that of the producer of the image is another? **GOMET.** That is exactly what I am asking. **PHILAL.** It would certainly be profane and unbefitting the divine essence to admit such a distinction within it; for where there is a distinction of essence in any thing, there is true composition <note>In philosophy, "composition" means being made of parts, which would contradict the belief that God is "simple" or perfectly one.</note> and the exclusion of absolute simplicity. **GOMET.** Therefore, the divine essence which produces the image of the intelligible thing in itself is one and the same as the produced image itself. **PHILAL.** Judge it so. **GOMET.** Does the same essence, then, produce itself? **PHILAL.** It is not even lawful to say that. Otherwise, the same thing would be prior in origin to itself. **GOMET.** Then you must either admit that God is not an intelligent being, or a distinction must be devised which neither multiplies the essence nor designates only a single numerical hypostasis <note>A technical term for a "person" or distinct individual existence within the Godhead.</note>, so that the relations of the producer and the produced—which are opposites—can be fittingly applied to the divine nature. **PHILAL.** Such a distinction must surely be given, which suggests unity on one hand and plurality on the other. Just as the Stagirite <note>Aristotle, born in Stagira.</note> says: whenever arguments occur that persuade toward contrary sides, then some third thing that partakes of both opposites is brought forward, by which the extremes are reconciled. **GOMET.** But what distinction do you think can be applied here, by which contradiction is avoided in these divine relations? Would a "distinction of reason" <note>A "distinction of reason" (*distinctio rationis*) is a distinction that exists only in our minds, not in the thing itself.</note> be enough for this? For example, when we want to prove that Socrates is not Socrates by distinguishing Socrates as the subject from Socrates as the predicate. In this way, God, as the producer of His own image in Himself, would be distinct from Himself as the produced image, such that there is no real distinction in divine matters, but only one made by the consideration of the intellect. **PHILAL.** A distinction of reason only removes a contradiction in our logic, but not a real one. By distinguishing Socrates into "Socrates as subject" and "Socrates as predicate," it removes nothing other than the contradiction of the concept whereby we say Socrates is not Socrates; no actual contradiction corresponds to this in the reality of the thing, because the subject and predicate here exist by the work of the intellect and differ only by reason. However, the "understanding" of God is produced in reality from the intelligent essence of God, and even if we set aside every operation of our own intellect, the "produced" is nevertheless distinguished from the "producer." Because, therefore, the producer and the produced in divine matters are distinct in reality, regardless of any act of our intellect, a distinction of reason is not sufficient to remove this contradiction. **GOMET.** Finally, I gather from your answers here that you judge it a wicked thing to say that the essence of the producer is one thing and the essence of the produced is another. Yet, a distinction of reason is not enough to remove the contradiction. What distinction, then, do you think must be devised, by which you do not multiply the essence in divine matters, yet you do remove the contradiction? **PHILAL.** The error committed in so great a matter is dangerous and much to be dreaded; therefore, lest I strike against the hard rock of error, I do not dare to put forward any opinion on this matter. But it will be your task (O man of heavenly mind) to unfold this mystery, just as you have the other secrets of truth...
