### ON CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE, BOOK I. ###

**GOMET.** I ask you, what great mistrust and fear has seized you, that you dare neither to remove this doubt nor to declare the proper distinction in divine matters? After all, one can experience and clearly see this kind of distinction in those things that are subject to our senses. Tell me, please, have you not also fathered a son according to the Law of Nature? **PHILAL.** Certainly. **GOMET.** Are you the same person as your son, or is there some difference? **PHILAL.** A difference, without a doubt. **GOMET.** Are you so distinguished from your son that there is absolutely nothing held in common between you and him? **PHILAL.** We are distinguished in such a way that we are nevertheless sharers of the same essence or nature; indeed, in terms of the degree of distinction, there is no greater coherence and unity than that between a son and a parent. This is because between the two of them there is a unity of species and essence, with a relationship to his immediate origin. **GOMET.** You answer then—and not without reason—that you are one with your son in essence, but you are distinguished as individual persons <note>Original: *supposita numero*—in Scholastic philosophy, a *suppositum* is an individual, distinct substance, often used interchangeably with "person" when discussing humans or God.</note>. This distinction does not destroy the true and simple unity of essence. **PHILAL.** That is exactly what I mean. **GOMET.** From this, therefore, you will easily be able to deduce the unity of essence in divine matters along with a real distinction of persons: namely, that the one producing is the same in essence as the produced image, yet not the same person, and not the same individual hypostasis <note>Original: *hypostasis*—a Greek term used in theology to denote the distinct "personhood" of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit within the one Godhead.</note>, just as a father is not the same individual as his image, the son. **PHILAL.** Therefore, just as an earthly father and son are two composite men, divided by number, so in divine matters, there will be composition in the one producing and the one produced, and there will be two gods in number, not just one. **GOMET.** In this, my dear Philalethes, you wander far from the path. In human affairs, a father and son are indeed two men because human essence is actually distinct from the person in whom that essence is grounded. Therefore, when the person is multiplied, the humanity is multiplied—just as a single, simple solar splendor <note>Original: *solaris splendor*—sunlight.</note> becomes manifold according to the multitude of openings and receptacles through which the solar ray is poured. But in divine matters (as we have taught), the hypostasis or person is the same as the divine essence itself. Therefore, the Deity <note>Original: *Deitas*.</note> always remains one in number, even if the personality is not the same. **PHILAL.** You have now certainly persuaded me that two persons are to be granted in divine matters, called Father and Son, with a unity of essence. But now, I beg you to explain in a few words how a third, which you call the Holy Spirit, is to be admitted at all.

<margin>Epilogue.</margin>
**GOMET.** You will easily understand the certainty of this if you recall the things explained just a moment ago. For we established that God exists as the best and most beautiful of all things, who, by understanding Himself, produces an image in Himself. Now, does not someone who contemplates the best and most beautiful of all existing things immediately break forth into love for that known thing? **PHILAL.** It is established—unless he be "an ass at the lyre" <note>Original: *asinus sit ad lyram*—a classical proverb describing someone who is tone-deaf to music, art, or reason.</note>; for the stronger the intellect is (as Averroes <note>The 12th-century philosopher Averroes.</note> says in the second book of *On the Heavens*, commentary 58), the more perfect the desire will be. **GOMET.** Therefore, God the Father, by understanding Himself as the best and most beautiful, reflects His love back upon Himself. So too the image itself (the Son), which is produced by the Father's understanding, is carried into love for the Father by a similar impulse, while contemplating the Father's supreme beauty. Thus, from the mutual contemplation of the Father and the Son, there proceeds a supreme delight and love. Insofar as this love is produced, it is actually distinct from the producer. However, the producer of this love is the Father together with the Son; therefore, the love is actually distinguished from both. And because love is nothing other than a breathing <note>Original: *spiratio*—a technical theological term for the "procession" of the Holy Spirit, related to the word for "breath" or "spirit."</note> or spiritual procession of the lover toward the beloved, it has pleased us to call this very thing by the name "Holy Spirit." We therefore judge with firm belief and understanding that God is three in hypostasis or persons, but one in essence. In the unity of essence, we call Him "God"; in the Trinity of persons, we call Him "Father, Son, and Holy Spirit." **PHILAL.** By the very skillful and clear light of reason, you have led me there step by step, so that what I thought just a moment ago was hidden and beyond the grasp of human intelligence, I now conceive easily and without any fear. First, however, we must lay this Peripatetic <note>The "Peripatetics" were followers of Aristotle, so-named because Aristotle allegedly taught while walking (*peripateo* in Greek) in the Lyceum.</note> foundation: that a plurality of Intelligences <note>In medieval philosophy, "Intelligences" were non-physical beings (often identified as angels) responsible for moving the celestial spheres.</note> can only be proven to exist because of the multitude of moving bodies. **PHILAL.** That is evident. One conjectures not only the plurality of the "movers," but even the various conditions of each mover based on the variety of the body's motion. Just as we say that the prolific seed of a living creature, and the spirit within that seed, contains within itself as many distinctions of powers and bodily virtues as there are members and organs that we know have emerged from that seed and spirit. Therefore, just as the first bodily essence relates to itself and to the order of other things belonging to the body, so too the first intellectual essence relates to itself and to other things that belong to the intellect. Since, in truth, the first bodily nature and mass is really one, yet consists of three principles—distinguished by a real difference from one another—namely **privation**, **matter**, and **form**; <note>These are the three principles of change in Aristotelian physics: Matter (the stuff), Form (the identity/shape), and Privation (the lack of a form that matter desires to have).</note> which are nonetheless the same as the bodily nature itself, separated from it by no real distinction. Therefore, it is necessary that the first intellectual nature (namely the Divine nature), which is the moving and efficient cause of that first bodily mass, contains this threefold distinction with a real unity of nature in an eminent and unsearchable way. Just as a "model" encompasses in a much more sublime way the individual parts that are present in a shadowy image. Whence these three principles of bodily nature (if you consider them rightly) regard themselves and the bodily mass itself with the same relationship by which the Divine Persons regard one another and the Divine nature itself, as can be clearly seen from the table provided here.

### OF CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE, BOOK I ###

...-ceive: So that thing in the divine essence which is the **opposite of privation** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "privation" is the absence of a quality that should naturally be present. By being the opposite of privation, the Divine Essence is pure "act" or fullness.</note> makes it so that the first intellectual essence can act upon all things; this we call the **Father**, and to him we attribute power. The second thing in corporeal substance is **matter**; which is indeed stripped of every perfection of being, yet it possesses the **germinal reason** <note>original: "seminariam rationem," a Stoic and Neoplatonic concept of "seed-logics" that allow things to grow into their specific forms.</note> of all the perfections of being, so that it might receive each one. Thus, in the first intellectual essence there is something which overflows toward every perfection of the creatures and contains their **Ideal reasons**, from which all things proceed through the power of the Father. This we name the **Son** and attribute to him **wisdom**, whose role it is to order all things—just as it was the nature of matter to be ordered by all things. The third thing in corporeal substance is **form**, which is drawn out from the potential of matter due to a "privation" by means of appetite—and not by love—which supplies the essence and all natural goods to the body. Thus, from the omnipotence of the incarnate Word, on account of the most rich perfection of God the Father, there proceeds through the Word and the conceived Mind not an appetite, but **love**. (For love belongs to the perfect and the giver; whereas appetite belongs to the imperfect and the receiver.) This third thing in the first intellectual essence is called the **Holy Spirit**. Just as those three things are distinct from one another and yet constitute one single corporeal essence in reality, so the three persons in the first intellectual essence are indeed distinguished among themselves, but are nevertheless fundamentally the same as the essence itself.

<margin>The steps from the first being to non-being, and from non-being to the highest being, meet each other on the horizon of eternity and time: namely, the rational soul. Job 38:14.</margin>

**PHILAL.** This table is indeed expressed in a brief and concise speech, yet a most sublime and vast meaning is hidden within it. For those who search out secret things know that the circuit of the universe is disposed by such a law and order that, by whatever degree higher and eternal things descend toward these lowest and decaying things, these lower things climb by an equal step and seek the heights, until their steps from both sides meet at the **horizon of eternity and time**, in which the rational soul is situated and established. Furthermore, your table brings to my memory the praise of a certain wise man, saying: "It is turned (namely, the earthly machine) like the clay of a signet or seal" <note>This is a reference to Job 38:14. The "seal" represents the divine pattern being pressed into the "clay" of the physical world.</note>. For the mass of the earthly body represents the clay, in which the image of the **Archetypal Man** <note>original: "Archetypi hominis," likely referring to the Platonic ideal of humanity or the Kabbalistic Adam Kadmon.</note> is signed and impressed. You know, however, that when the seal of a protruding figure is fixed into wax or clay, then that which is higher and more prominent on the seal is rendered deeper and lowest in the clay. But mysteries of this sort require a longer discourse than the logic of this compendium demands. Therefore, setting these things aside for now, we must return to the remaining examinations of this symbol. Indeed, the delay torments me until I have completed every detail regarding this path of life.

**GOMET.** Proceed then, my son; if you have any point where you hesitate, bring it into the open now.

**PHILAL.** The doubt that occurs to me now is this: although I now understand these mysteries of the Trinity to be in harmony with the truth and the order of things, yet the belief and knowledge of every truth is not absolutely required for true salvation. For instance, that the angles of a triangle are equal to two right angles is an indubitable truth, yet belief in it is by no means necessary for a blessed life. Therefore, I doubt whether belief in the Trinity is strictly required for the path of eternal salvation.

<margin>Believing in the Trinity in divine matters is necessary for salvation.</margin>

**GOMET.** This is quite clear from the logic of true salvation (which you know). For it has been shown by us, and granted by you, that true salvation of this kind consists solely in the contemplation of and adherence to God the Creator.

**PHILAL.** So I have judged.

**GOMET.** But does not the adherence and unification of two things demand conformity and likeness?

**PHILAL.** That is certain; for "like is a friend to like," as is taught in the ninth book of the *Ethics* <note>Aristotle’s *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book 9, Chapter 8, discusses how friendship is based on likeness and virtue.</note>.

**GOMET.** For a beatific adherence, therefore, it is fitting that the human intellect itself should make itself conformable to the divine intellect.

**PHILAL.** So it clearly seems.

**GOMET.** And it is made conformable when it adapts its own concept to those things which are chiefly present in the divine mind.

**PHILAL.** It is certain that human nature cannot be made like divine nature from any other source than from the conformity of the work of the intellect.

**PHILALETHES:** Thus at last (as I see) it must be professed; but soon another, and indeed a far harder obstacle <note>original: "scopulus," literally a "rock" or "cliff" in the sea; a metaphor for a difficult problem.</note> presents itself, for immediately in the Creed there follows the clause saying: *and in Jesus Christ, His only Son our Lord.* For two things are expressed by these words: one of which seems indeed unspeakable and altogether unthinkable—that the Son of God, who is Himself God, was Jesus Christ born from a woman’s womb. Thus, that the lowest mortal creature, man, has been made numerically the same <note>The philosophical concept of "numerical identity" means being one and the same individual thing, rather than just being similar or having the same nature.</note> as the Creator, the highest origin of all things. The other point is: even if it were granted and admitted that the same individual exists as both God and man, why is it permitted—let alone necessary for salvation—to believe in Jesus Christ, a frail and mortal man? Would it not be enough to believe in God the Creator of the universe, three and one, in whom alone all human happiness and eternal salvation are placed?

**GOMETIUS:** Your **Stagirite** <note>Aristotle, who was born in the city of Stagira.</note> does not speak inconsiderately in the second book of his *Divine Wisdom* <note>Referring to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*.</note> when he affirms that even the knowledge of manifest truth is hindered and clouded by the stain of corrupt habit. **PHILALETHES:** By what reason, and upon what **Peripatetic** foundation these things can be built, I can neither see nor devise.

**GOMETIUS:** Do you not know it is a commonplace in the school of the **Peripatetics** (as is handed down in the third book of *On the Soul*) that the "possible" or "material" intellect receives intelligible forms by the same law that corporeal matter receives sensible forms? For this reason it is called the "material intellect": because it corresponds by proportion to matter; and just as matter receives all forms, so the intellect receives all intelligible things. In short, what primary matter is in the order of natural things, the possible intellect is in the order of intelligible things.

**PHILALETHES:** 

<margin>
Just as primary corporeal matter is joined in personal unity to the best of sensible forms—namely, the rational soul—so primary intellectual matter, which they call the possible intellect, is joined in personal unity to the creator God, the best of intelligible forms.
</margin>
I know it indeed, and the **Cordovan** <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd), the famous commentator on Aristotle from Córdoba, Spain.</note> explained that very thing clearly in the same place, asserting that no difference exists between the matter of sensible forms and the matter of intelligibles (that is, between primary matter and the material or possible intellect) except that corporeal matter receives singular forms, while the intellect receives universal forms. For this reason, he says, the intellect is capable of knowing, whereas corporeal matter is not.

**GOMETIUS:** Does not corporeal matter receive and unite with sensible forms in such a way that, by a perpetual succession, it never ceases to lose one and receive another, until it reaches the most perfect in the range of sensible forms—namely, the intellectual form of man—and is united to it, under which it can be said, not absurdly, to rest?

**PHILALETHES:** Experience demonstrates that.

**GOMETIUS:** Therefore, the material intellect does not cease to run through intelligible forms until it applies itself to, and is united with, the most perfect form of intelligibles. But the most perfect of all intelligible forms is God; it will therefore follow, by necessity according to the order of nature, that the human intellect—which is called both possible and material—becomes one with the glorious God.

**PHILALETHES:** I do not deny this, since both Aristotle in the 12th book of *Divine Wisdom* and frequently his interpreter Averroes teach that the human intellect is united with that principle upon which heaven and nature depend. But the **Cordovan** intended this union to happen by a certain "coupling," just as a nurtured flame is attached to a wick; which coupling does not constitute numerically the same thing. For this reason, I do not yet see by what law it is right to admit that God and man are numerically the same.

**GOMETIUS:** If you revolve your mind with firm consideration upon the hinge we have established—namely, that by the same path the intellectual matter (that is, the human intellect) is united to intelligible forms as corporeal matter is united to sensible forms—you will see that God the Creator and man exist as the same numerical **suppositum** <note>In scholastic philosophy, a "suppositum" is the individual substance or "person" that underlies the attributes.</note>, or the same person or **hypostasis**. For in such a way, especially, corporeal matter itself is united with the best...

the intellectual soul, and constitutes one and the same being in number—let us say, Philalethes—although your body is frail and mortal; the intellectual soul, however, is immortal and everlasting. Wherefore it must be confessed that the intellectual matter itself (namely the human intellect) becomes one person in number with the best of intelligible forms, God the Creator. Furthermore, the union of the divine nature with the human form is far more in harmony with the order of things than the union of the soul with the body, because the body is fleeting and frail, while the soul is everlasting. Therefore, these two (the soul and body) are distant from each other by a longer interval—indeed, more than merely in kind, as noted in the *Metaphysics*, Book 10 <note>original: "Metaph. 10." Aristotle's Metaphysics, Book 10, discusses the nature of unity and difference.</note>—than the human intellect is from the divine mind, both of which are eternal beings. In things that have a shared "symbol" or common ground (as the **Stagirite** <note>Aristotle, born in Stagira.</note> taught you), the transition and union with one another becomes easier. This is what **Athanasius** <note>Refers to the Athanasian Creed, a Christian statement of belief.</note> seems to have felt when he says that God and man are one Christ, just as the soul and body are one man. Since, therefore, the union of the divine nature with the human form is the same as—and indeed much more perfect than—the union of the soul and the body, and since this latter union is a "personal" one <note>A "personal union" (or hypostatic union) means the two natures are joined in one individual person, rather than just being close or similar.</note>, it stands to reason that the former is also personal, and that one person is constituted from God and man; which was the point to be demonstrated.

**PHILALETHES:** Although you show excellently and upon the solid foundation of the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> that human nature is fused into one in number with the divine nature, yet this does not seem to agree with the words contained in the aforementioned clause [of the Creed]. For it says: *And in Jesus Christ the only Son of God.* Therefore, the Son of God who is man is "unique" or "only." From your argument, however, it is drawn that any mortal whatsoever could reach this personal unity with God.

**GOMETIUS:** And from what part of our discourse (tell me, I pray) do you think this is to be elicited?

**PHILALETHES:** Since you prove this personal unity of the human intellect with the divine intellect from the fact that the human and "possible intellect" <term>possible intellect: In Scholastic philosophy, the capacity of the human mind to receive or "become" the concepts it understands.</term> receives all intelligible forms in the same way that prime matter <note>The most basic, formless stuff of the physical world.</note> receives sensible forms; and since this way of receiving intelligible forms is present in each and every human being, it seems it must be concluded that any man whatsoever could turn out to be one in number with God. Therefore, the Son of God and man would not be "unique," but almost innumerable.

**GOMETIUS:** Look, you are again deserting our central point and rolling the same stone as before.

**PHILALETHES:** Why do you say that?

<margin>
It cannot (namely according to the order of nature) be given that there is a personal union of human nature with the divine nature, except in only one individual of the human race.
</margin>
**GOMETIUS:** Was not the solid and unshakable basis of our reasoning that intellectual matter relates to intelligible things in the same way that corporeal matter relates to sensible things?

**PHILALETHES:** Why not?

**GOMETIUS:** Now, corporeal matter regards sensible things in such a way that, although according to a "remote potency" (which exists in prime matter) any portion of matter could receive any sensible form whatsoever, yet it cannot do this according to a "proximate potency" <note>Gometius distinguishes between what is theoretically possible for human nature (remote) and what is actually possible for a specific individual based on their specific conditions (proximate).</note>, which results from the varying mixture of elements. For example, the portion of prime matter that is subject to the form of a man could not, according to its proximate potency, be subject to the form of an ox; nor could the proximate matter of a donkey be spread beneath the form of an ox; and the same must be judged concerning each case. Therefore, just as not every portion of matter is able, according to its proximate potency, to be united to the best of sensible forms (namely the human intellect) in a personal unity, so also not just any portion of intellectual matter (that is, the human intellect) can be united in personal unity with God the Creator according to the proximate potency which results from the connection of that same human intellect with such-and-such a body and organ. Finally, the multiple meanings of "potency" have made you waver.

<margin>
One potency is remote, the other proximate.
</margin>
Indeed, we call one "remote potency," which is inherent in the possible intellect or intellectual matter by its very nature. We consider another "proximate potency," which belongs to the intellect by what is added to it, and according to whether it is annexed to such-and-such an organ and such-and-such a mental image <note>original: "phantasmati," the sensory images from which the intellect derives abstract concepts.</note>. The first kind of potency for receiving every intelligible form is present in every human being. But the second kind of potency does not render everyone fit to grasp every intelligible form and every perfection...

<summary>Gometius uses Aristotelian metaphysics to argue that while all humans have the theoretical capacity to be united with God, only one individual (Jesus) possessed the specific, "proximate" potential for this personal union. This explains why there is only one "Son of God" despite the shared nature of the human intellect.</summary>

Therefore (to return to the point), that form which contains only a few acts and perfections within itself requires only small, previous potentials and dispositions in the receiving matter. But a form that encompasses many perfections requires more preparations in the receiving matter. Since the intellectual form of man is more eminent than all others, it requires all the bodily dispositions that correspond to those forms to be present beforehand in the <term>prime matter</term> <note>original: "materia prima," the most basic, formless substance that underlies all physical things.</note>. Because the intellectual form of man is more sublime than the entire corporeal machine, and conversely, prime matter itself is lower than the entire corporeal machine, these extremes cannot be joined except through intermediaries. Now, the entire corporeal machine acts as an intermediary between prime matter and the human intellect. <margin>Man is the epitome of the whole universe and a shortened map of the world.</margin>
Hence that wise Arab, <term>Algazel</term> <note>original: "Algazel," referring to the Persian philosopher and theologian Al-Ghazali (c. 1058–1111).</note>, asserted that man was the epitome of the whole universe and a shortened map of the world. *GOMET.* Do you admit, then, that corporeal matter is by no means united to the best form of sensible things unless that matter itself receives within it the image of the whole corporeal world? *PHILAL.* I judge that to be so without hesitation. *GOMET.* In the same way, therefore, intellectual matter is by no means joined in a personal bond with the best of intellectual beings unless it carves within itself the actual image of all <term>intelligibles</term> <note>Things that can be understood by the mind, rather than perceived by the senses.</note>. ->### PAUL RICIUS###<-

<margin>From the whole human race, only one individual can contain the full accumulation of human perfections.</margin>

...receives the forms and perfections of sensible things, it is proven that the matter of intellectual things (namely the human intellect) requires being associated in <term>personal unity</term> <note>original: "personali unitate," a theological concept referring to the union of divine and human natures in one individual person, most famously in the person of Christ.</note> with the best of all intelligible things. This is so that it may possess within itself the forms and perfections of all intelligible things (in its own way), from which the whole of human happiness results and proceeds. These are the things which your wisdom has taught me thus far; it remains now for you to explain the second assumption: namely, that only one individual in number can reach the peak of human perfection.

**GOMETIUS.** The induction of facts, as well as the order and relationship of men to one another, demonstrates this. For if you consider the individual practitioners of the arts and sciences, and those endowed with honest character, you will nowhere find two—let alone many—who are equal in the same industry and virtue without one excelling the other in some respect. If you observe two, for instance, who study the art of music: one excels in theory, the other in practice; one has a melodic voice, the other a hoarse one; this one alone is harmonic, the other rhythmic; this one plays the lute, that one the lyre; this one is agile of hand, the other slow. Finally, just as you will never find two mortals who exactly match in the same physical habit and temperament, so it is impossible for them to participate in the same skill with an equal share—as can be seen and experienced in every single thing.

Whence <note>original: "Stagirita," a common nickname for Aristotle, who was born in the city of Stagira.</note> the Stagirite also asserts in the tenth book of the *Divine Wisdom*: In any genus of things, there is given one that is greatest and the highest of all others. If, therefore, in any single human perfection the order of things does not permit the summit of that perfection to more than one individual, it is far more reasonable that the peak of *all* human perfections cannot be granted except to one. Added to this is the relationship and order of men to one another, which (as Aristotle testifies in the ninth book of his *Ethics*) must be maintained in human society in the same way we know nature maintains it among the members and organs of each individual. 

For in any single human being, we experience that all members do not participate in the power of the intellect immediately and without an intermediary. Rather, in a certain order, one serves the other until they reach the <term>cogitative power</term> <note>In medieval philosophy, the "vis cogitativa" was considered the highest physical faculty of the brain, acting as a bridge between the physical senses and the immaterial intellect.</note>, which holds the leadership among all the powers of the human body. This power alone is attached to the intellectual power without any intermediary. Nor (if you notice) do paired and double members hold an equal force and degree of perfection. For the feet (as is taught in the first book of *On the Motion of Animals*) were given by nature as a pair, yet they are not of the same rank: for she destined the left as a support for the right. The same judgment must be made concerning the hands, eyes, ears, nostrils, and every pair of members. 

There is, therefore, only one single bodily power that holds the highest place in the entire order of members and virtues; and through its mediation, all the remaining limbs of the body become participants in the intellect. If, therefore, you investigate the individual forms of things, and if you attend to the mutual order of individuals in the human race, you will clearly recognize that everything supports this opinion: namely, that there is only one in the entire race of mortals who accumulates within himself all the gifts of human virtues and perfections. 

For this reason, he who was to be the Son of God and man (in whom it is necessary that all human perfection be heaped together) could only be one in number. For just as the parts of an individual relate to each other, so do the individual members of the human race; because there is also a certain order among individuals. Moreover, the best order is that in which the origin of the first Being and the Pattern of all things shines forth—such as the order of the whole, which flows from the <term>ideal reason</term> <note>The "ratio idealis" refers to the divine blueprints or Ideas in the mind of God according to which the world was created.</note> that exists in the mind of the universal Maker. Since, therefore, it has been demonstrated that such an order exists in the parts of a single individual, it is probable, and much more so, that the same order exists among the parts of the entire human species—that is, among the individuals themselves, or among men. Therefore, just as in one man or individual all parts of the body are indeed united to the intellectual soul, but all others are united through an intermediary—the cogitative power alone being united immediately, through which all other parts manage to be united to the intellectual soul—so in the entire human species, the intellects of all men can indeed be united to the best form of intelligible things (that is, to the divine essence). But all are united through an intermediary: only one is united immediately, through whom all the others have the ability to be united to the divine essence—

# ON CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE, BOOK I. #

...that they may be united. For just as in a single individual all parts of the body communicate with the soul—or, to keep to our primary terms, just as <term>prime matter</term> <note>original: "prima materia"; in Aristotelian philosophy, the most basic, formless "stuff" of the universe that has the potential to become anything.</note> is united to the best of natural forms—so the human intellect is united to the divine essence. But prime matter is united to the best of natural forms (that is, the soul) through the <term>cogitative power</term> <note>original: "cogitatiuam"; in medieval psychology, this was the specific faculty of the mind that processed sensory information to make it ready for the higher intellect.</note> alone. Therefore, the human intellect is united to the divine essence through the only Mediator, the Word of God. 

And so, in this proportion, the divine essence corresponds to the soul; Christ to the cogitative power; and the Saints to the other parts of the body. Thus, the Saints are united to God through Christ, just as the parts of the body are united to the soul through the cogitative power. And just as the limbs are not united to the soul except through the cogitative power, so the saints are not united to God except through Christ. He is, for this reason, truly the Mediator between God and men, in whom is the communion and bond of the saints, and therefore their happiness. 

That I should call only the saints "citizens," and not all men, I have done for this reason: although a city does not consist of children, the elderly, or the idle (<note>original: "polit. 3"; a reference to Aristotle’s *Politics*, Book 3.</note>), but of citizens; so too that Jerusalem which is above, which is built as a city—as the Prophet says—does not consist of all men, but only of holy men. And just as in a physical body not everything belongs to the body (for some things are either useless or putrid and are rejected from the body), so in this context the wicked are excluded from the embrace of humanity. From all this, conclude that only one individual among all men is united immediately and personally with God; the rest are indeed united, but <term>mediately</term> <note>indirectly, through an intermediate step</note> through that one who is personally God.

**PHILALETHES.** Although you conduct this business wisely and in the <term>Peripatetic manner</term> <note>the style of the followers of Aristotle, who famously walked about while teaching.</note>, what we accepted as the base and foundation of our entire examination seems to struggle against this. I mean the foundation that intellectual matter (the human intellect) is joined to God—the best of intelligible forms—in the same way that corporeal matter is joined to the best of sensible forms, namely the human intellect. Since we see that a <term>personal union</term> of matter with the best sensible form occurs not in only one, but in every individual human being, it would follow by the same logic that a personal union of intellectual matter with God—the best of intelligible things—should occur in every human being. Thus, there would be many who are both God and man, not just one.

**GOMETIUS.** 

<margin>Prime matter is not exactly coupled to the human intellect except in one individual.</margin>

If you consider the condition of human nature more accurately, you will find that even corporeal matter itself is not truly or exactly coupled to the human intellect except in one single instance. We judge any form to be perfectly united to its subject only when we see the "supposit" (the individual being) of that form perfectly exercising its work. For we say each thing is what it is based on its ability to perform its own proper work (as your <term>Stagirite</term> <note>Aristotle, who was born in the city of Stagira.</note> taught in the fourth book of *Meteorologica* and the first book of *On the Parts of Animals*). 

Now, the proper work of the human intellect (as handed down in the third book of *On the Soul*) is "to become all things"—that is, to contemplate all intelligible things. Therefore, a person lacking the understanding of truth and the foolish must be called "human" only by an <term>equivocal name</term> <note>original: "æquiuoca appellatione"; a logical term meaning a word used for two different things, like calling both a living eye and a stone eye an "eye."</note> (as the <term>Cordoban</term> <note>Averroës, the famous 12th-century philosopher from Córdoba.</note> pleased to say in his introduction to the *Physics*). So too Aristotle, in the first book of the *Politics*, judged a man without prudence to be worse than a beast. Since, therefore, the most perfect operation of the human intellect (namely the contemplation of all intelligible things) can be found in only one single individual (as has been demonstrated), it follows that an exact union of corporeal matter with the best form of sensible things does not exist except in one single instance. 

All other mortals, however many they are, are ordered toward that one and look to him, just as the multitude of an army is ordered toward its leader, and as the forces of the entire human body look to the single cogitative power and offer it prompt obedience.

**PHILALETHES.** You truly surpass and conquer me manfully with these spiritual weapons. Unless I wished to deceive myself or rush headlong into error, I cannot resist them or escape their force. Therefore, I must fearlessly agree with you and accept your teachings with firm understanding and faith—provided that two matters, which seem to hold some difficulty, might be resolved by your usual kindness and...

### OF PAUL RICIUS, ###

<margin>The reason why it is necessary for salvation to believe in the man who is also God.</margin>
...you have explained with such prudence. First, why does the path of eternal salvation require belief in a God-man at all? Second, what reasoning dictates that such a man, who was simultaneously God, actually existed in the person of Jesus Christ, born of the Virgin Mary? **GOMETIUS.** It will not be difficult to make these things clear and evident to you, if you look at the logic of human salvation that we explained from the start. We asserted that salvation is nothing other than adherence to God the Creator. This is the same as saying that the extremes of a vast range of things are fused into one; for God is the first principle of all things, and man is the ultimate extreme <note>In the "Great Chain of Being," humans were often seen as the final, most complex point of physical creation, standing on the border of the material and spiritual worlds.</note> of all things. Now, separated extremes cannot be joined except through a "Middle" (<term>medium</term>). Do you not agree with us on this? **PHILALETHES.** Who could deny it? **GOMETIUS.** And a "Middle" is that which participates in both extremes. **PHILALETHES.** That is established. **GOMETIUS.** Therefore, the "Middle" between God and man is a single thing that exists as both God and man at the same time. **PHILALETHES.** So it would seem. **GOMETIUS.** Therefore, if anyone desires to be coupled to God, they must cling to that very Middle, or Mediator, who is God and man. Furthermore, "to believe" (as we explained before) signifies nothing other than to turn the mind toward, apply it to, and settle it upon the thing in which one believes. Since, therefore, Jesus the Son of the Virgin Mary is and was a Middle of this kind, it is necessary to believe in him for salvation. **PHILALETHES.** Although you seem to reason correctly and derive this conclusion, a doubt nevertheless creeps into my mind: if the extremes—namely God and any particular man—cannot be joined except through a Middle, then Jesus, the Son of the Virgin Mary, was a true man; therefore, he himself could not be made one with God the Creator except through a Middle that was truly God and man simultaneously. And then, concerning this very Middle, the same ambiguity would arise again. Either the question will go on to infinity, or you will be forced at last to admit a man who clings to the Glorious God without any personal bond (<term>personali copula</term> <note>Philalethes is using a classic logical trap: if everything needs a "middleman" to connect to God, then the Mediator would need a mediator too, creating an endless chain.</note>). And if those extremes could be joined without a middle, then the blessed coupling of man with God could similarly be granted without any Mediator at all. **GOMETIUS.** If you hold to the foundations already laid down and admitted by you, there will be nothing to doubt in this examination. For it has been shown that the one who is to turn out to be "one in number" with God must apprehend all <term>intelligible things</term> <note>original: "intelligibilium"; in Platonic and Aristotelian thought, these are the pure ideas or "blueprints" of reality that exist in the mind.</note>. That is, he must apply his mind to the underlying reasons and forms of all things. Now, he who applies his mind to all intelligible things does not adhere to God without a middle; rather, he adheres to God through the entire scope of the universe, which stands as the middle between himself and God. Therefore, in Christ the Mediator, the extremes are not joined without a middle (as you hesitate to believe), because he himself, through his understanding, encompasses the "Middles" of the entire range of things. **PHILALETHES.** From this, it seems another and far more contradictory point must be admitted: namely, that it is not at all necessary for salvation to believe in Jesus Christ, or any Mediator, if we attain salvation solely through the apprehension of all intelligible things. **GOMETIUS.** And we certainly admit, my dear Philalethes, that if every human being were capable of grasping all intelligible things, there would be no need for a Mediator. But because the unchanging order of things permitted this to only one person (as we discussed before), and the rest of mortals are less fit to form the image of the entire <term>microcosm</term> <note>original: "mycrocosmi"; the concept that a human being is a "little world" that perfectly reflects the structure of the entire universe.</note> within themselves, it is worth the effort for those who desire to be joined to God to cling to the one "Microcosm Mediator" in whom the extremes, God and man, are joined. **PHILALETHES.** I am now sufficiently persuaded by these points that it cannot happen otherwise than that a person must complete the path, and stop there, and fix their gaze. But that Jesus, the Son of the Virgin Mary, was such a person has not yet been made known to me from these arguments.

<margin>It is clearly shown that Jesus Christ existed as the Mediator, both God and man.</margin>
**GOMETIUS.** That is clear from the fact that we recognize all the conditions required for a Mediator to be fulfilled in Jesus Christ alone: namely, the highest physical balance, the highest purity of life and morals, the highest wisdom, the highest power to work miracles, and furthermore (as you will hear in what follows) the appropriateness of the time; and what is greater than all these and is ready at hand for us: that the very path of eternal salvation, which had been foretold long ago...

Philalethes questions the logic of needing a mediator, fearing an infinite regress, but Gometius explains that Christ uniquely encompasses all "middle" steps within his own intellect.</summary>

# ON CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE, BOOK I. #

...declared, has now been revealed and made open to us through the same Son of the Virgin Mary, Jesus Christ. *PHILALETHES.* Man of celestial mind, it is necessary to open and explain two things here more broadly. First, why the condition of the Mediator demands those spiritual gifts you just mentioned. Second, how all these things were fulfilled in Jesus Christ. *GOMETIUS.* We have already revealed through a long examination and discussion just a little while ago that the highest temperament of the body, the greatest purity of life and morals, and the peak of wisdom are to be attributed to the Mediator alone, who is both God and man. 
<margin>Wisdom <unclear>7</unclear></margin> <note>A reference to the Book of Wisdom in the Apocrypha, often associated with the nature of divine wisdom.</note>
That the highest power of performing miracles is owed to the same Mediator is clearly understood from the logical consequences of what was said. For the power of a man (who is also God) far and without limit surpasses the power of all creatures. Just as the organic body of the <term>microcosm</term> <note>The "small world"—a common Renaissance concept that the human body is a miniature reflection of the entire universe.</note> obeys every nod of the thinking power, so too the parts and members of the <term>macrocosm</term> <note>The "large world"—the universe as a whole.</note> obey the command of the Mediator. He holds the same position in the whole scope of things (as we showed before) that the thinking power holds in the human frame. Furthermore, the order of things and the perpetual series of causes declare that the presence of the Mediator requires a certain fitness of time. For just as we see the microcosm, so also the macrocosm (especially the <term>sublunary machine</term> <note>The physical world below the moon, which was believed to be subject to constant change and decay.</note>) is driven and varied by a certain cycle of times and periods of ages. Aristotle clearly affirms this in the first book of his *Meteorology* regarding the individual parts of the earthly globe. 
<margin>Aristotle, *Meteorology*, book 1.</margin> 
Since, therefore, the more perfect operation of the microcosm requires a more perfect period of age—and the more perfect age is that which Physicians call the "age of consistency" <note>The prime of life; the period when a person is fully matured but not yet declining.</note>—it follows that the more perfect operation and effect of the macrocosm must be assigned to the more perfect age of consistency of the world. And since the more perfect age of the microcosm is that which holds the middle of the whole period of human life... According to the course of nature, the middle years are from the thirty-sixth to the fortieth. This is because a span of seventy, or more rarely eighty years, usually measures the life of mortals. And because this age of consistency is more perfect and of greater strength, 
<margin>Aristotle, *Politics*, book 7, ch. 16.</margin> 
for this reason Aristotle, in the seventh book of his *Politics*, judged the best and "divine" (as he calls it) work of propagation to be especially suited to this age. Finally, if trust is to be placed in both ancient and more recent observers of the stars, and in some wise men of the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note>, who establish that the circuit of the eighth sphere <note>The sphere of the fixed stars.</note> is completed in seven times seven thousand years [49,000 years]; and if authority is to be given to the divine oracles, 
<margin>Genesis 1. Leviticus 25. Daniel 9.</margin> 
which announce this same thing in mystery through the seven days, through the weeks of seven days, and through the seven years, and through the weeks of seven years—where one hundred years in the macrocosm correspond to each single year in the microcosm—it follows that the more perfect age, the "age of consistency" of the world, from the beginning of sublunary things (according to the tradition of sacred history), is the six hundredth year beyond the third thousandth [year 3600] until the completion of the fourth thousandth [year 4000]. Since this age is the most perfect of the ages of the world, it is fitting that it produced a more excellent effect on this earthly globe. Therefore, since no effect more excellent than God and man himself as Mediator can be given in the world, it is proved that this age of consistency is suited to the most great birth of the Mediator. That it especially belongs to this Mediator to provide the common path of eternal salvation is clear from the fact that the Mediator (as we discussed before) must hold the primacy and highest place over the whole human race. It belongs to the highest of any category to influence and pour out power into the whole breadth of things contained under it. Just as it is the duty of the thinking power alone to distribute rational and chosen acts into the whole organic body. Finally, gather here three things to be attributed to the Mediator alone: the first concerns the internal gifts of the soul and body in the highest perfection. The second indicates the harmony of the time. The third respects the magnitude of the promised and longed-for effect. Since, therefore, it has been searched out and discovered that all these things were found in abundance...

# PAUL RICIUS, #

<margin>Three things that belong to the Mediator alone were found in Jesus Christ.</margin>
...were found to be in Christ Jesus, we judge most firmly and without any hesitation that He was the true Savior. *PHILALETHES.* Though I am now convinced that these three offices belong to only one Mediator, I do not know by what rule of logic it can be proven that they were fulfilled in Jesus Christ, the Son of Mary. *GOMETIUS.* You claim the teachings of the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for their focus on logic and empirical evidence.</note>, yet you neglect their well-worn foundation. *PHILALETHES.* To what end? *GOMETIUS.* That those things which are specific, historical events (as is taught in the first book of the *Physics* <note>original: "de Physico auditu." Referring to Aristotle's work on natural philosophy.</note>) are understood not by abstract reasoning or discourse, but only by the senses, faith, and the testimony of others—just as we understand that Socrates and Plato existed as wise men, born to certain parents, in a specific place and time. *PHILALETHES.* What method of teaching, then, can solve this question upon which the whole weight of your creed depends? *GOMETIUS.* This could not be known from any other source than the truthful and widespread authority and fame of those who knew the certainty of these deeds by touch and the "faith of the eyes" <note>An expression for eyewitness testimony.</note>. For if you turn through the writings and monuments of the ancient wise men, you will find they weave a consistent and identical history of Jesus Christ, testifying that He was born at such a time, place, and lineage, and celebrating Him with the highest praise and proclamations—just as we shall explain more fully, by the will of those above, in the following volume. 

Yet, among the rest, one inviolable argument for this certainty is given, drawn from a long and broad experience: Namely, that now nearly the entire multitude of men who are governed by the law of nature and reason (having despised and rejected the cursed worship of idols) worships and adores the one God, the creator of all things. And although many wise men, Prophets, and powerful Kings (throughout every age) desired nothing more, nor spent so much study and labor on any matter than to lead the human race from the unspeakable and most shameful worship of idols to the observance of the one Creator God, none of them—no matter how much they excelled in holiness of life, divine and human wisdom, or greatness of power—could accomplish or fulfill that wish, not even among their own small group of people. 

For the wise and God-beloved Abraham could not do this, nor his holy offspring Isaac, nor that heavenly and upright man Jacob; nor could Moses, the prince of all Prophets and full of God, who knew how to split the depths of the sea with the strike of a staff, and drown the huge cohort and troop of Pharaoh in the salt waves, and draw a spring of living waters from the rock—he who, for forty years in the solitude of the desert, nourished more than six hundred thousand men with the heavenly food of <term>manna</term> <note>Miraculous food provided to the Israelites in the desert.</note>. Even the great leader of the Israelites, Joshua, did not know how to achieve this—he who halted the currents of the greedy Jordan and led a vast army across on dry feet, who commanded the stars and the heavens to stand still, and who overthrew the high and impregnable walls of Jericho with the blasts of trumpets. I am silent about the powerful King David, the messenger of human salvation, and Solomon, the oracle of divine wisdom. I pass over Elijah, the temple of the Holy Spirit, who commanded the clouds to rain and flames to devour the burnt offerings, and commanded the spirit to restore life to the dead. Such things as his successor, Elisha—that heavenly power on earth—also knew how to perform. 

If, finally (lest my speech grow too long), you consider each of the most brilliant lights of the first <term>synagogue</term> <note>Used here to refer to the era of the ancient Jewish prophets and the biblical community of Israel.</note> and their writings and deeds, you will find openly that they could not recall and turn away even their own Jewish kin, let alone the huge and unrestrained multitude of barbarians and other foreign nations, from that wicked and deadly worship of idols. And this is no wonder, since the conversion of the entire human race to God the Creator and His worship and service cannot be achieved or fulfilled through the power or virtue of any creature (as you were made aware before). Since, therefore, it appears through long and wide experience that this saving work was effected and completed by the presence, teaching, and passion of Jesus Christ alone, we conclude by solid argument that Jesus, the Son of Mary, existed as the true Mediator of the human creature: both God and man. ...and believing in Him, look to the true path of eternal salvation. If you consider these individual things (my Philalethes) with your usual purity of mind, nothing uncertain or ambiguous will be left for you in this inquiry. **PHILAL.** Indeed, no one is so dull or lacking in reason that, while applying their mind to these teachings of yours—which are illuminated by a heavenly light—they would not embrace them all with firm understanding and solid faith. Come then, my father, and please finish and explain what remains. **GOMET.** If you gather your mental strength and, with your usual cleverness, weigh the other things contained in the Creed <note>original: "symbolo." Referring to the Apostles' Creed, the standard statement of Christian belief.</note>, you will easily be able to reach certainty regarding all the points that follow. First, there occurs the 

<margin>Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary. The order of things shows that Christ the Mediator must be born of a virgin.</margin>
clause saying: *Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit. Born of the Virgin Mary.* The truth of this follows clearly from the foundations already laid down. For since it is necessary, according to the Law of Nature, that he whom the Maker of the world endows with the highest perfection of the human race should possess the best constitution <note>original: "crasim." A term from ancient medicine referring to the healthy mixing of the four humors.</note> and bodily temperament; yet the order of things and nature does not allow the best temperament to proceed from a blood-born seed. Therefore, Christ the Mediator could not be produced and born from such a seed, because the highest temperament of a man requires the highest temperament of the father and ancestors, and a certain supreme harmony of the stars. However, it is fundamentally against the inviolable order of things for many people to possess this highest temperament; for in the harmony of the stars and the range of complexions (just as in any kind of thing), only one (as you know) is given as the highest and best, not many. Furthermore, if you were to argue that the father and ancestor were of the best and highest temperament, you would be forced by the same Law to proceed backward and attribute the highest temperament to all ancestors all the way to the beginning of the world. Since this is impossible, it is proven that no human offspring from physical seed can obtain the best constitution and temperament. **PHILAL.** I was hoping indeed that I could grasp and penetrate the remaining mysteries of the Creed with a short speech and little effort, but frequent obstacles and a multitude of rocks delay me and compel me to stop my feet quite often. For two things from what has been said trouble me now. First, by what law must one admit that there is a first parent on this earthly globe, and not rather say (as most of the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle, who generally believed the universe and the human species had no beginning but had existed eternally.</note> believe) that the order of ancestors goes back into infinity? Second, even if a "first-formed" man <note>original: "prothoplasten." Referring to the first human, Adam.</note> is recognized and admitted, what was to stop him from having obtained the highest temperament of the human frame and being able to perform the duty of the Mediator? **GOMET.** We know that a first parent must be given because it is necessary that this entire earthly globe had a beginning in time. 

<margin>It is not contrary to nature, nor to the order of things, for a human—just like many other animals—to be born from decay.</margin>
Hence, the manner of formation for the first parent was the same. According to the tenth book of *Problems* <note>A work of natural philosophy attributed to Aristotle.</note>, as we also see now by daily experience, mice, moles, small rats, and that kind of animal are born from a certain rot <note>original: "putredine." Referring to the theory of spontaneous generation, the historical belief that small animals could arise directly from decaying matter rather than from parents.</note>. For even that prince of Arabian wise men, Avicenna, in his fifteenth book *On Animals*, demonstrates with strong arguments that nothing prevents a human form—no less than that of other living things—from arising and being produced from a certain mixture of elements. Specifically, this happens when animals and things born of the earth are devastated and perish by a flood of waters or the heat of summer.

<margin>The arguments of Averroes to the contrary are refuted.</margin>
Nor do the clever arguments of the man from Córdoba <note>original: "Cordubensis." Referring to the philosopher Averroes.</note> in his eighth book of *Physics* <note>original: "de auditu." Referring to Aristotle's Physics.</note> work against this assertion. He thinks two inconveniences follow from this position. First, it would follow that any form could come from any matter, or anything from anything. Second, it would happen that the human species was created not by nature, but by chance. But neither (if you consider it) should be admitted. Not the first, because we do not admit that the matter prepared from rot or any heap of elements is a different species from that which arises from fertile seed; for we have proven that the forms of these matters are not different in species. For the form of a mouse born from rot is of the same specific essence as the form of a mouse that [is born] from a male...

He further defends the concept of a "first parent" and a beginning of time by citing the theory of spontaneous generation to show that life can begin from elements rather than an infinite chain of ancestors.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical defense of the Virgin Birth by Gometius. He is addressing the scientific and philosophical objections of the era, specifically regarding "spontaneous generation" versus sexual reproduction, to prove that a human (the Messiah) could be "conceived" through a divine/celestial cause rather than traditional biological means.</meta>

# PAUL RICIUS,

is born from the coupling of male and female: because we see that these [mice] possess the same function and the same physical form. Moreover, those things which have the same function surely possess the same nature and form; for we do not recognize the distinctions between forms from any other source than the variety of their work and movement. Clear experience demonstrates that both kinds of mice <note>The author is referring to the historical belief that mice could be born both through mating and "spontaneously" from decaying matter.</note> maintain the same functions. 

However, those who bring forward the opinion of Aristotle (from the first book of *On the Generation of Animals*) against our position—where he says that the genus of those born from putrefaction <term>putredine: the historical theory of "spontaneous generation" where life was thought to arise from decaying matter or elemental mixtures</term> is different from those propagated by prolific seed—these people misjudge Aristotle's meaning. For there (if you pay attention), the discussion is only concerning insect-like animals, whose nature is such that they arise from putrefaction; such creatures do not generate anything of their own specific kind <note>original: "uniuocum." In logic, a "univocal" generation produces an offspring of the exact same species.</note>, nor do they have male and female sexes. Our discussion here, however, concerns those whose birth is indeed by nature from the seed of propagation. For when such creatures are sometimes produced from a certain mixture of elements or putrefaction, Aristotle by no means seems to deny that a male and female, and an animal of the same species as those propagated naturally, can be produced and born. 

I confess, however (as the experience of the matter shows), that those born from putrefaction are less perfect in their functions than animals of their own kind generated from the coupling of male and female. The reason for this imperfection is the unsuitability of the decaying matter and the location; yet the fact that they are of the same univocal species is not taken away because of it. For it is a common saying in the Peripatetic <note>Followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy.</note> school that "more or less" does not change the species; just as a man who comes forth from the womb mutilated or crippled in body and spirit is not, for that reason, prevented from being called a "man" in the same sense. 

Therefore, since the opinion remains established—that the form of perfect animals generated from putrefaction is the same in species as the form of animals of the same genus produced through propagation—it follows that they also exist as the same species in their proximate matter. Thus, the defender of this opinion is by no means forced to agree that "anything can become anything," as the Cordovan <note>referring to the Islamic philosopher Averroes (Ibn Rushd), born in Córdoba.</note> contends. 

Furthermore, the identity of the efficient cause shows that their form is the same in species. Indeed, the true general efficient cause is not this specific individual [parent]. For (as the Cordovan himself proves in the second book of *On Generation*, Commentary 29, and in the eighth book of the *Physics*) the parent does not take the place of the primary agent, but only of the instrument and organ. He affirms that the true acting cause is "celestial heat," which (as he says in the seventh book of *Divine Wisdom*, Commentary 31) is measured by a certain divine art. Since, therefore, that celestial heat—which is the true cause of the generation of living things—is similar and the same in species, nothing prevents it from producing the same effect, even if not quite as precisely, using an instrument other than this individual human. For the skill of an Art is not bound precisely to one instrument, even if it operates more conveniently and aptly through one than another. 

From these points, you will also easily be able to gather that the second inconvenience mentioned by Averroes by no means follows from our position. 

<margin>We do not say that everything which happens rarely happens by chance and luck.</margin> 

Namely, the claim that the human species would then arise by chance or accident. For we do not say that whatever arises in fewer instances happens by chance; for example, the conjunction of Mars and Jupiter with Saturn in a single point of the zodiac happens rarely and only after a long time; yet no one would say this happens by chance, since nothing accidental or fortuitous can happen to the heavenly bodies. Rather, we assert that something happens by chance (as taught in the second book of the *Physics*) not simply because it happens rarely, but because it proceeds from such-and-such a cause in fewer instances—such as finding gold by the accidental striking of one's feet. 

In this way, even the birth of a human without the coupling of male and female, though it may happen rarely (and perhaps only once in the entire cycle of this world), is still by no means to be ascribed to accident or chance. For the stable and perpetual order of things requires that whenever the celestial stars (by the nod of the Supreme Creator) look upon each other with a certain "countenance of friendship" (so to speak) and harmony, then those stars send down the rays of their benevolent countenance into the undigested mass and chaos of sub-celestial things,

<meta>catchword: send down,</meta>

<summary>Gometius argues that species identity is determined by "celestial heat" and divine intent rather than just biological parents, allowing for the possibility of a human (Christ) being born through non-sexual means. He refutes Averroes' objection by distinguishing between rare, divinely-ordered events and mere random chance.</summary>

<margin>Just as nature does not suffer a vacuum, so the order of things does not permit a lack of the human race.</margin>

How much more fitting and reasonable it is, then, to believe that those sublime and spiritual celestial bodies—whose perpetual providence and care it is to preserve the perennial beauty of the world and to bring forth this fleeting image on earth from the Archetypal world <term>Archetypi orbis: the divine blueprint or "World of Ideas" from which the physical world is modeled</term>—would provide and strive with the greatest effort so that the beauty and adornment of the universe should not lack this noble and divine race of men? If you consider and examine these things yourself, you will easily understand that the order and beauty of things requires that a "first-formed" or primary man be given, born from a certain balance of elements without seminal propagation—a matter about which you were doubting just a moment ago. <margin>Because the first-formed man could not obtain the best balance, he was therefore unable to serve as the Mediator.</margin>

However, a terrestrial heap, although it may reach the limit of the human constitution, cannot nonetheless obtain the *best* balance. This is not due to the weakness of the agent <note>The "agent" here is the celestial or divine force acting upon the matter.</note> but (as we mentioned before) from the unfitness and sluggishness of the recipient. Furthermore, the condition and natural order of all other generated things shows this: for everything (as Aristotle argued in the tenth book of *Problems*) that is brought from non-being to being, or from disorder into order, is produced first as something dull and crippled (as if in the age of infancy). Then, it proceeds and profits gradually through the ages until it reaches the peak and state of its perfection, from which it declines again, tending toward its setting and corruption. Since, therefore, we have proved that this terrestrial globe was produced at a certain beginning of time from non-being to being, and from confusion into distinction, due to the state of the heavens at that time, it must be admitted that this earthly machine first came forth somewhat crude and less refined. From this, it follows that the balance of the human frame—which is recognized as the end and effect of the entire elemental structure—could not at that time come forth as the "best." And although the primeval man himself emerged mature and wise immediately from his origin (with no age of infancy or adolescence and no preceding teacher), nevertheless, that first-formed man—just as other things capable of birth—could not obtain the best balance. Not only do the truthful and divine oracles of the Prophets testify to this, but the writings and monuments of foreign nations also proclaim it everywhere when they recount and marvel at the rudeness and inertia of the earlier age of men. From that point, their modesty, wisdom, and virtue grew step by step in the course of time, until there should come the [fullness] of times...

<margin>That it was necessary for him to be born of a Virgin.</margin>

This is indeed much more in accordance with the Law of nature and the inviolable order of things than the procreation and birth of living creatures from mud and from a certain heap of elements in the womb and bowels of the earth; for a virginal womb has far more symbol and likeness with the conceived fetus than the foul and senseless element of the earth. Since, therefore, it has been explored that it was necessary for the Mediator to be conceived of the Holy Spirit and born of a Virgin; and since we have now plainly recognized that Jesus the Nazarene, born of Mary, stood forth as the Mediator, it must be firmly concluded that the same Jesus the Nazarene was conceived

namely, that there exist certain spirits of a rational nature, thrust down into this dark sublunary world <note>The region below the moon, which in ancient cosmology was the realm of change, decay, and elemental struggle.</note> and driven by the power of the stars, whom it has pleased people to call "demons." These spirits strive to secretly and craftily insert themselves into the minds of mortals and to allure and draw them into their own service. If anyone obeys them once and enters into treaties of servitude with them, they cannot thereafter, according to the Law of Nature, withdraw themselves from their command, unless they pay a heavy penalty for their rebellion and pay a fine according to the will of those same demons. And even if they are unable to deceive some faithful and wise person (devoted to God their creator) through any zeal or trickery, they nevertheless never cease for a single moment to place obstacles and various stumbling blocks (as the justice of things permits) and to weave snares. For just as with any existing thing, a desire for acting and producing something similar to itself—and for warding off and expelling what is repugnant—is implanted in a demon. This being admitted, we must say: the fault of the first parent could by no means be removed and abolished except by the bloody punishment and death of the Mediator, because (according to the order of things) the human race—enslaved to the service of the Prince of this world <note>A title for the Devil.</note> and the worship of idols—could not be redeemed and restored to its original liberty unless the author of rebellion and redemption himself paid the penalty and bore the punishment for the violated treaty. And although the power of the redeemer is unavoidable and immense, it was nevertheless not permitted to violate the right of the Prince of this world, nor to take away the servitude of the human race (which that Prince obtained by the law of nature) through violence and against the perpetual order of things. Finally, to explain the matter in a few words, I say that redemption could not happen without a fine and the penalty of punishment, unless he who redeemed had either destroyed the prince of demons himself along with his entire clientele, or transformed him into another nature.

faith, where he especially placed the seat and throne of glory. But he placed it (as I recounted a little before from the opinion of the Prince of the Peripatetics <note>The "Prince of the Peripatetics" refers to the Greek philosopher Aristotle. His followers were called Peripatetics—meaning "those who walk about"—because he famously taught while walking.</note>) at the axis of heaven; therefore, the mind of mortals who seek the path of eternal salvation must direct itself there.

<margin>He sits at the right hand of God the Father.</margin>

Furthermore, one must believe that Christ sits at the right hand of God the Father: because corporeal nature, as we discussed before, designates the condition of the exemplary and Archetypal nature as an image. It is established according to the Peripatetic dogma that "right" and "left" are attributed to the celestial body. Therefore, right and left must also be rightfully ascribed to the Archetypal principle, upon which heaven and nature depend, in a more sublime manner. Hence the entire school of the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, known for their focus on numbers and dualities like right/left or light/dark.</note>, as well as the ancient Allegorizers, enumerates right and left among the other principles of things. Pure and naked intellectual substances and the souls of the blessed reside at the right hand of God the Father, of all of whom Christ the Lord exists as head and prince; but on the left sit the virtues <note>original: "uirtutes." Here referring to spiritual powers or forces tied to the material world.</note> which are compelled by and subject to corporeal nature. And therefore, when the judge of all comes, he will say (as the author of truth speaks in Matthew 25) to those who are on the right: "Come, you blessed"; but to the goats, who are on the left, he will say: "Depart, you cursed." 

<margin>Thence he shall come to judge the living and the dead.</margin>

Regarding these matters, we shall endeavor to discourse more widely with the help of those above in the fourth volume of this work. However, that he is to come from there to judge the living and the dead will be conspicuous when the nature of the judgment has been understood and perfected. For the name of "judgment" suggests nothing else to us here but the consummation and end of things, toward which the things themselves are inclined and prone by nature or by acquired habit <term>habit: "habitus" in Latin, referring to a settled disposition or quality of character developed through repeated action</term>. Moreover, the consummation and end will accompany the future state <note>original: "statum." In medieval physics, this refers to the "stasis" or the moment when the celestial spheres stop moving at the end of time.</note> of heaven; therefore, we are compelled to admit the future judgment entirely. 

<margin>The end and consummation of things follows the state of heaven; but judgment accompanies the consummation and end of things.</margin>

That the consummation of things follows the state of heaven is apparent from the fact that the dissolution of all mixed things follows the state of heaven. For the efficient and preserving cause of mixing and mixed things (as we gather from the eighth book of *Physics* <note>original: "octauo de auditu," a common medieval title for Aristotle's *Physica*.</note> and the first of *Meteorology*) is the motion of heaven. Since, therefore, the dissolution of mixed things is nothing other than the conversion and translation of the mixable elements into that for which they yearn and aspire by nature or by contracted habit—and such a conversion becomes the ultimate end and consummation of each thing—therefore, a future judgment must undoubtedly be reckoned by the state of heaven. 

But the intellectual nature of man (though it be a substance lacking true physical mixture) nevertheless relates to all intelligible things like a blank slate <note>original: "tabula rasa." A philosophical concept where the mind is a blank slate upon which experience and learning write.</note> for receiving a beautiful and pure image. Therefore, it is entangled in many and various habits, both corporeal and intellectual, which reflect a certain spiritual kind of mixture, from which a various inclination and readiness of the soul results according to the variety of habits. For the habit which the anxiety for earthly things brings in twists the soul toward earthly things and the regions below, just like the demon who, although he was granted a naked and angelic nature from the beginning, was nevertheless thrust down and condemned to perpetual exile in this dark world of fleeting things by the malice and impiety of his will alone. 

Thus, and indeed much more easily, the human intellectual form—weighted down by the bulk of the body and enticed and defiled by earthly allurements—is banished from celestial company through the contracted habit of earthly things, enslaved to the most foul prison of this fleeting world. However, the habit which it acquires from mental exercise and work purifies the soul, lifts it up, and raises it to the fellowship of those above. Therefore, regarding these searched-for habits which sit more deeply and occupy the soul, they themselves convert and translate the soul to the celestial or earthly objects with which the habits themselves are concerned. But those habits which are less ingrained and fixed are gradually abolished and vanish entirely. Thus, when the period of heaven is completed and every mixture and concretion is dissolved, it will be necessary for the earthly habits joined and bound with celestial ones to be separated, so that those which more greatly prevail and are more deeply rooted may remain alone, the others which sit less deeply being abolished and cast out. Whence the remaining earthly habits will thrust the soul to the regions below; and the celestial
