saying: "When the scepter shall be taken away from Judah, he who is to be sent shall come." <note>original: "Quando auferetur sceptrum de Iuda, ueniet ille qui mittendus est" — a variation of Genesis 49:10.</note> In truth, that scepter was taken away at the arrival of Jesus of Nazareth; therefore, he who was to be sent came at that time. Nor is the sophistry of the Jews valid here, who seek an escape by contending that the scepter was taken from Judah a long stretch of time before the presence of Jesus of Nazareth—specifically when the Maccabees, who were of the tribe of Levi, obtained the royal scepter along with the priestly dignity. They also argue that for many decades after Jesus of Nazareth, their kingdom continued in the land of Israel. From these points, they infer that Jesus of Nazareth was by no means the one who was to be sent. For these wretched people are ignorant that the kingdom and scepter of Judah are so named not because the King himself must be of the lineage and blood of Judah. Just as the Roman Empire is not so named because those who commanded were always (as you know) from Roman stock, but because they were elected, admitted, and appointed to command by the Roman army and magistracy. So too was the kingdom called "of Judah" because the people, the magistrates, and the tribe of Judah—together with the appointed king—held the governance of the land of Israel. And although the tribe of Benjamin were also inhabitants of Judea at that time, the part belonging to Judah was more powerful and numerous; from which their entire land was called Judea.

Furthermore, the delusion of the Jews fails to consider that this chronological marker (until...) does not announce this hour, day, and year of the Savior's arrival with absolute precision. For the outcome of any event is given an internal beginning, progress, and status, which embrace a certain and varying space of time—just as the time of the Egyptian captivity, foretold by the mouth of Moses, declares. 

<margin>Genesis 15. Exodus 12.</margin>

the reckoning of the Jews from the beginning of the world to this very day (on which, of course, the writings of the present volume are published) numbers five thousand two hundred and ninety-seven years. <note>The Latin "nonaginta septem ultra ducentessimum & quintum millenarium" refers to the year 5297 in the Hebrew calendar.</note> But if the years of the Messiah are numbered (as the Talmudist asserts) from the beginning of the fifth millennium, it must be admitted regarding the time and days of the Messiah: that one thousand two hundred and ninety-five years have already passed, taking the starting point from the times of Constantine the Great, <note>Constantine the Great (r. 306–337 AD) was the first Roman emperor to convert to Christianity.</note> in whose time the grace of the Savior and the orthodox faith began most powerfully to spread and be established throughout the world. The second testimony of the Talmudists is in that same chapter *Helek*: <note>Chapter *Helek* is the eleventh chapter of the Talmudic tractate Sanhedrin, which discusses the afterlife and the coming of the Messiah.</note> where (on the authority of Rabbi Judah) it is written that in the age when the son of David comes, the house of assembly is turned into a brothel, and Galilee is devastated. From this one may clearly hear that the advent of the Messiah was to be hoped for at that time when the Jews still held magistracy and the governance of Galilee and the land of Israel; for immediately after the desolation of the Temple, the college of judges ceased to exist, and Galilee and all of Judea were overturned. The third testimony of the Talmudists is found in the great commentary on Lamentations called *Echa Rabbati*, <note>A collection of midrash (scriptural interpretations) on the Book of Lamentations.</note> where a story is told of a traveler from Moab who, when he saw a certain farmer plowing in a field, said to him: "Unbind your oxen, unbind your cup and your water jar, because the Messiah is born." So they say. Indeed, the ignorance of the younger Talmudists is so great and so stubborn that that Moses of Gerona <note>Rabbi Moses ben Nahman, also known as Nahmanides (1194–1270).</note> in his disputatious treatise against Paul of Burgos, <note>Paul of Burgos (c. 1351–1435) was a prominent Jewish convert to Christianity and bishop who wrote critiques of Jewish interpretation.</note> finding no other refuge in this place, did not shrink from saying that it would not be inappropriate to occasionally reject certain sayings of the Talmudists. Yet this is considered a crime and an unspeakable wickedness by the universal synagogue of the Jews. Finally, if you attend to the individual sayings of the Talmudists in that same chapter *Helek*, you will plainly and readily see that they all testify either that the advent of the Messiah to save has already passed, or that he will come at the end of the ages to judge. In the second place, it is shown that Jesus of Nazareth was the true Savior 

<margin>You may read all these things in the book which he titled *A Miscellany of the Talmudic Work*: where he recounts at length all those things which he has passed over here in silence.</margin>

by the very work of salvation which was effected through him. For especially that which (as is read in Deuteronomy 1) is required for the salvation of the human race, and for the sake of which the entire Law of the commandments was given to Israel, is nothing else than that they should serve God alone, the creator of all things, cling to Him in faith and love, and utterly eliminate the abominable worship of idols. "I," He says, "am your God, you shall have no foreign gods before me," and for this reason the Talmudists establish that whoever rejects the worship of idols shall be considered a keeper and worker of the entire Law. Conversely: whoever embraces the worship of idols is to be judged a transgressor and contemner of the whole Law. Therefore, although no authority of the first saints or prophets—nor their celestial virtue, nor any providence or ample power of the most potent and wisest kings—could remove and extirpate that lethal worship of idols from the single tribe of the Jews, Jesus of Nazareth himself, poor, mild, and humble of heart, Christ the Lord, has exterminated, utterly destroyed, and extinguished it from the entire circuit of the then-known world by the spirit of his mouth and by the virtue and work of his Apostles. This is according to that prophecy of Zechariah: "And it shall be," he says, "in that day, says the Lord of hosts, I will destroy the name of Idols from the earth, and they shall be remembered no more." Where, by the consensus of all, the letter speaks of the Messiah: it is concluded by a solid argument that this very Jesus of Nazareth, who suffered under Pontius Pilate, was the true and foretold Savior, in whose name every knee bows, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth: to whom be praise, glory, and honor. Finally, from the entire long examination of the aforesaid things, let it be resumed: that the faith of the eternal Trinity, and the sacraments of the Lord's incarnation, passion, resurrection, and redemption, have been fulfilled through Jesus of Nazareth, who suffered under Pontius Pilate: and that it is necessary to believe all these things for salvation: of which things the belief of the Jews explains nothing...

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'P' featuring a landscape scene within the letter's frame.</image-desc>
For it is an established and indubitable opinion among the Talmudists (in the *Book of the Senators*, <note>original: "Senatorum codice," referring to the Talmudic tractate Sanhedrin.</note> chapter *Helek*) <note>Chapter *Helek* (the eleventh chapter of Sanhedrin) is famous for discussing the afterlife and who has a portion in the world to come.</note> that every Israelite has a portion in the world to come; and since it has been found that every believer in Christ is a true Israelite, it will follow (from the assertions of the Talmudists) that the same person has a portion in the world to come. Indeed, he is called a "true Israelite" who professes the aforementioned thirteen or (according to the opinions of others) eleven foundations of the Mosaic Law, as witnessed by Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides (1138–1204), often called "the Egyptian" because he served the court in Cairo.</note> in the explanation of that chapter *Helek*, and by Rabbi Joseph Albo <note>Joseph Albo (c. 1380–1444), author of the *Sefer Ha-Ikkarim* (Book of Principles/Roots).</note> in the first tractate of the *Book of Roots*. <note>term: *Book of Roots* — Albo’s work which categorized Jewish faith into three primary roots: existence of God, divine revelation, and reward/punishment.</note> Moreover, every cultivator of Christian piety professes these very things; therefore, it must be admitted that such a person is a true Israelite. Furthermore, that every believer in Christ approves each individual root of the Jewish belief will indeed be easy to understand if you compare those roots of their faith which we have enumerated with the orthodox Creed. For you find that the contents of both creeds are precisely the same, either openly or by consequence. The remaining things, however, which the orthodox faith adds and supplies, although they are not at all included in the symbol of the Jews, do not conflict in any way (as you will hear in what follows). For there are five roots (if you pay attention) of the Jewish belief which clearly approve the same things as the orthodox faith: that God exists, that He is one, that He distributes rewards and punishes, that the Messiah is to be expected, and that there will be a future resurrection of the dead. 

Lest the similarity of words confuse the understanding of the matter, know that "Messiah" in the Hebrew idiom sounds like "Christ" or "Anointed." As in that passage of the Psalms: *and against His Christ* <note>Psalm 2:2.</note>—in Hebrew *Meshicho*, <note>original: "Messiho" with the letter 'het' (ח).</note> spelled with the letter *Het*. But *Moshia* <note>original: "Mossia" with the letter 'ayin' (ע).</note> designates "Savior," as in that passage of Judges: *They cried out to the Lord and He raised up for them a Savior* <note>Judges 3:9.</note>—in Hebrew *Moshia*, with the letter *Ayin*, which you should remember everywhere. Therefore, the Creed explains the first and second of these roots by saying: *I believe in one God.* It puts forward the third and fourth: *From thence He shall come to judge the living and the dead.* The fifth it explains in the Creed as *the resurrection of the flesh.* Nor does it hinder the fact that the root concerning the arrival of the Messiah-Savior is the same among the Jews and the believers in Christ. For although the Jews hope for Him as a Savior, while the orthodox faith hopes for Him to come as a Judge, that arrival—even if it is most especially for the purpose of judging—will nevertheless be for the salvation of the Jews. According to that word of the Apostle: *Blindness in part has happened in Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and so all Israel shall be saved.* <note>Romans 11:25-26.</note> Hence, in the twentieth book of *The City of God*, Augustine, among the other eight things that are to come at or around that judgment, also commemorates the faith of the Jews. This is also supported by the Chaldean edition <note>term: *Chaldean edition* — the Targum, an Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> (which has nearly equal authority among the Jews as the Hagiographa) where Hosea prophesies: *After these things (he says) the children of Israel shall return and seek the Lord their God and David their king.* <note>Hosea 3:5.</note> There the Chaldean interpreter, whom the Jews revere as an oracle, translates: *They shall obey the Messiah, the son of David their king, and they shall submit to the Lord and to His goodness in the last days.* Therefore, the root concerning the future Savior for the Jews does not deviate at all from the orthodox foundation. And indeed, nothing prevents the Jews, in the Last Judgment—during a long tract of time before the end of the ages—from accepting the orthodox faith, in which they may persevere until the end of the world. For it is uncertain (according to the tradition of the same Augustine and of wise theologians) for how many days or years this future judgment will be extended—the judgment of discussion, I mean—which could be drawn out for many years...

<meta>This page continues Paulus Ricius's attempt to reconcile Jewish theological principles (the "roots" of belief) with the Christian Apostles' Creed. On the previous page, he argued that five of the thirteen Jewish roots are explicitly found in the Creed; here he begins to demonstrate how the remaining eight are implicitly included by "concomitance" (logical necessity).</meta>

<header>ON CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE, BOOK II.</header>

...[fifty] year cycles, <note>original: "lustris," referring to the five-year periods or cycles used in Roman and later ecclesiastical dating; in this context, it refers back to the jubilees mentioned on the previous page.</note> but not the judgment of retribution and execution in which the order of the ages will finish and end. Therefore, it is manifest that five roots of Jewish belief are openly explained in the Apostles' Creed. It remains now for me to declare that the remaining eight roots of the Jews are included by concomitance in that same Creed.

Three of these roots—namely, that God is incorporeal, that He is the first of all, and that He alone is to be adored—immediately follow from the first foundation of faith, by which we believe in only one God. For since God is a being depending on no condition, whereas a body and whatever inheres in it depends on its parts and some efficient cause, God surely cannot be believed to be corporeal. The same argument applies to the primacy of God: for if He were not first, He would depend on another as a later thing depends on a prior. But He does not depend. Since, therefore, He is omnipotent and the first of all, He alone is surely to be adored. Moreover, He is adored by the act of believing, by which we do not only believe God and believe in God (for in this way even the demons believe and tremble) but we are carried toward Him in charity and hope and adhere to Him—which cannot happen unless the lust of carnal concupiscence has been restrained and subdued. 

Since certain *mycrologi* <note>A term derived from Greek meaning "triflers" or those who focus on minute, insignificant details at the expense of the whole; Ricius uses it to criticize certain contemporary theologians.</note> of our time consider this less, they despise all external works of virtues and commandments, and pronounce them as if futile and void (to the ruin and perdition of many), as we will explain more extensively in the third volume of this undertaken work, with Christ's help. 

Next, three roots of Jewish belief—concerning the gift of Prophecy, that Moses stood out as a Prophet, and that the Law was handed down from heaven—are necessarily pre-required so that we may believe in the holy Catholic Church. For unless it were believed that divine inspiration is given to mortals, announcing things present as well as future (which we choose to call Prophecy), it would indeed be useless and vain to believe in the holy Catholic Church for salvation, since by that same holy and Catholic Church, we understand nothing other than the assembly of Apostles and Prophets and other Saints joined together. 

According to that saying of Augustine in his Letter to Jerome: "Only to the Apostles and Prophets," he says, "this honor must be exhibited, that whatever they have said, these things themselves are believed to be true." But we believe and obey the synodal authority of the saints only insofar as we know it to consist with sound reason and the law of nature, or if it has been built and solidified upon the foundations of the Apostles and Prophets, or at least does not contradict them: <margin>Ephesians 2</margin> according to that word of the Apostle, *built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets.* 

Thus, unless we also believe that Moses stood out as God's Prophet, we could offer no firm and stable faith to the traditions of Moses. Nevertheless, although we have admitted the gift of Prophecy and Moses as God’s Prophet, nonetheless, because that holy and super-celestial Spirit is not always present to the Prophets—since we read that even Moses, the greatest of Prophets, and Peter, the prince of the Apostles, sometimes overstepped and wandered from the path of truth—therefore, unless we say that the entire Law of Moses was handed down from heaven, the minds of the faithful would surely waver and turn in doubt: whether all the holy things and warnings of the Law were entirely to be believed for salvation. Therefore, whoever professes the holy Catholic Church, he must also confess that the entire Law of Moses was handed down from heaven. 

But why the Law is said to be handed down "from heaven" and not rather "from God," according to that passage in Exodus: *You heard that I have spoken to you from heaven,* and in the Apostle to the Galatians: *The Law,* he says, *was given through Angels by the hand of a Mediator* <note>original: "per Angelos in manu Mediatoris," referring to Galatians 3:19.</note>—this is not the business of the present discussion to examine. 

The tenth root, that God has all things clearly seen, agrees with that article of faith: *to judge the living and the dead.* For no one can judge what he does not know; therefore He knows all things, because He judges all things. 

But the root which establishes the Law of Moses as unchangeable into another Law of God—although on the surface it seems to fight with the orthodox faith, which professes a new Law, a new commandment, and a new testament—nevertheless, if you look with right and sound understanding, you will find nothing whatsoever that disagrees with the foundations of faith in this. For that root suggests a twofold understanding...

<meta>This page continues Paulus Ricius’s argument regarding the relationship between Jewish "roots" of faith and Christian doctrine. Having established how the first five roots are explicit in the Apostles' Creed, he now addresses the concept of the immutability of the Mosaic Law and how it distinguishes between the moral Decalogue and temporary ceremonial laws.</meta>

### THE WORKS OF PAUL RICIUS

<note>The text continues an argument about why the Law is considered immutable.</note> ...either the law is believed to be immutable because all its mandates impose a yoke and bind us, such that they must be fulfilled in practice forever; or because no other Law of deeds has been handed down, or is to be handed down in the future, to replace the Law of Moses. The first idea is contrary both to Apostolic truth and to the very design of the Mosaic Law. For whoever subjects himself to the Law of Moses's deeds after the Law of faith and grace has been proclaimed is (as the Apostle <note>Paul</note> taught) subjecting himself to a curse and despising the grace of the Savior, who redeemed us from the curse by his own blood and the punishment of the cross. This same idea is also contradicted by the text of the Mosaic Law itself, which frequently reminds us that all the precepts of the Law (except for the <term>Decalogue<gloss>The Ten Commandments</gloss></term>) bind no one to their observance except while they held the kingdom and governance of the land of Israel. 

Indeed, they held power until the times of Christ the Savior, according to the prophecy of <note>The text attributes this to Balaam, though it is actually the blessing of Jacob from Genesis 49:10.</note> Balaam: "The scepter," he said, "shall not be taken from Judah, nor a leader or lawgiver from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent." Once he was sent, and had suffered under Pontius Pilate, the scepter was taken from them shortly thereafter; and together with the kingdom, the yoke and bond of the Law was loosened, just as the Law itself clearly forewarned, saying: 

<margin>Deuteronomy 4</margin> 
"Behold, I have taught you ceremonies and judgments as the Lord my God commanded me, that you should do so in the land which you are to possess." And a little further down: "He declared to you," it says, "his covenant which he commanded you, that you should do the **ten words** <note>original: "decem verba," referring to the Ten Commandments</note> which he wrote on two stone tablets; and he commanded me at that time to teach the ceremonies and judgments which you ought to do in the land which you are to possess." 

Thus says Moses. From this, observe two things worthy of consideration. First, the way in which he calls the "ten words" by the singular name of "his covenant," because the design of the entire Law hangs upon this one law of the Decalogue as if on a main hinge—just as the entire <term>School of Theologians<gloss>The Scholastic philosophers and theologians of the medieval universities</gloss></term> explains more extensively in the third volume of the *Sentences*. Even the dogma of the Talmudists—most especially the book of beliefs by **Rabbi Saadia** <note>Saadia Gaon (882–942), a prominent Jewish philosopher; the book mentioned is *The Book of Beliefs and Opinions*.</note>—demonstrates this with a long discourse. 

The second thing worthy of consideration is that these ten words were set forth and commanded to be observed perpetually, without any condition of time or place, because they flow from <term>natural law<gloss>Moral principles believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason</gloss></term> and are an image of the eternal Law implanted within us, necessarily pertaining to the whole human race. But regarding all the other mandates of the Law, he immediately attaches a condition of place and time, saying: 

<margin>Chapters 5, 6, 11, 22</margin> 
"Which you ought to do in the land which you are to possess." Outside of that land, however, they are not required at all, except perhaps out of love, not out of fear—as we read repeated frequently in various places in Deuteronomy. From these points, you may finally conclude that the first interpretation of the aforementioned "Root" <note>The Jewish root concerning the immutability of the Law.</note> can stand neither with orthodox piety nor with the design of the Mosaic Law. 

However, the second interpretation of that same Root does not clash or conflict in any way with the <term>Apostolic Creed<gloss>The Symbolum Apostolorum, the standard statement of Christian belief</gloss></term>, with the sacred scriptures, or with the traditions of the saints; rather, it plainly follows their traditions and dogma. For the Law is called such in an absolute sense because it binds a person to its decrees, which must be observed or fulfilled in external work; it judges and punishes the transgressor of these as a prevaricator. Only one such Law is believed to have been brought from God through Moses. 

But the Law of grace and faith (which we call "Law" by an improper, borrowed term) was revealed through Christ the Lord, and handed down and set forth to the entire race of mortals, according to that saying of John: "The Law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ." The wise architect, the Apostle Paul, also calls this the "Law of faith," while he calls the Law of Moses the "Law of works." Therefore, while the orthodox faith proposes a new commandment and testament, it proclaims only the Law of faith and grace. It puts forward no other Law of works handed down by God besides the Law of Moses—which, as far as the mandate of the Decalogue is concerned (which stands as the chief foundation of both divine and human law), certainly binds man to its observance forever. Yet all the other mandates of the Law reserve for themselves no further power of obligating or judging. For, as the Apostle says, "You have not received again the spirit of servitude in fear, but the spirit of adoption..."

He concludes that the Christian "Law of Grace" fulfills the Law of Moses without violating its "immutable" status.</summary>

...of the adoption of sons, in which we cry **Abba, Father**. To this the tradition of the allegorizing Talmudists <note>Scholars of the Talmud who interpret the text through symbolic or spiritual meanings</note> agrees, regarding that enigma in Ecclesiastes: *He who breaks through a wall, a serpent will bite him* <note>Ecclesiastes 10:8</note>. Whoever makes this Law void will be bitten by the venom and the <term>fuel of sin<gloss>fomes peccati; the underlying inclination toward sin</gloss></term>, which that cunning serpent <note>The Serpent in the Garden of Eden</note> instilled into the first-formed [Adam] and transmitted to his descendants. This serpent's venom (they say) is not destroyed until the coming of the Messiah. Once that venom is extinguished and destroyed, there will be the least possible need for the wall and partition of the Law, which was torn down through the blood of Christ the Messiah. And it came to pass (as the Apostle speaks) that out of the two, one was made: for then all shall be taught by God. According to that word of the Prophet: *The nursing infant shall play over the hole of the asp... because the earth is filled with the knowledge of the Lord.* <note>Isaiah 11:8-9</note>

Thus it is established that Christ did not bring forth a *new* Law, unless we wish to improperly call the new covenant of Christ a "new Law." Nor has the Law of Moses ceased, since we retain its chief part, its foundation, and its perfection—especially since the other laws bind no one except in the [Holy] Land itself, and therefore, being suspended outside the land, they take nothing away from the Law. When all these things are rightly perceived, it clearly follows that every faithful follower of Christ embraces and professes all the roots of Jewish belief; and therefore (according to the assertions of the Talmudists) every practitioner of Christian piety is a true Israelite and has a share in the **world to come** <term>world to come<gloss>Olam Ha-Ba; the afterlife or the future messianic age</gloss></term>.

### APPENDIX ON THE MUTABILITY OF THE LAW.

Regarding the objection the Jews raise here—that the Law of Moses is eternal and ought never to be changed—it seemed right to trace the matter a little further back. That the Law is indeed changeable is first evident from the fact that, as we said a little earlier, all laws except the **Decalogue** <gloss>The Ten Commandments</gloss> bind no one outside the Promised Land. Therefore, a Law is variable which binds or does not bind depending on the location.

Next, the same is clear from the nature of the one who receives the Law. For everything is received according to the manner of the receiver. But the receiver (that is, man) is changeable. Therefore, that which is received (the Law) is also changeable. Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>The famous 12th-century philosopher Maimonides</note> testifies in the third treatise of his *Guide* <note>The *Moreh Nevuchim*, or Guide for the Perplexed</note> that the Law is varied according to the nature of men; there he says that many ceremonial laws were handed down more because of the dullness of men and the habit of idolatry than because the Lawgiver [God] desired it. From this it is clear that the Law could have been handed down differently if the condition of the men receiving it had been different; likewise, it can be changed once the condition of men is changed. Therefore, the Law is changeable.

Thirdly, the same is clear from the Talmudic volume itself, in the book *Sanhedrin*, in the chapter *Those who are strangled* <note>original: "illu hen hanchenokin," referring to the Mishnaic chapter Elu Hen HaNenekin</note>, where it is read: "Master Johanan said: In all things which a Prophet tells you to transgress the Law, obey him, except for the worship of idols." In that same place they also add: "If the time requires some change in the Law, this can be done by any wise man, even if he is less than a Prophet." Rabbi Moses <note>Maimonides</note> also confirms this in his *Book of Judges*, in the chapter on the *Laws of the Rebellious* <note>Hilkhot Mamrim</note>. From this it is clear, by the testimony of the Rabbis themselves, that the Law can be changed according to the time.

Fourthly, the Kabbalists teach that the Law was given because of the venom instilled into Adam by the serpent. But the venom will cease when the Messiah comes. Therefore, what is clearer than that the Law will also cease then? As for the objection they raise from the second [book of the Law, i.e., Deuteronomy]:
> "The hidden things belong to the Lord our God, but the things revealed belong to us and to our children **forever**, that we may do all the words of this Law." <note>Deuteronomy 29:29</note>

Thus the Law might seem to be eternal. I respond: The Hebrew word *olam* <note>original: "olam"</note> does not always mean "eternal," but sometimes signifies a finite time, as in Exodus 21: *And he shall be his servant forever* <note>Exodus 21:6</note>, where Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the 11th-century French commentator</note> explains *olam* as the number of the **Jubilee**—that is, fifty years. In this place the Kabbalists also teach many hidden things concerning the revolution of the world, which they extract from the "sevens"—that is, seven times seven—and the Jubilee, which is the fiftieth year. As for what the Jews then proceed to say from the New Testament...

...to seek out certain points to prove the eternity of the Law, such as: *I have not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it* <note>Matthew 5:17</note>; also, *whatever they tell you, observe and do* <note>Matthew 23:3</note>; and, *the doers of the Law shall be justified* <note>Romans 2:13</note>; also, *circumcision is indeed profitable if you keep the Law* <note>Romans 2:25</note>; and, *the Law is holy and the commandment is holy* <note>Romans 7:12</note>; and, *we know that the Law is good, if one uses it lawfully* <note>1 Timothy 1:8</note> (and many other points to which, because they are so clear, it seemed unnecessary to respond). But I wished to refute three additional arguments which they <note>Jewish interlocutors or traditionalists</note> misuse to prove the eternity of the Law. 

The first argument is that the Law is eternal because its cause is eternal. For the final cause of the Law is to lead men back to their own perfection; and since this cause is eternal, therefore the Law is too. But the response is easy: not all laws are necessary for this. For the Rabbis themselves, as was said before, testify that many ceremonial laws were not needed except because of the <term>dullness of men<gloss>hebetudinem hominum; a lack of spiritual sensitivity</gloss></term> and for outward ornament. 

The second argument is that the Law perfects man in either body or soul, and since those two are always necessary, the Law must also be eternal. But the response is equally easy: those laws which pertain to the perfection of man are indeed eternal—not because Moses brought them, but because they are laws of nature. The others are not eternal. Thus, the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note> alone shall be eternal. 

The third argument is that the Law is a figure of eternal truth, and since this truth is eternal, the Law must be as well. In this argument, I concede everything, provided that the "figure of eternal truth" is found not in the literal sense of the Law, but in the allegorical sense. For thus <term>Rabbi Moses<gloss>Maimonides, the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher</gloss></term> and all others say that the letter of the Law is a small thing, an example compared to a candle that is bought for a tiny coin; but the allegorical sense is the certainty of the Law, like pearls. Yet these pearls are nonetheless found by the light of the candle: that is, through the letter of the Law. 

Thus it is sufficiently shown that the Mosaic Law in its entirety is not eternal. But someone might ask here: if this is the case, why do the Jews so obstinately insist on the outward observance of the whole Law? I respond first that they have been so persuaded by the Rabbis, as if a Law received from the ancients cannot be changed. Nor have the Rabbis only persuaded the common people of this, but also that if the Rabbis advise anything against the Law for the utility of the times, they should believe it to be true. Thus, regarding the passage in Deuteronomy 17: *You shall not turn aside from it...* etc., the <term>Talmudic gloss<gloss>Interpretive commentary within the Talmud</gloss></term> says: *If a wise man tells you that the right hand is the left, and the left is the right, you shall obey him.* So too in the book *Sanhedrin*, in the chapter *Dine Mammonos* <note>original: "Dine Mammonos"; referring to the section on civil laws or "Laws of Money"</note>, one reads that no one can be a judge unless he knows how to prove from the Law itself that "unclean" food is "clean," and so on. Notice there that by the Rabbis' own confession, the Law is variable. 

But observe the argument by which they persuade the common people that the Law is eternal. Since it is written in Deuteronomy 12 that the laws are not to be kept outside the Land of Promise, and yet the avoidance of idol worship must still be observed even outside the Land, they argue as follows: the avoidance of idols lasts even outside the Land, but the avoidance of idols is a "debt of the body" (for thus they divide the laws, as pertaining either to the cultivation of the land or to the "debt of the body"). Therefore, they claim, all laws regarding the "debt of the body" must be kept outside the Land. But they err. First, the logic does not hold from a particular case to a universal rule. Furthermore, the reason for the Law against idols is not the same as for other laws. For the Law on avoiding idols is necessary for salvation and pertains to the perfection of man as a human being—as they say in the Talmud, to worship idols is the same as denying the whole Law, and conversely, he who does not worship idols is as if he kept the whole Law. But the other laws are not necessary for salvation, nor do they pertain to the perfection of man—neither circumcision, nor food, nor <term>Unleavened Bread<gloss>Azyma</gloss></term>, etc. Otherwise, the saints before the Law <note>The Patriarchs like Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob who lived before the Mosaic Law was given</note> would not have been perfect or saved. Therefore, an argument from dissimilar things is invalid. They would conclude more correctly thus: "Whichever Law is as equally necessary for salvation as the avoidance of idols, that Law must always be kept; but there is no such law in the whole Mosaic Law except for the Decalogue. Therefore, etc." But enough on these matters for now.

# PAUL RICIUS, ON CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE, BOOK III. PREFACE TO THE THIRD VOLUME.

<margin>2 Timothy 3.</margin>
<margin>Matthew 5.</margin>
<margin>Peace and concord are to be placed before any mandates or legal institutes.</margin>
<margin>Hosea 4 and 10.</margin>
<margin>The deliberate and foreseeing intention of the author.</margin>

THE Prince of Peace and restorer of the world, Christ the Lord, among His most holy and salutary warnings, especially commends the observance of mutual love and peace: which, like an anchor and the highest hinge of human affairs, is that upon which the eternal blessedness of mortals and the entire happiness of this life depends. For God (says the Apostle) is not a God of dissension, but of peace <note>1 Corinthians 14:33</note>. And for that reason, Truth itself warned that unanimity and concord are to be placed before the sacred offering of the altar. *Leave* (He said) *your gift before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother* <note>Matthew 5:24</note>. Furthermore, divine concern so loathes and hates dissensions and schisms that it taught it is better to live even with the most wicked worship of idols than among contentions and discords. *Ephraim* (He said) *is a companion of idols; let him alone; their heart is divided, now they shall perish* <note>Hosea 4:17 and 10:2; original: "Particeps Idolorum Ephraim..."</note>. 

Wherefore the great and most pious Prince Constantine, writing to Alexander and Arius—who were disputing over the Trinity, the greatest sacrament of the faith, and rending the unity of the Christian flock—imposed total silence upon them, as can be clearly seen from that same letter of Constantine. I have seen fit to append this letter to the end of this Volume, so that the pious and prudent reader may reflect upon it, and know how to apply it to the turbulent and miserable condition of our own time, and take it in good part. Indeed, so many horrendous dissensions and formidable discords now attack and rage far and wide throughout the entire world of the Christian name, that unless counsel and diligent care are awakened more providently and maturely, it is to be feared that, with the momentum of the seditious breaking out even more widely a little later, we may experience the irremediable violence of Mars <note>A classical reference to the god of war, signifying armed conflict or civil war</note> and the slaughter of souls (may the heavens avert the omen!). 

These things take their origin from nowhere else than the distorted understanding of certain men and the unbridled lust of carnal desire. Although their amendment or correction requires the governance of divine providence and its severity and mercy, we—as the hired workers of that supreme Master of the House and <term>husbandmen<gloss>colonos; literally 'tillers' or 'tenant farmers'</gloss></term> bought by the price of His blood—must apply the diligence of our cultivation and our labor according to our strength. We shall therefore plant and water, but God, that celestial farmer, will give the increase. 

Having therefore already worked and cultivated the rough and parched field of the unbelieving philosophers, as well as the stony and sterile ground of the foolish Jews—now filled with richer and more fertile soil—we now, by the nod of the heavens, approach the task of purging and restoring the field of certain wandering believers, which is currently oppressed by the thistles and briars of error. 

Indeed, since the fallacy and error of those who go astray is recognized as manifold and great, if I wished to refute and extirpate them one by one, my strength would fail me and I would sink under the magnitude of the burden before the labor of the undertaken task was finished. Furthermore, the reader’s mind would grow weary of a longer speech spent in debating, especially since many have already taken up this duty and have tried with their hands and backs to fulfill that vow. Some of these, though they have handled the business vigorously, full of erudition and zeal, and have profited not a little in it, yet the debate of certain other <term>micrologists<gloss>mycrologorum; those who focus excessively on trivial or petty details</gloss></term>—who are like geese hissing among swans—is so crude, and their speech so insolent and slippery, that whatever the former may piously and providently teach, instruct, and repair, the latter immediately subvert and render void with their petulance and virulent rage, bringing back nothing in the end but the fable of the Hydra <note>A reference to the mythological beast that grew two heads for every one cut off, suggesting that their arguments only create more problems</note>. 

Therefore, for the sake of correcting and reconciling both disagreeing parties, I have judged it to be wiser and safer not to blunt the insolence and ignorance of those who stray by means of a trivial or direct rebuff. This is so that they do not, out of pride (as is the habit of human frailty) and a stubborn mind, resist even the recognized truth, and although conquered, refuse to yield and acknowledge their error. Instead, I have decided to propose and explain certain solid and principal **theorems** <note>Used here in the sense of fundamental, self-evident propositions or principles</note> granted and approved by all cultivators of the Gospel faith. By these, the minds of those wandering may be directed secretly and step-by-step toward the mark of truth and may, of their own accord, become conscious of what is right. Indeed, through these theorems, a reason and method will be given for soundly understanding and interpreting the sacred utterances. From there, it will also be possible to weigh what faith and what works provide, and which human authority is to be rejected or embraced. Finally, from this, you—the provident and pious follower of Gospel truth and its most honorable guardian—will be able to settle the lawsuits that now roam to the point of destruction in the sacred Commonwealth of Christians, and reduce discordant things into concord and peace, the best of all things. 

But since this seems a truly arduous task, far unequal to the strength of the weak, I turn to the heavens and the celestial Parent, and as a suppliant, I implore His spiritual grace and help in this manner.

# PAUL RICIUS: HERE THE AUTHOR PROMISES BOTH SILENCE AND ELOQUENCE.

<image-desc>A historiated woodcut initial 'Q' depicting a robed figure, likely a scholar or saint, kneeling in prayer or contemplation in an outdoor setting with a tree and a path leading toward a building.</image-desc>

WHO will set a guard over my tongue, and a Law of dictation over my mouth, lest slipperiness lead me into a precipice, and lest silence give birth to the fault of sluggishness? <note>This opening paraphrases Ecclesiasticus 22:27: "Who shall set a guard before my mouth, and a seal of wisdom upon my lips?"</note> For to remain silent while piety and the religion of truth are confounded by the mouths of the foolish is a great and inhuman vice of impiety; yet it is also an unspeakable impudence to speak where the mystery of truth is hidden away. For if human reason falters, wavers, and is deceptive regarding earthly things—which it touches more lightly—how then shall the fragile and muddy form of mortals, mere rot and worms, presume to speak of celestial things and the immortal King of the ages? And if He does not even trust His own saints, and finds depravity even in the sublime assembly of Angels, what firm or stable thing can a thin reed, shaken by the weight of filth, ash, and earth, attribute to itself? What, then, shall I, an unhappy and puny man <note>original: "homuncio"</note>, dare to do? What, finally, shall I provide for my miserable self, lest I transgress against another? Shall I speak? Or shall I remain silent? For silence is given over to sluggishness, and speech to impudence. Or perhaps I shall refrain from one and the other while I join them both, speaking and remaining silent at the same time? For whatever is mine in me shall remain silent, because it is all empty. But that which shines from elsewhere shall speak: the spirit of celestial and eternal wisdom, which perpetually cries out from without and calls its ministers to the citadel. He shall set a guard over my tongue, and a Law of dictation over my mouth. Therefore, let me hear what God may speak in me through the mouths of the saints, and what that living Word of God—more penetrating than any double-edged human intelligence—might advise me.

->FEAR GOD (HE SAYS), AND KEEP HIS COMMANDS,<-
->for this is the whole duty of man. Ecclesiastes, last chapter.<-

<margin>Why the author took the mandate of fear rather than love as the theme of this volume.</margin>
<margin>Ecclesiastes 16.</margin>
<margin>Romans 2.</margin>
We have taken the precept of fear as the theme of this work because of the poisonous and accursed error of certain people—the cause and fuel of all outrages and crimes—by which they despise and reject the external observance of the commandments and everything decreed by human prudence as if they were futile works of no benefit. They assert that he who presumes to carry back any merit through external works distrusts the mercy, passion, and merits of Christ the Savior, who Himself bore our infirmities and sustained the pains and dire tortures of death for the remission of all sins. From this, they drag the unwary multitude of the faithful toward the ruinous and incorrigible sin of presumption, plunging them into the abyss of eternal perdition by teaching that it is enough for salvation that each person hopes for divine mercy and firmly believes that, without any external work of penance, they obtain the pardon and remission of sins. They do not heed the warning of the wise man: that even the mercy of God is distributed and makes a place for each according to his merits. How much more shall His severity and justice do this, which (as the Apostle says) shall render to each according to his works. For no one follows Christ unless he takes up his cross, chastises his body, and brings it into the servitude of God's commandments. Since, therefore, this detestable and deadly sin of presumption can be removed and exterminated only by the fear of God (as you shall hear in what follows), the theme of this work is taken from that wise maxim: *Fear God, and keep His commandments, for this is the whole duty of man.*

->FOR THIS PURPOSE WAS EVERY MAN MADE, THAT<-
->he might cling to the source from which he flowed, the origin of eternal life.<-

<margin>Deuteronomy 30.</margin>
It is implanted by nature in all things that they should long for that upon which they depend, and that each should seek its own origin. The dust (says the wise man) returns to the earth from whence it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it. Hence Moses also says: *Cling to Him, for He is your life.* And the Apostle: *He who clings*

### HE ADHERES THROUGH LOVE.

For the whole basis of union and adherence is love and affection; therefore Moses also commanded love, so that adherence might follow from it. "You shall love," he says,
<margin>Deut. 30</margin>
"the Lord your God and obey His voice, and you shall adhere to Him." Just as
<margin>Luke 16</margin>
the servant who loves his master (as the Truth <note>original: "Veritas" — Ricius frequently uses "the Truth" as a title for Jesus Christ or the Gospel</note> says) adheres to him, and the one he hates, he despises. † But here, the task I have undertaken and the sequence of the matter require that I do not pass over in silence what a certain modern <note>original: "neotericus" — referring to contemporary Reformation theologians, likely Martin Luther or his followers</note> writer of no small reputation contends against this theorem in certain propositions disputed by him. He insults it quite insolently, asserting that it is "impiety" to believe that we obtain the remission of sins through the love of God. His reasoning is that to believe this is to believe that we have remission of sins because of our own work, not because of Christ. Thus, he claims, the merit of Christ would be removed and buried. These are his words. But I cannot wonder enough how
<margin>He departs from and contradicts himself.</margin>
this man, contradicting himself, calls it "impiety" that the remission of sins should follow because of or through our work, since the very act of faith—which is to believe in Christ the Savior—is also our work. Indeed, it is more "ours" than love is, since love also belongs to the Creator, who is Charity itself. It would therefore be impious (according to this hypothesis of his) to believe that we are justified through faith and obtain remission of sins—which, according to his own assertions and dogmas, is a most unfitting thing to hear and even execrable. However, since the whole mass of faith and piety, and almost the entire conflict now raging and venting its fury in the most holy Republic of Christ, hangs upon a distorted understanding of this theme, I have decided to wander a bit further here and repeat this examination from a deeper level. I say, therefore, that this conjunction "because of" <note>original: "propter"</note>, or "through" <note>original: "per"</note>, or any other causal word, designates a different mode of causality (according to the multiple types of causes): namely, the <term>final cause</term>, the <term>efficient cause</term>, the <term>formal cause</term>, and the <term>material cause</term>. <note>Ricius is using the classic Aristotelian framework of the "Four Causes" to resolve the theological dispute.</note> A "final cause" is like that in Matthew chapter five: *Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of [propter] justice.* An "efficient cause" is like that in John:
<margin>Chapter 15</margin>
*Now you are clean because of [propter] the word which I have spoken to you.* A "formal cause" is like that of the
<margin>Romans 8</margin>
Apostle: *He will also give life to your mortal bodies because of [propter] His Spirit dwelling in you.* A "material cause" or subject is like that of the Apostle to the Ephesians in chapter four:
<margin>Ephesians 4</margin>
*Alienated from the way of the Lord through [per] the ignorance that is in them, because of [propter] the blindness of their hearts.* Thus, all other modes and conditions of things must necessarily be reduced to one of these four modes. If, therefore, the causal word in this theme is to be understood as a final, efficient, or formal cause, then I securely agree with that opponent that it is false and impious to say that we obtain remission of sins "because of" our love for God—and not only because of love, but also because of faith, hope, or any work of ours. However, if the causal word indicates a mode of material causality or the "disposition of the subject," then it is just and pious to believe that because of our work—and especially because of love (which presupposes faith, as a form presupposes its matter)—we obtain the remission of sins. For just as no form or perfection is infused, so neither is the light of grace poured in, except according to the previous disposition and aptitude of the recipient. For "according to the measure,"
<margin>Matt. 7</margin>
(says the Truth) "with which you measure, it will be measured back to you," and to him who has (namely, preventing grace), subsequent grace shall be given, which justifies. To this relates that passage from Proverbs: *Reveal your works to the Lord, and your thoughts shall be directed.* And that of the Apostle: *The righteous judgment of God, who renders to each according to
<margin>Romans 2</margin>
his works.* For unless preparation and aptitude were required for justifying grace, all the commands of the Savior and the Apostles would have been frustrated and in vain—all those great counsels and warnings about Fasting, Almsgiving, modesty, the mortification of the flesh, and that whole kind—nor would the way be so narrow and the entrance so cramped to the kingdom of heaven. Here the adversary will perhaps say that all these are moral commands and the Law of nature...

<margin>
What the chief reason and cause of ceremonies is.

bound. <note>original: "verbum Dei non est alligatum" — a reference to 2 Timothy 2:9, meaning God's grace is not restricted by human rules.</note> However, because the Law of Nature prescribes things that are implicit and general, their specific explanation is required for the sake of the simple and unrefined among the faithful, who do not know how to maintain a proper measure. Such a divine or human explanation, or the determination of the Law of Nature, is nothing other than the institution of ceremonies. For example: to live soberly or to fast belongs to the Law of Nature. But to fast on this or that day, such as on the feast of the Apostles or the Blessed Virgin, pertains to ceremonies. Likewise, to indulge occasionally in rest belongs to the Law of Nature; but to be at leisure on the Sabbath or the Lord’s day is ceremonial. To help the poor and share the fruits of the earth with them belongs to the Law of Nature; but to distribute a tenth part <note>the tithe</note> to them is ceremonial. This same judgment should be applied to every single divine or human ceremony. Since, therefore, the determination of the Law of Nature is necessary for the common health of the Commonwealth, it is proven that some ceremonies, whether these or those, must absolutely be admitted. And if some ceremonies must be given: why, I ask, should we not rather embrace those which were established by the Synods of the Saints and by the leaders—men of wisdom and holiness—and observed and guarded for so many centuries (I except, however, the immoderate and destructive abuses of many today), rather than having each person presume to take away the old and decree the new according to his own whim? From such a thing follows nothing but stumbling blocks for the poor and the destruction of the entire commonwealth.

<margin>
He who has ears to hear, let him hear.
</margin>
For you know what that pagan <note>original: "Ethnicus"</note> Prince of the Peripatetics, <note>Aristotle, whose followers were called Peripatetics because they walked while teaching.</note> the master of moral and political life, warned in the second book of his *Politics*: it is certain, I say, that some errors of lawmakers and magistrates must be tolerated; for a person who proceeds to correct them will not do as much good as the habit of not obeying one's superiors will do harm. Consider these things, if you are wise. From these it must finally be concluded that, because of our works—by way of preparing and fitting the disposition of the receiver (but not by way of the primary agent, the end, or the form)—we obtain the remission of sins, and adherence to God, and justifying grace.

<margin>
Prevenient grace precedes every act of the will. Romans 9.
</margin>
Nevertheless, it is true that this very faculty of disposing oneself toward justifying grace (or of not rebelling against it) is also a grace, which they call "prevenient" <note>Prevenient grace is a theological concept referring to divine grace that precedes human decision.</note> grace, which precedes every act of the will and our every chosen work. Concerning this, the Apostle <note>St. Paul</note> writing to the Romans says: "It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy." <note>Romans 9:16</note> Yet that grace is "maimed and imperfect" (I speak to those who have ears) which does not immediately shine upon us from the Father of Lights, but rather through the series of secondary causes and the intervention of the work of nature. It is founded in this muddy mass <note>original: "lutulenta hac massa" — referring to the clay of human nature or original sin.</note> through which there is fashioned (as the Apostle speaks) from the same mass (namely, the remote and primary matter) a "vessel for honor," and through the lack of that same grace there is fashioned a "vessel of dishonor and wrath." This prevenient grace, therefore, although it is a gift of God, is nonetheless a less perfect gift and exposed (as you will hear in what follows) to various accidents of nature. But that "subsequent grace," by which we are justified immediately without any intermediary, is what James calls the "perfect gift" and the "best thing given," <note>James 1:17</note> which comes from above without any gap or any help from secondary causes, descending from the Father of Lights. Through this grace, we obtain the love of God, the remission of sins, and adherence to the origin of eternal life.

### CONFORMED THROUGH THE PURITY OF THE SOUL.

<margin>Ecclesiastes 7</margin>
For although the human soul is joined to a human body, remaining pure and conformed to the image and likeness of God from the very beginning of its creation, it is nevertheless deeply weighed down and turned away from the source of eternal life by the infection and weight of that same muddy body. Solomon said: "God made man upright, but he has entangled himself in many questions." <note>Modern translations often render this as "many schemes" or "devices."</note> For this reason, the Eternal 
<margin>Matthew 19</margin>
Truth <note>A common title for Christ in Renaissance theology.</note> taught that little children (because their souls are not yet so polluted) are more capable than others of the kingdom of heaven, and that their angels perpetually behold the face of the heavenly Parent. <margin>Matthew 18</margin>

To be converted and become like a little child is nothing other than to turn the soul away from the vain and filthy affections of earthly things, and to restore it to its innate purity, from which it may be able to achieve conformity, love, and adherence to the source of eternal life.

### cleanliness of the body and of life.

iniquities (that is, your filthy and intemperate works) have divided you from your God, and your sins have hidden His face from you." To this is added that teaching of Gospel truth: "The
<margin>Matthew 13</margin>
care of this world and the deceitfulness of riches chokes the word of God, and it is rendered without fruit." And because the purity of the soul requires cleanliness of the body and of life, 
<margin>Psalm 23 <note>Modern Psalm 24.</note></margin>
the Prophet sings: "Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in His holy place? He who is innocent in his hands and pure of heart." Hence also the man of God, 
<margin>James 4 <note>OCR says James 3, likely James 4:8.</note></margin>
James, says: "Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded." The mystery of Baptism itself designates this. For unless one is 
<margin>John 3</margin>
born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. For water signifies the cleanliness of the body and of life, while the Spirit shows the purity of the soul. Moses also places the entire system of good works and life in conformity and likeness, compressing it into this brief clause: "Be holy," he says, "for I am holy." The Wise Architect of faith <note>Referring to St. Paul.</note> explained this in clearer
<margin>Colossians 3</margin>
words to the Colossians, saying: "If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is; savor the things that are above, not those on the earth. Mortify your members, putting on the new man, who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of Him who created him." Indeed, the entire reason for conformity, love, and adherence consists in this image. It is therefore worth the effort that whoever desires purity of soul should cleanse his body from the plague of earthly lust and (as the Apostle says) mortify its members, presenting it as a living sacrifice, so that like the celestial bodies, they may become a seat and temple of the Holy Spirit and weapons of light.

### A diligent fear of God works the purity of the soul.

For since the cleanliness of the body and of life is nothing other than the sobriety and modesty of human works—whether toward oneself, toward God, or toward one's neighbor—which human weakness cannot perfectly grasp...

# PAUL RICIUS,
<margin>Wisdom 9</margin>
<margin>Proverbs 6</margin>

<margin>Faith is more perfect than the sum total [of other powers], because it is an act of a more perfect power and concerns a more noble object.</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 13</margin>
<margin>Ecclesiasticus 34</margin>
and knows no limit. Because the thoughts of mortals (says the Wise Man <note>original: "Sapiens" — likely referring to Solomon or the author of the Book of Wisdom</note>) are timid, and their providence uncertain, only the wisdom of God, which understands all things, leads a man (as the same author says) soberly in his works. Therefore, there is a need for divine instruction and direction through His commandments. A commandment (says Solomon) is a lamp, and the law is light; for this reason, Scripture (says the Apostle) is divinely inspired so that it may be useful for teaching, and that the man of God may be equipped for every good work. 

Wherefore, if you wish to enter into life (says the Truth <note>i.e., Christ</note>), keep the commandments of God. And because divine authority says: You shall fear the Lord your God, and Him only shall you serve. And that saying from the Psalms: Fear God and serve Him. And (as the Apostle says) work out your salvation with fear and trembling. Now, the fear of God works the purity of the soul—specifically, that fear which follows faith with love—because the purification of the soul consists in nothing else (as we mentioned before) than in wiping away the filth and rust of earthly thoughts, which stain and defile the soul, pure by its own nature, so that the image of eternal truth cannot shine back within it. 

Only that fear of God which follows faith with love performs this cleansing. For the fear of God (says the Wise Man) drives out all sin, and therefore he calls the fear of God—which places itself above all things—the crown and fullness of wisdom. I speak, however, of the fear that follows faith with love. For while all fear and love arise from some preceding knowledge of the senses, reason, or faith, the action of sense and reason, since it is grounded in "otherness" <note>original: "alteritate" — a philosophical term for the state of being different or separate from the divine unity</note> and motion, cannot reach that supreme and immutable Good. 

Faith, however, and firm belief (because it is the action of a more sublime power, grounded in a state of rest) attains that same supreme and immutable Good through that same faith. Certainly, true fear of God accompanies faith with love. I say "faith with love" because even the demons (as James says) believe, and it follows from their belief that they fear and tremble; yet such fear in no way purifies the spirit of a demon. This is because it proceeds from a faith that lacks love and adherence; rather, they fear with a dread of punishment. Of such faith the Apostle affirms: "If I have all faith, so as to move mountains, but have not charity, I am nothing." 

But faith with love gives birth to a fear—not a dread of punishment or the loss of any created thing—but a fear of deserting the supreme, desirable, and lovable Good. He who truly fears this dreads nothing else in the entire circle of the universe (according to the word of the Wise Man): "He who fears God shall fear nothing, and shall not be afraid, for He is his hope."

<margin>Why the authority of the ancients prefers fear, while the Truth of the Gospel commends love.</margin>
<margin>Luke 7</margin>
<margin>John 14</margin>

<margin>Note the mystery.</margin>
But before I begin my discourse on fear, I think it not out of place to resolve a question that silently presents itself here. The listener will doubt (and rightly so) that if the authority of the ancients <note>The "ancients" usually refers to Old Testament figures or Hebrew patriarchs.</note> makes so much of fear, why is it that the words of Christ the Savior and the Apostles are everywhere filled with the teachings of love, affection, and charity, rather than the precepts of fear? "Many sins are forgiven her," He says, "because she loved much." "He who loves me will be loved by my Father." "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word." Nor did He commit the pastoral care to Simon, son of John, until He had three times approved his love and affection. 

I consider it superfluous to recount how many places in the writings of John and the other Apostles report the commandments of charity, making no mention of fear. Indeed, John entirely excludes fear, saying that fear is not in charity, and perfect charity casts out fear. Know, therefore, first of all, and note the mystery: the love which Christ the Lord so often commands to his disciples is not that which Moses sometimes prescribes. That was surely for God the Father; but Christ commends the love of himself...

### ON CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE, BOOK III.

<margin>John 14</margin>

However, he cannot reconcile them unless he clings to both one and the other of the extremes. He clings to them through love; therefore,

<margin>John 17</margin>
Indeed, from this love follows what he says: 
> "I in them and you in me, that they may be perfected into one." 
Truly, such a unity could not be given to us—born as we are from corruptible seed—without a Mediator. For God is a consuming fire; 
<margin>Deuteronomy 4 <note>The original margin notes Deuteronomy 14, but the text "God is a consuming fire" is found in Deuteronomy 4:24</note></margin>
yet even with a Mediator, it is not easy. For the way is narrow and the entrance even narrower, where nevertheless, for the one who knocks through true faith and love, it is opened. 

<margin>Behold the great mystery of godliness.</margin>
Pay attention, I pray you, and listen diligently: for you have read how, when **Elisha** <note>original: "Heliseus"</note> sought to ascend to heaven from **Elijah** <note>original: "Helia"</note> through a whirlwind, he besought him (according to the Latin edition): "I pray that your double spirit may be in me." Here one should not listen to what many feel—that Elisha, a man of God, asked for such an enormous thing as a spirit twice as intense or extensive (as they say) as the spirit of Elijah. Rather, if you consider Elisha’s petition, it was that the double spirit of Elijah—or more correctly, that *doubleness* which was in Elijah's spirit—might be upon Elisha himself. 

<margin>John 14</margin>
Whether that is the **Paraclete** <note>from the Greek *parakletos*, meaning the Comforter or Advocate, referring to the Holy Spirit</note> who is another in essence, of whom the Truth <note>Christ</note> says: 
> "And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Comforter," 
or whether it is double only in effect, is not the place to discuss or explain here. Elisha therefore asks for the double spirit of Elijah, to which Elijah responded that he had asked a difficult thing: 
> "Nevertheless, if you see me when I am taken from you, it shall be so as you have asked; but if you do not see me, it shall not be." 

<margin>James 1</margin>
Consider, I beg you: although every spiritual gift comes from above from the Father of Lights, Elijah did not say to Elisha, "If you lift your mind on high to God, the giver of all honors," but rather, "if you see *me* when I am taken from you." This is according to that saying of John: 
> "What if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?" 
Then, surely, the Spirit who gives life will be present. For the flesh, insofar as it is flesh, profits nothing; but insofar as it is joined to the Spirit and seasoned with its salt, it does. Finally, because Elisha was capable of seeing Elijah rise and ascend to the heavens, crying out: 
> "My father, my father!"

And that other saying:

In him indeed (as the Apostle speaks) all things are restored, both those in heaven and those on earth, through his passion and the blood of the cross. 
<margin>You who are wise, understand.</margin>
The mystery of this cross also reveals that deed which the history of the Kings recounts shortly after the mysteries of Elisha. I mean that of the King of **Moab**, who offered his innocent firstborn son as a burnt offering upon the wall, which caused great indignation against Israel. See the glosses of the writers there and consider. To this also turns the story of the **Gibeonites**, who, when they had crucified seven innocent men from the lineage of Saul (whom David handed over for punishment), God was soon reconciled to the land—ponder these things within yourself. 

Finally, returning to where the greatness of the mystery and the sinister understanding of some regarding the sacred letters diverted us, we must say: 
<margin>The precept of fear was most fitting for the Jews; but the commandment of love for the followers of Christ.</margin>
It was not fitting for the leaders of the Jews to have any mandate or instruction for loving Christ the Mediator, who was not yet born in human form nor perfectly foreknown by them. Instead, the fear of God was most suitable for them, as they saw such great severity and terrible plagues upon the Egyptians. They also received the Law of the Decalogue <note>the Ten Commandments</note> in the solitude of the desert with great terror, amid horrendous thunders, lightnings, portents of flames, the sound of the trumpet, and the formidable voice of the Almighty. And whenever they committed some small offense, immediately, with no delay of long-suffering, they paid the penalty for their fault by the sword, by the swallowing of the earth, by the burning of flames, by the bite of serpents, or by the punishment of the gallows. But for the Apostles and other followers of Christ, who saw the Savior in the flesh, the commandment of love and all the ways of friendship and affection were most fitting. Since indeed he is of two forms...

<meta>Continuing from the discussion on the Mediator (Christ) as the bridge of love between God and humanity, Ricius now explores the nature of friendship and the transition from the "heavy yoke" of the Old Testament Law to the "liberty" of the New Testament through the gifts of the Holy Spirit.</meta>

# PAUL RICIUS,
<meta>catchword: ctu,</meta>

<margin>Friendship occurs either by natural instinct or from external circumstances.</margin>
Every bond of friendship is either by the instinct of nature or is adventitious <note>meaning something added from the outside, rather than being innate</note> from without. The first arises from an innate harmony and fitness of things—as it were, reciprocal—such as that between parent and child, brother with brother, or wife and husband. The other is superadded, based on what is good, useful, pleasant, and honorable. Both types of friendship are increased by familiar social interaction and by presence itself. Since, therefore, the friendship of Christ our Savior toward us contains all these incitements and causes of love in an accumulated and far more sublime way, who, I ask, is so impious or of such dull understanding that they would refuse or doubt that Christ the Lord is to be cherished with the highest zeal of affection and love above all other mortals and immortals? For as God, the propagator of the human race, He is to be loved as a parent; and as man and the firstborn Son of God, He is to be loved as a neighbor and a co-heir brother. Again, because in Him is the summit of all virtues, He is to be respected as the honorable good. Because through Him and in Him is eternal sweetness, glory, and joy, He is to be embraced as the supremely pleasant good. Because He is the restorer of the blessed life, He is to be pursued with the greatest desire as the supreme utility. This affection is urged and increased immeasurably by His presence, His familiar interaction, and His immense, unheard-of love, known through clear experience, by which He did not shrink from so many hardships of life for us, His brothers and neighbors—namely, the scourges and the punishments of a bitter death. Hence it is no wonder if we read that the teachings of Christ’s faithful saints more frequently commemorate the commands of love than of fear. For this reason, Christ the Lord said to His own: *I will no longer call you servants, but friends* <note>original: "Iam non dicam uos seruos, sed amicos." See John 15:15</note>.

<margin>1 Corinthians 1</margin>
And there is that saying of the Apostle: *God is faithful, through whom you were called into the fellowship of His Son.* Added to this is the fact that, when in the past the Jewish people were driven into the vile and filthy slavery of the Egyptians and defiled by their unrefined and barbarian customs, there was a need for a hard and rigid pedagogue <note>a strict teacher or guardian, usually for children</note> and a yoke of commandments to institute their education and the religion of true piety. By this, their ignorance and the untamed lust of the flesh would be restrained by the dread of lashes rather than by the bond of friendship. But the followers of Christ, now imbued with more refined manners and taught by the spirit of wisdom and understanding through Christ, the best teacher of life, could be educated and moderated by no pedagogue and no precept of slavery, but by the Law of liberty and love. For, as the Apostle says, *you have not received again the spirit of slavery in fear, but the spirit of adoption as sons, in which we cry out, Abba, Father* <note>original: "Abba Pater"</note>. For where the Spirit of the
<margin>Romans 8</margin>
Lord is, there is liberty. And if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the Law. To institute this true liberty of Christians, our mild and humble-hearted, good 
<margin>Matthew 11</margin>
Jesus calls to Himself, crying out: *Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you; for my yoke is easy, and my burden light.* Indeed, the observance of the Mosaic Law was of such great weight that it seemed an unbearable yoke to the Apostles, according to that saying of Peter:
<margin>Acts 15. The law of Moses imposes an unbearable yoke.</margin>
*Now therefore, why do you tempt God by imposing a yoke upon the necks of the disciples which neither we nor our fathers were able to carry?* Notice and consider, I pray you, in what way he says one "tempts God" when they strive to occupy a common multitude with an excessive burden of regulations; and you, who are wise, reflect on these things within yourself.

Having heard these things, we now turn by divine will to the examination of fear. *Fear* (says the Wise Man) *is nothing but a surrender of the helps of thought, a betrayal of the reinforcements of reason* <note>original quote from the Book of Wisdom 17:11, describing the nature of fear as a loss of rational support</note>. For an exact understanding of this and other scriptures—which attribute various and dissonant titles to fear—and also because the entire worship of piety and all the happiness of mortals depends on fear itself, I have wished to repeat this matter from a bit deeper down, and to proceed and 
<margin>In what way the gifts of the Holy Spirit shine forth in us step by step through clear experience.</margin>
wander more widely into it; and you, give me your ears. A manifold condition preoccupies the affection which we call the "fear of God," which can be experienced in any mortal who is not deprived of it. To this correspond the spirits of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and fortitude, of knowledge and fear (which are called "gifts"). And although these gifts are numbered as seven, the Prophet <note>Isaiah 11:2</note> expressed only six, as all the most ancient manuscripts of the original language <note>referring to the Hebrew Bible</note> demonstrate.

For first, to any man not born by chance, but by a certain instinct of nature...
