# ON CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE, BOOK III.

<margin>The gift of wisdom.</margin>
...by the act <note>continuing from the previous page: "by that act"</note> which we call **wisdom**, it becomes known that there is one thing given within the compass of all reality, upon which all things depend. For only the foolish and senseless man says in his heart: *There is no God.* <note>original: "Non est Deus"; a reference to Psalm 14:1</note> From there, the soul turns itself toward that which wisdom has conceived by the light of
<margin>The gift of understanding.</margin>
**understanding**, through which it perceives that the Supreme Being is unbegotten and immortal, supremely good, and supremely wise, almighty, and the like. Once this is known, the soul is soon
aroused, and a certain desire is raised up toward that very same Being, by which the soul is urged to revolve within itself (which we call **counsel**) whether by any Law it might be able to possess and enjoy
<margin>The gift of counsel.</margin>
His effusive goodness and the splendor of His wisdom. And when, by deliberating, it gazes upon His immense bounty and the sweetness of His mercy, immediately the faculty to carry out
<margin>The gift of fortitude.</margin>
the wish (which we call **fortitude**) arises; by this, with almost no fear, the soul presumes that it can become a sharer in its wish. But when, next, through the knowledge of shifting and
perishing things (which we call **science** <note>here meaning "knowledge" or "scientia," the systematic understanding of the created world</note>), it turns itself downward through circumspection
<margin>The gift of knowledge.</margin>
and considers its own unhappy lot—how it is exiled in this blind and most foul prison <note>a common Renaissance metaphor for the physical body or the material world</note>, surrounded by the filth and stench of earthly things, and by how great an interval it stands from His immense greatness and fearsome majesty—its presumption is soon turned into sloth and numbness, as if destitute of all hope. Thus the soul is tossed and fluctuates to and fro with anxious and wandering thought, offered arguments of distrust on one side and presumption on the other, until there arrives and places himself in the middle the author of consolation and peace: 
<margin>The gift of fear eliminates the vice of presumption and distrust alike.</margin>
the **fear of God**. This gift immediately settles every battle of thoughts and calms the turbulence of the soul; for it checks the audacity of presumption by considering the immense greatness of that supreme good and one's own despised and wretched insignificance, while it also eliminates the sluggishness and numbness of distrust by proposing the unfailing bounty and mercy of the supreme good, and announcing a confidence in help against the assaults of earthly things. These things standing thus and being rightly perceived, we have deemed that some further appropriate matters, worthy of being heard, should be added and built upon the foundation already laid. For **wisdom** and **understanding**, **counsel** and **fortitude**, **knowledge** and **fear**, which we mentioned a moment ago, are of a triple order.
<margin>The triple order of the gifts is worthy of all attention.</margin>
The first is the **order of nature**, to which is joined a certain amount of "auxiliary grace" (as they call it), which belongs to the following order, acting as a prelude and a nursery in the recipient. The second is the **order of received grace**, which exists as an expressed likeness and a certain image of the third order. The third order is the **exemplary order** <note>the "perfect pattern" or archetype</note> in the Giver of grace Himself: wisdom, and the true image of God. Therefore, the functions of the first order (because they also depend on the series of secondary causes) are defective and obscure, agitated in many ways by the variety of circumstances. But those of the second order are brighter and more exquisite, and less subject to the alteration of contingent things. Of the third order are the archetypes themselves: the **Brightness** <note>original: "Candor"</note>
<margin>Wisdom 8.</margin>
(as the Wise Man says) of eternal light, and a mirror without blemish, the image of God’s majesty and
<margin>Job 12.</margin>
goodness; with whom (says Job) is true **wisdom** and **fortitude**: and He Himself has **counsel** and **understanding**. The volumes of the Divine Scriptures are full of the truthful and clear testimonies of these three orders. Consider the **wisdom** of the first order: although it too—just like His other gifts of auxiliary grace—is wisdom (since all wisdom is from God), yet because it leans upon worldly thoughts and is bound by the frailty of the flesh and the wrappings of phantasms <note>sensory mental images that can cloud pure reason</note>, Paul calls it in his letter to the Corinthians "the wisdom of this world," "human," and "carnal," which is "foolishness with God." But the wisdom of the second order (of which the same Apostle speaks "among the perfect") he everywhere calls the "**wisdom of God**." James also
<margin>James 3.</margin>
labels the wisdom of the first order as "earthly" and "animal." The wisdom of the first order was also
<margin>Genesis 41.</margin>
the wisdom of the Egyptian sages, of Babylon, and of Tyre, and the wisdom of which it is written in
<margin>Jeremiah 9.</margin>
Jeremiah 9: *Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom.* And that saying: *I thought that the*
<margin>Job 32.</margin>
*multitude of years would give wisdom,* and other such things. But the wisdom of the second
<margin>Proverbs 2.</margin>
order is that by which a man is called **blessed** who finds wisdom—namely, that which was the wisdom of all the Holy Saints and Apostles, concerning which the universal...

# OF PAUL RICIUS,

<margin>

Just as with wisdom, so too a threefold order is given to faith, which offers mutual aid.
1 Corinthians 2.

</margin>
...the various doctrines of the Law, the Sacred Writings <note>original: "Agiographorum," referring to the *Ketuvim*, the third section of the Hebrew Bible</note>, the Prophets, and the Apostles are concerned. Sometimes Scripture encompasses both orders of wisdom under a single term "wisdom," and quite often the name of wisdom is transferred to any man distinguished by some skill, any office, or even by malice—a matter I leave to the reader's own investigation. Regarding wisdom of the third order, we read: *You have made all things in wisdom*; and *God founded the earth with wisdom*; and thus Scripture declares everywhere concerning the rest of the exemplary gifts. Regarding fear, that saying of Jacob is also expressed: *Unless the God of my father Abraham, and the fear of Isaac, had been with me*, and Jacob swore by the fear of his father Isaac. This must be understood in the same sense as the saying: *You, O God, are my hope*. From this, the very name of God, derived from a Greek word, signifies fear <note>The author likely refers to a Renaissance etymological theory connecting *Theos* (God) to *deos* (fear/dread)</note>. But you, remember this one thing: what I say about the orders of wisdom, understand by the same law regarding faith, which contains within itself wisdom, understanding, and the rest of the gifts through the act of believing. The first order is deficient, which they call **unformed faith** <note>original: "fides informis"; a theological term for belief that is intellectually held but not yet put into practice through love</note>, about which Paul says: *Let your faith not be in the wisdom of men*. And James calls it dead and idle. The second order of faith is more precise, which they call **formed faith** <note>original: "fides formata"; faith animated by charity and active in the soul</note>, of which it is said: *He who believes in me has life*. The third is that of which it is written: *All his works are in faith*. Many mortals indeed have been made, and are made, partakers of the first order of wisdom and faith. Fewer partake of the second, and very few of the third, whose summit was reached by the unique Restorer of the world <note>Referring to Jesus Christ</note>, in whom all things are reconciled and connected—the last things with the first—in God and the man Christ Jesus. These same orders provide mutual help; the prior is the preparation and nursery for the following, while the following is the fullness and perfection of the prior.

<margin>
Mark 4.
</margin>

<margin>The reason for the variety of attributes assigned to fear.</margin>

...the progress of that order is terminated in the final advancement, which is why the fear of God is read to be the "end of modesty." It is clearly established that the beginning of the next sequence takes its starting point from this very extreme and end. This fear, through which the wisdom of its own order is transferred to a more sublime order, exists as the "fullness" and "crown" of that same wisdom. Therefore, the Wise Man says: *the fear of God places itself above all things.* Indeed, this same fear will be the "beginning" of the wisdom of the following order. Since the beginning of any thing constitutes one and the same thing with the thing itself, the fear of God is rightly and deservedly called the "wisdom of God" itself. This same fear is read as the "fountain of life," both because fear is wisdom itself—the fountain of life—and because through the fear of God we attain wisdom, which is the fountain of life. It is also called "holy" (or more correctly, "clean" <note>original: "mundus"</note>), because the fear of God calls one back from all uncleanness and the filth of fleshly desire. It is also "enduring forever," in the same way as the fountain of life. It is the "piety of knowledge," <note>original: "scientiae religiositas"</note> because fear arises from knowledge, through which we recognize human weakness and the vanity of fleeting things that must be avoided and rejected. Upon this hangs the entire religion of true piety; hence, it is rightly called the "piety of knowledge." It "hates evil" and turns away from it, because it occupies the soul all day long, lest it think or act in a way that does not harmonize with divine piety and its paths. Fear also "neglects nothing," because it strives not only to flee from evil but to ensure that no good work—which looks toward conformity with and imitation of the origin of eternal life—is overlooked. "In the fear of the Lord is the confidence of strength," <note>Proverbs 14:26</note> namely the confidence of God’s help, which is the strength of the soul for repelling adversity; and because of this confidence, the fear of God "gladdens the heart." Therefore, if you apply your mind, you will easily be able to judge the reason and cause of these and similar attributes from the aforementioned teachings.

**F**ear arises from faith, which is joined with love <note>original: "dilectione," often translated as "charity" in a theological context</note>, as if by a certain touch of divinity. This is because while faith, through firm contemplation (as we said regarding the order of wisdom), presents the image of divine beauty, its goodness, and its sweetness, the entire desire of the soul is immediately raised toward it. By this, the mind itself is spurred to strive to approach that immense goodness by the act of believing with anxious care. And when, in that very effort, the soul perceives the greatness of such majesty and splendor through that same belief—and as if by a certain hidden touch—it notices itself hedged in on all sides by opposing things. Recognizing through that same faith that help can be provided from nowhere else but from that very Giver of all goods, God, whom it seeks, the soul is suddenly seized. Abandoning its own weak and fragile "little-man" self <note>original: "homuncionem," a diminutive for man, suggesting humility</note>, it places its refuge in God, the only helper. Just as Moses, after he had driven the "flock of the senses" <note>An allegorical interpretation of the flock Moses tended in Exodus</note> to the inner parts of the desert, and God had appeared to him, then hid his face in fear, abandoning himself and whatever had been humanly devised within him. For this reason, because fear draws its origin from the firmness of faith, the more effective and solid the faith exists, the more the soul is affected by a more vehement fear. Hence, holy men of God, while they approach more closely to Him with whom there is power and terror, and are moved by His breath and spirit, are shaken by a truly dreadful and ineffable dread. This is according to that experience of Abraham: while the deep sleep of God had fallen upon him, a great and dark horror invaded him. And that of the most holy Job in chapter 4: *Dread,* he said, *seized me and trembling, and all my bones were terrified; and when a spirit passed in my presence, the hair of my flesh stood up.* All of this is worked by that splendor of divine purity, which, like a "consuming fire," allows nothing filthy, nothing defiled, to be associated with it, just as light does not suffer darkness. The Truth) is against me: and he who does not gather with me, scatters: and therefore, the Apostle says, **everything that is not from faith is sin** <note>original: "omne quod non est ex fide, peccatum est"</note>, and the "wisdom of the flesh," which cannot be from faith, is called **death**. From all these things, conclude finally that the work of the commandments without fear is vain, and contains more fault than merit. Nevertheless, although it may be vain in itself, yet when related to something else, it provides much timely benefit. 

<margin>Some works precede faith, others follow. Acts 10.</margin>
For some external works of the commandments precede the true faith of piety, such as the works of Cornelius <note>Cornelius was a Roman centurion described in Acts 10 as a "devout man" whose prayers and alms were noticed by God even before his formal conversion.</note> and others, of whom Peter speaks thus: "In truth I have found that God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation, he who fears God and works justice is accepted by Him." 

<margin>Proverbs 22.</margin>
Concerning these works, the Wise Man also commands in Proverbs: "Direct," he says, "a youth according to his way; even when he grows old, he will not depart from it," and "if you strike him with a rod, you will deliver his soul from hell." Consider, I pray, of what great weight and benefit are those works which precede faith, since the Wise Man judged that by them a youth is delivered from hell. 

<margin>Works that precede faith deliver a youth from hell.</margin>
For works of this kind wipe away the contracted filth of the soul and make it passable and capable of receiving the supernal light. But those works which follow faith—which the Apostle calls "faith that works through charity" <note>original: "fidem, quæ per charitatem operatur"</note>—serve to ensure the permanence of the faith already conceived. 

<margin>Galatians 5.</margin>
<margin>Matthew 13.</margin>
They do this by guarding against those things which the Author of Truth warned us to flee, by which faith and the received word of the Lord are choked—namely, the "cares of the world" and the "deceitfulness of riches." Hence the Apostle James calls him who has faith without works a "forgetful and distracted hearer," enticed by his own concupiscence. But he who is a "doer of the work," he says, remains in the **perfect Law of liberty**, which is the eternal Law of faith, our mother, and the **celestial Jerusalem**. In the same sense, James, together with Paul, proves that a man is justified by works. 

<margin>James 2.</margin>
"You see," says James in the second chapter, "that a man is justified by works, and not by faith alone." 

<margin>Romans 2.</margin>
And Paul, in the second chapter to the Romans, says: "For it is not the hearers of the Law who are just before God, but the **doers of the Law** shall be justified." For they say that works justify to the extent that they lead to faith and make it perfect and permanent. James openly testifies to this when he says: "And by works was faith made perfect, and the Scripture was fulfilled, saying: 'Abraham believed God, and it was reputed to him for justice.'" Yet these works in themselves—if not related to the faith for which they prepare the soul, or which they prevent from being scattered once received—contribute nothing to justification by way of an efficient form or an end (as I have explained before).

<margin>Note the comparison, by which you can remove many ambiguities and distinctions.</margin>
Consider this: suppose some poor and upright priest, weak and ailing in his feet, is carried to a prelate on a **little donkey**. When the pious and merciful prelate sees him present, he immediately grants him a wealthy income. If you were to ask this priest, "Who bestowed such a great income upon you?" would you not call the little priest ridiculous and insane if he answered that the **donkey** gave him this income? This is true even though, without the donkey or some other vehicle, he could hardly or not at all have acquired the income. 

<margin>Ponder these things with yourself, and revolve them in a sincere mind.</margin>
From this, consider the twin grace bestowed on the poor man: one is an accessory grace from the one who gave the donkey; the other is the greater grace from the pious prelate, who distributed the income according to the merits and poverty of the petitioner. In a similar way, you shall judge concerning faith and works. He who is wise understands that the Creator of things gives the "gift of the donkey" through nature and prevenient grace <note>Prevenient grace is a theological term for divine grace that precedes human decision, "preparing" the heart to respond.</note>, but bestows the "income" through the Holy Spirit. 

You might say, perhaps, that according to this comparison, the Apostle Paul should be mocked for teaching that the "doers of the Law are justified," or James for asserting that "man is justified by works." I respond—and you, lend your ears—that the "active" and "passive" disposition (like all relative opposites) are given together; when one is given, the other must necessarily be given. However, what is attributed to one is not immediately to be attributed to the other. Therefore, because the deeds of the Law (as you have heard) concur toward justification "dispositively" or "passively," it is **true** to say: **"The doers of the Law are justified."** But it is **false and ridiculous** to say: **"The deeds of the Law justify."** Just as regarding that ailing priest, it is true to say that, having been carried by the donkey, he **is given**...

# BY PAUL RICIUS,

<margin>Just as it is aptly said: "We are justified by works," so it is ineptly and falsely said: "Works justify."</margin>
profit is granted, yet it is not the donkey’s carrying that grants the profit. In the same way, as it is truly and appropriately said, "from wood a stool is made," so it would be ridiculous to say, "the wood makes the stool." Thus it is aptly said, **Abraham was justified by works**, <note>original: "ex operibus iustificatus est Abraham"</note> but truly it is ridiculous to say that **works justified Abraham**. And for this reason, the divine word adds: **Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness** <note>Genesis 15:6; Romans 4:3</note>; therefore faith was credited as righteousness, and not works.

However, in a twofold way, works that precede faith lead toward justification. In one way, indeed, because the worker himself, by being intent on these works of darkness, avoids worse things and the "thorns" which stifle the word of God and recall the soul further away from divine fellowship. Just as a tutor <term>pedagogue: in the ancient world, a slave who escorted and supervised children</term> permits children to play with nut-shells, lest by wandering about they break the things that are in the house. Then also, and most especially, because from long habit of performing the commandments, if by chance he arrives at that fear which works through love, he may be able to fulfill the works of salvation more promptly and joyfully. The Wise Man says: **Direct a youth according to his way, and when he grows old, he will not depart from it** <note>Proverbs 22:6</note>. You, however, consider these things, and diligently revolve them within yourself.

For whatever the Prophet brings forth from the mouth of God, he sees and reads with a spiritual eye in the supernal wisdom of God. Wisdom, it says, establishes friends of God and prophets, by whose hands it directs the works of mortals; this Wisdom the Scripture calls the Eternal Law and the Book of the Commandments of God. It also calls the same the Book of Life, the Testament of the Most High, and that which commanded the Law to Moses. Whenever, therefore, a commandment, a Testament, or a Law is delivered by a Prophet through divine authority, a Double Testament, Law, or commandment must be heard. One is that which the Prophet promulgates through a book, written with a human pen for the instruction of mortals. The other is the archetype of that book—namely, the Book of Life, written by the finger and word of God. Paul clearly shows these two Testaments to the Galatians: one indeed on Mount Sinai, generating into servitude; the other, which is above and is free, our mother Jerusalem. The former he calls the law of deeds, the latter of faith; the former the law of death, the latter the spirit of life; the former a tutor, the latter a mother. The commandment of the former is not above you, nor in heaven, but is carnal, weak, and useless; the latter is the exceedingly broad word remaining in heaven, bright, illuminating, and eternal life. By a similar rule, the same Apostle declares a double man: the interior and he who is outside. He calls the former the "new man" and the latter the "old man"; the former spiritual, the latter animal. The latter must be stripped off, the former must be put on. The latter serves the Law of sin, the former the Law of God and of the mind; the works of the latter are death, those of the former are life.

<margin>Romans 7.</margin>
For the earthly and carnal man, since he lusts from his innermost nature and fights against the spirit, cannot be subject to the Law of God; therefore he is restrained only by an external bit <note>original: "chamo"</note> and the bridle of an earthly commandment, which the Apostle calls the Law of Death. "But now," he says, "we are released from the Law of Death, serving, namely, in the newness of the spirit." But where that spirit is not present, then there is need for a tutor and some law of deeds. The interior man, however, is blessed when he looks into the law (as James says) of perfect liberty, and remains in it. The perfect Law of Liberty, however (as we have said), is the Testament of the Most High: our mother who is free, the heavenly Jerusalem, from which, being born anew, we return to the origin of eternal life.

# ON CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE, BOOK III.

### *SINCE NEITHER OF THESE CAN EXIST <note>original: "horum alter sine altero"</note> or even act in this mortal life without the other: therefore the inner man cannot serve the Law of the mind, unless he who is outside also obeys the law of deeds.*

<margin>An irrevocable reason, because even external good works are required for eternal salvation.</margin>
<margin>Man is the bond of the universe, connecting the last things to the first.</margin>
<margin>Matthew 17</margin>
<margin>Galatians 5</margin>
<margin>Psalm 32 <note>Original cites Psalm 3.2, likely referring to the "bit and bridle" of Psalm 32:9.</note></margin>
<margin>A type <term>type: a symbolic person or event that foreshadows something later</term> of original sin, worthy of being known.</margin>
<margin>Ephesians 2</margin>
<margin>Ecclesiastes 10</margin>
For if the inner man could remain in this slippery and mortal life without the company of the outer man, he could certainly perform his work without the body's help and serve the Law of God with his mind. Nor would the <term>concupiscence: the strong desire for worldly or carnal pleasures</term> and lust of the flesh stand in the way in any part; whether we were drunk or sober, whether wanton or restrained, we would equally enjoy—in this valley of darkness where we journey away from the Lord—that blessed vision, not through mirrors and enigmas, but beholding the glory of God with a revealed face. Therefore, the counsels of God and men and the institutions of Laws would be in vain and empty, indeed false, for they intend nothing else, nor do they promise the kingdom of heaven in any other way, except to those who restrain the madness of the flesh and its battle against the spirit through sobriety, chastity, fasts, prayers, and things of that kind. 

However, you will weigh this with a clearer and firmer understanding if you look more deeply into the condition of human nature. For since the inscrutable order of divine wisdom fashioned the human race as the bond and unity of the universe—by which, as if on a certain horizon between eternal and passing things, the last might be joined to the first—it could not happen that its structure would not be a participant of both extremes. In man, the nature of heavenly and earthly things is fused into one (which was indeed most perfectly accomplished in the God and man Jesus Christ). This bond and connection is such that toward whichever part one side directs its forces, the other is drawn there too; nor is a middle ground given, because "no one can serve two masters" <note>Matthew 6:24</note> who are opposed to each other, for if he clings to one, he must despise the other. "He who is not with me," says the Truth <note>Ricius frequently refers to Jesus as "the Truth" (Veritas).</note>, "is against me; and he who does not gather with me, scatters" <note>Matthew 12:30</note>. Since, therefore, these parts of the human frame seek contrary and clashing duties—for the flesh lusts after nothing but transitory and muddy things against the Spirit, while the Spirit desires heavenly and eternal things against the flesh—therefore, unless the lust of the earthly man is restrained with a bit and bridle and reduced to servitude, it distracts the spiritual man and clouds his vision, preventing him from responding or becoming conformed to the image of God. 

For you know how, from the original fault of nature, perpetual enmities were placed between the woman (if you know the mystery) and the serpent and the offspring of both, and the serpent was cursed so that he is forced to creep on the ground with his chest and eat earth and slime, and to lie in wait for the heel of the woman and her seed. Although the power of "crushing the head" of the waylayer was given to them, nevertheless, for a more secure protection against his traps, the Law of the commandments was built as a wall and a fence; and the Wise Man says that he who breaks this fence, the serpent shall bite him <note>Ecclesiastes 10:8</note>. Therefore, against the traps of the "prudence of the flesh," and as a bit and bridle for taming lust, or as a <term>pedagogue: a tutor or guide for children</term> who shakes out the ignorance of little ones, a certain Law of commandments was given. When this law is kept with faith and love, it cooperates in many ways toward righteousness and life; in just as many ways, its transgression works toward wrath and death.

### *THE OBSERVANCE OF THE LAWGIVERS’ COMMANDS cooperates toward life in four ways, and its transgression toward death; in one way indeed it works toward life, not by the merit of the work itself, but by the merit of obedience: In another way, not by obedience, but by a threefold view of the work—because it is modest, because it is conformed to the work of the Creator, and because it lifts the mind to the things above.*

<margin>Romans 6</margin>
<margin>John 12</margin>
<margin>1 Kings 15</margin>
First, indeed, the observance of the Law cooperates toward righteousness and life, not by the merit of the specific work commanded, but from the obedience rendered to the command of the mandates. For the obedience by which one humbles himself and commits himself to the orders and pleasures of the commander adapts the soul and makes it capable of receiving the grace and love of the one who commands. For the Apostle says: "To whom anyone obeys, of him he is also a servant" <note>Romans 6:16</note>. And the Truth says: "Where I am, there also will my minister be" <note>John 12:26</note>. Therefore, obedience is better than sacrifices, <note>1 Kings 15:22</note>

h 3
<meta>catchword: sacrifices,</meta>

<summary>Ricius argues that the inner spiritual man cannot function without the outer physical man being disciplined by the Law. He describes man as a "bond of the universe" where the soul and body are so interconnected that the flesh's desires will inevitably cloud the spirit unless restrained by the "fence" of God's commandments.</summary>

...of the victim, by which alone Abraham, beloved of God, earned a perpetual blessing for himself and his offspring. Secondly, the commandment works together toward justice and life through the honesty and modesty of the deed, by which the madness of the flesh is governed and reduced to servitude, lest it prevail against the spirit. Indeed, such a work of modesty is to be carried out with the light of nature as a guide, even without the preceding authority of a commander; by this, even the gentiles (as the Apostle speaks), who do not have the Law, perform those things which belong to the Law by the sting of a pure conscience. Yet we are taught more exactly, and we "approve the things that are more useful" (as the Apostle says), being instructed through the Law of commandments more than by any searching of the human mind. Thirdly (a mode which accompanies the second), the commandment works toward life through the conformity of the work, and its harmony with the works of God the Creator, by imitating Him and walking in His ways. This conformity truly gives birth to love and divine fellowship. For because God is just, for the sake of conformity, He loves justice and the just. And "Be holy," He says, "for I am holy"; and "be merciful, because your heavenly Father is merciful." Fourthly, the commandment works toward life by the merit of diligence: for he who desires to be blessed must meditate on the Law of the Lord day and night without intermission. The human mind, entangled and distracted by external and carnal work, cannot accomplish this unless it perceives in that very earthly work some memorial and <term>simulacrum: a representation or image of something else</term> of a higher commandment and of the Law’s liberty. Thus, while one walks in the flesh, he may not work and wage war according to the flesh. For unless we do whatever we do in word and deed in the name of Jesus, and always keep God before our sight, the mind—forgetting the higher image—would immediately slip away and collapse. Because "you have forgotten" (says the Prophet) "the God of your salvation, therefore you shall be deserted." For he who is ignorant shall be ignored, and he who is ignored loses every protection and shield of salvation, according to that chief mystery of divine providence: "I will hide," He says, "my face, and it shall be for a devouring." <note>original: "Abscondam faciem meam, & erit in deuorationem." See Deuteronomy 31:17.</note> Pay close attention, I pray, for it does not read: "I will make him to be devoured," but rather "it shall be," namely through consequence, "for a devouring." "The foolishness of man" (says the Sage) "trips up his steps, and his heart seethes against God." For he who walks in opposition (or more correctly, by chance) submits himself to the elements of the world, and carries back a sevenfold weight of indignation and wrath according to the seven wandering bodies <note>The "seven wandering bodies" refers to the traditional seven planets of ancient astronomy, often associated with astrological fate.</note>. For when the helmsman is absent, he is credited as the cause of the sinking, whereas his presence is the cause of safety. If you weigh these things, you will easily be able to penetrate the secret of divine providence. This is supported by that word of James: "But he who looks into the perfect Law of liberty" (that is, the celestial Law, which is our free mother Jerusalem) "and remains in it, being not a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work, this man shall be blessed in his deed."

</margin>
To understand this matter, consider the commandment of the Sabbath: for since it cannot happen, according to the Law of nature, but that a man (and likewise a beast of burden) should indulge in leisure and alternating rest after long movements and labors, divine care established the seventh day. On this day (all servile work ceasing), the strengths of the body are restored, and at the same time the mind itself may recover its senses, mindful of the eternal Sabbath and the higher image of God. Otherwise, if one "sabbathizes" <note>To "sabbathize" is to observe the Sabbath rest.</note> only by the rest of the flesh and by idle leisure, without looking upon the higher Law of perfect liberty, he will be (according to James's warning) more miserable than blessed in this act of observing the Sabbath. For those who have known the mysteries—not crawling in the "letter that kills"—know by what Law the six days of labor (which consist of light and darkness) show the distinctions of the six <term>mobile things: refers to the changing material world subject to time and decay</term> which consist of the darkness of deprivation and matter and the light of forms, perpetually subject to transmutation and labor. And they know in what way the seventh day—for which the Scriptures offer no evening—announces a seventh and holy kind of substance, where no darkness, no transmutation, and no overshadowing of change turns, but rather the placid rest and state of eternal salvation. In the same way, one must judge the remaining commandments of the Law and the sacraments of orthodox piety, which serve as the pattern and shadow of heavenly things, because the "form of knowledge and truth" (as the Apostle says) is held in the Law.

## THE TRANSGRESSION OF THE LAW WORKS TOWARD DEATH, FROM
### *disobedience, immodesty, deformity of work, and the intermission*
### *of the spiritual secret of the commandments.*

<margin>Romans 6</margin>
<margin>Romans 3, 4</margin>
<margin>Galatians 2</margin>
For in as many ways as the observance of the Law works together toward life, in just as many contrary ways does the transgression of the same Law work toward death. First, from transgression and disobedience alone. For just as obedience gains favor, so disobedience breeds hatred. Indeed, through the disobedience of one, condemnation and death (says the Apostle) reigned in the world; this is considered not according to the depravity and immodesty of the work itself, but according to the contempt for the authority of the one giving the command. For sin is not imputed when there was no Law, because where there is no Law, neither is there transgression: for through the Law comes the knowledge of sin, whence we say that the Law works wrath and death: and that those who are of the works of the Law are under a curse <note>original: "sub maledicto esse"</note>, because the power of sin is the Law.

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 18</margin>
<margin>Romans 9</margin>
<margin>Isaiah 56</margin>
Second, the transgression of the Law works toward death, not in view of the one commanding, but from the immodesty and dissolution of the commanded work. For he who is soft and lax (says the Wise Man) in his work is the brother of him who destroys his own works. For when the reins of the flesh are loosened and relaxed, even with no mandate of the Law intervening, man will work nothing but sin and impiety. But the wage of sin is death: because there is nothing that divides and separates man from God (which division is death) except sin and iniquity: but he who sins without the Law, says the Apostle, shall perish without the Law.

<margin>Psalm 3</margin>
<margin>Ephesians 4</margin>
<margin>Psalm 91</margin>
In a third way (which accompanies the second way), the transgression of the Law works toward death from the deformity or depravity of the work. For just as imitating and walking in the ways of the Lord works love through conformity, so to turn aside and be alienated from His ways breeds repugnance and hatred through deformity: for God hates those who observe vanities. Moreover, those who are alienated from the way of God through ignorance observe vanities: and because God is upright, and His ways are upright: therefore, "woe" (He says) "to those who have forsaken the upright ways, and turn aside into crooked ways."

<margin>Galatians 6</margin>
Fourth, even if one were obedient, modest, and conforming in the outward work of the commandments, if he applies himself only to carnal and servile work: and does not lift his mind to the heights and the Law of imperfect liberty <note>Ricius often contrasts the "carnal" or literal Law with the "spiritual" liberty found in higher understanding</note>, to this man the commandment will work nothing toward life, but rather toward death because of intermission <note>original: "intermissionis causa," meaning a pause or neglect of spiritual focus</note>. For just as constant meditation on the heavenly Law of God works toward blessedness and life: so its intermission and forgetfulness (as James warned) leads to misery and death. For he who sows in the flesh (says the Apostle), from the flesh reaps corruption; but he who sows in the spirit, from the spirit reaps eternal life.

## THE COMMANDMENTS, WITHOUT THE OBSERVANCE OF WHICH
### *no one has access to the kingdom of heaven, are the*
### *precepts of the Decalogue.*

<margin>Deuteronomy 4</margin>
<margin>Deuteronomy 10</margin>
Access to the kingdom of heaven is open to no one without the fear of God: but the fear of God (as you have heard), without the observance of the commandments—which instruct the mind toward purity and the body toward cleanliness—cannot be perfected. But the commandments of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note> provide this, for they clearly tend toward this one thing: to turn the soul toward the Creator alone, and to recall it from every stain of carnal concupiscence. Therefore these very precepts of the Decalogue, because of their pre-eminent virtue, were delivered by the living voice of God before more than six hundred thousand listeners, and were inscribed by the finger of God on stone tablets, and (for this reason) deserve to be called by the singular name of "the Covenant" <note>original: "foederis"</note>. Whence also the Ark in which the tablets of the Decalogue were placed, we read, was named the Ark of the Covenant, because the primary covenant and eternal pact was entered into between God and the seed of Israel through this Law of the Decalogue.

<margin>Matthew 18</margin>
<margin>Luke 18</margin>
Wherefore also Christ the Lord, when asked which commandments they were that direct the one performing them to the kingdom of heaven, then replied with neither the commandments of Circumcision nor of Baptism, but only with those of the Decalogue. Saying, "You know the commandments: Do not kill, Do not commit adultery." And the rest—supply the remaining precepts...

### THE REMAINING INSTITUTES OF DIVINE LAW AND APOSTOLIC 
### sanction are nothing other than various expressions of the Decalogue, 
### to be administered according to the requirements of the matter, 
### just as the Law itself demonstrates through the 
### sacrament of circumcision.

<margin>Deuteronomy 4</margin>
Furthermore, there is no wise man who does not feel that all the other remaining mandates of the Law and Apostolic sanction are nothing else but an expression of the Law of the Decalogue. Indeed, the Law itself first declares that the observance of the Mosaic Law can be paused or removed according to the condition of the place or time. For it does not bind one to its observance except for as long as the Jews held the scepter and the kingdom of the land of Israel. He declared to you (it says) His <term>covenant</term> <note>original: "foedus"</note> which He commanded you to perform, the Ten Words themselves, which He wrote on two stone tablets; and He commanded me at that time to teach you the ceremonies and judgments which you ought to perform in 
<margin>The precepts of the Decalogue are separated from the rest of the Law's mandates by a fourfold distinction.</margin>
the land that you are to possess. Thus says Moses. Here, notice how he separated the Ten Words from the other mandates of the Law in a fourfold way: first, he enumerates them apart from, and not with, the rest of the mandates of the Law. Next, these very things were commanded by the proper voice of God to six hundred thousand listeners. Furthermore, he ascribes to them the singular title of "Covenant." Fourth and finally, no condition of time or place is attached to their observance. However, he encompasses all the remaining mandates under the names of ceremonies and judgments; these were not enunciated to the multitude by a divine voice, but (says Moses) "He commanded me to teach you," nor does he separately call them a covenant. Finally, in the last place, he adds: "which you ought to perform in the land that you are to possess." And we read that this last-attached condition of place was indeed often repeated by Moses. 
<margin>Deut. 4, 5, 6, 12, 21</margin>
By this it is plainly shown that the Law—aside from the Decalogue—can be 
<margin>Chapter 6</margin>
paused or removed according to the variety of place and time. Circumcision also bears witness to this; it is the principal sacrament of the mandates of the Law, which (as Joshua witnesses) we find was not observed at all for as long as they wandered in the desert, even while their teacher and leader was present (though for the sake of a hidden mystery). Regarding Apostolic sanction, there is no one who would deny that it can not only be paused, but even abolished or changed according to the necessity of the matter, since its observance rests upon human rather than divine 
<margin>Canon 2, question 6</margin>
authority. For it belongs to the same person to dissolve a Law as it does to establish it. Because of this, even the pontifical laws themselves decree that the decrees of the Apostolic See can be relaxed, tempered, and cease to be, according to the variety of time, person, and cause.

### AND THE LAW OF WORKS, SO IS BAPTISM THE TESTIMONY 
### OF THE NEW COVENANT AND THE LAW OF 
### THINGS TO BE BELIEVED.

<margin>Genesis 17, 1 John 5</margin>
For both circumcision and Baptism derive their origin from the first commandment of the Decalogue, by which the worship of one God is enjoined. They serve as a sign and perpetual testimony of the covenant and vow by which the receiver of the Law devotes himself to worshiping the one God, according to that saying: "You shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, so that it may be a sign of the covenant between me and you." One also reads concerning the testimony of Baptism: "There are three who give testimony on earth: the spirit, the water, and the blood," designating the washing and testimony of Baptism through water. <header>ON CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE, BOOK III.</header>

...testimony through a certain external work and a solemn deed of a contracted and inviolable covenant. Indeed, God himself, the prince and founder of the ages, likewise established a rainbow in the clouds as a sign of his pact <note>original: "pactum"</note> not to bring a disaster of waters upon posterity again. 
<margin>Genesis 9.
Genesis 31.</margin> 
So too did Jacob, beloved of God, when striking a treaty of friendship for himself and his descendants with his relative Laban; he erected a monument and a heap of stones as a memorial of the pact and a testimony of the covenant to be kept. So too 
<margin>Exodus 24.</margin> 
did Moses, the greatest of prophets, sprinkle the people with blood as a sign of the pact to keep the Law forever, saying: "This is the blood of the covenant which God has made with you." So too 
<margin>Joshua, last chapter.</margin> 
did Joshua, that strenuous leader of the Israelites, erect a very large stone under an oak as a testimony of the renewed covenant to worship God forever, saying: "Lest perhaps hereafter you wish to deny it, and lie to your God." By the same rule, one must judge concerning Baptism and any other solemn covenants and pacts. Therefore, just as it is at the will of the author to establish this or that testimony or sign of a covenant, so also divine providence, in its immense wisdom and power, is by no means bound to one or another <term>sacrament</term> <note>From the Latin "sacramentum," originally a soldier's oath of loyalty, here referring to a sacred rite that acts as a visible sign of inward grace.</note>, but can be changed or transferred to another sign according to His will. Thus, what circumcision formerly witnessed under a veil, the sacrament of Baptism now witnesses with faith revealed. For "circumcision and uncircumcision are nothing," says the Apostle, "but the keeping of the commandments of God" <note>original: "Circumcisio siquidem & præputium nihil est, sed obseruatio mandatorū Dei." See 1 Corinthians 7:19.</note>. By "commandments," he indicates the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note>. Otherwise, if he intended this to apply to all other mandates of God, the Apostle's sentence would directly conflict with itself; for he asserts that the observance of God's mandates is absolutely required for salvation, yet he teaches that circumcision is nothing, even though it was among the number of God's other mandates.

In this way, certainly, even Baptism—the testimony of the new covenant—is of no great importance regarding the kingdom of heaven insofar as it is only what we perform outwardly. For "bodily exercise" (although it is not useless) is profitable 
<margin>1 Timothy 4.</margin> 
"for a little," as the Apostle says, but "piety and faith" are what the sacrament of Baptism announces. For many (as I have handed down from the beginning) have been received into the <note>colony of the blessed</note> <note>A metaphor for Heaven.</note> without the water of Baptism, and countless others, having received Baptism, suffer eternal punishments. It matters little, therefore, if you transform whatever is external and circumstantial by divine authority, provided that you observe the covenant of the Decalogue itself and the goal of worshipping God—which can be removed or changed by no decree, not even a divine one. 

The same is handed down regarding the commandment of the Decalogue on the <term>Sabbatism</term> <note>The practice of keeping the Sabbath.</note>. For when a traveler is ignorant of which day of the week is being counted, it matters little (as the authority of the wise Pharisees declares) whether he keeps the Sabbath on the day of Saturn or the day of the Sun <note>Saturday or Sunday.</note>; so long as he rests on the seventh day (from whichever day he began to count) and sanctifies it, the mandate of the Decalogue will be satisfied. By this same law, the use of fringes on cloaks, and the words of the Law bound as a sign 
<margin>Numbers 15.
Deuteronomy 6.</margin> 
on the hands, and fixed between the eyes on the forehead and on the doorposts of the house, concerns divine worship and the first commandment of the Decalogue. These and similar things were commanded only for this purpose: that while we are occupied with the works of the flesh and the world, there may be a ready sign of admonition, lest forgetfulness of divine things, the Law, and the mandates of God seize us. 

Whence Moses subjoins to such mandates, saying: "And when the Lord your God has brought you in... and you have eaten and are full, take diligent care lest you forget the Lord your God, who led you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage." To this same worship and end are directed many works of the devoted faithful, serving for the constancy of prayer and the memory of the Lord's passion and the saints. For this reason, some carry in their hands a string of beads hanging from a cord <note>A rosary.</note>; others carry a cross; others a cord for a belt; others an <term>Agnus Dei</term> <note>A small wax disc or pendant blessed by the Pope, often bearing the image of a lamb.</note> (as they call it); others hang images of the saints on their walls, and things of that kind. If you were to transform any one of all these into another by divine or Apostolic authority—in the external work only—it matters little to salvation, provided the faith of truth and a mind of piety are preserved, as you shall hear in the following sections where I commemorate the sacraments of the New and Old Testaments. Therefore, just as with the aforementioned things, so it must be judged concerning each of the ten commandments, the observance of which...

These external forms can be changed by divine authority, whereas the core moral requirements of the Ten Commandments are eternal and essential for salvation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument regarding the immutability of the moral law (the Decalogue) while discussing the role of the Law as a guide for those not yet fully led by the Spirit. It emphasizes that only the Lawgiver has the right to change the Law and contrasts divine institutions with human ones.</meta>

# PAUL RICIUS,

<margin>
The changing of the Law belongs to no one except the Lawgiver or one to whom equal authority is given.
</margin>
...which both Christ the Lord and his herald the Apostle especially commend: because circumcision and uncircumcision are nothing, but rather the observance of the commandments of God. He calls the precepts of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note> "commandments of God" (as we have said), which were brought forth by the living voice of God and heard by the entire multitude. However, the power to change these belongs to no one except the very one who brought the Law, or to whom an equal authority has been committed. For if any person of Christian piety were to have obtained such an auxiliary grace of nature and super-celestial gifts of grace, by which they could measure human operations and acts through themselves (with no one teaching) and discern right from wrong and fulfill it in deed, then surely the power of changing would be given to anyone. There would be no need for an external measure, no need for the bridle of the Law or the muzzle of the precept. Because for the righteous and spiritual person, who (as the Apostle says) judges all things, the Law is not given <note>A reference to 1 Timothy 1:9: "the law is not laid down for the just but for the lawless."</note>.

<margin>
1 Timothy 1.
1 Corinthians 2.

Galatians 5.
</margin>
For he who is led by the spirit is not under the yoke of the Law, but of his own accord does those things which belong to the Law. But since most mortals are children, unskilled in spirit, and given over to carnal desire—as their manifest works of the flesh declare—therefore they must be fed on milk and vegetables. It is necessary that they have the Law of commandments as a <term>pedagogue</term> <note>From the Greek 'paidagogos', a tutor or guardian who escorted children to school; here, the Law acts as a temporary guide for the spiritually immature.</note> which explains the Decalogue and the Law of nature, expounding it according to the variety of things, times, places, and persons.

->*INDEED, THE SIGN AND TESTIMONY GIVEN DIVINELY*<-
->*is especially superior to the seal of a human covenant, because the latter contains no*<-
->*hidden energy. The former, however, deservedly acts secretly for the sake of obedience, modesty, conformity, and hidden meditation;*<-
->*it works for salvation beyond the limits of worldly cleverness,*<-
->*which we have recognized through the clear and once-successful*<-
->*experiment of Moses and Christ.*<-

<margin>
Deuteronomy 4:1.
</margin>
The Law itself declares how much divine traditions excel human institutions in those four ways by which the commandments work toward justice. According to that word of Moses: "For this is your wisdom and understanding before the peoples, so that hearing all these precepts they may say: 'Behold a wise and understanding people, a great nation.' Nor is there any other nation so grand that it has gods approaching it, just as our God is present for all our petitions." These are the words of Moses, which a long and manifest experience of the matter also declares. Indeed, from the beginning of the age until this very day, no sanction of Law, no institution of a republic, has been known or heard of which has established so many and such great men—no less in human than in divine wisdom and holiness of life—nor such a vast multitude of Prophets and miracle-workers as the Law of Moses had propagated. This Law also finally produced Christ the Savior, along with the sacred order of Apostles, as if the ultimate progress and end of the entire Law and the whole human race. I have deemed it unnecessary to assert the brilliance of their lives, their wisdom, and their wonderful works with a long testimony, since the entire circle of the lands now resounds with these, and all things are full of Christ. Therefore, he will be an altogether cursed and wicked little man <note>original: "homuncio"</note> who presumes to equate—much less prefer—commandments devised by human conjectures with divine sacraments and statutes. Therefore, let human prudence by no means dare to change what the divine Law once established: this is proven by what has been said before.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of Divine Law, specifically focusing on the four necessary conditions for a "Law of Works" to be considered divinely instituted. It builds on the previous page's argument that only God has the authority to change the Law, now demonstrating why the Mosaic Law is the only divine Law of Works ever given, while the Gospel of Christ introduces a Law of Faith.</meta>

# ON CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE, BOOK III.

no [act] is ascribed to virtue or vice, merit or guilt, unless it resulted from the consent of the will. Again, it is necessary that the Law be delivered openly and publicly: for if the consent of the multitude is required, the Law itself must undoubtedly be made known to the multitude. Nor is even this enough, unless, in the fourth place, all things belonging to the Law are delivered by the command and name of God; otherwise, the recipient of the Law would be tossed about in perpetual hesitation, wondering whether the contents of the Law were institutions of God or of man. Now, each of these points is confirmed by the testimony of the Scriptures if you attend to the manner of the Mosaic legislation. First, the Lawgiver God himself did not wish to promulgate the Law (if you take notice) through Moses until His divine authority had first been made known to the people, both by the use of signs and wonders and by the repeated experience of prophecy. <margin>Exodus 14</margin> "They believed," it says (namely after the crossing of the sea), "in God and in His servant Moses," and also by hearing the divine voice and the speech of God to Moses. <margin>Exodus 19</margin> According to that verse: "I will come to you in a thick cloud, so that the people may hear me speaking to you, and may believe you forever." In the second place, He requires the solemn vow and consent of the multitude: <margin>Exodus 24</margin> "Moses came," it says, "and having called together the elders, he set forth all the words which God had commanded." And all the people answered together: "All the things that God has spoken, we will do." Shortly after, having performed a solemn rite with the construction of twelve monuments <note>original: "titulorum fabrica," referring to the twelve pillars Moses built at the foot of Mount Sinai to represent the tribes</note> and the sprinkling of blood, they gave their consent to keep the Law in its entirety. This consent, we read, was repeated twice and thrice under the leadership of Joshua. In the third place, such a proclamation of that Law was made as has never been heard or believed by any mortal since the beginning of the world, where a numerous multitude of more than six hundred thousand men heard the voice of their God, the Lawgiver, in person, amidst so many admirable and terrifying signs and portents: <margin>Deuteronomy 4</margin> "Ask," he says, "of the ancient days, which were before you, from the day that the Lord God created man upon the earth, from one end of heaven to the other, if such a thing has ever happened, or has ever been known, that a people should hear the voice of the Lord God speaking out of the midst of fire, as you have heard and seen." Fourthly, the divine Law does not bind, nor do any oracles of the prophets, except to those things which are set forth and commanded by the mandate and name of God. <margin>Deuteronomy 18</margin> "I will put," he says, "my words in his mouth, and whoever will not hear his words, who speaks in my name, I will be the avenger." For you will nowhere find that the Jewish people gave their consent except to those things which God himself commanded. <margin>Exodus 19, 24</margin> Saying: "All things that God has spoken, we will do," and that Moses established nothing except by the mandate and name of God: <margin>Deuteronomy 4, 6</margin> "Keep," he says, "the commandments of the Lord your God, which I command you; and these are the precepts, ceremonies, and judgments which the Lord your God commanded that I should teach you, so that you might do them."

IF you rightly weigh those things which are required for a "Law of works" <note>term: "Lex factorum" - a technical term in theology referring to the Old Testament legal system based on external ritual and moral performance, as opposed to the internal Law of Faith</note> to be called divine, you will find many of them lacking in the Gospel and Apostolic tradition. <margin>Matthew 5</margin> "Therefore the Law," says John, "was given through Moses; but Grace and Truth were made through Jesus Christ." <margin>The Savior fulfilled the Law in two ways.</margin> Nor does Christ the Lord mention any other Law of works anywhere besides the Law of Moses, which he warned he had come not to destroy but to fulfill. For he fulfilled the Law in one way by bringing it to its supreme end, for the sake of which the entire Law had been delivered—namely, that the human race might be established in the worship of the one Creator God and the destruction of idols. This, however, Moses [achieved] with so many signs and portents, so dread...

<meta>This page continues the argument regarding the transition from the Mosaic Law of Works to the Christian Law of Faith, specifically refuting critics who claim that "fulfilling the law" refers only to ritual observance or prophetic prefiguration.</meta>

-># PAUL RICIUS<-

...punishments and threats could barely accomplish in the single people of Israel: but Christ the Lord accomplished that very same thing through the preaching of the Apostles without any severity or terror, by the spirit of gentleness and humility alone throughout the whole world (as experience testifies). He fulfilled the observance of the Law in another way (which the hypocrisy of the Scribes and Pharisees then observed only in the letter, not in the spirit) by showing that the completion of the Law consists more in restraining and pursuing the internal affections of the soul than in the external works of the flesh. This is clearly demonstrated by the context of the words there: for he adds to the statement about the completion of the Law: *unless (he says) your justice exceeds that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven* <note>original: "nisi abundauerit... iusticia uestra plusquã Scribarum & Pharisæorum, non intrabitis in regnum cælorum." See Matthew 5:20.</note>, and immediately (if you pay attention) he adds teachings in which he mentions nothing but spiritual affections of the soul to be avoided or pursued. And thus Christ the Savior did not in the least abolish the Law of Moses, but fulfilled it by a more perfect way of observing it—namely, by giving the spirit of faith and charity: for the *end of the commandment (as the Apostle says) is charity* <note>original: "finis enim præcepti... est charitas." See 1 Timothy 1:5. Ricius argues that "charity" or love is the ultimate goal toward which the Old Law was pointing.</note>.

¶ Here, however, that spiteful and insolent empty boaster <note>Ricius is likely responding to a specific contemporary critic, perhaps a traditionalist theologian or a former colleague, who accused his mystical interpretations of being heretical.</note> grows bold again, saying that none of the saints interpreted Christ's fulfillment of the Law in the sense that Ricius understands it, and that here "a snake lies in the grass" <note>A Latin idiom (latet anguis in herba) meaning there is a hidden danger or a deceptive argument.</note>. Let that foolish and worthless man read **Chrysostom** <margin>Chrysostom</margin> <note>Saint John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Church Father known for his "Golden Mouthed" oratory and biblical commentaries.</note> on this passage, saying that Christ said "I have not come to abolish the Law" for a twofold reason. First, so that he might incite his disciples by these words to his own example, so that just as he himself fulfilled the whole Law, so they might strive to fulfill it; finally, it was going to happen that the Jews would slander him as if he were abolishing the Law; before he incurred the slander, he satisfied the slanderers. Read the same man in the homily saying: Christ therefore fulfilled the Prophets by completing all things which were said about him through them; but he fulfilled the Law first by transgressing nothing of the legal requirements, and second by justifying through faith. Thus he spoke.

Pay attention, therefore, according to these words of Chrysostom: Christ the Lord commanded the disciples that, by his example, they should fulfill the whole Law. If, therefore, you were to say that such a warning from Christ should be understood as referring to external works and not rather to spiritual affection, then however many Apostles and elders there were, they would have been not only transgressors but even despisers of the Lord's word, since by both their works and their decrees they declared in many ways that the yoke and slavery of the Mosaic Law was to be removed and cast away. Pay attention further to the teaching of the same Chrysostom, who asserts that, in the second place, Christ the Lord fulfilled the Law by justifying through faith. It is established, however, that faith is nothing other than (excluding the worship of idols) adoring and worshipping the one God the Creator, who was incarnated and suffered, having been made man.

Again, consider from Chrysostom’s words that it must be heard in one sense that Christ the Savior fulfilled the Law, and in another that he fulfilled the Prophets. <margin>A solid argument that the primary purpose of the Law is not prefiguration.</margin> For if the ceremonial commands of the Law had been handed down chiefly for this purpose—to prefigure and announce the coming and acts of the Savior—he would have fulfilled the Law in the same way as he fulfilled the Prophets, by completing all the things which were pre-signified through figures concerning himself in the Law. But Chrysostom attributes this only to the fulfillment of the Prophets, and not of the Law. Add to this: if Christ the Lord fulfilled the Law only insofar as he was prefigured in the Law as God and man, to be born of a Virgin, to suffer, to rise again, and the like, in what way could he have incited his disciples to his own example (as Chrysostom taught), so that they too, under the same condition, might strive to fulfill the Law? Would they have had to become God and man? Would they have had to be born of a Virgin, suffer the cross, and soon rise from the dead? Truly, it is a thing unspeakable to hear.

Nor do I indeed deny—rather, I candidly approve—that a sense of figures is also contained in the Law. <margin>The Law undoubtedly contains figures within itself: yet the Law was not handed down primarily for this reason.</margin> For even those who, by the light of nature implanted in them, search into the secrets of sensible things, assert that it happens from a certain connection and series of causes that one gesture, word, or deed is a prelude and announcement of what follows. Nevertheless, they do not on that account presume that the preceding gesture, word, or deed exists *chiefly* for this purpose: to be held as a portent or a figure of what follows...

<header>ON CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE, BOOK III.</header>

...of the following: just as the mystery of the paschal lamb <note>original: "agni paschalis"</note> prefigured most especially the passion and redemption of the Savior, yet it was not instituted for this as its primary intention, but as a memorial (as the Law itself clearly declares) of the wondrous exit of the Israelite people from Egypt. 
<margin>You who are wise, Reader, pay attention.</margin>
For if the more powerful reason for the ceremonial commands and the chief intent of the Lawgiver had been that such commands were figures and precursors of future things: Why, I ask, did divine providence—which wants all to be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth—not say so through the mouth of Moses? Why did Christ the Lord—who willed to be born, scourged, spat upon, and suffer the punishments of a bitter death for the salvation of mortals—not say so? Why did not that herald of God, the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul.</note>, say so? Why, finally, did the first and most sacred synod of all the Apostles and the first saints, when treating with the highest scrutiny (as we read in their Acts) the release from the legalities, make absolutely no mention of this reasoning of prefiguration, nor even a word? Yet among so many and such great differences between Jews and Gentiles regarding legal observance, no reason for the calling away from legalities would have been more effective or more irrefutable than this reason of prefiguration—from which (in the opinion of all theologians) no effective argument can be drawn.

<margin>Saint Augustine against Faustus.</margin>
Listen, moreover, to Saint Augustine speaking against Faustus <note>Faustus of Mileve was a Manichaean who argued that the Old Testament was incompatible with the New; Augustine defended the continuity of the two.</note> in this way: I think it should also be accepted that what is said—*I have not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it* <note>original: "Non ueni soluere Legem, sed adimplere." Matthew 5:17.</note>—refers to the additions which belong to the statement of the ancient sentences, or to the way of living with them: for the Lord opened up the idea that even an evil urge to harm a brother is counted as a kind of homicide. These are the words of Augustine. By which you clearly hear that Christ the Lord fulfilled the Law because he added, against the hypocrisy of the Pharisees, a spiritual affection or urge (just as Ricius has taught) to be attended to in the Law, rather than the external work of darkness. Read the same author saying against Faustus: Faustus does not understand what it is to fulfill the Law: for the fullness of the Law is charity <note>In this context, "charity" (caritas) refers to the highest form of Christian love.</note>, which the Lord gave by sending the Holy Spirit to the faithful. These are his words. But what else is the operation of the Holy Spirit than to establish the minds of the faithful—after the worship of creatures is rejected—in the faith and love of the one creator God (who also became man)? <margin>Romans 5.</margin> *The charity of God* (says the Apostle) *is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit.* Let the petulant and ignorant man see, therefore, that according to the primary sense of the holy interpreters, Christ the Lord fulfilled the Law in the same sense that Ricius intended it to be understood. Because these aforementioned things contain within them some things worthy of attention, I recognized that they should be introduced and added here. Returning, therefore, to where the discourse diverged, let us say what that wise master-builder, the Apostle, reminded the Romans <margin>Romans 9.</margin>: that the Legislation belonged to the one people of Israel. He nowhere brings forward a law of works, except for the Law of Moses' commandments, which he affirms to be spiritual, good, holy, and formerly justifying. And although after the faith and grace of the Savior appeared, the Apostle did not constrain anyone to one or another rite for the necessity of salvation—thinking it sufficient that each person remain in whatever calling they were called, whether of circumcision or uncircumcision <margin>1 Corinthians 7.</margin>—he nevertheless did not judge the rite of the Jews to be as useful and expedient <margin>as for the Jews</margin> then for the Gentiles. For under the Law of faith and grace, although all things were lawful, yet *not all things* (he says) *are expedient*. <margin>1 Corinthians 6.</margin> Where the holy <term>glosses<gloss>interpretive commentaries written in the margins or between the lines of a text</gloss></term> say: those things which are lawful but not expedient are to be avoided not by the bond of the Law, but by the free benefit of love and the counsel of charity. <margin>1 Corinthians 10.</margin> For to eat things sacrificed to idols, or even to feed on the flesh of pigs or wolves, is perfectly lawful, but neither is expedient. The former on account of the stumbling block to another's conscience; the latter on account of its own inconvenience and the intuition of bad nourishment. 
<margin>The figurative sense of the Law is approved not so much for the sake of certainty as for the sake of pious exercise.</margin>
For we have certainly found that whatever the observance of the Law contains was four-foldly conducive to salvation, as the literal sense (from which alone an effective argument can be drawn) declares. But the mystic and figurative understanding is approved for the sake of pious and spiritual exercise rather than for the sake of certainty. For if you inspect individual commandments with the scrutiny of right reason, they are all true, and by the Law of Nature...

<header>PAUL RICIUS,</header>

you will clearly understand that a solid reason has been given for nature. If you desire to know more precisely <margin>Saint Thomas [Aquinas], Part 1, Question 103.</margin> about these things, unroll the excellent writings and monuments of Saint Thomas Aquinas on these matters. Furthermore, even if it is admitted that for certain commands of the Law—just as with the sacraments of the orthodox faith—a cause and evident reason may not appear, do you not think something more should be attributed to divine providence and the depth of its unsearchable wisdom than to the wavering and deceptive conjectures of human weakness? Consider, I ask, how many hidden qualities of foods the skill of natural philosophers has discovered through experience. The causes of these things could never be reached by any scrutiny or investigation of reason: for instance, that the meat of the turtle-dove sharpens the wit, the roe deer strengthens the heart, the peacock relieves the pains of colic, and the wood-pigeon treats the falling sickness <note>original: "Comitialem morbum," referring to epilepsy.</note>. The power of herbs and pigments demonstrates this through frequent experience. What, then, I ask, prevents it from being so that just as the turtle-dove sharpens the wit, the pig is an unclean animal that dulls the wit? Or that boiling a kid in its mother’s milk contains some hidden malice? Or that weaving cloth from wool and linen together (as the worshippers of idols were accustomed to do) possesses some deformity compared with works governed by divine and natural Law? Indeed, human presumption is a wondrous and stupendous curiosity, and far too daring.

<margin>A most apt and effective argument.</margin> Tell me, I ask, pious and perceptive Reader: if someone seized by a burning fever <note>original: "causonide"</note>, a continuous fever <note>original: "synocho"</note>, or any grave disease, calls for a doctor outstanding in learning and practice, would you not call that patient insane and delirious if they anxiously questioned and investigated every single thing the doctor administers? "Why this and not that? Why this weight? Why at this hour rather than another does he offer the medicine and antidote?" For you know very well that it is in the interest of the sick person—before committing themselves to the doctor's faith and work—to investigate with vigilant and solicitous care whether that doctor is approved by the testimony of all for his learning, experience, and integrity. Once this has been established, the patient immediately submits themselves entirely to his warnings and advice without any examination or wavering thought. If these things are to be considered by one who is sick in body when committing themselves to a transitions, fragile, and fallible little man as a doctor, consider for yourself what should be judged concerning the celestial parent, the healer of spiritual sicknesses, God and our Savior Jesus Christ, and His old and new antidotes and pigments of eternal salvation.

But here, perhaps, you will think and ask with hesitation: Since Paul taught the Corinthians that everyone should remain in the calling in which they were called—because for salvation (as the gloss <note>A "gloss" is a standard marginal or interlinear commentary used by medieval and Renaissance scholars.</note> there testifies) this or that, namely the Jewish or Gentile rite, neither helps nor hinders—why is it that the same Apostle so often rebukes the observer of the Jewish rite and <margin>Galatians 5.</margin> immediately excludes him from the grace and fellowship of Christ? Saying: "If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing; you are severed from Christ, you who are justified by the Law; you have fallen away from grace" <note>original: "Si circumcidimini Christus nihil uobis proderit... à gratia excidistis."</note>. Because by the works of the Law no flesh is justified before God: in these and many similar passages, Paul seems to blame the rite of the Law and hold it in contempt. Furthermore, the Epistle to the Hebrews itself declares that the Old Testament is carnal, weak, useless, and altogether near to perishing. It is indeed a wonderful thing and hard to hear if you say that one called in circumcision must remain in it. If circumcision profits him who observes the Law. If the utility of circumcision is great in every way, how can you say: "If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing"? If you affirm it is spiritual, how can you call it carnal? If good, if holy, how is it useless? If justifying, how is it weak? If not one iota or dot shall pass away until heaven and earth pass away, how do you judge it as near to perishing? Know, therefore, that there are many obscure sayings of the Apostle of this kind, which even in the time of the Apostles (as Peter testifies) were a precipice and a snare of the worst errors for many.

<margin>What is to be understood by serpentine prudence. Matthew 10.</margin> No other reason for this obscurity could be assigned except that "serpentine prudence" of Paul, of which Christ the Lord warned the disciples whom He sent into the midst of wolves. Saying: "Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves." For the serpent (if you pay attention), after the fall of human nature, strives for two things by its craftiness and cunning: one, to strike with lethal venom...
