<meta>This page continues the discussion on the divine rationale behind the Mosaic Law and the strategic approach of the Apostles, particularly Saint Paul, in reconciling Jewish tradition with the new Christian faith. It transitions from the physical properties of animals and plants to the spiritual "prudence" required to spread the Gospel among different groups.</meta>

->### ON CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE, BOOK III.<-

...[so that] it might strike the seed of Eve: the second, so that it may avoid the dangers of those for whom it lies in wait: to accomplish both, it seeks out cracks. So also the Spirit of Truth, after the restoration of the fall of nature, aims at two things: one, that it may save the weak and those wounded by the serpent with a sharp point <margin>❦</margin>; the other, that it may take care lest those whom it strives to save should trample upon the Spirit itself; it executes both through cracks and hiding places. For if you reveal the secrets of wisdom to the little ones and those weak in conscience, you scatter pearls before swine, whereby you commit two evils: you give the pearls to none other than swine, who waste away from hunger, and furthermore, you shamefully scatter and trample a precious gem. For this reason, the Holy Spirit, who was to move among wolves through the Apostles, seeks out hiding places and cracks after the manner of serpentine prudence. <margin>Song of Solomon 2</margin> For even the dove itself inhabits the openings of the rock and the hollows of the wall; it feeds the little ones with milk and the weak with vegetables: it hides the mysteries of solid truth in parables, or under some veil and within cracks, so that "seeing they may not see, and hearing <margin>❦</margin> they may not hear." <margin>Mark 4</margin> For you know (if you are wise) the mystery that "no one puts [new] wine into old wineskins, otherwise the wineskins burst, the wine is spilled, and the wineskins are ruined." <margin>Matthew 6</margin> <note>Though the margin cites Matthew 6, this reference to wineskins is found in Matthew 9:17.</note> Therefore, when this serpentine prudence toward men is joined with a dove-like simplicity toward the Creator, the Apostles, as men of God, were compelled to act between the Jewish synagogue and the crowd of Gentiles. From this, Paul also, like a wise Architect <term>Architectus</term> <note>original: "Architectus," here meaning a master-builder of the church.</note>, seeing the heresies of the Jews and Pagans disagreeing at the extremes, was compelled (in order to draw all to the unity of faith) to hand down the sacraments of the faith through word, writing, and deed, with a varied and manifold dissimulation. <note>In this context, "dissimulation" refers to "pastoral accommodation" or "holy tact"—adapting the presentation of truth to the listener's capacity.</note> According to that passage to the Corinthians: <margin>1 Corinthians 9</margin> "I became as a Jew to the Jews; to those under the Law, as if I were under the Law, though I myself was not under the Law; to those without the Law, as if I were without the Law. Finally," he says, "I have become all things to all men, that I might save all." Just as he did this in his deeds, so also it was necessary to practice this same kind of concealment in word and writing. For the Jews then adhering to the faith—and especially the Cerinthians and Ebionites <margin>Romans 10</margin> <note>The Cerinthians and Ebionites were early Jewish-Christian groups who insisted on the continued observance of the Mosaic Law, such as circumcision and dietary restrictions.</note> (however much they were rivals for justice and truth)—contended not according to knowledge, but out of servile fear and a dull and perverse ignorance <margin>Acts 15</margin> (as is clear from the Acts of the Apostles) that no one would be capable of the kingdom of heaven unless he were circumcised and subject to the Law of the commandments. On the other hand, the crowd of Gentiles, who were branches from the wild olive tree, unbridled and given to the lusts of the flesh, and puffed up with human and earthly wisdom, said that all faith in piety should be rejected rather than yield to Mosaic dogma and submit themselves to such a heavy yoke of commandments. Therefore, Paul, the wise Architect and teacher of the life of mortals, relying also on the counsel of the other Apostles, foresaw that this altercation would lead to a stumbling block for Christians and to the confusion and destruction of the poor and weak. He immediately interposed himself with that prudence which our own tempestuous times also require (I speak to those who have ears), and he granted something to the most rigid persistence of the opponents, and took something away, so that once the gap was broken and the middle wall of the enclosure was dissolved <margin>Ephesians 2</margin> (namely, the Law of the commandments, by which the sons of the kingdom were formerly distinguished from the sons of perdition), one might be made out of both. To the Jews indeed he granted that, according to the condition of the time, they might then embrace the mandates of the Law and approve them as more useful. In support of their opinion, <margin>Romans 2</margin> the Apostle brings forward in many places that the commandment is holy, good, spiritual, and justifying; but he rebukes the fact that they think no one becomes blessed through faith without the works of the commandments. As a foundation for this refutation, he extols faith alone, and shows in many ways that the carnal works of the Law are of little use and by no means justifying. In like manner, he grants to the Gentiles (as the Truth itself [Christ] testifies) that, while maintaining their liberty and without the external work of the Law's mandates, they can become participants in eternal salvation by the purity of faith alone. In assertion of this opinion, he teaches that the yoke of the Law's mandates empties grace and excludes the fellowship of Christ the Savior. Yet he refutes the opinion of the Pagans, by which they contended that the works of the mandates were empty superstition and of no moment for the kingdoms of heaven; and he disproves this with the same arguments and passages with which he strengthens that which he grants to the decrees of the Jews. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the "prudence of the serpent" and how the Spirit of Truth uses strategic concealment or "dissimulation" to protect the faith of the weak. It transitions into a specific defense of the Apostle Paul’s methods in teaching different groups.</meta>

<header>->### BY PAUL RICIUS, <-</header>

<margin>Dissimulation, in its proper place and time, is to be judged worthy of praise and a virtue.</margin>
...the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note>, by this kind of strategic agreement—carrying one thing on his face and another in his heart—could be blamed for lying. And where he passes down teachings that seem to openly conflict with one another, it might be thought that one is true and the other empty or false. Let such a profane and sacrilegious presumption be far removed from this herald of eternal truth and "vessel of election" <note>original: *uasa electionis*; a title for Paul from Acts 9:15</note>. For there is one kind of simulation where the truth is withdrawn by silence or covered by some veil, and another where a falsehood is expressed as truth. The first is not only blameless, but rather, in its proper place and time, is to be considered worthy of praise and a virtue. 
<margin>1 Kings <note>Known in modern Bibles as 1 Samuel 21</note></margin>
For even David, to escape the hands of King Achish, changed his behavior and feigned madness; and Christ the Lord, while going to Emmaus, pretended to be ignorant of the events in Jerusalem and acted as if he were going further. He also veiled the secret of truth in parables, so that "seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand." Therefore, Paul (if you notice) dissembles by keeping the truth silent, giving "milk" to the little ones <note>the spiritually immature</note> of the Jews and "vegetables" to the weak among the Gentiles. For with the Jews, he fulfilled the works of the Law, not revealing to the "little ones" with what sincerity of mind he did so, while they judged the Apostle himself to be just as subject to the Law of commandments as they were. Likewise, with the crowd of Gentiles, he performed no work of observing the Law; hence the multitude of Gentiles thought that Paul also despised the works of the Law as being of little or no importance. In the same way, one must judge his strategic agreement in word and writing. For since the commandment of the Law can be judged—under various respects and at different times—to be both profitable and unprofitable, justifying and not justifying, and other such contradictory things, he announced it through dissimulation: keeping silent in one place about the argument by which the commandment was to be judged useful, and in another, the argument by which it was proven useless. Thus, the opposite judgment regarding its uselessness must be made, just as it will be clearly evident to anyone who thinks rightly about the Apostle's words. If you desire to understand and penetrate his true and sincere mind accurately through so many entanglements of opinions, contemplate his words to the Romans:

<margin>1 Corinthians 3</margin>
To them—as to those wiser and more prudent than the Galatians (whom he calls "senseless") and the Corinthians (whom he calls "carnal" and not "spiritual," to whom he gave "milk" and not "solid food" <note>original: *escam*</note>)—to those Romans, I say, as with the other weaker Gentiles to whom the Apostle wrote, he wished to indicate the innermost decree of his mind. 
<margin>Romans 3</margin>
He does this more openly where he asks, saying: "But if our injustice commends the justice of God, is God unjust who inflicts wrath? I speak according to man" <note>original: *secundum hominem*; meaning from a human perspective</note>—according to man, that is, but not according to God. He says "injustice" to call back and dissuade people from the observance of the Law. On the contrary, this very "injustice according to man" and the "Gospel of the uncircumcision" <note>Paul's mission to the Gentiles</note> commends the true justice of the Law, which consists in the truth of faith, to the Gentiles. 
<margin>Romans 11</margin>
Compare these and the rest that follow there with his words further down, where he asks: "Have they stumbled so as to fall? Far from it," he says, "but by their lapse, salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to make them jealous. Now if their lapse means riches for the world, and their loss means riches for the Gentiles, how much more their fullness?" And a little later he adds: "For if their rejection is the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance be but life from the dead? If the first-fruits are holy, so is the whole batch; and if the root is holy, so are the branches."

<margin>Chapter 15 <note>Acts of the Apostles 15</note></margin>
These are his words. They are more openly supported by the single opinion of all the Apostles, which is written in their Acts: "Certain men coming down from Judea were teaching the brothers: 'Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.'" Then, when the Apostles met concerning this word, and to prevent the overthrow of the faith of the Gentiles, he showed in three parts that it was not right for the Gentiles to be restricted to the chief observance of the Law. First, because it is not necessary for salvation; and he declares this by experience and the constant testimony of God: "He who knows hearts," he said, "bore witness, giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us." Second, because the keeping of the Law is too difficult, adding: "Now therefore, why do you tempt God by putting a yoke upon the necks of the disciples, which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear?" Third (and most importantly), because now a way to the kingdom of heaven has been revealed that is far easier and safer through the grace of the Savior than through the observance of the Law. Adding: "But through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, we believe..."

# ON CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE, BOOK III.
<note>The title *De Coelesti Agricultura* (On Celestial Agriculture) refers to the cultivation of the soul and the growth of divine truth within the believer, using the metaphor of farming.</note>

...we believe we are saved, just as they are. And immediately James, with the entire order of the Apostles and Elders, approving Peter’s word, wrote to the faithful of the nations <note>the Gentiles</note> in this brief series of words: *Since we have heard that some going out from among us have troubled you with words, subverting your souls, to whom we gave no commandment, it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose no further burden upon you than these necessary things: that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what is strangled, and from fornication; by keeping yourselves from which, you will do well.* These are the words of the Apostles. From them, you can clearly deduce what the most urgent cause was for relaxing the observance of the Law, and what things were excepted and must necessarily be kept. You, a prudent reader eager for sincere truth, should diligently consider these things.

But here again, perhaps the listener will doubt, and not without reason: Since that same Prince of the Apostles, Peter (as read in their Acts), received from the Lord that nothing should be considered common or unclean. Christ the Lord Himself taught that what enters through the mouth does not defile a man, and that to one who gives alms, all things are clean. So too Paul says to Timothy: *Nothing is to be rejected which is received with thanksgiving*, because all things (as he writes to Titus) *are clean to the clean*. <note>original: *munda mundis*</note> 

Why then did Peter, with the entire and most holy synod of all the Apostles and Elders, decree it necessary to abstain from what is strangled and from blood? If all things are clean to the clean, for what reason do the decrees of the ancestors and saints forbid the consecrating of shrines where there are tombs of the dead? Why do they command the scraping of <margin>Concerning Consecration, Distinction 2. <note>A reference to the *Decretum Gratiani*, the foundational collection of Canon Law.</note></margin> walls and beams? If all things are clean to the clean, why is it not permitted, under heavy Anathema, to cover the shoulders of a corpse with sacred vestments? If all things are clean to the clean, why is it enacted: *He who has known the bed in chaste marital union should refrain from entering the Church, nor enter until he has first been washed?*

To these things I respond: if you rightly weigh what it signifies when we say someone is "clean," nothing in this matter will remain ambiguous to you. For Truth <note>Christ</note> taught that He is the true vine, whose branches He pronounces to be of three types: 
1. Some are already pruned and, clinging to the vine, they bring forth abundant and praiseworthy fruit. 
2. Others are utterly withered, <margin>The Evangelist suggests a threefold kind of branches.</margin> branches of no use, which are cast out into the fire. 
3. Others indeed cling to the vine, but are entangled with dry, rotten, and wandering sprouts; these must be cleaned and purged with anxious care so that they may fruit more abundantly and happily. 

The first are those whom Truth calls clean and blessed, saying: *You are clean through my word*, and *blessed are the clean of heart*. These the Apostle himself calls "clean"; they are called the "children of the bridegroom" who do not mourn in the bridegroom’s presence, and for them, through Him, nothing is common or unclean. <margin>Matthew 8. 1 Timothy 4. John 3.</margin> Neither principalities, nor any power of darkness—much less food or the touch of a sordid thing—is able to defile them; rather, they even cleanse defiled things and sanctify them through the word of God. 

However, for the withered and rotten branches—since they are unbelievers and already judged as children of Gehenna <note>hell</note>—nothing, no matter how sacred and pure, can be clean. 

But those branches that cling to the vine but are entangled with rotten, withered, or wandering sprouts, require the labor of pruning and repurging. Although external cleanliness of things may not be strictly necessary for them, if someone (like the Ebionites and Cerinthians) <note>Early Christian sects that insisted on strict adherence to Jewish Law.</note> decrees it to be absolutely essential and judges as a transgressor unto destruction anyone who neglects it, he judges and acts wrongly. Nevertheless, such external cleanliness cooperates in no small way toward the purity of the soul, and its neglect contributes to the defilement of the soul. For if such external cleanliness and sanctity of life were mere hypocrisy and vain superstition (as certain mockers of ceremonies and holy Canons insolently claim), then that testimony of divine authority would be a lie which says: *For this is your wisdom and understanding before the peoples, so that hearing all these precepts they may say: Behold, a wise and understanding people, a great nation.* <margin>Deuteronomy 4.</margin> On the contrary, they would be judged a foolish, superstitious, and vain people by the whole multitude of nations. Again, if this were empty superstition, the Divine Law would not have established and commanded its observance with such diligent and anxious care...

### PAUL RICIUS

<margin>Numbers 19</margin> ...observance, nor would He have punished transgressors with such severity—those whom He declares are deprived of divine help and the communion of the faithful and holy. <note>original: "fidelium sanctorumq; communione"</note> "He has polluted," He says, "the tabernacle of the Lord, and he shall perish from Israel." And this: <margin>Deuteronomy 23</margin> "The Lord your God walks in the midst of your camp to rescue you and to deliver your enemies to you; therefore, let your camp be holy, and let nothing filthy appear in it, lest He abandon <margin>Leviticus 11</margin> you." Divine authority clearly shows that these external impurities defile not only the flesh, but also the spirit and the soul, according to that saying: "Do not contaminate your souls, nor touch any of those things; I am your Lord, <margin>Leviticus 21</margin> be holy, for I am holy." <note>The Latin "sancti estote: quia sanctus ego sum" is a central refrain in the Mosaic Law, emphasizing that physical cleanliness reflects spiritual status.</note> Do not pollute your souls even with foods: "Do not pollute your souls," He says, "with cattle, or birds, or anything that moves upon the earth, which I have shown you to be unclean; you shall be holy to me, for I, the Lord, am holy." 

If the observance of these things is "vain superstition," then why, many centuries before the giving of the Divine Law, while men lived under the Law of Nature, <note>The "Law of Nature" refers to the period from Adam to Moses, before the Ten Commandments were written on stone.</note> was a distinction made between clean and unclean animals? It was so distinct that the just and wise man, Noah, preserved seven pairs of each of the clean animals from the destruction of the waters in the ark, but only one pair of the unclean. If it is "vain superstition," then some of the wise and holy men are mere chatterboxes and triflers—<margin>Prima [Secundae] q. 103</margin> and especially Saint Aquinas, who, by discussing each of these mandates at great length, showed their reason and cause to be consistent with the Law of Nature and strengthened by it. <note>original: "diuus Aquinas." Reference to Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae*, Ia IIae, q. 103, which discusses the "Ceremonial Precepts" of the Old Testament.</note>

Let those who philosophize in human terms about the secrets of nature tell me, I pray: do they not claim that a symbol and a certain disposition <note>original: "habitudinem"</note> of the receiving body are necessarily given for the sake of the form and the soul being received? And the more temperate that which receives is, the more excellent will be that which is infused by the Bestower of Forms. <note>The "Bestower of Forms" (formarum largitor) is a philosophical term for God, who provides the "form" or soul to the physical "matter" of the body.</note> And therefore, because the human soul’s "receiver" <note>the body</note> is clean and naturally approaches a balanced temperament, it deserved to receive a clean form capable of reason and intelligence. But the neighboring "receptacle" of reptiles, because it is subjected as something flawed and filthy, therefore brings forth filthy and defective animals.

Let those also tell me who contemplate the mysteries of sacred and sublime things: is not one spirit given as clean and another as unclean? And he who is unclean communicates with every filthy and obscene man, and with the most foul race of hags and sorcerers. <note>original: "lamiarum, & maleficarū generi." Ricius connects physical ritual impurity with susceptibility to demonic influence.</note> This is not done by the Clean Spirit, by whom it is commanded: "Be holy, for I am holy." And from this it happened that even the wise men of the Pagans of old, as well as the Jews—although they knew God as the supreme creator of all things—nevertheless changed His glory (as the Apostle says to the Romans) into the image of corruptible man, birds, and four-footed beasts. And this was for no other reason than that the unclean spirits of idols and images show themselves equally ready and dutiful—even easier for their worshipper—the more he indulges in the filthier works of the flesh, to which the muddy form of mortals is more prone than to sobriety and cleanliness of life, such as <margin>Joshua 24</margin> the Holy and Clean Spirit requires in every way.

This is according to the response of Joshua to the crowd of Israelites: "You will not be able," he says, "to serve the Lord; for He is a holy God, and a mighty rival <note>or "jealous God"</note>, and He will not forgive your crimes." For light (as you know) in its purest state banishes darkness far away; fire itself consumes rot and all filth. <margin>1 Corinthians 6</margin> Therefore, if you strive to make your mortal body a member of the glorious body of Christ (and like a heavenly element) a temple of God, you must keep it holy and clean from all corruption of rot and filth, and you must present it as a living and spotless sacrifice, according to the teachings of the Apostle. For this reason, although the observance of external cleanliness—through a certain and mystical understanding—serves as a shadow and figure of heavenly things, it cannot be considered "vain superstition" even according to the literal sense. Rather, these are the vine-branches <note>original: "palmites." This ties back to the book's title, "Celestial Agriculture."</note> which are not yet fully clean but are to be purged; though it may not be appropriate in every instance, it nevertheless provides some measure of conformity and aptitude for attaining exact purity of soul and for a fruitful clinging to the Vine, the source of eternal life. # ON CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE, BOOK III.

The synod of the Apostles prohibited blood and what is strangled: <note>Refers to the Council of Jerusalem in Acts 15, where early Christians were told to abstain from blood and strangled meat to maintain fellowship between Jewish and Gentile converts.</note> From which the decrees of the saints (which we have mentioned) rightfully exclude and banish from sacred and dedicated buildings the contagion of corpses and graves, and intercourse with those defiled by marital acts: as well as many other things of this kind which we shall explain elsewhere in their proper place and time. For to us who embrace the faith of truth, although all things are lawful: yet not all things (as the Apostle says) are expedient; <note>original: "omnia licent : Non tamen omnia... expediunt" — a reference to 1 Corinthians 10:23.</note> and therefore those things which are lawful (says the gloss of the saints) <note>A "gloss" is a traditional scholarly or theological commentary written in the margins or between the lines of a text.</note> and are not expedient, are to be avoided not by the bond of the Law, but by the free beneficence of love and the counsel of charity.

Therefore, we receive the Gospel narrative as from a faithful and truthful writer of deeds, not as a Lawgiver. These things are clearly evident from what has been said to anyone looking closely.

->*THE LAWGIVER, PROPHET, EVANGELIST, or Apostle, although at times they may hallucinate (as their own utterances testify) and be deceived where the spirit of the super-celestial God is not present: nevertheless, all their writings, which they suggest were produced for them by divine authority, are surely to be embraced with firm and sincere faith.*<-

<margin>Wisdom 9</margin>
For where the spirit of the super-celestial God is missing, nothing is left there but human wisdom, which is foolishness before God. For the thoughts of mortals (as the Wise Man speaks) are fearful and their providence uncertain: <note>original: "Cogitationes namque mortalium... timidæ sunt & incertæ prouidentiæ" — Wisdom of Solomon 9:14.</note> since even Moses the Lawgiver, the greatest of Prophets, was rebuked for his "foolish labor" by his father-in-law, a gentile man, and having rejected his own plan, he obeyed his father-in-law’s advice. <note>Referring to Jethro, a Midianite priest, who advised Moses on how to delegate judicial duties in Exodus 18.</note> So too, 
<margin>Leviticus 10</margin>
<margin>Galatians 2</margin>
regarding the burnt goat sacrifice, the same Moses, becoming angry without due consideration, yielded to the opinion of his brother Aaron: so also Peter, the prince of the Apostles, was seen to be blameworthy, whom the Apostle Paul did not hesitate to resist to his face. <note>Paul famously rebuked Peter in Antioch for refusing to eat with Gentiles (Galatians 2:11).</note> If therefore we know that the greatest of Prophets and the prince of the Apostles clearly strayed at times where divine authority did not intervene, consider for yourself what is to be judged of others, however much they may excel in wisdom and the purity of their lives. But where and when the authors of sacred utterance have hallucinated, or handed down some teaching by their own human authority, the sacred History itself announces, just as we have mentioned regarding Moses and the Apostle Peter. So, in the Fourth Book of Kings <note>In the 16th century, the books of 1 & 2 Kings were often called 3 & 4 Kings.</note> we read of Elisha, that God concealed it and did not reveal it to him regarding the Shunammite boy: so it is written of the old Prophet in the Third Book of Kings, that he deceived another Prophet who was then killed by a lion. And in the Acts of the Apostles, we read that a sharp disagreement arose between Paul and Barnabas, who had been set apart by the Holy Spirit for the ministry of faith. And the same Apostle confesses to the Corinthians that he has no commandment from the Lord concerning virgins: but has given his own counsel: so too must we judge many things of this kind. Truly all the rest of the writings and warnings of the sacred Canon are declared by the divine utterances themselves to have been handed down by God. Regarding the Law of Moses, it is written: the Lord said to Moses: "Come up to me, and stay there, and I will give you stone tablets, and the Law, and the commandments which I have written, so that you may teach the children of Israel." So also the Apostle Paul frequently prefaces in his Epistles (excluding the one to the Hebrews) and asserts that he is an Apostle of *JESUS CHRIST*. "For I do not dare," he says, "to speak of any of those things which Christ has not worked through me": and "my speech and my preaching were not with persuasive words of human wisdom, but in the demonstration of the spirit and of power." So also, the sacred History clearly declares that all the prophecies, counsels, and writings of the Prophets were handed down from divine revelation and command. Therefore, whatever warnings of any wise men or saints are not handed down by the command or name of God, nor by clear argument from those things which were uttered by divine authority, [they are not to be...]

For although the teachings of the holy and wise may deviate from the path of truth when that super-celestial spirit is absent: yet no one should rashly presume to despise the dogmas and institutes of the ancestors and elders. <margin>Deuteronomy 13</margin> <note>Though the margin cites chapter 13, the following text is a paraphrase of Deuteronomy 17:8-11.</note> According to that word of Moses: If you perceive a judgment to be difficult and ambiguous between blood and blood, cause and cause, leprosy and leprosy, and you see that words vary within your gates (more correctly, words between blow and blow, or matters of litigation within your gates), rise and go up to the place which the Lord your God shall choose, and you shall come to the Priests of the Levite lineage, and to the judge who shall be in office at that time. ### ON CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE, BOOK III.

...admitted that the decrees established [by the Church] do not bind the faithful of Christ under the penalty of mortal sin, it would follow that whoever transgresses those Canons would commit nothing more than a **venial sin** <term>venial sin: In Catholic theology, a lesser sin that does not result in complete separation from God, unlike a "mortal" sin</term>. Such a sin requires neither confession nor a penance of satisfaction; its entire guilt and punishment is wiped away simply by entering a consecrated Church and by the sprinkling of the sacred font <note>This refers to the use of holy water upon entering a church</note>. 

From this, something unspeakable and horrifying to hear would follow: namely, if anyone were to revive the errors and dogmas of **Arius, Mani, Pelagius** <note>original: "Arrij, Manichei, Pelagij." These were famous early Christian heretics: Arius (denied Christ's full divinity), Mani (taught dualism between light and dark), and Pelagius (denied original sin)</note>, and as many heretics as there have been since the beginning of time—errors which the authority of the sacred Word [the Bible] does not openly or precisely refute—then no matter how much they have been excluded and condemned by the **Councils of the Saints** and the decrees of the early **Popes**, the one who embraced them would be guilty of no mortal fault, but only a venial crime. 

I remain silent regarding the sacred solemnities of **fasts and feast days**, the celebrations of **Masses**, religious **vows**, **celibacy**, **marriages**, **blood-relations** <note>Rules regarding who is allowed to marry based on family proximity</note>, and several most pious rites of the **sacraments and ceremonies**. If one observes none of these but renders them all void, he would obtain pardon for his offense through the Lord’s Prayer alone and the sprinkling of the sacred font.

If, however, the defender of error says that although these individual points are not precisely laid out in the sacred Word, they nevertheless draw their root from it and establish their foundations there—then, contrary to his own hypothesis, it would follow that *no* Canon constitution is given which does not bind the Christian under mortal sin. For you will find no decree of the synods or the pious Popes, not even the smallest, which does not in some way have its origin in some passage of the New or Old Testament, as the **Apostle** commands: *built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets*. 

<margin>Ephesians 2</margin>
If no other foundation were given from the sacred Canon than this one, by which the **Truth** [Christ] commands: *The Scribes and Pharisees have sat upon the chair of Moses; therefore, do all things whatsoever they tell you,* this would be sufficient and entirely effective to bind the faithful of Christ to obedience to the Councils and the pious Popes under the penalty of mortal sin. 

<margin>Matthew 23</margin>
<margin>1. q. 1.</margin>
For if He said that those who sat upon the **chair of Moses** <note>original: "cathedram Mosis"</note> must be heard (as the decrees of the saints establish), how much more are those who reside upon the **chair of Peter** <note>original: "cathedram Petri"; the office of the Pope</note> to be heard! For *he who resists the power*, says the Apostle, *resists the ordinance of God*.

But let the sower of pestiferous error and heresy tell us: if the decrees of Councils and Popes have no power to bind under mortal sin from any other source except that they draw the foundation of their constitutions and traditions from the **sacred scriptures**, then every heretical dogma and error would have equal authority to bind the faithful! For there has never been a heretic or one wandering from the faith, from the beginning of the Christian religion to this day, who did not draw the source and fountainhead of his error from the Canon of the sacred Scriptures and strive to lead others back to it; no scholar is ignorant of this. 

Perhaps here the foolish dreamer <note>original: "hallucinator insipiens"</note> says: "Although the leader of a heresy strives to draw the root of his error from the sacred Word, he does this not through a true understanding, but through a distorted and wicked interpretation of the Scriptures." 

Then we shall ask this very man: "Tell me, I pray, who should be given as **judge or arbiter** to settle the dispute between opponents and discern the right interpretation of Scripture from the wicked one? Must an Angel, Prophet, or Apostle be sent from heaven for the sake of every man’s rash presumption and insanity to eliminate their individual errors and ravings and reveal the true sense of the Scriptures?" 

Turn over, then, the rulings of the Scriptures and the wise; turn them over and over again; consult the matter by the examination of reason: this faculty of judging and discerning must be committed to no one except the **synod and authority of the pious and wise**. 

<margin>¶</margin>
Whoever despises this, and deems the transgressor of its constitutions to be liable only to venial guilt, utterly subverts the governance of the entire commonwealth and the faith and religion of piety; such a person despises not man, but **God and His Holy Spirit**. *He who rejects you,* He says, *rejects me.* And *where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I [in the midst of them].*

<summary>Ricius argues that Church laws (Canon Law) must bind the faithful under the penalty of mortal sin; otherwise, heresy would be trivialized and religious order would collapse. He asserts that the Papacy (the Chair of Peter) holds a higher authority than the ancient leaders of Israel and that only the Church's collective wisdom, not individual interpretation, can rightly judge the meaning of Scripture.</summary>

<margin>Exodus 23</margin>
You will inquire and ask, since the same Moses commands by the mouth of God that we should not follow a multitude to do evil, nor should we yield in judgment to the opinion of the many which deviates from the truth: What, I pray, is the manner, what is the method for him who desires to walk the path of life and seeks the kingdom of heaven, for judging or discerning which multitude and which counsels of the elders or priests declare what is just, and which deviate and wander from the path of right? 

To this, if you are wise, you will understand that although Moses thought the opinion of priests and judges should be consulted and obeyed whenever something ambiguous occurred, he mainly explained those matters concerning **blood, legal causes, and leprosy** <term>leprosy: In the Mosaic Law, specific rituals and judgments were required to identify and handle skin diseases (Tzaraath), often involving social and religious quarantine</term>, and other disputes that usually occur between man and man. In these matters, one must not turn to the right or the left, but obey their command without further examination. 

Regarding those things, however, which concern the solid and unshaken truth of faith—about which the Law and the teachings of the Apostles leave no room for even a tiny or dangerous ambiguity or suspicion—Moses mentions nothing explicit in the aforementioned context. This is because in the foundations of faith, even if the judgment of the leaders should be consulted when something is obscure, the subject of the Law ought not to be bound by so tight a chain of obedience as in those other matters. The reason is that the sacred words pronounce those things that most concern the beatific faith openly and clearly, and this is rightfully so. 

For if the fleeting nature of perishable things lacks nothing and neglects nothing required for their existence and preservation, how much more is it fitting that the height of divine providence—which cares for **sparrows, ravens, and other birds of the sky, and for the lilies of the field** <note>These are references to the teachings of Jesus in Matthew 6 and Luke 12 regarding God's care for all creation</note>—should permit nothing to remain obscure or unexplained in those things which concern the eternal salvation of mortals. 

Human events, however—disputes, legal causes, operations, and acts that proceed from the shifting prudence of the flesh and earthly desire—undergo such variety and change that they cannot be explained by any divine sanction, let alone human law, since they are infinite. Therefore, the judgments of those things and the decrees of law cannot be expressed or enclosed by any limit of constitutions and opinions. And for that reason, divine authority established that even the conjectures and judgments of **unworthy** <note>original: "discolorum," literally "discolored" or "variegated," used here to mean priests who may be morally inconsistent or lacking in character</note> priests and judges holding the highest office must be obeyed without any dispute or any daring contradiction. 

But in those matters which concern the truth of faith, upon which the eternal salvation of men depends, one may not listen even to a Prophet of God or an Angel from heaven, if by their teachings the listener is turned away from God and from the faith of truth.

<summary>Ricius argues that while religious authorities must be obeyed in civil and legal matters where the law is complex, the fundamental truths of faith are made so clear by God that even an Angel should be ignored if they contradict the Gospel. He justifies the absolute authority of judges in human affairs by the infinite variety of human disputes, contrasting this with the clarity of divine providence regarding salvation.</summary>

Therefore, we must abide by the decrees of the ancestors and elders, as long as sense, reason, and authority do not establish the contrary. Neither the sound of the letter <note>original: "literæ sono"; referring to a strictly literal interpretation devoid of spiritual context</note> of the Law nor of the Prophets should be accepted when one of these three presents a conflicting testimony or experience. 
<margin>Deuteronomy 32</margin>
Moses, for instance, speaks to the dull earth just as if it were capable of hearing and understanding. "Let the earth hear," he says, "the words of my mouth." 
<margin>Deuteronomy 28</margin>
He also predicts that the heavens will become brass and the earth iron as a result of transgressing the Law. In the same way, Christ the Lord calls himself the "true vine" and the "light of the world," and Paul taught that He was the "rock." We do not accept any of these or similar things according to the literal tenor of the words (because both perception and reason declare the opposite), but we approve of them as being spoken through metaphor or likeness.

Moses also commands us to "circumcise the foreskin of the heart," and Christ the Lord commands us to be "born again." But because clear reason judges that the former cannot be done without self-slaughter, and the latter cannot happen under any physical condition, we therefore judge that these are by no means to be believed according to the literal understanding. 
<margin>Deuteronomy 4</margin>
Rather, the former signifies that we must circumcise the dullness of spirit in the heart, and the latter signifies that we must be reborn through purity of body and novelty of faith. Similarly, the invisible and immortal Creator of all things, God himself, calls himself a "consuming fire." To Him, the Scripture attributes now an eye, now ears, nostrils, fingers, hands, and feet, and various visible things of that kind. We know clearly that none of these things exist in God, as divine authority teaches: 
<margin>Isaiah 40</margin>
"Keep your souls carefully, for you saw no likeness on the day the Lord spoke," and that other passage: "To whom have you likened God, or what image will you place upon Him?" Sense, reason, and authority thus reveal that these things must be understood in a sense other than what the letter plainly pronounces.

By the same law of truth in faith, these three [criteria] build up the mind and lead it to cling firmly to what must be believed. For the sight of wonders and the hearing of the living voice of God brought the certainty of faith to the multitude of Israel and led them to enter into a perpetual covenant to observe the Law. Likewise, the first disciples of Christian piety and faith, seeing and feeling the flesh and bones of the most sacred body of Christ—
<margin>Luke 24</margin>
and Thomas by touching the marks of the nails with his fingers—gave faith to the Resurrection. 
<margin>John 5</margin>
So too all the other leaders who followed the Christian doctrine received the testimony of faith from the works of Christ the Savior perceived by sight. "If you do not believe me," He said, "believe the works; for those very works that I do bear witness of me, because the Father sent me." 

To this, it was worthwhile to join manifest reason, by which they might weigh the miracles of Christ as being the works of God and not of demons, or trickery, or madness. Reasoning against the impudence of the Pharisees, those who were of the faith argued that a demon does not have the power to enlighten the blind, nor is it the office of a demon to cast out a demon. 
<margin>Matthew 10</margin>
The truth argued from the mouth of Christ: "If Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself; how then shall his kingdom stand?" Nor did He consider the inviolable testimony of reason and sense sufficient to establish faith, unless He also added the authority of the Scriptures: 
<margin>John 5</margin>
"Search the Scriptures," He said, "for they are they which bear witness of me." Through these, the mystery and the sacrament of faith, hidden from eternity, were revealed. Therefore, just as these three provide faith in the truth, so they eliminate the error of falsehood. For we discern a false prophet from a true one by no other means than when we find by sense and experience that things have not happened as that prophet predicted. According to that...

# ON CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE, BOOK III.

### THE MEANING OF THE SCRIPTURES IS CONSIDERED PLAIN, so long as divine authority, sound perception, or manifest reason do not show otherwise elsewhere; for just as these things build up the truth of the written word and of faith, so they also eliminate what is false; by their certainty the faith of both Moses and Christ the Savior became known, and their

->Testaments<-

were established.

<margin>Deuteronomy 32. Deuteronomy 28.</margin>
We must, therefore, stand by the decrees of our ancestors and elders so long as sense, reason, and authority do not establish the contrary. For we should not settle for the mere sound of the literal word of the Law or the Prophets when one of these three—testimony, experience, or reason—shows an opposing truth. For instance, Moses addresses the "dull earth" as if it were capable of hearing and understanding, saying: *Let the earth hear the words of my mouth* <note>original: "Audiat terra uerba oris mei." From the Song of Moses in Deuteronomy 32:1.</note>. He also foretells that the sky will become brass and the earth iron as a result of transgressing the Law. Similarly, Christ the Lord calls himself the "true vine" and the "light of the world," and Paul taught that He was the "rock." We do not accept any of these or similar things according to the literal tenor of the words (because perception and reason both declare the opposite), but we approve of them as being spoken through metaphor or likeness. Moses also commands us to circumcise the foreskin of the heart, and Christ the Lord commands us to be born again. But because manifest reason judges that the former cannot happen without self-murder, and the latter <margin>Deuteronomy 4.</margin> cannot happen under any physical condition, we therefore judge that these are by no means to be believed according to the literal understanding. Rather, the former signifies a "circumcision" of a dull spirit in the heart, and the latter designates that we ought to be reborn through the purity of the body and the novelty of faith. So too, the invisible and immortal Creator of all things, God, calls himself a "consuming fire," to whom Scripture attributes now an eye, now ears, nostrils, fingers, hands, and feet, and that kind of visible anatomy <margin>Isaiah 40.</margin>—none of which, we clearly know, exists in God, as divine authority teaches: *Guard your souls solicitously, for you saw no likeness on the day the Lord spoke* <note>A reference to Deuteronomy 4:15, emphasizing God’s incorporeal nature.</note>; and again: *To whom have you likened God, or what image will you place upon Him?* Sense, therefore, along with reason and authority, makes it clear that these things must be understood in a sense other than what the literal word plainly pronounces. By a similar law, these three things establish the truth of faith and lead the mind to cling firmly to things that must be believed. For the sight of portents and the hearing of the living voice of God brought certainty of faith to the multitude of Israel, and led them to enter into a perpetual covenant to observe the Law. So too, the first nurslings of Christian piety and faith, seeing and feeling the flesh and bones of the most sacred <margin>Luke 24.</margin> body of Christ—and Thomas, by touching the marks of the nails with his fingers—placed their faith in the resurrection. Thus all the other primary followers of Christian doctrine received the testimony of faith from the works of Christ the Savior perceived by sight: *If you do not believe me,* He said, *believe the works: for those very works that I do bear witness of me, because the Father sent me* <margin>John 5.</margin>. To which it was worthwhile to associate manifest reason, by which they might weigh the miracles of Christ as being the works of God and not of demons, or of trickery, or of a madman. Those who were of faith reasoned against the impudence of the Pharisees, noting that a demon does not have the power to give sight to the blind, nor is it the office of a demon to cast out a demon. The truth argued from the mouth of Christ: <margin>Matthew 12.</margin> *If Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself; how then shall his kingdom stand?* Nor did He think the inviolable testimony of reason and sense was enough to establish faith, unless He also added the authority of the Scriptures: *Search the Scriptures,* He said, *for they are the things that bear witness of me* <margin>John 5.</margin>; through them the mystery was revealed, and the sacrament of faith hidden from eternity was made clear. Therefore, just as these three provide faith in the truth, so they also eliminate the error of falsehood: for we do not discern a false prophet from a true one by any other means than when we find by sense and experience that things have not happened as that prophet pronounced. According to that...

He cites examples like "circumcision of the heart" and Christ's miracles to show how sense, reason, and authority work together to confirm religious truth.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from page 107 regarding the criteria for interpreting Scripture. While the previous page established that literal meaning should be set aside if it contradicts sense, reason, or authority, this page provides specific tests for identifying false prophets and explains the theological concept of "newness" in the New Testament.</meta>

# PAUL RICCIUS,

<margin>Deuteronomy 18, 5; Psalm 113; Deuteronomy 4.</margin>
In the book of Deuteronomy, you shall have this sign: if that Prophet has predicted something in the name of the Lord and it does not come to pass, the Lord has not spoken it; therefore, reason proves that no faith should be placed in him. By this same rule <term>canon: a rule or standard of judgment</term>, we must judge those people who boast of a spiritual understanding of the scriptures and the gift of the Holy Spirit: if you recognize the fruits of the Spirit in them—charity, gentleness, self-control, chastity, and the rest which the Apostle Paul enumerates to the Galatians <note>Galatians 5:22-23</note>—then lend them your ears. But if you recognize among them contentions, quarrels, vainglory, impurity, gluttony, greed, and similar works of the flesh, be certain that the angel Satan has transformed himself into an angel of light <note>2 Corinthians 11:14</note>. For you shall know them (as the Truth itself says) from no other source than their fruits. Indeed, the incautious mind of curious people would everywhere succumb to the vanity of idols, were it not for the fact that the senses judge that mute idols are merely statues made of wood, stone, and metal—things which neither see, nor hear, nor throb with a pulse, nor show any work of intelligence or life. When the senses judge this, then solid reason immediately proves that these things are by no means to be worshiped. This is also supported by the solid and unshakable authority of the Decalogue <term>Decalogue: The Ten Commandments</term> and of all the Prophets and Apostles. Therefore, whoever you are who have ears for hearing, turn over and diligently search the Scriptures; examine every command and warning of Moses, the Gospel, and the Apostles. Whenever you find a saying where the common sense of all people and manifest reason are repugnant to the plain sound of the letter—and even more so if no clear authority is given elsewhere—do not listen to any of the commentators or dogmatists. Instead, be safe and certain that it must be understood in a sense other than what the letter shows on its face. Think fearlessly and clearly affirm that it must be heard through a metaphor, a likeness, a hyperbole, or any other figure of speech <term>tropo: a figurative use of language</term>.

->*CHRIST THE SAVIOR, AND EACH OF HIS SACRAMENTS,*<-
->*are called "new" not because of a novelty of command or of an external*<-
->*work, but from a new act of believing, which brings to life dead—*<-
->*and indeed even death-bearing—works,*<-
->*and renders them saving.*<-

<margin>Ezekiel 36; Ephesians 4; Mark 16; 1 John 2; 2 Corinthians 3.</margin>
You ought to pay attention to this: a thing is not always called "new" because of the novelty of its substance—as if it were made now when it did not exist shortly before, like new crops or new houses. Rather, we often read that something is called "new" because of a certain new quality coming upon the substance of the thing. This is according to that word of the Prophet: *I will give you a new heart* <note>Ezekiel 36:26</note>; and that of the Apostle: *Be renewed in the spirit of your mind* <note>Ephesians 4:23</note>. Sometimes we call something "new" solely in respect to the fact that the thing has just become known to someone, whereas it was hidden from them before. For example, in Mark 16: *they will speak* (he says) *in new tongues* <note>Mark 16:17</note>, even though the differences between languages have existed almost since the beginning of time. Likewise, we speak of the "new moon" <note>original: "neomenias seu nouilunium"</note> because it was not visible before. For the sake of this distinction, we find the same thing called both "new" and "old" at the very same moment. This is according to that word of John: *I am writing no new commandment to you, but an old commandment, which is the word that was heard from the beginning.* And again he says: *I am writing a new commandment to you, because the darkness has passed and the true light shines* <note>1 John 2:7-8</note>. For he calls the commandment "old" (if you notice) because it was heard from the beginning under darkness and a veil. But he calls it "new" because it was then first received with a clearer understanding, by the splendor of heavenly light and the removal of the veil. From these things you have discovered that not everything which "grows old" (as is written to the Hebrews <note>Hebrews 8:13</note>) is "near to vanishing." For example, the command of mutual love is indeed the oldest commandment of the Mosaic and natural Law, yet it will never perish in any age. Therefore, since that passage in Hebrews states without any condition that "what is becoming old is near to vanishing," it would be necessary for you to charge Paul with ignorance and contradiction, because...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the distinction between the Old and New Testaments. It argues that "newness" is a matter of spiritual transformation and faith rather than entirely new physical rituals, drawing parallels between Jewish purification rites and Christian sacraments.</meta>

### ON HEAVENLY AGRICULTURE, BOOK III.

...which is horrendous and cursed to hear: or it ought to be said that, just as we call a "new mandate" and a "new heart" by the novelty of revealed understanding, so too the Old Testament is considered "old" and "fading" by the antiquity and vanishing of the former darkness, servitude, and the spirit of fear by which people were bound—especially in the observance of the Law. Likewise, the New is proven by the new light of grace of the true and eternal Testament of faith. This by no means excludes, but rather fulfills and perfects (just as an end goal and a form perfect the raw material) the works of the commandments. Therefore, anyone who claims that the sacraments instituted by Christ our Savior are "new" simply because the external action is a novelty judges incorrectly. For the external practice of both baptism and the fraction (or the sacrament of the Eucharist) was a most ancient custom, and it remains so for the entire Synagogue of Israel.

But the sacraments are called "new" from the novelty of revealed faith, which brings to life the carnal, dead, and death-bringing works of the commandments, making them salvific <note>salvific: leading to salvation</note>. <margin>Genesis 9</margin> Just as killing a man is prohibited by the Decalogue <term>Decalogue: The Ten Commandments</term> and by the law of nature, as it is written: "Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed." <margin>Deuteronomy 17</margin> Yet elsewhere, the Law commands that the hands of the witnesses first, and then the people, shall kill the guilty party. <margin>Genesis 4, Numbers 28</margin> So too, Cain reported the curse of God because he killed his brother. Phinehas <note>Phinehas: A priest in the Hebrew Bible who was rewarded for his zeal in stopping a plague by killing a couple who had defied the law (Numbers 25)</note>, however, when he pierced through a fornicating man and woman, earned a covenant of perpetual priesthood. Therefore, what had been death-bringing to the former because of a distorted and wicked intention, was made salvific to the latter out of a zeal for piety. 

In the same way, he who partakes of the most holy body of the Lord with a polluted mind and unworthily eats the judgment of eternal punishment upon himself; but he who receives that same thing with the faith of piety and a pure heart is made a sharer in eternal life and the divine nature. We celebrate Passover, we celebrate Pentecost; those Jews also celebrate them with a dull mind and impure faith unto their destruction. We observe them with a sincere and revealed faith in the truth unto life. The Gentiles adored images and worshiped man-made statues; we also adore <note>original: "adoramus" - here used in the sense of venerating sacred images</note>, but they did so in the cult of demons unto perdition. The wise faithful, however, do so in veneration of the incarnate Word and the saints, unto eternal life. 

There are many arguments of this kind which clearly declare that the same type of work—which is considered old, dead, and death-bringing because of a lack of moderation and deformity (as if it were formless and mere matter)—is proven to be new, living, and justifying through right intention and true faith (as if by its "form" <note>Riccius uses the Aristotelian concept where "matter" is the physical act and "form" is the spiritual meaning or intent that gives it life</note>). <margin>The Jewish Synagogue observes a two-part baptism.</margin> For the Jewish sect is accustomed to using a double baptism and washing. One is to wipe away a stain from contact with a filthy or unclean thing. In this kind of baptism, they cleanse not only human bodies, but also chalices, jars, and other vessels and furniture used for food, drink, and other things whenever they have been contaminated by any uncleanness. If these items can withstand fire, they purge them with fire; if not, they cleanse them with the water of expiation and the washing of baptism (according to the mandates of the Law). <margin>Numbers 31</margin> 

The other is the baptism of repentance, by which (as the stated book or the Talmudists <term>Talmudists: scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</term> treat it) anyone who is a follower of a foreign faith and religion, when he decides to take himself to the true worship of God the Creator and to the Mosaic colony, is not admitted (if he is male) unless, together with the sacrament of circumcision, he receives the water of baptism. If it is a female, only baptism is required. And not only proselytes <term>proselytes: converts</term> who jump from a false religion to the Mosaic religion, but also any Israelite repenting of sin strives to be reborn through a new bodily cleanliness and the washing of baptism, just as they seek a novelty of a more honorable and spiritual life. 

By this kind of baptism, Judith was baptized in a fountain; Nehemiah was stripped for baptism; and now many repenting Jews do the same, especially on the Day of Atonement, which they keep with the highest solemnity on the tenth day of the September moon <note>Yom Kippur</note>. After many days of fasting and prayers before dawn, preceded by a confession of sins, they soon dip their entire bodies in the washing of baptism, with the water covering the crown of their heads. Truly, by this same law, the multitude of Jews were baptized by John in the Jordan, confessing their sins. By the same...

<meta>This page continues the argument that Christian sacraments are not entirely "new" in their physical form, but rather ancient Jewish customs transformed by a new spirit of faith. Ricius specifically links the Eucharist to the Jewish Seder and daily table blessings.</meta>

# PAUL RICIUS,

In the same way, one must judge the sacrament of communion and the breaking of bread <note>The Eucharist or Lord's Supper</note>. Regarding the external action, it should by no means be believed to be a new institution of a sacrament, since its use was most ancient. The Talmudists <note>Jewish scholars and compilers of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note> discuss this at length in the "Book of Blessings" <note>Referring to the Talmudic tractate *Berakhot*</note> regarding that verse of Moses: *You shall bless the Lord when you have been satisfied* <margin>Deuteronomy 8</margin>. Even today, the entire multitude of Jews carefully observes this: namely, whenever they recline at the table, the father of the family—or whoever among those reclining is of higher rank—before they taste any side dish or food, blesses the bread or cake, breaks it while blessing, and distributes a small portion of the morsel to each person. In a similar way, once the meal is finished, the person whose duty it is to give thanks takes the cup; when these thanks are finished, he blesses the cup and offers it to each individual. Nor should it be overlooked that whenever a solemn feast day occurs, in addition to the cup used after the meal for praise and thanksgiving, he also blesses another cup before the blessing of the bread and the tasting of the food, and offers it to each person. Luke is the only one among the Evangelists to mention this [first] cup <note>Referencing Luke 22:17, where a cup is mentioned before the bread, reflecting the sequence of a Jewish Passover Seder</note>. 

Consider, therefore, whether the "breaking" and "baptism" should be judged as a novelty of external action. If you weigh the words of the Apostle to the Corinthians, to whom he handed down the mystery of this sacrament, you will understand that they hint at the same opinion we have stated. Thus, the very same sacrament in its external action—which for the earliest saints was a seal under the cloud and veil of the future Passion (since the Lord’s Passion had not yet happened)—is now celebrated with true faith and the ardor of devotion as a memorial of that Passion already enacted, and as a sign and preparation for future glory, now that the understanding of faith and truth has been revealed. And just as we judge these matters, so must we judge all other sacraments of Christ the Lord and the Apostles. Having heard these things, remember: just as the commandment to love one's neighbor is most ancient and will never perish, it is nevertheless called "new"—not because of the external action, but by the novelty of faith, which renews, gives life to, and makes salvific <note>Leading to salvation</note> those works that were otherwise dead and death-bringing. Judge that this must be believed and firmly held concerning each of the sacraments and the novelty of the Savior’s testament.

<margin>Epilogue.</margin> Finally, from all that has been handed down here, take up this summary: through the observance of the commandments, faith and the fear of God are strengthened and remain; fear, in turn, provides purity of the soul; purity of the soul requires cleanliness of the body, from which conformity [to God] itself arises; conformity gives birth to love; love effects an adherence with the origin of eternal life. Since every human being was made for this purpose, that living Word of God most skillfully and providently warned: *Fear God* (he said) *and observe his commandments, for this is the whole of man.* <note>Original: "hoc est omnis homo"; a quote from Ecclesiastes 12:13</note>

->THE CONQUEROR CONSTANTINE, GREATEST AND<-
->PIOUS, TO ALEXANDER AND ARIUS.<-

<image-desc>A decorative drop cap 'I' (translated from the Latin 'D' for *Didici*) at the beginning of the text, featuring ornate foliage and scrollwork.</image-desc>

*I have learned that the origin of the present dispute arose when you (O Alexander) asked the priests what each of them felt concerning a certain passage written in the Law—or rather, what they felt regarding a vain portion of a certain question. And you, O Arius, rashly threw out a thought that should never have been conceived in the first place, or, if conceived, should have been consigned to silence. Because of this, discord has emerged between you, the holy mysteries are held in contempt, and the holy people, divided between both sides, are separated from the harmony of the common body. Therefore, let each of you, showing an equal willingness, obey that which your fellow-servant <note>Constantine refers to himself as a "fellow-servant" of God to show humility despite being Emperor.</note> justly advises. For it is neither worthy to ask such things, nor to respond to those who ask. Such questions, which are not proposed by the necessity of some Law, require only the time of useless leisure. And even if they are raised for the sake of intellectual exercise, we ought to keep them enclosed within our own minds and not carry them forward into public assemblies, nor rashly commit them to the ears of everyone. For how many men are there who can either perfectly perceive or worthily interpret the power of such grand and extremely difficult matters? And if someone were able to do this (though it is difficult), how many of the people would he persuade? Or who can endure the subtleties of such great questions without the danger of falling into error? Therefore, loquacity <note>excessive talking</note> must be avoided in such matters, lest perhaps, while our natural weakness fails to explain what is proposed, the minds of the listeners—being too slow of intellect to reach a perfect perception of the question—be led to the necessity of blasphemy or schism. Wherefore, let both the incautious questioning and the improvident response grant equal pardon to one another. For no conflict has been ignited among you on account of a supreme commandment of the Law, nor has any new heresy concerning the religion of God been introduced; rather, you hold one and the same reasoning, just as you also have one sign of communion. For while you contend with one another over very small and trifling causes, it is neither fitting, nor is it believed to be at all lawful, for so great a people of God—whom it is proper to govern by your prayers and wisdom—to be in discord. To remind your wisdom by a small example: You know that even the philosophers themselves are all united in one dogma, yet when they disagree on some part of an opinion, although they are separated by the character of their discipline, they nevertheless agree among themselves for the sake of the unity of the body. Since this is so, how much more is it just for you, the ministers of the Great God, to be in agreement with one another in the purpose of religion? Let us therefore consider with greater reason and think with more ample intelligence whether it is right that, because of small and vain contests of words, brothers should rise against brothers, and the honor of the Council be torn apart by you through impious contention, while you litigate with one another for such small and by no means necessary things. These things are vulgar, and more suited to the follies of children than to the harmony of the intelligence of sacred and wise men. Let us therefore willingly withdraw from the tempta-*

*...from diabolical [snares]: Our great God, the Savior of all, has shone forth a common light to everyone. By His providence, allow this effort of mine—as a servant of God—to reach its completion, so that I may recall you, His people, to synodal communion <note>original: "synodalem communionem"; referring to the formal unity of the Church as expressed in its councils</note> through my address, my ministry, and the persistence of my warning. For (as I have said) there is a certain single faith among you, and according to your own views, a single understanding of heresy; the precept of the Law with all its parts tends toward the purpose of a single will. Therefore, this matter which has stirred up contention between you, since it does not pertain to the power of the whole Law, should not cause a separation and sedition among you. I say these things not as if forcing you to agree in every way with this question—whatever its nature or quality may be. For the honor of the Council <note>meaning the collective body of church leadership</note> can be kept intact by you, and one and the same communion can be preserved for all, even if some small contention arises among you individually regarding a minor point. For we do not all desire the same thing in every matter, nor is there only one nature or one single will known among you. Regarding divine providence, let there be one faith, one providence, and one sense of God among you. But as for these frivolous questions debated between you, even if they are not reconciled into a single opinion, they ought to remain within the mind, with the ineffable nature of the thought preserved. Let the chief sacrament of our common charity, the faith of truth, and honor toward God and the religion of the Law remain unshaken among us. Return therefore to one another in friendship and grace; give back your embraces to all the people. Cleansing yourselves as if they were your own souls, recognize each other once more. For friendships are often sweeter when they are restored to harmony after causes of enmity. Therefore, give back to me peaceful days and secure nights, so that the joy of pure light and the gladness of a now-quiet life may be preserved for me. If not, I shall be forced to groan, and be perpetually weighed down by tears, and no longer find the light of day pleasing to behold. For it is time that the people of God—that is, my fellow servants—who are so unjustly and harmfully divided by your contention, be gathered together. Hear this, so that you may feel the magnitude of my sorrow: When I came previously to the city of Nicomedia <note>A significant imperial city in modern-day Turkey, where Constantine stayed before moving the capital to Constantinople</note>, I was hurrying to proceed quickly to the East. And while I was heading toward you and was already with you in spirit for the most part, I was held back by the news of this matter, lest I be compelled to see with my eyes what I judged impossible to reach my ears. Therefore, through your concord, open for me the paths to the East, which you have closed by your mutual contention. Quickly grant me the sight of yourselves and all other peoples rejoicing, and allow me to offer due thanks to God in favorable words for the common concord and liberty of all.*

## PREFACE TO THE FOURTH VOLUME.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut drop cap 'A' containing a landscape scene with hills and trees.</image-desc>

<margin>
James 2.
Chapter 4.
Colossians 4.
2 Corinthians 10.
</margin>
AFTER the uncultivated and neglected field of those practicing philosophy has been prepared and re-tilled; after the barren and rocky ground of the younger Jews has been cleared; and after the thorny field of certain wandering believers has been purged of thistles and weeds—it remains for me now to approach the fertile field of the faithful and devoted, to irrigate and enrich it. This field will be watered more abundantly when it has been adapted, with diligent care and study, to the spring of the super-celestial waters. Indeed, it will be more exquisitely prepared when the worker of the external labor performs everything in this dry and mortal soil—not according to the earthly sense and the letter, which kills—but rather through spiritual and mystical intelligence. For the letter (because it turns away and distracts from the heavenly life) kills; but the Spirit (as the Apostle says) gives life, and restores the soul to the origin of eternal life. Therefore, the greater the diligence and persistence with which one exercises the mind on higher things and fixes one's gaze there, the more copiously do the heavenly streams drip and irrigate, and God, the <term>Celestial Farmer</term> <note>original: "coelestis Agricola"; the central metaphor of Riccius’s work, portraying God as a gardener and spiritual study as cultivation</note>, generously gives the increase. 

However, the fragile and earthly condition of mortals does not know how to carry out this constant meditation and stability—or permanence of the mind—in higher things (as I have explained more extensively in the first and third Volumes), unless one looks upon the super-celestial patterns within these works of the flesh (without which human life and society cannot stand or be preserved). One must view them as if in a thin likeness and a shadowy image of the archetype, contemplating the commands of the eternal Law with unceasing thought. Otherwise, these earthly works separate and distract the soul from the rivulets of super-celestial waters and from the very origin of eternity. As James says: *But he who looks into the perfect Law of liberty and remains in it, being not a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work, this man shall be blessed in his deed.* 

Therefore, the happiness of the external work easily depends mostly upon this (if you consider it): that the doer of the work (like one looking into a mirror) looks forward to the exemplary Law of perfect liberty and remains in it. The Apostle, in the letter to the Galatians, calls this Law—through allegory or <term>Cabala</term> <note>original: "Cabalā"; Riccius uses this term to mean a tradition of mystical or allegorical interpretation of Scripture</note>—the heavenly testament and our free mother, who is the Jerusalem above. If, therefore, the worker of the deed looks less upon that Law of perfect liberty (of which this Law of commandments has a shadow, as is written to the Hebrews), and does not remain in it, he will surely be unhappy and wretched in his labor. For he who does not set God (as the Psalmist warned) before his sight and at his right hand, his soul soon slips, tends toward the precipice, and falls. For this reason, the Herald of Truth <note>meaning St. Paul</note> says: *Whatever you do in word or in deed, do all in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.* And the Apostle in 2 Corinthians 10 says: *Walking in the flesh, let us not war or work according to the flesh.* 

Those who use allegory know best how to perform and teach these things. They refer and raise every external work—and indeed all the words and elements of the sacred discourse—to the heavens. Thus, through this Law of working and contemplating, as if through celestial hoes and plowshares, the watchful tiller of the field digs into and clears this parched and dry soil, transplanting it to the rivulets and streams of super-celestial waters. From there, it brings forth fruit more abundantly in its own time, and its leaves (as the Psalmist sings) shall not wither, and whatever he does shall prosper. We, therefore, for the right and clearer understanding of this doctrine, have composed this fourth Volume on Celestial Agriculture, by which the student of faith and secret truth may be able to cultivate his fertile field more diligently, bring forth richer fruit, and fulfill it in deed and work, with the help and increase of God, the Celestial Farmer, to whom be glory and blessing forever.

This present Volume, then, embraces two things. First, it proposes an introduction, which, if neglected, no one will easily be able to reach a true and secret recognition of the teachings of the Cabalists or those who use allegory. It clearly shows what the name "Cabala" designates, what its necessity and goal are, by what reasoning it excels other doctrines, what its method and order of teaching are, and finally, what its primary parts are. Second, it adds a paraphrase and epitome concerning the sacred names and their attributes. I have rescued these from the library of the deluded Jews (like a most brilliant torch snatched from the hand of a blind man carrying a light) to be handed over to the enlightened minds of the faithful. I have touched upon them in a brief summary, through which the approach to the inner chambers of sacred discourse and the mysteries of the divine names will easily lie open. From this, any perceptive and diligent cultivator of Christian piety will be able, with little trouble, to be initiated into the doctrine of those who use allegory, and in it to profit and be instructed, by the help of divine grace and the nourishing, undivided Trinity. Having invoked its sublime and ineffable name, at which every knee bows, we begin the first part of this Volume. First, however, I have chosen to place here the following speech against a detractor of the Cabala, which brings no small light of understanding to the present task.
