# AN APOLOGETIC ORATION BY PAUL RICCIUS
## AGAINST A DETRACTOR OF THE
### CABALA.

<margin>Romans 14</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial P depicting a figure (likely Saint Paul) holding a sword in one hand and an open book in the other.</image-desc>Paul, the wise architect of faith and the supreme teacher of the life of mortals, warned very diligently and indeed by divine prompting: "Let us follow the things that make for peace, and let us guard one another in the things that make for edification" <note>original: "Quæ pacis sunt sectemur, & quæ ædificationis sunt, inuicem custodiamus"; a paraphrase of Romans 14:19</note>, removing the stones of offense and fitting them so that they may be part of the structure of the temple of the Lord, and making the members of a harlot into members of Christ. This is achieved by refuting those who wander and those who fight against God through sound doctrine—that which is according to piety—and by pointing out the path of eternal salvation. Indeed, every doctrine is according to piety which provides lessons of secret truth and holiness of life, and which either builds up or does not reject the foundations of the orthodox faith. He who despises such doctrine and strives to attack it, "languishing" (as the Apostle says) "concerning questions and battles of words and conflicts of men corrupted in mind," will certainly not be a listener of Christ or of Apostolic teaching, but a contaminator of the temple of the Lord and a corrupter of human salvation. 

Among all foreign and hidden <note>original: "Apocrypha"</note> teachings, none so clearly hands down the lessons of eternal truth and purity of life, and is equally consistent with orthodox piety, and is able to resist those who contradict from the "circumcision" <note>meaning Jewish scholars who did not accept Christ</note> and lead them to a clear acknowledgment of the truth, as the learning of the ancient Allegorizers, called the Cabala <note>Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition</note>. Its primary practitioners were undoubtedly the first Hebrews who were listeners of Christ and who embraced his sacred teaching and the piety of faith, yet remained zealots 
<margin>Chapter 21</margin>
for the paternal Law. As it says in the Acts of the Apostles: "You see, brother, how many thousands of Jews there are who have believed, and they are all zealots for the Law" <note>Acts 21:20</note>. Since there is no hidden teaching that so skillfully and easily directs all human acts and thoughts toward the heavens, and turns them toward the eternal and unchanging good itself, as this very tradition of the Cabalists (ancient indeed, but recently brought to light), it has pleased certain men of sublime genius, integrity, and learning to reveal something of this doctrine to the faithful and to Christians of sincere mind. These men include Mirandolano <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a famous Italian Renaissance philosopher who integrated Kabbalah into Christian thought</note>, a prince among the wise and the unique oracle of our age; and also Capnion <note>Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a German humanist and Hebrew scholar who used the pseudonym 'Capnion'</note>, distinguished for his faith, honesty, and varied learning. It also seemed right to me, as the newest worker and smallest member of the body of Christ, so that the doctrine of our Savior might be honored in all things (according to the Apostle's instruction), even among the unbelieving Jews, to write an <term>Isagogen</term> <note>Introduction; from the Greek 'eisagoge'</note> to this teaching and to translate its summary into the Latin tongue. 

However, I have heard that this work is being attacked, both meanly and shamefully, by a certain Master of Sacred Letters and Theological Wisdom named Hohenstratus <note>Jacob van Hoogstraten (c. 1460–1527), a Dominican inquisitor and fierce opponent of Reuchlin and the study of Hebrew texts</note>, who clings to contentious and frivolous word-battles. He proclaims it to be "playful perfidy," whereby he does not hesitate to profane the secrets of sacred speech and the solid testimonies of Christian piety, and to touch the pious doctrine and sincere faith of the best men with the brand of execrable treachery. I could hardly restrain my spirit, nor keep the silence of my tongue or pen, from weaving this brief oration against the man's criminal and useless censorship. Through this, a sincere and sharp-sighted seeker of secret things may clearly judge how inconsiderately and petulantly this man accuses the teaching of the Cabalists or allegorizers, and condemns it with a headlong judgment. For anyone handling their vast volumes can easily see how great and solid the testimonies for the faith this Cabalistic doctrine provides. Indeed, they state the mystery <note>original: "sacramentum"</note> of the Trinity in unity quite clearly: of the Father, the Son, and the Spirit; and of the only-begotten...

...begotten by eternal generation, concerning original sin, by which death entered the world, concerning redemption through the passion and blood of the Messiah, concerning his resurrection, concerning the Virgin, the nourishing Queen of Heaven, concerning the mystical body of the Church—in which the saints are the temple of God and the members of Christ—concerning the Judgment and the consummation of the world, concerning repentance and the remission of sins, concerning the resurrection of the dead, and concerning the gift of prophecy, knowledge, and wisdom. It treats of Allegory and the spiritual sense of sacred speech, by which the <term>Cabala</term> <note>The Kabbalah; Riccius argues that Jewish mystical traditions contain the same truths as Christian doctrine.</note> itself raises not only the words and individual elements of the words, but even the <term>tittles and points</term> <note>original: "apices, puncta"; referring to the small decorative strokes and vowel markings in Hebrew script</note> and whatever is added to them, toward sublime and divine oracles. From this, the human mind is exercised and established in heavenly matters through constant meditation. Furthermore, it hands down teachings concerning the power of languages and healings, the angelic hierarchy, and clean and unclean spirits.

And indeed, the Kabbalist performs this through three various modes of consideration; those who are unable to judge and discern between these modes involve themselves in inextricable knots of ambiguity and error. One of these modes of consideration is that which the context of the words and the literal understanding requires. Another is what the type of allegory demands. Yet another is that which the striving for prophecy and for clinging to the heavens requires. 

First, for example, in the first chapter of Genesis, the context of the letters and words requires us to seek the reason and cause why, in the works of the beginning, that unutterable <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter name of God (YHWH), often considered too sacred to pronounce.</note> name is nowhere mentioned, nor any of the holy names except that one which is also usually shared with creatures: the name <term>Elohim</term>. We read this name repeated thirty-two times <note>original: "bis & trigesies"; the number 32 is significant in Kabbalah, representing the '32 Paths of Wisdom.'</note> in those works of the beginning, even though creation is the work of the Creator God alone, to whom the unutterable name Tetragrammaton properly belongs. However, when the second chapter resumes the generation of heaven and earth, it prefixes the name Tetragrammaton to the name Elohim. "These," it says, "are the generations of the heaven and the earth when they were created in the day that the <term>Tetragrammaton God</term> <note>original: "tetragrammaton Deus, Elohim"; usually translated as "the LORD God."</note> made the heaven and the earth." And so thereafter, through the whole second and third chapters of Genesis, these two sacred names are brought forward as one. 

And although both designate the same essence of supreme simplicity, they do not announce the same aspect of that essence, nor the same condition of human understanding. Just as the name <term>El Shaddai</term> <note>original: "El sadai"</note> (that is, God) indicates this same essence in its incomprehensible unity—meaning "He who is sufficient" or "the Almighty"—the name Tetragrammaton shows the same. Yet, the name El Shaddai was made known to the Patriarchs, while the name Tetragrammaton remained hidden from them, according to that passage in Exodus: "I appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as <margin>Chapter 6.</margin> El Shaddai; my name Tetragrammaton (spoken and pronounced as <term>Adonai</term> <note>Riccius notes the Jewish practice of substituting "Adonai" (Lord) when reading the four-letter name YHWH.</note>) I did not indicate"—or more correctly, "I was not known to them by it." 

By this same law, one must judge each of the sacred names of God, searching for the cause why the Prophet now explains the name <term>Ehyeh</term> <note>original: "EHEIE"; the name "I AM" from Exodus 3:14.</note>, now the name <term>Yah</term> <note>original: "Ioh"</note>, and very often invokes the Tetragrammaton with the vowel points of Adonai, and sometimes with the points of Elohim. As in that saying of Moses: "Abraham said, Adonai, Elohim (Lord God), what will you give me?" Furthermore, many times he prays using the name <term>El</term> to obtain one vow, the name Elohim for another, the name <term>Sabaoth</term> <note>original: "Zeuaos"</note> for that one, <term>Shaddai</term> for this, and the name Adonai. No suitable searcher of sacred speech would be ignorant that the reasons and causes for these and similar distinctions must be sought. For even those who contemplate physical bodies and the natures of sensible things examine every small portion and the slightest accidents among them, seeking reasons and causes everywhere. Therefore, with a far more accurate zeal of diligence, the parts of that sacred speech—inscribed forever in the divine mind—must be inspected, their utterances examined, and every single element discerned. 

But reason itself demonstrates that, besides the literal sense, a spiritual understanding is given in every declaration of the Prophets. For first, we have it from the Law that we should "cleave to God." But no one can exactly cleave to God unless he knows God perfectly—that is, unless he knows all His works perfectly. Therefore, we know all the works of God from the Law; but because this does not happen through the literal sense, it is therefore necessary that beyond it...

# PAUL RICCIUS,

...the other remaining mode is the Allegorical. Furthermore, all the oracles of the Prophets have been inscribed in the divine mind from eternity. For the Prophets (as was the view of Augustine in his work *On Free Will*) read from the <term>Book of Life</term> <note>original: "libro vitae"; a biblical concept of a record of those destined for heaven, here used by Riccius to represent the divine blueprint of reality.</note>. It is well established that the things contained in the Book of Life are not uttered by a mortal voice nor recorded by a human pen—things which would be subject to perpetual decay and the changing of time and place—but rather, the writings of that Book are certain paradigms and <term>Ideas</term> <note>Riccius uses the Platonic concept of "Ideas" to explain how the Hebrew scriptures reflect eternal truths.</note>. These correspond to these fleeting voices and letters as models and eternal reasons inscribed in the divine mind. To these, the Allegorizing Kabbalist and the spiritual contemplator of sacred speech is most especially vigilant; his entire business and study revolves around them. 

This is plainly what the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> taught in his letter to the Galatians, declaring two testaments through allegory: one handed down on Mount Sinai, which is joined to the earthly and enslaved Jerusalem; the other given on the holy mountain, joined to that Jerusalem which is above, which is free and is our mother. The Kabbalists recount this very mystery of the Apostle in many places, though all who are profane are certainly far from a true understanding of it. 

It is clear, therefore, that beyond the literal sense of the Law there is another Allegorical or Kabbalistic sense, of which the literal sense is like an image. For the literal sense is entangled in the conditions of place and time; but the Allegorical and Kabbalistic sense pertains to eternal things, without any condition of time or place. 

To the literal and allegorical understanding of sacred letters, a third kind of contemplation is added, providing a <term>practical</term> <note>original: "practicam"; referring to the "Practical Kabbalah," which involves meditative techniques to achieve spiritual effects or insights.</note> rather than a theoretical action. By this, the imagination, reason, and mind—each in its own way—adhere to the things above. Through this adhesion, the gift of prophecy, the power of tongues and healings, and the spirit of interpretation, knowledge, and wisdom are infused in various distributions. According to this, different people may look to one gift more than another and strive for it, following that word of the Apostle: <note>original: "Aemulamini charismata meliora"; 1 Corinthians 12:31</note> *Earnestly desire the better spiritual gifts; but as for speaking in tongues, do not forbid it.*

However, the adhesion of the human mind to the things above requires the purity of those who adhere, and a correspondence and harmony between them and the eternal truth to which they cling. The Kabbalists—and those whom Scripture calls the "sons of the Prophets"—strive to achieve this by meditating on the sacred letters: namely, by contemplating their number, shape, position, permutation, combination, and the like, and by referring and raising these things to the heights and to the <margin>☞</margin> mysteries of eternal truth. 

This is not because the Kabbalist believes such interpretations everywhere represent the exact intended meaning of the Prophets and of sacred speech, but he intends this one thing: that through this harmonious and reciprocal exercise of the imagination, reason, and mind, the powers of the soul may be stripped of earthly thought, raised to the things above, and cling to them. 

And for this reason (if you take notice), the Kabbalists disagree in many ways in this genre of <term>glosses</term> <note>interpretive comments or annotations</note>; some meditate on the number, others the shape, and several on the position, permutation, and combination in manifold ways, thereby exercising the powers of the soul. For this reason, many of the younger students—no less among the Jews than among the Christian faithful—who study the teachings of the Kabbalists or Allegorizers, fail to notice the power situated in this kind of contemplation. They marvel at this discordant law of interpretation and involve themselves in many various and useless petty questions. They mistakenly take this third kind of contemplation for the second or first, thinking that everything explained by this very type of meditation tends toward the true understanding of the letter or the allegory, just like the first and second kinds of contemplation. In this, they wander far and stray from the right path, failing to notice that although the individual discoveries of this kind are harmonious and altogether necessary, the Kabbalists do not consider it necessary that the Prophet intended that specific meaning in that place in a literal or allegorical sense. 

For example, in contemplating the elements of the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter name of God, YHWH.</note>: some affirm that the letter <term>Yod</term> <note>The first letter of the Name, י.</note> was placed first among the letters of the Tetragrammaton because, by representing an indivisible point and unity, it designates the indivisible essence of the highest unity. Others suppose it is first for this reason: because it shows the number ten in units; which number ten is a certain unity, embracing the entire scope of numbers in its power, the beginning...

...beginning and end. Others, for this reason, presume that it is placed first among the elements of the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH. The first letter is "Iod" or Yod.</note> because, with its slender peak and a tip scarcely perceived by the senses, it announces the divine essence as indivisible and incomprehensible. The number ten <note>original: "denarius"; the letter Iod has the numerical value of 10.</note>, however, suggests the ten <term>Sephiroth</term> <note>The ten emanations or attributes in Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself.</note>: namely, the three persons of the divine essence and the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. Although these and similar things are discovered to be mysteries of solid truth—namely, that the divine essence is a supreme unity and simplicity, the beginning and the end, incomprehensible and threefold in persons, and that it is necessary for the gifts of the Spirit to be given—nevertheless, they do not think it is entirely necessary to believe that the Prophet intended to teach and suggest these things primarily through the letter *Iod* itself. We must judge in a similar way regarding other meditations of this kind, which are devised not so much for the understanding of the letter or the allegory, but solely for the purpose of exercising or preparing the soul and out of a desire for adhering to the things above. 

<margin>❀</margin> Therefore, whoever attends to this threefold genus of contemplating the Scriptures upon which the Kabbalists lean, and considers those testimonies of the orthodox faith and the most soul-healing lessons of life and good morals provided in them, and desires (by the Apostle's command) the doctrine of our Savior to be built up and honored in all things—such a person will certainly not presume the dogma of the Kabbalists to be a mockery or treacherous. Instead, they will extol it with celebrated praise and heraldry, and embrace and cherish it as a doctrine of piety. For it tends toward this one goal: to lift the souls of mortals from the fleeting shadows of this falling world to the celestial and immortal powers, and to lay open the way of eternal salvation.

Indeed, those things by which that rigid and fierce <term>Scourge of Kabbalah</term> <note>original: "Cabalæ oppugnator" or "Cabalæomastix"; a term for a dedicated critic or "whipper" of Kabbalah.</note> strives to blunt that dogma and persuade others of its "treachery"—how inconsiderate they are and unworthy of a wise man is easily recognized by anyone looking closely. To be silent about the many vain things which this man records to the shame and confusion of the Kabbalists in his fictional commentaries on "Kabbalistic treachery" (as he prattles), so that I do not occupy the kind ears of the reader with frivolous and less-than-fruitful readings, I have decided to bring forward only three points. These are the three upon which he himself chiefly leans in his epistolary preface to the Supreme Pontiff, **Leo X**, to refute Kabbalah as a blasphemous heresy and a mocking treachery. Once we have proven these to be vain and invalid, the nullity of his other arguments can be clearly judged.

First, therefore, this man lists as an error the idea that Abel, Abraham, Isaac, David, and also certain other Fathers before the flood, thought that they themselves, or someone from their offspring born of male and female seed, would be manifested as the restorer of the world. 

Second, that a divine revelation was made to the first parent <note>Adam</note> more after his ruin and fall than before, and that the light of grace shone more in him when he was already a transgressor than while he acted as an innocent. 

Third, that Adam and Eve burned with a mutual itch, filled with a procreative desire—a sudden and brutal itch that would have been more appropriate for cattle than for humans still perfected in the state of innocence. 

These are the points by which that man busies himself most to convict Kabbalah itself as a certain mocking and blasphemous heresy; however, how much they fail both in reality and in the form of the argument can be clearly seen from what follows. It brings me no small wonder what confidence and presumption allows someone to judge with such a headlong opinion and to condemn without fear that of which he is ignorant—not only of its foundations, but even of the force of the voice and the word. For there has never been any of the faithful who attained even the first rudiments of this dogma without cherishing and venerating it as a pious, secret doctrine consistent with the orthodox faith. The only author of this detraction has been unskillfulness and a puffed-up ignorance of the secret truth. 

Moreover, that this "Scourge of Kabbalah" wanders from the path in his very form of arguing is easily established by this: even if we were to call those three mentioned points (and other similar Kabbalistic lessons) erroneous and mocking, and even if we admitted that the Kabbalah of <term>Capnio</term> <note>A reference to Johann Reuchlin (1455–1522), whose Greek-derived nickname was "Capnio." He was the primary proponent of Christian Kabbalah in the Renaissance.</note> had said something wrongly (which I would by no means say), it is nonetheless not right to conclude from that that the dogma of the Kabbalists should be called a mocking treachery and a pestilential...

...spreading errors: just as it would be cursed and unspeakable to argue that because <term>Peter Lombard’s</term> <note>A 12th-century theologian whose book, the *Sentences*, was the standard textbook for medieval theology students.</note> book of *Sentences* (around which the entire machine of younger theologians turns as if on a hinge) deviates in many points from the true and common consensus of theologians, therefore the volumes of the *Sentences* and the dogmas of the theologians must be erroneous; so indeed it is a crude and equivocal quibble to say that <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>The Jewish mystical tradition. Riccius argues that true Kabbalah is a divine science, even if individual writers make mistakes.</note> is a "playful perfidy" <note>original: "ludicram esse perfidiam Cabalam"</note> because some writer of Kabbalah might announce certain things discordant with the truth or erroneous. For an "erroneous Kabbalah" is not Kabbalah at all, just as it is not right to call "false wisdom" by the name of wisdom. 

Furthermore, it is readily apparent to any intelligent person that this detractor not only reasons with false logic but also assumes false premises. For he presumes that it is a blasphemous heresy to attribute any ignorance regarding the inner secrets of the faith to any of the Holy Fathers and Prophets who flourished before the times of the <term>Incarnation</term> <note>The Christian doctrine that God became human in the person of Jesus Christ.</note>. No wise theologian is ignorant of how false and vain this presumption is. These theologians (as we mentioned in the second volume) feel with one mind that before the presence of Christ the Lord in the flesh, the articulated mystery of the incarnation was not known even to the ministering angels—through whom the ray of divine things is spread to us—much less to the Holy Fathers 

<margin>Ephesians 3</margin>
and Prophets, according to that word of the Apostle: *In other generations the mystery of Christ was not known, as it has now been revealed to his holy Apostles and Prophets.* <note>Quoting Ephesians 3:5. Riccius uses this to argue that revelation is progressive.</note> For if the first of the saints had known exactly the sacraments of faith and the incarnation, or the manner of the Savior being born of a Virgin, their silence would surely have to be attributed to the vice of negligence and ingratitude. They would have uttered that truth (upon which the redemption and eternal salvation of men depends) in such obscure and doubtful sentences, rather than teaching what they knew plainly and clearly. They would have rescued the poor and miserable children of Eve from such a great danger of conflicting opinions and heresies; and yet divine mercy wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. 

Indeed, the least of the disciples of Christ the Lord, after the <term>Paraclete</term> <note>The Holy Spirit.</note> spirit shone forth, penetrated the divine oracles with a clearer understanding than the Prophets—the authors of the prophecies themselves—and those who were holy from the beginning. For before the presence of Christ and the Holy Spirit, it was (as Isaiah says) like a vision of all things, like the words of a sealed book.

<margin>Chapter 12</margin>
As Daniel says: *The words are closed and sealed up until the pre-appointed time.* <note>Quoting Daniel 12:9.</note> 

<margin>John chapter 20</margin>
According to that in John chapter 20: *For they did not yet know the Scripture, that it was necessary for him to rise from the dead.* 

<margin>Luke chapter 24</margin>
And that of Luke 24: *Then he opened their minds, so that they might understand the Scriptures.* For the Spirit, the Paraclete (as John writes), *whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things.* 

Hence, Saint Gregory affirms that the knowledge of the saints grew with the increase of time, and the further away they were from the Savior’s coming, the less they perceived the sacraments of salvation. For this reason, in the seventh book of *The City of God*, <term>Augustine</term> <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most influential Western Church Fathers.</note> asserted that many spoke words of prophecy regarding the mystery of the incarnation which they themselves nonetheless did not know would actually happen. For none of the Holy Fathers, even if they did not clearly perceive every detail of the sacraments of the resurrection, held any of these things in contempt. It is one thing to think of a matter in a diminished way, and another to think of it perversely; for a diminished belief does not exclude the truth, whereas a false opinion does. He does not think perversely who believes a restorer of the world is given through the passion and blood of an innocent person, even if he does not contemplate the mode of his birth from a Virgin. But he believes falsely and toward his own destruction who rejects the birth from a Virgin and plainly despises it. 

Having seen all these things, it will be easy to understand that he commits no heresy or pestilent error who asserts: that Abel, Isaac, and other saints, before the incarnation of the Word, thought that they themselves, or someone else born from their own lineage and physical seed, would be revealed as the restorer of the world, because they did not consider nor understand the mode of the incarnation and redemption. 

The second point, by which that fierce attacker accuses the tradition of the Kabbalists...

<summary>Riccius defends Kabbalah against charges of heresy by arguing that spiritual knowledge is revealed progressively over time. He maintains that the Old Testament Patriarchs had true faith even if they lacked a modern, detailed understanding of the Incarnation.</summary>

enough; namely, the claim that revelation was clearer and more abundant in Adam once he had become a transgressor than while he acted as an innocent, is entirely fictitious. It is utterly foreign to the mind of the <term>Kabbalists</term> <note>Followers of Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition.</note>, who assert with one voice that the innocent "first-formed man" was gifted with a far loftier light of understanding than he possessed after the crime was committed. This is according to the <term>Chagigah</term> <note>original: "Hegiga"; a tractate of the Talmud dealing with Temple offerings and mystical visions.</note>: Adam reached from one end of the world to the other, but when he acted as a transgressor, he was made smaller. And there is the word of the Prince of Kabbalists, <term>Simon</term> <note>Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, the traditional author of the Zohar, the foundational work of Kabbalah.</note>, on Genesis 3, where it is read: *And the eyes of both were opened, and they knew they were naked.* Simon says: "They were opened" to recognize the previously unknown evils of the world; when they knew these, and noticed they were more perceptive in the apprehension of evil, they immediately recognized the guilt of their crime, because they had already lost the supernal splendor that had shone within them and were left naked. These are the words of Rabbi Simon. <term>Moses of Gerona</term> <note>original: "Gerundinus Moses"; also known as Nachmanides, a major 13th-century Jewish scholar.</note> says the same, as the volumes of divine ordinance prove. The commentaries of <term>Menahem</term> <note>Menahem Recanati, an early 14th-century Italian Kabbalist.</note> on the Pentateuch and the authority of all Kabbalists agree. Nor does the Kabbalah of the most learned <term>Capnio</term> <note>The Greek-style pseudonym of Johann Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous Christian Hebraist and supporter of Riccius.</note>, in the context of his words, seem to sound like what the detractor imagines.

As for the third point, which he counts among "pestilential errors and blasphemous heresies"—namely, that Adam and Eve burned with a mutual <term>urge</term> <note>original: "prurigine," literally an "itch" or "stimulation." Riccius is discussing natural physical desire.</note>, filled with generative longing—he asserts this is more fitting for beasts than for humans perfected in the <term>state of innocence</term> <note>The theological term for the condition of humanity before the original sin.</note>. Who, I ask, is so unthinking and such a crude observer of the Sacred Scriptures that he would reject—let alone consider it a blasphemous heresy—that Adam and Eve in the state of innocence were subject to all the affects naturally accompanying human nature, including the moderate and implanted allurements of nature? For even the Restorer of the world himself, the God-man Christ the Lord, willed to endure sadness and joy, sleep, wakefulness, thirst, hunger, and whatever follows the condition of human nature in his assumed body.

A moderate generative urge for the sake of propagation should no more be attributed to shame or vice than the urge of <term>black bile</term> <note>original: "atrae bilis." In ancient "humoral" medicine, black bile in the stomach was thought to trigger the sensation of hunger.</note> (called hunger) at the opening of the stomach for the sake of eating, or the urge of dry humor (which we call thirst) for the sake of drinking. Indeed, the movements of nature that are not ruled by the command of the will argue no crime, especially in a temperate body where nothing is desired except what the order of nature demands. For such a nature (as the Wise Physician says) needs no teacher to measure the quantity of what is offered. "The best nature," he says, "desires only as much as it can digest."

The same law must be judged regarding the act of propagation. In the state of innocence, they were not affected by the urge to propagate unless a proper <term>concoction</term> <note>A term from Galenic medicine referring to the body's processing of fluids and nutrients.</note> and quantity in the "seeds," as well as the proper time, demanded it, accompanied by the right moderation of reason. Neither the authority of Augustine nor Jerome, which he brings forward, prejudices our assertion in any way. For when they teach that the first humans "sowed" in Paradise without "heat," and thus commanded their genitals for propagation just as they commanded their feet for walking, this must be understood as referring to the *exterior* stimulation and the physical adaptation to the marital work, which they judge should not have happened without the command of the will. 

However, they do not think it at all foreign that nature was *inwardly* affected (given a proper balance of the "seeds") by some moderate incitement and generative ardor, just as nature and the order of things demonstrate. For just as food is not taken except by the command of the will—and a right and consulted will commands this least of all unless it senses the exact digestion of previous food—the will would certainly not know this unless the power of nature announced it through the sense of hunger. In the same way, the genitals in that state of innocence would not have adapted themselves to the marital work without the command of the will; but the will would not have commanded it unless the proper "concoction" of the "seeds" had first required it. The will would have perceived this in no way unless some internal natural incitement were felt. Therefore, in this sense, to say that Adam was affected by a generative urge in Paradise detracts nothing from that state of innocence; nor [does it detract from] the sacred

## INTRODUCTORY THEOREMS OF KABBALAH.

<margin>I.</margin> <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>From the Hebrew word meaning "reception."</note> is said to be that faculty which, through the <term>type</term> <note>A symbolic representation or prophetic blueprint.</note> of the Mosaic Law, suggests the secrets of divine and human things in an allegorical sense. It was chosen to be called Kabbalah (that is, "reception") because this manner of suggestion is received by no discourse of reason nor by the pen, but only by hearing and faith.

<margin>II.</margin> That this "type" lies hidden in the Law is demonstrated by the condition of the Lawgiver himself, as well as by the condition of the recipient.

<margin>III.</margin> For the giver of the Law, who is God the creator of all things, since He is eternal and immutable in every way, it is necessary that His speech be everlasting and immutable.

<margin>IIII.</margin> Yet the speech of the Law delivered through Moses and proclaimed to the multitude of the Jews is subject to change and various modes of transformation. Therefore, it is necessary that there be another Law of Moses, far different from the earthly one, belonging to the celestial and true Law of God.

<margin>V.</margin> Wherefore, one must infer that eternal Law of God as an <term>archetype</term> <note>The original pattern or "idea" from which copies are made.</note> and an "Idea" from this Law of commandments, as if from a certain shadowy image.

<margin>VI.</margin> Furthermore, since the recipient of the Law—man—is a <term>microcosm</term> <note>original: "paruus mundus" (small world); the idea that a human being reflects the structure of the entire universe.</note> made according to the condition of the universe and in the image and likeness of God, his perfection and salvation require that he reflect and imitate the <term>macrocosm</term> <note>original: "magnum mundum" (great world/universe).</note> and his Creator through deed and work.

<margin>VII.</margin> He will imitate Him, however, if he moderates his actions by a conforming and similar Law to that by which the world is ruled, and through which the Maker of things Himself founded and governs the universe.

<margin>VIII.</margin> Just as man, the microcosm, represents the likeness and image of the supreme Creator and the whole world at once, so it is fitting that the Law of this same microcosm should announce the eternal Law of the macrocosm. This could not be delivered and taught in the Law from any other source than through allegory and mystical understanding, which is Kabbalah.

<margin>IX.</margin> Although this dogma of the Kabbalists lies disorganized and as if under a certain ancient rust—owing to the ignorance and mental dullness of the younger Jews—nevertheless, in itself, it surpasses and far excels the tradition of many other allegorizers in authority, erudition, and also in the ease of adapting the mortal mind to the kingdoms of heaven.

<margin>X.</margin> It excels in authority because, just as Moses was the first proclaimer of the divine Law, so he was (undoubtedly) the explainer of its secret understanding. Since he was the greatest of all Prophets, his authority ensures that his tradition is to be preferred far above that of other allegorizers.

<margin>XI.</margin> It also excels in erudition because it considers the principles and elements of all divine and human things, one by one, connects them gradually, and reveals them in their proper order. We have not known this to be delivered so exactly by any of the allegorical interpreters until now.

<margin>XII.</margin> It excels also in the ease of adapting the soul to the kingdoms of heaven: for it opens the way and shows the path by which he who desires the celestial life may render himself conforming to the nature of the heavens and to the image of the <term>indivisible Trinity</term> <note>Ricius, as a Christian, interprets the goals of Kabbalah through the lens of the Christian Trinity.</note>, without an anxious, wandering, and stumbling investigation of reason.

<margin>XIII.</margin> Of this dogma, one part is theoretical, which considers the innermost secrets of things to be contemplated; the other part is active, which adapts the mind and the powers of the body for obtaining spiritual gifts and the comforts of this life.

<margin>XIIII.</margin> The theoretical part (just like other types of doctrines) announces higher things through the lowest, and hidden things through those more known to us.

He argues that man, as a microcosm, must use this knowledge to align himself with the divine macrocosm and the Trinity.</summary>

<margin>XV.</margin>
The things we discover through clear and constant experience in the most noble subjects are more familiar to us: from this, we see that all the commandments of the Law respond precisely, in number and proportion, to the parts of the human frame.

<margin>XVI.</margin>
For since man is threefold—existing at a great distance and distinction from one another as the **archetypal**, the **celestial**, and the **terrestrial**—the Law itself clearly outlines each of these. <note>Ricius is using the "Macrocosm-Microcosm" theory, where the human body reflects the structure of the entire universe (the "Celestial" world of stars and the "Archetypal" world of Divine ideas).</note>

<margin>XVII.</margin>
For just as any of these "men" consists of male and female, so also the Law (in its own way) embraces both the male and the female.

<margin>XVIII.</margin>
In the Law, the first four volumes of the <term>Pentateuch</term> <note>The first five books of the Bible: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers.</note> take the place of the male; however, the fifth volume, <term>Deuteronomy</term>, suggests the type of the female.

<margin>XIX.</margin>
The senses judge the male and female of the **terrestrial man** by their appearance and the variety of their functions; from there, through a similar relationship of actions, we ascend to the naming and cognition of the parts of the other two "men" in the highest realms.

<margin>XX.</margin>
The more brilliant machinery of the heavens represents the male of the **celestial man**; whereas the lunar globe, along with the elemental structure and the internal organs contained within it, represents the female.

<margin>XXI.</margin>
The male of the **archetypal man** is the sublime choir of angels; its female, however, is the "queen" or the heavenly host, which we have chosen to call the <term>animastic order</term>. <note>From the Latin "animasticum," referring to the realm of souls or the vitalizing principle of the world.</note>

<margin>XXII.</margin>
If you look at the male and female of each of these "men" separately, you will find each is composed of nine primary members. But if you consider the male with the female, and the female with the male as one (as they truly are), then you will clearly perceive that each of these "men" (just like the Law itself and the most sacred Names of God) is joined together by ten primary members.

<margin>XXIII.</margin>
The primary and eternal members of the Law are ten: the perpetually observed commandments of the <term>Decalogue</term>. <note>The Ten Commandments.</note>

<margin>XXIIII.</margin>
The members of the **terrestrial man**, which both perpetuate the species and preserve the individual, are also counted as ten: namely, the brain, lungs, heart, stomach, liver, gall [bladder], spleen, kidneys, the genitals, and the womb with its appendages.

<margin>XXV.</margin>
So too, the primary members of the **celestial man** announce ten parts: the intellectual or <term>Empyrean heaven</term> <note>The highest heaven, believed in medieval cosmology to be the abode of God and pure fire/light.</note>, the First Mover, the firmament, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon with the "viscera" contained within its sphere.

<margin>XXVI.</margin>
The members of the **archetypal man** are the ten orders of angels, which they call by the Hebrew names: *Haias Hakadesch* <note>Chayot HaKodesh/Holy Living Creatures</note>, *Offanim* <note>Wheels</note>, *Erelim* <note>Valiant ones</note>, *Hasmalim* <note>Glowing ones/Amber</note>, *Seraphim* <note>Burning ones</note>, *Malachim* <note>Messengers/Kings</note>, *Elohim* <note>God-like beings</note>, *Bene elohim* <note>Sons of God</note>, and *Cherubim*. The sacred school of theologians calls these orders: Seraphim, Cherubim, Thrones, Dominations, Virtues, Powers, Principalities, Archangels, and Angels. The tenth order is that which the <term>Kabbalists</term> <note>original: "Cabalei"</note>, along with many ancient theologians and Peripatetic [Aristotelian] sages, call the "animastic" order, and they name it with the Hebrew word *Ischim* (that is, "men").

<margin>XXVII.</margin>
Finally, all the groups of ten set forth here derive their origin from the ten most holy and exemplary Names of God, and all things look back and tend toward them; that is: *Eheie*, *Iah*, the *Tetragrammaton* pronounced as *Elohim*, *El*, *Eloha*, *Elohim Tetragrammaton Zeuaos*, *Elohim Zeuaos*, *Schadai*, and *Aedonai*. <note>Ricius is listing the ten Hebrew Names of God associated with the Sephirot: Ehyeh, Yah, YHVH, El, Eloah, YHVH Tzabaoth, Elohim Tzabaoth, Shaddai, and Adonai.</note>

<margin>XXVIII.</margin>
The Kabbalists call these ten Names of God the ten **Sephiros** (that is, "numerations"), to each of which they attribute various titles; I bring some of these forward here for the sake of example and clearer understanding.

<margin>XXIX.</margin>
To the **First Sephira** is ascribed the name *Eheie* [I Am], the Supreme Crown, Privation, Father, and Mind.

<margin>XXX.</margin>
To the **Second**, is ascribed the name *Iah*, Wisdom, the First-born Essence, and the Informless.

<margin>XXXI.</margin>
To the **Third**, the *Tetragrammaton* pronounced as *Elohim*, Prudence, the Spirit of God, Jubilee, the Great Trumpet, the Mother-Former, Conversion, the Redemption of the world, and the Life of the world to come.

<margin>XXXII.</margin>
To the **Fourth**, *El*, Grace, Magnificence, the Right Hand, Mercies, and the Higher Waters.

<margin>XXXIX.</margin> Finally, the Kabbalists refer every word and element of the Law and of sacred speech to these ten Sephirotic models. Thus, a wise and diligent seeker of the Scriptures, equipped with this skill for allegorizing, can easily be led by the hand, step-by-step, through the literal sense—as if through a thin image—and be raised up to a mystical and spiritual understanding. This can be clearly seen from the attached summary of the *Gates of Light* <note>original: "Portarum lucis"; a reference to the *Sha'are Orah* by Joseph Gikatilla</note> and various traditions of the Kabbalists.

<margin>XL.</margin> Of the Sephirotic models and the ten names of God, some belong to the Creator in Himself, unrelated to any creatures. Others belong to Him as they regard the creation. The former are the supreme crown, wisdom, and prudence (or understanding), the word, and love—or as we say, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The latter, however, are the remaining seven that follow: namely, the seven gifts that incline outward and constitute the very building of the world.

<margin>XLI.</margin> The Kabbalists call the three higher ones the Father, the Firstborn, and the Spirit of God. They assert that these show a simple and co-equal unity of essence (as stated in the compendium of divine order called the <term>Maereches elohus</term> <note>original: "Maereches elohus"; likely referring to the *Ma'arekhet ha-Elohut*, a 14th-century Kabbalistic text</note> and the following summary). However, they teach that the other seven are distinguished from one another—not because they are actually separate in the divine mind, but because we clearly judge that seven kinds of things exist separately in the creatures in which those models are reflected. Just as, on the other hand, we consider that the three principles of sensible things cannot be separated or disjoined from one another by any condition or force.

<margin>XLII.</margin> For we consider that the three principles of natural things—<term>privation, matter, and form</term> <note>Basic concepts of Aristotelian physics: matter is the "stuff," form is the "structure," and privation is the "absence of a form" that allows for change.</note>—are distinguished by a wide gap, yet we conclude that none of them can be given or exist separately, but they constitute one and the same corporeal nature. But the body itself, as well as the elements, minerals, plants, animals, rational beings, and intellectual beings—we find that each of these exists apart and acts by itself.

<margin>XLIII.</margin> These ten Sephirotic models (as the Gerundian Rabbi Moses <note>Moses ben Nahman, also known as Nachmanides</note>, the commentator Rachanates <note>Menachem Recanati</note>, and the compendium of divine order discuss) were grasped with a clear intuition by the first Adam as long as he inhabited the garden of pleasure.

<margin>XLIIII.</margin> But when, at the urging of the serpent and of Eve, he ate from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and "cut the branch from the root" <note>A Kabbalistic metaphor for heresy or causing division within the divine emanations</note>, and separated the "kingdom" from the "foundation," he was then banished from the garden of pleasure with all his offspring. Thus, he was left capable of perceiving only the seven lower Sephiroth. As for the three higher ones (as Rabbi Simeon <note>Simeon bar Yochai</note>, the *Gates of Light*, and the compendium of divine order hand down), no mortal is able to reach or behold them until the venom of the serpent has been removed.

<margin>XLV.</margin> The venom of the serpent is removed—whereby the Law of commandments is also made void—when the "conversion" occurs. This happens when possessions return to their original owner and the servant returns to his own kin. <note>An allusion to the Jubilee year in Leviticus, where debts were forgiven and slaves freed.</note>

<margin>XLVI.</margin> All these things happen when the pipes and channels respond to one another, and the great trumpet of the Jubilee sounds.

<margin>XLVII.</margin> The trumpet sounds when the seven "remissions" <note>The Sabbatical years</note> are completed, and from there the days of the Great Sabbath...

A day follows that has no evening, as testified by Rabbi Moses of Gerona <note>original: "Rabi Moses Gerundensis," also known as Nachmanides (1194–1270), a prominent medieval Jewish scholar and mystic</note>, Rabbi Simeon <note>likely referring to Simeon bar Yochai, the traditional author of the Zohar</note>, the eighth gate of the *Gates of Light* <note>original: "Portarum lucis," a reference to the influential Kabbalistic work *Sha'are Orah* by Joseph Gikatilla</note>, and the compilation of the divine order. <margin>XLVIII.</margin>
When each of these things has been completed, then the restorer of the world—the Messiah, Son of Joseph and Son of David—born of the Virgin, the Queen of Heaven and Gate of Paradise, rising from the dead, shall save the world. <margin>XLIX.</margin>
Finally, upon these things, as if upon a base and foundation, the entire theoretical doctrine of the Kabbalists rests, which is immediately followed by the practical and active part of the Kabbalah.

<margin>L.</margin>
The active doctrine of the Kabbalists (to put it briefly) intends nothing other than to join together the concepts of the mind, the images of the imagination, and the gestures of the body (as if they were the openings of earthly channels) with divine models and with angelic and heavenly powers (as if they were the openings of higher channels). Through this, the skillful follower of faith and piety may, with less anxiety and care, cling to God Himself—the Giver of all good things and the Father of Lights—and attain the benefits of both this world and the world to come with the highest happiness of life.

### APPENDIX TO THE FIRST THEOREM.

<margin>Chapter 72.</margin>
<margin>Chapter 40.</margin>
<margin>Chapter 43.</margin>

<margin>Proverbs 15.</margin>
For whoever wishes to receive the order of the universe (as the Egyptian Rabbi Moses <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the author of the *Guide for the Perplexed*</note> handed down in the second treatise of his *Guide*) from the wise solely by hearing will easily be able to build upon it. For he says that the concern of the Divine Law is to hand down true teachings about God and the order of angels, and thus to educate man so that he may perceive the entire world in its exact order. Often, the speech of the Prophets—using transposed letters <note>A reference to the mystical practice of rearranging the Hebrew alphabet to find hidden meanings</note> and other unusual signs—points to great secrets of wisdom. So he says. From these words, you may gather that the Kabbalistic listener receives and accepts the secrets of truth in two ways. One way is through firm belief, by which he accepts that the dependency and order of the universe actually exists just as the wise Kabbalist describes it. The other way is by accepting without hesitation that Moses himself hinted at this same order of things in the symbolic sense of the Law. This is supported by the authority of Rabbi Moses of Gerona in his commentary on Genesis, which he received from the Talmudists in the Book of Vows (commenting on the Psalm: *And you have made him a little lower than the Gods*). He says: There are fifty gates of understanding <note>original: "ianuæ prudentiæ," referring to the fifty levels of creation leading up to the divine</note>, all of which (save one) were handed down to Moses. The Law itself reveals these either openly or through certain signs, and no one is permitted to explain their meaning to those who are unworthy, and then only by speech, never in writing. Thus says the man from Gerona. By these "gates of understanding," he indicates the levels by which the entire order of things consists. But the "one" which he says was withheld is that third gate among the higher <term>Sephiroth</term> <note>The ten emanations or attributes of God in Kabbalah</note>, to which the name "Understanding" is specifically assigned, and which hints at the Trinity (as you have heard) within the unity of the Creator. Therefore, not even Moses, the greatest of Prophets, was worthy to penetrate this "Pentecostal" and incomprehensible gate of the Trinity. He only surveyed the "back parts" <note>original: "posteriora," referring to Exodus 33:23 where Moses sees God's back but not His face</note> (that is, the entire scope of created things), being faithful in all his house, but not in the One who built it. For He said: *You shall see my back parts, but my face shall not be seen.* But as to what and of what sort those fifty gates or levels and boundaries of things may be, neither the man from Gerona in this place, nor any of the Kabbalists, has openly expressed. For the providence of the first wise men was greatly concerned with covering the secrets of the Law and of reality with a manifold variety of riddles and veils, lest they be contaminated by the arrogance and ignorance of the profane. *Do not reveal secrets to a stranger,* says Solomon. Nor should "pearls be cast before swine," nor (as the Author of Truth <note>Referring to Jesus Christ</note> warned) should "what is holy be given to dogs, lest they turn and tear you to pieces." For he who hands over the hidden things of the Law and of wisdom to an unteachable and profane multitude is like one who releases the chains of a furious and captured wild boar, only to deck him in golden and precious necklaces; for the beast remains fierce and unrestrained.

# PAULUS RICIUS

...then the beast <note>Ricius often uses "belua" (beast) to refer to the unlearned or profane masses who lack spiritual discernment</note> scatters and breaks whatever chance offers to it, and even tramples golden ornaments, polluting them in filthy wallowing-holes; you, who are wise, should consider this. For this reason, the *Synteresis* <note>original: "Synteresis"; here used to describe the preservative wisdom or collective conscience of the ancient sages</note> of the ancients at first committed the Kabbalah to no written letters. But finally, when they saw the Jews being scattered everywhere, they handed down and taught a few things about the Kabbalah—lest it perish entirely—in such a way that it could be perceived and judged by men of insight, wisdom, and integrity, especially those who had previously received a part of this doctrine by oral tradition. At the same time, these things were left veiled and unknown to the profane, according to that praise of Solomon <margin>Proverbs 25</margin> (rendering the text word for word): "Apples of gold in silver carvings," he says, "is a word brought forth in its proper fitness." For to a hallucinating man, such golden apples seem entirely silver; but he who excels in sight and light notices through those very latticed coverings, and perceives the gold that shines and glows within. 

Therefore, the Apostle [Paul], that wise architect relying on "serpentine prudence" <note>A reference to the command in Matthew 10:16 to be "wise as serpents," suggesting Paul used strategic discretion in his teaching</note> (as I opened more extensively in the preceding volume), speaks wisdom only among the perfect; but he feeds the babes with milk and the weak with vegetables. He preaches the Gospel to the nations, but "privately to those who seemed to be something" <margin>Galatians 2</margin>. Wherefore Truth itself [Christ] warned that spiritual gifts must be veiled in parables, so that "seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand." And the Kabbalists say it is most profane if anyone speaks concerning the "Type of the Law" <note>The "Typus Legis" refers to the mystical or symbolic structure underlying the literal commandments of the Torah</note> when more than two or three are listening.

### APPENDIX TO THE SECOND THEOREM.

<margin>Deuteronomy 4</margin> That the secrets of things are suggested through the Law of Moses is shown by various authorities of the wise and the holy. Moses says: "This is your wisdom and understanding before the peoples, who, hearing all these precepts, shall say: 'Behold, a wise and understanding people, a great nation.'" Since wisdom is nothing other than the notion of the highest causes, and intelligence is said to be that by which we grasp the remaining consequences through the known causes of things, it is proven that the mandates of the entire Law suggest the knowledge of the highest causes and the cognition of the things hanging therefrom. To this the Apostle alludes: <margin>Romans 12</margin> "You trust that you yourself are a guide to the blind, a light to those in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of infants, having the form of knowledge and truth in the Law." 

This is also supported by that Talmudic saying which the Egyptian Rabbi Moses <note>original: "Aegyptius Rabi Moses," referring to Moses Maimonides (1135–1204), the famous Jewish philosopher and author of *The Guide for the Perplexed*</note> records in the preface to his *Guide*: "The literal understanding of the Law," he says, "is related to the sense of certainty hidden within it, just as a dark and gloomy house is related to a precious pearl hidden inside it," according to that oracle of Truth: <margin>Matthew 13</margin> "The kingdom of heaven," He says, "is like a treasure hidden in a field, which a man found and hid," etc. Consider these things yourself. 

But here, a trivial argument of the "smatterers" <note>original: "Sciolorum," a disparaging term for those with superficial or pretentious knowledge</note> seems to fight against us: "If that dogma of the Kabbalists," they say, "were of such weight (as you tell) in the sacred words, surely some of the Apostles and ancient sages would have brought it forth, or made mention of it somewhere. But because we read that none of them commemorated anything of this in their writings or sayings, it therefore seems ambiguous, suspicious, and least of all to be admitted." Thus they speak. But you, if you pay attention and correctly consider that reasoning, will find that it not only proceeds erroneously and falsely, but even assumes false and vain fictions. It proceeds falsely because Truth does not depend on human speech; it is not right to say that if a man (however much he excels in wisdom and spirit) does not bring something forth, it does not exist. Rather, on the contrary, a wise man does not speak that which does not exist. Therefore, it is a far too crude and inconsiderate argument to say: "The Apostle does not treat the Kabbalah, nor does he mention it, therefore he rejects and despises the Kabbalah." Just as it is shameful and far to be cursed to say: "Because the Apostle (namely on account of the rudeness of the nations) explains nothing, or not enough, concerning the sacred Virgin Mother of God, or concerning the individual Trinity, therefore they are not to be admitted." Because furthermore, the Apostle, Ambrose, Augustine...

<meta>This page continues Ricius’s argument that the Kabbalah is a valid spiritual tradition, comparing its historical secrecy and "late" emergence to the writings of Dionysius the Areopagite. He asserts that the Apostles practiced Kabbalah under the guise of allegorical interpretation.</meta>

### ON CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE, BOOK IV. <note>The title of Ricius's major work, *De Coelesti Agricultura*, uses a farming metaphor to describe the cultivation of the soul and the study of divine mysteries.</note>

If Jerome, or any of the ancient theologians, says nothing precise about the celestial and angelic hierarchy, which the most extensive volumes of Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher. In the Renaissance, his works were considered foundational for Christian mysticism.</note> now reveal, they should not for that reason be rejected—especially since many of the holy and wise faithful embrace and cherish these very things as celestial oracles. By the same law, one must judge that somewhat crude and vain argument against the Kabbalah. That this very argument adopts false and empty fictions is clearly evident to anyone looking closely: for it proposes that no Apostle, nor any of the first wise men, handed down or even hinted at anything concerning the doctrine of the Kabbalists. This is clearly seen to be false and fabricated by anyone who reads their writings diligently.

Indeed, the anxious concern and care of all the holy and wise men (as you know) aimed chiefly at this one thing: namely, to transfer the entire Law of Moses and the other Sacred Writings of the Prophets from a literal and earthly understanding to an allegorical and spiritual intelligence. As the Apostle [Paul] warned: *The letter kills, but the spirit gives life.* <note>original: "Litera occidit: spiritus autem uiuificat" — a famous quote from 2 Corinthians 3:6, central to the argument for looking beyond the literal meaning of Scripture.</note> Since, therefore, it has pleased them to call this spiritual and allegorical sense of the sacred word "Kabbalah," it is proven by a clear argument that the tradition of the Apostles, and the commentaries and interpretations of the wise and holy men regarding the Divine Scriptures, are occupied with all diligent study around the Kabbalistic doctrine. And therefore, the hater and contradictor assumes false things, being ignorant even of the name of Kabbalah.

Nor should the recent disclosure of this kind of Kabbalistic doctrine move you or make you suspicious, just as the late publication of the Areopagite’s volumes <note>Dionysius's works appeared in the 5th century but were claimed to be from the 1st century; their "late" arrival was a point of historical contention Ricius is addressing.</note> should not. For you know (as I related a little earlier) with what care and skill the provident early sages attempted to veil and cover the mysteries of faith and truth. They did this to guard against exactly what we now experience happening far and wide in this turbulent and miserable time of ours. For this reason, it was not permitted to publish the tradition of the first allegorists (or Kabbalists), just as it was not permitted to publish the monuments of Dionysius and give them to the common people. It was only lawful to open them secretly and under a pact of silence to provident men of wisdom and honest character. This lasted until—after the subsequent disturbance of affairs and the prevailing audacity of the seditious and tyrants—these secret and hidden volumes of the wise reached the hands of street-peddlers and the foolish. These people, out of a lust for profit and vain glory, dared to bring them into public, to violate them, and to corrupt them. 

The result is that now every individual who presumes to have some literacy—even little women, <note>In the 16th-century context, "mulierculae" (little women) was a dismissive term used to suggest that even those traditionally excluded from formal theological education were now debating complex dogmas.</note> butchers, and cobblers, and unrefined farmers—does not fear to argue and assert things about the greatest mysteries of faith, profaning everything with vain and most pernicious entanglements of opinion, leading the multitude of the weak onto a slippery slope and a precipice. 

And therefore, let no wonder seize you that the monuments of Rabbi Simon, <note>Rabbi Simeon bar Yochai, the 2nd-century sage traditionally credited with authoring the Zohar, the foundational work of Jewish Kabbalah.</note> the prince of the Kabbalists, and likewise those of the divine Dionysius, lay hidden for such a long stretch of time in hiding places and the fog of darkness. If you look into the Ecclesiastical histories as well as the histories of the Talmudists, and compare the writings of Dionysius with the doctrine of Rabbi Simon, you will plainly find that both were contemporaries, flourishing around the times of the Lord’s most holy Cross and the destruction of Jerusalem. The dictates of both also treat the secrets of things with an equal tenor and a similar law of contemplation, handing down a spiritual understanding of the sacred word. Their writings also remained hidden for nearly an equal space of years, and came forth into the light at almost the same time. If you pay attention, you will recognize—and you should consider—that this same thing happened (by what rivaling star or what hidden series of causes I know not) to the Justinian sanctions <note>The Code of Justinian, the foundation of Byzantine and later European law.</note> along with the codex of the Talmudists.

is the word of God, and a sharp discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart. <note>original: "est sermo Dei, & efficax discretor cogitationum & intẽtionum cordis" — a reference to Hebrews 4:12.</note> But since God alone, the King and Creator of all things, is the discerner of thoughts, the Word of God must be the same as God himself; and since He is immutable, it is necessary that His word also be immutable. ### APPENDIX TO THE FOURTH AND FIFTH THEOREM.

<margin>Psalm 18.</margin>
<margin>Proverb 12.</margin>
The Law has a shadow <note>original: "Vmbram" — following the Latin Vulgate's terminology for the Old Law as a precursor to the New.</note> (as written in the Epistle to the Hebrews) of the good things to come. He calls these "future goods" celestial and eternal, just as the same epistle declared shortly before, saying: *Those things which serve as a copy and shadow of heavenly things,* namely, of the higher Covenant and Law, which the Apostle in Galatians 4 calls our free and celestial mother, Jerusalem. Concerning this it is written: *The Law of the Lord is immaculate, converting souls.* <note>Psalm 19:7 in modern Bibles; Psalm 18 in the Vulgate.</note> Regarding the other Covenant delivered on Mount Sinai, he adds: *The testimony of the Lord is faithful, providing wisdom to the little ones.* For a testimony provides certainty about a thing not seen, which is received more safely and with more stable faith the more the one who bears the testimony is proven in wisdom and purity of life.

And you, who are wise, understand that faith and firm belief through the testimony of the Prophetic spirit perfect the sincere seeker of truth far more than a syllogistic and argumentative knowledge of a thing. For the condition of the mind that believes a thing through firm apprehension is more excellent and much more sublime than any force of reason, which judges the thing itself through wandering and wavering thought and movement. This is according to that saying of Solomon: *He who is good draws grace from God; but he who trusts in his own thoughts acts impiously.* <note>Proverbs 12:2.</note> For even if reason is a light inscribed in us from the divine light, it is nevertheless so disturbed by phantasms <term>mental images or sensory distractions</term> that unless it is guided by the Prophetic spirit, it always remains weak. Therefore, Solomon says in the same place: *A diligent woman* (that is, enlightened reason) *is a crown to her husband,* etc. 

Hence even the ancient wise men of the Pagans (as the Stagyrite <note>Aristotle, who was born in the city of Stagira.</note> handed down in the last chapter of the second book of *Sophistical Refutations*) thought they could instruct men not by giving them the art itself, but by giving them those things which come from the art. For a farmer inhabits a house built by another more easily and with less expense than one for whom it is worth the labor to build it from the very start of the foundations. I have said this also to prove that the Kabbalistic tradition from the Law of Moses, being taken from the Prophetic spirit, is more certain than the traditions of many philosophers, which flowed from uncertain reason—as you see that all things among philosophers are controversial and uncertain.

### APPENDIX TO THE SIXTH THEOREM.

<margin>Psalm 118, Ephesians 4.</margin>
It is common knowledge in the school of the wise (as you will hear more extensively in what follows) that man is a microcosm <term>a little world</term>, formed according to the condition and likeness of the universe. Because, therefore, man himself carries the image of the whole world in his condition and his "first perfection" (or "first act," as they call it), the logic of his ultimate human perfection requires the imitation and likeness of the operations and acts of the "great world" <note>The Macrocosm or the Universe at large.</note> and its Creator. For the perfection of man seeks for him to adhere to God. But adherence requires a likeness between those adhering, since nothing is a friend unless it is like its like. Whence that passage in Deuteronomy 10: *And now Israel, what does God* (namely the Tetragrammaton <note>The sacred four-letter name of God, YHWH, which Ricius emphasizes here.</note>) *your God ask of you, but that you fear your God and walk in His ways.* For blessed are they (says the Psalmist) who walk in the ways of God, just as they are miserable and lost who, through ignorance (as the Apostle says) and blindness of heart, are alienated from the way of God. And therefore he concludes and commands: *Be imitators of God as most dear children.* Thus also the Kabbalists, by reason of this likeness, all...

<meta>This page continues Ricius’s exploration of the "Eternal Law," moving from the nature of the Word of God to a comparison between the laws governing the universe (macrocosm) and the laws governing humanity (microcosm). He uses this philosophical framework to distinguish between universal moral laws and temporary ceremonial rituals.</meta>

[page 127]

->ON CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE, BOOK IV.<-

...explain the causes of all ceremonial matters. However, that similarity between God and the great world <term>macrocosm: the universe as a whole</term> exists in the secondary act <note>original: "in actu secundo" — a Scholastic term referring to the manifestation or operation of a thing, whereas "primary act" refers to its essential existence</note>, not in the primary act; and it is found in proportion, not in form or substance. Specifically, the same proportion that the soul has to its powers, operations, and organs, God has to his exemplary works and to the angelic and corporeal machinery of the universe. Likewise, just as there is a rational relationship among the powers, operations, and organs themselves, there is a similar proportion among these divine works. 

At this point, observe one thing and reflect upon it. For just as the Law of the great world—and its manner of operating in those things subject to the cycle of birth and decay—does not produce the same or a uniform effect in every individual, but instead forms one person tall in stature (for example) and another short, one upright and another bent with a protruding shoulder, making this one dark-skinned and that one fair, this one dull in sense and that one very sharp, and producing all those kinds of symptoms <note>original: "Synthomatum" — here meaning individual physical or mental characteristics</note> by which the variety and differences of individuals are established; nevertheless, in the primary members of the human frame, which are required in every way for the life and actions of mortals, the Law and nature of things never fail to adapt and grant those very members with a certain and limited size, number, and form, according to the necessity of each. 

In exactly the same way, the Law of the small world <term>microcosm: the individual human being</term>, even if it does not always or everywhere maintain the same manner and tenor in each of its six hundred and thirteen commandments <note>A reference to the *613 Mitzvot*, the total number of commandments found in the Torah in Jewish tradition</note>, because the word of God 
<margin>2 Timothy 2</margin>
(as the Apostle taught in 2 Timothy 2) is not bound to this or that specific work. However, the precepts of the Law of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note> lose none of their power through any variation of time or place, nor do they permit any mortal to be immune or free from their observance and bond of service. For instance, the commandment to worship God and honor one's parents binds everyone, always and everywhere, to its observance within a certain limit. Yet, to worship God or honor a parent through *this* or *that* precise rite of ceremony and observance does not reserve for itself the same binding power always or everywhere. The same judgment should be applied to the remaining mandates of the Decalogue, just as I opened more widely to the reader in the third volume of this work. Anyone who considers this rightly and without any arrogance could immediately remove and extinguish the many disagreements that currently wander and rage, even to the point of destruction, within the sacred republic of Christ.

### APPENDIX TO THE SEVENTH THEOREM.

<margin>Proverbs 8; Deuteronomy 30; Psalm 118</margin>
The Law by which the world was founded and by which it is governed—which the Kabbalists <note>original: "Cabalei"</note> (referring to that passage in Proverbs 8: *I was ordained from eternity*) declare existed before the constitution of the world—is the very Law which Augustine, in his first book on free will, says is the supreme reason of all things, inscribed in the divine mind. And that great Cordoban interpreter of Peripatetic doctrine <note>This refers to Averroës (Ibn Rushd), the famous philosopher from Córdoba known for his commentaries on Aristotle (the "Peripatetic")</note> calls it the "divine art," of which this Law delivered on the mountain in Arabia <note>Mount Sinai</note> has only a shadow (as I explained before). Regarding its commandment, it is written in Deuteronomy 30: *It is not above you, nor is it set in heaven.* But concerning that eternal Law, it is said in Psalm 118: *Your Law is the truth; I will keep your Law always, forever and ever; Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the Law of the Lord. I was ordained from eternity.*

### APPENDIX TO THE EIGHTH THEOREM.

For just as the great world relates to the small world, so the Law of the great world relates to the Law of the small world. But the machinery of the world is more excellent than man. Therefore, the Law of the former is superior to the Law of the latter. But note that there is a triple Spheristic Law <note>original: "Legem sphæristicam" — Law relating to the celestial spheres or the universal order</note>: One from the beginning, before the construction of the world, which is the uniform and immobile supreme paradigmatic notion of all things in the divine mind; the second (in the middle) is the "written" law, which is immobile but nevertheless manifold, and is the exemplary conception inserted into the angelic mind (which is called "written" because it is stable, like written characters); the third (at the extremity) is that uttered by the mouth, which is...

<meta>This page continues Ricius’s philosophical inquiry into the nature of Law. Having previously discussed the "Eternal Law" and how it manifests in the macrocosm (universe) and microcosm (humanity), he now shifts to the specific structure of the Mosaic Law. He categorizes the Law into three distinct levels—Ideal, Written, and Applied—and begins a historical defense of the Jewish oral tradition, tracing its lineage from Moses down to the compilation of the Mishnah to show its continuity and divine authority.</meta>
