<meta>This page serves as a collection of formal endorsements for Paul Riccius’s work. It follows the conclusion of Book IV, where Riccius applied mystical and philosophical interpretations to biblical themes. These letters from the theological faculties of Bologna and Padua provide the "imprimatur" or official approval necessary for a scholarly religious work in the 16th century.</meta>

## THE THEOLOGICAL ACADEMY OF BOLOGNA, TO THE MOST LEARNED LORD PAUL RICCIUS, SECRETARY TO THE MOST SERENE KING OF THE ROMANS, from the Doctors of the Theological University of Bologna.
->Sends many greetings.<-

*We have, due to a lack of time, skimmed through the books offered to us on **CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE** <note>original: "DE COELESTI AGRICVLTVRA"</note> rather than reading them as diligently as we had wished. Nevertheless, we were so delighted by the reading of this book that we have praised its pious and sound dogma as being in no way worthy of censure. We saw in it a clear intellect and a sincere soul intent on protecting, preserving, and increasing those things which pertain to Christian Law and doctrine; you venerate and extol divine matters in such a way that you do not abhor or think nothing of the laws of nature and philosophy. On the contrary, you ascend to the invisible things of God through those things which are seen to be made; you reach, taste, and open them as if by a preceding step. With your multifaceted knowledge of languages, you cast down, pierce through, and reduce to nothing the errors of the Jews and the Raving Heretics <note>The "raving heretics" likely refers to the early Protestant reformers, against whom Riccius’s work was often positioned.</note> using their own weapons, just like the sword of Goliath <note>A common metaphor in this period for using an opponent's own tools—in Riccius's case, his mastery of Hebrew and Jewish texts—against them.</note>. Therefore, since you reside as a secretary to the never-sufficiently-praised Ferdinand, the Most Serene King of the Romans, and have been the primary physician of his weary body and soul, it is fitting that just as your Prince cuts down wicked heresies with sword and fire, you—not unlike him in counsel—should similarly demolish and eradicate them through your writings and your book on **CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE**. Therefore, bring into the light this volume on **CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE** which you have written for the benefit of many and which has been approved by several universities, so that it may profit the many for whose salvation it was composed. Farewell. Given at Bologna, August 12, 1540.*

I, Brother Seraphinus of Bologna, Dean of the University of the Order of Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans.</note>, confirm this.
I, Brother Alexander of Bologna, of the Order of Hermits <note>The Augustinians.</note>, as above.
I, Brother Vincentius of Piacenza, Regent of Bologna and Inquisitor of Pavia, confirm and approve as above.
I, Brother Jacobus of Ortona, General Visitor of the Celestine Congregation and Regent of Bologna, approve as above.
I, Brother Thadeus of Bologna, of the Order of Servants <note>The Servites.</note>, confirm as above.

## THE THEOLOGICAL ACADEMY OF PADUA TO THE MAGNIFICENT AND MOST LEARNED PROFESSOR OF SACRED THEOLOGY, AND COUNSELOR TO THE MOST SERENE KING OF THE ROMANS, THE MOST WORTHY AND EXCELLENT LORD PAUL RICCIUS: The Doctors and Masters of the University of Theology of Padua, undersigned,
->Send many greetings.<-

*Since we can by no means deny those things which are requested justly and honestly—and especially when they concern the honor of God, the increase of divine worship, the defense of the Christian faith, and the destruction of heresies—we have therefore been requested on behalf of your Excellence to see, read, and consider the book on **CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE** published by your Excellency, and to judge whether it was composed in a Catholic and Christian manner. We have seen, read, and diligently considered it, and we find (as we attest by these presents and provide indubitable faith) that in all that pertains to the Christian religion and holy Catholic doctrine, the book itself is composed and published by your Excellence in a Catholic, faithful, and Christian manner, with the divine spirit breathing upon it and the grace of the Holy Spirit illuminating it. We praise and, as far as we are able, approve the excellence of your intellect and learning. Greatly extolling your exceptional zeal for the Christian religion and the Catholic faith, we exhort and indeed ask your Excellency, in the heart of Christ, that for the praise of God, the destruction of heresies, the increase of the Catholic faith, the salvation of souls, and for your own perpetual name and eternal glory, you should and must bring it into the light and have it printed as soon as possible. In witness of which, etc. Given at Padua in the Spiritual Palace, Wednesday, the 18th day of the month of August, 1540.*

## THE THEOLOGICAL ACADEMY OF FERRARA, TO THE MOST EXCELLENT LORD PAUL RICCIUS: GREETINGS.

It was not without spiritual delight that I read through the four volumes of *CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE* <note>original: "COELESTI AGRICVLTVRA"</note> published by your lordship, from which I have come to know the singular wisdom of your talent. I marveled at how weightily and ornately you revealed the truth of the divine oracles, and how you made clear the method of harmonizing them in a clear style, such that I judged you were speaking the very truth and divine wisdom itself. I recognize indeed the sharpness of your mind, and I do not doubt that the spirit of God has been found speaking within you. I praise the strength of your eloquence and the beauty of your speech. I praise the greatness of your soul, for I have experienced the splendor of God shining in you and your singular virtue. But even more, I have come to know that you will be a great champion of the Christian faith and a zealot for Christian truth—especially after reading these volumes—and I see how much effort you have spent so that (once all heretical depravity has been exploded and utterly uprooted) the faithful people may forever adhere to God and the Catholic Church. Farewell, divine man, and be mindful of me, your devoted servant.

->FROM THE GYMNASIO OF SAINT PAUL, BROTHER JOHN MARY<-
->Veratus of Ferrara, Carmelite, Dean of the University of<-
->Theologians of Ferrara.<-

I hold that this doctrine will be most useful in the Church of Christ our Redeemer because of the greatness and sublimity of such—if I may put it this way—wonderful doctrine of both Testaments; and I sign this with my own hand.

## THE THEOLOGICAL ACADEMY OF PAVIA, TO PAUL RICCIUS, Physician to the Most Serene Ferdinand, King of the Romans: Brother Julius Galacius and Brother Archangelus Lafranchoxius, Masters of Theological Wisdom and holders of the public chair in the venerable Academy of Pavia, send greetings in the Lord.

Several volumes of your dignity's *CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE* were presented to us, which we have turned over with repeated and diligent reading and with no small amount of delight. In these, with skillful and spiritual erudition and zeal, you lay open many celestial secrets and hidden mysteries of the Sacred Scriptures and the faith; you blunt the impious dogmas of those who wander in error, and you destroy vain and false foundations. Therefore, since no one (according to the warnings of the Truth) lights a lamp to hide it under a bushel, but sets it upon a lampstand so that it may give light to all who are in the house, we also exhort and beseech your lordship that you no longer allow your volumes on *CELESTIAL AGRICULTURE*—so full of spiritual sweetness and wisdom—to lie hidden and in secret. Rather, bring them forth into the light for the instruction and progress of many pious faithful, so that they may shine more widely and illuminate more clearly those who desire the secret truth, and lead those wandering back to the right path of faith and piety. For he who teaches and instructs many unto justice shall be (as the oracles of Daniel promise) like the splendor of the firmament and the brightly shining stars of heaven for all eternity. Farewell, from the Academy of Ticinum <note>Ticinum is the ancient Latin name for the city of Pavia.</note>, July 26, 1540 <note>original: "7. Calen. Augusti, M. D. XL."</note>.

Brother Julius, as above, with my own hand.
Brother Archangelus, as above, with my own hand.
Brother Augustine of the Lenten Order <note>original: "de quadrages."</note>, with my own hand.

# BY PAUL RICCIUS,
## A DISCOURSE ON THE COMMUNICATION OF THE
## SACRAMENTS,
## worthy of diligent reading.

About to speak on the mystery of the sacrament, I shall take my beginning from the reasoning behind its name, by the will of the individual Trinity. The word "Sacrament" <note>original: "Sacramentum"</note>, and the individual words related to it by analogy, announce an abundance of a thing or the completion of a work. If these words derive their origin from a noun signifying the substance of a thing, then they designate an abundance of what is inherent within it, such as "succulent," "vinolent" <note>meaning full of wine</note>, "luculent" <note>meaning full of light</note>, and that sort of thing. However, if they are derived from a verb, they show the efficacy and completion of a work, such as "oath" <note>original: "iuramentum"</note>, "testament" <note>original: "testamentum"</note>, and "instruction" <note>original: "documentum"</note>. The name "sacrament" should indeed be placed in this latter category: for it designates a work that renders the recipient holy <note>original: "sacrum"</note>; just as instruction <note>documentum</note> makes a listener learned, a testament <note>testamentum</note> makes one an heir, and an oath <note>iuramentum</note> makes one bound by a vow. From this, we read that the celestial secrets of the divine mind (which are holy by their very nature and exist as the cause and reason for all holy things) are most excellently called "sacraments."

<margin>Wisdom 2</margin>
The Wise Man said: "They did not know the secret <note>original: "sacramentum"; in many early Latin bibles, "sacramentum" was used to mean a divine secret or mystery</note> of God," where the discourse concerns the divinity, passion, and incarnation of the Word. And that saying of the Apostle:
<margin>Ephesians 1</margin>
"That he might make known to us the mystery <note>original: "sacramentum"</note> of his will." If you pay attention, you will see that the divine utterances pronounce the word "sacrament" under such a concept in many places. Sometimes the name of "sacrament" is also transferred to human secrets, such as that in the book of Tobit: "For it is good to hide the secret <note>original: "sacramentum"</note> of the king." Occasionally, it has even pleased people to call an oath itself a "sacrament" (because it consists of the attestation of a holy thing and indicates something imperfect or hidden); hence the oaths of soldiers were customarily called "military sacraments" <note>original: "militiæ sacramenta"</note>. However, our discourse here concerns the first way of naming sacraments.

Therefore, although the definition or description of a sacrament has been expressed in many ways by the holy school of Theologians, we know that all their sayings are explained in this brief theme: "A sacrament is a visible form of invisible grace, bearing its image and existing as its cause." If you desire to know the reasoning behind the parts of this theme individually, they must be sought from no other source than the knowledge of the "end" or "purpose" (upon which all inventions of nature and art depend). Hence, God, that highest author of sacraments and founder of laws, taught that He intended no other end from the work of the sacraments except that which would render the recipient fit for, and a participant in, eternal salvation.
<margin>John 3</margin>
"Unless," He says, "a man be born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God." And:
<margin>John 6</margin>
"Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in you." And:
<margin>Luke 13</margin>
"Unless you do penance, you shall all likewise perish." Certainly, one must judge in the same way regarding the remaining sacraments.

Since, therefore, the intention and end of a sacrament is to make the recipient a participant in eternal salvation, it makes one a participant indeed if it renders the person conformable to the thing to be participated in. It renders them conformable while it adapts the soul through the concept of eternal truth, and the body through the suitability of the physical work. It is necessary, therefore, that the condition of a sacrament provide both. For it instills and exercises the concept of eternal truth and faith through the comparison of the visible sign to the invisible light of grace itself. In view of this, in the aforementioned definition of a sacrament, it is placed as "a visible form of invisible grace." But the suitability of the physical work results from the symbol and similarity of the sign to the thing signified, for which reason it is added in the aforementioned theme that it "bears its image" (that is, a similarity of proportion). When both of these (namely, the thought of eternal truth and the suitability of the physical work) have been applied, the effect and end of the sacrament soon follow: namely, the participation in heavenly grace and the kingdom of heaven, in view of which is added...

[by teaching]: and existing as a cause—not indeed one that effects grace, but one that prepares and disposes the recipient—through the likeness and analogy of the sign to the thing signified. And for this reason, Augustine writes to Boniface: *If sacraments (he says) did not have a likeness to the things of which they are sacraments, they would not properly be called sacraments; for where likeness is lacking, no power can be given for consecrating and making the recipient a sharer in the sacred thing.* Indeed, just as contrary and clashing things exclude one another, so like-minded and related things embrace and meld into one. For by likeness alone (as Augustine taught in the seventh book *On the Trinity*) does one approach God, and by unlikeness one draws away from Him. For every animal (says the Wise Man <note>Refers to the author of the Book of Sirach/Ecclesiasticus 13:19</note>) loves its own kind, and all flesh joins itself to its like. Whence even those who investigate the secrets of nature through human inquiry believe that spiritual gifts are given to mortals through a harmonious condition and a certain way of thinking, just as the prince of the Peripatetics <note>A common title for Aristotle</note> himself testifies in the 8th book of the *Politics*: praising and approving the harmony of melodies in sacred celebrations, by which the mind of the listeners becomes a suppliant. Some in our time, wandering in delusion, mock these melodies—as well as the rites of other ceremonies—as if they were seductive pomp and vain superstition; they do not pay attention to the mystery of Saint Elisha, who, while the harpist played, was seized by the heavenly spirit of God <note>original: "super cœlesti Dei spiritu est arreptus"; see 2 Kings 3:15</note>. Hence also Proclus, the grave and faithful interpreter of Platonic doctrine, when he discusses the efficacy of sacrifices, says: *The ancients brought down divine powers to a lower place on account of a certain likeness; indeed, likeness itself is a sufficient cause for binding individual things to one another.* So too Iamblichus, the most studious and wise investigator of the cults, speaking of the symbols of the ancient Egyptians, writes: *Therefore, since they see that all higher things take delight in the likeness of lower things, and moreover desire to be filled with goodness from the higher things so as to imitate them as much as they can, they rightly offer a mode of action suited to the celestial powers... when they insert hidden mysteries into manifest symbols.* Iamblichus himself recounts many such things, consistent with orthodox piety and worthy of reading and attention. Furthermore, the ancient practitioners of Christian piety who use allegory (who are commonly called Kabbalists <note>original: "Cabalei"</note>) call this conformity and likeness of the mind and body being consecrated a "fitting together of certain channels" <note>original: "canalium coaptationem"; this refers to the Kabbalistic concept of the *Sefirot* or conduits through which divine light flows into the world</note>, imitating the sacred scriptures which frequently liken the supreme wisdom of God to a fountain of living waters. Therefore, since this very wisdom drips through the whole world via certain hidden streams of channels, as it were; but human nature, because it is weak and is kept away from the spring of super-celestial waters by the "turning sword" <note>original: "uersatili gladio"; a reference to the flaming sword guarding Eden in Genesis 3:24</note>, it is worthwhile (if you understand the mystery) that all the powers of the body and soul gather themselves into one, and upward, so they are not distracted by the allurements of earthly things. These powers (with the openings of the channels now joined to one another) should, through sense, imagination (or fantasy), and mind, correspond exactly to the pathways of eternal truth and heavenly wisdom. Otherwise, the mind of mortals will not be imbued with that nectar-like and super-celestial fluid, but will suck up the bitter waters of contradiction or breathe in empty air. For how much the conformity and likeness of visible and invisible things contains of hidden energy is testified not only by divine and human authority, but also demonstrated by many experiments perceived by the senses. For if you carefully consider the individual types of things that can be generated, you will find that each of their forms requires a certain previous disposition in the receiver so that it may actually constitute a single thing. For instance, the species and form of a horse is not born from the seed of a donkey or a pig, but only from a horse. Just as the planting of an acorn does not produce a citrus tree, nor does a nettle spring from the seed of lettuce; and we see that not only a corruptible nature, but also an immortal one, through analogy and its symbol with the mortal body, constitutes one thing in number. For indeed, the intellectual substance and form require a certain temperament of the organic body, by which the soul itself, in the center and on the horizon of all things, may bind [them together]...

### ON THE COMMON REASON OF THE SACRAMENTS ###

...joining the last things to the first. And not only this intellectual substance, which gives form to and constitutes a single individual in number <note>The human soul</note>, but the intellectual nature itself, which merely assists and breathes upon the mind of mortals (like an angel of light or a demon), requires a certain disposition and kinship in the recipient. For a filthy spirit and demon glides only into the souls of the filthy—such as the collection of sorceresses and hags, and other foolish men—in whom the phantastic or imaginary faculty prevails more, which obeys the command of the demon more readily than the intellectual power. But the holy and clean spirit of the angelic order offers itself only to purified souls and the minds of saints; it breathes upon them and clings to them.

Nevertheless, although we know for certain that individual things which must be associated and fused into one demand a certain analogy and conformity, nonetheless, what kind of symbol or analogy the order of things requires between individual adhering parts is unsearchable and incomprehensible to the human mind. For what could be that so persistent disposition of the magnet toward iron, by which it affects its contact so much that wherever the magnet itself is carried, it soon (despite the gap) pulls and carries the iron around with it? Or what is the kinship of the Heliotrope <note>original: *Heliotropij*; a plant that turns toward the sun, such as a sunflower</note> to the Sun, or the Selinotrope <note>original: *Selinotropij*; a plant traditionally believed to turn toward the moon</note> to the Moon, so that the one so anxiously emulates the circuit of the Sun and the other the Moon? And what is the correspondence of the rooster with the Sun, that he rejoices so greatly at its rising and approach to the horizon, and exults with song and the clapping of wings? Surely there is no wisdom so exact, no sharpness of mind so intense, that knows how to know these things precisely or explain them with voice or pen.

But if the analogies and primary reasons for these things—which consist of the work of a weaker nature and are subject to the senses—cannot be grasped or penetrated by the human mind, how is it that you, a weak and muddy mortal creature, do not blush to scrutinize, judge, and decide upon the sublime and hidden symbols of the sacraments, and their reasons (hardly known even to angelic minds), with your deceptive and wavering thought? Tell me, I pray, if you know and if you grant faith to the sacred word: what great force and energy was there in the placement <margin>Exodus 17</margin> and position of the hands of Moses, waging war against Amalek, so that when he lifted his hands, Israel conquered, and when he lowered them a little, Amalek overcame? And what great power was in the <term>septenary: the number seven or a group of seven</term>, by which (so that the walls of Jericho might collapse of their own accord) the divine authority had ordered seven priests to be used, seven trumpets, seven days, and seven circuits of the city of Jericho? Or what efficacy and force was in the gesture of the external body, by which <margin>3 Kings 17 <note>In modern Bibles, 1 Kings 17</note></margin> it was necessary that Elijah <note>original: *Elias*</note>, in order to raise the son of the widow of Zarephath, stretched himself out and measured himself three times over the boy? And to obtain rain, he bowed down on the top of Carmel and put his face between his knees? By which also Elisha <note>original: *Eliseus*</note>, wishing to restore to life the dead son of the Shunammite, lay upon the boy, putting mouth to mouth, eye to eye, and hand to hand? By which also the same Elisha had ordered the King of Israel to bring a bow <margin>4 Kings 13 <note>In modern Bibles, 2 Kings 13</note></margin> and arrows, and when he had brought them, said to the king: "Put your hand upon the bow," and when he had put it, Elisha placed his hands upon the king's hands, and said: "Open the eastern window," and when he had opened it, Elisha said: "Shoot the arrow," and he shot it, and Elisha said: "The arrow of the Lord's salvation, and the arrow of salvation against Syria in Aphek until you consume it." And he said: "Take the arrows," and when he had taken them, he said: "Strike the ground with the dart," and when he had struck it three times and stopped, the man of God was angry with him and said: "If you had struck five or six or seven times, you would have struck Syria until its destruction; but now you shall strike it three times."

Finally, what man is of such great wisdom and such clever talent that he has searched out and reported the cause by which the Restorer of the world himself—who spoke and things were made—Christ the Lord, provides spit and mud as an ointment for restoring light to the blind? If, therefore, the causes and analogies of these works—which respect the mundane benefits of men—are especially and most closely unknown and unsearchable to human cleverness, who is a man so inconsiderate and of such rash presumption that he would judge the inner secrets of the divine sacraments, which the Repairer and Founder of the world himself instituted, not for any use in mortal life, but for eternal life, which...

# PAUL RICIUS ON THE COMMON REASON OF THE SACRAMENTS #

...which "eye has not seen, nor has it entered into the heart of man" <note>original: *oculus non uidit, neq; in cor hominis afcendit*; a reference to 1 Corinthians 2:9</note>. Since He has established our salvation, who would dare to approach and comprehend it with an obscure mind and the subtleties of a stumbling reason—much less hold it in contempt and reject it? Even many of the wise among the Pagans <note>original: *Ethnicorum*; referring to non-Christian philosophers</note>, who were subject to the elements of the physical world, decreed that when they considered sacred matters, the entire use of reason and the laws of argumentation must be set aside. Instead, they claimed one must cling to such things by faith alone and by a firmness of mind. 

Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on theurgy and Egyptian mysteries</note> testifies to this when recording the ancient tradition regarding the power of the sacraments. He says: "The proper observance of the precepts and of divine works (which exceed all understanding), and the power of symbols and sacraments known only to the gods, provides us with a deifying union." The same author, when he describes the power of the divinity in sacred matters a little later, says: "In religion, no work of any miraculous efficacy can occur unless some member of the higher orders is present there as a spectator and accomplisher of the work. Human nature can neither receive a reason nor a discourse about the gods without the gods, much less is it able to perform divine works without them. For it is so weak and dull that it has no remedy for its own nothingness, except for a portion of divine light descending from above, without which nothing divine is done by us." 

Thus far Iamblichus. Therefore, let human nature be ashamed of its weakness, and let the vain and rash presumption of mortals restrain itself. For if man is unable to search out and comprehend the analogies and primary reasons for fleeting things—things that can be felt by the senses—he should not dare to inquire into, judge, or decide upon these sublime sacraments of eternal truth, which surpass all understanding, through the mere discourse of a fragile and wavering reason. 

Admittedly, it is worthwhile for one who desires the path of eternal salvation and wishes to learn it thoroughly to first become more secure and certain of the indubitable divinity and wisdom of the Master <note>Christ</note> through accommodating conjectures and arguments. Indeed, we read of many of the Prophets' listeners and the disciples of Christ the Savior seeking arguments and signs. However, once the divinity and wisdom of the Teacher has been recognized and established beyond all doubt, it will be considered mere curiosity—or rather, a cursed audacity—to question any saying, precept, or warning of that Author. 

If we read that those same holy followers of Christ and the Prophets sometimes doubted and sought reasons, you should not think this happened because they hesitated in any way regarding the truth or the divine wisdom of the Mediator. Rather, it was because they were seeking a way to understand and perform these mysteries, or perhaps a way to answer the objections of opponents. They were accusing their own ignorance and dullness rather than suspecting any fallacy, ignorance, or lack of power in the Master. 

Consider this: a sick person would be judged impudent and insane if, after entrusting the care of his failing body to a physician whom he already knew to be a man of the highest prudence, experience, and integrity, he nevertheless refused to take any medicine unless the doctor first explained the reasons for every single thing—why he administers this drug and not that one, why he uses a certain weight or measure, why at this hour and not another, or why he orders him to bleed this vein and not that one. 

How much more impudently and harmfully does a crude, blind, and insignificant man—surrounded by the most foul sicknesses of the soul—inquire after the causes and reasons for the most sacred and health-giving antidotes of the sacraments? These were handed down to us by Him who alone bore our infirmities, and in whom we place all our faith and certain hope of healing. As the Apostle <note>St. Paul</note> exclaims, His counsels are unsearchable, His senses and His ways are past finding out. This is Christ the Savior, the restorer and creator of the universe, God, who is holy and

-> blessed forever. <-

<summary>Ricius argues that because human reason is too weak to understand even natural mysteries, it must defer to faith regarding the sacraments. He uses a medical analogy to show that just as a patient trusts a proven doctor without demanding a technical explanation for every remedy, a believer should trust Christ’s "antidotes" (the sacraments) for the soul.</summary>

# BY PAUL RICIUS,
## ON THE SECRET PROVIDENCE OF GOD
### A BRIEF COMMENTARY ON the Psalm: "Blessed is the man."

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'H' containing a scene with a human figure and ornate foliage.</image-desc>
The human race is born for truth and eternal blessedness. However, it is quite impossible to achieve this within this slippery and fleeting structure of earthly things; instead, we attain it in the sublime and archetypal framework of the universe, and in the very highest of all goods. Indeed, all things that we perceive here through the senses are vain and very much like children's toys. While we are so greatly delighted by their charms, we are not (as we presume) enjoying the things themselves, but rather an empty and trifling shadow of them. We are like small children who are delighted by nothing weighty, nothing serious, nor any of the things we deal with in adult life, but rather by bubbles, rattles, the rattle of Archytas <note>original: *architæq; tabella*; referring to a toy mentioned by Aristotle, attributed to the philosopher Archytas, used to keep children occupied</note>, and playing with shadowy images on a wall. Anyone who dwells upon such delights of the senses and feeds only on earthly shadows is surely a child and utterly blind in mind; though his body bears a human likeness, his soul reflects the clear image of a beast. This is just as those divine oracles of David proclaim: <margin>Psalm 31</margin> "Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding" <note>This is Psalm 32:9 in modern numbering</note>. And also: <margin>Psalm 48</margin> "Man, who does not abide in honor, is like the beasts" <note>This is Psalm 49:20 in modern numbering</note>. Indeed, he is a foolish and dull-witted beast who—when he compares these playful and soon-passing pleasures of the body to the immense height of heavenly and spiritual things and the ineffable sweetness of the life above—does not immediately value these filthy and lethal charms of a falling world as worthless. Instead, as far as the miserable condition of nature allows, he should trample and drive away every irritation of wicked desire, turning his gaze toward the heavenly lights of the empyrean sphere. Let him reach out for, love, possess, and finally enjoy that sublime Good, Beauty, and Delight through the highest edge of an upright mind for ages without end. Since the entire intention of the Psalmist <note>original: *Psalmographi*; referring to King David as the traditional author</note> and his efforts are turned toward this single goal—to promote and lead the human race to the summit of blessedness—he placed this goal at the very beginning of the Psalms (like an archer marking his target). He opened the book right at its front with the concept of "blessedness," which the other following Psalms, as well as the entire words of the Prophets, look toward as the ultimate progress and end for mortals. We, therefore, will first attempt to open and unravel this first one in the order of the Psalms (by which we are made attentive, teachable, and well-disposed). We promise to provide only the literal understanding <term>literal sense (sensus literalis): the primary meaning intended by the author, as opposed to allegorical or mystical interpretations</term> of this and the other Psalms that follow, according to the sound of the words. We will not act as many interpreters are accustomed to—both Catholics and the wandering interpreters of the Jewish synagogue—who strive to fit the sound of the words to their own preconceived notions, rather than fitting their concepts to the sense of the words. The latter do this out of a stubborn and hostile contempt for Christian truth, while the former do it out of an immoderate affection for Gospel piety. For the orthodox truth does not need a beggarly or in any way forced persuasion; it is most richly proven from elsewhere, both by various experiences of nature and sensible things, and by the most evident teachings of sacred speech. All these things are ready at hand for one who looks diligently, and "all things are full of Christ." Therefore, the gifts of the Prophets are not to be extorted, but are to be accepted in their literal understanding (from which alone it is permitted to draw an argument). With these things having been tasted beforehand, we soon turn, by the nod of those above, to the first of the Psalms.

But because the Psalmist wished this first one in the order of Psalms to be a prelude and introduction to those following, he therefore depicted, by a certain brief argument and in figurative form, all those things which contribute to eternal salvation and the salvation of this age, as well as those things which give birth to the misery of both ages. It is as if he were to say: "Blessed will be he who flees evil and embraces good." To these things are also joined [the rewards] of the present age...

# PAUL RICIUS,

prosperity follows, just as the misery of this world and the eternal one follows their opposites. The cause and reason for all of this is that God Himself, the king and founder of all ages, is present to the good and hidden from the wicked.

<margin>Chapter 10. Matthew 12. Ephesians 4.</margin>
Therefore, this present Psalm proposes three things. First, the condition of the man to be made blessed—what he must cast aside and what he must keep. Second, it explains through a comparison how we attain success in this world through the same means by which we reach eternal happiness; and how, by neglecting these, we fall into every kind of unhappiness and misery. Third, it assigns the true reason and cause for all the things mentioned above. First, therefore, it records two things that the condition of blessedness absolutely demands: namely, to flee from evil (which must be observed first according to the order of nature) and to pursue good (which is naturally second). As to why it forbids walking with the ungodly, standing with sinners, or sitting with scoffers <note>original: *irrisoribus*; often translated as "mockers" or "scornful" in English Bibles</note>, the reason is this: because there are three kinds of faults among the wicked—corresponding to the three powers and operations of the soul—which are required for an act of virtue: namely, **willing**, **knowing**, and **being able**. 

The first of these they call the unamendable and unpardonable sin against the Holy Spirit, which proceeds from a depraved and impious **will**. For, as it is written to the Hebrews: "For if we sin willfully after we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remains no more sacrifice for sins." And that passage in Matthew 12: "Every sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven unto men: but he that shall speak a word against the Holy Spirit, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this world, nor in the world to come." 

The second kind of evil arises from a defect in **knowing** itself, or from affected ignorance, which they call a mortal sin (yet one that is amendable). The Apostle <note>Standard reference to St. Paul</note> hints at this in Ephesians 4, saying: "Having their understanding darkened, being alienated from the way of God through ignorance." And also in Romans 10: "For I bear them record," he says, "that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge." 

The third kind of evil is that which is born from the fragility and **impotence** of the flesh, which they call venial sin. Of this, the Apostle says: "For to will is present with me; but how to perform that which is good I find not. For I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind." For "to will" shows the rectitude of the will; the "law of the mind" designates the truth of the intellect; but the "other law" which is in the members announces the impotence of the flesh.

Take note of two things here: although the enticement of the senses is the chief fault in all venial sins—because the creature (as the Apostle says) was made subject to vanity, not willingly—nevertheless, not every sin arising from the sting of the flesh is venial. Indeed, many times that kind of fault produces a mortal sin when the work of the free will and the intellect accompanies it. 

Furthermore, you who are wise, pay attention to this: the motivating or executive power in a **theological work**—which proceeds from faith, hope, and charity—is primarily founded in the operative or practical intellect, though participating with the irascible power <note>term: *irascibilis*; in medieval psychology, the "irascible" faculty is the part of the soul that deals with courage, anger, and the pursuit of difficult goods</note>. In a **moral work**, however, the foundation is strongly in the irascible power, participating with the practical intellect. The reason is that theological virtue, since it is infused from above, coming from the Father of Lights, first meets the intellect and from there overflows into the irascible faculty. Moral virtue, on the contrary, taking its origin from sensory things, first meets the irascible faculty (which is raised up from there) and is illuminated by the practical intellect—reflect on this within yourself.

Therefore, three things to be avoided in the Psalm correspond to these three kinds of evils and sins: **Walking** with the ungodly, **standing** with sinners, and **sitting** with scoffers. For with the impious man—who is occupied by that very pestilence and the curdled mass of all evils, impiety—it is not permitted for anyone even to walk, much less to stand, and far less to sit; for he pollutes instantly and leads to eternal destruction, with all hope of salvation taken away. But with the sinner—who is occupied by the second kind of evil—although walking is by no means to be permitted, the slippery nature of mortals does not allow it to be forbidden entirely. Since there is no man (as Solomon says) just on the earth, who does good and does not sin. And if we say (says John) that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves. For a just man falls seven times in a day...

### ON THE PSALM, BLESSED IS THE MAN. 201

the just man: yet soon after a fall he will rise again. This is permitted to the ungodly man only in the smallest degree and only by a miracle; for if a sinner lingers in his headlong fall, he will eventually fail to rise at all. It would, therefore, be beyond the limits of the human condition not to walk at all in the way of sinners, but what must be forbidden is "standing"—which could be easily avoided, according to the habit of nature and by "preventing grace" <note>original: *praevenienti gratia*; a theological term for grace that moves a person toward God before they have even turned toward Him</note> (as they call it). As for scoffers and jesters—into which the third kind of evil-doers throws us back—walking or even standing with them at times is by no means forbidden; indeed, it should be entirely permitted so that the tired powers of the soul may occasionally recover. But to "sit," and to provide a great deal of leisure for mocking actions, creates an obstacle and removes the hope of eternal salvation.

The first kind of evil must therefore be cast aside at the very beginning, as he warned by saying: **Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly.** <note>original: *Beatus vir qui non ambulauit in conſilio impiorū*</note>] He attributes "counsel" to the ungodly because the ungodly person—whom not only his own crimes but also those of others delight—strives to pollute others with deadly suggestions and sweet poison, dragging them onto slippery ground.

He mentions that the second kind of evil must be avoided: **And has not stood in the way of sinners** <note>original: *Et in via peccatorum non ſtetit*</note>] He calls it the "way" of sinners because this fleeting and empty world is an open path of sinners through which the entire race of mortals must pass. We are driven to go into the way of sinners by the Law of nature; however, to "stand" there is committed to the command of the will.

He declares that the third kind of evil must be fled: **And has not sat in the chair (or seat) of scoffers.** <note>original: *Et in cathedra (uel ſede) deriſorum non ſedit*</note>] For walking and standing with scoffers does not take away the hope of eternal salvation; but to sit and spend a great deal of leisure in scurrilous and mocking acts immediately excludes one from the kingdom of heaven.

But since it is not enough to achieve blessedness merely to flee from evil—for in that way even beasts and every kind of wild animal would participate in eternal salvation, since they are guilty of no crime—it is also required that the human mind itself, which is the part of mankind superior to the beasts, should exercise its own action. Its action consists solely in the operation of the will and the intellect. The operation of the will is to wish or to desire; the operation of the intellect is to meditate. The desire of the will demands the highest good, and the intellect seeks the highest intelligible thing, which is nothing other than the Word of God, Wisdom, or the eternal Law of God. And the highest good which the will desires is the very same thing as the eternal wisdom and Law of God. The Psalmist teaches these actions of the human mind, in which the second condition of the man to be made blessed consists, by saying: **But his will is in the Law of the Lord.** <note>original: *Sed in Lege Domini voluntas*</note>] More correctly, "his desire": that is, the act of the will concerning the heavenly Law, as if it were the highest beauty and good. **And on His law he will meditate.** <note>original: *Et in Lege eius meditabitur*</note>] This is the operation of the intellect concerning the heavenly Law, the first of all intelligible things. Moreover, he calls divine wisdom the "Law of God" because, just as the law given to men is a certain measure and a moderation of all the acts of the microcosm <note>the human being seen as a miniature version of the universe</note>, so also divine wisdom is the order by which the motions and acts of the macrocosm <note>the great world or universe</note> and the entire world are directed. Nor should one understand here by "the Law of God" the law of commandments written with a human pen, for to fulfill this Law, the thought of the mind alone is not enough, but the very performance of the work is required. The heavenly Law, however, requires the pure and diligent meditation of the mind, according to that saying of the Psalmist: **I shall live because your Law is my meditation.** <note>original: *Viuā quia Lex tua meditatio mea*</note> And that: **I have longed for your salvation, O Lord, and your Law is my meditation.** Truly, he who gasps for the eternal Law of God and meditates upon it will likewise honor the Law given by God to mortals, and will meditate upon it as an image of the eternal Law. It seems, therefore, that these things have been sufficiently explained: what the condition of the man to be made blessed is, both what should be cast aside and what should be pursued. Then he adds: **And he shall be like a tree.** <note>original: *Et erit tanquam lignum*</note>] The very similarity of a man to a plant declares that the observance of these things will result in the prosperity of this world as well, just as misery follows their contempt. For man (as it pleased the Prince of the Peripatetics <note>Aristotle</note>) is called an "inverted plant," because his root is planted in the heavens, just as a tree's is in the earth. Therefore, the prosperity of a plant—whether human or a fruit-bearing tree—depends on nothing else but being near the channels, and

*And he shall be*] namely, that man who flees from evil and follows after good:

Transplantation is the moving of a tree from the place where it was sown to another, so that it may take root more firmly; thus the mind of men was sown in an earthly and squalid body, where it receives no increase unless it is turned toward and transplanted into the things above. 

Therefore, just as the planting of a shrub in earthly things refers to human planting in heavenly things, so indeed the effect which results from the supernal <note>meaning "heavenly" or "from above"</note> planting will be represented by the effect of the earthly planting: *which will give its fruit in its season*] when it has grown to its perfect magnitude; it will give its fruit at the proper time, neither prematurely nor too late. *And its leaf*] which is the covering of the fruit: *shall not fall off*] because of the constant moisture by which it is nourished. *And whatsoever*] namely, adventitious things, and those less intended by nature, such as flowers, gum, and shoots: *he does, shall prosper*] thus, following that exact human transplantation into the things above, the successes of the gifts of the soul, the body, and external goods accompany it. The goods of the soul bear the likeness of the fruit; the body represents the leaf of the tree; and external things are likened to the adventitious parts.

When he says: "Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord," it refers to that phrase: "Blessed is the man whose will and meditation is in the Law of the Lord." Next, where it is added: *And he shall be like a tree*] he shows by this likeness that the happiness of even this world accompanies trust in the Lord. (**Transplantation**) as I taught before, designates the sacrament of spiritual regeneration.

Just as waters do not at all affect the dryness of a tree that has not been transplanted, but rather the heat causes it due to the absence of waters; so too the sad events of this world are not caused by the heavenly waters, but by a foreign series of causes which

<meta>This page continues the commentary by Paulus Ricius on the first Psalm. Having previously discussed the righteous man as a thriving tree, Ricius now contrasts this with the fate of the wicked and the sinner, drawing on his background in both Jewish exegesis and Christian theology.</meta>

### ON THE PSALM: BLESSED IS THE MAN.

...they fear when the heat comes; but they are like stubble, which is incapable of any transplantation or nourishment, and is miserably driven here and there by the whirlwind of the winds. And if by chance it were driven by any means to the streams of water and became a partaker of moisture, it could nevertheless by no means achieve long-lasting endurance; for in a short time it rots, and is soon reduced to corruption and dust. So too the impious <note>original: *impius*; refers to one who is godless or lacks reverence</note> man, if perhaps by a certain series of causes—with divine providence so permitting—he enjoys some earthly happiness, it will certainly not be long-lived; instead, flattering fortune will immediately change her face: *I saw* (says Job) *the fool with a firm root, and I cursed his beauty immediately.* <margin>Job 5.</margin>

Now you should notice that here only the "impious" is mentioned, by saying: *Not so the wicked*, but he remains silent regarding the "sinner." But where he mentions the misery of the future age, he names both the impious and the sinner together, when he says: *Therefore the wicked shall not rise in judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous.* The reason is that a sinner—as is clear from what has been said—is not so immediately and utterly uprooted from the heavens (like the impious man), and therefore is not to be compared to stubble, which, being completely uprooted, can thereafter partake of no sprout or long-lasting greenness. But (according to the teaching of Jeremiah) a sinner is like a tamarisk <note>original: *myricæ*; a hardy shrub found in arid, salty places, often used in scripture to represent the desolate</note> in the desert and a salt land, which, although it is not immediately uprooted and withered, nevertheless after some space of time (unless in the meantime it has been transplanted to the flowing waters) is consumed by decay or drought, so that no hope of fruitful transplantation can remain thereafter. Thus indeed it happens that in this dark and passing light, the sinner may obtain prosperous outcomes—something which the order of things by no means permits to a man of total impiety. For this reason, he mentions only the "impious" here and wraps the "sinner" in silence; however, in the misery of the future world, he condemns both equally and says: *Ideo nõ resurgent impij in iudicio, & peccatores in congregatione iustorum* <note>Therefore the wicked shall not rise in judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous.</note>. For from the fact that neither the impious nor the sinners are transplanted to the streams of water, it follows that they cannot be replanted, nor rise in judgment—that is, in the resurrection of the righteous. *For all of us*, says the Apostle <note>St. Paul</note>, *shall rise, but we shall not all be changed.* Only the elect, of course, shall be changed into glorious bodies. Therefore, the context of the letter is to be read as follows: Therefore the impious and the sinners, when they are judged, although they may rise, yet it will not be in the congregation of the righteous: *For the Lord knows the way of the righteous, and the way of the wicked shall perish.*

Here, in the third and final place, he assigns the greatest cause of all the things predicted, just as if he were to say: the reason why the righteous man is like a tree transplanted to the streams of water, and happy both in this and the future age—while the impious man is like stubble and subject to perpetual misery—the reason, I say, is: because God *knows*; that is, he adheres to the way of the righteous (as in that passage: *But Adam knew his wife Eve* <note>Ricius is explaining that "to know" in a biblical sense means an intimate union or attachment, not just intellectual awareness</note>) and because he does not "know" the path of the impious, it is therefore frustrated and perishes. *For if anyone is ignorant* (says the Apostle), *he will be ignored*: he who is ignored will have the face of the Lord hidden from him; but he from whom the face of the Lord is hidden is devoured by the living creatures of the earth and perishes. For just as our knowledge of heavenly things is a certain bond and union with the heavens—a union which the prosperity of things follows—so our ignorance of heavenly things produces a gap and a divorce, which is accompanied by devouring and the misery of both this and the future age: because his face is hidden, by whose presence we are protected from every outcome of evil. 

Now the cause by which the spirit of God adheres to one and not the other is "assimilation" <term>assimilation: the process of the human soul becoming like God through contemplation</term> itself: for like adheres to like. Moreover, assimilation happens through the conformity of our concept to the divine concept; this conformity results from the fact that we conceive, according to our small measure, the same things that are in the divine mind, which we read are called the Word of God, the Wisdom of God, and the eternal Law of God. Therefore, by meditating on the eternal Law of God, conformity of concept is born; from conformity comes assimilation; from assimilation comes adherence; from adherence comes the prosperity of sensible things and the perfected happiness of the eternal age. Hence it is written:

> Let your mercies come to me, and I shall live:
> because your Law is my meditation.

<meta>This page transitions from Ricius's biblical commentary on the Psalms to a new philosophical and theological treatise. Ricius is defending his views on the nature of the heavens—specifically whether the stars and planets possess souls—after being criticized during a public debate in Ingolstadt.</meta>

PAUL RICIUS,
A COMPENDIUM ON THE SOUL OF THE HEAVEN, ACCORDING TO THE
DOCTRINES OF THE PERIPATETICS AND THE SAINTS:

# AN APOLOGETIC PREFACE.

<margin>A dispute took place at Ingolstadt in the presence of Matthew Lang, Cardinal of Gurk.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' featuring scrolling foliage and floral patterns.</image-desc>
Indeed, "holy simplicity" <note>original: *Sancta rusticitas*; a phrase used by St. Jerome to describe a simple, unlearned faith that is virtuous but lacks the dialectical tools to defend itself against error.</note> (as Jerome says) is only of benefit to itself; and as much as it builds through the merit of a good life, it does just as much harm if it does not resist those who destroy. For indeed, an excess of silence and tolerance is to be avoided and blamed no less than an unbridled boldness in disputing and speaking—especially in those matters where we might allow the sacred inner chambers of truth to be attacked and profaned by our silence. Therefore, since a literary discussion recently happened to me at Ingolstadt <note>original: *Auripolis*; the Greek-styled name for Ingolstadt, meaning "City of Gold."</note> with a very celebrated assembly of learned men, and our conversation happened to break out into an examination of the celestial body (namely, whether it is animate or inanimate) through some sequence of discourse and talk; after a long and inextricable contention held on both sides, a certain devotee of divine wisdom did not shrink from asserting with an open face that the position which considered the celestial bodies to be animate was execrable and straying from the faith everywhere. Furthermore, in his writings, he contended that this same assertion was exotic and ridiculous, using the sting of sarcasm <note>original: *scommatum*; sharp jokes or gibes</note> more than the sharpness of reason. In this, he opposes many of the saints and the leading men of orthodox piety, and shamefully disparages my own assertions in this matter. Therefore, lest I myself seem to acknowledge error and guilt by immoderate silence, and so that I might cut away this pestilential plague with which he touched me, I have printed this concise and very brief little compendium. In it, one may see clearly and without any question that this opinion of ours regarding the Soul of the Heaven asserts nothing (as that man charges) wrongly or alien to orthodox piety; rather, it will be judged to be consistent in every way with both reason and the traditions of the saints. Nevertheless, in every point I commit myself to the lights of the most illustrious Church, which is ruled by the Spirit that does not err, denying myself and bringing my intellect into captivity in obedience to Christ—who alone may judge me, not any human day—in whom I hope, in whom I may be wise, and may I live forever and ever.

---

->**IT PROMISES ARGUMENTS THAT ARE NOT ENTIRELY**<-
->**DEMONSTRATIVE, YET ARE VALID.**<-

---

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'I' containing an illustration of a man standing in a landscape with a cityscape and mountains in the background.</image-desc>
THEREFORE, INQUIRING into what should be thought regarding the soul of the celestial bodies according to the dictates of reason and the Peripatetics <note>original: *Peripateticorum*; followers of Aristotle's philosophy, so named because Aristotle taught while walking about.</note>, and what should be asserted according to the foundations of orthodox truth, we shall attempt to clearly prove the three Themes which are soon presented in this brief examination. However, we must first state that I have not said that I will demonstrate the third in this order of Themes by an absolute and unshakeable law of syllogizing; otherwise, our presumption would be judged more rash than pious or studious. Indeed, that wise architect of the Peripatetic doctrine <note>referring to Aristotle</note>, while seeking the cause of the variety of motions of the celestial bodies in the second book of *On the Heavens*, clears himself of such presumption with a long series of words, and asks, as it were, for pardon to be given because he attempts such lofty examinations and undertakes the scrutiny of those things which are distant from us by an almost immense interval, and because he has brought forth reasons of such small sufficiency concerning them. So too Augustine, a man of both divine and human wisdom, speaking of this examination of ours (in his commentary on the second chapter of Genesis) says: "Now, however, always preserving the moderation of pious gravity, we ought to believe nothing rashly concerning an obscure matter." With what face, then, and with what lack of moderation of mind, should I myself—certainly a fragile and sluggish explorer of sublime things—dare to devise and bring forth the most solid reasonings for a position of this kind, which might demonstrate it fearlessly? Nevertheless, we shall attempt (with the Holy Spirit as guide) to express those things by which we are drawn toward the affirmative rather than the negative opinion of this inquiry.

### FIRST THEME.
It matters nothing to the orthodox faith whether one says the celestial bodies are animate or inanimate.

### SECOND THEME.
It seems more consistent with the utterances of the prophets and saints to admit the affirmative part of this inquiry than the negative.

<meta>Catchword: THE THIRD.</meta>

<meta>This page continues Paul Ricius’s defense of his philosophical position regarding the "Soul of the Heaven." Having introduced the controversy on the previous page, Ricius now begins his formal argument, citing major Church authorities—Augustine, Thomas Aquinas, and Duns Scotus—to prove that the idea of celestial bodies having souls is compatible with Christian faith.</meta>

COMPENDIUM ON THE SOUL. 205 BOOK THREE.

->*Reason and the perceptible order of things declare that celestial bodies exist as animate beings—that is, by a soul which informs the heaven itself (in its own way).*<-

->*It neither contradicts nor follows from the foundations of faith to say the heaven is animate.*<-

The first theme is therefore demonstrated by both reason and the authority of the saints. For in matters that neither contradict the foundations of faith nor are drawn by evident consequence from any of them, it matters nothing whether one admits one of the opposing views or the other. The position concerning the soul of the heaven is of this kind, which is clearly found by anyone examining the individual foundations of faith and the sayings of sacred scripture. Therefore, regarding this inquiry, to call either side true or false can neither add to nor take away from the solid and unshakable truth of faith.

->*The authority of Augustine, Thomas, and John Duns Scotus proves the same.*<-

Many and most illustrious men of divine wisdom, both ancient and modern, affirm this position either explicitly or as a clear consequence. First, consider the sayings of that most shining star, Aurelius Augustine; for he says in *Enchiridion* <note>original: *Enchiridion 43*; a handbook on Christian faith, hope, and love. Modern editions usually locate this in chapter 58.</note> 43:

> Nor do I hold it as certain whether the Sun, the Moon, and the animate stars belong to the heavenly city, although some appear to be glowing bodies but not intelligent ones. If the celestial bodies are animate, their souls belong to the society of those Angels; where, for the solution of many arguments, note that the souls of the heaven and the celestial bodies are not in the genus of human souls, but of Angels, and are themselves Angels.

The same author in *On Genesis* <note>original: *super Genes. 2*</note>, book 2: It is also usually asked whether the visible lights of the heavens are only bodies or if they have certain spirits as their rulers, and if they have them, whether they are also vitally inspired by them just as flesh is animated by the souls of animals, etc. But now, while always preserving the moderation of pious gravity, we ought to believe nothing rashly about an obscure matter, lest perhaps what truth may later reveal—although it can in no way be adverse to the books of either the Old or New Testament—we might hate it simply because of the love of our own error. Again, in the *Retractations* <note>original: *Retractationū 11*; a work where Augustine reviewed and corrected his earlier writings.</note> 11:

> But, he says, that this world is an animal <note>original: *animal*; in this context, the term refers to a "living being" possessing an *anima* (soul), following the Platonic concept of the *Anima Mundi* or World Soul.</note>, as Plato thought and many other philosophers, I could not track down by certain reason, nor did I know it could be persuaded by the authority of divine Scriptures. Therefore, I noted as rashly said anything of mine from which that could be accepted, even in the book *On the Immortality of the Soul*; not because I confirm this to be false, but because I do not comprehend it to be true, that the world is an animal.

Thus he spoke. From these passages, we clearly gather that Augustine does not consider it a trivial matter or one alien to the foundations of faith (as that man <note>referring to Ricius's opponent at Ingolstadt mentioned on the previous page.</note> contends) to say that celestial bodies are animate and that their souls are placed in the assembly of angels. We also gather that this position cannot be adverse in any way to the sayings of the Old or New Testament. That passage from the *Retractations* provides the most stable strength and invincible foundation for our position, because no one is ignorant that the book of *Retractations* serves as the censor and judge of all those things which he himself had written before. So also Saint Thomas of Aquino, when he declared in *Against the Gentiles*, book two, that Aristotle believed an intellect was united to the celestial body as its form, adds the following:

> Moreover, what has been said about the soul of the heaven, we have not said as though asserting it according to the doctrine of faith, to which it pertains nothing whether it is said this way or otherwise.

Similarly, in *Quodlibet* 12, we read the same man saying: "But I say, following Augustine's *Literal Commentary on Genesis*, that it does not matter to the faith whether the celestial body is animate or not." Likewise, the man of divine insight, John Duns Scotus, in Book 1, Distinction 4, Second Part <note>original: *1 4. Distinctione secunda*; likely a reference to his commentary on the *Sentences*.</note>, says:

> As for the animation of the celestial body, it seems to be in doubt.

And a little further down, when he had supported the same position with the manifold opinion of Augustine, he adds (speaking briefly):

> if the heavens are inanimate: this is a matter of belief and not concluded by reason: because no

<summary>Paul Ricius argues that the question of whether celestial bodies (stars and planets) have souls is a matter of philosophical inquiry rather than a fixed dogma of faith. He supports this by quoting St. Augustine, Thomas Aquinas, and Duns Scotus, all of whom treated the "animation" of the heavens as a permissible, if uncertain, theological position.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Paul Ricius’s argument regarding the "Soul of the Heaven" (Anima Cœli). On the previous page, he cited Augustine to show that the animation of celestial bodies is a permissible belief. Here, he extends this to other Scholastic and Patristic authorities like Duns Scotus and Bernard of Clairvaux, arguing that such a belief is neither heretical nor contrary to reason.</meta>

PAUL RICIUS,

is the condition in that body, appearing so perfectly and manifestly to oppose the animation of the body. These are his words. Here you see Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a highly influential Franciscan priest and philosopher-theologian of the High Middle Ages.</note> himself doubting about the soul of the heaven, yet not plainly disapproving of it. By these things we clearly understand that in no part does it contradict reason or belief to admit an animate heaven.

->*The same is to be ascribed to several of the saints by way of consequence.*<-

Furthermore, we know that many of the saints say the same by way of consequence; namely, those who doubt and consider it no inconvenience for angels to be naturally united to bodies and to persist in them. Indeed, if an intellectual substance is naturally fit to seek the companionship of a body, it will undoubtedly be more inclined and prone toward a sublime and eternal body than toward an earthly one subject to corruption; for like adheres to like more than to the unsuitable. Although the entire school of younger theologians <note>Refers to the later Scholastics who moved away from the idea of celestial souls in favor of "extrinsic movers" (angels pushing the spheres from the outside).</note> contends otherwise, not without merit, refusing to believe that angels inhabit bodies by nature. However, that many of the ancients felt this way about the angelic nature is declared by their own words. I will remain silent for now regarding Dionysius, Augustine, Gregory, and Damascene <note>The "Four Great Doctors" or similar high authorities: Pseudo-Dionysius, Augustine of Hippo, Gregory the Great, and John of Damascus.</note>, to whom (according to Thomas in his *Questions on Evil*) <note>Thomas Aquinas, *De Malo* (Disputed Questions on Evil), where he discusses the nature of spiritual substances.</note> one may not unreasonably adjudge this assertion according to the sound of their words. But because their words can be twisted to another meaning, I pass over them in silence. 

Yet let us hear the wise and God-filled Bernard <note>Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian abbot and mystic.</note> saying in his sermons on the Song of Songs: "As for angelic bodies, whether they are truly natural to the spirits themselves as ours are to us men, and whether they are animate like men—though immortal—I do not wish for you to inquire from me. For the fathers seem to feel differently, and it is not clear to me which of the two I should teach, and I confess my ignorance; but I do not think that the knowledge of these things contributes much to our progress." Thus says Bernard. Since he holds this as an open problem, and confirms that other saints do as well, and that knowing whether angels naturally unite bodies to themselves does not much affect the perfection of salvation, it is much more reasonable to suspect that the Soul of the Heaven is united to it by its own nature. The assertion of this thing (or its opposite) matters little to the way of salvation, and thus by consequence we prove, according to the teachings of Bernard and other ancients, that it is not entirely foreign to call the celestial bodies animate. Nor can it be entirely heretical. For that is heretical whose contrary is handed down in Scripture either expressly or by way of consequence; but it is established in no place in Scripture that the heaven is inanimate. Therefore, it is not heretical to say it is animate. From all this, it must be firmly concluded that it matters nothing to the truth of the orthodox faith whether one admits celestial bodies to be animate or inanimate. As for the authorities and reasons that seem to prove the opposite, we shall strive to untie every knot of ambiguity in the examination of the following conclusion.

## SECOND THEME.

### *It seems more consistent with the utterances of the prophets and saints to admit the affirmative part of this inquiry than the negative.*

### *If the celestial body were inanimate, the Prophet, by remaining silent, would have given cause for the permanence of the cult of idolatry.*

One may build this theme upon the multiform opinion of the Saints and Prophets; and first, I show that they agree with the words of the Prophets by a double law of syllogism: first, by the destruction of the contradictory; second, demonstratively (as they call it) and directly. Therefore, one must first argue that the heaven, according to the Prophet, is not "not animate," therefore it must be animate. For if the heaven were inanimate, the Prophet, by remaining silent about that fact, would have been the cause of strengthening or permitting the cult of idolatry. For (as is handed down in the second book of *The Physics*) <note>original: *De auditu*; refers to Aristotle’s *Physica*, often called *De naturali auditu*. The analogy describes "accidental" causality: the absence of a pilot causes a shipwreck because his presence would have prevented it.</note> the absence of a sailor is the cause of a sinking, just as his presence is the cause of safety. In this way, ignorance and silence regarding the inanimation of the heaven is the cause of the permanence of the cult of idolatry,

Having previously established that Scholastic thinkers like Duns Scotus did not explicitly rule out the idea, he now turns to the Biblical Prophets to provide negative proof: the fact that they never mock the stars for being "inanimate" suggests they believed the celestial bodies possessed life.</meta>

### A COMPENDIUM ON THE SOUL OF THE HEAVEN ###

...the knowledge and explanation of which would have been the reason for its removal. Since it would be absurd to think that a Prophet—who was concerned with all diligent zeal and anxious care to remove the cult of idolatry—would have remained silent about the very thing whose knowledge or belief would have provided the most powerful reason for despising and rejecting such a cult, it can easily and by solid reason be gathered that the celestial body is not inanimate.

That the Prophet remained silent on this point is clear to anyone who carefully examines all the words of the Prophets, especially those places which most strongly demand an expression of this matter—namely, where they most earnestly accuse and forbid the worship of the stars and the heavens. For you will never hear a Prophet give as a reason for his rebuke that the celestial stars do not see, do not hear, nor understand. Yet, wherever they rebuke the worship of statues, they always bring this very reason forward.

For example, in **Deuteronomy 4**: *You shall serve gods who were fashioned by the hands of men from wood and stone, who do not see, nor hear, nor eat, nor smell.* <note>original: "Seruietis dijs, qui hominum manu fabricati sunt ligno & lapide, qui nõ uident, nec audiunt, nec comedunt, nec odorāt."</note>

And that passage in the **Psalms**: <margin>Psalm 134</margin> *The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works of the hands of men: They have a mouth and do not speak, they have eyes and do not see, they have ears and do not hear.* <note>This is Psalm 135 in modern Bibles, though the Vulgate numbered it 134.</note>

And that of **Isaiah chapter 44**: <margin>Isaiah ch. 44</margin> *They are their own witnesses: because they do not see, nor do they understand.* Again: *hiring a goldsmith to make a God, but even when one cries out to him, he will not hear, nor save them from tribulation.*

We read that the Prophet cried out these things and many of this kind in his reproach of images and statues. But regarding the Sun and the Moon, and the other stars of heaven, he did so not at all. Yet, no one is ignorant that, for the purpose of removing their worship, this would have been the most exquisite of all other reasons.

When the Prophet rebukes the worship of the stars, he assigns a different cause—not that they do not hear or do not understand—but that the people of Israel were not "attributed" to them <note>The term "attributed" (attributi) here refers to the ancient idea that different nations were assigned to the governance of specific stars or angels, while Israel was reserved for God alone.</note>, nor subject to them as the rest of the nations are, since they are a people chosen as the inheritance of the Most High. Or, he forbids it because the Lord did not command the worship of the stars, as it is written:

<margin>Deut. 17</margin> *The man or woman who does evil in the sight of the Lord your God, and transgresses His covenant, so as to go and serve alien gods and adore them—the Sun, and the Moon, and all the host of heaven—which I have not commanded.*

Again: <margin>Deut. 29</margin> *They abandoned the covenant of the Lord which He made with their fathers when He led them out of the land of Egypt, and they served alien gods and adored those whom they did not know, and to whom they had not been attributed.*

And also: <margin>Deut. 4</margin> *Lest perhaps, lifting your eyes to heaven, you see the Sun and the Moon and all the stars of heaven, and being deceived, you adore and worship them, to which all the peoples are attributed (or which He distributed to all peoples) who are under the whole heaven; but the Lord took you and led you out of the iron furnace of Egypt, so that He might have a people of inheritance.*

And although here, where we read: *And to whom they are attributed*, the Latin edition <note>Referring to the Vulgate, the standard Latin Bible of the time.</note> has: *which He created for service*, the **Hebrew Truth** <term>Hebraica veritas (the original Hebrew text of the Bible, often cited by Renaissance scholars to correct Latin translations)</term> nonetheless declares the same thing that we have interpreted: *And to whom they had not been attributed.*

Indeed, I think it is most worthy of wonder that the translator rendered the same word from the Hebrew manuscript in a uniform sentence correctly in **Deuteronomy 29**—*to whom they had not been attributed*—yet in **Deuteronomy 4**, he produced it corruptly as *which He created for service*, since it matters much to the secrets of truth whether the series of letters stands in this way or that.

Furthermore, the Hebrew Truth reveals that same mystery in **Deuteronomy 31** which the Latin edition also obscures. For it is read there in Hebrew: *And he shall go whoring after the alien gods of the land into which he shall enter*; but the Latin edition explains it as *after alien gods in the land*.

This is again declared in **4 Kings** <note>This is 2 Kings 17:25-27 in modern Bibles.</note>: *The Lord sent lions among them, and behold, they killed them, because they were ignorant of the rite of the God of the land.* There too, the understanding of the truth is dulled by the Latin edition.

Such a search demands a deeper and wider investigation, but I wanted to mention it here so that these things might become known to you: that there are many sacred words of the Prophets which, when you read them in the Hebrew manuscript, allow you to perceive sublime and great sacraments of the orthodox faith from which the Latin edition either casts a shadow or remains entirely silent. Anyone skilled in the Hebrew language will bear witness to this truth; indeed, even those who are only in its cradle...
