...[table] and touched upon only the first rudiments. From these points, you may finally conclude that the primary reason the Prophet rebukes the worship of the stars is that God’s chosen people are not subject or beholden—as other nations are in some way—to any celestial divinity, but only to the King of Ages, the invisible and immortal God. If the stars were inanimate, no argument would have been more effective or sufficient for calling people away from this worship than their lack of life. The ignorance of this fact, or silence regarding it, would have allowed this cult to persist. Since this would be absurd and completely foreign to the prophetic spirit—which was a rigid defender against the worship of idols—it seems consistent that the celestial bodies are not inanimate. Therefore, according to the sense of the Prophets, one may believe they are animate, which we set out to show from the beginning by destroying the contradictory view.

### THE PROPHET PLAINLY, OR ACCORDING TO PROBABILITY,
### suggests in a three-fold way that the celestial bodies are animated.

I declare this again through a proper way of syllogizing <note>logical reasoning using premises to reach a conclusion</note>: that which the Prophet expresses either plainly, or by way of consequence, or according to probability, and nowhere affirms the opposite, should be ascribed to the mind of the Prophets. Such is the position on the **Soul of the Heaven**. For if you examine the various utterances of the Prophets, you will understand this is included in their words in three ways: First, by explaining the nature of the soul; Second, by inferring it as a consequence; Third, by declaring it through the proportionality and similarity of their operations.

### SOLOMON EXPLAINS THE NATURE OF THE SOUL,
### and calls it "spirit."

Solomon first explains the nature of the soul in the book of Ecclesiastes: *The spirit,* he says, *goes circling through all things.* <note>original: "Lustrans uniuersa in circuitu pergit spiritus"</note> Here, he could have meant nothing else by "spirit" than the body of the heaven itself, or that power by which the celestial body is constantly revolved. Since he would not have wanted the body itself to be understood by the word "spirit," he designates the moving power of the heaven, which he calls the soul. That he does not mean the solar or celestial body itself is shown by two reasons. First, because the literal sense—from which alone one can draw an argument—does not allow "spirit" to be understood as "body" without some compelling reason or manifest authority. Second, because it would be a clear triviality and a useless repetition, since he had just before spoken of the exact rotation of the heaven: *The sun rises and sets, and returns to its place; and being reborn there, it circles through the south and turns toward the north.* <note>Ecclesiastes 1:5-6; original: "Oritur inquiens Sol & occidit, & ad locum suū reuertitur, ibiq; renascens gyrat per meridiem, & flectitur ad aquilonem."</note> Since the discussion is not about the local motion of a body, he speaks of the spiritual course of the soul, by which the soul surveys all the universal patterns <term>exemplaria: the divine blueprints or archetypes of things</term> that exist in the divine mind. For just as he previously commemorated the cause of perpetual generation and the change of things—namely, the circulation of the heaven and the sun—so now he announces the cause of that celestial circulation, which is the spiritual circulation of the soul. From the soul’s connection with the celestial body follows the physical movement of the heaven. Just as in us, the passions of the soul produce a sensible effect in the body through the soul's bond with the organic body—for example, sadness and intense anxiety make the body lazy, sluggish, and almost immobile, while joy makes it agile, alert, and ready for movement—so too the concepts of the heavenly soul overflow into the celestial body itself. I discussed this at greater length in the first volume of my work, *On Celestial Agriculture* <note>original title: "De Coelesti Agricultura"</note>, which I will recall shortly in a brief series of words. Therefore, following the appropriate and literal sense of Scripture, the discussion there is not about the body, but the spirit by which the revolution of the heaven is produced. 
<margin>Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book 3</margin>
Even **Augustine**, in the third book of *On the Trinity*, seems to have called this the "spirit of life," asserting that the bodies of the world are ruled by a rational spirit of life. 
<margin>St. Thomas, *Opuscula* 10</margin>
And **St. Thomas Aquinas** taught that this very interpretation of the text should be upheld in his tenth *Opusculum* <note>a small scholarly work or treatise</note>.

<header>COMPENDIUM ON THE SOUL OF THE HEAVEN.</header>

### THE PROPHET AFFIRMS THAT THE HEAVEN IS ANIMATED, BECAUSE HE DECLARES IT MORE EXCELLENT THAN THAT WHICH IS ANIMATED.

**S**econd, as a logical consequence, we infer this from the sayings of the Prophets: for the Prophet taught that the heaven and the stars are absolutely more perfect than man. Now, that which is simply more perfect than an animated being <note>original: *animato*, meaning a creature with a soul or life</note> must itself be animated; we speak here of absolute perfection. For nothing prevents an inanimate thing from being more perfect than a living one in certain ways—not by the perfection of nature and substance (which we call absolute perfection), but according to something external, such as an "accident" <term>accident: a philosophical term for a non-essential quality, like color or brightness</term>. For instance, a star is more perfect than a man in its splendor and the length of its existence, but not in its specific form and substance. Thus, nothing stands in the way of a man being more excellent than the stars and angels through the perfection of grace, even if not by nature. For we read in Job 15: *The heavens are not pure in His sight, how much more abominable and useless is man.* <margin>Job 15.</margin> Therefore, whoever declares the heavens to be absolutely more perfect than man must also profess that they are animated.

Nor should it be said that the heaven is called more excellent only because of the angels who inhabit it. After all, mention was made of the angels just a moment before, saying: *Behold, among His holy ones no one is unchangeable,* where by "holy ones" <note>original: *sanctos*</note> we all understand the angels. Nor should it be said that the heaven is more excellent than man simply because of its permanence. A long duration of existence does not grant absolute perfection; otherwise, a plant—or even the most useful metals and stones—would be simply more excellent than a man because they last longer. Added to this is the fact that the very form of man, by which he exists as man, is itself immortal and everlasting. Again, as the same Job says: *Can a man be justified compared to God, or can one born of a woman appear pure? Behold, even the moon does not shine, and the stars are not pure in His sight; how much more is man but rottenness, and the son of man a worm.* <margin>Job 25.</margin> So too said David, the messenger of salvation: *When I see your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars which you have established: What is man that you are mindful of him, or the son of man that you visit him?* Since the heaven is more excellent than man, and nothing inanimate could be more excellent than man, it seems we must firmly believe the heaven is animated.

### *THROUGH A LIKENESS OF PROPORTION AND OPERATION, the Prophet calls the intellectual substance father and mother, husband and wife, son and daughter, bridegroom and bride, virgin, King and Queen.*

**T**hird, the Prophet indicates the same thing through a likeness of proportion and operation. If you attentively weigh the sacred words of the Prophets, you will find that they reveal the spiritual and intellectual substance <note>referring here to the heavenly bodies or divine entities</note> through many different names. For he calls it now father, now mother, now husband, now wife, son, daughter, bridegroom, bride, virgin, King, and Queen. He calls it "Father," as in Jeremiah 3: *I have become a father to Israel*; and in Hebrews 12: *Shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits?* He calls it "Mother" in Isaiah 50: *Where is this book of your mother’s divorce, by which I sent her away?* and in Galatians 4: *But the Jerusalem which is above is free, which is our mother.* This statement by the Apostle opens the sense and understanding of all the things we mention here; consider it within yourself with careful meditation. <margin>Jeremiah 31. Hebrews 12. 2 Corinthians 11. Hosea 2. Revelation 21. Exodus 4. Isaiah chapter 62. Jeremiah 31.</margin>

He calls it "Husband," saying: *Return, O children, says the Lord, for I am your husband.* And in 2 Corinthians 11: *I have betrothed you,* he says, *to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.* He calls it "Wife" in Hosea 2: *Judge your mother, judge her, for she is not my wife*—namely, as she was before. And in Revelation 21: *Come, and I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb.* He calls it "Son" in Exodus 4: *Israel is my firstborn son.* "Daughter" in Zechariah 9: *Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; shout, daughter of Jerusalem.* "Bridegroom," "Bride," and "Virgin" in Isaiah 62: *And as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you.* And John says: *He who has the bride is the bridegroom.* And Jeremiah 31: *I will build you, and you shall be built, O virgin of Israel.* And that passage in 2 Corinthians 11: *For I have betrothed you to one...*

### JEREMIAH CLEARLY SEEMS TO INDICATE THAT THE SOUL OF HEAVEN IS GIVEN,
### since he frequently proclaims a "Queen of Heaven."

<margin>Jeremiah cap. 44.</margin>
For we read in the seventh chapter of Jeremiah: *The children gather wood, the fathers kindle the fire, and the women knead the dough, to make cakes for the queen of heaven.* The same Prophet repeats this title quite often. However, what he wished to be understood by "queen of heaven" is the subject of various and wavering opinions among the commentators. For the interpretation hesitates whether it refers to the Moon, or the host of heaven, or Juno, or Berecinthia <note>Another name for Cybele, the Phrygian "Mother of the Gods"</note> (as the interlinear gloss judged), who is called the wife of Saturn and the mother of the gods. But no student of the Scriptures, and no diligent seeker of truth, will be able to agree with these little glosses, which adapt the words to a preconceived concept rather than forming the concept from the words. For what does the "queen of heaven" have to do with the Moon, or the host of heaven, or Juno herself, and that sort? Would he not have more easily and clearly proclaimed "the Moon" or "the host of heaven" or any other 
<margin>

and 2 Kings 3.

Jeremiah 50.

</margin>
kind of idol here, just as he does openly elsewhere? For instance, in Deuteronomy 4 and 17, and 2 Kings 3, where he names Baal, the Sun, the Moon, the host of heaven, the twelve signs, the idol Molech, Astaroth, Chemosh, and Milcom; and in 4 Kings, Beelzebub; and 3 Kings 2, Ashtoreth; and Jeremiah 50, Bel; and Numbers 25, Baal-peor. Therefore, he who teaches that something other than the power by which the heaven is ruled should be understood by "queen of heaven" twists the text rather than explaining it. This creates various and inextricable tangles for the intellect and produces every kind of ignorance of the Scriptures when we strive to drag the sacred words away from their literal meaning without any manifest authority or reason compelling us to do so. The Prophet, therefore, expresses neither the host of heaven, nor the Moon, nor Juno, nor a king and ruler, but by the feminine title "queen," he designates the soul of heaven. This is because she alone, in the entire archetypal machine <note>A term for the cosmic structure as designed by God</note>, reflects a feminine disposition.

found in the margin of the sacred canon, it is certain that some secret lies hidden there, just as in that great mystery of the Passion indicated by the Prophet Zechariah: *And they shall look* (he says) *upon me whom they have pierced.* <note>original: "Et aspicient ad me quem confixerunt." Zechariah 12:10.</note> There, in the standard text, it is written *Elai*—that is, "to me"—but in the margin it is read as *Elou*, which sounds like "to him." By this, the Prophet wished to suggest that although God, who speaks through the Prophet's mouth, declares Himself to be pierced, it is not according to His nature as God, but insofar as He is man; therefore, the margin reads "to him," namely, to the man as man. The same law must surely be applied here: for although one might adore the celestial bodies and their works, it is not according to them being bodies, but insofar as a soul dwells within them—the gracious queen of heaven. Nor is the veneration <term>dulia; the lower form of veneration given to saints or angels</term> of this queen forbidden, but only <term>latria; the supreme worship reserved for God alone</term>. Yet even the adoration of *dulia* is to be avoided, lest in the long progress of time, the lower veneration pass over into the supreme worship of *latria*. 

However, if you—as some argue—contend that it is not permitted to draw an argument from the words of Jeremiah because the Prophet is speaking about the worship of speechless idols (which he himself refutes and in no part affirms), or that Solomon speaks from the persona of fools rather than from the nature of the thing itself, and therefore no conclusion can be reached from either side regarding our proposal—to this we say that the Prophet does not refute the opinion of those asserting that there is a "Queen of Heaven" in the celestial realms. Rather, he only rebukes the worship of her with *latria*, just as he often rebukes the adoration of the stars, but not their existence. For if the opinion concerning the soul of heaven were false, as we mentioned before, the Prophet would have to be blamed for neglect or even dense ignorance for wrapping this falsehood in silence. The same must be said regarding the words of Solomon; for although the inquiry might perhaps prove the opposite of the truth in itself, the reasons are nonetheless taken from the very nature of things. It would be unseemly and indeed far-fetched for divine eloquence to express a lie or a falsehood in any way without a refutation. Thus, this kind of argument can offer no obstacle at all to our assertion. Finally, having heard and understood all these things, it is proved that the Prophetic sentiment admits that celestial bodies are animate.

### SAINT JEROME AND
### Albert the Great clearly affirm the same.

Very many testimonies of other saints and wise men are established, primarily that of Saint Jerome, who says in the first chapter of Ecclesiastes: *The spirit goes circling round and returns into its circuits.* <note>original: "Girans girando uadit spiritus." Ecclesiastes 1:6.</note> Either he named the sun itself "spirit" because it is an animal that breathes and flourishes, completing its annual orbits in its course—by which he clearly indicates that the celestial stars exist as animate beings—or, as Albert, Thomas, and the rest of their followers do not doubt, this sentiment should be ascribed to Jerome. Second is the testimony of Albert's four contemporaries, clearly stating that a soul is given to the heaven, though not under the same condition as in a creature that is born and corruptible. For he says: "But if we wished to bring the philosophers back to the same point, we would say with the saints that there are certain Intelligences <term>Intelligences; non-material beings, often identified with angels, who move the celestial spheres</term> in the spheres serving the primary motion of the orbits. Those Intelligences are called the 'souls of the spheres,' though not in the same sense as the souls of men, because they do not come into action through the abstraction of mental images." <note>original: "phantasmatibus." In medieval psychology, "phantasms" were the sensory images the human mind uses to think; Ricius argues celestial souls are "purer" because they don't need these images.</note> And a little lower he says: "We concede, however, that the Intelligence which is called the 'soul' and 'motor' of the sphere is not called a 'soul' according to the same definition as the human intellect, but in a prior and posterior sense." Thus, a little later he says: "According to the philosophers, who do not contradict certain saints who deny that the heaven has a soul except in name only—those who shrink from the name 'soul'." These are Albert's words. From these you openly gather that there are Intelligences in the orbits themselves which he calls souls; but they differ from our souls because they are not sensitive—that is, understanding and abstracting through mental images—and he affirms that such was the meaning even of the saints who deny that souls are given to celestial bodies.

## THOMAS AQUINAS CLEARLY SHOWS
## THE SAME THING.

**T**he third point of evidence is the tradition of the Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential philosopher-theologian of the Middle Ages.</note>, who says in the sixth article of his work *On Spiritual Creatures*: He affirms that the soul of heaven is joined to the orb, and is in reality distinct from those un-joined <term>intelligences; purely spiritual beings, often identified with angels, who guide the movements of the stars</term> that move them as an "end." For he says:
> Thus there will be a twofold order of spiritual substances: some united to celestial bodies as movers, while others will be entirely abstract, acting as the ends <note>original: "fines"; in Aristotelian philosophy, the "end" or "final cause" is the goal or purpose that inspires a movement.</note> of these motions.

This is his view. Nor does it follow that because he said souls are joined to the orb as "movers," he denies that they provide some inherent perfection to the heaven by way of a <term>form; the internal principle that gives a thing its specific nature and life</term>. Rather, he stated they were united as "movers" to exclude the type of union found in the "form" of lower things, just as he himself explains in that same passage:
> To say further that celestial bodies are animated in the same way as lower bodies—which are given life and sensation through a soul—is contrary to the incorruptibility of celestial bodies.

Again, at the end of his determination of that same question, he says:
> It must be said that they have ruling spirits, by which they are nevertheless not animated in the same way that lower animals are by their souls,

and he resumes this same opinion wherever he treats these questions. Furthermore, in the seventh question of the first part, he examines the position of Damascene <note>John of Damascus (c. 675–749), a Syrian monk and Church Father.</note> and the foundations upon which it rests. Examining these foundations, he says that among those who claim the heavens are animate and those who claim they are inanimate, there is little or no difference found in the reality of the matter, but only in the words used. And immediately before this, he says:
> Thus it is clear that celestial bodies are not animated in the same way as plants and animals, but equivocally <note>original: "aequivoce"; meaning the word "animated" is used in two different senses.</note>. If such an equivocation exists, it is like the way the word "body" is predicted of both celestial and earthly things: for the condition by which the celestial soul provides form is as far removed from the condition of the soul of perishable things as the celestial soul and heaven itself are removed from the earthly soul and earthly bodies,

as I shall show more extensively a little further down. However, when he says in that same seventh question:
> It is not necessary for the soul to be united to the body as a form, but through a contact of power <note>original: "contactum virtutis"</note>, just as a mover is united to the thing it moves,

he is speaking to explain the foundation of Damascene, who thought the soul was united to the celestial body for no other reason than to move it. Many wise men (as you will hear in what follows) do not accept this, and we agree with them. Even if we were to say the soul is united to the celestial body solely for the sake of moving it, it would still be worth examining whether "contact of power" is sufficient for a thing that is moved primarily of itself. For a thing's proper motion is its own proper action, and the action of a thing is primarily through the thing's own form. Therefore, either the celestial body would have no action of its own, but only a "passion" <note>In this context, "passion" means being acted upon by an outside force rather than acting from within.</note>—which is utterly contrary to this, the most noble of all bodies—or the power through which it performs motion is inherent to it as a form. But these matters seem to belong rather to the topic that follows.

## THE SAME IS DECLARED BY AUREOLUS
## AND THE SONGS OF THE HOLY CHURCH.

**T**he fourth point comes from that most famous man of theological wisdom, Aureolus <note>Peter Aureolus (c. 1280–1322), a Franciscan theologian known for his original and often controversial views.</note>, who in the second book of his *Sentences*, through a long series of arguments, strives strenuously to prove that a soul stands within the celestial orbs as a form. He does not think it foreign to implore their prayers <note>original: "suffragia"</note> and to venerate them with the worship of *dulia* <note>The type of veneration given to saints, as opposed to "latria," the worship reserved for God.</note>, except for the fact that a "scandal" might easily be caused among the "little ones" (the common people). They might pass from the adoration of *dulia* to *latria* (as we read frequently happened in prior centuries) and change the glory of the incorruptible God into the image of some creature. Thomas asserted this same distinction in article 8 of *On Spiritual Creatures*, where, in response to the argument stating:
> If celestial bodies are animated, it will be lawful to implore their prayers:

he says this is not permitted, specifically so that the occasion for idolatry might be removed. Nor should it be doubted that this intention of avoiding the occasion of idolatry led certain Catholic wise men to deny the "soul of heaven" more in word [than in belief]...

He explains that theologians often hedged their language about celestial souls primarily to prevent the common people from falling into planetary idolatry.</summary>

...and pious, and with a veiled face rather than a sincere mind—especially among the Greek people, from whom the worship of idols could scarcely ever be thoroughly uprooted. However, in this century, in which the "fullness of the nations" <note>A biblical reference to Romans 11:25, suggesting the era when the world has been fully converted to Christianity.</note> has now entered, all suspicion is far removed; hence, with a revealed face, we in no way fear to express the nature of the matter. A fifth strong point, providing a stable foundation for all others, is the testimony of the entire Roman Church, which in the Preface of the celebration of the Sacrament <note>The "Preface" is the introductory prayer to the Canon of the Mass.</note> chants these words: *through whom the angels praise your Majesty, the Dominions adore it, the Powers tremble, the Heavens and the Virtues of the heavens, etc.* <note>original: "per quem Maiestatem tuam laudant angeli, adorant dominationes, tremunt potestates, coeli coelorumque virtutes."</note> where, by "the virtues of the heavens" (as Saint Thomas witnesses in his 12th *Quodlibet* <note>A "Quodlibet" was a formal Scholastic debate where a teacher answered "any question" posed by students.</note>), the Church seems to have intended the souls of the heavens. If, finally, you diligently leaf through the library of all the saints, you will clearly understand that some accept the soul of the heaven and speak their opinion according to either side, among whom Saint Augustine is recognized as the standard-bearer and leader. Others, indeed, openly contend for the affirmative side; the foremost of all these was the assertion of Saint Jerome, in whose assembly (according to the views of Saint Thomas) the 4th book of Gregory’s *Dialogues* can be placed—indeed, even the prophecy of Jeremiah and the oracles of Solomon. You will hear no one utterly denying it, except for John of Damascus or Basil among the Greek sages, who had some other followers. Yet, if you pay attention, these deviate but little from our path, as we shall explain shortly, more abundantly, by the will of those above.

### HE COMMEMORATES THE ARGUMENTS 
### THAT SEEM TO BE OPPOSED.

Lest any room for resistance remain for our adversaries, we shall soon attempt to resolve certain points by which they strive toward the opposite of our conclusion. First, therefore, they bring forward the words of Augustine in the 11th book of his *Retractions* <note>The *Retractationes* was a work in which Augustine reviewed his earlier writings to correct or clarify his views.</note> saying: *Something of this sort was said by me, by which it (namely, that the world is a living being) could be accepted; I noted that even in the book on the immortality of the soul, this was spoken rashly.* Through these words of Augustine, Bonaventure, in the 2nd book of the *Sentences*, presumes to establish the opposite of our conclusion, asserting it to be erroneous and against the tradition of the saints—and indeed of the philosophers—to say that celestial bodies are animated. And if some of the saints, such as Jerome in his commentary on the first book of *Ecclesiastes*, seem to say this, Bonaventure wished their sayings to be understood metaphorically. Second, the opinion of Jerome is brought forward in his books on Origen’s *Peri Archon* <note>Greek for "On First Principles," a controversial foundational work of Christian theology.</note>, where among Origen's other errors, he condemns the fact that he called the heaven animated. Third, John of Damascus says in his second book: *Let no one think the heavens or the lanterns [stars] are animated, for they are inanimate and without sensation.* Fourth, several again oppose us with Augustine in his book *On the Knowledge of the True Life*, saying of the stars: *Those who judge them to be rational, or at least sensible bodies, are rightly counted among the irrational, as they themselves lack sense.* Fifth, if souls of the heavens were granted, there would be three orders of those to be judged in the Judgment: namely, of angels, of men, and of celestial souls, which is clearly contrary to the tradition of all the saints. There are also certain other "clever" men, adding a vast crowd of arguments so that a multitude of words and futile arguments might supply their defect of sharpness and genius; such as when they say: *If the heaven were animated, the heaven would also need to be saved.* For the response is the same: because the souls of heaven are in the same order as the Angels—that is, perpetually blessed. But having set these aside, let us proceed.

### HE RESOLVES THE OBJECTED ARGUMENTS.

For one who looks rightly, the solution to these arguments will be by no means laborious. For first, the authority of the 11th book of the *Retractions* declares itself and resolves every mode of ambiguity, adding to the aforementioned opinion: *Not because I confirm this to be false, but because I do not grasp it to be true, that the world is a living being.* As for the saying of Bonaventure himself, it never...

<meta>This page continues Paul Ricius’s defense of the theory that celestial bodies possess souls. Having addressed general patristic caution in the previous page, he now systematically deconstructs specific objections raised by Saint Jerome, John Damascene, and Saint Augustine, using the logic of Scholastic heavyweights like Thomas Aquinas and Duns Scotus.</meta>

<page-num>214</page-num>
<header>PAUL RICIUS,</header>

I cannot help but wonder that he brought forth such a word of Augustine to strengthen his position, and that he taught that the saying of Saint Jerome must be heard metaphorically: for who would ever be such a commentator as to wish to explain the literal understanding of words through metaphor, and to explain riddles and obscure things through even darker ones? For in this way, it will be easy to call any fantastic ravings true, and to prove things that are true to be false. Thus, it is certainly playful—and contrary to the sense of Albert, Thomas, Scotus, and others—to say that Jerome spoke that [commentary] on Ecclesiastes 1 <note>original: "Ecclesiasticis 1" refers here to Jerome’s commentary on the Book of Ecclesiastes, specifically regarding the movements of the sun.</note> not by asserting it, but by reciting the opinion of others, since the context of the words there clearly demonstrates the opposite. Moreover, it is far more irrational to take up the vain documents of others and nowhere refute them, but everywhere keep silent about the true understanding of the matter. 

Secondly, it will be easy to resolve the point of Jerome in the books *On First Principles* <note>original: "periarchon"; referring to Origen's *De Principiis*, a controversial foundational text of Christian theology.</note> if you rightly consider the sequence of the speech there: for he does not blame Origen for saying the celestial stars are animated, but for saying that they were surrounded by these thick and perishable bodies because of certain faults, in the same way as men are. For he says: *That the Sun also, and the Moon, and the stars are living beings—indeed, that in the way we men are surrounded by these bodies which are thick and heavy because of certain sins, so also the lights of heaven received such and such bodies that they might shine more or less, and that demons are clothed in airy bodies because of greater faults.* These are his words. From which you understand that Jerome refutes not the position itself, but the *manner* of the position. 

The third document of Damascene <note>John Damascene (c. 675–749), a Syrian monk and Church Father whose *The Orthodox Faith* was a standard theological textbook.</note> (who indeed was the first and only one in the holy and vast monastery of the ancient theologians, together with Basil) seems to have asserted with a firm opinion the opposite of our conclusion. It allows for a two-part response: namely, that they affirmed this position either out of an inattentive investigation (as it pleased John Scotus <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major Scholastic philosopher known as the "Subtle Doctor."</note>) or with a certain limitation that agrees with us, just as Saint Thomas of Aquino judged. For in the 14th distinction of the second [book of the *Sentences*], the foundation upon which Damascene relies is wavering and of minimal strength. The same John Scotus maintained this, saying: *But another Greek, namely Damascene, asserted that the heavens are not animated. The reason he gives for this is that such a soul would be united to such a body in vain, since it has no sense-perception, and consequently acquires no perfection from the body.* But that (says Scotus) *does not seem appropriately said, that a power is united to matter so that it may acquire perfection from the matter, but rather so that it may communicate perfection to the matter; indeed, more principally so that the whole composite may be perfect from them.* These are his words. And thus Damascene (according to Scotus) declined into this opinion from an inattentive investigation of the foundation. 

The second and more agreeable response is that of Saint Thomas in his sixth [article] *On Spiritual Creatures*: for he says, *Damascene does not altogether deny that celestial bodies are animated, but he removes the idea that celestial bodies are animated in such a way that spiritual substances are united to them as forms, just as they are to corruptible animals.* These are his words. Therefore, he does not deny it entirely, but only that they are animated like earthly animals—which I myself also affirm (as do all who ascribe souls to the celestial orbs). Even the aforementioned words of Damascene seem to sound the same, by saying: *For they are inanimate and insensitive.* For it would be vain and trifling to add "insensitive" if he had said the celestial stars were altogether inanimate, since that which is inanimate must also lack sense. Therefore, with the intention of limiting the claim, he connects "insensitive," as if he had said: *they are inanimate by such a soul as that of perishable living things, which necessarily require sense for the permanence of their life.* 

In the same way, in the fourth place, one must respond to the sayings of Augustine, who from the same foundation we have now brought forward, added: *or at least sensible*; and this his other recorded sayings clearly declare, and especially those in the first [book] of the *Retractions*. 

The fifth point indeed (as Saint Thomas handed down in the sixth [article] of *On Power*) gave a greater occasion to many of the younger [scholars] for refusing to believe that celestial bodies are animated. That is resolved through a single clause of Augustine in the *Enchiridion* <note>Augustine’s "Handbook" on Faith, Hope, and Love.</note>, saying: *If we posit that the celestial bodies are animated, there will not for that reason be three orders of those to be judged in the judgment: because those souls are counted among the angels.*

<header>COMPENDIUM ON THE SOUL. 215</header>

...and these points are sufficient for an intelligent person to resolve the aforementioned issues. Thus, with divine assistance, we proceed to the examination of the third Theme.

## THIRD THEME

<margin>Commentary 14.</margin>
Reason and the observable order of things demonstrate that the celestial bodies exist as animate beings—that is, possessing a soul which <term>informs: In Scholastic philosophy, to "inform" means to give a specific nature or "form" to matter, making it a functional, living thing.</term> the heaven itself in its own particular way. This theme requires two points to be clarified. First, that the celestial body is animate; second, that the soul informs the heavens in its own unique way, and not in the manner of perishable <note>original: "caducorum"; literally things that fall or decay, referring to the "sublunary" world of change.</note> things. 

Regarding the first point: although it is a sentiment approved by almost all philosophers, I will demonstrate it using the very definition of the name for the sake of a clearer understanding of what follows. We say that something is "animate" if it performs some act of living by its own power. As Aristotle taught in the second book of *On the Soul*, we find a fourfold act of living: namely, understanding, sensing, self-locomotion, and <term>vegetating: the basic biological functions of nutrition and growth.</term> 

Since the heavens perform the act of movement by their own power—specifically a circular, continuous, multiple, and regular movement—it therefore performs an act of living. Consequently, the heavens must be animate. Nor should it be said (as some argue) that when Aristotle lists that fourfold act of living there, he only intends to speak of the souls of corruptible things, and not at all of the soul of the celestial bodies. For if you pay close attention to his words there, you will clearly understand that Aristotle is showing the soul not only of perishable things but also of celestial ones. For immediately after listing that fourfold act of living, he adds: "It is possible for this (that is, the faculty of nourishing) to be separated from the others; but for the others (that is, the other powers of living) it is impossible in mortal things." 

A little further below, he says: "Those mortal things which possess reasoning also possess all the rest." By these words, Aristotle clearly taught that in the souls of immortals, the other three powers (or some of them—for instance, reason and motion) can be separated from the power of nourishing. Therefore, his discourse there concerns not only perishable things, but indeed the celestial ones as well. Similarly, in his work *On the Movement of Animals*, he calls the motion of the heaven the "motion of an animal," asserting that there is a certain animal that is always moved by an "always-mover." Thus, according to <term>Peripatetic: The school of philosophy following Aristotle, so named for his habit of walking while teaching.</term> doctrine, it must be firmly concluded that the heaven is animate; and so we have completed the first part of our position.

->THE SOUL IS THE CELESTIAL BODY'S FIRST<-
->principle of living: Therefore, the soul is the<-
->celestial body's form, or act.<-

<margin>Commentary 3.</margin>
The second part of this Theme requires two further explanations: first, by which the truth itself is shown; and second, by which those who strive against it are resisted and their objections dissolved. The truth of our proposition is proved through a fourfold discourse, starting from this very firm foundation: That which is the first principle of living is the <term>form or act: "Form" is the organizing principle; "act" (or actuality) is the state of being fully realized as a living being.</term> of living bodies. The soul is of this kind; therefore, the soul is the form or act of celestial bodies. 

By this same rule of logic, Aristotle shows in the second book of *On the Soul* that any soul is the "act" of a physical body. According to the opinion of the <note>original: "glossatorum"; the medieval commentators who wrote explanatory "glosses" on authoritative texts.</note> commentators, this is a demonstrative reason based on the effect <note>original: "à posteriori"; reasoning from known effects back to their causes.</note>. This aligns with the statement of Averroes <note>The influential 12th-century Andalusian philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> in the second book of *On the Heavens*: "The recipient of the form which is united with it is the incorruptible celestial body, from which follow the corporal dimensions and other accidents found in it; and therefore the form and the thing formed are numerically the same within it." 

Likewise, the Blessed Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> concludes in the second book of *Against the Gentiles* that, according to the Aristotelian tradition, one must say the intellect is united to the celestial body according to its substance as a form—though not in the same mode of union by which a sensible form is united to the matter of perishable things.

<page-num>216</page-num>
<header>PAUL RICIUS,</header>

## THE HEAVEN IS A MORE PERFECT BODY, THEREFORE
### *its form—namely, the soul—is also more perfect.*

---

The same point is demonstrated, secondly, from the arrangement of the celestial body: for the form of a fundamentally perfect body is itself fundamentally more perfect. This is because matter (the subject) and form correspond to one another in mutual proportion (as is taught in the eighth book of divine wisdom <note>This likely refers to Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*, often called "Divine Wisdom" or "First Philosophy" in this period.</note>). Since the celestial body is the most perfect body, its form must also be the most perfect of bodily forms. This kind of <term>form: In Scholastic philosophy, the 'form' is the organizing principle that gives a thing its essence and life; for a living being, the soul is its form.</term> is the soul; therefore, one must conclude that the form of the heaven—which moves, lives, and understands—is indeed a soul. Furthermore, if this small, earthly body, which is opaque and in constant flux, is made a participant in an intellectual and divine nature within itself and according to its whole being, then this must be attributed far more greatly and more precisely to the ethereal and incorruptible celestial body.

At this point, however, some people object by citing the words of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the hugely influential 13th-century theologian.</note> in the 70th question of the *First Part* <note>original: "70. quæst. primæ," referring to the *Summa Theologica*.</note> regarding a similar argument. For he says: "Nothing prevents something from being more noble in an absolute sense, while not being more noble in a specific respect." Therefore, even if the form of the celestial body is not more noble in an absolute sense than the soul of a living creature, it is nevertheless more noble in respect to its function as a form: for it perfectly fulfills its matter so that there remains no <term>potentiality: the capacity or possibility for matter to become something else.</term> for any other form, which the human or animal soul does not do. These are his words. 

But I would believe that these statements of the holy doctor (as we touched upon above) were brought forth to explain the foundations of Damascene <note>John of Damascus, an 8th-century Church Father.</note> rather than as his own firm assertion. This is because such a response seems flawed in many ways. First, a logical error of <term>equivocation: using the same term in different ways to mislead.</term> is committed in the form of the reply, because the argument concludes regarding perfection in an absolute sense, while the answer is given regarding perfection in a certain respect <note>original: "secundum quid."</note>. For when it is argued that the form of a more noble body is more noble, the sense is that the form is more noble by that same nobility by which the body is noble. Since the celestial body (because it possesses more "being-ness" and "actuality") is absolutely more noble than earthly bodies, its form must also be absolutely more noble than the forms of perishable creatures. This nobility is not measured by the *way* it informs the matter, but according to its level of "being" or "actuality."

Furthermore, it seems to imply a contradiction to say that a form is "less perfect" and yet "totally fulfills its matter" so as to leave no potential for another form. For a form cannot fulfill the entire potentiality of matter unless that form contains within itself all the possible "actuality" that can inhabit the receiving subject. Such a form must be the most noble of all forms inhabiting matter, not "less perfect." 

If you were to say that it is not by the merit of the form that matter is totally fulfilled, but rather by the nature of the matter (which has no potential for any further form), then far greater inconsistencies follow. First, that perfection which consists in the "way of informing" would not be attributed to the form, but only to the matter—thus no excellence would be granted to the celestial form, even though you affirm it is more perfect in a certain respect. Second, it would follow that celestial matter is of lesser perfection than the matter of perishable things. For matter as matter—whether celestial or earthly—is defined by its potentiality; matter is substantiated (as Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to European university study.</note> says) through its "capacity to be" <note>original: "per posse."</note>. If, therefore, the potentiality of celestial matter looks toward no other form than this one—which you say is absolutely less noble than the soul of perishable animals—then celestial matter would be absolutely more ignoble than earthly matter, the opposite of which your own hypothesis and the nature of the thing itself demonstrate. 

Moreover, even if we were to admit that the celestial form fulfills the celestial matter by its own merit, the same impossibility would follow: no substantial form fulfills matter except that form which the potentiality of the matter "desires." If, therefore, the celestial matter or subject by its nature desires a form that is absolutely of lesser perfection than the forms of perishable animals, then the celestial matter or subject would be more ignoble...

He challenges Thomas Aquinas's view, asserting that if the heavens' form (soul) were inferior to earthly souls, it would lead to the logical absurdity that celestial matter is inferior to earthly matter.</summary>

## "ANIMATED" IS A DENOMINATIVE TERM

->predication : Denominative predication comes from a thing inherent by<-
->way of form : Therefore the soul inheres in the celestial<-
->body as a form.<-

<margin>Commentary 39.</margin>
The same is concluded, thirdly, from the nature of "denomination" <note>In Scholastic logic, "denomination" refers to naming a subject based on a quality or form it possesses (e.g., calling a man "learned" because he possesses "learning").</note>: For according to everyone’s opinion, the celestial body is called "animated." Now, "animated" is a denomination derived from "soul" <note>original: "anima"</note>. Since denominative predication <note>The act of describing something based on an inherent property.</note> arises from an intrinsic thing that inheres by way of a <term>habit: A stable disposition or quality; in this context, a lasting internal state rather than a temporary action.</term> or form—for as Averroes says in the 12th book of *Divine Wisdom* <note>Referring to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*.</note>, that which is "concrete" signifies a form or habit by connoting the subject in which it inheres—we thus say a man is "cloaked" or "helmeted" because the cloak or helmet is carried by the subject in the manner of a habit. Conversely, if it were permissible to call the heaven "animated" solely because of a mover acting as a mover from the outside, then it would be more fitting to say a tunic or a helmet is "human-ized" rather than saying a man is cloaked or helmeted. For the man himself is the mover and carrier of the helmet and tunic, but the tunic is not the mover of the man. In the same way, it would be permissible to call a wagon pulled by an animal "animated," or to call a man "donkey-fied" because he is carried and moved by a donkey. Since all these things are absurd and ridiculous, it would certainly be wicked to call the heaven "animated" based solely on the gaze of an external mover; therefore, we are compelled to admit that the heaven is so named from something existing within it by way of form.

## A CONNECTING MEDIUM MUST BE GIVEN

->the extremes, namely intellect and body : That which shares in<-
->the extremes is called a medium; such is<-
->the soul of heaven.<-

The same is shown, fourthly, from the order of things and the bond of the universe: Since extremes are not joined except through a <term>medium: A middle ground or link that shares characteristics with two opposing things.</term>. In the wide scope of existing things, the greatest distance lies between intellect and body; therefore, they are not joined except through a medium. We call a "medium" that which shares in the nature of the extremes. It is clear that the soul is such a thing, because in its essence it shares in eternity—like the other pure and naked intellects—but in its operation it shares in time and motion, like physical beings. For this reason, Averroes said in the second book of *On the Heavens* that the soul of the heaven is similar to a natural form and similar to an abstract form. So too the *Book of Causes* <note>original: "libellus de causa"; a famous medieval Neoplatonic text often attributed to Aristotle or Proclus.</note> judged that the soul must be placed on the "horizon" of eternity and time; for if there were not that genus of soul which the Academics <note>The followers of Plato.</note> call the "bond of the universe" <note>original: "vinculum universi"</note>, there would be no exact union of the world or connection of things.

<margin>Commentary 71.</margin>
And therefore, listen to the "Corduban" himself <note>Averroes, who was born in Córdoba, Spain.</note>, who declares the soul (in the 2nd book of *On the Heavens*) to be the "spiritual bond of the sphere." This soul constitutes the universe as "one" more truly and greatly than the soul of perishable things unites its own organic body. For he says: "It is a marvel how this power (namely the soul of perishable things) is divided among members of dissimilar parts; it is not a marvel how it is divided among parts or members of similar matter (namely, such as are the parts of the celestial sphere)." For the division of the soul in these (perishable things) is ingeniously achieved through ligaments; but there in the celestial bodies, it is without such ingenuity, being natural. Therefore, it does not need a ligament there to become one moved thing as it does here. Wherefore, a "bound animal" and a "divine animal" that is not bound are not called "one" except <term>equivocally: Using the same word to mean different things; for example, a "real" lion and a "painted" lion are both called lions, but in different senses.</term>. These are the words of Averroes; if you are wise, consider them and revolve them in your mind. Finally, by this fourfold means of syllogizing—namely, from the nature of the name, from the body’s...

<header>218 PAUL RICIUS,</header>

...by its disposition, its naming, and the order of things, we are convinced that the heaven is animated by way of a form <note>In this context, a "form" is the internal principle that gives a thing its essential nature and life, much like the soul is the "form" of a human body.</note>.

## HE RECORDS THE ARGUMENTS
### which strive for the contrary.

It now remains only to dissolve the objections of the opponents, which seem to be quite powerful. First, they argue that if any intellectual substance is united to the heaven as its form, it would certainly cause the formal effect of a form within it. Now, the effect of a "forming form" is "to be" or "to exist." Therefore, the celestial body would have its existence through the soul, and not at all from itself. It would follows then, that by its own power, it would be inclined toward "non-being," and would therefore be <term>generable and corruptible: Subject to being born, aging, and eventually decaying or dying.</term>

Second, if the heaven is a subject existing in its own right, and similarly the soul itself is a substance existing in its own right, then two things that each exist "in act" <note>Meaning they are already fully realized, independent things.</note> do not make a single unified being. Therefore, the soul is not united to the celestial body in the manner of a form. Nor would the celestial animal be more perfect or more "one" than a terrestrial animal—the opposite of which we have already brought forward from the opinion of Averroes.

Third, if an intellectual soul were united to the heaven as a form, it would have to be so that the soul itself might gain some perfection from such an inherence. But it gains no perfection from it, neither in its being nor in its operation. Regarding its own proper operation, the celestial soul does not use the senses, and consequently uses no bodily organ; nor does it need to be a form to exercise motion, because it could move the heaven by the power of its will alone, without needing to inhere as a form.

Fourth, if the heaven were animated, I ask: how do celestial souls differ from human ones? If you respond that they differ because humans use "phantasms" <note>Mental images or sensory impressions used by the mind to form thoughts.</note> to gain knowledge, but celestial souls do not, I would say in turn that this does not constitute a specific distinction between species. For if "knowing through phantasms" and "knowing without them" were distinctions of species, then Adam in Paradise and his son Abel would differ in species; for Adam in Paradise did not need a phantasm to know, whereas Abel knew nothing without one. Therefore, it is false that the heaven is animated. There are many other arguments that seem to oppose this position, but from those with which we refute the aforementioned, all others can be dissolved at will.

## HE SOLVES THE ARGUMENTS
### which were objected.

<margin>Commentary 61.</margin>
I seek, however, one inviolable foundation. Once this is laid down, all the aforementioned objections—and whatever others of this kind there may be—will be utterly unable to build a case against us. This is the foundation, I say, upon which the book *On the Heavens*—indeed, the entire science of nature as well as divine science—rests: Namely, that as much as the condition of the motion of one thing differs from the condition of another, so much do the principles of those moving things (and the modes that belong to them) differ. Since, therefore, circular motion <note>The movement of the stars and planets.</note> differs in its very genus from straight motion <note>The movement of earthly objects, like a stone falling or fire rising.</note>, the principles and modes of those moving things—specifically their power, matter, form, composition, and union—must also differ in genus. 

For this reason, Averroes establishes in the second book of *On the Heavens* that the propositions we have at hand regarding the dispositions of the heaven are few, and are spoken of almost <term>equivocally: Using the same word to mean two very different things; for example, calling both a living man and a marble statue "an animal."</term> This is because they are drawn from the animated things found here on earth; when we speak of "animated" regarding both earthly and heavenly things, the word is used almost equivocally. These are his words there. And a little lower (as we recorded before), he says: "Wherefore, a 'bound animal' [terrestrial] and a 'divine animal' that is not bound [celestial] are not said to be one thing except equivocally." Union, moreover, is a mode of being which (as we said) is spoken of almost equivocally regarding the higher beings and the generated beings, just as their very entity or essence is. Having seen this, we reply to the first objection by denying the conditional statement that "if an intellectual substance is united to the heaven as a form, it will give the heaven its existence." For although this is true of the forms of things that can be generated (whose matter does not have existence from itself)...

...[does not] exist [merely for a time], but rather passes from form—with its always insatiable power—to another form; <margin>3</margin> this, however, is not admitted in the celestial body, whose matter or subject has, of itself, the quality of existing. Yet, from another source (namely, from the soul), it receives the quality of being alive and intelligent, just as from light and a transparent medium <note>original: "diaphano"</note> a single thing is made by its very nature: namely, a luminous body. This is true despite the fact that the transparent medium is a body "in act" <note>In Scholastic philosophy, "in act" means something that is already fully realized and exists in its own right.</note>, yet it is luminous only in "potency" <note>Meaning it has the potential to be lit up.</note>. If light were a spiritual substance, as some of the ancients contend, a single thing would nonetheless be formed from the transparent body and the light by their very nature. 

But you will immediately object to the second point, saying: if the celestial matter or subject is a being "in act," and similarly the soul is a being existing by itself, it will not be possible for one single being to be made from them. <margin>7</margin> To this I respond that from two beings "in act"—insofar as they are "in act"—a single thing is not made; rather, it is made insofar as one, beyond its actual being, possesses the potential for a more perfect existence, just as the example of the transparent medium and the light declares. 

But not yet satisfied with these points, you resist again: if from two things existing "in act" in any way whatsoever a single thing were made, the proper being of each would be destroyed. For a thing exists only insofar as it is "one"; therefore, that which has lost its own unity will also lose its own being. Thus, while the soul "informs" <note>To "inform" (informat) means to provide the essential character or life-force to matter.</note> the heaven, it would destroy itself, which is utterly absurd. 

I respond that in created things on earth, when two things existing "in act" are fused into one, both are destroyed because they are subject to contrary qualities which cannot endure one another but instead drive each other out. But in the higher realms, where there can be no battle of contraries but only proportion and a relationship of the imperfect to the more perfect, nothing prevents the abundance of one perfection from supplying the defect of the other. It does this not by destroying the other, but by assuming it into the fellowship of its own unity and perfecting it. This is just as the wise Catholic thinkers declare that the most sacred and ineffable Word of God <note>The "Word" (Verbum) refers to Christ in the theology of the Incarnation.</note> took on human nature: for there, in one person by number, there are two "beings in act," namely the divine and the human. If you were to say there is only one "being" there, there would be only one form and one act, which could only be the divine nature; thus God would be like one part of a composite, or the form of His own creature, which seems quite inappropriate—though some of the younger thinkers have considered this not at all foreign. But these things are too sublime and beyond the limits of our little compendium, though the logic of the analogy and example led us to them. 

From these points and the previously established foundation, understand that just as perishable things are separated from eternal things by a long interval, so too are their modes of union. One cannot transfer a valid argument from the one to the other. Therefore, nothing prevents us from establishing that the heaven and the soul—both existing "in act"—are a single being "in act" by their very nature. Because of the conflict of contraries, this can by no means happen in earthly things. And for this purpose, we added to our diagram (if you noticed) the phrase "in its own way," by saying: "He who informs the heaven itself (in its own way)."

But you will ask: what sort of "mode of informing" is this for the heavens? I respond: it is such as follows the very essence of the heaven. If you, therefore, will make me more certain about the nature of the heaven, I will immediately make you understand its mode of informing. You might say: the nature of the heaven is neither heavy nor light, neither created nor corruptible, and things of that sort. And I, by the same law, shall say: this mode of informing or union is not according to the mode of informing a nature that is light, nor heavy, nor generable, nor corruptible. Finally, it ought to be enough for you that nothing appears in things subject to the senses that would prohibit this union of the soul with the celestial body, and the sensible order of things proves this in many ways.

To the third point, we say (just as John Scotus <note>Referring to the philosopher John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308) in his commentary on the *Sentences*.</note> affirms in Book 2 of the *Sentences*) that the soul is not united to the celestial body in order to grasp any perfection in its primary operation (which is the act of understanding), but rather in its secondary operation: so that it may bring forth the forms it conceives in the angelic and divine mind into a sensible existence. Moreover, since it exists on the horizon of the body and of pure intellect...

[intellect], or of eternity and time) possesses a certain innate readiness for the fellowship of the body, insofar as it is a bond and a spiritual—as **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), a medieval Andalusian philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to Western thought</note> says—tie of the universe, uniting and linking the last things with the first. Truly, I have considered it unnecessary to weave here a history of the gatherings of the **Pythagoreans** and the **Platonic** school, as well as the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, known for walking while teaching</note>—both Arab and Greek—and furthermore of the ancient **Kabbalists** <note>original: "Cabaleorum"; practitioners of Jewish mystical tradition</note>, or those who allegorize about the soul of the heaven, who unanimously strive toward and support this opinion of ours. It would indeed be marvelous, even incredible, that so many of the most brilliant lights of human wisdom throughout the ages would have been deceived by such a harmonious opinion concerning the soul of the heaven. If you think that trust should be placed in **Albert the Great** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a dominant figure in medieval science and theology</note> himself, a man of the highest erudition, unroll his twelfth book of *Divine Wisdom* <note>original: "diuinæ sapientiæ"; likely referring to his commentary on Aristotle's Metaphysics</note>, where he summarizes the sayings of almost everyone we have mentioned regarding this inquiry of ours.

To the fourth objection, it is responded that a specific distinction is taken not from the actual state, but from the aptitude. Therefore, although **Adam** in Paradise did not actually know through phantasms <note>Mental images derived from sensory experience. Scholastic thinkers debated how Adam processed information before the Fall</note>, he was nonetheless always capable of that mode of cognition. But the soul of the heaven never knows in such a way that it understands the unknown through the better known by means of a **syllogism** <note>A logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</note>; rather, it revolves from one intelligible archetype to another by a certain discursive process. 

Finally, with all these things rightly perceived, certainly no one—unless they are an unrefined investigator of things and scriptures, or a stubborn and puffed-up respecter of persons—would presume this position of ours to be erroneous, or deviating from Apostolic truth, let alone exotic or absurd (as that detractor snarls). For the most shining stars of the orthodox faith and divine wisdom declare that this matter in no way affects the foundations of the faith. Whether it is true in reality or not, they either remain in doubt or plainly affirm that which both reason dictates and the dogma of almost all philosophers proclaims. Therefore, for those who sincerely desire the truth, since I think these things will suffice, I shall cut the rope of my speaking, and here

# PAULUS RICIUS,
## PREFACE TO THE TREATISE ON THE SIX HUNDRED
### AND THIRTEEN MANDATES OF THE 
### MOSAIC LAW.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' within a circular frame depicting a figure in a landscape, likely a biblical or classical scene.</image-desc>

**H**ow much the prior and ancient Synagogue of the Jews flourished in wisdom, prophecy, and wondrous works is declared not only by the authority of the followers of Moses, but also by the unstained authority of the Apostles, and announced by the most ample monuments of the nations. These affirm that the ancient Jewish people penetrated all the hidden places—no less of the falling world than of the heavenly one—and knocked upon the summits of celestial wisdom. For as we read in the *Preparation for the Gospel* by **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a Christian historian whose "Praeparatio Evangelica" preserves many fragments of lost pagan and Jewish works</note>, both **Theophrastus** and **Porphyry**, men most distinguished in doctrine and wisdom, say that the Jews are philosophers by nature. **Megasthenes** also, a man most skilled in history, says: "All things which the ancient Greeks wrote concerning nature, others wrote before them. For we know that the **Brahmins** <note>original: "Brachmanas"</note> among the Indians, who are also called Jews, practiced philosophy much earlier." In the first volume of *On the Good*, **Plato** and **Pythagoras** testify to the same, saying: "What the Jews once discovered, the Greeks themselves later set forth." To this is added the assertion of the Pythagorean **Numenius**, who says that Plato is nothing other than "Moses speaking in the Attic tongue." Nor was it only natural and divine philosophy that they pioneered; **Abraham** first taught the Egyptians arithmetic and the knowledge of the stars, from whence the lineage of these disciplines flowed to the Greeks. With these and other similar writings of philosophers, poets, and historiographers, and the praise of oracles, **Eusebius of Caesarea**, and **Josephus** in his work *Against Apion*, build this opinion concerning the Jews. To this, indeed, the very restorer of the world, **Christ the Lord**, provides solid and inviolable testimony, he who wished to be born from the Jewish lineage along with the entire choir of Apostles. And that great man, than whom no one born of woman is greater, **John [the Baptist]**, was a Jew, born of his father **Zacharias** and mother **Elizabeth**. Moreover, the holy virgin **Mary**, the mother of God and gracious Queen of Heaven, was born a Jewess of her father **Joachim** and mother **Anna**. What of **Peter**, the gatekeeper of the Empyrean realm and prince of the Apostles: was he not himself a Jew under the circumcision and the Law of Moses? And the Apostle **James the Greater**, a man of integrity, was a Jew; likewise **James the Less**, surnamed the Just, was a Jew. **Matthew** the Levite, herald of the incarnate Word, was a Jew. What of that celestial trumpet, the pupil of the fierce **Gamaliel**, the Apostle to the Gentiles, **Paul**—was he not himself an Israelite according to the flesh, of the tribe of Benjamin? What of **Mark**, the chosen priest of God? Of **John**, the sublime son of Zebedee? Of **Andrew**, the brother of Peter? Of the great Levite **Barnabas**? What shall I say, finally, of each individual Apostle, and of nearly all the authors of Christ from the circumcision, who like wiser architects first laid the solid and unshakable foundations of the orthodox faith? Those whom the Spirit later stirred up from the Gentiles attempted, like assistants and laborers, to build upon their foundations and add the outward features. From that accustomed and ancient lineage and spiritual spring, so many rivers of wisdom burst forth, so many buds of the prophets blossomed, the lights of Christ shone back, and the oracles of the Apostles were brought forth on high. Therefore, if the stock and the root are holy, as the Apostle writes, then the branches are also holy; if the first-fruit is good, so is the whole mass. <margin>Romans 11</margin> For he from the Gentiles who believes is, he says, a branch of a wild olive which is grafted into the natural olive. But the Jew who is a worshiper of Christian piety exists as the root and the rich olive. For however much a shoot of the wild olive might become a partner in the richness of the olive, it is nevertheless compelled to taste somewhat of "wild-olive-ness" (if I may put it that way). But the branch of the natural olive, replaced in its natural stock, recovers its full flavor and resumes that power into itself from every side, which is not infected by any alien scent, nor dulled by any foreign taste. Whenever, therefore, anyone is converted by sincere faith from the Jewish darkness to the most brilliant lights of Christ, a branch of the natural olive is grafted into its own natural richness, which no stain of outward things and no taste of Gentilism is able to contaminate. Let the scorpion, therefore, cease to rise up with its poisonous wound, and let the barking of the rabid be silenced—those who, by no light of reason and no spirit of faith or truth, but with a dull and incredulous brow, a polluted mind, and a deceitful tongue, strive to defile the riches of others with their own poverty. Let them hear the Apostle commanding that no one presume to boast against the branches of the natural olive; <margin>Romans 11</margin> for if you boast, he says, "you do not support the root, but the root supports you; therefore, do not be haughty, but fear." That very thing is proved by the great excellence in every kind of discipline and the perpetually memorable authority of the **seventy-two translators** <note>The "Septuagint" (LXX), the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note>, of whom **Eleazar** the High Priest chose only six from each tribe. Whence **Augustine** not without justice (as also the authors of the **Talmud**) judged that these translators were driven by a divine and, as it were, prophetic spirit; for, separated into seventy-two small cells for the span of seventy days, they translated the entire Law of Moses from the Hebrew idiom into the Greek tongue with one sequence of writing and the same context of words and letters, just as if there had been one and the same craftsman. For this reason, it is rightly ascribed to divine skill rather than human investigation. It is otherwise, however, with the manifold editions, both Greek and Latin, which, since they were produced only by human industry and error <note>original: "hallucinatione"</note>, differ from one another and from the Hebrew original with such variety that (as Saint **Jerome** testifies) they have rightly given the adversaries occasion for mockery and calumny. Since, therefore, we have proved by so many solid arguments that the palm of spiritual warfare is owed to the rank of the first Jews alone, I thought it would not be out of place to bring forth here in what sequence the tradition of the ancient Jews was propagated, and how it gradually succeeded and preserved its own energy as it was poured into the listener by the living voice. But because I have recounted that more extensively elsewhere, I have decided not to repeat it here, except to briefly resume one point now on account of several objections which might perhaps leave the reader’s mind in doubt. We gather a fourfold heresy of the **Pharisees**: some indeed were persistent rivals of the Law and the worship of God (while shortly before the time of the Passion the Jewish crowd raged against one another with bloody seditions and slaughters), and having left the Judean fatherland again, they wandered as vagabonds among the nations; these, being ignorant of the cross and passion of Christ, were held guilty of no crime.
