->### PREFACE.<-

...accused and proved them guilty of every kind of disgrace and crime. There were those who, through a lust for power and a fury of anger and vengeance, shed the innocent blood of Christ in a cruel execution. I have learned that their testimony and names have been deleted and excluded from the <term>Talmudic</term> <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism</note> book of the Pharisees, just as they are from the Book of Life. Others, due to the depth of the mystery, neither embrace nor worship the faith of Christ and the Sacrament of the cross, yet they do not go so far as to curse or condemn it. Others still—and these were indeed innumerable, as the Acts of the Apostles record—followed the faith of Christ while simultaneously contending with a stubborn mind that the Mosaic Law must be observed as an eternal shadow and image of the Law, not indeed out of fear of punishment, but out of love for exemplary virtue; this was, for a time, permitted to them.

Therefore, I think it should be attributed to pride and a rustic sort of "holiness" (which benefits only itself) rather than to piety and prudence, to despise the teachings of the Pharisees of this latter sect as if they were futile and senile ravings. For if great men of the Church embrace and examine with the highest scrutiny the boastful and deceptive dogmas of certain philosophers, what prudent person of Christian piety will shrink away or be annoyed if we also bring forward something of the erudition of those to whom wisdom, religion, and the worship of the Most High God first became known? These are people who, with diligent nighttime study and the greatest zeal, philosophize upon the sacred gifts of the Prophets.

If, in their garden, some wild things, thorns, or briars should sprout up, we shall reject and cut them away, lest they disfigure the most pleasant orchard of our own [faith]. But those things that are more refined and fragrant with piety and doctrine, we shall venerate; we shall collect them like ambrosia and manna from the vast solitude of the desert.

<margin>
These things are handed down to you in another order. But meanwhile, it is clear that the author erred not a little in the calculation of time.
</margin>

Having prefaced these things, it must be said that there are twin teachings upon which the Jewish Synagogue relied in the past and still relies today. One is the <term>Written Torah</term> <note>original: "tora sehebich taf"; Hebrew: Torah she-bi-khtav</note>, that is, the Law which is called "in writing." The other is the <term>Oral Torah</term> <note>original: "tora sceba alpe"; Hebrew: Torah she-be'al peh</note>, that is, the Law which is delivered by mouth. The former is the Law of Moses expressed in the five volumes of the Pentateuch; the latter is the explanation of that same Law.

The leaders of the <term>Talmudists</term> <note>original: "Talmudeorum"</note> assert (in the first chapter of *Berakhot* <note>A tractate of the Talmud concerning blessings</note>), regarding that passage in Exodus 24: "I will give you the stone tablets, and the law, and the commandments," that Moses learned the explanation of the Law on Mount Sinai by the same spirit through which he had received the Law itself. This explanation proposes two primary meanings: the literal and the allegorical (in the Hebrew word, <term>Kabbalistic</term> <note>original: "Cabaleum"</note>). It was not permitted to commit either of these to written characters. The literal sense could not extract every individual human act and its rights into writing, because such acts, being infinite or varied, cannot be closed within any rule or limit. The allegorical sense, however, *could* have been written, but it was not *permitted*, so as not to give solid food to the weak or provide [heavy] meat to infants. Thus, it was not permitted to publish either the spiritual or literal understandings of the Pentateuch to the common people, whether by voice or pen.

This was the case as long as Israel held the scepter and the kingdom. But when, after the destruction of Jerusalem and the kingdom, they were dispersed through the world as wanderers and vagabonds, and they realized that religion was being disturbed and the secrets of truth were being obliterated because of the cruel tyranny of foolish nations, it seemed right to the entire assembly of the Pharisees to commit such literal and spiritual explanations of the Law to writing and published books, as far as could be done. They chose to call the sum of these the <term>Talmud</term>. It declares the literal understanding of the Law openly, but the allegorical understanding is covered by a manifold variety of veils.

How the chair of Mosaic tradition arrived from Moses down to the publication of the Talmudic book, passing from one listener to another, I have thought it not out of place to repeat here in a few words. However, if you recall those things which I reviewed in the second volume of this work concerning the various and different types of Pharisees, let the ambiguity of the name not confuse the correct understanding of the matter. For we read in the traditions of the ancient wise men of the Jews, which they call the <term>Chapters of the Fathers</term> <note>original: "pirke auos"; Hebrew: Pirkei Avot</note>, that Moses received the Law on Mount Sinai and delivered and explained it to Joshua; Joshua to the Elders; the Elders to the Prophets; the Prophets to the men of the Great Assembly. The last of these was the High Priest Simeon the Just, of whom the highest praises are sung in the book of Ecclesiasticus. Luke also calls him Simeon the Just in the second chapter of the Gospel.

He delivered the Law to Antigonus of Soho. He to Joseph the son of John, and the other Joseph the son of Joezer. Both Josephs delivered this to the most famous Nittai [of Arbela] and to Joshua the son of Perachiah. The younger Talmudists falsely affirm (due to the ambiguity of the name) that Jesus Christ our Lord was a student of this Joshua, which is false. For in the chapter *Helek* <note>A chapter in the Talmudic tractate Sanhedrin</note> of the Talmudists, there is testimony that this Joshua flourished in the time of Hyrcanus (whom they call Jannaeus). Hyrcanus (as the history of Flavius Josephus teaches) held the kingdom of Jerusalem and the Priesthood together for a space of nearly one hundred years before Pontius Pilate—but more on these things elsewhere.

Nittai of Arbela and Joshua therefore delivered this to Judah the son of Tabbai and Simeon the son of Shetach. Both of these delivered it to Shemaiah and Abtalion. Again, to Hillel and Shammai, concerning whom Josephus records many excellent things. These delivered it to Rabbi Jochanan the son of Zakkai. Thus far in the *Chapters of the Fathers*.

Then, from various writings of the Talmudists, they collect those things which follow, just as the Egyptian Rabbi Moses <note>Maimonides (1138–1204)</note> in the preface to his *Mishneh Torah* <note>original: "Deuteronomij sui"</note> and Rabbi Isaac in his *Astronomical Narration* recount. A fellow student and colleague of this Rabbi Jochanan was Rabbi Simeon, whose son was that elder Gamaliel, at whose feet the Apostle [Paul] heard the Law.

<margin>Acts 22.</margin>

This same Gamaliel explained the Law to his son, also named Rabbi Simeon, and he to his own son Rabbi Judah, whom because of the greatness of his wisdom and the honesty of his life, he calls the Holy Rabbi. The Emperor Antoninus, surnamed Pius, enjoyed his companionship and constant familiarity (as the Talmudists relate in the last chapter of the book of *Blessings* <note>Berakhot</note>). This same Rabbi Judah, in the one hundred and twentieth year after the destruction of Jerusalem, was the first to arrange the explanation of the Mosaic Law in a compendium called the <term>Mishna</term> <note>The first major written collection of the Jewish oral traditions</note>, and he began to give it to the common people; the entire assembly of the Jews embraces it as if delivered by the mouth of Moses.

The same Rabbi Judah delivered the explanation of the Law and his book to the other Jochanan, who, in the three-hundredth year after the desolation of the Temple, explained that compendium of the Mishna more widely and in a clearer style in one volume, which they call the Jerusalem Talmud. The colleagues of this Rabbi Jochanan were Rav and Samuel, whose student was Rav Huna. He had Rabbah as a student; Rabbah had Rava; his student was Rav Ashi, who, excelling in erudition, modesty of life, honors, and worldly glory, began to forge the Babylonian Talmud in the year 436 after the destruction of the Temple. However, being prevented by death, he could not complete the undertaking, which his son named Mar, together with his colleague Maremar, afterwards finished. That Talmudic book contains the glosses and commentaries of the aforementioned compendium of the Mishna. Also all the new things according to the [requirements] of the time and place...

->### PREFACE.<-

...its requirements established, it encompasses several mysteries of sacred speech, as well as some notable crimes and historical events. It was published in the year 4,365 from the beginning of the world (according to the Jewish calculation), and in the 436th year from the destruction of Jerusalem. This codex <note>The Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism containing laws and traditions</note> was received with the highest veneration by the entire community of Jews exiled throughout various regions of the world, to be preserved and followed in practice, and they still retain it today. Finally, the Egyptian Rabbi Moses <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher</note> enumerates forty generations from Moses until the <term>Talmudic</term> <note>Relating to the Talmud</note> codex was given to the common people; whoever desires to hear about these in more detail should seek the beginning of his commentary on Deuteronomy. Regarding the younger men who followed the Talmudists, although many outstanding men of exceptional erudition and probity existed among them, the authority of none of them is easily admitted except insofar as he follows the dogma and footsteps of the Talmudic codex. Therefore, I judged it less appropriate to explain their order. It pleased me, however, to recount here the aforementioned times and succession of the Talmudic canon, because I recognized that many things pertaining to the <term>Kabbalistic</term> <note>Jewish mystical tradition</note> dogma are scattered and handed down in various places of that codex. And although after the times of <term>Hillel and Shammai</term> <note>Two famous leaders of opposing schools of Jewish thought in the 1st century BCE</note>, the chief Pharisees, the opinions of the Talmudists vary in many constitutions concerning the appendices of the divine mandates, you will nevertheless find absolutely no differences of opinion in the very foundation of the matter. For instance, no one contends whether the <term>Shema</term> <note>original: "lectio scema"; the central prayer in the Jewish prayerbook</note>—that is, "Hear, O Israel"—should be read in the evening and the morning. They do, however, doubt which of the morning and evening hours is more suitable for the reading: whether before or after the rising and setting of the sun. Nor does anyone ask whether a lamp should be lit on the evening of the <term>Preparation</term> <note>original: "parascenes"; referring to the eve of the Sabbath or a festival</note>, since no Jew is ignorant that this has been established; but as to which oil or fat is more suitable for the lamp, one thinks and ordains one way, and another another; the same judgment applies to the rest. Finally, having looked through these matters in this way, we soon prepare ourselves to explain the 613 mandates of the Mosaic Law (according to the series of the Talmudists and the Rabbi Moses of Coucy <note>original: "Chuzensis Rabi Mosis"; a 13th-century French scholar who authored a famous work on the 613 commandments</note>) by God's command. And this indeed according to the understanding affirmed by the unanimous school of the Talmudists; however, it is not the business of the present work to assign the reasons or causes of all these things. At another time, life permitting, I will attempt to unlock the natural and Theological or Kabbalistic cause of each individual mandate. Now, however, if I recount only the bare history of the mandates, I think it will be sufficient for the requirement of the proposal. But if anywhere the madness of the younger Israelites should object, we shall strive to argue against it for the sake of truth and with our best strength, and to pull it down as much as the series of this little compendium allows, first imploring the help of the indivisible Trinity, that it may favor these little readings of ours and grant them grace and understanding, Amen.

## MOSAIC PROHIBITIONS
### Mandates of the Law.

<margin>Exod. 20.</margin>
1. *You shall have no other gods before me.*
You shall not presume that any other God is given in the entire scope of things besides me.

<margin>Levit. 22.</margin>
2. *Do not profane my holy name.*
The name of God is profaned when he who professes doctrine and the worship of piety lives incautiously and with the unbridled lust of the flesh.

<margin>Deuter. 12.</margin>
3. *You shall not do so to the Lord your God.*
That is, do not overturn His altars; for it is written: Overturn all the places in which the nations have worshipped, scatter their altars, and break their statues, burn their groves with fire, and crush their idols, destroy their names from those places: You shall not do so to the Lord your God. From this it follows that it is not permitted to delete the holy names of God, nor even a single letter of which they consist.

<margin>Deut. 6.</margin>
4. *You shall not tempt the Lord your God.*
He tempts God who says: I will fulfill the mandate of the Law, and from that I will observe whether rewards follow.

<margin>Levit. 19.</margin>
5. *You shall not have hatred for your brother in your heart.*
But rebuke him with an open face; if he asks for pardon, indulge him.

<margin>Ibidem.</margin>
6. *You shall not bring shame upon your neighbor by rebuking him.*
Although you may have been offended by him, nevertheless in those things which concern the worship of God, if he is not corrected by hidden reprimand, then he must be rebuked openly for the crime.

<margin>Deuter. 23.</margin>
7. *Do not mistreat a servant who has fled to you.*
But allow him to dwell with you.

<margin>Exod. 22.</margin>
8. *You shall not harm the widow and the orphan.*

<margin>Levit. 19.</margin>
9. *You shall not be a slanderer.*
That is, a secret calumniator among your people.

<margin>Exod. 23.</margin>
10. *You shall not accept a false report.*
Unless it is attested by evidence.

# PAULUS RICIUS,

Not even with the adoration of <term>dulia</term>. <note>Dulia is a theological term for the honor or veneration given to saints and angels, as opposed to "latria," which is worship reserved for God alone.</note>

<margin>Numbers 15.</margin>

That is, you shall not grant persistent faith to your own thoughts, nor shall you indulge the enticements of the senses.

Even if you do so without the intention of worshiping.

<margin>Exodus 20.</margin>
20. *You shall not make for yourself a carved image.*

Even if you do not worship it yourself.

But because both of these commandments of the <term>Decalogue</term> <note>The Ten Commandments</note> are indispensable and to be kept perpetually, Jewish ignorance foully disparages the rite by which the Christian faithful fashion, cherish, and adore images of the saints. They judge Christians to be transgressors of the Decalogue, which openly commands: *You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor shall you adore it.* 

Indeed, some try to resolve this question and approve the veneration of carved images by pointing to the images of the **Cherubim** <note>Angelic figures placed atop the Ark of the Covenant</note> established in the Holy of Holies over the Ark of the Covenant. But this argument and solution to the question is less effective against such disparagement. For just as the Law itself counts it a mortal sin to cook or to kindle a fire on the Sabbath day, yet commands that very thing to be done in the Tabernacle. In a similar way, although divine precept might abominate the carving of images as an unspeakable and implacable crime, the Law clearly describes and commands the images of the Cherubim. 

Added to this is the fact that the argument does not apply in the same way here as it does there. For in that case, absolutely no danger of any stumbling block was imminent, because no one was permitted to approach the threshold of the Holy of Holies except the High Priest, once a year. Here, however, at every single moment, the incautious multitude of the faithful moves and prays among sculptures and images. 

Therefore, there is a double dissimilarity because of which the presumption of sculptures is not permitted based on the images of the Cherubim. First, because the Law openly prohibits the former, but openly commands the latter. Second, because in this case the minds of the weak can be contaminated, whereas in the other, not at all. 

It must be said, therefore, that when the Decalogue commands: *You shall have no foreign gods before me,* the remainder which is subjoined—namely, *you shall not make for yourself a carved image*—does not constitute a separate commandment, but is an explanation of the first. Just as one reads regarding the commandment of the Sabbath: *Remember to keep the Sabbath day holy,* and soon it is added: *Six days you shall labor and do no work.* These certainly do not sanction two different commandments, but explain what the first implies. Otherwise, we would be asserting that more than ten commandments of the Decalogue were given. 

Standing upon this, you will be able to easily untie the knot of this ambiguity. First, from the canon of the <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the body of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note> which says: whenever a general opinion is brought forth on a matter, the clearer understanding of which is thereafter expressed individually, then each individual thing expressed preserves the condition of the proposed theme. For the universal (as the logicians teach) is always present in its particulars. Since, therefore, the general and chief commandment of the Decalogue is *You shall have no foreign gods before me,* the rest of its clauses respect that same commandment. Thus, when it is subsequently commanded: *You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness,* it must be understood: *if you do these things so that they may be foreign gods to you.* The same must be judged of the following parts. 

Christian worshipers do not worship statues as "foreign gods," but insofar as they refer back to the Creator (who is worshiped with <term>latria</term>), or because they designate saints (who are adored with <term>dulia</term>).

# ON THE COMMANDMENTS OF THE MOSAIC LAW.

Fifthly, even the glorious humanity of Christ is not admitted to be worshiped by itself with <term>latria</term> <note>Latin: *latria*; the highest form of worship, reserved for God alone.</note>, but rather with <term>hyperdulia</term> <note>Latin: *hyperdulia*; a level of veneration higher than that given to saints (*dulia*) but lower than that given to God, typically reserved for the Virgin Mary or, as argued here, Christ’s human nature.</note>. Therefore, a practitioner of Christian piety is by no means to be judged a transgressor of the Decalogue. 

Secondly, the question is resolved by the fact that the images of the saints which we honor are not truly "carved images," idols, or likenesses. For a thing is not truly an idol or an image unless an angelic, celestial, or living power from beneath the heavens shines forth within it. For just as a painting is not a true likeness or image of its subject if any of the members—and especially the head—are missing, so a stone or bronze body is to be considered far less of an image (no matter how much it resembles the subject in outward lines and variety of colors) if a spiritual power is not infused into it. Indeed, the more important part of a likeness is the spirit of the thing itself. 

For as it pleased Augustine in books 7, 8, and 18 of *The City of God* (following the Apostle in <margin>Romans 1.</margin> Romans 1), the structure of idols was intended for some image of a human or another kind of living creature, in which an angelic, animal, or celestial power, or a demonic or heroic spirit, might reside. Since, therefore, the carved works and likenesses that we venerate in sacred buildings participate in no spiritual power at all, it follows that they are called "images" inaccurately and by a borrowed term. For this reason, the adoration of them does not render the commandment of the Decalogue void. 

Yet there remains a certain scruple by which the mind wavers and is offended. Since the worship of idols is held to be the most wicked among the entire genus of crimes, we must take every precaution against any work, cult, or act by which the incautious mind of the "little ones" might easily be offended or endangered. As the Apostle says: *If anyone sees someone who has knowledge reclining in an idol's temple, will not his conscience, since it is weak, be "built up" to eat things sacrificed to idols? And the weak brother will perish in his conscience. Therefore, if food causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat.* If, therefore, food offered to idols—which (as the Apostle says) does not commend us to God—is to be avoided for the sake of the weak, how much more should we avoid the wicked and pestilential adoration of images, which more than other crimes pollutes the soul of mortals and immediately turns it away from its Creator? 

And although in the third book of the *Sentences*, Saint Thomas [Aquinas] shows by a threefold reason (collected in the third part of the *Consecration*) that the cult of images is permitted: 
First, so that the unlearned may be taught by them as if by books; 
Second, so that the mystery of the Incarnation and the examples of the saints may stick more firmly in the memory; 
Third, because a more vehement affection is stirred by those things which lie before the senses. 

Nevertheless, the mind of the inquirer is by no means satisfied by these reasons. This is because we know that the cult of images was established by none of the Apostles, nor by any canonical decree, but was rather rejected with the greatest contempt, according to the word of the Apostle: *And they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the image of a corruptible man.* And again: *Flee from the worship of idols*—that is, of images. And: *When you were heathens, you were led away to mute idols.* And: *That they abstain from the pollutions of idols.* Finally, we read this in various places where the text clearly demonstrates that not only the internal worship of the mind, but also the external worship of the body must be avoided, lest it produce a scandal by which the weak are endangered. 

Furthermore, the suspicion of idolatry, which arises from the freedom allowed to images, is more harmful and damaging than the ignorance, forgetfulness, and lukewarmness of devotion that result from a lack of images. For "ignorance of disposition" (as they call it), which judges wickedly and wrongly, is more pernicious than "ignorance of negation," which thinks nothing at all about the matter. 

Therefore, it must be said that the ritual of images has crept into the most sacred Church of Christ—like a wild grape in a fruitful vineyard, or tares in a well-cultivated field—out of a corruption of custom. Indeed, it is a vain labor to suddenly and utterly uproot the long-standing custom of the masses. For just as the Jews of old, when accepting the truth of the faith, were nonetheless captured by the bond and snare of their Law and custom, and preferred to abandon faith in Christ the Savior rather than the earthly works of the Law; so also the Gentiles, given over to the unbridled lust of the flesh, preferred to neglect the eternal salvation of the soul rather than undergo the burdens of circumcision and other parts of the Law. Thus, for the common salvation of both...

But because both of these commandments of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note> are indispensable and to be kept forever, Jewish ignorance basely slanders the rite by which the Christian faithful make, honor, and adore images of the saints. They judge Christians as violators of the Decalogue, which openly commands: "You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor shall you adore it." 

Some indeed attempt to solve this question and approve the veneration of carved images by pointing to the images of the <term>Cherubim</term> <note>Angelic figures with wings</note> established in the Holy of Holies over the Ark of the Covenant. But this is an ineffective argument against the slander and a poor solution to the question. For just as the Law itself counts it a mortal sin to cook or light a fire on the Sabbath day, yet commands that very thing to be done in the Tabernacle; in the same way, although divine precept abhors the carving of images as an unspeakable and unpardonable crime, the Law clearly describes and commands the images of the Cherubim. 

Furthermore, the argument does not work the same way in both cases. In the Tabernacle, there was absolutely no danger of anyone being offended or misled, because no one was allowed to enter the threshold of the Holy of Holies except the High Priest once a year. Here in the world, however, the unwary multitude of the faithful is constantly surrounded by carvings and images and prays among them. There is, therefore, a twofold difference why one cannot justify the presumption of carved images by citing the images of the Cherubim. First, because the Law openly forbids the former, but openly commands the latter. Second, because in this case the mind of the weak can be contaminated, but in the other case, not at all.

It must be said, therefore, that when the Decalogue commands: "You shall have no other gods before me," the part that follows—namely, "you shall not make for yourself a carved image"—does not constitute a separate commandment, but is an explanation of the first. Just as we read concerning the commandment of the Sabbath: "Remember to keep holy the Sabbath day," and soon after it is added: "Six days you shall work and you shall do no work." These do not ordain different commandments, but explain what the first one implies; otherwise, we would have to assert that more than ten commandments were given in the Decalogue. 

Standing by this principle, you will easily be able to untie the knot of this ambiguity. I take the first point from the canon of the <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Jewish legal scholars and commentators on the Talmud</note>, which says: "Whenever a general opinion is uttered about a matter, and then a clearer understanding of it is expressed in particulars, those particulars keep the condition of the main theme." For the universal (as the masters of logic teach) is always present in its particulars. 

Since, therefore, the common and chief commandment of the Decalogue is "You shall have no other gods before me," the remaining clauses of it respect that same commandment. Thus, when it is later commanded "You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness," it should be understood as: "if you make these things *so that they may be other gods to you*." The same must be judged regarding the words that follow. Christians do not worship statues as "other gods," but insofar as they represent the Creator, who is worshiped with <term>latria</term>, or because they designate the saints, who are honored with <term>dulia</term>.

<meta>catchword: Quin- (But/Nay)</meta>

<summary>Ricius argues that the biblical prohibition against images is not an absolute ban but a clarification of the law against false gods; since Christians do not view icons as gods, their use of images is valid. He critiques the common defense involving the Ark's Cherubim, preferring a logic-based and Talmudic interpretation of the Decalogue.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Ricius’s exploration of the Mosaic Law, specifically the transition from the strict prohibition of "carved images" in the Decalogue to the Christian use of icons. # ON THE COMMANDMENTS OF THE MOSAIC LAW.

Indeed, not even the glorious humanity of Christ is admitted to be worshipped with <term>latria</term> <note>original: "latria"; the supreme worship due to God alone</note> for its own sake, but is instead to be venerated with <term>hyperdulia</term> <note>original: "hyperdulia"; the highest level of veneration, above that of the saints but below that of God</note>. Therefore, a practitioner of Christian piety is by no means to be judged a transgressor of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note>. Secondly, the question is resolved by this fact: the images of the saints we venerate are not "true" carved images, idols, or likenesses. For nothing is truly an idol or an image unless an angelic, celestial, or living sub-celestial power shines forth within it. Just as a painting is not a true likeness or image of its subject if it lacks members—and especially the head—so a stone or bronze body should be considered much less of an "image" (no matter how much it resembles the subject in its external lines and variety of colors) if no spiritual power is infused into it. After all, the most important part of the original subject is the spirit of the thing itself.

As it pleased Augustine in books 7, 8, and 18 of *The City of God* (following the Apostle in the book of Romans), <margin>Romans 1.</margin> the structure of idols was made in the likeness of a man or some other kind of living creature so that an angelic, animal, or celestial power—or perhaps a demonic or heroic spirit—might assist it. Since, therefore, the carvings and statues that we venerate in sacred buildings share in no spiritual power whatsoever, it follows that they are called "images" inaccurately, using the word loosely. For this reason, their veneration does not render the commandment of the Decalogue void.

Yet there remains a doubt by which the mind wavers and is offended. Since the worship of idols is held to be the most wicked among the entire class of sins, every precaution must be taken against any work, worship, or act by which the unwary minds of the "little ones" <note>Referring to the "weak in faith" or the uneducated</note> might easily be offended or endangered. This follows the word of the Apostle: *If anyone sees someone who has knowledge sitting at a table in an idol's temple, will not his conscience, since it is weak, be "built up" to eat things sacrificed to idols? And the weak brother will perish in his conscience. Therefore, if food scandalizes my brother, I will never eat meat.* If, therefore, food sacrificed to idols—which (as the Apostle says) does not commend us to God—must be avoided for the sake of the weak, how much more should we avoid the wicked and pestiferous adoration of images, which defiles the soul of mortals above all other sins and immediately turns it away from its Creator?

Now, although Saint Thomas [Aquinas], in the third book of the *Sentences*, shows through a threefold reasoning that the veneration of images is permitted: first, so that they may serve as books to instruct the uneducated; second, so that the mystery of the Incarnation and the examples of the saints may stick more firmly in the memory; and third, because a more powerful emotion is stirred by things subjected to the senses. However, the inquiring mind is by no means satisfied by these reasons. This is partly because we know that the worship of images was established by no Apostle nor by any canonical decree, but was rather rejected with the utmost contempt, according to that word of the Apostle: *And they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into an image of corruptible man.* And: *Flee from the worship of idols*—that is, images. And: *When you were Gentiles, you were led to dumb idols.* And: *That they abstain from the pollutions of idols.* Finally, we read this in various places where the text clearly demonstrates that not only internal mental worship but also external physical worship must be avoided, lest it cause a scandal by which the weak are endangered.

Furthermore, the suspicion of idolatry that arises from the permission of images is worse and more damaging than the ignorance, forgetfulness, and lukewarm devotion that result from a lack of images. For an "ignorance of disposition" (as they call it), which judges wickedly and wrongly, is more ruinous than an "ignorance of negation," which thinks nothing of the matter at all. Therefore, it must be said that the ritual of images has grown into the most holy Church of Christ—like a wild vine in a fruitful vineyard or tares in a well-cultivated field—arising from a corruption of custom. Indeed, it is a vain anxiety to try to pull up a long-standing custom of the masses suddenly and fundamentally. For just as the Jews of old, when receiving the truth of the faith, were yet captured by the bonds and snares of their Law and custom, and preferred rather to abandon the faith of Christ the Savior than the earthly works of the Law; so the Gentiles, on the other hand, given over to the unbridled lust of the flesh, preferred to neglect the eternal salvation of the soul rather than undergo the burdens of circumcision and other requirements of the Law. Hence, for the common [salvation of both...]

<summary>Ricius explores the tension between the prohibition of idols and the Christian use of images, arguing that while Church icons lack the "demonic spirits" of pagan idols, their use is a "wild vine" or "corrupt custom" that persists mainly because old habits are hard to break.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Ricius’s theological exploration of the role of images in the Christian faith compared to the strict prohibitions of the Mosaic Law. In the previous page, he argued that Christian icons are not "idols" because they lack the "spiritual power" or demonic infusion that pagans attributed to their statues. Here, he discusses how the Apostles and the early Church used "custom" to transition converts from paganism to Christianity.</meta>

# PAUL RICIUS,

For the salvation of the entire assembly of the Apostles <note>referring to the Council of Jerusalem described in Acts 15</note>, it was decided to allow the Jews the observance of the Law for a time, and to permit the Gentiles its abrogation; yet neither of these was required for mortal happiness, but was instead demanded by **custom** alone. Since, therefore, the power of custom is such that (according to the proverb of the wise) it "begets a second nature," it was impossible for the ritual of images—which the pagan multitude of the nations had practiced for many centuries—to be abolished instantly. For that frenzied crowd would have preferred to abandon the most sacred religion of Christ rather than their vain worship of idols. For this reason, divine concern took pity on the poor unbelievers and chose to permit this worship which is applied externally, so that the worship which is within might be more easily and cautiously directed and transferred to the faith of truth.

For the weak discernment of the common people gazes more upon the external act of the body than the manner and form of the action, even though an act claims its type and name not from the deed itself, but from its manner. For instance, the union with a woman, in and of itself, is neither shameful nor honorable; rather, it is made wicked if done solely out of fleshly desire, without marriage, or if polluted by menstruation. However, it is honorable if done with the vow of procreating, or in a ratified marriage where she knows herself to be pure. The saying of the Apostle also points to this: *In Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision avails anything, but faith.* <note>Galatians 5:6</note> And also: *Let each one remain in the calling in which he was called.* <note>1 Corinthians 7:20</note> On this, the <term>gloss</term> <note>a standard medieval scriptural commentary</note> of the saints says: "For salvation, the Jewish or Gentile ritual neither helps nor hinders." This is supported by the Apostle saying: *To those who are under the Law, I became as if under the Law; to those who were without the Law, I became as if without the Law... I have become all things to all men, that I might save all.* <note>1 Corinthians 9:20-22</note>

Since, therefore, an action in itself is neither shameful nor honorable, but the manner of acting gives the action its name, by the same rule, this kind of external veneration of images should be lightly esteemed in itself. However, internal adoration—by which the mind itself deserts its Creator and makes itself subject to a creature—must be avoided by all means. Therefore, when the leaders of the saints permitted the external veneration of carvings (just as they permitted the observance of the Law to the Jews) it was so that they could transfer and exchange the internal worship of idols for faith in Christ and eternal truth more safely and with less trouble. At that time, while the external worship was preserved, the dull and stubborn multitude yielded to the faith of internal piety. If, by chance, some souls of the weak are put at risk by this, no offense or harm could happen to the wise and learned because of it.

But this one thing—saving the reverence due to hidden things—I do not fear to judge and approve: now that the orthodox faith of Christ has been brought to its fullness and the worship of idols has been utterly destroyed, it would be not only pious but also fitting and praiseworthy (unless the corruption of custom resisted this too) to build temples and sacred houses without images. This would indeed exalt the minds of men toward the empyrean and super-celestial spirits of the saints, and not toward corporeal images made by hands. Thus, every stumbling block for the weak and the danger of most wicked error would be avoided. Furthermore, many of the detractor Jews, who loathe the worship of images above all else, could be induced and persuaded to embrace the pious religion of Christ. Nevertheless, in all things I commit myself to the sacred and unshakable decrees of the Church (which is ruled by a Spirit that does not err); I go with her, I think with her, I live and shall rest in her for eternal ages.

-># CONCERNING THE COMMANDMENTS OF THE MOSAIC LAW.<-

25. *It shall not be built again, namely that overturned city.* <margin>In the same place.</margin> <note>Referring to Deuteronomy 13, regarding a city that has turned to idolatry.</note>
26. *And he shall by no means do anything similar to this matter again.* <margin>In the same place.</margin>
That is, let him not dare to persuade even one of the faithful, let alone a multitude, to follow foreign gods.

27. *You shall not yield to him, nor love him.* <margin>In the same place.</margin>
Namely, the one who attempts to turn you toward idols.

28. *Let your eye not spare him.* <margin>In the same place.</margin>
Namely, that you should wish to free him from the punishment of death.

29. *Nor shall you listen to him.* <margin>In the same place.</margin>
That is, so that you might provide him any help.

30. *Nor shall you pity him.* <margin>In the same place.</margin>
Namely, not even with any favorable word.

31. *Nor shall you conceal him.* <margin>In the same place.</margin>
That is, do not remain silent about anything in the testimony of his crime.

32. *By the name of foreign gods you shall not make mention.* <margin>Exodus 23.</margin>
The Latin edition <note>the Vulgate</note> says "you shall swear" <note>original: "iurabitis"</note>: that is, you should utter nothing in the name of idols, even if the matter were true and just. But if some cause happens to require the pronunciation of these names, then some epithet of contempt for the idol must be added. This is just as the stubborn ignorance of the later Talmudists <note>Jewish scholars of the Talmud</note>—when they think that Christians (on account of the veneration of images) worship foreign gods—pronounces all the names of Christ the Savior and the saints with an ignominious and blasphemous voice, about which there will be more extensive discourse in what follows.

33. *You shall not listen to the words of that Prophet.* <margin>Deuteronomy 13.</margin>
Namely, the one who prophesies and predicts in the name of idols, no matter how many wonders and signs he may have performed.

34. *Nor let a Prophet speak presumptuously in my name things which I have not commanded.* <margin>In the same place.</margin>
Namely, whether he speaks those things which the Spirit of God did not command at all, or whether he arrogates to himself those things which He commanded to another.

35. *You shall not fear to put the False Prophet to death.* <margin>In the same place.</margin>
36. *Let there not be found among you one who consults an Of.* <margin>In the same place.</margin>
The Latin edition says "pythons" <note>original: "phytones"</note>, but this is a common name for seers. *Of* <note>Hebrew: 'Ob' (אוב), a medium or spirit of the dead</note>, however, shows a certain peculiar Law of divining. For as it is written in the book *Sanhedrin*, in the fourth chapter <note>A tractate of the Talmud dealing with legal procedures</note>, there are four capital punishments. *Of* is the spirit of a deceased person which speaks with a whisper and a low voice from the middle of the armpits, or from the skull of the deceased, according to that saying of Isaiah: "And like a python's"—that is, *Of*—"your voice and your speech shall mutter from the ground." And that in the Book of Kings: "Divine for me by a python"—namely *Of*—"and raise up for me whom I shall tell you," and she raised up Samuel.

37. *Do not turn to the Ovos.* <margin>Leviticus 19.</margin>
The Latin edition translated less aptly, "do not turn aside to mages" <note>original: "magos"</note>. For *Of* and *Ovos* designate the same thing, except that the latter expresses many <note>the plural form</note> and the former one. This differs from the prior commandment in that the former prohibits consulting and inquiring, while this prohibits the practice and work. These differ not a little: for he who inquires indeed hears the responses of the spirit, but perceives nothing by sight. The practitioner, on the other hand, sees the image but hears no speech.

38. *Nor let him consult an Ideoni.* <margin>Deuteronomy 19.</margin>
The Latin edition here also less aptly provides "diviners" <note>original: "divinos"</note>. For "diviner" indicates a python, a soothsayer, an augur, a haruspex, and a follower of any sort of omen. *Ideoni* <note>Hebrew: 'Yidde'oni' (ידעוני), often translated as wizard</note>, however, designates a certain specific kind of prophesying. For there is (as Moses of Coucy <note>A 13th-century French rabbi, author of the 'Sefer Mitzvot Gadol'</note> records on the authority of Rabbi Simeon, and the Jerusalem Talmud affirms) an animal called *Jiddua* very similar to the human form. From the middle of its navel, a sort of cord is produced by which (like a gourd) it is fixed to the soil of the earth, and as far as the length of the cord extends, the savage animal snatches and devours everything all around. Hunters do not know how to capture it unless they sever the cord with a strike of arrows, by which...

Nor did the command intend to forbid the structure itself, but rather the erection of the pillar.

But with the Gentiles, in whose number they include the faithful of Christ...

-># ON THE COMMANDS OF THE MOSAIC LAW.<-
<u>u</u>
<meta>catchword: safe</meta>

...they wish to be understood, not at all. According to the Egyptian Rabbi Moses <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the "Egyptian" Rabbi because he lived in Fustat/Cairo.</note> (who in the *Book of Knowledge* <note>original: "Madaa"; the first book of Maimonides' *Mishneh Torah*</note>, in the section on idolatry) says: "Christians are worshipers of idols, with whom it is not permitted to associate or to enter into a peace treaty, but one must strive to recall them from their error." Thus he spoke. However, the great interpreter of the Law, the Prophets, and the Talmudic code, Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi (1040–1105), the most famous commentator on the Torah and Talmud.</note>, relying on the traditions of the ancients, asserts that the nations of this time—especially the worshipers of Christ—do not worship idols, as they only follow the custom and usage of their fathers in external worship.

<margin>Leviticus 19.</margin>
### § 1. *You shall not practice augury.*
Augury <note>The practice of predicting the future through signs.</note> here does not designate a prophecy through the chirping of birds, but through certain signs of nature or events; for instance, when a staff falls from the hand or a morsel of food from the mouth of one beginning a journey, he predicts an unlucky trip. By the same law, it is forbidden to take any omen in any business to be undertaken, as when you propose to yourself, saying: "As soon as I leave the threshold of my house, if I meet a friend, I want to be safe <note>original: "tutus"; connecting to the catchword.</note>, because that day will make my wishes fruitful." Yet they say that one who, by hesitating and with fear, sets ominous signs for himself, is not at all to be judged a transgressor for that reason, since we read that Abraham’s servant Eliezer presumed that kind of omen <note>Refers to Genesis 24, where Eliezer asks for a sign from God to identify Isaac's future wife at the well.</note>.

<margin>Deuteronomy 18.</margin>
### § 2. *Let there not be found in you those who divine by pieces of wood.*
The Latin edition <note>The Vulgate Bible.</note> asks for "soothsayers" <note>original: "ariolos"</note>: The name "soothsayer," although it is said to come from the divination that used to happen near altars <note>Latin "ara" (altar).</note>, shows any kind of prophecy in a broader sense. Here, however, it is taken for a certain law of divining which the insane multitude of nations once practiced with pieces of wood <note>Xylomancy.</note>. For having taken a small part of wood, from which the bark was removed on one side but left on the other, the wood was then thrown into the air twice. If on the first throw the white and debarked face of the piece appeared turned upward on the ground, and on the second throw the bark-covered and dark side showed itself, it announced a safe and favorable outcome for the things to be done. If, however, the darker face appeared first and the white one second, they predicted a black and unhappy fate. But if the side with bark showed itself on both throws, it indicated a future success somewhere in between. Against these the Prophet Hosea cried out: <margin>Hosea 4.</margin> "My people consult their wood, and their staff reports to them."

<margin>Leviticus 19.</margin>
### § 3. *Nor shall you observe times.*
The Latin edition says "dreams" <note>original: "somnia"</note>: for it translates the same word *me’onen* <note>original: "meonem"</note> as "dreams" here, and in the Second Book of Kings as "soothsaying," though in both places it is less appropriately rendered. Since *ona* (from which the word *me’onen* derives its origin) designates a time or hour, as in that passage of Exodus: "And he shall not diminish her hour" <note>Exodus 21:10; standard English translations usually say "marital rights."</note>; although there (as the learned Nicholas of Lyra <note>A 14th-century Franciscan theologian known for his literal biblical commentary.</note> testifies) it is interpreted far from the sound of the literal text as the price of chastity. He "observes times" who distinguishes certain hours, days, and months as unlucky, and some as happy for performing something. There are some, however, who think that *onen* indicates a prestigiatory art <note>Illusionism or sleight of hand.</note> that mocks the senses.

<margin>Deuteronomy 18.</margin>
### § 4. *Nor let there be found one who is joined by incantation.*
The Latin edition says "enchanter" <note>original: "incantator"</note>; in Hebrew it is written *chover* <note>original: "houer"</note>, which means an "associate" or "to be joined," as in: "I am an associate of all who fear You." For even today, exorcists are accustomed to gather reptiles, snakes, and other kinds of vipers into one place with certain muttering voices, according to that saying of David: <margin>Psalm 57.</margin> "Like deaf asps that stop their ears, so that they do not hear the voice of the charmers." And where the Latin translator connects "and of the sorcerer enchanting," the Hebrew text has *chover chavarim* <note>original: "houer heuarim"</note>: that is, "of one joining joinings," or "coupling couplings." Consider this well.

<margin>Deuteronomy 18.</margin>
### § 5. *Nor let there be found among you a sorcerer.*
Sorcery <note>original: "Maleficium"</note> is the harmful work of demons against humans; for the understanding of which it must be known that the crafty nature of demons exerts itself against the human race in three ways: Either by the malice and deceit of the will; or by a higher power...

-># PAULUS RICIUS<-

by the command of [someone] safe: or attracted and enticed by him who, either by nature or by a wicked and impious pact, has made himself inferior to a demon. In the first way, therefore, the demon himself, by his own nature, secretly glides into the fantastic power <note>original: "phantasticæ uirtuti"; referring to the faculty of imagination</note> and suggests himself to it; yet the mind and reason itself resists this, if it so wills. For the enemy is weak, and does not conquer except the one who is willing. However, the higher power, by whose command the demon is forced to obey, is the Creator of all things, God himself, or angelic power, or a man to whom divine authority has been given, by which the demon is driven to inflict punishment upon a man for the purging of his crimes. The lower power, by which a demon is attracted, is either the fantastic force <note>The imagination</note>, which is naturally weaker than the demon and exists as its attendant, or the intellect, which is indeed by its own nature free and higher than the demon; yet, by indulging the irreparable lust of the imagination and the senses, it offers itself as subject to the demon's tyranny as if in slavery. By this third Law <note>The law against sorcery</note>, therefore, the most fragile and unstable female sex fulfill their shameful and filthy desires. Since, therefore, "a sorcerer shall not be found in you," the Law mandates—and the meaning is—that there shall not be found one who, by imprecation or sacrifice or any other service, seeks help from a demon. For although the demon mostly administers external goods and bodily comforts, heals illnesses, and shows dangers to be avoided, it nevertheless leads the soul away from its origin, and finally twists it toward the obscene crimes of hags <note>original: "lamiarum"; often translated as witches or female night-monsters</note>. Nevertheless, the Talmudists <note>original: "Talmudei"</note> do not think it is so unspeakable and execrable to subjugate a demon by the power and names of Almighty God or the angels and saints, and to use their service, except that the fear which they strike when provoked and the imminent danger do not allow one to dare and attempt it. For as the Author of Truth speaks: "No one enters the house of a strong man to plunder his vessels, unless he first binds the strong man." <note>A reference to Matthew 12:29</note> But the binding of the strong man itself consists only in the power of the Most High or of those who are led by the spirit of God.

<margin>Deuteronomy 18.</margin>
56. *Nor let there be found among you one who consults the dead.*
They consult the dead who, macerating themselves with a thin diet and fasting, keep vigil at the tombs of the dead during the night, so that, inspired by a sordid spirit, they may receive the expected answers. Here, as it is written in the chapter *There are Four Capital Punishments* <note>A reference to the Talmudic tractate Sanhedrin</note>, Rabbi Akiva <note>original: "Rabi Echiua"; a leading 1st-century Jewish sage</note> sighed, saying: "If an unclean spirit is infused through the spontaneous affliction of the flesh, how much more abundantly could one become a partaker of the pure spirit through purity of life?"

<margin>Leviticus 19.</margin>
57. *Nor shall you round the hair of your head.*
<margin>Ibidem.</margin>
58. *Nor shall you destroy the corners of your beard.*
The Latin edition says, "nor shall you shave your beard." Why the Latin translator translated it thus, I do not see; for in Hebrew it is read *taschis* <note>tashchit</note>, which without any ambiguity sounds like "you shall destroy." Indeed, the universal synagogue of the Jews, both now and in ancient times, judges that to destroy the corners of the beard is a crime and against the decrees of the Law. They say the "corners" are the upper and lower extremes of the jaws. To "destroy" the hair designates scraping it away with a razor, which, however, is permitted to be done with scissors.

<margin>Deuteronomy 22.</margin>
59. *A woman shall not be clothed in male attire.*
<margin>Ibidem.</margin>
60. *Nor shall a man use female clothing.*
For both give birth to debauchery, incest, and adultery.

<margin>Leviticus 19.</margin>
61. *Neither shall you make any figures or marks upon yourselves.*
They make marks <note>original: "stigmata"</note> and figures who engrave some image into the skin and flesh and fill it with dye or any kind of tincture, as the worshipers of images are accustomed to do.

<margin>Ibidem.</margin>
62. *Nor shall you make any cutting in your flesh for the dead.*
(The Latin edition says "incisuram" [an incision].)

<margin>Deuteronomy 14.</margin>
63. *Nor shall you make any baldness for the dead.*
The Law itself soon declares the cause of this, as well as of the prior inhibition, saying: "Because the Lord has chosen you to be a peculiar people to Himself, out of all the nations that are upon the earth." Moreover, such a peculiarity cannot be discerned or judged from anything other than the distinction of actions and habits.

### CONCERNING THE COMMANDMENTS OF THE MOSAIC LAW. ###
u 2
<meta>catchword: to be venerated</meta>

<margin>Deuteronomy 8.</margin>
64. **"Take care lest you forget God, namely the Tetragrammaton <note>The sacred four-letter name of God, YHWH</note> your God."**
That is, take care, when the flatteries of fortune smile upon you, that you do not, with an exalted mind, forget God himself, the giver of all good things, nor wish to ascribe the success of your affairs to your own prudence and skill.

<margin>Exodus 20.</margin>
65. **"You shall not do any work on the Sabbath day."**
Namely, cultivation of the land, wool-working, shoemaking, hunting, cooking, butchery, tanning, writing, building, craftsmanship, transport, and that sort of thing. Nor only the aforementioned, but the Talmudic authorities <note>original: "Talmudei"</note> decree that all works which assist these are to be avoided; for example, not only is lighting a fire forbidden, but even touching a lit lamp, or indeed the candlestick itself with the hand, is a sin. Not only is it forbidden to cook, but it is not permitted to eat of food prepared on the Sabbath unless death is imminent. For when the danger of life is imminent, it is permitted to set aside not only the Sabbath but all the statutes of the Law, with the commandments concerning fornication, murder, and the worship of idols excluded, which must never be violated at any time. From this also—just as they do regarding images—the insolence of the Jews takes the opportunity to mock, asserting that the faithful of Christ are transgressors of the Law of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note>, which mandates the celebration of the Sabbath day as a solemnity and clearly commands ceasing from all work on it. But they pay little attention to the commandments of the Decalogue, since it establishes six days for working, but for rest it appoints the seventh—not this or that specific day, but it looks toward every seventh day. For "Sabbath" indicates not *Sabbatum* (Saturday) or the day of Saturn, but "rest." What mystery the Law itself designates in the septenary numbers, however, is not the business of the present work to express.

<margin>Exodus 16.</margin>
66. **"Let no one go out of his place on the seventh day."**
Namely, outside the limits of the city. Moreover, the authority of the ancients declares that the boundaries of the city are contained within a space of two thousand cubits or paces <note>This refers to the "Sabbath limit" or *techum shabbat*, the distance one is permitted to walk outside a settlement on the day of rest</note>.

<margin>Exodus 35.</margin>
67. **"You shall not kindle a fire in all your dwellings on the Sabbath day."**
From this the Talmudists <note>original: "Talmudei"</note> derive that it is not permitted to inflict a capital punishment by fire on the Sabbath day, and by the same law, it is to be judged concerning any punishment or any fine.

<margin>Leviticus 16.</margin>
68. **"On the tenth day of the seventh month, you shall do no work."**
The lunation of September constitutes the seventh month of the Hebrews, which revolves while the Sun illuminates Libra. But it is called the seventh because then the seventh circuit of the Moon after the Sun's entry into Aries is completed. For the Law (as you will hear in what follows) reckons the first of the months as the circuit of the Moon in March, while the Sun revolves through Aries. For by this very same reasoning, the ancient Romans named September from "seven" <note>original: "septem"</note>, because that month stands as the seventh after the rains of March; thus it is to be reckoned for October, November, December, and the remaining months, except that a later age, greedy for new things, by the desire for vain glory, transferred all the decrees of the fathers into foreign ones: most of all, however, the Roman nation, which always (as Cicero writes in the *Oration for L. Flaccus*) with a furrowed brow <note>original: "abducto supercilio"; suggesting a look of disdain or haughtiness</note> was adverse to Jewish customs. This indeed envious arrogance, even after the incarnation of the Word (as the Apostle witnesses in Romans), has increased greatly, and has left many dangers (I speak to those who have ears) up to this very day in the Church Militant. But returning to the order of the months, let us say: For (as Macrobius reports in the first book of the *Saturnalia*, and Isidore in the sixth of the *Etymologies*) the month of July used to be called *Quintilis* <note>The fifth month</note> because it was the fifth after March, and August was called *Sextilis* <note>The sixth month</note> because it was the sixth from March. Of these, Julius Caesar usurped the former, and Augustus Caesar the latter, for his own memory and glory. Just as the courses of the Moon were once measured, so too was the beginning of the months, which used to be taken from March. The same Julius Caesar changed this into this Law which the Roman Church also now follows. Enough concerning these things. Now, the tenth day of the seventh month is what Moses calls the Day of Atonement <note>original: "propitiationis diem"; refers to Yom Kippur</note>, and it is to be venerated no differently than the feast of the Sabbath...

He also provides a historical and astronomical explanation of the Hebrew calendar, comparing it to the ancient Roman calendar before the reforms of Julius Caesar.</summary>

# PAULUS RICIUS #
### Page 232 ###

...is to be venerated, except that this day (as the following commandment shows) is dedicated solely to spiritual exercise: while the Sabbath day is given both to that and to the indulgence of the flesh <note>Physical rest and the enjoyment of food</note>.

<margin>Leviticus 23</margin>
69. **"And every soul that is not afflicted on this day shall perish from among its people."**

This is handed down in the book *Yoma* <note>original: "ioma"; a volume of the Talmud concerning the Day of Atonement</note>, in the chapter "The Day of Atonement" <note>original: "iom ha Kipurim"</note>. The affliction commanded on the tenth day of the seventh month is fulfilled through fasting, going barefoot, and abstaining from sexual intercourse, ointments, and every kind of carnal delight. Moreover, the Law of the fast is such that if anyone, from dawn until the twilight of night, consumes food the size of an olive <note>original: "oliuę magnitudinis"</note>, the fast is judged void and invalid.

<margin>Ibidem</margin>
70. **"On the first day of unleavened bread, you shall do no servile work."**

The first day of unleavened bread <note>Passover; original: "azymorum"</note> is the fifteenth day of the March lunation, while the Sun travels through Aries. <term>Servile work</term> <note>Work typically performed by servants or for commercial gain, such as farming or crafts</note> is interpreted to exclude whatever pertains to the preparation of meals and the requirements for celebrating the festival; this rule applies to all solemn days (except the Sabbath and the Day of Atonement).

<margin>Leviticus 23</margin>
71. **"Nor shall you do any servile work on the seventh day of unleavened bread."**

What the ceremonies of unleavened bread are, and what the <term>offering of the sheaf</term> <note>The "Omer" offering of the first barley; original: "manipuli oblatio"</note> entails, the commentaries on the affirmative commandments will teach.

<margin>Ibidem</margin>
72. **"Nor on the fiftieth day after the offering of the sheaf of the first fruits of the harvest shall you do any servile work."**

This kind of solemnity is called the Feast of Weeks <note>Shavuot</note> and the feast of Pentecost <note>meaning "fiftieth day" in Greek</note>, because the Law was promulgated on the fiftieth day after Israel’s departure from Egypt.

<margin>Ibidem</margin>
73. **"Nor on the first day of the seventh month shall you do any servile work."**

This solemnity is the day on which the beginning of the year is taken; however, the order of the months and the year is not the same now. For among the months, the first to be counted is that which runs while the Sun moves through Aries <note>the month of Nisan</note>, in memory of the Israelites' departure from Egypt. Yet it is not called the first month of the year; rather, that is the first month of the year which occurs while the Sun revolves through the sign of Libra <note>the month of Tishrei</note>, from which the Egyptians also take the beginning of the year.

<margin>Leviticus 23</margin>
74. **"Nor on the fifteenth day of the same seventh month shall you do servile work."**

This festival is the *Sukkot* <note>original: "scenopegia"; literally "the pitching of tents"</note> or dedication of tabernacles, which we will explain more extensively in its proper place.

<margin>Ibidem</margin>
75. **"Nor on the eighth day of the festival of tabernacles shall you do any servile work."**

For the Festival of Tabernacles <note>original: "Scenopegia"</note> is celebrated for seven days (just as the solemnities of unleavened bread last eight); yet only on the first and last day must one cease from servile work. For the ancients write (in the book *Chagigah* <note>original: "hegiga"</note>, in the chapter *En Dorfin* <note>likely referring to "Ein Doreshin"</note>) that the days which fall between the first and last of these solemnities are also to be venerated, nor is servile work permitted on them, unless delay would result in loss.

<margin>Exodus 13</margin>
76. **"Leaven shall not be eaten on the day of the departure from Egypt."**

<margin>Ibidem</margin>
77. **"Neither leavened bread nor leaven shall be seen with you."**

That is, for the seven days of unleavened bread throughout all your borders.

<margin>Exodus 12</margin>
78. **"For seven days leaven (the Latin edition says 'leavened') shall not be found in your houses."**

For in Hebrew it is read as *se'or* <note>original: "se'eor"</note>, which means leaven <note>the fermenting agent</note>; but leavened <note>the fermented product</note> is called by the Hebrew word *chametz* <note>original: "hemez"</note>.

<margin>Exodus 12</margin>
79. **"You shall not eat anything mixed with leaven (the Latin edition says 'leavened')."**

A distinction is to be noted among the four commandments just mentioned. The first forbids the eating of leavened food. The second and third prohibit not only the eating, but also the keeping of it in the home or throughout the entire region. By the fourth, not only leaven itself, but whatever has been made with leaven, is to be rejected. Between the second and third, there is a threefold dissonance in the text. For the former prohibits the *sight* [of it], the latter the *finding* [of it]; the former mentions leaven and leavened bread, the latter only leaven; the former in all...

<meta>This page continues the list of negative commandments following the discussion of the Passover feast. It concludes the theological reasoning for the prohibition of leaven and transitions into laws concerning sexual morality, marriage, and domestic life.</meta>

<header>ON THE MANDATES OF THE MOSAIC LAW.</header>

...in all borders, but this [prohibition of leaven] applies only in houses. To bring forth the cause and reason for all these things requires a deeper investigation than the present task allows. For the Cabalist <note>A practitioner of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah)</note> ponders the same archetype that the wise Theologian considers in the Sacrament of the Eucharist. For he who desires to be snatched from Egyptian servitude and to be received as an inhabitant of the Promised Land must shake out the leaven and whatever tastes of leaven. For we, groaning in this tabernacle <note>The human body; a reference to 2 Corinthians 5:4</note>, do not wish to be stripped, but to be further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life. But truly, that which is mortal in you is by no means swallowed up by life as long as you permit any leaven to be found in your borders. For a little leaven (as the Apostle speaks <note>St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 5:6</note>) corrupts the whole mass. For this reason, even the small wafer of the host to be consecrated must be free from the mixture of leaven; otherwise, it cannot be further clothed with the glorious body of Christ, and what is mortal cannot be swallowed up by life. Consider this yourself.

<margin>Deuteronomy 23</margin>
80. **"There shall be no harlot among the daughters of Israel, nor a male prostitute among the sons of Israel."**
A harlot <note>original: "meretrix"</note> is she who, of her own accord and without a ratified marriage, defiles her bed; a male prostitute <note>original: "scortator"</note> is he who solicits this very thing. The Chaldean edition <note>The Targum, an Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> translated this here as: "No one of the sons of Israel shall marry a slave woman, nor shall any of the daughters marry a slave bought from the nations."

<margin>Exodus 21</margin>
81. **"He shall not diminish the girl’s food, clothing, or her time."**
The Latin edition <note>The Vulgate</note> says: "And he shall not deny the price of her modesty." The girl’s food and clothing do not fall under a fixed limit but must be moderated according to the status of the girl and her husband, as well as the conditions of the place and time. To not "diminish her time" is to pay the conjugal debt at its proper times; here, the ancient tradition of the Talmuds has set a limit for the conjugal debt. Specifically: those who are at leisure <note>Gentlemen or those without labor</note> should close no day without visiting the marriage bed; a manual laborer should do this twice in the space of a week; a donkey-driver who binds bundles, once in the space of seven days; once in the cycle of a month for those who transport loads by camels; and once every half-return of the Sun <note>Every six months</note> for a ship-master.

<margin>Deuteronomy 24</margin>
82. **"The first husband shall not be able to take back his divorced wife."**
For there is (as you will hear in the following) a Mosaic constitution: when someone discovers indecency in his wife, he may give her a bill of divorce. If she then passes to another, and that second husband also dismisses her with a divorce, the first cannot take her back again as his spouse.

<margin>Deuteronomy 25</margin>
83. **"The wife of one who died without children shall not marry anyone other than the brother of the deceased."**
If, however, the brother of the deceased does not wish to take her as his companion, then the woman—having observed the Law of Unshoeing <note>The ceremony of Chalitzah, where the widow removes her brother-in-law's shoe to release them from the obligation of marriage</note>—may marry another at her own discretion. What the Law of Unshoeing entails is declared in the assertive mandates.

<margin>Deuteronomy 22</margin>
84. **"A man may not divorce a girl with whom he has lain for all the days of his life."**

<margin>Leviticus 19</margin>
85. **"You shall not prostitute your daughter."**

<margin>Deuteronomy 22</margin>
86. **"He shall not be able to divorce a virgin whom he has defamed for all the days of his life."**
A husband defames a virgin when he falsely complains that he did not find the signs of virginal modesty <note>Proof of virginity</note>.

<margin>Numbers 5</margin>
87. **"He shall not pour oil upon the offering to be offered by a woman suspected of adultery."**

<margin>Ibidem</margin>
88. **"Nor shall he put frankincense on it."**

<margin>Leviticus 18</margin>
89. **"You shall not reveal the nakedness of your father."**
To reveal nakedness <note>original: "turpitudinem reuelare"</note> is to have illicit intercourse with a woman, or to be mixed in any way with a male. While the present mandate prohibits exercising this indecency with the father, and although a general and common mandate regarding this unspeakable crime is delivered a little later, the Law wished to express this separately because of the horrific shame of it occurring with a parent.

# PAULUS RICIUS <note>Paulus Ricius (c. 1470–1541) was a philosopher and physician, a Jewish convert to Christianity who sought to reconcile Jewish tradition with Christian theology.</note>

<margin>In the same place <note>Referring to Leviticus 18.</note></margin>
90. *You shall not uncover the nakedness <note>original: "turpitudinem," literally "shame" or "foulness," referring to sexual relations.</note> of your uncle.*
Here, likewise, male-on-male sexual union is to be understood, and the reasoning is the same as the previous commandment.

<margin>In the same place.</margin>

That is, you shall not uncover her nakedness, even after the uncle has died.

<margin>In the same place.</margin>

Even if your father married her in an invalid union.

<margin>In the same place.</margin>

That is, even after the death of your son.

<margin>In the same place.</margin>

The written law <note>original: "canon"</note> does not explicitly state this, but it is proven by a "from the stronger" argument <note>An argument *a fortiori*: if a granddaughter is forbidden, a daughter is even more so.</note>.

<margin>In the same place.</margin>

<margin>In the same place.</margin>

<margin>In the same place.</margin>

Provided, of course, the marriage was valid.

(That is, outside of marriage.)

<margin>In the same place.</margin>
107. *Nor your mother’s sister.*
<margin>In the same place.</margin>
108. *You shall not take your wife’s sister as a rival wife <note>original: "pellicatum."</note> while she is still living.*
The term "rivalry" <note>original: "pellicatus"</note> is named from the word for "concubine" or "rival wife" <note>original: "pellex."</note>. A *pellex* is what they call a second wife whom a bigamist marries while the first is still alive, as if the latter has "pushed out" <note>original: "pepulerit," a wordplay on *pellex* and *pellere* (to drive away).</note> the first. However, when the first wife dies, one is permitted to join her sister to himself in marriage.

<margin>In the same place.</margin>
109. *You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother’s wife.*
That is, even if the brother is deceased.

<margin>In the same place.</margin>
110. *Nor that of your uncle’s wife.*
Even when the uncle is dead.

<margin>Leviticus 18.</margin>
111. *You shall not approach a woman during her menstrual impurity to uncover her nakedness.*

This applies not only as long as the menstrual blood is flowing, but also when nothing remains; it is still forbidden to approach her for the duration of a week—indeed (according to the decrees of the more recent Talmudists), it is not even permitted to touch her. Finally, the Law prohibits twenty-four "shames" (including the one concerning the Priest's daughter), for all of which the common punishment is the **extermination of the soul** <note>original: "animae exterminium," referring to the Hebrew penalty of *Kareth* (divine excision).</note>. Seven are condemned by the extermination of the soul alone; ten, however, undergo the punishment of **burning** in addition to the extermination of the soul; the remaining seven are overwhelmed by the punishment of **stoning**. Those punished by burning include: a priest’s daughter, a wife's daughter, a wife’s granddaughter by her daughter, a wife’s granddaughter by her son, a wife’s mother, a wife’s maternal grandmother, and a wife’s paternal grandmother with her daughter, with her daughter's daughter, or with her son's daughter. Those struck by stones include: the mother, the stepmother, the daughter-in-law with a male, with a beast, a woman submitting to a beast, and a betrothed girl. By the extermination of the soul alone: a sister, a father's sister, a mother's sister, a wife's sister, a brother's wife, a father's wife, and a woman polluted by menses. These are the laws of Moses. The Talmudic constitution, however, added twenty others (which they call secondary nakednesses). The first maternal line: grandmother, great-grandmother, great-great-grandmother, and so on back to the origin of the world. Second: the great-grandmother who is the mother of the maternal grandfather. Third: the paternal grandmother, specifically the wife of the paternal grandfather. Fourth: the mother of the great-great-grandfather, and so on to the beginning of the generations. Sixth: the wife of the maternal grandfather. Seventh—

<margin>In the same place.</margin>

The Ammonites and Moabites are nations descended from the twin daughters of Lot (begotten by their own father). To "not enter the assembly" means not to join in marriage with the people of God; whereas "to enter" means to be joined in marriage within that same people.

<margin>In the same place.</margin>

<margin>In the same place.</margin>

That is to say, until the third generation. However, the third generation is admitted. One is called an Edomite who is born from the lineage of Esau, the brother of Jacob, who was surnamed Edom.

<margin>In the same place.</margin>
117. *A <term>mamzer: a person born of an illicit or incestuous union</term> shall not enter into the assembly of God.*
A *mamzer* is one who is born from any of the aforementioned shameful unions. Here it should be noted that whenever the Law prohibits someone’s entry into the assembly of God, it is understood that even if they were to reject their paternal rites or paganism and commit themselves to the observance of the Mosaic Law, their entry is still not to be admitted—nor even that of their children—but only to the third generation; that is, it is permitted to the grandson or granddaughter. 

However, we shall not exceed the limits of this compendium if we mention something of the ceremonies and rites by which foreigners were accustomed to enter the covenant of the Mosaic Law. Three things (as recorded in the second chapter of the tractate *Peah* <note>A tractate of the Mishnah/Talmud; Ricius is likely referring to the procedures for conversion often discussed in the context of legal status.</note>) were required of any of the Gentiles who wished to hand themselves over to divine worship and the observance of the Law: circumcision, baptism, and sacrifice. After the destruction of the Temple, however, since the rite of sacrifice ceased, the remaining two apply to the male. For a female, only baptism is required. For a male, neither baptism while still possessing a foreskin, nor circumcision without baptism, will be of benefit. 

Nor is every newcomer who seeks the faith and the law of truth admitted immediately on the spot; rather, he must first be warned of the heavy burden of the Mosaic Law and the dreaded punishment for those who fall short. If, despite these things, he requests the observance of the Law and faith with a constant mind, then he is admitted with the great and solemn applause of all. First, they circumcise the foreskin of his flesh. If he should already be circumcised due to an ulcer, a wound, or from birth, they nonetheless strike a small wound from which some blood may break out. When he has subsequently recovered from the wound, he is then cleansed in his whole body by the washing of baptism while three witnesses stand by. 

Regarding the manner of baptizing, it was the custom of the Jews then, as it is now, to dip the body into a collection of spring water or rainwater, so that the waves of water cover the entire crown of the head. By this law of baptizing, Christ the Savior was dipped in the Jordan River. By the same law, Judith was dipped in a fountain; so also Nehemiah <note>This likely refers to a tradition or a specific reading of Nehemiah 4 or similar texts regarding ritual purification.</note> was stripped with his brothers for baptism. Finally, so also Paul, that wise master builder <note>original: "architectus," a reference to 1 Corinthians 3:10.</note>, taught that we are buried together in the baptism of Christ. But the Church, sparing us, changed the ancient rite of baptizing into the custom which we use today.

<margin>In the same place.</margin>
118. *One wounded by the crushing of the testicles shall not enter the assembly of God.*
<margin>In the same place.</margin>
119. *Nor one whose male organ is cut off.*

112. *You shall not join in marriage with the seven nations.*
There were seven nations who were the previous inhabitants of the land of Israel: the Hittite, the Girgashite, the Amorite, the Perizzite, the Canaanite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite.
