113. *An Ammonite shall not enter the Assembly <note>original: "Ecclesiam"; in this context, the Hebrew "Qahal," referring to the legal and religious community of Israel.</note> of God.*
<margin>In the same place.</margin>
114. *Nor a Moabite.*
The Ammonites and Moabites are nations that trace their origin from the twin daughters of Lot (begotten by their own father). Not to "enter the Assembly" means not to join in marriage among the people of God; whereas "to enter" is to unite in marriage within that same people.

<margin>In the same place.</margin>

<margin>In the same place.</margin>
116. *Nor the Egyptian.*
Specifically, they are excluded only until the third generation. The third generation, however, is admitted. One is called an Edomite who is born of the lineage of Esau, the brother of Jacob, who was surnamed Edom.

<margin>In the same place.</margin>
117. *A <term>Mamzer</term> <note>A Hebrew term referring to a child born from an forbidden union, such as incest or adultery. This status carried legal restrictions in Jewish law.</note> shall not enter into the Assembly of God.*
A Mamzer is one who is begotten from one of the aforementioned "shameful acts" <note>original: "turpitudinum"; referring to the forbidden sexual unions listed in Leviticus 18.</note>. Here, however, it must be noted that whenever the Law prohibits someone's entry into the Assembly of God, it is understood that even if they rejected their paternal rites or paganism and devoted themselves to the observance of the Mosaic Law, their entry is still not to be admitted—not even their children’s. Entry is permitted only to the third generation, namely the grandson or granddaughter. Here, we shall not exceed the limits of this compendium if we mention something of the ceremonies and rites by which foreigners were accustomed to enter the covenant of the Mosaic Law. Thus, three things were required (as is handed down in the second chapter of the book <term>Pe'ah</term> <note>A tractate of the Talmud; while Pe'ah deals with agricultural tithes for the poor, the rituals for conversion are famously detailed in the tractate Yevamot, though Ricius cites Pe'ah here.</note>) for any of the Gentiles who wished to commit themselves to divine worship and the observance of the Law: circumcision, baptism, and sacrifice. After the desolation of the Temple, however, as the rite of sacrifice ceased, the remaining two apply to the male. For the female, only baptism is required. For the male, neither baptism with a foreskin nor circumcision without baptism will be of benefit. Nor is any newcomer who seeks the faith and the same truth admitted immediately and on the spot; but first, he must be warned of the heavy burden of the Mosaic Law and the dreaded punishment for transgressors. If, despite these things, he demands the observance of the Law and the faith with a constant mind, then he is admitted with the great and solemn applause of all. First, they circumcise the foreskin of his flesh; and if he was already born circumcised or was circumcised due to an ulcer or wound, they nevertheless make a small wound from which some blood may break out. When he has recovered from the wound, then, in the presence of three witnesses, he is cleansed in his whole body by the washing of baptism. For it is the custom for those being baptized, both formerly and now among the Jews, to dip the body in a collection of flowing or rain water, so that the waves of water cover the entire crown of the head. By this law of baptizing, Christ the Savior was dipped in the Jordan River. By the same law, Judith was dipped in a spring; so too Nehemiah was stripped with his brothers for Baptism; and finally Paul, the wise architect, taught that we were "buried together" in baptism with Christ. But the Church, sparing us, changed the ancient rite of baptizing into that custom which we use today.

<margin>Leviticus 22</margin>
120. *In your land, you shall not do this at all.*
Namely, to crush or cut off the testicles of cattle <note>a prohibition against the castration of animals</note>.

<margin>Leviticus 21</margin>
121. *A priest shall not take a harlot as a wife.*

<margin>In the same place.</margin>
122. *Nor a profane woman.*
The Latin edition says "a vile prostitute." He calls her "profane" regarding a priest, meaning a woman born from an invalid marriage <note>a woman born from a union forbidden to the priesthood, known in Hebrew law as a "Challah"</note>.

<margin>In the same place.</margin>
123. *Nor a divorced woman.*

<margin>In the same place.</margin>

<margin>Leviticus 21</margin>
125. *Nor shall he profane his seed.*
Here the Latin edition differs significantly. He "profanes his seed" who mingles and procreates outside of marriage.

<margin>Leviticus 18</margin>
126. *He shall not approach his near of kin to reveal her nakedness.*
That is, neither by embraces, nor kisses, nor any gesture which could incite one to shameful acts.

<margin>Leviticus 11</margin>
127. *You shall not eat an unclean animal.*
Of cattle and beasts, there are ten kinds which may be eaten; the Law rejects all the rest. The unclean is distinguished from the clean when it lacks one of two things: namely, the <term>cloven hoof</term> or <term>chewing the cud</term>. Thus, since the pig divides the hoof but does not chew the cud, and the hare chews the cud but does not divide the hoof, the Law judges both—and whatever is of that kind—to be filthy and abominable.

<margin>In the same place.</margin>
128. *You shall not eat of unclean birds.*
The Law mentions twenty-four kinds of unclean birds, and whatever is not forbidden and explained there is permitted for food. However, because many of the birds named in the Law rarely come into human use, certain signs are given by which the unclean is distinguished from the clean: namely, any bird that is predatory and feeds by trampling, and which gulps down and devours a captured animal while it is still half-alive, is to be judged unclean and abominable.

<margin>In the same place.</margin>
129. *You shall not eat the flesh of unclean aquatic creatures.*
Fish are unclean if they lack scales and fins. Scales are those things which adhere to the skin of the fish; fins are those with which it swims.

<margin>Deuteronomy 14</margin>
130. *Every creeping thing among the winged creatures shall be unclean; you shall not eat them.*
An animal "creeps" either by its belly alone contracted into wrinkles, or even with tiny feet, slithering on the ground almost with its chest.

<margin>Leviticus 11</margin>
131. *Every thing that creeps upon the earth (namely, the non-winged) shall be an abomination, and shall not be taken as food.*

<margin>In the same place.</margin>
132. *Do not contaminate your souls with every creeping thing that creeps.*
Namely, even in the water; the Latin edition says nothing of this.

<margin>Deuteronomy 14</margin>
133. *Whatever dies of itself, you shall not eat of it.*
"That which dies of itself" <note>original: "morticinium," referring to carrion or "nevelah"</note> is that which perished either by disease or by a wound (one not inflicted according to the Law of slaughter). What the Law of slaughter is will be explained in its proper place.

<margin>Exodus 22</margin>
134. *You shall not eat meat torn in the field.*
The Latin edition: Meat "pre-tasted" by beasts.

<margin>Exodus 21</margin>
135. *You shall not eat the meat of a wild ox (namely, one that gores with its horn).*

<margin>Deuteronomy 13</margin>
136. *You must not eat the life with the flesh.*
That is, a limb cut off while the animal is still living <note>a reference to the "Ever Min HaChay" prohibition</note>.

<margin>Leviticus 7</margin>
137. *You shall not take the blood of any animal as food.*
Specifically of birds and cattle; however, it is permitted to consume the blood of fish.

<margin>In the same place.</margin>
138. *You shall not eat the suet (Latin edition: "fat") of sheep, ox, and goat.*
We call it <term>suet</term> <note>original: "arvinam"</note> whenever the fat adheres to the membranes in such a way that it cannot be separated; however, that which is covered by the flesh and adheres to it is usually called <term>fat</term> <note>original: "adeps"</note>.

<margin>Genesis 32</margin>
139. *The sons of Israel do not eat the nerve of the hip.*
The sciatic nerve <note>original: "neruum sciæ"</note> is inserted into the joint of the hip, which serves as a hinge for the thigh and foot to perform the movement of walking.

<margin>Exodus 23</margin>
140. *You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk.*
Even if you do not intend to eat it.

<margin>Exodus 34</margin>
141. *You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk.*
Meaning, that you may not eat it; and not only a kid, but any animal; and not only in its own mother’s milk, but in the milk of any animal. It is a divine violation not only to boil it, but to mix it with any kind of seasoning.

<margin>Leviticus 23</margin>

This refers specifically to the day of Pentecost.

<margin>In the same place.</margin>
143. *Nor parched grain.*
Parched grain <note>original: "polentam"</note> here refers to grains toasted by fire and husked by rubbing them with the hands.

<margin>In the same place.</margin>
144. *Nor porridge.*
He calls porridge <note>original: "pultes"</note> those grains broken by a pestle or a millstone.

<margin>In the same place.</margin>

Meaning that when you have sown your vineyard with mixed seed, the crops produced there may not be taken for use; for nothing that has been <term>sanctified</term> <note>set apart for holy use or rendered "taboo" by religious Law</note> is permitted to be converted to one’s own personal profit.

<margin>Leviticus 19</margin>

<note>This refers to "Orlah," the prohibition against eating fruit from a tree during the first three years after it is planted.</note>

They profane the holy things who eat of the crops from which the <term>firstfruits</term> and <term>tithes</term> have not yet been removed.

<margin>Exodus 34</margin>
148. *You shall not eat of things sacrificed.*
Meaning, sacrificed to idols. Nor may you drink the wine of their libations; because of this, the foolish among the Jews determine that wine which a Christian <note>original: "Christicola," literally "Christ-worshipper"</note> has touched is profane and abominable.

<margin>Leviticus 22</margin>
149. *An ox and a sheep shall not be sacrificed on the same day with their offspring.*

<margin>Deuteronomy 22</margin>

But once the young are taken, you must let the mother go.

<margin>Leviticus 19</margin>

# ON THE COMMANDMENTS OF THE MOSAIC LAW

...is spoken of. Indeed, the Law itself shows through frequent warnings how execrable and abhorrent the pollution of the dead is. For it says: *Whoever touches the corpse of a human soul* <note>original: "humanae animae morticinium"; This phrasing reflects the Hebrew "nefesh met," where "soul" or "breath" refers to the person, even in death.</note> *and has not been sprinkled with water, he shall defile the tabernacle of the Lord and shall perish from Israel.* Again: *All who enter the tent of a man who dies, and all the vessels that are there, shall be polluted.* Furthermore: *Whoever touches a bone of a corpse or a grave shall be unclean.* In short, the Mosaic Law detests no impurity as much as the contagion of the dead. This is partly because the foolish superstition of the ancient gentiles used to inhabit the tombs of the dead to consult and worship their spirits, and partly because nothing more stains and corrupts the spiritual strength of mortals than the foul and poisonous exhalation of the dead. Hence the saying of the Apostle: *Touch no unclean thing.* And that of the Gospel: *Whitewashed tombs full of dead men's bones and all filth.*

You will perhaps ask, and not without reason: if the pollution of corpses is so execrable, why is it that the temples, shrines, and altars of the saints are everywhere strewn and filled with foul and pestilential corpses of the dead, even in those places where the most sacred mysteries of the glorious body of Christ are celebrated? This question is not solved by the fact that the Apostle, in the Letter to the Romans, judged *all things to be clean,* and to Titus said, *To the pure, all things are pure.* For in those passages he is speaking of food, which does not recommend us to God. Although all things are permitted by the license and liberty Christ gave us through the blood of the cross, yet (as the Apostle says) *not all things are expedient.* To settle this matter and question in a few words: know that the reasoning for this and for the veneration of images is one and the same; consider it well.

<margin>Leviticus 21</margin>
236. *The High Priest shall not be defiled even for his father or his mother.*

<margin>Ibid.</margin>
237. *And he shall not go in to any dead body at all.*

<margin>Exodus 20</margin>
238. *You shall not take the name of God—that is, the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The sacred four-letter name of God in Hebrew (YHWH).</note>—of your God in vain.*

The name of God is taken in vain in four ways. First, when one denies by oath that which everyone else affirms, for example, by swearing that the city of Jerusalem is nowhere to be found in the world. Second, by swearing to something that the nature of things does not allow at all, such as an ox flying through the air, or wanting to devote oneself to seven continuous days of vigils and fasting. Third, by swearing that he will transgress one of the commandments of the Law. Fourth, by swearing that something is true whose opposite or falsehood cannot even be imagined, such as swearing that "two is two."

<margin>Leviticus 19</margin>
239. *Neither shall you perjure yourselves in my name.*
That is, in whatever sacred name, claiming you have done what you did not do, or will do what you will not do.

<margin>Ibid.</margin>

That is, you shall not deny a loan given to you.

<margin>Ibid.</margin>
241. *Neither shall you be fraudulent, every man against his neighbor.*
That is, do not deny a deposit <note>An item or sum of money left in your care for safekeeping.</note>.

is spoken of. Indeed, the Law itself shows through frequent admonition how execrable and abhorrent the pollution of the dead is: for it says, *Whoever touches the corpse of a human soul and has not been sprinkled, he shall pollute the tabernacle of the Lord and shall perish from Israel*; and again, *all who enter the tent of a man who dies, and all the vessels that are there, shall be polluted.* Furthermore, *whoever touches the bone of a carcass or a grave shall be unclean.* In short, the Mosaic Law detests no impurity as much as the contagion of the dead, both because the foolish superstition of the ancient nations used to inhabit the tombs of the dead and to consult and adore their spirits, and also because nothing stains and corrupts the spiritual powers of mortals more than the putrid and poisonous exhalation of the dead. Hence that saying of the Apostle: *Touch not the unclean thing.* <note>original: "Immundum ne tetigeritis" - quoting 2 Corinthians 6:17.</note> And that of the Gospel: *Whitened sepulchers full of dead men’s bones and all filthiness.* <note>original: "Dealbata sepulchra plena ossibus mortuorum & omni spurcitia" - quoting Matthew 23:27.</note> You might perhaps ask, and not without reason: if the pollution of corpses is so execrable, why are the temples, shrines, and altars of the saints everywhere scattered with and full of foul and pestilential corpses of the dead, even in those places where the most sacred mysteries of the glorious body of Christ are celebrated? This question is not solved by the fact that the Apostle, in the letter to the Romans, judged *all things to be clean.* <note>Romans 14:20.</note> And to Titus, he said: *To the clean, all things are clean*; <note>Titus 1:15.</note> for there he is speaking of food, which does not recommend us to God. But although all things are permitted by the license and liberty which Christ gave us through the blood of the cross, nevertheless (says the Apostle) *not all things are expedient.* To finally conclude this matter and question in a few words, know that the logic for this and for the veneration of images is the same; consider it well.

<margin>Leviticus 21.</margin> 236. *The High Priest shall not be defiled even for his father or his mother.*
<margin>Ibidem.</margin> 237. *And he shall not go in to any dead body at all.*
<margin>Exodus 20.</margin> 238. *You shall not take the name of God (that is, the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The sacred four-letter name of God, YHWH, which was not to be spoken aloud in common speech.</note>) of your God in vain.*

The name of God is taken in vain in four ways. First, when one denies by oath that which everyone else affirms as the opposite—for example, by swearing that the city of Jerusalem is nowhere to be found in the world. Second, by swearing something that the nature of reality absolutely does not allow, such as that an ox flies through the air, or that one wishes to persist in seven days and nights of continuous vigil and fasting. Third, that one will transgress one of the commandments of the Law. Fourth, to swear that something is true whose opposite or falsehood cannot even be imagined by anyone, such as swearing that "two are two."

<margin>Leviticus 19.</margin> 239. *Nor shall you perjure yourself in my name.*
<gloss>That is, by any sacred name, swearing that you have done what you have not done, or that you will do what you will not do.</gloss>

<margin>Ibidem.</margin> 240. *You shall lie to no one.*
<gloss>That is, you shall not deny a loan given to you.</gloss>

<margin>Ibidem.</margin> 241. *Neither shall you be fraudulent, every man against his neighbor.*
<gloss>That is, you shall not deny a deposit entrusted to you.</gloss>

<margin>Numbers 30.</margin> 242. *He who knows his word shall not make it void.*
<margin>Numbers 6.</margin> 243. *One abstaining by a vow shall abstain from wine and everything that can inebriate.* <note>These verses refer to the vow of the Nazirite, a person who consecrated themselves to God for a specific period.</note>
<margin>Ibidem.</margin> 244. *And from fresh grapes.*
<margin>Ibidem.</margin> 245. *And from grape seeds.*
<margin>Ibidem.</margin> 246. *And from dried grapes.*
<margin>Ibidem.</margin> 247. *And from the skins of grapes.*
<margin>Ibidem.</margin> 248. *He shall not go in to a dead person.*
<margin>Ibidem.</margin> 249. *Nor shall he be defiled at the funeral of his father, or mother, or brother, or sister.*
<margin>Ibidem.</margin> 250. *A razor shall not pass over his head.*
<margin>Leviticus 27.</margin> 251. *Everything that is consecrated to God shall not be sold.*
<margin>Ibidem.</margin> 252. *Nor can it be redeemed.*
<note>Specifically by the same person who consecrated his property.</note>

<margin>Exodus 22</margin> 253. *You shall not delay to offer your tithes and firstfruits.*

<margin>Leviticus 22</margin> 254. *No stranger shall eat of the sanctified things.*
"Stranger" here designates every Jew who is not born of the priestly lineage.

<margin>Ibidem</margin> 255. *Neither a sojourner nor a hired servant of a priest shall eat of them.*
Namely, of the sanctified things. "Sojourner" here designates one bought by a priest forever (that is, until the Jubilee), whereas "hired servant" designates one hired for a limited time.

<margin>Ibidem</margin> 256. *A priest’s daughter married to anyone from among the common people shall not eat of those things which are sanctified, nor of the firstfruits.*

This is not explicitly stated in the Law, but is concluded by analogy from the law of the Passover lamb.

<margin>Deuteronomy 12</margin> 259. *You may not eat within your gates the tithe of your grain.*
But you shall eat all these things before God in the place which God shall choose, namely in Jerusalem.

<margin>Deuteronomy 26</margin> 261. *Nor of the oil.*

From this they conclude it is by no means permitted to eat tithes while in a state of ritual impurity.

<margin>Ibidem</margin> 263. *I have not eaten of it in my mourning.*
From this it is proved a sacrilege to eat of sacred things on the day of the death of parents, a sister, a brother, or a child.

<margin>Ibidem</margin> 264. *Nor have I spent any of these things on a funeral matter.*
For he profanes sacred things who spends them for the use of the unclean. Hence the Talmudists <term>Talmudei</term><note>Scholars and teachers of the Jewish Talmudic tradition.</note> decree that he most greatly defiles sacred things who bestows the firstfruits of tithes, and whatever pertains to sacred matters, upon an ignorant and wicked priest.

<margin>Deuteronomy 12</margin> 265. *You may not eat the firstfruits of your hands except before God, your God.*

<margin>Leviticus 25</margin> 266. *You shall not sow your field (namely, in every seventh year).*

<margin>Ibidem</margin> 270. *He to whom something is owed by a friend, or neighbor, or his brother, shall not be able to demand it back in the year of release.*

<margin>Ibidem</margin> 271. *Beware lest an impious thought perhaps creep into you, and you say in your heart that the seventh year of release approaches, and you turn your eyes away from the poor man.*
Namely, so that you refuse to provide a loan.

<margin>Leviticus 25</margin> 272. *You shall not sow.* <note>original: "Non feretis," likely a printer's error for "seretis" (to sow).</note>
Namely, in the Jubilee year.

<margin>Ibidem</margin> 273. *Neither shall you reap what grows from its fallen fragments.*

<margin>Ibidem</margin> 274. *And you shall not gather the firstfruits of the vintage.*

<margin>Ibidem</margin> 275. *The land shall not be sold forever.*
But in the year of Jubilee, it shall return to its original owner.

<margin>Deuteronomy 18</margin> 276. *The Priests and Levites shall have no part (namely of the spoil) or inheritance with the rest of Israel.*

<margin>Leviticus 25</margin> 277. *The Levites shall receive nothing of possession in the midst of their brothers.*

<meta>This page transitions from the discussion of the 365 negative commandments (prohibitions) to the affirmative commandments of the Mosaic Law. The previous page ended with prohibition number 346. Ricius here concludes the section on prohibitions and begins a new numbered list for the positive requirements of the Law.</meta>

->PAVLVS RICIUS,<-

Namely, in everything that I command you. From this, those who are Israelites according to the flesh <note>A common Renaissance term for the Jewish people, contrasting with "Israelites according to the spirit," or Christians.</note> argue for the perpetual observance of the Mosaic Law, because that to which nothing must be added or subtracted must be invariable and remain eternal. But they, in their usual manner, go out of bounds and wander from the right path. For it is not the intention of the Law that none of the commandments should be omitted in any place or time; indeed, even today, the Jews offer no libations, they do not burn whole offerings, they do not slay victims—in short, they fulfill nothing of the rite of sacrifice, nor anything of the commandments depending on the cultivation of the land. 

Instead, as the Talmudists teach in the commentary called the *Siphra* <note>The *Sifra* is an ancient Jewish legal commentary on the book of Leviticus.</note>, when the Law commands "You shall not add nor diminish," the meaning is that the condition and mode of performing each commandment, which the Law expresses precisely, must be observed. For example, for the solemnities of the Feast of Tabernacles <note>original: *scenopegiæ*. This refers to Sukkot, the festival where four specific plants (the *lulav* and *etrog*) are bound together.</note>, it is commanded that a bundle be gathered from four things growing from the earth; if, therefore, you join a fifth to these, you will be a transgressor of the precept "do not add." If you bind it from only three, you will be a transgressor of the precept "do not diminish." The same is to be judged concerning individual matters, but these things are discussed more widely elsewhere. Thus far, we have considered enough concerning the 365 prohibitive commandments of the Law, according to the purpose of this compendium; now, by God's will, we shall approach those which are commandments of things to be done.

### AFFIRMATIVE COMMANDMENTS OF THE MOSAIC LAW.

<margin>Exodus 20.</margin>
1. *I am God (namely the Tetragrammaton) your God, who led you out of the land of Egypt.*

The Tetragrammaton <note>The sacred four-letter name of God in Hebrew, often represented as YHWH.</note> is a name incommunicable to creatures, which sounds like "the giver of being," he who imparts the gift of existence to all. This first commandment of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note> suggests two things to be believed: namely, that there is a God who gives being (that is, the creator of all beings), and that this God is *your* God, who led you out (that is, one who has care for human affairs).

<margin>Deuteronomy 6.</margin>
2. *Hear, O Israel, God (namely the Tetragrammaton) our God, is one God.*

That is, one must also believe that He is one; here the mystery of the indivisible Trinity is openly handed down. <note>Ricius, as a Christian Kabbalist, often interprets Jewish scripture and tradition as containing hidden proofs for Christian doctrines like the Trinity.</note>

<margin>In the same place.</margin>
3. *You shall love God (the Tetragrammaton) your God with all your heart.*

Wherever "your God" is read, one should hear "He who provides for you and is the moderator of your affairs."

<margin>In the same place.</margin>
4. *You shall fear God (the Tetragrammaton) your God.*

Fear is of two forms: one is servile, the other filial. The former is like that of a small child, the latter like that of an adult toward a parent. The former precedes love; the latter is the companion of love, which is the subject of the discussion here.

<margin>Leviticus 22.</margin>
5. *I shall be sanctified in the midst of the children of Israel.*

He sanctifies God who, for the sake of the worship of true piety, is shaken by no terror or fear, dreads no tortures, and does not shrink from the punishments of death.

<margin>Deuteronomy 18.</margin>
6. *A Prophet from your nation and from your brothers like me, God (the Tetragrammaton) your God will raise up for you; him you shall hear.*

You shall not observe spirits of divination <note>original: *phytones*, referring to the "Pythonic" spirit of the Oracle at Delphi.</note>, nor soothsayers, nor dreams, nor auguries; consult only the oracles of the Prophets.

<margin>Deuteronomy 13.</margin>
7. *You shall follow God (the Tetragrammaton) your God.*

That is, you shall walk in His ways. His ways are order and justice, which we perceive existing in the nature of things.

<margin>Deuteronomy 10.</margin>
8. *To Him you shall cling.*

In this clinging, the whole reason for blessedness consists.

<margin>Leviticus 19.</margin>
9. *You shall love your friend as yourself.*

<margin>Deuteronomy 10.</margin>
10. *And you shall love the stranger.*

He calls "stranger" one who embraces the covenants of the Law out of the insane superstition of the Gentiles. <note>A reference to a *ger tzedek*, or a righteous convert to Judaism.</note>

<meta>catchword: 11. Argue.</meta>

<summary>Ricius concludes the 365 negative commandments and begins the affirmative ones, starting with the Ten Commandments and the duty to love and fear God. He argues that the Law’s prohibition against "adding or subtracting" refers to the specific ritual methods of the commandments rather than the Law’s eternal immutability in all times and places.</summary>

### ON THE COMMANDMENTS OF THE MOSAIC LAW.

11. *Rebuking, you shall rebuke (that is, many times) your neighbor.*
<margin>Leviticus 19.</margin>
Because unless you do this, you will be guilty of the crime: for (as the Talmudists say) the children of Israel are mutual guarantors for one another, so that when one offends, another may pay the penalty. <note>This refers to the Jewish legal principle "Kol Yisrael arevim zeh bazeh"—all Israel are responsible for one another.</note>

12. *Teach these words of mine (namely of the Law) to your children.*
<margin>Deuteronomy 11.</margin>
For he taught that the tenderness of children should be instructed not with the enticing and obscene fictions of the poets or the seduction of words, but in the mandates of the divine Law and the sacred utterances of the Prophets. For the sort of things a child’s soft nature hears, such things he speaks and fulfills in action: as the adolescence is, so is the youth, so is the more mature adult age, and finally such is the resulting government and order of the entire human society. Therefore, he who allows the weakness of children to be soothed by this deadly song of the Sirens <note>A classical reference to the seductive and dangerous songs of the sirens in Greek mythology, used here to represent secular or pagan literature.</note> and by sweet-tasting poison, removes every good thing. To avoid this virulent plague of the Republic, Moses says: *Teach these words of mine to your children.* Indeed, it is for no other reason that the Jews more persistently cherish the Law, except that from their very cradles they are imbued with the documents and warnings of the Law and the Prophets; to which Jerome (writing to Paulinus) alluded: "I pray you, dearest brother, to live among these (namely the gifts of the Prophets and Apostles), to meditate on these, to know nothing else, to seek nothing else—does this not seem to you a dwelling place of the heavenly kingdom here on earth?"

13. *Rise up before the grey head.* <note>i.e., honor the elderly.</note>
<margin>Leviticus 19.</margin>

14. *Overthrow all the places in which the nations worshiped.*
<margin>Deuteronomy 12.</margin>

15. *They shall confess their sin.*
<margin>Deuteronomy 21. <note>The marginal citation "Deut 21" is unusual here; confession of sin is typically linked to Numbers 5 or Leviticus 5.</note></margin>
For if a sinner performs repentance, offers a sacrifice, and restores dishonest gain or what was unjustly taken, yet dies having neglected confession, he carries the penalty of eternal damnation—consider this.

16. *You shall strike the inhabitants of the city (namely, one turned toward idols) with the edge of the sword.*
<margin>Numbers 5. <note>The marginal note cites Numbers 5, though this command regarding idolatrous cities is found in Deuteronomy 13.</note></margin>

17. *Reconsider in your heart: that just as a man instructs his son, so the Lord your God <note>original: "Deus Tetragrammaton," referring to the four-letter holy name of God, YHWH.</note> instructs you.*
<margin>Deuteronomy 8.</margin>
That is, if fortune (as they call it) looks upon you with a cloudy face, reconsider that this has been brought upon you by divine correction.

18. *You shall meditate (namely on these words of mine) while sleeping and while rising.*
<margin>Deuteronomy 6.</margin>
From this, the entire Synagogue of the Jews observes with the greatest zeal and study that it should perform the short reading of the *Shema* <note>original: "scema" (Hear), the central prayer of Judaism: *Hear, O Israel...*</note>—in which the mystery of the most Holy Trinity is hinted at—in the evening and the morning, with a living voice and attentive meditation. <note>As a Christian convert, Ricius often interprets Jewish prayers through a Trinitarian lens.</note>

19. *And you shall serve him (namely God) with all your heart.*
<margin>Deuteronomy 10.</margin>
They determine that the service of the heart consists in prayer alone, which (as is handed down in the book *Berachos* <note>The Talmudic tractate Berakhot, which deals with blessings and prayers.</note>) requires a certain fitting together of time, place, body, and mind. The times are indeed fixed: morning, noon, and evening, according to that verse of the Psalms:
<margin>Psalm 54. <note>Psalm 55:17 in modern English Bibles.</note></margin>
*Evening, morning, and at noon I will talk and declare.* But the younger multitude of the Jews fulfill the noon and evening hours together in the evening. Let the place not be elevated, but on level ground, purged of all filth, and removed from the sight of women. Let the body also be clean and neat, let the face turn toward the east, standing with feet close together; let him fix his gaze on the ground and raise his heart on high; and let the mind be empty of any outside image; and first let it recount the praises of the Creator, then let it implore with devotion, and finally let it give thanks.

20. *Thus you shall bless (namely you Priests) the children of Israel.*
<margin>Numbers 6.</margin>
For it is established that on solemn feasts the Priests should bless Israel in the great and ineffable name, the Tetragrammaton, by pronouncing that same Tetragrammaton in the sanctuary with its own characters; but outside, only by the surname *Adonai*. <note>original: "Edonai." It was Jewish practice to substitute the name "Adonai" (Lord) for the four-letter name of God when outside the Temple.</note>

21. *And you shall bind (namely my words) as a sign upon your hand.*
<margin>Deuteronomy 6.</margin>

22. *And they shall be as a frontal ornament between your eyes.*
<margin>Ibidem.</margin>
These twin signs are to be bound to the left arm and hand, and to the forehead, from which...

<meta>catchword: Namely</meta>

...four small readings from the Law, written according to a specific Law, and prescribed to be covered and bound together with a certain leather. <note>original: "tuor de Lege..." This refers to the *Tefillin* or phylacteries—small leather boxes containing Torah verses worn during prayer.</note> The first reading is that from Exodus: *Sanctify to me.* <note>Exodus 13:1-10</note> The second in the same book: *And when he shall have brought you in.* <note>Exodus 13:11-16</note> The third, that from Deuteronomy: *Hear, O Israel.* <note>Deuteronomy 6:4-9</note> The fourth: *If then you will obey.* <note>Deuteronomy 11:13-21</note>

<margin>Deuteronomy 6.
Deuteronomy 6.</margin>
23. *And you shall write them (namely those words of mine) on the doorposts of your house and on your gates.*

Indeed, in obedience to this mandate, they are accustomed to fix to the doorposts a parchment sheet enclosed in a reed, inscribed with two of the aforementioned readings along with certain divine names (following the same ritual as the previously mentioned ornaments). <note>This describes the *Mezuzah*.</note> They venerate this by the touch of their fingers and a kiss when leaving or entering the house.

<margin>Deuteronomy 31.</margin>
24. *Now therefore, write for yourselves this song.*

Namely, the Law. <note>The Torah is often poetically referred to in the tradition as a "song."</note> From this, the Talmudists—in the *Book of the Elders* <note>original: "codice senaturum," referring to the Talmudic tractate *Sanhedrin*.</note> in the chapter *The High Priest* <note>original: "capite cahen gadol"</note>—derive that it pertains to every one of the children of Israel to write for himself a Pentateuch (with the same reverence as the forehead and hand ornaments) <note>Referring to the scrolls inside the Tefillin.</note> or, if written by another, to purge it of errors with his own hand.

<margin>Deuteronomy 17.</margin>
25. *He (namely the king) shall write out a copy of this Law.*

The sense is that he should write out not only that volume of the Pentateuch which is titled Deuteronomy, but the entire Law doubled: one because he is an Israelite, the other because he is a king. The former he may set aside, but the latter he should carry about with him both abroad and at home.

<margin>Numbers 15.</margin>
26. *They shall make for themselves fringes on the four corners of their cloaks.*

The fringes here are threads woven of wool, eight in number, tied together on each of the four corners of the cloak. <note>These are *Tzitzit*, the ritual fringes worn by Jewish men.</note>

<margin>Deuteronomy 8.</margin>
27. *When you have eaten and are satisfied, you shall bless God,* (The Tetragrammaton) <note>The four-letter divine name, YHWH.</note> *your God.*

<margin>Leviticus 12.</margin>
28. *On the eighth day the infant shall be circumcised.*

<margin>Exodus 20.</margin>
29. *Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day.*

<margin>Exodus 23.</margin>
30. *On the seventh day you shall rest.*

<margin>Leviticus 23.</margin>
31. *A Sabbath of rest is the tenth day of the seventh month.* <note>This refers to *Yom Kippur*, the Day of Atonement.</note>

<margin>Leviticus 16.</margin>
32. *You shall afflict (on that day) your souls.* <note>A biblical idiom for fasting.</note>

<margin>Exodus 12.</margin>
33. *The first day of unleavened bread shall be holy and solemn.* <note>The start of Passover.</note>

<margin>Leviticus 23.</margin>
34. *The seventh day of unleavened bread shall also be most celebrated and holy to you.*

<margin>Leviticus 23.</margin>
35. *And you shall call this day most celebrated.*

Namely, the day of Pentecost, on which the offering of new fruits is made. <note>Known as *Shavuot*.</note>

<margin>In the same place.</margin>
36. *On the first day of the seventh month, there shall be a Sabbath for you.*

This is the day on which (according to the computation of the Hebrews) the beginning of the year is taken. <note>*Rosh Hashanah*, the Jewish New Year.</note>

<margin>In the same place.</margin>

Namely, with both praises and the giving of thanks.

### ON THE MANDATES OF THE MOSAIC LAW.

Namely, during the days of the Feast of Tabernacles <note>original: "Scenopegię" — from the Greek for "tent-pitching," referring to the festival of Sukkot.</note>, during which they live under the cover of willow branches or the green twigs and leaves of any trees.

<margin>Exodus 30.</margin>
45. *Every person who passes over to be counted shall give half a shekel.*
A shekel <note>original: "Siclus"</note> (as explained in the Talmudic book *Shekalim*, that is, "of weights") was first taken as the weight of twenty denarii, but now twenty-four. A denarius consists of sixteen grains of wheat. Therefore, every year, anyone who passes to the numbering (that is, those who have reached twenty years of age) should offer half a shekel.

<margin>Exodus 12.</margin>
46. *This month shall be for you the beginning of months.*
From this (in the second chapter of *Rosh Hashanah* <note>original: "rosh ha-shehena," the Jewish New Year tractate</note>), the Talmudists decree that the New Moon or the new month must be judged by sight. If, on the thirtieth day of the month, the horns of the Moon do not shine forth due to the turbulence of the air, then they celebrate the new month on the thirty-first day, and take the beginning of the following month from there. Such observation of the new moon was practiced by the Jews as long as they held the governance of the land of Israel. But after their expulsion and dispersion throughout the world, they established certain rules and fixed tables by which the lunar, solstitial, and leap-year cycles can be found and announced in their proper order and at fixed times.

<margin>Deuteronomy 4:16.</margin>
47. *You shall observe and fulfill them, for this is your wisdom and understanding before the peoples.*
From this, the Talmudists conclude that the calculation of the movements of the luminaries <note>The sun and moon</note> must be thoroughly learned and observed.

<margin>Deuteronomy 24.</margin>
48. *If a man takes a wife and becomes her master.*
From this, they teach (in the book *Kiddushin* <note>original: "chi dušchim" — the Talmudic tractate on betrothals</note>) that marriage is contracted in three ways: namely, by the price of silver, by conjugal union, and by documents.

<margin>Genesis 1.</margin>
49. *Increase and multiply.*
From this, they derive (in the chapter *He who comes upon his sister-in-law* <note>original: "habaal ieuimto," referring to a chapter in the tractate *Yebamot*</note>) that no one is exempt from the Law of propagation—unless he has entirely surrendered and devoted himself to God—until he has fathered both a son and a daughter.

<margin>Deuteronomy 24.</margin>
50. *He shall write a bill of divorce and give it into her hand.*
For when a wife becomes hateful to her husband because of some uncleanness, then the Law and the bond of marriage is dissolved through a bill of divorce, and each is able to pass on to a second marriage.

<margin>Deuteronomy 25.</margin>
51. *The brother shall take the wife of his deceased brother who is without children.*
If the brother is unwilling to take her as his wife, he is compelled to fulfill the Law of "unshoeing" (which is described immediately below). <note>This refers to the Law of Levirate marriage.</note>

<margin>Ibid.</margin>
52. *She (the wife of the deceased) shall take the shoe from his foot.*
For when the brother of the deceased refuses marriage with his brother's wife, then in the presence of the elders, the woman shall take the shoe—woven with a certain specific craft—from the foot of the brother-in-law <note>original: "leuiti," likely a slip for "leviri" (brother-in-law)</note>, and shall spit in his face, saying: "So shall it be done to the man who will not build up his brother's house."

<margin>Exodus 22.</margin>
53. *If anyone seduces (namely, by the charms of words) a virgin, he shall have her as his wife, or he shall pay money according to the measure of the dowry by which virgins are usually endowed. If he seizes her (namely, by force) and lies with her, he shall give fifty shekels to the father and shall have her as his wife.*

<margin>Ibid.</margin>
54. *A man who has slandered [his wife] shall have her all the days of his life.* <note>Meaning he cannot divorce her.</note>

<margin>Numbers 5.</margin>
55. *A man whom a spirit of jealousy has stirred up against his wife shall bring her to the Priest.*
Who shall give her a certain cursed liquid to drink; when she has drained it, if she has been defiled and is guilty of adultery, her belly shall immediately turn into a swelling and her thigh into rot. If she is innocent, then she will be unharmed, dear to her husband, and fertile.

<margin>Leviticus 21.</margin>
56. *The High Priest shall take a virgin as his wife.*

<margin>Ibid.</margin>
57. *A Priest may be defiled (that is, he may celebrate the funeral rites) for the deaths of blood relatives and close kin.*
Which is by no means permitted for those who are not blood relatives.

<margin>Deuteronomy 14</margin>

That is, learn thoroughly the signs by which these may be distinguished. <note>These signs refer to the requirements of chewing the cud and having completely split hooves, as defined in the kosher laws.</note>

That is, it will be permitted to eat them. <note>This refers to certain types of locusts or grasshoppers which were considered permissible (kosher) for consumption.</note>

61. *Everything that has fins and scales you shall eat.*

<margin>Deuteronomy 12</margin>

The condition of the sacrifice <note>original: "Immolandi" — here referring specifically to ritual slaughter, or "Shechita"</note> is that the passages of the throat are to be cut: in a bird, indeed, one of the two, namely the esophagus <note>original: "meri," from the Hebrew "mer'i"</note> or the trachea only. In cattle, however, it is necessary to slaughter through the greater part of both. The Law requires many additional accessories for slaughter, such as: who, how much, with what [instrument], where, when, how, and of that sort, which it seems hardly appropriate to recount here.

63. *He shall pour out its blood (namely, the blood of the slaughtered animal) and cover it with earth.*

Namely, so that he who killed his neighbor not by will, but by chance, may flee to them. <note>These are the "Cities of Refuge," designed to protect accidental killers from blood vengeance.</note>

### ON THE COMMANDMENTS OF THE MOSAIC LAW.

<margin>Exodus 21</margin>
84. *The Master shall redeem a (Hebrew) maidservant who has been sold (the Latin edition says 'dismiss').*

That is, he shall allow her to be redeemed.

<margin>Ibidem</margin>
85. *But if he betrothes her to his son.*

Here they establish that a purchased maidservant is to be betrothed to either the father or the son. <note>Under Mosaic Law, a Hebrew girl sold into service by her father was intended to eventually marry either her master or his son, rather than remaining a permanent slave.</note>

<margin>Leviticus 25</margin>
86. *You shall possess servants from the nations that are around you forever.*

That is, until the Jubilee. <note>In this legal context, "forever" often refers to the completion of the fifty-year Jubilee cycle, at which point certain social and economic statuses were reset.</note>

<margin>Exodus 22</margin>
87. *He who receives money or a vessel for safekeeping (add: for free), and it is taken by theft, he shall swear that he has not extended his hand toward his neighbor’s property.*

That is, he shall swear that he has not committed fraud, nor provided the opportunity for the theft, and thus he shall restore nothing for the stolen item.

<margin>Ibidem</margin>
88. *If he receives a thing for safekeeping (namely, not for free, but for a fee), and it is taken by theft, he shall restore the loss to the Master.*

<margin>Deuteronomy 24</margin>

<margin>Deuteronomy 23</margin>

<margin>Exodus 22</margin>

<margin>Ibidem</margin>

This refers to the garment with which he is covered during his nightly rest.

<margin>Ibidem</margin>
93. *If (that is, because) you give money as a loan to my people.*

From this we are taught that a loan is to be given to the needy.

<margin>Ibidem</margin>

<margin>Numbers 27</margin>

<margin>Deuteronomy 16</margin>

<margin>Exodus 23</margin>
97. *Judgment is to be made according to the majority (namely, in a court).*

The Latin translation says otherwise.

<margin>Exodus 21</margin>
98. *He shall be avenged with vengeance.*

That is, by the sword.

<margin>Leviticus 20</margin>
99. *He shall die the death.*

That is, by strangulation.

<margin>Ibidem</margin>
100. *He shall burn alive with them: that is, he shall be consumed by fire.*

<margin>Deuteronomy 22</margin>
101. *The people of the city shall overwhelm him with stones.*

Under these four methods of inflicting death, the punishment of the gallows is also included, because no guilty person is hung unless he has first paid the penalty of death by one of these methods. <note>In Jewish law, hanging was not a method of execution but a public display of the body after certain types of execution—specifically stoning—to serve as a deterrent.</note>

<margin>Deuteronomy 21</margin>
102. *And he shall be hung on a gallows.*

<margin>Ibidem</margin>
103. *One sentenced to death shall be buried on the same day.*

<margin>Ibidem</margin>
104. *The judge shall lay him down and have him beaten in his presence.*

For he who has been a transgressor of any prohibitive mandate (in cases where neither death nor the "cutting off" of the soul is decreed) is struck with up to forty lashes. <note>In practice, the limit was set at thirty-nine lashes to ensure the biblical limit of forty was never accidentally exceeded.</note>

<margin>Leviticus 19</margin>
105. *Judge your neighbor justly.*

<margin>Exodus 23</margin>
106. *You shall flee from a lie.*

<margin>Leviticus 5</margin>
107. *He who has seen or is aware, unless he indicates it (namely, by the law of testimony), shall bear his iniquity.*

<margin>Deuteronomy 13</margin>
108. *Search and investigate diligently (namely, the witnesses).*

<margin>Deuteronomy 19</margin>

Namely, regarding vows; for the vow of a girl is committed to the will of her father, while the vow of a married woman is committed to the judgment of her husband, so that he may either reject or confirm it. The vows of others, however, can be released by only one wise man, or by three <term>common persons</term>. <note>The original uses "idiotis," which in a legal/ecclesiastical context refers to laypeople or those not specialized in the Law, rather than a lack of intelligence.</note>

Meaning the hair of him who has made a vow or has been a <term>Nazirite</term> (one abstaining from wine and other things).

On the day of purification (according to the Latin edition), he shall shave it immediately.

The condition for this is the same as for an animal.

<margin>Ibidem</margin>

That is, it is not permitted for it to come into profane use, but it shall be strictly the possession of the Priests, and it can neither be redeemed nor sold.

### CONCERNING THE COMMANDMENTS OF THE MOSAIC LAW.

Specifically, that which the Levite receives from the laity must in turn have its own tenth part handed over to the Priests. <note>This refers to the *Terumat Maaser*, or the "tithe of the tithe," which Levites gave to the Priests from the tithes they collected.</note>

<margin>in the same place</margin>
135. *The tithe of the children of Israel, which they offer to God <term>Tetragrammaton</term>, I have given to the Levites as a possession.* <note>The "Tetragrammaton" is the four-letter name of God, YHWH. Original: "Decimam filiorum Israël... offerunt Deo Tetragrammaton."</note>

<margin>Deuteronomy 14</margin>
136. *Tithing you shall tithe (the Latin edition says "with a tithe you shall set apart") all the fruits of your sowing.* <note>original: "Decima decimabis... decimā separabis."</note>

The Law commands that a double tithe be given annually: one for the Levites, and another which the owner who pays the tithe sets apart for himself, so that he may eat it in Jerusalem. There is also a third kind of tithe, which they call the "tithe of the poor," to be extended only to the poor among the laity and the Levites; this is not given every year, but only in every third year in place of the second tithe. The first discussion was of the first tithe, and now the discourse concerns the second.

<margin>in the same place</margin>
137. *In the fourth year (namely, from the time of planting), all their fruit (specifically of the trees which you have planted) shall be sanctified.*

That is, it is not permitted to eat of it, except in the place which God has chosen, namely, in Jerusalem. However, for the first three years from planting, it is not lawful to take any fruit of this kind at all. <note>This refers to the law of *Orlah* (the first three years) and *Neta Reva'i* (the fourth year).</note>

<margin>Deuteronomy 26</margin>
138. *You shall speak in the presence of God <term>Tetragrammaton</term> your God: I have brought that which is sanctified.*

The discourse here concerns the confession which must be made after the second tithes have been offered. <note>Known as *Vidui Maaser*, a formal declaration that one has distributed tithes correctly.</note>

<margin>Exodus 23</margin>
139. *The firstfruits of the produce of your land you shall bring into the house of the Lord.*

"Firstfruits" here indicates the early-ripening fruits of the land, which are commanded to be brought to the house of God. You may gather from this a fourfold offering of produce: First is the fruit that matures earliest. Second is the firstfruits of the winepress and the threshing floor. Third is the tithe for the Levites. Fourth is the second tithe, which belongs to the poor <note>in the designated years</note>.

<margin>Deuteronomy 26</margin>
140. *You shall go to the priest, and say: I profess today.*

This is the confession of the firstfruits, whereas the previous one was for the tithes.

<margin>Numbers 15</margin>
141. *Of the firstfruits of the dough (specifically from the pottage) you shall set aside a cake.* <note>The commandment of *Challah*, where a portion of dough is given to the Priest.</note>

This shall be handed over to the Priest; if he is not in a state of ritual purity, it shall be consumed by fire.

<margin>Deuteronomy 18</margin>
142. *They shall give to the Priest the shoulder, the jaws, and the stomach.*

Specifically from a slaughtered beast.

<margin>in the same place</margin>
143. *The firstfruits of the wool from the shearing of the sheep you shall give to the Priest.*

<margin>Exodus 24</margin>
144. *The firstborn of your sons you shall redeem.*

Specifically by giving five shekels to the Priest.

<margin>Exodus 13</margin>
145. *The firstborn of a donkey you shall exchange for a sheep.*

That is, for its redemption you shall give a sheep.

<margin>in the same place</margin>
146. *But if you do not redeem it (specifically the donkey), you shall kill it.* <note>By breaking its neck.</note>

<margin>Leviticus 25</margin>
147. *In the seventh year there shall be a sabbath of rest.*

Namely, from the cultivation of the earth. <note>The *Shmita* or Sabbatical year.</note>

<margin>Exodus 23</margin>
148. *The fruits of the seventh year the poor of your people shall eat, and the beasts of the field.*

This refers to the produce which the ground brings forth of its own accord in that year.

<margin>Deuteronomy 15</margin>
149. *To whom anything is owed by a friend in the year of remission, he must release it.*

That is, he may not demand the debt, unless perhaps some agreements had intervened by which (according to the decree of Hillel) this mandate is set aside. <note>original: "Hilelis sancitum." This refers to the *Prosbol*, a legal instrument instituted by the sage Hillel the Elder to allow debts to remain enforceable past the Sabbatical year to ensure the poor could still receive loans.</note>

<margin>Leviticus 25</margin>
150. *You shall also number seven weeks of years.*

That is, seven times seven, up until the fiftieth year.

<margin>in the same place</margin>
151. *And you shall sanctify the fiftieth year, and you shall call it a remission.*

<margin>in the same place</margin>
152. *You shall sound the trumpet in the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month.*

Namely, of the fiftieth year, which is also called the Jubilee.

<margin>in the same place</margin>
153. *A man shall return to his possession, and every one shall return to his ancient possession.*

# THE PREFACE OF PAUL RICIUS,
## TO THE COLLECTION OF THE TALMUDIC EDITION.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'M' featuring floral and leaf patterns.</image-desc>
The late Divine Emperor Maximilian <note>Maximilian I (1459–1519), Holy Roman Emperor, who was a patron of Ricius.</note> once advised me to translate those ancient and obsolete volumes of the Mosaic tradition (which it has pleased them to call the <term>Talmud</term> <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishnah and the Gemara.</note>) from their Hebrew hiding places into Latin speech. This was so that their obscure and nearly inextricable doctrine could be more clearly and with less effort understood and judged by his sacred and provident Majesty, as well as by other seekers of sincere truth. This was truly an honorable and fruitful task, worthy of all obedience, though it is a work of immense labor (if I may say so). Due to the vast number of volumes, the long sequence of texts, and the thick fog of words and sentences, it would require many years to complete the work. Nevertheless, since it was not permitted for me to refuse the edict of the Imperial Majesty—who is to me like a unique divinity on earth—nor was it right to altogether neglect a duty that is turned toward the strength and use of orthodox piety, I decided to publish something regarding the Talmudic compendium, called the <term>Mishnah</term> <note>The first major written collection of the Jewish oral traditions; the core text of the Talmud.</note>, around which all Talmudic studies and their entire structure revolve. I have set out to "pluck the flowers" of their vast and wide commentary in some way. I have not done this by rendering word for word, lest the speech of our edition should stretch too long and concern itself with less profitable matters, but according to the requests of his Majesty, who desired to touch upon only the arguments and the inner beginnings of the Talmudic doctrine. I deemed it sufficient if I brought forth only a summary of the clauses and the main headings of the matters. This I have performed so far for the introduction of the <term>Egyptian Rabbi Moses</term> <note>Maimonides (1138–1204), also known as Rambam, a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and scholar who lived in Egypt.</note> and for the "Book of Senators" <note>original: "librum Senatorum," likely referring to the Talmudic tractate *Sanhedrin*, which deals with the high court and legal procedures.</note>, using certain "little flowers" gathered from the Talmudic commentary as a sort of preliminary, though in a somewhat reversed order (promising more important things hereafter, if it seems advisable and if the celestial powers permit). In these, as in other works published by me, I have thought it best to consult faithful interpretation and diligence rather than the allure of words and the sweetness of the ears. First, therefore, we shall here approach in a brief compendium those things which the Egyptian Rabbi Moses opened in a long context of speech as a prologue to the book of the Mishnah. Through this, the intention, name, author, parts, method of teaching, order, and finally the utility and end of the Talmudic doctrine may become known. We take our beginning from the method and order by which Moses himself, the master of all Israelites and wise men, taught the explanation of the Law.

---

# THE PROLOGUE OF THE EGYPTIAN RABBI MOSES, TO THE BOOK OF THE MISHNAH
## *MOSES’ METHOD AND ORDER OF TEACHING.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' depicting Moses teaching a group of seated men.</image-desc>
First, therefore, his brother Aaron <note>original: "Aheron"</note> entered the study-chamber of Moses with a desire to learn. Moses soon explained to him a section of the Law, along with all the little notes <note>glosses or oral explanations</note> belonging to it. Once these were received, Aaron immediately took his place at the right side of Moses. Then, his two sons, Eleazar and Ithamar, approached, to whom Moses delivered with precision everything he had first opened to his brother. Then one of them stepped to the left of Moses, and the other to the right of their father Aaron. When this was done, the seventy Elders entered immediately to hear the same things from Moses that Aaron and his twin sons had learned. Finally, in the last place, the entire teachable and studious multitude of the Israelites approached. To them, he himself recounted for a fourth time each individual point already explained three times by the mouth of Moses. Thus, Aaron heard all the instructions delivered by the living voice of Moses four times, his sons three times, the Elders twice, and the rest of the multitude once. When Moses then departed, Aaron himself took up and repeated those things he had received to all those standing by. When he, in turn, withdrew, both of Aaron's sons, Eleazar and Ithamar, delivered the same things anew to the Elders and the other listeners. When they departed, the seventy Elders interpreted everything once more to the multitude of listeners. The result was that each person who entered the study-tabernacle of Moses received the explanation of the Law through a fourfold repetition of the lesson.

<summary>Paulus Ricius introduces his Latin translation of the Mishnah, commissioned by Emperor Maximilian I, and begins with Maimonides' account of how the Oral Law was originally transmitted from Moses to the people of Israel through a system of fourfold repetition.</summary>

<header>CONCERNING TALMUDIC DOCTRINE.</header>

### WHAT MOSES TAUGHT.

Thereafter, the assembly of listeners indeed began to instruct one another, committing the "roots" <note>The fundamental principles or core rules of the commandments.</note> of the mandates to small scrolls, and revolving and weighing their meanings in both mind and speech, according to the dogmas received from Moses. For all things (as the Sages hand down) both the individual and the common institutions of the Law, as well as the commentaries, were delivered together to Moses on Mount Sinai. For example, the mandate of <term>Scenopegiæ</term> <note>original: "Scenopegiæ"; the Feast of Tabernacles or Sukkot, from the Greek for "tent-pitching."</note> prescribes in Leviticus: "You shall dwell in booths," it says, "for seven days." But as to who is bound by a mandate of this kind, and from what materials, in what form, of what size, and in what manner the booths ought to be constructed, the letter of the Law is entirely silent. However, Moses revealed these very things by word of mouth, teaching that a precept of this sort does not concern the female sex, nor those suffering from ill health, nor those undertaking a journey. Thus, it is certainly not permitted to construct the covering of the booths from stones, nor from wool-work, or silk, or any other household gear—not from pillows, mattresses, or that kind of bedding—but only from things growing from the earth. It is likewise only lawful to take food, drink, and sleep during those seven continuous days within the booths. Furthermore, their size must be no less than seven handbreadths in length, the same in width, and ten in height. Therefore, just as the mandate of the Feast of Tabernacles was delivered to Moses on Mount Sinai together with these appendages of its own, so must it be judged concerning each of the six hundred and thirteen commandments, along with all the accessories annexed to them: namely, that the listeners received the "roots" of the precept in writing, but learned the annexed details as they were explained by mouth.

### MOSES COMMITS THE LAW TO WRITING,
->*and meets his blessed final day.*<-

And when the fortieth year of the Legislation was turning, on the New Moon of the eleventh month <note>The month of Shevat.</note>, Moses called the entire people together as one. Announcing that the day of his death was near, he admonished them: if any teaching of the Law had fallen from anyone’s memory, or if anyone pondered some unexamined or difficult question, they should bring it forward. With a prompt and benevolent spirit, he wished to repeat and clarify those very things. Indeed, Moses himself performed this, according to his promises, until the seventh day of the twelfth month <note>The month of Adar.</note>, reviewing everything that had been forgotten and resolving all questions. And as his final day now flew closer, he took it upon himself to commit the Law delivered by God to writing, and he inscribed the volumes of the <term>Pentateuch</term> <note>The first five books of the Bible (Torah).</note> thirteen times upon parchments. From the first to the very last element of the Law, he delivered one of these to each of the twelve tribes to be preserved and followed in their works. The thirteenth, however, he granted to the tribe of the Levites. Then, on the seventh day of the twelfth month, at the midday hour, ascending Mount Horeb <note>Here referring to Mount Nebo, often associated with the Sinai/Horeb complex in this tradition.</note>, he withdrew himself to those above and completed his most blessed day. This passing, although to us mortals it seemed a change from life into death—robbing us of this very radiant light—nevertheless, in truth, no plague of disease had invaded him, nor did the dire corruption of death touch him; rather, he passed into a loftier goal of perennial glory and eternal joy.

### BY WHAT MEANS THE DOCTRINE OF MOSES
->*passed down to posterity.*<-

When Moses had closed his final day, he transferred the scepter of teaching and ruling to Joshua, the minister of Moses. Joshua delivered all things heard from the living oracle of Moses to the Elders; the Elders to the Prophets; the Prophets to the men of the Great Synagogue <note>A legendary assembly of 120 scribes, sages, and prophets from the start of the Second Temple period.</note>, the last of whom was Simeon the High Priest, who was called "the Just." He committed these same things to Antigonus of Sokho; and finally, by this sequence of teaching, one after another explained the interpretations of the Law down to Rabbi Judah, who, on account of the singular purity of his doctrine, life, and character, was called "the Holy Master" by the mouths of all. He [gathered] all the things transmitted to posterity by the voice of Moses, and all those things which, according to the times and places...

<header>->PAULUS RICIUS’S EPITOME,<-</header>

...and having added those things which the necessity of the persons required, he fused them into one volume, which he wished to be called the **Misna** <note>original: "misna"; the Mishnah, from a Hebrew root meaning "to repeat" or "to study," referring to the oral transmission of the law.</note> (which signifies a repeated reading).

### HE SOLVES A SILENT QUESTION, AND DECLARES WHAT 
### the contents of this book are.

Lest your thoughts wander in uncertainty, and you silently ask yourself: "If all things contained in the present Volume were delivered to Moses on Mount Sinai, whence, I pray, comes such great disagreement among the sages of the **Talmud** <note>A central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishnah and the Gemara.</note> and such a manifold and varied assertion from them?" Know, therefore, that whatever was delivered by the mouth of Moses was preserved by his successors without any distinction or dispute. However, regarding those things which Moses did not explicitly teach, there are some in which there is, was, and shall be no controversy among the assembly of the Israelites. Yet others differ in many ways and are subject to a variety of questions, in which some, leaning on different reasons, decree different things. Finally, to encompass the matter in a few words, all mandates or statutes founded in the Mosaic Law are divided into five very broad categories. 

The **first category** concerns all mandates explained by the mouth of Moses, which consist either of the literal sequence of the text or of some law of argumentation. Regarding this kind of mandate, there was never any contention within the synagogue of the Talmudists. 

The **second category** consists of all those mandates or decrees which are said to have been delivered to Moses on Mount Sinai. And these, although they consist of no explicit precept of the Law nor any argument therefrom, are nevertheless held as valid without any question. 

The **third category** is of those things which were not delivered by the mouth of Moses, but were explained by a certain law of syllogism <note>Logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two or more premises.</note>; therefore, this kind of sanction receives manifold distinctions of opinion. Nevertheless, those things which the more numerous part of the sages affirms, the successors embrace and observe. 

The **fourth category** is of the institutions which the Prophets and men outstanding in wisdom sanctioned at various courses of time—not because the Law so dictated, but so that they might be like a fence and a rampart for the Law, lest through easy transgression, the radical mandates of the Law might be rendered void. 

The **fifth category** is of the constitutions and customs of those things which seem to pertain less to an express mandate of the Law, but were approved by a synod of many Prophets or sages, or by long-standing custom, for the common welfare of the Israelites.

### HE ENUMERATES THE PRIMARY PARTS OF THE BOOK.

Therefore, all the things comprised within these five categories of constitutions and decrees, the present book, the **Misna**, has touched upon in a compendium. The author wished for it to be divided into six primary parts, and for these to be called **Sedarim**: that is, "Orders." 

1. The first is **Seder Zeraim** <note>original: "Seder Zeraim"; the Order of Seeds.</note>: that is, the Order of Seeds, which treats of things growing from the earth, of things sown and grafted promiscuously, of the release of the land and its uncircumcision <note>The "preputio" or "uncircumcision" of the land refers to *Orlah*, the prohibition against eating fruit from a tree during its first three years.</note>, of first fruits and tithes, and other crops to be distributed. 
2. The second part is called **Seder Zemanin** <note>original: "Seder Zemanin"; the Order of Times (usually called *Seder Moed*).</note>: that is, the Order of Times, which considers the seasons of the year, feast days, and the various conditions of their observance. 
3. The third is called **Seder Naschim** <note>original: "Seder Naschim"; the Order of Women.</note>: that is, the Order of Women, which examines the laws and statutes of marriage, the bill of divorce, and all those things which concern spouses. 
4. The fourth is named **Seder Nesikim** <note>original: "Seder Nesikim"; the Order of Damages.</note>: that is, the Order of Damages, which treats all things regarding lawsuits, exchanges, and the mutual commerce of men. 
5. The fifth is called **Seder Kedoschim** <note>original: "Seder Kedoschim"; the Order of Holy Things.</note>: that is, the Order of Holy Things, which explains the law and ritual of sacrifices and offerings. 
6. The sixth is called **Seder Teharos** <note>original: "Seder Teharos"; the Order of Purifications.</note>: that is, the Order of Expiations, which declares the norm and observance of pollutions and cleansings. 

Furthermore, he partitions each of these orders into **Massechtos**: that is, volumes or tractates; the volumes into chapters; and the chapters into lessons, as we shall explain in their proper places, life permitting.

### HE INDICATES THE PARTS OF THE ENTIRE TALMUDIC WORK, 
### and its intent.

But because the things contained in the present Volume are delivered in a very brief context of words and with an understanding that is far too obscure, so much so that the investigation of all later students was focused only toward the correct [understanding] of these...

<header>ON TALMUDIC DOCTRINE.</header>

...is occupied with understanding, whence among its various decrees a manifold and nearly inextricable contention has arisen. Therefore, it seemed best to **Rav Ashi** <note>original: "Rau aschi"; a 4th-5th century Babylonian sage credited with the primary redaction of the Babylonian Talmud.</note>, the latest of the Talmudic sages, to forge several commentaries into a compendium of the **Mishnah** <note>The first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions.</note>. He wished to call the sum of these the **Talmud** (which signifies "instruction" or "discipline"). Its entire intention is to reveal the latent meaning of the words of the Mishnah and to provide a clearer understanding of its clauses; it also strives either to reconcile dissenting opinions entirely or to prove one over the other. Finally, all the commentaries of the Talmudists consist of a fourfold method. 

The **first** is to explain individual points which the compendium of the Mishnah encompasses, and to examine whatever might be ambiguous or manifold among the commentators by recording the arguments upon which each relies. 

The **second** is that, whenever he finds a variety of opinions regarding the sequence of words, their gloss, some new statute, or an explanation compiled for the Mishnah itself, he brings forth a firm judgment and a ratified sentence in favor of one of the parties. 

The **third** is that by which they announce those things which later Talmudists learned by following from the present book, and they set forth the things decreed and added after the publication of this compendium. 

The **fourth** is that by which he inserts conversations or homilies in appropriate places. If these are heard according to their outward sound and common conception, they seem like certain playful things wandering far from the right path of reason. If, however, one applies his mind more perceptively to that type which lies hidden within and under the riddle, he will truly penetrate the sublime and recondite oracles of wisdom. These are delivered veiled in the covering of riddle and allegory, lest dreamers and the ignoble rabble defile the sacraments of truth, and the unclean pollute the clean. This is also done so that those who are eager for pure truth and strong in intellect may more vigorously gird their strengths for the contemplation of secret things, and more accurately lift their minds to the heavenly ones and the lights of eternal wisdom. 

Thus far, therefore, we have encompassed in a paraphrastic and concise oration those things which **Rabbi Moses the Egyptian** <note>Maimonides (1138–1204), the famous Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note> set forth in a more copious discourse in his Preface to this book. Now, however, we proceed to explain, by divine will, certain principal and fruitful matters gathered from the commentary on the **Book of the Senators** <note>The tractate Sanhedrin, which deals with the high court and legal procedures.</note>.

### EXCERPTS WORTHY OF KNOWLEDGE FROM THE GLOSS OF THE CODE OF THE SENATORS, CALLED *SANHEDRIN*, FROM THE CHAPTER *HELEK*.

It is asked: why does he who denies the future resurrection of the dead have no part in the world to come? It is answered, by the opinion of **Rav Jonathan**, that in all things (as is gathered from the fourth book of Kings) God matches measure for measure.

->RICIUS.<-

The clear and untainted authority of the Gospel teaches this, saying: "With what measure you mete, it shall be measured to you again" <note>Matthew 7:2.</note>. Indeed, in the entire order of things, one may plainly perceive this: that as much perfection and action is bestowed upon each thing as there was prior disposition in the receiver. Faith in the resurrection disposes and renders the believer capable; the denial of it constitutes the unbeliever as unfit and incapable of the resurrection itself.

->TALMUD.<-

He who offers the firstfruits to an ignorant Priest shall be accounted as if he had offered them to a ravenous lion. **Cleopatra** <note>A legendary figure in the Talmud, often depicted in dialogue with Rabbi Meir regarding life after death.</note> questioned **Rabbi Meir**: "When they rise," she said, "will they rise naked or clothed?" He responded: "A grain of wheat declares this very thing: for it is buried naked in the earth, and it rises up clothed in many ways. Therefore, those who are buried in the tomb clothed shall undoubtedly rise clothed."

->RICIUS.<-

The Apostle concurs with this in the first letter to the Corinthians, for he says: "Someone will say, how do the dead rise, and with what sort of body will they come? You fool..."

<meta>catchword: Insipiens (You fool)</meta>

<header>PAUL RICCIUS’ EPITOME,</header>

<note>The page opens with a quote from the Apostle Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:36–37, used here to bridge Christian and Jewish thought on the resurrection.</note> **You fool, what you sow is not brought to life unless it first dies; and what you sow, you do not sow the body that is to be, but a bare grain.**

->TALMUD.<-

When Caesar asked **Rabbi Gamaliel** <note>Gamaliel II, a leading sage of the late 1st century CE.</note> by what means the deceased, once reduced to dust, might rise again, the daughter of the same Gamaliel immediately stepped forward. She entreated her father to allow her to answer Caesar’s question. With his consent, she said to Caesar: "If there are two potters, one of whom fashions from water and the other from mud, which of these craftsmen do you consider superior to the other?" Caesar replied: "I judge him to be the more excellent creator who fashions from water." Then she said: "If He forms from water, can He not more easily fashion from the slime and mud of the earth?"

->RICCIUS.<-

By "water," she signifies the prolific seed of man, which resembles a watery liquid. It is as if the daughter implied that if the power of nature itself (under the guidance of the supreme Creator of all things) forms a human being from a watery seed, it will certainly more easily cause the same to rise from the slime of the earth.

->TALMUD.<-

A certain heretic asked **Rabbi Ami** <note>A 3rd-century scholar in the Land of Israel.</note> whether those who "sleep" <note>A common euphemism for the dead.</note> could truly rise. "For they are dust," he said, "and what power of reviving can be within dust?" Rabbi Ami responded: "The example of the mouse (if you take notice) will give you understanding. For now you see in the field a mouse, one part of which is earth and the other is flesh, which immediately crawls at tomorrow's light, and its entire mass has already become flesh." <note>This refers to a common ancient belief in "spontaneous generation," specifically that certain mice were formed from the earth after rain.</note> The Patriarch **Abraham** handed over "unclean names" (that is, the names of unclean spirits) to the sons of his concubines, as it is written: *And to the sons of the concubines, Abraham bestowed gifts.*

->RICCIUS.<-

For it is written: *And Abraham gave all that he possessed to Isaac himself.* By this, he implies the sacred names of God, the manner of worshipping God, and the super-celestial lights of the world. But to the sons of the concubines, he bestowed "gifts" of unclean spirits, from which the worship of idols was sown among the nations and throughout the whole world. But you might say (and not without cause) that since no kind of sin is so deadly, leading to eternal destruction, as the worship of idols, it seems a wicked thing to believe that Abraham—a man of the highest wisdom and holiness, who first after the disaster of the waters <note>The Great Flood.</note> instituted the worship of the one Creator (according to that passage in Genesis: *Abraham truly planted a grove in Beersheba, and there he called upon the name of the eternal God*)—would have instructed his offspring and posterity in the execrable adoration of idols and demons. 

However, anyone who has touched the inner chambers of sacred eloquence will very easily understand that the sons of the concubines were not assigned to the supreme Creator God, but were subject to foreign powers <note>original: "numinibus"; divine or semi-divine wills.</note>. Truly, the legitimate progeny and seed of **Isaac** is attributed to the one immortal King of all ages, God, and not to foreign gods, according to that passage in Deuteronomy: *And they served foreign gods, and adored those whom they did not know, and to whom they had not been assigned.* On these matters, I have written more extensively elsewhere.

->TALMUD.<-

**Antoninus** <note>A Roman figure, often identified in Jewish tradition with Marcus Aurelius, who frequently dialogues with "Rabbi" (Judah the Prince).</note>, while conversing on various matters with **Rabbi**, brought forward this question concerning judgment. "It seems," he said, "that both parts of the human frame—namely the soul and the body—could rightfully absolve themselves from the rigor of judgment. For the body casts all blame for the sin upon the soul, because as soon as the soul departs, the body lies sluggish, devoid of sense and life. The soul, on the other hand, rebukes the body itself, contending that every fuel for sin proceeds from it, because once the soul is loosed from the bond of the body, it soon flies upward to the heavens and proceeds to the dwellers above." Thus spoke Antoninus. To whom Rabbi said: "I will give you a fitting parable..."
