<meta>This page continues the discussion of the resurrection of the dead from the Talmudic tractate Sanhedrin. It moves from simple analogies of creation to a famous parable about the partnership of body and soul, followed by a philosophical dialogue between "Antoninus" and "Rabbi" concerning the movement of the sun.</meta>

# ON TALMUDIC DOCTRINE. 263

so that the certainty of the proposed question might become more clearly known. Imagine a householder who entrusted a garden to the care of two guards, one of whom lacked the ability to walk, and the other the power of sight. Now, the lame man <note>Latin: *loripes*, literally "strap-footed" or "club-footed."</note>, who had healthy vision, saw certain precious fruits hanging from a tree. Allured by their delightful appearance and sweet fragrance, he said: "Alas, my companion, what beautiful and pleasant fruits I see hanging here on the tree! I would pluck them if I had your power of walking." To which the blind man replied: "And I likewise would not hesitate to pluck those fruits if I had your power of seeing." Therefore, after their opinions had been tossed back and forth for a long time on how to satisfy their desire, the lame man finally said: "I see no better plan than this: that I, who have healthy vision, should ride upon your shoulders, since you are strong in your gait and feet. Thus, by bringing aid to one another, we may together achieve the wish of us both."

When these two had thus conspired and satisfied their lust by the very act of seizing the fruits, the householder entered the garden. Noticing that the early fruits which had been hanging from the tree were plucked, he indignantly demanded of the guards who had stolen such things. When each of them pleaded ignorance and claimed they were innocent—the lame man because he had no power to walk, and the other because he was deprived of his eyes—the perceptive and considerate householder, already aware of the deed, refuted them both. He argued that although neither of them could have been the doer of the crime separately, they were nonetheless joined together in the offense as one. Therefore, making one sit upon the shoulders of the other, he compelled them to undergo punishment together, just as they had committed the crime together. In this same way, the Craftsman of the world, the just judge and arbiter, will ultimately join the soul to the body, so that those who transgressed by mutual aid may be punished together and receive their penalty.

Antoninus <note>In the Talmud, "Antoninus" is a Roman emperor (often identified as Marcus Aurelius) who frequently engages in philosophical debates with Rabbi Judah the Prince.</note> asked again: "Why does the Sun rise in the east and proceed to the west?" To which the Rabbi replied: "The same question would certainly remain if the Sun turned from the west toward the east." But Antoninus said: "My primary question is this: Why does the Sun descend into the west?" The Rabbi responded: "It seeks the west for this reason: to speak its greeting and peace to its Creator and to adore Him, as it is written: *And the host of heaven worships you.*" <note>original: "Et te cœli militia adorat." A quote from Nehemiah 9:6.</note> To this, Antoninus said: "Why, I ask, is it not enough for the Sun to reach the middle of the sky, and then, having given its greeting, depart?" The Rabbi responded: "This is done in this way for the sake of workers and those traveling on the road."

->RICCIUS.<-

Regarding the understanding of this saying, **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Referring to Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo itzhaki, 1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator on the Talmud.</note> says: "If the Sun were to depart suddenly from the middle of the sky, sudden darkness and the gloom of night would overtake the workers and those traveling on the road."

Rabbi Solomon here, in his usual manner, follows not the spirit but the shadow of the letter. For no one is so crude or so lacking in intelligence as to say that the Arch-Talmudist gave such a tasteless and silly answer to Antoninus—a man who was otherwise wise, most skillful in nature, and an investigator of sublime things. Rather, that wise Talmudist (in the manner of the Prophets and the Gospels) displays the very sacraments of truth under a parabolic veil. On the surface, he shows empty little fables and, as it were, the ravings of old women; but in the secret depths, he opens up the high and hidden oracles of truth. This can be gathered from the present model of the Rabbi's answer to Antoninus, and from there one may take an argument for other enigmas of the Talmudists.

Therefore, Antoninus’s first question concerns the motion of the heavens: why it is circular and not straight, like the element of fire which, seeking the heights, does not then turn itself back downward. This is what Antoninus indicates when he says: "My primary question is: why does the Sun descend into the west?" (Add here: "and not remain in the middle of the sky.") The second question is why the motion is circular and not simply moving forward, like the movement of perishable living creatures; this is what Antoninus hints at by saying: "Why does it not depart as soon as its greeting is given?" To these questions, the Rabbi assigns a two-fold cause for why the heavens are carried in a circle—a cause which the unanimous school of the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, who believed the heavens moved in perfect circles.</note> also affirms. The first cause is so that the heavens may be likened to the Creator, who by His immense power encompasses and surrounds the entire universe at once. This the heavens imitate and achieve through their constant rotation...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the dialogue between "Rabbi" (Judah the Prince) and the Roman Emperor "Antoninus," moving from astronomical allegories to the biological and spiritual nature of the soul and the mechanics of the resurrection.</meta>

# THE EPITOME OF PAULUS RICIUS, 264
<note>Paulus Ricius (c. 1470–1541) was a Jewish convert to Christianity, a physician, and a Kabbalist who translated many Jewish texts for a Christian audience.</note>

...resists. And indeed, the Rabbi calls this imitation "giving peace" and "adoring," because likeness and imitation alone provide peace, union, and connection to all things. There is, however, another reason for this circulation: so that all the movable things of this falling world (which he calls "workers" because they are driven by constant operation and motion) and all things created and perishable (which he calls "travelers" because they proceed on a perpetual path from birth to decay without any pause) might endure. I say these perishable things persist through the constant movement of the Sun and other stars in the never-failing cycle of generation. For no constant motion could be given according to the order of nature except that which is carried in a circle. Wisely, therefore, the Rabbi answers that for the sake of "giving peace" or "adoring," and on account of the "workers" and "travelers," the Sun revolves in a perpetual circuit.

### THE TALMUD.

Again, the Rabbi is asked by Antoninus: "Is the human soul infused at the moment of conception, or at the hour of formation, which occurs about forty days after the hour of conception?" The Rabbi answers: "At the hour of formation." To which Antoninus says: "That is a strange and incredible thing to say! For we see that meat, if not sprinkled with salt, can hardly be kept for three days without rotting (implying that the mass of blood and the embryo could not be preserved for a space of forty days within the closed womb without the spirit and soul acting in the place of salt)." Therefore, the Rabbi yielded to Antoninus and admitted that the soul is infused at the very moment of conception; and he was not ashamed to confess that he had learned the true understanding of this question from Antoninus.

Furthermore, Antoninus asks: "Does the <term>kindling of desire</term><note>Latin: *fomes concupiscentiæ*; in Jewish thought, this refers to the *Yetzer Hara* or the inclination toward evil/physicality.</note> creep into a human at the hour of formation, or rather at the hour of birth?" The Rabbi answers: "It creeps in at the hour of formation." But the emperor says: "If the matter were as you think, the fetus would immediately struggle and do violence to the mother's womb, and once the formation was complete, it would break out of the uterus." The Rabbi yielded again, asserting that he had penetrated the correct understanding of this examination through Antoninus's reasoning. 

Those who rise <note>referring to the Resurrection of the Dead</note> will rise with their ailments, but they will be healed immediately and regain good health. Samuel says: "The age of the Messiah (which they call the world to come) differs in nothing from the present age, except that there will then be no imperial power." Rabbi Eleazar taught: "A man who excels in knowledge is to be compared to one who has seen the house of the Sanctuary <note>the Temple in Jerusalem</note> standing before him." (Ricius adds: The reason is that the Spirit of God dwells in the wise man as if in the house of a sanctuary.) The Talmud continues: Such a man will also excel in outward wealth. But he who lacks knowledge will wander as an exile through the world, and no consideration of piety should be shown to him. He who provides food to such a person will bring back nothing but hardships; however, he who does not bring help to a student of wisdom will perpetually lack success.

He who, having taken a meal, leaves no morsel on the table, will see no outcome of prosperity. He who is deceitful in speech shall be considered an idolater. He who gazes upon his own private parts, the strength of his "bow" or "sinew" <note>a euphemism for virility</note> shall be cast down. Always be mild, and you will always be safe. These are the words of Rabbi Eleazar. 

It is written, as Rabbi Josiah says: "The Grave (or Hell) and the opening of the womb [are alike]" <note>referring to Proverbs 30:16</note>; because just as the womb takes in and then gives back what was taken in, so also the grave hides the dead within itself and restores them to life. Indeed, this restoration to life will happen with a great sounding of the trumpet, just as the birth from the womb demonstrates; for that which the womb took in secretly (at conception), it brings forth with a great cry during labor. Therefore, if the grave received them with wailing and the sound of lamentation, how could it not bring them forth again with the resonance of trumpets? 

The House of Elijah taught: "The righteous who rise shall not thereafter be reduced to dust." If you ask, "What then shall the righteous who rise do during the thousand years in which the world shall be renewed?" The answer is: "The Holy One, blessed is He, will add wings to the righteous like those of eagles during that interval of time, with which they shall meanwhile be carried over the face of the waters."

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Jewish tradition as presented by Paulus Ricius. # ON TALMUDIC DOCTRINE.

## RICIUS.

In this passage, the "House of Elijah" <note>A reference to the *Tanna Devei Eliyahu*, a midrashic work often cited in the Talmud regarding the age of the world.</note> seems to allude enigmatically to that verse from the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>: *And they reigned with Christ a thousand years; the rest of the dead did not live again until the thousand years were finished.* <note>original: "Et regnauerunt cum Christo mille annos: cæteri mortuorum non uixerunt donec consumentur mille anni." (Revelation 20:4-5)</note> And a little later: *And I saw,* he says, *a new heaven and a new earth.* <note>Revelation 21:1</note> However, Saint Aurelius Augustine <note>Bishop of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational Christian theologian.</note> judged this statement in the Apocalypse to hint at a spiritual rather than a physical resurrection—an interpretation which perhaps the Talmudic author himself wished to suggest here.

## RICIUS S.

Since the stubbornness of the modern Israelites <note>Ricius, as a convert, often critiques his contemporaries while praising the "ancient" sages.</note> originates from their false and erroneous understanding of the Messiah, and since in no other place in the Talmudic codex is the discourse on the Messiah so varied, rich, and consistent with orthodox truth as in this present chapter, *Helek* <note>The 11th chapter of Tractate Sanhedrin, famous for its discussions on the afterlife and the Messianic age.</note>: I have therefore decided to linger here for a short while to explain several Talmudic themes concerning the Messiah. By these, you will be able to clearly judge the folly of the moderns and their affected ignorance (which is the root of all evils). For many of the ancient Talmudists, although they were zealous for the Law, nevertheless diligently embraced and cherished the orthodox faith of Christ, as we gather from the Acts of the Apostles.

## THE TALMUD.

It is written concerning the Messiah in the Book of the Senators <note>The Sanhedrin, the supreme council and court of ancient Israel.</note>, in the chapter *Helek*: *And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom, and he shall fill him with the spirit of the fear of the Lord.* <note>Isaiah 11:2–3</note> (In Hebrew this is read as *va-hericho*, which sounds like both "a millstone" and "a scent.") <note>The word וַהֲרִיחוֹ (*v’haricho*) literally means "his smelling/delight." Ricius is noting a phonetic similarity to terms for grinding or burdens.</note> From this, Rabbi Alexander wished it to be understood that God burdened the Messiah with the weight of the commandments and a multitude of afflictions, as if by the weight of a millstone. Rava, however, judged it was written so that it might be understood that the Messiah would perceive the certainty of things as if by a sense of smell. Thus it is immediately added: *He shall not judge by the sight of his eyes, nor reprove by the hearing of his ears.* <note>Isaiah 11:3</note> For this reason, in times past, when Bar-Koziba held the kingdom for two and a half years and boasted that he was the Messiah: the sages gathered together and entered into counsel to scrutinize whether Bar-Koziba was the true Messiah or a false one. When they understood (according to the oracles of the Prophets) that the Messiah would grasp the knowledge of truth as if by smell, and they recognized that this was not at all true of Bar-Koziba, they judged him a false Messiah and guilty of death. <note>Bar-Koziba (Bar Kochba) led the Jewish revolt against Rome (132–136 AD). His name was changed from "Son of a Star" (Kochba) to "Son of a Lie" (Koziba) after the revolt failed.</note>

## RICIUS S.

The Talmudic author here openly proclaims the infused fullness of wisdom and the passion of the Messiah. Rava demonstrates this infused wisdom by asserting that the Messiah will perceive the certainty of things not by hearing or sight, but by smell. This is because he does not learn through human teaching (which is learned by hearing) nor through experience (which is produced by sight), but by smell alone, which is carried out by a certain thin and hidden spirit. Rabbi Alexander explains the Passion <note>The suffering of the Messiah.</note>, as is clearly evident to anyone looking at his statement. Bar-Koziba is that leader of the Jews whom Eusebius calls "Bar-Kochba" in the fourth book of his *Ecclesiastical History*.

## THE TALMUD.

Rav Menachem asked the Rabbi himself: had he heard when the "Son of the Fall" was coming? To which the Rabbi replied, "Whom, I ask, do you call the 'Son of the Fall'?" He responded, "The Messiah." But the Rabbi said, "Good heavens! You call the Messiah the 'Son of the Fall'?" Menachem replied, "I do indeed, because it is written: *In that day I will raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen.*" <note>Amos 9:11. The Hebrew term *Bar Nafli* (Son of the Fallen) is a Messianic title based on this verse.</note> Finally, answering the questions, the Rabbi said: "In the age in which the Son of David comes, there are few students of wisdom; the strength and appearance of men are reduced to wasting and dryness by groaning and sorrow; many kinds of distress and dire events occur; and before one has passed, another soon rushes in."

->RICIUS.<-

Pay attention for a clearer understanding of the things already said and those yet to be said. According to the orthodox faith, a twofold coming of the Messiah or Christ is believed. The first, which has already passed, was for the purpose of redemption. The second, which is to come at the end of the age, is for judgment. In this second advent, we admit the future salvation of the Jews (as the Apostle Paul taught) <note>A reference to Romans 11:26, "And so all Israel will be saved."</note>. Therefore, if you consider all the themes here to be interpreted regarding the Messiah’s coming, you will clearly understand that almost all of them testify that either the advent of Christ has passed, or it will occur at the consummation of the age. Therefore, the present saying may be heard as referring to either of these comings, because a lack of wisdom, tribulation, and sad turns of events occurred during the first advent and will occur in the last, just as the following sayings of the Talmudists declare. Moreover, it seems fitting that the Talmudic author calls the Messiah the "son of the fall" <note>original: "filium casus". This likely refers to the "fallen hut of David" from Amos 9:11, which Ricius interprets as a reference to Christ’s suffering</note>, by which he might signify the passion and resurrection of Christ, just as Truth itself [Christ] brought forth from his own mouth: *Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.* <note>John 2:19</note>

->TALMUD.<-

In the week (as the masters teach) of the coming of the son of David, in its first year that which is written is fulfilled: *I will rain upon one city, and upon another I will not rain.* <note>Amos 4:7</note> In the second, the arrows of famine are sent forth. In the third, a horrendous famine attacks, and death rushes upon men, women, and little children, and even upon the righteous and men famous for their deeds; the Law <note>The Torah.</note> is blackened and given over to oblivion. The fourth year turns between abundance and scarcity. In the fifth, there is rich abundance and satiety, and all kinds of joy, and the Law is restored to those who study it. In the sixth, there are shoutings <note>original: "uociferationes"; referring to rumors of the Messiah's coming.</note>. In the seventh, wars; at the conclusion of which comes the son of David. But when Rabbi Joseph asked, since many such weeks have already passed, why has the son of David not yet come? To this Abaye responds, saying: Were there shoutings in the sixth, and wars in the seventh? Was there such a succession of these things exactly as described? *With which your enemies have reproached, O Lord, with which they have reproached the footsteps of your Christ.* <note>Psalm 89:51. Ricius uses "Christi" where the Hebrew text of the Psalm says "Messiah" or "Anointed One."</note>

->RICIUS.<-

This saying about the Messiah seems to pertain to the second advent at the end of the age, which Gospel truth itself plainly taught: *You shall hear,* it says, *of battles and rumors* <note>original: "opiniones", here meaning rumors or reports</note> (that is, the shoutings of battles). Note one thing further worthy of attention: where it is added at the end of this saying, *with which your enemies have reproached, O God*, Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> confesses, forced by the truth, that it is clear to him why such a concluding phrase of the Psalmist was added, even though the Talmudist explains nothing for its understanding. However, it must be firmly believed that some followers of Christ, from the ancient assembly of the Talmudists, added this clause, by which they might designate the Jews' reproach and contempt for Christ, and signify that the first advent has already passed.

->TALMUD.<-

The assembly of Rabbi Judah judged the age in which the son of David comes: the house of the council is turned into a brothel, Galilee is devastated, and the border of Gyblin <note>likely Gebal or Gaulanitis</note>; the inhabitants become fugitives, wandering from city to city, and there is no one who takes pity on them; the wisdom of the scribes is held in contempt, and those who fear God and abhor sins are given over to vilification; the whole race of men becomes impudent, with the impudence of a dog, and finally no truth is cherished in word or deed, as it is written: *Truth is forgotten, and he who departs from evil is made a prey.* <note>Isaiah 59:15</note>

->RICIUS.<-

Because mention is made here of the house of council, Galilee, Gyblin, the inhabitants of the border, and the sages of the Jews: Therefore it seems to hint at the first advent of the Messiah, because the house of council, Galilee, Gyblin, the inhabitants of the border

Similarly, there are currently neither wise men nor scribes among the Jews, nor will there be any in the future, except perhaps for a brief course of time at the final advent of Christ, which, as we mentioned above, will provide an occasion of salvation for the Jews.

### TALMUD.

"The age," says **Rabbi Nehorai**, "in which the son of David comes, the young will treat the elders with contempt, and the elders will stand in respect before the young; a daughter rises against her mother, a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law, and a son is not restrained by shame in the presence of his parent; finally, the race of men becomes as impudent as a dog." "The age," says **Rabbi Nehemiah**, "in which the son of David comes, the audacity of men will be great, the high price of provisions will give birth to snares and deceit; the vineyards will produce fruit, yet wine will be at a high price, and the entire kingdom will be converted to heresy <note>original: "hæresim". In the Talmudic context, this refers to 'Minut', often interpreted by medieval Christians as a reference to their own faith or a general collapse of religious authority.</note>, nor will any correction from the elders be of use." The masters handed down a tradition saying, as it is written: *He will see that the hand is weakened* <note>Deuteronomy 32:36</note>, which is to say, that the hand of traitors will grow strong; or in another sense, that men will fail in the study of wisdom; or in another sense, until money has vanished from the purse; or in another sense, until no hope of redemption remains any longer. When **Rabbi Zeira** found the masters discussing the coming of the son of David, he implored them not to draw out his coming for too long, because there are three things that appear suddenly: the Messiah, a found object, and a **lizard** <note>original: "lacertus". The Talmudic source (Sanhedrin 97a) usually lists a "scorpion" (*akrab*); Ricius or his source text uses the Latin for lizard or arm.</note>.

---

### RICIUS.

The orthodox truth also affirms this: *That day,* he says, *will come upon you suddenly.* <note>Luke 21:34</note> And elsewhere: *Lest when he comes suddenly, he finds you sleeping.* <note>Mark 13:36</note> Therefore, if you compare these things with the Gospel doctrine, you will find them all in harmony, and you will weigh them as things to come at the consummation of the age and the second advent of Christ.

---

### TALMUD.

<margin>1,000 years make a single Lord’s Day.</margin>
"The world lasts for six thousand years," says **Rav Kattina**, "and for a thousand years—the seven thousandth—there will be desolation, because it is written: *And God alone shall be exalted in that day* <note>Isaiah 2:11</note> (for a 'day,' a thousand years are understood, the sum of which makes one Day of the Lord)." **Abaye**, however, believed the future desolation of the world would last for two thousand years, because it is written: *He will revive us after two days, and on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live.* <note>Hosea 6:2</note> The tradition of the wise supports the word of Rav Kattina, asserting that every seven years (according to Moses) one seventh year is a remission; and thus seven thousand years remit the seven-thousandth, because it is written: *And God alone shall be exalted in that day.* And it is written: *A psalm of a song for the Sabbath day*—that is, the day which is entirely a Sabbath; and it is written: *For a thousand years in your sight are like yesterday.* <note>Psalm 90:4</note>

---

### RICIUS.

**Augustine** discussed this <term>Sabbatism</term> <note>The idea of a thousand-year "Sabbath" or rest at the end of the world’s 6,000-year history.</note> and the six days of the world’s revolution in the second book of *The City of God*; he does not think this opinion should be rejected as alien, but he judges the position of those who promise carnal pleasures and the allurements of the senses in the seventh millennium to be profane and ridiculous. For Augustine says in the aforementioned place: "The opinion that once six thousand years (as if six days) are completed, a seventh 'Sabbath' follows in the last thousand years, would be tolerable in some way if it were believed that some spiritual delights would be present for the saints in that Sabbath through the presence of the Lord. For we also once held this opinion; but when they say those who have then risen will spend their time in immoderate carnal feasts, in which there is so much food and drink that they not only keep no modesty but also exceed the measure of belief itself, such things can in no way be believed except by carnal men." Thus says Augustine. By these words he alludes to that Talmudic enigma concerning the **Leviathan** and the **Great Wild Ox** <note>Behemoth</note>, which are to be prepared for the righteous to feast upon together in the end times; but those who [understand the spiritual sense] of the words...

# PAUL RICIUS’S EPITOME

...weighs [these things] with discernment, he will understand that the Talmudist in these matters intends an allegory (as we mentioned above) and not a literal understanding, just as Truth itself <note>A common title for Christ in Renaissance theology.</note> speaks of spiritual delights through the mouth of Christ using the metaphors of feasts, banquets, and weddings. "Let us feast," says the Apostle, "not with leaven" <note>1 Corinthians 5:8</note>; so also it is written in the Apocalypse: "If anyone hears my voice, I will enter to him, and sup with him, and he with me" <note>Revelation 3:20</note>. And that saying of John: "I have food to eat which you do not know" <note>John 4:32</note>. Therefore, do not believe it foreign that the ancient doctrine of the Talmudists handed down the spiritual sacraments of things presented under various veils of allegory and type.

## TALMUD

"For six thousand years," says the school of Elijah <note>original: "conuentus Eliahu". This refers to a famous tradition in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 97a) attributed to the School of the prophet Elijah.</note>, "the world shall persist: of which two thousand years are void, two thousand years are the Law, and two thousand years are the Messiah; but because of the multitude of our sins, that which we see to be lacking is missing."

## RICIUS

This Talmudist suggests two solid foundations of Gospel truth. First, that the observance of the Law has now ceased. Second, that the coming of the Messiah has already passed. He explains the first openly when he announces that the Law was to be kept for only two thousand years, the end of which already passed, according to the Talmudists' own calculation, about one thousand three hundred and thirty years ago. And although from the incarnation of the Word to this very day, one thousand five hundred and thirty-seven years have passed <note>This provides a specific date for Ricius's writing: 1537 AD.</note>, the observance of the Law was not yet entirely cast out, but was permitted in the beginnings of the Church until the times of Constantine the Great; this seems to agree plainly with the Talmudists' calculation concerning the abrogation of the Law. 

The Talmudist also proves the second foundation of truth by asserting that the times of the Messiah would be two thousand years, taking their beginning from the time when the observance of the Law ceased—namely, at the end of the fourth and the beginning of the fifth millennium—wherefore the sum of the years of the Messiah and the abrogation of the Law will be the same. But because the fullness of the nations and of faith was not reached until the observance of the Law was entirely emptied out, therefore those years in which the Mosaic Law had not yet entirely ceased are not counted in the times of the Messiah. They therefore calculate the true times of the Messiah from Constantine to this very day, namely, about one thousand three hundred and thirty years. With this agrees that passage of the Apocalypse, that God feeds the woman (that is, the Church of the saints) for one thousand two hundred and sixty days <note>Revelation 12:6. Ricius is interpreting these "days" as years in a prophetic timeline.</note>. 

However, regarding what is added in the text—*And because of the multitude of our sins, that which we see to be lacking is missing*—this was not the saying of that same school of Elijah. Rather, the compiler or some younger Talmudist—lest he be forced to admit the coming of the Messiah had passed—undoubtedly added this clause erroneously. 

Furthermore, where he announces two thousand years as "void" <note>original: "inane". In Hebrew, this corresponds to "Tohu" or chaos.</note>, he does not mean that for two thousand years there was a total lack and vastness of created things; otherwise the Talmudist would refute himself with an evident contradiction. For saying the world would last six thousand years, and then asserting two thousand of those same six thousand were a wasteland, is the same as if he had said the world would last six thousand years and yet also only four thousand years. Rather, he calls the world "void" for two thousand years because the human race was untaught and unformed around the world's beginnings, without the Law, the cultivation of morals, or any political governance. It was as if the whole race of mortals was frustrated and empty, according to that Mosaic saying: *God regretted that he had made man on the earth* <note>Genesis 6:6</note>. For we call that "void" which does not attain its proper end and its prefixed goal of perfection.

## TALMUD

The world, as the pious **Rav Yehuda** learned from Elijah, is to remain for no less than eighty-five jubilees <note>A jubilee is a 50-year cycle; 85 jubilees equals 4,250 years.</note>, and in the final jubilee the son of David shall come. **Rav Hanan** related to **Rav Joseph** that he had found a man...

### ON TALMUDIC DOCTRINE

[He told of] a man carrying a volume written in the Assyrian character <note>original: "Assyrio charactere"; this refers to the standard square Hebrew script used in sacred scrolls.</note> and the holy tongue, who was asked where that volume had come to him. He replied: while he was serving as a mercenary soldier in a Roman cohort, he found it in the Roman treasuries. In that volume it was written: from the creation of the world, in the two hundred and ninety-first year beyond the fourth millennium <note>The year 4291 of the Hebrew calendar, roughly 531 AD.</note>, the world will fail; there will be partly the battles of dragons and partly the wars of Gog and Magog <note>Biblical figures representing the enemies of God’s people in the end times.</note>; and the remainder shall truly be the days of the Messiah. Nor will the Creator of the world himself renew the age until seven thousand years have passed. But Rav Aha <note>A Jewish scholar of the late 3rd century.</note> contended that this was said to happen after five thousand years had passed.

->RICIUS.<-

A Jubilee contains a space of fifty years. John commemorates the battles of dragons and the wars of Gog and Magog in many places in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>. However, while Elijah affirms that the world shall remain for eighty-five Jubilees, he does not count the years of the beginning, which they call "void and empty" (as mentioned just before) because of the great crimes of mortals; and thus he seems to differ very little from the previous statement. By a similar law, when the Talmudist says here: "the world shall fail," the sense is that the race of men will decline into evil. So too Rav Aha himself presumes the world is to be renewed after five thousand years, not counting the two thousand prior years. For the renewal of the world, according to Rav Katina, occurs after seven thousand years; from which, if you subtract the two thousand years in which the void lasted, five thousand will remain.

->TALMUD.<-

This clause, says Rabbi Jonathan, penetrates and descends even to the abyss: "For the vision is yet for a certain time, it will bring forth to the end and will not lie; if it makes a delay, wait for him: because coming he will come, and he will not be late" <note>Habakkuk 2:3.</note>. For these sayings are not to be understood in the way the Teachers interpret that phrase of Daniel: "until a time, and times, and half a time" <note>Daniel 12:7.</note>. A "time," says Rabbi Solomon <note>Known as Rashi (1040–1105), the most famous Jewish commentator of the Middle Ages.</note>, designates the four hundred years of the Egyptian captivity; "times" truly shows a doubling of the Egyptian captivity, namely a period of eight hundred years. "Half a time" indicates two hundred years, which together constitute a sum of one thousand four hundred years. Thus he speaks. Nor is the clause to be understood in the way Rabbi Samlai explained that passage of the Psalms: "You have fed them with the bread of tears, and given them tears to drink in a third measure" <note>Psalm 80:5.</note>; or the measure (the sense is, says Rabbi Solomon) of the duration of the third captivity is triple the time of the two preceding captivities. For the Egyptian captivity was four hundred years, and the Babylonian was seventy; when these are brought together into one and repeated three times, the sum of one thousand four hundred and ten years results. Thus says Rabbi Solomon. Nor are the words of the clause to be understood in the way Rabbi Akiva <note>One of the most influential Jewish sages of the 2nd century AD.</note> took that passage of Haggai: "Yet one little while, and I will move the heaven and the earth" <note>Haggai 2:6.</note>.

->RICIUS.<-

Rabbi Akiva, the Chief Pharisee, a man of great testimony and wisdom, thought a certain man named Bar Kokhba <note>original: "Barchusiuam"; Simon bar Kokhba, leader of the Jewish revolt against Rome (132–136 AD). His name means "Son of a Star."</note>—who took up the royal scepter for himself while Hadrian was Emperor, shortly after the time of Christ our Savior—to be the Messiah. He believed this oracle of Haggai was a prophecy about the same Bar Kokhba, who was nevertheless overthrown in the third year of his reign in a savage and miserable slaughter. And thus Rabbi Akiva himself, however much he excelled in wisdom and purity of life, was led by that same spirit of error to worship the false messiah Bar Kokhba as the true Savior, just as he had judged the true Messiah, Jesus of Nazareth, to be a false prophet.

# THE EPITOME OF PAULUS RICIUS,

### TALMUD

Rav <note>original: "Rau"; a title for a Babylonian rabbinic teacher.</note> says that all the set times for the coming of the Messiah have already passed, and the matter now depends on nothing else but repentance and good works. Rabbi Eliezer <note>original: "Rabi Eliasaris"; a prominent scholar of the late 1st century.</note> supports this assertion, saying: If Israel repents, their redemption will happen; if they do not repent, there will be no hope of salvation. To this Rabbi Joshua responded: If Israel does not repent, they would indeed have no redemption; nevertheless, the most Holy One (blessed be God) will set over them a king as cruel and raging as the most wicked Haman <note>The villain of the biblical Book of Esther, who plotted the genocide of the Jews in Persia.</note>, by whose monstrous cruelty and the dread of punishments they will finally be turned toward acting well and piously.

### RICIUS

The Talmudist here openly taught that all set times—and consequently the first coming of the Messiah—have passed. He shows that the future redemption will occur through repentance and conversion, though driven more by impulse and fear than by a love of the truth. We see this happening to many Israelites in our own time, and it will happen even more frequently in the future, and not without reason. For just as a youth is driven to the study of letters—not out of a love for virtue, but enticed by small gifts and the charms of toys, or terrified by the threats of the switch <note>original: "ferulæ"; a rod or cane used for discipline in schools.</note>—so too is it necessary to instruct the children and those who are blind in Christ Jesus in one of these two ways, and to establish them in the worship of true piety. Similarly, Moses enticed the vast and unrefined people of Israel with tangible and bodily delights rather than those of the eternal age, transforming them toward the true worship of God by promising flowing streams of milk and honey rather than the kingdoms of heaven. Thus, finally, their restoration is to be hoped for (according to the Talmudic tradition): not indeed out of a desire for orthodox piety—due to their stubbornness and the thick darkness of their minds—but out of fear and the dread of punishment. Although this fear may be worldly and "of the switch" at the beginning, it will thereafter become a filial and diligent love for the eternal truth, under the protection of the heavenly spirit.

### TALMUD

Rav Abba established that no prophecy concerning redemption is clearer than that of Ezekiel: *But you, O mountains of Israel, shall shoot forth your branches and yield your fruit to my people Israel.* <note>Ezekiel 36:8.</note> This same redemption of Israel is clearly gathered, according to Rabbi Eliezer, from that passage of Zechariah: *Before those days there was no wage for man, nor any wage for beast; neither was there any peace for him who went out or came in because of the affliction.* <note>Zechariah 8:10.</note> Samuel handed down the tradition that the son of David <note>A standard messianic title.</note> will not come until there has been a great and intolerable cost for provisions. According to Rabbi Henina, the son of David will not come until not even a tiny fish can be found to bring help to the sick.

### RICIUS

Whether you understand all these things literally or according to an allegory, they are to be expected at the consummation of the age.

### TALMUD

Rabbi Hama established that the son of David will not come until the small branch of sovereignty ceases from Israel. <note>This refers to the total loss of even minor self-governance.</note> From the opinion of Rabbi Henina, he recounted that the son of David will not come until the "haughty in spirit" cease from Israel. And according to Rabbi Samlai, on the authority of Rabbi Eliezer, the son of David will not come until all judges and officers <note>original: "iudices & apparitores"; referring to the Jewish legal and administrative infrastructure.</note> cease from Israel. Ulla says: Israel shall not be redeemed except through justice. If you see a generation, says Rabbi Johanan, or an age that is afflicted by heavy and perpetual hardships; if you see a generation upon which distress rushes with headlong event and, as it were, the force of a torrent, expect [him]...

him. He also said: The Son of David <note>A common title for the Messiah in Jewish tradition, referring to the promised redeemer from the lineage of King David.</note> does not come except in a generation that is either entirely righteous or entirely wicked. Rabbi Alexander, on the authority of Rabbi Joshua, asked: With what correct understanding can that passage from Daniel—"Behold, one like a son of man was coming with the clouds of heaven" <note>Daniel 7:13</note>—be reconciled with that of Zechariah: "Poor and riding upon a donkey" <note>Zechariah 9:9</note>? To this he replied: The meaning of the aforementioned clauses is that if they are pure and deserving, he will come with the clouds of heaven; if not, he will be riding upon a donkey.

### RICIUS

Since the scepter of ruling was taken away long ago—namely, shortly after the time of the Lord’s Passion <note>The suffering and death of Jesus; Ricius argues that the loss of Jewish sovereignty in the 1st century proves the Messiah has already come.</note>—one must admit that the first coming of the Messiah has already passed. For two comings of the Messiah are shown here: the first, on account of the guilt of sin, is in the guise of a poor man and a servant for the purpose of redemption. The second, once original sin has been deleted, will be with the clouds of heaven and in commanding majesty, for the purpose of judgment. Consequently, that second coming will be for the redemption of the Jews.

### TALMUD

King Sabar <note>original: "Rex Sabar"; likely referring to the Sasanian King Shapur I, who appears in various Talmudic dialogues.</note> used to mock Samuel, saying: "You assert that the Messiah will come upon a donkey; I, however, promise him a swift horse, distinguished with trappings, if he so desires." To which Samuel replied: "Do you perhaps have a hundred-colored donkey, such as the Messiah's donkey will be?" Rabbi Joshua asked Elijah <note>The prophet Elijah, who in Jewish folklore is a frequent messenger between heaven and earth.</note>, who was standing at the gate of paradise, when the Messiah would come. Elijah replied: "When it shall be pleasing to this Lord of ours." And Rabbi Joshua himself asserted that he then saw two, and heard the speech of three.

### RICIUS

The Talmudist here openly enunciates the mystery of the Trinity in unity, since Elijah indicates only one "Lord of ours." Yet the Rabbi himself affirms that he saw two and heard the speech of three. He said he knew two by sight, but three by hearing, perhaps because the third person—the Holy Spirit—is perceived by faith alone, which comes from hearing. The other two, however, can be investigated by reason in some way (as theologians discuss). Or perhaps it is because the mission is to be ascribed to only two persons, but not at all to the person of the Father. But these matters are of a deeper inquiry and outside the limits of our proposal. Let it be enough for you to have accepted how he affirms the Messiah—whom he calls "our Lord"—to be three and one according to the opinion of the Talmudists. By the "donkey," one should understand the symbolic chaos of all moving things, <term>Matter</term> <note>original: "Materia & hylen"; Ricius uses both the Latin and the Greek philosophical terms for the primal substance of the universe.</note>, which one alone rides and dominates: the Messiah, in whom there is no fuel for sin. And it is "hundred-colored"—taking a specific, certain number to represent an uncertain one—because <term>Hyle</term> <note>The Greek term for matter; Ricius argues the donkey represents the physical world's endless variety of forms.</note> assumes the variety of all colors, that is, of sensible forms, through a certain succession.

### TALMUD

The same Rabbi Joshua, finding Elijah again standing at the entrance of the cave of Rabbi Simeon bar Yochai <note>A famous 2nd-century sage and mystic.</note>, asked when the Messiah would come. To him Elijah said: "Go and ask him yourself." But when the Rabbi inquired, "In what place shall I find him?", he replied: "At the gate of Rome." To which the Rabbi said: "And by what sign shall I distinguish him from the others?" He replied: "He sits in the midst of the poor who are suffering from illness, all of whom untie all their bandages at the same time and then bind them all up again together. But the Messiah alone unties them one by one, and immediately binds the same one again with the medicine applied, lest, if he should be called suddenly—namely, to redeem—he might be forced to delay, occupied by the binding of several wounds." Therefore, the Rabbi went to the Messiah and, greeting him, said: "Peace be unto you, my Master and Teacher." To which the Messiah replied: "Peace upon you, son of Levi." But he said: "When are you coming, Lord?" He replied: "Today." And so, having received the response, the Rabbi returned to Elijah. When Elijah asked him what the Messiah had reported to him, he replied, saying: "Peace to you, son of Levi." To these things, he said...

# THE EPITOME OF PAULUS RICIUS

...waits for light in vain with blinded eyes, just as Rabbi Auhu responded to a heretic asking about the arrival of the Messiah: that the Messiah would come when darkness covers the wicked, as it is written: *Behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and a mist the peoples.* <note>Isaiah 60:2. This passage is often used in Jewish tradition to describe the spiritual state of the world before the redemption.</note> According to the opinion of Rabbi Eliazar, the years of the Messiah will be forty, because it is written: *For forty years I shall take up that generation.* <note>Psalm 95:10. Traditional Jewish exegesis often used numerical values or specific timeframes from scripture to calculate the Messianic era.</note> However, Rabbi Eliazar ben Azaria determined that the years of the Messiah would be seventy. This is because it is written: *And on that day Tyre shall be forgotten among the cities for seventy years, like the days of one king* <note>Isaiah 23:15</note>—namely, the pre-eminent king, who is the King Messiah. But the Rabbi <note>Likely referring to Judah ha-Nasi, often called simply "Rabbi" in the Talmud.</note> asserted that the years of the Messiah would endure for three ages or generations, because it is written: *They shall fear you as long as the sun and before the moon, throughout generation and generations.* <note>Psalm 72:5</note>

Rabbi Hillel asserted that there would be no future Messiah for Israel, because his rule had already passed in the time of Hezekiah. <note>King Hezekiah of Judah (8th century BCE). Hillel’s controversial view was that the prophecies of the Messiah were fulfilled during Hezekiah’s reign.</note> But Rabbi Joseph refuted him, saying: "May the Lord forgive Rabbi Hillel; for Hezekiah reigned while the first house of the sanctuary <note>The First Temple in Jerusalem, destroyed by the Babylonians.</note> was standing, but Zechariah prophesied concerning the Messiah at the time of the second sacred house, saying: *Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: Behold, your king comes to you, just and a savior.*" <note>Zechariah 9:9</note> Another teacher, following the opinion of Rabbi Eliazar, handed down that there would be four hundred years of the Messiah, because it is written: *Make us glad according to the days in which you afflicted us, and the years in which we have seen evil*—namely, in the Egyptian captivity, the years of which were four hundred. For it is written: *And they shall bring them into servitude, and shall afflict them for four hundred years.* <note>Genesis 15:13</note>

But according to the Rabbi, the days of the Messiah are three hundred and sixty-five years, according to the number of the days of the Sun. For it is written: *Because the day of vengeance is in my heart, and the year of my redemptions has come.* <note>Isaiah 63:4</note> But here (as Rabbi Johanan says) it is written "in my heart," as if he had said: "To my heart alone have I revealed this secret; but to my limbs, not at all." And according to Rau Lachis, the sense is: "I have revealed it to my heart, but to the ministering angels, not at all." Abime judged the days of the Messiah to be seven thousand years, because it is written: *And as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you.* <note>Isaiah 62:5</note> Such a joy is customarily held for seven days of a wedding. <note>Comparing the seven days of a wedding feast to seven millennia of divine joy.</note> Rau Jehuda reported, from the opinion of Samuel, that there would be as many days of the Messiah as the days that have passed from the beginning of the world until that day. For it is written: *That your days and the days of your children may be multiplied in the land which the Lord swore to your fathers to give them, as the days of heaven over the earth.* <note>Deuteronomy 11:21</note> Rau Neheman determined that the days of the Messiah are as many as those from the days of Noah until that day. Concerning which it was said, through the mouth of Isaiah: *For this is as the days of Noah to me: for as I have sworn that I would not be angry with you, nor rebuke you.* <note>Isaiah 54:9</note>

-> R I C I V S <-

That assertion of Rabbi Johanan squares with the Gospel: *But of that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, but the Father alone.* <note>Matthew 24:36</note> Regarding the days and years of the Messiah, the tradition of the Talmudists is vague and multifaceted, as you have heard. Nevertheless, they all lean upon the same foundation: that before the completion of the age, the kingdom of Israel is to be restored and will endure for some course of time under the rule of the Messiah. The orthodox faith <note>Meaning Ricius's Roman Catholic perspective.</note> does not reject this in the least, though maintaining reverence for the divine secrets. For from the opinion of the Apostle in the letter to the Romans, we have it as a certainty that there will be a future salvation for the Jews at the second coming of Christ. <note>Romans 11:26: "And so all Israel will be saved."</note> But by what Law, and for how long a span of time before the completion of the age this will be, we acknowledge that it was perceived by none of the wise (as Augustine testifies in the twentieth book of *The City of God*), nor has it been sufficiently investigated how long the judgment of discussion will last. Therefore, nothing prohibits the Israelites—whom the Apostle calls "natural branches"—when they have been grafted back into their natural richness, from attaining a higher degree of salvation than those from the "wild olive" of the Gentiles who, by divine mercy, were made companions of the natural olive. <note>A reference to the metaphor in Romans 11:17-24, where Paul describes the relationship between Jewish "natural branches" and Gentile "wild olive shoots."</note> And from being "members of a harlot," they are made "members of Christ"; regarding which, attend to the words of the Apostle in the eleventh chapter of Romans for a fuller understanding, and revolve them diligently in your mind. # ON TALMUDIC DOCTRINE

...who calculate the times of the completion of the age: however, they review these things by various means and conjectures rather than by solid truth. Hence Augustine, in the twentieth book of *The City of God*, writes: "Here," he says, "it is usually asked when this (that is, the final persecution by the Antichrist, and his destruction by the presence of Christ) shall be. This is asked quite impertinently; nevertheless, some have said that four hundred, others five hundred, and others even a thousand years could be completed from the ascension of the Lord until his final coming. Indeed, they use human conjectures; nothing certain is brought forward by them from the authority of canonical Scripture. Truly, he who says: *It is not for you to know the times and the moments, which the Father has put in his own power,* <note>Acts 1:7</note> loosens the fingers <note>A metaphor for stopping someone from counting or calculating.</note> of all those calculating this matter." Thus says Augustine. However, no view harmonizes more with the order of things, the Mosaic enigma, and the course of the stars, than the assertion of the "sabbatizers"; <note>The "sabbatizers" refers to those who believed the world would last 6,000 years (corresponding to the six days of creation) followed by a 1,000-year "Sabbath" or Messianic age.</note> but more on these things elsewhere. So much for the Messiah.

## SOME REMAINING MATTERS
## of this chapter follow, worthy of memory.

->TALMUD<-

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba <note>original: "Hiabar Aba"</note> said: All the prophets prophesied only concerning the time of the Messiah. The same Rabbi said: All the prophecies of the Prophets were spoken only concerning those who repent. But as for the rewards of the just and holy men, *no eye has seen a God besides you.* <note>Isaiah 64:4</note> Rabbi Abbahu <note>original: "Ahu"</note> truly judged that even men of the highest justice and integrity cannot reach the rank or place of the penitent. It is asked: what is that which "no eye has seen"? Rabbi Joshua <note>original: "Iosue"</note> answers: this is the wine preserved in its clusters since the six days of the beginning. Resh Lakish <note>original: "Reslakis"</note> asserts, however, that what "no eye has seen" is Eden (that is, pleasure); but if you ask where Adam was placed? He answers: not in Eden, but in the garden itself. You might say, do not Eden and the garden designate the same thing? It is denied. Because it is written: *And a river went out of Eden to water the garden.* <note>Genesis 2:10</note>

->RICIUS<-

Rabbi Joshua (who a little before commented on the Messiah with Elijah) now also calls the spiritual delights of the future age by the metaphor <note>original: "typo"</note> of wine preserved in its clusters since the beginnings of the age. By "celestial wine," which we shall enjoy hereafter, he designates the wisdom of God, which *no eye has seen a God besides you.* This is according to that saying of the Apostle: *We speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, which is hidden... as it is written: What eye has not seen, nor ear heard.* <note>1 Corinthians 2:7–9</note> The Talmudic author asserts that this wisdom is the wine preserved in its clusters since the beginning of creation, to distinguish it from human wisdom, which has already been "pressed out" and corrupted by the multiform defilement of fantasies. From this, the Kabbalists <note>original: "Cabalæi"</note> teach that the sin of Eve was nothing other than that she pressed out the grapes for her husband; <note>A Kabbalistic allegory suggesting that Eve prematurely sought "hidden knowledge" before it was ready or permitted.</note> for the six days of the beginning show the six degrees of things subject to corruption and motion. The seventh day, however, is the Sabbath and rest, subject to no corruption or change. Therefore, these things, accepted according to the allegory in the manner of the Kabbalists, suggest indeed sublime and hidden sacraments of truth; a similar judgment must be made regarding many of their sayings that follow.

->TALMUD<-

He who has learned the Law, says Rabbi Joshua, and does not repeat it, is like one who sows but does not reap. Again, he who has learned the Law and allows it to be abolished by forgetfulness, is like a woman who, when she has given birth to offspring, immediately places it in the tomb. To every man, says Rava <note>original: "Raua"</note>, anxiety and labor are incumbent; but happy is he whose lot is labor in the Law. He who busies himself in the Law for the love of the Law, says Rabbi Alexander, reconciles peace in the heavens above and the earth below. And it shall be reckoned (says Rava) as if he had built a dwelling for himself among the transitory things below and likewise in the heavens above. Such a man, says Resh Lakish, shall be like a protector of the whole world. And he himself (says Levi) hastens the time of redemption. He who [brings] his neighbor's son to the Law...

# EPITOME OF PAUL RICIUS
<meta>catchword: RICIUS.</meta>

...established the Law. He, says Resh Lakish <note>original: "Reslakis"; a 3rd-century scholar known for his strength and his transition from a bandit to a prominent rabbi.</note>, should be considered its propagator. Indeed, as Eleazar <note>original: "Eliazar"</note> says, he shall be judged as a Lawgiver.

->RICIUS.<-

By "Law" here, the Talmudist does not understand the letter, but the spirit that lies hidden within; according to that saying of the Psalmist:
> Open my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your Law. <note>Psalm 119:18</note>

->TALMUD.<-

It is written in the book of Ben Sira <note>An ancient Jewish work of ethical teachings, also known as Ecclesiasticus or the Wisdom of Sirach. Though not part of the Hebrew Bible, it is frequently cited in the Talmud.</note>, a thin beard shows a wise man, but a thick one shows a fool. He who blows into the cup (namely to clear away the foam) is not thirsty. He who asks for food to be eaten with bread, takes away his bread too (because he is not truly hungry). A forked beard shows a man than whom no one is more cunning. A wicked woman is a leprosy to her husband; let him cast her out of the house, and he will be healed of the leprosy. A beautiful woman is salvation to her husband, and the number of his days will be reckoned as double. Do not be ensnared by a beautiful woman; turn away your eyes, and do not feast with her husband or drink frequently with him, for many perish because of the face of a beautiful woman.

Do not permit many to enter your house. Let your friends be many, but reveal your secret to scarcely one in a thousand. Even from her who lies in your bosom, guard the doors of your mouth. Do not be anxious about tomorrow, for you do not know what the day may bring. Sad are the days and nights for the poor man; for his roof is low (since he lacks the power to build high) and his vineyard is higher than all others (because out of poverty he cultivates the mountain peaks), from which the rain of other roofs drips onto his; and the cultivation of his vineyard, and the crops already in the earth, are driven by the force of the winds into the vineyards of others. (All these are from the book of Ben Sira, which the Talmudists count among the apocryphal books.) He who murmurs an exorcism with spitting to heal a wound has no portion in the world to come <note>The Hebrew term *Olam Ha-Ba*, referring to the afterlife or the Messianic era.</note>, because the excrement of spit defiles the holy names of God. On the Sabbath day, as the masters teach, it is permitted to utter exorcisms for snakes and scorpions; however, it is a sin to consult demons. But according to Rabbi Yosi <note>original: "Rabi Iosi"</note>, the consultation of demons should be avoided on other days as well as the Sabbath. However, Rabbi Huna <note>original: "Rabi Huna"</note> does not approve of this opinion of Rabbi Yosi. Nor did Rabbi Yosi himself think the service of demons should be avoided for any other reason than imminent danger. Just as they say happened to Rabbi Isaac: for he, in order to escape the harm of a demon rushing at him, was swallowed by a cedar tree, which then gaped open and vomited him back out. The masters established that among the types of demons, it is lawful to consult the "princes of oil and eggs" <note>Ancient forms of divination using the surface of oil or the patterns in eggs.</note>, though that kind often deceives the questioner with a lie. Exorcists are accustomed to utter the murmur itself into the oil of a vessel, but not into the oil with which the hand is anointed; hence it is permitted to use the oil of the hand for anointing, but not the oil of the vessel. For Rabbi Isaac, son of Samuel, when staying at a lodging, the host brought oil in a vessel, and when he smeared his face with it, his face immediately swarmed with boils of phlegm and bile. As he went out to the market, a woman met him and said: "The spirit Hamas has blown upon you," and that same woman restored him to health shortly after by performing some ritual. He who uses any of the created things for his own benefit while neglecting the blessing, is considered (as Rav Hanina <note>original: "Rau Henina"</note> taught) to have extorted it from God and from the Congregation of Israel, because it is written:
> He who robs something from his father and mother is a partner of a destroyer: <note>Proverbs 28:24</note>
for "Father" signifies the most holy God, as it is written:
> Is he not your father? Who possessed you. <note>Deuteronomy 32:6</note>
So also "Mother" designates the Congregation of Israel, according to that saying of Solomon:
> Hear, my son, the discipline of your father, and do not forsake the law of your mother. <note>Proverbs 1:8</note>
It is asked, what kind of spirit was that of which it is written:
> I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets. <note>1 Kings 22:22</note>
Rabbi Yohanan answered: It was the spirit of Naboth the Jezreelite (as Ravina <note>original: "Rauina"</note> says). The Lord said, "Go out from my wall," because it is written:
> He who speaks lies shall not be established in the sight of my eyes. <note>Psalm 101:7</note>
To this is applied that saying of Rav Papa <note>original: "Rau popa"</note>, as the proverb goes:
> He who is overcome by an excessive desire for vengeance destroys his own house.

# ON TALMUDIC DOCTRINE. 277

### RICIVS.

A great and celestial mystery is touched upon here concerning the soul when it is released from the bond of the body. For Naboth the Israelite, because he refused to give his vineyard to King Ahab, was killed with stones by the order of Queen Jezebel (as we read in 3 Kings <note>original: "3. Regum"; in the Latin Vulgate, 1 Kings is titled 3 Kings.</note>). Because his soul departed at the very end of his life with a burning desire for vengeance, it became a "lying spirit" in the mouth of the Prophets to fulfill that lust for revenge. 

By what reasoning and by what testimony of truth it is right to believe this, the mystery is shown by the Pythoness <note>The Medium or Witch of Endor who summoned the spirit of Samuel at the request of King Saul.</note> who was consulted by Saul regarding Samuel. Samuel was a "truthful spirit" to Saul, just as Naboth was a "lying spirit" to Ahab. However, as it is expressed in 1 Kings <note>original: "primo Regum"; referring here to 1 Samuel.</note>, Samuel appeared with a certain restlessness, whereas Naboth performed his task with the greatest eagerness.

### TALMUD.

Four types of men, says Rav Hisda <note>original: "Rau Hista"; a prominent 3rd-century Babylonian scholar.</note>, are excluded from the presence of Glory: scoffers, those who speak lies, flatterers, and slanderers. It is written: *No evil shall happen to you* <note>Psalm 91:10</note>; that is, you shall not be terrified by nightmares or wicked thoughts at night; *no plague shall approach your dwelling*, meaning that you will have no son or disciple who publicly turns away from the faith, such as Jesus the Nazarene was.

### RICIVS.

Since mention is made here of Jesus the Nazarene—as is done in various places in the Talmud—who, by the symbolism of his name, seems to hint at Jesus our Savior, this foolish and deadly presumption has provided the Jewish madness with an occasion for disparaging and blaspheming the super-heavenly sacraments of orthodox piety. Therefore, I have decided to immediately subjoin the history of this kind of "Jesus the Nazarene," which the Talmudist mentions a little further down in this very chapter *Helek* <note>A famous chapter in the Talmudic tractate Sanhedrin dealing with the afterlife and the Messiah.</note>. From this, you will clearly understand by what an evident fallacy of equivocation <note>Ricius is arguing that the "Jesus" mentioned in the Talmud lived in a different historical period and is not the same person as Jesus Christ.</note> and uncorrectable error they are deceived. For it is read a little later:

### TALMUD.

It is proper (as the masters teach) to repel with the left hand but to draw in with the right hand one who has done wrong. One should not be like Elisha, who pushed away his servant Gehazi with both hands, nor like Rabbi Joshua ben Perachiah <note>original: "Rabi Iosue Ben Praheia"; a leader of the Sanhedrin in the 2nd century BCE.</note>, who pushed away Jesus the Nazarene with both hands at once. 

For when King Yannai <note>Alexander Jannaeus, a Hasmonean king known for persecuting the Pharisees.</note>, driven into a rage, ordered the masters to be slaughtered, Rabbi Joshua went away, taking flight to Alexandria in Egypt. But a little later, when the King’s rage had cooled, Simeon ben Shetach <note>original: "Simon Ben Sota"; a famous scholar and contemporary of Joshua ben Perachiah.</note> wrote back to the same Rabbi Joshua, announcing that the time demanded he return to holy Jerusalem. Obeying these warnings, he soon set out on the journey toward Jerusalem. 

When he was received at a certain splendid inn along the way, he said: "O! How fine and how pleasant this inn <note>original: "hospitium"; this term can refer to both the lodging and the hospitality/hostess.</note> is!" Then Jesus, thinking the master was speaking of the hostess of the inn, said: "She has squinting (or round) eyes." To which the Rabbi replied: "Wicked man! Do you think of such filthiness?" And immediately, with the blast of four hundred trumpets, he ordered him to be proclaimed anathema <note>A formal curse or excommunication.</note>. And although Jesus frequently asked for pardon and to be taken back into the number of disciples, the master could in no way be inclined to indulge him. 

Finally, a little later (while the Rabbi himself was occupied with prayer and the reading of the *Hear, O Israel* <note>original: "audi Israël"; the Shema, the central prayer of Judaism.</note>), Jesus approached the master again. The Rabbi, whose mind was now pacified, intended to grant the petitioner's wish and signaled to him with his hands to wait until the end of the reading. But Jesus, thinking the wave of the hands was a sign of rejection and indignation, immediately went away in a rage. And he straightway set up a brick stone and worshipped it with the cult of idolatry. When the Rabbi, with a concerned mind, urged him to repentance and to the worship of true piety, he refused with a stubborn face, asserting that he had learned from his master,

# EPITOME OF PAUL RICIUS.

from the master: that for he who leads the multitude of the people to transgression, no opportunity for repentance is left to him. Moreover, he recounted that Jesus the Nazarene practiced magic, instigated outrages, and turned the multitude of Israel away from the true worship of the Creator.

### RICIUS.

That there is no mention here of Jesus the Nazarene who suffered under Pontius Pilate, our Savior, will be easy to recognize once we have demonstrated that the times of Pontius Pilate are far removed—by more than a hundred years—from the times of King Jannai. For Jannai (as is handed down in the book *Berakhot*, in the chapter on the morning prayer) was Jonathan, the son of Simon the Maccabee, who was also called Hyrcanus (as is read in the thirteenth book of Josephus’s *Antiquities*). If, therefore, you calculate the time from Hyrcanus—also called Jonathan the Maccabee or Jannai—to the times of Herod and Pontius Pilate, you will find an interval of about one hundred and ten years. From this, you may easily prove that the Jesus the Nazarene who was a pupil of Rabbi Joshua is not the same as the Jesus the Nazarene who suffered under Pontius Pilate, Christ our Lord. 

Even if the blind persistence of the younger Israelites contends that the Talmudist here implies Jesus the Savior, it is nonetheless consistent that the Talmudist himself was deceived by error. This is just as that "Chief Talmudist" Rabbi Akiva <note>Rabbi Akiva (c. 50–135 CE) was a leading Jewish scholar who famously supported Bar Kokhba as the Messiah.</note>—a man of remarkable wisdom and celebrated life by the testimony of all—honored the Pseudo-messiah <note>referring to Simon bar Kokhba, leader of the Jewish rebellion against Rome.</note> as the true Restorer of the human race, as we mentioned a little earlier. By that same fallacy and mist of ignorance, he judged Christ the Nazarene, the true Redeemer of the world, to be a Pseudo-messiah. It is no wonder then, when the blind lead the blind, if both fall into the pit.

### TALMUD.

It is asked by Rabbi Simon: when it is written, *From the impious their light is taken away, and the uplifted arm shall be broken* <note>Job 38:15</note>, why is it that the letter *ayin* (ע) in the word <term>מרשעים<gloss>Mersaim; "from the wicked" or "from the impious"</gloss></term> hangs outside the sequence of the other letters? <note>In traditional Hebrew scrolls, the letter *ayin* in this specific verse is written "suspended" above the line.</note> The answer is: that he who is destitute in this lowest and fleeting world shall also be rendered destitute in the celestial realms.

### RICIUS.

When the letter *Ayin* (ע) is removed by syncopation from the middle of the word *Mersaim* (as is read in the Hebrew text of the aforementioned clause), there remains *Meresim* <note>Ricius is playing on the Hebrew words *Resha'im* (wicked) and *Rashim* (poor/destitute).</note>. Then the word signifies not "the impious," but "the destitute"—namely, those destitute of mind. For when the human mind itself grows sluggish and fails to contemplate or consider the beauty of this fleeting world, it becomes destitute and ignorant of the secret things in the celestial realms. From this, one falls into impiety and into the misery of the world to come. For, as the Apostle says: *the invisible things of God are clearly seen by the creature of the world through those things which have been made* <note>Romans 1:20</note>. Therefore, he who does not notice the manifest things that lie beneath the senses in this machine of fleeting things has certainly not earned the right to penetrate the invisible things in the heavens. But you, take note of how many spiritual gifts lie hidden in the very manner of writing and the context of the Hebrew letters, which can be taught and understood only from the Hebrew original.

### TALMUD.

Two Israelites (as the Masters recounted when commenting on the cleverness and insight of the sons of Israel) were captured on Mount Carmel. During their travels, one said to the other: "I deduce that the camel which has gone before us lacks the light in one of its eyes. Moreover, because it is burdened, it carries a jar of wine in one side and oil in the other. Furthermore, of the two who are leading the camel, one is an Israelite and the other is a Gentile." Then their captor, following the tracks and listening to their conversation, said: "Hah! You stiff-necked people, how? By what rash conjecture do you presume these things you have narrated?" They responded: "That the camel lacks the light in one eye we concluded from the fact that it grazes on the grass on only one side of the road and path."

[The camel] grazes [on one side], but on the other side not at all. Again, when we see drops dripping from flasks, some indeed sink to the bottom, while others float on the surface; we therefore understand one to be a flask of oil, and the other a flask of wine. Furthermore, concerning those who lead the camel: since we observed one relieving himself shamelessly right in the path, but the other outside the path in a hiding place, we knew one to be a Gentile and the other an Israelite. The captor, wishing to be more certain of this matter, set out on foot and followed the camel and its companions with a swift pace. When he discovered the matter was exactly as the captives had said, and recognized their great insight with the highest admiration, he greeted them both with a kiss of peace, granted them gifts and freedom, and restored them to their fatherland with glory and honor.

He who passes over insults offered to him in silence shall pass over a thousand evils that threaten him. Seven slippery places do not cause the innocent to fall, but the wicked is overwhelmed by one. While the love of a couple glows, they lie together on the blade of a sword; when it cools, a bed of sixty cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of measurement, roughly the length of a forearm (about 18 inches).</note> does not suffice for them. It is written: *A king by justice builds up the land, but a man of first fruits destroys it* <note>original: "Rex in iudicio erigit terram, & uir primitiarum dissipat eam" (Proverbs 29:4). Ricius interprets "man of first fruits" as a poor judge who depends on small offerings.</note>: as if to say: A judge who abounds in wealth like a king builds up and strengthens the land; but if he is needy (like a priest who lives on the small amount of the first fruits), he will destroy it. He who appoints an unfit judge in a city will be regarded as if he had planted an idol to be worshipped in Israel. No wise man should inhabit a city in which one of these ten things is missing: namely, a college of judges, a treasury for alms, a house of prayer, a bathhouse, a place for nature’s requirements <note>A public latrine.</note>, a physician, a bloodletter, a scribe, a butcher, and a teacher of children. 

At the time when Solomon had married the daughter of Pharaoh, Gabriel descended and fixed a reed in the sea, from which a reef arose, upon which the great city of Rome was built. Mar Sutra <note>A Talmudic sage.</note> first said: The Law was given to Israel in Hebrew characters and in the holy tongue, which in the times of Ezra was changed into the Aramaic language and Assyrian characters. But a little later, retaining the Assyrian characters, they chose the holy tongue for themselves, leaving the Hebrew characters and the Aramaic tongue to the "idiots." By "idiots," according to Rav Hisda, are meant the Cuthean people <note>The Samaritans.</note>, who fear the Creator and worship idols at the same time. But the Rabbi <note>Likely Judah the Prince, the redactor of the Mishnah.</note> asserts that from the beginning the Law was given and written in the same characters in which it is written now. He claims that due to the transgressions of the Israelites, it was changed into another kind of script, and when they were led back to repentance, the original characters were restored. However, Rabbi Simon son of Eleazar asserted that at no time was the manner of speaking or writing ever changed. 

A woman, says Rabbi Samuel, is something unformed, and therefore she adheres to no mortal with so stable a bond as to him who makes her a "formed vessel" <note>This refers to a Talmudic concept regarding a woman's first marriage and its spiritual/physical bond.</note>, which is perfected by the first man and husband. Neither does a man die except to his wife, nor a wife except to her husband. There is a proverb: though a famine should rage throughout the world for seven years, it never touches the door of a man skilled in any craft. Whoever adds, diminishes. A rich man who does not enjoy his riches is a mouse lying upon gold. It is a sin to betray what the wise discuss in the literary school. Whence Rav Ami immediately expelled and cast out one of the students who had betrayed a certain secret handed down twenty-two years earlier in the literary cloister. 

A physician of Tyre by name says: The Egyptians allow no cow or sow to be led away from Alexandria unless they first remove its womb, so that it may not conceive. It is written: *God spoke once, but we heard two things*: because from one and the same clause of the sacred word we receive various teachings; but from several clauses, we never understand one and the same thing. # PAUL RICIUS’S EPITOME
