...from the master, because he who leads a multitude of people to transgress is left with no opportunity to repent. Mar, however, recounted that Jesus the Nazarene practiced magic, instigated crimes, and turned the multitude of Israel away from the true worship of the Creator.

->RICIUS<-

It will be easy to recognize that there is absolutely no discussion here regarding our Savior, Jesus the Nazarene who suffered under Pontius Pilate, once we demonstrate that the era of Pontius Pilate is far removed—by more than a hundred years—from the times of King Jannai <note>Alexander Jannaeus, a Hasmonean King of Judea who ruled from 103 to 76 BC.</note>. For Jannai (as is passed down in the book *Berakhot*, in the chapter on the morning prayer) was Jonathan, the son of Simon the Maccabee, who was also called Hyrcanus (as is read in the thirteenth book of Josephus’s *Antiquities*). If, therefore, you calculate the time from Hyrcanus (or Jonathan the Maccabee, or Jannai) to the times of Herod and Pontius Pilate, you will find an interval of about one hundred and ten years. From this, you can easily prove that the Jesus the Nazarene who was a student of Rabbi Joshua is not the same as the Jesus the Nazarene who suffered under Pontius Pilate, Christ our Lord. 

Even if—as the blind stubbornness of the younger Israelites contends—the Talmudist hints at Jesus the Savior here, it is nonetheless consistent that the Talmudist himself was deceived by error. This is just like that Arch-Talmudist Rabbi Akiva, a man of remarkable wisdom and celebrated life by everyone's testimony, who (as we mentioned a little earlier) worshiped a False Messiah <note>Rabbi Akiva famously supported Simon bar Kokhba as the Messiah during the Jewish revolt against Rome (132–136 AD).</note> as if he were the true Restorer of the human race. By the same fallacy and cloud of ignorance, he judged Christ the Nazarene, the true Redeemer of the world, to be a False Messiah. It is no wonder then, when the blind lead the blind, if both fall into the pit.

->TALMUD<-

It is asked by Rabbi Simon: when it is written, *Light is taken away from the wicked, and the high arm shall be broken* <note>Job 38:15</note>, why is it that the letter *Ayin* <term>ע</term> in the word *Mershaim* <term>מרשעים</term> (meaning "from the wicked") hangs outside the alignment of the other letters? <note>In traditional Hebrew scribal practice for this verse, the letter Ayin is written "suspended," or slightly higher than the rest of the word.</note> It is answered that he who is poor in this lowest and falling world shall also be rendered poor in the heavens above.

->RICIUS<-

When the letter *Ayin* <term>ע</term> is removed from the middle of the word *Mershaim* (as read in the Hebrew text of the aforementioned phrase), *Meresim* remains. In that case, the word does not mean "the wicked," but rather "the poor"—specifically, poverty of the mind. For when the human mind grows sluggish and fails to contemplate or consider the beauty of this "falling machine" <note>Ricius uses the word "machine" (machinae) to describe the complex, physical structure of the created universe.</note>, it becomes poor and ignorant of the secret things in the heavens. From this, one slides into impiety and the misery of this age and the age to come. For, as the Apostle <note>Saint Paul, in Romans 1:20.</note> says, "the invisible things of God are clearly seen from the creation of the world through those things which have been made." Therefore, he who does not notice the manifest things which lie beneath the senses in this world of falling things, certainly has not earned the right to penetrate the invisible things in the heavens. Take note, then, of how many spiritual gifts lie hidden in the very manner of writing and the context of the Hebrew letters, which can be taught and understood only from the Hebrew original.

->TALMUD<-

Two Israelites (as the Masters recounted when commenting on the cleverness and insight of the children of Israel) were captured on Mount Carmel. In the course of their travel conversations, one said to the other: "I suspect the camel which preceded us is missing the sight in one of its eyes; and in one flask, because it is heavy, it carries wine, and in the other oil; moreover, of the two who lead the camel, one is an Israelite, and the other a Gentile." Then their captor, following their tracks and listening to their conversation, said: "Hah! You stiff-necked people! From where and by what rash conjecture do you presume to tell such things?" The captive responds: "That the camel lacks the light in one of its eyes, we gathered from this: that it grazes on the grass on only one side of the path and track..."

...is grazed upon, but on the other side not at all <note>The captives deduced the camel was blind in one eye because it only ate the grass on one side of the path</note>. Again, when we see that of the droplets dripping from the flasks, some indeed sink to the very bottom, while others are seen to float on the surface, we understand from this that one flask is of oil and the other of wine <note>Oil floats on water/residue, whereas wine or water-based liquids soak in</note>. ## ON CERTAIN OTHER CHAPTERS
### *Excerpts worthy of reading.*

He who passes over insults brought against him in silence shall see a thousand evils that threaten him pass by. Seven slippery pitfalls do not cast down the innocent, but the impious man is overwhelmed by just one. While the love of a married couple is burning, they can sleep together on the blade of a sword; but when it grows cold, a bed of sixty cubits <note>About 90 feet</note> is not large enough for them. It is written: *A king by justice establishes the land, but a man of first-fruits tears it down* <note>A Latin rendering of Proverbs 29:4</note>. It is as if one wished to say: A judge who abounds in wealth like a king establishes and strengthens the land; but if he is poor (like a priest who lives on the meager offerings of the first-fruits), he will tear it down. He who appoints an' improper judge in a city will be regarded just as if he had planted an idol to be worshiped in Israel.

No wise man should inhabit a city in which any one of these ten things is lacking: a college of judges, a treasury for alms, a house of worship <note>original: "Ecclesiasticę ædes"</note>, a bathhouse, a place for the requirements of nature <note>A public latrine</note>, a doctor, a bloodletter, a scribe, a butcher, and a teacher of children. 

At the time when Solomon had married the daughter of Pharaoh, Gabriel descended and fixed a reed in the sea, from which a reef arose, upon which the great city of Rome was built <note>A Talmudic legend from Sanhedrin 21b suggesting that Solomon's marriage to a foreign princess planted the seeds for the eventual rise of Israel's conqueror, Rome</note>. 

First, Mar Zutra <note>original: "Marsutra"</note> says: The Law was given to Israel in the Hebrew character but in the holy tongue, which in the times of Ezra was changed into the Aramaic tongue and Assyrian characters. But a little later, retaining the Assyrian characters, they chose the holy tongue for themselves, leaving the Hebrew characters and the Aramaic tongue to the "idiots" <note>The word "idiotis" here refers to commoners or the unlearned; the text explains this refers to the Samaritans</note>. By "idiots," according to Rav Hisda <note>original: "Rau Hisda"</note>, the Cuthite people <note>original: "Chusini"</note> are meant, who fear the Creator and worship idols at the same time. 

Rabbi <note>Judah the Prince</note>, however, affirms that from the beginning the Law was given and written in those same characters with which it is written now. But due to the transgression of the Israelites, it was changed into another kind of writing, and when they were led to repentance, the original character was restored to them. But Rabbi Simon, son of Eleazar, asserted that at no time was the manner of speaking or writing ever changed.

A woman, says Rabbi Samuel, is something unformed, and therefore she does not cling to any mortal with such a stable bond as to him who made her a formed vessel; this is perfected through the first man, her husband. Neither does a man die except to his wife, nor a wife except to her husband. 

There is an adage: even if a famine should rage everywhere through the world for seven years, it never touches the door of a man skilled in any craft. 

Whoever adds, subtracts. 

A rich man who does not enjoy his riches is like a mouse lying upon gold. 

It is a sin to betray what the sages treat in the literary school. For this reason, Rav Ammi <note>original: "Rau Ami"</note> immediately expelled and eliminated one of the disciples who had betrayed something of a secret that had been handed down in the literary cloister twenty-two years earlier.

A physician of Tyre by name says: The Egyptians do not allow any cow or sow to be taken away from Alexandria unless they first cut out its womb, so that it might not conceive <note>To maintain a monopoly on their livestock</note>. 

It is written: *God has spoken once, but we have heard two things* <note>Psalm 62:11</note>; because from one and the same clause of the sacred word we receive various teachings; but from several clauses, we never understand one and the same thing. 

A woman standing with her feet upright is unfit for conception; nevertheless, they confirmed this Law for Shealtiel <note>original: "Saltiliellū"</note>, the parent of Zerubbabel <note>original: "Serubabellis"</note>, in the Babylonian prison. And for that reason, he is named Zerubbabel... <note>The text cuts off mid-word "nuncupatur"; Zerubbabel's name was traditionally interpreted as "conceived in Babylon"</note>

<header>EPITOME OF PAULUS RICIUS,</header>

...it is said that he was conceived or born in Babylon: whose proper name was Nehemiah, son of Hachaliah. When wine enters, a secret departs <note>A common Latin and Hebrew proverb: *In vino veritas* / *Nichnas yayin, yatza sod*.</note>. The faces of mortals (as the Teachers hand down) are not granted exactly the same image; nor should one man, seeing another's wife or home as splendid, claim it for himself and contend it is his own. According to the opinion of Rabbi Meir, there are three things by which individual men differ most from one another: voice, appearance, and thought. God, the Creator of the world, fashioned man as the final creature on the sixth day. He did so like a <term>Master of the Feast</term><note>Latin: *Architriclinus*. The head steward of a banquet who prepares everything before the guests arrive.</note>, who, having first spread the dining couch, set the table, and sumptuously prepared everything, is accustomed to introduce the guests last of all. To this Solomon alluded, saying:
> Wisdom has built a house for herself, she has hewn out seven pillars, she has sacrificed her victims, she has mixed her wine and set her table, she has sent out her handmaids.
So it is written there. For the Wisdom of women building a house shows the measure or meter of the Creator, by which He established the universe. The seven pillars which she hewed out are the seven days of the beginning; the victims, the diluted wine, and the table are the seas, rivers, and whatever has come into use for this world. The handmaids whom she sent are Adam and Eve. The earth from which the first-fashioned Adam was made was gathered from the entire terrestrial engine (as it pleased Rabbi Meir to say), as that verse of the Psalms testifies:
> Thine eyes did see my unformed substance. <note>Psalm 139:16.</note>
Now, the eyes of the Lord, as it is written elsewhere, are carried over the whole orb of the earth. Rav Hoshaya <note>original: "Rau Osia"</note> judged that the trunk of the first Adam's body was from the land of Babylon, his head from the land of Israel, and the remaining limbs of his body were compacted from other regions of the world. Rav Aha said there are twelve hours in a day: in the first, the earth for Adam was gathered; in the second, he became an unformed mass; in the third, his limbs were stretched out; in the fourth, a soul was cast into him; in the fifth, he rose to his feet; in the sixth, he gave names to things; in the seventh, Eve was given to him in marriage; in the eighth, two ascended the bed, but four descended <note>An allusion to the immediate birth of Cain and his twin sister</note>; in the ninth, the commandment was given to him; in the tenth, he became a transgressor of it; in the eleventh, he was judged; and finally, in the twelfth, he was cast out of paradise and departed, as it is written:
> Man did not abide in honor. <note>Psalm 49:12.</note>
Beasts have no power over a man unless he appears like a beast, for it is written:
> He is become like the beasts that perish.
The stature of the first-fashioned Adam reached from one end of the world to the other; but when he became a transgressor, the Creator reduced him to a smaller size by the laying on of hands. But according to Rabbi Eleazar, the first-formed man touched the firmament with his height. The speech of the first Adam (as it pleased Rabbi Judah) was in the Aramaic tongue. To him, as Resh Lakish hands down, the glorious Creator of the world showed the generations of all ages, and all men of truth and wisdom. According to the opinion of Rabbi Judah, the first Adam fell into heresy. But according to Rabbi Isaac, he sinned in this: that he "nourished his foreskin" <note>A rabbinic idiom meaning he attempted to conceal his covenant with God or acted like a gentile</note>. Rav Nahman affirms he sinned because he rejected the primary origin of all things. In those same passages of the Sacred Scriptures where the depravity of heretics strives to be insolent and to twist the sound of the letter to a foreign meaning, a response is immediately subjoined by which their stubbornness is blunted. For example, it is written:
> Let us make man in our image:
By which heresy contends there is a plurality of gods. But that is proved false by what the text immediately subjoins:
> And God created man in his own image,
which implies the express unity of God. Thus far concerning these things; there follows a brief summary of the *Mishnah* regarding the Book of the Senators, called the *Sanhedrin*.

Others are judged by a senate of twenty-three consuls, such as those regarding the person and criminal judgments. Others are judged by the great [council] of Jerusalem of seventy-one...

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological descriptions of Jewish tradition as interpreted by the author. The previous page concluded with a discussion of the creation of man and symbolic interpretations of the "Master of the Feast." This page shifts focus to the structural and legal functions of the Jewish Senate and the specific rights and restrictions of the High Priest and the King.</meta>

-># ON TALMUDIC DOCTRINE.<-

The council of Senators <note>Referring to the Great Sanhedrin, the highest judicial and religious assembly in ancient Israel.</note> handles matters that concern an entire tribe, a <term>false prophet</term><note>Latin: *Pseudoprophetam*. One who claims to speak for God but promotes idolatry or violates the Law.</note>, or the High Priest. Other matters are first treated by a council of three, then investigated by five, and finally settled by seven—such as the calculation of the <term>intercalary month</term><note>Latin: *mensis embolismi*. A leap month added to the lunar calendar to reconcile it with the solar year.</note> and the counting of years. Other things, such as the <term>laying on of hands</term><note>Latin: *manuum impositio*. Known in Hebrew as *Semikhah*, the ceremony for ordaining judges or leaders.</note> to confer judicial and senatorial insignia, are performed by five. Other matters are judged by ten, in whose number one Priest is included, such as the valuation of fields for sale or redemption, and other matters of that kind.

### TO WHAT THE HIGH PRIEST AND THE KING ARE BOUND, AND FROM WHAT THEY ARE EXEMPT. CHAPTER II.

The High Priest judges and is judged. He gives testimony, and testimony is given concerning him. He is subject to the <term>Law of the Unshoeing</term><note>Latin: *Discalciationis Legi*. Known as *Chalitzah* (Deuteronomy 25:9), a ritual involving a widow and her brother-in-law if he refuses to marry her after his brother's death.</note> with the wife of his deceased brother, just as the brother of the deceased fulfills the same Law with the High Priest’s wife. The widow of a deceased High Priest may be joined in marriage to the High Priest’s brother, but the widow of a deceased brother is not joined in marriage to the High Priest <note>Under Jewish law, a High Priest was required to marry a virgin and was forbidden from marrying a widow.</note>. The High Priest does not follow the funeral procession, nor does he recline on the ground for the <term>funeral feast</term><note>Latin: *silicernium*. A meal for mourners.</note> like other mourners, but sits upon a small stool while the entire multitude sits on the ground.

The King, however, does not judge, and is by no means judged. He gives no testimony, nor is testimony given concerning him. He does not undergo the Law of the Unshoeing, nor does his brother observe it with the widow of that same deceased king. He is not joined in marriage to a deceased brother’s wife, nor is a brother joined to the widow of a deceased king; however, a king is permitted to be joined to the widow left by another king. He follows a funeral procession at his own discretion, and at the funeral feast he reclines on a bench (which some call the <term>couch of fortune</term><note>Latin: *cubile fortunae*.</note>), while the whole multitude sits on the ground. He wages discretionary wars with the consent of the Great Senate. He may tear down walls (to make a path open for himself) and whatever structures he pleases according to his will. From the soldiers' plunder, he reserves a portion for himself first. He may not take more than eighteen wives. His supply of horses must not be greater than his equestrian rank requires. He should not be anxious to amass a heap of silver and gold, except as the needs of the military and the state demand. He shall write for himself a copy of the <term>Pentateuch</term><note>Latin: *pentateuchum*. The first five books of the Bible (the Torah).</note> of the Law, which he shall keep with him abroad, and in camp, and at home, kept hanging from his neck. It is not permitted to ride upon the king’s horse, nor to sit upon his throne, and it is a sacrilege to use the royal scepter. One may not approach or look upon the King while he is having his hair cut, or while he is naked in the bath.

### BY WHAT MEANS JUDGES ARE TO BE CHOSEN, AND IN WHAT WAYS WITNESSES AND JUDGES MAY BE DISQUALIFIED; AND BY WHAT LAW WITNESSES ARE TO BE EXAMINED. CHAPTER III.

In <term>cases of mammon</term><note>Latin: *iudiciis mammonis*. Legal disputes regarding money or property rather than capital crimes.</note>, which are decided by three, either of the litigants chooses one judge, and both judges choose a third. But if the litigants admit their own relative, or the relative of the other party, or even ignorant and unrefined cowherds as judges, they are not given the power to refuse or reject the judges after the sentence has been passed. 

However, those who are marked by impiety, or by shameful or unjust gain, are disqualified: namely, those who engage in dicing <note>Gambling with dice.</note>, in usury, or in <term>pigeon racing</term><note>Latin: *venatorium columbarum volatum*. A prohibited form of gambling.</note>, and those who trade in the produce of the <term>year of release</term><note>Latin: *remissionis anno*. The Sabbatical year (Shmita) in which the land was to lie fallow and commercial trade in its natural growth was restricted.</note>, and similar things. For none of these (if they have studied no other mastery or craft) is admitted to judge or to bear witness. It is also not lawful for blood relatives or in-laws to judge or to give testimony. Close companions and enemies may give testimony, but they may by no means judge. 

In the examination of witnesses, the elder or more distinguished in rank is called into a separate room first. Unless he confirms the certainty of the loan from his own sight or from the mouth of the debtor, his testimony is considered void. After the examination of the first witness is completed, the second follows; if his words agree with the words of the former, the judges immediately discuss the matter itself and conclude the judgment according to the opinion of the majority. Once the sentence is passed, a space of thirty days is left for the debtor to object; after these have passed, nothing thereafter...

->## SUMMARY BY PAULUS RICIUS.<-

...subsequently admitted to the opposition of the opinion. By a similar law, when a debtor, after a sentence has already been finalized, is asked: "Do you have anything to say in contradiction?" if he responds that he has nothing to oppose, but later attempts to establish something against the sentence in any way, he will in no way be able to rescind the power of the sentence already passed.

### THE DIFFERENCES BETWEEN JUDGMENTS OF MAMMON AND OF PERSONS. THE MANNER AND ORDER OF THE SENATORS. CHAPTER IV.

Cases of <term>Mammon</term> <note>Latin: *Mammonis*. This refers to civil cases involving money, property, or financial disputes.</note> are judged by three men, but actions concerning persons or souls <note>Referring to capital cases where the life or physical person of the accused is at stake.</note> are decided by a senate of twenty-three. In cases of Mammon, it does not matter whether the opinions of those who convict or those who <term>acquit</term> <note>Latin: *justificant*. Literally "justify" or "declare righteous," used here in the sense of a legal acquittal.</note> are brought forward first. In those matters that concern the person (or a criminal judgment), the opinions of those who acquit are pronounced first, and then those who convict. In the former, a majority of one is sufficient either to acquit or to convict; in the latter, however, a majority of one acquits, but a majority of two is required to convict. In the former, once a sentence has been passed, it is permitted to raise an opposition to convict as well as to acquit; in the latter, however, once the sentence is finalized, it is permitted to raise an objection only to acquit, but not to convict. In the former, the power of arguing or teaching is given equally to all legal experts, however minor, both to convict and to acquit. Here, however, it is permitted only for the sake of acquittal.

In the former, it is lawful for the same person who argued for conviction to then argue for acquittal. Likewise, conversely, one who first argued for acquittal can afterwards teach toward conviction. Here, however, it is by no means permitted for one who has once taught for acquittal to then argue for conviction. In the former, the examination is conducted by the light of day, and the sentence is brought forth at night. Here, however, it is lawful to complete both the examinations and the sentences only by the light of day. In the former, they discuss the cases on the same day and bring forth the sentence in whichever direction is opposed; here, however, the examination is conducted on the same day and an acquitting sentence is pronounced, but they finalize a convicting sentence on the following day, and not on the day of the examination. For this reason, examinations of cases are forbidden on the eve of the Sabbath or any solemn day.

In determining the rites of expiation and pollution, the judge of higher rank explains his own opinion first; but in judgments regarding the person and the soul, the one who is junior in dignity and wisdom pronounces his sentence first <note>This was done so that junior members would not be intimidated or influenced by the opinions of the more prestigious judges.</note>. All <term>proselytes</term> <note>Latin: *proseliti*. Converts to Judaism.</note>, and even those of illegitimate birth, are fit to determine cases of Mammon; but judgments of souls are settled only by Priests and Levites, as well as those Israelites related by marriage to the Priests. It was the custom of the Senators to sit together in the shape of a semicircle, so that they might look at one another in a shared view, with two scribes assisting (one at the right of the Senators, the other at the left), writing down the words of those who convict and those who acquit.

In the Hall of the Senators <note>Latin: *Senatorum Basilica*. Likely referring to the Chamber of Hewn Stone where the Sanhedrin met.</note>, there were three other rows of students of wisdom, who all sat on the ground in steps according to the excellence of each; from these, some were promoted to the Senatorial rank (when the matter required it), so that when one from the first of the three rows was chosen for the Senatorial rank, another from the second row took the place of the one co-opted into the college of Senators, then another from the third row filled the place in the second, and finally another from the public assembly was taken to act in the third row. Thus it happened that when one was removed from the Senatorial rank, each of the other three ranks would climb one step higher.

Terror must be struck into those giving testimony in personal cases, lest they presume to testify by mere estimation (however much the signs may appear) or by the mouth of another’s testimony, or by the report of a truthful man, but only by the certainty of sight; and they must be forewarned of the rigorous examination by which their words are to be discussed and winnowed. For personal judgments differ from judgments of Mammon by a very great interval: for he who condemns someone to a loss of Mammon by false testimony shall indeed be purged of the fault if he restores the sum of Mammon to the innocent; but from the crime of shedding innocent blood, the false witness shall not be freed...

ON TALMUDIC DOCTRINE.
A 4
<meta>catchword: ...is led</meta>

...you can testify forever. For whoever destroys a single Israelite, or saves a single soul, it is judged as if he had destroyed or saved the machinery of the whole world. The divine ingenuity is worthy of the highest and unspeakable praise; for if a man produces countless coins from one mold, each reflects the exact same image. But the Creator of all ages Himself formed the vast and immense race of mortals from the single mold of the <term>protoplast</term> <note>From the Greek *prōtoplastos*, meaning "first-formed."</note> Adam, yet not one of them precisely mirrors the image of another.

### BY WHAT LAW WITNESSES ARE TO BE EXAMINED, 
### and how the sentence is to be brought forward in judgment. CHAPTER V.

Witnesses giving testimony are examined with seven inquiries, namely: In which seven-year <term>Jubilee</term> cycle <note>The Jubilee cycle consists of seven sets of seven years, followed by a fiftieth year of release.</note>, in which year, in which month, on which day of the month and of the week, at what hour of the day, and in what place they saw it done. They are additionally asked whether they knew the one guilty of the crime and whether they pre-warned him to abstain from the crime <note>This refers to the requirement of *hatra'ah*, a formal warning that must be given to a perpetrator immediately before a crime for them to be liable for capital punishment.</note>. Regarding idolatry, they are asked which of the idols he adored, and with what worship. The law is not the same for the "inquiries" and the "interrogations." For if one of the witnesses responds that he does not know something in an <term>inquiry</term> <note>Latin: *inquisitione*. These are the *Hakirot*, or essential questions regarding time and place.</note>, the testimony will be void. However, regarding an <term>interrogation</term> <note>Latin: *interrogationem*. These are the *Bedikot*, or supplementary questions to test the consistency of the witnesses.</note>, if one, or even two of the witnesses, should assert that they do not know, the testimony will nonetheless be valid and acceptable. Yet in the case of interrogations as well as inquiries, if one contradicts the other, the testimony will be void. If one of the witnesses wishes to bring forward something for <term>acquittal</term> <note>Latin: *justificandum*. Literally "to justify" or declare the accused innocent.</note>, or if any of the order of the <term>students of wisdom</term> <note>Latin: *studiosorum sapientiæ*. These were disciples of the sages who sat in rows before the court to observe and learn.</note> wishes to bring forward something for condemnation, the faculty of speaking is not granted to them. But if one from their order promises that he will say something that may acquit, access is granted to him, and they soon place him in a seat among the session of the Senators <note>The Latin *Senatorum* refers to the members of the Sanhedrin, the supreme rabbinic court.</note>, nor do they allow any of the college of Senators to depart until the completion of that day. If he brings forward things worthy of being heard, he shall be listened to, just as ears must be given to the one who is himself exposed to judgment if he mentions things worthy of hearing for his own acquittal. Therefore, if they bring forward those things which are sufficient for acquittal, he is immediately left free. But if they declare less than what is sufficient for acquittal, the pronunciation of the sentence is suspended until the following day, and meanwhile the Senators, two or three at a time, revolve the matter itself throughout that entire night, abstaining from wine all that day and night, and living on light food. Entering the courtroom again in the morning, they bring forward the sentence, first those who acquit, and then those who condemn. Nor is it lawful for him who previously acquitted to condemn thereafter; it is permitted, however, for him who condemned on the previous day to acquit on the following day. If, therefore, from a convention of twenty-three senators, there are twelve who acquit and eleven who condemn, he is immediately released without punishment. If, on the other hand, there are twelve who condemn and eleven who acquit, or eleven acquitting and likewise eleven who condemn, and one affirms himself to be uncertain and ignorant of the sentence to be carried, then senators are added to the previous number in pairs up to seventy-one. Of these, if thirty-six are for acquittal and thirty-five for condemnation, they pronounce the sentence of acquittal. But if thirty-six are for condemnation and thirty-five for acquittal, they then weigh and revolve the matter among themselves until one of those condemning finally adheres to the sentence of those acquitting.

### BY WHAT LAW THEY EXECUTE THE JUDGMENT 
### after the sentence has been passed. CHAPTER VI.

Once the sentence of condemnation is finished, the one about to die is soon led from the courtroom to the place of punishment and execution. And meanwhile, the gatekeeper of the courtroom carries a linen cloth in his hand, to be raised (as the situation requires) as a signal. Another, indeed, sits upon a horse far from the courtroom, yet at such an interval that he can see the gatekeeper looking out at the door of the courtroom with the linens, so that if in that space of time while the guil... <note>The text cuts off mid-word; the Latin "re-" continues as "reus" on the next page.</note>

<header>PAUL RICI'S EPITOME,</header>

...is led. If anyone, for the sake of the acquittal <note>original: "iustificationem," referring to legal exculpation</note> of the condemned, should presume to bring forward any legal warnings, a signal would immediately be raised with cloths <note>The use of flags or cloths as signals to stay an execution is a specific procedural detail in the Talmud (*Mishnah Sanhedrin* 6:1).</note> by a man mounted on a horse in view of the court. Immediately, the judges and officers would be informed so that they might halt their pace for a little while and suspend the punishment of the condemned. Indeed, even if the condemned man himself, who is about to undergo the punishment of death, promises that he has something to say for his own acquittal, he is brought back to the judgment hall even four or five times, provided that he utters something worthy of a hearing. If, therefore, they receive something from him sufficient for acquittal, they reverse the sentence; and he whom they had judged worthy of death a little while before, they now release unpunished. But if they find nothing legally sound for acquittal, they lead the guilty man out again to punishment, with a herald going before him who proclaims by shouting: "This guilty man is being led to be stoned because of such a crime committed by him, based on the testimony of such and such witnesses. If anyone presumes to have anything regarding his acquittal, let him come forward and produce it." 

And when he arrives at the place of execution, at an interval of about ten cubits, he is admonished to perform a confession (as those about to die by judgment are accustomed to do). For all who confess have a portion in the <term>World to Come</term> <note>original: "futuri saeculi" (the world to come/Olam Ha-Ba), the Jewish concept of the afterlife.</note>. If he does not know how to confess, it will be enough to say: "May my death be the remission of all my sins." And when he comes closer, to the space of four cubits from the place of execution, then if it is a male, he is produced naked and covered only at the thigh; if a female, she is produced clothed in a garment. 

The place of stoning, however, was a structure twice the height of a man, higher than the ground, from which the guilty man was cast down by the push of one of the witnesses onto a stone spread on the ground. If he has not yet expired from this fall, immediately the second witness would fall upon his chest <note>original: "præcordia"</note> with a stone. If he did not yet succumb to death from this blow, then the entire multitude of bystanders brought the completion of death by the throwing of stones. It was not permitted for the college of Senators <note>The Sanhedrin.</note> to condemn more than one person to death on the same day. 

Once overwhelmed by stones, a male—but not a female—was immediately hung upon a gallows. The manner of hanging was that a beam was fixed in the ground, at the top of which was inserted a small piece of wood in a semi-forked shape, by which the guilty man himself was suspended with his hands folded. But <term>Rabbi Yosi</term> <note>A prominent 2nd-century CE scholar (Tanna) often quoted in the Talmud.</note> wanted the hanging to be done against a beam leaning against a wall (in the manner of butchers). When the hanging was finished, the corpse was taken down from the gallows and buried in a tomb apart from the others killed by judicial punishment, until the flesh was consumed. Then the bare bones, having been collected, were placed in his own or his father’s sepulcher. Thereupon, the relatives and kinsmen of the deceased go to the judges and witnesses and give them words of greeting, declaring that they bear no hatred against them for the death inflicted, because they clearly recognize that all things were carried out by a right judgment and truthful testimony.

### ON THE FOUR KINDS OF JUDICIAL DEATH,
### and which of the delinquents are killed by stones. CHAPTER VII.

The Senate <note>The Sanhedrin.</note> judges with a fourfold kind of punishment: by stones, by fire, by the sword, and by strangulation of a noose. Regarding the rite of stoning, the things already said above demonstrate it. 

The Law of Burning, however, is that the guilty person is pushed into manure <note>original: "simo," likely a misprint or variant for "fimo" (dung/manure). In the Talmud, the person is placed in dung to keep them upright for the execution.</note> up to the armpits. They cast a hard cloth around his neck, wrapped in a softer cloth; then two people—one on this side, the other on that—tighten the folded cloth until, forced by the necessity of breathing, he opens his mouth wide. Into his mouth a glowing metal rod <note>In the Talmudic description of *serefah* (burning), this is often described as pouring molten lead down the throat so as to burn the internal organs without scarring the body.</note> is immediately inserted, which, penetrating the chest and viscera, instantly burns out the breath of life and consumes it with heat. 

Death by the Sword is inflicted by the amputation of the head. 

Strangulation by a noose is also carried out with a hard cloth wrapped in a softer one, not only until the mouth opens, but until the breath of life is extinguished (like a closed flame). 

Different people are condemned to different punishments of death. For he who has committed incest and disgrace with his mother, with a stepmother, a daughter-in-law, or with a beast, is overwhelmed with stones. So too is the blasphemer, and he who offers his offspring to the idol <term>Molech</term> <note>An ancient Near Eastern deity associated with child sacrifice.</note>, he who consults the spirit of <term>Ou</term> <note>A medium or "ghost" (*Ob* in Hebrew).</note> and the <term>Iedani</term> <note>A "knowing spirit" or familiar (*Yidde'oni* in Hebrew).</note>, the profaner of the Sabbath, he who has cursed his parents, the corrupter of a betrothed girl, the instigator...

->ON TALMUDIC DOCTRINE. 285<-

...to the worship of idols, a subverter of the city, an evildoer, and a rebellious son. They call one an "evildoer" <note>original: *maleficum*</note> not a mere conjuror who deceives the senses, but one who actually commits evil deeds in reality.

### ON THE DEATH OF THE WICKED AND THE RIGHTEOUS,
### ON SLEEP, WINE, AND REST; WHO SHOULD BE PROTECTED, AND HOW
### THE INNOCENT ARE TO BE SAVED FROM THE IMPIETY OF THE PERSECUTOR. CHAPTER VIII.

The rebellious son is not surrendered to death solely for his current fault, but to prevent more shameful crimes in the future <note>The Talmudic reasoning is that a "wayward and rebellious son" is executed for what he will eventually become, as his current trajectory leads inevitably to violent crime.</note>. For the death of the wicked is beneficial both to themselves and to the world. Conversely, the death of the righteous brings loss to both themselves and the world. Sleep and wine are beneficial for the wicked and for the world, but for the righteous, it is the opposite <note>The logic here is that while the wicked sleep or are drunk, they cease from harming others or sinning.</note>. The tranquility of the wicked harms themselves and the world, but the rest of the righteous aids both. Those must be protected whom someone pursues with the intent of killing, or with the lust of natural filthiness, or to ravish a betrothed woman—even if it cannot be done otherwise (if no other way is possible) than by the destruction and death of the pursuer <note>This refers to the legal principle of the *rodef* (pursuer), where lethal force is permitted to save a victim from murder or rape.</note>.

### THOSE CONDEMNED TO FIRE, THOSE CONDEMNED TO THE SWORD, 
### AND THOSE TO BE KILLED WITHOUT A JUDICIAL SENTENCE. CHAPTER IX.

Those who are judged by fire <note>original: *incendio*; in the Talmudic context, this involved pouring molten lead down the throat rather than a pyre.</note> are: one who has sexual relations with a mother and her daughter, a priest’s daughter, his own or his wife’s daughter, his own or his wife’s granddaughter, or his mother-in-law or great-mother-in-law. Homicides and the subverters of men who pollute a city by leading it to worship idols are put to death by the sword. However, a murderer is by no means punished with the sword unless the one he killed was an Israelite, even if only a month old; moreover, it must be done not by accident, but by intent, and with such weapons or projectiles as are fit for inflicting death. He who is guilty of two kinds of death is afflicted only with the more severe one. 

One who, for a capital crime, has once paid the penalty with forty lashes minus one <note>The standard Jewish corporal punishment consisting of 39 lashes.</note> and falls back into the same crime from the start—even a murderer whose deed cannot be proven by all the conditions of testimony—is thrust into a narrow dungeon <note>original: *ergastulum*</note> barely the height of a small man, in which he can neither lie down nor sit, but can only stand on his feet. No food is allowed him except barley, until his belly swells, his bowels burst, and he finally perishes by a wretched death. 

A man who has stolen a censer or that type of sacred vessel, or who has blasphemed the Name of the Tetragrammaton <note>The sacred four-letter name of God, YHWH.</note>, may be killed on the spot by anyone zealous for piety <note>This refers to "zealot justice," where an individual acts without a formal trial in specific cases of public desecration.</note>. A priest <note>original: *flamen*</note> who, being defiled, handles the sacred rites, is not brought to judgment; instead, the chosen of the priests dash out his brains outside the courts of the temple. A stranger <note>original: *alienigena*; referring to a non-priest.</note> who ministers the sacred rites in the sanctuary will be condemned to death not by human judgment, but by divine judgment.

### THOSE STRANGLED BY A NOOSE, AND CONCERNING THE
### TRIPLE SENATE OF JERUSALEM. CHAPTER X.

He is strangled by a noose who strikes a parent, who has kidnapped an Israelite man, an elder who rebels against the senate, a false prophet, a prophet of idols, an adulterer, and witnesses who bear false witness concerning fornication against a priest’s daughter, and he who pollutes the priest's daughter herself. 

There were three orders of senators in Jerusalem: one at the gate of the mountain of the house of the sanctuary; another at the gate of the court; the third in the very inner chamber of the court, built of squared stones <note>This is the *Lishkat HaGazit* or Chamber of Hewn Stone, where the Great Sanhedrin met.</note>. And whatever was ambiguous and needed to be untangled throughout the whole assembly of Israel was first referred to the Senate sitting at the gate of the mountain. If they did not know how to resolve it, they proceeded to the second order at the gate of the court. If that group could not define the cause either, then all went together to the third—which they call the Great Order of Senators—in the inner chambers of the court. To its traditions and decrees the entire multitude and synagogue of Israel offered obedience without any resistance.

<header>THE EPITOME OF PAULUS RICIUS,</header>

# CHAPTER ELEVEN, CALLED HELEK.

<note>original: *Helek*. This is the Hebrew word for "portion," referring to the "portion in the world to come" discussed in this chapter.</note>

->*Who they are who have no portion in the world to come: And on the punishment of the subverted city.*<-

All Israel has a portion in the world to come <note>This famous opening from the Mishnah (Sanhedrin 10:1) suggests a universal baseline of salvation for the Jewish people, which is then narrowed by specific exclusions.</note>. For it is written: *And your people, all of them righteous, shall inherit the land forever.* However, those who are devoid of the world to come include those who deny that the resurrection of the dead is established by the Law <note>The "Law" here refers to the Torah. The Talmudic argument is that if one denies the Torah teaches resurrection, they forfeit their own resurrection.</note>. Additionally, those who refuse to believe that the Law was delivered from heaven, and those who adhere to the opinions of the Epicureans <note>original: *Epicureorum*. In a Jewish context, this term (Apikoros) refers generally to skeptics or those who despise the sages, rather than strictly followers of the Greek philosopher Epicurus.</note>. Rabbi Akiva also said that he has no portion in the world to come who whispers an incantation over a wound to heal it, and whispers the sacred name of God while spitting, for instance by saying: *I will put none of the diseases upon you which I put on Egypt: for I am the Lord <term>Tetragrammaton<gloss>The four-letter, ineffable name of God (YHWH).</gloss></term> your healer.* Rabbi Saul <note>likely referring to Abba Saul</note> also excluded him who pronounces the name of the Tetragrammaton according to its written characters <note>The Name was only permitted to be spoken in the Temple; elsewhere, it was substituted with "Adonai."</note>. There are three kings and four commoners <note>original: *idiotæ*, meaning private citizens or those without official religious rank.</note> who are not participants in the world to come: the kings are Jeroboam, Ahab, and Manasseh. But Rabbi Judah asserted that King Manasseh does have a portion in the world to come, because it is written: *And he prayed to him, and He heard his prayer, and brought him back to Jerusalem into his kingdom.* To this, the opponents respond that He brought him back indeed to his kingdom, but by no means into the life of the world to come. The four commoners are Balaam, Doeg, Ahitophel, and Gehazi. The generation that perished in the disaster of the waters <note>The Great Flood of Noah.</note> has no portion in the world to come, because it is written: *My spirit shall not remain in man forever.* It is as if he said: there shall be neither judgment for him, nor spirit. The generation whose languages were confused and divided <note>The builders of the Tower of Babel.</note> has no portion in the world to come, because it writes: *He scattered them from that place over the face of the whole earth.* A little after it adds: *The Lord scattered them over the face of the whole earth:* for He scattered them in the present age, and thereafter in the world to come. The men of Sodom have no portion in the world to come, because it is written: *But the men of Sodom were very wicked and sinners before God.* They were indeed very wicked in this age, and very great sinners toward the world to come; nevertheless, they shall rise in the judgment. But Rabbi Nehemiah contends that neither of these generations will rise in the judgment, because it is written: *Therefore the wicked shall not rise in judgment, nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous.* "The wicked shall not rise"—that is, the generation of the deluge—"in the judgment"; "And sinners in the assembly of the righteous"—that is, the men of Sodom. To this the others respond: They shall not rise to life in the assembly of the righteous, but they shall rise in the assembly of the wicked. The spies of the land of Canaan have no portion in the world to come, because it writes: *Those who brought an evil report of the land died and were struck down in the sight of God.* They died indeed in this age, and were struck down in the future. The generation that fell in the desert has no portion in the world to come, nor shall they rise (according to the teachings of Rabbi Akiva) in the judgment, because it writes: *In this wilderness they shall be consumed and there they shall die.* But Rabbi Eliezer thought that it was said of this very generation in the Psalms: *Gather to me my holy ones, who have made a covenant with me over sacrifice.* The assembly of Korah (namely, the one stirring up sedition against Moses) shall not rise, nor shall it ascend at the last, because it writes: *And the earth covered them, and they perished from the midst of the multitude:* for they were covered by the ground in the present age, and perished from the midst of the multitude in the world to come. But Rabbi Eliezer thinks that passage of the Book of Kings was spoken of them: *The Lord kills and brings to life, he leads down to the grave and brings back.* The Ten Tribes (whom Sennacherib the King of the Assyrians sent into exile) shall not return in the future, just as Rabbi Akiva taught, because it writes: *And he cast them into a foreign land, as it is this day.* For just as a day that has passed never returns, so they shall not return. However, Rabbi Eliezer felt that just as the day turns into darkness and passes back again into light, so also the ten tribes who now live in darkness shall at the last rise into the light. The men of a city turned away to the worship of idols <note>Known as the *Ir Ha-Nidachat* or "Apostate City."</note> have no portion in the world to come, because it is written: *Children of Belial have gone out from your midst and have led away the inhabitants of their city.* They are not, however, to be judged to death unless the city is subverted...

<header>ON TALMUDIC DOCTRINE.</header>
<sig>QVII.</sig>

<note>original: *aversae*. This refers to the "subverted" or "wayward" city described in Deuteronomy 13, which has been led away into idolatry.</note>...if the inhabitants have turned away, and those who belong to the same tribe and make up the greater part of the city are the ones subverted, and if these subverters are men and not women. But if women, or children, or those who are not inhabitants of the city, or a smaller part of the city were subverted, then those who have turned away are not judged by the Law usually applied to a subverted multitude. Instead, they are condemned as private delinquents, each of whom requires the testimony and warning of two witnesses. And in this regard, the punishment for private individuals was more severe than for the multitude: for the punishment of private individuals was carried out by stoning alone without a monetary fine. However, a multitude is judged by the sword, along with the loss of their wealth. Mule-drivers and carriers, who wander from place to place, are to be protected from the strike upon the subverted city, because it is written: *You shall surely strike the inhabitants of that city with the edge of the sword, destroying it utterly, and all that is in it, and its cattle.* From this, it is gathered that the property of the righteous which is found inside the city perishes; however, those things which were outside remain unharmed. But the wealth of the impious, both what is outside and what is inside, is destroyed, for it is written: *And you shall gather all its spoil into the middle of its street.* If the city itself lacks streets, one must be built; but if there is a street outside the city, all the spoils must be brought there, because it is written: *You shall burn the city with fire, and all its spoil, to consume it as a whole burnt offering to the Lord your God.* From the fact that the letter of the text specifies "its spoil," it was intended that spoil dedicated to sacred use be excluded and saved. Therefore, they decreed that consecrated items found in the city must be redeemed; and that the first fruits (namely, those not yet offered to the Priest) must be left to spontaneous decay. Second tithes <note>The "Second Tithe" (Maaser Sheni) was a portion of produce to be eaten by the owner in Jerusalem; here, the law discusses its disposal if the owner's city is destroyed.</note> and the Volumes of Holy Scripture <term>Hagiographa<gloss>The third section of the Hebrew Bible, including Psalms and Proverbs</gloss></term> are to be hidden away so that they do not come into use. Rabbi Simon taught that it was said: *You shall consume it as a whole burnt offering to the Lord your God.* By this, he suggests that he who rightly judges a subverted city with judgment shall be regarded just as if he had offered a complete and pleasing burnt offering. It is written thereafter: *And it shall be a perpetual mound; it shall not be built again,* meaning it is a sin to cultivate gardens or orchards in that place, as was the opinion of the Galilean Rabbi Jose. But Rabbi Akiva affirms, from what is read—*It shall not be built again*—that one should not hear this as a prohibition of every structure, but only of that which is similar to the prior building; it does not prohibit cultivating gardens or orchards there. The clause is added: *Nothing of that accursed thing shall cling to your hand,* because as long as the impious inhabit the world, anger and fury turn within the age; once they are driven out and eliminated, distress, fury, and anger are soon removed, and tranquil peace is lived everywhere throughout the world.

# OF PAULUS RICIUS,

## ON THE NINE-FOLD ORDER OF DOCTRINES,
## AND ON THE COHERENCE AND CONNECTION OF THE
## WHOLE PERIPATETIC DOCTRINE, TO THOSE
## zealous for sincere truth, a Compendium.

### *PREFACE ON THE NOVENARY ORDER*
### *of Doctrine.*

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'V' featuring a man sitting amongst scrolling vines and foliage.</image-desc>
The contemplation of truth is not the accumulation of words, nor does it receive increase according to the multitude of arguments; for there is but one cause of a single kind for one thing to be contemplated, and one effect through itself primarily. For this reason, regarding the order of doctrine—in the understanding of which many Moderns <note>original: *Neoterici*. Ricius refers to contemporary scholars or "New Men" who he feels lack the clarity of the ancients.</note> miserably grope and stumble about—I wish to take up a clearer discourse and will endeavor, by the will of the heavens, to achieve this in a brief Compendium. Nor does my intention seek anywhere to "expand the phylacteries" <note>A biblical metaphor (Matthew 23:5) used here to mean Ricius does not want to make his books unnecessarily long or ostentatious.</note> of my volumes by recounting history in other doctrines, or by setting up a wrestling-match of arguments in them with strained strength; instead, we propose to explain the obscure and hidden truth. Indeed, just as the straight is the index of itself and of the crooked, so also the exposed truth presents itself as the judge of itself and of falsehood. Since Galen touches upon the business of this examination in the introduction to the *Microtechnos* <note>Galen's *Ars Medica*, a foundational medical textbook in the Middle Ages and Renaissance, often called the "Small Art."</note>; therefore, I will explain that very thing according to the context of the words: first, however, I will show in a few words what doctrine is, what order is, what its necessity and excellence are, and finally how many kinds of order are given in doctrine.

<vocab>Talmudica doctrina (Talmudic doctrine), Paulus Ricius (Humanist scholar and physician), Peripatetici (Followers of Aristotle), Compendium (A concise summary), Neoterici (Modern scholars), Galenus (Ancient Greek physician), Microtechnos (Galen's Art of Medicine), Anathemate (Something cursed or set apart), Rabi Simon (Simeon bar Yochai), Rabi Ekiua (Akiva ben Joseph)</vocab>

It then introduces a new philosophical work by Paulus Ricius on the "Nine-fold Order" of knowledge, aiming to clarify the organization of doctrine for contemporary students.</summary>

# THE COMPENDIUM OF PAULUS RICIUS,
<meta>catchword: necessity; faint show-through from verso</meta>

-> WHAT LEARNING IS. <-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' depicting a seated figure, likely a scholar or saint, inside a square frame with floral motifs.</image-desc>**LEARNING**, as far as it concerns us and the nature of the thing, is an **intellectual habit** <note>original: *habitus intellectiuus*. In Renaissance philosophy, a "habit" is not a routine behavior, but a stable, acquired quality of the mind—a state of "having" knowledge.</note>, gathered from several knowable things, which we explain by voice and in writing, as if by certain signs. I say "from several knowable things" because, just as we do not call someone a geometer simply because they have mastered one geometric conclusion—just as we do not call the conclusion itself "geometry," but rather "geometric"—nor do we call someone a **Doctor** <note>The Latin *Doctor* literally means "Teacher."</note> by the absolute title from the single act of teaching one conclusion. In this same way, we have not called a single demonstrated conclusion "learning." 

The reason is this: a habit takes its name from the act, and the act from the object. And just as an object is not called such, nor is it simply such, because its smallest part exists as such, but because it is such according to all or most of its parts—for example, a feverish person is not said to be "cured" simply because their nausea, suffering, and the onset of shivering have been removed. Thus, the person who removed these things, or knows the Rule for removing them, is not yet called a healer or a physician. But he will be called "cured" when the thirst, the headache, the loss of appetite, the damage to other faculties, and finally that foreign heat that occupies the heart and viscera, has vanished. And he who has driven away such symptoms and weakness, or knows how to drive them away, truly deserves to be called a healer and physician. 

If, therefore, we are to use names as the majority or the wise use them, it follows that whenever we read the name of "learning" in a simple utterance, we are referring to the habit of not just one, but many conclusions. This is proved by the discourse of Galen <note>Galen of Pergamum (129–216 AD) was the most influential physician and medical philosopher of antiquity.</note> here (as the very series of words shows), especially in this passage: *For all things are easily memorable enough through the dissolution of the limits.* For if he had called the concept of a single conclusion "learning," it would be absurd to say "all things are easily memorable." Indeed, the **syncategorema** <note>A logical term for words like "all," "none," or "every" that modify the subject or predicate.</note> "all" indicates not just one, but many knowable things. 

Furthermore, since the tenacity of memory for one thing is equal to that of another single thing, the ease of remembering would not be greater in the "definitive" order of learning than in the "resolutive" or "compositive" orders—yet Galen taught the opposite in that same place. From this, the error of those who think that the way of learning should be heard solely through the order of demonstrating and defining is first uncovered. Since the method of demonstrating and defining can be exercised concerning a single conclusion, nothing at all would stand in the way of the ease of memory being equal in the compositive and resolutive orders as in the definitive, because a single conclusion, whether demonstrated or defined, produces a firm and stable concept. Galen, however, attributes the ease of memory only to definitive learning. Moreover, because learning shows the habit of many knowable things, the method of demonstrating will not be the primary order of learning; for such an order only relates the thing sought to the "middle term," but does not consider the relationship of many knowable things or sought-after things to each other—to which we have shown the name of "learning" is properly accommodated, as you will be able to understand more clearly a little later.

**ORDER** is a suitable proportion of several things according to what comes before and what comes after. And for that reason, it is written in the first book of *On the Parts of Animals*: *All things that exist by nature are arranged in a certain order, so that this is first, and that is second.* I say "suitable proportion" because even disorder is a proportion of some things, but it is by no means a "suitable" one. # ON THE THRICE-TRIPLE ORDER OF LEARNING.

...the multitude of knowable things produces. For just as the same matter cannot exist under several actually sensible forms, so neither can a sense be informed by several sensible things, nor can the **reason** be simultaneously informed by several **intelligible species** <note>original: *specieb[us] intelligibilibus*. In Scholastic philosophy, a "species" is the mental image or form that allows the mind to recognize a thing.</note>; rather, one must come first, and another later. Where there is a "before" and an "after," there is also **order**. Since, therefore, all learning requires several things to be known, it is necessary that it also respect order.
<margin>Commentary 24.</margin>
The excellence of order is so great that **Aristotle**, in the third book of *On the Heavens*, declares it to be the nature of sensible things—not because order is the essence or substance of a thing, but because it is the arrangement of things, which the form of the thing immediately follows. Hence, **Plato** said that an unordered being is a non-being. And in the *Timaeus*, he wished for the world to be called "created" because it was reduced from disorder into order, the example and likeness of which is demonstrated by the arrangement of letters. For example, the letters **m. l. a. a.**, placed in this way, offer no defined concept in Latin speech; but if you arrange the same letters in a suitable series, such as **a. l. m. a.**, they show something **holy** <note>original: *sanctam*. The word *alma* means nourishing or kind, often associated with the divine (as in *Alma Mater*).</note>; yet if you transfer them into another order, such as **m. a. l. a.**, they then designate something **evil** <note>original: *malam*.</note>. Therefore, the same elements indicate no concept at all without the harmony of order, but when placed in one suitable order or another, they announce opposites: namely, now the holy, now the evil. Since, finally, nature constitutes nothing unordered, and learning is an imitator of the nature of things, it is proven that learning also consists of a certain fixed order. Added to this is the fact that order—as we read in the book *On Memory and Reminiscence*—renders learning itself easier to understand and remember. The reason is this: those things that possess order look toward one another by a certain innate **symbol** <note>original: *symbolo*. Here used in the sense of a shared token or connecting link.</note>. Since the transition is easier between things that share a symbol, it must be concluded that the transition of memory is far easier from one thing to another when they possess order than when moving toward something lacking order. Thus far regarding learning and order. We shall soon endeavor to explain how many kinds of order there are in learning.

### THE VARIOUS KINDS OF ORDER IN LEARNING.

There are three genera of orders given in learning. First, the **order of things sought**, which by primary reasoning we call the "order of learning." Second, the **order of means**, which we call the "order of demonstrations." Third, the **order of the means to the thing sought**, which it has pleased us to call the "order of demonstrating." Again, we know that each of these is divided into a triple order, like a genus into species: namely, into the **resolutive** <term>original: *resolutiuum*. An analytic method that works backward from a goal to the principles needed to achieve it.</term>, which excels the others in origin, certainty, and nobility; the **compositive** <term>original: *compositiuum*. A synthetic method that builds up from principles to a conclusion.</term>, which is later in certainty and origin; and the **definitive**, which is last in origin and certainty. Any perfect learning must employ these three genera of orders, though the same learning cannot consist of every species of these genera at once. Indeed, it stands that the order of demonstrations may be resolutive, the order of learning definitive, and the order of demonstrating compositive—or vice versa, and interchangeably, as the nature of the division allows. 
Having set these things down as a preface, we shall soon attempt to prove them with reasons and support them with examples.

## THAT THREE GENERA OF ORDER ARE GIVEN IN LEARNING, 
## and the reasoning behind each name.

That three genera of orders are given in learning can be seen from the elements of which learning consists. For every branch of learning consists of **things sought** and **means**. Where there are things sought and means, a triple relationship is necessarily observed: namely, of things sought to things sought, of means to means, and of the means to the thing sought. Since, therefore, order is nothing other than the suitable relationship of things according to a "before" and "after," it follows that if there are such suitable relationships (that is, ones that imitate nature), there are as many genera of orders as there are common relationships of this kind. Since three have been found, there are certainly three [genera] of orders in learning...

# PAUL RICIUS’S COMPENDIUM,

...it is necessary that [three] genera emerge. Of these, we call the first the **order of teaching** <note>original: *ordinem doctrinae*</note> (specifically concerning the **things sought** <note>original: *quaesitorum*</note>). This is because that which we are taught deserves to be named "teaching" more than the means by which we are taught; for everything should be named from its internal essence rather than from something added to it. We are taught the things sought, and the means are those things by which we are taught. Therefore, the name "teaching" fits better when we look at the mutual relationship of the things sought rather than the means.

Second, we have assigned the **order of demonstrations** to the category of **means** <note>original: *mediorum*, referring to the "middle terms" in a logical syllogism</note>, because the "means" contains the entire power of a demonstration. Indeed, this order deals with several means or several demonstrations. However, the **order of demonstrating** <note>original: *ordo demonstrandi*</note>, which we subjoin immediately, can belong to only one demonstration regarding a thing sought. I use the term "demonstration" here to refer to whatever leads to the knowledge of one of the four "things sought" <note>The four traditional Aristotelian questions: whether a thing is, what it is, what qualities it has, and why it is.</note>. By extending the vocabulary in this way, I have chosen to call a **definition** a demonstration, because it "shows" what a thing is.

The third order (which revolves between the things sought and the means) we call the **order of demonstrating**. This is because the vigor of demonstrating consists in nothing other than the relationship <note>original: *habitudine*</note> of the means to the thing sought. If this relationship were lacking, no act of demonstrating would be possible. Therefore, as many distinctions as this relationship undergoes, just as many demonstrations lie beneath it.

->EACH OF THE THREE KINDS IS<-
->completed in a triple order of species.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' with floral scrollwork within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>That each of these kinds is further divided into a threefold order is evident from this: in every thing, one finds the **whole** and the **parts**, or that which takes the place of a whole and a part. This is seen in simple substances which, even if they do not possess a real distinction of parts, possess a formal distinction, as they say. Where there is a whole and parts, a triple relationship and a triple order are entirely visible: either you begin from the whole and go to the parts, or from part to part—and this in two ways: namely, from a part that is prior by nature to a part that is posterior by nature, or by a reversed path from a posterior part to a part that is prior by nature.

A fourth order—namely, from the parts to the whole—is not granted. To proceed from the parts to the whole implies a two-fold meaning: either one proceeds to the whole from the parts taken all at once, or from one after another. If from the parts taken all at once, it is the same as the first order, because parts taken together are nothing other than the whole. Even if you say (as some opinions hold) that the whole is distinct from its parts, such a process would still not help the **order of teaching**. The process of teaching goes from things more known to us toward things less known. Since the whole is always more known than the parts, a progression from the parts to the whole would be useless, because it would go from the less known to the more known.

Remember this: whenever I say the whole is "more known" than the parts, always understand it in a **formal sense**—that is, taking the whole as a whole and the parts as parts. For the parts of a definition are more known than the thing defined, but not insofar as they take on the role of a "part"; for no part can be said of the whole by itself. However, any part of a definition acts as a whole, because it designates the thing defined by a distinct concept before the definition is even completed. Thus, a process from the parts taken together toward the whole cannot provide an order of teaching. If you say the process is from parts taken not all at once, but individually and step-by-step toward the whole, it will emerge as the same as the second or third progression.

But this one thing must not be overlooked: there are two types of **priority of nature**. One is from thought, or intention, or reason, which **Aristotle** hints at in the first book of the *Metaphysics*, saying: "that which is posterior in generation is prior in nature." And in *On the Parts of Animals*: "form is prior by nature, matter is posterior." Another priority of nature is given in **operation**, about which he speaks in the first book of the *Posterior Analytics*. He says: "Things that are further from the senses are prior in an absolute sense." Regarding this, one also reads in the beginning of the *Physics*: "It is necessary to proceed from things more certain to us—that is, the more confused and universal things—into things more certain and prior by nature." To understand these, **Averroes** <note>original: *Auerrois*, the famous 12th-century Islamic commentator on Aristotle.</note> says in his second commentary on *The Physics* <note>original: *de auditu*</note>: "The first in thought is the last in action; and the first in action is the last in thought." For nature, in operat-

...[gather]ing the effect from causes, and the whole from the parts; therefore, nature, in its operation, encounters the causes before the effect, and the parts before the whole. To us, however, it is the opposite: the whole is known to us before the parts, and the effect before the causes. ### DIGRESSION ON THE FIRST THING KNOWN.

Let not those things disturb you which seem less consistent in the readings of Aristotle. In the preface to the *Physics* <note>original: *physicorum libri praefatione*</note>, he says that things more universal are better known to us. Yet in the *Posterior Analytics* <note>original: *posterioribus... Analeticis*</note>, he affirms that things less universal are better known to us. These are less known and posterior to nature, even though (according to our aforementioned view) in both cases he is speaking of priority in operation. At the start of that same *Physics*, he teaches sometimes that composites—which are particulars—and sometimes that universals are better known. Again, in both the *Analytics* and the *Physics*, we read that what is better known to us is not the same as what is better known to nature. 

Now, he seems to have established the opposite by determining that the "particular whole" is better known to us than its parts, and that it is likewise better known to nature, because the particular whole is posterior in generation to its parts. But that which is posterior in generation is prior in nature (says Aristotle); therefore, the same whole is better known both to us and to nature. If you hold to the aforementioned distinction regarding the twofold priority of nature, and this small distinction which we add below, you will not need to wander through so many diversions and steep bypasses. 

Although this discussion on the "first thing known" seems to exceed the limits of our task, I thought this doubt should be removed so the reader's mind is not left wavering. Be forewarned: that *which* we understand is one thing; that *by which* we understand is another. It is a common saying (gathered from *Metaphysics*, book 2) that things stand in the same law regarding their knowable truth as they do in their existence. But in the existence of sensible things, the thing *which* exists is one thing, and that *by which* it exists is another. <margin>Commentary 24.</margin> For that which exists (as Aristotle taught in *Metaphysics*, book 7) is the composite itself, and whatever integral parts are within it. That *by which* it exists, however, is the rationale and the form, and whatever formal parts or rational principles are within it.

Having perceived these things, we say and assert three points: 
**First**, what is known first to us is less universal; but that *by which* it is first known is more universal. 
**Second**, comparing the "whole-which" and the "whole-by-which" to one another: the "whole-which" (that is, the composite) will be posterior and less known to nature in thought than the "whole-by-which" (that is, the specific form). In operation, however, it is the reverse. 
**Third**, we say that the "whole-which" and the "whole-by-which"—each being related to its own parts (the "whole-which" to its component parts, the "whole-by-which" to its formal parts)—are always more universal and more remote from the whole, and thus better known to nature in its working and producing. In thought, however, they are more unknown and posterior. But the less universal thing—namely the whole itself, and that which is closer to the whole—is posterior to nature both in thought and in operation.

For a clearer understanding of these things, it must be said: because the intellect conceives nothing (according to the course of nature) except what the common sense offers to it, therefore what is first sensed is first understood. The singular composite whole is sensed before its parts. For Aristotle says the whole is better known according to the sense; therefore, the whole or the singular universal is understood before its parts. <margin>Commentary 51.</margin> And Averroes <note>A 12th-century philosopher known as "The Commentator" on Aristotle.</note> taught this in the introduction to the *Physics*, saying: "From the fact that this universe (that is, the whole) is better known to the senses than its causes, it is the reason why universal things understood are better known to the intellect than the parts understood." These are his words. 

The reason why the whole offers itself to the senses and intellect before the parts is this: both sensitive and intellective knowledge are of some distinct being, insofar as it is distinct. Hence matter, because it is indistinct, is unknowable except through **analogy** <term>analogy: understanding an unknown thing by its relationship to a known thing</term>. But as we read in *Metaphysics*, book 12, nothing distinguishes except an **act** <note>original: *actus*, the state of being "actually" something as opposed to just having the potential</note>. Therefore, that which is first offered to us as an act is itself known first; and the whole is offered first. For (as is written in the first book of *On the Heavens*), the whole and the perfect are the same; but the perfect is the same as an **existing act**,
