# PAUL RICIUS'S COMPENDIUM.
<meta>catchword: common</meta>

...[being in] act; therefore, any whole, insofar as it is a whole, exists in **act**—that is, in a complete state. The parts, however, exist in **potentiality** or in a diminished state of act. But since there are many parts by which a whole is fashioned, which neither the senses nor reason can conceive all at once, it is necessary to conceive them in succession: first one, then another. Moreover, that which is closer to the "first conceivable thing" is conceived first. The first thing we can conceive is the composite whole; therefore, the part that is closer and more immediate to the whole is conceived first. Such a part is one that is more singular. Conversely, a part more remote from the whole—which is more universal—is conceived later. By "universal," I do not mean a concept that reason fashions within itself, but rather the foundation and the underlying nature which impresses a universal concept upon us.

For example, when I see Socrates, a likeness of the whole is formed in me before the image of his face, arms, and hands. From there (provided no gap of space or other object prevents it), the whole of the face, arms, and hands is conceived before their <term>homogeneous parts (parts made of the same substance throughout)</term>, namely the skin, flesh, nerves, and bones. Furthermore, these homogeneous parts become known before their internal temperament <note>original: *complexio*</note>, and this temperament before the elements. The elements are known before the matter and the form <note>Aristotle's theory that all things are made of matter (potential) and form (the defining essence)</note>.

In this progression, we always advance from the less universal to the more universal. For Socrates, who first offers himself as a whole, is entirely "incommunicable" <note>Unique to himself; cannot be shared by others</note>; he cannot, as Socrates, produce a concept in us that could apply to anyone else. But the face, arms, and hands are indeed "communicable"—not that these specific parts can be shared, for they are individual and singular, but they instill such a concept that is not incompatible with being applied to any human being. For a face, arms, and hands belong to every person, whereas the personhood of Socrates is shared with no one.

Again, the concept impressed by skin, flesh, nerve, and bone is even more communicable, because we recognize that this belongs not only to humans but to any perfect genus of living creatures. Likewise, a temperament <note>original: *complexio*</note> is more universal, as it exists not only in living things but also in every individual mixed body. Finally, matter and form are the most universal, as they constitute every single natural body.

Conclude, therefore, that what is understood first is less common and exists closer to the senses. However, that the *means* by which we first understand is more universal is demonstrated by both reason and the experience of knowing. Reason is drawn from the way the senses know and from the way nature acts.

First, the argument is as follows: The intellect understands under an "intelligible aspect" <note>original: *ratione*</note> in the same way the senses first conceive under a "sensible aspect." For just as the intellect first understands what is first offered to the sense, so too the intellect conceives it under an intelligible aspect similar to the sensible aspect by which the sense perceives it. But the sense-object first offers itself to the sense under a more common sensible aspect; therefore, the intelligible object is offered to the intellect under a more common intelligible aspect. 

For instance, the formal object of sight—the aspect under which it sees visible things—is color. Since color contains many different variations, <margin>Commentary 1, 44.</margin> there is necessarily some less common aspect than the general "aspect of color" (such as whiteness, blackness, and the like) which the sense judges equally. For the sense judges (as Averroes <note>The famous 12th-century Moorish philosopher who commented on Aristotle</note> writes in *On the Soul*, book 2) its own sensible object and the differences within that object. Yet the sense first judges universally under the common aspect of its sensible object before judging under the specific aspect. Thus, the intellect also first judges under a more common intelligible aspect.

This reason is also drawn from the way nature acts: those things which act by nature first produce what is more potential and imperfect before producing what is distinct in act and perfect. Both the sensible and intelligible object act upon the power of comprehension by the pure force of nature. For this action precedes every act of the will; therefore, it first impresses a sensible or intelligible <term>species (a mental image or form)</term> that is more potential and indistinct. Since such a species is more common, it follows that both the intellect and the sense conceive their object first under a more common species or aspect, and later under a less common one. By these points, it is finally proved that the means by which we first understand is more universal. 

The same is shown by experience, which we perceive daily in our own process of knowing. For whenever I see Socrates, I first conceive of him through the common sense...

# ON THE THREEFOLD ORDER OF TEACHING.

...[in a] common [way], under the concept of the first <term>common sensible (a quality like size or movement that can be perceived by more than one sense)</term>, namely as having dimension, or magnitude, or as a "quantum" [quantity], without whose concept no sensible thing can be perceived. Soon the intellect conceives the same thing under the concept of the first <term>intelligible (a concept understood by the mind rather than felt by the senses)</term>, namely as **being** <note>original: *ens*</note>, without whose concept no intelligible thing is intelligible. But because the mind judges that "being" to be extended in space, it therefore conceives it as a **body**.

Next, the senses judge that "Socrates is moving," which follows the common sensible of motion; and soon reason supposes that he is **animate** [alive]. Again, the senses judge that this very thing which moves has an **upright figure**, which is the third common sensible. The other two common sensibles, namely **number** and **rest**, consist in privation (as <term>Aristotle (the Greek philosopher whose logic dominated medieval thought)</term> taught), and then reason judges that this very thing is a **man**. 

From there, when the senses perceive the specific mode of these sensibles—namely, that he is of a certain size, performing a certain action or movement, and having a certain figure—and joins these with other common and specific perceptions, reason immediately perceives that this is **Socrates**. And thus, finally, if you look more clearly at this way of knowing, you will plainly see that nature proceeds with the same step in its physical operations as the human mind and senses do in their way of knowing.

Therefore (to summarize the matter briefly), when someone asks you what is known first and what is known later in Socrates, say: the **whole individual Socrates** is known first; the face, arms, and hands later. Then the flesh, nerves, and bones. Even later, the temperament <note>original: *complexio*, referring to the balance of bodily humors</note>; then the elements; and finally **matter and form**. And so, the less universal always becomes known first.

If, however, the person asks under what concept or reason Socrates and the individual things we mentioned are presented first and later, respond: they are always presented first under the **more universal** concept. For "being" (insofar as it is being) is more universal than "corporeal being" [a physical body]. A body is more universal than a "moving and animate being." And these are more universal than "upright stature" and "man." These, in turn, are more common than "three-cubits tall," "fast," "lean," and "Socrates." In a similar way, when the face, arms, hands, flesh, bone, and that sort of thing offer themselves under various concepts, the one under the more universal concept always becomes known first. 

And so the first of the three points we proposed is now sufficiently stated. 

The **second point**—namely, that the <term>formal whole (the "whole-by-which" a thing is what it is, like the soul or the design)</term> is better known in thought than the <term>material whole (the "whole-which" is the actual physical object)</term>, and vice versa in physical operation—is apparent from this: the formal whole is like an **end** [a goal]. The material whole is the composite itself, which acts as the material and is ordered toward that end. Therefore, since the end is first in thought and reason, but last in the finished work, and since those things ordered toward the end are first in the physical operation but last in the mind's intention, it follows that: the **formal whole** is first in thought but last in operation; the **material whole** is the opposite.

The **third statement** is concluded by the same argument. For a "whole," insofar as it is a whole, holds the rank of an **end**. The **parts**, however, hold the rank of those things that lead to the end; and a part that is closer to the whole will be closer to the end, while one further from the whole will be further from the end. Since, therefore, the end is first in thought but last in operation, it follows that the **whole** is first in thought, and what is closer to the whole is earlier in thought but later in the physical work. Conversely, what is further from the whole will be first in operation and later in being known.

Since, therefore, what is further from the whole is **more universal**, and what is closer is **less universal**, it is concluded that: in any whole, the **more universal** is later in thought and first in operation. The **less universal** is first in thought and later in operation. 

Having established these things, you can easily untie every knot of this ambiguity. For in the <term>*Posterior Analytics* (Aristotle's book on how we gain scientific knowledge)</term>, where the author treats "intentions" (or things as they are understood), the discussion is about how a thing is understood. And regarding the priority of knowledge for nature in its operation—by which priority (as we showed in the third statement) the **more universal** is always better known to nature. # PAULUS RICIUS'S COMPENDIUM.

...is better known to us (as the first saying commemorates). Just as <term>Averroes (the 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to Renaissance thought)</term> more clearly testifies in that place. For he says: "That which is prior by nature is not prior to us in knowledge in all things: because sensible, composite things are prior in knowledge to us, while simple things, from which composites are made, are better known to nature." 

And these simple things are far removed from the senses—that is, the mind grasps them later—if they are among those things whose nature allows them to be perceived by sense. In short, things far from the senses are **universal things**. Things near to sense, and better known to it, are **particular things**: that is, composite existing realities. Thus says Averroes. 

If you examine these words correctly and diligently, you can easily understand that the opinion of almost everyone mentioned is contained within them. The beginning of the <term>Physics (Aristotle's foundational work on the natural world)</term> points toward the same meaning: "The same things," it says, "are not known to us and known simply [by nature], but composite things are better known to us." For here, the discussion is also about **that which is known** <note>original: *de eo quod cognoscitur*</note>, and about priority in the operation of nature. 

But when it is immediately added there: "Wherefore it is necessary to proceed from universals to particulars," then the discussion concerns **the way by which we know** <note>original: *de eo quo cognoscimus*</note>. The reason why <term>Aristotle</term> first spoke about the *what* and now speaks about the *how* we understand, is because there are two primary and most noteworthy processes and orders of teaching (as you will hear in what follows). 

The **process of demonstration**, which turns between the thing sought and the "middle" <note>the "middle term" in a logical argument that connects a subject to its properties</note>; and the order or process to which the **order of teaching** <note>original: *ordo doctrinae*</note> is especially and appropriately assigned, by which the things sought regard one another in turn. Regarding both of these processes, Aristotle wished to hint at what Averroes, the commentator, clearly declares in the same place, saying: "And the reason why it was necessary for the demonstrations of this science to be **signs** <note>logical proofs that move from an effect back to its cause, rather than from cause to effect</note> is to go from what is better known to us toward what is more hidden. We must also proceed in teaching from universal things to particulars." Thus says Averroes. 

Therefore, the first process properly regards the *object* which is known in natural things. For the natural craftsman <note>the scientist or researcher</note> contemplates nothing except as it exists with sensible matter and motion; such is the composite object itself. The second process, however, because it respects only the order and distinction of teaching, therefore does not concern the **what** itself, but the **how** we understand. For the distinction and order are not made by the *what*—that is, the material substance and foundation—but by the **formality** <note>the specific perspective or logical framework from which something is viewed</note>, or the reason, and the *how*. 

For example, both the <term>Logician</term> and the <term>Philosopher</term> treat the **predicaments** <note>Aristotle's categories of being, such as quality, quantity, and place</note>; they do not differ in the variety of the foundation or the *what* itself, but are distinguished only by different ways of considering them. The Logician considers these things as they fall under a concept; but the **Metaphysician** considers them as they suggest **simple essences** <note>original: *simplices quidditates*</note>. Again, the natural philosopher and the practitioner of medicine both consider the human body, but the former considers it as a part of a "mobile being," while the latter considers it as something "healable by art." In the same way, both the physicist and the contemplator of the stars <note>astronomer</note> examine the same mode and the same figure, but the physicist looks at these as the attributes of a natural body, while the astronomer contemplates them as having a certain quantity, proportion, or aspect. The same rule applies to other judgments. 

Therefore, if you ponder these things diligently within yourself, you will be able to very easily solve and explain everything that seems doubtful or contradictory in these readings of Aristotle. The second point (namely, how the same thing appears better known to us and to nature) is also clearly established from the aforementioned distinction between the **how** and the **what**. For the "whole" (as the second saying commemorates) is twofold: there is the **what** itself (the composite whole) and the **how** itself (the formal whole or the specific form). 

Therefore, when Aristotle writes that what is "later in generation is prior in nature," his intention is not regarding the priority of the *what* (the physical object), but as the *how* and the formal reason. For the **formal whole** is prior by nature (as we explained before) to the **composite whole**. And therefore, the priority of the thing which Aristotle says is later in generation refers to the formal whole. Since that is later and less known to us (as we have said) than the composite whole, because it is less universal than the parts. But speaking of the composite whole, then nothing prevents

## ON THE THREEFOLD ORDER OF DOCTRINES. 295

...not that the same thing is better known to us and to nature in thought: for as is concluded in the second saying, the whole, when related to its own parts, is always "better known to nature" than the parts are. But our knowledge of the whole differs from the knowledge nature has of that same whole in this: we first conceive of the thing that is a whole, but not under the concept of its "wholeness." Instead, we see it under a general concept—which some call **confused knowledge** <note>original: *noticiam confusam*</note>. For example, in conceiving of Socrates or "man," what I conceive is a whole (namely, a man), but I do not first conceive of him specifically *as* a man, but rather as a body. Nature, however, conceives of man first under the concept of wholeness—that is, as a man—which others call **distinct knowledge**. If you reflect on this yourself, you will easily be able to judge the threefold order of any kind, and you will be able to avoid and remove so many entanglements of questions and laborious examinations.

Returning, then, to where the discourse led us, we must speak. It has now been shown that a two-part <term>priority of nature</term> exists: namely, in thought and in operation, when we assert that there is one order starting from the part which is "prior by nature" toward the part which is "posterior [later] by nature." Here, the discussion concerns **priority in thought**. We read that <term>Aristotle</term> frequently called this "priority by nature," and often "priority by reason" <note>original: *prioritatem ratione*</note>. For example, in the second book of *On the Soul*: "Acts are prior to powers according to reason." And in *Metaphysics*, book 9: "Act is prior to power by reason." Elsewhere, however, he calls the same thing "priority by nature," such as: "That which is later in generation is prior in nature." Moreover, it is established (and read in *Metaphysics* 9) that what is later in generation is the **act**. Therefore, the same "act" will be prior by nature, which he just before established as prior by reason. And in *On Interpretation*, book 2: "Those things which are in act along with possibility are prior by nature and posterior in time." Finally, summarize from all these things mentioned here: 

Since in every thing there appears a "whole" and "parts," a threefold relationship and a threefold order of knowing is discerned in every thing. The first proceeds according to the **being** <note>original: *esse*</note> that the thing has in the <term>efficient cause</term> (the maker). The second, according to the being it has in the **making** <note>process of becoming</note>. The third, according to the being it has as a **finished product** <note>original: *in facto*</note>. The first "being" exists only in **knowing**. The second in **operating**. The third in **preserving**. Again, the first mode of proceeding is from the part that is prior by reason or nature: namely, from the **end** <note>the goal or purpose</note>, which is the principle of all other parts in thought. The second is from the part that is posterior by nature and reason (namely, the **matter**, which is the principle in operating) toward the part that is prior by reason: namely, the end. The third is from the **whole** to the **parts**: because the form of the whole unites, activates, and preserves the parts. We call the first **Resolutive**. The second, **Compositive**. The third, **Definitive** or the unbinding of the term.

### BY WHAT REASON IS ONE ORDER OF DOCTRINE CALLED 
### resolutive, another compositive, and another the unbinding of the term.

WE call that the **Resolutive order** which proceeds from the part that is prior by reason or nature toward the part that is posterior by reason or nature: namely, from the end toward those things that exist for the sake of the end. We call it "resolutive" for this reason: because "to loosen" <note>original: *soluere*</note> means nothing other than to untie the bond of a joined thing. Since parts are joined and bound together in a whole, he who separates the parts is said to **dissolve** the whole itself. Moreover, "resolution" is, as it were, a "loosing again" <note>Latin *re-solutio*</note>. This is because the parts—which existed loose and free in their own region before they came into a composition—having been reduced into a composition, were made "exiles" and held by the bond of the composition. Therefore, it was not without reason that it pleased the ancients to call the segregation of these parts "resolution." Since the **end** <note>the goal</note>, by its virtue, contains in a much more eminent way all the things that are destined for that end, he who steps gradually from the end toward those things which the end requires, in a certain way "loosens" the whole into its parts. Wherefore, the authority of the ancients thought this very progress should be aptly named **Dissolutive** and **Resolutive**. It is called Dissolutive when it first takes its beginning from the notion of the end (as in the *Analytics* and the discovery of any art). But it is called the Resolutive order when we have first made a Compositive one (as in almost all natural doctrine)...

THE COMPENDIUM OF PAUL RICIUS,

once this is completed, we return from the end to those things which are ordered toward the end (as Aristotle does in his work *On the Parts of Animals*). This will be called the **resolutive order** <note>original: *ordo resolutivus*; also known as the analytical order, where one breaks a goal down into the steps needed to achieve it</note>, because those things which were gathered into one through the compositive order are again distributed into individual parts through the resolutive. While this stands, the reason for the compositive can be easily assigned: for the things that the resolutive order thinks out separately, the compositive order fuses into one. Thus, <term>Averroes</term> <note>The influential 12th-century Islamic philosopher and commentator on Aristotle</note>, the faithful interpreter of Aristotle, in the second book of the *Metaphysics*, calls the path that goes from the prior to the posterior "dissolutive," and the path from the posterior to the prior "compositive." The reasoning behind the name of the third order—namely, the **definitive order** <note>original: *termini dissolutivi*; here referring to the order of definition or delimitation</note>—is also clear. For when we have already gathered the parts into one by composition, we then immediately behold the whole itself as it now exists in actuality. Wishing to comprehend it exactly, we are compelled to look at the parts, which only a **definition** <note>original: *diffinitio*</note> embraces; this could not be tracked down or constructed from anywhere else except through division—that is, through the "dissolving" of the term into its components. You will understand each of these things we have reviewed regarding the naming of the orders more clearly if you look upon the examples that follow with attentive meditation. And first, concerning the order by which questions relate to one another, which we call the "order of teaching" for a specific reason.

### EXAMPLES OF THE THREEFOLD ORDER OF TEACHING (THAT IS, OF QUESTIONS).

Let it be, for the sake of example, our intention to hand down medical teaching. Since this requires a multitude of questions, it is appropriate (if you expect perfect teaching) that you arrange the questions in a certain agreeable series. As the preceding points teach, this happens in one of three ways: namely, by following the footsteps of nature in thinking things out, in acting, or in preserving. In thinking things out, you begin from the notion of the **end** <note>The *finis* or goal</note>, which, as we said, is the principle of both nature and art according to reason. Moreover, the end of the entire medical art, which moves us to the scrutiny of the art, is health itself—namely, the disposition by which the operations of the human body emerge unimpaired. This is what nature itself intends as the immediate end of man. For "each thing," says Aristotle in the second book of *On the Heavens*, "exists for the sake of its work." Therefore, it is necessary to treat how many and of what sort the operations of the human body are. Because, truly, operations proceed from **powers** <note>original: *uirtutibus*; the faculties or "virtues" of the soul/body</note>, powers are carried through the **members** <note>The organs and limbs</note>, members are fashioned from the **humors** <note>The four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>, and humors are produced from the complexion of the **elements** <note>Earth, air, fire, and water</note>. Therefore, it is necessary to consider how many and of what sort each of these are. If you treat these in the same order in which they are commemorated here, discovered starting from the notion of the "end," it will be a resolutive order of this kind, and you will be imitating nature not in its operation, but in its way of thinking. 

However, take note here: in things whose discovery does not depend on art or on our work, but on the work of nature, the first "resolutive" order (which arises from the notion of the end) cannot occur. This is because we are initially ignorant of nature's end *as* an end, and therefore what the end requires is hidden from us. At last, however, after we have come to know the individual parts of a thing and compared them to one another, then for the first time nature's end becomes known to us. For our order of knowing concerning the beings of nature is contrary to nature's own order of knowing. Nature knows its own work first resolutively, second compositively, and third definitively. We, however, do the opposite. We contemplate the work of nature first in a **definitive** order, second in a **compositive** order, and third in a **resolutive** order. For our reason behaves just as if some inhabitant of a very temperate region (where, because of the extreme mildness of the air, one always lives under the open sky) were to come into our region and behold the structures of so many houses and buildings with wonder. He would first, without doubt, contemplate the whole fabric together with its parts. From there, he would consider in what way the parts were joined and gathered into one. Thirdly, he would consider for what end there is such a variety of parts and such a construction of the whole—which conception is the last for the observer, but truly the first for the builder. In the very same way, our foreign reason behaves in contemplating the fabric of the builder, Nature. Whence <term>Galen</term> <note>The famous 2nd-century Roman physician and philosopher</note> said in the third book of *On the Constitution of the Art of Medicine*: "We are the ones who contemplate a house already made," namely, the human body itself, which first...

through **Anatomy**, which is the dissolution of the whole into its parts in a definitive way through causes (specifically material causes), we gain knowledge. In those things whose existence depends on our own voluntary work, we proceed by the same process that nature follows in its own work. And because **Analytic reasoning** is a certain type of reasoning—and an art that is not entirely inventive (like one who constructs a dwelling or builds a house) but rather corrects and supplies the defects of nature’s work—it was therefore discovered and organized in a **resolutive** <note>original: *resolutive*; the process of "resolving" or breaking a finished product back down into its requirements or causes</note> manner. Thus, any doctrine, insofar as it depends on will and art, is discovered in a resolutive order, as seen in the beginning of the *Physics* <note>Aristotle’s work on natural philosophy</note>. However, its execution is either **compositive** <note>original: *compositiva*; building up from simple parts to a complex whole</note>, as in natural things, or **definitive**, as in divine things. But where the final work and the end goal of nature have already become known to us, there we proceed in a resolutive way (just as nature itself does), which you should consider carefully. Finally, returning to where we digressed, we must conclude that the progress from the end goal to the things that lead to that end is "resolutive," and is the first order used by both nature and art. If, however, you walk in a retrograde direction, taking your starting point from where we established the end—namely, beginning with the **elements** from which nature fashions a **complexion** <note>original: *complexionem*; the specific balance of bodily qualities like heat and moisture</note>, then moving to the complexions from which the **humors** are made, and then the members and the virtues—and lastly ending with the operations (by which law the **Prince Abu Ali** <note>The Latinized name for the Persian physician Avicenna, referring here to his *Canon of Medicine*</note> published the first book of his *Canon*), this will be the **compositive order**. If indeed you proceed by the path of the **Microtechnes** <note>original: *Microtechnes*; referring to the "Small Art" or *Ars Medica* of the Greek physician Galen</note>, you will produce a **definitive** order (or an order that dissolves a term into its components), and you will be a follower of nature—not indeed in thinking things out, nor in operating, but in preserving.

## ON THE TRIPLE ORDER OF DEMONSTRATIONS
### Examples of *A Priori* Reasoning <note>Reasoning from cause to effect</note>.

The following examples clarify the first order, in which the "means" or intermediate steps regard one another, which we have called the order of demonstrations in a broader sense. Thus, if the question is asked whether a **fever** is present, since this requires several demonstrative means (whether they be causes or effects), they must receive a three-form arrangement of order. First, I will give you examples of the "means" which are the causes of the thing being sought; for instance, I show that a fever is present because there is a heat of **putrid humor** around the heart. I prove that such heat is present because there is found a **prevention of ventilation** <note>original: *eventationis prohibitio*; the body's inability to release internal heat through the skin</note>, because there is a **blockage** <note>original: *opilatio*</note>, because there is a multitude of **gross humors**, because of excessive eating, because of immoderate appetite, and because of a **malice of the complexion** <note>A harmful imbalance of the body's primary qualities</note>. All these things joined together are a sufficient demonstrative means of the question through the cause. If, therefore, you proceed by the same series in which these very things are placed here to establish the certainty of the question, the order itself will be **resolutive**, beginning from the end and proceeding toward those things which are directed toward the end. For of these causes we have just brought forward (according to the intention of common or fallen nature), the end is the fever itself, toward which the putrid humor is ordered, for which the prevention of ventilation is required, for this the blockage, and so on by stepping backward all the way to the "malice of the complexion," which was produced by a celestial ray, the surrounding air, or any other depraved disposition. If, however, you walk by a reversed order of the means (the path nature follows in its operation), then the **compositive order** emerges: namely, there is a fever because there is a bad complexion, because there is immoderate eating, and so on until you reach the heat of putrid humor around the heart. If, however, the question was "What is a fever?", the first manifestation will be the proper definition or description of the fever; from there, the definition of its individual parts, and so on step by step until you arrive at the parts that cannot be further defined. By such a law, the **definitive** (or "term-dissolving") order will come forth—namely, from the whole into the parts. For there is no process from the definition to the thing defined unless a division of the **genus** into **differences** <note>The logical process of taking a general category and splitting it into specific types</note> has first been made, which is nothing other than proceeding from the whole into the parts. Thus you will judge clearly in what way the means demonstrate the question from the prior through this threefold order.

PAUL RICIUS'S COMPENDIUM,
ON THE ORDER OF DEMONSTRATIONS,
"of the fact" <note>original: *quia*; a logical term for a demonstration that shows *that* something is true based on its effects, rather than *why* it is true based on its cause</note>, an example.

However, if the "middle terms" <note>the links in a logical argument</note> sought are effects, a threefold order of demonstrations will arise by the same law. For example, one might argue that a fever is present because there is an impairment of all bodily functions; and this impairment exists because there is a weariness or failure of all strengths; and this exists because of the consumption of the nourishing moisture; and this, in turn, because of an immoderate or external heat around the heart. These middle terms demonstrate that a fever is present through conjecture and by looking at the effects. If you arrange these in the same order as we have listed them, the process will be **resolutive** <note>analytical; breaking the end result down into its preceding conditions</note>—namely, moving from the end goal to those things intended for that end. For just as the goodness of a regulated nature provides for the existence and operation of things with a final intention, so conversely the malice of a fallen nature intends the corruption of things, which results from the injury and failure of operations. 

If, however, you proceed by the opposite path, reasoning that a fever is present because there is immoderate heat around the heart, which leads to the consumption of nourishment, the failure of strength, and finally the impairment of all operations, then the order will be **compositive** <note>synthetic; building up from the cause to the final effect</note>. For this is how nature proceeds in its work, intending the injury and corruption of the sick person. 

Furthermore, when you demonstrate that a fever is present through a description of the fever itself, the process will be **definitive** or the "dissolution of the term." This is because it moves from the whole to the parts—namely, from something acting as a "genus" to those things acting as "differences." For just as a true definition consists of a genus and a difference, which are the intrinsic and essential causes of the defined thing’s existence, so when the causes are hidden, there is a need for certain accompanying traits (which act like the genus and difference) to reveal the thing itself.

### ON THE THREEFOLD ORDER OF DEMONSTRATING,
### examples.

The examples of the "order of demonstrating" (which operates between the middle term and the thing sought) are: the "demonstration of the cause" <note>original: *propter quid*; showing *why* something is the case</note>, the "demonstration of the fact" <note>original: *quia*; showing *that* something is the case</note>, and the definition. The common school of younger students brings this up here, although they sometimes give examples of "demonstrations" and other times examples of the "order of demonstrating." You, who are wise, judge for yourself how far they wander from the right path. 

Therefore, the "demonstration of the cause" creates a **resolutive** order. The "demonstration of the fact" creates a **compositive** order. The definition creates a **dissolution of the term**. The name "resolutive order" fits the demonstration of the cause because the process there moves from a part that is prior in nature or thought—namely, the end goal—to those things ordained toward that end, as can be seen from the example of provident nature. 

For the order of wisdom intends to produce something for the unity and completion of the universe, by which the higher things are connected with the fleeting things, and the last with the first. However, according to the order of things, this cannot happen except through some mediating form that participates in both—such as the **rational soul**. Since the soul is more sublime than an ethereal body, it cannot inhabit these dark and mortal bodies without a suitable medium. Therefore, a medium similar to the "element of the stars" (as <margin>Chapter 3.</margin> Aristotle speaks in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*) must intervene. 

Whether this is a tiny body and "ethereal clothing" as the Academics <note>the followers of Plato</note> believed, or whether it only corresponds to the celestial element by proportion, as the Stagirite <note>Aristotle, born in Stagira</note> taught, it perpetually revolves and produces heat. Since the fuel of this heat is the **radical moisture** <note>original: *radicalis humor*; the vital fluid thought to be the basis of life and longevity</note>, and the moisture is consumed unless it is restored by heat, restoration is achieved by a moisture suitable to it, namely **blood**. Blood is produced from food and drink. To be chosen appropriately and transformed into the restoring moisture, food requires the animal, vital, and natural "virtues" <note>powers or faculties of the body</note>. These organic virtues require bodies, which draw their origin from the humors and elements. Having perceived all these things, nature soon arrives at the knowledge of man and his four causes, which relate to one another in this order: first, in thinking, the **end** occurs—namely, the connection of fleeting things...

# ON THE THRICE-THREEFOLD ORDER OF DOCTRINES.
<meta>catchword: Demon-</meta>

...connection with the higher realms, from which nature, in the second place, devises a form consistent with this connection. Thirdly, it fashions the matter suitable for receiving this form—namely, the <term>organic body</term> <note>a body organized with specific parts to perform life functions</note> according to the series mentioned before. Fourthly, it conceives of the rational form <note>the human soul</note> to be joined and gathered to its organic body; from this, in the final place, follows the human composition and that "bond of the universe." Although this bond was first in thought, it is the last to be completed in the actual work. 

As for what we judged in the preceding sections—namely, that the causes of matter and form are prior in nature to the composite whole during the process of operation—this makes sense (as I have just now warned) regarding matter and form as the "what" <note>the actual components</note>, but not as the "whereby," or the material condition (as they call it), rather than the formal one. For matter does not take on the character of matter except while it is subject to form, nor does form take on the character of form except while it actuates matter; these things can only happen after the composition is complete. Therefore, in the eyes of nature during operation, the composite whole is prior (in its formal condition) to the matter and form, even though it is the last thing in the order of thought. 

You, therefore, for an exact understanding of the order of nature and doctrine, weigh these things in the balance and turn them over with repeated investigation. Finally, conclude that whenever we show an effect through a cause, we always proceed from the end—or from that which is closer to the end—to those things which are ordered toward the end. This process will be **resolutive** <note>analytical; moving from the final result back to the necessary steps</note>, which is why we rightly call this the order of demonstrating. When, however, you demonstrate a cause through its effect, it will be the **compositive** order <note>synthetic; building up from the basic elements to the result</note>, because you are proceeding from a part that is later in nature to a part that is prior. 

And just as both the resolutive and compositive processes are observed in the relationship of the effect to the four types of causes, and in the relationship of the four types of causes to one another, so too may one experience these same processes among the causes of any single genus. For example, in the genus of the <term>material cause</term> <note>what a thing is made of</note>, there is the ethereal body of the soul (or something proportioned to it), then natural heat, then <term>radical moisture</term> <note>a vital fluid thought in the Middle Ages to sustain life and heat</note>, and then the blood that restores what has been dissolved. All of these constitute a demonstration of "why" <note>original: *propter quid*</note>, because the matter which is closer to the form always acts as an end to the more remote matter. Likewise, in this same genus of material cause, by proceeding backward, the order becomes compositive; this can easily be judged in the other three genera of causes as well. 

If, however, the question is "what is it?", where the answer is given through a definition, the order becomes **definitive** (or the "dissolution of the term"), moving from the whole to the parts. For a definition consists of a <term>genus</term> <note>a general category</note> which is narrowed down to a specific <term>difference</term> through division; and division is the breaking down of a whole into parts. From these things, therefore, through the relationship of the "middle term" to the thing sought, gather the threefold order of demonstrating. These, along with the aforementioned orders of things sought and middle terms, constitute the **thrice-threefold order**. Thus, I believe I have sufficiently explained what I proposed from the beginning, as far as this compendium is concerned.

### EVERY GENUS OF ORDERS MUST BE USED, BUT NOT 
### every species of every genus is necessary for every doctrine.

Every doctrine requires these three genera of orders for its perfection. For if the proper relationship of the things sought (which we especially call the "order of doctrine") were missing—such as in a <term>quodlibetical</term> <note>original: *quodlibetica*; a style of academic debate where questions are asked at-will without a fixed structure</note> doctrine, which passes from one type of question to another without any order—the collection of all those questions would still be a doctrine, but it would not be an ordered one. In a similar way, if the proper relationship of the "middle terms" to one another were absent, no perfect knowledge of the thing sought could be had, nor could it be called a doctrine. By the same law, one must judge if the appropriate relationship between the thing sought and the middle term is missing. 

Therefore, one must admit that there is a relationship between the things sought, the middle terms, and both toward each other, and that a threefold genus of the order of doctrine is given. Nevertheless, not all species of these three orders—namely, the resolutive, compositive, and definitive—are to be expected in every doctrine. For sometimes (as in Galen’s <term>microtechnes</term> <note>referring to Galen's *Ars Medica* or "Small Art," a foundational medical textbook</note>), the order of the doctrine is **definitive**, while the order of the demonstrations is **resolutive**.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion regarding the three types of logical "orders" used in scientific teaching. Having just explained the relationship between matter and form in the "bond of the universe," Ricius now focuses on interpreting the specific words of Galen's preface to the Microtechne (The Small Art), specifically how Galen classifies the methods of teaching knowledge.</meta>

->PAVLVS RICIUS’S COMPENDIUM<-

The order of demonstrating is compositive: for the most part (as in the <term>Analytics</term><note>Aristotle’s works on logic and reasoning</note>) the order of teaching is resolutive. The order of demonstration is compositive, while that of demonstrating is definitive. Thus, they alternate according to what the nature of the division allows, which can be clearly seen by anyone who examines what has been laid out before. Thus far, it has been explained what doctrine is, what order is, and its necessity and excellence; how many types of order there are; and furthermore, regarding the first thing known, that one must use three kinds of orders simultaneously in every doctrine, though not every specific variety of those kinds. Now, however, we shall attempt to complete the understanding of the preface to the <term>Microtechne</term><note>Latin for "The Small Art," referring to Galen’s *Ars Medica*, a foundational medical textbook</note> according to the sequence of the text, under the protection of the heavens.

### EXPLANATION OF GALEN’S WORDS.

Galen says: "There are three doctrines in all, which are held in order," where the discussion concerns the order in which they relate to one another as subjects of inquiry, as we showed a little while ago. For if the intention here were to speak of the "order" or "mode of demonstrating," Galen would have surely promised falsely that he would provide a <term>definitive doctrine</term><note>A method of teaching based on defining the essence of a subject</note> here especially. For in the second treatise of this work, for example, he demonstrates this conclusion through a <term>compositive process</term><note>A method starting from causes and building toward effects; synthesis</note>: namely, that a large head, combined with a good shape and the correct arrangement of the neck and other bones, is a sign of a well-composed brain. He gives the reason: because it was able to regulate a great deal of matter, which could only happen through the intensity of its power. That it was able to regulate much matter is the effect of the intensity of that power; therefore, as is clear from what was previously stated, this is recognized as a compositive process. 

So too, in the third book of this work, he employed a <term>resolutive process</term><note>A method starting from the goal or effect and working back to the causes; analysis</note>, where he strives to demonstrate that the medical art looks toward six healthy causes. This inquiry encompasses two things. First, whether the preservation of health requires an art. Second, whether it requires knowledge of the six healthy causes. Both of these are shown through the <term>final cause</term><note>The purpose or goal for which something exists</note>. The first is shown thus: the intention to preserve a thing that nature can alter requires an art. Nature can alter health; therefore, an art of preservation is required there. The second is shown thus: the end of the art is to preserve health. Health is not preserved except by the management of the causes that can alter it. The management of causes is not perfected unless it is known what kind and how many these causes are. The causes are six: therefore, it is necessary to know the six healthy causes. 

Conclude, therefore: Since Galen uses both the compositive and resolutive modes of demonstrating, yet promised only the definitive one, he did not mean the "order of demonstrating" nor the "order of demonstrations" when he spoke of the "definitive order." Furthermore, an argument is drawn to show that this discussion concerns the "order of doctrine" that occurs between subjects of inquiry, based on Galen’s words: "Which are held in order." For the "order" being discussed here can be separated from some doctrines (such as <term>quodlibetical</term><note>Refers to "whatever you like"; informal or unstructured academic debates</note> doctrines), but the "mode of demonstrating" cannot be separated from any doctrine. Therefore, the order discussed here is not the mode of demonstrating. 

Galen’s own words declare that the order discussed here can be separated. For unless there were some doctrine held without order, it would have been a superfluous and trifling statement to say "those which are held in order." Just as it is irrational to say, "Every man who is rational is capable of laughter," since no irrational man exists; and how full of playful and "holy rusticity" <note>original: "sancta rusticitate"; a sarcastic way of calling an error simple-minded or clumsy</note> is the assertion of <term>Trusianus</term><note>Pietro Torrigiano (c. 1270–1350), a famous commentator on Galen</note> regarding the <term>vertebrae of the back</term><note>original: "spondylibus dorsi"</note>. Because he laid a wavering and weak foundation, whatever he built upon it collapsed; for once one inconsistency is admitted, many others follow. For he will think that the "order of doctrine" is nothing other than the "mode of demonstrating." Since he knew this mode of demonstrating to be inseparable from doctrine, he was forced to twist Galen's words—which seem to suggest this mode can be separated from doctrine (where he says: "which are held in order")—away from their proper meaning, saying: "When Galen said there are three ordinary doctrines, he seems to suppose there are some inordinate ones; but perhaps he said 'three are ordinary doctrines' in the same likeness as when one speaks of the 'vertebrae of the back': for this is not said [because...]"

<summary>Ricius interprets Galen's classification of the three teaching methods—compositive, resolutive, and definitive—arguing that they refer to the arrangement of subject matter rather than just logical proof. He critiques the commentator Torrigiano for confusing these concepts and rendering Galen's distinctions redundant.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of Galen’s "Microtechne." In the previous pages, Ricius established that there are three primary methods of teaching (doctrine): the resolutive, the compositive, and the definitive. Here, he begins by critiquing a previous commentator—referred to as "the Monk"—regarding the definition of terms, specifically using an anatomical analogy about the spine to illustrate how specific context (order) defines a subject.</meta>

### ON THE THRICE-THREEFOLD ORDER OF DOCTRINES.

...it is said, because <term>spondyli</term><note>The Greek-derived term for vertebrae or circular joints</note> are found elsewhere than in the back, but this manner of speaking rather suggests that they are proper to the back. These are the words of the Monk. But if you look at the common use of the word, you will greatly mock the ignorance of this statement. For the whorl of a spindle is also called a *spondylus*, and in the writings of <term>Athenaeus</term><note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian</note> it refers to a kind of salted fish. In <term>Pliny</term><note>Pliny the Elder, author of Natural History</note>, Book 27, it refers to a genus of fish and serpents, and the like. Therefore, consider whether the name "of the back" was added for the sake of specific property or to avoid ambiguity, and judge the same regarding the "doctrine held in order." For just as a *spondylus* can exist without a back, so too can doctrine be given without order. Finally, conclude that the discussion here is solely about the order of doctrine, which turns between one inquiry and another. I have chosen to digress here for a moment so that studious youth may be warned and more cautious, lest they trust too much in outward appearance, or place their faith in a multitude of words rather than their correctness. Now let us pass to the remaining words of Galen that follow.

> **[The first indeed (he says) is from the notion of the end, which comes about according to dissolution.]**

He calls the "resolutive way" first because it excels in certainty, perfection, and origin. In **certainty**: because (as the following explains) this alone shows the rational basis for every individual part. In **perfection**: because it inheres in the subject of perfection, namely the intellect. In **origin**: because (as we have just been taught) an agent always thinks out the plan of the whole work before beginning the task; this plan or art is woven together from the notion of the end according to its individual parts, which is most evidently clear in an agent acting through art and through nature alike. For Nature (as is taught in the second book of *The Physics*<note>original: "de auditu"; the Latin title often used for Aristotle’s Physics</note>) acts for the sake of an end in whatever it does. Whence in the third chapter of *On the Constitution of the Art of Medicine*, Galen says: "God and nature, just like one who first built a house, thus foreknow the parts." These are Galen’s words. He does not mean, however, that nature itself possesses the faculty of knowing, but is directed by a knowing and unerring spirit, which is the true agent; for these sensible and fleeting bodies are nothing but the aids and instruments of the efficient cause. From this it must finally be concluded that the doctrine by which we proceed from the knowledge of the end according to <term>dissolution</term><note>Here meaning "resolution" or the breaking down of a whole into its constituent parts</note> is prior in perfection and origin. It is said to be "according to dissolution" because the end (as we showed before)—and whatever is prior in nature according to reason—contains within its power all things that the end requires, just as the whole contains its parts. Since, therefore, division is the same as the dissolution of a whole into parts, the deduction of the parts from the end will likewise be the same as dissolution.

> **[The second indeed is that which comes from composition according to the resolution of things found.]**

He calls the "compositive way" second because it is posterior to the resolutive in certainty and origin, yet prior to the definitive. It is second in **certainty** because it does not provide the rational basis for the individual parts as does the one from the notion of the end, and thus it is less certain than the resolutive. Yet it is **prior** to the definitive because it moves from part to part as things distinctly known. The definitive, however, moves from a confused thing confusedly known to something distinct—that is, from the whole to the parts. That this compositive way is also second in **origin** is easily established; for as soon as the plan of the work is thought out, the discovered small parts are gradually fused into one, and finally, from the gathering of these, the whole emerges in the third place, from which the definitive process takes its beginning. For we recognize (as we mentioned before) that a threefold mode of being is given in created things: first in the **maker**, second in the **making**, and third in the **thing made**. These relate to each other such that what is last to one is the beginning to the other; in the same way, the three orders of doctrine behave, according as each order follows the footsteps of nature. He says:

> **[According to the resolution of things found.]**

This is because the composition is made of such things as were discovered through resolution, yet not in the same order, but in a retrograde (reverse) order, as can be seen from the examples above. Here, too, phantoms deceive the Monk, by which he asserts that the second doctrine (namely the compositive) also comes about from the notion of the end. And although Galen’s words do not say this, the Monk judged it should be added. How far this wanders from the truth, you who are wise should consider from our previous words. I rebuke the Monk, not because other modern thinkers offer better things, but because this "good shepherd," while walking through steep places, leads the whole flock of students into a precipice...

<meta>This page continues the technical commentary on Galen’s "Art of Medicine" (Microtechne). On the previous page, Ricius began discussing the three orders of teaching: the resolutive (starting from the end), the compositive (starting from the elements), and the definitive (the dissolution of the definition). Here, he analyzes the various names given to the third method—the definitive—and its historical development.</meta>

# COMPENDIUM BY PAULUS RICIUS,

leads: strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered. <note>original: "percute igitur pastorem, & dispergentur oues." A biblical allusion (Zechariah 13:7) used here to illustrate how a whole is broken by striking its core.</note> *The third indeed, says Galen, is by the dissolution of the term, which we now insist upon.*] Why he calls the definitive method the "third" is clear from what has already been said. It is called "by the dissolution of the term" <note>original: "ex termini dissolutione"</note> because, just as the method that proceeds from the notion of the end dissolves that which is a "whole" in potentiality and distinct knowledge into its rational parts, so too the definitive method dissolves a whole that is "actual" but only confusedly known into its actual parts. 

*It is permitted, however, he says, to call this kind of teaching not only the "dissolution of the term," but also the "opening," as some have named it.*] Dissolution and "opening" <note>original: "apertio"</note> differ in this: dissolution is the segregation of things joined into one, whereas "opening" does not entirely segregate them, but provides a way to enter into a closed thing. For he who defines a term does not utterly segregate its parts—for the complete segregation of parts is the destruction of the whole—but rather "opens" it so that the concept of the mind can penetrate the essence of the thing. To judge "confusedly" is to look at a closed thing from the outside; but to know "distinctly" is to perceive what is inside once it has been opened up. 

*Or "resolution."*] As we have said, "resolution" <note>original: "resolutio"</note> differs from "dissolution" in that dissolution is merely the segregation of joined things. Resolution, however, is the segregation of those things which also existed separately beforehand. For he who carries out the process of resolution must have previously known, in a separate way, all those things into which he now dissolves the term itself. For instance, before Galen declared that "medicine is the science of the healthy, the sick, and the neutral," <note>Galen's famous tripartite definition of the subject of medicine.</note> it is certain that he already knew each of these individually, as the medical art and faculty requires. He then re-collected and condensed them into three, and those three into one. As <term>Porphyrius</term><note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) whose "Isagoge" was a standard textbook on logic.</note> says, those who ascend must collect the multitude into one. Thus, he who "opens" a term separates those things which he had also inspected separately before; therefore, it was not wrongly decided to call this "resolution," as if it were a "re-solution" (solving again). 

*Or "definition."*] For a true division is of the whole into its essential parts, and this is the same as defining. 

*Or, as others call it, "explanation."*] "Explanation" <note>original: "explicatio"</note> extends to more things than "definition" does, because it also applies to a "description," which is expressed through proper accidents. For a defined thing implies not only the essential parts of the thing, but also those accidents that exist within it by its very nature. For example, a "human" contains within itself not only the "rational animal," but also an upright stature, the capacity for learning, and other such things. Here, however, "explanation" is taken as the account that explains the essence of the thing. 

*Or "exposition," as others say.*] "Exposition" <note>original: "expositio"</note> sounds even broader than "explanation," because it designates the knowledge of the name and the thing not only through essential concomitants, but through any attributes whatsoever. The followers of <term>Herophilus</term><note>A Greek physician in Alexandria (335–280 BC), often called the "father of anatomy."</note> attempted to create this kind of teaching, as did Heraclites and Eritheus; and the Herophilians, certain followers of <term>Erasistratus</term><note>A Greek anatomist and royal physician (c. 304–250 BC).</note>, and Athenaeus of Attalia also attempted the method according to composition. 

*However, no one before us wrote of that which begins from the notion of the end.*] He says "no one before us," meaning specifically in the assembly of physicians. For Aristotle also handed down this doctrine in his *Analytics* and in his books *On the Parts of Animals*. In the *Analytics*, the "end" (which is knowledge itself) is present in everyone by a natural desire, and from its notion he demonstrates all the primary parts of the analytical doctrine. In the book *On the Parts of Animals*, although the end is by no means evident to us by nature, it finally becomes known through the more common parts of philosophy already established. For the "end" of all nature is the soul; from the knowledge of the soul, he demonstrates with solid reason that the individual limbs or parts of the animal must be granted in the book *On the Parts of Animals*. 

*From which all arts consist according to reason.*] So too Aristotle speaks in the first book of *On the Parts of Animals*, saying: the cause which we signify by the phrase "for the sake of which" is the reason. Reason is the principle, equally in things constituted by art as in those by nature. For if you wish to learn an art through reason, you can achieve it from no other source than from the notion of the end. The "compositive" and "definitive" methods, although they can provide the art, do not do so according to reason. For example, the Architect, the Manufacturer, and the Inspector of the finished work all perceive the art, but the Architect does so through resolution, the Manufacturer through the composition of the work, and the Inspector through the disso...

He emphasizes that while earlier physicians used composition and dissolution, Galen (following Aristotle's lead in philosophy) was the first to apply the teleological method (starting from the "end") to medicine.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical commentary on the three methods of medical instruction. This page explores why this method is particularly effective for learning and memory compared to the resolutive and compositive methods.</meta>

### ON THE THREEFOLD ORDER OF TEACHINGS.

...the dissolution [of the whole], and definitive doctrine, one acquires such an art. Regarding the understanding of this, Galen said in *On the Constitution of the Art of Medicine*: "We, however, are those who contemplate a house already built, namely the human body itself; therefore, through Anatomy, it is necessary to dissolve the whole into its parts." [*But that indeed we have passed over elsewhere.*] <note>Ricius is quoting Galen here.</note> namely that which proceeds from the notion of the end, elsewhere—specifically in the book *On the Constitution of the Art of Medicine*. 

But notice (as is clear from what was said before) that "proceeding from the notion of the end" has a double meaning: namely, in **discovering** or in **pursuing** the order. To find the order, in most of Galen’s works (just as in the traditions of anyone creating an ordered teaching), one proceeds **resolutively** <term>resolutio: the analytical process of breaking a goal down into its necessary requirements</term>, as can be seen in the *Physics* and in the beginning of the first *Canon*. Other parts of the volumes are arranged in a **compositive** and **definitive** order; only the entire book *On the Constitution of the Art of Medicine* proceeds in a resolutive order throughout. For there, wishing to hand down those things of which the entire art of healing consists, he takes his origin from the notion of the end, namely from **health**. 

For from this it is necessary that we contemplate the whole body: the whole through its parts via **Anatomy**, and Anatomy through the knowledge of formation, magnitude, number, and position. Moreover, it must be considered which of such parts can be healed and corrected or not; he even introduces there (not as a primary intention, but for the sake of example) a comparison to the elements. Then he shows that if health is to be preserved and sickness avoided, it is necessary to know the natural disposition and the sicknesses of each part. From there he proceeds to find what must be known regarding the curative part, and finally completes each thing (up to the end of the book) in the same order. 

The reason why that entire volume—whereas his other volumes use the resolutive order only in the preface—is because that whole compendium considers nothing other than the art itself. Therefore, it is carried out solely from the notion of the end. Other volumes consider the art only in the preface (namely the order which follows the art); therefore, they proceed resolutively only there. In the rest of the volumes, they consider the things of nature which do not depend on our work. Thus, they proceed either compositively or definitively. Ponder all these things yourself, and *you will clearly weigh how great the hair-splitting <note>original: "mycrologia," a term for overly-detailed or trivial analysis</note> of the commentators is. Here, however, we shall produce a **definitive** teaching.*] 

He produces a definitive teaching in ordering the things sought—namely, by proceeding from the whole into the parts. In verifying the things sought, he sometimes defines, sometimes demonstrates through the effect, and sometimes demonstrates through the cause. 

[*How much this [definitive teaching] is left behind by that which happens according to resolution, it is yet so much more abundant in dignity and reason for the comprehension of the whole art and the memory of those things which pertain to the parts.*] He assigns the reason why he chose the definitive method here, though it is indeed more "uncertain" than the others; it is because this kind of definitive teaching, by encompassing the scope of the whole art and entrusting the contents to memory, far excels the resolutive. 

[*For all things are easily enough remembered from the dissolution of the term, because the best term (which they even call the "substantial" term) contains within itself the main chapters of the whole art.*] He states the reason why the definitive teaching excels the other two types in memory: by arguing that it is easier to remember one thing than many, and the more something participates in unity, the more it facilitates memory. 

The definitive teaching participates more in **unity** than the resolutive and the compositive. Because it proceeds from the **whole**, and from the "one" containing all parts in itself in actuality. The resolutive, however, proceeds from a part, which is the whole and the "one" containing parts only by virtue <note>i.e., potentially</note>, not in actuality. The compositive indeed proceeds from a part, which contains parts neither by virtue nor in actuality, but in a remote and "seminal" potential, just as "primary matter" in a way embraces the whole composite. Since, therefore, the actual union of parts is in the thing defined itself—from which the process in the definitive teaching occurs—and since unity provides the ease of remembering, it follows that the definitive teaching excels the resolutive and compositive in the ease of memory. I say it contains, and the best term unites all parts.] 

The **definition** is called the **term** <note>original: "terminus"</note>: because just as a boundary [term] leaves nothing outside itself, so if a part of the thing...

<meta>This page concludes Paulus Ricius's commentary on the methods of teaching and defining medicine, specifically finishing the section on the definitive method. It then transitions into a more philosophical oration regarding the cosmic order of learning, connecting Aristotelian (Peripatetic) thought with a theological worldview.</meta>

of which it is the limit; otherwise, it would not truly be called its limit. In this way, a definition is best assigned: it will contain the whole substance of the thing and all its parts, leaving nothing out that the definition does not include. And such is a **substantial definition**. For just as in being and in being known—as is gathered from the first book of *On the Soul* <note>Referring to Aristotle’s *De Anima*.</note>—substance contains accidents by virtue of its essence, and not vice versa; so too a substantial definition contains the description, but not the other way around. For accidents accompany the substance, but substance does not arise from accidents. Therefore, Galen adds, saying: [*On the contrary, those who divide by what they call notions define things by their accidents; but these others consist of the substance itself.*] <note>original: "Econtrariò diuidentes his quas notiones appellant, & illi fiquidem ab accidentibus diffiniunt rebus: hi verò substantia ipsa consistunt."</note> He calls descriptions "notions" because they work only through markers—that is, signs—which are secondary and flow from the substance itself. [*The treatment of the universal medical speculation according to its parts has been written by us in many other works.*] So far, he has commemorated the orders of teaching and what has been discussed here; therefore, he explains that the material to be treated here is the medical faculty, and he touches upon it with a preceding summary. But because the material of this book concerns the entire art of medicine, lest anyone think that the art itself is delivered here in its completeness, he warns, saying: [*The treatment according to the part—that is, according to the individual parts required for the completion of the universal medical art—has been delivered in many other volumes.*] [*Which it is profitable to use for the three teachings.*] That is, whoever wishes to learn the medical faculty according to all three orders of teaching <term>doctrinarum ordines: the resolutive, compositive, and definitive methods discussed previously</term>, it is profitable for them to seek this from the other parts we have written in medical doctrine; from the present work, however, we attain only the **definitive** teaching. Therefore he says: [*But now we shall begin from the definitive, adding only this much: that only the main chapters, like conclusions, will now be stated according to the explanation of the things demonstrated.*] For the reader might say to himself: "If the treatment of the universal medical speculation according to every part has been delivered elsewhere, what then remains to be treated in the present work?" Answering, he says that although all things have been shown elsewhere, it remained for the sake of memory to repeat the chapters of all the explicitly demonstrated things in the manner of conclusions. We say "in the manner of conclusions" because here not only are the conclusions brought forth, but also their demonstrations; nevertheless, they maintain the proportion of conclusions because, just as a conclusion implicitly contains those things which the premises announce, so too our treatment here contains by virtue everything that the entire medical speculation explains piece by piece. Thus, finally, by the will of immortal God, we close here the treatise on the **ninefold order** <term>nouenarius: a system organized into nine parts or levels</term> of doctrine; to Him be glory, praise, and blessing.

# THE ORATION AND THEMES FOLLOW REGARDING THE THREEFOLD ORDER, WHICH
## CLEARLY SHOW THE
->threefold order of the Peripatetic doctrine, and its<-
->connection and<-
->coherence.<-

->*An Oration on the Threefold Order of Doctrine.*<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring scrolling floral motifs within a square border.</image-desc>
WHEN I consider more deeply, and revolve the order of nature and of things more and more in my mind, I see that the true opinion is that which places God Himself—the best and greatest—as the individual and unchangeable center of **four circles**. These circles, I say, are the **Mind**, the **Soul**, **Nature**, and **Hyle** <term>Hyle: a Greek term used in philosophy to refer to primordial, unformed matter</term>, which embrace and surround the entire machine of the world. For Ideas shine in the Mind, Reasons glow in the Soul, Seeds shine forth in Nature, and Hyle flashes with Forms. ### ON THE TRIPLE-THREEFOLD ORDER OF TEACHINGS. 305

C 3

...took their origin. Since, therefore, the light of reason innate within us flows not from the dark abyss of empty matter, but from the fountain of supernal light, and has fallen by a certain force into this **Egyptian servitude** <note>A common Renaissance metaphor for the soul's imprisonment in the physical body or the material world, referencing the Israelites' captivity.</note>—tossed about by the constant whirlwind of the senses—there, as an exile from the Father of Lights and held fast by the bond of this opaque body, it anxiously desires and seeks a return and an embrace of its own beginning. 

But since that wealthy Giver of all good things is ready to bestow, and our reason is ready to receive, yet only the allurements of the senses overshadow the desired effect and prohibit it, weak human reason was endowed with an innate desire for knowing. Indeed, science seems to consist in nothing other than the removal of the obstacle of the senses, because science is nothing else than the **knowledge of universals** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "universals" are general concepts or essences that exist beyond specific, individual objects.</note>. The universal, however, lacks place and time; and where these (I mean place and time) are absent, no sensory faculty—neither the exterior nor any part of those within—is able to exercise its work. 

Hence **Plato** too (as is read in the introduction of *Alcinous* <note>Alcinous was a Middle Platonist philosopher; this refers to his "Handbook of Platonism."</note>) says: [*Philosophy is the release of the soul from the body*] <note>original: "Philosophia, inquit, solutio animæ à corpore est"</note>, from which it is proved that science is nothing other than the loosening of the bond of the senses, so that once the hindrance is removed, the mind itself may emerge as a partner and sharer in the paternal light. 

Since, therefore, the perfection of every thing depends on the return to its beginning, and human reason attains this return through science, it is worthwhile to discern by what path and in what ways we may acquire science, which we shall explain in this brief oration; to which you should diligently lend your ears. 

There is, then, a twofold way by which we acquire science: one is of **grace** (as they call it), and the other of **practice** <note>original: "operationis"</note>. The way of practice is that by which we attain it through natural investigation and work. That of grace, however, is that by which we possess it without work and beyond the limits of nature. The wise **Aristotle** showed this bipartite way with these words: [*Intellectual virtue,*] he says, [*has its generation and increase mostly from teaching*] <note>original: "Intellectualis, inquit, uirtus plurimum ex doctrina generationem habet"</note>. But what is "for the most part" is not "always"; therefore, intellectual virtue is not always acquired through teaching. He who does not attain science through teaching must find that it consists either in faith alone or in the grace of the supernal light. 

This is by no means rejected by the great interpreter of the Peripatetic doctrine, **Averroes**, in his book *On Union*; it is approved by the distinguished **Algazel** of the Arabs, and the prince **Avicenna** confirms it. **Maximus Abubachar** <note>Referring to the Andalusian philosopher Ibn Tufail (Abubacer) and his work *Hayy ibn Yaqdhan*.</note> demonstrates it plainly in his book titled *The Gazelle*. Nor should our "**Melchizedek Plato**" <note>An honorific title likely suggesting Plato was a "priest-king" of wisdom, linking him to the biblical figure Melchizedek.</note> be omitted, who in many places (most clearly in the *Meno* and the *Theages*) proves this opinion: [*Truly,*] he says, [*the human race never ceases from evil unless either legitimate philosophers rule, or those who govern philosophize by some divine lot.*] 

The same was taught by the sacred and inviolate authority of the **Apostle Paul**, who often repeats this twofold mode of salvation (in Romans 4): [*To him who works, wages are not counted according to grace, but according to debt.*] And to the Ephesians: [*For by grace you are saved through faith, and this is not of yourselves: for it is the gift of God, not of works, lest anyone should boast.*] So says he. By these words, he wished two things to be heard. First, that the way of salvation is biform: namely, by works and by grace. Second, that through works we attain salvation as if by debt—by "debt," I say, not from the nature of the work performed, but by the eternal ordination of God so predestining it. Through grace, however, it is not by debt, but by gift. 

Now, truly, as to what is "grace freely given," what is "grace making pleasing," what is "operating grace," what is "cooperating," what is "prevenient grace," what is "subsequent," and others of that kind—it is not the business of the present inquiry. Rather, we here pursue the way of practice and of acquiring science by one's own investigation. 

Practice, therefore, is bipartite: one of the mind, the other of the body. That which is of the mind, they call **intellectual virtue**. That which is of the body, they call **moral virtue**; and these are mostly accustomed to accompany one another. For intellectual virtue follows the moral, just as joy accompanies the abundance and temperament of the spirit. Yet moral virtue follows the intellectual, just as laughter follows joy. Whence moral virtue is observed in different ways: that which precedes the intellectual, and that which follows it. For that which precedes is observed by the Law and the impulse of fear. But that which succeeds the intellectual is observed by the spirit of love: hence that saying of the Apostle...
