...of the Apostle to the Romans, chapter 8: *You have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you have received the spirit of adoption as sons, in which we cry out: Abba, Father.* <note>original: "Non accepistis spiritū seruitutis..." – Paul Ricius is quoting the Vulgate Bible to emphasize that the Christian relationship with God is based on love and family, not fearful servitude.</note> And to the Corinthians, book 2: *Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty.* And to the Galatians, chapter 2: *If you are led by the spirit, you are not under the Law.* <note>The text cites Galatians 2, though this famous verse is found in Galatians 5:18.</note> 

If you desire to know how moral virtue accompanies the spirit of wisdom and love, hear **Averroes** <note>A prominent 12th-century Islamic philosopher from Spain whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to European universities.</note> in the introduction to his work *On Hearing*, where he brought forth this opinion of **Alexander** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, an ancient commentator on Aristotle.</note>: "When the wise have known justice existing in the substance of things, they then love to be made like that nature, and to acquire that form, from which it is also necessary for them to be just." 

From this comes that opinion of the **Kabbalists** <note>original: "Cabaleorū" – Ricius was a famous bridge between Jewish mystical tradition (Kabbalah) and Christian thought.</note>, by which they teach that the Law of Moses—because it intends to render man conformed to the whole **macrocosm** <note>term: macrocosm (the "great world" or universe as a whole, which Renaissance thinkers believed was mirrored perfectly in the "microcosm" of the human body)</note>—therefore contains in its commands acts of both mind and body that correspond in proportion to the acts of the universe. 

The reason for all these things is this: just as the vain and shadowy beauty of a woman affects and ravishes the onlooker with love, and impels him to adapt and adorn himself in his every action according to the likeness and service of the girl; so too, and indeed far more eminently, the **divine beauty** shining through the universe itself—the pattern and reason for this vain beauty—draws and impels its contemplator toward the imitation of its works and service to its ways, through the intimate ardor of the spirit.

By these things, finally, he proves that whatever is done voluntarily and by the right dictate of reason is shown to be done in the "spirit of adoption of sons." This is also clearly affirmed by the opinion of **Saint Ambrose** <note>A 4th-century Bishop of Milan and Father of the Church.</note> on that saying of the Apostle: *No one can say: "Lord Jesus," except in the Holy Spirit,* saying: "Truth, by whomever it is spoken, is from the Holy Spirit." 

You, then, revolve these things in your mind and consider them diligently. Conclude, therefore, that the way of acting is one thing for the mind, and another for the body. Of the body’s actions, some are by the bond and fear of the Law, others by the spirit and love of prudence. Again, as far as we are concerned, the operation of the mind is threefold. First, that which finds the method by which doctrine and science are constructed. The second constructs it. The third neither finds the method nor constructs, but uses what has already been constructed by another, the understanding of which the art itself declares. 

For the craftsman learns those things belonging to an art in a threefold order. First, by beginning from the **end** <note>term: end (the "final cause" or the purpose for which a thing is made)</note>, from the notion of which he gradually thinks out all the things that the end requires, as **the Philosopher** <note>In the Renaissance, "The Philosopher" almost always refers to Aristotle.</note> first testifies in his *On the Parts of Animals*: "That cause," he says, "seems to hold the principality which we signify by the phrase 'for the sake of which': for this is the reason." Reason, moreover, is the principle equally in establishing things of art and things of nature. Nature and art, therefore, proceed equally from part to part—namely, from the "end," which is prior in reason to all things but posterior in operation—to the part that is posterior in reason but prior in operation. <note>In philosophy, you "think" of the goal first (it's prior in reason), but you "do" it last (it's posterior in action).</note> 

The second order is that by which the craftsman and manual operator does not "invent," but composes and executes what has already been invented; he likewise moves from part to part, but by a reversed path: because he goes from the part that is last in reason but first in work, toward the part that is prior in reason but posterior in operation.

The third is the order by which the worker neither invents nor executes the art, but learns the art by gazing upon those things that have been invented and structured by art. This is clearly demonstrated by the art of building a house. For since the intemperance of the air is varied and manifold—storms, whirlwinds, rains, hail, showers—which oppose the nature and safety of mortal life in many ways, provident human ingenuity is forced to think out some covering and dwelling by which it can be protected and guarded from these and other rushing evils. And since there are various exercises and uses for a human which cannot be fulfilled in the same place, it therefore thinks out various places for this dwelling: the vestibule, the portico, the hall, the bedchambers, and the kinds of places that the various uses of a family require. Thus, once the form or figure of the house is pre-conceived, it immediately adapts material that is neither fragile nor soft—which would be unable to resist the rushing evils—but hard and solid, such as bricks packed with lime, beams, boards, nails, and similar things. Hence, the "end" which it first conceives is the protection itself from imminent evils; second, for the sake of this, it thinks out the dwelling to be inhabited; third, it conceives the form itself, harmonious with the proposed end; fourth,

### ON THE THREEFOLD ORDER OF TEACHINGS.

...provides suitable material for this, by which process and order the invention of the art occurs. While he carries this out, first he prepares the material, second he builds the form, third he inhabits the dwelling, and then fourth—which was the first goal—he achieves his purpose, namely being protected from the corruptions of the air. Therefore, both of these processes move from one part to another; however, this one moves from the part which is prior in reason and is **resolutive** <note>original: "resolutiuè" – This refers to the "analytic" method, which starts with the end goal (a finished house) and works backward to find the necessary steps.</note>; the other moves from the part which is posterior in reason and is **compositive** <note>original: "compositiuè" – This refers to the "synthetic" method, which starts with raw materials and builds them up into a whole.</note>. 

When the house has finally been constructed, he first conceives of it as a whole, from which he then descends into the parts, contemplating their substance, order, and assembly. Indeed, it is innate for us to conceive of the whole first (because it is already completed) rather than the parts, which exist only in potential. It is easy to see that all these things hold true in the practice of art itself. If you rightly consider this threefold conception, you can clearly see it arises from the triple order of nature: namely, **before the work**, **while working**, and **after the work**—specifically in the stages of inventing, executing, and preserving.

Having explained all these things, you will easily be able to gather that threefold operation of the mind. For that which discovers the method of knowing is the art of reasoning through logic <note>original: "ars syllogizandi"</note>, which **Aristotle** rightly calls not "science" but the "mode of science" in his *Metaphysics, book 2*. The discovery of this, as with other arts, could only be established **resolutively** from the notion of the end goal. This aligns with the opening premise of **Galen’s** *Microtechne* <note>term: Microtechne (Galen’s "Ars Medica," a foundational textbook of medieval medicine)</note>, where he says that all arts consist of a rational order through the teaching that begins from the notion of the end goal, which he calls the "resolutive" method. He says, "according to reason," because it is possible for an art to consist of two other modes, though not according to reason; for only the reason of the end goal can assign the logic of the work. Indeed, the entire faculty of logic <note>original: "syllogistica facultas"</note> is discovered from the very act of "knowing," which is the final intention of logic, as the *Prior* and *Posterior Analytics* clearly demonstrate. These works are named "Analytics" for no other reason than that they could only be established through a resolutive process.

In the same way, the art by which nature operates was discovered by this same process of order. For nature, with a final intention, aims at the most specific species, though it reaches them last. Hence that saying from *Metaphysics, book 1*: *What is posterior in generation is prior in nature.* <note>original: "Quod generatione posterius est, natura prius est" – A central Aristotelian idea that the "final form" of a thing is the primary reason for its existence, even if it is the last thing to appear in time.</note> 

However, because we are beings produced by the art of nature, and are posterior to that art itself, we are least able to perceive the art of nature directly. Instead, we contemplate the execution of that art and the things produced by it. Therefore, none of the natural sciences can be conducted **resolutively**, since resolution depends entirely on the notion of the end goal. We are initially ignorant of nature's end goal and its art; we conceive of it only later, by inspecting nature’s execution and the things that come from nature. 

Just as someone who is ignorant of the end goal and the art by which a house is built will by no means know how to construct a house, yet by watching the builder’s execution or by contemplating the already constructed house and its parts, he is able to learn the art itself **a posteriori** <note>term: a posteriori (reasoning that derives theories from observed facts or results, rather than from starting principles)</note>. 

From this comes that second operation of the mind in us, by which science is birthed, by executing the mode or the art that was discovered resolutively. And where the first operation takes its beginning by "resolving" (breaking down), this second one reaches its end by "composing" (building up). For the final thing expected from the entire scope of the sciences is the very act of truly knowing—from which, as if from a notion of the end goal, the doctrine and art of logic is woven. 

Hence that saying of **Galen** in the same introduction to the *Microtechne*: "The second," he says, "is the teaching which comes from the composition of things discovered through resolution." From this, one can clearly understand why **Aristotle**, in the entire scope of natural teaching, proceeds in a **compositive** order, except *in the book On the Parts of Animals*. In that case, the universals of all things consisting of nature were seen "a posteriori," from which the end goal of all nature was already known: namely, the **soul**, which is the end goal of the animated body and of all things capable of being generated. From the soul, he concludes all those things that are ordered toward that end.

The third operation of the mind is that which neither discovers the mode of constructing science, nor constructs the science itself, but gazes upon it once it is already constructed. It proceeds naturally from the whole into the parts, conceiving the essence <note>original: "quidditatem" – the "what-ness" or defining nature of a thing</note> and the connection of each part. Galen, when establishing the order of his teaching, calls this the **definitive** method. In this mode, one does not seek the rationale of the order (which depends on knowing the end goal), but only the knowledge granted by evidence and trust...

...definition provides; indeed, he established this order in Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*, where, breaking down the whole of existence into parts, he then treats each one gradually and step by step. Since order serves not only memory (as Aristotle taught in *On Memory and Reminiscence*) but also leads to an easy understanding of the matter, the Prince of the Peripatetics <note>A traditional title for Aristotle, referring to his "walking" school of philosophy.</note> employed a triple order of teaching, which shows the mutual relationship of the things sought in the *Analytics*, *Physics*, and *Divine Works* <note>original: "diuinis" – referring to the *Metaphysics*, which deals with divine or first principles.</note>. To understand this more clearly, I will subjoin these Theorems, by which you can clearly grasp not only this triple order but also the coherence and connection of the entire Peripatetic doctrine.

## THEOREMS BY WHICH WE ACQUIRE THE METHOD OF KNOWING THROUGH ANALYSIS.

I. <image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'O' featuring floral scrollwork.</image-desc> All men by nature desire to know.
II. *He who by nature desires to know is able to achieve it by nature.*
III. *And although he is able to achieve it by his own nature, Art <note>Here meaning formal method or technical skill.</note> nevertheless provides help to many.*
IIII. *Art, or the method of knowing, is the faculty we call **Logic**.*
V. *Logic, which teaches the method of knowing, proposes nothing other than to moderate the concepts of reason.*
VI. *Concepts are moderated if they are made to conform to things perceived from the outside.*
VII. *They become conforming if we conceive of the thing in the same way the thing itself exists.*
VIII. *Furthermore, every thing is to be conceived through the "being" of its cause.*
IX. *Therefore, it is necessary that we conceive of the thing itself through a knowledge of its cause.*
X. *The means by which we know a thing through its cause, we call **demonstration**.*
XI. *Demonstration shows unknown things from things that are better known.*
XII. *Things are "better known" either equally to nature and to us, or to nature but not to us, or to us but not to nature.*
XIII. *That which is better known to nature, but not to us, produces no demonstration.*
XIIII. *That which is better known to us but not to nature makes a **demonstration of the fact** <note>original: "demonstrationem quia" – knowledge that something is true without knowing the underlying reason why.</note>. This is not a true demonstration.*
XV. *That which is better known to nature and to us is given in two ways. Either the same thing is better known to us and to nature, but not in the same way (because it is not according to the relationship it has to the unknown thing); or it is the same thing, and in the same way.*
XVI. *The first type makes a **demonstration of the reasoned fact** <note>original: "demonstrationem propter quid" – knowing both the fact and the specific cause that makes it so.</note>: because I know the thing through the cause, yet I am ignorant that this is the cause of the thing.*
XVII. *The second constitutes **simple demonstration**: for I know the thing through the cause, and I know that it is the cause.*
XVIII. *Simple demonstration grants us that which is "to know" in the absolute sense, in which the whole perfection of the human race consists; and this was the goal first envisioned, which we execute last.*

## THEOREMS BY WHICH THE METHOD OF ORGANIZING DOCTRINE IS DEVISED, AND FOR FINDING THE SUBJECT OF ANY DOCTRINE, BOOK, OR INQUIRY.

XIX. The human race, just like individual things, desires its own proper perfection or end.
XX. *It achieves this while it obtains those things which its own nature seeks.*
XXI. *It obtains these while it receives them in actuality from its own principle <note>The source or origin of its being.</note>.*
XXII. *It receives them when it is joined to that principle.*
XXIII. *It is joined when it is made similar to it.*
XXIIII. *It is made similar when it exercises the act of knowing.*
XXV. *It exercises that act when it gazes upon the causes of things.*

XXVI. *The soul perceives while it seeks these things.*
XXVII. *It seeks while it doubts.*
XXVIII. *It doubts when it wonders.*
XXIX. *It wonders through a certain flight of the soul from that which is repellent.* <note>In this context, "repellent" refers to things that are confusing or contradictory to the mind's natural desire for order.</note>
XXX. *That which is repellent is whatever stands in the way of the soul’s perfection, both primary and secondary.*
XXXI. *Multiplicity, magnitude, and motion stand in the way of the soul (because the soul is one, indivisible, and unmoving).*
XXXII. *The **observer of natural things** <note>The Natural Philosopher or Physicist.</note> wonders at motion together with multiplicity and magnitude. The **Mathematician** wonders at multiplicity with magnitude. The **Metaphysician**, full of wonder, contemplates multiplicity without magnitude and motion in **being** <note>original: "ente"; the basic state of existence.</note>.*
XXXIII. *Being in itself embraces many things.*
XXXIV. *Since reason cannot investigate many things at once, it investigates the first thing.*
XXXV. *It inquires into that which offers itself as more wonderful first.*
XXXVI. *Mobile being <note>original: "ens mobile"; objects that are capable of change or movement.</note> offers itself as wonderful first, and as more repellent.*
XXXVII. *Mobile being consists of many things that are within it.*
XXXVIII. *No being offers itself according to all its parts at once.*
XXXIX. *It offers itself first according to that which is first within it.*
XL. *That which is the cause of the prior work is first within.*
XLI. *That which spreads itself more widely or commonly is the cause of the prior work.*
XLII. *Simply mobile being spreads itself more widely than that which is mobile in place, and those things which follow.*

### THEOREMS BY WHICH WE ACQUIRE THE SCIENCE OF NATURE IN A COMPOSITIVE ORDER—NAMELY, BY PROGRESSING FROM THE PART TO THE PART, ACCORDING TO THE EXECUTION OF NATURE.

XLIII. That is **mobile** <note>changeable</note> which becomes something out of something; not out of just anything, but from something naturally suited to become it.
XLIV. Since a thing can only happen from something naturally suited, **nothing can be made from nothing**, according to the dogma of the philosophers.
XLV. Since something cannot be made from nothing, it is necessary that **Mobile Being** consist of three principles distinct in reality: namely, **privation** <note>the absence of a form</note>, **matter**, and **form**.
XLVI. **Privation** is non-being mixed with being. **Matter** is being mixed with non-being. **Form** is being devoid of privation.
XLVII. Matter desires to cling to **form** (as if to a "good").
XLVIII. Since matter cannot fulfill this desire for all forms all at once, it is necessary that this happens through the succession of **motion**.
XLIX. **Motion** is the perfection of a being in potentiality <note>original: "perfectio entis in potentia"; the Aristotelian definition of movement as the process of a possibility becoming a reality.</note>, insofar as it is in potentiality.
L. A being in potentiality is moved toward **act** <note>completion or reality</note> by another.
LI. In those things which move and those which are moved, there must be a **first**.
LII. The **First Mover** is neither a body nor a power within a body, but moves with infinite vigor as the goal and the efficient cause of the first mobile thing.
LIII. The **first mobile thing** is the heaven, constructed from a soul that effects motion and a body that is moved, which is carried in a circle according to nature.
LIIII. That which is carried in a circle, insofar as it exists as uniform in nature and motion, adapts this **sublunary matter** <note>matter found on Earth, beneath the moon's sphere</note> to the first and homogeneous form of perishable things.
LV. The first substantial and homogeneous form of sublunary things is **corporeal nature**, which we confess to be co-eternal with matter.
LVI. With this corporeal form interceding, and the instruments of heaven cooperating, and the variety of corruptible bodies assisting—not as the efficient cause, but rather (according to the views of Aristotle in the second book of *On Generation*) as something less than an instrument—matter is adapted and disposed toward forms distinct in number, species, and genus.
LVII. Once matter is adapted, the agent or **giver of forms** <note>original: "dator formarum"; the divine or external source that gives a specific identity to an object.</note> from the outside immediately limits and informs it.

LVIII. He <note>Referring to the Creator or Nature</note> indeed finishes it with six distinct forms according to their kind, namely: elemental, imperfect mixed, mineral, vegetable, brute animal, and finally the rational form.

LIX. The rational form, however, consists through the material or potential intellect; even though this intellect is potential, we prove that it is neither matter, nor mixed with matter, but an abstracted substance. <note>In Scholastic philosophy, the "potential intellect" is the capacity of the human mind to receive knowledge, which is considered "abstracted" because it does not depend on a physical organ for its highest functions.</note>

LX. Because it is an abstracted substance, it is therefore always understanding in actuality.

LXI. But although by its own nature it always understands in actuality, when it provides form to the human body, it understands at times, but at other times not at all.

LXII. It understands when the thinking power offers a phantasm <term>phantasm: a mental image or representation derived from the senses</term> to it.

LXIII. Since the phantasm is not intelligible by its own nature, an active power must be granted within us which makes what is potentially intelligible into something actually intelligible.

LXIV. Things that are actually intelligible give birth to the "intellect in habit" <note>original: "intellectum in habitu"; this refers to knowledge that is acquired and stored in the mind, ready to be used.</note>, from which the "acquired intellect" is produced.

LXV. Once the acquired intellect is produced, and the attachments of phantasms are deleted from it, the active intellect is joined with us, by which we look upon abstract things and achieve adherence with the highest of all goods.

---

### THEOREMS, BY WHICH WE ACQUIRE METAPHYSICAL
### wisdom in a definitive order, namely by proceeding
### from the whole into the parts.

---

LXVI. We acquire adherence to the **Highest Good** if we know it.

LXVII. We know it if we comprehend that the scope of the universal being and its attributes depend on that source.

LXVIII. We comprehend this very thing if we relate the parts and attributes of being <note>original: "entis"; the concept of "Being" or "Existence" in general.</note> to one another.

LXIX. There is a fourfold partition of being. It either has its origin in a thing and remains in the thing itself; or it arises from the intellect and remains in the same; or it takes its origin from a thing but is stored in the intellect; or it arises from the intellect and remains in a thing outside.

LXX. That which arises within and is bounded and remains outside is considered by the maker of artificial things and the investigator of morals.

LXXI. That which has its origin in a thing outside and remains within are the "intelligibles" or species of things, which we gaze upon through a reflected act by the acquired intellect.

LXXII. That which takes its origin within and is stored there is a "being of reason" <term>ens rationis: a concept that exists only in the mind, such as logic or mathematical categories</term> which the logician treats.

LXXIII. That which both arises and remains in a thing outside is what the particular sciences consider individually; the Metaphysician, however, considers it in general, insofar as he contemplates **being**.

LXXIV. Being insofar as it is being is, by its own definition, something that is in all things analogically.

LXXV. If you inspect its essence, you will recognize that "one" (as if its primary property) accompanies it.

LXXVI. If, however, you relate its essence to that which first fits the definition of being (namely the intellect), you will perceive that "truth" follows it.

LXXVII. But if you compare it to the "will," which is constantly present in the intellect, you will soon discover that "goodness" belongs to it.

LXXVIII. Therefore, "One" describes being as undivided insofar as it is undivided; "True" as it is apprehended by the intellect; and "Good" as it is willed.

LXXIX. But since what is willed and apprehended depends not on an absolute but a relative definition of being, being itself receives parts and distinct attributes.

LXXX. For insofar as it is independent, it emerges as **substance**. Insofar as it is dependent, it emerges as **accident**. <note>"Substance" is that which exists in itself (like a tree), while "accident" is a quality that must exist in something else (like the greenness of the leaves).</note>

LXXXI. Again, as independent, it is "one." Because it is dependent, it is "many."

LXXXII. From this side comes **actuality**, from that side **potentiality**.

LXXXIII. From this side **prior**, from that side **posterior**.

LXXXIV. From this side **cause**, from that side **effect**.

LXXXV. From this side **universal**, from that side **particular**.

LXXXVI. *On one side the infinite, on the other the finite.* 

LXXXVII. *On one side the necessary, on the other the contingent. We recognize that these belong to being as modes attributed to it, rather than as parts.* <note>In philosophy, a "mode" is a way something exists (like being "necessary"), whereas a "part" is a component of its substance.</note>

LXXXVIII. *The parts—not the modes—which first narrow down the definition of "being," are substance and accident.* 

LXXXIX. *The definition of substance is to not exist within another thing. The definition of an accident, however, is to exist within a subject.* <note>For example, a "tree" is a substance because it exists on its own; "greenness" is an accident because it must exist within a subject like a leaf.</note>

XC. *Because an accident exists within another, but a substance does not, substance is the more powerful part of being.* 

XCI. *Of this substance, one part is immobile and another is mobile. For mobile substance, there must be a "matter" that is subject to opposite states.* 

XCII. *This subject matter is "being," not in actuality, but in potentiality; in eternal things, this potentiality relates to "where" they are <note>meaning their location or orbit</note>, while in things that can be created and destroyed, it relates to their "form."* 

XCIII. *Whatever exists in potentiality requires a mover to lead it into actuality.* 

XCIIII. *Regarding the "univocal mover" which we perceive with our senses: since it perpetually undergoes birth and decay, it is necessary that another perpetual mover exists.* <note>original: "generationem & corruptionem"; the standard Aristotelian terms for the birth and death of physical things.</note>

XCV. *That which moves perpetually is not mixed with any potentiality or matter.* 

XCVI. *To that which no potentiality is joined, it is "actuality" primarily understanding itself; from this, it secondarily understands and cares for all other things. This is a life that is most delightful and perfect—a mover that is both desired and understood, upon which nature and the heavens depend for their existence and their motion.* 

XCVII. *Since the heavens flow from such a mover as if from an efficient cause, it is necessary that there are as many "motors" as there are celestial movements.* 

XCVIII. *I say these motors are of two types: one is joined to the body, which we call a "soul"; the other is separate in its very reality, which we call an "intelligence."* 

XCIX. *Even though there are many motors, these nevertheless (just like the things that move by themselves) possess a unity of order among themselves. They are like an army directed toward a single leader, upon whom all things depend, from whom they flow, and back to whom they return.*

# PAUL RICIUS’S BOOK
# ON THE METHOD OF THE PREFACE, AND
# ITS CONSTITUENT PARTS.

## A THREE-PART OPINION ON THE
## parts of a preface. CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>Decorative initial Q containing an illustration of two figures in scholarly or clerical attire seated and engaged in discussion, one pointing toward the other who holds a document or book.</image-desc>

Younger students ask why, according to the opinion of Averroes <note>A famous 12th-century philosopher from Muslim Spain whose commentaries on Aristotle were essential to Western universities.</note>, the commentators <note>original: "glosfatores"; scholars who wrote explanatory notes (glosses) on authoritative texts.</note> of a preface assert there are eight parts: namely, the **intention**, the **utility**, the **order**, the **division**, the **proportion**, the **way of teaching**, the **name of the book**, and the **name of the author**. Rhetoricians, however, assert only three parts: namely, **docility**, **benevolence**, and **attention**. <note>In rhetoric, these three goals aim to make the audience ready to learn, well-disposed toward the speaker, and focused on the topic.</note> Again, they ask why not even all the commentators observe the same rules, since Severinus Boëtius <note>A 6th-century philosopher who bridged the gap between Classical and Medieval thought.</note> in his work on Porphyry, and John the Grammarian <note>A 6th-century commentator on Aristotle, also known as Philoponus.</note> in his work on the *Prior Analytics*, announce only six parts. 

To solve this doubt, a certain modern commentator, in his preface to the book by Averroes called the *Destruction of the Destruction* <note>original: "destructionem destructionum"; Averroes's famous defense of philosophy against the attacks of theologians.</note>, says: "One type of preface is moral or rhetorical, while another is physical and technical. The moral type intends three things, but the physical and technical type proposes eight." Another commentator on this passage says: "One preface belongs to the author, and another to the commentator. It is the author's job to pronounce three things, but the commentator's job to pronounce eight." 

We, however, assert that a physical preface intends three things no less than a moral one, and an author’s preface no differently than a commentator’s. But because a listener is not led to these three goals except through certain persuasive means—of which the exact total is eight—the author does not explain them all individually, but rather folds them together. Since the duty of a commentator is to show in a more ample and clear discourse those things which the author treats in a clouded manner, it therefore falls to the commentator to bring forth the eight parts in a clear speech within the preface. For the author, it is enough to perform these very things through his actual work and deed.

LVIII. Indeed, he <note>Likely referring to Aristotle or the creator/nature</note> concludes this hierarchy with six distinct types of forms: the elementary, the imperfect mixture, the mineral, the vegetable, the animal, and finally, the **rational form**.

LIX. The **rational form** consists of the "material" or "potential" intellect. Although this intellect is "potential" <note>meaning it has the capacity to learn but is not born with all knowledge</note>, we prove that it is neither made of matter nor mixed with matter, but is an **abstract substance**.

LX. Because it is an abstract substance, it is therefore always "thinking in act" <note>original: *intelligens actu*; meaning its essence is pure intellectual activity</note>.

LXI. But while it always thinks by its own nature, when it provides the form for a human body, it sometimes thinks and sometimes does not.

LXII. It thinks when the "cogitative power" <note>the faculty of processing thoughts</note> presents it with a **phantasm** <note>original: *phantasma*; a mental image or sensory representation</note>.

LXIII. However, since a phantasm is not inherently understandable by its own nature, there must be an **agent power** within us that makes what is "potentially understandable" into something "actually understood."

LXIIII. These "actually understood" things give birth to the "intellect in habit" <note>stored knowledge or dispositional learning</note>, from which the **acquired intellect** is produced.

LXV. Once the acquired intellect is born and the attachments to sensory images are removed, the **agent intellect** <note>the "Active Intellect" in Aristotelian thought</note> is joined to us. Through this, we perceive abstract things and achieve a bond with the **highest of all goods** <note>referring to God</note>.

### THEOREMS BY WHICH WE ACQUIRE METAPHYSICAL
### wisdom in a definitive order, proceeding
### from the whole into the parts.

LXVI. We achieve a bond with the **Highest Good** if we know Him.

LXVII. We know Him if we understand that the entire scope of universal being and its attributes depends upon Him.

LXVIII. We understand Him, moreover, if we relate the parts and attributes of "being" to one another.

LXIX. There is a fourfold division of **Being**:
1. It either originates in a thing and remains in that thing.
2. It originates in the intellect and remains in the intellect.
3. It originates in a thing but is stored in the intellect.
4. Or it originates in the intellect and ends in an external thing.

LXX. That which begins inside the mind and ends in the world is the concern of the **maker of artificial things** <note>crafts and engineering</note> and the **investigator of morals** <note>ethics</note>.

LXXI. That which originates in an external thing but remains inside the mind are the "intelligible species" <note>the concepts or essences</note> of things, which are viewed through a reflected act of the **acquired intellect**.

LXXII. That which originates inside and remains there is the **being of reason** <note>original: *ens rationis*; purely mental concepts like categories or logic</note>, which the logician treats.

LXXIII. That which originates and remains in an external thing is what the **particular sciences** consider individually; however, the **Metaphysician** considers it in common, insofar as he contemplates "being" itself.

LXXIIII. **Being insofar as it is being** <note>original: *Ens in quantum ens*</note> is, by its proper definition, something that exists in all things by analogy.

LXXV. If you look at its essence, you will recognize that **The One** <note>unity</note> accompanies it as its chief property.

LXXVI. If, however, you relate its essence to that which first recognizes the nature of being (namely, the intellect), you will perceive that **The True** <note>truth</note> follows it.

LXXVII. If you relate it to the **Will**, which always follows the intellect, you will find that **The Good** <note>goodness</note> belongs to it.

LXXVIII. Therefore, **The One** refers to being as "undivided"; **The True** refers to being as "grasped by the intellect"; and **The Good** refers to being as "desired."

LXXIX. But since being "desired" or "grasped" depends not on the absolute nature of being but on its relationships, being is sorted into disjointed parts and attributes.

LXXX. Insofar as it is independent, it emerges as **Substance**. Insofar as it is dependent, it emerges as **Accident** <note>a quality that exists only within a substance, like "redness" in an apple</note>.

LXXXI. Again, as independent, it is **One**. As dependent, it is **Many**.

LXXXII. On one side is **Act**, on the other is **Potency**.

LXXXIII. On one side is **Prior**, on the other is **Posterior**.

LXXXIIII. On one side is the **Cause**, on the other the **Effect**.

LXXXV. On one side the **Universal**, on the other the **Particular**.

# PAUL RICIUS’S BOOK ON THE NATURE OF THE PROEM, AND ITS PARTS.

## A TRIPARTITE OPINION ON THE PARTS OF THE PROEM. CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'Q' depicting three scholars in academic robes engaged in a formal debate or consultation inside a vaulted hall.</image-desc>
Younger students ask why—according to the opinion of **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd, the 12th-century Andalusian philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to university life</note>—the commentators (or "glossators") of an introduction <note>original: *prooemium*; the formal preface to a book</note> claim there are eight parts: namely, the **intention**, the **utility**, the **order**, the **division**, the **proportion**, the **method of teaching**, the **title of the book**, and the **name of the author**. Yet, the rhetoricians claim there are only three: namely, **teachability**, **goodwill**, and **attention**. Furthermore, they ask why even the commentators do not all follow the same rule, since **Boethius** <note>original: *Severinus Boëtius*</note> in his work on Porphyry, and **John the Grammarian** <note>original: *Ioannes Grammaticus*; likely John Philoponus</note> in his commentary on the *Prior Analytics*, declare there are only six parts. To solve this doubt, a certain modern commentator, in his preface to Averroes' book titled *The Destruction of the Destruction* <note>original: *destructionem destructionum*; the *Tahafut al-Tahafut*, a famous defense of Aristotelian philosophy</note>, says: one type of introduction is moral or rhetorical, and another is physical and technical. The moral type intends three things, while the physical and technical type proposes eight. Another commentator on this passage says: one introduction belongs to the author, and another to the commentator. The author's task is to declare three things; the commentator's task is to declare eight. We, however, assert that the physical introduction intends three things no less than the moral one, and the commentator’s no less than the author’s. But because a listener is not led to these three things except by certain persuasive means—of which the exact total is eight—the author does not explain them all, but rather implies them. Since the duty of the commentator is to show in a broader and clearer speech those things which the author treats obscurely, it therefore falls to the commentator to bring forth the eight parts in clear oration in the introduction. For the author, it is enough to fulfill these parts through his actual work and deeds.

<header>THE BOOK OF PAULUS RICIUS,</header>
<meta>The catchword "uocet" indicates the first word of the next page completes the word "prouocet" (to call forth/provoke).</meta>

### EVERY INTRODUCTION AIMS AT THREE THINGS, AND ASSIGNS THE
### cause for this. CHAPTER II.

It must be said first, therefore, that the introduction—no matter what kind it may be—aims at the same three things. Secondly, there are a total of eight means by which we are led to these three aims. The truth of the first point is shown by this logic: those things which share the same goal must also share the same essential methods ordered toward that goal. For the same cause produces the same essential effect; and since the goal of every introduction is the same, it follows that the things which naturally produce this goal are also the same. That the goal of every introduction is indeed the same is obvious to anyone inspecting individual prefaces; for the introduction of any branch of knowledge strives for nothing else than to lead the listener to perceiving or doing something. For "all sciences," as Aristotle says, "participate in some way in Rhetoric." <note>Aristotle discusses this in the beginning of his *Rhetoric*, noting that rhetoric is a counterpart to dialectic and used in all fields to persuade.</note> Since, therefore, there are three things ordered toward the goal of an introduction, it is concluded that every introduction intends these same three things: for each one intends the goal itself, and simultaneously the means by which that goal is reached. 

Now, we show that three things are required for this goal based on the three stages of human operation (insofar as it is human): **knowledge**, **desire**, and **choice**. We can prove this same point from Theology, and even from the actions of uneducated men and beasts alike. This is evident from moral or human operation because, as we gather from the *Ethics* and the third book of *On the Soul*: <note>referring to Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics* and *De Anima*</note> No one who acts according to a purpose executes his work unless a consulted will first commands it; nor does the will command unless the will first desired that very thing; nor does it desire except what the reason has first recognized. 

If you pay attention, this very **pre-knowledge** suggests nothing other than **receptivity** <note>original: *docilitatem*; in rhetoric, *docilitas* refers to making the audience "teachable" or ready to receive information</note>, because it makes the worker fit to correctly learn what is to be done or perceived; for this reason, it is necessary that he becomes receptive—either by himself or from another teacher—and foreknows what must be executed before the work is done. So it is also with **desire**: because it signifies **goodwill** <note>original: *beneuolentiam*</note> toward the thing to be done or perceived; therefore, once receptivity is established, he must immediately become well-disposed toward the matter at hand. 

Again, even when the reason has conceived the idea and the will has desired it, the person does not yet gird himself for the effect unless the consulted will itself commands it, and intends its powers toward pursuing the pre-conceived and willed work. This act of commanding—because through it we tend toward the work—we have chosen to call **attention** <note>original: *attentionem*</note>. Therefore, pre-knowledge creates a **receptive** person, desire creates a **well-disposed** person, and the act of command creates **attention**. 

Theological action confirms the same, consisting of three virtues: **faith**, **charity**, and **hope**. For through **faith**, as the schools of Theologians have agreed, a firm conception of things not seen is shown, which provides **receptivity**. **Charity**, however, is the mental desire and love (stemming from divine grace) for the thing believed, which makes the believer or worker **well-disposed** to complete the work. **Hope** also, as we gather from the third volume of the *Sentences*, <note>Refers to Peter Lombard’s *Sentences*, the standard medieval theological textbook.</note> is a certain stretching out of desire toward a good that is high and possible; this is exactly what **attention** implies, for attention results chiefly from the magnitude and difficulty of the thing to be attained. Aristotle also ascribed this to "choice" in the third book of the *Ethics*: that is, to the consulted and commanding will, which in moral action is called **attention**. Thus, faith provides receptivity, charity provides goodwill, and hope itself provides attention.

The behavior of the uneducated also demonstrates this; for even without any formal dictates of counsel, they exercise these three things to obtain their wishes. A poor man, for example, so that you might hold out a morsel to him, knocks at the door and cries out: "Give bread to the poor, for the love of God!" When he knocks at the door, he makes you **attentive**; while he cries "Give bread to the poor," he makes you **receptive** <note>docile</note> by letting you know what he seeks; and when he utters "for the love of God," he makes you **well-disposed** to the task. 

And it is not only the human race that knows how to do this by the industry of nature, but even the kinds of beasts. A dog, for instance, so that you may offer him food, barks, holds out his jaws, and wags his tail. By barking, he makes you **attentive**; by holding out his jaws, he makes you **receptive**; and by wagging his tail, he fawns and pro-

<header>CONCERNING THE METHOD OF THE INTRODUCTION.</header>

...calls forth <note>The word completes "provocet" from the previous page.</note> goodwill. Since, finally, in any operation that must be carried out, three such things must be provided, and the purpose of an introduction is nothing other than to turn the listener toward doing or perceiving something, we firmly conclude that the duty of every introduction is to intend and execute these very three things: and this is the first point which we undertook to clarify.

### THE MEANS BY WHICH WE ATTAIN THE THREE DESIRES 
### OF THE INTRODUCTION ARE EIGHT. CHAPTER III.

In the second place, it must be explained that there are a total of eight means by which we reach these three goals. This is demonstrated by the fact that if any of those eight is missing, the mind hesitates and carries out the work itself with anxiety; however, when these same things are known beforehand, nothing remains that might delay the listener from embarking on the task, as is clear to anyone inspecting each of these eight. Indeed, no one of sound mind presumes to take up the duties of investigation unless they aim at a specific branch of knowledge. For no one (says Aristotle) will attempt to do anything if they are not going to reach a conclusion; therefore, to attain knowledge of a matter, the first thing needed is the **intention**. <note>original: "intentione". In this context, it refers to the "aim" or "objective" of the study.</note> Since, however, that by which any branch of knowledge is first distinguished is the name of that science or book—for the first perception of anything to be learned is the knowledge of its name—it is therefore necessary to announce the proper **name** of the science or book in the second place. Again, lest any part of that science or book be left unexamined, you ought to know in advance how many inquiries are to be scrutinized in that science; for this reason, the **parts** of the doctrine should be placed third. Furthermore, since such parts cannot be investigated all at once, but one must come before and another after—and where there is a "before" and "after," there is also **order**—therefore, the order of the doctrine is expressed in the fourth place of the introduction. Once these things are known, one must know in advance the **way and kind of demonstrating** (the method), without which no doctrine is constructed; this is placed fifth. When these have been noted, nothing further remains that contributes to the **docility** <note>The quality of being "docile" or "teachable"—the listener's readiness to receive instruction.</note> of the listener. Yet, one does not yet perform the act of inquiry itself unless they understand that something honorable, pleasant, and useful will come from it, by which they may be drawn into a desire for the doctrine; thus, the **utility** of the doctrine must be placed sixth. Even once the utility is known, we do not immediately pursue the work of investigation unless we also command our powers and direct them toward the act; this is achieved with greater diligence and zeal the more the greatness and difficulty of the matter are set before us. Now, the authority of the creator suggests the greatness of the work, which is why the **author's name** is usually explained in the seventh place in an introduction. Finally, proportion announces the difficulty: for when we understand, for example, that this book *On Hearing* <note>original: "de auditu". This refers to Aristotle’s *Physics*, traditionally titled *Physica Auscultatio* or "Lectures on Nature".</note> serves as the foundation of natural science, we immediately apply ourselves more attentively and with greater diligence and study. Hence, in the eighth and final place, it is necessary to grasp the **proportion** <note>Meaning the relationship or status of this specific book within the wider field of study.</note> of the book. 

And although utility also contributes to **attention**, just as proportion and the name of the book contribute to **docility** and **goodwill**, nevertheless, if you consider each of these eight individually, you will clearly understand that five of them—namely, the intention, the name, the parts, the order, and the way of doctrine—primarily regard **docility**. One regards **goodwill**, namely utility. Two regard **attention**, namely the proportion and the name of the author. All of these together are the means through which we achieve the three goals of any introduction.

With these things thus revealed, those arguments which we brought forward at the beginning can be very easily solved. For the rhetorician, the philosopher, and the commentator <note>original: "glossator". A scholar who writes explanatory notes (glosses) on a text.</note> alike—the author—all intend three things; but as for the means that contribute to these, some explain them outright, while others wish them to be understood implicitly. For in the beginning of the *Physics* <note>original: "physicorum"</note>, from the sequence of the text, the intention, the name of the book, the parts, the method, the order, and the proportion can be heard from Aristotle. The intention, name, and proportion are understood from the fact that he says it is clear that those things which concern the principles of the science—which one must first attempt to determine concerning nature. Indeed, the intention is understood when he says it must be attempted to determine...

## PAUL RICIUS'S
# COMPENDIUM ON INVESTIGATING AND ESTABLISHING
# THE SUBJECTS OF THE SCIENCES:
### *And first, concerning the intention and order of the treatise. CHAPTER I.*

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial D depicting two figures in a landscape setting.</image-desc>
Intending to speak about the subjects of the sciences, we will first examine what the common nature of a "subject" is in a branch of knowledge. From there, we will look at the nature of the subject from which a science is named. In the third place, we will ask what is the principal subject of natural science <note>Physics</note>, mathematical science, and divine wisdom <note>Metaphysics or Theology</note>. Fourth, we will ask what is the relative order of these subjects to one another. Fifth, we will explain in an analytical order what the mutual relationship of the parts is within the same science.

### **WHAT THIS NAME "SUBJECT" AND "SCIENCE" DESIGNATE,** *and what the "formal reason" of a subject designates. CHAPTER II.*

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial P depicting a figure sitting on a bench in a natural environment.</image-desc>
First, however, it must be stated what we understand by "subject," by "science," and by the <term>formal reason</term> <note>The "formal reason" (formalis ratio) is the specific aspect or defining characteristic that makes something a subject of study.</note> of a subject. By **subject** here, we do not mean it only in the sense of a subject being spoken of in relation to a predicate, as it is used by Aristotle in the first book of the *Prior Analytics*. For this kind of "subject" belongs to every proposition in which one thing is said of another, whether it is a principle known through itself or something knowable through reasoning. Instead, we take "subject" here as it designates the *subject matter* of a science. By **science**, I mean a <term>habit</term> <note>In scholastic philosophy, a "habit" (habitus) is a stable quality or disposition of the mind acquired through practice or study.</note> acquired by the correct discourse of reason, whether it consists of a single demonstrated conclusion or a collection of many; it is concerning such a common subject of science that our inquiry here lies. By the **formal reason of a subject** in science, we understand the disposition which, when present, establishes the subject and allows it to be known as a subject, and which, when removed, takes away both the being and the knowing of the subject. I say "and in knowing" to distinguish it from the reason given through its own "accidents" <note>Secondary characteristics that are not part of the essential definition.</note>, which is not a formal reason. For example, if this reason or definition is granted—namely, "an animated, sensitive, capable-of-laughter substance"—a human being is established. This is because the "passion" <note>An attribute or property (like laughter) that follows from a thing's essence.</note> is not separated in being from the subject; however, it is not established as far as *knowing* is concerned, because a thing is not truly known except through its own specific difference. Moreover, if a "material reason" is granted, such as "an animated sensitive substance," a human being is not established, neither in being nor in knowing. The "formal reason," however, establishes both.

# ON THE INVESTIGATION OF THE SUBJECTS OF SCIENCE

...to be the subject of a science, about which a property <note>original: *passio*; in Scholastic logic, this refers to an essential attribute or characteristic that is "suffered" or possessed by a subject and can be proven to belong to it.</note> is principally shown. This position rests on the word of Aristotle, who says: regarding the subject, it is necessary to know beforehand *what* it is and *that* it is, which seems to imply the same thing: that the properties of a subject are demonstrated through the definition of that subject. Although this position intends to speak only of the subject from which a science (aggregated from many conclusions) receives its name, the authority of Aristotle that it cites speaks of the subject of every knowable conclusion. But however it may be, their position is false, and it rests on a false understanding of Aristotle's words. 

The position is false, namely the assertion that the formal definition of a subject is the "demonstrability of its property." This is because a subject of science is given without any consideration having been made regarding the property and its demonstrability in the thing. This is evident from the fact that a science is given concerning a thing where the property is in no way considered—namely, the science of the essence <note>original: *quidditate*; literally the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing.</note> of a thing, which precedes the science of its property. But where there is science, there is a conclusion, a question, and (as you will hear from what follows) a subject about which the question revolves. Therefore, a subject is given even when the property is completely neglected. 

Furthermore, it is manifest that the knowledge of the essence—even without knowledge of the property—is truly called "science." This is because the definition of "knowing" truly applies to its action: namely, to know a thing through its cause. This is according to the second book of the *Posterior Analytics*: "Questions are equal in number to those things which we truly know." Since, therefore, one—and indeed the most powerful—question is "What is it?", it follows that the knowledge of "what it is" exists as true science. Hence, in the third book of the *Metaphysics*, Aristotle says: "Though people know the same thing in many ways, we say that he knows most of all who knows what the thing is."

Nor is there weight in the argument of certain people who refuse to call knowledge of a thing's essence "science" because Aristotle, in the sixth book of the *Ethics*, wished for science to be a "demonstrative habit" <note>A "habit" here refers to a stable disposition or intellectual capacity.</note>. Since a demonstration cannot be had regarding the essence of a thing, they say it is not science; therefore, the subject in the conclusion or question "What is it?" cannot be called the subject of a science. For those who argue this way pay too little attention to the fact that a "demonstrative habit" refers not only to that which we acquire through a demonstrative syllogism, but to any habit resulting from even a small amount of discourse—such as division and composition—by which the "What is it?" is shown. We use these methods, as Averroes <note>Averroes (1126–1198) was a highly influential Andalusian philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle shaped Western thought.</note> says, in those matters that require only a modest intuition. 

For this reason, it should not be doubted that knowledge of a thing's essence may rightly be called true science. Therefore, the subject about which an essential predicate is spoken is truly a subject, even if the property is neglected. Thus, the formal reason for a subject being a subject is not the demonstrability of a property concerning it, and so the false position of these people is refuted. That they also rely on a false understanding of Aristotle's words is apparent from the fact that in that passage, Aristotle is not speaking of the "essence of the thing" <note>original: *quid rei*</note>, but of the "meaning of the name" <note>original: *quid nominis*</note>. For a little earlier he says: "As for other things, it is necessary to understand what is meant by the name." And when he subsequently adds, "Regarding the subject, both *what it is* and *that it is* [must be known]," his intention there is undoubtedly, as we have said, regarding the definition of the name. 

The very process of Aristotle bears witness to this, for throughout his individual volumes, he examines and scrutinizes the intrinsic principles of the subject which constitute the essence of the thing within that same volume. Therefore, he did not intend for that subject [the essence] to be already known beforehand. Conclude, then, that the formal definition of the subject of a science is not the "demonstrability of its property"—that is, the subject of a science is not known through the fact that a property is demonstrated of it, because a subject is given even without consideration of the property. 

The opinion of certain others assigns three essential conditions to a subject: 
1. First, that it is known *what* it is and *that* it is. 
2. Second, that through its essence, the properties of that subject are demonstrated in the science. 
3. Third, that all other things determined in the science are reduced to it and considered because of it. 

This assertion also seems foreign to the truth, because either the first or the second condition fails. For if they are speaking of the "essence of the thing," then the first condition is false; because, as is [clear] from what was previously held...

# A COMPENDIUM ON INVESTIGATING AND ESTABLISHING THE SUBJECTS OF THE SCIENCES;

### And first, on the intent and order of the treatise. CHAPTER I.

Intending to speak about the subjects of the sciences, we will first examine the common definition <note>original: *ratio*; can mean reason, definition, or nature.</note> of a "subject" in a science. Next, we will look at the nature of the subject from which a science receives its name. In the third place, we will ask what is the primary subject of natural science, of mathematics, and of divine wisdom <note>Metaphysics or Theology.</note>. Fourth, we will ask what is the order of these subjects in relation to one another. Fifth, we will explain, in a resolutionary order <note>A method of analysis that breaks a complex whole into its constituent parts.</note>, the mutual relationship of the parts within the same science.

### WHAT THIS NAME "SUBJECT" DESIGNATES, WHAT "SCIENCE" IS, and what the "formal reason" of a subject means. CHAPTER II.

First, however, it must be stated what we mean by "subject," by "science," and by the "formal reason" of a subject. By **subject** here, we do not mean it only in the sense that a subject is spoken of in relation to a predicate—as Aristotle uses it in the first book of the *Prior Analytics*—for this kind of subject belongs to every proposition in which one thing is said of another, whether it is a self-evident principle or something knowable through reasoning. Rather, we take **subject** here in the sense that it designates the "subject of a science" <note>The specific object of study for a field, such as "numbers" for arithmetic or "nature" for physics.</note>. By **science**, I mean a habit or skill acquired by the correct discourse of reason, whether it be of a single demonstrated conclusion or an aggregate of many; it is regarding such a common subject of science that our question here is concerned. By the **formal reason** of a subject in a science, we understand the essential disposition which, when present, makes it a subject and allows it to be known as a subject; and when taken away, its being and its status as a subject are removed. I say "and in being known" to distinguish it from a definition given through "proper accidents" <note>original: *propria accidentia*; characteristics that are not part of a thing's essence but always accompany it, like "the ability to laugh" for a human.</note>, which is not a formal definition. For example, if you provide the definition "an animated, sensing substance, capable of laughter," a "human" is established because the property is not separated in existence from the subject. However, the human is not established in terms of being *known* <note>original: *cognosci*</note>, because a thing is not truly known except through its "proper difference" <note>The specific essential quality that distinguishes a species from others in its genus.</note>. But if a "material definition" is given, such as "an animated sensing substance," a human is not established, neither in being nor in being known. The **formal reason**, however, establishes both.

For one side asserts that the formal and subjective reason of a subject is its "susceptibility to" or "demonstrability of" a property <note>original: *passionis*; an attribute that can be proven to belong to a subject.</note>, judging that this should be established...

This is attested by Aristotle’s own process, for throughout his individual volumes he examines and scrutinizes the intrinsic principles of the subject—which constitute the essence of the thing—within that very same volume. Therefore, he did not intend for that subject [the essence] to be known beforehand. <meta>This page continues the discussion from page 315. Paul Ricius is concluding his critique of previous theories regarding the "subject of science" (the focus of a field of study) before presenting his own definition, which links the process of learning to the human lifecycle and the "agent intellect."</meta>

# PAUL RICIUS,

is established, it is necessary to know beforehand regarding a subject only what its name signifies <note>original: *quid nominis*</note>, and not what the thing itself is <note>original: *quid rei*</note>. If, however, the discussion concerns what the name signifies, the second condition will be false: because the meaning of a name can be assigned and limited by any quality proper to the thing, yet such a limitation is by no means sufficient to demonstrate a property <note>original: *passionem*; a technical term in Scholastic logic for a demonstrable attribute.</note> of that thing. Since, therefore, both aforementioned positions appear invalid, we shall soon attempt to explain the third opinion, which we ourselves approve.

#### THE TRUE POSITION CONCERNING THE FORMAL 
#### REASON OF THE SUBJECT. CHAPTER 4.

Let us say, then, that the formal reason of the subject of a science—or that which makes it a subject—is nothing other than a disposition by which something is presented as questionable <note>original: *dubitabile*</note>. Thus, when someone asks what the true nature of a subject of science is, one must respond: "a questionable being," where "being" <note>original: *ens*</note> acts as the genus <note>the broad category</note> and "questionable" acts as the specific difference <note>the unique characteristic that defines this sub-type</note>. That this is the true nature of a subject is apparent from the fact that, once this is established, the subject is established and known precisely as a subject; and when it is removed, the being and knowledge of the subject are also removed. For as soon as a disposition exists in a thing that renders the thing itself questionable, a question arises regarding that thing, either in act or in potentiality; consequently, that thing, when presented to the intellect, is made the subject of a question and of science. But once the disposition is removed, there will be no doubt about that thing, and therefore neither a question nor science, and for that reason, no subject of science. For that which is a "non-questionable being" must be a matter of either first principles or of "infused knowledge" <note>knowledge given directly by God rather than learned through study</note>, about neither of which (as we mentioned in the first chapter of this section) are we speaking here. Since, therefore, the disposition by which a thing is questionable is such that, when it is present, the subject is present and known, and when it is absent, the subject is removed, it is concluded that the formal reason of the subject of a science—or the subjective reason of the subject—is the disposition by which a being is presented as questionable. Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*, Book 1, tends toward this: "For because of wonder <note>original: *admirari*</note>, both now and at first, philosophers began to philosophize." That is, to search out the causes of things; and this because wonder suggests doubt, doubt suggests inquiry, and inquiry suggests science. For Aristotle says that those seeking the truth without doubt at the start are like those who do not know where they ought to go. If, however, someone should hesitate, saying: "Since wonder precedes doubt, it seems more appropriate to establish the formal reason of the subject as 'wonderability' (the disposition by which something is wonderful) rather than 'questionability,'" especially since Aristotle’s words seem to sound this way, asserting that philosophers began to philosophize solely because of wonder. To this, it must be said: although the objective disposition by which something is wonderful is the same thing as the disposition by which it is questionable, they differ in their mode. Something is called "wonderful" insofar as it contains something within itself that is repugnant to the intellect, producing a kind of fear and, in a way (as you will hear in what follows), a retreat and flight. But it is called "questionable" not insofar as it causes flight or repugnance, but insofar as it brings a struggle to the mind and rouses it toward knowing. For "to doubt," properly taken, designates nothing other than an indeterminate knowledge wavering between two opposites. For the human intellect is first, by its own nature, established in total ignorance; second, it wonders; third, it doubts; fourth, it seeks; fifth, through reasoning, it achieves science; sixth, it understands through the attained intellect; seventh, it is joined and, as if on the seventh day of the Sabbath, it rests in the <term>Agent Intellect</term> <note>original: *intellectu agente*; in Medieval philosophy, this is the "active" part of the mind or a higher cosmic intellect that makes knowledge possible.</note>. Clear experience demonstrates the truth of this in us: for instance, the age of infancy is lived in a state of ignorance (what they call "negation"), and the child is not affected by wonder in any natural thing. But as the years of adolescence begin, one soon begins to wonder and strives, as if from a repugnant thing, to take flight; yet one does not yet doubt, but stands somewhat astonished. However, as the more mature age of youth approaches, thirdly, one prepares oneself to struggle against this, and is established, as it were, in the very middle of ignorance and science...

ON THE INVESTIGATION OF THE SUBJECTS OF SCIENCE. 317

...by doubting. Fourth, as one's years settle into adulthood, one does not cease to inquire and to cast off the portion of ignorance until, in the fifth place and by the right course of reason, one reaches the goal and attains knowledge or understanding as a habit <note>original: *in habitu*; in Scholastic philosophy, a "habit" is not a routine, but an internalized skill or state of being that allows one to act or understand readily.</note>. At this stage, one does not yet taste wisdom clearly, but rather obscured by the haze of phantasms <note>original: *phantasmatum*; these are the mental images or sensory impressions that the mind uses before it reaches pure, abstract understanding.</note>. Finally, in the sixth place, one possesses what they call the "acquired intellect" <term>acquired intellect (intellectus adeptus): the state where the human mind is fully actualized and capable of contemplating higher truths.</term>. The cognition of this state is of such clarity that (on the testimony of Averroës <note>Averroës (Ibn Rushd) was a 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational for Western Scholasticism.</note> in the third book of *On the Soul*) it may only be called "knowledge" by an equivocal name. Through this acquired intellect, one is finally joined and clings to the "agent intellect" <note>The "agent intellect" was thought to be the divine or universal force that turns potential thought into actual knowledge.</note>, in which union the blessed life and the total rest of the Sabbath consist. But more on these matters elsewhere.

Returning therefore to where we digressed, I respond to the doubter: wonder <note>original: *admiratio*</note> itself signifies no judgment, but a mere passion or feeling. A subject of study, however, requires a judgment or prior knowledge. Therefore, the "wonderful" (insofar as it is wonderful) could not formally constitute the subject. Although the thing that is the subject exists, it does not exist *as* a subject simply because it is; rather, the formal reason of a subject is that it is questionable <note>original: *dubitabile*; something that can be debated or investigated.</note> insofar as it is questionable. 

Nor should it be argued that "questionability" cannot be the formal reason of a subject in science because it is not interchangeable with the thing defined—on the grounds that not every questionable thing is a subject of science (for example, whether the diagonal of a square is commensurable with its side, and things of that sort). For he who argues thus does not notice that the subject of a science is not named by that science in its *actual* state, just as the "questionable" does not always constitute a subject in *act*, but rather in *aptitude* <note>In other words, a subject is defined by its potential to be investigated, even if it hasn't been solved yet.</note>. In this way, everything questionable is "knowable." For we doubt concerning that whose certain cause we do not know; yet whatever has a cause can certainly be known and understood through inquiry and the movement of the mind from cause to effect. Conclude firmly, then, that the formal reason of a subject, in any mode of science, is its questionability—the disposition by which a thing is open to doubt. 

Thus far we have discussed the subject in general; it remains now to speak of the subject by which a science, aggregated from many habits, possesses its distinction and unity.

## CONCERNING THE SUBJECT FROM WHICH SCIENCE TAKES ITS NAME AND UNITY. CHAPTER V.

One must first know that science exists in two forms (as I have discussed more extensively in the section on the nine orders of doctrines). One mode is that where the questions sought maintain no connection or order among themselves; such is the teaching they call "quodlibetical" <note>original: *quodlibeticam*; literally "whatever you like," referring to academic exercises where any question could be proposed for debate.</note>. The other mode is that which is woven together by some systematic order of doctrine. 

The first of these is not truly "one" science, because it is not ordered, nor does it have an analogy <note>A shared relationship or proportion.</note> to a single thing. The second, however, is truly one science, because it contains one subject to which all the other inquiries of that science look. Our discussion here concerns the subject of science in this second sense. We say it grants distinction and unity to a science because science refers to "form." Form is that by which a thing has unity and distinction; therefore, it is fitting that the knowable subject itself grants unity and distinction to the science. 

Having seen this, we must state: the subject by which a science (composed of many parts) claims unity and distinction for itself is the "adequate and primary questionable thing" of that science. I call "adequate" that which is such that nothing is treated in that science unless it has at least an analogous relationship to it; nor is there anything having an essential order to such a subject that the science does not treat. By "primary," I mean "according to itself"—that is, the science considers nothing except insofar as it has an order to that subject, as will be taught more fully a little later in the sixth chapter of this Compendium. 

In this definition of the subject, the "questionable" plays the role of the *genus* <note>The broad category.</note>. For, as I explained previously, the common nature of a subject is the very disposition by which a being exists as "questionable." "Adequate" and "primary," however, hold the place of the *differences* <note>The specific qualities that narrow down a genus into a specific species.</note>, because through "adequate," it is distinguished from any partial part of the same science...

...subject of a science than to a more common or less common subject of another science, from which science takes neither its unity nor its distinction. For the distinction and unity of a thing come through its form; and the form must be adequate and convertible <note>original: *convertibilis*; in logic, two terms are "convertible" if they refer to exactly the same things, like "human" and "rational animal."</note> with the thing of which it is the form. By the first principle we added to the description, it is necessary that such a subject of science be distinguished from the adequate but less principal subjects of that same science. For example, there are many "passions" <note>original: *passiones*; in Scholastic philosophy, these are properties or attributes that necessarily follow from the essence of a thing.</note> convertible with "mobile being," such as "placeability" and "divisibility," which the natural philosopher considers. Because these are convertible with mobile being, they deserve to be called the adequate subjects of natural science; however, they are not the *primary* subject. This is because they are not considered insofar as they are placeable or divisible—neither of which is the primary reason for wonder and doubt—but insofar as they are "mobile." For every primary subject is adequate, but not every adequate subject is primary. As for what some add—that the subject of a science must be the "first thing known" in that science—this is redundant. This is already implied by the word "questionable" itself; for if something is "questionable," it is necessary to have prior knowledge of what its name means and that it exists. For doubt, as I explained before, holds the middle ground between ignorance and science. A middle ground tastes of the nature of the extremes; therefore, doubt arises simultaneously from ignorance and from some preceding cognition or science. Finally, conclude then that the formal definition of a subject, from which a science takes its name, is that it is the adequate and primary "questionable thing" of that science. Now, by the will of God, we proceed to establish the subjects of natural science, mathematics, and divine wisdom.
