### ON THE THREE SUBJECTS: NATURAL, MATHEMATICAL,
### AND DIVINE WISDOM. CHAPTER VI.

In determining the subjects of the three sciences, let this tripartite conclusion be ours: The subject of Natural Science is **mobile being**; of the Mathematical discipline, **quantitative being**; of Metaphysical wisdom, **being as being**, both simple and manifold. For an exact understanding of these, it must be noted (as previous points show) that nothing is a "subject" except insofar as it is questionable, and it is not questionable except because it is "admirable" <note>original: *admirabile*; meaning something that causes wonder or "awe" due to its complexity or nature.</note>. Therefore, whatever produces wonder in things is exactly what is suited by nature to constitute both doubt and a subject. Consequently, there will be as many kinds of subjects as there are kinds of admirable things. Now, the common kinds of admirable things are the three primary "common sensibles" of the common sense <note>The "common sense" (*sensus communis*) was a faculty theorized to unify the inputs of the five individual senses into a single perception.</note>: namely, **motion, magnitude, and number**. It is therefore necessary that these three commonalities follow the kinds of subjects and sciences. That there are only these three common kinds of admirable things is demonstrated by both reason and experience, the mistress of all things. The reason is taken from the nature of wonder itself: for wonder (since it is a species of fear) is a certain flight of the intellect from something "repugnant" <note>original: *repugnante*; meaning something that contradicts the intellect's own nature or expectations.</note> to it. Therefore, there will be as many admirable things as there are common kinds of things that are repugnant to the intellect. Since there are three such kinds of repugnance, you must admit these are the kinds of admirable things. That there are three such kinds of things repugnant to the intellect will be clear to you when you know the number and nature of the internal conditions of the intellectual soul and the end <note>The "end" or *finis* is the ultimate goal or purpose.</note> which the soul seeks. Truly, as we gather from the first and third books of *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle's *De Anima*.</note>, the internal gifts of the intellectual soul are **immobility, impartibility** <term>impartibility (impartibilitas): the quality of having no parts; being a simple, indivisible unity.</term>, and **unity of essence**. These same conditions belong far more eminently to the End toward which all operations of the intellectual power are directed—namely, to the Creator of all things himself. As is shown in the twelfth book of *Divine Wisdom* <note>Metaphysics.</note> and the eighth book of *On Hearing* <note>Physics.</note>, the conditions of immobility, impartibility, and unity belong to Him hyperbolically. Therefore, since motion is repugnant to immobility, magnitude to impartibility, and number or multitude to unity, it is by right and merit that when one of these is presented to the intellect, the intellect itself immediately takes flight as if from something repugnant: it draws back and wonders. From this, the soul, having been provoked, begins to doubt, and that repugnant...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the relationship between the intellect and the "common sensibles" (motion, magnitude, and multitude) as the foundations of the three major sciences. ->## ON THE SUBJECTS OF SCIENTIFIC INVESTIGATION.##<-

...striving to push forward by searching and inquiring, until it reaches the thing suitable to it and its end. It resolves motion into rest, magnitude into the incorporeal—that is, the indivisible power—and finally multitude into the one principle and leader of all things. Because these three "common sensibles" <note>original: *comunia sensibilia*; in Aristotelian philosophy, these are properties like shape or motion that can be perceived by more than one sense (like sight and touch), unlike color which is only seen.</note> are repugnant to the intellect, three kinds of wonders emerge from them, and consequently three kinds of doubts. From these, three common subjects of the sciences are established. 

The first of these (specifically the one which wonders at motion) we shall call **natural science** <note>Physics</note>, because nature is the principle of motion. The second, which wonders at magnitude, we call **mathematical** or "exercising" science, because it exercises the mind and renders it fit for the contemplation of abstract and divine things. Finally, the third, which wonders at multitude, we name **Metaphysics**, because it transcends the boundaries of nature. 

However, let it not escape your notice that although natural science wonders at motion or "mobile being," motion nevertheless follows magnitude and multitude by its very nature. For as is taught in the sixth book of the *Physics* <note>original: *sexto de auditu*; a common Latin title for Aristotle’s Physics</note>, motion results from the continuity of the mobile thing (magnitude) and the multitude and difference of its boundaries or forms. Thus, it was impossible for the natural philosopher not to wonder at and treat magnitude and multitude simultaneously with motion. Indeed, it is taught in the first book of the *Physics* that the principle of science is the multitude of things, just as it is motion; hence, anyone who says that being is one and immobile denies the principles of knowing and does away with science entirely. 

Therefore, although the natural philosopher considers multitude and magnitude, his primary wonder and inquiry concerns motion, or "mobile being." So it is with **Mathematics**: because it contemplates magnitude, and through division it contemplates multitude or number; but it wonders at and treats magnitude more, because magnitude is more resistant to multitude. It neglects motion, however, because it has already considered it in natural things and reduced it to a state of rest. And although the Astronomer <note>original: *Astrologus*; in this period, the terms for astronomer and astrologer were often used interchangeably</note> and the Musician look at motion, they do not examine it as motion, but rather examine the quantity and proportion of motion and sound. 

To summarize, since there are three types of things in beings that are repugnant to the intellect—namely multitude, magnitude, and motion—there are three primary common sensibles. (For "figure," which is the fourth common sensible, is the limit of magnitude; and "rest," the fifth common sensible, is the privation of motion). For this reason, we conclude there are three types of wonders, three types of doubts, three types of subjects, and finally three types of sciences. One of these, the first for us, wonders at *mobile being*; the other, the second for us, wonders at *extended being*; the third wonders at *multiplex being*. For if you pay attention, the first philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> always proceeds by dividing, which can be seen everywhere, especially in the fifth volume of the *Metaphysics*. 

Nor does any investigator of these three sciences stop his search until he has removed every repugnance in things and applied to himself those things that are suitable and symbolic. For the natural philosopher, as is shown in the *Physics*, does not cease his scrutiny of motion until he reaches rest and a "mover that is not mobile." Nor does the Mathematician stop measuring the magnitude of all the bodies in the world until he applies an indivisible or unextended nature. And the divine philosopher <note>The Metaphysician</note> completes his examination of the vast multitude of beings in the unity of a principle, like a leader in a great army.

But here a modern commentator <note>original: *neotericus glossator*; Ricius is likely referring to contemporary Scholastic rivals who adhered strictly to standard interpretations of Aristotle</note> will immediately rise up, disparaging and crying out that I am fashioning a new and unheard-of dogma—one which neither Aristotle nor his faithful interpreter Averroes would approve. This is especially so regarding the subject of divine wisdom <note>Metaphysics</note>, which Aristotle asserted was "being insofar as it is being" <note>original: *ens in quantum ens*</note> and Averroes asserted was the "genus of abstract things." No one has ever presumed that "multiplex being" <note>original: *Ens multiplex*</note> is the subject of any science.

<meta>This page continues the argument from page 309, where Ricius identifies the three "common sensibles"—motion, magnitude, and multitude—as the foundations for Physics, Mathematics, and Metaphysics respectively. # PAULUS RICIUS, #

is better known to everyone, and nothing regarding this is questioned; therefore, it cannot establish the subject of a science. When, therefore, Aristotle in the fourth and sixth books of the *Metaphysics* teaches that the science of Metaphysics contemplates "being insofar as it is being," <note>original: *ens in quantum ens*; the classic definition of the subject of metaphysics—studying existence itself rather than specific types of things.</note> he implies that there is something marvelous within it. For, according to Aristotle’s own testimony, it is only because of "wondering" <note>original: *admirari*</note> that it happens that men philosophize. 

However, such a wonder cannot be magnitude or motion, since these do not apply to the entire scope of "being." Indeed, in abstract things <note>Non-physical realities like God or the soul.</note> there is neither magnitude nor motion. Therefore, it must be the third sensible: **multitude**. This is present in all things insofar as they are beings. In sensible things, there is a multitude in essence, because they consist of several essences—namely matter, form, and accidents. In abstract things, however, there is a multitude of powers, reasons, and exemplary "paradigms." <note>original: *paradigmatum*; the ideal patterns or archetypes of things.</note> 

For, as Aristotle taught, the **One** and the **Many** <note>original: *unum & multum*</note> are convertible properties of being. Every single thing is both "one" and "many"—not only separately, as many think, but joined together. Insofar as something is manifold, it is marvelous; but insofar as it is one, it produces no wonder. Thus, "being insofar as it is being" does not become a knowable subject for any other reason than the vast multitude of beings. The intellect does not stop investigating the causes of this multitude until it reaches the supreme unity of God, and refers and reduces all things back to Him. 

Aristotle, however, remained silent and did not explicitly add "manifold" to "being insofar as it is being" because he wanted this to be understood as self-evident. For the principle of every science is a multitude of things, just as the peculiar principle of natural science is motion—I say not only as the "efficient" cause, but as the subject and the matter. If there were only one single being, there would be no wonder in things, nor any subject to doubt; there would be no opposition, no definition (since there would be no difference between things), and no demonstration (since things would have no distinct attributes). 

Since every science of things presupposes a multitude, it is therefore necessary that the subject of Metaphysics also implies a multitude. For just as all other sciences deal with being not "as being," but as a *certain kind* of being, so they all wonder at multitude not as it belongs to "being," but as it belongs to the "movable" or the "continuous." <note>That is, Physics studies the multitude of moving things; Mathematics studies the multitude of shapes/lines.</note> Metaphysics, conversely, treats being not as a "certain kind," but according to what it is as being; and it wonders at multitude not as movable or continuous, but as it pertains to being as being. 

Furthermore, it is false to say that the subject of Metaphysics (by which the unity of the science is grasped) is "abstract substances." <note>A reference to a major medieval debate: is Metaphysics the study of *God* (abstract substance) or the study of *Existence* (being as being)?</note> If that were so, it would not be a "common science" shared through the "analogical community" <note>The idea that "being" applies to God and humans in similar but different ways.</note> of the subject, which Aristotle taught First Philosophy must have. This is because the genus of abstract things does not include all other sciences, nor does it give them their scientific principles; otherwise, there would have to be a specific genus of sciences considering "being as being," for the types of sciences are divided like the types of things. 

Yet, I would not call the opinion of Averroes <note>The 12th-century Islamic philosopher known as "The Commentator" on Aristotle.</note> false for asserting that abstract substances are the subject of Metaphysics. This is because Averroes speaks of the "subject" in one way, and we in another. We, along with Aristotle, intend the "subject" by which the distinction and unity of a science is grasped. Aristotle suggests this clearly when he says in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics* that a science does not only have unity by looking at things defined in the same way, but also by looking at things that have different relationships to a single nature—just as there is one single science of all "healthy" things. 

Here it appears Aristotle intends the subject by which a science has its unity; and such a thing is "being insofar as it is being," which is present analogically in all things, just as "healthiness" is present in everything pertaining to health. Averroes, however, is not speaking of the "adequate" subject (which provides the distinction and unity), but of the "partial" yet more "principal" subject. Aristotle himself occasionally hints at this, as when he says a little further down: "The science of the first is always and principally that upon which other things depend, and because of which they are named." For this reason, in the twelfth book, Aristotle judged the theory of Metaphysics to be about "substance"—that is, as the principal part of the subject. 

To ensure that you understand more exactly this distinction of subjects—which causes the minds of younger students to stumble and wander off course—one must know when certain things are...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on how the "three common sensibles"—multitude, magnitude, and motion—serve as the specific subjects for the three major branches of philosophy. The author is concluding his argument on why a science takes its name from its most noble part and is about to explain the hierarchy of these sciences.</meta>

<header>ON THE INVESTIGATION OF THE SUBJECTS OF SCIENCE.</header>

When several parts immediately constitute a whole, then the whole itself receives its name from the more noble part. Now, the parts constituting a whole are divided into two types: they are either **essential parts**, such as the soul and the organic body (each of which is an essence in itself), or they are **integral parts**, such as the powers of the soul (none of which is an essence by itself). Just as an essential whole—namely, a living animal—is named after its superior essence, which is the soul, so too does an integral whole take its name from its superior integral part. For example, it is called a "sensitive soul," <note>The soul responsible for sensation and perception.</note> not because other powers are absent—such as the nutritive, vegetative, locomotive, appetitive, and the like—but because the power of sensation is the superior virtue. Therefore, the entire essence of the soul takes its name from the sensitive power. 

Just as a whole composed of matter and form is named after its **form** as the more noble of its essential parts, rather than after its matter, so it is with science. Because (as we touched upon before) science is defined in relation to the "knowable subject" <note>original: *scibile subiectum*</note> as its goal and form, the unity and distinction of a science are derived from its subject as its more noble essential part. But since that same subject, in turn, consists of integral parts (of which one is more excellent than the other), and the whole takes its name from the more noble part, the science of **Metaphysics** is sometimes said to be about "abstract things" <note>Non-physical or divine realities.</note> or about "substance" as its superior integral part. However, the science as a whole is named after the entire subject. Reflect on these things yourself.

## CHAPTER VIII. HE RESUMES WHAT WAS STATED IN THE EPILOGUE, AND SHOWS HOW ARISTOTLE, PLATO, AND PYTHAGORAS EACH CONSTRUCTED THEIR OWN DOGMA THROUGH THE COMMON SENSIBLES.
->*Aristotle, Plato, and Pythagoras each constructed*<-
->*their own dogma. CHAPTER VIII.*<-

Finally, gather from all this three things that are resistant to intellectual nature. <note>He means three things that provoke wonder because they are difficult for the mind to grasp immediately.</note> From these, three types of wonders, three types of doubts, three types of subjects, and finally three types of sciences are given, according to the number of the three "common sensibles": <note>original: *sensibilia communia*; qualities like shape or motion that are perceived by more than one sense. Ricius uses them as categories for all knowledge.</note> namely, **multitude**, which Metaphysical wisdom admires and treats within "being" as being; **magnitude**, which the investigator of the Mathematical discipline admires and considers within "extended being"; and **motion**, which the inquirer of Natural Science <note>Physics.</note> admires within "mobile being." 

Although Aristotle taught all these things in various places, he touched upon many of them in this very brief closing of the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*: *Every science,* says Aristotle, *which belongs to one genus—namely, being—pertains to one sense and is one science.* <note>original: *Omnis unius generis, scilicet entis, unius sensus & una scientia est.*</note> And according to the variety and similarity of proportion among these three wonders (the common sensibles), Aristotle, Plato, and Pythagoras proceeded along different paths. For Aristotle, although he neglected none of these three, proceeded in a peculiar way via the path of **motion**; Plato via the mathematical path of **magnitude**; and Pythagoras set out through number and the path of **multitude**. Yet all of them turn toward the same end, since all things are present in all things in their own way: sensible things are found in the "abstracts," <note>The physical world reflects the divine world.</note> and heavenly things are found in the "sensibles." Finally, in each of these genera, the paradigm of the Creator himself and the image of divine reasons shine forth. Thus far we have spoken of the three types of subjects from which the unity and distinction of the sciences are taken; now, however, something must be said regarding the order of these same parts.

## CHAPTER IX. ON THE ORDER OF THE THREE SCIENCES
->*toward one another. CHAPTER IX.*<-

The order of these can be very easily weighed from the instructions previously held. Since the subject of a science results from wonder and doubt, it is necessary that whatever offers itself as "wonderful" first is also the first to be "doubted," and thus the first subject of some science. But that which most strongly "resists" <note>challenges the understanding</note> offers itself as wonderful first; for a more powerful virtue operates more quickly and earlier than a weaker one. Hence, in the *Introduction to Physics*, <note>original: *proœmio de auditu*; referring to Aristotle's *Physica*, often called the "Lectures on Nature" or *De Auditu*.</note> Aristotle calls that which is "more known" <note>to us</note> by the name "previously known" a little further down. # PAULUS RICIUS

...motion is more remarkable to nature than magnitude, and magnitude more than multitude. Therefore, **mobile being** <note>original: "ens mobile"; refers to physical things that undergo change or movement</note> is more an object of wonder to us than **extended being** <note>original: "ens extensum"; things that have physical dimensions or space</note>, and this is more so than **manifold being** <note>original: "ens multiplex"; things that exist as a plurality or variety</note>. For this reason, the science whose subject is mobile being <note>Natural Science or Physics</note> will be prior for us than the science whose subject is extended being <note>Mathematics</note>; and this in turn is prior to the **divine science** <note>Metaphysics or Theology</note>, whose subject is manifold being. 

Furthermore, to explain why it offers a stronger resistance to the mind, motion is viewed in a twofold way: first, because a certain deprivation and corruption follow motion; and second, because it implies two other resisting categories within itself, neither of which implies motion. For everything that is mobile is also extended and manifold, but not everything that is extended and manifold is mobile. Indeed, there is a multitude of separate things <note>referring to immaterial beings or abstract numbers</note> that do not involve motion at all. Likewise, in the mathematical entity and "formal subject" (as they call it), multitude and magnitude are present, but motion is not. Therefore, since only mobile being contains within itself a triple kind of resistance <note>multitude, magnitude, and motion</note>, it follows that it is more remarkable and prior to us. Consequently, natural science will be prior to us than divine science. 

By this same law, mathematical doctrine follows natural science in order, because extension is more complex than mere multitude. This is because extended being encompasses two types of complexity: namely, extension and multitude. Every extended or continuous thing must be divisible, and thus manifold; however, not every manifold thing is continuous. Finally, third in order for us is manifold being, which retains only one kind of complexity—namely, multitude. As we mentioned before, in the 12th book of **Aristotle's Metaphysics**, this multitude is reduced to a single Prince <note>the Prime Mover or God</note>, upon whom all things depend, and from whom all things flow and ebb.

---

### ON THE ORDER OF THE PARTS WITHIN THE SAME
### science relative to each other. CHAPTER X.

The order of the parts of any science relative to one another can be investigated in this way: That part of the same science is prior for us in knowing which is prior for nature in its operation. Such a part is that which is more general, and therefore prior in operation. For there is a twofold priority in nature: one is **absolute** <note>original: "simpliciter"</note>, namely in knowing; the other is not absolute, but **in operation** <note>original: "in operando"</note>. 

The **end** <note>the goal or purpose</note> is absolutely first in knowing, being prior to the things ordered toward that end; however, in operation and execution, it is the reverse: that which leads to the end comes first, while the end itself is the last thing achieved. The truth of the aforementioned conclusions receives its strength from what has already been established. For just as that science is prior whose subject offers itself as more remarkable, so one part of a science is prior to another if its particular subject is found to be more "investigable" <note>original: "dubitabile"; literally "doubtable" or "open to inquiry"</note> first. 

Now, the mind first perceives that which nature, as the operator, produces first. For as a thing stands in its sequence of being, so stands its motion in the soul—as Aristotle says in his 8th book <note>referring to the *Physicorum Auditu*, or *Physics*</note>. The reason for this is that everything acts according to its natural aptitude and the mode of its nature. But the mode of nature is to be **indistinct** before being **distinct**, and to be **in potency** before being **in act** <note>a core Aristotelian concept where "potency" is the capacity to be something, and "act" is its realization</note>. This is because a transition from one extreme (non-being) to the other (perfect being) cannot occur except through a middle point. The middle point between absolute non-being and perfect being is **confused** and **potential being** <note>something that exists but hasn't yet taken its final, specific form</note>. 

Since an object presented to the intellect moves the intellect like a natural agent, it does so according to the mode of nature. Therefore, it first produces that which is potential and confused, and later that which is in act. Because a general thing, when related to a more specific thing, is indistinct and potential, it follows that the more general part is prior—both for nature in its operation and for us in our knowing—than the less general part. 

Thus, the more general part is treated first in science because it is known first; reason pursues it first through inquiry. For example, something is known by us as "simply mobile" <note>in a general sense of change</note> before it is known as "mobile in place" <note>specifically moving from point A to point B</note>. This same order exists in nature’s production, because everything that is mobile in place is simply mobile, but not everything that is simply mobile is mobile in place. Therefore, we inquire about "simply mobile being" in the book of *The Physics* <note>original: "de auditu libro"</note>. Next, a thing is presented as mobile in place before it is presented as mobile through generation or alteration, which is also prior in nature. For everything that can be generated or altered is mobile in place, but not every mobile thing...

Thus, that which is mobile through the movement of generation and alteration is known to us earlier, and is earlier in the operation of nature, than that which is mobile through the movement of mixing. ### THEME.

<margin>Ezekiel 33</margin>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'M' depicting a person sitting in a landscape with classical buildings and a tower in the background.</image-desc>
**M**y confidence and presumption today might indeed be considered great and ill-advised, in that I—a man weak and unrefined in learning and eloquence—would dare to approach and attempt those things which, for a long time now, no sacred authority of the Great Popes, no ample power of the most mighty Emperors, Kings, and Princes, nor the skill and perfected speaking ability of the most learned orators has been able to achieve or complete. Truly, in our time, we have arrived at such a point of crisis, and (alas!) such a point of calamity and turbulence, that with no authority of Popes, Emperors, Kings, or Princes leading the way, and no eloquence of orators persuading us, the situation itself warns, urges, and compels us. Unless that highest Pope of the heavens, the Emperor of the world, and the King and Creator of all ages, God—who for the salvation of mortals did not even spare the blood of His only-begotten Son—unless, I say, He looks upon the most foul lot of His flock with swift clemency and mercy, soon nothing else is to be expected but the fall and ruin of faith and religion, and the dreadful destruction, devastation, and desolation of the Roman Empire.

Behold the watchman, the most religious Prince and King Ferdinand <note>Ferdinand I (1503–1564), who was at the front lines of the conflict with the Ottoman Empire</note>, who announces the coming, the coming and hastening sword of the most savage and raging Tyrant to you, the leaders of the Holy Empire, to you, the most learned magistrates, and to all you peoples of Germany; he does this lest that eternal Judge, the just avenger and champion of the innocent, should require from his most innocent hand the blood of Christians which might be shed through the delay and sluggishness of others. Indeed, my soul shudders, my mind is stunned, and my very heart trembles and shakes as I think to myself—let alone expressing it with the living voice of a speech—of the wretched and formidable slaughter and the dire shipwreck which I see immediately threatening us due to the discord and lethargy of Christians. Behold, faith is now confounded, religion is slipping away, morals are corrupted; there is no mutual love among princes or peoples, no respect for honor flourishes, but rather a lust for dominating and a greed for possessing.

...greed, and the anxieties and pursuits of the belly <note>The author refers to gluttony or carnal materialism</note> flourish: frauds, robberies, arsons, and weapons.
Meanwhile, that most savage tyrant of the Turks <note>Likely referring to the Ottoman Sultan, Suleiman the Magnificent (r. 1520–1566)</note> follows, rages, and furies; he is the disturber and betrayer of the entire world, and a most thirsty plotter and enemy of Christian blood. He devastates everything with fire and sword, subverts kingdoms, and overwhelms the faith. Finally, by his fury and madness, almost the entire banks of the Ister <note>The ancient name for the lower Danube River</note> and Danube, and nearly the whole Illyrian land <note>The Balkans, specifically the coastal and mountainous regions of modern Croatia and Bosnia</note> are now—alas!—drenched with the blood and gore of innocent Christian youths, the elderly, mothers, and infants. He prostitutes the wives of noblemen, defiles virgins, takes them captive, sells them, tortures them, and subjects them to the yoke of filthy slavery. If anyone were to consider and think upon this monstrous, miserable, and unbearable yoke which this most foul race of Barbarians has placed upon the necks of Christians, I believe no one would be so inhuman or so rigid a follower of the Christian name as to not break out into groaning, mourning, and a fountain of tears.

For if you look back at the times of the great and pious Constantine <note>Emperor Constantine the Great (r. 306–337 AD), who legalized Christianity in the Roman Empire</note> and attend to his memorable deeds, you will clearly understand that the sacred faith and religion of truth then shone throughout the entire regions of Asia, Africa, and Europe like the clearest ray of the Sun. There was no race, no nation of the known world, that did not obey the empire of the Christians, that did not fight under the banner of the cross, and did not bow the knee at the sublime and inscrutable name of Jesus. There was deep peace and secure rest for every nation of the Christian name—a holy nation, a chosen race, and a people for His possession <note>original: "gens ſancta, gens electa, & populus acquiſitionis"; a reference to 1 Peter 2:9</note>—until Satan, the tempter of evils, stirred up that horrendous monster of Arabia, the asp and dragon Muhammad <note>original: "Mahumetum"</note>. By a diabolical instinct, with a counterfeit faith and feigned sanctity, he began to lay snares for Christian souls. With briars and most sharply piercing thorns, he attempted to block the path and way for the travelers of Christ. By obstructing the narrow gate of eternal salvation, he compelled them to walk the broad way full of all filthiness and crimes. Under the appearance of a deadly and ruinous liberty, he allured the rude and barbarian people of almost all Asia and Africa to their own destruction and perdition.

For the dull and ignoble rabble, otherwise prone to the belly and the life of cattle, is usually drawn much more easily into the service of those who loosen the reins of lust and passion than they are to obey the warnings of those who aim for religion and the purity of life and morals. We ourselves experience this far and wide in this calamitous age, to no small disgrace of the Germans and to the loss of souls and bodies. Indeed, they are like children who more readily and happily obey any idle and petulant man who gives them little gift-apples and rattles <note>original: "xeniola poma & crepitacula"</note>, granting them unbridled license to wander and run about to their own misery and ruin, rather than obeying an upright and learned <term>pedagogue</term> <note>pedagogue: A teacher or tutor, historically one who also oversaw a child's moral conduct and discipline</note> who strives to restrain childish restlessness and madness with the threats of the rod and the cane, and to instruct them toward grasping virtue, the safety of life, and the increase of glory.

Let us now return to where the speech departed. By these fallacies of the impious Muhammad, by these frauds and deceptions, this evil crept in step by step. It gathered so much strength to itself everywhere by moving forward that it now occupies both the rising and the setting of the Sun <note>Meaning the East and the West</note>. There is almost no region of the sky, no part of the <term>sublunary machine</term> <note>In the science of the time, this refers to the physical world beneath the moon, which was believed to be subject to change, decay, and chaos</note>, which does not appear infected by this deadly plague and contaminated by the foul rite of the Muhammadans. Wherever we turn our eyes, wherever we run in our thoughts, the enemies, persecutors, and defilers of the faith from the Muhammadan dregs surround us on all sides. We are so compressed into a narrow space that, from the once so vast circumference of the Christian world, not even one corner of Europe remains in which we might live safely from the incursions of the enemies and the desolators of the Christian name. Indeed, if I wished to recount each slaughter and disaster in order from the beginning of the Christian calamity, and to enumerate all those things which we have lost up to this day through our own sloth and ignominy, the day would surely pass and the night would go by, nor would our speech have an end. Let all Asia and all Africa therefore pass by; let us be silent about the old disgrace and the more recent ones too—Constantinople, once a Christian...

### AGAINST THE MOST SAVAGE RAGE OF THE TURKS

Instead, let us mourn and weep for those things which we saw happen only a short while ago, and which have been before our eyes in these present years. We saw—not yet six years have passed—Rhodes, that distinguished island of Europe, the protector and pillar of the Tyrrhenian Sea, of all Italy, and of the coasts of inner Spain and Gaul, conquered and captured to the great shame and slaughter of Christians, and reduced to the wretched slavery of the Barbarians. A little later, we saw Belgrade—which the Greeks call the "White City" <note>original: "Gręcanica albam"</note>—the unique bulwark and rampart of the Pannonian kingdom <note>Hungary</note> and the German Empire, overcome through our own discord and laziness in a bloody siege, lost, and forced into becoming a Turkish colony. I remain silent regarding so many incursions, arsons, captures, slaughters, and the extermination of so many thousands of souls throughout Illyria, Carniola, and Pannonia, which are miserable and horrific to hear.

Most recently, we saw the mournful and lamentable ruin and desolation of the renowned Kingdom of Hungary, celebrated throughout the whole world, which is the shield and fortification of the entire Christian military. There, that savage enemy of the Christian name raged with such atrocity, such fury and madness, against Christian blood that I believe I cannot tell of it, nor can you hear it, without the sharpest torment of the heart, without sorrow and groaning. There we saw the most powerful and innocent King Louis <note>Louis II of Hungary (r. 1506–1526), who died at the Battle of Mohács</note>, fighting piously and strenuously for the Cross of Christ, overthrown and taken away in the first flower of his youth in a most foul conflict and battle. In a single moment—O treacherous, O impious and cruel fates!—in a single moment, I say, we saw him stripped of both life and kingdom. His numerous and well-equipped army was routed, scattered and destroyed as if to total slaughter. 

How many orthodox and leading prelates, how many strenuous leaders of noble lineage were butchered there! One was transfixed by a spear and carried through the camp; another was impaled on a stake; another had his throat cut; another was cut in half; another fixed to a gallows; another swallowed by a whirlpool of water; another consumed by flames; another buried alive. Others were afflicted with various horrific and unheard-of new tortures of death. Yet that impious man, not yet satiated by the blood of so many slain, soon attacked and raged everywhere through the fields, the countryside, towns, and cities. Everywhere there were fires, wounds, torments, and slaughter. That treacherous man keeps no promises, no treaties of peace. Against the laws of nature, against the rights of human piety, he slaughters infants—infants snatched from their mothers' breasts and arms! He stabs them in their cradles or shatters their necks against the wall. He strangles the mother; he casts the elderly parent headlong from the roof; he cuts the youth in half or tortures them with dire and horrific torments. If he holds any in prison or chains, he leads them shackled through rapid torrents or drags them by the neck through impetuous rivers—not for any human or honorable use, but for punishments, or for a filthy slavery more bitter than any death. 

Could any human ear, much less a Christian one, or any mortal sense, hear or think upon such truculent, such impious and unspeakable crimes without sorrow and sighs, without groaning and wailing? Indeed, no race is so wild, so rigid, no nation so uncultivated and barbarian, that it would not pour out its wealth, bodies, strength, and soul for the safety of its fatherland and the security and peace of its people. Furthermore, even mindless and most lowly creatures—cranes, ants, bees, and their kind—sweat through perpetual and hard labors to protect the life and safety of their flock; they diligently follow and care for their own duties, they clash, they fight, and (as Maro <note>The Roman poet Virgil</note> says) "seek a beautiful death through wounds." But the holy race of Christians—a wise and divine animal, foretold by the oracles of so many prophets, established by the Cross of Christ, solidified by the preaching of the Apostles, strengthened by the blood of martyrs, refined by the laws and doctrines of the saints, and protected by the religion and arms of divine Emperors, Kings, and Princes—now, to its own desolation, to its own miserable destruction and slaughter (O, the shame!), lies so lazy, so sleepy, stupid, and senseless. ...Christendom's eyes <note>original: "Christiani orbis oculi"</note>, let us pass over the horrendous destruction of Trebizond, Euboea, and Illyria <note>Trebizond fell in 1461, Euboea in 1470; these were major Byzantine and Venetian strongholds</note>; let us instead lament and weep for those things which we saw happen only a short while ago, and which are turned before our eyes in these present years. Most recently, we saw the mournful and tearful ruin and desolation of the illustrious Kingdom of Hungary, celebrated throughout the whole world, which is the fortification, shield, and defense of all Christendom. There, that savage enemy of the Christian name, with such atrocity, such fury and madness, raved against Christian blood that I believe it cannot be told by me, nor heard by you, without the sharpest torture of the heart, without mourning and groaning. How many orthodox and pious bishops, how many strenuous leaders of noble lineage were butchered there? One was pierced by a spear and carried through the camp; another was impaled upon a stake; another had his throat cut; another was sliced in half; another was fixed to a gallows; another was swallowed by a whirlpool of water; another was consumed by flames; another was buried alive; and others were afflicted with various horrendous and unheard-of punishments of new kinds of death. Yet that impious man, not yet sated with the blood of so many slain, soon attacked and raged everywhere through the fields, the countryside, the towns, and the cities. Everywhere there were fires, wounds, tortures, and slaughters. That treacherous man keeps no promises, no treaties of peace; and against the laws of nature, against the rights of human piety, he snatches infants—infants!—from their mothers' breasts and arms and cuts their throats, stabs them in their cradles, or dashes them against a wall with broken necks. He strangles the mother, casts the elderly parent headlong from the roof, cuts the youth in half, or agonizes them with dire and horrendous tortures. If he holds any in prison or in chains, he leads them linked together through rapid torrents, or drags them by the neck through impetuous rivers—not for any human or honorable use, but reserved for punishments, or for a foul slavery more bitter than any death.

Could any human ear, much less a Christian one, or any mortal sense, hear or contemplate such truculent, such impious and unspeakable crimes without mourning and sighs, without groaning and wailing? Indeed, no race is so fierce, so rigid, no nation so uncultured and barbarian, that it would not pour out its wealth, its bodies, its strength, and its soul for the safety of its fatherland and for the security and peace of its people. Nay, even the dullest and most lowly creatures—cranes, ants, bees, and their kind—toil in perpetual and hard labors to protect the life and safety of their flock; they diligently follow their duties, taking care, clashing, fighting, and, as Virgil <note>original: "Maro," referring to Publius Vergilius Maro</note> says, "seeking a beautiful death through wounds." But the wise and divine animal, the holy race of Christians—foretold by the oracles of so many prophets, established by the cross of Christ, solidified by the preaching of the Apostles, strengthened by the blood of martyrs, cultivated by the laws and doctrines of the saints, and protected by the religion and arms of divine Emperors, Kings, and Princes—now lies (O, for shame!) so sluggish, so sleepy, stupid, and senseless toward its own desolation, toward its own miserable ruin and disaster. For adamant is harder than any metal or stone—

-> ### THE SERMON OF PAULUS RICIUS ### <-

...nnot be worn down <note>original: "confectum," continuing from the previous page's "caede" (slaughter)</note>. Even the diamond, which is harder than anything else, is softened and melted only by the blood of a goat. Yet the hearts of men of Christian piety are so harsh, so rigid, and so hard that they cannot be worn down, softened, or bent in any way by such a great and never-sufficiently-deplored slaughter, blood, and gore of innocent Christians. O wretched, O wretched and thrice-wretched bride <note>The Church is traditionally described as the "Bride of Christ."</note>, entrusted to such attendants <note>original: "paranymphis," referring to the leaders and guardians of the Church</note> who not only neglect and despise her defense against slanderers, but some of whom, moreover, profane her with their painted dogmas and false, wicked doctrines. They never cease for a single moment to scatter and subvert her with unbridled—as they call it—Christian liberty and lust.

Where, where now is that ancient glory of the Germans, and that strength formidable through all ages, and that proven virtue? We read that by this virtue, the German tribes—the hardest in war—were never conquered or subdued, not even by the Romans, the masters of the world, though they were attacked more than once with cruel intent. Where, where now is that former moderation of the Germans in their way of life, that very nurturer of peace and concord, that expeller of dissension and rivalries—the virtue of frugality and parsimony? 

By this virtue the Germans, above all other mortals (if we are to believe the accounts of history), were despisers of gold and silver—those greatest of plagues. By this, they also spurned all elegance in clothing and cast away the allure of fine garments; by this, they also despised and were ignorant of the use of wine, not permitting it to be imported from elsewhere. They believed that by its intemperance and luxury, the mind was dulled, and men became soft and effeminate toward labor. 

Where, finally, is that former fervor of the German faith? Where is the persistent guarding and observance of religion, for which the exceptional honor of the Empire <note>The "Translatio Imperii," the medieval theory that the right to rule the world passed from the ancient empires (Assyria, Persia, Macedonia, Rome) to the Germans</note>—which first passed from the Assyrians, Persians, and Macedonians to the Romans—at last migrated to the Germans? It came to them as those who were held more worthy than other nations, to whom Christ’s banner and the guardianship and steering of His republic should be entrusted. 

Has such glory of the Germans, memorable in every age, been extinguished? Has so much splendor of strength and fortitude vanished, that no power of repentance remains, no expectation of recovering former honor and praise? May the heavens far and wide avert such a thing! Indeed, if there is ever any future hope of restoring the falling Christian world, if any confidence is given to restoring orthodox piety to its former appearance and vigor, I believe this lies most especially in the protection, virtue, and help of the Germans. 

For the seeds of faith, religion, and military discipline are innate to the German lineage. Although these have not yet grown together due to the obstacles of dissension, the lust for pomp, and the intemperance of living—which cloud, suffocate, and corrupt this noble sowing—they will nevertheless easily rise again into their former vigor and bloom if you remove these three: the root and fuel of all evils. 

I think it would not be worthwhile to show through a long series of words and speech how much trouble, loss, and ruin discord, envy, and rivalry bring to human society, or how much safety and sweetness of life concord and love bring forth. The matter itself demonstrates it openly and clearly. The order of nature and of things, and even the behavior of beasts, teaches it, and sacred authority warns of it in many ways. For divine authority values concord and unanimity so much that it decreed it should be placed before even the observance of religion and the sacrifice of the altar: *If you offer your gift at the altar,* it says, *and there you remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother* <note>Matthew 5:23-24</note>. 

Conversely, divine concern abhors discord and hatred to such an extent that it taught that even the unspeakable worship of idols should be considered a lesser crime than dissension and discord. *Ephraim is a partner of idols,* it says, *let him go; their heart is divided, now they shall perish* <note>A combination of Hosea 4:17 and 10:2</note>. *For every kingdom,* says the Truth <note>i.e., Jesus Christ</note>, *divided against itself shall be laid waste: and every city or house divided against itself shall not stand* <note>Matthew 12:25</note>. 

The wise man Sertorius <note>Quintus Sertorius (c. 126–73 BC), a Roman general who used a famous parable involving two horses to teach his soldiers that unity is strength</note> taught this very thing by a clear experiment: for he brought out two horses into the middle, one solid in strength and in the flower of its years, the other weak with decay and years...

-> ### AGAINST THE MONSTROUS MADNESS OF THE TURKS ### <-

...finished <note>original: "confectum"</note>. Thereupon, he <note>Referring to the Roman general Sertorius, who used this demonstration to teach his army about unity.</note> handed the tail of a weak and filthy horse to a young man and a man of great strength to be pulled out; but the tail of a flourishing and robust horse he entrusted to a weak and old little man to be plucked. Then the young man, relying on his own strength and seeing the weakness of the sickly horse, tried incautiously, rashly, and finally in vain to tear out the whole tail at once in one continuous pull. But the old man, considering the matter more perceptively, divided the tail of that flourishing and robust horse into tiny portions and scattered them, extracting them bit by bit with frequent pulls, so that in a short space of time, that sickly old man completely plucked the entire tail of the robust horse with no trouble or labor. By this, that wise man warned that any strength, however small and thin, if it is harmonious and joined together, cannot easily be conquered or overcome even by a more solid and greater power; conversely, even a strong and very great power, if it is disjointed and scattered, can be oppressed, subjugated, and extinguished by any small and weak hand. 

The wise instinct of beasts teaches the very same thing, which that vigorous leader of leaders, **Cocio** <note>This likely refers to a contemporary or legendary military leader, possibly a variation of Scanderbeg (Gjergj Kastrioti), who was frequently cited in anti-Ottoman literature using this specific anecdote of the dogs and the wolf.</note>, showed in an assembly of the princes of that nation by a prudent act: for he allowed two very fierce dogs to clash and rage against each other, and when he saw they were in a sharper contest and a more ferocious madness, he ordered a wolf to be secretly let in against them. When the dogs saw the wolf, all their strife was immediately set aside, and they turned with a concordant pact to drive away the wolf. If, therefore, brute and dull animals do not hesitate to lay aside private contest and hatred to rise up against a common enemy: you, a man who possesses reason, a worshiper of Christian piety, a moderator of public affairs—think and consider what you owe, and what concerns you. 

The order of nature and of things teaches the same: that everything which nature itself shapes and produces is born of concord alone, and she preserves what is born. Although this clearly appears in each and every thing that consists of nature's work, it is possible to see and experience this more evidently in our human frame: where, if you take away concord and the mutual help of the limbs, it is necessary that the whole mass of your body soon be reduced to decay and corruption. 

No doubt you know the **Wise Man's Fable** <note>Referring to the famous fable of Aesop, "The Belly and the Members," famously used by Menenius Agrippa to quell a Roman plebeian revolt.</note>, which I now earnestly ask you to attend to: The feet and hands complained about the tranquility of the internal organs and the leisure of the belly, and lamenting their own perpetual movements and agitations, they finally entered into a plan by which they decreed they would impart no work or service from then on to the organs and the belly. The belly and the emptied organs asked for the food usually supplied to them by the feet and hands; they refused with dull stubbornness. At last, through long hunger and the lack of restoration, the innate heat was dulled and the force of nature slipped away; the hands and feet themselves, stumbling and already sensing the fall of nature, were anxiously worried and hurried to give all effort and provide help. But it was far too late; their power of moving and stirring was already prostrated, and the belly lacked the faculty of digesting food. It finally happened, from that stubborn disagreement of the members, that a little while later all the joints of the body became filthy, the heat was extinguished, the spirit flew out, and finally the whole frame was turned into a rotting corpse. 

If you pay attention, the Fable clearly designates the calamity of our time, where the feet and hands—that is, the rural inhabitants <note>original: "coloni"</note>, craftsmen, and commoners—grow insolent with wicked rashness against the organs and moderators of the Commonwealth. For the crude Farmers and commoners seek the duties and rudders of Princes and magistrates; Butchers and Bakers take upon themselves the ministries and works of the Priesthood; Shoemakers and cobblers boast themselves as interpreters of laws and sacred canons; and little women—O insanity, O madness!—little women do not hesitate to philosophize and pass judgment on the mysteries and hidden sacraments of the faith. Beware, I say, beware, and I say again beware—and may the heavens avert the omen—lest you too (unless you come to your senses more maturely and quickly, and restrain your mind from contention and malice, and let each member of your commonwealth exercise that duty which divine sanction and the order of nature has distributed to each) may soon experience a similar exit, which the aforementioned frame of disagreeing members miserably felt. -> ### THE ORATION OF PAULUS RICIUS ### <-

The most ruinous stain upon the Commonwealth, how much it now occupies the entire German nation, and how far this nation degenerates from the frugality and modesty of its ancestors, there is no one who cannot judge. For rare indeed is that man—even if he boasts of only a small degree of nobility, or acts as a wealthy citizen, merchant, or craftsman—who does not disdain woolen garments unless they are woven from the exotic and foreign fleeces of Britain or Ireland <note>original: "Britannię aut Hibernię"</note>. Rare is he who does not think it shameful to be covered in sheep or fox skins, or who is content with a cap and cloak of common wool, unless he shines in a garment lined twice or thrice with all-silk <note>original: "holoſerico"</note> and purple marten or sable <note>original: "Martina aut Sebelina"</note> fur (as they call it). He revels in a cap—what they call a beret <note>original: "birethum"</note>—imported from Lyon in France, bordered with scarlet and adorned with gold buckles and winding purple ribbons. This variety of luxuries is open to the blasts, the rains, and the burning rays of the sun. He also sports a doublet <note>original: "diploi-de"</note> and breeches <note>original: "caligis"</note> with a base of reddish or crimson-patterned silk, which shines through six hundred slits and cracks, as well as a fine linen undershirt <note>original: "byſsina interula"</note> with a gold-embroidered neck and hem; in such pride and pomp does he behave wantonly. 

I am silent regarding the insatiable lust of the table and delicacies, where you are not content with three or four dishes, nor with one or two varieties of wine and other drinks. Nor do you consider it enough to sit at the table two or three times a day, unless you also gorge yourself on a sleep-inducing nightcap of Punic <note>Carthaginian</note>, Falernian <note>a famous Italian wine</note>, or Cretan wine, and that whole sort, by which you surely consume your entire income, profit, and all your fortunes; at the same time, you overthrow the power and strength of both body and soul. You become weaker in strength, poorer in substance, slower toward the works of religion, duller in counsel, and more powerless for military preparation. 

O wicked and scandalous display! O cruel, impious, and empty luxury, which scatters the houses of the illustrious, destroys the kinships of the nobles, ruins kingdoms, and subverts every sublime empire—and yet there is no one who guards against you, who rejects or despises you! If a virulent plague corrupts your finger, if poisonous ulcers defile your hand or foot, you do not hesitate to consume the whole finger, hand, or foot with iron and fire so that you may guard and keep the remainder of your little body unharmed. Yet for the safety and protection of the entire Christian Commonwealth—which you see trembling in the final crisis of extermination and devastation because of your exorbitant luxury and unbridled lust for pomp—not even one, O the disgrace! O the shame!—not even one nightly cup, not one little dish, nor the smallest flattering garment, nor the pomp of dress or pride do you think should be cut away or tempered. 

But if no piety, no religion, nor the glory of your ancestors and the splendor of virtue moves you, this single example of the most pious King Ferdinand <note>Ferdinand I (1503–1564), Archduke of Austria and later Holy Roman Emperor, who was on the front lines against the Ottomans.</note> ought to bend, entice, and draw you. (Let all enticement and stroking flattery be far away; I speak from the facts themselves, which far surpass and excel all this praise; God, who is the searcher and knower of secrets, knows it.) For that most religious King Ferdinand, born of such a great lineage and high blood, established in so sublime a watchtower of scepters and kingdoms, in the flowering years of his youth—having nonetheless trampled the heat of youthful spirit, rejected pleasures, and spurned the allurements of all delights—shudders at no adversity or inconvenience whenever it concerns religion and the public good. He fears neither heat, nor cold, nor winds, rains, or hail. He is broken by no vigils, no hunger, nor any anxious labors whatsoever. Instead, like a skillful and vigilant watchman of the Christian flock and a strenuous vanguard of the Cross, he does not fear to descend into the line of battle against the Cross-bearer <note>likely referring to the Ottoman Sultan as a rival claimant to power</note> and the furious exterminator of the Christian world, and to cast his troops, wealth, strength, and soul in defense of the flock committed to him. 

But I seem to hear the voice of one whispering and murmuring to himself, saying: "And what wonder is it that King Ferdinand moves his arms, collects troops, and directs all his strength and efforts against the enemy, since it is now in his interest, and it falls to him above the other potentates of Germany to restrain the fury and onset of the impious Tyrant <note>The Ottoman Sultan, Suleiman the Magnificent</note>, who even now penetrates, burns, and lays waste to the vitals of his kingdoms of Pannonia <note>modern-day Hungary</note>, Croatia, and Dalmatia, and attacks the garrisons and defenses <insert>bulwarks</insert> of those kingdoms?"

occupies the fortifications. But the other German Princes, magistrates, and peoples are still far from the enemy; the foe does not yet knock at their doors, nor touch the borders or thresholds of anyone else. These are the things you think to yourself, these are the things you mutter, these are the things you say. O improvident, O vain voice, unworthy of a man! For if you say that one should not resist, nor prepare for war, until you see the enemy's vibrating sword and blade drawn against you, and until you feel the gasping heat of the flames and the abyss of the conflagration—what distinction, I ask, will you make between a human and a beast of burden? What difference between a provident and rational creature and a wild animal? Since there is no species of beast so sluggish or stupid that, when it sees or feels a man or a wild animal attacking, it does not immediately rise up, grow fierce with its teeth, strike with horn and hoof, or wound its pursuer with its claws. Or who is so reckless and lacking in counsel that he does not judge, and does not see openly, that if that horrendous monster <note>Referring to the Ottoman Sultan, likely Suleiman the Magnificent.</note> should once more break into Hungary (which he will do unless your religion, prudence, and arms resist him, since he already occupies the keys, citadels, and garrisons of that kingdom), he will immediately rush into the Austrian provinces, and devastate everything with sword and fire with his usual cruelty and rage? And what then, I ask, will stand in his way? Who will close the path? Who will block the entrances? Instead, immediately, like the broken levee of a great river whose force can be contained by no mass or barrier, that impious tyrant will soon attack through the regions of Bavaria, Swabia, the Rhine, and the Saxons. He will grow fierce and fill everything with ruin and slaughter—so much so (may the heavens avert it) that the Rhine and the Elbe <note>original: "Albis"</note>, just like the Danube <note>original: "Danubius & Ister"</note>, will be stained by the slaughter of innocent Christians and redden with blood and gore. 

But even if it were granted—though no prudent person would say so—that this fierce tyrant, after subduing Hungary and overturning Austria, should halt his step there and not turn the fury of his sword against you, does it seem humane to you, let alone pious and Christian, to wink with lowered eyelids at the ruin and destruction of your people? And like a cowardly and stupid man, to look upon and watch the calamity of others with your hands folded in your lap? If you saw your neighbor's roof seized by fire at your very doors, and his house, furniture, wife, and infants being devoured by the cruel flame, would you not be reckoned an impious and wicked man? If you did not immediately cry out, rouse the neighbors, call for help, and fly there yourself with a swift foot, bringing aid with hand, back, and all your strength? 

If the Evangelical truth <note>A reference to the Gospels; specifically Luke 14:5.</note> declares that a sheep or an ox that has fallen into a pit must be pulled out; if it commands by the mouth of Moses <note>Exodus 23:5.</note> that you should lift up and relieve a donkey lying under an overwhelming burden; will you shrink from snatching a faithful man and a vast multitude of the Christian name from this deep pit of distress and abyss, and from protecting and rescuing them from the truculent hand of the slaughterer who thirsts for your blood? For these people, Christ the Savior did not shrink from spit, whips, the cross, wounds, blows, and finally the punishments of a bitter death. You, who promise to be a servant of Christ, who pledge to be a hearer and a doer of the word—will you shrink from this? 

Let this unspeakable cruelty and horrendous impiety be far from the innate fellowship and sweetness of the Germans <note>The author here makes a pun on the word *Germani* (Germans) and *germanitas* (brotherhood/kinship).</note>, who are called "Germans" for no other reason than that they embrace and cherish one another with mutual kindness and love, as if joined by brotherly blood. By the merit of this former benevolence and fraternal concord, there was once no nation in the world, no race however hard and fierce in war, that restrained the onset and violence of tyrants with such virtue and glory, or protected its genuine liberty as the Germans did.

For what people, what race or nation repressed the force of Alexander the Great, the master of the world, and restrained his onset so that he did not cross the banks of the Danube, except the Germans?

Darius, son of Hystaspes, and Cyrus, the most powerful Kings of Asia, when crossing the Danube, did not dare to touch the Germans.

The legions of Octavian Augustus were destroyed to the point of extermination among the Carisci <note>Likely a reference to the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest, though "Cariscos" specifically refers to a Germanic tribe, sometimes associated with the Carystians or simply used here as a general tribal descriptor.</note> by the Germans.

<meta>This page concludes the oration of Paulus Ricius, continuing his urgent appeal to the German estates. Having previously warned of the immediate threat to the borderlands, he now invokes the martial history of the German people and the sacred duty of the Holy Roman Empire to defend Christendom against the Ottoman advance.</meta>

<page-num>330</page-num>
<header>PAUL RICIUS ON THE MOST MONSTROUS RAGE OF THE TURKS</header>

The Germans also drove Tiberius <note>Tiberius (reigned 14–37 AD), the second Roman Emperor, who led several campaigns in Germania.</note> into flight and beyond his own borders when he attacked them with the force of arms. Later, the Germans could not be overcome or defeated by Vespasian, who would become the Great Emperor, even after thirty-two battles had been joined. As for the long-standing tyranny of the Lombards, which no power of Kings or Princes and no strength could blunt or restrain, the Germans overcame and extinguished it. Finally, so great and so sharp was the German virtue in war and fighting that a proverb was born among their neighbors: *He who wishes to fight poorly, let him fight the Germans.* <note>original: "Malè qui pugnare uelit, cū Germanis pugnet." A testament to the fearsome reputation of German warriors in the Renaissance imagination.</note>

If, therefore, in earlier centuries—while the Germans still served the elements of the world and worshiped the mute idols of the nations, not yet having attained the royal scepter nor the summit of the Empire—they always protected their liberty and the tranquility and peace of their people with manly audacity, unshaken spirit, and strength against Kingdoms, Empires, and the incursions and attacks of the most ferocious nations; then how much more fittingly, how much more opportunely, and how much more gloriously must you now fight! For now you are instructed by the highest religion and the greatest faith in truth, established in Divine laws and customs, decorated with Imperial Majesty, and fortified by military discipline and arms above all other nations. You must fight against the most atrocious sword of a Raging Tyrant, against the slave-like and most filthy dregs of all mortals, who seeks not only to lay waste to fields and homes and plunder your household goods, but seeks your life and the blood and bones of your sons, mothers, and infants. He aims for the extermination of your most sacred faith and religion; he seeks your Principalities and your Empire, not to possess them, but to ruin, delete, and extinguish them. This has been heard more than once from the impious and polluted mouth of this tyrant: that he does not wish to withdraw his hand, his steel, and his fire from the Christian people, nor can he be satiated with Christian blood, until he removes and exterminates their Empire, and utterly deletes and extinguishes its memory and name.

Come then, arise, you nobles of the Holy Empire, you most wise Magistrates, and all you people! Come and seize your arms, your missiles, and your swords, and break off your delays before the shadows fall from the mountains and the sudden and indelible darkness of calamities seizes you. Already the ax is laid to the tree; <note>A reference to Matthew 3:10, signaling imminent judgment or destruction.</note> already that pestilential plague has crawled all the way to your thresholds. If you delay but a little, it will be all over for your faith, your religion, your Empire, and your Principalities. Come, therefore, and arise while there is time, while a little of the day still shines, and follow King Ferdinand, <note>Ferdinand I (1503–1564), King of Bohemia and Hungary, and later Holy Roman Emperor, who was the primary defender of the Habsburg lands against Suleiman the Magnificent.</note> that most pious standard-bearer of the Cross, who will not fear to set his scepters, kingdoms, troops, fortunes, and strengths against the enemy for the sake of religion, for the Christian people, and for your Empire. Come, finally, for the sake of the faith of Him who hung for us upon the cross; come for the religion for which the saints underwent the dire torments of death; come for the Empire, the Principalities, and your Magistrates, which the Ottos, the Henries, the Fredericks, <note>Ricius invokes the great medieval dynasties: the Ottonians, the Salians, and the Hohenstaufens.</note> and your other ancestors attained and protected by religion, by arms, and by their own blood. Come for your own blood and the gore of your sons, your wives, and your innocent little ones, which that monstrous and furious enemy of God and nature seeks and thirsts for.

Come finally, and lay aside dissension and malice; lay aside pride and the lust for display; lay aside luxury and intemperance of living, so that those innate seeds of virtue may unite within you and rise again into the former bud and flower of your glory and splendor. Then you will be healthier in body, wealthier in substance, more vigilant in the practice of religion, more perceptive in counsel, better fortified for the apparatus of war, and finally, in all your conduct, actions, and successes, you will be more fortunate and more blessed for all time.

# TO CHARLES PERRENOT
## OF GRANVELLE
<note>Charles Perrenot de Granvelle (1524–1567) was the Abbot of Faverney and brother to the powerful Cardinal Granvelle, a leading advisor to the Spanish Habsburgs.</note>
-> To the most distinguished and most Reverend Abbot of Faverney, and a most worthy Councilor <-
-> of the private councils of **PHILIP**, King of Spain, <-

## JOANNES CAROLUS SARACENUS.

---

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'M' depicting a person seated outdoors in a landscape with buildings in the background, enclosed in a rectangular frame with decorative foliage.</image-desc>

Truly, most excellent Charles, it is considered a **GREAT** <note>original: "MAGNVM"</note> thing indeed—and not without justice—by mortals that, among all the kinds of living things placed in this lower world by the generosity of God the Best and Greatest <note>original: "Dei Optimi Maximi," a common Renaissance formula for the Judeo-Christian God derived from the titles of Jupiter.</note>, [man] has obtained the human condition and human dignity. But it seems to be far greater and more distinguished that, after nature has co-opted you into such an illustrious order, you then confirm the supreme nobility and excellence of the human race—not just in face and outward appearance, but also in mind and internal form—first by adorning your appetite with the best character and virtues, and then finally by instructing your intellect with the liberal arts and disciplines. But that thing finally exists as the greatest, and in my judgment almost divine, when you have attained both of these goals: when the powers handed to you by nature, as well as all the virtues acquired by yourself with the greatest labor and highest study, are finally returned for the benefit of other men and the common good. For that you are a man, you owe to nature; that you turn out prudent and wise, you owe to art; and finally, that you benefit the human race, you surely owe to the divine power. Whence it is no wonder if a man—refined at last by nature, by art, and by divinity itself—seems to embrace the supreme perfection and beauty of all things within himself, as if in a certain <term>microcosm</term>. <note>The "microcosm" or "little world" is a central Renaissance idea that the human being reflects the structure and qualities of the entire universe (the macrocosm).</note> Since, therefore, these three aforementioned conditions—which are accustomed to render the human race as illustrious and conspicuous as possible—were observed by me day and night, I soon felt certain most burning torches cast into my mind, which wonderfully kindled and inflamed it to seize that part of perfection and beauty in which it is lacking. Wherefore, when my mind itself [observed] that it had first attained a certain purest and heavenly nature by the favor of the divine power, and then [attained] the liberal ar- <note>The text breaks here; the catchword "tium" at the bottom of the original indicates the word is "artium," completing the phrase "liberal arts."</note>

### PREFACE.

*...[of arts] and disciplines, he perceived that he had acquired a knowledge of things themselves, as well as a command of languages—perhaps not exact or perfect, but at least moderate—and girding himself for what remained, he finally decided to contribute something to the common use of human society and the shared benefit of all studies. To this most holy and pious deliberation, a recent opportunity seems to have been offered, such that no more convenient or opportune one could have ever occurred. For when, in recent days, I came across the dialogues of **Leo the Hebrew**, that most learned and erudite man, which are titled **ON LOVE** <note>original: "de AMORE"</note>, I noticed they were read by very few because they were originally written by the author himself in a language neither particularly splendid nor elegant, nor common to all scholars <note>Leone Ebreo originally wrote his work in Italian (the "vulgar" tongue), which Sarrazin, as a humanist scholar, considers less "splendid" than Latin.</note>. Moreover, seeing that they were in many places corrupt, distorted, and mutilated, I deemed it quite intolerable to let such a disgrace stand. Therefore, serving first the common utility of all, and—to tell the truth—being somewhat intent on my own praise and glory, I eagerly and promptly took up this noble burden, which many most learned men perhaps refused to undergo as being too troublesome and laborious.*

*Thus, I have illustrated these proposed dialogues—which in my judgment embrace nearly the whole of **Aristotelian** and **Platonic** philosophy along with the divine and hidden knowledge of the Sacred Volumes <note>The "Sacred Volumes" refers to the Bible and religious scriptures.</note>—in a Latin style, which (unless my mind deceives me) is sufficiently proper and elegant, as the nature and condition of the subjects treated here require. Furthermore, by prefixing summaries to each dialogue and inserting most beautiful and useful **Annotations** in their places, I seem to have made them significantly more expanded and enriched. Moreover, I have clarified obscure passages, discarded the superfluous, emended the corrupt, restored the imperfect, and finally most diligently purged this entire Work from numerous errors. Lastly, I resolved to undergo with a strong and constant mind every kind of labor or inconvenience that might have deterred anyone’s mind from such a noble undertaking, so that I might consult and provide for the whole community of scholars to the best of my abilities.*

*I did this all the more willingly because, out of the almost innumerable multitude of books written in various and diverse languages by the Greeks, the Hebrews, or many other foreign authors, I believe one can scarcely be found that deserves the splendor and light of Latin literature as much as this one. For what kind of doctrine or erudition can be imagined by anyone that you will not find treated here abundantly and copiously? What science, I ask, so arduous, or what discipline so hidden will you bring forward, whose common principles at least, and certain noble foundations, you do not see laid down here? What argument so famous, or what matter so splendid or clear will you find, of which you can show me no mention was made here? Finally, what notable dispute of the ancients, or what noble controversy of the old philosophers and theologians will you cite, which I cannot show you was here either subtly disputed to the core, or finally excellently decided and settled?*

*Indeed, you will find the natures, powers, and virtues of all things—of whatever order or condition they are said to be, whether simple or compound, celestial or elementary, divine or human, spiritual or corporeal, higher or lower—described and treated here so learnedly, eruditely, splendidly, and elegantly, that from a studious and attentive reading of this nearly divine work, you will rightly judge that you have both reaped the greatest benefit and felt a certain supreme delight. And certainly, it is no wonder. For we see such an argument proposed for treatment in the present volume that no other more common, more illustrious, or finally more holy could ever have been devised. I call this a "common" argument: for what, I ask, is found in the whole universe of things more ample or more common than **love** itself?*
