<meta>This page continues the preface by Jean-Charles Sarrazin for his Latin translation of Leone Ebreo’s "Dialogues on Love," moving from his personal motivations to a philosophical praise of Love as the universal binding force of the cosmos and human society.</meta>

-># PREFACE.<-

What else besides love could have ever possessed the power to compel so many opposite and contrary natures—required for the very constitution of the world—into one, and to keep them so closely joined and bound together even to this present day? It is believed that through the mediation of Love, God created the world, and the world itself returns to God; through Love, the celestial intelligences move the heavenly spheres, and the heavens follow the spiritual movement of those intelligences. By the works of Love, the movements of the Heavens themselves, however diverse and opposing they may be, are seen to breathe together in harmony, all watching over the perpetual preservation of the lower world. By the tightest and most indissoluble bond of Love, I say, the elements endure the rule of the heavens, and the celestial bodies tolerate their proximity to the elements with a peaceful mind. Because of Love, these same elements—though marked by contrary natures and qualities—not only tolerate one another most comfortably in their own regions, yielding one to another and gladly submitting, but all are also seen to descend together in harmony to produce the various kinds of mixed bodies. Why should I say more to you? The force and power of Love is even able to finally couple and join those things which are considered the most remote and contrary of all, such as <term>act and potency</term> <note>These are technical Aristotelian terms: "potency" is the capacity to become something, while "act" (or actuality) is the fulfillment of that potential.</note>, as well as spiritual and corporeal nature; this can be perceived by each of us in that wonderful mixing of form and matter, and primarily in the fellowship of the divine intellect and the human body.

Rightly, therefore, did **Plato**, in his *Symposium*, after discussing Love eloquently and at length, pronounce that this greatest God spreads himself most widely through all things, both divine and human. Rightly, too, did **Aristotle** judge the force and commonality of love to be so great that he left a testament stating that even **prime matter** <note>The most basic, formless substance of the universe in Aristotelian philosophy.</note>—which, as the most imperfect of all things, seems entirely removed from any kind of affection or appetite—is affected by a remarkable love for "form" itself. Finally, **Virgil** spoke excellently, who, as if he bore the great force and power of love with an uneasy mind, seems to have burst forth into that poem as if in anger:

> Wicked Love, to what do you not drive mortal hearts? <note>original: "Improbe amor, quid non mortalia pectora cogis?" (Aeneid 4.412)</note>

In another place, we find he also said:

> Love conquers all, and let us yield to Love. <note>original: "Omnia uincit Amor, & nos cedamus Amori." (Eclogues 10.69)</note>

Not without merit, therefore, do we seem to have long ago commended the subject of the proposed dialogues with the praise of its breadth and commonality. To this, we have judged that another point should be added, taken from its excellence and nobility. For what could you ever find more noble or more illustrious than Love itself? We see that, driven by the love of their very Fatherland, so many most famous and brave men exposed themselves to certain death, and by this means left an everlasting memory of themselves to posterity. What of the **Horatii**, the **Bruti**, the **Pisones**, the **Decii**, the **Scipiones**, and almost countless others who, inflamed by a great love of their country, performed noble and admirable deeds and finally underwent death itself with a prompt and eager spirit? The praises of these most excellent men have been celebrated everywhere by Poets, Historians, and Orators, and seem to have been consecrated to immortality; you will surely find that love was the chief cause of all these things. 

Indeed, I will add this further: those who were most outstanding in military practice and the science of war, but turned both toward the destruction and ruin of their country—as **Coriolanus**, **Sertorius**, **Sulla**, and **Caesar** are said to have done among the Romans—surely rendered the glory and splendor of their virtues weaker and more obscure by such great disgrace. It is as if virtues themselves, if they are destitute of due and appropriate love, are usually turned into vices, and intolerable ones at that. What more? Even **Eloquence**, which **Cicero** calls the companion of peace, the associate of leisure, the foster-child of well-constituted states, and finally the light of genius—unless it be joined with love and charity for the Fatherland itself—surely seems to be like a certain fury, equipped with arms and torches, to be detested and cursed by everyone to the highest degree. Therefore, Eloquence and military virtue, which alone (as Cicero testifies) can place us in the highest rank of dignity, if both are associated with Love itself, [excellent]...

He supports his argument by citing classical authorities such as Plato, Aristotle, and Virgil, as well as the examples of Roman heroes and villains.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the preface by Jean-Charles Sarrazin, following his discussion of Love as the unifying force of the universe. -># PREFACE.<-

*...truly noble and most excellent men. But if they are separated and divided from Love, they are usually rendered wicked and most villainous. These things indeed stand as a great proof of the excellence and nobility of love. Yet, if we bring forward the study of the virtues and of wisdom itself to confirm our proposition, it will seem that hardly anything greater remains that could be desired or experienced in such a distinguished subject. How conspicuous, I ask, and how illustrious does this kind of love usually make the human race? Driven by a wondrous love for wisdom itself, Pythagoras* <note>Pythagoras (c. 570–495 BCE) was an ancient Ionian Greek philosopher and the eponymous founder of Pythagoreanism.</note> *is remembered to have finally left behind his homeland, parents, kinsmen, and friends to first visit the Egyptians and diligently pore over the writings and commentaries of those most ancient priests. Afterward, he betook himself to the Persians, and there learned astrology and many other sciences from the Magi—a race of the wisest men. Then he sailed to Crete and Lacedaemon* <note>The ancient name for the city-state of Sparta.</note> *and learned the laws and institutions of these two most famous cities. Finally, he descended into Italy and traveled through almost the whole of <term>Magna Graecia</term>* <note>original: "magnam Græciam"; literally "Great Greece," the name given by the Romans to the coastal areas of Southern Italy that were extensively populated by Greek settlers.</note>. *What else, I ask, could have separated and pulled this noble man away from the love of his country, from the embraces of his parents and kinsmen, and finally from the most pleasant company of his friends? What could have propelled him, wandering through so many regions and peoples of Asia, Africa, and Europe, even to the most remote shores of the world like some exile, except for a certain most ardent devotion to wisdom? Indeed, he himself seems to have confirmed this: when some asked about his art and condition, he replied that he was not a "wise man," but rather a "philosopher"—that is, a student and most devoted lover of wisdom itself.* <note>The term "philosopher" (philosophos) literally means "lover of wisdom." Tradition credits Pythagoras with coining the term to express humility before the vastness of knowledge.</note> *We see that the divine Plato, also seized by this noble and most excellent love, left his household gods* <note>original: "penates"; a Roman term for the guardian spirits of a household, here meaning his family home.</note> *and soon approached the Egyptian priests, receiving from them geometry, astrology, and theology. Finally, sailing to Italy, he diligently learned the precepts and dogmas of Pythagoras from Archytas and Timaeus. Now, that a man captured by the immense love and beauty of wisdom should desert his country, postpone his parents, despise his kinsmen, and leave his friends behind might perhaps seem great to someone, yet not new or incredible. So be it. But what shall we say of Democritus?* <note>Democritus (c. 460–370 BCE) was a Greek philosopher influential in the development of atomism.</note> *Who, since he loved wisdom most vehemently, is said to have left behind his very large inheritance and the vast wealth passed down from his ancestors so that he might embrace wisdom more easily and unencumbered? In this way, he most gladly exchanged the goods of fortune for the goods of the mind. I could indeed recount innumerable examples of the most distinguished men who, seized by a most excellent and almost divine love for wisdom, are said to have set all things aside to possess it. But these examples, added to those above, seem more than enough to celebrate the splendor and name of Love, just as we proposed. Only one thing is seen to remain for us at present: after we have demonstrated that the subject of this work is both most universal and as illustrious as possible, let us finally show that it is also most holy and worthy of the highest honor and reverence, so that we may appear to have fully and abundantly fulfilled all we have promised. To confirm this, what more noble or more fitting example, I ask, can be brought forward than the example of CHRIST himself? Who, as the Holy Volumes relate, when the entire human race had fallen into the most fearsome anger and vengeance of the Divine Power because of the ingratitude and arrogance of our first parents, was driven by a most vehement and incredible love to expiate human crimes. To soothe and appease the most just anger of the Divine Parent toward his children, he is remembered to have descended to earth, taken on mortal form, and voluntarily devoted himself through that admirable sacrifice of the CROSS for the sake of the impunity and salvation of the entire human race. A great, or rather the greatest, proof and specimen of love is thought to have been given then by both Father and Son, when each took pity on the unfair lot and condition of mortals: the Father exposed the Son to certain death, and the Son, striving to comply with the Parent, [faced] death itself with a brave and constant*

<meta>This page continues the preface by Jean-Charles Sarrazin. Having previously discussed philosophical examples of love (like Pythagoras), he now moves to the theological foundations of Love (Charitas) in Christian scripture and tradition, eventually turning to dedicate the work to a patron named Charles.</meta>

-># PREFACE.<-

...he seems to have endured with a steady mind. Nor is God found to have only confirmed the divinity of love by a brilliant and admirable example of this kind; but He is also found to have most greatly commended it to mortals as something wonderfully leading to the attainment of blessedness. For He declared that the entire Law and, moreover, the whole doctrine of the Prophets are concluded and contained, as if in a certain summary <note>original: "Compendio"; a concise treatise or abstract.</note>, in the study and love of God and neighbor alone. From which divine source Paul seems to have received that eulogy of love; he, to use the Apostle's words, is read to have boldly declared that the entire Law ultimately consists and is ended in the love of one's neighbor. These things are thought to provide the greatest help in proving the divinity and sanctity of Love. 

But what of those things, I ask? What, I say, shall we again significantly say concerning charity <note>The author uses both "Amor" (love) and "Charitas" (charity/divine love). In this context, charity refers to the highest, most selfless form of love.</note>—that most ardent zeal and love toward God and neighbor? How nobly Solomon declared that charity covers and hides all sins. How magnificently we find Paul also speaking of it everywhere, who left those divinely written words to the Corinthians:

> *If I speak with the tongues of men and of Angels, but have not charity, I shall be like clanging brass; and if I should most greatly excel in prophecy, and in the knowledge of all mysteries, and furthermore in science, faith, and miracles; but fail in charity alone, I shall judge that I have profited nothing. And if I distribute all my resources for the benefit and use of the poor, and if I finally undergo death itself eagerly and promptly, know that, being destitute of charity alone, I shall perceive no utility at all from such noble and admirable works.* <note>A translation of 1 Corinthians 13:1-3.</note>

With what more illustrious or effective words could anyone have ever commended the sanctity and reverence of love? Furthermore, a little later, the Apostle, having made a comparison of those three divine and most spiritual virtues—namely, Faith, Hope, and Charity—is seen to have placed Charity far above the other two. Elsewhere we read that this most holy man called Charity the "fruit of the spirit itself," the "bond of perfection," and the "most holy end of all commandments." 

But we find that no one has ever expressed the piety and divinity of love better or more illustriously than John: who said that God himself is charity, and that he who remains in charity remains in God himself, and carries the divine power perpetually with him. From this, our theologians seem to have chiefly accepted that the **HOLY SPIRIT** is defined as nothing other than the mutual love of the Father and the Son, and a certain mutual benevolence of both. 

These things are certainly judged, in my opinion, to be sufficient for opening and clarifying the divine and most holy nature of love, as we have already proposed. But, that our discourse may return to the point from which it began: since it is now established that the subject of this work is so common, so illustrious, and so divine; and since all understand that it has been treated here quite splendidly and elegantly, nothing more seems to remain for me now, except to exhort the whole body of scholars, and you especially, most noble Charles <note>Likely Charles de Lorraine or a similar high-ranking patron of the 16th century.</note>, to an attentive and constantly repeated reading of such a noble and almost divine work. I have persuaded myself to choose you from the number of many illustrious men to whom I might offer and dedicate this noble gift as a most weighty testimony of my singular zeal and respect for you. 

For I perceive that none of those conditions or virtues, which are thought by all to bestow full and absolute happiness upon a man, are lacking in you. First, indeed, if you seek nobility of lineage, it is handed down that you have such a parent who, excelling most greatly in prudence, knowledge of human affairs, and experience, is remembered to have been always summoned as a Leader into all his councils by the most warlike and most fortunate **EMPEROR** <note>The "Imperator" likely refers to Holy Roman Emperor Charles V, suggesting the patron's father was a high-ranking advisor at court.</note>. Furthermore, you seem to be thronged and surrounded by a band of brothers like a most noble crown, such that I believe another more excellent or illustrious can scarcely be found. Likewise, if you bring forward the abundance of riches and wealth, I believe no one will ever find the liberality and munificence of fortune lacking in you...

...to be sure, they are most noble and excellent. But if they are separated and divided from it, they are usually rendered depraved and most wicked men. These things certainly stand as proof of the excellence and nobility of love. Truly, if we bring the pursuit of virtue and of wisdom itself to the confirmation of our proposal, it will seem that hardly anything greater remains that could be sought or desired in such a distinguished subject. I ask you, how conspicuous and how illustrious is this kind of love accustomed to render the human race? Pythagoras, driven by a wonderful love of wisdom, is remembered to have finally left his fatherland, parents, relatives, and friends to travel first to the Egyptians, where he diligently studied the writings and commentaries of those most ancient priests. Afterward, he betook himself to the Persians, and there learned astrology and many other sciences from the Magi <note>original: "Magis"; a class of Zoroastrian priests and wise men in ancient Persia.</note>, a race of the wisest men. Then he sailed to Crete and Lacedaemon <note>The ancient name for Sparta.</note>, and there learned the laws and institutions of these two most famous cities. Finally, he descended into Italy and traversed almost the whole of Magna Graecia <note>original: "magnamque Græciam"; literally "Great Greece," the name given to the coastal areas of Southern Italy colonized by Greeks.</note>. I ask, what else besides a certain burning pursuit of wisdom could have separated this distinguished man from the love of his fatherland, from the embraces of his parents and relatives, and from the most pleasant company of his friends? What else could have driven him through so many regions and peoples of Asia, Africa, and Europe to the most remote shores of the world like some kind of exile? This is something he himself seems to have confirmed; when some people asked about his art and condition, he responded that he was not wise, but rather a **philosopher**—that is, a student and lover of wisdom itself. We see that the divine Plato, seized by this same noble and excellent love, also left behind his household gods <note>original: "penates"; a reference to the Roman/Latin concept of domestic guardian spirits, here used to mean his home and family life.</note> and soon went to the Egyptian priests, from whom he received geometry, astrology, and theology; finally sailing to Italy, he diligently learned the precepts and dogmas of Pythagoras from Archytas and Timaeus.

But for a man captured by the immense love and beauty of wisdom to desert his fatherland, set aside his parents, despise his relatives, and leave his friends might perhaps seem great to someone, yet not new or incredible. So be it. But what, finally, shall we say of Democritus? He is said to have left behind the vast patrimony and enormous wealth handed down to him by his ancestors so that he might embrace wisdom more easily and readily; in this way, he most willingly exchanged the goods of fortune for the goods of the mind itself. I could surely review innumerable examples of most distinguished men who, seized by an excellent and almost divine love of wisdom, are said to have put all things aside in order to possess it. But these examples, added to those above, seem more than enough to celebrate the splendor and name of Love, just as we proposed. Only this remains for us at present: that after we have demonstrated the subject of this work to be both most common and most illustrious, we should finally show it to be also most holy and worthy of the highest honor and reverence, so that we may appear to have fully and abundantly fulfilled all that we have promised.

In confirmation of this matter, what more distinguished or more appropriate example, I ask, can be brought forward than that of **CHRIST** himself? As the sacred volumes record, when the entire human race had fallen into the most fearsome wrath and vengeance of the divine power because of the ingratitude and arrogance of our first parents, Christ is remembered to have descended to earth, taken on mortal form, and—driven by a certain most vehement and incredible love—voluntarily devoted himself to that wonderful sacrifice of the **CROSS** for the sake of the impunity and salvation of the whole human race, in order to expiate human crimes and to soften and appease the most just anger of the divine Parent toward His children. A great, indeed rather the greatest, proof and specimen of love is thought to have been given then by both the Father and the Son in very deed; when both pitied the unfair lot and condition of mortals, the Father exposed His Son to certain death, and the Son, striving to obey the Parent, [met] death itself with a brave and constant...

# PREFACE.

...is seen to have endured with a steady mind. Nor is God found only to have confirmed the divinity of this kind of love by such a distinguished and admirable example: but He is also found to have recommended it as much as possible to mortals as wonderfully conducive to attaining happiness: since He pronounced that the entire Law, and moreover the whole doctrine of the Prophets, are concluded and contained as if in a certain Compendium <note>original: "Compendio"; a concise summary or shortcut.</note> in the study and love of God and neighbor alone. From which Paul seems to have received that divine eulogy of love, who—to use the words of the Apostle—is boldly read to have brought forth that the entire Law ultimately consists and is bounded in the love of one's neighbor. 

These things are thought to provide the greatest help for proving the divinity and holiness of Love. But what about those things, I ask? What, I say, shall we say again of charity, which signifies a certain most ardent study and love toward God and toward our neighbor? How excellently Solomon pronounced that charity covers and hides all sins. How magnificently we find Paul also speaking of the same everywhere: who left those divinely written words to the Corinthians: "If I speak with the tongues of men and of Angels, and have not charity, I shall be like sounding brass: and if I should excel greatly in prophecy, and in the knowledge of all mysteries, and also in science, faith, and miracles: but should be lacking in charity alone, I shall judge that I have profited nothing: and if I should distribute all my resources for the benefit and use of the poor, and if I should finally undergo death itself eagerly and promptly, know that, being destitute of charity alone, I shall perceive absolutely no utility from such distinguished and admirable works." With what more illustrious and effective words could anyone have ever commended the sanctity and reverence of love? Furthermore, a little lower, the Apostle, having made a comparison of those three divine and most spiritual virtues—namely, Faith, Hope, and Charity—seems to have placed Charity far before the other two. Elsewhere also we read that this holy man called Charity the fruit of the spirit itself, the bond of perfection, and the end of all commandments. 

But we find that no one has ever expressed the piety and divinity of love better or more illustriously than John: who said that God himself is charity, and that he who remains in charity remains in God himself, and carries the divine power perpetually with him. Whence our Theologians seem to have especially received this: that THE HOLY SPIRIT is defined as being nothing other than the mutual love of the Father and the Son, and a certain mutual benevolence of both. These things are certainly judged, in my judgment, to be sufficient for opening and elucidating the divine and most holy nature of love, just as we have now proposed. 

But, so that our discourse may be brought back to where it began: since it is now established that the subject of this Work is so common, so illustrious, and so divine; and since all understand that it has been treated here quite splendidly and elegantly, nothing further seems to remain for me now, except that I should exhort the whole community of all scholars, and you especially, most noble Charles <note>original: "Carole"; likely a specific patron or dedicatee from a noble family.</note>, to the attentive and diligently repeated reading of such a distinguished and almost divine work: you whom I have persuaded myself to choose from the number of many illustrious men, to whom I might offer and dedicate this distinguished gift as a most serious testimony of my singular devotion and respect toward you. For I perceive that you certainly lack none of those conditions or virtues which are thought by all to bestow full and absolute happiness upon a man. First indeed, if you require nobility of lineage, that parent is recorded to have existed for you who, excelling greatly in prudence, knowledge of human affairs, and experience, is remembered to have been always employed as a Leading Prince in all his councils by the most warlike and fortunate EMPEROR <note>original: "IMPERATORE"; likely referring to Charles V, the Holy Roman Emperor.</note>. Furthermore, you seem to be supported and surrounded by that band of brothers as if by a most noble crown, than which I believe another more excellent or more illustrious can hardly be found. Likewise, if you bring forward an abundance of riches and wealth, I think no one will ever find fortune's liberality and munificence lacking in you,

# PREFACE.

...I suppose. If you also demand beauty and elegance of body, everyone understands that a certain noble appearance, combined with the highest gravity and kindness at once, was granted to you by nature. Finally, if it is pleasing to descend to the character and virtues of the soul, who does not perceive, commend, and admire the innocence and integrity of your life—who, I say, the honesty and easy nature of your character, and finally your teaching and erudition? I certainly remember, when you were staying at the Gymnasium <note>original: "Gymnasio"; here referring to the University of Padua, a premier center of Renaissance learning.</note> in Padua years ago, with what diligence you frequented the gatherings and lectures of those most learned men. I remember, I say, how successfully you then labored day and night in the study of the liberal arts and disciplines. I remember, finally, with what joy and delight of men you spent five years in that most excellent Gymnasium, and with what sorrow of all students, and with what grief of nearly everyone, you finally departed from it. 

Since I hold all these things best in my memory, and since an incredible devotion and the highest inclination of your soul toward me is added to those things already mentioned, what wonder is it if I have decided and decreed to dedicate these watches and midnight labors of mine to you alone, as one most worthy of this gift and most loving of me and all my affairs? Receive, therefore, with a glad and cheerful heart, most excellent Charles, this remarkable monument—unless I am mistaken—of my respect and devotion toward you. Indeed, if I perceive that this has been pleasing and delightful to you, as I hope, I shall certainly strive hereafter to reveal to mortals my immense devotion toward you with greater evidence and more ample signs, and with the greatest eagerness to celebrate your name and, so to speak, consecrate it to immortality. Farewell.

->VENICE, on the Calends of January <note>January 1st</note> in the year 1564 from the birth of the Virgin.<-

### TO THE READER.

<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut initial 'E' featuring a classical or biblical scene with a seated figure in a landscape with architectural elements and trees in the background.</image-desc>

Behold for you, kind and honest reader, a clear and, unless I am mistaken, quite elegant interpretation of those Dialogues concerning LOVE, which treat the subject so learnedly and eruditely. In this work, I confess I felt no small amount of labor in serving equally the sincerity and truth of the matters themselves, as well as the propriety and sweetness of the speech, while also preserving both of these pure and untainted. However, how much I have profited in both, I leave to be judged by you alone as a man most loving of fairness; and I expect from you the palm of victory and the crown of this whole struggle and contest of mine, just as from a most just judge, if I shall seem to you to have deserved it. 

But I wish you to be warned of this one thing first: that this work, like a most fertile spring, overflows with such varied and manifold doctrine of almost all the sciences, that in this great variety and diversity of subjects treated, it was necessary to use some vocabulary which is not found at all among the ancient and most approved writers. <note>The author is defending his use of "New Latin" or technical terms that wouldn't be found in the classical works of Cicero or Virgil.</note> For we see that the ancients did not encompass all kinds of sciences in Latin speech; and if those most excellent men had done so, they would certainly have been forced both to devise new names and to fashion proper words most accommodated to the natures of the things themselves, however unheard of they might perhaps be. 

Therefore, most kind reader, I beseech you, let no such scruple cast into your mind hinder or retard your soul as it hastens toward the diligent and studious reading of so remarkable a work. Rather, once this matter is despised and looked down upon as being of very little importance—and once several errors have been diligently purged and amended, which were admitted through the carelessness of the printers in the first edition (as usually happens)—immediately run through this whole work like an Olympic stadium, from the starting gates <note>original: "carceribus"; the stalls where horses or runners waited for the start of a race.</note> to the finish line, as they say, with the greatest speed. Persuade yourself most firmly of this: that in the very brief circuit and compass of these three proposed Dialogues, almost the entire doctrine of both Aristotle and Plato (however widely it spreads itself), as well as nearly the whole of moral, natural, and divine Philosophy, is concluded and bounded as if in a most elegant Compendium.

->ON LEONE EBREO'S FIRST DIALOGUE CONCERNING THE NATURE AND ESSENCE OF LOVE<-

# FIRST DIALOGUE ON THE NATURE AND ESSENCE OF LOVE
## Summary:
### Prefixed by JOANNES CAROLUS SARACENUS.

First, this work thoroughly treats the difference between love and desire, declaring the essences and natures of both these passions of the will. It then reviews the three kinds of goods—namely, the useful, the pleasant, and the virtuous <note>original: "honestum"; in Renaissance philosophy, this refers to things that are morally good or honorable in themselves, distinct from things that are merely useful or pleasurable.</note>—and demonstrates how love and desire relate to these in various ways. It shows that while wealth contributes greatly to moral and social life, it presents no small obstacle to the contemplative and speculative life. Furthermore, it teaches that moral virtues require a "middle ground" <note>referring to the Aristotelian "Golden Mean," where virtue is the balance between two extremes.</note>, whereas intellectual virtues allow for a praiseworthy "excess." It separately disputes several other goods that possess a confused and mixed nature, such as health, children, marriage, power, dominion, empire, honor, fame, and glory. Then, the discourse turns to the friendships usually formed among men for the sake of utility, pleasure, or virtue; it highly commends virtuous friendship, placing it far above the other two types. Turning afterward to divine love, the author pursues the subject with a solemn and brilliant discourse, teaching that the Divinity itself is the beginning, middle, and end of all virtuous acts; he also shows that God, the best and greatest, is understood only imperfectly by the human intellect and is loved only slightly and weakly by the human will. Having completed these points, he begins a discussion on human happiness. Rejecting many errors, he concludes that happiness is situated in wisdom and in the "agent intellect" <note>original: "intellectūs agentis"; a technical term in Aristotelian philosophy for the part of the mind that transforms potential knowledge into actual understanding.</note>—that is, in the pure and sincere knowledge we hold of God and the divine intellect. Or, to use the language of the philosophers, it lies in the most blessed union of our potential intellect with that divine and agent intellect. He enumerates the five dispositions of the intelligent soul and describes each individually. He extols wisdom above all else, laments the ignorance and weakness of human nature, and reveals two ways our intellect reaches an understanding of spiritual things. He declares more than sufficiently that the ultimate happiness of man consists neither in riches, nor pleasures, nor arts, nor craftsmanship, nor moral virtues, nor in a state of mind separated from action, nor in the distinct and separate knowledge of many things. Rather, it consists solely in the actual and joined understanding of one single thing—namely, God, the best and greatest—and in the clearest vision of Him, and in the very act of that most intimate union and unified divine knowledge. He demonstrates that this divine union and happiness can be obtained and continued by us much more easily after death than in this present life. Next, he transitions to pleasures, showing that bodily pleasures quickly turn into a hateful kind of surfeit and disgust, whereas spiritual pleasures do not. He admires the skill and providence of nature. He testifies that the external and imperfect union of bodies strengthens and more tightly binds the internal and perfect union of souls. He divides and distinguishes love into two types: the imperfect, which arises from desire; and the perfect, which proceeds first from right and knowing reason and subsequently induces desire. He elegantly interprets the form of Cupid as sung by the poets, as well as his powers and marvelous effects, and the wretched and unjust condition of lovers. Finally, he demonstrates that true and perfect love assumes strength and growth through the mutual embrace of bodies, and that such love—scorning and despising the warnings of ordinary reason—follows and embraces a certain new and extraordinary reason as its leading guide.

PHILO: I feel that the knowledge of you, O Sophia <note>The names are symbolic: Philo means "Lover" and Sophia means "Wisdom."</note>, has stirred my soul to love and to a certain desire.

# LEONE EBREO ON LOVE,

...to be loved; those things, however, which we lack, are said to be desired: so that desire precedes love, and love follows desire. Thus, the beginning and birth of love is the end and death of desire itself.

PHILO: What, I pray you, led you to this opinion?

SOPHIA: Various examples of things that are loved and desired. Who does not see that lost strength is desired, but not at all loved? And once recovered, desire departing, it is only loved? Wealth, inheritances, and pearls <note>original: "uniones"; referring to large, high-quality pearls often used as examples of great material value.</note> are said to be desired before they are possessed, not loved; but once possessed, they are loved and no longer desired.

PHILO: Although strength and riches cannot be loved when we lack them because we are without them, we nevertheless love to acquire and obtain them.

SOPHIA: This is indeed an improper use of speech, as if someone saying they love a certain thing intended the name of "love" to signify a certain inclination and propensity of the soul toward possessing that thing.

<margin>Love is for the thing itself being loved; desire, however, seems to be for the possessing and attaining of it.</margin>

For love is of the beloved thing itself, while desire is for its possession and attainment; nor do these two motions of the soul seem able to meet as one.

PHILO: The reasons you bring forward, Sophia, show the sharpness of your wit rather than the truth of your opinion. For unless we desired what we love, we would be desiring that which is in no way loved, and consequently that from which our nature is alienated and shrinks—which indeed seems to be utterly self-contradictory.

SOPHIA: I am not mistaken as you think, Philo. For I say that I desire that which, although I cannot love it while it is absent, I shall greatly cherish once it is present and desire has been extinguished. Yet I am not led by this to admit that I desire what I either loathe or love.

<margin>The loved thing is present, whereas the desired thing is absent.</margin>

For the loved thing is present, whereas the desired thing is absent. What more illustrious example of this can we bring than that of children? Parents are said to desire them when not yet born, not love them; and once born, to love them and no longer desire them.

PHILO: The example of parents and children does indeed seem to favor your opinion. But what will you answer regarding the example of a husband and wife? For each of them, or at least one, both desires and loves the other before they are joined together. After their union, desire is always seen to perish, and sometimes even love; yet in many cases, we see love not only flourish but also frequently increase. Does this example not seem more fit to confirm my opinion than the one you brought earlier was to refute it?

SOPHIA: I feel my mind so distracted by the variety and opposition of these examples that I am beginning to adhere to your opinion, not entirely, but only in part.

<margin>Love exists either for those things which are truly good, or for those things judged to be good by us.</margin>
<margin>Every good is lovable.</margin>
<margin>The good exists in three forms: the useful, the pleasant, and the virtuous.</margin>
<margin>Love exists in three forms: that of the useful, the pleasant, and the virtuous.</margin>
<margin>Pleasant things, before they are obtained, are simultaneously desired and loved; once they are possessed, we often see both desire and love for them extinguished.</margin>

PHILO: I shall speak, therefore, of what is common. Love exists either for those things which are truly good, or for those things judged to be good by us; for whatever is good is lovable <term>lovable: in this context, "amabile" means worthy or capable of being loved</term>. Therefore, since there are three species of goods—the useful, the pleasant, and the virtuous—there will also be said to be three species of love: the first will be rightly called the love of the pleasant; the second, of the useful; and the third, of the virtuous. Of these three, the two extremes—namely, the useful and the virtuous—must be loved both before and after their acquisition, whenever they are possessed. The pleasant, however, is no longer loved after its enjoyment. For whatever things bring pleasure to our imperfect senses are by nature such that, once possessed, they induce satiety rather than love. Therefore, goods of this kind, while they are desired before they are obtained, are simultaneously loved; but after they have been fully obtained and are possessed without any controversy, desire is extinguished, and frequently love as well. From this, you must concede that it is possible for love and desire to be found together.

SOPHIA: These reasons, in my opinion, although they sufficiently confirm your view, do not entirely do away with mine which opposes yours, nor do they prove it false. In what way, then, can truth be opposed to truth itself, and any opposition be found between two truths? I wait to hear your determination on this ambiguity, which disturbs my mind in no small measure.

PHILO: I would indeed prefer, Sophia, to obtain some relief from my calamities from you rather than to solve and explain your enigmas; but I perceive that you very cunningly...

<margin>
*Refutation of this opinion.*
</margin>
**SO.** Their sentiment also seems foreign to the truth: for we see many things desired everywhere which, since they lack essence <note>original: "essentia"; here referring to the actual existence or presence of the thing.</note>, cannot be loved. Hence, love is for existing things, but desire is for non-existing things. For by what reasoning can we ever love offspring or health unless we have first obtained them, even if we are held by the greatest desire for them? Therefore, I am led to this opinion: that love and desire are two contrary affections of the will; yet you just said they could be found together. What solution, I pray, will you bring to this difficulty?

**PH.** If love is only of existing things, why will desire not also be of them?

**SO.** Because as love presupposes the essence of things, so desire presupposes their privation <note>original: "privationem"; the state of lacking or being without something.</note>.

**PH.** For what reason does love presuppose the essence of things?

<margin>
*The human mind is like a mirror and a pattern, or rather a certain image of things themselves.*
</margin>
**SO.** Because knowledge must necessarily precede love: for nothing could be loved unless it were first known under the aspect of "the good" <note>original: "sub ratione boni"; a Scholastic term meaning perceiving something as being beneficial or desirable.</note>: moreover, nothing comes down into our knowledge unless it first exists in reality. For the human mind is like a mirror, and a pattern, or rather a certain image and likeness of things themselves, so that nothing can be loved unless it first exists.

<margin>
*Nothing can be loved unless it first exists.*
</margin>
**PH.** You speak the truth: but for the same reason, desire will also regard the essence of things: for we seek nothing unless we first apprehend it as a good, whence the philosopher <note>original: "philosophus"; typically referring to Aristotle, whose definition of the Good was foundational to Renaissance thought.</note> defined that "the good" is what all things desire. By the same argument, therefore, we will be able to demonstrate that both love and desire are for existing things.

<margin>
*The good is that which all things seek.*
</margin>
**SO.** Certainly, knowledge seems to precede desire no less than love: but in defense of my opinion, I would declare that knowledge is not only of existing things, but also of non-existing things: since the difference between the existing and the non-existing is judged by the intellect, it is necessary that both of these be first known by it separately. Love might therefore be said to presuppose the knowledge of things that are; but desire, the knowledge of things that are not, and which we lack.

<margin>
*Both love and desire necessarily presuppose the knowledge of the thing under the aspect of "the good."*
</margin>
**PH.** Knowledge under the aspect of "the good" must precede both love and desire of the thing loved or sought: for if the thing loved or sought were presented under the aspect of "the evil," it would induce flight rather than love and pursuit: hence each of these two affections of the will seems to presuppose the essence of the object, both on the part of the thing and on the part of the knowledge.

**SO.** If the essence of things preceded desire, then when we judge something to be good and desirable, it would surely follow that our judgment would always be true: the falsity of which...

who does not see the truth of this? since many things which we consider good are, by their very nature, evil. It would seem, therefore, that we must say that desire does not always assume the actual essence of the things sought.

<margin>Loves and desires are rendered diverse and manifold according to the diversity of judgments.</margin>
**PH.** This is seen to occur no less in love than in desire: for those things which we think are good and lovable often turn out to be evil and things to be avoided. Hence, just as right desires and honorable loves proceed from true and correct judgments—from which all virtues, temperate actions, and noble deeds are later derived—so too do evil desires and dishonorable loves take their origin from false and perverse judgments, from which, at last, all human vices and errors are accustomed to emerge as if from a kind of cesspool.

<margin>Both love and desire require the essence of a thing for themselves.</margin>
Therefore, each of these two <term>affections</term><note>The word "affectuum" refers to states of mind or emotions that "affect" the soul.</note> requires the essence of the thing for itself.

**SO.** I cannot fly so high with you, Philo; let us seek more humble ground again. I seem to see very clearly that none of those things which we most greatly seek, and which cannot properly be called "loved," actually exist.

**PH.** Indeed, we always wish for those things which we do not have; however, we are by no means said to seek those things which are non-existent. Rather, desire is usually for those things which do exist, but which we are unable to possess.

**SO.** We frequently appetite not only these, but also those things which do not exist in reality at all, wishing that they might be, though we do not desire to "possess" them as such: as when we desire rain in summer, clear skies in winter, the return of a friend, and similar things. All of these, because they do not exist, we wish to happen only for our own benefit, not for the sake of possessing them; yet they will not, for that reason, be said to be "loved" by us. I believe it has been more than sufficiently proven, therefore, that desire is for non-existent things.

<margin>Desire, even if it does not assume an actual essence, frequently assumes a possible essence of a thing.</margin>
**PH.** That which lacks all essence is nothing: and "nothing" can neither be loved, nor sought, nor finally possessed. But those things you just listed, even if they lack a present essence when they are desired, can nevertheless exist: and this is certainly what is desired in them—that they be transferred from a <term>possible essence</term> to an <term>actual essence</term>. Just as with those things which already are, but are not yet held by us, we are accustomed to wish only for their possession.

<margin>Men are accustomed to desire either the actual essence of a possible thing, or the present possession of a thing already existing in act.</margin>
Therefore, men desire either that those things which are not "in act" <note>original: "actu" - meaning currently real or active rather than just potential.</note> be led to an actual essence, or that they might acquire for themselves the possession of things already existing in act which they currently lack. By what reasoning, then, do you affirm that desire sometimes assumes the essence of a thing and sometimes its <term>privation</term><note>A "privation" is the absence of a quality or thing that should naturally be there.</note>, and that it seeks the entire and perfect completion of its essence? For this reason, desire and love are founded upon the essence, not the privation, of things.

<margin>Things that are to be loved as well as sought require three conditions: essence, truth, and goodness.</margin>
For things that are both to be loved and sought require three conditions following one another in a certain order: first, **essence**; second, **truth**; third, **goodness**. These three conditions, joined together, infuse in us the love and desire for them. For these two affections of our minds could not be excited at all unless the things were first judged to be good: but this judgment would never occur unless they were first known to be true: and finally, this knowledge clearly assumes the essence of the things themselves. For first, a thing exists; second, it is impressed upon the intellect; third, it is judged to be good; and in the last place, it is cherished and wished for.

<margin>Being, the true, and the good are convertible with one another. The difference between being, the true, and the good.</margin>
And for this reason, <term>the Philosopher</term><note>A standard historical reference to Aristotle.</note> says that **being**, **truth**, and **goodness** are <term>convertible</term><note>In medieval philosophy, these are "transcendentals" that refer to the same reality but from different perspectives.</note> among themselves, differing only in this: that essence consists in the thing itself; truth, after it has been impressed upon the intellect; and goodness, when we finally descend from the intellect and the **will** through love and desire—as if through certain mediating steps—toward the acquisition of the thing itself. You see, therefore, that love and desire equally assume the essence of things.

**SO.** Yet many things which exist neither in the one who wishes nor in themselves are often seen to be sought by us, such as children and health by those who lack both: to which things, indeed, the name of "desire" only, and not "love," can be applied.

**PH.** That which is wished for, even if it is lacking to the one wishing and does not exist in itself, is not found to be destitute of all essence, as you think: but it must certainly exist in some manner; otherwise, it could neither be known as a "good" nor finally be wished for. This is indeed what happens to a sick person seeking health, which [exists] in many healthy [people]...

He refutes Sophia's idea that we can desire things with no reality, explaining that we desire the "possible" to become "actual."</summary>

Therefore, he who lacks them, both knowing and judging them to be a certain good, desires them with his whole heart. From this, these and similar types of existence can sufficiently impress the <term>species</term><note>In this context, "species" refers to the mental image or form of a thing that the mind perceives.</note> of health upon the sick, and the image of offspring upon those who most greatly desire them. Therefore, it is common to both love and desire that they are directed toward things which exist in some way, and which are judged as good by the intellect; but these two <term>affections</term><note>States of being moved or influenced by an object.</note> seem to differ in this: that love indiscriminately embraces all goods, both those already possessed and those whose possession we do not yet have; desire, however, is only for those things which we do not possess at all.

**SO.** You seem to agree with the opinion of those who claim that everything which is wished for is loved, and that love is a certain <term>genus</term><note>A general category that contains various sub-types.</note> commonly encompassing all things judged to be good—and that those things which are craved but not possessed, as well as those possessed but not craved, are loved indifferently. I, however, think it is in no way possible for someone to love those things which he does not have, and which exist in no way, even if he vehemently craves them. For the essence which you said such things obtain in others does not seem sufficient either to impress a knowledge of itself or to win over benevolence for itself, since we do not love the children of others, but our own; nor do we love the health of another, but our own. Indeed, if these things are lacking to us, how can they ever be said to be loved, even if we have desired them vehemently?

**PH.** we have nearly hit the mark of truth. For although it is commonly affirmed that things which are craved are also loved as goods, nevertheless—unless we perhaps wish to misuse the name of love—things which lack their own essence (such as children and health for those who crave them) will never be called "loved," if we are speaking of love existing outside the soul and among the number of real things.

<margin>Love is twofold: true and imaginary.</margin>
<margin>Imaginary love concurs with desire into one thing, but true love does not.</margin>
However, because of a certain obscure existence of things dwelling only in the imagination, "imaginary love" will apply to all those things which are desired. From this imaginary existence, a certain love arises whose subject is not the thing itself which is craved (since that thing has no existence at all on its own part), but only a certain concept formed by the <term>phantasy</term><note>The "phantasy" or "imagination" was considered a specific faculty of the mind that produces mental images.</note> from its general essence. Such a love is said to have a subject only improperly, nor is it a true love, since it lacks a subject consisting truly and outside the soul; rather, let it be called a certain obscure, fictitious, and imaginary love. From this, it is finally deduced that desire is for those things which we cannot pursue with proper and true love.

<margin>Of lovable things, some are loved and desired at the same time; some are loved but not desired; finally, some are desired but not loved at all.</margin>
Therefore, making a division, let us say that three species of things which are loved and craved are found. The first of these is of things which are loved and desired at the same time, such as virtue, wisdom, and a learned man, when these are distant from us. The second is of those things which are loved but not desired, such as all the goods which we have already attained and possess. The third is of those things which are craved without any love, just as children and strength when we lack both of them, and similar things not having their own <term>consistency</term><note>The "consistency" or "standing" of a thing refers to its independent reality or substance.</note>. Therefore, whatever goods are judged to be and truly consist in reality, when they are lacking, they excite both love and desire in us at once; but when they are possessed, they induce love, not desire. Those things, however, which are not only lacking to us, but do not even have their own existence in themselves, kindle desire alone, separate from love.

**SO.** I have properly understood the meaning of your mind, and I confirm all of it except for one thing: I see that many things exist outside the intellect which, while not yet held, are indeed craved, yet are not loved until after they have been acquired by us. For then they are no longer craved, but only loved. For example, riches, houses, lands, gems, and similar things existing in the power of others are indeed only desired, not loved; but after they have been acquired by us, and the desire departs, they begin to be loved.

<summary>Philo distinguishes between true love for existing things and "imaginary love" linked to desire for non-existent things, while Sophia argues that external possessions like wealth are only loved once they are owned.</summary>

...to be loved. Therefore, before they are acquired, they are only longed for, not loved; after their acquisition, they are loved only, and no longer longed for. 

**PHILO.** We are certainly in agreement on the matter itself, even if we seem perhaps to disagree because of the variety of examples. You will not find me saying that all things which are desired while existing outside the intellect are simultaneously loved; rather, I simply stated that desire joined with love requires the essence of the things sought to exist outside the soul. For this reason, I did not bring up the example of wealth, nor of sumptuous houses, nor of fields, nor of precious stones, but rather of virtue, wisdom, or some distinguished man in whom these qualities reside. For goods of this kind are equally loved and sought after when they are lacking. 

**SOPHIA.** I pray you, give me the reason for this distinction found in desired things that have their own consistency outside the soul—why some of them are desired and loved at the same time, while others are only sought after with no intervening love.

<margin>The lovable exists in three forms: the useful, the pleasant, and the honorable.</margin> 
**PHILO.** The reason for the difference depends on the diversity of the "lovables" themselves. Since these—as you know very well—exist as either <term>useful</term><note>Latin: *utilia*. Refers to material goods or tools used to achieve an end.</note>, <term>pleasant</term><note>Latin: *iucunda*. Refers to things that provide sensory or emotional delight.</note>, or <term>honorable</term><note>Latin: *honesta*. Refers to moral or intellectual virtues that are good in themselves.</note>, they are seen to behave in different ways regarding love and desire. 

**SOPHIA.** Unless it would be troublesome for you, I greatly desire to hear the difference between love and desire as it is derived from these three objects. For the sake of clearer teaching, I would like you to devise two common definitions: one for love and one for desire, each encompassing their various kinds.

<margin>Desire is a certain voluntary affection so that a thing, which is judged to be good and is lacking, may either exist or be possessed.</margin> 
**PHILO.** It is not as easy as you think to encompass all kinds with a single common definition of either love or desire, because their nature is rendered various and manifold according to the variety of their objects. Nor can we bring forward any example of the ancient philosophers who provided a single common definition for them. Nevertheless, as much as I can gather from what has been said, I would define **desire** as a voluntary state of mind <note>original: *affectus*</note> so that a thing, which is judged to be good and is lacking, may either exist or be possessed.

<margin>Love is a certain voluntary affection for enjoying, as closely as possible, a thing judged to be good.</margin> 
**Love**, on the other hand, I would commonly define as a voluntary state of mind for enjoying, through the greatest possible union, a thing judged to be good. From these two definitions, you will perceive not only the difference between these two states of the will—since one, as I said, wishes to enjoy the thing joined to itself in reality, while the other wishes either that the thing exist or that it be possessed—but you will also understand that desire is always for those things which are lacking.

<margin>Desire is always for those things which are lacking. Love can be equally for those things which are either already possessed or not at all.</margin> 
Love, however, can be equally for things that are either already possessed or not possessed at all. For this kind of state of the will, which consists in enjoying things in the closest union, extends both to those things we lack and to those we already possess; for it determines for itself neither the possession of the thing alone, nor its privation alone, but is common to both. 

**SOPHIA.** Although those definitions might require a fuller explanation, they seem to be more than sufficient for understanding the reason for the difference that depends on the variety of the three objects: the useful, the pleasant, and the honorable, in both love and desire. Therefore, continue the journey you have begun.

<margin>Useful goods can never be loved and desired at the same time.</margin> 
**PHILO.** Useful goods, such as riches, can never be loved and desired at the same time. Rather, when they are not held, they are longed for but not cherished <note>original: *diliguntur*</note>, for they are in the power of others. But after they have been acquired, as desire fades, love for them arises as for things that are our own, and we enjoy them in the closest union as our property. However, in the case of useful goods, it very frequently happens that although the desire for what we already possess is extinguished, new desires for other similar things held by others are immediately kindled.

<margin>Useful goods are longed for before they are possessed, but not cherished; once held, they are cherished and no longer longed for.</margin> 
Hence, those who are ensnared by the love of useful goods have almost infinite and always new desires; as one dies away, another larger and more burning than the first soon arises. For this reason, their wills are never filled by such desires, and a greater possession is always accompanied by a greater desire. They seem most rightly compared to those who try in vain to drive away thirst with a false potion: for the more they drink, the more they thirst.

<margin>Desires for useful goods proceed into infinity.</margin> 
Moreover, the immoderate desire for these useful goods is properly called **greed** <note>original: *cupiditas*</note>; but moderation in [them...]

### DIALOGUE I.

<margin>In the desire for useful goods, greed is the excess, negligence is the defect, and the middle ground—rightly called so—is the desire for only what is necessary.</margin>
The desire for only what is necessary is called <term>sufficiency</term><note>Latin: *sufficientia*. The state of having enough to meet one's needs without excess.</note>, and it is a most excellent virtue. For this reason, the wise judge that man to be truly rich who lives content with what he has. Just as greed for the superfluous is one extreme that exceeds this distinguished virtue, so the other extreme—failing to seek what is necessary—is called <term>negligence</term><note>Latin: *negligentia*. In this context, it refers to a lack of proper care for one’s material well-being.</note>.

<margin>Among the wise, he is held to be truly rich who lives content with his own.</margin>
**SOPHIA.** What are you saying, Philo? Did not many philosophers believe that riches should be utterly despised? Did some not even abandon them? 

**PHILO.** This was the opinion of the <term>Stoics</term><note>A school of philosophy that taught that virtue is the only good and that external things like wealth are indifferent.</note> and the <term>Academics</term><note>Followers of the school of Plato, who at various times emphasized skepticism or the superiority of the soul over the body.</note>. However, this contempt for riches and the great disregard for necessary things—which those philosophers praised in words and confirmed by their lives—should not be called "negligence." This is because it is directed toward the <term>speculative life</term><note>The "contemplative life" focused on study, meditation, and the search for truth rather than physical action.</note> and the internal, contented contemplation of things. They perceived that riches were a great hindrance to this most noble kind of life, because they occupy the whole mind and turn it away from speculation and contemplation, in which the highest perfection and greatest happiness consist.

<margin>Riches are held in little value by the Stoics and Academics, but they are highly esteemed by the Peripatetics.</margin>
On the other hand, the <term>Peripatetics</term><note>The followers of Aristotle, known for a more balanced view of physical goods and moral action.</note> believe that riches should be acquired with great zeal, since they are necessary for leading a life according to virtue. They say that although riches are not virtue itself, they are nonetheless a kind of instrument highly suited for practicing many virtues. For we could never exercise <term>liberality</term><note>The virtue of being generous with one's money.</note>, nor <term>magnificence</term><note>The virtue of spending large sums of money appropriately for great and noble causes.</note>, nor piety, nor charity without riches.

<margin>In the opinion of the Peripatetics, riches are certain instruments necessarily required for attaining many virtues.</margin>
**SOPHIA.** What? Is a certain preparation and readiness of the mind to perform actions not enough to acquire these virtues, even if wealth is lacking? Why should a poor man not also be able to be studious and virtuous? 

**PHILO.** Preparation alone, separated from action, does not seem sufficient at all. For the virtues listed are <term>habits</term><note>Latin: *habitus*. A stable disposition of the soul acquired through repeated action.</note>

<margin>Virtues are habits of acting rightly.</margin>
of acting rightly, which are finally acquired through the long-continued exercise of good and laudable actions. Since, therefore, these actions cannot be performed without the "goods of fortune" <note>External goods such as wealth, health, and status.</note>, it follows that those virtues can by no means be acquired without such goods.

<margin>The virtues of good and laudable actions are finally acquired through long practice.</margin>
**SOPHIA.** Did the Stoics not also know this? And how did the Peripatetics fail to see that riches lead the intellect away from that highest happiness which consists in contemplation? 

**PHILO.** The Stoics do indeed concede that moral or civil virtue cannot be acquired without external goods of fortune. But in the judgment of the Stoics, human happiness is by no means to be placed in those things, but rather in the intellectual and contemplative life. For the sake of this life, not only are riches to be undervalued, but even the civil virtues that flow from them. These are not exactly turned into vices,

<margin>External goods of fortune, especially riches, are most necessary for leading a life of moral or civil virtue, as well as for human actions. For contemplation, however, they are found to be a hindrance rather than a help.</margin>
but are rather to be converted into more excellent virtues that are closer to ultimate happiness. No learned Peripatetic would ever deny this. These two sects do not seem to differ in anything except that the Stoics, preferring the more excellent to the less noble, utterly neglected "useful goods," which certain moral virtues use as necessary instruments. In this, they certainly showed the greatness and generosity of their souls: in seeking ultimate happiness, they directed the gaze of their eyes toward the light of the Sun, not toward the glow of a lamp—especially since they had discovered that external goods often provide the material for vice rather than for virtue. 

The Peripatetics, however, while knowing that riches were not at all necessary for those most famous and excellent men <note>i.e., the contemplative philosophers.</note>, taught that other virtues existed which, though noble, were inferior to those, and that some of these required the goods of fortune. Both schools, therefore, agree that the vice of "negligence" consists primarily in this: that men cease to desire the goods of fortune necessary for exercising certain moral virtues, even if those virtues do not lead to contemplative blessedness. This vice, which inclines toward a "defect," is the opposite of greed, which urges toward "excess." In the middle of these two extremes resides a certain distinguished virtue concerning the desire for useful things; it seeks only what is necessary for exercising the virtues, and it is called "sufficiency." 

**SOPHIA.** Just as a middle virtue and two extreme vices are found in the *desiring* of useful goods, is the logic the same for useful things after they are *possessed*? 

**PHILO.** Precisely. Regarding riches...

<meta>This page continues Philo’s explanation of how love and desire apply to different types of "goods." # LEONE EBREO ON LOVE,

<margin>In the case of possessing useful goods, an excessive love of riches is called <term>greed</term><note>Latin: *avaritia*.</note>, a deficient love is called <term>prodigality</term><note>Latin: *prodigalitas*.</note>, and a moderate or middle love is called <term>liberality</term><note>Latin: *liberalitas*. The virtue of using one's wealth balanced by reason.</note>.</margin>
...of those things which have already been gathered and are possessed, the excessive love is called greed, and it exists as a base and shameful vice. For when the love of one’s own wealth exceeds a laudable moderation, it leads to both an excessive preservation of money beyond what is just and good, and a meager distribution of it below what is honorable and commanded by reason. However, moderation in loving such things, combined with a fitting distribution of them, produces that middle virtue called liberality. On the other side of this sits the opposite extreme: one who lacks a proper love for their own resources and pours them away without any regard for reason; this is the contrary of greed and is called prodigality. Therefore, both the greedy man and the prodigal man are depraved and evil, as both follow extremes in the valuing of useful goods. But the liberal man, walking the middle path between these extremes, is rightly praised as good and obedient to the commands of reason. We have thus revealed how love and desire are said to revolve around the excess, the defect, and the middle point of useful goods.

**SOPHIA.** This discourse pleases me greatly. Now I would like to learn in what way "pleasant things" are said to be loved and longed for, as this discussion will be far more suited to our current purpose.

**PHILO.** Just as in the case of "useful goods" a proper and true love is never found at the exact same time as desire, so, on the contrary, in "pleasant things" desire is seen to be always joined with love. For all pleasant things that are lacking are both longed for and craved—and simultaneously loved—before their enjoyment is fully achieved. 

The drunkard, before he has gorged himself to the point of satiety, both desires and loves wine equally. One addicted to gluttony, before he has filled his belly with food, pursues a sumptuous table with no less love than desire. And generally, whoever is thirsty loves and longs for drink at the same time; whoever is hungry does the same for food. Likewise, a lover, before he is joined with the woman he loves, both intensely craves her and greatly loves her; the same happens for a woman toward a man. 

However, the specific condition of these kinds of goods is that after their most pleasant use, as the desire vanishes, the love itself very frequently vanishes at the same time, and often turns into hatred and loathing. For he who just a moment ago was affected by an incredible craving and pleasure for eating and drinking, after being satisfied, not only no longer craves or loves the food and wine, but rather loathes and scorns them. 

<margin>Before they are possessed, pleasant things are desired and loved at the same time; but once they are had, as the desire and love frequently vanish together, they leave behind a loathing of themselves and a certain hateful satiety.</margin>

<margin>Some men are extremely intemperate in their pleasures.</margin>

<margin>The desire for pleasant things is properly called <term>appetite</term><note>Latin: *appetitio*. A physical or sensory craving.</note>.</margin>

<margin>The desire for useful things is called <term>ambition</term> or <term>covetousness</term><note>Latin: *ambitio aut cupiditas*.</note>.</margin>

<margin>In the craving and enjoying of pleasures, the excess is commonly called <term>luxury</term><note>Latin: *luxuria*. In this context, it refers to debauchery or lewdness.</note>, but more specifically <term>incontinence</term> or <term>intemperance</term>; the defect is called excessive abstinence; and finally, the middle ground is called either <term>continence</term> or <term>temperance</term>.</margin>

We see the same thing happen in other matters which bring pleasure to the senses in a raw and coarse way. For the desire for all such things is usually very easily extinguished by a certain hateful satiety; thus these two affections of the will regarding pleasant things live and die together, as if bound by an unbreakable chain. 

Some people, however, are found to be so intemperate in pleasures (not unlike others are in profits) that they never wish to be satisfied; such are those devoted to the belly and to lust. This type of person hates satiety itself, and returns with unspeakable greed to the desires and loves of those same, or similar, pleasures. 

The desire for pleasant things is properly called "appetite," just as the desire for useful things was called "ambition" or "covetousness." An excess in the appetite for pleasures and an immoderate indulgence in them is called "luxury," which indulges too much in gluttony and the private parts, and most especially embraces a soft and idle life; those who are contaminated by this vice are called "luxurious." If reason, after struggling for a long time against this sharp enemy, finally succumbs, they are called <term>incontinent</term><note>Someone who knows what is right but lacks the willpower to do it.</note>; but if they surrender immediately without any fight, they are called <term>intemperate</term><note>Someone who has lost the moral compass to even struggle against their desires.</note>. 

Just as luxury regarding pleasant things corresponds to greed and covetousness regarding useful things, so I judge that "excessive abstinence" should be called the other extreme in these matters. This can rightly be compared to prodigality and negligence in the former case; for while one of them neglects the care of money conducive to living honorably, the other neglects the pleasures necessary for life...

### DIALOGUE I.

...to protect the body, as well as to preserve health, one should completely abandon and leave behind [excesses]. A certain moral virtue claims for itself the middle ground between luxury and excessive abstinence. If reason emerges superior after a long battle with appetite, it is called **continence** <note>original: *continentia*; the state of resisting temptation through effort.</note>; but if the appetite yields and obeys reason without any struggle, it will be named **temperance** <note>original: *temperantia*; a more perfected state where one's desires are naturally aligned with reason.</note>. Both of these consist in the moderation of pleasures by omitting the superfluous and choosing the necessary. Some have called this virtue **fortitude** <note>original: *fortitudo*; usually meaning physical courage, but here applied to the strength of character required for self-control.</note>, saying that he is truly brave who conquers himself. Indeed, pleasure is much more deeply ingrained in human nature than utility, as it preserves the body in its proper state and best disposition. Therefore, if anyone reduces the excess of pleasures to a moderate level, he is rightly thought to have won an illustrious victory over a most powerful and rebellious enemy.

<margin>Temperance is not without reason called fortitude by some. He is truly brave who conquers himself. Pleasure is much more innate to human nature than utility.</margin>

**SOPHIA.** You seem to have spoken rightly about those pleasures that are to be loved and sought. However, a certain ambiguity can be drawn from your previous words: perhaps someone might falsely think that pleasant things are sought and loved only when they are missing, but not after they are in our power. For although this is true of desire, it is not found to be true of love; for while pleasures are being acquired, they are loved, but not before they are obtained, because love for them seems to consist in the very perception of the delights themselves.

**PHILO.** From the tasting of pleasures, appetite and desire are stirred no less than love; however, only those things that are missing are said to be craved and desired.

**SOPHIA.** What on earth is this contradiction? For if pleasures are not only loved while they are held, but also desired—and appetite always refers to a lack—it follows that what is already held is actually missing and not held.

**PHILO.** It is indeed true that pleasures are loved and desired while they are being perceived. However, neither of these two emotions remains after their perception is complete; for then, as we have already said, both are extinguished. But in the act of acquiring them, something is always missing until satiety <note>original: *satietas*; the point of being completely full or satisfied.</note> is reached; moreover—

<margin>The perception of pleasant things, continued until satiety, is always connected with a sense of lack. In pleasant things, when the need or lack is completely removed, desire and love for them are likewise taken away.</margin>

—at the very beginning of acquisition, the knowledge and sense of lack are increased by the pleasant proximity of the object. Because of this greater sense and knowledge of lack, the appetite is driven more fiercely, and love is made more ardent. Thus, it is not surprising that when one part of a pleasure is acquired, the appetite becomes sharper and more biting because of the intense sense of what is still missing. But if satiety arises from an excessive continuation of pleasures, the need is completely removed, and with it, desire and love are taken away, replaced by a certain disgust and hatred. Therefore, let us conclude that love and desire do not follow or accompany pleasures that have already been fully obtained, but rather precede pleasures that are yet to be fully acquired.

**SOPHIA.** You have said more than enough about pleasant things regarding these two emotions. But now that the similarity and difference between useful and pleasant things have been explained (since both relate to love and desire), and the reason for their agreement is clear, I cannot figure out the cause of their difference. Why is it that with useful things, love and desire are never joined—

<margin>The reason why useful things are first desired and later loved, while pleasant things are desired and loved at the same time, depends on the different ways of enjoying these two kinds of sought-after and loved things. Utility consists in the continuous possession of a thing.</margin>

—but while something is sought, it is not yet loved, and once desire leaves, love succeeds it; yet in pleasant things, the opposite happens: as long as the thing is desired, it is loved, and when desire dies, love also vanishes? For what reason is such a great dissimilarity and contrast found in two such similar species of love?

**PHILO.** The reason for the difference arises from the different ways of enjoying these two classes of sought and loved things. Since utility consists in the continuous possession of a thing, the longer a thing is possessed, the longer the fruit is perceived from it. For this reason, a thing can hardly be loved before its possession; once it is obtained, desire ceases and love takes its place—a love that is preserved perpetually along with the perpetual possession of the thing itself. If, however, possession has not yet been acquired, or is lost after acquisition, we are said to crave the thing, but not at all to love it. But pleasures—
