<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Philo and Sophia. In the previous section, Philo discussed how temperance and fortitude allow a person to moderate physical pleasures. He now moves into a deeper psychological analysis of how we experience pleasure versus utility, and begins to introduce the highest form of love: the love for the "Honestum" (the virtuous or honorable good).</meta>

### LEONE EBREO ON LOVE,

<margin>Pleasure consists in a certain movement that is always joined to deprivation and lack.</margin>
Indeed, [pleasures] consist neither in possession, nor in habit, nor in their perfect acquisition, but rather in a certain movement always joined to deprivation and lack. When these two—deprivation and lack—are removed, both the pleasures themselves and the desire and love for them immediately fail. 

**SOPHIA.** It seems consistent to say that the desire for a delightful thing signifies a deprivation; but the love for a present thing is rather considered at the moment of enjoyment. 

**PHILO.** You have questioned this most subtly, Sophia, and you spoke rightly that the true love of a delightful thing should have no meaning of "lacking" <note>Philo is distinguishing between the "desire" for something we don't have and the "love" for something we are currently enjoying.</note>. 

<margin>In seeking pleasant things, a certain imaginary pleasure is perceived; but in seeking useful things, a certain interior sadness is usually felt.</margin>
But it should not escape your notice that in the very act of seeking the pleasant, a certain imaginary delight arises, even if we have not yet obtained it. This, however, is not at all the case with the desire for useful goods; on the contrary, men are made sad by the lack of them. The greatest proof of this is that those seeking pleasant things are seen to be joyful and cheerful, while those gasping for money <note>The "useful" good.</note> are very frequently observed to be sad and melancholy.

<margin>In the absence of both, the pleasant surpasses the useful; but in the presence of both, the possession of the useful is much more powerful than the pleasant.</margin>
The reason for this effect is certainly that, in the absence of both, the pleasant has a far more effective power than the useful to excite the imagination <note>original: *phantasiam*; the faculty of the mind that forms mental images.</note>. In the present possession of both, however, the useful exists as much more powerful than the pleasant itself. Thus, in the pleasant, an imaginary pleasure arises from the sense and appetite of the person who lacks it, and from the present and true pleasure, the sense and appetite of the lacking person are fulfilled. For this reason, the pleasant things themselves are both loved and sought indifferently at both times. But the difference consists in this: when pleasures are absent, the appetite is more intense than the love; but when they are present, love is more vehement than the appetite. 

**SOPHIA.** The truth of this matter can also be confirmed by the fact that we perceive a certain present delight from dreams of things that bring enjoyment. Sometimes, even while awake, we feel no small pleasure from the most intense activity of the imagination concerning such things. This efficacy cannot be shown at all in the imagination of useful things. But it only remains for you to explain, having made a comparison of these two species of love, which of them is more extensive and universal, and whether both are ever found together in one and the same lovable thing.

<margin>The pleasant is far more common and universal than the useful.</margin>
**PHILO.** The pleasant is far more common and universal than the useful. For not everything that delights also brings utility; because those things from which the senses perceive pleasure frequently affect the body, its strength, and its faculties with no small detriment. Nevertheless, all useful things usually bring us delight—both before their acquisition (if indeed their utility has been known and perceived by us), and much more after acquisition, and especially in the very moment of acquisition.

<margin>A far greater pleasure is felt from the recent acquisition of riches than from their long-term possession.</margin>
However, a much greater pleasure is felt in acquiring useful things than in continually possessing them. For every delight seems to proceed from a comparison to that which we lacked; hence it consists more in the acquisition than in the possession of riches. 

**SOPHIA.** You have handled the two lower species of love and desire very well. Let us now, therefore, turn ourselves to the third, which is the most excellent and noble of all.

<margin>From seeking and loving virtuous things, men attain the greatest praise. Love and desire for virtuous things consist primarily in two ornaments of our intellect: virtue and wisdom.</margin>
**PHILO.** From seeking and loving virtuous things <note>original: *honesta*; the "Honestum" refers to moral excellence, honor, or that which is good for its own sake rather than for pleasure or profit.</note>, men are indeed raised up to the stars. For loves and desires of this kind render that part [of us] most excellent—that part by whose merit man attained his proper essence, and which, receding furthest from the darkness and gloom of matter, approaches the divine and purest light. This is called the intellectual soul <note>original: *anima intellectiua*.</note>, which alone among all human powers and faculties rescues itself from foul and miserable mortality into immortality. 

<margin>The virtuous precedes the useful and the pleasant in dignity for two reasons.</margin>
Therefore, the love and desire for virtuous things consist primarily in two ornaments of our intellect: virtue and wisdom. Upon these, as if upon bases and foundations, is built the truly pleasant divine "honesty" <note>The state of being virtuous/honorable.</note>, which precedes both the gain of useful things and the delight of pleasant things in dignity for two reasons. First, because pleasant things are in the senses, useful things are in the imagination, and virtuous things are in the intellect—a faculty far nobler than the other faculties of the soul...

<summary>Philo and Sophia distinguish between the "pleasant" and the "useful," noting that while the pursuit of pleasure can be joyful, the pursuit of utility (like wealth) often brings sadness. Philo then introduces the "Honestum" (the virtuous or honorable), the highest form of good which resides in the intellectual soul and leads to immortality.</summary>

### DIALOGUE I.

<margin>The useful and the pleasant are ordered toward the honorable itself as toward an end.</margin>
...are placed in a more noble rank. Secondly, it is because the useful and the pleasant are referred to the honorable <note>original: "honestum"; in this context, it refers to moral virtue, wisdom, and that which is inherently good and worthy of honor.</note> as toward an end. For riches <note>The "useful" good.</note> are acquired for the sake of enjoying pleasures; pleasures are ordered toward the health and comfort of the body; and the body serves as an instrument for the intellectual soul in its own proper actions proceeding from virtue and wisdom. <margin>In the honorable, the end of man is placed and alone located.</margin> From this it follows that the "end" or ultimate purpose of man is found in honorable actions endowed with virtue and wisdom. These actions excel all others in nobility and induce more excellent loves and more praiseworthy desires in the souls of men. 

**SOPHIA.** You have clearly shown how much the honorable excels the useful and the pleasant. But now our purpose is to pursue the difference between love and the desire for honorable things, as well as to reveal in what way both agree with the love and desire for useful and pleasant things. <margin>The agreement of the honorable with the useful and the pleasant.</margin> 

**PHILO.** This is certainly what I wanted to open up, if you hadn't interrupted me. Honorable loves and honorable desires partly agree with the useful and pleasant taken together; partly they agree with the pleasant and differ from the useful; partly they agree with the useful and differ from the pleasant; and finally, they differ from both.

**SOPHIA.** Address each individual part of your proposed division. 

**PHILO.** Honorable, useful, and pleasant desires agree in this: that all are said to refer to those things which we lack. For just as useful and pleasant things are sought because we are deprived of them, so too wisdom and the virtues are greatly desired when they are not possessed. <margin>In what way the honorable agrees with the pleasant and differs from the useful.</margin> Indeed, in this respect the honorable and the pleasant are so similar to each other that in both, desire is found joined with love. For things that bring pleasure, as well as wisdom and the virtues, are both desired and loved at the same time before they are acquired. This condition reveals not only the agreement of the honorable with the pleasant, but also the distinction between the honorable and the useful: for useful things are only sought <note>i.e., we want to obtain them.</note> before their acquisition, but they are not yet loved.

**SOPHIA.** What reason can be given for this similarity between the honorable and the pleasant, and for the difference of the honorable from the useful? <margin>The reason why honorable and pleasant things are sought and loved at the same time, while useful things can by no means be sought and loved at the same time.</margin> 

**PHILO.** At first glance, honorable things, when they are not held, seem only to be sought and not loved; for virtue and wisdom, before they have been acquired by us, are seen to have no true or solid essence that exists as worthy of love. 

**PHILO.** <note>The speaker tag is repeated in the original text.</note> Useful things, unless actually possessed, are entirely foreign to those desiring them, and therefore, even though they truly exist in the world, they cannot be loved. Pleasant things, however, as we said, before they are held, create a desire that excites a certain movement and a "pre-taste" of pleasure in the imagination <term>phantasia</term><note>The "phantasia" was considered the faculty of the mind that forms mental images of sensory things.</note>. Even if this essence is thin and obscure, it is a subject sufficiently suited to receive the love established within the lover himself. 

The desire for wisdom, virtues, and honorable things induces a similar—or rather, a more illustrious—essence into the intellect. For to desire wisdom and virtue can, not undeservedly, be called a kind of wisdom and virtue itself, and to long for honorable things is itself a most honorable state. Since the desire for honorable things (which are sought but not yet held) fashions these kinds of interior essences in the intellect—which is the highest and noblest faculty of the soul—it is right that an unwearied and swift love should accompany that desire. This love follows the desires for honorable things far more readily than it follows pleasant ones. Therefore, when both honorable and pleasant things are lacking, we find desire associated with love; this never happens with useful things.

**SOPHIA.** Enough on these points; now turn your speech to revealing the other two parts that remain. <margin>In what way the honorable agrees with the useful and differs from the pleasant.</margin> 

**PHILO.** In things that are already possessed after their complete acquisition, the honorable and the useful agree in being loved. For just as useful things are loved after they have been obtained, so wisdom and the virtues of honorable things are wonderfully loved when they are possessed. In this respect, the honorable differs from the pleasant: for almost all men, once they are filled with pleasures to the point of satiety, immediately turn their love for those pleasures into hatred and disgust. <margin>The honorable is twice over repugnant to the useful and the pleasant.</margin> The honorable, therefore, differs from the useful and the pleasant taken together in this: that it is both longed for when not yet acquired, and completely loved when acquired...

### OF THE LOVE OF LEO THE HEBREW

...may always have the desired love accompanying it, which certainly happens to neither of the other two. Furthermore, it possesses another distinguished difference from both: for the virtues concerning the **useful** and the **pleasant**—in loving and seeking them—choose for themselves a **middle path** <note>This refers to the Aristotelian "Golden Mean," where virtue is the balance between two extremes.</note>, leaving aside the extremes as if they were the sources of nearly all vices, and in that middle they remain. But with **honorable** goods, the more their love and desire exceed, the greater the praise and the truer the name of virtue they deserve. He who desires and loves them too little stands as one full of vice; and if anyone should desire or love them for no reason at all, he should be called not only vicious but even inhuman. For the **honorable** is the true good, since 

<margin>The Good is defined as that which all men seek.</margin> 
according to the Philosopher's <note>Referring to Aristotle, who famously began his *Nicomachean Ethics* with this definition.</note> opinion, the "good" is defined as that which all men seek. Moreover, by a natural instinct, all men desire to know. 

**SOPHIA.** I have heard this 

<margin>All men by natural instinct desire to know.</margin>
difference explained by others in a somewhat different way. 

**PHILO.** In what way do they explain it? 

**SOPHIA.** They say that in honorable things, virtue consists in the extreme of **excess**, while vice consists in the extreme of **deficiency**. For the more the honorable itself is sought, loved, and acquired, the more excellent and illustrious the virtue becomes. On the other hand, it must be considered a great vice if someone is touched by very little or no love and desire for honorable things at all. But in useful and pleasant things, the opposite happens: for virtue consists in seeking, loving, and pursuing them only a **little**; vice, however, is placed and located in the excess of these feelings. Therefore, virtue regarding the **honorable** is found in the maximum love of it, and vice in the minimum; whereas the **useful** and **pleasant**, if they are loved a little, tend to introduce virtue, but if they are loved beyond measure, they introduce vice. 

**PHILO.** The opinion of those people seems to be true not entirely, but only in part. For the idea that virtue regarding the useful and pleasant 

<margin>In common and moral life, virtue consists in the middle path; vices, however, consist in the excess and deficiency of seeking and loving useful and pleasant things.</margin>
proceeds from a small amount of love and pursuit of them is true in one sense, but false in every kind of life. For in common and moral life, virtue resides in the **middle path** <note>original: "mediocritate"</note> of both seeking and loving them, and is not placed in either of the two extremes. For a love of them that is too great, as well as one that is nonexistent or less than is fitting, is blamed as a vice, just as we said above according to the opinion of the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note>. But those who follow the **intellectual and contemplative life**, in which the highest happiness is placed, judge the care for riches and the desire for pleasures to be vicious—not only when they are excessive, but even when they are moderate. For the contempt of these things is especially necessary for deep and intense contemplation, and the care for goods of this kind is no small hindrance to that class of men, since far fewer comforts are 

<margin>In the intellectual and contemplative life, however, both a vehement and a moderate love and desire for these same goods is blamed as a vice; whereas a more restrained desire is usually praised as a distinguished virtue.</margin>
required in the contemplative life than in the moral life, a point which the Stoics <note>A school of philosophy that advocated for self-control and detachment from worldly desires.</note> demonstrated with many arguments. Therefore, in matters of character (morals), virtue resides in the middle of the useful and pleasant; but in contemplation, it chooses for itself the extreme tending toward deficiency <note>Meaning the contemplative person should desire worldly things as little as possible.</note>. In morals, both extremes are vicious; in contemplation, only the extreme of excess is blamed. 

**SOPHIA.** I recognize the truth of both opinions. But I would greatly desire to understand the reason for this difference, by which the honorable is distinguished from the useful and the pleasant. 

**PHILO.** The reason for the diversity can be given as this: just as an immoderate appetite for pleasures and an unquenchable greed for riches sink our intellect and cast it headlong into the deepest place of matter, obscuring the brilliance of the mind with the darkness of the senses; so, on the contrary, an insatiable and burning love for wisdom and honorable virtues transforms the human intellect into the **divine**, and converts our fragile body, subject on all sides to decay, into something **angelic**. 

**SOPHIA.** Do you not think that moderation and the middle path in useful and pleasant things are themselves "honorable"? 

**PHILO.** They are undoubtedly honorable, since they are called virtues. 

**SOPHIA.** If, therefore, they are honorable, why is their excess vicious? For you just said that the virtue of honorable things shines in excess, not in deficiency or in the middle. Yet on the other hand, you affirmed that in useful and pleasant things, excess is a vice. Truly, this is a manifest contradiction. 

**PHILO.** Since...

### DIALOGUE I.

...though you may excel in sharpness of mind, wisdom must be sought by you with all your might.

<margin>The reason why moral virtues regarding **pleasant** and **useful** things consist in a middle way, whereas intellectual virtues shine most **honorably** in their excess.</margin>
Those virtues found within the realm of the **useful** and the **pleasant** do not take the name of "virtue" from their own nature. For the delights of **pleasant** things reside in the senses, and the conveniences of external **useful** goods reside in the phantasy <note>In Renaissance psychology, the "phantasy" or imagination was the internal sense that processed images from the physical senses.</note>; these are entirely foreign to the pure and spiritual substance of the intellect. Since the intellect is the origin of **honorable** things, it follows that the further the love and desire for them extends, the more excellent and worthy the virtue is judged to be. However, **useful** and **pleasant** things can only participate in intellectual reason when the love and desire for them is brought back to moderation and a "middle way" <note>This refers to the Aristotelian concept that virtue is the balance between two extremes (e.g., courage is the mean between cowardice and recklessness).</note>. In this moderation—devised by the intellect—consists the virtue seen in their use. If we turn away from that middle path, either toward more or toward less, we immediately fall into vice. For loves of this kind, unless they are determined by reason, are evil and perverse, and belong to brute animals rather than to man. But the middle path prescribed for them by reason is virtue itself; and the more intensely and vehemently men long for, love, and pursue this middle path, the more they excel in virtue. For that love and appetite should no longer be called "pleasure" or "gain," but rather it proceeds toward the moderation of both, which exists as an intellectual and **honorable** virtue.

*SO.* Regarding the difference between the love and the desire for things that fall under the will, and furthermore regarding the reason for this difference, you have abundantly satisfied my requests. Now I ask this of you: to which of the three aforementioned species should certain things—which are both loved and sought—be reduced? Such as health, children, a husband, a wife, power, dominion, empire, honor, fame, and glory. For although things of this kind are both cherished and longed for, it is not clear whether they should be placed in the category of the **useful**, the **pleasant**, or the **honorable**. On one hand, they seem **pleasant** because of the delight perceived in acquiring them; on the other hand, since after their acquisition and stable possession their love is preserved unharmed—with no satiety and no boredom intervening—they might be thought to differ from **pleasant** things and agree with the **honorable** or the **useful**.

<margin>Health is primarily referred to as **pleasant**, yet it is also seen to be **useful** and **honorable**.</margin>
*PH.* Health, although utility follows from it, ought properly to be numbered among **pleasant** things. Nor is it contrary to reason that some **pleasant** things are also **useful**, just as many **useful** things bring delight, and in both categories, some **honorable** things are found. Health, therefore, is primarily **pleasant**, yet it is also **useful** and **honorable**. Because of this, neither satiety nor any boredom ever takes hold of us regarding it, as happens with other things that bring only pleasure. For those other things, when they are possessed, are not valued as highly as they were before they were acquired, when they were still longed for. Another reason can be given for why we never grow weary of health: namely, because the pleasure proceeding from it is not perceived only by the external and coarser senses (whose delight is quickly turned into boredom), as it is not found in tasting food, nor in sexual touch, nor in smelling scents. Nor does it only delight the external and more spiritual senses (which are satisfied more slowly), as it does not consist in hearing harmonic sounds and sweet voices, nor in seeing beautiful and artistic figures; rather, it insinuates itself into all human senses, both external and internal, even into the phantasy itself. When health is lost, it is desired not only by the sensory appetite, but also by the will itself, enlightened by the light of the intellect. Therefore, we can call it an **honorable** pleasure, although because of its long-lasting possession, we often do not value it as highly as is proper.

*SO.* So much for health; now pass on to children.

<margin>Children <note>The original Latin margin likely contains a typo "Libri" (books) for "Liberi" (children), as the text clearly discusses offspring.</note> seem to be a certain good mixed from **honor** and **pleasance**.</margin>
*PH.* Children, although they are sometimes desired for the sake of utility—so that they may possess and preserve our riches, and acquire even more—nonetheless, the love and desire for them also participates in **pleasance**. For this reason, it is found differently in brute animals than in humans. For the [pleasure] of brutes...

<summary>Philo explains that while "the honorable" (virtue) is better in excess, "the pleasant" and "the useful" must be moderated by reason to be virtuous. He begins to categorize complex goods like health and children, noting that health is a unique pleasure that never causes boredom because it involves both the senses and the intellect.</summary>

### LEO THE HEBREW ON LOVE,

pleasures do not pass beyond the five external senses. In the human race, however, although parents feel the greatest pleasure from seeing and hearing their children, the goal of parental desire is not merely the possession of children. Their chief delight consists in the imagination <note>Original: *phantasia*. In Renaissance psychology, the imagination was considered an "internal sense" that processed and stored images from the physical world, making it more spiritual than raw sight or touch.</note> and in thought itself, which is a faculty of the soul far more spiritual than any of the external senses. For this reason, long-standing familiarity with children does not bring satiety or boredom to the minds of parents. This occurs all the more because children are desired by parents not by a sensible appetite alone, but also by the will and the rational mind—which governs nature without error—directing that desire. 

<margin>Living creatures, so that they may achieve at least a specific immortality, apply themselves vehemently to the procreation of offspring.</margin>
For as the Philosopher <note>A common reference to Aristotle, specifically his idea in *On the Soul* that mortal beings participate in the eternal and divine through reproduction.</note> affirms, since nature has denied individual perpetuity to fleeting animals, they seek to achieve the specific immortality <note>Original: *immortalitatem specificam*. This refers to the immortality of the "species" rather than the individual person.</note> granted to them through the procreation of children. Hence, since the pleasure parents take in their children differs from other things that bring only pleasure, it happens that parents never hate their children once they are born, nor are they ever weary of them. In this matter, children are like health: love is not diminished because one possesses them; rather, they are loved most especially then, and they are guarded with no diligence omitted. This arises from the desire and hope for future immortality. Therefore, since the pleasure taken in children is honorable, it always has joined to it a continuous love—the most faithful companion of all honorable things—which was also the case with health. **SO.** This part being perfected and finished, it is now time to pass to the love of a man for his wife, and of a wife for her husband. 

<margin>Conjugal love is seen to be especially pleasant, yet it is also associated with both honor and utility.</margin>
**PH.** It is agreed among all that the love of spouses is pleasant, but it ought to be joined with honor. By the nature and reason of honor, once pleasure has been obtained, their mutual love is not only preserved but is even always increased. Furthermore, in conjugal love, the useful is connected with the pleasant and the honorable, since each of the spouses always receives mutual benefits from the other, which contributes greatly to the perpetual preservation of goodwill. Therefore, since the love of spouses is pleasant, it is continued until the final day of life because of the partnership formed by pleasure with honor, or with utility, or rather with both at once. **SO.** To which of the species mentioned above should the love and appetite for power, dominion, and command be reduced? 

<margin>The love and desire for ruling has both utility and pleasantness joined to it.</margin>
**PH.** The love and desire for ruling participate in both utility and pleasantness. However, because these kinds of pleasures do not delight the external senses in some thick or crude way, but rather delight the imagination and human thought internally in a spiritual manner—especially since they have utility joined to them—men can never be satisfied by their long-standing possession. On the contrary, once dominions, kingdoms, and empires have been acquired, they are loved vehemently and preserved with the greatest anxiety and skill. This is not because they participate in honor—for how can the lust for command ever be honorable?—but because the human imagination, in which these pleasures reside, is not captured by satiety in the same way as the coarser senses. Indeed, nature can scarcely be satisfied, and even less so because the desire for ruling looks toward utility in addition to pleasantness. By virtue of this utility, powers are not only loved after they have been acquired with the greatest zeal, but are also guarded with the utmost diligence; men devote themselves to their increase with an insatiable greed and unbridled lust. **SO.** It remains for you to say in what category of love honor, glory, and fame should be placed. 

<margin>Honor is twofold: one indeed false and counterfeit, which is reduced to the pleasant; the other truly legitimate and genuine, which embraces a certain pleasantness mixed with honor.</margin>
**PH.** Honor is twofold: one kind is false and counterfeit, the other is legitimate and genuine. False honor flatters power; legitimate honor rewards virtue. The counterfeit kind, which the powerful demand and seek, is reduced to the pleasant; but because it does not delight a satiable sense, but only an insatiable imagination, no boredom intervenes (as happens with other pleasures). Indeed, even if it lacks honor, yet...

### DIALOGUE

even though it may truly exist as something entirely alien to every kind of virtue <note>Original: *honestatis*. In this context, *honestas* refers to moral integrity or the quality of being "honorable," often used as a synonym for virtue itself.</note>, nevertheless, once it is compared, it is continued and preserved with an insatiable desire for its own increase. True honor, however, since it is the reward of virtuous deeds, although it is pleasant by its very nature, the pleasure arising from it is mingled with virtue. From this, both by reason of virtue and because it clings firmly to the imagination <note>Original: *phantasiæ*. Nor is it enough for the imagination if a person achieves glory and honor throughout the entire course of life, unless they also ensure that their name remains on earth for a long time after death, which is properly called fame. <margin>Honor is the reward of virtue, yet it should not be considered the proper or fitting end of virtue.</margin> Truly, even if honor is said to be the reward of virtue, it should not be thought of as the fitting end of honorable and earnest actions, nor ought we to live rightly for the sake of attaining it. For the end of virtue consists in the perfecting of the intelligent soul, which is first rendered healthy, purged, and clear through earnest actions, and is afterwards adorned with a certain divine painting by the most splendid colors of wisdom. Therefore, the end of pure and clean virtue can consist neither in the opinion of men—who are accustomed to place glory and honor in writings and monuments that preserve the memory of illustrious men—nor in the internal pleasure of the imagination, which ambitious men are accustomed to take from fame and glory. These rewards are certainly owed to virtue, yet they are not to be considered the fitting ends of noble actions. Virtue indeed ought to be praised for its own goodness, but one should not act from virtue for the sake of acquiring praise. Indeed, even if it receives an increase from praise, it would degenerate not a little from its own excellence and nobility if it proposed praise itself as its proper and appropriate end. However, because of a certain connection by which pleasures of this kind are joined to virtue, they are not undeservedly highly valued and loved, and their continuous increase is desired by men. 

**SO.** You have indeed liberally satisfied my requests, and I now clearly recognize that all the things you have enumerated belong to the pleasures of the imagination. <margin>Friendship usually flows from three sources: utility, pleasure, and virtue.</margin> They differ, however, in that in some of them utility, in others virtue, and in some both are joined together with pleasure; from this it happens that however long their possession may be, it never brings about satiety or boredom. Now I wonderingly desire to understand about human friendship and divine love: what kind they are, and what conditions they require. 

<margin>Only virtue and integrity are able to create stable and never-dissolvable friendships; utility and pleasure cannot.</margin> **PH.** Friendships are contracted among men sometimes for the sake of utility, sometimes for the sake of pleasure. But from these two causes, a relationship never arises that is either stable or perfect; for once these things are taken away, the friendships that were built upon them soon collapse and dissolve. <margin>Friendship drawn from virtue is far to be preferred over friendship made for the sake of pleasure or utility.</margin> But that is surely the true and absolute friendship which is joined by the firm and indissoluble bond of virtue and integrity. This alone, out of all kinds of human friendships, exists as worthy of the highest praise and commendation, since it binds the minds of friends so tightly and unites them so closely that the advantages and disadvantages of one are common to both. Sometimes it also brings greater joy or sadness to the friend than to the one to whom these things actually happen, and occasionally one is accustomed to take on a portion of the other's troubles to relieve the friend and lift them up when prostrated by adversity; for miseries shared with friends are felt much less. <margin>A true friend is defined as another self.</margin> Hence the Philosopher <note>Aristotle, in the *Nicomachean Ethics*, where he discusses the nature of the "perfect friendship" based on the good.</note>, providing the most common definition of honorable friendships, said that a true friend is another self. This signifies that in true friendship, a person lives a double life established in two different persons: that is, both in their own person and in the person of the friend. By this reasoning, the friend exists as another self, and each of the friends encompasses two lives united together within themselves—both their own life and the life of the other friend. They pursue each person with equal love and carry out one and the same care for both lives. <margin>Honorable friendship is also commended by the Sacred Volumes and commanded to mortals.</margin> Therefore, honorable friendship...

D

<margin>The reason for such a close union and indissoluble bond between two friends who love each other for the sake of virtue.</margin>
The Sacred Volumes <note>A reference to the Bible, specifically Leviticus 19:18 and the Gospels.</note> command friendship to mortals in these words: *Love your neighbor as yourself.* Truly, they intend for friendship to join two souls into one, and for that same love to be planted in the minds of both friends. The cause of this close union and indissoluble bond is the mutual virtue or wisdom of the two friends. Since this wisdom is spiritual, alien to matter, and entirely separated from bodily qualities, it removes the diversity of persons that arises from our physical nature. It creates a certain unique essence for the friends, located in their minds, which is preserved through a wisdom, love, and will common to both. This essence is so free from all diversity and discrepancy that it is as if their subject were only one soul shared between two persons, neither divided nor multiplied by their number. Briefly, then, it seems we must say that honorable friendship <note>Original: *honestam amicitiam*. In this context, "honorable" refers to a friendship based on moral excellence (the Aristotelian "friendship of the good") rather than utility or pleasure.</note> is accustomed to making two persons out of one, and only one person out of two.

<margin>Honorable friendship is accustomed to making two persons from one, and only one from two.</margin>
<margin>Divine love is not only honorable, but also the source of all honor and virtue.</margin>
SO. You have summarized many things regarding human friendship in a few words. Let us now ascend to divine love: for I desire to hear something of that, as it is the greatest and most supreme of all. PH. Divine love not only participates in honor, but it contains within itself, in the most excellent way, the honor of all things and of the entire love of the universe. Indeed, divinity is the beginning, the middle, and the end of all honorable actions.

<margin>Divinity is the beginning, middle, and end of all honorable actions.</margin>
<margin>The human intellect seems to be a small ray of God’s immense clarity fitted to man.</margin>
<margin>The human intellect necessarily needs the illumination of divine light to acquire and exercise honorable and wise habits.</margin>
<margin>God is said to be the twofold beginning of all honorable things, both in terms of their potential and their actualization.</margin>
SO. If He is the beginning, how can He also be considered the middle and the end? PH. He is called the Beginning because the thinking soul depends on Him. This soul performs all human and honorable actions, and it exists as a small ray of God's immense clarity fitted to man to render him rational, immortal, and happy. To act rightly and honorably, this thinking soul must be a participant in the divine light. For although it descended as a ray of divine light from God, the Best and Greatest, clear and conspicuous, it is nonetheless bound to a body and obscured by the darkness of matter. It can in no way reach the illustrious habits of virtue or the lucid concepts of wisdom unless it is illuminated anew by that divine light for the acquisition of such great things. Just as the eye, though clear by nature, is unable to look upon colors, figures, and other visible things unless it is illustrated by the light of the sun—which, distributed through the eye, the visible body, and the distance between them, creates the act of vision—so too the human intellect, though lucid by nature, is so hindered and darkened by its association with a coarse and thick body in honorable and wise actions that it necessarily requires the illumination of divine light. This light brings the intellect from potentiality into action <note>A Scholastic concept where "potential" is the capacity to do something, and "act" is the actual doing of it.</note> and illustrates the species and forms of things proceeding from thought—which stands between the intellect and the images of the imagination <note>Original: *phantasiæ*. These are the mental pictures we form of physical objects.</note>. This finally renders the person actually intelligent, prudent, and wise, inclined toward all honorable actions and utterly resistant to the dishonorable, so that with all imperfection removed and all darkness put to flight, the person is seen as perfect and lucid on all sides. Therefore, God is called the Beginning for two reasons: since all honorable things proceed from Him, both regarding their potential and their actual exercise. Since God is the supreme over all, pure and highest goodness and honor, as well as infinite virtue, it is necessary that all other inferior virtues, honors, and goodnesses be derived from Him as the true beginning and the shared origin of every individual perfection.

<margin>God is said to be the most fitting middle of all earnest and honorable actions, both in terms of help and example.</margin>
SO. It is indeed right and just that the first principle of all honorable things be placed in the highest Creator, and no one has ever doubted this. But it remains a matter of debate how He himself can be called their middle and end. PH. Divinity itself is a very fitting middle, so that through it all earnest and honorable actions may come to light. For divine providence is inclined and disposed toward those who have acquired some portion of divine virtues...

<summary>Philo explains how honorable friendship merges two souls into a single essence and begins an exploration of Divine Love, defining God as the beginning, middle, and end of all virtue. He uses the analogy of the sun and the eye to show how the human intellect requires divine illumination to achieve wisdom.</summary>

# DIALOGUE IV.

G 3

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page.</note> ...to exist, and the more they have attained a larger portion of them <note>Referring to virtues or perfections.</note>, the more it cannot be doubted that these virtues provide the greatest momentum to such excellent men for performing and perfecting honorable actions. We can also interpret God as the "middle" <note>Original: *medium*. Here meaning both the central point and the means or instrument through which something is achieved.</note> for achieving honorable acts in another way: for since He contains all virtues and excellences in Himself in a most outstanding manner, He offers an example for imitation to all who desire to act out of virtue. For what greater charity and clemency can be imagined than the divine? What greater liberality is there than that which provides an abundance of itself to all created things? What more perfect justice than that seen in divine governance? What greater goodness, firmer truth, deeper wisdom, or more absolute prudence than that which is known to be in God?

<margin>We are able to know God not perfectly as He truly exists, but only through His actions.</margin>
Yet we can know Him not perfectly, as He truly exists, but through His actions, which are seen in the creation and preservation of things. Hence, if one diligently considers divine virtues, their imitation will be the best path and the most fitting means to lead us toward all honorable and studious actions and wise thoughts, as far as human strength can reach. Therefore, God not only shows paternal love in procreating humans, but also performs the duty of a most excellent teacher by stirring and instructing them to embrace all honorable things through His distinguished and most manifest examples.

**SO.** I am greatly rejoiced that almighty God is not only the beginning but also the middle of all our happiness. Now I would like to understand in what way He is the end.

<margin>God alone exists as the supreme and ultimate end of all human actions.</margin>
**PH.** God alone exists as the ultimate and supreme end <note>Original: *finis*. In classical philosophy, the 'end' is the goal or purpose for which a thing exists.</note> of all human actions: for useful things are ordered toward the acquisition of suitable pleasures; necessary pleasures are directed toward the convenience of life and the preservation of health; these two ultimately serve the perfecting of the soul. For the soul soon attains its perfection through studious habits, and then through true wisdom, the end of which consists in the knowledge of God—who is indeed the highest wisdom, the highest goodness, and the common origin of all good things.

<margin>Love surpasses the knowledge that precedes it.</margin>
Moreover, from the knowledge of this most excellent object <note>Meaning God, as the object of our contemplation.</note>, an immense love, full of excellence and honor, is stirred within us. For things are honorably loved only insofar as they are known to be good. Thus, love for God ought to excel any honorable love and any studious action.

**SO.** I remember you saying elsewhere that because God is infinite and contains all kinds of perfections within Himself, He can hardly be known by the human mind, which is always seen to be finite and limited. For that which is known must first be comprehended; but by what means can the infinite ever be comprehended by the finite, or the immense by the small? Since He is not known, how can He be loved? For you have already said that a thing must be known before it is loved.

<margin>Just as the human mind knows God imperfectly, so too the human will loves Him only weakly and slightly.</margin>
**PH.** The immense God is loved to the extent that He is known. And just as He cannot be perfectly known by mortals, nor His wisdom penetrated by the human intellect, so He is never loved by men as much as His excellence and the nearly innumerable benefits bestowed upon the human race require. Our will cannot be capable of such great love; but it is enough for human minds to know God, if not according to His dignity, then at least according to their own strength. Nor does our will love God according to His merits, but with as much love as it can pursue.

**SO.** Is any faculty given to know something that is not comprehended by the knower himself?

<margin>A thing known is often received by the knower according to the strength of the knower himself, not according to the dignity of the thing known.</margin>
**PH.** It is enough for that portion of the thing which is known to be comprehended, and for the thing known to be received by the knower according to the strength of the knower, not according to the dignity of the thing known. Do you not see the human form impressed and marked in a mirror, not according to human perfection, but according to the powers and capacity of perfection of the mirror itself, which represents only images and not the essences of things? Fire [is not received] according to its burning nature by the eye...

<summary>Philo explains that God is the source, the exemplar, and the ultimate goal of all virtue. He addresses the paradox of how a finite human mind can know and love an infinite God, using the metaphor of a mirror to show that we perceive God according to our own capacity rather than His full essence.</summary>

<margin>
The human intellect understands God only according to its own strength and capacity, and not according to the immensity of divine essence and wisdom.
</margin>
...is received, for then it would burn the eye itself; but it is seen only according to its color and shape. Indeed, what clearer example of this matter can be brought forward than the entire celestial hemisphere being encompassed by the single pupil of the eye? This pupil is of such smallness that some wise men have thought it to be indivisible <note>original: *indiuisibilem*; referring to a geometric point that cannot be further split</note>, and unable to undergo any natural division. The eye, therefore, gazes upon visible things according to its own power, size, and nature—not according to the full nature of the things themselves. By this same reasoning, our small intellect encompasses the immense God; namely, according to the strength and capacity of the human intellect, and not according to the immensity of the divine essence and wisdom. Furthermore, from this thin sort of knowledge, there follows a certain love for God that corresponds to the weakness of the human will, but which does not match the infinite goodness of the Best God Himself.

**SOPHIA.** Tell me, I pray, is desire also joined with our love for God?

**PHILO.** 
<margin>
Our love for God is never found lacking a vehement desire to acquire that knowledge of God which we currently lack.
</margin>
Indeed, our love for God is never found to be without an ardent desire to acquire that knowledge of God which we lack. Hence, as the desire increases, the love for the known Divinity also grows. Since the divine essence infinitely exceeds human knowledge, and God's goodness exceeds human love by an infinite proportion, for this reason, a most vehement, ardent, and even most happy desire to increase one’s knowledge and love of God always flows into the souls of men. This increase can extend into infinity because of the nature of the object being known and loved; however, perhaps in consideration of human strength, it remains finite and stands at that degree which men cannot transcend. Alternatively, once the intellect has reached its highest goal, when it sees how much of the journey for knowing God still remains to be completed and realizes it cannot traverse it, a certain trace of desire remains. Yet, because of the excellence of the loved object being beyond human strength and faculties, the soul exists in a state of bliss. 

<margin>
The souls of the blessed feel no trouble or bitterness whatsoever from the desire for that divine knowledge which they lack.
</margin>
For the desire for that divine knowledge which is lacking does not bring any disturbance or bitterness to the souls of the blessed, since it is not granted to human strength to proceed any further. On the contrary, the blessed take the greatest pleasure from the fact that they feel they have already reached the ultimate perfection appointed and suitable for them, both in knowing and in loving God.

**SOPHIA.** Since you have made mention of human happiness <note>original: *beatitudine*; often translated as "blessedness" or "supreme happiness"</note>, I would like you to judge for me what it consists of.

**PHILO.** 
<margin>
Human happiness is by no means to be placed in useful goods, as some have falsely persuaded themselves.
</margin>
There have been various opinions among men concerning the subject of happiness. Many have placed it in the possession and abundance of useful goods <note>meaning material wealth or external resources</note> lasting until their final day. Truly, the falsehood of this opinion is detected by the fact that external goods are referred back to internal ones, since the former depend on the latter. Happiness, however, must be placed in the most excellent goods; and it must be the end of all other things, not ordered toward another higher purpose, since all things are done for the sake of attaining happiness. Furthermore, external goods are placed in the hand and judgment of fortune, whereas happiness must be established within the power of the human person.

<margin>
Human happiness is by no means placed in sensible and common pleasures, as the Epicureans falsely thought. Human happiness must undoubtedly be established in nobility, and in the habits and acts of the intelligent soul.
</margin>
Others, however, have held a different opinion and said that happiness consists in bodily pleasures. These are called Epicureans <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Epicurus; in this period, they were often characterized (sometimes unfairly) as being solely focused on physical indulgence</note>, who preach the mortality of the soul and wish to attribute happiness to man through nothing other than common pleasures. But it is clear that this opinion is also deceptive because the pleasure of the senses, when it turns into satiety and disgust, destroys itself. True happiness, however, ought to bring perpetual delight and perfect pleasure to men. Furthermore, we have already said that the end of pleasure which delights the senses is moral excellence <note>original: *honestum*; referring to what is noble or virtuous</note> itself; but happiness has no higher end; indeed, it exists as the most excellent end of all human actions. Therefore, it must be concluded that happiness is undoubtedly to be placed in moral excellence and in the acts and habits of the...

<margin>The habits of the intelligent soul are said to be five: Art, Prudence, Intellect, Science, and Wisdom.</margin>
...of the intelligent soul, which excel all other human habits <note>original: *habitus*; in Renaissance philosophy, a "habit" is not a repetitive routine, but a stable quality or "disposition" of the mind acquired through practice.</note> in dignity, and exist as their well-suited goals: and by whose benefit man deserves the name of man, and precedes the other animals by a very long interval. **SOPHIA.** Which and how many are those habits of the intelligent soul? **PHILO.** Five: Art, Prudence, Intellect, Science, and Wisdom. **SOPHIA.** How are they defined?
<margin>Definition of Art.</margin>
**PHILO.** Art is the habit of producing things according to reason, which are handled by the hands and require the operation of the body. This habit includes all the mechanical arts <note>mechanical arts: physical crafts and trades, as opposed to the "liberal arts" of the mind.</note> that use a physical instrument. <margin>Definition of Prudence.</margin> Prudence is the habit of acting according to reason, which is concerned with good morals, and encompasses all the virtues whose actions proceed from the will through its two primary affections, love and desire. <margin>Definition of Intellect.</margin> Intellect is the habit and principle of understanding those common principles which are immediately known by everyone through the light of nature and are granted to be true, provided the meaning of the words expressing them is correctly understood: such as, that good is to be pursued, evil is to be fled, that contraries cannot coexist in one thing, and others similar to these, in which the intellect soon exercises its first action without the help of reasoning. <margin>Definition of Science.</margin> Science is the habit of knowing conclusions that are deduced from the aforementioned principles, and it contains the seven liberal arts: in which, with the help of reasoning, the intellect shows its middle operation.
<margin>Definition of Wisdom.</margin>
Wisdom is a habit consisting of intellect and science together, and it encompasses all principles and all conclusions that signify things existing outside the soul. This alone ascends to the highest knowledge of incorporeal and spiritual things, and is called theology <note>original: *θεολογία* (theologia)</note> by the Greeks, which we interpret as the science of divine things. <margin>Wisdom is called "theosophy" by the Greeks and "First Philosophy" by the ancients.</margin> It was also called "First Philosophy" by the ancients <note>Aristotle famously referred to the study of the highest causes and divine things as "First Philosophy."</note>: because it is first and as it were the head of all sciences, in which the intellect, now most disposed toward perfection, consumes its universal and strongest powers in the final place. **SOPHIA.** In which of these five habits does happiness consist? <margin>Human happiness is to be placed neither in art nor in the works of art, but rather in actions emanating from virtue or wisdom.</margin> **PHILO.** All concede that it is placed neither in art nor in the works of art: for these seem more suited to never obtaining happiness than to eventually acquiring it: but blessedness is rather to be placed in actions emanating from virtue or wisdom: for in these two, true happiness consists. **SOPHIA.** Explain in detail which of these two habits—virtue or wisdom—bestows ultimate happiness upon us. <margin>Moral virtues are necessary to attain happiness: however, the proper subject and home of happiness is wisdom itself.</margin> **PHILO.** Moral virtues are indeed necessary means to attain happiness: however, its proper subject is wisdom, which we could never attain without preceding moral virtues: for he who lacks virtue will never turn out wise, just as, conversely, a wise man is found at no moment of time to be destitute of virtue: so that in this way virtue is the way to acquire wisdom, and wisdom itself is the proper home of happiness. **SOPHIA.** There are many modes of knowing, and different kinds of sciences according to the multitude and diversity of things known, as well as the variety of modes by which things are known by the intellect. <margin>Moral virtue is a certain way necessarily required for wisdom.</margin> Tell me, therefore, in how many and in which of these is happiness placed—whether it consists in the knowledge of all things, or of some, or of only one: and what thing of such great excellence can be found, whose knowledge alone can lead the human intellect to supreme blessedness. <margin>The opinion of some who think human happiness is situated in the knowledge of all things and sciences, together with the reasoning and foundation of this opinion.</margin> **PHILO.** Some think that happiness is situated in the knowledge of all sciences and all things, with not even one missing. **SOPHIA.** What argument do they bring forward to confirm their opinion? **PHILO.** They say the intellect is from the start in a state of pure power for understanding, and this power is not restricted or forced into a narrow space by any specific kind of thing, but is commonly and universally spread out to understand all things: and as Aristotle affirms, our intellect is of such a nature that it can...

# LEONE HEBREO ON LOVE,

<margin>Two proper functions of the active intellect.</margin>
...is to understand all things, just as on the contrary the nature of the active intellect <note>original: *intellectus agentis*; in Aristotelian philosophy, the part of the mind that transforms sensory information into abstract concepts</note> is said to exist as that which creates the intelligible forms <note>original: *species intelligibiles*; the mental "blueprints" of things</note> and illuminates our intellect with them. For making all things intelligible, and impressing them upon the potential intellect <note>original: *intellectui potestatis*; also known as the "possible intellect," the capacity of the mind to receive knowledge</note>, or illuminating it with them, are the proper functions of the active intellect. Since, therefore, the potential intellect is said to be that which is led back from its own dark potentiality to a luminous act by the active intellect, it follows that its supreme perfection and happiness consist in this: that it eventually be found to have been entirely translated from potentiality to the act of all things that exist. For since its most universal power regards all things, its perfection and its happiness must be placed in knowing all things, so that no potentiality and no defect at all remains within it. And this, they say, is the supreme blessedness and the most happy end of the human intellect—a goal in which they affirm our intellect, having been

<margin>That most happy coupling of the potential intellect with the active intellect.</margin>
entirely liberated from potentiality, has been translated completely into act. And then it is united in every way with the active intellect that illuminates it, and is converted into it, all potentiality having now been removed, which previously was the cause of all their diversity and contrariety. By this reasoning, therefore, the potential intellect is entirely led into act; this translation, or rather union, is its highest perfection and its true blessedness. And this is indeed called by the Philosophers the "happy coupling" <note>original: *fœlix copulatio*; a technical term for the soul's mystical or intellectual union with a higher intelligence</note> of the potential intellect with the active intellect. **SOPHIA.** The reasoning of those men seems to me no less effective than it is profound, but in my judgment it demonstrates that happiness is impossible to attain rather than attainable. **PHILO.** For what reason? **SOPHIA.**

<margin>Man is by no means able to acquire for himself a perfect and absolute knowledge of all things and all sciences. He laments the ignorance and weakness of human wit.</margin>
Because if a man cannot be blessed before the knowledge of all things, he will never be able to be blessed; for it is quite impossible for any man to acquire for himself the knowledge of all things, both because of the brevity of human life and because of the almost innumerable abundance and multitude of things existing in the universe. **PHILO.** This is indeed true, and it is manifest that no man can be found who has knowledge either of all things together or of each thing separately. For in the different regions of the earth, such varied species of land animals and birds, as well as other mixed types, are found that no man could travel the whole world to see and know them all. Much less, even if he could diligently survey the sea and its depths, would he ever acquire a perfect knowledge of fish; for far more species of aquatic animals are found than of terrestrial or winged ones. From this, men are accustomed to wonder whether there exists a greater number of eyes or of hairs—for they judge that the eyes of fish are contained in a number no smaller than the hairs of terrestrial animals. Nor is it necessary for me now to explain the incomprehensible knowledge of celestial things: for who will ever perceive the number, natures, and properties of the stars of the eighth sphere? <note>the "eighth sphere" in the Ptolemaic system is the realm of the fixed stars, beyond the seven planets</note> The multitude of these stars forms those forty-eight celestial figures, twelve of which are placed in the Zodiac—that almost immense and most famous path which the sun and other planets traverse. Twenty-one figures ascend from the equator toward the Northern region, toward the arctic pole always visible to us, which the common people call "Boreal"; the remaining fifteen figures incline toward the southern region from the equator toward the antarctic pole, which is always hidden from us. No one doubts that in that southern region of the sky, around the antarctic pole, many stars are found forming certain figures unknown to us, since they always complete their courses under our hemisphere—the disposition and site of which lower hemisphere remained hidden from men for a long time until the present age.

But now, through the new and unusual voyages of the Portuguese and the Spanish, which have been recorded in literary monuments, it has become known to us in great part. ->D I A L O G V E 357<-

<margin>The specific difference of things is unknown to us.</margin>
...is unknown to men: our knowledge of these things is far less than if a single drop of water were compared to the entire Ocean. Moreover, I skip over many things—not only things foreign to us, but even our own—which, even if we see them, we remain ignorant of. Because of this, many have not hesitated to affirm that the **specific differences** <note>original: *differentias proprias*; in logic, the essential characteristic that defines a species, like "rationality" for humans</note> of things are unknown to us. Whether this opinion is true or false should not be determined at this present moment. It is certainly and undoubtedly true that many things are found in the universe which, because they are neither seen by the eyes nor perceived by any sense, can hardly be understood by us.
<margin>Nothing is in the intellect that was not first in the senses.</margin>
For as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> confirms: **nothing is in the intellect that was not first in the senses.**

*SO.* What are you saying? Are not spiritual things grasped by the intellect, even if they are neither seen nor felt at all?

<margin>Spiritual things can be understood by us in two ways.</margin>
*PH.* Spiritual things are pure and sheer intellects, and that intellectual light exists in our own intellect through union and its own nature, just as it exists in itself. It does not imitate sensible things—which first require the work of the intellect to be made "understandable" before they are received within it, just as a thing is usually received in something different from itself. For all things of this sort, because they consist of matter, are rightly said to be unable to be found in the intellect unless they were first in the senses, known in a certain material way, so to speak.

*SO.* Do you believe that everyone who reaches the understanding of spiritual things understands them through that unity and agreement which they have with our intellect?

<margin>Spiritual things are known by us first from their effects which are seen or felt; then finally from the natural and intellectual affinity which the human intellect, established in supreme perfection, maintains with them.</margin>
*PH.* I do not dare affirm this for certain, even if that were the true and perfect knowledge of them. Truly, however, spiritual things can be understood by us in another way too: from their **effects**, I mean, which are seen or felt. For example, when we conclude from the continuous rotation of the heavens that the "mover" <note>the intelligence or force that moves the celestial spheres</note> is neither a body nor a physical power, but a spiritual intellect entirely separated from matter. For unless the motion—which is its effect—first stimulated our senses, that mover would not be known by our intellect at all. This knowledge is followed by another, more perfect understanding of spiritual things, which arises because our intellect, when it actually understands the intellectual knowledge existing within itself, is raised up to know them. This is due to the same nature and intellectual unity which actual intelligence rightly shares with spiritual things.

<margin>What the philosophers understood by the "understanding of all things," wherein human happiness resides.</margin>
*SO.* I have understood this very well. But let us not interrupt the sequence of the subject already begun. You admit that happiness cannot possibly consist in the knowledge of all things, for this knowledge exceeds human powers. Now, since our happiness should in no way be placed in the perfect and absolute knowledge of all things, I would like to understand by what reasoning some wise men placed it there.

<margin>Universal knowledge of all sciences can only be acquired by one man with the greatest difficulty.</margin>
*PH.* Those most excellent men do not place happiness in knowing every single thing particularly and individually. Rather, by the "understanding of all things," they mean the perception of all **sciences** <note>the organized branches of knowledge</note> concerning all things, treating them in such an order and universality that—by explaining the common principles of all things and opening up every mode of their existence—they bring about a universal knowledge of everything, even if some details escape the senses.

*SO.* Can this universal knowledge of all sciences be acquired by just one man?

<margin>Happiness consists not in the habit alone, but rather in the act of knowing.</margin>
<margin>Human happiness consists in the actual understanding of only one thing.</margin>
*PH.* It can indeed, but the power to achieve it is far removed from the actual doing of it. Therefore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says that all sciences can be found partly easily and partly with difficulty: for among all men collectively they are found easily, but in one man alone they are found with difficulty. For happiness is not placed in the mere collected knowledge of many and diverse things at once. As the Philosopher testifies, **happiness consists not in the mere habit** <note>original: *habitu*; the state of possessing knowledge or a skill</note> **but in the act of knowing.** A wise man overwhelmed by sleep is not happy, but he is happy when, while awake, he freely enjoys the understanding of things. <meta>This page continues the dialogue on the nature of human happiness and the intellect. ->LEONE EBREO ON LOVE<-

<margin>To attain happiness, a person must first be practiced and especially perfected in all types of sciences for a long time.</margin>
For although many habits of knowledge <note>original: *habitus scientiarum*; refers to the internalized skill or state of knowing something</note> are possessed at the same time, no more than one thing can be understood in a single act. That is to say, happiness cannot be placed in the knowledge of all things or many diverse things, but must be found in the knowledge of only one thing. However, it is true that to reach happiness, a person must first be long-practiced and especially perfected in almost every kind of science. Specifically, one must be skilled in the art of demonstrating and dividing truth from falsehood in all understanding and reasoning—which is called **Logic**. One must also be practiced in **Moral Philosophy**, which teaches the use of both prudence and the active virtues; and in **Natural Philosophy**, which deals with matters subject to motion, change, and alteration.

<margin>The division of the Mathematical sciences is taken from their subject matter.</margin>
One must also study **Mathematical Philosophy**, which deals with numbers and measures existing in the highest category of quantity. If this science considers numbers absolutely, it creates **Arithmetic**; if it considers the number of sounds, it creates **Music**. Likewise, if it deals with measure simply, it produces **Geometry**; if it deals with the measure of celestial bodies and their motions, it produces **Astrology** <note>In the Renaissance, the term "astrologia" often encompassed what we now call astronomy.</note>.

<margin>Wisdom and the study of First Philosophy contribute as much as possible to human happiness.</margin>

This science deals with all things that exist, but it is primarily concerned with those things that have been granted a more noble and excellent essence. This alone deals with spiritual and eternal things.

<margin>The essence of spiritual and eternal things is far greater and more manifest by its nature than the essence of bodily and corruptible things.</margin>
The essence of these spiritual things is far greater and more manifest by its nature than the essence of bodily and corruptible things, even if they are less known to us than bodily things because they are not, like the latter, exposed to our senses. Hence, our intellect, in knowing those spiritual things, holds the same relation

<margin>Our intellect’s relation to knowing spiritual things is like a bat’s eye to discerning the light of the Sun.</margin>
as the eye of a bat to the light of the Sun and the discerning of other visible things. **SO.** What is this knowledge, and of what thing, that alone is able to lead a man to happiness? Your previous reasoning—by which you concluded that happiness consists in the actual knowledge of all things and sciences to which our intellect's power refers—seems to demonstrate this. Since the human intellect is endowed by nature with the ability to understand all things, its complete and absolute happiness should be situated in the actual knowledge of everything. <margin>Truth cannot possibly contradict truth.</margin>
Your argument seems well-suited to the conclusion you draw; however, reason demonstrates that truth cannot contradict truth, but rather one must agree with the other as much as possible. You should not be unaware that happiness is placed in the knowledge of only one thing, as it cannot consist in knowing individual things separately. Therefore, to acquire happiness, the knowledge of all things must be embraced simultaneously in the understanding of only one thing, which contains everything in the universe within its own scope. When this one thing is known, all things are known together in one and the same act, far more perfectly than if each were known separately and individually.

<margin>The nature of the intellect.</margin>
<margin>The difference between the potential intellect and the active intellect.</margin>
**SO.** What thing is found to be of such great excellence that, while it is one, it embraces all things at once?

**PH.** The intellect by its own nature has no determined essence, but declares all things to exist together. If it is the **potential intellect** <note>original: *intellectus potestatis*; the mind's raw capacity to learn or receive information</note>, it will be all things potentially; for its own essence is nothing other than knowing all things potentially. But if it is the **active intellect** <note>original: *intellectus in actu*; the mind when it is actively thinking or has mastered a subject</note>, it will be pure essence and pure form, containing all grades...

</margin>

In Him, all things consist in a spiritual manner without any division or multiplication, as if in the simplest unity. He is truly happy—or rather, the most abundant fountain of all happiness. All things need Him; He alone needs nothing. By gazing at Himself, He knows all things, and seeing, He is seen by Himself. His perfect vision, if it were perhaps shared with anyone, would be the highest unity. And even if things do not grasp Him in His entirety, they nevertheless know a portion of Him adapted to their capacity. The human or angelic intellect, contemplating Him according to its capacity and strength, contemplates all things simultaneously in Him with a certain supreme perfection. # DIALOGUE I.

<margin>Human happiness consists in the clear and lucid cognition of the actual intellect held by the human intellect.</margin>
...it will contain the essences, forms, and acts of the universe within its own essence, unity, and purest simplicity. Whoever, therefore, knows that actual intellect alone, truly knows the sum of all sciences and all things in an excellent manner, by which a person is made blessed.

PHILO: Some say this is the **Agent Intellect** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the *intellectus agens* is the active force that allows the human mind to move from potential to actual knowledge</note>, which, when joined with our potential intellect, produces a spiritual and clear vision—that consummate vision of all things existing simultaneously in act. <margin>Two philosophical opinions regarding human happiness are recounted.</margin>
from which human happiness is thought to flow as if from a most fertile fountain. In this state, the thing understood, the act of understanding, and the one who understands are seen to be one and the same, without any difference or diversity of knowledge. Furthermore, they add that when our intellect is found in this state, it shares one and the same essence with the Agent Intellect, all division or multiplication between them having been removed. These are the views held by the more illustrious philosophers regarding our happiness. However, it seems best to set aside the arguments that each sect brings forward to confirm its own opinion or to dissolve the views of its adversaries, as this would lead to an excessively long dispute that does not serve our present purpose.

<margin>The third and true opinion regarding human happiness is said to be that it rests in the pure and sincere cognition we have of the Agent Intellect—that is, God—and His intellect.</margin>

In that Intellect, all things exist without controversy, primarily and far more perfectly than in any created vision. He is the first essence, by whose participation all things exist. all intellects, acts, forms, and perfections depend, and toward whom they are directed as to their most perfect end. <meta>This page continues the dialogue from page 359, where Philo had begun explaining that the peak of human happiness is found in the contemplation of the "actual intellect"—the divine source of all knowledge.
