-># LEONIS HEBRÆI ON LOVE<-

<margin>Human happiness consists in the knowledge and vision of God.</margin>
...it is. It is enough that you are not unaware that our happiness is placed in the knowledge and vision of the Divine, in which all things are seen in the most perfect manner. SOPHIA: This is more than enough for me. But a certain doubt occurs to my mind: for I remember having understood elsewhere that happiness is not defined by knowing God, but by loving Him and enjoying Him with the greatest pleasure.

<margin>A question long and much debated by the wisest men: whether human happiness is primarily defined by knowing God or by loving Him.</margin>
PHILO: Since God exists as the true and unique object of human happiness, He is loved by us through a certain knowledge, and He is known through a certain love. Regarding these two acts—whether the proper act of happiness itself lies in the knowledge or in the love of God—there has been a great controversy among the wise. But now, setting aside such a difficult dispute, let us say that both of these two acts concur to complete our beatitude <note>Supreme blessedness or ultimate happiness</note>. SOPHIA: I most greatly desire to understand the reasons that led the wisest men to such different opinions.

<margin>Arguments of those who maintained that human happiness consists primarily in loving God.</margin>
PHILO: Those who say happiness consists in loving God use this argument: namely, that beatitude must be placed in the final action of our soul directed toward God, because an action of this kind is the soul's ultimate moving end <note>original: "postremus mobilis ipsius finis" - the final goal that prompts the soul to action</note>. Since, therefore, it is necessary first to know and then to love the divine power, it follows that happiness consists not in knowledge, but in the love of God as the ultimate act. They also bring forward pleasure <term>delectatio</term> as a very weighty witness in confirmation of this opinion; for pleasure is considered the most important part of happiness and is an affection of the **will**. Thus, they say that the truly happy act is to be referred primarily to the will and to love itself: for in this, and not in the intellectual act (which shares in joy much less than love does), they judge pleasure to reside.

<margin>Arguments of others who said human beatitude is primarily situated in knowing and understanding God.</margin>
Others, on the contrary, argue with this reason: namely, that happiness is found in the more principal and more spiritual power of our soul. Therefore, since the **intellectual faculty** is said to be more principal and more abstracted from matter than the will, it follows that beatitude is by no means to be placed in loving God, which is indeed an act of the will. Nevertheless, they say that love and pleasure later follow that knowledge as a kind of addition, but neither of them should be established as the principal end. SOPHIA: Both of the arguments brought forward seem effective to me. Now I would like to understand your determination. PHILO: To determine a matter disputed with so many arguments by both the ancient philosophers and our theologians on either side is certainly no easy task. But to satisfy your wish, I will not be reluctant to offer my opinion in such a difficult matter, having only prefaced this: that you are procuring the eternal misery of my mind <note>Philo often uses this dramatic language to describe the "pain" of intellectual labor or his unrequited love for Sophia</note>. SOPHIA: I only wish for you to explain this: for after we have been filled to satiety with divine things, we shall then speak more purely and sincerely about our friendship.

<margin>Three true and necessary propositions for determining this difficult question: whether the proper act of happiness itself should be placed in the intellect or the will.</margin>
PHILO: One of the true and necessary propositions is that happiness consists in the final action of our soul as its true end; another is that it is placed in the nobler and more spiritual power of our soul, which is indeed the intellective power. We also cannot deny that love presupposes a preceding knowledge; however, it does not follow from this that love is the last action of the soul.

<margin>Knowledge is twofold: one before love, separated from the known object; the other after love, coupled with the known object.</margin>
For it must be known that there are two ways of knowing all those things which are loved and desired. One exists **before** the love proceeding from it, and knowledge of this kind does not have the power of perfectly uniting. The other exists **after** the love, taking its origin from it, which unifying knowledge is nothing other than a certain fruition <term>fruitio</term> <note>The enjoyment of a thing possessed</note> of perfect coupling and union. For the first knowledge of bread induces a love and desire for it in the hungry; because unless the bread were previously known by the eyes, it could certainly never be loved or desired. But by the benefit of this love and desire, we finally arrive at a true and proper knowledge of the bread itself, and one that is most highly united, which is the end of the desire—and this is had when we eat it. For the true knowledge of bread...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from page 360, where Philo is explaining to Sophia the relationship between knowledge and love. He is addressing how love acts as a bridge between an initial, imperfect understanding and the ultimate, perfect union with the divine.</meta>

->### DIALOGUE I ###<-

<margin>Love and desire are a certain medium leading us from imperfect happiness to perfect knowledge.</margin>
...knowledge <note>The Latin text begins with the end of the word 'cognitio'.</note> is perceived by tasting it. The same happens to a man toward a woman; he who loves her, knowing her only by sight, desires her, and from this love he later descends to a united knowledge, which is the end of the desire itself. The same can be shown in all other things that are loved and sought: for in each case, love and desire are a certain bridge that leads us from imperfect knowledge to perfect unity. This unity exists as the true end of love and desire—those two affections of the will—which are accustomed to transfer us from a rough and separate understanding to the enjoyment of a perfect and joined knowledge. When you have looked into the inner nature of these two affections of the will, you will recognize that they are not far removed from the mind's desire and love, even though we spoke of love earlier as a common subject in another way.

<margin>Love is a certain most vehement desire to enjoy the greatest union with that thing which is judged to be good.</margin>
Therefore, love can truly be defined as a certain desire to enjoy, with the greatest union, that thing which is considered good. For this reason, although desire (as I have said elsewhere) presupposes the absence of the thing sought, I now affirm to you for certain that even if a thing is judged good and is already possessed, it can still be desired—not indeed to have it, since it has already been acquired, but to enjoy it with a certain united knowledge. This enjoyment, when it is not yet present, can be most vehemently desired.

<margin>Love and desire can best come together as one.</margin>
This desire is indeed called love, and it is either for things not possessed which we seek to have, or for things already possessed which we long to enjoy in union. Each of these is properly called desire, but the second is more properly called love. Therefore, we define love as the most vehement desire to enjoy the loved thing in the closest union, or to turn oneself toward the loved thing to acquire a greater unity.

<margin>How the human intellect finally reaches that most happy coupling with the divine intellect.</margin>
To return, therefore, to our purpose, let us say that the knowledge of God must precede—that knowledge which can be held by us concerning an immense and supreme thing. Recognizing His perfection, because we are able to know it neither fully nor completely, we love Him; and we desire to enjoy Him with a certain union joined to our knowledge, which is as perfect as our strength allows.

<margin>Love and desire can best both precede and follow that most happy union of man with God, though in different ways.</margin>
From such great love and so vehement a desire, it happens that we are drawn into such contemplation that our intellect is raised up so far that—by a certain divine grace and the breathing of a singular favor from the Divinity—it is carried toward a higher and more sublime knowledge than fits human strength and human speculation. Then, it is sometimes so united and coupled with the supreme God that our intellect is perceived to be a divine reason and part rather than a human form. At that time, its desire and love are filled with much greater joy than when it moved within the earlier knowledge and the preceding love.

<margin>The act of that most happy coupling with God seems to surpass all delight, pleasantness, and joy.</margin>
Yet, in that happiness exceeding the human condition, love and desire could remain—not indeed to have that united knowledge, for we would have already attained it, but for the continuation of the enjoyment of that divine coupling, which is truly the truest love. I would not dare to pronounce that any pleasure is perceived in that act of beatitude <note>Supreme blessedness</note> except while it is being acquired. For then, from the acquisition of the longed-for thing which we previously lacked, we would be affected by great pleasantness, because most pleasures seem to flow from the filling of a defect and from the attainment of a sought-after thing.

<margin>Human happiness consists only in the act of that inward coupling and that united and divine knowledge.</margin>
But in the act of enjoying that most happy union, no trace of defect would remain; rather, the intellect would then rest entirely in unity. This most happy rest would surpass all delight, pleasantness, and joy. In short, happiness consists neither in the act of knowing God (which generates love in us) nor in the love that follows this knowledge, but only in the act of intimate coupling and that united and divine knowledge. This knowledge is judged to be the highest perfection of the created intellect; that act is its ultimate and blessed end, and in that state, our intellect deserves to be called divine rather than human.

<margin>The Sacred Volumes [speak] of the human intellect...</margin>
Wherefore the Sacred Volumes <note>Refers to the Bible or holy scriptures</note>, after they have commanded us that we ought first to know the perfect and pure unity of God:

# LEONE EBREO ON LOVE #

<margin>
[The Law] celebrates divine union as the highest possible state and promises it to mortals as the ultimate happiness.
</margin>
...then, so that we might prefer the love of Him over the gain of desire, the pleasure of appetite, and all the honor of the soul and the rational will, they finally add: *Therefore, be joined to God.* <note>original: "Ideò cum Deo copulaminis." A reference to the biblical concept of 'cleaving' to the Divine (Deuteronomy 10:20).</note> Elsewhere also, they promise us ultimate happiness in these words alone: *And you shall be joined to God.* Nor does it promise anything else—not long life, not eternal glory, not supreme delight, not immense joy, nor infinite light, nor other things similar to these. For the name "union" <note>The Latin 'copulatio' here refers to a spiritual and intellectual 'cleaving' or 'uniting' rather than a physical act.</note> is more proper than the others, and more suited to signify blessedness; for union contains the universal good and the universal perfection of the perceiving soul, inasmuch as it provides the soul with true happiness.

<margin>
That divine union and blessedness is very difficult for us to possess in the present life, and it can by no means be continued for long.
</margin>
But in this present life, that happiness is not so easily obtained. Even if it were perhaps acquired by some among us, it could not be so easily continued. This happens because, while we live, our intellect has a certain connection and a kind of bond with the matter of this most fragile body. For this reason, a man who, while acting in human affairs, reaches such a sublime union, cannot continue it for long because he is hindered by the bond of the body; rather, after the union, he returns to recognize corporeal things just as before. However, at the departure of the soul's life, when it persists longer and more intensely in divine union, it deserts the body entirely, remaining with the uniting Divinity in supreme happiness.

<margin>
After death, however, it is both easily acquired and perpetually continued by the most excellent souls.
</margin>
After its separation from the bodily bond, since the soul is of such excellence and every hindrance has been removed, it enjoys its most happy union with the divine light forever. In this, it imitates the manner of the angels, the <term>separated intelligences</term> <note>In medieval philosophy, these are spiritual beings (like angels) that lack physical bodies and move the celestial spheres.</note>, as well as the movers and the celestial orbs, each of whom perpetually participates in that same union with God Himself according to the degree of their dignity. These things which we have said so far concerning spiritual matters ought to seem sufficient to you, O Sophia. Now, returning to me, I wish you would devise some remedy to expel the sickness of my soul, contracted from the passions of the will, and to preserve the frame of this body.

SOPHIA: First, I want you to declare to me what kind of love you pursue me with. Since you have shown me that many kinds of love, endowed with various and differing natures, are found among men, and you have reduced them all to only three species, it would be very pleasing to me if you would now reveal by which of the aforementioned species your love for me is encompassed.

PHILO: O Sophia, I am neither able to perceive nor do I know how to explain the kind of my love for you. I feel its greatest powers, yet I do not truly know them. Since love itself has reduced all the faculties of my soul into servitude and has utterly deprived me of my former liberty, it—like a King, or rather a most cruel tyrant—knows me, its subject, very well. But how shall I, a servant and captive, ever know my master and Prince? This much only I know: the desire and love with which I feel myself affected are centered upon the <term>pleasant</term>. <note>Philo refers to the Aristotelian categorization of love into three types: the Useful, the Pleasant, and the Virtuous (or Honest).</note>

<margin>
Philo’s love for Sophia is chiefly concerned with pleasure and delight.
</margin>
SOPHIA: If it is so, you certainly ought neither to implore any help from me to relieve your miseries, nor to accuse me of not satisfying your will. For you have already shown that when our appetite is filled with pleasures long lusted after, not only does desire vanish, but love itself is usually extinguished and even turned into hatred.

PHILO: You do not judge it enough to gather sweet and wholesome fruit for yourself from our conversation, unless—may God not permit it to happen—you take from the same source something bitter and deadly to hand back to me to taste as a reward for my labors. Nor will you ever win the praise of gratitude or piety from this so impious retribution, since you threaten to bring death and a most cruel end to me with the very same weapons with which I did not hesitate to fight for the defense of your safety and life.

SOPHIA: If you think your benevolence toward me and your love for me is something worthy, as I believe it is, I would indeed act unworthily if, by yielding to your desire, I were to [extinguish] that love now...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Sophia and Philo. In the previous pages, they discussed the nature of the "union" with the Divine as the ultimate end of human desire. Here, the conversation shifts to the psychological and physiological nature of satiety—why some pleasures become boring or disgusting while others remain eternally fresh.</meta>

# DIALOGUE I. 363 #

...to extinguish or lull that which is kindled and burning would surely be cruel both to myself and to you. I would be depriving you of the love with which you pursue me and defrauding myself of your goodwill. However, by refusing to satisfy your lust <note>The Latin 'libidinem' refers to physical desire or passion.</note>, I will show myself faithful to both of us, since only in this way can your most sweet love for me, which is worthy of the highest praise, be preserved unharmed.

**PHILO.** Either you are mistaken, or you are trying to lead me into error by laying a false foundation that is not at all conducive to love. You make me the author of the claim that love perishes once the desired object is obtained, and that hatred succeeds it. This is certainly most false.

<margin>Not every pleasant thing, once possessed, brings satiety.</margin>
**SOPHIA.** Why is it false? Did you not just say that it is a property of pleasant love that its fullness turns into a disgust full of hatred?

**PHILO.** Not *every* pleasant thing brings satiety once it is possessed. For virtues and sciences, once they have been acquired, bring the greatest pleasure to our minds and are never found tiresome; on the contrary, their increase is continually sought and desired. Nor is this seen to happen only in noble matters, but even in things whose nature has no share in virtue at all. For power, wealth, and honors, once they are possessed, continue to delight and never bring about their own disgust; indeed, the more of them we have, the more we desire to have.

**SOPHIA.** You certainly seem to contradict your earlier statements.

<margin>Pleasures of taste and touch, once possessed, quickly bring satiety—that is, disgust.</margin>
**PHILO.** I remember saying above only this: that the pleasures of the external senses—specifically the "imperfect" ones like taste and touch—bring satiety and disgust. But the pleasures of the other three external senses, like sight, hearing, and smell, do not lead them to satiety or disgust so quickly or so easily. Hence Solomon says that the eye is never satisfied with seeing, nor the ear with hearing. <note>original: "oculum uidendo & aurem audiendo nunquam exatiari." A reference to Ecclesiastes 1:8.</note> Much less is the fancy or the imagination <term>phantasia: the faculty of the mind that forms images of external objects</term> seen to be satisfied by the things that delight it, such as honors, wealth, dominion, and other similar things, which are always sought by men with the greatest zeal.

<margin>But the pleasures of smell, hearing, and sight, likewise of the imagination, and finally those of the intellect, are seen to satisfy men much later, or never.</margin>
The pleasures of the mind and intellect are even more insatiable when exercising scholarly actions and wisdom. Men can never be fully filled or "saturated" by these pleasures; thus, they are considered by men to be more excellent and outstanding.

<margin>The more pleasures consist in the spiritual power of our soul, the less satiety and disgust they bring to our minds.</margin>
**SOPHIA.** I am easily persuaded that the more delights consist in the spiritual power of our soul, the less satiety and disgust they bring to our minds. But since you, following common and vulgar footsteps, wish to take those pleasures from my company which delight the sense of touch—which above all others quickly falls into a great and hateful satiety—you should not be surprised if I seem to entirely resist your desires.

<margin>The reason why nature prescribed much narrower limits for touch and taste than for sight, hearing, and smell.</margin>
**PHILO.** Nature has circumscribed much narrower limits for touch and taste (which were given to us not only for preserving the life of the individual man, but also for perpetuating the human species through the benefit of reproduction <note>original: "humana specie similis generationis."</note> arising from touch) than for sight, hearing, and smell. This was done for this reason: because these three senses are necessary neither for the individual essence of man nor for the succession of the species. Rather, they are ordered only for the convenience and utility of men and more perfect animals. Therefore, just as their essence is by no means necessary, they require no limit or prescription in their action. For just as men are not deprived of life because they do not see, hear, or smell, neither do they lose their life because they exercise the sense of seeing, hearing, or smelling for a long time and very frequently—unless perhaps by accident. Taste and touch, however, are necessary for human life and posterity; for if these were taken away, life would be taken from everyone. Thus, the very frequent and repeated exercise of them would, in a very short time, exhaust...

<sig>H 2</sig> <meta>catchword: ...the person.</meta>

<summary>Philo explains to Sophia that while physical pleasures like touch and taste lead to rapid satiety and boredom, higher pleasures—those of the intellect, virtues, and the "superior" senses—are essentially insatiable. He argues that nature limits the physical senses because they are tied to survival, whereas the intellectual faculties are limitless.</summary>

# LEONIS HEBRAEI ON LOVE, #

...[it would lead to death], since mortals are seen to perish from too much food and too much drink no less than from hunger and thirst. For the same reason, frequent sexual intercourse, as well as heat or cold—all of which relate to the sense of touch—would quickly lead a man to his end. Since the actions of these two senses <note>The senses of taste and touch.</note>, because of their necessity for preserving both the personal and the successive existence <note>Latin: *successiuam essentiam*. This refers to the survival of the species through reproduction.</note> of mortals, are followed by a greater pleasure than the others, nature had to set a certain limit on their operation. This was so that if men were perhaps carried headlong by excessive delight into an immoderate use of them, they might at least be restrained by a natural law, lest untimely death and the dissolution of the individual should follow the excess of such pleasures.

<margin>The skill of nature and its wondrous providence.</margin>
Thus we see that nature has applied no less wisdom and diligence in establishing a limit and end for the senses of taste and touch for the safety and preservation of individuals—going beyond the common law of the other senses—than it did in procreating those same individuals and bringing them into the light by granting them existence. And although the lover's appetite, having attained copulation and union with the beloved object, is seen to be satisfied and diminished, yet for that reason...

<margin>The intimate love of souls is by no means dissolved because of the external union of bodies; rather, it is strengthened and bound more tightly.</margin>
...the intimate love residing in the innermost parts of the heart is not extinguished. Rather, because of that external union of bodies—whatever its nature—it is more strengthened and more tightly bound. This union, by removing the division and diversity of the two lovers as much as possible, turns one into the other and makes only one out of two. Since internal love is more united and more perfected by that bodily union, it burns with a continuous desire to enjoy the beloved object in reality with the greatest unity, which is indeed the true definition of love.

<margin>The end of perfect love does not consist in the external and imperfect union of the body; nevertheless, mutual and physical embraces of the lovers bind and constrain their perfect internal love more tightly.</margin>
**SOPHIA.** So you admit that the end of your desire is placed in the sense of touch, the most imperfect of all senses. Since you have already declared love to be something spiritual, I am indeed surprised that you place the end of such a sublime thing in such a base and lowest of all the senses.

**PHILO.** I by no means admit that the end of perfect love is placed in the action of such an imperfect sense. But I assert that this act does not dissolve perfect love, but rather constrains and binds it more tightly through mutual embraces. These are sought primarily for two reasons: first, because they are seen to be noteworthy signs of the mutual love between the two lovers; and second, because since the souls are united as much as possible by spiritual love, the bodies also seek to enjoy a granted unity following the example of the souls, so that no division remains and a completely perfect unity exists. Especially since, because of a certain fittingness of symmetry <note>Latin: *symmetriam*. Philo refers to the physical harmony or proportion between bodies that reflects spiritual harmony.</note>, spiritual love is also increased and rendered more perfect by bodily union—just as the knowledge of prudence is said to be absolute when its own appropriate actions follow it. In summary, then, let us say...

<margin>Perfect love is defined as the transformation of the lover into the beloved, joined with a desire that the beloved also be transformed into the lover.</margin>
...the true and proper definition of the perfect love of a man for a woman, or a woman for a man, is the transformation of the lover into the beloved, with a certain desire that the beloved also be transformed into the lover. But if the love is equal and fair on both sides, it will be defined simply as the transformation of each of the two lovers into the other.

**SOPHIA.** 
<margin>The most vehement love of David's son for his sister Tamar, and his incest.</margin>
Even if your reasons are as plausible as they are subtle, they nevertheless seem to contradict experience, which must be given greater weight than the reasons themselves. Many are seen to have loved, but after they obtained those corporeal and most sweet embraces they so greatly desired from the women they loved, not only did the desire perish, but the love itself died away completely, and sometimes was even turned into hatred. We see this happened to Amnon <note>original: "Amoni"</note>, the son of David, who loved his sister Tamar <note>original: "Athamarem"</note> so vehemently that he fell into a very serious illness because of his love...

# DIALOGUE I. #

...and led into the greatest danger of his life. After he had satisfied his lust through the cunning and force of Jonadab, the Sacred Scriptures report that he was immediately seized by such a great hatred for his sister that soon after the incest was committed, even as the bright day was dawning, he drove her out of the house. <note>A reference to the story of Amnon and Tamar from 2 Samuel 13. Amnon’s "love" was actually a fleeting lust that turned to loathing once satisfied.</note> PH.

<margin>Love is found to be of two kinds: one which perishes and vanishes along with desire; the other, however, is the parent of desire itself, which is not only preserved unharmed but seems to become greater and more vehement day by day.</margin>
Love is found to be of two kinds. The first is generated by desire and sensory appetite—namely, when we are driven to love a person because of a desire for them. This love is imperfect, since it proceeds from a faulty and fragile beginning; it is, in a sense, a son deriving its origin from desire as if from a father. It was with this kind of love that Amnon <note>Original: *Amon*</note> loved Tamar <note>Original: *Athamarem*</note>, in whose case that which you just said frequently happens: once the desire or sensory appetite vanishes after satiation, the love also soon vanishes. For when the cause—namely, the desire itself—is removed, the love is also taken away as its effect, and it even often turns into hatred, as is clear from the previous example. The second kind of love is said to be that which does not arise from desire or sensory appetite, but rather induces desire and appetite for the beloved person, and in a way gives birth to it. For whenever we love perfectly, we are driven by the force and vehemence of love to desire a spiritual and bodily union with the beloved person. Thus, just as that first love was the son of desire, so this second love is the parent and father of desire itself. This second love, once it has obtained the desired object, does not vanish even if the appetite and desire are lost. For although the effect is removed, the cause is not therefore taken away—especially because, as I have said elsewhere, a perfect desire is never lost, namely the desire to enjoy the most intimate union with the beloved person. For this desire is always joined with perfect love and necessarily follows from its nature and essence. However, that impure and imperfect desire, as well as the sensory appetite for sexual union <note>Latin: *sexuum commiscendorum*</note>, languishes and slackens after intercourse because of the limit prescribed by nature in the embracing of bodies. Though these bodily embraces can by no means be continuous, they nevertheless increase and bind the internal love of souls rather than diminish or dissolve it. For this reason, you should by no means dismiss or criticize my perfect love for you because of the defect found in imperfect love. For the love with which I have always pursued you is not at all the offspring of desire; rather, desire draws its origin from love, as a son from a father. And for this reason, at the beginning of my speech, I said that love and desire were stirred in my soul from the knowledge of you. I did not wish to put desire before love, because my love for you does not proceed from desire at all; indeed, it precedes desire just as a father precedes a son. SO.

If your love for me was procreated neither by appetite nor by desire, and did not derive its origin from leisure <note>Latin: *ocio*. In classical literature, "idleness" (otium) was often considered the breeding ground for romantic passion.</note> or human error, as they say, I beg you not to keep silent about its parent and father. For it is not to be doubted that all human love is generated and born; and whatever is born necessarily requires a parent. For neither can a son be found without a father, nor an effect without a cause. PH.

<margin>True and perfect love is seen to stir desire indeed, but it proceeds from right and knowing reason.</margin>
The true and perfect love I have for you is the parent of desire, but it is the offspring of reason, and was procreated from right and knowing reason. For when I perceived that you were endowed with virtue, intellect, and a certain singular beauty that draws the souls of men no less toward sweet love than toward the highest admiration, my will caught fire with an incredible desire for you—a desire which reason previously judged to be just and right, seeing that you are most worthy to be loved in every kind of virtue. This zeal and this love stood as the most powerful cause for my being transformed through an added desire, so that you too might be transformed into me; thus, with every difference between lover and beloved utterly removed, we might both be entirely the same, and because of the equal perfection of love on both sides, our two souls might be joined into one, which indeed [indifferently]...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Philo and Sophia regarding the nature of love. Philo is explaining how true love, though born from reason, eventually transcends and even defies it. He uses the classical imagery of Cupid to illustrate the irrational and piercing nature of deep affection.</meta>

# LEO HEBRAEUS ON LOVE, #

...that they might serve two bodies, supplying them with life and strength. A portion of this sensible desire excites the appetite for bodily union, so that the bodies also, joined together, might in some way—according to their own powers—attain that unity of souls which penetrate each other from every side. Consider therefore, O Sophia, that by a certain succession and order, love first descends from the knowing reason, and then from love my desire follows. For this reason, I began my speech above with these words: namely, that the knowledge of you excited love and desire in me. For your lovable qualities, once they were known to me, kindled love; and that love, in turn, excited desire. 

**SO.** How can you assert that true love proceeds from reason? For I remember having often understood that perfect love can be governed or restrained by no reason; and for that cause, men call love "unbridled," because it completely rejects and despises the command and moderation of reason.

<margin>
True and perfect love is procreated only by right, knowing reason; however, it does not afterward consent to be ruled or governed by it.
</margin>

**PH.** You have indeed understood truly; and I declared that love is only *procreated* by reason, not, however, directed or restrained by it. Rather, I assert this to you: after love has been fathered and brought into the light by the knowing reason, it in no way consents to be ruled or governed by it. Instead, like an untamed colt, it kicks back against its own mother and becomes so "unbridled," as you just said, that it drags the lover headlong toward manifest loss and destruction. For he who loves another vehemently has no care at all for himself, which is indeed most foreign to all reason and equity. For since love is a kind of charity <note>Here "charity" refers to *caritas*, or selfless, sacrificial love.</note>, it ought to begin with oneself; but how is this rule observed by us when we frequently love others more than ourselves?

<margin>
The form of Cupid as described by painters and poets, through an elegant interpretation.
</margin>

Since love is deprived of all reason after its birth, it is depicted as blind. And because it desires the beautiful—taking its origin from the reason that discerns the beauty, goodness, and worth of the beloved person as if from a mother—for that reason Cupid <note>Original: *Cupidinem*</note> is imagined to be the son of Venus, who possesses the most beautiful eyes. Furthermore, they represent Cupid as naked; for vehement love, on account of the soul's greatest and most unbearable torments, can neither be disguised by reason nor hidden by prudence. They declare him to be a boy because he is destitute of prudence, nor does he commit his own governance to the care of prudence. He is depicted with wings because he insinuates himself most swiftly into our souls, and induces them—despising themselves or divided from themselves—to seek out the beloved thing with the greatest speed.

<margin>
The lover, according to the opinion of Euripides, lives in another's body. The wounds of love and of an arrow are most similar to each other.
</margin>

And for this reason Euripides <note>A famous Greek playwright known for his psychological insight into human passion.</note> affirms that the lover lives in another's body. They attribute arrows to Cupid because he shoots from afar and sets the heart itself as his target to be struck. The reason for this can also be given: the wounds of love and of an arrow are remarkably similar to each other. Both have a narrow opening on the outside, but are seen to penetrate to the most hidden and deepest parts. Both seem difficult to see, more difficult to treat, and most difficult to heal. Both, as far as external appearance is concerned, seem of no consequence, but in reality, they are most heavy within and often turn into some incurable evil. And just as a wound inflicted by an arrow cannot be healed even if the bow that sent it is broken, or the archer himself is split in half; so too, no kind of pleasures provided either by fortune or by the beloved person for the lover's consolation, nor—what is even greater—even the inevitable death of the beloved person herself, seems to be a sufficiently fit or convenient remedy to perfectly cure or entirely close the wound inflicted by a true and vehement love. Therefore, let it not seem strange to you if perfect love, though it is the son of reason, is nonetheless neither directed nor ordered by it. 

**SO.** On the contrary, I am filled with the greatest wonder as to how love, being entirely foreign to the rule of reason and prudence, can ever be praiseworthy. For I thought the difference between virtuous <note>Original: *studiosum*, implying an earnest or noble pursuit of virtue.</note> and vicious love consisted only in this: that one of them submits to the command of reason...

<summary>Philo explains the genealogy of love, arguing that while it is born from the rational recognition of beauty and goodness, it eventually becomes an uncontrollable force that defies reason. He uses the classical allegory of Cupid (blind, naked, winged, and armed) to illustrate love's irrationality and the deep, enduring nature of its "wounds."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Philo and Sophia. Philo is explaining that while love is born from reason (the recognition of beauty or worth), once it becomes "perfect" or "intense," it transcends the control of its parent, reason. He is currently refuting Sophia’s suggestion that true love should remain under the command of the rational mind.</meta>

# DIALOGUE I. #

...[that it] might be subjected to its command and obey its mandates; but that the other, having shaken off the yoke of reason, should be carried headlong, completely loose and free. Now, however, I doubt which one should be called "perfect love."

<margin>
The vehemence and madness <note>original: *furor*</note> belong not only to "vicious" or bad love; rather, it is said that a certain property exists for any intense love, whether it be honorable or base.
</margin>

**PH.** Your perception was not quite right: for vehemence and madness are not properties exclusive to vicious love. Rather, they are characteristics of any effective and intense love, whether honorable or base—except that madness joined to honor makes virtue even greater, whereas when it is glued to baseness, it drives men to greater insanity and error. Who will ever deny that the most vehement and unbridled desires are found in honorable loves? What can be brought forward that is more honorable than divine love? And what is more ardent or swift than that? Yet, one cannot say that such a person obeys the "governing and preserving reason" in any way, since many who are captured by divine love neglect themselves and hand over their lives to the greatest dangers and most certain death. Many also despise themselves out of an exceeding love for God, just as, conversely, the unhappy man—by loving himself too much—despises God. Finally, to conclude this matter, how many men, inflamed by a desire for virtue and glorious fame, have wished to end their lives and trade them for death? Such a most noble deed in no way agrees with "common reason"; rather, for the sake of embracing honor, it sets aside everything, even life itself, than which we hold nothing dearer. I could also list many for you who did not hesitate to meet death with a cheerful and willing spirit for the safety of honorable friends, but I will skip these examples so as not to seem too tedious to you. Furthermore, the vehement love and headlong devotion of a man toward a woman incurs no less praise, provided it proceeds from true knowledge and right reason, which judges that woman to be worthy of being loved; for love of this kind participates no less in honor than in pleasure.

**SO.** Nevertheless, it would be very pleasing to me if your love were ruled and restrained by the reason that fathered it, and which moderates all distinguished men.

<margin>
True and perfect love is by no means tempered by reason; rather, it drives reason out.
</margin>

**PH.** Love that is tempered by reason usually exerts no force upon the lover, and it usurps the name of love without the effect. For true love constrains both reason and the lover himself with a certain wondrous violence and incredible force; more than any other human impediment, it disturbs the mind and judgment. It deletes the memory of all other things and occupies the whole man by itself. It makes a man entirely "alien" to himself and "addicted" <note>In the sense of being legally bound or devoted</note> to the beloved person: fleeing pleasures and social habits, seeking solitudes, 

<margin>
The greatest powers and admirable effects of love.
</margin>

melancholic, full of soul-torments, hedged in on all sides by cares, vexed by afflictions, distracted by various desires, living on hope, stimulated by despair, lost in thought, torn apart in cruel ways, afflicted by suspicions, pierced by the arrows of Jealousy <term>Zelotypia: a Latinized Greek term for romantic jealousy</term>, continually tortured, passing time in perpetual labors, and surrounded on all sides by an escort of almost innumerable pains: always dwelling in hardships, fears, and injuries. What more shall I say to you?

<margin>
For the sake of love, lovers die while living, and live while dying.
</margin>

For the sake of love, lovers die while living, and live while dying <note>original: *vivendo moriuntur, & moriendo vivunt*—a classic Renaissance paradox of the "living death" of the lover</note>: and what brings even greater wonder is that, although the torments arising from it are savage, inhuman, and intolerable, the mind neither hopes, nor desires, nor manages to be freed from them. Indeed, if anyone gives the lover a piece of healthy advice or offers faithful help, they are regarded as a most bitter enemy. Does it seem to you, O Sophia, that in this blind and tangled labyrinth, the Law of reason or the norm of prudence can be discerned by men?

**SO.** Gentler words, I pray: for it does not escape me that lovers abound much more in words than in actual hardships.

<margin>
The powers of love can be perfectly understood and judged by no one except by one who has experienced them.
</margin>

**PH.** Indeed, this is the clearest sign that you have never experienced them: for by the magnitude of the pain, which lovers...

<sig>H 4</sig>
<meta>do per-</meta>

<summary>Philo argues that true, intense love (including divine love and the pursuit of honor) naturally transcends and even subverts human reason, leading the lover into a state of "living death" and emotional turmoil that cannot be understood by those who have not experienced it.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Philo and Sophia. Philo is responding to Sophia's skepticism about the intensity of his suffering, arguing that true love is an all-consuming force that disables reason rather than being governed by it.</meta>

# LEONE EBREO ON LOVE, #
<meta>catchword: would [procuraret],</meta>

<margin>
Those who truly love can least of all feign or lie. The most miserable and unfair condition of lovers.
</margin>
...is perceived, no one can believe it unless they have at some time experienced it. If the sickness of my soul could infect others by touch alone, you would confess that not only is what I tell you and suffer in reality true, but much more than true; for what I feel, I neither know how to explain, nor can I remain silent, nor have I yet expressed even the smallest part of my suffering through speech, however bold or intense. How could you lead your mind to think that in the midst of such affliction—when all the lover's strengths are broken and weakened, the mind disturbed, reason confused, memory occupied, imagination <note>original: *phantasia*</note> alienated, and the senses clouded by immense pain—the tongue alone would remain free to compose fables? My speech has only sketched what words are able to signify and what the tongue has the power to express. If this can be understood by those who have, to their great detriment, experienced the adverse and hostile powers of Cupid <note>The Roman god of desire, used here to represent the overwhelming force of passionate love.</note>, and who have tasted the most bitter sweetness of love, and who neither knew how, nor wished, nor were able to refuse its sweet poison from the start: for I, God is my witness, have neither the words nor the means to explain matters so difficult and unusual. I feel the burning of the spirits, the consumption of my heart, and a universal fire in all my parts. Would you not think that one placed in such miserable and unfair fortune would, if he could, claim his freedom? But he cannot; for he is deprived of liberty not only to free himself, but even to seek or desire liberty itself. How then can one who lacks all liberty be governed by reason? For any servitude of the body at least leaves the will free and unconstrained;

<margin>
Love alone binds and fetters the will itself.
</margin>
love alone, by an unbreakable knot, binds and fetters our wills first to the beloved thing, and then our whole selves to the will itself. **SO.** It is not to be doubted that lovers are tossed by many disturbances until they have achieved their desire; but all that storm then turns into the greatest tranquility, so that by this logic, the cares and desires of lovers stem from a thing not yet in their power, rather than from love itself.

<margin>
Love, which proceeds from reason, is not lessened or vanished after bodily embraces; rather, it takes on strength and increase.
</margin>
**PH.** In this, as in other things concerning love, you show yourself to be unrefined and inexperienced. For the love of those whose torture is lessened after the pleasure perceived from the mingling of bodies does not come from reason, but from sensory appetite. Their sicknesses and disturbances (as I said above) savor of the flesh rather than the spirit, and for this reason they are distinguished from those deeper pains felt by lovers whose love depends on reason. These latter obtain no remedy for their pain nor relief for their love from the pleasures of bodily embraces; indeed, I tell and assure you that their punishments are far greater and more intolerable after the union of bodies than they were before their coupling.

<margin>
A most elegant reason is given why, in love proceeding from reason, it very frequently happens that after lovers have obtained the beloved thing, their ailments grow and are redoubled.
</margin>
**SO.** Why do their ailments grow and redouble after they have obtained the beloved? **PH.** Because love of this kind is a desire for the perfect and absolute union <note>original: *copulationis*</note> of the lover with the beloved person. This will never be achieved unless both have first entirely and completely penetrated one another. In souls, which are spiritual, this can indeed happen; because incorporeal spirits, being pure minds, can penetrate each other through the most effective actions, and be united together, and even be converted one into the other. But in different and distinct bodies, each of which requires its own determined place, this union—and, so to speak, penetration—can never be perfectly acquired. Therefore, it always leaves a continuous and perpetual desire in the lover, whose mind, while seeking an entire and absolute conversion of itself into the beloved person...

<summary>Philo argues that "rational love" is a profound spiritual bond that physical intimacy cannot satisfy; because bodies cannot occupy the same space, the physical act only intensifies the lover's desire for an impossible total union.</summary>
<keywords>Leone Ebreo, spiritual union, rational love vs. sensual appetite, bondage of the will, Cupid, bodily limitation, Phantasia</keywords>

# DIALOGUE I. #

...[it] would, it despises and holds its own person in contempt, living in perpetual unhappiness and misery because of the lack of a perfect union of bodies. The desire for this impossible union of bodies, which remains perpetually in the lover, can never be restrained or coerced by reason, will, or prudence. **SO.** I am already beginning to agree with your arguments to some extent. However, it still seems absurd and improper to me that in man, or in the universe of all things, love—or any other good—could be found that is not governed by the mind; since it is agreed among everyone that every good and laudable thing is directed by the rule of the mind and governed by its command: for things are said to possess as much dignity as they are thought to participate in reason. How then do you affirm that perfect love is not ruled or governed by reason? **PH.** Since this is the only doubt remaining to you, I will set out to explain only this in today's discussion.

<margin>Two types of reason are found in man: one ordinary, the other extraordinary.</margin>
Sophia, you should by no means be ignorant that two species of reason are found in men: which we shall call "ordinary" and "extraordinary." The intent of the first is to rule and preserve a person in an honest life, toward which end all <margin>In true and perfect love, the lover, having spurned and despised ordinary reason, proposes extraordinary reason as the one to be followed.</margin> other things are directed; whatever things hinder a person’s good life are immediately disapproved and cast out by reason. This is indeed that reason which, as I have already said, can establish neither a rule nor any limit for perfect love: because that love plots the harm and destruction of the lover's own person, and of his life and way of living well and honestly—along with great loss—so that the lover may more easily and quickly obtain the beloved person. Indeed, the purpose of extraordinary reason is to enjoy and possess the thing loved, and it is touched by no care for preserving its own interests; rather, it puts them in second place so that it may finally obtain the beloved. And rightly so, since the more ignoble <note>Lower or less valuable.</note> must always be postponed for the sake of acquiring a more excellent possession.
<margin>The beloved is more perfect and noble than the lover himself.</margin>
For as the philosopher <note>Likely referring to Aristotle, often called "The Philosopher" in medieval and Renaissance texts.</note> affirms, the beloved exists more perfectly than the lover himself, acting as the end <term>end (finis): the ultimate goal or purpose toward which an action is directed</term>, because it is toward the attainment of the end that things are directed and referred. Moreover, the lesser and more ignoble ought by right to work for the sake of acquiring the better and more excellent: which can be confirmed by both a natural and a moral example.
<margin>He confirms the difference between ordinary and extraordinary reason with two examples: namely, natural and moral.</margin>
Natural, because we see any person expose their arm—as if it were the less noble part—to receive and slow down a blow coming from above, in order to defend the head. By a similar reasoning, because as soon as the lover and beloved have come together into one, the beloved exists as the nobler portion of that union, while the lover is the more ignoble; it should be no wonder if, by the persuasion of nature, the lover—in order to finally obtain the beloved—refuses to undergo no difficulty, however arduous, and no labor, however intolerable. He pursues the beloved as a true and most excellent end, with the greatest care and highest diligence, neglecting and despising his own affairs as if they belonged to another. An example of the moral kind would be this: just as the first reason impels us to save money for our own use so that with its help we can lead a right and comfortable life; but the second commands us to distribute wealth among others, taking the person into account, directing it toward the exercise of liberality <note>The virtue of generosity or giving freely.</note> as a nobler end. In the same way, the first reason suggests we procure utility and honest pleasures; but the second seems to exhort us to weary the soul and body with continuous vigils and labors for the sake of joining and coupling ourselves with the most noble person, most worthy of our love. **SO.** Which of these two types of reason, in your judgment Philo, should we follow? **PH.** The second is certainly worthier and more eminent, just as the <margin>Extraordinary reason is to be followed, as it is more eminent than ordinary reason.</margin> prudence of a liberal man in spending and distributing money according to the precept of virtue attains far greater praise than the prudence of a miser in accumulating it...

<meta>catchword: do [accumulando]</meta>

<summary>Philo explains the paradox of love and reason by distinguishing between "ordinary reason" (self-preservation) and "extraordinary reason" (pursuit of the beloved). He argues that because the beloved is more noble than the lover, it is rational to sacrifice one's own well-being to achieve union with the beloved.</summary>

# LEO THE HEBREW ON LOVE, DIALOGUE I. #

...in accumulating and gathering wealth because of the many and diverse necessities that occur in human life: for although men are praised for their prudence in acquiring riches, they are seen to be much more prudent and worthy in distributing them generously. Whoever, however, holds within themselves a worthy and excellent love that proceeds from reason, but does not enjoy it, can certainly be compared to a tall tree, overflowing with branches and blooming in perpetual youth, yet suffering from the defect of sterility.

<margin>
True and perfect
love seems to be
the most certain
sign of an
outstanding and
excellent character.
</margin>
And undoubtedly, he who remains completely unrefined and devoid of an outstanding and excellent love is deprived of many virtues, and indeed the most illustrious ones. If anyone, however, turns toward a bestial and lustful love—one which does not proceed from reason carefully weighing the qualities and merits of the beloved thing, but is instead excited only by sensory appetite—his love must be compared to a tree that produces fruit which is actually deadly, even though its outer skin promises the greatest sweetness and delight. But that first and most excellent love, which is chosen by reason, brings the highest pleasure not only to the sensory appetite but also to the spiritual mind, joined with a certain insatiable, soulful zeal.

<margin>
A certain
preparation for the
following
Dialogue.
</margin>
If you ever come to know, O Sophia, how much importance love has in the whole and universal world—not only in your body <note>original: "corpore o", likely a typo for "corpore tuo"</note>, but much more in spiritual love—and by what logic there is nothing, from the highest and First Cause <note>The "First Cause" refers to God, the source of all existence in Neoplatonic and Aristotelian thought.</note> (which grants essence and life to every individual thing) down to the lowest and last of all things, that does not participate in love, you will hold it in much greater veneration. Then you will attain a nearly complete and perfect knowledge of its genealogy <note>The "genealogy of love" refers to its origins and how it descends through the different levels of reality.</note>. **SO.** Do not refuse to reveal this also for my sake. **PH.** We shall reserve the discussion of this arduous and hidden matter for a more opportune time. For already the hour suggests that you grant some rest to your soft and delicate body, and that you refresh your spirits—perhaps too tired and exhausted by this long dispute—with peaceful and sweetest sleep. But leave me to my accustomed wakefulness; for though I shall seem to remain alone, I will not be alone, since my mind carries you with me everywhere. From your company and the contemplation of you, my mind perceives no less pain than pleasure.

<meta>This page serves as the "Argument" or summary of the second dialogue of Leone Ebreo's "Dialogues on Love." It bridges the previous discussion on individual human love to a broader investigation of love as a universal, cosmic force. The translator, Giovanni Carlo Saraceno, outlines the upcoming topics including the love between elements, the nature of the "World Soul," and the concept of man as a microcosm.</meta>

## ON LEO THE HEBREW’S
# SECOND DIALOGUE CONCERNING THE COMMUNITY OF LOVE, 
# AND ITS VAST 
# UNIVERSALITY,
### THE ARGUMENT,
->Composed by **GIOVANNI CARLO SARACENO**.<-

He proposes at the beginning to speak about the community of love. Then, having approached this so arduous and distinguished a subject, he shows that living beings love one another for five reasons: he demonstrates that these are found in the human race in a far more perfect and noble manner than in other species of animals, even if contrary things sometimes happen due to some external impediment. He then adds two more reasons for love specific to the human race, which are not shared with any species of brute animals: he traces the natural and innate propensity of two humans to pursue each other either with the greatest love or intense hatred back to both their physical temperaments <note>The humors or biological makeup of a person.</note> and to the celestial aspects and figures <note>The astrological alignment of the stars at birth.</note>. He adds that knowledge, as well as appetite and love, are of three kinds: natural, sensible, and rational. He declares that all of these are found together in the human race, while only the first two are found in brute animals, and only the first is found in bodies devoid of life.

Furthermore, he testifies that bodies lacking sensation are directed and illuminated toward their own goals and toward recognizing, loving, and seeking their own regions either by the Soul of the World <note>original: "anima Mundi"; the vital spirit that animates the entire universe.</note> or by universal nature, which knows and enlightens. He reveals that the love of the elements is derived from those same five reasons from which the mutual love of living beings also flowed. He assigns the cause for the site and placement of the elements; he traces the reason for elementary qualities to their distance from or proximity to the celestial body. He examines the cause of why so many noble kinds of mixed things are seen to be born only on the earth, and not in any of the other elements; using an elegant comparison, he calls the earth "mother" and all mixed things, whether animate or inanimate, "children."

Next, besides the four elements, he teaches that a certain matter common to all things that are generated and perish is found, whose zeal and benevolence toward all forms he describes very beautifully; he confirms that from this matter—no differently than from a mother or a stepmother—the birth and death of all lower things proceed. Afterward, he seems to transfer the generation of mixed things to Heaven as the acting cause, and to the elements as the proximate matter. He also reviews various orders and different classes of forms, each always more excellent than the last, which the elements deserve to serve once they have been joined and mixed into one through their mutual friendship. He shows that these elements were reduced to the greatest equality and highest unity in the composition of a human being, and he gradually descends to the opinion of Empedocles <note>A Greek philosopher who believed the universe was governed by the opposing forces of Love (attraction) and Strife (repulsion).</note> concerning the birth and death of lower things.

Then he turns to declaring the zeal and benevolence of Heaven, both toward prime matter as a husband toward a wife, and also toward all these lower bodies as a parent toward children. He considers that the dews and rains have the character of celestial seeds falling upon the earth. To produce these most excellent seeds, he affirms that the whole celestial body—like a kind of "great animal"—works together with all its parts. He compares the seven planets both with the seven members of the human body required for the production of seed, and also with the seven parts of our head serving sensation and knowledge. He demonstrates that for Heaven, as a most perfect living being, not only two directions of position should be assigned (as Pythagoras <note>An ancient philosopher who focused on number, harmony, and the soul.</note> wrongly thought), but all six (as Aristotle <note>The "Philosopher" whose logic and physics dominated Medieval and Renaissance thought.</note> rightly believed).

Furthermore, he brings forward that most difficult question concerning the rising and setting of Heaven, which, after many opinions of others have been rejected and refuted as false, he seems to determine in such a way that he declares the right and left parts of Heaven, or the true East and true West, should be referred not to some certain and defined part of the celestial body, but rather to two various and opposite kinds of celestial motions: namely, the diurnal <note>The daily rotation of the sky.</note> and the wandering <note>The movement of the planets.</note> motion. Afterward, he approaches that so arduous and illustrious commentary on why man is accustomed to be called by the wise a <term>microcosm</term> <note>original: "μικροκόσμος", meaning a "little world" that reflects the order of the entire universe.</note>, and he pursues this at great length. Next, he turns his speech toward declaring the mutual love of the Heavens among themselves and their mutual benevolence; and he interprets the concord and harmony of the celestial motions most excellently according to the opinion of Pythagoras. He concludes that there are two principal causes of the mutual love of the Heavens themselves. This part being finished and completed, he turns to explaining and unravelling the myths of the Poets: first, he brings forward five reasons why the ancients were driven to involve and hide the secrets of nature in poetic fables; he also assigns the reason why in the most skilled philosophy of Plato...

<summary>This page provides a detailed outline of the Second Dialogue, describing love as a cosmic force that moves everything from inanimate elements to celestial bodies. It highlights the Renaissance concept of the microcosm, where the human being reflects the structure and harmony of the entire universe.</summary>
<keywords>Leone Ebreo, universal love, World Soul, elements, microcosm, celestial motion, Aristotle, Pythagoras, Empedocles, astrology</keywords>

# LEO THE HEBREW ON LOVE, DIALOGUE I.

accumulating and gathering [wealth] because of the many and diverse necessities occurring in human life. For although men are praised in the name of prudence for acquiring riches, they are seen to be much more prudent and worthy in distributing them liberally. Whoever holds within themselves a worthy and excellent love, one proceeding from reason, but does not enjoy it, can rightly be compared to a tall tree, exuberant with branches and flowering in perpetual youth, but suffering from the fault of sterility.

<margin>True love seems to be the most certain judgment of a superior and excellent mind.</margin>And undoubtedly, he who is entirely ignorant and devoid of superior and excellent love is destitute of many virtues, and the most illustrious ones at that. If, however, someone turns to a bestial and lustful love—which does not proceed from reason carefully weighing the conditions and merits of the beloved thing, but is excited only by sensory appetite—his love must be compared to a tree actually producing lethal fruit, but which promises the greatest sweetness and pleasantness in its outer bark. But that first and most excellent love, which is chosen by reason, brings the highest pleasure not only to the sensory appetite, but also to the spiritual mind, joined with a certain insatiable devotion.

<margin>A certain preparation for the following dialogue.</margin>For if ever, O Sophia <note>The name Sophia means "Wisdom" in Greek.</note>, you learn how much weight love carries in the whole and universal world—not only in corporeal things, but much more in spiritual ones—and by what logic it flows from the highest and first cause <note>The "First Cause" refers to God in the Neoplatonic and Aristotelian traditions.</note> (which grants essence and life to each thing) down to the lowest and last of all things, such that there is nothing that does not participate in love, you will hold it in much greater veneration. Then you will attain an almost complete and perfect knowledge of its genealogy <note>Philo suggests that love has a "family tree" or origin story that explains how it connects the divine and the material worlds.</note>.

**SOPHIA:** Do not refuse to reveal this also for my sake.

**PHILO:** <note>Philo's name means "Lover" or "Friend" in Greek.</note> We shall reserve the treatment of this so difficult and hidden matter for a more opportune time. For now the hour suggests that you grant some rest to your soft and delicate body; and that you refresh and restore with calm and sweet sleep your spirits, perhaps too tired and fatigued by this long discussion. But leave me in my accustomed wakefulness; though I shall seem to remain alone, I will not be alone, since my mind carries you everywhere, and from your company and contemplation perceives no less pain than pleasure.

# ON LEONE EBREO’S
# SECOND DIALOGUE CONCERNING THE COMMUNITY OF LOVE, AND ITS BROAD UNIVERSALITY,

## THE SUMMARY,
### BY
## GIOVANNI CARLO SARACENO
### composed.

---

He proposes at the beginning to speak about the community of love. Then, having approached this arduous and noble matter, he shows that living creatures love one another for five reasons. He demonstrates that these reasons are found in the human race in a far more perfect and noble way than in other species of animals, even if an opposite result sometimes occurs due to some external obstacle. He then adds two reasons for love that are unique to the human race and not shared with any species of beasts: he traces the natural and innate inclination of two people to pursue one another with either the greatest love or intense hatred back to their physical temperaments <note>The "temperament" refers to the balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) which were thought to determine personality.</note>, and also to celestial aspects and planetary figures. He adds that knowledge, appetite, and love are all threefold: natural, sensible, and rational. He declares that all of these are found together in the human race, while only the first two are found in beasts, and only the first—natural love—is found in bodies that lack life.

Moreover, he testifies that bodies devoid of sense are directed and illuminated toward their own proper goals and regions by either the Soul of the World or by universal nature, which knows and guides them. He reveals that the love of the elements <note>The four classical elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note> is derived from the same five reasons from which the mutual love of animals flows. He assigns the cause for the placement and arrangement of the elements and traces the nature of elemental qualities to their distance from or proximity to the celestial body. He examines the cause of why types of so many noble "mixtures" <note>In Renaissance science, "mixtures" or "compounds" refers to any physical object created by combining the four elements, such as minerals, plants, or animals.</note> are seen to be born only on the Earth and not in any of the other elements. Using an elegant comparison, he calls the Earth "mother" and all mixed things—both animate and inanimate—her "children."

Beyond the four elements, he teaches that a certain common "matter" is found in all things that are born and perish; he clearly explains its desire and benevolence toward all forms. He confirms that the birth and death of all lower things proceed from this matter, as if from a mother or a stepmother. He then attributes the generation of mixed things to Heaven as the "acting cause," and to the elements as the "immediate matter." He also reviews the various orders and different classes of forms—each one always more excellent than the last—with which the elements deserve to be clothed when they are joined and mixed into one through mutual friendship. He shows that these elements were brought to the greatest equality and highest unity in the composition of a human being. Finally, he gradually moves into the opinion of Empedocles <note>A Greek philosopher who famously argued that the universe is governed by two opposing forces: Love (attraction) and Strife (repulsion).</note> regarding the birth and destruction of lower things.

Next, he turns to declaring the care and benevolence of Heaven, both toward "prime matter" <note>The fundamental, formless substance of the universe.</note> as a husband toward a wife, and toward all these lower bodies as a parent toward children. He considers that the dews and rains falling upon the earth function as celestial seeds. He affirms that the entire celestial body, like a great living animal, concurs with all its parts to produce these most excellent seeds. He compares the seven planets both to the seven members of the human body required for the production of seed, and to the seven parts of our head serving sense and knowledge. He demonstrates that for Heaven, as a most perfect living being, one should apply not only two directions of position (as Pythagoras wrongly thought), but all six (as Aristotle rightly judged).

Furthermore, he brings forward that most difficult question regarding the rising and setting of Heaven. After rejecting and refuting the opinions of many others as false, he determines that the "right" and "left" parts of Heaven—or the true East and West—refer not to a specific, fixed part of the celestial body, but rather to two different and opposite types of celestial motions: the "diurnal" <note>The daily rotation of the sky.</note> and the "erratic" <note>The movement of the planets, which appear to "wander" compared to the fixed stars.</note> motion. Afterward, he approaches that arduous and famous discussion of why man is usually called a <term>microcosm</term> <note>original: "μικρόϰοσμος", meaning "little world"—the idea that the human body reflects the structure of the entire universe.</note> by the wise, and he follows this idea at length. 

Next, he turns his speech toward declaring the mutual love and benevolence between the Heavens themselves. He provides an excellent interpretation of the concord and harmony of celestial motions according to the opinion of Pythagoras. He concludes that there are two primary causes for the mutual love of the Heavens. Having completed this part, he turns to explaining and unravelling the fables of the Poets. ### OF LEONE EBREO CONCERNING LOVE, DIALOGUE I.

Whoever contains within themselves a worthy and excellent love, proceeding from reason, yet does not enjoy it, can certainly be rightly compared to a tall tree, overflowing with branches and blooming with eternal youth, but suffering from the vice of sterility.

<margin>True and perfect love seems to be the indicator of a most outstanding and excellent soul.</margin>

And without a doubt, he who exists entirely ignorant and devoid of an outstanding and excellent love is destitute of many virtues, and indeed the more illustrious ones. If, however, someone turns toward a bestial <note>original: *ferinum*, literally "of wild beasts"</note> and lustful love—which does not proceed from reason carefully weighing the conditions and merits of the beloved object, but is excited only by sensory appetite—his love ought to be compared to a tree actually bearing lethal fruit, but which promises the greatest sweetness and pleasantness through its outer skin. Truly, that first and most outstanding love, which is chosen by reason, brings the highest pleasure not only to the sensory appetite but also to the spiritual mind, joined with a certain insatiable zeal.

<margin>A certain preparation for the following Dialogue.</margin>

For if ever, O Sophia, you recognize how great an importance exists in the whole and universal world—not only in corporeal love, but much more in spiritual love—and by what reason from the highest and first cause <note>A Neoplatonic reference to God as the source of all being</note> (which grants essence and life to individuals) down to the lowest and last of all things there is nothing that does not participate in love, you will hold it in much greater veneration, and then you will attain an almost complete and perfect knowledge of its genealogy <note>original: *genealogiæ*; the "Genealogy of Love" is a major theme in the following dialogue, exploring the cosmic origins of love</note>.

**SO.** Do not refuse to reveal this also for my sake.

**PH.** We shall reserve the treatment of this so arduous and hidden matter for a more opportune time. For now the hour suggests that you grant some rest to your soft and delicate body, and that you might recreate and refresh your spirits—perhaps too weary and exhausted by the long discussion—with calm and sweetest sleep. Leave me, however, in my customary vigil; though I shall seem to remain alone, yet I will not be alone, since my mind carries you yourself everywhere, and perceives no less pain than pleasure from your company and contemplation.
