# ON THE SECOND DIALOGUE OF LEONE EBREO
# CONCERNING THE COMMUNITY OF LOVE,
# AND ITS VAST
## UNIVERSALITY,

## THE SUMMARY,

<sig>A'</sig> <note>This is a printer's signature mark, used in the 16th century to help bookbinders assemble the pages in the correct order.</note>

### Composed by
### GIOVANNI CARLO SARACENO.

He proposes at the beginning to speak of the community of **LOVE**. Then, having approached this so arduous and distinguished matter, he shows that living beings love one another for five reasons: he demonstrates that these are found in the human race in a far more perfect and noble way than in other species of animals, even if, due to some external hindrance, the opposite sometimes occurs. He then adds two reasons for love that are unique to the human race and not shared with any species of brute beasts: he traces the natural inclination of two humans to pursue each other with either the greatest love or intense hatred back to their biological temperaments, as well as to celestial aspects and configurations <note>This refers to the astrological belief that the positions of stars at birth influence human attraction.</note>. He adds that cognition, appetite, and love are all threefold: natural, sensory, and rational. He declares that all of these are found together in the human race, while only the first two are found in brute beasts, and only the first—natural love—is found in bodies devoid of life. Furthermore, he testifies that bodies lacking sensation are directed and illuminated by the Soul of the World <note>original: *anima Mundi*, a concept where the universe itself is a living being with a soul</note>, or by universal nature which knows and enlightens, so that they may recognize, love, and seek their own ends and proper regions. He reveals that the love of the elements is derived from those same five reasons from which the mutual love of living beings also flowed. 

He assigns a cause for the site and placement of the elements; he reduces the reason for the qualities of elements to their distance from or proximity to the celestial body. He examines the cause of why so many types of noble mixtures are seen to be born only on the earth, and not in any of the other elements; and, employing an elegant comparison, he calls the earth "mother" and all mixed things—both animate and inanimate—her "children." Next, besides the four elements, he teaches that a certain common matter is found in all things that are generated and corrupted <note>In the philosophy of the time, "corruption" meant the breaking down or death of a physical thing.</note>, and he beautifully explains its devotion and benevolence toward all forms: and he confirms that the birth and death of all lower things proceed from this matter, not unlike a mother or a stepmother. 

Afterward, he seems to transfer the generations of mixed things to the Heaven as the acting cause, and to the elements as the immediate matter. He also reviews the various orders and different classes of forms—each one always more excellent than the last—by which the elements, through their intervening mutual friendship, deserve to subsist together as one. He shows that these elements were reduced to the greatest equality and highest unity in the composition of man; and he gradually descends to the opinion of Empedocles <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher who taught that Love and Strife are the forces that move the four elements.</note> regarding the birth and death of lower things. 

Next, he turns to declaring the devotion and benevolence of the Heaven, both toward "prime matter" <note>The most basic substance of the universe before it takes any specific shape.</note>—as a husband toward a wife—and also toward all these lower bodies, as a parent toward children. He considers that the dews and rains have the quality of celestial seeds falling upon the earth: he affirms that the entire celestial body, like a certain "greatest animal," concurs with all its parts to produce these most excellent seeds. He compares the seven planets both with the seven members of the human body required for the production of seed, and also with the seven parts of our head serving sensation and cognition. 

He demonstrates that for the Heaven, as for a most perfect living being, not only two directions of position (as Pythagoras wrongly felt), but all six (as Aristotle rightly judged) must be applied. Furthermore, he proposes that most difficult and confused question concerning the Heaven, which he seems to determine—after rejecting and refuting several opinions of others as false—by pronouncing that the right and left parts of the Heaven, or the true East and true West, should not be referred to some fixed or defined part of the celestial body, but rather to two different and opposite types of celestial motions: namely, the daily and the wandering motion <note>original: *diurnum atque erraticum motum*, referring to the daily rotation of the sky versus the movement of the planets.</note>. 

Afterward, he approaches that arduous and illustrious meditation on why man is accustomed to be called by the wise a <term>microcosm</term> <note>original Greek: *μικρόκοσμος*, meaning "a small world" or "a world in miniature."</note>, and he pursues this at great length. Then, he turns his discourse toward declaring the mutual love and benevolence of the Heavens among themselves: and he most excellently interprets the concord and harmony of the celestial motions according to the opinion of Pythagoras. He concludes that there are two primary causes of the mutual love of the Heavens themselves. This part being finished and complete, he turns to explaining and clarifying the fables of the Poets: and first, he brings forward five reasons why the ancients sought to wrap and hide the secrets of nature in poetic fables; he also assigns the reason why, in treating philosophy, Pla-

<meta>This page continues the "Argumentum" (Summary) of the Second Dialogue. The opening line completes a sentence begun on the previous page regarding how Plato and Aristotle approached the use of myths and poetry to convey philosophical truths.</meta>

...having set aside the poetry, he <note>Referring to Plato</note> retained only the myth; Aristotle, however, boldly disregarding both the poetry and the commentary, substituted for them a brevity and obscurity of speech. Then he interprets quite elegantly the many different names of the Gods devised by the poets, as well as their marriages, adulteries, kinship, and descendants. He also demonstrates that the Platonic Ideas <term>Platonic Ideas: In Plato's philosophy, these are the eternal, perfect patterns or "blueprints" of which everything in our physical world is just a reflection.</term> wondrously agree with the divine deities of the poets. Next, he brings forward many of the poets' own fables along with their most learned and hidden allegories; in this matter, many wondrous properties of natural things are explained, and many opinions of philosophers and theologians are treated in an ornate and clear fashion. 

Having allegorically explained and interpreted the poets' stories, he examines the specific natures of the celestial signs as well as the planets. He diligently inquires into which celestial aspects <term>aspects: In astrology, the specific angular relationships between planets that were believed to determine their influence on Earthly events.</term> are said to be favorable and which unfavorable. He further discusses at length the friendly and hostile conjunctions of the planets, as well as their beneficial and harmful influences. Moreover, he follows with a long and subtle discourse on the specific houses <term>houses: Twelve divisions of the sky in astrology, each representing a different area of life (like health or wealth), where planets are said to have more or less power.</term> of the planets themselves; he demonstrates that their contrary and opposite natures match perfectly with the opposition of their houses, just as, conversely, planets of friendly and similar natures seem to have been assigned friendly and non-hostile houses. 

Finally, he elevates his speech to the interpretation of the love of spiritual beings, which he shows to be far more perfect and excellent in them than in physical bodies. He teaches that spiritual beings themselves carry two kinds of love: one toward higher things, the other toward lower things. He places the love of higher things for lower things and of lower for higher far above mere benevolence. He also asserts that the lack and imperfection seen in lower things detracts somewhat from the excellence and dignity of the higher, just as, conversely, the perfection of the lower (according to their capacity and condition) usually makes the higher more brilliant and visible. Furthermore, he adds that the higher beings are led to love the lower by a most excellent kind of love, by which they themselves pursue other even higher things. 

With these things established, he moves on to that arduous and most difficult question: what is the end <note>original: "finis" (purpose or goal)</note> for whose sake each intelligence <term>intelligence: In Renaissance science, "intelligences" were spiritual beings or angels believed to be responsible for moving the celestial spheres and keeping the planets in their orbits.</term> is said to rotate its own celestial sphere. In this matter, having cited and rejected two different and contrary opinions of the Arab philosophers <note>Referring to medieval thinkers like Avicenna and Averroes, whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to Renaissance science.</note>, he concludes that the end, driven by whose love each intelligence moves its sphere, is God, the Best and Greatest. He first declares, as a matter of the greatest importance, how it is possible for the individual intelligences, in rotating the spheres entrusted to their care, to attain divine union and supreme happiness. So that we may better understand this, he demonstrates that two "ends" (purposes) are found in things: the common and the private. He testifies that the common end, even if perhaps by its own nature it is sometimes less noble than the private one, must always be placed before the private, however noble that may be. 

Finally, he gathers and concludes that love, like a certain common bond, binds and ties together the entire universe, and that through the mediation of love, each individual thing acquires first its essence and finally the happiness that is its due and ->proper state.<-

## SECOND DIALOGUE:
### BY GIOVANNI CARLO SARACENO

#### SOPHIA AND PHILO,
->The Speakers.<-

Greetings, oh Philo: do you answer nothing? You certainly seem mute. *PH.* She who clearly procures my death and destruction now prays for my health with flattering words. Oh, greetings, Sophia: what do you require of me? *SO.* I thought this a timely hour for you to pay what you owe. *PH.* Do I owe you anything? You will find that I owe you neither benefit nor benevolence, since you have bestowed upon me only sorrows and innumerable tortures of the soul. *SO.* Your debt is not one of gratitude, but of a promise, by which men are bound most of all to pay. *PH.* I remember promising you nothing else but that I would love you perseveringly, and that I would bear your injuries and insults with a calm mind until I am carried across the Lethean river by Charon. <note>original: "Letheum flumen à Charonte." In Greek mythology, Charon is the ferryman who carries souls across the rivers of the underworld; Lethe is the river of forgetfulness.</note> And if even in those regions the soul remains endowed with some sense of things, it will preserve the love and memory of you together with the tortures following both, for eternity. There is no need for you to remind me of this debt, since it is paid daily. *SO.* Either you have truly forgotten, or you pretend and feign forgetfulness. Yet it is fitting for the debtor no less than the creditor to remember a contracted debt. Do you not keep in memory that in previous days, toward the end of our discussion on love and desire, you promised me you would speak amply and at length on the origin and genealogy of love? Have you forgotten that promise so quickly? *PH.* Oh, oh, at last I barely remember. You should not wonder at all, Sophia, if you alone occupy my entire memory, that I so easily forget past things. *SO.* I ought to recall it to you only from foreign things, not from my own. *PH.* Of things pertaining to you, I keep only those in memory which are accustomed to affect my soul with love and sorrow; the rest, even if they are yours, nevertheless cause me no disturbance.

<margin>The order of the future discussion.</margin>
*SO.* However it may be, I forgive the forgetfulness, but I wish to demand the promise. Therefore, using the opportunity of the time, let us sit under this shade so that you may more conveniently narrate the birth of love and its first origin.

<margin>The origin of any thing precedes its universality on the part of the thing itself, but not on the part of our knowledge.</margin>
*PH.* If you desire to understand the birth of love, first in the present conversation we must speak of its universality and its wide community; otherwise, we will treat its birth later. *SO.* Does not the origin of anything precede its universality? *PH.* It precedes indeed on the part of the thing itself, yet not on the part of our knowledge. *SO.* For what reason?

<margin>The universality of love is far more manifest to us than its origin.</margin>
<margin>We are raised from things known to us to the knowledge of things unknown to us.</margin>
*PH.* Because the universality of love is far more manifest to us than its origin: and we are raised from known things to know things unknown. *SO.* You truly declare that the universality of love is clear and manifest enough to us: for no sex of men and no age is found which is devoid of love; indeed, indifferently, both males and females, and the old and the young are seen to love; and infants themselves in that first and rough knowledge are seen to love their mothers and nurses. *PH.* Therefore, you judge that the empire of love should not be extended beyond the human race? *SO.* On the contrary, it also runs throughout all irrational living creatures that have the power of generating, as in

females and males, toward children and parents. *PH.* Love, which is found among humans and the other animals, is usually born not only from procreation, but also from other causes; nor does it consist in these alone, but truly extends and expands to much more. *SO.* First, tell me what other causes of love are found in living beings besides generation; then, you shall reveal by what logic love exists in things that lack a soul <note>original: "animam," referring here to the 'anima' or life-force/soul that distinguishes living beings from objects.</note> and the power to reproduce. *PH.* I will fulfill both in order. Animals—aside from the fact that they love things suitable to them by the guidance of Nature so that they may pursue them, just as they conversely hate things unsuitable to them so that they may flee them—also love each other for five reasons.

<margin>Living creatures love each other mutually with love for five reasons: because of the appetite and pleasure of reproducing; because of the succession of offspring; because of some notable benefit conferred or received; because of the affinity of the same or at least a similar species; because of continuous use and long-standing habit.</margin>
First, because of the appetite and pleasure of reproducing, as with males and females. Second, because of the succession of offspring, as with parents toward their children. Third, because of a benefit, which generates love not only in the one receiving it toward the one conferring it, but also in the giver toward the receiver, even if their loves are distinguished by their type. For we see that if a dog or perhaps a goat should nourish an infant or any animal of a different species, both of those living creatures pursue each other with the greatest mutual love. Fourth, because of the affinity of the same, or at least a similar species: for you will see animals of the same species that do not live by prey dwelling together because of mutual love; even predatory animals, though they do not share their prey and rejoice in solitude, fleeing society, nevertheless—because of a certain natural love and an innate ferocity that is not terrifying to their own kind—never exercise their deadly venom against animals of the same species. In different species of animals, some similarity is also found which fosters friendships between them, as happens between the dolphin and man; just as, conversely, other animals are found that carry on natural and perpetual enmities among themselves, such as the basilisk <note>original: "Regulus seu basiliscus." A legendary serpent king said to kill with a single glance.</note> and man, who indeed kill each other by sight alone. Fifth, because of continuous use and long-standing habit: which joins with mutual benevolence not only animals of the same species, but even those of different and hostile species; just as we see a dog joined in friendship with a lion, and a lamb with a wolf, because of frequent association. *SO.* I have clearly understood the reasons for the friendship or benevolence of brute animals; now I would desire you to explain the causes of human love.

<margin>The mutual love of humans is seen to proceed from the same five reasons as those of brute animals, yet with the light of reason additionally accompanying each one of them.</margin>
*PH.* From the same five reasons just enumerated, the mutual love not only of animals but also of humans arises: but the use of reason makes them more intense or relaxed, or right or crooked, according to the diversity of our goals. *SO.* I pray you, explain these differences in each of the five reasons already mentioned. *PH.* The first cause, which is taken from the desire and pleasure of reproducing, instills a love in humans that is more intense, more stable, and more "proper" <note>meaning more specific to the individual</note> than in the rest of the animals, which indeed is usually more hidden through the use of reason. *SO.* Do not be burdened to declare these differences one by one. *PH.* Love proceeding from this first cause—

<margin>In the human race, the love of men for women seems to be more intense, more stable, more proper, and also more hidden than the devotion of males for females in other species of animals.</margin>
—is said to be more intense in humans because they love more vehemently and seek out women for themselves with greater anxiety than other animals seek females; so much so that, for the sake of obtaining their favor, they are often accustomed to set aside and refuse food, sleep, and all rest whatsoever. It is also more stable: because devotion and love are preserved longer between a man and a woman than among other animals, to such an extent that neither satiety, nor absence, nor any obstacle at all can dissolve it. It is also more "proper" <note>Specific or individualistic.</note>: because each of us has a greater propensity and application toward a specific woman than a male has toward a female in individual species of animals. And although in some of them a certain proper and particular application is seen, in humans it is far more perfect and more determined. Finally, this first love is more hidden in us than in other animals: because reason restrains and coerces its excess, and judges it to be shameful unless it is tempered by reason. More humans are killed and consumed by the enmities, ambushes, and right hands of other humans than by any other executioner, whether accidental or natural. Moreover, greed and the care for superfluous things dissolve the natural love of the human species.

<margin>[The fourth cause is] shared in two forms: one arising from the harmony of nature and temperament, the other originating from intellectual virtues.</margin>

at the very first meeting, it reconciles them in friendship. Since such sudden and mutual goodwill cannot be traced back to any certain cause, it is usually attributed to a similarity in the physical temperament of their bodies. In truth, it proceeds from a likeness and a certain harmonic proportion. Conversely, some people pursue each other with the greatest hatred for no apparent reason, which flows from a diversity and contrariety of their temperaments <note>In Renaissance medicine, "temperament" or "complexion" referred to the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—within an individual.</note>.

<margin>The natural propensity of two humans to either love or hate one another is attributed by physicians to temperaments, but by astrologers it is customarily traced back to celestial aspects and figures.</margin>

Astrologers, however, provide a celestial explanation for this phenomenon. They say that the inclination and propensity of two people to love one another proceeds from the same or very similar aspects and figures of the planets and zodiac signs dominating the birth chart <note>original: "genitura," referring to a natal horoscope</note> of both individuals. Conversely, they attribute innate hatred and the contrariety of natures to a dissimilar and hostile disposition of the stars. This explanation for the love and friendship of humans can indeed be given by us, but it applies very little to other animals. **SO.** What then is the other form? **PH.** The second form originates from moral and intellectual virtues, which are accustomed to lure us in a wonderful way to love excellent and distinguished men. Our souls are most easily captured by their distinguished form and beauty through an honorable love <note>original: "honesto amore," referring to *honestum*, or moral virtue, as opposed to mere utility or pleasure</note> that is far superior to all others. For men who are studious of the good pursue each other with a more vehement love of perfection—and therefore a greater love—for the sake of virtue and honor alone, rather than for utility or pleasure, which are the two fonts from which all five previously mentioned reasons flow. This love alone claims for itself the name of "honorable" and is born from right reason; for this reason, it is not found at all in animals that lack reason. **SO.** I have understood very well how many causes of love can be given for both humans and beasts; but all of these can only be applied to living things, and in no way to bodies that lack life. Yet you said a while ago that love is common not only to animals but also to inanimate <note>original: "insensibilis," meaning lacking the faculty of sensation</note> bodies, which seems to me to be entirely alien to the truth. **PH.** Why alien to the truth? **SO.** Because nothing can be loved unless it is first known, and inanimate bodies do not have even the smallest faculty for knowing. Furthermore, love arises from the will or appetite, and ends in sensation itself. Therefore, since inanimate bodies lack will, appetite, and every kind of sense, by what logic can they ever be said to love?

<margin>Cognition, appetite, and love are each three-fold: natural, sensible, and rational or voluntary.</margin>

**PH.** Cognition, as well as appetite, and therefore love also, exists in three forms: natural, sensible, and rational (or voluntary). **SO.** Follow through with each part of your proposed division.

<margin>Natural cognition, appetite, and love are found in inanimate bodies.</margin>

**PH.** Natural cognition, appetite, or love is said to be that which is found in bodies lacking sense—namely the elements <note>The four elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note> and those things composed from the meeting of the elements, such as metals, many types of stones, as well as plants, herbs, or trees. For all things of this kind have a certain natural knowledge of their own ends and an innate propensity to achieve them. Just as heavy bodies seek the lower region by descending, and light bodies seek the upper region by ascending, they do so as if seeking their own proper place, known to them beforehand and vehemently desired. This propensity, appetite, and love is called "natural" by everyone everywhere, and it truly exists as such.

<margin>Sensible cognition, appetite, and love are seen to be innate to the entire genus of beasts.</margin>

Next follows sensible cognition, appetite, and love, which is innate to the entire genus of beasts for the purpose of pursuing what is useful and rejecting what is harmful. By this logic, animals seek with great zeal food, drink, the temperateness of the weather, mating, rest, and other familiar things which must first be known, then desired and loved, and finally moved toward in order to be grasped. For unless the animal first knew these things, it would never afterwards desire or love them; and if it did not desire them, it would never work to acquire them; and if these were not obtained, death would immediately follow.

<margin>Neither sensible cognition should be called rational, nor should sensible appetite or love be called voluntary for any reason.</margin>

But this kind of cognition is not rational, nor should such an appetite or love be called "voluntary," since the will always follows reason itself. Rather, these are certain actions of the sensing faculties; and for this reason, sensible cognition and love—or to speak more properly, appe-

# SECOND DIALOGUE
<page-num>377</page-num>

<margin>Rational knowledge and voluntary love are found in the human race alone.</margin>
...are customarily called. Finally, rational knowledge and voluntary love are found in humans alone. For the former flows from the light of reason, while the latter is governed by the command of that same reason, which Divine Goodness has shared with man alone among all created and perishable bodies. **SO.** You have placed voluntary love only in humans, and not at all in beasts or unfeeling bodies. But you have placed sensible love or appetite in animals lacking reason, and not at all in unfeeling bodies. Finally, you have attributed only natural love and appetite to the lower, unfeeling bodies. Now I desire to know this: is natural love found in animals joined with their own specific sensible love? And are both—that is, the natural and the sensible—associated with the voluntary or rational love that is unique to humans? **PH.** You have questioned rightly, and you seem to have guessed the truth:

<margin>A lower form of love always follows a nobler one; however, the more excellent does not conversely accompany the inferior.</margin>
for a lower love always follows a nobler one, but conversely, the more excellent does not always accompany the inferior. Therefore, in humans, sensible love—which seeks what is friendly to life and flees what is hostile—is joined with rational or voluntary love:

<margin>In the human race, sensible and natural love are joined together with rational or voluntary love.</margin>
and in them is also found the natural inclination of unfeeling bodies, by virtue of which, if one of us falls from a height, he will strive toward a lower place by the impulse of nature and the example of heavy bodies <note>In the Aristotelian physics of the time, "heavy" elements like earth and water naturally moved downward toward the center of the universe, while "light" elements like fire moved upward.</note>.

<margin>In beasts, natural love is also joined with sensible love.</margin>
We see this same innate inclination everywhere in beasts; led by nature, and in the manner of heavy bodies, they are carried toward the center of the universe as to their own proper place, known and desired by them only through the light of nature.

<margin>The reason why natural and sensible inclinations have customarily been called 'loves'.</margin>
**SO.** Why do you call these natural and sensible inclinations "love"? For love truly seems to be an affection of the will, and among all lower things, only humans were gifted with a will. Therefore, those higher aptitudes should be called "appetites" rather than "loves." **PH.** Things are best known from their contraries.

<margin>Things are best known from their contraries.</margin>
<margin>The science of contraries is one.</margin>
For as Aristotle testifies, the science of contraries is one <note>original: "eadem est scientia contrariorum." A common philosophical maxim meaning that to understand a concept, one must also understand its opposite—for example, medicine studies both health and disease.</note>. Therefore, if the contrary of those inclinations is truly called "hatred," each of them will rightly be named "love." For just as in the human race voluntary hatred is opposed to voluntary love, so in the genus of animals, hatred of things that oppose their well-being is the contrary of their love for those things that preserve it. Animals are seen to flee one and pursue the other, because hatred seems to persuade them toward the flight of one, and love toward the pursuit of the other. By no dissimilar reason, natural love and natural hatred are seen in unfeeling bodies: such as the love of heavy things for obtaining a lower place and fleeing a higher one, just as, conversely, light things love the upper region and hate the lower. Therefore, just as hatred is found in each of them, so is love. **SO.** How can it be that what lacks the faculty of knowing could ever be said to love? **PH.** On the contrary, it does know, since it loves some things and holds others in hatred. **SO.** How can you attribute knowledge to these lower bodies, which are utterly destitute of reason, sense, and imagination? **PH.** Even if they lack those three powers of knowing, they are nevertheless directed either by Universal Nature—which knows and governs all these lower things—or they are enlightened by the Soul of the World <note>original: "anima mundi." A Platonic concept suggesting that the universe possesses a guiding spirit that directs the movements of all things.</note> with a certain direct and never-erring knowledge of those things necessary for the preservation of their own nature. **SO.** But in what way can that which is entirely devoid of sense love anything?

<margin>Unfeeling bodies are directed to know and desire their own ends and proper places, and are enlightened by the light of either the Soul of the World or the knowledge of Universal Nature.</margin>
**PH.** Just as these lower bodies are rightly directed by the providence of nature to know their own ends and proper places, so too are they enlightened by the light of that same nature in loving, desiring, and seeking them when they are violently held in a foreign region. Thus, just as an arrow—not by its own knowledge, but by the skill of the archer who directs it—strives toward the intended target, so these lower bodies are rightly carried to their proper places, not by their own notice, but by the direct knowledge infused into the Soul of the World and into the universal nature of all lower things by the First Creator...

# LEONE EBREO’S ON LOVE
<page-num>378</page-num>

<margin>The love of the elements and of other lifeless bodies for their own regions, and their hatred for alien and hostile regions, is seen to have a certain correspondence with the love and hatred of living creatures, who embrace what is useful and proper and reject what is foreign and harmful.</margin>
...and they are carried toward their proper boundaries with the greatest speed. Just as the flight of an arrow proceeds from the knowledge, love, and desire of the craftsman, so too the inclinations and efforts of these unfeeling bodies are directed and tempered by a natural knowledge and love. **SO.** This kind of love and knowledge found in bodies destitute of a soul is very much approved by me. But I would like to understand this further: is there any other love or desire seen in them besides that for their proper places, for the sake of which light things ascend and heavy things descend? **PH.** The love by which the elements or other lifeless bodies seek their own regions, and the hatred by which they flee from hostile and contrary ones, are seen to have a certain correspondence with the love and hatred of living creatures in embracing useful things and rejecting harmful ones. But another reason for this similarity also exists: for just as quadrupeds love the earth, fish the water, birds the air, and the Salamander (as it is said) the fire, as their own native lands and proper homes, so also the elements display the greatest love for their own natural regions. I tell you and affirm, moreover, that besides this first kind of love, all five types of mutual benevolence—which we have already declared to exist in living creatures—are also found in the elements. **SO.** All of them? **PH.** All of them, I say. **SO.** May it not be too burdensome for you to go through each one.

<margin>Love derived from the similarity of species is found in the elements no differently than in living creatures.</margin>
**PH.** I shall begin with the last one, as it is more manifest than the others: namely, the harmony of the species. You will see that parts of the earth that have been divided from the whole earth are moved toward it with a most effective love, so that they may be joined with the whole. Stones also, which were frozen in the aerial region <note>This refers to hail or perhaps meteorites, interpreted through the lens of ancient physics.</note>, are soon carried to the earth. Rivers also, and other kinds of water generated at the boundaries of the earth from vapors that exhale and turn into water, run down toward the sea and the entire watery element because of a love for their species as soon as they have attained a fitting quantity. Furthermore, aerial vapors or winds born in the depths of the earth, seeking an exit so that they may be joined with their own element, finally burst forth with a terrifying noise and the greatest movement of the earth itself <note>A common Renaissance explanation for earthquakes: trapped wind escaping the earth to return to the air.</note>; they display a supreme benevolence toward their own kind. Finally, fire, whether it was generated in the innermost reaches of the earth or in this foul and misty sky <note>original: "tetro & caliginoso cœlo." Philo refers to the sublunary world, the realm of change and decay below the moon, which was considered "dark" compared to the ethereal heavens.</note>, continually seeks the higher regions, driven by the love of its species. **SO.** I have understood the love of the elements for their own species very well; now turn yourself to explaining the other reasons.

<margin>The love derived from companionship is seen to exist in the four elements no differently than in living creatures.</margin>
**PH.** I shall now approach the fourth reason for love, which is derived from companionship, since it stands out more clearly than the rest due to a certain harmony of the elements with their natural places. **SO.** What companionship can we attribute to the elements and similar bodies? **PH.** It pleases each of the four simple bodies—namely earth, water, air, and fire—to live and dwell near this element but not near that one. Earth flees the approach of heaven and fire most of all, and rejoices to stay in the center <note>In the geocentric model, the Earth is at the center, the point furthest from the outer celestial spheres.</note>, the most remote of all places from the celestial body. It delights in the proximity of water and air, granting the higher place to each of them and choosing the lowest for itself. But if it should ever be above them, it immediately strives for the bottom, and never stops until it has attained the greatest possible distance from heaven. **SO.** Why does the earth hate and flee from heaven so much, when all good proceeds from heaven?

<margin>The reason why the earth, among all the elements, exists as far as possible from heaven.</margin>
<margin>The reason why water sits between the upper air and the land.</margin>
**PH.** Because it is heavier and thicker than all the elements, and because of a certain laziness and an ingrained sluggishness within it, it rejoices and delights in rest more than any of the others. Therefore, since heaven is perpetually moved with no intervening rest at all, the earth—in order to securely enjoy rest and stability—recedes as far as it can from it, and finally attains its longed-for rest in the center as the lowest point of all, defended and fortified on one side by water and on the other by air. **SO.** So much for the earth; now pass on to water. **PH.** Water also shares in sluggishness and heaviness, though less so than the earth...

### DIALOGUE II

<margin>...the lower thing was placed in the middle.</margin>
...of the earth, but more than the other two elements: and for that reason, she herself also avoids interaction and use of the heaven, lest she be moved quickly in the likeness of air or fire; she seeks the lower parts, desiring proximity to the earth and the air. Indeed, she remains below the air while embracing the earth, loving both with equal devotion. But she holds fire in the greatest hatred, and carries on perpetual enmities with it; for the sake of these, she flees from it, nor can she tolerate its neighborhood or company in any way.

<margin>The reason why air, placed under fire and above water and earth, obtained the middle place among the rest of the elements.</margin>
**SO.** What do you say concerning the air? **PH.** Air, because of its lightness and subtlety, is delighted by the celestial nature and its society, and contends with the greatest zeal to enjoy it; it seeks the heights, yet it does not touch the heaven itself. For it is not endowed with that same purity as fire, which claims the first place among the elements for itself. Therefore, it is eager to be subject to fire, and rejoices to be the boundary of water and earth: yet it does not agree to be placed under them, but rather above them. It follows the very swift rotation of the heaven most readily, and it agrees perfectly both with fire and with water. Whence, since these two elements <note>fire and water</note> exist as contraries and enemies to one another, the air itself was placed in the middle as a friend to both, lest these two most bitter enemies might sometime exhaust and consume themselves in perpetual war.

<margin>The reason why fire occupied the middle place between the hollow circuit of the Lunar body and the rest of the elements.</margin>
**SO.** It remains for you to speak of fire. **PH.** Fire surpasses all elements in thinness, lightness, and purity: it loves none of them except air alone, in whose proximity it delights; yet it is placed in a worthier and higher seat. It loves the Heaven <note>the celestial spheres</note> wondrously: nor does it ever or anywhere rest, unless after it has been joined with it. This is surely that "social love" <note>original: "amor socialis," referring to the bond that holds the physical universe together</note> which is seen in the four elements.

**SO.** I am glad of it. But why did you not also insert the reason and cause of the elementary qualities <note>the four primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry</note> into this proposal?

<margin>The reason for the elementary qualities is referred to the distance or proximity of the celestial body.</margin>
**PH.** Because such knowledge pertains very little to social love; however, since it will bring the greatest importance to what follows, I will try to render it to you. The Heaven, by its continuous motion and the flashing rays of the Sun and other planets, as well as the fixed stars grazing the eighth sphere, heats this lower globe of rude and lifeless matter, which fills the entire capacity and cavity of the lunar sphere.

<margin>The reason why fire is hot and dry, as well as being the lightest.</margin>
Whence the first portion of this globe, which exists closer to the heaven, since it is heated more vehemently, is thinned out to the greatest degree and obtains the greatest purity: and it is rendered so light and hot that all moisture is consumed and squeezed out by the vehement heat, and it remains arid, from which fire comes forth into the light.

<margin>The reason why air is considered hot and moist, as well as light by its own nature.</margin>
Furthermore, the vital heat of the heaven, penetrating further into the second portion of this globe which follows fire, heats it also; yet not so much that it can resolve its moisture: whence air is procreated of a hot and moist nature. By reason of the heat, it turns out pure, thin, and light, only a little less so than fire, having now attained the primary parts of heat.

<margin>The reason why water is seen to be cold and moist, as well as heavy.</margin>
But when the celestial heat is extended into this globe beyond the air, it is not of such power that it can create a hot element; on the contrary, because of the excessive distance from the heaven, that element remains cold, yet not so much that it is deprived of moisture; it also exists as heavy because of the thickness proceeding from the cold, and it seeks out sloping places. This element of a cold and moist nature is called "water" by us.

<margin>The reason why earth is seen to be cold and dry, as well as the heaviest.</margin>
Lastly, from the greatest distance from the heaven, such a piercing cold <note>original: "horror," used here to mean the shivering or shrinking quality of extreme cold</note> invades the parts of this globe nearest to the center of all the others, that it forces together and constricts all moisture, from which a most thick and heavy body is made, as well as cold and dry, which indeed we call "earth."

<margin>The reason why air and fire pursue heaven itself with the most vehement love, but earth and water with a more relaxed love.</margin>
Therefore air and fire—which, because of their proximity, drink in the most abundant heat, life, and health for lower bodies from the starry fountain—love the heaven vehemently: and wherever they exist, they approach it, and are moved perpetually in a circle along with it. The remaining two elements, namely earth and water, because they have obtained little heat and life from the celestial power, also love it little, nor do they care for proximity to it; but rather, so that they may enjoy a certain and stable rest, and not be led around perpetually together with it, they flee from it most greatly.

**SO.** If the earth is the lowest,

# LEO THE HEBREW ON LOVE

...[the earth] and exists as the most ignoble <note>In the context of Renaissance natural philosophy, "ignoble" refers to being physically base, heavy, and furthest removed from the "noble" or divine heavens.</note> of all elements; it is distant from the origin of life—that is, from heaven itself—by a longer interval than the rest. Why then are so many vicissitudes of things carried out upon it rather than in any of the other elements? For example, there are so many kinds of stones, some of which are large, conspicuous, and beautiful; some, moreover, are clear and precious. There are also metals: not only the more common ones like iron, lead, copper, tin, and Mercury, but even the glowing and highly valued ones like gold and silver. There is the wonderful variety of flowers, trees, and fruits that come forth from the earth, and such a great multitude and diversity of animals, all of which venerate the earth as their common mother. For although some plants and almost innumerable kinds of living creatures arise in the sea, and many species of birds fly through the air here and there, nevertheless, all living things acknowledge the earth’s munificence and liberality toward them; they rely upon her especially as a firm and stable seat. This seems to prove the excellence and nobility of the earth above all: that in this element alone, we see the human species—by far the most perfect and excellent of all things contained within the embrace of the heavens—being born and dwelling. This species cannot be produced or placed in any of the other three elements. By what reasoning, then, did you just pronounce that the earth is the basest among all four elements and approaches more closely to death?

<margin>
The reason why in the earth alone—though she is the most ignoble of all elements and most remote from heaven—so many kinds of the most noble mixtures are seen to be born.
</margin>

**PH.** Although the earth, because of its greatest distance from the celestial body, is by its nature thicker, colder, and lower, and participates in life less than the remaining elements, it nevertheless remains immobile at the center. Because its individual parts are most firmly and tightly joined and united at that center, it receives all the rays and influences of the stars, planets, and celestial bodies as they converge and gather into one. These influences, carrying with them the virtues of the other three elements in addition to their own, are able to create so many great "temperaments" <note>A "temperament" or "complexion" refers to the specific balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—that defines a physical substance.</note> through which the individual things you just listed are born on earth. This could not happen in the regions of the other three elements. None of them is a common receptacle for all those celestial and elementary virtues; rather, they all unite in the earth. These virtues pass through and are dispersed by the other elements, but they stay and join together in the earth alone—partly because of its density, and partly because, being located at the center, it receives the impact and strike of all rays most strongly. For this reason, the other elements can rightly be called the "harlots and concubines" of the celestial body; but the earth alone is its proper and legitimate wife. This is because the celestial seeds—for the generation of all or at least most mixtures <note>A "mixture" refers to any complex physical body, like a plant or animal, composed of the four elements.</note>—are received into the most fertile womb of the earth, and she, displaying a mother’s love, cherishes and nourishes her numerous and beautiful offspring.

**SO.** You have explained my uncertainty excellently. Now let us return to the main point. Tell me whether the remaining reasons that reconcile mutual friendship among humans and beasts are also found in the elements and other bodies devoid of sense and life. To recap, the third was benefit, the second was posterity, and the first was the appetite and pleasure of generating.

**PH.** The principle of benefit <note>original: "Ratio beneficij"</note> in the elements seems to exist alongside the benefit received, and ultimately with the logic of their generation. For the offspring loves the parent as a benefactor, and the parent loves the offspring as a beneficiary. In those things generated from the elements, the principle of succession is found quite purely and distinctly. This is proven by the example of those things born in the region of the air from vapors ascending from the land and sea. For if such vapors are moist, they are converted into rain, snow, or hail; these soon descend with a certain "amorous impulse" to find the sea and earth as their common mother. If, however, those vapors are dry, winds and fiery impressions <note>Fiery impressions often referred to meteors, lightning, or other atmospheric phenomena believed to be composed of "dry" or "exhalations."</note> are generated from them...

<margin>
Love seems to exist both from a benefit received and finally from the reason of their generation: for the generated loves the generator as a benefactor; the generator, however, loves the generated as a beneficiary. But in these things which are generated from the elements, the reason of succession or origin taken up in the elements and in mixtures is found quite elegantly.
</margin>

### DIALOGUE II

<margin>All composite things, both animate and inanimate, venerate the earth as their common mother in the manner of children; they are, in turn, loved by her with a maternal affection as if they were her dearest offspring. <note>original: "Omnia mixta tam animata quàm inanimata terram uelut communem matrem filiorū more uenerantur..."</note></margin>
And indeed, the winds, blowing vehemently, strive toward the air; while fiery things, seeking the highest and first of all the elements, climb even higher. Both are driven by a love for their own origin and the element from which they took their beginning, as if from a father. Stones and metals, too, which derive their origin from the earth, are seen to be carried swiftly toward her whenever they are outside of her, never resting until they return. The Earth, moreover, shows the greatest charity by generating, retaining, and conserving them. Furthermore, plants, herbs, and trees pursue the earth, their common mother and creator, with such great love that they never wish to depart from her unharmed; rather, they most zealously embrace her with their roots as if with arms, like infants at their mother’s breasts. The Earth, performing the duty of a pious and diligent mother, does not merely give birth to them—kindled as she is by the greatest charity and enormous love—but she also strives greatly to nourish them and keep them alive by pressing her own internal <term>humor</term> <note>In ancient science, "humors" or fluids were the vital juices—like sap or blood—that sustained life.</note> to the outer surface. In this, she surely imitates a human mother, who sends milk from her vitals to her breasts so that she may provide suitable nourishment for her small children. And if, perhaps by the injury of the seasons or the inclemency of the weather, she becomes too dry and parched, she strives for rain from the sky and air with suppliant vows and most humble prayers. She even risks her own vapors—from which, as they rise, rain-water is made—to purchase and obtain nourishment for her plants and her living creatures. What mother could ever show greater piety and charity toward her children?

**SOPHIA:** It is indeed a marvel that the earth, an inanimate body, should have such great care for her children. We ought to respect much more the one who made the earth so vigilant and hardworking for the safety of her children. It only remains for you to adapt that first reason for the mutual love of animals—which is taken from the desire and pleasure of generating—to the elements and to bodies that lack all sense.

<margin>The love of generating is found quite distinctly in the elements, and moreover in the common matter of all lower things. <note>original: "Amor generandi in elementis, & in cōmunissimā insuper rerū omnium inferio rum materia distinctè admodū reperitur."</note></margin>
**PHILO:** The love of generating is found more extensively and abundantly in the elements and the matter of these lower things than any other love of the higher things.

**SOPHIA:** Why did you just mention "matter" in addition to the simple bodies (the elements)? Is there some other matter of these lower things besides the four elements, from which everything else generated in this lower world is seen to be born?

**PHILO:** This is true indeed; but since we see these same elements being generated everywhere, something must surely be found from which *they* are generated.

**SOPHIA:** From what? Surely one element is generated from another. For we frequently see water made from air, air from water, fire from air, and air from fire. The same must be said of the earth.

<margin>The four elements themselves are the matter and subject of the things that are generated from them. <note>original: "Rerum, quæ ex elementis generantur, ipsamet quatuor elementa sunt materia atq; subiectum."</note></margin>
**PHILO:** This is also true. But of the things generated from the elements, the four elements themselves are the matter and subject; in the thing born from them, these elements remain and are seen, joined and united together by a certain wonderful craftsmanship and power. However, in the mutual generation of the elements, we cannot simply lay one down as the "matter" for the other. For when fire is turned into water, fire does not remain in the water; rather, the fire is "corrupted" <note>In philosophy, "corruption" is the technical term for the ending of one thing's existence so another can begin.</note> and water is generated. Therefore, it is necessary to assign some common "matter" to the elements in which their individual changes can take place—a matter which, for example, having previously put on the form of air when prepared by a suitable alteration, now puts off that form of air and is clothed in the form of water. We must feel exactly the same way about the other exchanges of the elements.

<margin>Prime matter was discovered by natural philosophers because of the mutual exchanges of the four elements.</margin>
<margin>"Chaos" signifies confusion.</margin>
This is called **Prime Matter** by philosophers, and was called **Chaos** by the ancient sages, which signifies "confusion." This is because all things that are generated are contained within it by a certain potential and are folded together confusedly; from this same source, individual things come forth into the light distinctly and in an ordered series.

**SOPHIA:** Truly, what kind of love can be attributed to this matter?

<margin>Prime matter loves all forms as a woman loves a man. <note>original: "Materia prima formas omnes ut fœmina mas"</note></margin>
**PHILO:** According to the opinion of **Plato**, Matter appetites and loves all the forms of things that are generated, just as...

# LEONIS HEBRÆI: ON LOVE

<margin>Matter pursues the thing with enormous love.</margin>
...it pursues the thing with enormous love, as a female pursues a male. Since its appetite and desire are so far-reaching and wide-ranging that they cannot be satisfied by the presence of only one form, it is held by a great love for other forms which it does not possess; and therefore, leaving the former, it immediately takes up another. Since it can by no means receive all forms at one and the same time, it receives them one after another in a certain succession. Indeed, it encompasses all forms in all its parts together; but because each of those parts desires to enjoy the love of all forms as much as possible, it follows that it is constantly carried from one to another in a certain preserved order; for a single form is hardly able to satisfy its nearly immense and insatiable appetite and love. Therefore, just as from Prime Matter <term>materia prima</term> <note>The formless "stuff" that underlies all physical reality in ancient philosophy.</note> the continuous generation <note>original: "generatio"</note> of forms that it lacks proceeds as if from a cause:

<margin>The generation and corruption of all lower things seems to proceed from Prime Matter as if from a common root.</margin>
so, from that same matter, the perennial corruption <note>original: "corruptio"</note> of the forms it does possess seems to flow forth as if from a spring.

<margin>Prime Matter has been called a prostitute by some, not without merit.</margin>
For this reason, some call matter a "prostitute" <note>original: "meretricem"</note>; because it has no single or stable lover; rather, when it lies with one, it strives to leave it and prostitute itself to another. Yet, because of this "adultery," this lower world is filled and adorned with such a great and admirable diversity of things and elegant forms. Therefore, the love of generating implanted in this Prime Matter, and the perpetual desire for new marriages, and the pleasure which various and different couplings bring to it, is the cause of the unceasing generation of these lower things.

<margin>The love of generating composite things is infused into the four elements.</margin>
**SO.** I seem to have understood the love, appetite, and insatiable desire of Prime Matter very well. I would now like to know what kind of love of generating can be found among the four elements, which are so greatly contrary to one another.

**PH.** The mutual love of the four elements themselves—though they are opposed to one another—seems to be a significant cause of the generation of all composite things <note>original: "mixtorum," referring to physical objects made of multiple elements.</note> that consist of them.

**SO.** By what reasoning?

<margin>The Heavens are the chief cause that the four elements, though contrary by their own nature, are mixed together and joined into one.</margin>
**PH.** Because although the elements inhabit different and separate seats due to their hostile natures—since fire and air, because of their heat and lightness, fly upward to escape the lower place, while earth and water, because of their coldness and weight, strive downward against the upper region—nonetheless, through the interceding kindness and favor of the Heavens <note>original: "cœli," referring to the celestial spheres and their influence.</note>, and because of the movements and divine power of its rays, they come together in friendship. Thus they are mixed, so that all things eventually coalesce with one mind into one body and one quality. This friendship is suitable and well-adapted so that that first subject <note>Prime Matter</note> may obtain, through the power of heaven, other forms far nobler and more excellent than the elementary ones, possessing more and different perfections. Yet, the elements are always seen to remain in a mixture of this kind as the proper matter and the immovable foundation of the whole structure.

<margin>The orders or classes of forms in which the elements, through their mutual friendship, deserve to be clothed when joined and mixed into one.</margin>
**SO.** By what forms are the elements distinguished through their mutual friendship? And how many levels of such forms are there?

**PH.** The first and simplest class of friendship is occupied by the forms of inanimate mixtures, such as stones; some of which are dark, some clearer, and some brilliant and famous. To these, the earth gives hardness, water gives clarity, air gives transparency <term>diaphaneitatem</term> <note>From the Greek for "showing through"; the ability of light to pass through a stone.</note>, and fire gives splendor and light; as is clearly seen in precious stones.

<margin>In the composition or mixture of metals, water holds the primary position.</margin>
Furthermore, from this first and harmonious mixing of the elements, metallic forms proceed. Some of these metals are coarser, like iron and lead; others are cleaner and more elegant, like copper, tin, and Mercury; and finally, some are seen to be brilliant and shining, like silver and gold. In all of these, however, that water holds the primary place is shown by this strongest argument: they are liquefied and dissolved by fiery heat.

<margin>The more the elements joined together have conspired into a closer society and been reduced to a more equal balance, the nobler and more perfect a form they seem to receive.</margin>
Stones and metals seem to agree in this: that they receive a more perfect form of the mixture the more the elements are brought to a greater friendship and a more equal balance <term>temperamentum</term> <note>The "tempering" or proportion of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that determines a thing's nature.</note>. For if the contrary elements have conspired into a tighter bond of necessity and a more equal fellowship, having [overcome] their excesses...

<summary>Philo explains how Prime Matter's "insatiable" desire for new forms drives the cycle of birth and decay, using the metaphor of a prostitute to describe its lack of permanence. He then describes how the Heavens force the four contrary elements into a "friendship," creating stones and metals based on the balance and proportion of their mixture.</summary>

### DIALOGUE II

...with the elements constrained on all sides, they achieve not only the forms of simple mixtures, but others far more noble and excellent: the living forms. First, they receive vegetative forms <note>original: "uęgetantes"; these are the most basic forms of life responsible for growth and nutrition</note>, by which we see plants sprout, be nourished, and increase in size, and produce others like themselves by an almost divine power through their seeds and branches. In this way, all species of plants are generated; the imperfect ones are called herbs, while the perfect ones are called trees. Among them, one species is granted a more perfect form and a nobler way of acting than another, depending on how much the elements of contrary natures have come together with greater love, more equality, and a more intimate friendship to create that specific composition. This is the **second degree** of the friendship of the four elements.

But if an even more intense and vehement love joins them with greater harmony and equality, they do not only receive the forms of a mixture, nor merely of a nourishing, growing, and generating soul; rather, they are also clothed in the forms of the **sensitive soul** <term>anima sentientis</term> <note>The "sensitive soul" refers to the level of life possessed by animals, allowing for sensation and movement.</note>, which grants them feeling, local motion, imagination, and appetite. By virtue of this friendship, all species of earthly, aquatic, and winged animals come into the light. Some of these, due to their imperfection, participate in no motion and no sense except for touch alone; the more perfect ones, however, are endowed with all the senses and motion itself. One species excels another in its own operation just as much as the elements came together in greater friendship and a more harmonious and equal union to form that species. This is the **third order** of the elements' love.

The **fourth and final degree** of friendship and mutual love of these same simple bodies is said to be when the elements have attained the greatest equality and the highest perfection of which they are capable in their mixing. In this state, they do not only receive the mixed, vegetative, sensitive, and motor forms, but they also deserve to be clothed in a form that is supremely pure and removed from the foul and hideous uncleanness of these generatable and corruptible bodies. This form, which belongs to the celestial and eternal bodies, is called the **intelligent soul** <note>original: "anima intelligens"</note>, and among all lower things, it is found in the human species alone.

<margin>
The reason why, of all things that are born and die, only man deserves to receive an eternal and intellectual form.
</margin>

SOPHIA: But why was man alone—since he was formed from the same contrary and corruptible elements as everything else—granted by the supreme God an eternal and intellectual form, proper to the celestial bodies, contrary to the common law of other mixtures?

<margin>
In the composition of man, the elements were reduced to the greatest equality and highest unity.
</margin>

PHILO: Because in man alone, the mutual love of the elements is of such equality, unity, and perfection that all their discords and enmities are suppressed and calmed. Being joined together in one harmony, they produce a body that is free and released from any kind of contradiction or opposition, as similar as possible to a celestial body that lacks all contraries. For this reason, man is clothed in that intelligible and eternal form which alone deserves to give life to the heavenly bodies.

SOPHIA: I do not recall ever hearing of this kind of "friendship" of the elements before. I only know that according to the greater or lesser balance of their temperament <term>complexio</term> <note>A technical term in medieval medicine and philosophy referring to the specific "blend" or balance of the four humors and elements in a body.</note>, the bodies composed of them are granted greater or lesser perfection.

<margin>
The temperament of the elements is not without merit called their friendship.
</margin>

PHILO: The temperament of the elements *is* their friendship. For how could contraries, having set aside their hatreds and bitter enmities, come together as one and live together in harmony, unless a very great love and mutual friendship intervened? Some have called this friendship harmony, concert, and concord; and rightly so, for just as enmity seems to cause discord, so friendship produces concord.

<margin>
Empedocles attributed the birth and death of lower things to six causes: namely, the four elements, friendship, and enmity.
</margin>

From this, that man Empedocles <note>A Greek Pre-Socratic philosopher who famously proposed that the universe is governed by the two forces of Love (Philia) and Strife (Neikos) acting upon the four elements.</note>, a man of the greatest authority among philosophers, attributed the birth and death of all lower things to six causes: the four elements, friendship, and enmity. For in truth, the friendship of the four elements, which are naturally contrary to one another, produces all the generations of the bodies composed of them, and their enmity brings about all the deaths of these...

<meta>catchword: deaths of these...</meta>

He concludes that the human soul is unique because the elements in the human body reach a state of perfect harmony that mimics the eternal heavens.</summary>

# LEONE EBREO ON LOVE

<margin>
A summary of what has been said thus far.
</margin>

...produces <note>original: "efficit"; the first syllable likely appeared on the previous page</note> corruption. For just as the four degrees of love we enumerated above—which are seen in the embraces of the elements—are the causes of the four ways that bodies are composed or generated from them, so too must we understand four identical types of hatred among those same elements, from which the death and dissolution of mixed bodies proceed. Therefore, just as all evil or destruction arises from the hatred and enmity of these four elements, so whatever good or birth there is depends on their love and friendship.

**SOPHIA.** It is with the greatest pleasure of my mind that I have heard you explain, so learnedly and eloquently, these various kinds and reasons for love found in this lower world—a world dedicated to the birth and corruption of things. You have shown it not only in humans, but in beasts, plants, and inanimate mixtures, as well as in the four elements and in that Prime Matter <term>materia prima</term> <note>the fundamental substance that exists before it takes on any specific form</note> common to all things. And I truly perceive that just as one species of animal is a friend to another and delights in its company, while it hates and flees from another, so some species of plants love one another and grow together. Indeed, if they are joined together, they germinate much better and more fruitfully; yet others carry out the greatest enmities among themselves, and if placed near each other, they destroy one another. We also see certain metals born and mixed together in the same vein of the earth, while others are not. The same judgment must be made concerning gems. Furthermore, we see the magnet so greatly cherished and loved by iron that the iron, taking no account of its own heaviness and weight, immediately rushes to find it. In short, I see no body found under the embrace of the heavens that is not affected by some love, desire, or appetite—whether it be natural, sensible, or voluntary—exactly as you have said. 

However, it would seem quite absurd to me if the celestial bodies and those spiritual intellects <note>often called "Intelligences," these were thought to be the spiritual beings that moved the planets and stars</note> were said to love or cherish anything, since none of those affections that belong to these mortal and

Love in the celestial bodies and the intelligent spirits is found to be far more eminent, perfect, and excellent than in these lower things.

perishing bodies ought to be placed in them.

**SOPHIA.** It would be very pleasing to me to learn this. For the principal and most common origin of love seems to be generation <note>the act of being born or produced</note>; since this is entirely alien to eternal things, how can we ever attribute love to them?

**PHILO.** Although they were never born and will never be destroyed, and are truly not subject to birth or death, the generation of these lower things proceeds from the Heavens as if from a true and legitimate father. Just as we have already declared that the mother of this same

->### DIALOGUE II<-

<margin>Heaven is to the earth just as the male is to the female, for it seems to pour forth its most fruitful seed into her.</margin>
**SOPHIA.** By what reasoning does the heaven influence the earth with the power of procreation? **PHILO.** The entire celestial body exists as the male, surrounding and embracing the earth from all sides. The earth herself, although she delights in rest and stability, is nonetheless stirred and awakened by the great motion of her husband, being moved at least a little. In truth, the moisture, the spirit, and the natural heat—namely, water, air, and fire—are set into motion by the masculine movement of the celestial body. In the same way, these three things are stirred in a woman during the "storm" of intercourse by the movement of the male, even if she herself displays no outward bodily motion; rather, she remains quiet and unmoved so that she might better and more conveniently receive the fertile seed of the man.

<margin>The seeds that the earth receives from her celestial spouse are the dews and the rains.</margin>
**SOPHIA.** What sort of seed does the heaven send down into the earth, and how is it able to send it? **PHILO.** The seeds that the earth receives from her celestial spouse are the dews and the rains. By the power of the rays of the Sun, the Moon, and the other planets—as well as the fixed stars—these seeds produce and bring forth all species and all individual bodies composed of the elements in the earth and the sea, following one of those four ways I mentioned above.

<margin>The heaven is compared to the human body. The stars of the eighth sphere are like homogeneous members, while the seven planets, no differently than heterogeneous members, concur in the procreation of dews and rains, which are like the world's semen.</margin>
**SOPHIA.** What things specifically are said to form this most wonderful seed? **PHILO.** The whole heaven, by its continuous motion, is said to form that seed, just as the entire human body commonly contributes to the formation of sperm. And just as our whole body is composed of homogeneous members <note>original: "membris homogeneis"; parts where every piece is the same substance, like bone or gristle</note>—that is, those of the same nature, such as bones, nerves, veins, membranes, and cartilage, besides the flesh that fills the intervening spaces—so the vast mass of the eighth sphere <note>the firmament containing the "fixed" stars</note> is composed of fixed stars of diverse and different natures. These are divided into five magnitudes and a sixth type of "cloudy lights" <note>likely referring to nebulae or the Milky Way</note>, with the substance of a certain transparent body connecting those scattered flames and filling those intermediate places.

<margin>Seven members are especially required for the making of human sperm: the heart, brain, liver, spleen, kidneys, testicles, and penis.</margin>
**SOPHIA.** And what role do the seven planets play in the procreation of this worldly seed? **PHILO.** The seven planets exist as the seven heterogeneous <note>organic or complex parts made of different tissues</note> members, holding the primary roles in the formation of this seed, just as seven specific parts of a human contribute to the generation of sperm.

**SOPHIA.** I pray you, declare them all. **PHILO.** The making of human sperm is first attributed to the heart, which bestows spirit along with natural heat upon it as its form. Next, the brain provides moisture to it as its matter. Thirdly, the liver, by a certain sweet concoction <term>concoctio</term> <note>a Renaissance medical term for the "cooking" or refining of bodily fluids through heat</note> and by contributing a purer part of the blood, renders it finished and elaborated. Fourthly, the spleen, after it has diligently purged it of the dross of black bile <note>original: "atrae bilis"; one of the four humors, associated with melancholy</note> by its inborn power of attraction, makes it thick, sticky, and airy. Fifthly, the kidneys—by a powerful concoction, especially with the addition of yellow bile which is steadily and copiously supplied to them from the gall—communicate to it a certain sharpness, pungency, and heat. Sixthly, the sperm receives its final touch and that divine power of generating from the testicles. Seventhly and in the final place, it is transmitted through the penis into the receiving female.

<margin>The correspondence of the seven mentioned members required for making human sperm with the seven planets in procreating dews and rains, which are like the seeds of the world.</margin>
**SOPHIA.** I have certainly understood very well the way these seven organic members contribute to the generation of human seed. But what correspondence and similarity can they have with the seven planets? **PHILO.** In the same way, the seven planets of the celestial body contribute to the making of the worldly seed. **SOPHIA.** In what manner? **PHILO.** The Sun is the heart of heaven itself, the origin of natural and vital heat, drawing vapors out of the earth and sea. From these vapors, rains and dews—the most fertile seeds of the world—are both generated and, once born, carried down to the earth, both by the power of the solar rays and aspects, and by the change of the four seasons of the year proceeding from the Sun's own motion. The Moon is the celestial brain, set over the seminal moistures; because of her changes, the winds change and rains descend. She is said to generate the nocturnal moisture and dew, which is the most suitable food for nourishing seeds. Jupiter is the celestial liver, doing much for the generation of waters, the healthfulness of the air, and the fitness of the seasons by his mild and temperate heat and moisture. Saturn is the spleen of heaven itself, which by its inborn cold and dryness...
