...thickens the heavier vapors and makes the waters icy cold; it stirs up winds suited to bringing down rain. It also tempers and blunts the excessive power of heat that thins and dissolves bodies. Mars in the heavens corresponds to the gall bladder <note>original: "felis", likely "fellis"</note> and the kidneys; with its sharp heat, it greatly aids the rising of vapors and melts the waters, making them flowing, thin, penetrating, and endowed with a "seminal heat" most suitable for fertility. This prevents the excessive cold of Saturn and the Moon from making the seed unfit or useless for the generation of things due to a lack of heat. One might not wrongly call Venus the "testicles" of the heaven; for she brings the greatest impetus to generating the best waters, which are quite suitable for making things fertile, because she was granted a certain tempered moisture, perfectly refined, and best suited for the generation of earthly things. Hence, because of the proportion and proximity 
<margin>Reason why the poets imagined that Mars and many Venus loved each other.</margin>
of the kidneys and testicles found in the making of human seed, the poets imagined that Mars and Venus loved each other most. For one bestows a sharp heat, while the other grants a certain praiseworthy moisture to the seed itself. Celestial Mercury can rightly be called the penis <note>original: "coles"</note>, appearing now moving forward, now backward <note>A reference to "retrograde" motion in astronomy.</note>; sometimes he stirs up rains, and at other times he suppresses them. He is especially excited by the approach of the Sun and the aspects of the Moon, just as the penis itself is seen to be extended and erected because of the desire and impulse of the heart, as well as the imagination and memory of the brain.

<margin>
Heaven and earth are seen as spouses, and both love the things generated from them just as parents love their children; likewise, generated things seem to love heaven and earth as children love their parents.
</margin>
Therefore, you can now see, **SOPHIA**, that heaven itself is most loving of the earth, just like a spouse, since it moves with all its members—both its organs and its tissues <term>homogeneous members: tissues like bone or flesh that are the same throughout, as opposed to complex organs</term>—and strives with all its strength to pour its seed into her, and in her to generate and produce so many and such diverse things. Do you not see that such diligent care and such wonderful providence could not continue unless it were preserved by the most fervent and perfect love of the heaven (as the generating husband) toward the earth and the other elements, and "prime matter" itself (as his own woman, lover, or wife)? And unless heaven maintained a fatherly benevolence and charity toward generated things (as its own children) in both nourishing and preserving them? Earth too, and matter, seem to love heaven as a beloved spouse or lover from whom they receive many benefits. Generated things also are seen to love heaven itself as a caring father, providing and looking out for the health of his children.

Therefore, by the bond of this mutual love, the entirety of physical bodies is joined and bound together, and the world itself is stabilized and adorned. What clearer or more effective argument can be brought to demonstrate the community of love than this? **SOPHIA.** The marital and mutual love of earth and heaven is indeed wonderful; and certainly the specific conditions of wife and husband found in the earth and heaven induce no less admiration, along with the seven planets having the greatest similarity and correspondence with the seven nobler members that come together for the procreation of human seed. But I remember having understood elsewhere that, according to the opinion of astrologers, the seven planets refer to and represent seven members of man—not those that serve generation as you just listed, but rather those external ones located in the head that serve sensible and internal knowledge. **PHILO.**

<margin>
The seven planets retain some correspondence and similarity with the seven parts of our head serving sense and knowledge.
</margin>
It is indeed truly said that the seven planets signify the seven parts of our head serving sense and knowledge. For the Sun seems to represent the right eye, and the Moon the left, since both exist as the "eyes of heaven." Saturn is said to represent the right ear, and Jupiter the left (or sometimes the reverse). Mars is declared to refer to the right nostril, and Venus to the left (or vice versa). Mercury presides over the tongue and mouth; for he was designated the Prince of eloquence and learning. But this is no obstacle to the fact that, as astrologers testify, the dominion of the seven planets also extends to the seven members of the human body working in the preparation of seed, which I listed above—

The liver and spleen, the moderators of the seed, are the ears with which it hears, and are called Saturn and Jupiter. The penis transmitting the seed is the Mercurial tongue, directing and governing knowledge. In man, however, and in other perfect animals—although images and certain likenesses of heaven exist—it was necessary for the members of cognition to be separated and distinguished from the members of generation: the former placed in the higher seat of the head, and the latter thrust down to the lower place of the body, yet with their agreement and proportion maintained. **SOPHIA.** So far, I acquiesce to what you have said. ->### LEO HEBRAEUS ON LOVE ###<-

<margin>Pythagoras used to attribute the six differences of a living being—namely, right and left—to the heaven.</margin>
...used to attribute to a living being: he called the half of the heavens extending from the equator to the Arctic pole (which we call the North) the "right" side. He did so because he observed that from the equator toward this pole, the stars placed in the eighth sphere <note>In the ancient Ptolemaic system, the eighth sphere contained the "fixed stars" as opposed to the wandering planets.</note> were far more numerous, larger, and brighter than those seen from the equator toward the other pole. Furthermore, he believed these stars produced more and more excellent effects in the northern region of the earth situated beneath them. The other half of the heaven, however, which extends from the equatorial line to the Antarctic pole (unknown to us <note>At the time of these classical theories, the Southern Hemisphere was largely unexplored by Europeans.</note>), he called the "left" side.

<margin>Aristotle applied all six differences of position to the heaven, just as if it were a most perfect living being.</margin>
*Aristotle*, however, agreeing and confirming that the heaven is a certain perfect living being, did not only attribute to it those two aforementioned animal parts (right and left). Beyond these, he also assigned the other differences of a perfect living being: namely, the front and back (called the face and the rear), as well as the upper and lower (called the head and the feet). For in a perfect animal, all six of these parts are undoubtedly seen as divided and distinct. The right and left parts presuppose the other four, and could never be found without them: for right and left are the parts that measure the width of a living body; the upper and lower (namely the head and feet) are the parts defining its length (and length, by the order of nature, precedes width); and the front and back (the face and the rear) are the parts defining the depth of a sentient body, which dimension exists as the foundation of both length and width.

<margin>Aristotle judged that right and left in the heaven should be determined not by the two poles, as Pythagoras did, but rather by the East and West. Aristotle depicted the entire celestial body in the form of an animal.</margin>
Therefore, since right and left are found in the heaven, as *Pythagoras* himself felt, it is necessary that it also be endowed with the other four parts of the remaining two dimensions: that is, with a head and feet designating length, and a face and shoulders designating depth. *Aristotle* adds further: that neither our pole should be called "right," nor the other "left," as *Pythagoras* wished. This is because the difference between these two parts, and the excellence by which one surpasses the other, is not found in the nature of the celestial body itself, but rather in its position and the relationship it has toward us. Perhaps even in that half unknown to us, the heaven abounds and overflows with a greater number of stars, and the earth with more regions—a fact which, in our own time, the wondrous voyages of the *Portuguese* and *Spanish* <note>original: "Lusitanorum & Hispanorum"</note> have partially shown to be true. Led by these reasons, the Prince of the Peripatetics <note>Aristotle; the "Peripatetics" were his followers, named for his habit of walking while teaching.</note> placed the "right" in the East and the "left" in the West. He depicted the entire celestial body in the form of an animal, having its head at the Antarctic pole (always hidden from us) and its feet at the Arctic or Northern pole. By this reasoning, the right side extends toward the East and the left toward the West. The "face" of the heaven is said to be the upper, visible hemisphere, while the "back" is called the lower and hidden hemisphere. Therefore, since the whole and universal world is a "man," a perfect living being encompassing both male and female together, and it is established that the heaven is one of these two—complete and absolute in all its parts—we must surely assign the masculine and virile sex to the heaven, and the feminine sex to the earth, the other elements, and primary matter. We must conclude, as we said above, that both were joined and bound forever in conjugal love and mutual benevolence by God, the Best and Greatest.

**SOPHIA.** I am greatly pleased to have learned this similarity between the heaven and a living being, and the six innate and differing parts of an animal, which you have so aptly and skillfully assigned to the celestial body, following the doctrine of *Aristotle*.

<margin>Plants seem to have obtained only two differences of position: upper and lower, namely the root and the foliage.</margin>
However, I clearly perceive that plants participate only in the difference between the head and the legs: since the root serves as the head, and the foliage as the feet. In this upper and lower part, they represent an inverted animal:

<margin>A plant represents a certain inverted animal.</margin>
the remaining four differences can by no means be fitted to them, for they are not seen to have a face, nor a back, nor a right, nor a left side.

<margin>She brings forward that most difficult question concerning the East and West of the Heaven.</margin>
But from the fact that *Aristotle* calls the East the "right" and the West the "left" of the heaven, a certain doubt occurs to me: for the rising and the setting are not one and the same for all inhabitants of the earth...

He also touches upon how the Age of Discovery voyages are expanding classical understanding of the globe.</summary>

### DIALOGUE II ###

->K 3<-

...it seems to be; on the contrary, our east is called west by those who live beneath us and are referred to as the <term>Antipodes</term> <note>Literally "those with feet opposite," referring to people living on the opposite side of the globe.</note>. Our sunset is their sunrise. Because of the round shape of the world, individual parts of the heaven from east to west are called "east" by some inhabitants of the earth and "west" by others. Which, then, of these countless sunrises will be worthy of being called the "right hand" of heaven? And why should one be more deserving of this name than another? Furthermore, if any sunrise at all could be called "right," then one and the same place would exist as both "right" and "left" simultaneously. Do not leave this significant question unsolved.

*PHILO.* The difficulty you have proposed certainly demands a more difficult solution.

<margin>He refutes the opinion of some who argued that the celestial sunrise and sunset should be centered on those who inhabit the middle of the habitable earth.</margin>
Some say that the celestial sunrise, which should be called the "right," ought to refer to those who inhabit the middle of the long stretch of the habitable earth, bounded on either side by the east and the west. They persuade themselves that only half of the earth's length is uncovered by water and inhabited, while the other half is entirely surrounded by water and uninhabitable. *SOPHIA.* Is this opinion true? *PHILO.* Not at all. For it has been discovered that the greatest portion of the world traveled from east to west stands above the waters, and that individual regions have their own sunrises. Neither of these can be called "more right" than the other, especially since the same part that rises for one region sets for another. From this diversity, it would follow that one and the same sunrise would happen to be both right and left, just as you have so excellently deduced. For this reason, others have said that the sign of <term>Aries</term> <note>The Ram, marking the Spring Equinox in the Northern Hemisphere.</note> should be called the right hand of heaven, and the sign of <term>Libra</term> <note>The Scales, marking the Autumnal Equinox.</note> the left. *SOPHIA.* By what reasoning were they led to this? *PHILO.* Because when the Sun runs through Aries, plants sprout and turn green, and the world is renewed and adorned; thus, the great power of that planet <note>In the pre-Copernican system, the Sun was classified as a "planet" or "wandering star."</note> is shown and declared to the human race. But when the Sun occupies Libra, plants wither and the world itself grows old; the empire of the Sun seems to diminish, and its strength is seen to be broken and weakened.

<margin>He refutes the opinion of others who thought the sign of Aries should be called the right and the sign of Libra the left of heaven.</margin>
*SOPHIA.* Even if this were perhaps granted to them, Aries should not be called the "right" nor Libra the "left" for that reason. Neither the former always stays in the east, nor the latter in the west; rather, both of them are seen indifferently, now at the sunrise and now at the sunset. When it rises for one person, it sets for another. Aristotle, however, always calls the east the "right" part of heaven and the west the "left." *PHILO.* You have rightly refuted their opinion, which is proven false by an even greater fact: the Sun entering Aries does not show itself as kind and beneficial to all inhabitants of the earth. For those who inhabit the other half of the earth beyond the equator—who always have the <term>Antarctic pole</term> <note>The South Pole.</note> high above them and are called the <term>Antichthones</term> <note>A classical term for "dwellers on the opposite earth," or the Southern Hemisphere.</note>—receive the use and benefit of spring when the Sun is in Libra, which is when it begins to approach them. They feel the discomforts of autumn when the Sun passes through Aries, for it then deserts and leaves them, producing events in those regions that are different and contrary to ours. By this reasoning, the same part of heaven would be called both "right" and "left" depending on whether it referred to us or to them. But in a living animal, the right and left are always seen to be right and left, no matter the perspective. *SOPHIA.* That is certainly true. Indeed, I remember understanding that those who have settled their homes beyond the <term>torrid zone</term> <note>The tropics; ancient geography often held that the heat at the equator was an impassable barrier.</note> toward the south pole truly enjoy spring while we feel autumn, and are vexed by the cold of autumn while the warmth of spring soothes us. Nevertheless, Philo, I beg you again and again to bring some solution to the difficulty I proposed. *PHILO.* The commentators of Aristotle could think of no other solutions besides the two already mentioned. Since they recognized the weakness of both, they abandoned the rest and chose the one that faced fewer objections. You, Sophia, should rest your mind upon the opinion and authority of these most learned men. *SOPHIA.* I do not follow the genius of others, but my own; and I feel that each of the two explained solutions is [unsatisfactory] not only to me, but also to you...

...is hardly satisfying. So that I may be convinced, you must either admit that your Aristotle was wrong, or you must devise a better solution than the ones you offered before.

**PHILO.** Since my mind has long been devoted to you and focused on your every word, I must satisfy all your requests, and I am compelled to open all the thoughts of my soul to you 
<margin>The true solution to the proposed difficulty.</margin>
readily and generously. I believe Aristotle should be understood in another way; he explained with great subtlety the functions of the six aforementioned directions—both in the heavens and 
<margin>Right and Left in the Heavens, according to Aristotle's opinion, should not be referred to any fixed or defined part of the celestial body, but rather to two different and opposite types of celestial motions. Thus, the diurnal motion—the motion of the <term>Primum Mobile</term> <note>The "First Moved" sphere in Aristotelian cosmology, which carries all the stars from East to West every 24 hours.</note>—is called "right," while the motion of the planets is most rightly called "left."</margin>
in every "perfect" animal. He left it in writing that the "vertex" or the head—where the length of an animal begins—is that part from which the first origin of motion proceeds. For from the head, or the brain, the nerves and the spirits that provide motion undoubtedly descend. He says the "right" is that part which is seen to move first, as happens in almost all men. Finally, the "face" or the front part is named as that toward which the motion of the right side tends. The remaining three directions are the opposites of these and serve the motion in an opposite way. **SOPHIA.** I follow this very well. But let us get to solving the difficulty. **PHILO.** Aristotle says that the "right" of heaven is that part from which the Sun, the other planets, and all the stars are seen to rise, and for that reason, it has claimed for itself the name "East." In my opinion, the philosopher judges that this name should not be granted to any single, fixed, or determined part of the celestial body; rather, he thinks it can be applied to all parts without distinction, specifically because they "rise" and proceed toward the west. This does not apply, however, insofar as they move in the contrary direction—the planets' own motion—which strives from west to east. For this kind of <term>erratic motion</term> <note>The slow movement of planets (the "wanderers") against the background of the fixed stars.</note> is "left," and takes its beginning from the left side, much like the left hand of any of us. Conversely, the other motion from east to west—regardless of which celestial parts or revolutions we consider—is rightly called "right" and said to begin from the right. Since the "vertex" of heaven is placed in the <term>Antarctic</term> <note>Aristotle argued the South Pole was the "top" of the universe because motion originates there.</note> and the "legs" in the Arctic, as Aristotle says, it is absolutely necessary that since the entire heaven and all its parts are always led around from East to West, the diurnal motion begins from the right, and the erratic motion from the left. The "face" is the upper hemisphere lying between the East and the West, which the heaven seeks with its "right" motion. The "back," however, is said to be those parts of the celestial body that lie hidden behind the East and are divided from the visible parts by the intervention of the horizon line. 
<margin>In heaven, only two differences of position—namely the upper and the lower—are physically divided and separate. The other four differences are distinguished not by physical reality, but only by the logic of motion.</margin>
**SOPHIA.** I am very glad to have understood this. But this solution seems to imply that in the heavens, only two parts—the upper and lower, or the head and legs—are actually divided and separate, which are indeed called the poles. The other four directions are distinguished not by physical reality, but only by the logic of motion. Have I perceived this correctly? **PHILO.** Most correctly indeed. **SOPHIA.** But what is the reason for such a great difference—that in animals all six parts physically differ, but in the heavens they do not?

**PHILO.** Naturally, this happens because an animal walks in a straight line from one place to another, and its parts of length and width physically differ and are distinct. In the celestial body, 
<margin>The reason why all six differences of position in living animals are physically different, while in Heaven only two differ, and the other four are distinguished only by the logic of motion.</margin>
which revolves into itself and returns in a circular motion, it is necessary that those four parts physically coincide. They are assigned to every portion of heaven indifferently in a certain succession, and are distinguished only by the logic of their position and the path of the motion itself. But the "vertex" and "feet" of heaven—namely, the two poles—because they do not change and one is never transferred into the place of the other, but they remain stable and unmoved forever, they are physically different and divided, just as we see happens in animals. **SOPHIA.** But if the same sign of the zodiac is both East and West when referred to different provinces, it will undoubtedly follow that the same part is both right and left. **PHILO.** You do not perceive it correctly; for even if physically the same portion of heaven rises for certain peoples and sets for others, nevertheless, by the logic of the motion which the whole celestial mass and its individual parts...

### DIALOGUE II ###

...they resolve this by stating that this portion commonly arises when it exists in its own East: and by reason of that motion, it always remains on the right, and is never changed to the left. This is because neither the whole heaven, nor any of its parts, is ever seen to move in any opposite or contrary motion to this right-handed motion in its incredibly swift course, nor is it seen to retreat or run back. This is unlike what we see happening with the <term>seven wandering stars</term> <note>The seven "planets" of the ancient world: the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>, whose own proper motion is called "left." They are said to move left because they run back and retreat; by this second motion, they resist the first and right-handed motion of the celestial body, thereby producing and preserving the diversity of lower and contrary things, and their continuous generation.

**SOPHIA.** You have conducted yourself excellently and have most skillfully untied the knot I proposed. But I desire to learn this from you in addition: for what reason have the philosophers said that man alone exists as a certain marvelous <term>image</term> <note>original: "simulachrum"</note> of the entire universe? I mean an image both of the lower world—always shaken by birth and death—and also of the celestial, as well as the spiritual, angelic, and divine worlds. 

<margin>He demonstrates that man was called a <term>microcosm</term> <note>original: "μικροκόσμον"</note>, or "lesser world," by the wise.</margin>

**PHILO.** We shall depart somewhat from our purpose of speaking about the community of love; but because this also seems to be deduced from the argument of our previous discussion, I will attempt to declare it to you briefly and concisely. All those three worlds that you enumerated—the mortal, the celestial, and the intelligible—are included in man as if in a <term>microcosm</term> <note>From the Greek "mikros" (small) and "kosmos" (world/order).</note> by a certain divine craftsmanship. They are found to differ in him not only in power and action, but are also distinguished by the members, parts, and locations of the human body.

**SOPHIA.** Explain each one separately.

<margin>The human body is divided into three principal parts, which correspond by a certain wonderful proportion to the three worlds: namely, the elemental, the celestial, and the angelic.</margin>

**PHILO.** The human body is divided into three parts, no differently than the universal world: of which the first occupies the lowest seat, the second the middle, and the third the highest. The first part, taking its beginning from a certain membrane or small cloth-like tissue that divides our middle body crosswise—which is called the <term>diaphragm</term>—extends down to the legs. The second part, placed above the first and beginning from the diaphragm, ascends upward to the head. The third, the highest of all, is the head itself.

<margin>A comparison of the lowest part of the human body, which serves nutrition and generation, with the elemental world or these inanimate organs.</margin>

All those members that serve nutrition and generation inhabit the first seat: such as the stomach, liver, gall, spleen, <term>mesentery</term> <note>The fold of membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall.</note>, intestines, kidneys, testicles, and penis. This part of the human body can be compared with the lower world, which is subject to generation. 

<margin>The four humors are seen to be very similar to the four elements.</margin>

For just as in that world the four elements—fire, air, water, and earth—are generated from <term>primary matter</term>, so in this lowest part, the four humors are themselves produced from food (which can be called the "primary matter" of all four humors). These are: **yellow bile**, which is hot, dry, and subtle, being very similar to fire; **blood**, which is hot, moist, and perfectly tempered, agreeing with air; **phlegm**, which is cold and moist, representing water; and the **melancholic humor** <note>Also known as "black bile."</note>, which is cold and dry, corresponding to earth. 

And just as animals are made from the four elements—which, besides being nourished and growing, also participate in sense and motion—and just as plants are made (which, though lacking sense and motion, are only nourished and grow), and other types of inanimate mixtures come into the light (which, lacking the faculties of sense, motion, nutrition, and growth, can rightly be called the "dregs" of the elements, such as stones, mushrooms, salt, and metals), so also from the four humors procreated in this first and lowest seat, certain members are made that are nourished, grow, feel, and move: such as the nerves, membranes, muscles, and brawny parts of the arms. Others are produced that are by their own nature destitute of sense and motion, yet are nourished and grow: such as bones, cartilages, and veins. 

Furthermore, from food and the four humors, other things are generated that participate in no sense or motion, nor are they nourished or grow, but exist as the dregs and superfluities of food and humors: such as dung, urine, sweat, nasal mucus, and earwax. And just as in the lower world certain living things are generated from rot, many of which are infected with poison, so also from corrupt humors, many species of diseases proceed, some of which are like poison...

...form the human being itself. And just as in the lower world—through the intervention of celestial power—that remarkable and spiritual animal called "man" is born, so too from the more refined and subtle vapor of the <term>humors</term> <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile) believed to determine health and temperament.</note>, thin and pure spirits are generated. <margin>The remarkable proportion and similarity of the middle part of the human body—assigned to the heart and both lungs—to the celestial world.</margin>
**PHILO.** The second seat of the human body, which is located above the <term>diaphragm</term> <note>original: "septum transuersum"</note> and reaches up to the throat, was assigned to the spiritual members: the heart and both lungs, right and left. In the right lung, three distinct and separate lobes are seen, and in the left, two. This second portion of our body is seen to correspond to the celestial world.

<margin>The heart in man is seen to be most similar to the Eighth Sphere and the First Mover in heaven.</margin>
The heart is very similar to the <term>Eighth Sphere</term> <note>The celestial sphere containing the fixed stars.</note>, which shines with almost innumerable stars, and to that portion of the entire heaven that exists above it, called the <term>First Mover</term> <note>original: "primum mobile"; the outermost moving sphere that imparts motion to all others.</note>. This First Mover grants equal, regular, and circular motion to all others; by its perpetual and unfailing movement, it preserves all the bodies of the universe. Every other motion, whether of the planets or the elements, derives its origin from it, provided it is continuous. For the same reason, the human heart always moves in a circle and uniformly; it never rests, and by its continuous and equal motion, it provides life to the entire body. It is the primary origin of the unfailing breath of the lungs and the constant pulse of all the arteries. In the heart reside all the spirits and all human powers, not unlike the sparkling stars in the eighth sphere, of which some are large, some medium-sized, and some small; indeed, such a great multitude of celestial forms is observed there.

<margin>The reason why the seven planets are called "wandering."</margin>
Immediately following the starry sphere and the First Mover are the seven <term>wandering planets</term> <note>The Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>, so called for this reason: because they seem to "err" or wander in their motion. This is because they are thought to sometimes move straight forward, sometimes backward, sometimes quickly, and sometimes slowly; yet all follow the First Mover.

<margin>The two lungs in the human body are seen to correspond perfectly with the seven planets in the celestial body.</margin>
Similarly, the lungs are like the attendants and ministers of the heart, serving its needs through their frequent and constant motion. Since they are like the "sponges" of the celestial part of our body, they sometimes dilate and sometimes contract, using a respiration that is now hurried, now slow—doubtless imitating the unequal motion of the wandering stars in this way. And just as the two most famous lights of the world, the Sun and the Moon, are said to be the leaders of the seven planets' care for the universe—with three planets (Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn) placed in the higher region along with the Sun, yet above it; and the remaining two (Venus and Mercury) placed in the lower region together with the Moon, yet above it—so the right and principal lung represents the Sun, and is therefore distinguished into three parts <note>The three lobes of the right lung.</note> which are contained by it like parts of a whole. The left lung, representing the Moon, is divided into two portions <note>The two lobes of the left lung.</note> like a certain whole. All of these, when collected together, complete the number seven <note>Counting the five lobes and the two lungs themselves to match the seven planets.</note>. Furthermore, just as the celestial world continually rules and preserves the lower world by its light and motion—communicating vital heat, spirit, and motion through the intervention of its rays—so the heart, together with both lungs, protects and governs the entire body by sharing heat, vital spirits, and its continuous motion through the intervening arteries. Therefore, the similarity between the heavens and the second seat of the human body is seen to be perfect and fitting in every way. **SOPHIA.** The correspondence between the spiritual members and the celestial world—which influences this lower world with its divine power in a marvelous way—is approved by me, having been explained by you no less eloquently than learnedly. Now [describe] the proportion of the spiritual world with the human body...

# DIALOGUE II #
<page-num>393</page-num>
<header>DIALOGUE II. 393</header>

...let us see the proportion.

<margin>
A very learned comparison of the human head with the spiritual and angelic world.
The spiritual world is divided into three orders: soul, intellect, and divinity.
In man, the soul (the senses residing in the brain as their first origin) corresponds to the **Soul of the World**; the **potential intellect** corresponds to the **Universal Intellect**; and the **active intellect** corresponds to **Divinity** itself by a wonderful proportion.
</margin>
**PHILO.** The human head, which is the highest part of the body, is the image of the spiritual world. According to the opinion of the divine **Plato**, with **Aristotle** not disagreeing, the spiritual world is divided into three orders: soul, intellect, and divinity. The **Soul** <note>original: "anima"</note> is that from which the movement of the heavens proceeds, and which guards and governs the nature of the lower world, just as nature itself governs primary matter. The human brain represents this, along with its two faculties that provide sense and voluntary motion; both of these are contained within our sensing soul, which is most similar to the **Soul of the World** <note>original: "animae mundi"; the Neoplatonic concept of a spiritual force that animates the physical universe.</note> that governs and moves the bodies of the universe. Next, the **potential intellect** <note>original: "intellectus potestatis"; also known as the possible intellect, it refers to the human mind's capacity to receive and process knowledge.</note> is situated in man; this is his final form, and in a certain proportion, it corresponds to the **Universal Intellect**, in which all the angelic minds are found. Finally, the **active intellect** <note>original: "intellectus agens"; the faculty that illuminates the mind and turns potential knowledge into actual understanding.</note> also resides in man himself; if the potential intellect is ever joined with it, it immediately becomes actual and most perfect, full of God, and united with the most sacred divinity. Indeed, when this **actual intellect** is found in man, it can be likened in part to the divine principle from which all things take their origin, and toward which the entire universe is directed as its ultimate end, finally resting in it. These things we have discussed familiarly among ourselves concerning the correspondence of man with the whole universe—adding the reason why he was called a **microcosm** <note>original: "microcosmos"; meaning "little world," the idea that man is a miniature reflection of the entire universe.</note> by the ancients—seem to be enough for you, **Sophia**. Some other similarities also intervene, but to recount them all would be too long and foreign to our current purpose. What we have just said will be of greatest use to us when we speak of the birth and origin of love; for then you will understand how all things seen in the world do not follow one another with love by chance—whether the highest following the lowest, or the lower following the superior—because all things concur together like parts to compose a single, whole, and perfect body.

**SOPHIA.** The flow and connection of our speech seems to have carried us so far that we have wandered somewhat from our original purpose. Let us now return to it. If I have understood correctly, Philo, you have shown with how much love heaven is held toward the earth—following the likeness of a man begetting—

<margin>
An epilogue of the things said so far.
The vehement and wonderful love of the heavens toward all things composed of the earth and the matter of the elements, like that of a father toward his legitimate sons.
</margin>
and toward the primary matter of the elements, as if toward his own woman or wife receiving his seed. From this, there subsequently arises the second love of heaven toward all things composed of the earth and elemental matter, like the love of a father toward his legitimate sons. Indeed, the greatest proof of this is the immense care and diligence we see heaven employ in preserving, nourishing, and rewarding them; for it sends down rain-water onto the earth to nourish the plants, and produces plants as suitable food for animals, referring both of these ultimately to the utility and convenience of man, who is like the eldest and most excellent son. Furthermore, heaven creates the series and succession of the four seasons of the year—spring, summer, autumn, and winter—providing in this way for the birth, preservation, and growth of things, and affecting the air with various qualities to sustain the life of these lower creatures and to bring their temperatures back to a praiseworthy moderation.

<margin>
The zeal and benevolence of lower things toward Heaven, as children toward a common parent.
</margin>
That these lower things also love heaven as a true and most pious parent is proven most strongly by the fact that animals are seen to be joyful and cheerful as the Sun approaches and the day dawns; just as, conversely, they are seen returning to their own homes sad when night comes on and obscures the splendor of heaven with its shadows. I am not unaware that this difficult and illustrious matter could be treated by you even more fruitfully and copiously; but what you have said so far about the mutual and conjugal benevolence of heaven and earth—and about the paternal and maternal charity of both toward created things as toward common children—and about the love of the offspring toward the earth and heaven as common parents—seems to me to be more than enough. Now I would vehemently desire to know this: whether the celestial bodies, besides the love with which they pursue the lower world, love each other mutually and in turn? For since the birth [of things]...

# LEO HEBRAEUS ON LOVE #
<page-num>394</page-num>
<header>LEO HEBRAEUS ON LOVE,</header>

...[offspring] would be judged the most powerful cause of love, and these things are in no way subject to it: no reciprocal love, and no mutual benevolence, would seem to intervene between them for this reason.

<margin>
The Heavens pursue not only lower things, but also one another with the greatest love and remarkable benevolence.
</margin>
**PHILO.** Even if the heavens are devoid of reciprocal and mutual procreation, they are not therefore deprived of perfect and reciprocating love: which is chiefly proven by their concord and harmonic agreement <note>original: "concordia & harmonica eorum conuenientia"</note>, proceeding from true friendship and true love. For if you, O **Sophia**, were ever to consider the concord and harmony of the motions of the celestial bodies: both those that rush with the greatest speed from the east to the west <note>The diurnal motion of the whole sky.</note>, and others that, on the contrary, move from the west to the east at a more relaxed and slower pace—some slowly, others most slowly—and the way in which they sometimes move forward, sometimes backward, and sometimes appear to stand firm and unmoved at the points of progression and regression; and how they sometimes travel toward the north, sometimes toward the south, and sometimes through the middle of the zodiac itself; and how the Sun, alone among all the planets, never departs from the middle and straight path of the zodiac, nor ever deflects its journey toward the north or the south; likewise if you were ever to comprehend in thought the number of the celestial spheres, and their various and diverse motions, measures, forms, positions, their own poles, and the **eccentrics** and **epicycles** <term>eccentrics and epicycles: mathematical models used in ancient astronomy to explain why planets seem to speed up, slow down, or move in loops; they involve circles whose centers are offset from the Earth.</term> revolved around their own centers which are different from the center of the world, now ascending, now descending: and if, moreover, you were to penetrate into the force and virtue of the two motions of the Sun, the eastern and the western: and if you were to embrace in your mind many other things besides, which pertain to celestial knowledge and which (lest we seem too wordy) shall be wrapped in silence by us: you would surely be struck with amazement at the marvelous harmony of diverse bodies and different motions concordant among themselves, and at the musical concord; and you would celebrate the Governor of the universe with the highest praises. For what greater or more evident judgment of mutual love and mutual benevolence of the celestial bodies can be brought forward than such great concord and agreement preserved and continued in such manifold diversity and difference?

<margin>
The concord and harmony of celestial motions.
</margin>
<margin>
The most elegant opinion of **Pythagoras** concerning the sweetest harmony and musical concord of celestial motions.
</margin>
Whence it was not without merit that **Pythagoras** said that the motions of the celestial bodies produce excellent and sweetest voices, responding and consenting to one another in a marvelous way by harmonic proportion and musical art: he declared that this celestial concord distributes to all things weights, numbers, and measures suited to their natures by a certain and most just Law; he assigned to individual spheres and individual planets their own tone and their own voice, and most skillfully declared the harmony proceeding from them all.

<margin>
The reason why celestial harmony cannot be perceived by human ears was usually attributed by **Pythagoras** both to the vast distance and to continuous habit.
</margin>
As to why a concord of this kind is neither heard nor perceived by us, he attributed the reason and cause to the vast distance intervening between heaven and the human race: or he brought forward continuous habit, which does not allow that divine sound to be felt by us, just as it is said to happen to those who dwell by the sea, who, because of long custom, are unable to hear the enormous crash of the waves, which is most distinctly perceived by others who have recently come to the shore. Since, therefore, all concord proceeds from love and friendship, and that concord is seen to be greater, more stable, and more perfect in the celestial bodies than in the lower ones, it surely follows that a greater and more perfect love and friendship is found in those than in these.

**SO.** The common concord and mutual agreement of the heavens seems to me to be an effect and a certain sign rather than the cause of their love. But I would vehemently desire to understand the reason for the reciprocating benevolence of the celestial bodies: for since no procreation and no succession produced by the help of generation can be attributed to them—which indeed is judged to be the most powerful cause of mutual love among animals and men—I perceive no other of the reasons which can be suited to them quite aptly: no voluntary benefit bestowed by one upon another, because things pertaining to the heavens always observe one and the same tenor...

<summary>Philo argues that the complex yet harmonious movements of the stars and planets are proof of a "perfect and reciprocating love" between celestial bodies, invoking Pythagoras's theory of the music of the spheres. Sophia agrees that this harmony exists but questions what the underlying cause of this love could be, since celestial bodies do not procreate like humans.</summary>

# DIALOGUE II #
<page-num>395</page-num>
<header>DIALOGUE II.</header>

...[matter]; nor any agreement of species: because I remember often understanding that neither species, nor genus, nor individual <term>species, genus, individual</term><note>These are the hierarchical categories of Aristotelian logic used to classify all things.</note> is properly found in them. For even if they perhaps participate in the heavens, each of the celestial bodies was allotted its own proper species, different from every other; much less is there a social bond. For when the series and order of the celestial motions are diligently perceived and considered, we see those divine fires sometimes joined and sometimes separated; yet neither can a conjunction <note>original: "coniunctio"</note> bring about a new love between them, nor can a separation dissolve their former friendship. This is because in the heavens, these things are effected only by the order of nature, with no inclination or propensity of the will intervening.

**PHILO.** Although we cannot quite fit any of those five reasons—which join both humans and beasts in mutual friendship—to the celestial world, we shall perhaps find in it those two reasons that belong to the human race alone.

**SOPHIA.** How so?

**PHILO.** The chief reason for the love of the celestial bodies is a similarity of nature <note>original: "naturae similitudo"</note>, which in humans was called by us earlier an "agreement of temperament." 
<margin>The reason why celestial bodies pursue each other with mutual love and mutual benevolence seems to be twofold: one taken and derived from similarity of nature, the other from some remarkable virtue of the celestial bodies.</margin>
Among the heavens, planets, and stars, there exists such a similarity of nature and essence that they correspond to one another in their motions and actions with such proportion that their entire multitude and diversity conspire into a certain harmonic unity <note>original: "harmonicam quandam... unitatem"</note>. For this reason, they seem to be various members of one and the same perfect and organic body, rather than distinct and separate bodies. And just as from different voices—one deep, another high—a complete and sweet-sounding song is formed, and if one of them fails or errs, that entire concord and harmony is dissolved; so too, from the celestial bodies—differing both in size and in the speed or slowness of their motions—a certain musical proportion and unity is established because of their affinity and agreement. This unity is so great and of such a kind that if the smallest particle were taken away, the whole universe would collapse. 

Therefore, this similarity of nature must be considered the most powerful cause for the celestial globes to love one another—not as diverse or distinct persons, but as members of one and the same body. For just as the heart, kindled with the greatest love for the brain and the other members, supplies them with life, natural heat, and spirit; and the brain sends down nerves into the remaining parts, and with them sense and motion; and the liver distributes the veins together with the blood into the whole body because of the immense love with which the parts pursue one another and the whole itself—which love indeed surpasses and excels the benevolence of any other person by a vast interval—so the portions of the celestial body seem to love one another with a certain marvelous agreement of nature. And since they all strive toward the same goal and refer their actions to the same end, one serves another, and all provide some use and convenience to one another, so that they complete and perfect the whole. 

Another reason proper to human love might also perhaps be accommodated to the heavens, which proceeds from virtue <note>original: "virtute"</note>. Since each celestial body excels in some virtue—which contributes greatly both to the essence and safety of the others, and even to the whole heaven and the universe—it is necessary that this kind of virtue, known and perceived by the other globes, should infuse into the rest a vehement love toward the heaven distinguished by this virtue. I will even add this besides: that their mutual benevolence proceeds not from any singular benefit to one small part of the world, but from a common and most ample benefit conferred by each of them upon the university of things <note>meaning the "entirety" or "totality" of the universe.</note>; if this were undoubtedly withdrawn, the universe itself would immediately collapse and be dissolved. And truly, good and studious men embrace one another with this remarkable love, namely because they consult the advantage and convenience of the whole human race, and not because of some singular benefit that they have conferred on this person or that, as we often see happen in useful matters. Hence, since the celestial bodies [are] the perfection of all animals...

<summary>Philo argues that celestial bodies exhibit love through a "harmonic unity," functioning like the organs of a single body (heart, brain, liver) to sustain the entire universe. He posits that their mutual benevolence stems from their shared nature and the individual "virtues" they contribute to the cosmic whole.</summary>

# LEO THE HEBREW ON LOVE #
<page-num>396</page-num>
<header>LEO THE HEBREW ON LOVE,</header>

...that they are most holy, everyone confesses with one voice; both of these reasons for love are found in them, which are also found in the human species—being superior to other living creatures. **SO.** If, therefore, the celestial bodies love each other as vehemently as you declare, it seems it should be believed that the poets did not without reason compose those fables about the loves of the heaven-dwellers <note>original: "cœlicolarum," referring to the gods</note>, such as those of Jove <note>Jupiter</note> and Apollo. Yet I find two things hard to accept: first, that the poets attributed certain lustful loves to the gods themselves, such as those of males for females—devising marriages for some, but for many others, adulteries and outrages—and second, that they said other
<margin>Poets are permitted to lie much.</margin>
gods were furthermore procreated from their union and intercourse. Both of these things are entirely foreign to the divine and celestial nature. But, as it is said, poets are permitted to lie much. **PH.** Nor do they themselves seem to have written these things rashly or falsely, as you persuade yourself. **SO.** Do you think such things ever happened among the celestial gods? **PH.** Certainly; and you too, if you understand them correctly, will confess them to be true. **SO.** To attain the understanding of such obscure matters would be most pleasing
<margin>The fictions of the poets are accustomed to involve and encompass many intentions and allegorical senses.</margin>
to me. **PH.** The ancient poets involved not just one, but many intentions—which they call "senses"—in their poems. First of all, for the sake of providing a common and easier meaning, like an outer bark <note>original: "corticem exteriorem"</note>, they run through the famous and memorable deeds of illustrious persons in a kind of History. Afterward, they involve in the same fable a moral sense conducive to the active life of men, extolling virtues and depressing vices, like an inner bark closer to the marrow. Furthermore, within the same fiction, they include some true understanding of either natural, celestial, or divine things—separately, or two together, or all three joined—like the marrow of the fruit covered by the rinds. These secret senses, corresponding in some proportion to the marrow or the internal organs, 
<margin>What the allegorical senses are usually called.</margin>
are called allegorical. **SO.** It seems to me a matter of no small weight or poor wit to signify and embrace so many, so diverse, and so profound meanings in just one historical narration, whether it be true or false. I would wish that you might reveal and illustrate this wonderful and almost incredible thing with some brief example. **PH.** I want you to hold it as certain, Sophia, that those ancients cultivated their wits no less in skillfully explaining arduous and most high matters of the sciences than in knowing them perfectly. 
<margin>The fable of Perseus, celebrated by the poets, presents five allegories: historical, moral, natural, celestial, and divine.</margin>
Hear this example of that thing, which is quite suited to our purpose. The poets tell the story that Perseus, the son of Jove, killed the Gorgon and, having achieved his vow, flew to the ether <note>the upper atmosphere</note>, a part of heaven higher than the rest. The historical significance is said to be this: that a certain Perseus, considered a son of Jove because of his heroic virtues descending from that most happy planet <note>The planet Jupiter was traditionally associated with kingship and benevolence</note>—or perhaps truly deriving his origin from one of those Kings who ruled in Crete, Athens, or Arcadia and were called "Joves"—killed the Gorgon, a tyrant of the lands. For "Gorgon" among the Greeks signifies "earth" <note>A common Renaissance etymological association</note>. Hence, both because of this greatest benefit bestowed upon the human race and because of his illustrious virtues, he was enrolled by mortals into the number of the heaven-dwellers. The moral sense will be of this kind: that Perseus, a most prudent man and son of Jove—that is, excelling in the best morals and outstanding virtues by the kindness of that planet—having routed and overcome the foul and earthly vices signified by the name of the Gorgon, ascended to celestial and divine virtues. The first and natural allegory, however, will be this: that the human mind, the daughter of Jove—that is, of God—having fought down and killed the "Gorgonic" or earthly nature, immediately flew up to understand celestial, sublime, and eternal things, in the contemplation of which the wise have placed human happiness and perfection. We shall say the second allegory, sought from the fountains of astrology, is this: that the celestial nature, the progeny of Jove, after it has brought about the mortality and death of these lower and earthly bodies through its continuous motion, [shines] with the most illustrious and greatest...

# DIALOGUE II #

<page-num>397</page-num>
<header>DIALOGUE II.</header>

Once victory was reported over them, and their foul and hideous mortality was left behind, he hastened toward the upper dwellings and preserved his immortality whole and untouched. Finally, the last and **metaphysical allegory** <note>metaphysics here refers to the study of things beyond the physical world, like spirits and God</note> is conjectured to be this: that the angelic nature—born of Jove (that is, God, the Best and Greatest, and the creator of all things)—having defeated and cast off corporeal and earthly matter (which is designated by the name of the **Gorgon**), escaped into heaven. For the **angelic intellects** <note>spiritual beings or "intelligences" believed to move the planets</note>, separated from body and matter, are indeed thought to be those who perpetually lead the celestial spheres in their circles. **SO.** It is indeed a marvel that in very few words, simply narrating some historical action, so many secret and hidden meanings—each more excellent than the last—are involved and encompassed. But tell me, I pray, why did the ancients not open their doctrines more freely and clearly? **PH.** Persuaded by many

<margin>
The ancients, driven by five reasons, strove to involve and hide the secrets of nature and of God, the Best and Greatest, in poetic fictions; especially for their excellence and nobility, because of a certain pleasure joined with ease, for the lasting and untouched preservation of intelligible things, and for the common utility.
</margin>

reasons, they were unwilling to do so. First, because they judged it hateful to the secrets of nature and the divine power to betray or open them to the common crowd. They certainly felt this most rightly: for to treat true and profound knowledge too widely and broadly is nothing else than to communicate it with rude and foolish men. In their minds, no differently than the best wine in a tainted and faulty jar, knowledge is spoiled and corrupted. Once this "adultery" of knowledge began, a universal corruption of all doctrines throughout the whole world followed; this grows greater day by day as knowledge is passed, as if from hand to hand, from one rude mind to one even ruder. This kind of plague and corruption of the liberal arts took its origin from a too easy and excessively clear interpretation of the sciences. In our own time, because of the wordy and talkative speech of more recent philosophers, it has proceeded so far that you can hardly find any pure "intelligible" truth <note>a truth understood by the mind rather than the senses</note> without it being tainted and corrupted. But those ancients used the greatest artistry to wrap the mysteries of wisdom in the **bark** <note>original: "corticibus," meaning the outer shell or literal story</note> of fables, so that only those wits suited to perceiving divine and intelligible things—minds that preserve knowledge rather than corrupt it—might be able to enter therein. **SO.** I favor this opinion wonderfully; for without a doubt, arduous and excellent things are to be committed only to fit and distinguished minds. If they were perhaps entrusted to the foolish and the dim, they would degenerate greatly from their own excellence and nobility. But hurry to the other reasons for poetic fables. **PH.** Four additional causes for this matter can be brought forward. Of these, **brevity** itself holds the second place, encompassing many meanings in few words. Brevity contributes greatly to preserving and retaining the memory of things, especially when this artistry is used: so that men reading some historical action that is treated briefly may immediately remember the doctrine of all the overflowing senses that are involved under the veil of those same words. The third reason is so that the **pleasure** of historical and fabulous reading may be mixed with intelligible truth—the easy with the difficult—so that our weak intellect, charmed by the delight and ease of the fables, may be led gradually and by a most sweet method to perceive the truth of the sciences. This is no different than how **schoolmasters** <note>original: "pædagogi"</note>, when beginning to instruct boys in studious and honorable disciplines, are accustomed to start from the easier things. We see that the ancients achieved this with the greatest praise; for the fictions of the ancient poets provided a most convenient "dwelling" for both of the things just mentioned at once: since the lie, the pleasure, and the "bark" occupy the exterior of the fable, while the truth, the sense, and the "fruit" occupy the interior. The fourth reason is deduced from the **preservation** of intelligible things, lest as the years circle by, they themselves should change according to the diversity of human minds. For the histories in which the ancients encompassed the mysteries of the sciences, because of the certainty and stability of their terms, cannot undergo even the slightest change. To achieve this better and more easily, they composed those histories in rhythmic words and metrical feet...

# OF LEO THE HEBREW ON LOVE #

<page-num>398</page-num>
<header>LEO THE HEBREW ON LOVE,</header>

...described them as being bound by a fixed measure <note>original: "certa mensura," referring to poetic meter</note>, so that they could never be corrupted or depraved: for the rhythmic meter of poems leaves no entrance or opening for vice or corruption. Thus, neither the diversity or weakness of minds, nor the carelessness or error of writers, can adulterate or corrupt the sciences handled in this way. The final reason is that, like a single meal prepared with different flavors to satisfy the differing tastes of all the guests, the weaker minds perceive only the stories of the poems along with the elegance and melody of the verse; the stronger minds, beyond this, uncover the moral sense; and others, even sharper than the first and second groups, penetrate beyond the history and morals into the allegorical senses—insinuating themselves not only into natural philosophy, but even into astrology and theology. To this end, we can also connect the fact that since all kinds of people feed indifferently on these poems as if they were common food, it happens that they are perpetually preserved in the mind of the multitude. For more difficult things are known by the few, and the memory of the few is quickly and very easily obliterated—as if some later age should follow which, through the misfortune and unfairness of the times, should lead men away from the study of the sciences. We see this has happened in many provinces and among certain religions, as with the Greeks and Arabs, who, although they once flourished in learning, are now seen to have lost their sciences either entirely or for the most part. The same also happened to Italy during the storm of the Greeks, which now seems to have recovered some portion, however small, of ancient learning. Therefore, so that the sciences are not brought into such danger, the most effective and timely remedy is to entrust them to the fabulous and historical songs of the poets; because of the sweetness and delight of the verse, these are learned by heart by everyone, and are always and everywhere sung by every sex, age, and condition of people with the greatest cheerfulness of mind.

**SO.** The reasons you have given for poetic fables are most highly approved by me. But tell me, I pray, why did Plato and Aristotle, the princes of philosophers, despise the custom and practice of the ancient sages? For one of them, although he admitted the use of the fable, nevertheless neglected verse and always used prose <note>original: "soluta oratione," literally 'loosened speech,' meaning prose</note>; while the other despised both fable and verse, and treated the sciences with philosophical and continuous prose.

<margin>Only the powerful are accustomed to overturning and breaking through laws.</margin>
**PH.** It is not the weak, but only the powerful who are accustomed to overturning and breaking through laws. The divine Plato, when he decided to amplify and expand the sciences, broke only the single bond of verse,

<margin>The reason why, in writing philosophy, Plato used only fables and not metrical speech; but Aristotle neglected both fable and verse in his writing.</margin>
while leaving the other bond of the fable untouched. Thus, he was the first of all to violate, in some part, the law of preserving the sciences; however, since he used a fabulous style for what was false <note>referring to the use of myths to cloak truth</note>, he seems to have provided more than enough for their preservation. Aristotle, more daring and most eager to propagate the empire of the sciences, wished—by a new method and an unusual example—to cut the other bond of the fable as well. He completely broke the ancient law that preserved the sciences, using prose and a most learned style in treating the secrets of philosophy. Nevertheless, he seems to have been clever and shrewd in this, because he devised a way of speaking so brief, so significant, and so learned, that it alone takes the place of both verse and fable for the preservation of knowledge.

<margin>The marvelous brevity and obscurity of Aristotle in treating the sciences.</margin>
Hence, when Alexander, King of the Macedonians and a student of Aristotle, wrote to his teacher saying he was filled with wonder that he had published the hidden books of sacred philosophy, Aristotle replied that those books were partly published and partly not published: they were published only to those who had heard and learned their interpretation from him.

<margin>The serious and sharp response of Aristotle to Alexander, King of the Macedonians.</margin>
From these words you can perceive the difficulty of Wisdom <note>original: "Sophia"</note> and the great art of Aristotelian speech. **SO.** I do indeed look upon it with awe. But it seems absurd to me that such a great philosopher said no one could ever understand the books written by him unless they had first learned their explanation from him; especially since, after Aristotle had departed this life, many philosophers...

## DIALOGUE II. ##

<page-num>399</page-num>
<header>DIALOGUE II.</header>

...there succeeded those who understood either all, or at least most, of his writings. For this reason, he himself seems to have been not only a liar but also arrogant: for if his doctrine is true and sincere, why shouldn't it be understood by perceptive minds, even if they are far removed in time? For writing was instituted not for the benefit of those present, but for the utility and convenience of those absent and for posterity. What, then, could hinder Nature from being able to form and procreate such minds as are capable of understanding the writings of Aristotle, even though he has now been dead for nearly two thousand years?

*PHILO:* That saying of Aristotle would certainly be absurd unless it held another sense and a different meaning.

*SOPHIA:* Please, explain it.

<margin>Whom Aristotle was accustomed to call his listener.</margin>
*PHILO:* The Philosopher calls his "listener" someone who, wherever and whenever they may exist, observes and imitates the method of understanding and philosophizing practiced by Aristotle himself. He intends to signify that his writings do not make just *any* man a philosopher; rather, they serve only the one who, by God’s grace, has obtained a mind highly disposed to philosophical knowledge, just as Aristotle himself was. Such a person will indeed understand his most learned writings, but others will not at all—just as it used to happen in that genre of writing which wrapped philosophical meanings in the fabulous stories of the poets.

<margin>Aristotle deserves praise for his handling of philosophy, yet he seems to deserve some blame by accident.</margin>
*SOPHIA:* Therefore, Aristotle incurs no mark of blame if he liberated philosophy from the difficulty and bondage of both verse and fable; for he so fortified and walled-in his doctrines that he left an entrance or access to them for no one except the most excellent minds and perceptive spirits.

*PHILO:* Certainly, he committed no crime himself: because, trusting in the greatness of his own genius, he supplied by another method what he seemed to have taken away. However, he might perhaps be blamed in this: that by his example he made others bolder in writing philosophy in plain prose <term>soluta oratione: literally "loosened speech," referring to prose rather than rhythmic poetry</term>. Later, making no distinction and always explaining his most holy mysteries more diffusely and copiously, these followers communicated philosophy indifferently to the fit and the unfit, the sharp and the dull-witted. From this, pure and elegant wisdom was so torn apart, deformed, and trampled underfoot by everyone from all sides that it can hardly be recognized, and it exists as something utterly unlike itself.

*SOPHIA:* Enough of this; let us now return to interpreting the fabulous loves of the inhabitants of heaven <note>original: "cœlicolarum," referring to the gods</note>.

*PHILO:* First, we must reveal who and how many are the Gods celebrated by the poets; then, their loves are to be explained.

*SOPHIA:* Rightly so; therefore, first of all, explain the names and meanings of those Gods.

<margin>Jupiter is the prince and supreme God of the poets.</margin>
*PHILO:* The prince and supreme God of the poets is that First Cause producing all things and preserving the universe of things. He is commonly called Jupiter by them, as if he were a "helping father" <note>original: "iuuans pater," a traditional but linguistically creative etymology for Iuppiter</note>, because, like a most kind parent, he provides help to all, since he fashioned each thing from nothing

<margin>Jupiter is commonly called a "helping father" by everyone.</margin>
and granted to each an essence suited to its capacity. The Romans, moreover, called him the "Best and Greatest" <note>original: "Optimum Maximum"</note> because all good things and all the essences of things flow and proceed from him.

<margin>Jupiter is rightly called "Best and Greatest" by the Romans, and "Zeus" by the Greeks.</margin>
The same was called Zeus <note>original: Ζεὺς</note> by the Greeks, as if from the word for "living" <note>original: ζῶν (zôn)</note>, because all things received life from him—or rather, he himself is the most excellent life of all things. Nevertheless, by this supreme name of Jupiter, certain created things were shared by the Almighty God as being more excellent than the rest. For instance, in the celestial world, he earned the title of the second of the seven planets, because he pours into the lower world the greatest happiness, the most brilliant splendor, and the best effects.

<margin>The name of Jupiter is found to signify many things among the poets.</margin>
And men in whose births he holds the primary and chief parts are always seen to turn out better, more excellent, and more outstanding than others by the gift of this beneficial star. In the sublunary world, moreover, the element of fire is also called Jupiter: because it is clearer and more active than all the other elements, and is supremely vital; since all these lower things, as Aristotle agrees, live and are nourished by an igneous quality—that is, by heat itself.

### DIALOGUE II

...affections possess their own proper Ideas. According to the greater or lesser communication of these Ideas, such qualities are found more or less intensely in human beings. For this reason, the poets placed Fame, Love, Grace, Desire, Pleasure, Strife, Toil, Envy, Deceit, Obstinacy, Mercy, and other similar things among the number of the Gods. This is because each of these was endowed with its own Idea and its own incorporeal principle, as we have already said, by merit of which it acquired for itself the name of a God or Goddess.

**SO.** Although virtues seem to have Ideas because of their supreme excellence, how can vices and the corrupt affections of the soul participate in them?

<margin>
Evil is converted into good because it also necessarily contributes to the preservation of the universe.
</margin>
**PH.** Just as among the celestial Gods some are good and fortunate, such as Jupiter and Venus—from whom various kinds of blessings and happiness always proceed—and some, on the contrary, are harmful and disastrous, such as Saturn and Mars—who are considered the authors of all evils and hardships—so too among the Platonic Ideas, <note>Platonic Ideas are the eternal, non-physical templates or archetypes of all things in the physical world.</note> some exist as principles of goods and virtues, while others are principles of evils and vices. This is because both are necessary for the preservation of the universe; by reason of this necessity, evil itself is even converted into good. For whatever parts come together to constitute the totality of things must undoubtedly be counted among the number of good things, since the universe itself is conceded by all to be not only good, but the very best. Therefore, evil and corruption are no less required than good and generation <note>original: "generatio" - the process of coming into being or birth.</note> to complete the essence and perfection of the World. Each seems to be a kind of disposition and preparation for the attainment of the other. You should not, therefore, feel any wonder if both have been allotted that divine principle—namely, an Idea separated from matter.

**SO.** But I remember often understanding that vices and evils are pure privations, <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "privation" is the absence of a quality that should naturally be present, rather than a "thing" in itself.</note> and that they proceed from the defect of primary matter and its imperfection through the "contagion" of its potentiality. By what reasoning, then, can they have those divine principles?

<margin>
According to the opinion of the Platonists, Ideas are also set over primary matter and its imperfections.
</margin>
**PH.** Even if we were to follow in the footsteps of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, who walked while teaching.</note> and admit this to be true, we would nevertheless never deny that the same matter proceeded from the divine mind and was established by divine decree. All its affections and defects are directed by and proceed from the supreme wisdom of God, since both the former and the latter necessarily concur in the constitution of the lower world and especially of the human species itself. For this reason, proper Ideas were also set over them by God the Best and Greatest—acting as principles not of matter, but of action and form—which complete and perfect the essences of those imperfect things that are always joined with privation and which contribute to the composition of the universe.

**SO.** You have certainly satisfied my request in abundance. Returning now to the subject, tell me, I pray, whether the poets communicated the divine name to other things as well.

<margin>
Finally, the divine name is usually adapted by poets to illustrious and most excellent men.
</margin>
**PH.** They finally applied it to men—not to all, certainly, but only to those who were distinguished by heroic virtues and who performed illustrious, great, and memorable deeds similar to those of the divine.

**SO.** Is it only by reason of this similarity that mortal men attain the divine name?

**PH.** They are called Gods not by reason of their mortality, but only by consideration of their immortal and eternal intellect.

**SO.** If all men are participants in intellect, why do they not all receive the divine name?

<margin>
The poets attributed divinity itself to the most outstanding men for various and diverse reasons.
</margin>
**PH.** Indeed, not all are seen to possess an intellect equally excellent and divine. Rather, we know the degree and excellence of our souls from our actions. Hence, those distinguished men were not undeservedly called Gods. Some of them, because of their supreme excellence, obtained the names of the celestial Gods, such as Jupiter, Saturn, Apollo, Mars, Venus, Mercury, Diana, Cœlus (the Heavens), Polus (the Pole), Æther (the Ether), and the various images of the many stars forming the Eighth Sphere. <note>The "Eighth Sphere" in the ancient cosmos refers to the sphere of the fixed stars, beyond the seven planetary spheres.</note> Some, however, were held to be sons of these...
