<margin>
The myth of Demogorgon, explaining its length as well as the unusual manner of this kind of procreation.
</margin>
...I shall strive to explain. We read in the poet Pronapides <note>Pronapides was a legendary Greek poet, often cited in Renaissance works as the teacher of Homer, though his existence is debated by modern scholars.</note> in his *Protocosmus*, that Demogorgon—while surrounded only by Eternity and Chaos, and while resting most happily in that eternity—sensed a great tumult stirred up in the belly of Chaos itself. Therefore, to bring aid, he reached out his hand and opened that belly. From there, Strife <note>original: "litigium"</note> immediately came forth. Because it was endowed with a foul and deformed face, and while it stirred up the greatest disturbances and strove to fly upward, it was soon thrust down into the depths by Demogorgon. However, while the one in labor was still miserably burdened and oppressed by sweats and burning sighs, Demogorgon would not withdraw his hand until he had led Pan out of her belly, together with three sisters who are called the Fates <note>original: "Parcæ"</note>. Moved by the great beauty and excellent form of this Pan, he placed him in charge of the household affairs; and he ordered the three sisters to follow him as attendants, handmaidens, and servants. Then Chaos, having been unburdened and freed from the weight of such a great mass, at the persuasion of Demogorgon, placed her son Pan upon the paternal throne. This is the myth of Demogorgon sung by the poets, even though Homer in the *Iliad* attributes the procreation of Strife and Discord to Jove as her father; he asserts that because she gravely offended Juno at the birth of Eurystheus and Hercules, she was cast down by the Goddess from heaven to earth. They add, moreover, that Demogorgon fathered the Pole <note>original: "Polum," referring to the heavens or the celestial axis.</note>, Python, Earth, and Erebus <note>Erebus represents the personification of darkness.</note>. **SO.** I ask you to declare to me the meaning of this myth.

<margin>
The allegory of the myth of Demogorgon just explained, which quite elegantly signifies all things emanating from the supreme creator and proceeding from prime matter.
</margin>
**PH.** Truly, it seems to signify the generation and procreation of all things emanating from the supreme creator, with whom they wish Eternity to have always been joined in indissoluble fellowship. For he alone can truly be called eternal, who is the beginning and cause of all things, and always was, and always will be, with no succession of time seen in him at all. They say that Chaos also held the third place in that eternal fellowship; because Chaos, as Ovid so excellently sang, is the common, mixed, and confused matter of all things. The ancients used to say that this matter was eternal together with God, and from it—acting in the role of a true and best parent—He procreated and formed all things according to his will and judgment. Indeed, the matter of all things that were created seems to be their common mother, both in word and in reality. Whence the ancients declared that there are only two first and most ancient parents of all things—one of whom holds the character of the father, the other of the mother—and that they are eternal and unbegotten. Nevertheless, they intended God to be the primary cause, while Chaos was an attending and accompanying cause. Indeed, Plato also seems to have held this view in the *Timaeus* concerning the new and recent manner of things procreated by the supreme God out of eternal and confused matter.

<margin>
Chaos proceeded from God by a certain eternal generation; all other things, however, were effected by God from Chaos by a new and temporal generation.
</margin>
But perhaps someone might rebuke the ancients: for since God is held by all to be the common father of all, it is necessary that he also brought into the light the matter from which the rest were then created. Truly, those most excellent men intended to signify that when Chaos is said to have been the companion of the Best and Greatest God in that eternity, it proceeded from Him by a certain eternal generation. And God afterwards made all other things out of Chaos by a new and temporal <note>In this context, "temporal" refers to things that exist within time and are subject to change, unlike the eternal nature of God.</note> generation; in which matter they agreed with the Platonic opinion. However, even though Chaos emanated from God, they said it was his companion, both because it flowed from God from eternity and is always seen together with him, and also because it concurs with God for the procreation and generation of things like a certain wife and companion to him.

<margin>
The reason why the poets feigned that Chaos itself was the companion of God.
</margin>
Since, therefore, Chaos was produced by God with no intermediary existing, while all other things drew their origin from God and out of Chaos (that is, out of matter), Chaos is rightly called the companion of God. Nor is it repugnant to this that it came forth from the divine power from eternity; just as Eve, although she was formed from Adam, was always held by him as a companion and wife; and even among their descendants, a certain fellowship and affinity intervened between both of them. **SO.** The ancients, by this myth, [taught] the generation of the universe by almighty God...

# LEO HEBREW ON LOVE #

...proceeding from a Father, as it were, and from Chaos or matter as from a mother. Truly, I would desire to understand not just the general sense of this fable, but also the meaning of each individual detail: such as what is meant by the tumult stirred up in the belly of Chaos, the application of Demogorgon’s hand, and the birth of Strife <note>original: "Litigium"</note> and the others.

PH. The noise and tumult which we said Demogorgon sensed coming from the belly of Chaos itself is the power and appetite of matter to give birth to divided and separated things; such division usually produces noise and tumult. The hand of Demogorgon applied to open the belly of Chaos is the divine power, which brought the common and universal potential of Chaos into a separate and distinct act: for this is undoubtedly what it means to open the belly of one who is pregnant and to lead out the hidden offspring. In performing this generation, however, they chose to have him use not a limb adapted for propagation, but a hand—following a new and unusual example. This was to indicate that the first procreation and production of things was by no means common or customary, like the natural generation that succeeded creation later; rather, it stood forth as something marvelous and "monstrous" <note>In this context, "monstrous" (monstruosam) refers to something outside the natural order or a divine marvel, rather than something inherently evil.</note>, requiring the use of the hand, the most powerful instrument.

They say that Strife <note>original: "Litigium"</note> was the first to emerge from the belly of Chaos: for before all else, the division of things proceeded from prime matter. Though all things were previously found joined and confused within it, once the time for birthing had passed, they were divided and distinguished by the hand of Demogorgon—that is, by the supreme power of God. That division is called "Strife" because it involves the four opposite and contrary elements <note>The four elements are Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note>. It is depicted with a foul and dishonorable face because division and opposition themselves usually introduce defect, just as, conversely, union and concord introduce perfection.

They say that when Strife strived to fly upward, it was cast down from heaven to earth by Demogorgon: this is because, in the opinion of the Peripatetics <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle; they believed the heavens were made of a "fifth element" (ether) and were immune to the change and conflict found on Earth.</note>, no discord or opposition is found in heaven. For this reason, celestial bodies are not at all subject to mortality, unlike these lower bodies: because in the heavens no diversity or opposition is seen, whereas in the lower world it is greatest, and is considered the primary cause of the death and dissolution of things. Furthermore, when they pronounce that Strife was driven from heaven to earth, they intend to signify that heaven is the cause of all diversity and the battle of lower things, while remaining itself free from any opposition or discord.

SO. If heaven lacks every kind of opposition, how is it able to produce it?

<margin>Three reasons are assigned as to why celestial bodies send opposite effects into the Lower World.</margin>
PH. Three reasons for this matter can be brought forward: first, the opposition of effects which proceed from the planets, stars, and celestial signs; second, the opposition of celestial motions, one of which strives from East to West, while the other conversely moves from West to East—one proceeding toward the North, the other toward the South; finally, the contrary positions of the lower bodies located within the Lunar sphere: for those closer to heaven are seen to be lighter, while those further from it and closer to the center are heavier. From this first opposition, all the remaining differences and diversities of the elements are derived.

<margin>Plato, following the opinion of the most ancient Hebrews, judged that Heaven consists of water and fire.</margin>
We could also bring forward that ancient and Platonic opinion in confirmation of this matter: that the stars and planets were made of fire because of their most abundant light, while the celestial orbs were made of water because of their great thinness and transparency. Hence the Hebrews called Heaven *shamaim* <term>original: "scamaym"; a Hebrew word for the heavens/sky</term>, which they interpret as being from *esh* and *mayim* <term>original: "maini"; Philo is referencing the Hebrew words for fire (esh) and water (mayim)</term>: that is, fire and water. Following this opinion, we might perhaps say that strife and opposition ascended to the heavens at the very first beginnings of the World because celestial bodies consist of fire and water; but they did not remain there. Rather, they devolved from heaven to the lands as if to their own proper and convenient habitation, where the succession of generation is perpetually continued by the mediation of contraries.

SO. It seems absurd to me that the contrary natures of elements, such as fire and water...

<meta>catchword: and water</meta>

He explains that while the heavens are harmonious, they cause diversity and opposition on Earth through their varying motions and the combination of fire and water.</summary>

# DIALOGUE II #

...and of water be placed.

<margin>
Plato held that the celestial bodies consist of the same matter from which the lower bodies are made, and thus by their own nature they could eventually be corrupted—a point he considered later.
</margin>
PH. If the primary matter <note>original: "materia prima"</note>—as these thinkers, along with Plato, believed—is common to both the celestial and the lower worlds, why is it that some opposition of the elements is not found in the heavens as well? SO. Why then do the celestial bodies not decay in the same manner as the lower bodies? PH. Plato indeed conceded that the heavens could be corrupted by their own nature; however, because of the divine power of the intellectual forms <note>These are the "blueprints" or spiritual realities that give shape to matter.</note> actually existing and informing the heavens, he held that they were indissoluble. This is all the more true because the celestial elements must be considered far purer than the lower ones, and as it were, the very "souls" of the sublunary things. Nor are the elements seen to be mixed in the heavens as they are in the lower mixed bodies; for the heavens have claimed for themselves only the luminous part of fire and only the transparent part of water. Hence, although Strife <note>original: "Litigium"</note> hurried toward the heaven as soon as it touched the vital airs, it was nevertheless soon thrust down into the lower world, where we see this "god" residing today as if in his own court. For this reason, the fable adds that when Chaos was still burdened and oppressed by sweats and burning sighs even after Strife had been brought forth, Demogorgon extended his hand further and led Pan out of the mother’s womb along with three sisters who are called the Fates <note>original: "Parcae"</note>. By those labors and torments which the poets say Chaos and the primary matter endured while giving birth to Strife, we are to understand the contrary natures of the four elements: thus, by that oppression and weight, he seems to signify the earth (which is heavier than the other elements); by the sweat, water; and by the burning sighs, air and fire. Therefore, so that divine power might bring help and salvation to these great labors and torments arising from the battle and discord of opposites, it drew from the womb of Chaos a second son, Pan—whose name among the Greeks means "The All" <note>original: "totum"</note>. By Pan, they wish us to understand universal nature, which orders and governs all things that were brought forth and produced into the light from Chaos, and which simultaneously pacifies and brings into accord these contrary natures. Hence they say Pan was born after Strife: because concord succeeds discord, and indeed takes the place of discord.

<margin>
The three Fates are said to signify the three orders of time: namely the present, the past, and the future.
</margin>
They say that with Pan, the three Fates <note>original: "Parcae"</note> were born together, who are named Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos, and are said by Seneca to preside over destiny. By these they signify the three orders of time—present, past, and future—which they believe were established to follow the God of universal nature. For they interpret Clotho as the turning of present things, and she winds and draws out these present threads of life. Lachesis signifies the production of the future, and she diligently prepares and guards those linen threads which remain to be spun and twisted. Atropos—which you might translate as "unalterable" or "irrevocable"—figures the past, which can by no means return; she has already spun and finished these threads committed to her. Furthermore, they are called *Parcae* by a certain irony <note>A common medieval and Renaissance etymology: *Parcae quia nemini parcunt*.</note>, because they "spare" (*parcunt*) no one. They add, moreover, that Pan was placed upon his father's throne by the command of Demogorgon, because nature carries out the divine order and promptly and faithfully executes the administration of things entrusted to it. Afterward follows the birth of the sixth son, namely Polus <note>The Pole/Firmament</note>, representing the ultimate sphere which turns upon two poles, the arctic and the antarctic; then the seventh, Python, representing the Sun; afterward the eighth, being female, was allotted the name of Earth <note>original: "Tellus"</note>, and is seen to signify the center of the world.

<margin>
The progeny of Earth, namely Night, Fame, and Tartarus, along with an elegant explanation of the meaning of these three children.
</margin>
The poets furthermore sang that Earth <note>original: "Tellurem"</note> gave birth to Night, because night itself is produced from the shadow of the earth. Through Night we can also understand the death and privation of lucid forms proceeding from the darkness of matter. They even added that Fame is the daughter of Earth, because the earth preserves the fame and name of mortals after they have met their final day. Finally, they say the mother Earth gave birth to Tartarus—that is, the underworld—as a son, because all generated bodies eventually return to the lower belly of the earth. They affirm that Earth gave birth to these, and many other children, by herself alone without the cooperation of any man: because all things of this sort are defects and privations of essence...

<summary>Philo interprets the birth of Pan (Universal Nature) and the Fates (Time) as the divine imposition of order and harmony upon the discordant elements of Chaos. He further explains how Earth produced Night, Fame, and the Underworld as "privations" that arise from matter itself without an active creative cause.</summary>

In this sublunary world <note>The region below the moon, which in ancient science was the realm of change, birth, and death.</note>, it is the very matter of things that can be generated, and it is the cause of generation and corruption, as well as every variety and change of the lower bodies. In man, however—whom we have already demonstrated to be a "little world" <note>original: "mundum exiguum," the concept of the human as a microcosm reflecting the universe</note>—it is the appetite and desire for acquiring new things. they say Erebus had many children, such as Love, Grace, Labor, Envy, Fear, Deceit, Fraud, Persistence, Want, Misery, Hunger, Complaint, Disease, Old Age, Pallor, Darkness, Sleep, Death, Charon, Day, and Ether.

**SO.** Who do they say was the mother of so many children?

**PH.** Night <note>original: "Noctem"</note>, the daughter of the Earth; it is said that Erebus lay with her to produce all this offspring.

**SO.** Why do they believe this whole brood was born of Erebus and Night?

**PH.** Because all these things proceed from an inherent power and "night-like" deprivations <note>original: "privationibus," a philosophical term for the absence of a quality or form</note>, both in the great sublunary world and in the small human world.

**SO.** In what way?

**PH.** Love, or desire, has its origin in inherent power and lack; for matter, as the Philosopher <note>Commonly referring to Aristotle</note> testifies, desires all those forms which it lacks. **Grace** is the quality of the desired or loved thing itself, which persists in the mind or appetite of the one who desires. **Labors** are defined as the torments and anxieties of the lover so that he may finally achieve the object of his desire. **Envy** is said to be a certain anguish of the soul, because of which the wretched lover greatly envies the advantages and pleasures of the possessor. **Fear** is either the fear of losing what was just acquired (for whatever is obtained by us can also be lost) or the fear that we can never attain what we long for. **Deceit** and **Fraud** are the appropriate and adapted means for obtaining the desired thing. **Persistence** is that which we use in pursuing the same. **Want**, **Misery**, and **Hunger** are the deprivations of those who desire. **Complaint** is the lamentation and grieving of lovers, because they either cannot attain what they vehemently desire, or they have lost what was already held and acquired. **Disease**, **Old Age**, and **Pallor** are certain dispositions toward the loss and destruction of things acquired by the will or the power of generation. **Darkness** and **Sleep** are the first losses of things; **Death**, however, is the final corruption. **Charon** brings about the forgetfulness <note>original: "oblivionem"</note> that follows the loss and destruction of the acquired thing. **Day**, in the universe, exists as a luminous form which the power inherent in matter can finally reach, and it is the human intellect itself; in man, however, it is the most luminous virtue and wisdom, toward which the wills and desires of the perfected are raised. **Ether** is 그 celestial spirit endowed with intelligence, in which the power of matter and the human will can participate at the highest level. Perhaps these two last-born children of Erebus, Day and Ether, could also signify those two celestial natures: both the luminous nature of the stars and planets, which is called **Day**, and also the transparent nature of the spheres themselves, which is called **Ether**.

**SO.** What similarity or suitability do these two celestial natures have with Erebus, whom you have already asserted to be the matter of things that are generated and mortal? And for what reason do you claim they were born from him?

**PH.** Because many of the ancients, and Plato along with them, maintained that these celestial natures consist of the matter of the lower bodies; hence, among all the children of Erebus, they obtained a more excellent

</margin>

**PH.** The poets say that **Pan** has two horns on his head reaching up to the sky, a fiery face, and a long beard hanging down to his chest...

### DIALOGUE II. ###

->...they handed down.<- He carries in his hands a staff and a pipe made of seven hemlock stalks joined together. He is dressed in a many-colored skin. His limbs are described as lowly, deformed, and disordered, and he is said to have the legs of a goat. Long ago, when Pan and Cupid entered into a very serious dispute over who held the greater power, Pan was finally conquered and overcome by Cupid. As a result, he burned with a most intense and powerful love for a certain Arcadian virgin and nymph named Syrinx. While Pan pursued the nymph and she fled from the god, it happened that they both reached the river Ladon. There, the maiden, having implored the help of the other nymphs, was transformed into marsh reeds. When the god heard the sweet sound of the wind <note>original: "zephyro," referring to Zephyr, the West Wind</note> blowing softly through them and striking them gently, he was wonderfully delighted by that harmony. Wanting to show his great love for the nymph, he took seven of those reeds, joined them with wax, and formed from them a pastoral pipe—a most sweet-sounding instrument.

**SO.** What allegorical meaning did the poets intend to signify by this fable?

<margin>
An allegory explaining both the figure of Pan and his intense passion for Syrinx, which beautifully represents the universal nature that rules and arranges the World itself.
</margin>

**PH.** Beyond the literal story of a man from the forests of Arcadia who, being a great lover and a student of music, was the first to invent the pipe made of seven reeds joined with wax, the ancients undoubtedly wrapped another higher and more hidden meaning in the aforementioned story. Specifically, among the Greeks, "Pan" signifies "All" <note>original: "Pan apud Graecos totum significans"</note>; he represents universal nature, which rules and arranges the entire world. The two horns that rise from his forehead and reach up to heaven represent the two poles, the Arctic and the Antarctic. The skin sprinkled with various colors that he wears represents the eighth sphere <note>In the ancient model of the universe, the eighth sphere was the firmament containing the fixed stars.</note>, which is distinguished by almost innumerable stars. His fiery face seems to represent the seven planets. For the face, as we said earlier, is marked by seven principal organs that have the greatest similarity to the seven wandering stars: namely, two eyes, two ears, two nostrils, and the mouth. His shaggy hair and the long beard hanging down upon his chest are said to refer to the rays of the Sun, the planets, and the stars, which hang down into the lower world to bring about all generations and mixtures of matter. His lowly and disordered limbs can be likened to the elements and the lower bodies, which appear crude and deformed when compared to the heavenly bodies. His feet are said to be those of a goat because, just as goats never walk in a straight line nor keep any order in their movement—always seen wandering and being carried here and there—so too in this lower world, things are seen to move and change from one species or essence into another without any fixed law, but rather in an oblique and disordered way. The heavenly bodies, however, are entirely free from this confusion and error. Unless my mind deceives me, we seem to have followed the poetic figure of Pan and its interpretation quite diligently.

**SO.** Very diligently indeed. But now, proceed to interpret the meaning of that most intense love with which the god loved Syrinx, as it is more suited to our current purpose.

**PH.** They add, moreover, that this universal nature—so excellent, powerful, wonderful, and distinguished—was by no means devoid of love. Therefore, they say he loved a pure and incorruptible virgin: that is, the stable and perpetual order of things. Nature prefers better and more perfect things over the lower and imperfect. Yet, while Nature desired to attain this certain and most constant order, the order fled from her. This is because this lower world is seen to be not at all stable, but subject to perpetual changes without any order, just like the feet of goats. The speed and flight of this maiden was halted and blocked by the river Ladon. This is because the Heaven, which resembles a river in its continuous and perpetual motion, contains and restrains the unstable and slipping stability of the changeable bodies of the lower world—even though the heaven itself is seen to be unstable in some part due to its own eternal motion. Truly, the heaven...

# LEO HEBREUS ON LOVE #

...that mobility is ordered and eternal, and she is rightly called an **uncorruptible virgin** by the poets, since her deformities and diversities possess a unified and harmonious proportion—just as we said earlier when we spoke of the musical and most sweet harmony <note>original: "concentu," referring to the "Music of the Spheres"</note> of the heavens. These are the river reeds into which Syrinx is said to have been transformed; indeed, these reeds, with the spirit driving them, produce a harmonious and most sweet sound. This is because the intellectual spirit revolving the celestial spheres composes their concordant and musical sounds.

The fact that Pan fashioned a pipe out of seven reeds signifies nothing other than the gathering of the seven spheres of the Planets, and the magnificent and wonderful melody produced as they are led around. For the same reason, the ancients said that Pan carries a staff and blows a pipe: because the nature of the seven Planets uses perpetual and equal motions to bring about the continuous changes in the sublunary world <note>The "sublunary world" refers to the Earth and everything below the moon, which was thought to be subject to change and decay, unlike the eternal heavens.</note>. Here is a brief and concise interpretation for you, O Sophia, of the love with which Pan pursued Syrinx.

**SO.** Indeed, I have heard it with the greatest delight. Now I would like to understand the generations, marriages, affairs, and loves of the other celestial Gods, along with their allegorical meanings.

**PH.** I will not explain all of them, so that we may avoid a long speech and boredom, but I will briefly set forth some that are more elegant and notable than the rest. The origin of the heavenly dwellers <note>The gods.</note> proceeds from **Demogorgon** <note>In Renaissance mythology, Demogorgon was considered the primordial creator or grandfather of all the gods.</note>, and from **Aether** and **Day** bound together in a fraternal and conjugal society—who were born either from Erebus, the son of Demogorgon,

<margin>An allegory explaining the birth of Coelius, or Heaven. The poets held that this God was born from Aether as his father and Day as his mother.</margin>
or, as others have felt, from Demogorgon himself. They say that from the joining of both <note>original: "arborum," likely a printer's error for "amborum" (both), referring to Aether and Day.</note>, **Coelius** (or Heaven) was born. The gentiles <note>Non-Christian ancients.</note> gave this name to **Uranus**, the father of Saturn, because he so surpassed and excelled others in the splendor of his virtues and the strength of his intellect that he seemed celestial rather than human. He was thought to have drawn his origin from Aether and Day because he expressed a spiritual and ethereal nature through his intellect, and represented divine light through his virtues. This allegorical sense is not at all obscure.

<margin>Heaven consists of two natures: ethereal and luminous.</margin>
For Heaven, which surrounds, embraces, and comprehends all things, is said to be the son of Aether and Day because it consists of two natures: one ethereal, because of its very thin and spiritual transparency; and the other luminous and divine, because of the most abundant and copious light of the stars with which it is filled. **Aether**, however—as the principal part of heaven, embracing all the spheres in its magnitude, and because (as **Plotinus** affirms following **Plato**) it penetrates and spreads through the entire universe, which he believes is full of a certain ethereal spirit—obtained the title of "father."

<margin>According to Aristotle's opinion, a star is a denser part of its own sphere.</margin>
But the **Stars**, because they are related to heaven much like individual limbs are to a whole body, are very similar to a woman and a mother—whom the **Sacred Volumes** <note>The Bible, specifically the account of Eve's creation from Adam.</note> relate had her first origin from man as a part from the whole. We could offer another reason for this: because the aether is far thinner and more spiritual than the most luminous bodies of the stars and planets. This is why **Aristotle** says the stars are capable of receiving and preserving light only because of their dense and solid bodies, a quality which nature denied to the spheres themselves because of their transparency and thinness.

<margin>According to the mind of Plotinus, Aether penetrates all bodies in the universe because of its extreme thinness.</margin>
Furthermore, Plotinus thinks the thinness of the aether is so great that it penetrates all bodies of the universe, both above and below. Being joined and intertwined with them, it does not make them any larger, because this interior spirit nourishes and preserves all bodies without their mass receiving any additional weight.

<margin>An allegory of the birth of Saturn himself, whom the poets reported was born to Heaven and Earth.</margin>
Therefore, Aether is rightly likened to a husband providing the spirit, and Day to a wife supplying the matter; we have already said that Heaven itself consists of these two natures.

**SO.** But whom did Heaven procreate?

**PH.** **Saturn**.

**SO.** Which mother is said to have given birth to such a great son?

**PH.** Saturn, the King of Crete, was the offspring of Uranus and **Vesta**. Because Uranus was called "Heaven" due to his excellence and superiority, Vesta his wife obtained the name of "Earth": therefore

### DIALOGUE II ###

...because, as a most fruitful mother, she brought forth many offspring, especially Saturn, who labored most greatly in the study of earthly things and was the first to devise many useful things for farmers. He is simply called "Heaven" because, no differently than a parent, he embraces all the other 

<margin>Several similarities existing between Saturn and the Earth.</margin>

Planets. Nevertheless, many similarities exist between Saturn and the earth: first, he is of a leaden color approaching an earthy hue; second, just as the earth is thicker and more sluggish than all the other elements, so Saturn completes his own motion more slowly than all the wandering stars <note>The "wandering stars" is the literal translation of "planetae."</note>. It is said that Saturn takes thirty years to traverse his own circles, Jupiter twelve, Mars two; the Sun, Venus, and Mercury take one year; and the Moon is said to travel her own path in the space of one month. Furthermore, 

<margin>The nature and influence <note>original: "exfluxus"</note> of Saturn.</margin>

Saturn also seems to agree with the earth in the temperament and constitution which he sends down into bodies—namely, a cold and dry one. He usually makes the men over whom he rules melancholic, sad, grave, sluggish, and leaden in color; he makes them devoted as much as possible to agriculture, buildings, and earthly studies. He is said to preside over all things in whose composition the earth holds the primary parts. They depict him as an old man, sad, with a deformed appearance, contemplative, meanly dressed, and carrying a scythe <note>original: "falciferum"</note>. This is because the men he rules are seen to be endowed with these sorts of conditions and are greatly prone and inclined toward agriculture, which uses the scythe as its most convenient tool. He bestows a keen wit, deep thoughts, true science, good counsel, and constancy of soul because of the nature of his celestial father, which is most perfectly mixed with his terrestrial mother. 

<margin>Saturn best represents a celestial nature in the soul and a terrestrial nature in the body.</margin>

Finally, he owes the benefit and divinity of souls to his father, while he owes the destruction and deformity of bodies to his mother. For this reason, he is also said to signify poverty, death, the grave, and things hidden under the earth, with all bodily care and ornaments utterly cast aside. Hence, the poets did not without merit imagine that Saturn was accustomed to devour all his male children, but by no means the females: because he himself destroys all individual things <note>Male children here represent individual, distinct forms or "active" things that perish over time.</note>, yet he preserves the earthly and maternal roots of things. Rightly, therefore, was he called the son of Heaven and Earth by the ancients. 

**SO.** But is Saturn not said to have had children?

<margin>Cronus is rightly proclaimed by the poets to have been the son of Saturn and Ops.</margin>

**PH.** Several indeed, both male and female: such as Cronus <note>Philo is distinguishing between Saturn the god/planet and Cronus as the personification of Time.</note>, who signifies defined time, or some circuit of time, such as a year, which measures and completes the Sun's own circular motion. Now, Cronus is said to have been the son of Saturn because the greatest and most lasting circuit of time which a man can see and observe—given the brevity of his life—belongs to Saturn himself. As we have already said, it is completed and filled in the space of thirty years, whereas the proper revolutions of the other planets are finished and perfected in a shorter time. 

**SO.** What wife is Saturn said to have had, or who was the mother of Cronus? 

**PH.** The wife of Saturn and the common mother of Cronus and the other children is said to have been Ops, the sister of her husband, born of Heaven as her father and Earth as her mother, just as 

<margin>What Ops signifies.</margin>

he was also born. 

**SO.** By "Ops," do they wish for something else to be understood than the lawful wife of Saturn who ruled over Crete? 

**PH.** Allegorically, *Ops* sounds like "work" <note>Philo is making a wordplay on the Latin "Ops" (the goddess) and "Opus/Opera" (work or labor).</note>, and she seems to signify the labors of the earth, which are seen both in cultivating fields and also in building cities and houses. 

<margin>Ops is not without reason fashioned by the poets to be the sister and wife of Saturn.</margin>

Moreover, she is rightly called the wife and sister of Saturn. She is his sister because she is born of Heaven, which is considered the most powerful cause of both the cultivation of fields and of terrestrial dwellings; thus the same parents—namely, Heaven and Earth—begot both Ops and Saturn. She is also his wife because agriculture and buildings proceed from Saturn as the active agent, and from Ops as the one suffering and receiving <note>In classical philosophy, the "agent" is the one who acts or provides the form, while the "patient" is the material that receives the action.</note>.

<margin>Historical and allegorical sense of the fable which shows Saturn being expelled from his kingdom by his son Jupiter.</margin>
**PH.** We shall say the historical sense of this fiction is that after Jupiter liberated Saturn from the servitude of the Titan, having taken away the kingdom, he drove him into Italy, where he reigned together with Janus and laid the first foundations of Rome, and there as an exile he exchanged life for death. The poets called Latium <note>The region of Italy where Rome was founded.</note> the "underworld": both because in those superior or early times it was inferior to Crete in both riches and nobility (for which reason the King, compared to his own Kingdom, called it the underworld), and also because in truth Italy lies lower than Greece, since it inclines more to the west. Men have everywhere been accustomed to call the East "the upper" and the West "the lower" <note>Ancient geography often mapped the rising sun as 'up' and the setting sun as 'down'.</note>. Allegorically, however, it is to be understood that when Jupiter holds the principal place in the birth or action of any person, he snatches the dominion and empire from Saturn, and forces him to yield to virtue and be inferior. ->### DIALOGUE II ###<-

...even if at first, in the beginning of the generation of things and the conception of living creatures, Saturn reigns—that is, the seeds are preserved under the earth and the sperm is condensed with the divine help of this Planet intervening—nevertheless, in the progress, growth, and adornment of things already arisen and brought to the light, Jupiter is seen to claim the kingdom for himself and holds the primary role. Having expelled his parent Saturn from power, he is seen to banish him to the underworld; that is, into blind and dark places where the seeds of things, over which Saturn is rightly thought to rule, lie hidden in the beginning of generation.

**SO.** The interpretations you have devised for those things said to have happened to Jupiter and Saturn together seem indeed to be sharp and most plausible. Since these matters have held such subtle and elegant meanings, I judge that those things which the poets have related concerning the victories and virtues of Jupiter—especially concerning his justice, generosity, and piety—will hold much more subtle and elegant meanings still.

<margin>He interprets Jupiter's beneficent nature and his illustrious actions quite elegantly.</margin>

**PH.** You judge rightly indeed: for they say that he first showed mortals the way of living well and honorably, whereas before, men were accustomed to sacrifice humans and feed on their flesh; they say the God withdrew them from this most impious and inhuman custom. Truly, they intend to signify that the celestial Jupiter, on account of his greatest kindness, forbids men from every kind of cruelty and ferocity, and pours piety into them, and preserves and extends their lives—as well as protecting and freeing their bodies from almost innumerable dangers.

<margin>Jupiter is called *Zeus* <note>original: "Ζεύς"</note> by the Greeks, as if from *zoe* <note>original: "ζωή"</note>, which is to say, life.</margin>

Hence he is called *Zeus* by the Greeks, as if it means "life." They add, moreover, that he established laws, taught piety, and dedicated temples to the immortal Gods: because the celestial Jupiter is accustomed to make the men subject to him moderate, lovers of equity, and as devoted as possible to divine worship. They also declare that he subdued the greatest part of the whole world: which he distributed among his brothers, sons, relatives, and friends, and reserved for himself only Mount Olympus, in which he resided as if in a court; and with almost countless men flocking from everywhere to the God, seeking divine judgments, he rendered the laws and administered complete and incorrupt justice. They certainly signify that this most beneficent Planet confers victories, riches, and possessions upon his men, along with a liberal distribution of them; and that he himself, having attained a certain purified substance and most pure nature by divine favor, was entirely foreign to all greed and filth: and he makes men just, and most loving of virtue and equity. For this reason, the Hebrews called him *Sedech* <note>original: "Sedech," a transliteration of the Hebrew *Tzedek* (צדק), meaning "justice"</note>, as if you were to say "Justice."

<margin>All Hebrews call Jupiter *Sedech*, as if justice.</margin>

**SO.** All those allegories of Jupiter, which you have interpreted so learnedly and eruditely, have brought me the greatest pleasure. But what will you say about this God's various and diverse loves, rapes, and adulteries?

<margin>The allegorical sense of why the poets feigned that Jupiter joined his sister Juno to himself in marriage.</margin>

**PH.** Historians report that Jupiter first joined his sister to himself in marriage—the daughter of Saturn and Ops, brought into the light in one and the same birth with him. In rendering the allegorical sense, some think Juno signifies earth and water, and Jupiter air and fire; but some others think Juno signifies air, and Jupiter fire: which elements indeed seem to be joined by brotherly charity and conjugal benevolence. Others think that by the name of Juno, the Moon should be understood. Each, however, interprets the fables of Juno according to their own opinions.

**SO.** But you, O Philo, what do you think should be understood by the name of Juno?

<margin>The element of fire was obscure and unknown to the ancients.</margin>

**PH.** Certainly the Power that rules and governs this lower World and all the elements, especially the air, which surrounds and encompasses the water, and is seen to penetrate the earth everywhere: for the element of fire was obscure and unknown to the ancients; indeed, the ancients believed the air touched the Lunar sphere, even if its upper part, contiguous to the heavens, acquired a greater heat than the lower part on account of their continuous motion. Hence, on account of the air's greatest commonality and dignity in the elementary world, it was consecrated to Juno; she herself is thought to be the Goddess and power moderating and governing the entire World attributed to generation and the elements, just as Jupiter is the ruler and moderator of the celestial bodies...

...the moderator <note>Referring to the planet Jupiter</note> is held in the highest veneration by mortals—and not without reason, since he is more beneficent and more excellent than the other planets. He occupies the second seat as the most worthy after the first; however, the first seat was granted to his father Saturn out of reverence and piety as the most worthy of all, for Saturn is seen to signify the celestial intellect that produces the soul. Similarly, Opis <note>A Roman goddess of the earth and fertility</note>, the wife of Saturn and mother of Jupiter and Juno, designates the earth and prime matter. Jupiter obtained the middle place in the ethereal regions; he is seen to be the prince and common parent of the other planets (excepting only Saturn), of the Heaven, and of his sister Juno, who encompasses and moderates all bodies found between heaven and the center of the earth. Moreover, because the celestial world and the elemental world touch one another with no intermediary existing between them, they are said to be siblings. They are asserted to have been brought forth in the same birth because both were procreated simultaneously from the father (Intellect) and from the mother (Matter), as Anaxagoras <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who taught that "Mind" or "Intellect" (Nous) ordered the universe</note> felt. This is also confirmed by the authority of the Sacred Volumes <note>The Bible, specifically the book of Genesis</note>, which, in treating the creation of things and the beginning of the world, report that heaven and

<margin>The reason why Juno is said to have come forth from the mother's womb before Jupiter.</margin>
earth were created from one principle and seed by the best and greatest God. However, Juno is said to have come forth from the mother's womb first because it is a very ancient opinion that the procreation of the universe began from the center and crept upward in a certain succession to the outermost circumference of heaven, not unlike how a tree rises gradually from the lowest earthly root to the highest ethereal branches. This can indeed be confirmed by the most weighty testimony of the Psalmist <note>Referring to the Book of Psalms</note> who says: "In the day that God created the earth and the heaven," <note>original Latin: *Die, quo Deus terram cœlumq; creauit*</note> placing the lower before the superior in the order of procreation through such a context of words. These two worlds are also said to have been joined in marriage; for, as I have already said above, the entirety of the heavens maintains the same proportion to the community of the elements as a husband to a wife—since the former are seen to act upon the latter, and the latter receive the actions flowing down from the former.

<margin>Jupiter and Juno have the same etymology: for both are so named from "helping."</margin>
Even the name of Juno has one and the same origin as Jupiter: that is, from "helping" <note>original Latin: *iuuando*</note>. For both help greatly in the generation of things—he as the father, she as the mother. She is also called the Goddess of Marriages and "Lucina" <note>A title for Juno as the goddess of light and childbirth, who brings children "into the light"</note> to those in labor, being that most excellent power which tempers and moderates the lower world, the conjunction of the elements, and the generation of things.

<margin>Why Juno is considered the Goddess of Marriages and Lucina to those in labor.</margin>
**SO.** You have said enough concerning the marriage of Jupiter and Juno; now proceed to interpret their progeny, namely the female Hebe and the male Mars.

<margin>The allegory of that fable which recounts that Juno conceived by the work of Apollo and gave birth to Hebe.</margin>
**PH.** They say that Apollo, the son, while once staying with his father Jupiter, gave his stepmother Juno wild lettuces to eat. Because of this, the Goddess—who had previously been spoken of poorly for her barrenness—immediately conceived and gave birth to a daughter, Hebe. On account of her extraordinary beauty, Hebe was placed in charge of youth and was later joined in marriage to Hercules.

**SO.** What is the allegory of this little fable?

**PH.** When the Sun, who is called Apollo, dwells in the house of his father Jupiter—that is, in Sagittarius, the first and principal domicile of Jupiter—and from there runs through to Pisces, the second habitation of the same Jupiter (a notable work of the Zodiac), he completes a journey that encompasses the entire interval of time between mid-November and mid-March. Because of the excessive cold and constant rains of those months, Juno (designating the elemental sphere) is made pregnant. And this is surely what is signified when it is said that Apollo served the Goddess wild lettuces to eat, which are undoubtedly a very cold and moist food. These two qualities <note>cold and moisture</note> seem to stir and move the earth, which had become barren from the intemperance of the previous autumn, and to bestow upon the roots and seeds of things a certain power of generating or germinating, which is called "conception." Hence, in the next spring, as the Sun leaves Pisces and enters Aries, the earth is seen to bring forth so many and such beautiful offspring. Moreover, because at that time plants turn green and all things are renewed, Hebe is proclaimed to be the Goddess of Youth; for she [represents] that power of germinating...

<margin>The allegorical sense of why Hebe is said to have been joined to Hercules in his mother’s name <note>The Latin *matris nomine* (in the name of the mother) likely refers to Hebe being the daughter of Juno, who eventually adopted Hercules as her son upon his deification, or it may be a scribal error for *matrimonio* (in marriage).</note>.</margin>
They say she later became the wife of Hercules himself. This is because excellent men, famous and distinguished for their virtues, are called "Hercules." We see their fame preserved perpetually fresh and whole <note>The name Hebe is the Greek word for "Youth" or the "prime of life."</note>, never dying or growing old.

<margin>The allegorical sense of why Mars and Hebe are said to be siblings, both drawing their origin from Jupiter and Juno as if from parents.</margin>
PH. Mars, as you know well, is a very hot and almost burning planet; he sends down abundant heat into the <term>sublunary world</term> <note>The region below the moon, consisting of the four elements (earth, water, air, and fire) where things are born and die.</note>. This heat, when mixed with the moisture signified by Hebe, produces many and very diverse offspring in this lower world, which is designated by the name Juno.

Therefore, elemental Juno, with the concurrent power of celestial Jupiter, gave birth to these two most noble offspring, Hebe and Mars—namely, moisture and heat—by whose union all subsequent generations of mixed things followed.

They add, moreover, that just as Hebe signifies the most common generation of the world by reason of moisture, so Mars, who has an innate property of burning and destroying, seems to foreshadow the death of things, which usually proceeds from summer heats that squeeze out all moisture.

Consequently, these two children born of Jupiter and Juno represent the rising and falling of lower things.

Since destruction emanates from celestial causes only by accident—for the causes themselves perform only their own duty and intention by generating—they claimed that Juno gave birth to Mars by a "striking of the womb." For corruption usually follows from a defect or striking of matter, and not as a target or end proposed by the <term>agent</term> <note>The 'agent' refers to the active celestial force, which intends only to create life; death is a byproduct of material limitation.</note>.

SO. I have greatly enjoyed the allegories of the marriage of Jupiter and Juno and their legitimate progeny which you have now explained. Now, I would desire to understand something of their secret loves and adulterous offspring, such as when Jupiter is said to have lain with Latona, Alcmena, and many others.

<margin>The fable of Latona, who was Ravished by Jupiter and greatly hated by Juno, explaining her misery, flight, and long wandering, as well as the birth of Apollo and Diana.</margin>
PH. The poets tell the tale that Jupiter was once captured by love for the maiden Latona and made her pregnant. When Juno took this poorly, she not only stirred up the most serious hatred against the wretched woman in all lands, so that no woman would grant her refuge out of mercy, but she also ordered a serpent of marvelous and unusual size, named Python, to pursue her everywhere.

For this reason, as she fled both the divine wrath and that threatening serpent, after a long wandering she finally reached the famous island of Delos. There, having obtained hospitality from the citizens of Delos, she is said to have given birth to Diana and Apollo.

Indeed, since Diana came out first, she assisted her laboring mother by performing the duty of a midwife <note>Original: *Lucinae officio*, referring to Lucina, the goddess of childbirth.</note> at the birth of Apollo.

After Apollo reached the vital airs, equipped with bow and arrows, he killed that serpent Python and remarkably avenged his mother's injuries.

SO. I ask you to interpret the allegorical sense of this fable.

<margin>An allegory declaring the fable of Latona, skillfully relating it to the storm of the Great Flood.</margin>
PH. By her [Latona] is signified that during the time of the Flood <note>A reference to the Great Flood (like that of Noah or Deucalion) which was a common theme in Renaissance allegorical interpretations of myths.</note>, the air was rendered so cloudy and dark by the vapors of the water—because of the vast and continuous rains that fell then, covering the earth—that neither the Sun nor the Moon could spread their light into this lower world. Because of the extreme density and thickness of the air, the rays of neither planet could penetrate it.

Therefore they say that Latona—whom they interpret as the circumference of the heaven where the Milky Way is seen—conceived by her lover Jupiter. And when she desired to bring forth and return the light of the Moon and Sun to the universe after the Flood, Juno (who signifies the air, water, and earth) was heavily incensed against both the husband and the mistress because of that conception. She tried as hard as possible to hinder Latona’s birth and the rising of the Sun and Moon in the lower world with her thick and dense vapors, so that no place on earth offered any entrance or path for these lights, nor could they be seen.

Furthermore, the serpent Python represents the abundant moisture that remained on the earth after the Flood, which, with vapors always and continuously rising, it...

seemed to pursue her: those who, by condensing the air and making it thicker, allowed neither the lunar nor the solar rays to arise or be seen. Moreover, they called that immoderate moisture "the Serpent" <note>original: "Serpentem." The name Python is often etymologically linked to the Greek verb *pythein*, meaning "to rot," referring to the slime left after the Great Flood.</note>, inasmuch as it brings plants and terrestrial animals toward rot and destruction. Finally, on the island of Delos—where the air first became pure because of the dryness of the receding waves—Latona gave birth to Diana and Apollo. For the Greeks believe that after the flood, the Moon and Sun first shone upon the inhabitants of Delos <note>The name Delos means "manifest" or "visible" in Greek, fitting the allegory of light appearing.</note>. They say that Diana preceded her brother Apollo in birth, because the Moon shone first by night, and the Sun followed on the next day. Hence the Moon seems to have prepared the air to receive the maximum splendor of the Sun, acting as if she had brought aid to her mother in labor, just as Lucina <note>The Roman goddess of childbirth, here identified with the Moon/Diana.</note> does. They then relate that Apollo, once born, pierced the serpent Python with arrows: because once the Sun showed himself to be seen by mortal eyes, he immediately put to flight and dissipated with his most effective rays that moisture which was greatly hindering the generation of animals and plants. **SO.** What, I ask, is called the bow of Apollo? **PH.** We could interpret it as the circuit of the solar body itself, from which rays are sent out like arrows from a bow. We could also bring forward another more ancient, more learned, and wiser allegory regarding the birth of Diana and Apollo. **SO.** I pray you, do not be silent about it.

<margin>Another allegory explaining the same fable of Latona, elegantly adapting it to the creation of the two luminaries at the beginning of the world.</margin>
**PH.** The fable just recited seems to signify the creation of the two luminaries at the world's beginning, and it agrees in a wonderful way with the Mosaic writings <note>Referring to the Book of Genesis in the Bible, attributed to Moses.</note>. **SO.** By what reasoning? **PH.** Moses recorded in his writings that before God created and ordered the celestial world occupying the upper seats and the terrestrial world assigned to the lower regions, the terrestrial orb with all the elements was utterly confused and entangled; there existed a dark and obscure abyss. But with the divine breath breathing over the waters of the abyss, light immediately arose, and the first night preceded the day; the day followed afterward. This indeed seems to be signified by the birth of Latona, who represents the celestial substance. Since Jupiter—namely the supreme God, the creator of all things—was held by the greatest love for her, he filled and impregnated her with the shining bodies, specifically the Sun and the Moon. But when Juno—namely the confusion of the elements—resisted the divine will, those most bright bodies could not penetrate her with their rays; rather, they were attacked on all sides by the elemental globe and compelled to retreat. Furthermore, the abyss of waters, which is represented by the name of the serpent Python, brought a great impediment to the heavens, so that they could not give forth or show the most clear light of the Sun or Moon to the lands. Finally, at the island of Delos—which signifies that small portion of the earth first uncovered from the waters at the origin of the world, rising above the waves like an island—the celestial lights showed themselves to be seen. This was both because it rose above the waves and because in that part of the world the air was not very thick or dark. Whence the Holy Books testify that after light and darkness—namely night

<margin>The order of the world's creation.</margin>
and day—were created on the first day: then on the next, God formed and extended the <term>ethereal firmament</term> <note>The "expanse" or sky that separates the waters above from the waters below.</note>, and separated the air and waters from the Earth. On the third day, he soon opened the earth and began the generation of plants. Finally, on the fourth day—represented by Latona giving birth among the Delians—the Sun and Moon illuminated the Earth, which was now visible and open. From this sequence of works and times, it can be understood that in the cycle of the six days of the world's construction, the conception preceded on the first day, but the birth and offspring finally came forth on the fourth day. They granted the prior place in birth to Diana, and feigned that she played the part of the midwife at Apollo’s birth, because at the beginning of creation, night precedes day, and the lunar rays, by a certain wonderful providence of God, prepared the air to receive the solar ones. ### DIALOGUE II. 415

...Python <note>original: "Pythonem." Referring to the monstrous serpent slain by Apollo.</note>: that is, they add that he killed the abyss. They say this because the Sun, by the almost divine power of its rays, dried the earth more and more each day, purified the air, and dispersed the water. It consumed that raw and undigested moisture remaining from the abyss, which was a great obstacle to the generation of living creatures, even if it did not hinder the growth of plants, which are naturally more moist. For this reason, on the fifth day of creation—which followed the rising and presence of the heavenly lights—winged and aquatic creatures were brought forth and created, as they are considered less perfect. Finally, on the sixth and last light of creation, God formed man as the most perfect and complete of all lower things. This happened when the celestial lights, and especially the Sun, had so arranged the elements and tempered their mixture that from them that animal could be made in whom spirit is found joined and mingled with body, divine nature with earthly nature, and eternity with mortality in a wonderful composition.

**SO.** I do not remember ever hearing an allegory more elegant or learned than this. I believe I have perfectly understood the similarity you have shown it shares both with the creation of the universe as narrated by Moses in the Holy Volumes <note>Refers to the Book of Genesis.</note> and with the successive and continuous series of the six days of work. It is truly marvelous that such arduous and sublime matters could be concealed or hidden under the veils of human stories. <margin>The allegory of the myth of Jupiter’s adultery with Alcmena under the form of Amphitryon, and the discussion of the birth of Hercules himself.</margin>
**PH.** The Poets feigned that Jupiter, ensnared by love for Alcmena, lay with her after assuming the form of her husband Amphitryon, from which union Hercules is said to have come forth. Indeed, among the Greeks, men who were most worthy and excellent in virtue were usually called "Hercules," as you know. These men are born to mothers endowed with a praiseworthy composition of both body and mind—beautiful, honorable women like Alcmena, who is said to have possessed the finest character and remarkable physical beauty, and to have loved her husband uniquely. Jupiter is very easily captured by love for this kind of woman, upon whom he is accustomed to pour his virtues largely and copiously. Thus, they seem to conceive primarily from Jupiter, while their husbands serve only as the physical instruments in the act of conception. This is precisely what is signified when it is said that Jupiter lay with the wife while assuming the appearance of her husband, Amphitryon. For the seed of Amphitryon alone could never have produced a Hercules from Alcmena unless power and virtue had also arrived via the influence of the heavenly Jupiter. Because he proceeded from the greatest and divine virtues of that most beneficial Planet <note>Jupiter was known in Renaissance astrology as the "Greater Benefic," the most helpful and positive planetary influence.</note>, Hercules was considered the true and proper son of Jupiter, but the son of Amphitryon in name only. The same must be felt regarding all excellent and famous men who deserve the name of Hercules: it is exactly as we said of that most outstanding son of Alcmena.

**SO.** Did Jupiter not also burn with love for other women? Is he not said to have had many children by them?

<margin>The reason why the poets attributed many loves to Jupiter himself. Jupiter seems to infuse various and different kinds of love into men according to the condition of the other planets with which he is joined. The allegory of the love with which Jupiter pursued Leda.</margin>
**PH.** Furthermore, the poets attributed many loves to Jupiter because that Planet is by nature most benevolent, and it renders men wonderfully fit and inclined toward friendship and love. And although his love seems to look toward honor alone as its proper and fitting goal, yet when he has commerce with some other Planet in the horoscopes <note>original: "natalibus," referring to birth charts or planetary alignments at birth.</note> of men subject to his power and virtue (whom the poets call his "sons"), he renders their minds inclined to love and cherish honorable things mixed with those qualities that savor of the nature of that other Planet. In this kind of love, he is imagined to have loved Leda, with whom he is said to have practiced the arts of Venus <note>original: "Venerem exercuiße," a euphemism for sexual union.</note> while clothed in the form of a swan. Thus he was captured by Leda, and soon he captured Leda herself, who, heavy with divine seed, gave birth to Castor and Pollux together in the same labor. The poets fashioned the story that Jove assumed the form of a swan for this reason: to indicate that purity and clarity of mind, together with sweetness and elegance of speech, possess the greatest power to stir up love and win over friendship.

<margin>Allegories of many of the loves of Jove.</margin>
Sometimes, however, Jove sends into the minds of his followers an honorable love, yet one that is not open or manifest, but internal and hidden—and, so to speak, "cloudy." Such was his love for the daughter of Inachus <note>Io.</note>, with whom they say the God had relations while wrapped in a cloud. 

But if Jove should be associated with Venus, he will stir up a certain love that tends toward pleasure. For this reason, they say he loved Europa and carried the girl away after she was deceived by the appearance of a most beautiful bull, because in truth the sign of the Bull <note>Taurus.</note> is the home of Venus itself. 

But if he should have some commerce with Mercury, he will induce a love in the minds of men looking toward utility; for Mercury is indeed thought to be the diligent provider and administrator of resources and substance. For this reason, they say Jove was ensnared by love for Danaë and obtained and seduced the maiden through the most clever invention of a golden shower; for the generous distribution of money is the most powerful reason for the powerful and wealthy to be loved by the weak and needy, who expect and receive such things with the greatest greed, as if they were rain falling from Heaven. 

But if he is joined with the Sun, he will impress upon our minds a vehement love for reigning, dominating, and obtaining the highest ranks of dignity. This is what they signify when they say that Jove, in order to possess Asteria, transformed himself into an Eagle. 

However, if he is joined with the Moon, he will pour forth a tender and pious love, like that of a mother or a nurse toward a son or a pupil. Hence, they say he loved Semele, the daughter of Cadmus, and took the girl by assuming the person of Beroe, her nurse. 

But if he should be attached to Mars, he is seen to excite a burning and consuming love; for this reason, they have passed down the story that he ravished Aegina by taking the terrifying form of a lightning bolt. 

When, however, he joins himself to Saturn, he is thought to bestow a certain love composed of the honorable and the base—partly human and intellectual, and partly bestial and impure. From this, the poets sang that he was captured by the outstanding beauty of Antiope and enjoyed her love by assuming the form of a Satyr, which represents a human in its upper parts and a goat in its lower parts. This was not done randomly, since the sign of the Goat <note>Capricorn.</note> is said to be the seat of Saturn. 

Furthermore, if he is coupled with a feminine sign, he will induce a womanly love; for this reason, they say he obtained Callisto by feigning a female appearance. But if he enters a masculine sign, especially Aquarius, which is the home of Saturn, he is seen to bring about the greatest propensity for the love of boys. For this reason, the ancients recorded that he loved Ganymede, a most handsome boy, and having raised him up to heaven, transferred him into Aquarius, the house of Saturn. 

I could explain to you learned, whole, and perfect allegories for all the loves of Jove mentioned here, as well as others besides; but we shall pass over them, lest we seem more inquisitive or talkative than is right and good. You must only be aware of this: all the loves of this God signify various species of loves and friendships, and different kinds, which proceed and are poured forth from Jove when he holds dominion and leadership in the horoscopes of men. These diverse propensities for loving and inclinations of minds—which he bestows upon his people partly by his own nature, and partly because of the different powers of the many celestial signs to which he is joined—are seen to be signified through his numerous and manifold progeny. Their history reveals those who participated in Jove's virtues in different ways, along with the manner of that participation...

We find many things fashioned by the poets regarding Venus; they sometimes call her the "great generation of more excellent things," referring all dominion over them to her as if to a mother and Queen, and saying she was born of Heaven and Day as her parents.

They contend that she bore twin loves <note>Eros and Anteros (Love and Reciprocal Love).</note> and three sisters, who are called the Graces, by Jove. By this they wish to signify that the love of lower things proceeds from two beneficial and kind parents who are called the <term>Fortunes</term> <note>In traditional astrology, Jupiter is the "Greater Fortune" and Venus is the "Lesser Fortune," both being planets believed to have a positive influence.</note>: that is, from Jove the Greater Fortune, and Venus the Lesser Fortune. However, they assigned the name of father to Jove as the male and superior, but the name of mother to Venus as the female and inferior. Furthermore, Jove’s love is honorable, spiritual, perfect, and masculine; whereas the love of Venus is pleasant, sensible, imperfect, and feminine. For this reason, the poets called the bright and pure love of both planets "twin," both because it is composed of the honorable and the pleasant simultaneously, and also because the true and absolute love of two lovers ought to be twin and mutual. These two parents joined together are also said to have fathered the Graces, since love is never found destitute of the "grace" <note>Here "grace" implies both charm and mutual favor/gratitude.</note> of both parties. The same also happens when Venus looks upon <note>In astrology, an "aspect" or "looking upon" occurs when planets reach specific geometric angles to one another.</note> Mars. They also depict her surrounded by a <term>cestus</term> <note>A magical girdle or belt said to make the wearer irresistible.</note> amidst marriages and weddings, to signify the great union and indissoluble bond with which Venus binds and ties lovers to one another.

<margin>Doves consecrated to Venus.</margin>

<margin>The myrtle sacred to Venus.</margin>
We could also give this further reason: because the leaves of the myrtle, following one another two by two, represent a twin and reciprocating love, as we have already said. Furthermore, the berries of the myrtle are stained with a dark color, by which it is signified that love produces sad and melancholic fruits.

<margin>The rose dedicated to Venus.</margin>
From the flowers, Venus is said to have chosen only the rose, both for its wonderful beauty and most pleasing scent, and also because it is hedged about on all sides by sharp thorns, just as love sits in the midst of hardships, pains, and unbearable tortures of the soul.

...she did not hesitate to prostitute her friendship and offer the use of her body to many. Because of her extraordinary beauty and dazzling appearance, everyone called her Venus, as she reflected that most bright and famous planet on earth. Furthermore, they persuaded themselves that the Celestial Venus <note>The "Celestial Venus" refers to the planetary or divine influence, as opposed to the historical woman being described here.</note> had infused her with great royalty, supreme beauty, and an immoderate lust for coupling. For it is said to be the nature of that planet to send down a life of pleasure and concupiscent desires into this lower world. Hence, the Cyprians are recorded to have been the first to worship Venus as a divine power and to have built temples in her honor. However, the poets, through a certain new and unusual method of birth, signified her origins quite subtly.

<margin>
The myth recounting the monstrous birth of Venus herself.
</margin>
They say that Saturn once cut off the testicles of his father Coelus <note>Original: *Coelio*, the personification of the Heavens.</note> with a sickle; or, with the story varying slightly, they imagine that Jupiter cut off the testicles of his parent Saturn with his own sickle. When these were thrown into the sea, they say Venus was born from their blood together with the foam of the sea; and for this reason, they depict her naked, floating in the sea within a seashell.

<margin>
The allegory explaining the unusual birth of Venus.
</margin>
**SO.** What allegory can be asserted for such a monstrous origin? 

**PH.** The testicles of Coelus signify the power of generating, which descends from heaven into this lower world. Venus is the proper instrument of this power, since she is said to truly bestow the appetite and the force of generating upon living things. They add that Saturn cut off Coelus's testicles because Saturn is called <term>Chronos (χρόνος): the Greek word for "Time"</term> by the Greeks, which signifies Time—the primary cause, clearly, of generation in this sublunary world <note>The "sublunary world" is the Earthly realm below the moon, characterized by change, birth, and death.</note>. For it is necessary that things existing in this realm and subject to time, since they are not eternal, must have had a beginning and been born. This can also be proven by this reasoning: because time corrupts the things subject to its rule, and whatever is corrupted must necessarily have been born previously. Hence, Time (understood as Saturn), with Venus mediating, brought generation from heaven into the lower world. This world is given the name of the "sea" because of the constant change from one form to another, aided by the perpetual cycle of generation and corruption.

<margin>
Generation always requires preceding corruption. Saturn's nature seems to be corruption, just as Venus's is generation.
</margin>
The sublunary world received this benefit of generation because the testicles of Coelus were cut off with a sickle: for generation always requires a preceding corruption <note>In ancient philosophy, "corruption" refers to the breaking down or decay of a thing, which is necessary for new things to be formed.</note>. Furthermore, Saturn's own nature seems to be that of corrupting, just as Venus's is of generating; thus, birth proceeds from the latter and death from the former as if from causes. Yet both are necessary: for unless prior things were corrupted, subsequent things could not be born at all. For this reason, they say Saturn used the sickle—which he usually employs to overturn and corrupt all things—to cut off the manhood of his father Coelus and threw it into this worldly sea. From these, Venus was born, who bestows the power of begetting upon lower beings, joined with the power of corruption due to the cutting off of the heavenly testicles. 

Those who believe the severed testicles were not from Coelus, but were Saturn’s own, intend to signify that Saturn—because he was castrated by his son Jupiter and thus remained unfit and unable to produce offspring—is a great hindrance to generation itself. However, the instruments of begetting of which Saturn was deprived are said to have formed Venus, the complete and absolute cause of generation. The authors of this second opinion also seem to signify that Saturn begins the process after the first conception following intercourse; for it is his role to congeal or condense the seed, and for this reason, he rules and dominates in the first month of conception. But soon, in the second month, Jupiter begins to form and shape the fetus, appearing to usurp the domination and command of the conception for himself. And this is surely what they mean when they say the manhood of the father Saturn—who plays the primary part in the conception—was cut off by his son Jupiter, and that Venus was born from them. For she stands as the prince of all generation, and especially in the fifth

...she exercises her dominion in that month <note>original: "mense"; referring to April, the month of Venus</note>, granting both perfection and beauty to the offspring. For this reason, they imagined that she was born from the blood of the testicles and the foam of the sea: because a living creature is procreated from the bloody seed of the male supplied by the testicles, and from the subtle and foamy sperm of the female. <note>Renaissance biology often debated the nature of "female sperm" and its role alongside menstrual blood in formation.</note> Alternatively, the foam should be understood as human sperm because of its whiteness, and the blood as the menstrual flow of the woman which provides nourishment to the fetus. Furthermore, they depict the goddess naked: because love can by no means be concealed or hidden, and because she leads one toward the love of the flesh; and also because lovers ought to be open, sincere, and "naked" in their intentions. She is also seen swimming in the sea: because the love of procreating is spread through all parts of this lower world—which represents the sea due to its continuous and constant change—and because lovers are found to be mobile, unstable, doubtful, and inconstant, tossed by storms and tempests no differently than a sea agitated by the winds.

**PH.** They say that Venus
