The story of Mars and Venus, treating love and adultery in a very elegant manner.
</margin>
was once married to Vulcan. Disdaining him because he was both deformed in appearance and lame in both feet, the most beautiful goddess was inflamed with a vehement love for the vigorous warrior Mars. While she was carrying on a quiet and clandestine affair with him, she was seen by the Sun <note>Sol</note> and immediately reported to Vulcan for adultery. Vulcan secretly surrounded the bed where the two lovers were lying with iron nets of the finest thread, catching them naked and unaware, and binding them together most tightly. Therefore, Vulcan called all the gods together, especially Neptune, Mercury, and Apollo, and showed them Mars and Venus naked and constrained by the iron bonds. The gods, moved by the unworthiness of this spectacle and affected by shame, are said to have covered their faces. Only Neptune offered such humble prayers to Vulcan that he finally obtained the release of Mars and Venus from him. From then on, Venus pursued the Sun and his entire lineage with a perpetual and implacable hatred, so that all the daughters of Apollo <note>Referring to figures like Pasiphae and Phaedra, who suffered from cursed or monstrous lusts.</note>, having the divine power turned against them, were defiled and corrupted. 

**SO.** What then do you think should be said concerning such lusts and adulteries of the celestial gods? 

**PH.** Not only is there hidden science, but also the greatest utility to be perceived from the allegory of this story. For it signifies that immoderate lust eventually brings the greatest detriment not only to all the faculties and virtues of the human body, but also displays a certain defect in the very act of coupling, along with a diminishing of one's solitary strength. 

**SO.** Explain the whole matter more broadly and diffusely. 

<margin>
A most learned allegory explaining the adultery of Mars and Venus.
</margin>
**PH.** Venus figures as human concupiscence <note>desire or lust</note> emanating from the planet Venus, which, because of the effective and powerful influence of this planet upon the births of its subjects, exists as something vehement and stirred up. This Venus is said to have married Vulcan—namely, the deity of the "inferior fire"—which in man is called "natural heat," <note>Natural heat (calor naturalis) was considered the internal warmth that governed digestion, life, and procreation.</note> providing the limit and the act of desire, and always adhering to it just as a husband to a wife. 
<margin>
He interprets the origin, nature, and conditions of Vulcan allegorically.
</margin>
They relate that this Vulcan was born of Jupiter and Juno. Because he was a lame boy, he was despised by his parents and cast down from heaven to the earth; Thetis lifted him up and nourished him, whence he later became the Smith of Jupiter, put in charge of forging thunderbolts. This signifies that the natural heat of humans and living creatures had its origin from Jupiter and Juno: because it seems to participate in something heavenly mixed with matter. For this reason, it is adorned with the natural, animal, and vital virtues by the merit of Jupiter and the heavens. However, because of the mixture of matter, it is found in human bodies to be neither eternal, nor equal in power, nor always consistent, unlike the heat of the Sun and other celestial stars. Rather, according to the changes of age and the diversity of human dispositions, it increases and decreases, rises and falls, just like a limp. And this is surely what is to be understood when it is said that Vulcan, because he was lame, was thrust down from heaven to the lands: for heat and all other qualities of heaven are seen to remain in one and the same consistent way perpetually, never "limping" like the inferior qualities.

<meta>This page continues the allegorical interpretation of the myth of Vulcan catching Mars and Venus in a net, explaining it through the lens of Renaissance physiology and the relationship between natural heat, moisture, and sexual desire.</meta>

->### LEO HEBRAEUS ON LOVE,###<-

Thetis, who represents the Ocean, providing milk signifies nothing other than the fact that the <term>natural heat</term> <note>original: "calor naturalis"; in Renaissance medicine, this was the vital warmth that fueled digestion and life</note> of both living creatures and the earth is nourished by moisture and vitality. This heat is stronger or weaker depending on whether the innate moisture corresponding to the heat is more abundant or more thin. They claim that Vulcan was a smith and craftsman hired by Jove because he appears to serve as a fit minister for many wonderful works that represent the nature of Jove—those works which make the human body illustrious and remarkable. Therefore, when desire (*Venus*) is joined in marriage with natural heat (*Vulcan*), she is ensnared by a most powerful love for *Mars*, who signifies the seething lust for intercourse. For *Mars* is thought to influence a raging, unbridled, and untamed libido. Because of this, they hold that he was not sired from the seed of Jove, nor did he participate in any virtue of that beneficial star; rather, they assert he erupted outward from the striking of Juno’s womb. By this, we ought to understand the deadly poison of maternal flows <note>original: "maternorum profluuiorum"; a reference to the belief that menstrual blood was toxic or influential in the formation of "hot" temperaments</note>. Indeed, because of the sharp stings of *Mars*, the force and power of Junonian matter is seen to greatly exceed the reason of Jove himself.

<margin>
The great friendship between Mars and Venus is confirmed by Astrologers.
</margin>
Therefore, desire (*Venus*) is accustomed to falling in love with the ardor of *Mars*. For this reason, Astrologers judge these two planets to be the closest of friends, and they believe that the favorable aspect of *Venus* restrains and coerces the wickedness of *Mars*. However, when these two lovers are coupled together and indulge in excessive and immoderate luxury, the *Sun*—representing the clarity of human reason—accuses them most gravely before *Vulcan*. The *Sun* shows him that because of this immoderate luxury, the natural heat is gradually weakened. Thus, *Vulcan*, warned by the *Sun*, captures and binds both adulterers with very thin nets that escape the sharpest sight of our eyes, leading to their great disgrace. For when the natural heat succumbs, the strength of libido also fails. Immoderate desires, stripped of their liberty and robustness, are bound and grow faint; they are seen to remain empty and naked of effect, with shame mixed with repentance added on top. *Vulcan* then offers both of them, caught in adultery, to be seen by the *Gods*. This means that the natural heat communicates its own defect and weakness to all the faculties of the body, which are called "divine" because of their distinguished duties. When the innate heat fails, these faculties suffer the greatest inconvenience and detriment. Three *Gods* in particular are called by name, acting as the three Princes of the human faculties: *Neptune*, *Mercury*, and *Apollo*. *Neptune* is seen to designate the "nourishing soul" along with all its natural virtues and powers proceeding from the liver; it receives the abundance of moisture it necessarily requires from *Neptune* <note>the liver was associated with the element of water/moisture in humoral theory</note>. *Mercury* is thought to represent the "sensing soul," which encompasses sense, motion, and cognition descending from the brain; they recognize *Mercury* as its prince. *Apollo* is thought to represent the "vital and pulsing soul," which transmits the spirits and natural heat through the arteries into the entire body, taking its origin from the heart. For as I remember saying above, the heart in the human body is seen to hold the same position as *Apollo* (the Sun) holds in the world. Consequently, many inconveniences and disgraces follow immoderate libido in the heart, brain, and liver, and in all the virtues and faculties emanating from each of them. No one except *Neptune* can appease *Vulcan* and repair his lost strength: for he signifies the nourishing virtue, which alone is able to recover the consumed natural heat through the moisture of food, and to restore the exhausted powers of *Venus* to their wholeness. They reported that *Venus* <note>original: "Cytheream"</note> held the entire family of the *Sun* in the greatest hatred, and that she took revenge for her own injuries through the debaucheries and adulteries of his daughters, upon whom she impressed a "Venereal" nature and "Venereal" habits. For love is the sharpest enemy of reason, and luxury is opposed to prudence. Not only does it refuse to obey reason, but it is also accustomed to overturning and corrupting all of reason's counsels and judgments. Whence reason, degenerated from its own right nature and clothed in a depraved and foreign one, considers all actions that proceed from libido to be good and con- <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; "con-" likely leads to "convenient" or "consistent".</note>

<margin>
The allegorical meaning of why Cupid is recorded by the poets as having been procreated from Venus and Mars. He explains the noble character and conditions of Cupid allegorically.

PH. You grasp the matter perfectly: for truly Cupid, who exists as a certain affection of love and absolute concupiscence, is procreated from Venusian <term>lust</term> <note>original: "libidine"</note> and the ardor of Mars. For this reason, they depict him as a boy, naked, blind, winged, and shooting arrows. He is a boy because love is always increasing, and is seen to be incontinent and untamable, not unlike an infant. He is naked because he can by no means be hidden or disguised. He is blind because he is so darkened and hindered by <term>perturbation</term> <note>original: "perturbatione"; in Renaissance psychology, a 'perturbation' was an emotion or passion that disturbed the equilibrium of the mind</note> that he is in no way able to look upon or discern the clearest light of reason which opposes him. He is winged on account of his great velocity: for the thoughts of a lover hasten most swiftly toward the beloved person, and there they find rest and a most happy life. The arrows of Cupid are said to be those with which he seeks out and pierces the hearts of lovers. Furthermore, the wounds inflicted by weapons of this kind are narrow, deep, and incurable; they are often inflicted like arrows by the most piercing rays that exit from the eyes of the lovers themselves.

SO. Tell me, I pray, Philo, for what reason did Venus bear Hermaphroditus from Mercury?

<margin>
The birth and power of Mercury. The insignia of Mercury. The various and different influences of Mercury, according to how he is joined with other planets and looks upon them differently. The versatile nature of Mercury. Certain men called Mercury on account of their excellence. The allegorical sense of why Mercury is said to have been born from Heaven and Day as if from parents, or in the opinion of others is the son of Jupiter and the nursling of Juno; he is also the brother of Venus, the messenger of Jupiter, and the interpreter of the Gods: and he is said to carry a woven rod in his hands as his own emblem.
</margin>

PH. I believe you are not unaware that the poets relate that Mercury was born of Heaven <note>original: "Cælo"</note> and Day, and that he had Venus as a sister. Others believe him to be the son of Jupiter and the nursling of Juno. Men think that this god presides over eloquence and the sciences—especially the mathematical ones, such as arithmetic, geometry, music, and astrology—and that he also presides over medicine, trade, and thievery; moreover, that he is the messenger of Jupiter and the interpreter of the Gods. Finally, a rod entwined with a serpent <note>original: "Virga... serpente circūntexta"; the caduceus</note> is believed to be the insignia of this divinity. From these principles, many fables sung by the poets about Mercury took their origin. But, setting aside lies and following the truth, let us say that the celestial Mercury—according to the various positions and different dispositions he obtains in the births of men—influences various and different properties or propensities in them. Hence, if he is powerful and has obtained a favorable <term>aspect</term> <note>original: "aspectum"; the angular relationship between planets in astrology</note>, he undoubtedly confers eloquence, elegance, and sweetness of speech, as well as learning and talent in the mathematical sciences. If he looks upon Jupiter rightly, he will grant a great propensity for philosophy and theology. Looking upon Mars rightly, he makes the best physicians; but wrongly, he procreates thieves or the worst physicians, especially when the Sun is <term>combusting</term> him <note>original: "comburente"; in astrology, a planet is 'combust' when it is so close to the Sun that its power is said to be weakened or scorched</note>. From this the fable arose that Mercury drove away the cows of Apollo, and from Chione had a son, Autolycus, a notorious thief. Joined with Venus, he usually produces poets and musicians; with the Moon, merchants and businessmen; associated with Saturn, he is judged to provide profound knowledge and the prophecy of future things. The reason for this diversity can be brought forward: that Mercury, endowed with a versatile nature, is easily changed into the nature of the other planet with which he is mixed. Hence, having obtained a mixture with a masculine planet, he turns out male; but joined with a feminine one, he is turned into a female. Among men, moreover, many have claimed the name of Mercury for themselves, especially some very celebrated physicians and most wise men among the Egyptians, who were participants in "Mercurial" virtues. Because this planet is seen to be bright on all sides, the poets feigned him to be the son of Heaven and Day; for he seems to participate in celestial substance together with the light of day, since the light of all planets proceeds from the Sun, which creates the Day. He is said to be the brother of Venus because both were born from the same parents, both are always found to be joined and close together, both complete their courses in the interval of the same time (namely, one year), and finally, both always travel near the Sun and never recede far from it. Others concede that Mercury was indeed fathered by Jupiter on account of his divine wisdom and virtue, but they believe he was afterwards raised by Juno: this is because human wisdom first proceeds from divinity, and is then perpetually preserved in the writings of men, which are understood by the name of Juno. They call him the messenger of Jove because he announces and foretells things that are to come and those to be accomplished by almighty God. Hence, both for this reason and because of his supreme eloquence, he is called the **interpreter of the Gods**. Mercury’s rod signifies the uprightness of natural talent <note>original: "ingenij"</note>, through which he instills the acquisition of the sciences into men. The serpent intertwined around the rod designates acute and subtle reasoning, which revolves and turns around that upright talent. Or rather, through the rod should be understood the intellect of the wise man dwelling on the contemplation of the sciences, and through the snake, the intellect of the prudent man turning and returning around the actions of the moral virtues. For the serpent, on account of its cunning and shrewdness, is seen to be very similar to <term>prudence</term> <note>original: "prudentiæ"; here meaning practical wisdom or discretion</note>, while the rod, on account of its straightness and precision, is seen to be like science. **SO.**

<margin>The fable of the theft by Mercury, the anger of Apollo, and the reconciliation of both: containing their mutual gifts together with its most learned allegory.</margin>
I remember having understood elsewhere that Mercury received his rod from Apollo. **PH.** They say that Mercury once secretly stole Apollo’s cows, and since no one but Battus had noticed this theft, the God is said to have bought the shepherd’s silence with the gift of a single cow. But since Mercury feared the peasant’s faith was uncertain and doubtful, he returned to Battus with his form and voice changed; having promised a bull if he would reveal the author of the theft, he discovered the secret that had been entrusted to the treacherous old man. Therefore, Mercury, fearing the anger of Apollo, turned the shepherd into stone. However, when Apollo, who was skilled in divination, finally learned of both the theft and the thief himself, he was moved by fury and drew his bow against Mercury, who, immediately dissolving into the breezes, excellently eluded the anger and the blow of the divine power. Afterwards, when the dispute between them was settled, Mercury is said to have given the **Lyre** <note>original: "Cytharam"</note> to Apollo as a gift, and Apollo gave the **rod** to Mercury. Some, however, with the story slightly varied, have passed down that Mercury sensed Apollo’s anger in advance and secretly stole the arrows from his quiver; noticing this, Apollo, although he burned with heavy anger, could not contain his laughter upon seeing Mercury’s cunning, and he forgave the injury he had received. Hence both honored themselves with mutual gifts—namely, the rod and the Lyre—and confirmed their friendship, which was restored to its full integrity. **SO.** What significance is offered for this fable? **PH.** Certainly this: that those of a "Mercurial" nature <note>referring to people born under the influence of the planet Mercury, often associated with cleverness, trade, or diplomacy</note> are indeed poor, but they are accustomed to devise innumerable tricks and deceits to draw off riches and wealth from the treasuries of Kings or governors. For to them, representing the nature of Mercury on account of their shrewd and versatile talent, royal business and secrets are most often committed. And this is surely signified when it is said that Mercury drove away Apollo’s herds. For Apollo designates Kings and Princes, upon whom he bestows such dignities. The cows seem to represent the riches and wealth of the powerful. If it should ever happen that the princes discover the robberies of their ministers and are heavily incensed at them for that reason, the ministers, immediately fleeing to the shrewd and cunning devices of Mercury, escape the threatening anger of their masters. By removing the causes of punishment and soothing the angry Princes with the greatest skill and the use of ornate words, they seem to recover the favor of the powerful for themselves. Also, the lowly condition of this class of men usually renders them safe or secure from the threats and injuries of Princes, since they are seen to not resist or fight back in the slightest. In this they certainly imitate Mercury, who is smaller than the other planets, and on account of his smallness suffers less trouble and detriment from the Sun's rays, and less scorching than any of the others. Whence not rashly did **Plato** frequently say that power and wisdom are to be coupled together: for wisdom seems to moderate power, and power seems to extol wisdom. We might also perhaps adapt this sense to the reconciliation of **Mercury** and **Apollo**, and the mutual gifts of both: because when these two planets, at the moment of someone's birth, occupy a fortunate seat and the domicile of a praiseworthy sign, and have conspired in some perfect conjunction or society: they bestow upon the **Mercurial** and wise man riches, wealth, and dignities; and likewise upon the **Solar** and powerful man they grant wisdom, prudence, and eloquence.

**SO.** You seem to have said enough regarding the origin, nature, and deeds of **Mercury**. Now there remains for you to open up that which I requested a while ago: namely, by what reasoning **Hermaphroditus** was brought into the light from the conjunction of him and **Venus**.

<margin>The allegorical sense of why the poets testify that Hermaphroditus was brought to light from the conjunction of Mercury and Venus.</margin>
**PH.** This is surely best declared by **Ptolemy** in the *Centiloquy* <note>original: "Centiloquio"; a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms</note>: for that Prince of Astrologers says that if, at someone’s rising, **Venus** is dwelling in the house of **Mercury**, and **Mercury** in the domicile of **Venus**, and much more so if the bodies of both planets are joined together, they render that person inclined and prone to a beastly lust that is repugnant to nature: so much so that some are afraid neither to lie with males, nor to act and be acted upon at the same time, performing the office of male and female at the same moment of time. Moreover, this kind of monstrous and double lust is hiddenly expressed by the name of **Hermaphroditus**, because it signifies a person participating in both sexes. That he was procreated from the mixing and intercourse of **Mercury** and **Venus** agrees best with true and natural reasoning: for these two planets, since they exist as different and greatly contrary to one another, cannot be tempered together well or conveniently, because **Mercury** claims the whole <term>intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectum"</note> for himself, while **Venus** claims the entire body for herself. Therefore, it is not at all surprising that the conjunction of these two so different natures produces a new, monstrous lust that is adverse to nature.

**SO.** You seem to have spoken most abundantly of the loves, marriages, and offspring of the inhabitants of heaven: and of their natures, as much regarding the common parent of all, **Demogorgon**, as of the two celestial parents, **Aether** and **Coelius**, and also of the five planets which proceed from them in a certain series: **Saturn**, **Jupiter**, **Mars**, **Venus**, and **Mercury**. Now I would desire to understand something concerning the children of **Latona** and **Jupiter**, namely **Apollo** and **Diana**; although few things can be told of **Diana**, who is handed down as having always lived a solitary and virginal life. Therefore, only the love of **Apollo** for **Daphne** remains for you to explain and clarify, whom the poets fable was turned into a laurel while fleeing the God.

**PH.** We seem to have treated the birth of **Apollo** and **Diana** fully and diffusely, if I am not mistaken, further above. Approaching what remains, therefore, let us say that **Diana** is feigned by the poets to be a virgin for this reason: because on account of the immoderate coldness of the **Moon**, women over whose births she dominates are seen to lack the heat and fire of lust.

<margin>The attributes of Diana sung by the poets are interpreted allegorically and indeed learnedly.</margin>
She is called the Goddess of Mountains and Fields because the **Moon** provides the greatest assistance for sending forth the buds of herbs and trees, upon which the wild animals of the forest feed. She is called a Huntress because she favors nocturnal hunts with her copious light. The guardianship of the roads is committed to her because she renders journeys easier and safer with her nocturnal splendor. She is depicted equipped with a bow and arrows for the reason that the rays flowing down from the **Moon** are often seen to bring no small detriment to living things, especially if they have insinuated themselves after the manner of arrows through narrow cracks in walls or windows. She is carried in a chariot by white stags, as if by the swiftest of all four-footed animals—

### PHILO ON LOVE ###

It rejoices in whiteness, as that is its own proper color. It is called **Luna** because it shines new in the twilight of the night. It is called **Diana** because, when old, it precedes the day and shines brightly before the rising of the Sun, and also because it is often seen during the day.

<margin>The allegorical sense of why Apollo is considered the God of wisdom and especially of medicine; why he plays the Lyre <note>original: "Cytharam"</note> given to him by Mercury and presides over the Muses; and why he loves the Laurel and the Crow as sacred to him; and finally, why he is thought by the Poets to go about equipped with a bow and arrows.</margin>

**SO.** I wait to hear the meanings of these things.

**PH.** He is called the God of wisdom for two reasons: first, because he claims for himself the rule of the heart and renders the spirits <note>original: "spiritus"; in Renaissance medicine, these were subtle vapors that carried life and thought through the body</note> of human knowledge and wisdom pure and bright by supplying them with abundant material; and second, because by the most fertile light of Phoebus’s lamp <note>the Sun</note>, those things that fall under our sight—from which our knowledge and wisdom are for the most part derived—are seen and discerned. 

It is gathered from two arguments that he presides over medicine: first, because the almost divine power of the heart and the innate heat proceeding from the heart preserves the health of the entire body and expels various and different kinds of diseases. Second, because the heat of the Sun, being truly gentle and temperate, heals and dissolves old diseases contracted from the intemperance of winter and autumn; for during those two seasons of the year, the Sun's strength is felt to be weak and thin due to the deadly cold, and therefore innumerable diseases infest human bodies at those times, which are later seen to be healed and recover their former strength when the spring heat arrives. 

He is said to play the **Lyre** and preside over the **Muses** for a twofold reason: first, because he effects a harmony of the pulses <note>the rhythmic beating of the heart</note> from the heart into the whole body by the benefit of the spirits diffusing themselves, which harmony experienced physicians immediately discern by touch alone. Second, because the Sun—as the greater, brighter, and more principal of the planets, and like the commander of them all—tempers and moderates that divine harmony composed from the diversity of celestial motions which, as I have already said, **Pythagoras** judged to be placed in the sweetest concert of voices <note>the "Music of the Spheres"</note>. 

And for this reason, the Poets judged that the **Lyre** should be attributed to **Apollo**. They said that **Phoebus** received it from **Mercury** because **Mercury** indeed provides the concord and harmonic measure, but the Sun, as the chief of the planets, was placed in charge of the celestial melody. This is not without merit, since he is observed to keep a greater order and a more certain rule in his motion than any of the others: for he always travels through the middle of the Zodiac, never deflecting from it even the slightest bit, and always proceeds on a straight path. For this reason, his motion is rightly considered the measure of the motions of others, just as his light is the origin of the lights of others. 

This, then, is undoubtedly what we must understand when the Poets testify that he is the leader of the **Muses**, who are said to be nine in number: because the number nine also encompasses the celestial spheres <note>typically the seven planets, the fixed stars, and the first mover</note> which emit that sweetest and divine concert, from which he, like a most skilled master of music, seems as it were to compose that entire song and melody of the heavens. His arrows are called his rays, which, either because of their excessive heat or because of a foul disposition of the air, are often accustomed to bring damage and destruction; hence they think that he also brings about pestilence.

<margin>The nature and honor of the Laurel.</margin>
From among the trees, they consecrated the **Laurel** to **Apollo**: first, because the **Laurel** is of a hot and aromatic nature and enjoys perpetual greenness; and second, because the temples of famous poets and triumphing emperors are seen wreathed with laurel garlands, all of whom are considered subject to the Sun, who confers wisdom and bestows empires and victories.

<margin>The wondrous property of the Laurel.</margin>
For another reason also the **Laurel** is consecrated to **Phoebus**: namely, because **Apollo**, since he is the God of wisdom, is accustomed to flow divination into the minds of men. Regarding the **Laurel**, it has been handed down to memory...

<margin>The fable of Apollo’s vehement love for Daphne, the Nymph’s flight, and her conversion into a Laurel: an explanation.</margin>
**PH.** While in the presence of **Cupid**, **Apollo** was boasting too insolently of the power of his bow and arrows—with which he had killed that pestilential serpent named **Python**—and he seemed to despise **Cupid's** bow and arrows as if they were merely childish weapons, not at all suited for performing great deeds. **Cupid**, bearing this insult with a resentful mind, is said to have wounded **Apollo** with a golden arrow and **Daphne**, daughter of the river **Peneus**, with a leaden one. Whereupon **Apollo**, immediately inflamed with love for the maiden, pursued her in a swift race, just as men are also accustomed to love gold vehemently and pursue it. But **Daphne**, holding **Apollo** in the greatest hatred and refusing to undergo his love as if it were a most heavy and leaden burden, fled from the pursuing God for a long time. But when the girl felt herself sought by **Apollo** and even now being caught, she implored the help and aid of her father **Peneus** and other rivers: who, in order to free the maiden from the hands of **Phoebus** <note>original: "Phœbi"; another name for Apollo as the sun god</note>, are said to have transformed her into a **Laurel** tree. After many repeated embraces of this tree, which was trembling with fear, the God finally, deceived by the foliage, adorned his Lyre and quiver with it and called the **Laurel** his own tree: from which great devotion and incredible love of the God, **Daphne** is narrated to have felt the greatest joy. **SO.** The fable is indeed most elegant and ingenious, but what is its significance?

<margin>The Allegory, learnedly and eruditely explaining Apollo's burning love for the Nymph, the Nymph's flight, and her metamorphosis into a Laurel.</margin>
**PH.** By this fiction, the Poets wished to indicate the immense and most widely spreading powers of love, which reach even to the **Sun**, the proudest and most powerful God of all the inhabitants of heaven. For this reason, they elegantly imagined that he had insolently boasted that he had pierced the threatening and all-devouring serpent **Python** with his bow and arrows—which signify his most effective rays. This serpent, as we have already said, seems to foreshadow the flood of waters which flowed around and inundated the entire earth on every side, and which greatly hindered the generation and nourishment of men and other earthly living creatures. The **Sun**, by the emission of his burning rays as if they were arrows, dried up and finished this overflowing of waters, and bestowed the most noble gift of existence <note>original: "essentiam"</note> upon all who lead their lives on earth. However, so that you may understand, **Sophia**, what may properly be called the bow of **Apollo**—besides the fact that we can interpret it as the course and outer circuit of the **Sun** itself, by which that most beneficent star freed the whole race of living things, and especially of men, from the cruelty of the most cruel **Python** (that is, from the flood of waters)—I wish to bring forward another truer explanation more consistent with reason: namely, that by the bow of **Apollo**, that

...clouds are produced by diffusion, the difference and dissimilarity of which, in greater or lesser thickness according to the varied capacity of the clouds, produces that admirable diversity of colors; it follows surely that the solar bow <note>The rainbow, or Iris</note>, by the arrangement of divine providence, provides the greatest security to mortals against a flood. **SO.** By what 
<margin>The reason why the Rainbow we see is thought to make us safe or secure from a flood.</margin>
reasoning, I pray, does the Sun promise us security from the waters through that most beautiful bow? **PH.** When the traces of the Sun create that arched shape, they are by no means impressed upon thin or clear air, but rather upon air that is thick and humid. If this air were perhaps too thick or dense, such that it could once again produce a new deluge because of a massive multitude of rains, it would never be capable or powerful enough to receive the Sun’s impression nor to form the shape of the bow. Therefore, the impression of that bow seen by us provides the greatest proof that the clouds are not endowed with such thickness that they can send a deluge down upon the earth. This is indeed the certainty and security that the solar bow provides to the human race against the flooding of waters. The cause of this must be entirely attributed to the force and power of the Sun, which renders the clouds so pure and thin that, by impressing its own circuit and image upon them, it leaves them powerless and unfit to stir up a new deluge. 

Hence the Poets wisely and prudently sang that Apollo killed the Python <note>original: "Pythonem." In mythology, Python was a monstrous serpent born of the mud after the Great Flood; scientifically, it represents the pestilential mists and rot dried up by the Sun’s heat.</note> with his bow and arrows. Yet, after this illustrious and magnanimous deed was performed, though the God walked about boastful and proud, imitating his solar nature, he was nevertheless unable to escape the strike of Cupid. For by Love, he not only compels lower things to love higher things, but also leads the highest things down to love the lowest. For this reason, Apollo is said to have loved Daphne, the daughter of Peneus, who signifies the natural moisture of the earth proceeding from the rivers that irrigate it. The Sun seems to pursue this sort of moisture with a certain supreme benevolence, and by sending down his burning rays and converting the moisture into vapor, he strives to attract it to himself. 

We might moreover add this: that the exhalations of lower bodies are carried upward to 
<margin>The heavens, according to the opinion of the most ancient poets, are nourished by vapors.</margin>
nourish the celestial bodies; for there exists an ancient opinion of the poets that the heavens are fed by vapors ascending from the terrestrial and humid globe. But since they speak metaphorically rather than literally, let us set aside their opinion and say that the planets, and especially the Sun, perform their own duty of governing and preserving this lower world—as well as the whole universe—by the benefit of the exhaling humid vapors. Hence the Sun, in order to acquire supreme perfection and attain the greatest praise by fulfilling his proper and most noble duty, vehemently loves moisture as the material and instrument of his perfection and praise, and endeavors to attract it to himself. 

But that moisture flees the Sun as if he were plotting its ruin and destruction. Furthermore, the solar rays compel the exterior moisture to leave the surface of the earth and betake itself through hidden passages to subterranean places. Once it has arrived there, with the Sun’s power always pursuing it so that it can flee no further, and with the 
<margin>The excellent temperament and mixture of the Laurel.</margin>
intervening help of the celestial Gods who preside over the generation of things, and the concurring aid of the terrestrial rivers defending it from the Sun’s forces and 
<margin>Peneus, a river of Thessaly, abounds in Laurels.</margin>
persecution, it is finally converted into trees and plants. The Poets add that Daphne was afterwards transformed into a Laurel, because in the Laurel—on account of its excellence, longevity, perpetual youth, fragrance, and heat—there is seen a far more praiseworthy and excellent mixture of solar rays with terrestrial moisture than in other trees. They added that she was born from the river Peneus because the meadows irrigated by this river abound with an almost innumerable multitude of Laurels. 
<margin>Only the celebrated Poet, triumphing Emperors, and most powerful Kings are crowned with the Laurel.</margin>
They related that Apollo adorned his lyre and quiver with the leaves of this tree to signify that only celebrated Poets (who are designated by Apollo’s lyre) and fortunate emperors, as well as the most powerful Kings (who are rightly signified by Apollo’s quiver), should be crowned with it; since the Sun bestows famous names, happy victories, and lofty triumphs...

### DIALOGUE II.

...[the Sun] is thought to truly and properly bestow light: they were accustomed to be crowned with laurel wreaths as witnesses of their perpetual honor and glorious fame. Just as the Laurel is preserved for a long time, so the memorable name of the wise and triumphant endures for a long age; and just as the Laurel enjoys perpetual greenness, so the fame of illustrious men is seen to be always young and green, never growing old or becoming dry. And just as the Laurel is warm and fragrant by nature, so the glowing minds of excellent men send forth the sweetest scent of virtue even to distant regions, and diffuse it with the greatest speed to the furthest and unknown shores.

<margin>
They were accustomed to call the Laurel "honorary" as if it were gold <note>original: "Laurus quasi aurum"</note>.
The Laurel was called "praises" <note>original: "laudes"</note> by the ancients.
The reason why the Laurel is thought to be unable to be touched or harmed by heavenly lightning.
</margin>

Hence people called this tree "Laurus" because it seems to hold the same dignity among trees that gold <note>Latin: *aurum*</note> holds among metals. But the ancients called it "Praise" <note>Latin: *Laudes*</note>, either because its praises were sung by poets, or because the temples of those who merited eternal and divine praise used to be crowned with the sacred leaves of this tree. Indeed, this remarkable and most excellent tree is sacred to the Sun, and for that reason, it cannot be touched or harmed by heavenly lightning; because the name of virtue can neither be erased by the length of time or injury, nor can it ever be consumed by the motions or changes of the heavens—which, like lightning, dissipate and extinguish all other things of this lower world through age, corruption, and oblivion.

<margin>
The celestial spheres are said by Astrologers to be nine in number.
The reason why the highest sphere is called "Diurnal" <note>The Daily Mover</note> by Astrologers.
</margin>

**SO.** Regarding the loves of the heavenly dwellers—both the celestial spheres and the seven wandering stars <note>The planets</note>—you have abundantly satisfied my requests. But concerning the loves of earthly and human deities, as being matters of small importance and not contributing much to wisdom, there is no need for you to labor. However, it would be very pleasing to me if you, leaving aside the fables and inventions of the poets, would reveal what the wise Astrologers have perceived regarding the mutual loves and mutual enmities of the celestial spheres and planets.

<margin>
The division of the circuit of the first mover and the sphere of stars into 360 degrees and twelve signs.
The Zodiac is so called by Astrologers as if it were a "circle of animals."

**PH.** I will complete some part of what you have asked as briefly as I can; for to explain the whole would certainly be too long and difficult. The celestial spheres, to whose understanding Astrologers have been able to reach, are said to be nine. Seven, being closest to this lower world, carry around the seven wandering stars, which are called planets. Of the two remaining higher ones, the eighth shines with an almost innumerable multitude of fixed stars that are seen; the ninth and last is called "Diurnal" <note>The *Primum Mobile* or First Mover</note> because in the space of one day and night—that is, twenty-four hours—it runs through and completes its entire circuit, and in that same interval of time, it revolves all the other celestial spheres along with itself. The circuit of these two higher spheres is cut into three hundred and sixty degrees; and it is usually distinguished by twelve signs, each of which encompasses thirty degrees. This circuit is called the "Zodiac," as if you were to say a "circle of animals"; for those twelve signs are seen shaped in the forms of animals, which were assigned these names: Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces.

<margin>
The names of the twelve signs of the Zodiac.
The various and opposite natures of the twelve signs of the Zodiac, which are in some way similar to the elements.
Concerning the love and hatred of the twelve signs of the Zodiac, considered both from their favorable and unfavorable aspects <note>Astrological positions</note>, and also from their similar or conflicting natures, treated according to the opinion of Astrologers.
</margin>

Of these signs, three are hot and dry, being of a fiery nature: Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius. Three are cold and dry, representing the earth: Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn. Three, endowed with heat and moisture, are referred to the air: Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius. Finally, three, having cold and moisture inherent in them, are seen to imitate water: Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces. These signs are found to have friendship and hatred among themselves; for each set of three of the same temperament divides the heavens into three equal parts, and they are said to be distant from each other by a space of one hundred and twenty degrees, and therefore they are joined together in the greatest and indissoluble friendship. For example: Aries with Leo and Sagittarius; Taurus with Virgo and Capricorn; Gemini with Libra and Aquarius; Cancer with Scorpio and Pisces. For the "trine" aspect <note>The 120-degree angle between signs of the same element</note>, by the agreement of the same nature concurring below, establishes a perfect friendship between them. But those signs which [divide] the Zodiac into six equal...

<header>428 LEO HEBREW ON LOVE,</header>

<margin>The trine aspect signifies the greatest friendship, and the sextile a moderate friendship between the signs.</margin>
Those signs which divide the circle and are distant from each other by an interval of sixty degrees <note>This is the "sextile" aspect, creating a hexagon within the zodiacal circle</note> possess neither the greatest nor an absolute friendship, but a moderate and imperfect one. Such are Aries and Gemini, Gemini and Leo, Leo and Libra, Libra and Sagittarius, Sagittarius and Aquarius, and Aquarius and Aries. These signs, when considered in this way, share a similarity of gender in addition to the harmony of the sextile aspect: for they are all masculine and endowed with the same active quality, since they are all either joined by heat and fiery dryness, or associated with aerial moisture. Indeed, fire and air are seen to have a certain moderate compatibility and friendship within the order of the elements. The same similarity is found among the other six signs of an earthy and watery nature; for they too are joined by a certain moderate friendship, such as Taurus with Cancer, Cancer with Virgo, Virgo with Scorpio, Scorpio with Capricorn, Capricorn with Pisces, and Pisces with Taurus. All of these are seen to have a sextile aspect, being sixty degrees apart, and are feminine in nature, formed with the same active quality—namely, coldness—even if a difference is later found between them in their passive qualities (dryness and moisture), just as exists between earth and water. For this reason, their friendship is also called moderate and imperfect.

<margin>The opposition is thought to bring about the most severe enmities, while the square aspect brings more tolerable ones.</margin>
However, if the signs of the zodiac are opposite to one another and maintain the greatest possible distance—namely, one hundred and eighty degrees—they are said to practice the most severe enmities and carry out capital hatreds against each other. This is because they occupy entirely opposite and contrary positions; when one of them is ascending, the other is descending, and while one is exerted above the earth, the other will be hidden beneath the earth. And although they always agree in their active quality <note>In this system, signs 180 degrees apart share the same "temperature" (both hot or both cold) but differ in "moisture"</note>—since both are either hot or both are cold—they differ greatly in their passive qualities, since one is affected by moisture and the other by dryness. Therefore, the discord of the passive qualities, combined with the opposition of position and aspect, divides them, inflicting the greatest and most capital enmities. Anyone can clearly see this in the relationships between Aries and Libra, Taurus and Scorpio, Gemini and Sagittarius, Cancer and Capricorn, Leo and Aquarius, and Virgo and Pisces. But when signs are distant from each other by a fourth part of the zodiac—that is, by a space of ninety degrees <note>The "square" aspect</note>—they will carry only moderate enmities, both because their distance is half of an opposition, and because their natures disagree in both qualities: the active and the passive. For if one is endowed with a hot, dry, and fiery nature, the other has obtained a watery, cold, and moist temperament; and if one is affected by heat and moisture (the aerial qualities), the other rightly approaches an earthy temperament of cold and dryness. This is seen if Aries is compared with Cancer, Leo with Scorpio, or Sagittarius with Pisces: for one represents fire and the other water. It is also seen if Gemini is compared with Virgo, Libra with Capricorn, or Aquarius with Taurus: for one of them has attained an aerial nature, and the other an earthy one. Sometimes, however, signs of this order disagree only in their active quality, such as when heat falls to one and cold to the other; the relationship of Taurus to Leo, Virgo to Sagittarius, Capricorn to Aries, Cancer to Libra, Scorpio to Aquarius, and Pisces to Gemini can provide the greatest evidence of this fact.

<margin>The friendship of the planets is judged by Astrologers chiefly from the trine and sextile aspects, while their enmity is judged from the opposite and square aspects.</margin>
For all these signs which have just been mentioned are found to have an opposition of active qualities only, and a square aspect signifying a moderate enmity. **Sophia:** I have correctly understood the love and hatred of the twelve celestial signs, both perfect and imperfect. Now I would like to understand whether these same things are found among the seven planets as well. **Philo:** The planets are said to love one another when they look upon each other with a favorable and benign aspect—for instance, in a trine aspect requiring a distance of one hundred and twenty degrees. This trine aspect is seen to indicate perfect love and the highest goodwill between them;

# DIALOGUE II.

...be given: or when they obtain a sextile aspect, which is half of a trine—namely, a distance of sixty degrees—which sextile aspect is thought to signify a relaxed love and a moderate friendship between them. But if, by an opposite aspect, they are turned toward one another at the longest distance that can be imagined in the heavens—namely, one hundred and eighty degrees—they will be most inimical and will pursue each other with implacable hatred; for a contrary aspect is accustomed to induce hatred, enmity, and their greatest opposition. Finally, if they have a square aspect <note>original: "quadratum aspectum"</note>, which is half of an opposition—namely, ninety degrees—they will bear tolerable hatreds and moderate enmities; for these things are seen to be proper to the square aspect.

**SO.** You have said, if I am not mistaken, that among the aspects, the trine and the sextile frequently signify love, while the opposite and the square signify hatred. Now I greatly desire to learn whether their conjunction <term>conjunction: when two planets appear in the same degree of the zodiac</term> is judged to be friendly or inimical.

<margin>The conjunctions of the planets are said by astrologers to be pleasant or odious according to their various and diverse natures.</margin>
**PH.** The conjunctions of two planets are thought to be pleasant or odious according to their various and diverse natures. For if two benefic planets—namely, Jupiter and Venus, who are called "fortunes" by astrologers—are coupled together, they will pursue each other with the greatest love and a certain supreme benevolence; and if the Moon is joined with either of them, she makes a happy and friendly conjunction. But if the Sun joins with either of the same, he will contract an inimical and harmful partnership, for by burning them <note>The technical term is "combustion," occurring when a planet is too close to the Sun, theoretically weakening its influence</note> he renders both of the aforementioned planets weak and useless; and although he himself might seem to take some benefit from such a partnership, it is not much, however, because of their burning. Mercury is happily and amicably associated with Jupiter; with Venus, he is coupled lovingly indeed, yet not altogether correctly. Joined with the Moon, he effects a moderate friendship. But glued together with the Sun, he is burned by him, and the assembly of both is little friendly—unless perhaps their bodies were united in a certain most perfect ratio <note>Likely referring to "Cazimi," or being in the "heart" of the Sun (within 17 minutes of arc), which was thought to strengthen a planet</note>; for then their conjunction would undoubtedly be the best and most friendly, and the powers of the Sun would be doubled, as if the Sun were doubled in the sky. The coupling of the Sun and Moon <note>A New Moon</note> is thought to be extremely odious, although the bodily and most absolute union of both is judged by some astrologers to be friendly and to contribute much to hidden secrets. The conjunction of two unhappy planets, which are called "malefics"—namely Saturn and Mars—with any of the others is odious, except only for the coupling of Mars with Venus, which is accustomed to excite immoderate lust and raging love. The connection of Saturn and Jupiter is held to be pleasant for Saturn, but hostile for Jupiter. But the embrace of Saturn or Mars with the Sun, just as it is inimical to the Sun, is thought to be harmful to them as well; because the Sun then burns both, and is also seen to weaken his own powers. Moreover, the meeting of both with Mercury or the Moon is both worst for the latter and inconvenient for the former.

**SO.** Just as conjunctions are said to be good or bad according to the natures of the planets coming together, do benign or malignant aspects take the same differences as conjunctions from the diverse natures of the two planets looking at each other?

<margin>Benefic and likewise malefic aspects of the planets are accustomed to receive increase and decrease from the differences in the natures of those looking at each other.</margin>
**PH.** Benefic and likewise malefic aspects undoubtedly receive increase and decrease from the differing natures of the planets looking at each other. For when two "fortunes," Jupiter and Venus, are seen to have a trine or sextile aspect, they portend the greatest happiness. But if they obtain inimical aspects—namely, the opposite or the square—they seem to presage no inconveniences, but fewer and more difficult prosperities. Similarly also, when any of them looks at the Moon, or Mercury, or the Sun with a pleasant aspect, he announces a happiness suitable to his nature. But if he is turned toward any of those three with an unlucky and inimical aspect, he will signify that little good will happen, and that it must be acquired with difficulty. But when the two mentioned fortunes look upon the two misfortunes—namely, Saturn and Mars—with a laudable aspect, they signify moderate goods, with fears...

# LEONE EBREO ON LOVE

...nevertheless, they bestow these gifts surrounded by certain troubles and inconveniences. But if they happen to look upon one another with a perverse and unjust gaze <note>original: "intuitu... aspectu"</note>, they are said to confer evils under the appearance of goods. Mars and Venus, however, are set apart from this number; they were endowed with such harmonious and fitting temperaments that whenever they obtain a fortunate aspect, they are seen to confer many benefits and the greatest happiness upon lovers. Likewise, when Jupiter and Saturn achieve a favorable and happy aspect, they promise things that are laudable, profound, and divine, and most far removed from the senses. Furthermore, Jupiter, by his own gentleness, softens the harshness of Saturn; and Venus, when rightly placed, tames the cruel and wicked nature of Mars. On the other hand, Mercury, when looking rightly upon Mars or Saturn, promises little good, but when looking upon either perversely, he promises much evil; this is because he most easily turns into the nature of whichever planet he is mixed with. Mercury, looking rightly at the Moon, predicts happiness, but looking unfairly, he predicts misery. Two "malefics" <note>Saturn and Mars are traditionally called "infortunae" or "malefics" in astrology.</note> looking unhappily upon the Moon are the worst; looking prosperously, they are not good, but merely less evil. The same judgment must be made regarding the aspects of the two malefics to the Sun. Friendly aspects of the Sun and Moon are judged to be the best; and they are accustomed to soften and restrain all the inconveniences and all the excesses of Mars and Saturn. Yet the unfriendly aspects of these same planets promise many difficulties, and none or very few good things, to mortals. Here is for you a brief and concise treatment of the diversity of the celestial aspects.

**SO.** What you have said regarding the love and hatred both of the twelve signs and of the seven planets individually among themselves seems more than enough. But tell me, I pray, whether the planets also follow one sign with greater or lesser love or hatred rather than another.

<margin>Each planet seems to love its own houses and hate those of others.</margin>
**PH.** Certainly: for the twelve signs are said to be, individually, the shrines or houses of the seven planets. Each planet seems to love its own dwellings and hate those of others. The reason for this can be given: because when any of the planets stays in its own house, its virtue exists more robustly and powerfully; but when it is found in the houses of others, and especially in the houses of its enemies, its strengths are weakened and diminished.

**SO.** In what order are the twelve celestial houses distributed among the seven planets?

<margin>The proper houses of the planets.</margin>
**PH.** The Sun and Moon are said to have chosen two celestial houses for themselves: the Sun chose Leo, and the Moon chose Cancer. To each of the remaining five planets, two dwellings fell: to Saturn, Capricorn and Aquarius; to Jupiter, Sagittarius and Pisces; to Mars, Aries and Scorpio; to Venus, Taurus and Libra; to Mercury, Gemini and Virgo.

**SO.** What reason can be devised for this assignment of the celestial houses?

<margin>The reasoning devised by the ancient astrologers—who placed the Sun beneath Venus and Mercury—for accommodating and distributing the seven planets like guests into the twelve celestial signs as if they were their own houses.</margin>
**PH.** It follows the sequence and arrangement of the planets observed by the ancients. For Saturn, being higher than the others, is said to inhabit Capricorn and Aquarius as seats suitable to himself because of his extremely cold nature. For while the Sun runs through these two signs—consuming that whole interval of time which extends from the middle of December to the middle of February—colder and more intolerable frosts and more savage storms are seen to infest the lands than at any other time, which two inconveniences are most suited to the nature of Saturn. Since Jupiter holds the second place after Saturn, he took for his use two houses bordering Saturn’s houses: Sagittarius, which precedes Capricorn, and Pisces, which follows Aquarius. Mars, who succeeds Jupiter, chose two contiguous houses for his habitation: Scorpio, preceding Sagittarius, and Aries, following Pisces. Venus—who, according to the opinion of the ancients, is placed in the fourth seat after Mars—took for herself two roofs near her lover <note>A reference to the mythological love between Venus and Mars.</note> to inhabit: Libra before Scorpio, and Taurus after Aries. To Mercury, to whom the ancients granted the fifth place next to Venus, there fell two dwellings joined to those of Venus <note>original: "Cythereæ," an epithet for Venus.</note>: Virgo preceding Libra, and Gemini following Taurus. The Sun—to whom the ancients assigned the sixth place after Mercury—proposed for his own habitation Leo, which precedes Virgo, Mercury's primary sign. For the Moon, who is the seventh and last of the planets, Cancer remained to be inhabited, a seat placed after the Mercurial Gemini.

### DIALOGUE II

...happens. Therefore, not rashly indeed, but by a certain and stable Law, they are said to have chosen for themselves different houses of the zodiac.

**SOPHIA.** The order you just brought forth certainly seems admirable, and most consistent with the position of the planets devised by the ancients, who judged that the Sun should be placed below Venus and Mercury. But to the opinion of more recent Astrologers, who wanted the Sun to be placed below Mars and above Venus, the aforesaid reasoning could by no means be adapted.

<margin>The reasoning of more recent Astrologers, who thought the Sun to be in the middle between Mars and Venus, establishing and placing the seven planets like seven Princes in the twelve celestial houses as if in twelve courts.</margin>
**PHILO.** We could very well adapt the order already explained to this opinion as well, starting not indeed from Saturn, but from the Sun and Moon as from the two principal lights of heaven, and as if leaders of the others: for these two seem to play the primary roles in the preservation of the lower World.

**SOPHIA.** I do not yet understand this sufficiently.

**PHILO.** Just as before we took our beginning from Capricorn—where the winter solstice <note>The point in the year when the sun reaches its lowest point in the sky, marking the beginning of winter.</note> occurs and the days begin to grow gradually—so now we will begin from Cancer, the boundary of the summer solstice, where the longest days of the whole year reach their desired goal. Indeed, because Cancer mimics the nature of the Moon through its inherent coldness and moisture, it is fittingly called the domicile of the Moon herself. But Leo, which is next to it, is called the palace of the Sun, both because it is hot and dry and thus approaches the Solar nature, and also because we experience the Sun's greatest force and power while it traverses this sign.

<margin>The reasoning for the house of the Sun itself is preferred by more recent Astrologers in the assignment of celestial houses.</margin>
**SOPHIA.** Do you then place the Moon before the Sun?

**PHILO.** This should bring you no wonder; for in the most holy creation of the World, night is also placed before day. And as we said above, the poets sang that Diana <note>The goddess of the Moon.</note> performed the duties of a midwife <note>original: "Lucinae partes"</note> at the birth of Apollo <note>The god of the Sun.</note>. Therefore, it should be no surprise if Cancer, the palace of the Moon, precedes Leo, the court of the Sun. Next to these two signs, two houses were further constructed for Mercury, who exists closer to the Moon than the other planets (the Moon occupying the first and lowest seat). Whence Mercury, obtaining the second place in this new order, was allotted two domiciles: namely, Gemini before Cancer, and Virgo after Leo. Venus, succeeding Mercury in the third and higher place, established her houses next to his: namely, Taurus before Gemini, and Libra after Virgo. Mars, the fifth, superior to Venus and the Sun, built his houses near those of Venus: Aries before Taurus, and Scorpio after Libra. Jupiter, the sixth, encompassing Mars, built his domiciles touching those of Mars: Pisces before Aries, and Sagittarius after Scorpio. To Saturn, the seventh, surrounding Jupiter and the highest of all planets, the two remaining nearby houses remained: Aquarius before Pisces, and Capricorn after Sagittarius. These two signs indeed touch each other because they are the last, and are most distant from the two domiciles of the Sun and Moon—namely Cancer and Leo <note>The Latin text here reads "Cancro uidelicet & Capricorno," but contextually refers to the "Luminaries" (Sun and Moon) whose houses are Cancer and Leo. Saturn's houses, Capricorn and Aquarius, are opposite to these.</note>—and are positioned directly opposite to them.

**SOPHIA.** I gladly acquiesce to the order of the planets in occupying the twelve houses of the zodiac, and I concede that each of them rightly loves their own houses and hates the contrary ones, as you said. <margin>The opposition of the signs perfectly corresponds and responds to the diverse and contrary natures of those planets to whom these signs were assigned as their own houses. The various temperaments and clashing influences of Saturn and both Luminaries.</margin>
**PHILO.** They respond very well indeed, because the contrariety of the planets wonderfully agrees with the opposition of their signs and places. **SOPHIA.** In what way?

**PHILO.** Because just as life proceeds from the luminaries—since the Sun is said to provide natural heat and the Moon radical moisture <note>In medieval science, "radical moisture" was the essential fluid within living beings that sustained life and acted as fuel for natural heat.</note>, by which two qualities animated bodies live and are nourished—so on the contrary, Saturn seems to procure death and the destruction of lower things by his inherent contrary qualities, namely cold and dryness. Also, the two houses of Mercury, Gemini and Virgo, [are opposed to] the two [houses] of Jupiter...

### LEONIS HEBREI ON LOVE

...[Jupiter’s houses] are opposed to the dwellings [of Mercury], Sagittarius and Pisces, because of the contrary influences of these two planets.
<margin>The different and contrary influences of Jupiter and Mercury.</margin>
**SOPHIA.** Which influences?
**PHILO.** Jupiter inclines our minds toward the acquisition of great riches and wealth; for this reason, men subject to the rule of Jupiter generally appear wealthy, magnificent, and opulent. Mercury, however, because he is seen to provide the greatest propensity for investigating subtle sciences and unearthing the doctrines of hidden things, leads the minds of his followers away from the pursuit of material possessions.
<margin>The reason why it often happens that the wise are poor and the wealthy are ignorant.</margin>
From this, it frequently happens that the wise are poor and the wealthy are ignorant. Indeed, the knowledge of the speculative intellect is acquired through study, whereas wealth is acquired through the labor of the active life. Since the human soul is only one, when it exercises its active power, it leaves behind the speculative; and when it applies itself to contemplation, it disregards human affairs. Thus, such excellent and "Mercurial" men lead a poor life, because they understand a certain "learned poverty" <note>The philosophical idea that intellectual or spiritual wealth is superior to material riches, often requiring the rejection of the latter.</note> which is undoubtedly to be preferred far above the wealth and treasures of the rich. Therefore, the houses of Mercury are rightly said to be opposed to the houses of Jupiter for those who, at their birth, have the houses of one of these two planets ascending above the earth while the houses of the other are descending below the ground. Thus, it is rare that those subject to the rule of Jupiter recognize Mercury as their Prince, or that those who find Mercury propitious also see Jupiter as being kind to them. Two dwellings of Venus remain, Taurus and Libra, which are opposed to the two tents of Mars, Scorpio and Aries, because of the contrary temperaments of those planets.
**SOPHIA.** For what reason do you declare these two wandering stars <note>In ancient and medieval astronomy, "wandering stars" referred to the planets, from the Greek 'planētes'.</note> to be contrary? On the contrary, they seem to have the greatest friendship and similarity between them; for as you yourself said above, Mars is said to have loved Venus, and they are both thought to agree with each other perfectly.
**PHILO.** Their opposition is by no means concerned with clashing influences, as is the case with Jupiter and Mercury; rather, it is understood to involve only contrary temperaments, like that of Saturn and the Luminaries <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note>. For if the Luminaries and Saturn, as we have already said, possess a difference of influences along with the opposition of their temperaments,
<margin>The opposition of Mars and Venus is not at all about clashing influences, but only concerns contrary temperaments.</margin>
Mars and Venus differ only in the complexions of their qualities. Mars exceeds the mean in heat and dryness; Venus, however, has attained a praiseworthy temperament of cold and moisture, though the excess of these two qualities does not imitate that of the Moon. Therefore, Mars and Venus, like two contraries serving a perfect mixture, seem to agree with one another. From their conjunction, most temperate effects arise, especially in generating and nourishing; for the former is said to contribute heat as the active cause of both actions, and the latter contributes temperate moisture as the passive cause of both. And although the heat of Mars is so vehement that it turns into a burning fire, it is nonetheless perfectly tempered by the praiseworthy coolness of Venus and rendered fit for performing vital duties. Thus, the opposition of qualities brings no hindrance to these two planets following each other with mutual love, so that they may temper each other and produce the most noble effects. By reason of these contrary qualities, they were allotted opposite houses of the zodiac.
**SOPHIA.** This reasoning for the opposition of the signs, deduced from the hatred and contrary effects of the planets to which the signs are assigned as houses, pleases me greatly. But tell me, I pray, is any logic of the love and friendship of the planets perceived in the order and placement of the signs, just as their hatreds and enmities can be inferred from their opposition?
<margin>The love and friendship of the planets seems to agree wonderfully with the order and placement of their signs.</margin>
**PHILO.** Truly, the same logic exists for both, which is found to be especially true in the case of the Luminaries. For you will see that no houses of Jupiter—the "Greater Fortune" <note>In traditional astrology, Jupiter is known as the 'Greater Benefic' or 'Greater Fortune', and Venus as the 'Lesser Benefic'.</note>—look upon the houses of the Sun and Moon with a hostile aspect. But you will see that the seats of Saturn—the "Greater Misfortune" <note>Saturn is traditionally the 'Greater Malefic'.</note>—examine the dwellings of the Luminaries with an opposite and poisonous aspect. Therefore Sagittarius, the first house of Jupiter, admires Leo, the palace of the Sun (the greater Luminary), with a trine aspect <note>A trine is an astrological aspect of 120 degrees, traditionally considered the most harmonious and loving connection between two points.</note> displaying the greatest love; and Pisces, the second habitation of Jupiter, [admires] Cancer, the guesthouse of the Moon (the lesser Luminary)...

### DIALOGUE II. 433

...they look upon them with a trine aspect <note>A trine aspect occurs when two planets or signs are 120 degrees apart, generally considered a very harmonious and "loving" relationship in astrology.</note>, which is a sign of the most intense love. Similarly, no house of Mercury was allotted a position adverse to the Sun’s Royal Palace or the Moon’s lodging, because Mercury is joined to both of them with the greatest familiarity. On the contrary, Gemini, the first seat of Mercury, admires Leo (the Sun’s court) with a sextile aspect <note>A sextile aspect (60 degrees) represents moderate friendship or "moderate love."</note>; and Virgo, his second house, looks upon Cancer (the Moon’s dwelling) with an equally friendly sextile aspect.

There remain the bedchambers of Venus (the minor fortune) and the tents of Mars (the minor misfortune) <note>In traditional astrology, Jupiter and Venus are "benefics" (fortunes), while Saturn and Mars are "malefics" (misfortunes). Venus and Mars are considered "minor" compared to Jupiter and Saturn.</note>. Just as these two planets seem to influence the same things, so too do the houses of both retain a moderate love toward the Sun and Moon. For Aries, the first house of Mars, holds a trine aspect toward Leo, the Sun’s palace, because both the planet and the signs are endowed with the same temperament—namely, hot and dry. However, it holds a square aspect <note>A square aspect (90 degrees) indicates tension, challenge, or "moderate enmity."</note> toward Cancer, the Moon’s domicile, because Mars and his house, Aries, being hot and dry by nature, are opposed to the Moon and her domicile, Cancer, which are endowed with a cold and moist temperament.

Scorpio, however, the second seat of Mars, has obtained a trine aspect of perfect love toward Cancer, the Moon’s lodging, because both signs consist of a cold and moist temperament. But toward Leo, the Sun’s royal palace, it holds a square aspect due to the opposition between the heat and dryness found in Leo and the cold and moisture perceived in Scorpio. 

The bedchambers of Venus seem to observe almost the same order regarding the seats of the Luminaries. For Taurus, the first seat of Venus, gazes upon Cancer (the Moon’s hospice) with a benign sextile aspect, because both seem to agree in coldness. However, it admires Leo (the Sun’s temple) with a square aspect—a sign of moderate enmity—as if it were contrary to itself by reason of heat. Similarly, Libra, the second house of Venus, looks upon Leo with a pleasant sextile aspect because both participate in heat. But it terrifies Cancer with a square aspect, signifying a diminished hatred, as Cancer is adverse to it by reason of coldness. 

Therefore, these two planets, Mars and Venus, are placed in the middle between Saturn and Jupiter; and for that reason, their domiciles are seen to have partly friendships and partly enmities with the dwellings of the Sun and Moon. We could add many more reasons for these celestial loves and hatreds, but lest our discourse seem too long and obscure, we shall pass over them.

**SOPHIA.** Before you set a limit to this discussion, I would only wish to understand this: do the planets pursue the celestial signs with any other kind of love or hatred, besides that which is considered in the good and bad aspects?

**PHILO.** Certainly—firstly, for the sake of declaring their power in action. For example: the Sun in Aries, the Moon in Taurus, Saturn in Libra, Jupiter in Cancer, Mars in Capricorn, Venus in Pisces, and Mercury in Virgo (even though this is said to be one of the two houses of Mercury).

<margin>The triple authority of the planets.</margin>
Furthermore, the planets have a triple authority <note>Also known as "triplicity," where a group of three planets shares rulership over the signs of a specific element (Fire, Earth, Air, or Water).</note>, which three individual planets are thought to hold in common over certain signs. For instance, the Sun, Jupiter, and Saturn are accustomed to exercise their authority in the three signs of a fiery nature, which are numbered among the six masculine signs: that is, in Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius. The authority of Venus, the Moon, and Mars is seen in the feminine signs: that is, in the three earthy signs (Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn) and the three watery signs (Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces). Saturn, Mercury, and Jupiter have extended their authority to the three remaining masculine signs: Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius. To avoid boredom, it seems best to refrain from assigning the causes for this allotment of authority. I will only add this: that the three masculine planets in masculine signs, and the three feminine planets in feminine signs...

# LEONE EBREO ON LOVE,

<margin>
The love of the planets for their "faces."

The planets exercise a threefold authority. Each decan is ruled by a different planet, which is said to have "dignity" or influence there.</note>: for each ten degrees of the zodiac are said to be the "face" of a certain planet. For example, the first ten degrees of Aries are traditionally called the face of **Mars**; the second, of the **Sun**; and the third, of **Venus**. Proceeding in this same way, following the order of the signs and planets through to the last ten degrees of Pisces (which are again called the face of Mars), one must move step by step. Another kind of love is found among the planets—with the exception of the Sun and Moon—regarding their **terms** <note>Also known as "bounds," these are specific, unequal segments of a zodiac sign assigned to the five non-luminary planets. Moreover, all planets are said to love **luminous** and favorable degrees, while they are said to hate those that are **obscure** and lowly. Likewise, they seek out conjunction with certain **fixed stars**, especially those of the first or second magnitude <note>Magnitude refers to the brightness of a star; first-magnitude stars are the brightest in the sky.</note> that are endowed with abundant light. Conversely, they flee as much as they can from the company and meeting of stars believed to have a nature contrary to their own. The zeal and benevolence of the planets (excepting the Sun and Moon) toward their own terms.

<margin>
Planets seem to love some stars and hate others.

Or rather, because they are separated from matter, have they remained free and loosed from the chains of love?

<margin>
Love exists first and more properly in the Intelligible World than in the Sensible World; indeed, it seems to have been translated long ago from spiritual things into corporeal ones.
</margin>
**PHILO.** Although love is spread through all bodies fashioned from matter, it must not be thought of as belonging to them alone. On the contrary, just as essence, life, intellect, goodness, beauty, and every other perfection proceed from spiritual things and are derived from the incorporeal into the corporeal—whence it happens that all excellences and superiorities are found in spiritual things before they are found in corporeal ones—so too does **love** seem to belong first and more properly to the **Intelligible World** <note>The "Intelligible World" is the realm of pure thought and divine ideas, which Neoplatonic philosophers believed was more "real" than the physical "Sensible World."</note> than to the Sensible World, and it appears to have been translated from the former into the latter.

**SOPHIA.** By what reasoning?

**PHILO.** Does any argument to the contrary of this opinion occur to you?

**SOPHIA.** This at least is ready at hand: you have already shown that love is the **desire for union**, and the desire for a sought-after thing necessarily supposes **privation** <note>original: "privationem." In Aristotelian philosophy, "privation" is the lack of a quality or form. One cannot desire what one already possesses in full.</note>. Since this privation seems to not fit spiritual beings at all, but rather to be a property only of matter, it follows that love should not be attributed to them. Furthermore, another reason can be brought to confirm this: those things which consist of matter, being imperfect, vehemently desire union with spiritual things as their perfections; but in what way can **perfect** things ever be said to seek out a union with **imperfect** ones?

<margin>

Thus, the **lower** (as something less noble) loves the **higher** (as something more excellent) and desires union with it. For this reason, all those intelligent and divine spirits greatly desire the **Supreme and most perfect God**, from whom (no differently than from a most fertile fountain) their entire essence and blessedness is derived; and they strive with all their might to participate in His intelligence.

**SOPHIA.** We could perhaps interpret those most blessed spirits loving one another in the sense that the lower is said to love the higher.
