### DIALOGUE III

Just as lower things are said to love higher things because of a desire for them—so that, through the closest possible union, they might acquire and attain the perfection they lack—so too must we consider that higher things love lower ones and wish to join with them so that the lower things may become more perfect. 

<margin>Not only do lower things love higher things and corporeal things love spiritual ones; but conversely, higher things are said to love lower ones, and spiritual things love corporeal ones, in an inverse relationship.</margin>

However, this kind of desire does not imply a lack in the higher being who seeks, but rather a lack in the inferior being who is in need. For the superior intelligence, by loving the inferior, desires to supply that part of its own perfection which the inferior lacks. It is with this most noble kind of love that spiritual things pursue corporeal things—even those infected by the "contagion" of matter—so that by communicating their own excellence to the lower things, they may fill their void, and by joining with them, make them more perfect and more visible.

**SO.** Which of these two types of love seems to you to be older and more praiseworthy: that of the superior intelligence for the inferior, or that of the inferior for the superior?

**PH.** Certainly that of the superior for the inferior, and of spiritual things for corporeal ones.

**SO.** Why?

**PH.** Because one of these loves is seen to be about receiving, while the other is about giving. 

<margin>The love of superiors for inferiors, and of spiritual beings for corporeal ones, is seen to be far more perfect and excellent than the zeal and benevolence of the latter for the former.</margin>

Spiritual and superior things are said to love corporeal and inferior things as parents love their children; while the latter love the former as children love parents. And who is found of such coarse and dull wit that they would not admit a father’s love far exceeds the love of the son? Furthermore, we said above that the spiritual world loves the corporeal world as a male loves a female, and the corporeal loves the spiritual as a female loves a male. Truly, though I may seem offensive to you in saying it, the male seems to love far more perfectly by giving than the female does by receiving. Even among humans, benefactors <note>Those who give a gift or favor.</note> are seen to love their beneficiaries more than the reverse: for the beneficiaries usually love for the sake of their own advantage, but the benefactors love for the sake of virtue alone. One of these two loves has utility as its goal, while the other looks only to honor. Who ever doubts that honor is to be preferred over utility? Therefore, we seem to have said quite rightly that the benevolence of spirits toward bodies is far more excellent and perfect than the love of bodies toward spirits.

**SO.** I give my assent to what you have said so far. However, two further doubts occur to my mind. First, because desire implies a lack and a deficiency of the thing sought on the part of the one desiring and loving—not, as you seem to suggest, a perfection in the lover that is lacking in the beloved. You have already placed the lack in the inferior, who is sought and loved by the superior. Second, I remember often hearing that the things loved are, by the very fact that they are loved, more perfect than the lovers. For love is said to be for "the good," and the beloved is surely the end and the goal set by the lover; and the goal of all things is declared to be the most noble part of those things related to it. How, then, did you just pronounce that the imperfect is loved by the perfect?

**PH.** The two difficulties you propose are not to be looked down upon. Nevertheless, approaching the solution to the first, let us say that in the sequence of the universe, lower things depend on higher ones, and the corporeal world depends on the spiritual. Therefore, a defect in the lower would also prove an imperfection in the higher; for a fault in the effect is thought to signify some weakness in the cause. 

<margin>In the sequence of the universe, a defect in the lower also signifies some imperfection in the higher; and a fault in the effect is rightly thought to signify some weakness in the cause.</margin>

Thus, when the cause is seen to love the effect, and the superior the inferior, it surely seeks the perfection of that inferior thing. It strives to join with it so that it may correct and amend its defect. For when the effect is perfect, the cause itself is preserved as free from every kind of fault or blame, and remains safe. Hence, when the inferior is not joined to the superior, not only does the inferior lead an imperfect and miserable life, but a certain stain is also burned into the superior, and its perfection and dignity are somewhat diminished. A father can never be called "happy" if his son is miserable and wicked. For this reason, the ancients believed that depraved and wicked men most seriously wound and, in a way, contaminate divinity itself; just as, on the contrary, just and good men are seen to extol and lift it up...

### LEO THE HEBREW ON LOVE

<margin>The superior, when joined to the inferior, not only perfects the inferior as much as possible, but also completes and confirms its own perfection in every way.</margin>
For this reason, the wise have said not only that the lower loves the higher and vehemently desires its union, but also that the higher loves the lower and strives as much as possible to join itself to it. This is done so that each may fully achieve the perfection suited to its capacity, and so that the universe of things may be bound together step by step in a sequence, coalescing into one through an indissoluble bond of love. This wondrous bond joins the corporeal world with the spiritual world, and lower things with higher ones. Indeed, such a connection—or more accurately, a union—was proposed as the primary and principal goal by the Supreme Architect <note>The "Supreme Architect" refers to God as the creator and designer of the universe.</note> and Omnipotent God when He ordered the variety of the universe and joined its multitude into one. **SO.** You have excellently explained one of the two previous ambiguities; now proceed to the second. **PH.** Aristotle seems to have solved the second difficulty quite subtly.

<margin>The goal, for the sake of which each intelligence moves its sphere, seems to be nobler than the moving intelligence itself, according to Aristotle's opinion.</margin>
<margin>The order of the four causes, ranked by their excellence and nobility.</margin>
<margin>The "End" is not undeservedly called the "cause of causes."</margin>
<margin>The love of celestial souls for the spheres subject to them, and of higher things for lower things, as well as spiritual things for corporeal ones, takes its origin from a certain higher love, by which these lovers pursue other superior goals.</margin>
After he demonstrated that those spirits which perpetually move the celestial bodies—the intelligent souls <note>original: "animas intelligentes," referring to the spiritual entities believed to guide the planets.</note>—are entirely free from matter, he then added that they move the heavens for the sake of a certain goal or purpose fitting to their souls. He concluded that this goal is ultimately nobler and more excellent than the mover itself. And this is not without merit: for the goal <term>End</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "End" or "Final Cause" is the "why" of a thing, considered the most important reason for its existence.</note> of any thing is undoubtedly more noble than the thing itself. Philosophers have devised four causes for natural things: Matter, Form, the Agent (who is said to move and create the thing), and the End (which impels the agent to act). Of all these, Matter is the most ignoble. Next, Form surpasses Matter in dignity. Thirdly, the Agent is considered superior to both, as it is their cause. Finally, the End is proclaimed to be more noble and excellent than all three together, and specifically more so than the Agent itself; for the Agent is moved for the sake of the End. Therefore, the End is not undeservedly called the "cause of causes" <note>original: "causa causarum"</note>. From this, it is inferred that the goal for which each celestial and intelligent soul revolves its assigned sphere is more worthy and excellent than not only the moved celestial body but even the moving soul itself. According to Aristotle's view, since this most noble goal is vehemently loved and sought by the soul of heaven, that intelligent soul—set on fire and inflamed by this great love—perpetually moves its assigned celestial sphere with a steady desire and insatiable zeal. It is seen to love that sphere and provide it with a most noble life, even though the sphere, as an inferior to a superior, appears to yield as a body to an intellect. This love of the celestial soul for the sphere subject to it takes its origin, of course, from that love with which the loving soul pursues a higher and more excellent goal beloved by it. It desires to enjoy eternal union with this goal, and to be so perfectly joined and united with it, just as a lover is accustomed to be connected with the person they most vehemently love. Therefore, Sophia, you can now see that higher things love lower things, and spiritual things love corporeal things, because of their own most ardent zeal toward other things higher than themselves. Since they wonderfully desire to enjoy union with those higher things, they are seized by a great love, through which they are then seen to bestow many benefits upon the things subject and beholden to them. **SO.** Tell me,

<margin>Diverse opinions of philosophers regarding what that "End" is said to be, for the sake of which each intelligence moves its sphere.</margin>
I pray, Philo: what things are found to be so much more excellent than the intelligent souls that they can imprint such an ardent love and such a vehement desire for union upon them? For these souls seem to believe they have attained blessedness once they have finally achieved that union. It is for the sake of attaining this that they move the celestial spheres perpetually, with the greatest care and diligence, without even the slightest interruption. Furthermore, I require an explanation from you as to how higher things, by loving lower things, more easily attain union and coupling with those other higher things. For the cause of this effect truly seems hidden and obscure to me. **PH.** As for your first question, the interpreters of Aristotle have searched for what things of such great excellence and dignity might be found to serve as the goals of intelligent souls...

### DIALOGUE II

<margin>The opinion of the Arabs, who assigned two intelligences to each celestial orb: they said one acts as a soul and active cause, while the other acts only as the "end" or goal for which the orb moves.</margin>
...those to whom the care of moving the celestial orbs was delegated—and who deserve to be called more noble—have labored greatly over this. The first opinion is said to have belonged to the Arabs—specifically Al-Farabi, Avicenna, Al-Ghazali—and our own Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>original: "Raby Moyses Aegyptij"; this is Maimonides, the famous Jewish philosopher.</note> in his *Guide* <note>original: "Morhe"; referring to the *Moreh Nevukhim* or *The Guide for the Perplexed*.</note>. All of these men unanimously affirm that two intelligences are assigned to each celestial orb. One of these moves its orb as an **acting cause**, and they call it the "intelligent soul" and mover of that orb. The other intelligence, however, moves that same orb as an **end** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "end" or "final cause" is the goal or purpose for which something is done. Here, the sphere moves because it loves and desires to imitate the perfection of this higher intelligence.</note>, for the sake of which the first intelligence (which rotates the orb) perpetually turns the heaven committed to its care, desiring that higher intelligence as something more excellent than itself.

**SO.** How then can the well-worn and celebrated opinion of the Philosophers be sustained? For Aristotle declared that there are as many angels—or separate celestial intelligences driving the wheels of heaven—as there are orbs being moved by them. This Arab opinion seems to double the multitude of intelligences when compared to the number of the orbs.

**PH.** They say that this statement of Aristotle, and the number established by the Philosopher, should be explained and interpreted as referring to two *species* of intelligences: namely, the movers and the ends, taken separately. For there must be as many "moving" intelligences as there are orbs, and likewise as many other intelligences as there are "ends" for those movers.

**SO.** By doubling the number of intelligences, these excellent and most learned men seem to be doing some violence to Aristotle's words. But what will they say regarding the **Prime Mover** of the supreme heaven, whom we believe to be God? Would it not be highly inconvenient and utterly absurd to establish some higher "end" or goal above Him?

<margin>The Arabs, who placed two intelligences over each celestial orb, did not want God to be the Prime Mover.</margin>
**PH.** The sect of Arab philosophers by no means agrees that the Supreme God is the Prime Mover. For if He were, God would be called a "soul" applied only to the movement of a single orb, just as the other moving intelligences are. Such an equality and specific application would not suit the magnitude and universality of the Greatest Being. Instead, these famous men held that God is that most excellent **End**, for the sake of whom the Prime Mover rotates the *Primum Mobile* <note>The "First Moved" or outermost sphere of the universe in medieval astronomy.</note>.

**SO.** Do all other philosophers confirm this opinion?

<margin>The opinion of Averroes, who assigned only one intelligence to each celestial orb: this single intelligence acts as both the agent and the end that rotates its orb; as the "end" of its own motion, it is far more noble than it is as the "worker" or producer of that same motion.</margin>
**PH.** Not at all. For Averroes <note>A widely influential 12th-century Islamic philosopher from Spain, known as "The Commentator" on Aristotle.</note> and others who later interpreted Aristotle said that there exist exactly as many intelligences as there are orbs—neither more nor fewer—and they further granted that the Prime Mover is God. Averroes judged it not at all absurd for God to be the soul and form that grants essence to the supreme heaven by being dedicated to moving one orb. This is because celestial souls are entirely devoid of matter; and since His particular orb encompasses and completes the entire universe of bodies, and by its motion turns all the others, it is by the highest right that the intelligence perfecting, moving, and informing it is the Supreme God, and nothing else can exist beyond Him. Simply because He is seen to move—just as each of the other intelligences is—does not mean He should be made equal to them. On the contrary, He is seen to be far more excellent and superior to them, just as His orb occupies the first and highest place among all the orbs of the other intelligences. And just as the power of His orb contains and encompasses all the lower heavens, so His power embraces the powers of all other movers.

<margin>Averroes believed God Himself was not only the "end," but also the "efficient cause" that rotates the supreme orb of all.</margin>
If He were made equal to the others simply because He shares the common name of "mover," then by following the previous opinion, He might also be thought equal to them when He is called the "End" of the supreme mover, just like the intelligences of the other order. Finally, Averroes adds that it is not fitting for a Philosopher to establish more intelligences than philosophical reason allows; for in the sciences, we ought to follow only the guidance of reason, not even in the smallest...

### PAGE 438

...departing from it. **SO.** This second opinion certainly seems more moderate than the first. But how would one respond to the authority of Aristotle, and to reason itself, which dictates that the "end" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "end" (Latin: *finis*) is the goal or purpose for which an action is performed. The "mover" is the agent that performs the action.</note>—whose impulse moves the orb by drawing it through love—must be judged more excellent than the mover itself?

**PH.** Averroes <note>original: "Auerroës"; the influential 12th-century Andalusian philosopher known for his extensive commentaries on Aristotle.</note> believes the Philosopher's [Aristotle's] words should be understood as follows: that one and the same moving intelligence, in its continuous motion, exists as its own proper and fitting "end." For it seems to rotate its orb for no other reason than to fulfill its own perfection. Thus, in the sense that it is the "end" of the movement, it is far more perfect and noble than it is in its capacity as the agent that actually performs the movement. Therefore, Aristotle seems to have compared two types of causes that coincide in the same intelligence—the acting cause and the final cause—rather than two different and distinct intelligences, as the first group of thinkers believed.

**SO.** It would certainly be strange if the Philosopher intended to indicate with such words that the same intelligence is more perfect than itself!

**PH.** I also judge it a rash claim to say that Aristotle's words—which signify an absolute and simple comparison between two things—should be narrowed and restricted to different aspects within one and the same intelligence. Thus, even if Averroes' view is found to be very true regarding the Supreme Mover—who, being God, must be considered the appropriate "end" of His own action and motion—and although it is true that among causes, the "end" must always be placed before the "acting cause," the Arab philosopher's opinion does not seem to fit Aristotle's actual words.

**SO.** What then do you think the Philosopher's intention was?

<margin>The author's own opinion: he believes that God moves only the supreme orb as both its final and its acting cause. However, he considers the other lower intelligences to rotate their orbs merely as acting causes, setting God Himself before them as the most common "end" of their own movements.</margin>

**PH.** He meant to show that the "end" of all celestial movers is a certain highest and supreme intelligence, which all lower ones love most vehemently and strive greatly to be united with. In this intelligence, their total and supreme happiness is placed—the one whom mortals most venerate as God and the Prince of Gods.

**SO.** Do you perhaps believe that God is the "first mover"?

**PH.** To review everything required by such a difficult subject would be far too long and painstaking, and by preferring one opinion over another, we might risk being called arrogant. However, even if I were to grant for the sake of argument that Aristotle believed God to be the first mover, I would say the Philosopher intended God to be the "end" of all those movers, and more excellent than all of them over whom He is superior. Therefore, you could never infer from Aristotle's words that God is more excellent than Himself, even though the Divine Power acquires a greater nobility from being the common and most ample "end" of all things than from any other cause or condition found in Him; for all things are referred to the "end" as if to the complete fulfillment of perfection.

**SO.** Do you then deny that other movers rotate their own orbs to fulfill their own perfection, which, as Averroes testifies, they strive greatly to enjoy?

**PH.** Not at all. Rather, I most firmly assert that the celestial souls vehemently desire to be united with God so that they may complete their own perfection. Hence, their final "end" and ultimate intention consists in their own perfection. Since this perfection is found in achieving divine union, we must necessarily admit that it resides in the Divinity itself as the ultimate "end," rather than in the souls themselves. Therefore, Aristotle pronounced the Divinity to be a more excellent and eminent "end" for the celestial souls than their own individual goals. This statement by Aristotle should by no means be stretched—as Averroes seems to have thought—to refer to the inherent and permanent perfections within the moving intelligences themselves.

<margin>The happiness and bliss of the human intellect finally consists in divine union.</margin>

**SO.** Should the bliss and ultimate "end" of our own intelligent souls be placed in divine union for the same reason?

**PH.** Most certainly. For their ultimate "end," final perfection, and true bliss are found not in the souls themselves, but rather in a certain turning of them toward higher things, and finally in a divine union extre-

# DIALOGUE II
### PAGE 439

...must be restored. Thus, although the Supreme God is called the most common end of all things and the true and complete bliss of all intellects, we should not, for that reason, deny that the proper perfections of the intelligent souls exist as their own final ends. For when the act of happiness <note>original: "fœlicitatis"; referring to the state of ultimate fulfillment or blessedness</note> arrives, the intelligent soul seems to dwell no longer in itself, but in God, who—through the mediation of His union <note>original: "copulatione"; in Neoplatonic thought, this refers to the mystical joining of the soul with the Divine</note>—renders that soul most happy. And this is surely its final end and its highest bliss; it by no means consists in itself alone when deprived of this blessed union. **SO.** You have explained the first of the two proposed ambiguities quite subtly and with an incredible degree of agreement from my own mind. Now, proceed to solve the second.

**PH.** Indeed, you wish for me to interpret for you by what logic an intelligence—by loving and moving a corporeal orb that is far more ignoble than itself—can ascend and be raised to the love of the Most High God, and even reach His most happy union. **SO.** That is precisely what I require of you.

<margin>He treats that arduous and most difficult question: namely, by what logic the intelligences achieve divine union by loving and moving their own orbs.</margin>
**PH.** That ambiguity certainly seems difficult, and all the more so because the proper and internal action of an intelligence separated from matter <note>A "separated intelligence" is a spirit, like an angel or celestial mover, that does not have a physical body like a human does.</note> consists in understanding itself, and in perceiving all things together with its own most perfect knowledge. This is because the divine essence shines most clearly within it, like the Sun in a mirror. That essence not only encompasses the essences of all things in a most excellent way, but also exists as their supreme cause. It is in this most outstanding and internal action—and by no means in the circling of celestial bodies—that their happiness and final end seems to reside. For the action of moving the spheres is considered a crude and accidental <note>original: "aduentitia"; meaning something added from the outside or secondary to their essential nature.</note> task of the intelligences. **SO.** I am glad you have made the wound wider and more visible <note>A metaphor for clearly defining the problem.</note>, so that you may then be able to heal it more safely and easily.

<margin>He elegantly compares the universe of all things to a single individual and one person consisting of many members.</margin>
Therefore, bring forth some healing remedy. **PH.** I remember telling you elsewhere, Sophia, that the universe exists as a kind of single individual, or a single person; and that every essence—whether corporeal or spiritual, whether eternal or fleeting—holds the status of the limbs and parts of this great individual. Thus, since God has assigned a certain end common to the whole to the universe and all its produced parts, and simultaneously assigned ends proper and suited to each individual part, it follows surely that both the whole and the parts are said to be perfect and happy when they rightly and absolutely execute those duties for which they were created, formed, and directed by the Supreme Architect of things.

<margin>The end of the whole World consists in unity. The ends of the individual parts contributing to the composition of the whole World are said to be two: the proper and the common.</margin>
The end of the whole is indeed the unity primarily intended by the divine architect as the most absolute perfection of the universe. But the end of each part is not only its own proper perfection when considered distinctly and separately; it is also that it should serve the perfection of the whole rightly and fittingly. For the common end is intended first and foremost by the Divinity itself, and the individual parts were formed, ordered, and devoted to the whole more for the sake of that common end than for their own proper ends. Hence, if the parts served the perfection of the universe either not at all or poorly, they would surely suffer from greater vice and misery than if they had been deprived of their own proper actions. Therefore, the parts seem to acquire greater happiness for themselves from the common end than from their own proper ends. In this regard, they certainly resemble the human body: the perfection of its parts—for example, the eyes or the hands—does not consist only or even primarily in the eyes being lovely or the hands being beautiful, nor in the eyes seeing most sharply or the hands being nimble and expressive. Rather, it is judged to lie chiefly in this: that the vision of the eyes and the action of the hands are directed toward the safety and benefit of the entire body.

<margin>The common end of all parts of the World is seen to far excel the individual ends of each.</margin>
And they achieve a far greater excellence and distinction by serving the whole body rightly than they do through beauty, loveliness, or their other proper perfections. Hence it often happens that for the defense and safety of the whole person, a part...

...prompted by nature, the part is immediately offered to imminent danger and boldly exposed: for which purpose the arm seems to give the most certain proof, being ready and prepared to bravely receive the blow of a sword for the preservation of the head. <note>Leo uses the analogy of the arm protecting the head to illustrate the "law of the whole"—where a part sacrifices its own immediate comfort for the survival of the entire organism.</note> Therefore, this same law being diffused throughout the entire universe, an Intelligence <term>Intelligence: in medieval and Renaissance philosophy, these are spiritual beings—often identified with angels—that govern the movements of the celestial spheres.</term>—by moving a celestial orb—achieves a greater happiness than by its own internal and spiritual contemplation, which is otherwise considered its own proper action. This is so even though the act of moving the orb is external and corporeal, because it is necessarily required for the existence of the universe. And this is surely what Aristotle <note>Referring to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*, Book XII, where he discusses the "Unmoved Mover" and the celestial movers acting out of love for the divine.</note> seems to have understood when he said that an Intelligence moves its orb by looking toward the order and the common good of the universe, on account of a certain higher and more excellent end, namely the divine power. For while the Intelligence loves and leads its orb in a circle, it gathers and binds together the unity of the universe; through this mediation, it is said to properly attain divine love, grace, and union <note>original: "copulationem"; a technical term in Neoplatonism for the soul's mystical joining with God.</note>. Indeed, this divine grace and union preserves the World itself in a vigorous and unharmed state; moreover, the wise rightly consider this to be the ultimate goal of the Intelligence and the highest happiness it ever seeks.

*SO.* I certainly favor this solution wonderfully. And for that same reason,

<margin>
Intelligent souls are associated with human bodies for this reason: so that the universality of all things may be gathered and bound as tightly as possible by the bond of unity.
</margin>
I believe our intelligent and spiritual souls were associated with such transitory and fragile bodies so that the divine order of binding the universe of things together—and of tying them with the bond of unity—might more clearly shine forth and be preserved.

*PH.* You think rightly indeed. For since our souls are spiritual and intelligent, they can receive no utility or convenience suited to their nature from their association with this fragile and mortal body; rather, they would achieve a far more fertile and abundant state through their own internal and pure action of understanding. However, solely on account of their love and piety toward the Maker of the World, they have applied themselves to bodies, drawing down that life, celestial intelligence, and divine light from the superior and eternal World into this inferior and transitory one. This is done so that even the lowest and earthly portion of the entire world should not be utterly destitute of divine grace and immortal life, nor should any part of this "great living creature" <note>A reference to the "Anima Mundi" or World Soul; the Platonic idea that the universe itself is a single, living organism.</note> be found that does not participate in life and intelligence, just as the whole itself is seen to participate.

<margin>
The human soul, according to whether it has guarded the body committed to it rightly or wrongly in the present life, will—after the fall of the body—either hasten to inhabit celestial and ethereal homes, or be banished forever to dark and gloomy dwellings.
</margin>
Hence, if our soul, while shut in this prison <note>A common Neoplatonic metaphor: the body as the "prison" of the soul.</note>, contributes some momentum toward preserving the unity of the world's universality in its allotted portion (as the divine order requires, which we said God proposed to Himself as a common and principal end in producing things), then the soul itself shall also enjoy divine love. After it has been loosened and freed from its bodily chains, it will immediately fly away to find God, the author of its final happiness and its own highest blessedness. But if it should poorly administer the duty enjoined upon it, it will seem neither to have loved God, nor to be ever about to participate in the divine union. Tormented by this deprivation—no differently than by dire and eternal punishments—it will be consumed by perpetual grief and sorrow. For though it could have ascended into heaven by ruling and governing the body committed to it prudently and wisely, it will see itself banished forever to dark and gloomy dwellings because of its sluggishness and depravity, away from the divine union and its own supreme blessedness—unless perhaps, by the eventual shining of divine piety, it finally obtains from Him some timely remedy for such great miseries and hardships.

*SO.* Far be it from us to ever fall into errors of this kind! Rather, having a propitious divinity, let us strive to fulfill and execute His most holy will and the order established by Him.

*PH.* May God grant and favor your most pious prayers; but this can by no means happen without love.

*SO.* Love truly seems not only common to the whole world and all its parts, but also most especially necessary, since nothing at all that is devoid of love can be called happy.

### DIALOGUE II

<margin>Love bestows not only happiness upon the whole universe, but its very essence as well.</margin>
If love were taken away, happiness would also be removed; indeed, neither the universe as a whole nor its individual parts would hold together if we were to abolish love. _SOPHIA:_ Why is that? _PHILO:_ Because the essence <note>original: *essentia*; the fundamental nature or "being" of a thing</note> of the entire world and of all things placed within it consists in their absolute and most perfect connection, composition, and unity—as if they were the limbs of a single individual. Otherwise, division would dissolve and ruin the world. Therefore, since the universe is cemented and grows together, and since its many and diverse parts are joined and bound together only through the mediation of love, it follows that love is the most vital principle for the existence of both the world and everything contained within it.

<margin>Love acts as a common bond, joining the higher with the lower, the lower with the higher; spiritual things with corporeal things, and bodies with spirits; the eternal with mortals, and the fleeting with the perpetual; it joins the Creator with his own creations, and the things established by him with the Founder himself.</margin>
_SOPHIA:_ I beg you, show me this as well: how can love provide life to the world and manage to compose just one thing out of so many diverse elements? _PHILO:_ Anyone could very easily deduce this from what has been said before. The Supreme God is seen to have displayed the greatest love in the making and preservation of the world, and he retains that love today; by compelling all its parts into one and binding them most tightly, he has constrained them with an indissoluble bond of unity. And this was not done randomly: for since God is said to be "the One" and the simplest Unity, whatever proceeds from him must also be absolutely one, endowed with a perfect unity that is consistent with itself. From the One, only one can proceed; and from pure Unity, a perfect union must flow. Furthermore, the spiritual world is connected to the corporeal <note>physical or bodily</note> world by the bond of love. For how could those Intelligences <term>Intelligences: spiritual beings or angels thought to guide the stars and planets.</term>—which are secluded from matter—or those angelic minds ever be joined with celestial bodies to provide them with the essence of their form and the life of their soul, unless they pursued them with a certain intense love? In what way, too, would human intellects enter mortal bodies and gift them with reason, unless compelled and driven by love? Nor would the Soul of the World ever be coupled with this sublunary <note>The "sublunary" region refers to the Earth and its atmosphere, which medieval science believed was subject to change and decay, unlike the eternal heavens above the moon.</note> globe of mortality, unless it experienced the powers of love. Likewise, lower things cling to higher things through the mediation of love—just as the corporeal clings to the spiritual, and mortals to the eternal—and the whole universe clings to the supreme Creator, whom it loves wonderfully. It intensely desires to be united with him and to be made blessed by participating in his divinity. _SOPHIA:_ That is certainly so: for love seems to be a kind of vital spirit diffusing itself into all regions of the world, and it can be called a bond tying and connecting the entire globe.

_PHILO:_ Since you think so magnificently of love and its "commonality"—which we have discussed so copiously and richly today—there is nothing more we need to say on that. _SOPHIA:_ It remains for you to speak of its birth, just as you promised me. You have explained very well how it exists as a common property of all things, and you have explained its individual conditions; I understand most clearly that nothing at all can be found that has not, at some point, tasted from the cup of love. What remains is for you to attempt an explanation of the origin of love, and at least some portion of its good and evil effects. _PHILO:_ I admit that I owe you an account of love's birth, but you never made mention of its effects. However, time now seems to be against us both; with the falling shadows of night, it is hardly suitable for us to begin a new argument. Therefore, let us defer this discussion to another day. But tell me, I pray, O Sophia: how can it be that while love commands everyone in common, you alone think little of the powers of this most potent King? _SOPHIA:_ And you, Philo—do you love me? _PHILO:_ Who can give a greater or more certain proof of this than yourself? _SOPHIA:_ If love, as you have said many times, is usually mutual and twofold, you must admit one of two things: either your love for me is feigned and fake, or I am hiding and disguising my internal goodwill toward you. _PHILO:_ I would patiently endure your speech having as much deception as mine has truth; but I suspect we are both lying, for it seems that love can by no means be feigned or disguised for very long. _SOPHIA:_ If your [love]...

# DIALOGUE II OF LEO THE HEBREW ON LOVE

...true love exists within me, nor can I be without it. _PHILON:_ Because you do not dare to affirm it, lest you be proven to have spoken falsely, you try to persuade me with the suspicions of arguments. I assert that my love for you is indeed true, and not at all feigned, but it is sterile. This is because, like the finest seed entrusted to an unfruitful field, it is unable to produce any fruit like itself; it has the power to bind me only, but not you in the least.
<margin>Love seems to be endowed with the nature of a magnet.</margin>
_SOPHIA:_ Why should it not? Does not love, endowed with the nature of a magnet, join diverse things, connect distant things, and draw heavy things together? <note>The magnet was a common Renaissance metaphor for the hidden "sympathies" that bind the universe together.</note> _PHILON:_ Although love excels the magnet in its power of attraction, whoever has no inclination at all toward loving is seen to be heavier than iron itself and more resistant. _SOPHIA:_ You can hardly deny that love joins lovers together. _PHILON:_ That is indeed true when both deserve the name of "lover." But we are allotted different and distinct titles: for to me, it seems, has fallen only the name of "lover," but not "beloved"; whereas to you has fallen only the name of "beloved," and not at all that of "lover." By what means, then, will love ever unite us? _SOPHIA:_ Who could ever believe that the lover is not loved?
<margin>Sophia most elegantly compares herself to Daphne, and Philo to Apollo.</margin>
_PHILON:_ I play the part of Apollo, and you imitate the hardness of Daphne. <note>In Greek mythology, Apollo pursued the nymph Daphne; to escape him, she was transformed into a laurel tree.</note> _SOPHIA:_ Then Cupid must have struck you with a golden arrow, and me with a leaden one. <note>According to Ovid, Cupid's gold-tipped arrows sparked love, while his lead-tipped arrows repelled it.</note> _PHILON:_ I would wish this were not so, but I grieve most of all that it has happened: for to obtain your goodwill would be more pleasing to me than any weight of gold, yet you refuse to receive my love for you, treating it as a mass heavier than lead itself. _SOPHIA:_ If I were playing the part of Daphne, I would have been turned into a Laurel sooner by the dread of your speech than the nymph was by the fear of Apollo’s arrows. _PHILON:_ A speech must be weak and feeble if it cannot produce an effect similar to the splendor of the eyes and a single strike—namely, mutual love and returning goodwill. Nevertheless, as far as the part of resisting is concerned, you seem already to have been transformed into a Laurel, since you will not move from your spot, nor change your purpose, nor be moved by prayers. Nor will you come forward even a little to meet the desires of a lover who approaches you more and more every day. You also imitate the perpetual greenness and the perpetual scent of the Laurel; yet its fruit is accustomed to affect the tongue of the taster with no other flavor than a bitter and unpleasant one, joined with a certain biting sharpness. For this reason, you certainly seem to me to have turned into a Laurel. A most evident sign of this metamorphosis is the sound of my weak lyre, <note>original: *cythara*; the stringed instrument of Apollo, here representing Philo's poetic and philosophical discourse.</note> which would produce no harmony at all if it were not adorned by your beautiful brows. <note>A play on words: Apollo’s lyre was traditionally adorned with laurel leaves (Daphne).</note> _SOPHIA:_ I would be ill-spoken of for impudence if I affirmed my love for you, and for impiety if I denied it. I want you to persuade yourself of what you judge to be more in accordance with reason and consistency, even if fear should perhaps twist and turn your mind toward the opposite opinion. But now, since night herself, weary and exhausted by the day’s labors, invites the bodies of mortals to take rest and sleep, let us use this opportune time and go to bed, to return tomorrow. Meanwhile, apply yourself diligently to caring for your body, and take care that your promises do not slip from your memory.

---

<meta>This page serves as the preface or "Argument" for the Third Dialogue of Leone Ebreo's (Judah Leon Abravanel's) work. It follows the second dialogue, which discussed the universality of love, and prepares the reader for a deep investigation into love's origins. This summary was written by the Latin translator, Giovanni Carlo Saraceno.</meta>

# ON THE THIRD DIALOGUE OF LEO THE HEBREW
# CONCERNING THE ORIGIN OF LOVE,

## A SUMMARY,

### Prefixed by
### GIOVANNI CARLO SARACENO.

After he has spoken sufficiently and more than enough in the first discussion regarding the essence and nature of love, and in the second regarding its universality, in this third discussion he proposes to investigate and treat its origin. However, before he approaches such a difficult and illustrious matter, he first establishes a most beautiful discussion regarding amorous ecstasy <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "ecstasy" (from the Greek *ekstasis*) refers to the soul literally "standing outside" the body during intense spiritual contemplation.</note>, using a certain philosophical introduction. He shows that, on account of strained and vehement contemplation, this state induces a much greater alienation and stupor—and calls a person much further away from external senses and movements—than sleep itself. He also demonstrates that if this state is repeated too often or continued longer than is right and good, it brings about the ruin and death of the body; indeed, some of the most excellent and holy men of old are found to have died by this most sweet kind of death. <note>This refers to the "Death of the Kiss" (*mors osculi*), a concept in Jewish mysticism where the soul departs the body in a moment of supreme divine love.</note>

He then passes to declaring the condition and essence of our soul, and he seems to attribute the reason why the soul itself moves so easily and readily from bodily things to spiritual ones, and then returns from spiritual things to bodily ones, to its double and ambiguous nature. Next, he teaches that the Sun is a most skillfully crafted image of the divine intellect, and the Moon is an image of the World Soul. <note>The *Anima Mundi* or "World Soul" was believed to be the link between the physical universe and the divine mind.</note> Furthermore, he elegantly explains the correspondence and similarity between the eye and the human intellect. He declares that the name of "light" fits the divine intellect more truly and appropriately than it does the Sun or the other stars, and that the light of the stars flows and emanates from that intelligible light; he confirms with six arguments that this light is by no means received into a transparent and clear body like a quality in a subject. <note>He argues that light is not just a physical property of the air, but something more fundamental and metaphysical.</note>

He commends the sense of sight above all else, contending that it far surpasses the other senses in its instrument, its object, its medium, its action, and its knowledge; because of the great excellence of this sense, he finally calls it the "observer of the intellect and of intelligible things." He demonstrates that the Sun holds the same proportion to the divine intellect as the eye does to the human intellect; and, with the terms transposed and exchanged, that the Sun holds the same proportion to the eye as the divine intellect does to human reason. Moreover, he judges that three things especially must concur to produce perfect and absolute vision: namely, the reception of the "species," <term>species: the visual form or "likeness" of an object that travels through the air to the eye</term> the emission of rays, and a certain comparison of the species impressed upon the eye with the external object that produced it.

He also shows that the celestial bodies—by the benefit of the Sun and other stars, acting as though they were certain most brilliant eyes—perceive these lower things most sharply and discern them perfectly; he also testifies that the heavens distinctly comprehend and perceive the objects of the other senses as well. Afterward, attempting to interpret the great similarity between the Moon and the World Soul, he teaches that the soul is placed in the middle between intellect and body for the same reason that the Moon is placed between the splendor of the Sun and the darkness of the earth. He seems to adapt all the cycles and changes of the lunar body in receiving the solar rays—along with its eclipse—to the soul so skillfully and elegantly that we might not undeservedly call the physical Moon a "bodily soul," and the soul a "spiritual Moon." He also confirms, by the example of our most holy fathers, that a defect of the Sun corresponds perfectly to an eclipse of the intellect, and that on account of the most tight coupling of the soul and the intellect itself, the body is led to its death in a certain most sweet manner.

Finally, he concludes that the genuine love by which the soul pursues both the intellect and the body itself is very similar to the twin love of the Moon, both toward the Sun and toward the lower world. With all these things completed and perfected—presented as a sort of preamble—he sets out to inquire into the origin of love as the thing chiefly intended by him. First, he proposes five questions to be examined which lead us toward understanding its origin: namely, *whether*, *when*, *where*, *from what*, and *why* love arose.

However, before he approaches the determination of any of these mentioned questions, he thought we should first be reminded that the existence of love itself—being a thing found and manifest among all people—seems to require the help of no demonstration whatsoever. Bringing forward the most common definition of love, he adds that it is "simply to be with the desire for something." Having utterly removed the opinion of certain theologians who devised a new and ridiculous difference between these two affections of our minds, he concludes that love and desire are entirely in agreement with one another; both of them suppose a certain mode of existing and signify a certain lack or "privation" of the things themselves. He further adds a wonderful order in which the affections of our minds are accustomed to follow one another. He demonstrates that any love—whether we take it to be animal, human, or divine—is always entangled and associated with desire, even if divine love is later seen to differ greatly from human love, and divine desire from mortal desire. Next, having been raised from these lower kinds of love to divine love as the most noble and excellent of all, he treats it in a different way in relation to the divine power than in relation to things themselves...

# ON THE THIRD DIALOGUE CONCERNING LOVE,

## A SUMMARY,

He demonstrates that love is appropriate to created beings. He contends that it signifies the defect and imperfection of the created things—which are vehemently loved by God—rather than a defect in the Creator who loves them so greatly. He testifies that this divine love can be rightly compared with the love of a father for a son, a teacher for a student, and between devoted friends. He shows that although the divine nature does not reject that specific and properly-named love which Plato defines as a certain "desire for the beautiful" and depicts as a "great spirit" <note>original: *daemon*. In Platonic philosophy, a daemon is a mediating spirit between gods and mortals, not an evil "demon."</note>, it also encompasses that common and generic love which Aristotle believes consists in "wishing good to someone."

He also addresses the reason why love, in its most common sense, is called a desire for the **Good**, but in its proper sense, a desire for the **Beautiful**. He attributes this to the different natures of the Good and the Beautiful: for the Beautiful seems to belong only to the lover <note>The lover perceives beauty, but the beautiful object does not necessarily "gain" from being beautiful.</note>, whereas the Good seems to be something common to both the lover and the beloved. Furthermore, he teaches that God attains either no perfection at all, or only an external and relative perfection, from the fitting perfection of created things.

But when he has touched upon the different natures of the Beautiful and the Good, and has deduced two different species and definitions of love from them, he concludes that the distinction between the two is chiefly located in three points:
1.  By the name of the "Beautiful," the appearance (*species*) rather than the essence of a thing is designated; but by the name of the "Good," the essence is signified more than the appearance.
2.  The Good, being more universal, encompasses more things than the Beautiful itself.
3.  A "middle ground" is found between the Beautiful and the Ugly, but no middle ground exists between Good and Evil.

Here, taking the opportunity offered to him, he begins a most beautiful disputation concerning beauty itself. Having first provided its definition, he testifies that beauty is perceived and discerned neither by touch, nor taste, nor smell, but only by sight and hearing, and by those other faculties of our soul further removed from matter and bodily conditions—namely, by the imagination (*phantasia*), then the intellect, and finally, more and more by the mind.

With these foundations laid, he prepares to determine the first of the proposed questions. He pronounces that love arises from the lover and the beloved as if from two causes and two superior principles, with this distinction: that in the procreation of love, the beloved concurs as the active force, form, and end (no differently than a father); while the lover concurs only as the "matter" (no differently than a mother). This is despite the fact that common people frequently call the lover the "active" cause and the beloved the "passive" cause, being more intent on describing the "slavery" of love than its actual generation.

He strives especially to persuade us that every lover, insofar as they love, is always inferior and less noble than the thing loved, insofar as it is loved. He brings forward the example of God loving Himself as the most excellent and celebrated confirmation of this matter. From this, he concludes that divinity shines forth far more excellently and brilliantly in the beloved than in the lover. He demonstrates that the example of Alcestis and Achilles <note>Alcestis died to save her husband; Achilles chose death to avenge his friend Patroclus. Both are classic examples of the sacrificial power of love.</note>, which might seem to some to detract from the excellence and dignity of the beloved, does not contradict these points in the slightest.

Not content with these, he proceeds to greater things. Since there are two kinds of love (excepting the divine): namely, that of lower beings toward higher ones, and that of higher beings toward lower ones, he clearly declares that both signify some defect or privation in the created things themselves. However, he shows us that divine love is as far removed as possible from any kind of disturbance, defect, or imperfection that might stain divinity itself. It does not imply a lack in the God who loves, but rather a privation or a mark of some fault observed in the things loved by God. These points seem sufficient for resolving the first of the mentioned questions.

Approaching the second question, he first reviews three opinions regarding the origin of the World that are more notable than the rest:
1.  That of the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note>, who assert the eternity of the World.
2.  That of the **Academics** <note>The followers of Plato.</note>, who ascribed a temporal beginning to the World out of eternal matter.
3.  That of the **Faithful**, who believed that the World once had a temporal origin out of nothing by God, the Best and Greatest.

Next, he brings forward the arguments of the Peripatetics, drawn from the fountains of both Nature and Theology, by which they strove to confirm the perpetuity of the World, and he attempts to dissolve and weaken them in defense of the faith. He also explains Plato's reasons, which impelled him to introduce the eternity of formless Chaos and to grant a temporal procreation of the World already formed from the pre-existence of that formless Chaos. In this section, he runs through that famous controversy: whether the celestial bodies consist of the same matter as lower things and can by their nature eventually be corrupted (as Plato thought), or whether they should be said to be neither made of matter nor subject to death (as Aristotle felt). Here, despising the authority of those Platonic interpreters who wished the heavens to be naturally mortal but perpetually preserved by God, he divines that Plato's mind was that the heavens are not only naturally dissolvable, but would eventually be destroyed after a long age had passed.

Hence, the author seems to be led gradually and step-by-step to the opinion that Plato—together with the **Cabalists** <note>original: *Cabalistis*. Practitioners of Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition.</note>, whom he shows deduced this opinion both from the Mosaic account of the World's creation and from several other authorities of the Sacred Volumes—wished the labor and rest of the lower world to be terminated in a span of seven thousand years, but the age and perpetual motion of the higher world in forty-nine thousand years <note>These numbers correspond to the Sabbatical cycle (7) and the Jubilee cycle (7x7=49) applied to the age of the universe.</note>. Thus, the dissolution of the celestial World and the entire universe follows the greatest revolution of the eighth sphere, while elemental corruption (arising from the excess of one of the four elements, especially fire or water) follows the approach and retreat of that same eighth sphere as its chief cause. For this reason, following this most noble and illustrious opinion of the most ancient theologians, Plato seems to have thought the World is renewed and perishes an infinite number of times, and to have placed a perpetual connection of infinite Worlds succeeding one another in this manner.

Here, having seized the opportunity, he breaks out into praise of that divine discipline which the Hebrews called **Cabala** (meaning "reception"), and of those most wise men, the Cabalists. He repeats their origin, series, and succession from another principle...

<meta>This page continues the "Argument" or summary of the Third Dialogue of Leone Ebreo’s "Dialogues on Love." The previous page established that love exists in God as a "desire for the beautiful" and a "wishing of good," transitioning now into the cosmological implications of this love.</meta>

# SUMMARY. 445

...it reveals. He also marvelously extols the number seven <note>original: *septenarium*. In Renaissance thought, the number seven was considered sacred, representing the harmony of the spiritual (3) and the material (4).</note>, and further opens and discloses the great agreement between the **Platonists** and the **Cabalists** <note>The Cabalists were practitioners of Jewish mysticism; Leone Ebreo sought to harmonize their teachings with Greek philosophy.</note>; he defends them remarkably well against the arguments of the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle, who argued for a world without beginning or end.</note> who assert the eternity of this world. Afterward, approaching the resolution of the second difficulty proposed above, he takes his beginning from God’s love for Himself as the most principal of all things, concluding that this love is eternal, just as God Himself is eternal. 

He shows that the divine and most simple unity is perceived by the human intellect—and not without reason—under a triple form and a triple relationship: namely, as the **Lover**, the **Beloved**, and **Love** itself; and likewise as the **Thinker**, the **Thought**, and the **Act of Thinking**. Indeed, he contends that this Trinity does not detract from that divine unity, but rather confirms and establishes it as much as possible. From this self-loving unity, he demonstrates that three most noble offspring—namely, the first intellect, the first matter, and the entire universe—derive their origin and come into the light as if from a supreme parent. 

Setting aside God’s internal love for Himself, God’s love toward the universe of things established by Him is seen to claim the first place. In the procreation of these things, the divine power acts as the supreme and most universal parent; however, the first intellect and first matter seem to concur as secondary parents, or rather as the most noble instruments of the supreme craftsman. Furthermore, three loves are said to have necessarily flowed together for the constitution of the World: 
1. The first is the love of God for the World and for both of the World's parents. 
2. The second is the love of both parents of the World—namely, **Chaos** and the **First Intellect**—who love each other with the greatest affection. 
3. The final love is that of all the parts of the World’s constitution, both for one another and for the whole itself. 

If we follow the opinion of **Aristotle**, all three mentioned loves have existed eternally; if we move toward the sentiment of **Plato**, some had no beginning, while others had a temporal origin in the past; finally, if we cultivate faith and piety, it appears that all of them began at some point in time. 

So much for the second question. Turning now to the third: we assert that love first arose when it approached the procreation of the World within God; then it passed through to the highest intellect and first matter, which are distinguished by a kindred benevolence; soon it flew to the angelic region, and from there approached the entirety of the heavens, finally descending into the lower world. 

The reason why the love seen in the assembly of **angels** is usually placed above the loves of other parts of the World as being greater, nobler, and more excellent is said to be this: because angels are thought to have a much greater and more abundant knowledge of the beauty they lack <note>original: *deficientis pulchritudinis*. The idea is that angels are closer to God and thus more aware of the gap between their own beauty and God’s infinite beauty.</note> than all other things. Everyone confesses with one voice that this condition—knowledge joined with a lack of beauty—provides the greatest help in exciting love and desire. Indeed, if anyone considers it rightly, they will find that the knowledge of a form one lacks not only equals the lack itself but far exceeds and surpasses it in inducing love and desire. 

The lack of divine beauty seen in the angelic and lower worlds appears to be both equal and unequal. They are equal because both are distant from the immense beauty of God by an infinite span. Yet they are called unequal because the greater and more abundant knowledge the angels have of the divine beauty they lack is thought to increase their "lack"; whereas the smaller and thinner knowledge of it in lower beings is thought to diminish their "lack" through the very nature of their species. 

Nor should it hinder us in any way when we say that, although God’s beauty is infinite and immense, one created thing nevertheless approaches closer to the Creator than another and is frequently said to be more similar to Him. For although divine beauty is infinite by its own nature, it was distributed to created things according to a certain finite and limited measure—to some more generously, to others more sparingly. Likewise, although the image and likeness of the divine form is infinite, it appears to have been expressed in created things according to a finite measure. 

Although we have stated simply that angels, if compared with lower beings, suffer not only an equal but even a greater "lack" than they do, let us nevertheless remove all ambiguities by applying a distinction: we shall say that the kind of "lack" that brings about deprivation is smaller in angels, but the other kind—which provides knowledge and kindles love and desire—is found to be greater in angels than in lower beings. Conversely, in the sublunary realm <note>The region below the moon, i.e., the Earthly world subject to change and decay.</note>, this latter kind of lack is weaker, while the first kind is more intense. 

But if someone asks for a reason why the knowledge of divine beauty held by mortals is not as clear and conspicuous as that held by angels—especially since angels behold and know God directly, while mortals are least able to perform this—we are instructed to answer thus: because angels possess an **actual intellect** (or rather, they are actual intellects themselves), whereas humans have only attained a **potential intellect**. If this human intellect ever becomes "actual" by being coupled with the **Agent Intellect** <note>original: *intellectu agente*. In medieval philosophy, the "Active Intellect" is the power that allows human minds to grasp universal truths.</note>, it still cannot contemplate the divine form directly; instead, it can only behold the supreme beauty of God in the Agent Intellect as if in a purified and most lucid mirror. 

This is indeed that happiness which the philosophers determined was the only kind to be sought by the human race. But the **Theologians**—bringing forward the example of **Moses** especially, who alone of all the prophets is said to have both seen God and spoken with Him familiarly—said that the human intellect can climb higher. They argued it can be joined and coupled not only with the Agent or Angelic intellect (as the philosophers seemed to want), but even with the Divine Intellect itself. 

We should not doubt that the human intellect, once freed from the bonds of the body, flies far more easily and unhindered toward this supreme blessedness, and persists in it longer than when it is mixed or entangled with the body. 

But to return to divine beauty: we assert that it is comprehended by no created intellect—neither human nor angelic—according to its own merit and excellence, but only according to the capacity and strength of the intellect knowing it. For the infinite can never be fully or completely perceived by the finite, nor the immense by the limited. 

The knowledge and vision of God, the **Best and Greatest**, is judged to be threefold: 
1. The first and lowest of all is held by the human intellect. 
2. The second and middle belongs properly to the angels. 
3. The third and most excellent is attributed to God alone, and to no one besides Him. 

The two higher types of knowledge are seen to be far inferior to the divine object; but the last is so only because of the greatest union of the knower with the thing...

# ON THE THIRD DIALOGUE OF LOVE

...it seems to equal the divine object itself because of its known harmony and likeness, as well as the exactly identical nature of these loves. Regarding angels, we are first reminded that even though their condition is most excellent, it does not reject or flee from every kind of love, desire, power, or motion. Their love and desire, though directed straight toward the infinite beauty of God, does not strive for something that cannot be attained at all. For any desire, provided it is said to be innate to nature, sets before itself something that can eventually be acquired. Indeed, the avoidance of death and the immortality of this bodily frame—so greatly desired by us—seems neither entirely vain nor completely false, as is demonstrated by several arguments. 

But if both angelic and divine nature are found to share in love, why did **Plato** depict love itself in the form and character of a "great daemon"? <note>In Greek philosophy, a *daemon* is a mediating spirit between gods and humans, not an evil spirit.</note> No other reason seems to have moved such a great philosopher to do this, except that he then proposed to investigate only the principle of *human* love—not at all angelic or divine love—which he rightly judged to be beautiful only in potential, but by no means in actual fact. 

To know how love, starting from the Angelic World, was soon distributed into the Celestial World and finally into the Lower World, we must recall two opinions of the most distinguished men on this difficult matter. The first of these, attributed to **Avicenna**, **Al-Ghazali**, **Maimonides** <note>original: *Raby Moysi*. Moses Maimonides, the preeminent Jewish philosopher.</note>, and many others, is described such that divine beauty and love, beginning from God the Best and Greatest, descend not all at once, but through a certain continuous series and succession through all the intervening intelligences and spheres, step by step, down to primary matter. From there, like a circle, it gradually ascends through all intermediate forms back to God Himself, from whom it took its beginning. The other view, which **Averroës** <note>An influential Islamic philosopher from Spain known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> seems to have followed, is this: that the immense beauty of God is diffused immediately, without the help of any intermediary, into the entire universe of created things—though with a choice made for each and their condition preserved. Love, also sent from the divine, is communicated immediately by God to all parts and particles of the world without requiring the work of any intermediary, though in different degrees and proportions. These points are considered more than enough regarding the third of the proposed questions. 

Now the author himself responds learnedly and excellently to the fourth question in a close-fought argument. The meaning of this very long dispute seems, in my judgment, to be this: First, he reviews various opinions of poets regarding love and allegorically interprets its parents as handed down differently by them. He also gives a most elegant reason why the poets placed two different and very dissimilar **Cupids** <note>Roman gods of desire; here representing different types of love.</note> over only two kinds of goods—namely, the *useful* and the *pleasant*—while the third kind of good, called the *honest* <note>meaning "virtuous" or "morally upright"</note>, completely ignores and rejects the empire of Cupid. He also assigns several reasons why love is said to be "twin." 

Next, he recounts that fable of the **Androgyne** <note>A primordial human being that was both male and female.</note> treated so extensively by **Plato** in the *Symposium*, through which the prince of all philosophers seems to have most skillfully described the origin of human love and its parents. He shows more clearly than light that Plato derived this fable from the **Mosaic account** of the world's creation. In this matter, the Prophet <note>Moses</note> is seen to have deliberately contradicted himself, as if on purpose. Indeed, no better or safer way can be found to harmonize the words of Moses than by tracing the creation of man described by Moses back to the fable of the Androgyne treated by Plato. He demonstrates that the different order kept by both in the sequence of the narrative comes to nearly the same thing, and that both are highly consistent with the truth. 

Afterward, attempting to penetrate the secret and hidden meanings of the Mosaic narrative, he brings forward two allegories—one especially subtle and elegant—regarding the creation of the first parents, the crime committed by both, and the punishment imposed on each for the crime. Then, he seems to adapt almost the same allegory to the fiction of the Androgyne explained by Plato, showing the greatest sharpness of wit and supreme craftsmanship. From this, he concludes that Plato meant to signify by the story of the Androgyne that all human loves and all their desires come into the light from the harmonious division of the intellect and the body, as if from a male and female. 

But since this most convinced philosopher expressed only the birth and parents of *human* love, he adds that the love encompassing the entire universe of bodies was thereafter fathered by **Porus** and **Penia** <note>Resource/Plenty and Poverty/Need, the parents of Love in Plato's *Symposium*.</note> as if by parents. The author soon opens and discloses many hidden meanings of this fable, as is his custom. Then, searching for the most ancient parents of the love that surrounds the universe of all created things—leaving Plato aside and dismissing the fictions of the poets—he demonstrates that it draws its origin from the **beautiful beloved** as if from a father, and from the **knowledge of the beautiful** joined with its absence noticed in the lover as if from a mother. 

He concludes that this opinion, having overcome many difficulties, is the truest, and that for the procreation of as many loves as are found, the two parents already mentioned finally come together into one. Hence, Plato not undeservedly pronounced love to be the desire for the beautiful and for birthing and bringing forth offspring very similar to the father. Since beauty seems to play the primary role in establishing the essence and definition of love itself, he rightly extols it as much as possible. Considering its nature, he teaches that every beloved is loved and every lover loves, and that beauty itself exists as the beginning, middle, and end of any love—even if we take God’s love for Himself. However, so that we may more clearly perceive the essence and nature of beauty, he decides to repeat what he has already said: that it is least perceived by the impure and more imperfect senses, such as touch, taste, and smell; but rather, it is always more and more known and apprehended by the spiritual and more excellent faculties of our soul, such as hearing, sight, imagination, intellect, and finally the mind. He teaches that the nature of beauty is spiritual and exists as far as possible from bodily stain and impurity—even if the common people, neglecting the truth of things, falsely persuade themselves that beauty belongs to bodies and is only adapted to the praise of incorporeal things through a certain likeness. On the contrary...

<meta>This page continues the summary of the "Third Dialogue on Love," transitioning from the discussion of angelic and divine love to the nature of beauty, the relationship between matter and form, and the reconciliation of Platonic and Aristotelian thought regarding Ideas.</meta>

### ARGUMENT. 447

...it happens more often that bodily deformity belongs properly to the nature and condition of things, whereas beauty seems rather to be distributed and diffused into bodies from incorporeal sources like a certain spiritual gift. Furthermore, the author refutes that common opinion—to which some ignoble philosophers later gave their assent—which considers beauty itself to be truly and properly situated in the harmonious proportion of parts, both among themselves and in relation to the whole; he rejects this as entirely false and deceptive. 

Once that theory is discarded, he demonstrates that all ugliness in bodies must be attributed to matter, while their elegance and loveliness must be referred to form as its proper author. He shows that when matter exceeds the form, bodies are rendered less beautiful and more ugly; conversely, when the form overcomes the matter, bodies emerge as less ugly and more elegant. From this, it can very easily be seen that a certain supreme beauty resides in the forms themselves when they are entirely separated from matter, and a far greater beauty exists in these than in bodies which consist of ugly matter and a graceful form. 

The elegance and beauty of bodies—both natural and artificial—proceeds chiefly from the form introduced into the matter, either by the skill of nature or the industry of the artist. This is a major argument for us: that beauty itself is defined as a certain "formal grace" <note>original: *gratia formalis*. A central Neoplatonic concept where beauty is a divine radiance rather than just physical shape.</note> which, when known and perceived by a lover, brings him the greatest pleasure and compels him, gradually and by a most sweet reasoning, to love it. 

Furthermore, he recounts three levels of beauty:
1. The lowest is assigned to bodies consisting of matter and form.
2. The middle is accommodated to the forms themselves which adorn such bodies.
3. The highest is truly owed to the **Ideas**, from which the aforementioned forms flowed down to perfect and work upon the matter. 

He pursues the beauty and elegance of these Ideas with the highest praise, testifying that they far surpass the forms entangled in matter. These Ideas reside first in the Divine Mind, and soon after in the **World Soul** <note>original: *anima Mundi*. In Neoplatonic thought, the spirit that animates the entire universe.</note> as if in their own proper dwellings, though they possess a far greater unity and simplicity when hidden in the Divine Mind than when translated to the World Soul. 

In addition, he explains the agreement and likeness which the human soul seems to have with the World Soul (which is set in charge of care), and which the human intellect has with that divine and most simple Intellect. He most elegantly compares visible light with intellectual light, and the harmony perceived by the sense of the ears with the harmony seen in the World Soul. 

He reveals that our soul is full of innate spiritual forms of all things, according to the opinion of **Plato**, and with **Aristotle** <note>The author is attempting to reconcile the two great philosophers, suggesting they aren't as different as they seem.</note> not disagreeing; these forms, though they seem almost to lie hidden because of the mass and impurity of the body, are later seen to be gradually uncovered and, as it were, illuminated by the help of the senses. In this greater or lesser shadowing and obscurity of the forms marked upon our souls, he believes we find the reason why some people attain an understanding of things more easily, some more with difficulty, and others not at all. He also attributes to this the reason why men feel the greatest labor in perceiving some things, and in others either none or very little. 

He teaches us that the principal duty of human minds is situated in this: that they should recall and separate spiritual beauties distributed in bodies from the darkness of matter and bodily foulness as much as possible. By this means, our intellect will more easily and readily reach the understanding of those most excellent forms which exist entirely apart from the contagion of matter and the stain of the body. 

Afterward, he treats the "middle condition" of the soul, showing that it exists between the intellect and the body, and that it carries two "faces" with it: one looking toward the intellect, and the other looking toward the body. He believes that from the various changes and dispositions of these two faces of the soul, all diversity of human loves is derived—whether in loving and pursuing bodily or spiritual forms more vehemently, more weakly, or moderately. Finally, he concludes that human happiness is placed in the most sharp contemplation and most vehement study of spiritual forms; as these are the most noble of all, our entire knowledge of bodily forms must be raised up and referred to them. 

Then he returns to declare and reveal the interior nature of beauty, testifying that it is contained and preserved entirely in the **Idea** as if in its own principle, and that it soon dissipates and diffuses into the whole universe of bodies, flowing out from it no differently than from a most fertile fountain. Here, quite conveniently and opportunely, he explores the essence or definition of the Ideas, demonstrating that they are certain divine "pre-motions" necessarily required for the procreation of the World. He does not believe that Aristotle entirely did away with Ideas when they are explained and accepted in this way, even though Aristotle everywhere professes himself to be a most bitter enemy of the Ideas. 

He opines that the controversy between Plato and Aristotle regarding these separate forms arose from a diversity of names and a varying method of philosophizing, rather than from a difference in the things themselves. He believes these two most wise men were saying different things but feeling exactly the same. He considers that both attained nearly equal praise: the former by exalting the Ideas, and the latter by depressing them. 

Next, although Ideas seem to be many when compared with the forms fashioned in their likeness, he judges that they are reduced to a supreme and most simple unity—once any appearance of multitude, division, or diversity is removed—since they are defined as the most beautiful examples of all created things set aside in the Divine Mind. He confirms with a famous example of the **Sun** how Ideal unity can be joined and connected with the multitude of things that differ among themselves and are expressed in its likeness. By bringing forward that same example, as well as another regarding intellectual concepts, he explains very clearly how the Divine Idea is impressed and distributed into various things by certain different ratios. 

He also thinks it should by no means be passed over in silence that the Idea of the whole World, and of all created things, seems to be so joined and entangled with the Divine Essence that it exists as one and the same with it, and is not distinguished from it in any way. However, he demonstrates that we should not conclude from this that the Divine Essence is situated in some kind of relationship to external works. For a richer teaching and easier understanding of this matter, he recounts two opinions of the most excellent philosophers: the first of which, ascribed to **Aristotle**, holds that the divine form and essence agree entirely into one and the same thing with wisdom itself, the first intellect, and Ideal beauty...

<meta>This page continues the summary and analysis of the "Third Dialogue on Love."
