->### ON THE THIRD DIALOGUE ON LOVE. ###<-

...by the very thing known, the suitability and likeness, as well as because of the completely one and the same nature of both, it seems to equal the divine object itself. Regarding angels, we are first reminded that although their condition is most excellent, it does not reject or flee from every kind of love, desire, power, and motion; nor does their love and desire—even if directed straight toward the infinite beauty of God—strive for a thing that cannot be acquired at all. For any desire, provided it is said to be implanted by nature, proposes for itself things that can eventually be obtained. Indeed, the avoidance of death and the immortality of this bodily frame, so greatly desired by us, seems to be neither entirely vain nor altogether false, as is demonstrated by many arguments.

But if both the angelic and divine natures are found to be participants in love, why did Plato represent Love itself in the form and habit of a certain **great spirit**? <note>original: *magni cuiusdam dæmonis*. In the Platonic tradition, a 'daemon' is a mediating being between gods and men, not an evil entity.</note> Surely that great Philosopher seems to have been driven to do this for no other reason than because he then proposed to investigate only the principle of *human* love, and by no means angelic or divine love; he rightly judged that human love is beautiful only in potential, but not at all in actual fact. 

Furthermore, so that we may know by what means love, having first begun from the Angelic World, was soon distributed into the Celestial World, and finally into the Lower World, we must recall two opinions of most distinguished men on this difficult matter. The first of these is said to be attributed to **Avicenna, Al-Ghazali, Rabbi Moses** <note>Maimonides</note>, and many others: namely, that divine beauty and love itself, beginning from God the Best and Greatest, falls down not all at once, but through a certain perpetual series and succession observed through all the intervening intelligences <note>celestial beings</note> and through all the interposed spheres, step by step, down to **prime matter** <note>the basic, unformed substance of the universe</note>. From there, following the example of a circle, it returns again to God himself, from whom it took its beginning, by ascending gradually through all the intermediate forms.

The other opinion, which **Averroes** seems to have followed, is this: that the immense beauty of God is immediately diffused, without the help of any intermediary, into the whole universe of created things—yet with a choice made for each individual thing and its condition preserved. And love, likewise sent from heaven, is immediately communicated by God the Best and Greatest to all parts and particles of the World itself, though in different degrees and proportions, without the work of any intermediary being required. And these things are considered more than enough regarding the third of the proposed questions.

To the fourth question, the author himself now responds learnedly and excellently in close combat; the sense of this very long dispute seems to be, in my judgment, as follows. He first reviews the various opinions of the poets regarding love, and allegorically interprets its parents as handed down differently by them. He also gives a most elegant reason why the poets placed two different and very dissimilar **Cupids** in charge of only two kinds of goods—namely, the *useful* and the *pleasant*—while the third kind of good, which is called the **honest** <note>the morally good or noble</note>, completely ignores and rejects the rule of Cupid. Furthermore, he assigns many reasons why love is declared to be **twin** <note>referring to the Common and Heavenly Aphrodite/Eros</note>. 

Then he recounts that myth of the **Androgyne** treated so widely and diffusely by Plato in the *Symposium*, through which the prince of all philosophers seems to have described the origin of human love and its parents with great artistry. He shows clearer than light that Plato derived this myth from the **Mosaic** <note>biblical</note> account of the creation of the world. In this matter, the Prophet <note>Moses</note> is seen to have deliberately contradicted himself and, as if by design, to have opposed his own work; certainly, no better or safer way can be found to harmonize and reconcile the words of Moses than by reducing the creation of man described by Moses to the myth of the Androgyne treated by Plato. He demonstrates that the different order preserved by both in the sequence and context of the narrative almost agrees on the same point, and that each of them is most highly consistent with the truth.

Afterward, attempting to penetrate into the secret and hidden senses of the Mosaic narrative, he brings forth two allegories—but one especially—regarding the creation of the first parents, the crime committed by both, and the punishment enjoined upon each for the crime perpetrated. This allegory is so subtle and elegant that nothing more subtle or elegant could even be imagined. Afterward, he seems to display the greatest sharpness of wit and supreme artistry by adapting almost the same allegory to the fiction of the Androgyne explained by Plato. From this, he concludes that Plato signified that all human loves and all their desires came to light from the harmonious division of the **intellect** and the **body**, as if of male and female. 

But since this most serious philosopher expressed only the birth and parents of human love, he later adds that the love encompassing the whole universe of bodies was procreated from **Porus and Penia** <note>Resource and Poverty</note> as if from parents; the author himself soon opens and reveals many hidden senses of this myth, as is his custom. Then, searching for the most ancient parents of the love that encompasses the universe of all created things—leaving Plato behind and dismissing the fictions of the poets—he demonstrates that it drew its origin from the **beautiful beloved** as if from a father, and from the **knowledge of beauty** together with its absence perceived in the lover as if from a mother. After overcoming and conquering many difficulties, he finally concludes that this opinion is the truest, and that the two parents already mentioned come together and agree for the procreation of however many loves are found. 

Whence Plato not undeservedly pronounced love to be the desire of the beautiful, and of bringing forth and setting out offspring most like the father. But since beauty seems to play the primary role in establishing the essence and definition of love itself, he rightly extols it as much as possible. With beauty taken into account, he teaches that every beloved thing is loved, and every lover loves; and he teaches that beauty itself exists as the beginning, middle, and end of any love, even if we take the love of God for himself. 

But so that we may perceive the essence and nature of beauty more distinctly, he decides to repeat those things which he has already said: that it is by no means known or apprehended by the **impure and more imperfect senses**, such as touch, taste, and smell, but only by the **spiritual and more excellent faculties** of our soul, such as hearing, sight, imagination, intellect, and finally the mind, always more and more. He teaches that the nature of beauty is spiritual and exists as far removed as possible from bodily stain and impurity; although the common people, neglecting the truth of things, falsely persuade themselves that beauty belongs properly to bodies and is adapted to the praise of incorporeal things only through a certain likeness. Indeed, on the contrary...

# ARGUMENT. 447 #

...it happens more that bodily deformity belongs properly to nature and its physical condition; beauty, however, seems rather to be distributed and diffused from incorporeal things into bodies as a kind of spiritual gift. He refutes as utterly false and deceptive that common opinion—to which several ignoble philosophers later gave their assent—which considers beauty itself to be located truly and properly in the agreeable proportion of parts, both among themselves and in relation to the whole. Once this view is exploded, he demonstrates that all ugliness in bodies is to be referred to matter, while their elegance and grace are to be referred to **form** <note>In this philosophical context, "form" refers to the internal organizing principle or "blueprint" of a thing, rather than just its external shape.</note> as their proper author. Furthermore, when matter exceeds form, bodies are rendered less beautiful and more ugly; conversely, he shows that when form overcomes matter, bodies emerge as less ugly and more elegant. From this, it can very easily be seen that a certain supreme beauty resides in the forms themselves when they are entirely separated from matter, and a far greater beauty exists in these than in bodies composed of ugly matter and decorative form.

The elegance and beauty of both natural and man-made bodies proceeds chiefly from a form introduced into matter, either by the skill of nature or the industry of the artist. This is certainly the greatest proof for us that beauty is defined as a certain formal grace; when this grace is known and perceived by a lover, it brings him the greatest pleasure, and gradually compels him to love it through a most sweet reasoning. Moreover, he reviews three levels of beauty: the lowest is assigned to bodies composed of matter and form; the middle is granted to the forms themselves that adorn such bodies; and the highest is truly owed to the **Ideas**, <note>Platonic "Ideas" or "Forms" are the eternal, perfect archetypes of all things existing in the divine mind.</note> from which the aforementioned forms flowed down to perfect and work upon matter.

He follows the beauty and elegance of the Ideas with the highest praise, testifying that they far surpass the forms entangled in matter. These Ideas reside first in the divine mind, and soon after in the **World Soul** <note>original: *anima Mundi*. A Neoplatonic concept of an intrinsic spirit that brings life and order to the entire universe.</note> as if in their own homes—though they obtain a far greater unity and simplicity when hidden in the divine mind than when they are translated to the World Soul. Furthermore, he explains the agreement and likeness that the human soul seems to have with the World Soul (which is charged with care), and that the human intellect has with that divine and most simple Intellect. He most elegantly compares visible light with intellectual light, and the harmony perceived by the sense of the ears with the harmony seen in the World Soul.

Moreover, he reveals that according to Plato’s opinion—with Aristotle not disagreeing—our soul exists full of innate spiritual forms of all things. Although these forms seem to remain hidden because of the mass and impurity of the body, they are seen to be gradually uncovered and, as it were, illuminated with the help of the senses. He believes that the reason why some people attain an understanding of things more easily, some with more difficulty, and others not at all, should be attributed to this greater or lesser shadowing and obscurity of the forms sealed within our minds. He also attributes to this the reason why men feel the greatest effort and inconvenience in perceiving some things, while in others they feel none or very little.

He teaches us that the chief duty of human minds is situated in this: that they should recall and separate, as much as possible, the spiritual beauties distributed into bodies from the darkness of matter and bodily foulness. By this means, our intellect, being more easily unencumbered, will finally reach the understanding of those most excellent forms which exist entirely foreign to the contagion of matter and bodily stain. 

He then treats the middle condition of the soul, showing it to be between the intellect and the body, and that it carries two faces: one looking toward the intellect, the other toward the body. He believes that from the various changes and dispositions of these two faces of the soul, all the diversity of human loves is derived—whether in loving and pursuing bodily or spiritual forms either more vehemently, more weakly, or moderately. Finally, he concludes that human happiness is placed in the sharpest contemplation and most vehement study of spiritual forms; as these are the most noble of all, our entire knowledge of bodily forms must be raised up and referred to them.

Next, he returns to declare and reveal the interior nature of beauty, testifying that it is contained and preserved entirely in the **Idea** as its principle, and from there, no differently than from a most fertile spring, it emanates and is soon dissipated and diffused into the university of all bodies. Here, very conveniently and opportunely, he explores the essence or definition of the Ideas, demonstrating that they are certain divine "promotions" <note>In this sense, "promotions" refers to the outward movement or procession of divine creative power.</note> necessarily required for the procreation of the World. He does not believe that Aristotle fundamentally did away with Ideas when they are explained and accepted in this way, even though Aristotle himself everywhere professes to be a most bitter enemy of the Ideas. 

He forms the opinion that the controversy between Plato and Aristotle concerning these kinds of separate forms took its origin from a diversity of names and a varying method of philosophizing, rather than from a difference in the things themselves. He believes these two most wise men felt exactly the same thing, though they spoke differently; he considers that both attained almost equal praise—the former by extolling the Ideas, and the latter by depressing them.

Next, although the Ideas seem to be many when compared with the forms fashioned in their likeness, nevertheless, since they are defined as certain most beautiful examples of all procreated things set apart in the divine mind, he judges that they have been reduced to a supreme and most simple unity, once the appearance of multitude, division, and diversity is removed. He confirms that this Ideal unity can be joined and connected with the multitude of things that differ among themselves and are expressed in its likeness, using a famous example of the **Sun**. <note>Just as one sun illuminates many different objects simultaneously without losing its own unity, one divine Idea informs many different physical things.</note> By bringing forward this same example, and another regarding intellectual concepts, he explains beautifully how the divine Idea is impressed upon and distributed to various things through certain different reasons.

He also considers it by no means something to be passed over in silence that the Idea of the whole World and of all procreated things seems to be so joined and intertwined with the divine essence that it exists as one and the same thing with it, not distinguished from it by any reasoning. However, he demonstrates that we must not therefore conclude that the divine essence is situated in a mere relationship to external works. For a richer teaching and easier understanding of this matter, he reviews two opinions of the most excellent philosophers: the first of which, ascribed to Aristotle, holds that the divine form and essence agree entirely as one and the same thing with wisdom itself, the primary intellect, and Ideal beauty...

is established. The other opinion, however, attributed to Plato, considers that the highest wisdom, the first intellect, and the Ideal form flow directly from God himself and differ somewhat from him. For this reason, Plato thought that God himself should not be called beauty or wisdom, but rather the **Supreme Fair** and the **Supreme Good**—or rather the author of true and primary beauty and highest wisdom. He rightly judged that the name "beauty" belongs to the intellect and wisdom rather than to God, who is the origin of that very intelligence and wisdom. He demonstrates at great length—and it is no wonder—that this opinion of Plato’s accords most closely with the authority of the Sacred Scriptures, and was received primarily from Moses and Solomon. 

He also brilliantly discusses that remarkable and most ancient love between the **Supreme Fair** and the **Supreme Beauty**, as if between a man and a woman <note>original: "quasi inter uirum & mulierem amore"</note>. From this love, the entire universe of all procreated things and all subsequent kinds of love flowed, as if from a single highest principle. He urges us above all to reject bodily and base forms and embrace only the knowledge of incorporeal things. Among these, we should observe a certain order, ascending from lower to higher things as if by steps, until we reach the supreme form of all things. Carried from there to the **Supreme Fair** itself, we may finally come to rest in Him, as the most excellent author of human happiness. And here, the discussion of the fourth ambiguity proposed above seems to end.

Finally, boldly approaching the fifth point—which proposed to investigate the very end <note>The "end" (*finis*) refers to the goal or purpose.</note> of love—he judges that it is situated chiefly in pleasure. Seizing this opportunity, he inquires into the difference between love and desire, judging that the latter is distinguished and separated from the former as a species is from its genus. From this, he decrees that pleasures which are both good and beautiful are the proper goals of **love**; however, pleasures that are merely good but not beautiful belong not to love, but rather to **desire** (which he calls sensory appetite) separated from love. 

Afterward, he most excellently interprets the meaning of the saying that all love and all appetite always strive toward the good. He reviews the various and differing natures of pleasures, explaining most diligently which are to be pursued and which avoided, and which are good in reality versus those that are only good in appearance. Furthermore, he offers a fourfold division of pleasures, from which he elegantly derives a division of desires and of those who desire them. 

Moreover, he demonstrates that **union** <note>original: "Copulationem"</note>—the intense desire for which he has already defined as love—perfectly coincides with pleasure, which he recently determined to be the goal proposed for every love. He concludes that pleasure is the most common end of all loves, even though Aristotle, following popular opinion as if contradicting this view, claimed that love is of the useful, the pleasant, or the honest. He thinks it must be especially noted that the love of useful and pleasant goods, when reduced to a praiseworthy moderation, seeks utility and pleasure from **matter**, but seeks honesty from **form**. Therefore, the moral virtues, which deal with these kinds of goods, achieve a certain mixed rather than pure or sincere honesty. But the intellectual virtues, which are seen to occupy themselves with certain divine goods far removed from the commerce of matter, embrace only a pure and intellectual honesty with a certain lover-like affection. 

Furthermore, he declares that the Platonic partition of love into the **feral** (bestial), **human**, and **divine** accords wonderfully with the Aristotelian division into the **depraved**, **moral**, and **intellectual**. Having completed this, he moves closer to determining the fifth of the proposed questions. He sets forth several points he believes will be of great use: namely, that the target and intention of every love—both of lower things for higher and higher things for lower—ultimately consists in the pleasure that the lover receives from the perfection and beauty of the beloved object. However, this intention is rendered manifold according to the diversity of the two mentioned species of love. 

He notes that God’s love for the entire universe of procreated things rests not on a love God has for himself, but rather on the beauty and perfection of the things God loves. In the Divine Power, as in a most excellent parent, two species of love seem to reside: one directed toward His own form and His own wisdom, which was intensely intent upon the procreation of the world and its perpetual preservation even to this day as its proposed goal; the other, however, directed toward the produced universe, striving to recall the already-created world to its final perfection as its ultimate end. He judges that the end of the world’s procreation is situated in the world’s greatest possible agreement and likeness with its Divine Model. 

The final perfection of the already-procreated world—by which it finally returns to the Creator from whom it is said to have first come—is thought to reside in actual and united intelligence joined with a most ardent love. This is the understanding that the procreated intellect (the highest and most noble part of the world) possesses regarding the unity of form, wisdom, and beauty. With all these points laid down as a foundation, he concludes that the proposed ambiguity should be determined thus: the enjoyment of the Creator himself is granted by a certain divine liberality only to the intellectual nature (as the supreme and most excellent part of the whole world) and exists as the final and most common end of all loves found in the universe of created things.

He then undertakes the explanation of a certain **Admirable Circle**, which encompasses in its circuit the various essences of all things and the diverse kinds of all loves. He testifies that it is divided into two semicircles: the first, beginning from God the Best and Greatest, descends step by step through all the classes of angels, then through all the celestial orbs, and finally stops in "prime matter," which is most opposed to divinity. The second semicircle, taking its start from this first subject (matter), touches the elements, inanimate mixtures, plants, animals, and the human race. In humans, it strives upward from the nourishing soul to the sensitive soul, and from there to the intelligent soul. Ascending step by step from lower to higher intellectual acts of this most excellent soul, it finally returns to the supreme Creator from whom it began. Indeed, the first semicircle of loves, since it falls from more perfect to less perfect things (or from more beautiful to uglier things), provides for the procreation and preservation of things; the second semicircle, however, since it strives from the more deformed to the more beautiful, and from the worse to the more excellent, looks toward the per-

<meta>This page continues the summary of the third dialogue of Leone Ebreo's *Dialogues on Love*, specifically concluding the philosophical "argument" or summary before beginning the actual dialogue text between the characters Sophia and Philo.</meta>

# 449 #

<header>SUMMARY.</header>

He demonstrates that Love strives most especially for the restoration of things and their return to their own principle. He also adds this: that things created from their most intimate union with the supreme Creator feel the greatest pleasure <note>original: "uoluptatem"</note>, which he declared to be the common end of all loves. These matters having been explained, he begins a discussion of intellectual pleasures and intellectual loves, demonstrating that both are as far removed as possible from the nature of mere passion, and he assigns to each its own proper definition. He also declares, as a particularly difficult and hidden matter, in what way we can attribute pleasure and love even to God, the Best and Greatest <note>Latin: "Deo quoque Optim. Maxim." — a common Renaissance phrasing for God</note>, and he offers two most elegant definitions of divine love and divine pleasure. Afterwards, he turns his discourse to declaring that the pleasure perceived by a lover from the union with the beloved object is the common end of all loves that can be brought forward—not only of those by which lower things pursue higher things, but also, much more so, of those by which higher things pursue the lower. Finally, he strives to demonstrate this through many reasons and to confirm it with several examples and the authority of the Sacred Volumes: that not only the world’s most ardent desire for its Maker, but also the Creator's incredible love for the whole of all created things, concurs as the most powerful cause for this—so that the world itself, by the help of its intellectual nature, may finally be joined with God, the Best and Greatest, and at last return to its own principle. Once all these things are finished and completed, he finally seems to embrace in a very brief Epilogue those matters which he treated more diffusely and widely throughout this entire third discussion. However, so that he might perhaps relieve and refresh the mind of the listener—which might be overwhelmed and fatigued by the sharp contemplation of so many great things—he finally introduces Sophia and Philo conversing in the manner of lovers. There, he assigns a certain acute reason why Philo alone, contrary to the common law of other lovers, receives only pains, torments, and sicknesses along with many soul-crushing agonies as the proper and fitting end of his love, rather than pleasure; he laments, with a certain lover’s passion, that this must be attributed to Sophia’s cruelty and hardness. He also highly extols the beauty of his beloved’s mind and the grace of her body, showing that, raised up by these two wings as it were, she approaches divine beauty more closely than is fitting for human lot or condition. Therefore, he concludes at last that it is not at all surprising if he himself pursues the distinguished and almost divine beauty of Sophia with such vehement love and great zeal.

**SOPHIA.** Philo, Philo! Do you not hear me, or do you simply not wish to respond?
**PHILO.** Who calls me?
**SOPHIA.** Do not hurry so; listen for a moment.
**PHILO.** It is you, O Sophia? Intent on other things, I had not perceived your arrival.
**SOPHIA.** Where are you heading so intently, that you neither speak, nor hear, nor see your friends as they pass by?
**PHILO.** I had left the house to serve the necessities of my more ignoble part <note>A reference to the physical body and its mundane needs, as opposed to the "noble" soul</note>.
**SOPHIA.** Do you call that part "ignoble" which, even with eyes wide and ears open, robs you of the power of seeing and hearing?
**PHILO.** That part possesses as much excellence and nobility in me as it does in any other person, yet I do not believe it should be valued more than is fair and just; nor are the occurring necessities of such great importance that they ought to lead my mind away from all other things. Therefore, the business I was going to attend to did not, as you think, cause this alienation of my mind.
**SOPHIA.** Then let it not seem heavy or troublesome to you to explain the reason for your preoccupation.

<margin>A most pleasant refuge for a mind affected by weariness and satiety.</margin>

**PHILO.** My mind, affected by weariness and satiety with human actions and necessary, sordid occupations, has this only refuge: to be driven back into itself.
**SOPHIA.** And what goal does it propose for itself there?
**PHILO.** The end and outcome of my thoughts is by no means hidden from you.
**SOPHIA.** If it were not hidden from me, I would certainly not ask for it; by asking, I show that I am entirely ignorant of it.
**PHILO.** So be it; yet I would scarcely have believed it was unknown to you.
**SOPHIA.** Why?
**PHILO.** Because one who holds the cause ought also to know the effect.
**SOPHIA.** But in what way...

<margin>The manner and custom of beautiful women.</margin>
...in what way do you think I understand the logic of your meditations? **PHILO.** This I know for certain: that you are better known to yourself than anything else is known to you. **SOPHIA.** Even if I know myself—though not as perfectly as I would wish—I would never have judged that the cause of your hidden thoughts should be blamed on me. **PHILO.** All you beautiful and beloved women are accustomed to pretending very well that the tortures of your lovers, though perfectly known to you, are a mystery. But just as you excel others in the beauty of your body and the greatness of your soul, I would desire that you also love the truth above all others. Since you have attained a beauty that is absolute, pure, and entirely free of any blemish, I swear by Hercules <note>A common Renaissance exclamation, "me hercule," used to emphasize sincerity.</note> that it pains me to see the common error of your sex leave a mark or stain of dishonesty upon you. **SOPHIA.** I see now, Philo, that in order to escape my accusations, you have devised this most clever method of slandering me in turn. But whether I know your mind's disturbances or remain ignorant of them, let us set aside this dispute and tell me this first: for what reason were you walking along just now so deep in thought? **PHILO.** Since you wish to review with me those things which you already know best, I tell you that my mind was turned toward the contemplation of the beauty formed within you, and toward the most pleasing image of that beauty impressed upon itself. This contemplation forced me to abandon my external senses. **SOPHIA.** Ha! You have made me laugh. How can it be that an image of something—which, when present, cannot even penetrate open eyes—is so powerfully impressed upon the mind? **PHILO.** You speak the truth, Sophia: for unless your extraordinary and most brilliant beauty had prepared a path for itself through the eyes, it would never have slipped into the senses and the imagination later. Nor would it ever, by penetrating into the depths of the heart, have decided to reside forever in the mind as if in a temple dedicated to itself, with your image most effectively carved and impressed upon it. Indeed, the rays of the Sun passing through the celestial bodies and the elements closest to them do not reach the earth with such speed as the likeness of your form flew to occupy the innermost chambers of my heart and mind. **SOPHIA.** If these things you say were true, they would cause even greater wonder; for while I have always been so intimate and familiar to your soul, and have exercised such absolute and long-lasting command over all its powers (as you yourself proclaim), yet now the doors of seeing and hearing are scarcely open to me. **PHILO.** Would you accuse me of being asleep? **SOPHIA.** Not at all, because sleep, by hindering the actions of the senses, would be more than enough to excuse you. **PHILO.** That same logic,

which just now took away my sense, provides my defense. **SOPHIA.** What thing can be found so powerful that it can take away the powers of sensing in the same way as sleep, which is the image of death? **PHILO.** Ecstasy <note>From the Greek "ekstasis," meaning to stand outside oneself; a state of being so overwhelmed by emotion or thought that one is oblivious to the world.</note>, or the alienation of the mind proceeding from amorous meditations, which seems to possess greater power than the very image of death itself. **SOPHIA.** By what reasoning can inward thoughts recall and lead men away from their senses more than sleep itself, which forces the body to lie like a kind of lifeless corpse? **PHILO.** Sleep is thought to preserve and provide life rather than snatch it away or take it; this is not at all what happens in amorous ecstasy. **SOPHIA.** How so? **PHILO.** Sages have said that nature devised sleep for living creatures in two ways and for two ends:

<margin>Sleep seems to have been established by nature for two ends: both for the rest of the senses and exterior movements, and the refreshment of the spirits; and also for the perfect concoction and digestion of food.</margin>
first, so that the organs of the senses and external movements might rest, and their spirits <note>In the medical theory of the time, "spirits" were subtle fluids that carried sensory information and life-force through the body.</note> which perform and oversee these duties might be refreshed, lest they should eventually be dissolved or consumed by constant labor and long hours of wakefulness. Second, so that nature might use the help of the spirits and innate heat to perfectly concoct <note>original: "concoquendum." In Renaissance medicine, digestion was viewed as a process of "cooking" food in the stomach.</note> and digest food. Nature, by inducing sleep to allow the rest of the senses and external movements, draws the spirits to the internal and hidden parts of the body, so that it may devote all its strength to nourishing and refreshing the living creature. The truth of this matter is confirmed especially by this evidence: that

<margin>A most elegant reason why the Heavens are never seen to sleep or rest.</margin>
the Heavens, since they neither take any food nor feel the slightest labor in their continuous motions, are seen to be always awake and never at rest. Therefore, sleep seems to bestow life upon living creatures rather than having any agreement or similarity with death. But the alienation of the mind from lov-

<margin>The extreme intensity and great harm of amorous ecstasy.</margin>
...from amorous meditations, there follows a deprivation of the senses and movement that is not natural, but rather a kind of violence. This state brings no pleasant rest to the senses, nor does it refresh the body’s exhausted strength; on the contrary, it seems to hinder digestion and to dissolve and consume the entire body. Therefore, if I could aptly and properly excuse my blindness and silence by claiming I was falling asleep, then this alienation of the mind and amorous ecstasy <note>The term "ecstasy" here refers to a "standing outside" oneself, a trance-like state where the soul is focused entirely on a single object.</note> ought much more to clear me of the crime you charge against me. **SOPHIA.** Do you mean to say that men sleep more by being awake and thinking than by lying in soft beds? **PHILO.** I mean, at least, that they feel less. For when ecstasy arrives, the spirits <term>spirits: subtle substances thought to act as the bridge between the soul and the physical body</term> are drawn back to the innermost parts of the body no less than they are in sleep. They leave the senses robbed of the faculty of feeling and the limbs destitute of motion. For the mind, in order to sharply contemplate some object it vehemently loves and desires, is so forced into itself that, being entirely occupied and dwelling in that contemplation, it becomes alienated from all other things. This is exactly what you saw happen to me just now, as I was contemplating your most beautiful image, to which—as if to some divine power—all my thoughts are directed. **SOPHIA.** It is certainly a marvel that thoughts can induce a stupor no different from the deepest sleep. For while we think, we usually retain the ability to speak, hear, and move ourselves; indeed, without some prior deliberation, actions of this kind can be fulfilled neither perfectly nor in an orderly fashion. **PHILO.** It is undoubtedly that same mind to which the governance of the senses
<margin>The gathering of the mind into itself.</margin>
and the direction of a person's voluntary movements have been entrusted. 
<margin>The reason why our bodies are deprived of both sense and motion while we are contemplating.</margin>
Thus, so that it may perform its duty better and more conveniently, the mind must travel from the internal to the external parts of the body—specifically to arrange the organs suited for performing actions and to meet the objects of the senses spread around it on the outside. At such times, we are able to think and simultaneously see, hear, and speak without one hindering the other. But when the mind is forced within itself so that it may contemplate the beloved object most effectively and intimately, it flees from the exterior parts. Deserting sense and motion, it retreats into that proposed meditation with almost the entire multitude of its powers and spirits. It leaves no power to the body except that which, if it were lacking, would cause the body itself to perish: I mean the vital force <note>Latin: *uim uitalem*</note>, by whose benefit the heart is constantly moved and the spirits, running everywhere through the arteries, frequently breathe so that they may draw in the external cooling air and expel the internal, boiling air. Only this vital faculty is seen to remain, along with a certain tiny portion of the nutritive faculty; for the greater part of it is occupied and completely hindered by the focused speculation. For this reason, a small amount of food usually suffices for those in contemplation for a long time. 
<margin>A small amount of food usually suffices for those in contemplation for a long time.</margin>
Just as sleep—when the nutritive faculty is strengthened and corroborated—is most harmful to the mind's right thoughts, obstructing them and casting a kind of darkness (because the vapors <note>It was a common Renaissance belief that the "vapors" of digestion rose to the brain and clouded the imagination.</note> from the concoction of food constantly seeking the brain often stir up various wandering dreams, confusing and disturbing the imagination itself), so too does deep and most vehement meditation take away and interrupt the sleep that is most conducive to a living creature's nourishment and the digestion of food. **SOPHIA.** You are asserting that sleep and contemplation are partly similar, because both force the spirits to the interior parts by deserting sense and motion, and partly contrary, since one hinders and expels the other. **PHILO.** That is exactly how it is. For both seem to agree in some things and differ in others; they desert and leave behind the same things, but they acquire and obtain different things. **SOPHIA.** In what way? **PHILO.** Because
<margin>The similarity and difference between sleep and amorous ecstasy.</margin>
sleep and meditation alike deprive and snatch away the senses and motions together. However, sleep seems to impede and, as it were, bind the powers of feeling and moving by strengthening the faculty of nutrition, while meditation does so by supplying strength to thought. Furthermore, both are seen to be similar in this: that they lead the spirits back from the outermost to the innermost parts of the body. But they differ in this: that sleep moves toward the lowest seats of the body located beneath the breast, namely to the stomach...

namely, where the organs serving nutrition—the stomach, liver, intestines, and other similar parts—reside, it contracts the spirits <term>spirits: the "vital spirits" or "pneumata," believed to be subtle vapors that carried life and sensation through the body</term>. All gathered there together, they apply themselves with all their might to concocting food and nourishing the living being. But contemplation leads these same spirits to the highest of all parts of the human body located above the chest, namely to the brain itself—the most excellent seat of thought and the royal palace of the mind—so that, all joined together in a close-knit rank, they may make a greater and more vehement assault upon the proposed meditation.

<margin>
The contraction of spirits, although common to both sleep and amorous ecstasy, is directed toward different ends.
</margin>
Furthermore, the contraction of spirits, although it is common to both, is directed toward different ends: for sleep introduces them so that it may also bring in natural heat along with them. It strives to drive these forces into one place as much as possible, so that it might effect a stronger and more perfect concoction or digestion. But meditation strives to contract the spirits not to bring in innate heat, but rather to join all the powers and faculties of the soul into one, and to lead the soul itself to the highest unity, so that it might render the soul stronger and more robust for the sharp and focused meditation on the thing most vehemently loved and desired.

<margin>
Sleep takes away contemplation, and contemplation takes away sleep, and not without reason.
</margin>
Since, therefore, so many differences intervene between sleep and contemplation, we have rightly said that one takes away and hinders the other. Truly, regarding the loss of the senses and movement, sleep and meditation seem to be equal or level; although perhaps we might consider meditation to inflict a greater force and violence than sleep. **SOPHIA.** I do not yet quite see how one who is thinking loses their senses just like one who is sleeping. For you yourself will not deny that a lover seized by ecstasy is thinking and speculating sharply, two things which are undoubtedly connected to the senses. But in a man overwhelmed and weighed down by the burden of sleep, none of these are seen to remain, but only the faculty of nutrition, which has no commerce at all with the senses; indeed, it is found even in plants, which are destitute of the power of feeling.

<margin>
Intimate and vehement contemplation induces a much greater alienation and stupor than sleep itself.
</margin>
**PHILO.** On the contrary, if you pay close attention, you will judge that the opposite should be said. For although sleep takes away the sense of seeing, hearing, tasting, and smelling, it does not take away the sense of touch; for those who sleep are accustomed to perceive cold and heat. The imagination <note>original: "phantasia"</note> also wanders about many things here and there, and although it seems to stray and wander widely with no order preserved at all, nevertheless most of its dreams derive their origin from present disturbances. But the mind’s vehement and intent contemplation takes away the sense of cold and heat along with the rest, and deletes the memory and thought of every single thing, except only for that which the mind has proposed for its own speculation. Indeed, the meditation on this one thing alone is referred not to the lover or the contemplator, but only to the person loved and thought upon. For the lover, seized by such sharp meditation, does not seem to remain within himself, but to have already left himself and entered into that thing which he so vehemently desires and contemplates. For no care or memory of himself touches the lover established in ecstasy and sharply speculating on the thing for which he is held by the greatest love. Intent neither on his own benefit nor his preservation, he exercises no action agreeable to nature, or sense, or motion, or reason. Rather, utterly despising himself and holding himself as nothing, he is dedicated and devoted only to the thing loved and thought upon, and is entirely transformed into it. For since the essence of the soul is established in its own action, whenever it is coupled or rather united with some object through the intervention of sharp contemplation, it is soon transferred into it and converted into its substance; it should not then be called the soul or essence of the lover, but the truest image <note>original: "species"</note> and most absolute act of the loved person. For this reason, men seized by amorous ecstasy seem to be called away from themselves much more than by sleep. By what reason, then, Sophia, did you think I should be rebuked, simply because I neither saw you nor spoke to you first?

### DIALOGUE III. ###

<page-num>453</page-num>

It would be most pleasing to me to understand this more clearly. What reason, then, can be offered as to why the senses cannot perform their own duties when the mind is thinking quite sharply? For the mind does not seem to require any withdrawal of the senses in order to observe more intently; the senses ought not to intrude or mix themselves into the mind's almost divine actions at all. Nor is an abundance of innate heat seen to be necessary for contemplating things, in the same way it is for "cooking" <note>original: *decoquendis*; refers to the digestive process which was viewed as a form of heat-based cooking</note> food. Furthermore, the spirits <term>spirits: the *spiritus*, or subtle vapors believed to carry life and sensation through the body</term> required for sensation should not be thought to provide any great help to the understanding of things, since the mind, being incorporeal by its own nature, seems to require no aid from spiritual bodies to perform its own duties. Why, then, did you say that sharp meditations require the leisure and holiday of the senses, and are accustomed to drive them away, take them away, and contract them?

<margin>
The reason why sharp meditations, by taking away both movement and sensation, contract and lead back all the spirits to the brain.
</margin>
**PH.** The soul, by its own nature, is indeed one and indivisible. However, by distributing its power throughout the whole body and reaching even to the exterior and extreme parts of the living creature, it is rendered fit and accommodated to exercise many actions of sensing, moving, and nourishing, according to the multitude and diversity of the organs. Thus, the soul is cut into many different powers. In this matter, the soul proposes to imitate and rival the Sun: although the Sun is seen to be one, yet because of the diffusion and vast multitude of its rays, it is divided and multiplied almost immensely, just as the number and variety of the places it illuminates seems to demand.

<margin>
The mind is called the "heart of the heart" and the "soul of the soul" by the wise.
</margin>
Therefore, when the spiritual mind—which is called the "heart of the heart" and the "soul of the human soul" by the wise—is kindled by a most vehement desire to more sharply observe an inward and sought-after object, it is driven into itself. It recalls the soul, which was dispersed throughout the whole body, back to itself and collects it into an indivisible unity. Along with the soul, the spirits are also contracted, even though they are not at all necessary for contemplation. They settle either in the middle citadel of the whole head, where thought resides, or in the center of the heart, the soul's own dwelling place of desire. Because of this violent and sudden contraction of the spirits to the brain or to the heart, the eyes are deprived of sight, the ears of hearing, and the other organs of sensation and movement. Moreover, even the internal members suited for nourishing the living creature become cold and fail in performing their constant and necessary ministries—that is, in digesting and distributing nourishment. For this reason, the human body, reduced to a certain extreme poverty and want due to the loss of these spirits, obeys only the vital faculty of the heart, to which the perpetual guardianship of the whole common life has been delegated, as we have said elsewhere. This vital faculty <note>original: *uitalis facultas*; the basic force that keeps the body alive regardless of thought or sensation</note> sits among the other virtues of the human body, carefully placed according to both its location and its dignity, and it joins the upper parts with the lower parts just like an intervening bond.

<margin>
He demonstrates that the vital faculty, by condition of both place and dignity, holds a middle position between the highest and lowest parts of our body. He testifies that the soul can leave the body and leave it lifeless because of extremely sharp and vehement contemplation.
</margin>
**SO.** How can you claim that this vital power joins and couples the highest and lowest parts of our body like a common bond, both in its location and its condition of dignity?

**PH.** The vital faculty is placed in the heart, occupying a middle seat in the chest between the belly (the lowest part of man) and the head (the highest portion). Therefore, it follows that the faculty itself is also in the middle between the lower part designed for nutrition, which is located in the belly, and the upper part consecrated to cognition, which resides in the head. Through the mediation of this vital power, the two extreme parts and powers of man are bound together. Unless this common bond of the middle power had been placed by nature in between, the mind and soul would be dissolved from the body during the most vehement meditations; the mind itself would immediately fly away, and the body would lie lifeless.

**SO.** Could we sometimes, when contemplating most sharply, lift the mind so high that it would carry away even this bond of life with it?

**PH.** Certainly, a desire so vehement and a contemplation so inward could occur that it would entirely unburden and liberate the soul, which is weighed down by the mass of the body and reduced, as it were, to slavery. In such a case, the spirits would be dissolved because of their stirred-up and violent rush into a very narrow space, so that the soul...

### OF LOVE, BY LEO HEBREW ###
<page-num>454</page-num>

<margin>The sweetest kind of death.</margin>
...the soul, having embraced the desired and contemplated object with a certain amorous affection, would utterly leave behind and desert the lifeless body. **SO.** This kind of death should certainly be considered the most sweet. **PH.** In this very way, our most holy fathers met their final day; while they were contemplating that divine and most excellent Beauty with the greatest and most sharp zeal, with all the powers of the soul turned toward it and consumed in that thought, they left the body lifeless.

<margin>Moses and Aaron, most sharply contemplating the divinity, died most happily joined with it.</margin>
For this reason, when the Sacred Volumes <note>original: *sacra Volumina*; referring to the Torah/Hebrew Bible</note> make mention of the death of two of our most holy fathers, Moses and Aaron, they affirm that they died "by the divine mouth." This metaphorical way of speaking was later judged by the wisest interpreters to be explained thus: that both died kissing the divinity—that is, they were carried away into the heights by an ecstasy or amorous contemplation and a divine union. <note>This refers to the *Mors Osculi* or "Death of the Kiss," a Jewish mystical concept where the soul of the righteous is drawn out of the body by a divine kiss.</note> **SO.** It certainly seems a wonder that our soul at one moment descends to know corporeal things, and at another betakes itself so easily and readily to the contemplation of spiritual things; and since the soul is one and indivisible, how it is seen to run with such incredible speed between things so contrary and distant as the corporeal and the spiritual. I would wish, Philo, for some reason to be devised by you that might lead my understanding to a grasp of this admirable tossing and turning of our soul. For how is the human mind able now to leave the senses, now to resume them—at one time to contemplate, and at another to cease from contemplation, as you yourself said just now?

<margin>The soul differs from the intellect as a mutable thing from a stable one.</margin>
<margin>The soul's nature is double and ambiguous, seen as a participant in both spiritual intelligence and corporeal change.</margin>
**PH.** It is by this very name that the soul is seen to be lower than the separate intellect. For the intellect is always found to behave in the same way; it is never carried from one thing to another, nor does it ever proceed from itself toward foreign things. But the soul, which yields to the intellect and depends upon it, does not persist long in the same condition. Rather, since it is placed in the middle between the intelligible and the corporeal world (for it is like a medium and a certain bond connecting both together), it was therefore allotted a double and ambiguous nature, being a participant both in spiritual intelligence and in corporeal change. Otherwise, how could it render bodies animate? Hence it happens that the soul very often goes out from its own intelligence toward corporeal things: partly to preserve the living body safely by means of its nourishing faculties, and partly to recognize exterior objects through the intervening work and power of the senses, which are most necessary for life and contemplation. Sometimes, however, it returns to itself and recurs to its own intelligence, and is gathered and joined with the separate and higher intellect. From there, it returns again to corporeal things, and from them back again to the intelligible, according to the succession of pressing necessities and differing inclinations.

<margin>The reason why Plato declared the soul to be composed of "the same and the other," as well as of the visible and invisible; and to exist as a self-moving number, moving perpetually in a circle.</margin>
For this reason, Plato thought the soul to be composed of "the same and the other," <note>original: *ex sese & alio*; a reference to the "Same" and "Different" in Plato's *Timaeus*</note> and of the visible and the invisible; he defined it as existing as a "self-moving number." By these words, that most weighty philosopher intended to signify that the nature of the soul is not at all simple and always like itself, such as the pure and unmixed intellect is. Rather, its essence embraces many and diverse natures: it is neither solely corporeal nor only spiritual, but is continually transferred from one to the other. Furthermore, Plato added that it moves perpetually "in a circle"—not because the soul is moved from place to place through the body itself, but because it is moved by a certain spiritual reason and a succession of actions from itself and returns into itself. That is, it proceeds from its intelligible nature to its corporeal nature, and from the body returns again to the intellect. **SO.** I seem to have grasped the manifold and different nature of the soul, so learnedly and eruditely treated by you. But it would be most pleasing to me if you would illustrate this obscure and difficult matter with some apt and fitting example. **PH.** What more illustrious and suitable example can be brought than the two principal lights of heaven <note>The Sun and the Moon</note>, which the supreme Creator of all things constructed in the image and likeness of the intellect and the soul?

He cites Platonic definitions of the soul's dual nature before preparing to use the Sun and Moon as allegories.</summary>

### DIALOGUE III ###

<margin>
The Sun and the Moon seem to represent the divine intellect and the Soul of the World as if they were most artfully crafted images.
</margin>

**SO.** What are those things said to be? **PH.** I speak of the greater light set over the day, and the lesser light placed over the night. **SO.** Do you mean to signify the Sun and the Moon? **PH.** Precisely those. **SO.** What correspondence do these celestial bodies seem to have with the intellect and the soul? **PH.** The Sun stands as an image of the divine intellect—the principle and common origin of all other intellects—while the Moon represents the Soul of the World, <note>original: *animam Mundi*; a philosophical concept where the entire universe is seen as a living being with a soul.</note> from which all other souls proceed. **SO.** In what manner? **PH.** It is surely not hidden from you that the created world is divided into the corporeal and the spiritual (or incorporeal). **SO.** This I certainly know. **PH.** Furthermore, you know very well that the corporeal world is "sensible" <note>perceptible by the senses</note> and the incorporeal world is "intelligible." <note>accessible only to the intellect</note> **SO.** I am not ignorant of this either. **PH.** You ought also to observe that of the five senses, only the sight of the eyes grants the name of "sensible" to the corporeal world, just as the incorporeal realm claimed the name "intelligible" because of the vision of the intellect. **SO.** Are the remaining four senses to be considered superfluous and unnecessary? **PH.** Only

<margin>
Sight is considered to provide far more than any of the other senses toward achieving knowledge and understanding of things.
</margin>

vision is able to perceive all bodies generally. Hearing, indeed, provides the greatest help in attaining knowledge of things, yet it does not acquire it from the things themselves as sight does; rather, it receives knowledge passed down by another who knows, through the use of the tongue—one who either saw the thing themselves, or understood it after it was first seen by another. From this it follows that sight precedes hearing, and the ear frequently relies upon the eye as the first origin of human intelligence. The other three corporeal senses <note>touch, taste, and smell</note> are entirely unrefined, coarse, and thick; they are ordered toward the perception and use of things that contribute to the life and health of living creatures, rather than toward the knowledge of the intellect. **SO.** Yet we see that animals, though destitute of intellect, have been gifted with sight and hearing. **PH.** This is indeed true, because they also require these two senses for the preservation of their bodies' needs. But in 

<margin>
In man, these two senses—sight and hearing—are ordered not only for the safety of the body, but also for the knowledge of the mind. The eye cannot behold things unless it, the object, and the intervening medium are filled with solar light.
</margin>

man, beyond the utility which both seem to bring to the health and safety of the body, they are additionally required for the knowledge of the mind. ...just as sensible vision, along with its medium and its object, is illuminated by the Sun itself. I believe it is now clear that the Sun, which is visibly seen in this corporeal world, is rightly called the image and likeness of that divine intellect which presides over the Intelligible World <note>The "Intelligible World" refers to the realm of ideas and spiritual truths accessible only to the mind, as opposed to the "Sensible World" perceived by the senses.</note>.

<margin>The name of Light seems to belong more truly and appropriately to the divine intellect than to the Sun.</margin>
**SO.** I entirely agree with this comparison between the Sun and the divine intellect. And although the name "light" seems to belong truly and properly only to the Sun, nevertheless, the influence of the divine intellect can also be called "light" quite aptly and conveniently due to a certain analogy.

**PH.** On the contrary, the name "light" applies more truly and appropriately to the intellect than to the Sun.

**SO.** Why?

**PH.** Because, just as the faculty of understanding provides a knowledge that is more excellent, more perfect, and more true than the power of sensing, so too the light illustrating intelligible vision seems to be more perfect and truer than solar light, which is adapted only for illuminating the sight of the eyes.

<margin>Solar light is nothing other than a certain shadow of intelligible light, or an intellectual splendor communicated to the most noble body.</margin>
Indeed, I will go so far as to boldly claim that solar light should be considered neither a body, nor an affection, nor a quality or accident of a body—as certain ignoble philosophers have falsely persuaded themselves <note>Philo is likely critiquing certain materialist interpretations of Aristotelian physics which categorized light as a simple "accidental quality."</note>. Rather, it is nothing other than a certain shadow of intelligible light, or its splendor communicated to the most noble body <note>By "noblest body," he refers to the Sun or the celestial spheres.</note>. For this reason, Moses, the prince of prophets, said when describing the beginning of the World’s creation that when all things were huddled together in that foul and gloomy Chaos (or in a certain blind and most dark abyss), the divine breath produced light by gently breathing upon the immense whirlpool of waters. The meaning of these words, in my judgment, is that on the first day of creation, visible light itself proceeded from the divine and most luminous intellect—light which was subsequently applied to the Sun, the Moon, and the other stars on the fourth day.

**SO.** Tell me, I pray, Philo, how can the light of bodies be called something incorporeal and almost "intelligible"? For if it exists corporeally, by what reasoning will you deny that it is either a body or at least a quality or accident of a body?

<margin>The light of the Sun and the other stars is by no means an accident, but rather exists as a certain spiritual form.</margin>
**PH.** The light of the Sun ought to be considered not an accident, but rather its spiritual form <note>In Scholastic philosophy, a "form" is the essential nature or "soul" of a thing, whereas an "accident" is a non-essential trait like color or weight.</note> which proceeds from and is shaped by the intelligible and divine light. This light, being then transmitted to the other stars, also exists as their perfection and spiritual form; but the primary role must be granted to the Sun, which has already occupied it most abundantly.

<margin>Divine and intelligible light is imparted to different bodies in different ways.</margin>
This same light is afterward communicated and imparted to fire and other luminous bodies residing in the lower world <note>The "lower world" refers to the sublunary sphere, or Earth.</note> as a form in a corporeal manner. However, this light of luminous bodies, derived from intelligible light, is received into transparent and clear bodies—for instance, into air or water—as a kind of separable and spiritual "act" <note>original: *actus*; a state of being or operation</note>, but by no means as a corporeal act according to the condition of a quality or affection.

<margin>A transparent body exists as a vehicle for light rather than its subject.</margin>
Therefore, a transparent body exists as a vehicle for light rather than as its subject <note>In logic, a "subject" is that in which a quality inherently resides (like the apple is the subject for the color red); a "vehicle" merely carries it without the light becoming a part of the air's substance.</note>.

**SO.** Why is that?

<margin>He demonstrates with six arguments that light is by no means received into a transparent and clear body like a quality into a subject.</margin>
**PH.** Because if light were received into a transparent medium as a quality into a subject, it would surely be affected by the six conditions of a quality. First, a quality generally spreads itself through a subject by a certain succession <note>i.e., it takes time to spread</note>, which does not apply to light, which is seen to penetrate the entire transparent medium instantly. Second, the arrival of a quality is seen to change the natural disposition of the subject, yet the transparent subject undergoes no change at all when light arrives. Third, a quality requires a determined space to be extended into a subject; but light is accustomed to diffuse into the transparent medium without being circumscribed by any limit or boundary. Fourth, we see that when the cause producing and introducing a quality is removed, the subject retains and preserves that impressed quality for a long time—hot water removed from the fire can provide us with most certain proof of this; but you will see the transparent medium lose all light the moment the illuminator is removed. Fifth, a quality moves together with its own subject; but light, insofar as it is seen to illuminate the transparent, does not move in the slightest due to the movement of the air or water where it resides. Sixth, multiple qualities of the same species affecting the same subject are confounded, mixed together, and composed into one; but multiple lights can by no means be joined into one: for when we are walking or strolling by two or more lamps, two or more...

In medieval philosophy, the "diaphanous" refers to substances like air or water that are capable of transmitting light.</note> or in an illuminating body is neither a quality nor a physical affection, but rather a certain spiritual act that perfects the transparent medium when the source of light is present, and vanishes when it departs.

<margin>Light relates to the transparent medium in the same way that the intellect, or the thinking soul, relates to the body itself.</margin>
Nor does light assist the transparent medium by any other reason than the intellect or the thinking soul assists the body; it is joined and coupled with the body by its presence and, so to speak, by a certain essential reason, yet it is by no means mixed with it. From this it follows that the mind is rightly said neither to be changed because of the body's changes, nor to die because of its destruction.

<margin>Intelligible light is truly and properly called "light."</margin>
Therefore, we must consider that "intelligible light"—which illuminates both the corporeal and incorporeal World by an essential reason and illustrates our soul for the completion of intellectual vision—has obtained the name of "light" truly and properly.

<margin>From intelligible light proceed all other lights infused into bodies.</margin>
From this intelligible and most excellent light is derived Solar light, which we see illuminating the corporeal World as its act and form. Moreover, ocular vision is thought to proceed from this same source, so that through its mediation we are able to perceive absolutely all bodies—not only those contained in this lower and decaying World according to the condition of the other senses, but even the divine and immortal bodies placed in the ethereal regions.

<margin>Of all the senses, sight alone is able to lead man to the knowledge of incorporeal and intellectual things.</margin>
For sight, the prince of incorporeal things, seems to provide intellectual knowledge to man; since from the fact that we see the stars and heavens perpetually revolving, we conclude that their movers are intellectual and incorporeal, and that their supreme maker and creator is most wise and most powerful. This is indeed confirmed by the most weighty testimony of David, who says: *When I contemplate your heavens, the work of your hands,* etc. (Psalm 8). **SO.** You seem to have preferred sight over all the other senses considered together; yet I clearly discern that the others—especially touch and taste—are more necessary for the life of living beings and humans than sight.

<margin>Sight is not so much for the physical or sensible life, but rather is most conducive to the spiritual and intelligible life compared to others.</margin>
**PH.** I also confirm that they are indeed more necessary for the physical and sensible life; but sight is far more conducive to the intelligible and spiritual life. For this reason, it seems to excel the others in its instrument, object, medium, and act.

**SO.** I pray you, interpret these four excellences you have mentioned.

<margin>Sight excels the other senses in its instrument, its object, its medium, and in the act itself.</margin>
**PH.** Who does not perceive how much the organ of vision surpasses the instruments of the other senses in clarity, purity, and craftsmanship? Since the eyes are seen to be neither like other parts of the body nor fleshy, but shining, transparent, and spiritual, reflecting the splendor of the stars, and excelling the other members of the human body in beauty and grace. Their greatest and almost divine craftsmanship can be most easily perceived from the composition of the seven humors or tunics <note>In Renaissance anatomy, based on Galen, the eye was thought to be composed of seven distinct layers (tunics) and fluids (humors) that acted as the mechanism for sight.</note>, which is accustomed to fill our minds with far greater admiration than the structure of any other member or organ. Furthermore, the object of vision is considered to be the entire corporeal sphere—both the celestial and the elementary—whereas the other senses are able to perceive only the smallest portion of the lower sphere. Moreover, the media of the other senses are said to be situated and placed either in flesh (as in touching), or in vapor (as in smelling), or in moisture (as in tasting), or in violently struck air (as in hearing). But the medium of seeing is seen to be luminous, spiritual, and transparent, since all philosophers confess that the air itself exists perfected and completed by the light of the stars. This light, which is properly its noble and conspicuous form, so excels all other parts of the world just as the eye seems more brilliant and excellent than all other members of the sensing body. Finally, the actions of the other senses are usually extended to only a very few affections of the bodies being perceived...

# LEONE EBREO: ON LOVE #

For the sense of smell only perceives sharp vapors, taste perceives the flavorful fluids of food and drink, and touch perceives the intensities of physical qualities through a coarse, common, and imperfect method of impression. For this reason, the "images" produced by these three senses are seen to bring about real physical changes and immediate disturbances within their respective sense organs. Although hearing is more spiritual than these and reaches further to perceive distant objects, it is only capable of perceiving the heavy and sharp "striking" of the air caused by the powerful vibration of two bodies hitting one another. Furthermore, for hearing to perform its duty correctly and conveniently, it requires a continuous and moderate distance; the images that excite this sense seem primarily to demand the physical striking of bodies and local motion. 

But the eye discerns things situated at the furthest edge of the World and in the high heavens, as well as all bodies both far and near, through the benefit of light. It receives their images without any intervening physical touch. Moreover, it recognizes distances, colors, lights, sizes, shapes, numbers, positions, motions, and many other minute distinctions of the physical World. It is as if the eye 
<margin>The eye is not without reason called the observer of the intellect itself and of intelligible things.</margin>
was granted to man by nature as the "eye of the intellect" and the most excellent and diligent observer of intelligible things. Driven by this very reasoning, **Aristotle** did not hesitate to declare that we love sight more than the other senses, 
<margin>Sight alone seems to provide us with a far richer knowledge of more things than all the other senses combined.</margin>
because it provides us with a far richer knowledge of more things than all the other senses collected together. 

Therefore, just as in man—who is called a <term>microcosm</term> <note>original: "μικρόκοσμος"—literally "little world." The Renaissance idea that the human being is a miniature map of the entire universe.</note>, or a "little world"—the eye seems to hold the same relationship among all parts of the body as the intellect holds among all the faculties of the soul, and is considered its image and servant; so too, if we look at the "Great World" <note>The Macrocosm or the universe as a whole.</note>, we shall find the Sun shining and reflecting among all bodies just as the Divine Intellect shines among all those most blessed spirits. We will undoubtedly find the Sun to be the "express image" of God, the Best and Greatest <note>original: "Dei Optimi Maximi"</note>, and the closest attendant to the King of the World. 

Furthermore, just as the light and vision of our eyes proceeds from the light and vision of the intellect, and serves that intellect by recognizing and examining the many differences between things, we must likewise understand that the abundant light and most splendid appearance of the Solar body emanates from the true and primary light of the Divine Intellect, 
<margin>The Sun represents and reflects the Divine intellect by the same logic that the eye represents the human intellect.</margin>
serving that same Divine source. Therefore, you can now perceive, **Sophia**, the reason why the Sun is truly and properly said to represent the Divine Intellect, to which it also seems very similar in terms of form and beauty. For just as the sum of all beauty and grace resides in the Divine Intellect—in which the entire universe is considered to be harmoniously arranged and most beautifully shaped—so the Sun is seen to be the most shapely and elegant of all bodies, adorning and illuminating all things.

**SO.** I believe I have perfectly understood that the Sun and the eye are most excellent images of the Divine and human intellects, respectively. I certainly perceive that the human intellect and the physical eye have obtained a very great correspondence and similarity with the Sun and the Divine Intellect. However, in one point only, the human eye and the celestial Sun show a certain discordance that does not seem to fit the human and Divine intellects: for our intellect seems to agree with the Divine in two things: namely, in "understanding" and in "illuminating." For just as the Divine Intellect not only understands all the "species" <note>In this context, "species" refers to the Platonic Ideas or the essential forms of things.</note> of things residing within it, but also grants to all other intellects a light adapted to the capacity of each from the most intense light of its own immortal Ideas or forms; so too, our intellect seems not only to have an understanding of all common species, but also to bring a fitting light to all the other virtues <note>Faculties or powers of the mind.</note> that serve human knowledge. Thus, although their knowledge deals with individual things entangled in matter, they are nonetheless directed by the most certain rule of a right and prudent intellect.

### DIALOGUE III ###

<margin>Vision seems to consist not only in the form <note>original: *specie*</note> received from the object as it passes through a medium to the eye, but also in rays emitted from the eye through that medium to illuminate the object.</margin>

This comparison cannot be easily applied to the Sun and the eye, since we see that the eye perceives but does not illuminate, while the Sun illuminates but does not perceive. *PH.* In this regard, we might find that the Sun and the eye actually agree. For the human eye is capable of seeing not only because of the common light of the transparent medium <term>diaphanum|The transparent substance, such as air or water, that allows light to pass through</term>, but also because of a certain unique illumination from shining rays that travel from the eye to meet the object. These rays, emitted from the sharp focus of the eyes, are certainly not enough on their own to light up the medium and the object; yet, without their help, the general light of the transparent medium alone could never bring the act of seeing to completion. *SO.* Do you really believe the eye sees by sending out its own rays toward the object? *PH.* Indeed. *SO.* In this, you certainly seem to disagree with the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy</note>, because **Aristotle**, having rejected this opinion, believed that vision occurs because the "species" <note>The visual form or image</note> of the object is introduced into the pupil of the eye, and not because rays are emitted from the eyes, as **Plato** is said to have believed. *PH.* In my judgment, **Aristotle** proved nothing against **Plato**. For it seems to me that both must necessarily occur together to produce and complete a vision: first, that rays are emitted from the eyes to perceive and illuminate the object, and second, that the image entering the pupil represents the object from which it came. Yet, these two opposing movements are not considered enough to fulfill vision; a third and final condition is required. After the eye has sent its rays to the object and received the image back, it must consider and judge the agreement and similarity of the image impressed upon it with the external object that produced it. In this third and final action, the perfected nature of vision is situated and achieved.

<margin>Three things are primarily required to produce perfect and absolute vision.</margin>
<margin>The Sun does not only illuminate things exposed to it, but it also discerns them with great sharpness and looks upon them most clearly.</margin>
*SO.* You seem to be introducing new doctrines and some paradoxes. *PH.* On the contrary, this is considered an ancient and long-held opinion. Just as we said that the eye does not only discern things but also "illuminates" them before it sees, so too I want you to be persuaded that the Sun not only illuminates the bodies before it but also perceives them. For among all the senses, men believe that sight is found in the celestial bodies in a more excellent and perfect way than in any living creature, whether rational or irrational.

<margin>The Heaven itself, through the Sun and other stars, sees the things exposed to it very sharply, no differently than if through most splendid and purified eyes.</margin>
*SO.* Do you really think the heavens see just as we do? *PH.* In fact, they perceive things far more sharply and distinctly than we do. *SO.* Were they also adorned and decorated with eyes like living creatures? *PH.* What more splendid and pure eyes can be seen than the Sun and the other stars? You will often find them called the "eyes of God" in the Sacred Volumes because of their magnificent vision, especially where the Prophet designates the seven planets with these words: "Those seven lights of God, which are spread over all the earth." <note>original: "Septẽ illa Dei lumina, quæ in omnes terras diffunduntur."</note> Furthermore, we find another Prophet speaking this way: "By the starry heaven, which is His body, and is full of eyes." <note>original: "Per cœlum stellatum, quod ipsius corpus, & oculorum plenum existit."</note> The Sun is also commonly called an "eye," which is why people very frequently refer to the "eye of the Sun." These celestial eyes are believed to see as many things as they illuminate, and through the work of sight, they perceive and know all the bodies of the sensible World and all their changes.

<margin>The reasoning by which celestial bodies are able to apprehend and perceive the objects of the other senses besides sight.</margin>
*SO.* But if the heavens were gifted only with sight, how will they perceive the objects of the other senses? *PH.* Regarding those things that consist only in the pure physical experience of the senses, the celestial bodies do not acquire knowledge of them in the same way we do. Thus, they do not experience flavors through taste, nor physical qualities through touch, nor vapors through smell. However, since they are said to be the most excellent "causes" of the elemental natures and qualities from which these sensations arise, they do not know them by "crude Minerva" <note>Latin: *crassa Minerva*—an idiom meaning a rough, plain, or unrefined understanding</note> but through a most noble and eminent knowledge of the causes themselves. Additionally, they perceive them through sight,
