...they perceive those things which are accustomed to bring in and produce such affections and effects.

<margin>The very sharp hearing of the heavens.</margin>
**SO.** But what do you think should be said concerning hearing? Do they hear? **PH.** Most certainly, though not with a specific instrument adapted for perceiving sounds. For we observe that the heavens are endowed only with the organ of vision. But since they see and take notice of the gestures of any whole body, as well as the motions of the lips, the tongue, and the rest of the vocal organs, they excellently guess and understand their meanings. This is not unlike what some very sharp-sighted men are able to do: by diligently observing and considering only the motions of the mouth and lips, even if they cannot hear the spoken voices at all due to some impediment, they nevertheless perceive the meaning of the speech solely from the gestures and motions they have seen. If mortal eyes perform such a wonderful feat, then the lights of the greater and shining stars, and especially the Sun, will be able to perform the same much more easily and perfectly.

<margin>The power and excellence of solar light.</margin>
Regarding the excellence of this Solar light, setting other things aside, I will tell you only this: that it penetrates into all the bodies of the world, even down into Tartarus <note>A reference to the deepest part of the underworld in classical mythology, used here to mean the very center of the Earth</note>, as anyone can perceive from the Sun’s natural and vital heat reaching to the center of the earth. Furthermore, with its noble and bright vision, it comprehends all the bodies of the sensible world, their qualities, acts, and affections, with the utmost sharpness and distinction.

<margin>A most learned comparison of the divine and human intellects, as well as the Sun and the eye.</margin>
Therefore, just as our intellect is very similar to the divine intellect in two ways—namely, in seeing and in illuminating things—so too do the human eye and the celestial Sun seem to agree in these same two ways. And with the terms transposed and exchanged, just as our eye and our intellect agree in two things, I mean in seeing and illuminating; so we seem to have already shown abundantly that the Sun and the divine intellect conspire in these same things. **SO.** You have spoken more than enough about the similarity between the Sun and the divine intellect. Now, it would be most pleasing to me if you would explain and declare that correspondence which you said above exists between the Moon and the World Soul <term>Anima Mundi|The "World Soul," a Neoplatonic concept of an intrinsic spirit that animates the entire universe</term>.

<margin>The greatest similarity between the Moon and the World Soul.</margin>
**PH.** Just as the soul is placed in the middle between the intellect and the body—and is thought to be composed both of intellectual unity and stability, and of bodily diversity and change—so too we say that the Moon holds the middle place between the Sun (the image of the intellect) and the earth (which represents bodily grossness and impurity to the highest degree). We say it is composed partly of the Sun’s unique and stable light, and partly of the manifold and changeable nature of terrestrial darkness. **SO.** I grasp the whole matter. **PH.** Since you are persuaded that you have perfectly understood what I have said, I pray you, interpret the meaning of my speech. **SO.** It is evident to everyone that the Moon resides in the middle between the Sun and the earth; for the lunar sphere is seen to be situated and placed below the Sun and above the earth, in the middle of both—especially following the opinion of the ancients, who wished for the Sun to immediately embrace and surround the Moon <note>This refers to the pre-Copernican, geocentric model of the universe where the Moon's sphere was closest to Earth, followed by the Sun or other planets</note>. Furthermore, the dark and obscure spots which are very frequently seen in the middle of the Moon's globe when it is full clearly and most plainly show that the lunar body is composed of Solar light and terrestrial opacity; hence you seem to have said not without merit that its light is mixed with darkness. **PH.** You have explained one part of what I said, and indeed the easier part; but you have not touched upon the other and principal part even in the slightest.

<margin>He shows with several arguments that the lunar body holds a middle place between solar light and terrestrial shadows.</margin>
**SO.** You, then, proceed to interpret what remains. **PH.** Leaving aside that part which you grasp so well, we declare that the light itself, or rather the illumination of the lunar globe—because it is seen to be neither as copious nor as rich as the Sun's, but remiss and modest—exists as a middle ground between the most brilliant light of the Sun and terrestrial darkness. We also see that the globe of the lunar body itself is partly bright and partly opaque; for it has been observed by the ancients that one half of the Moon (excepting only during an eclipse) is always illuminated by the Sun, while the remainder remains opaque and dark due to the lack of Solar rays.

For it seems the Sun has not yet finished its midday course. **PH.** We see that the Moon, with its round body, imitates a sphere; and always, unless an eclipse <note>original: "defectu," referring here to a lunar eclipse where the Earth's shadow intervenes</note> gets in the way, it receives light from the Sun on the front half of its globe that is turned toward it.

<margin>He demonstrates that one half of the Moon is always illuminated by the Sun, while the other remains dark (except only during an eclipse).</margin>

Indeed, the back half of the globe, which does not face the Sun at all, always remains dark and obscure. **SO.** You truly seem to contradict common sense, which does not agree that half of the Lunar globe is always illuminated, but only rarely so—specifically at the time of the full moon. Otherwise, light does not occupy an entire half of the Moon, but sometimes a larger portion of that half and sometimes a smaller one, according as the Moon waxes or wanes. Moreover, it is sometimes thought to have lost its light entirely, namely when it is found in conjunction <note>The "New Moon" phase, when the Moon is positioned between the Earth and the Sun</note> with the Sun, as well as on the day preceding and following that conjunction. **PH.** So indeed it appears to the senses; but in reality, the Sun always illuminates an entire half of the Lunar globe (I except only an eclipse). **SO.** Why then is our sense unable to discern this truth? **PH.** Because since the Moon moves constantly, sometimes approaching the Sun and sometimes receding from it, it receives solar light in many different ways and proportions due to various and differing aspects <note>The relative positions of the heavenly bodies as seen from Earth</note>. This light, which must always illuminate one half of the Moon, is carried around now from the upper to the lower part, and now from the lower to the upper part of the Lunar body. **SO.** Which part of the Moon do you call the "upper," and which the "lower"? **PH.** We are

<margin>Which part of the Moon is customarily called the lower or upper part by Astrologers.</margin>

accustomed to call "lower" that part which inclines toward the earth and seems to look at us; we observe this face most easily when either the whole of it or at least some portion of it drinks in the solar light. We call "upper" that part of the Moon which is turned toward the solar orb situated in a higher place; we are never able to see the whole of that part, nor any portion of it, however much it may be shimmering. Therefore, once every recurring month, the entire lower half of the Lunar globe is filled by the Sun, and then

<margin>He explains the various changes and transformations of the Lunar body in receiving the solar rays.</margin>

we see it full of light. This usually happens on the fifteenth day after the conjunction of the two lights <note>The Sun and the Moon</note>, for then the Moon and Sun are positioned diametrically opposite one another. At other times, the entire remaining half—namely, the upper half—is illuminated. This usually happens when the two lights come together as one; for then the Sun, illuminating the entire half of the Moon turned toward it, leaves the lower half that inclines toward us entirely obscure and dark. Then, for the space of two days, we seem to be deprived of Lunar light. On the remaining days of the month, the halves of the Lunar globe illustrated by solar rays are seen to behave in various ways. For after the conjunction, the light gradually leaves the upper parts (unknown to us) and steps by step approaches to illuminate the lower parts (conspicuous to us), as the Moon recedes further and further from the Sun day by day. Yet always a complete half of the Lunar body is penetrated on all sides by solar rays. However, as much light as is missing from the lower part is restored to the upper; and for this reason, it does not always happen that we see a full half of the Lunar globe illuminated. This kind of flow and alternation of light from the higher parts of the Moon to the lower ones lasts until the fifteenth day; for then the entire lower part facing the human race is bright, and the entire upper part is dark. Then, the light gradually deserts the lowest parts of the Lunar star and rises step by step to illuminate the upper parts, until—with the entire upper half (invisible to us) being occupied and illustrated—the other part situated and placed toward us is utterly lacking in light and [shrouded] in darkness...

<summary>Philo explains the mechanics of lunar phases to Sophia, arguing that while the Moon always has one hemisphere illuminated by the Sun, our changing perspective makes it appear to wax and wane. He defines the "upper" (hidden) and "lower" (visible) halves of the Moon and how the solar light shifts between them over a monthly cycle.</summary>

...be filled from every side. **SO.** I have very well perceived the order and alternation of both light and darkness observed in the two halves of the lunar globe. Furthermore, I have understood the way and order in which light progresses from the upper to the lower parts of the lunar body, and then returns from the lower back to the upper. But I cannot yet see what correspondence or connection these things have with the proposed similarity between the Moon and the soul.

<margin>He demonstrates that the soul holds the same relationship to the intellect and the body as the Moon does to the Sun and darkness.</margin>

<margin>He explains the various changes and alternations of the soul, now moving from the intellect to the body, and now from the body back to the intellect.</margin>

**PH.** The light of the intellect is always pure and stable; but when it is then poured into the soul, it immediately becomes changeable and mixed with darkness. For the soul consists of intellectual light and corporeal opacity, just as we have already shown the Moon to be composed of solar light and a bodily, foul darkness. Furthermore, the light of the soul undergoes the same changes, proportions, and alternations as that of the Moon. For it is transferred now from the upper to the lower part—the part that seems to face us—and now, conversely, from the lower back to the upper part. For the soul sometimes uses the entire light of knowledge derived from the intellect to manage corporeal things, leaving its upper and noblest part (which faces the intellect) completely filled with darkness. This undoubtedly happens when the soul, entirely lacking in contemplation and the most excellent knowledge of things separated from matter—and finally lacking true wisdom—has applied and entangled itself in the pursuit of bodily actions, appearing shrewd and clever <note>original: "astu-ta," implying a practical, worldly cunning or skill</note> in exercising and managing them.

<margin>He elegantly interprets the similarity of both the conjunction and opposition of the two luminaries: the intelligible <note>the intellect and soul</note> and the sensible <note>the sun and moon</note>.</margin>

And just as astronomers <note>original: "Astrologi"; in this period, the study of the stars and their philosophical meaning were not yet separate disciplines</note> judge that the Moon's appearance is hateful and most hostile to the Sun when it is full and opposite to it, so too when the soul pushes all the light imparted to it by the intellect down to the lower part facing the body, it is thought to be opposed to the intellect, most contrary to it, and to have retreated as far as possible from it. But the opposite occurs when the soul receives the light communicated to it by the intellect into its upper and incorporeal part, which faces the intellect itself and is joined with it—just as the Moon is coupled <note>original: "copulatur," referring to the astronomical conjunction</note> with the Sun at the time of their meeting. Nevertheless, the soul remains obscure and dark in its lower part turned toward us—like a kind of spiritual Moon—because it abandons and neglects corporeal things out of affection for that divine coupling. For when the soul is raised into deep and intense contemplation of things abstracted from matter and coupled with the intellect, it neither looks toward bodies nor is touched by any care at all for administering corporeal things rightly and prudently. However, so that the entire corporeal mass does not eventually perish and go to ruin, the soul—imitating the Moon—gradually leaves its union with the intellect and step by step communicates intelligible light to the lower and corporeal part. It seems to acquire as much light for itself as it takes away from the upper part. Since a perfect union of the intellect and soul cannot exist at the same time as the care for corporeal things, it follows that the soul, setting the example of the Moon before it to imitate, gradually withdraws its light and knowledge from divine things and transfers it more and more each day to illuminate and recognize corporeal things, until it has perfectly and fully completed its duty in their prudent and right administration, at which time contemplation is altogether postponed and abandoned. In this, the soul seems to emulate the Moon on the fifteenth day after conjunction, when we see the part turning toward us full of light, and the part turned toward heaven filled with darkness. You will further see the soul reflect the Moon’s example in that it also, just like the Moon, gradually takes its light away from the lower and mortal world and translates it step by step to the upper and divine world, until it finally returns to that complete and intellectual union, with the corporeal part entirely darkened and wrapped in thick gloom. Therefore, the light of the soul derived from the intellect and its darkness (which is opposite to that light) are seen to change and be transferred from one part to the other in turn, by the same logic as the light received by the Moon from the Sun and the darkness opposite to it. **SO.** With a certain incredible wonder...

<summary>Philo explains how the human soul mimics the phases of the Moon, alternating its focus (light) between divine contemplation of the intellect and the practical management of the physical body. He argues that total devotion to one side leaves the other in darkness, necessitating a cyclical movement to maintain the life of the body while seeking spiritual union.</summary>

*PH.* Most certainly. 
<margin>
He shows that the two square aspects of the Moon to the Sun are very similar to two changes of the soul.

For the Moon is then said to hold two **square aspects** <note>original: "quadratos aſpectus"; a square aspect or quadrature occurs when two celestial bodies are 90 degrees apart.</note> to the Sun when its upper half and its lower half have divided the light between themselves in two equal parts. For this reason, astrologers are accustomed to attribute a meaning of "moderate enmity and strife" to the square aspect; and rightly so: for since two contrary parts of the lunar body—namely, the upper and the lower—exist as equally powerful and luminous, they seem, as it were, to litigate over which of them will seize the remaining portion of the light that is lacking. In the same way, when an equal portion of intellectual light falls to the upper part of the soul, which is called **reason** or **mind**, and the lower part, which is called **sensible**, both seem to contend and dispute among themselves for leadership: namely, whether reason shall rule over sense, or sense over reason. 

*SO.* But how can we fit and adapt these two lunar quarters to the soul? 

*PH.* Very well indeed: for the first of them follows the conjunction, and then the lower part begins to exceed the upper in light. The same thing happens to the soul while it proceeds from union toward opposition <note>In this allegory, "union" or "conjunction" is the soul's focus on the divine intellect, while "opposition" is its focus on the physical body.</note>: for when it happens that both parts participate equally in light, you will see the lower part thereafter conquering and surpassing the upper—that is, the **sensible** overcoming the **rational**. The second of the two proposed lunar quarters follows the opposition: and then the light begins to illuminate the upper part (which is more hidden from us) rather than the lower part (which is visible to us) of the lunar body. We see the same thing occur in the soul while it returns from opposition toward intellectual union: for after both its portions are seen to be equally luminous, the lower part is soon forced to yield and succumb to the upper—that is, the **sensible** to the **rational**.

*SO.* Truly, this most elegant appendix to those things you taught above should by no means have been omitted. Proceed, I pray, to the four remaining favorable aspects of the Moon and Sun: I mean the two **sextiles** and the two **trines**, to be adapted to the changes of the soul itself. 

*PH.* The first of the

This happens so that while the abundance of bodily things continues, some intellectual ray may be joined with them. This is considered by astrologers to be the second aspect of perfect and absolute friendship. The other of the two **sextile aspects** <note>original: "sextilium aspectuum"; a sextile occurs at 60 degrees, considered a favorable but less powerful influence than a trine.</note> of the Sun and Moon, which we have already proposed, is usually formed on the twenty-fifth day after the conjunction of the luminaries; it follows the second square and precedes the coming conjunction. Similarly, when the soul turns from bodily things to spiritual ones, it can make reason not only equal to sense, but even superior to it, without sense resisting at all. Directed and illuminated by the bright and upright mind, the soul seems to sufficiently look after and serve the necessities of bodily things. But because bodily things are then seen to be empty and thin, astrologers who divine the outcome of things intended this aspect to portend a maimed and weak friendship. After this fourth and final aspect, which is quite suited for reconciling love, if the soul strives toward spiritual things, it finally attains **divine copulation** <note>original: "diuinam copulationem"; here meaning the mystical union or "marriage" of the soul with the divine Intellect.</note>, in which its supreme perfection and happiness is placed, and the misery and diminution of bodily things is set aside.

things have died by the divine favor of the deity: all of whom the Sacred Volumes <note>Refers to the Hebrew Bible</note> testify died by "kissing the divinity." <note>original: "diuinitatem exosculantes." <margin>
The reason why both the soul of the World and the soul of man seem to undergo so many changes—sometimes ascending to the intellect, and sometimes descending to the body—is to be attributed to a dual love: namely, that by which the soul pursues both the intellect and the body itself.
</margin>

is moved, or for what reason do you call it "dual"? **PH.** Since the highest and most excellent form and beauty reside in the divine intellect, the soul—which we can rightly call a splendor <note>original: "fulgore"</note> emanating from the intellect—is seized by a most vehement love for that greatest beauty from which it takes its origin. By adhering and leaning upon it alone, the soul strives to acquire its ultimate happiness: just as we see everywhere that the female, being imperfect, loves the male from whom she expects her own perfection, and desires to be coupled with him. To this highest species of love, another immediately succeeds, by which the soul is said to love the corporeal World placed beneath it, as a male loves a female. This is so that the soul might perfect the world by imparting and imprinting upon it the beauty it received from the intellect when it was seized by that higher love. It is as if the soul wishes to give birth and return to the corporeal World the beauty of the intellect it has already conceived; or as if it scatters the seeds of beauty entrusted to it into the corporeal orb as if into a most fruitful field; or as if a most skilled craftsman, having already received the species and forms of intellectual beauty, looks to adorn and perfect the raw and deformed bodies. We see this happen not only with the Soul of the World in relation to the divine intellect in the Great Orb <note>The Macrocosm or universe</note>, but also with the human soul compared to its own intellect in our "small orb" <note>The Microcosm or individual human being</note>. Therefore, since our soul is affected by a dual love, it is seen to hold a maximum inclination and propensity both toward the intellect (the highest origin of all other forms and singular beauty) and toward the various and different beauties expressed and formed in bodies. Sometimes it happens that the soul, seized by a most vehement love of intellectual beauty, completely forgets the amorous inclination it usually bears toward the body, so much so that it departs and is separated from it entirely. This "loosening" of the soul from the body is usually accompanied by that most happy death originating from [divine] coupling, just as we said above when we spoke of the Solar Eclipse. At other times, however, we see the opposite happen: the soul, enticed and soothed by an immoderate and excessive love of corporeal beauty, utterly deserts and abandons that most excellent love of intellectual form. It recedes far from the supreme intellect so that it becomes entirely corporeal and loses all intellectual light and beauty—just as we sufficiently discussed above when dealing with the Lunar Eclipse.

<summary>Philo explains the "Dual Love" of the soul: an upward love for the Divine Intellect (seeking perfection) and a downward love for the material body (seeking to impart beauty). The "kiss of death" is described as the soul's ultimate "Solar Eclipse," where it is fully absorbed into divine light.</summary>

But if the soul turns aside toward corporeal love, the opposite occurs: for if it deflects only slightly toward it, and the intellect tries to resist the senses, the man will receive the name of **incontinent**; if, however, he runs excessively into it, he will be ill-reputed under the name of **intemperate**.

**SO.** This explanation of the soul's changes—taken from the two kinds of love, one for intelligible beauty and the other for corporeal beauty—is highly approved by me. And from this I believe it happens that, just as two various and different loves are found among men, so too two different and very unlike beauties are seen among them: namely, the **intelligible** and the **corporeal**. Furthermore, I also perceive how much intelligible beauty excels corporeal beauty, and how much better and finer it is to make the intellect beautiful and graceful rather than the body. I ask you further: can these two amorous inclinations you just mentioned—one toward the Sun and one toward the Earth—also be applied to the Moon, as if it were a kind of "corporeal soul"? If so, we could assert even more boldly that the Moon is a perfect and absolute image of the soul.

<margin>
The double love of the Moon itself: one indeed for the Sun, like a female for a male; the other for the lower and earthly world, like a male for a female.
</margin>

**PH.** Certainly. For the love with which the Moon pursues the Sun himself—from whom light, life, and every perfection suitable to her proceeds—represents the devotion of a **female for a male**; indeed, so that she may fully and absolutely possess this love, she seems to hasten with a swift and rapid pace to meet and embrace the Sun. Furthermore, any of us can very easily see that the Moon loves the lower and earthly world as a **male loves a female**, so that she may fill and perfect it with the light and influence received from the Sun. For this reason, the lunar phases are found to have the greatest similarity and agreement with the soul's changes; but to avoid a wordy and long-winded speech, it will be best to pass over those examples. I wish only to add this before I put an end and limit to this matter: just as the soul, affected by a double love, carries light from the intellect into the corporeal world, so too the Moon, led by a twin love, directs the solar light down into the lower world.

**SO.** You have indeed performed excellently in putting the finishing touch on such a steep and difficult matter, and you have certainly satisfied all my difficulties and requests in abundance.

**PH.** Because of the reasons brought forward, does it now seem right to you that our soul, carried away by a most vehement love and desire for the sharp contemplation of some object, is able to desert the senses and all corporeal powers at once?

**SO.** Most certainly. **PH.** You seem, therefore, to have accused and charged me rashly and unjustly at the beginning. For when you perceived some time ago that I was distracted and alienated from the senses by sharp thought, my mind—having summoned and drawn together all the powers and faculties of the soul from every side—was so intent on sharply contemplating the most elegant **simulacrum** <note>A mental image or internal representation.</note> of your beautiful form, that with sight, hearing, and almost every movement deserted and abandoned at once (retaining only the appearance of movement, which is common even to irrational animals), it drove and pushed me in that direction which I had previously intended to reach. Therefore, you ought to blame yourself rather than me, for you closed the doors against yourself and blocked the way.

**SO.** Nevertheless, in this at least you seem to be unjust: that you think your image of me should be preferred to myself. **PH.** This

**SO.** But at least by that reasoning you will confess that I am useful and healthy for you, because I transfer and lead your mind away from sad and dire thoughts to happy and milder ones.

**SO.** Why?

<margin>An elegant comparison between poison and the image of Sophia most vehemently impressed upon Philo’s mind.</margin>
For just as a poison, once swallowed, straightway proceeds to attack the central and most fortified citadel of a living creature's life; and never departs from there until it has consumed all the spirits <note>In Renaissance physiology, "spirits" (spiritus) were subtle vapors that carried life and sensation through the body.</note> residing within; and, with the pulses of the arteries gradually compressed and the extremities of the body slowly chilled, it finally undermines and dissolves the creature's life—unless perhaps a learned and experienced physician applies some powerful and opportune remedy to the wretched patient whose life is in danger—likewise, the distinct and solid image of you, which I feel has already penetrated into the inner shrines <note>original: "adyta"</note> of my mind, seems never about to withdraw its step from there, all the powers and spirits of my soul having been forced together into one place toward it. Indeed, it would utterly cut off and abolish my life, were it not that your outward appearance, shed around me, delayed and prolonged my life by refreshing and restoring my spirits and senses, and snatching my body from the jaws of death.

**SO.** Since, therefore, I declared that I bring you a healthy medicine, I do not seem to have been a liar; for if the image of me while absent offers you a lethal poison to taste, then I, being present, seem to repair your life by offering an antidote.

**PH.** You have devised an interpretation far removed from the truth: for I would think it should be said that you have instead snatched a prey from the most cruel and violent hands of your own image; and in this way, you have excellently avenged the injury done to you by the blocking and denying of your entrance and approach. Nor do I judge that you were led by any benevolence or charity, but rather by fear, to prolong the threads of my life. For if they had been cut, the deadly powers of that lethal poison, which you once gave me to drink, would have long ago been consumed and exhausted.

<margin>The pain is greater, the longer it lasts.</margin>
Hence, since you desire to inflict upon me constant and perennial tortures, you in no way allow the venom of your image to immediately overwhelm and finish me; for pain is usually greater the longer it lasts.

**SO.** I can devise no way, O Philo, to explain your enigmas and to harmonize and reconcile the conflicting or dissenting opinions you have brought forward; for at one time you assert that I am divine and vehemently desired by you, but at another time that I am a wicked and poisonous woman.

<margin>Lovers certainly ought neither to praise nor to blame love itself.</margin>

This is especially true because since love (as rumor holds) is also placed in the number of the celestial and spiritual **Gods**, he ought by no means to hate the **Truth**, who is preached to be connected and always joined with divinity itself, and the sister of all the Gods. **PHILO.** We shall spend today only in treating the origin of love diffusely and copiously; but at another time we will explain its good as well as its wicked actions, if it seems best. But if by some chance I sense that such great freedom in speaking is hateful and odious to love, I will interpose Truth, his sister—and you at the same time, born of that same source and most similar to **Venus** his mother—as two mediators most fit for settling our disputes and appeasing the divinity that is hostile to me. **SOPHIA.** For such great faith as you show you have in me, I give you the greatest and innumerable thanks, and I liberally promise you my help and mediation. But lest we consume the day vainly and uselessly, now

### DIALOGUE III. 473 ###

...you ask. Then, having granted the birth of love, you ask when it came forth into the light: and whether its succession and origin were eternal or temporary; and if it is admitted to be temporary, when it began—specifically, whether at the very beginning of the World, under that most general procreation of all things, or afterward. Third, you seek the place of so illustrious and distinguished an origin: and you desire to understand which of the three worlds first received this most noble infant—whether the lowest and terrestrial, or the celestial and starry, or rather the spiritual, which is to say the angelic and divine. Fourth, you long to know its parents: whether it issued from a father alone, or from a mother alone, or rather from both joined and coupled together; and of what place and rank its parents are said to be—whether they savor and redolent of a divine nature, a human one, or some other kind; nor would you less willingly learn the genealogy and origin of those parents themselves. Fifth and lastly, you ask the end <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "end" or "final cause" refers to the ultimate purpose or goal for which a thing exists or is created</note> of love’s arising, and for what use it was produced and introduced into the World; and not without reason, since the end is said to be that most excellent cause for the sake of which all things subject to time and change were brought forth into the light and sired: for the end of a generated thing is first intended by the producer, even if it is the last thing acquired by the thing generated. Do I seem to have recited correctly and from memory, **O Sophia**, the five uncertainties regarding the origin of love just proposed by you?

<margin>
The end is the most excellent of all causes.
</margin>

**SOPHIA.** Most certainly. I, for my part, proposed these controversies to be settled only briefly and implicitly; you, however, seem to have expanded and explained them in such a way that I have conceived in my mind and soul the greatest hope of learning subtle and wondrous solutions. For just as wounds that are opened and carefully inspected are healed better and more easily: so too are distinct and explained difficulties settled more conveniently and perfectly. Therefore, proceed with alacrity upon the task I have so vehemently sought.

**PHILO.** You should by no means be ignorant, Sophia, that since we have proposed the questions pertaining to the origin of love for examination, it must first be assumed that love exists, and then its essence <note>The "essence" refers to the fundamental nature or "what-it-is-ness" of a thing, as opposed to its "existence" (that it is)</note> ought to be brought back to memory.

<margin>
That love exists ought to be assumed as a certainty, as a thing most manifest among all people.
</margin>

**SOPHIA.** I judge it to be a manifest thing that love exists: indeed, every one of us frequently experiences its being; and I think no one can be found who exists entirely devoid or empty of this affection of the soul. **PHILO.** I rejoice greatly that you confess the essence of love and have felt its powers: for I was afraid that you, being perhaps inexperienced, might demand from me some reason demonstrating that love exists—a thing which could surely be persuaded only with the greatest difficulty to a cold person, not at all prone to loving, such as you used to boast yourself to be.

**SOPHIA.** In this matter, I seem to have removed some part of the labor from you.

**PHILO.** In this also, no differently than in other matters, I will most willingly comply with your wish; but I scarcely remember enough of those things we said.

**SOPHIA.** Yet you profess yourself to be mindful! If you forget your own affairs so easily, how will you be able to retain or preserve those of another in your mind?

**PHILO.** If the memory exists as something entirely intent upon and addicted to the affairs of another, how shall I be able to care for or remember my own? And if I forget my very self so easily, by what reason shall I remember a previous disputation?

**SOPHIA.** It seems a wonder indeed that those things which you then devised and spoke so promptly have now fallen utterly from your memory.

**PHILO.** When I was talking with you at that time, my mind was composing reasons, and my tongue was expressing in words what had already been thought; but my eyes and ears, working together in another and contrary way, [turned toward] your most beautiful appearance...

# LEONE EBREO ON LOVE #

...together with your graceful gestures, your composed words, and that most sweet, subtle manner of speaking, [these things] then imported and introduced [those ideas] into my soul. Indeed, they were all so tenaciously and deeply impressed upon my memory that their traces can be seen and endure even to this day. These [thoughts] should be considered mine alone, yet entirely belonging to another. If anyone wished to understand those things that proceed from you, as I have just listed, I could certainly set them forth promptly and from memory. But as for those things which have already departed or slipped from my mind and memory through my own speech, let whoever wishes remember them.

*SO.* However the matter stands, the truth always remains one and the same. Therefore, if you spoke the truth the other day, even if your memory now fails to repeat it exactly, your mind will still supply that same truth to your tongue once more.

*PH.* I certainly affirm that this can happen; however, the manner, the arrangement, and the order will vary to some extent. Moreover, some things that were said by me then and have since slipped from my memory might perhaps be omitted.

<margin>Love, taken in its most common sense, is defined as the desire for something.</margin>
*SO.* Do as you please; for a variation in the form or arrangement matters little in my judgment, provided the meaning remains exactly the same. I, too, as the most faithful guardian and preserver of your words, will not find it troublesome to add or correct whatever I perceive you have omitted or changed due to a lapse in memory.

*PH.* Since you so vehemently long to understand what love is, I will attempt to define it for you in a plain and most common way. Love, therefore, taken in its common sense, is said to be the desire for something.

*SO.* This definition is indeed plain and clear. But we could make it even shorter by saying that defining love simply signifies "desiring." For since love itself is said to be desire, it is necessarily understood to be the desire *for* something desired; for we are also accustomed to always refer love to the thing loved.

*PH.* What you say is true; nevertheless, a lucid explanation of any matter should by no means be criticized.

*SO.* That is true. But since you have defined love generally as desire, you must admit that all love is desire, and yet not every desire is love.

<margin>A definition and the thing defined are always interchangeable.</margin>
*PH.* Certainly; for a definition is always interchangeable with the thing defined, and the scope of both is always equal and the same.

*SO.* Why then did you previously say that love is not always desire? You relied on the reasoning that love often refers to things that exist and are already possessed by us—just as when we are said to love our parents, our children, our present health, and wealth already acquired. Desire, however, is always accustomed to look toward things that either do not exist, or, if they do exist, are not yet possessed by us. For men are seen to desire everywhere things that are missing—those that do not exist, so that they may exist; and those not held, so that they may be held. But we see that things or persons we love always exist, and are mostly even possessed by us. Indeed, we are never moved to love things that do not exist at all. In what way, then, as if your opinion had changed, do you now affirm that all love signifies desire?

<margin>Love and desire were described and designated above by certain different definitions.</margin>
<margin>Desire, no less than love, presupposes some mode of existence; and likewise love, no less than desire, presupposes some lack of the things themselves.</margin>
*PH.* This brings to mind another point: that we previously defined love in a different way than desire. We then said that desire is a voluntary affection for a thing that is judged good but lacks existence or possession; whereas love is a voluntary affection for enjoying most closely a thing that is judged good and is [currently] present. But we added this afterward: even if desire frequently refers to things we lack, it nevertheless—no less than love—presupposes some mode of existence. For although the longed-for thing is said to be lacking to us, it nonetheless exists in others, or in itself (if not in act, then at least in potential); and if a true and solid essence was perhaps denied to it, it at least possesses an imaginary essence that rests in the mind itself. Furthermore, we demonstrated that even if love is often seen to be for things already possessed, it always—no less than desire—presupposes some defect or lack in them. This happens either because the lover has not yet attained a perfect union with the beloved object, and therefore loves and hungers to be perfectly joined with it; or because the lover, even if they possess the beloved thing and enjoy it in the present, certainly lacks the *future* enjoyment of it, and therefore hungers for that.

<summary>Philo and Sophia debate the technical definition of love, concluding that love and desire are inextricably linked because even when we possess what we love, we still "desire" its continued presence or a more perfect union.</summary>

### DIALOGUE III ###

<margin>Love and desire are found to be entirely the same.</margin>
<margin>Love is defined as a certain affection of desire for the most absolute union with the beloved object.</margin>
Wherefore, having carefully examined and looked into the matter, it is found that desire and love are the same thing—even if common and everyday speech seems to assign various and different conditions to each of them, just as you yourself have said. For this reason, toward the conclusion <note>original: "sub calcem," literally 'at the heel' or end</note> of that first discussion, we determined that love is the desire to attain the most absolute union with the beloved object. Furthermore, we assigned the reason why all desire is called love, and all love is called desire. Therefore, remaining firm in that same opinion, we now define love, taken in its most common sense, as being the desire for something. **SO.** Since love and desire are two different names, which are also frequently seen to signify various and different things, I do not see why you say they agree in meaning. For although the same thing can be both loved and longed for, these two terms seem to signify two diverse and distinct affections of our minds directed at the same object: since one impels us to love the thing, and the other to seek it out <term>appetite: the natural inclination or drive toward a perceived good</term>. **PH.** I believe that long-standing custom in speech has led you to this opinion.

<margin>Some more recent theologians, led chiefly by two reasons, have placed a certain inherent and natural difference between love and desire.</margin>
There have also been found some more recent theologians <note>Likely referring to Scholastic thinkers like Thomas Aquinas, who distinguished between the stages of the "passions of the soul"</note> who placed a certain inherent and natural difference between the two, saying that love is the principle and origin of desire; for it is because we first love a thing that we then gradually begin to long for it. **SO.** By what reasoning were these men persuaded to think that love is the beginning of desire? **PH.** First, they define love as a certain approval by our mind of a thing that is considered good. Then, they say that from this kind of approval of the pleasing thing, desire is awakened; and this desire hurries and strives toward the beloved object as toward its appointed goal. Therefore, they finally conclude that love is the beginning of the motion of the appetite. **SO.** The love which these very grave men seem to have understood is only for those things which we lack and do not possess at all; for only these are followed by the movement of desire. But regarding the love of things we have already acquired and possess—which can by no means be the beginning of the motion of the appetite itself—what did these men think?

<margin>Two species of love established by these theologians: one precedes desire, while the other follows it.</margin>
**PH.** Just as they defined the love of a thing we lack as the mind's approval of the beloved object and the beginning of the motion of the appetite, they also say that the love of a thing already acquired and possessed is nothing other than the joy and pleasure perceived from the enjoyment of the beloved object. They call this the end or limit, or the final rest of the motion of the appetite. **SO.** It seems, then, that these men have divided love into two species: one of which is the beginning of the motion of the appetite and concerns things not yet possessed; while the other is called the end and limit of joy and pleasure, concerning things already possessed. Since this second species of love follows desire, it is clearly distinguished and joined from it. Yet the first species does not seem to differ or be separated so much from desire, since both concern things we lack. Did these illustrious men confirm the difference and distinction between these two disturbances of the mind—namely love and desire—with any even more evident argument? **PH.** They brought forward another reason to strengthen their opinion, based on the contrary passions of these two mental disturbances, which differ greatly from one another. For they believe that hatred is opposed to love, and the flight <note>original: "fuga," the act of recoiling or avoidance</note> from a hated thing is opposed to desire. Therefore, just as they wish love to be the beginning of desire, so they wish hatred to be the beginning of flight. And just as hatred and flight are two affections natural to our minds so that we may shun evils, so they think love and desire are two opposite affections of our minds so that we may pursue goods. Furthermore, they add that just as joy and pleasure are the end of love and desire, so sadness and pain must be the cause and end of hatred and flight. And just as hope comes between love and desire, and between joy and pleasure... (for hope regards future and distant goods, while joy...

### LEO THE HEBREW ON LOVE ###

just as pleasure and joy are said to regard good things that are present and joined to us, so too is fear placed in the middle between sadness (or pain) and avoidance (or hate). For fear looks toward future and distant evils, whereas sadness and pain arise from evils that are present and close at hand. For this reason, the theologians I just mentioned completely separate and distinguish desire from love. They distinguish it first from that which they have established as the beginning of desire, which they call "approval" <note>original: *approbatio*, the internal recognition that something is good</note>; and they also distinguish it from that which they say is the end and limit of desire, which they name joy and pleasure. **SO.** This difference between desire and love devised by those most serious men seems indeed sharp and ingenious; but why do you, Philo, neglecting their opinion and scorning their authority, contend that love and desire are the same? **PH.** They themselves, deceived by the variety of words and following a common error, labor to distinguish and double these same affections of the soul.

<margin>He completely rejects and explodes the opinion of the aforementioned theologians, who said that love and desire were two various and different affections of the soul.</margin>

**SO.** In what way? **PH.** They claim that the essences of love and desire differ, even though their substance is the same; and they have devised a certain new and ridiculous difference between the love of a thing not yet possessed and the love of a thing already acquired. **SO.** If you also concede that our love is an "approval" of the beloved thing from which desire soon proceeds: you certainly cannot deny that love is distinguished from desire just as the beginning of a motion is distinguished from the motion itself. **PH.** The approval of a thing dear to us ought to be considered not as love, but as the *cause* of love, just as it is the cause of desire. For love seems to signify nothing other than the desire for a pleasing thing, or for a thing approved by us. Therefore, approval joined with desire enters into the definition of love, but otherwise it does not. Love and desire, therefore, are in reality one and the same; both presuppose a preceding approval of the thing that pleases us. And just as desire—if one wishes to call it a "motion"—is the soul's movement toward the very thing craved, so too love must be considered the soul's movement toward the very thing loved. But the "approval" stands as the common principle <term>principle: the starting point or source of an action</term> for both movements, as much for loving as for craving. **SO.** If love and desire were entirely the same, their opposites would never be said to be different: yet we see that hate is very clearly opposed to love, and avoidance <note>original: *fuga*, literally "flight" or "fleeing from"</note> is opposed to desire.

<margin>It appears that not "flight," but rather "alienation of the will" is properly and truly opposed to desire.</margin>

**PH.** No student of the truth would ever admit this. For flight is an action of the body, and is not contrary to desire itself, but to the *pursuit* that follows desire. The true and proper opposite of desire is the alienation of the will, which concurs as one with hate, the opposite of love. For this reason, love and desire—just like their opposites—will be entirely one and the same thing. **SO.** I perceive that love and desire, as well as their opposites, agree in substance; but the loves for things already possessed and those not yet acquired seem to be diverse and different, just as the aforementioned theologians thought.

<margin>Love differs greatly from joy, gladness, and pleasure: it appears to be entirely one and the same with desire.</margin>

**PH.** They *seem* so, but they are not actually different. For the love of those things which we possess is neither the pleasure taken from the enjoyment, nor the gladness perceived from the possession, as those men falsely judge. The possessor of a beloved thing does indeed perceive no small gladness and pleasure from the possession itself; but joy (or gladness) and pleasure must not be considered exactly the same as love. For love signifies motion, or at least the principle of motion; whereas joy and pleasure seem to signify the rest, the end, and the limit of that motion. Furthermore, these are seen to have opposite directions: for love strives from the lover toward the beloved thing, but joy is derived from the beloved thing into the lover himself. This is even more true because joy presupposes the present possession of the thing, while love presupposes its absence and privation; and being joined with desire, love is always found to be the same thing. **SO.** Nevertheless, we are often said to love things we already possess and which we do not lack. **PH.** We do not lack the *present* possession of them, but we are uncertain about their stable and perpetual continuation, and we are said to lack this certainty. Not content with present possession, we vehemently crave and love that permanence. Whence it happens that present possession [is...]

### DIALOGUE III. ###

...is said to bring joy and pleasure, while future things seem to affect us with desire and love. Therefore, the same love exists for a thing already acquired as for one not yet obtained, and it is identical to desire. It differs greatly, however, from pleasure and joy, just as pain or sadness is seen to differ from hatred and alienation. For we are affected by pain from present and near evils, but by hatred from future and distant evils.

<margin>A marvelous order of certain affections of the soul.</margin>
**SO.** What order, then, do you think should be assigned to these affections of the soul? **PH.** Love and the desire for good things seem to have obtained the primary place; to which the hatred of evils and the alienation of the mind from them are opposed. Hope follows love and desire, referring to future goods that are currently separated from us; to which fear is opposed, which looks toward future and separate evils. Whenever hope is joined to love and desire, we are immediately moved to pursue the beloved good; just as when fear accompanies hatred and alienation, we are at once incited to flee the hated evil. Finally, the end is joy and pleasure perceived from a present and joined good; to which pain and sadness, felt from present and near evils, are seen to be opposed. This last affection of the soul, namely joy and pleasure perceived from goods, is our primary intention; for it is for the sake of attaining joy and delight that we are accustomed to love, seek, hope for, and pursue good things. Therefore, when these are finally held and obtained, the soul finds its most happy rest; and it seems to love that present state and vehemently desire it to be preserved forever, or at least for a long time.

<margin>He concludes that the essence of love and desire is one and entirely the same.</margin>
Therefore, for those who philosophize correctly, let us say that the essence of love and desire is always and altogether one and the same; although we frequently hear people, following common usage, calling one type of love "desire" rather than "love," and another "love" rather than "desire."

<margin>He lists several different names that converge with love into one and the same meaning.</margin>
Nor do only these two words signify the same thing, but others besides: for what we love, we are also said to prize, to esteem, to wish for, to long for, to will, and finally to desire. All these words and others like them, though we use each for one species of love rather than another, are the same in substance and signify the same thing: namely, a common and vehement desire for those things we lack. For what is already possessed, insofar as it is possessed, is no longer longed for or loved; but it is said to be loved and longed for because it dwells in the mind under the appearance of a good.

<margin>Several different degrees of love and desire, of which one immediately follows the other.</margin>
Whence it follows that just as it is in the mind, it should be found outside the mind—the same in act as it is in potential. And if it perhaps exists in act but is not yet possessed by us, we are said to desire and love the possession itself; and if by chance we do possess it, we desire the constant and perpetual enjoyment of it, which future enjoyment does not yet exist and is then lacking to us. In this way, a father and son are seen to love one another; for they desire to enjoy each other's company and safety always in the future, just as they do in the present. Similarly, those who are healthy love health, and the wealthy love riches; for they desire not only their increase, but also a future enjoyment similar to the present.

<margin>According to Plato's opinion, love is defined as the appetite for the everlasting possession of good things.</margin>
Therefore, love, no less than desire, must always refer to those things that we lack in some way. Whence Plato defined love as the appetite for the everlasting possession of good things; by the name of "everlastingness," that most serious philosopher elegantly and aptly signified a continuous lack <note>original: *defectum*. Philo argues that wanting something "forever" implies you "lack" all the future moments of that possession right now</note>.

<margin>Both love and the desire for things loved and sought suppose some mode of existence.</margin>
**SO.** Even if some species of continuous lack accompanies love, it nevertheless supposes the essence of the thing: for love always seems to be of existing things, just as desire seems to be of things we lack, and often of things that do not exist. **PH.** You say truly that love is of existing things: for that which entirely lacks essence can hardly be known—

### LEONE EBREO ON LOVE, ###

...to me; but by what logic will something unknown ever be loved? As for your addition—that the desire for things that do not exist at all is for them *to* exist—I do not consider that to be absolutely or simply true. For the mind cannot know what is found nowhere, and what cannot be known can by no means be desired. Therefore, what is sought must first be grasped by the mind; and what is held in the mind must also be found outside the mind—if not in actual fact, at least in potentiality, lying hidden in its own causes. Otherwise, our knowledge would be deceptive and useless. For this reason, we must finally conclude that love and desire completely coincide as one.

**SO.** You have excellently declared that love is desire, and that it is concerned with those things that, even if they possess some manner of existence, we currently lack in either present possession or future enjoyment. However, a certain ambiguity still keeps me in suspense and perplexed. For even if I grant that all love is desire, I would not yet admit that every desire is love. For love seems to spread and extend only toward living things, or those things which are able to perfect us in some way—for example, toward health, virtue, riches, wisdom, honor, and glory. For all things of this kind are usually both loved and desired. But there are many other things besides, and many more accidental things and actions, which, when we lack them, are never said to be "loved," but only "desired."

<margin>
The common people frequently use a name with a broad and common meaning to express only one of its specific types; this is found to have happened with the name "love" as well.
</margin>
**PH.** Lest the long-standing use of words deceive you, look again and again. For the common people frequently use a name with a broad and common meaning to express only one of its specific types; we see this happening with the name "love" as well. **SO.** I ask you to provide some example of this. **PH.** The name "Knight" <note>original: "equitis"</note> was devised by the ancients to signify any man sitting upon a four-legged beast; but usage later introduced the habit of calling by this name only those who are seen to be experienced and agile in engaging in equestrian combat. Likewise, the name "Merchant" <note>original: "mercatoris"</note> is thought to apply indifferently to every buyer; but now only those seem to have taken and claimed that name for themselves who, prompted by greed, practice and profess the art of buying and selling. 

So it is (to finally return to where we digressed) that although "love" is a certain common name most suited to signify all things that are sought, it is usually referred only to worthy persons and more distinguished things that have obtained a more noble and stable essence than the rest. Other things, which have attained a weaker and more obscure essence, even if they are in truth loved, are not said to be "loved," but only "desired." For although I would not say that I love a thing that does not yet exist, I will love it *so that* it may exist; and if I have not yet attained it, I will certainly declare that I love to attain it. For this is also the proper intention of one who "desires"—to long for and seek the essence of a thing if it does not exist, or its possession if it is not held. 

Nevertheless, since love seems to be a most excellent name, it is chiefly referred to already existing persons and more distinguished things that can make us perfect and are already possessed by us. We will say that we "appetite," "wish," or "desire" other things rather than "love," "affect," or "cherish" them; for those superior things seem to be far more excellent and stable objects of love. Furthermore, the common people are accustomed to apply the name "love" to the things themselves, but "desire" to their generation and acquisition, even though one and the same meaning exists deep within both.

Among brute animals also, love and desire seem to completely converge into one.
</margin>

...whatever they love, they never wish to lose. Therefore, love seems to entirely agree and align with appetite and desire.

But if the divine nature is abhorrent to any defect, however small, it will truly never desire anything: for you have just safely confessed that desire is for things we lack.

<margin>

</margin>

**PH.** You are indeed approaching great—nay, rather the greatest and most difficult matters. **SO.** I pray you, interpret what you intend to signify more clearly and lucidly.

Likewise, divine love for those things which were created, and divine desire, ought by no means to be compared with the human. For if both are attributed to us, they exist as certain affections of the soul and suppose the privation <note>The state of being deprived of something or lacking it.</note> of something; but if they are referred to God, they are seen to be the highest and absolute perfections of all things. 

**SO.** This I certainly believe; but I would wish you to come closer to explaining the previous difficulty. For if you grant that God is endowed with love and desire, you must also confess that he loves and desires; but if desire falls within the Divine nature because in some way it is lacking to itself, then God will truly desire.

<margin>

</margin>

Therefore, Divine desire neither implies that God suffers, nor that he himself is in need of another; rather, because of his immense perfection, he loves and seeks that those things which were created by him might either reach the highest degree of perfection due to them and currently lacking, or, once those things are held and acquired, that they might enjoy them perpetually with no disturbance or trouble intervening. So that created things might better and more easily reach this end, God refuses to provide them with no kind of help or benefit. Does this response satisfy you, Sophia? 

**SO.** It pleases me, yet it does not entirely satisfy. 

**PH.** What more do you wish? 

**SO.** I would truly like to understand what induces us to attribute love and desire to God because of the defects of others, when he himself lacks nothing at all. For this seems altogether unjust and impious.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Philo and Sophia. In the previous section, Philo argued that God’s love does not imply a lack or defect, despite his earlier definition of love as a desire for what one lacks. # LEONIS HEBR. ON LOVE, #

...is impossible; for in what way can that which is unknown ever be loved? As for your point that desire is for things that do not exist at all—so that they might come into existence—I do not believe this to be absolutely or simply true. For that which is nowhere to be found cannot be known, and that which cannot be known cannot be desired at all. Therefore, what is sought must first be apprehended by the mind; and what exists in the mind must also be found outside the mind—if not in actuality, then at least in potentiality, lying hidden within its causes. Otherwise, our knowledge would be false and useless. Therefore, we must finally conclude that love and desire converge entirely into one.

**SO.** You have very well explained that love is desire, and that it concerns those things in which—even if they participate in some mode of being—we lack either present possession or future enjoyment. However, a certain ambiguity still keeps me in suspense and perplexed: for although I may concede that all love is desire, I will not yet admit that all desire is love. For love seems to be extended only toward living things, or those things which in some way are able to perfect us—for example, health, virtue, riches, wisdom, honor, and glory; for all things of this kind are usually both loved and sought. But many other things besides, and many accidents, as well as many actions, are found which, when we lack them, are never said to be loved, but only to be desired.

<margin>
The common people <note>original: *vulgus*</note> frequently use a name with a broad and general meaning to express only one of its specific types; this is found to have happened also with the name of love.
</margin>

**PH.** Take care, again and again, lest the long-standing use of words deceive you. For the common people frequently use a name with a broad and general meaning to express only one of its specific types; we see this happens also with the name "love." 

**SO.** I pray you, provide some example of this. 

**PH.** The name "Knight" <note>original: *equitis*, which literally means "horseman"</note> was devised by the ancients to signify any man sitting upon a four-legged animal; but usage later introduced the practice that only those who are seen to be experienced and agile in engaging in equestrian battles are called by this name. Likewise, the name "Merchant" <note>original: *mercatoris*</note> is thought to apply indifferently to every buyer; yet now only those seem to have claimed and vindicated it for themselves who, persuaded by greed, practice and profess the art of buying and selling. 

So indeed—to return at last to where we digressed—since "love" is a certain common name best suited to signify all things that are sought, it is usually applied only to worthy persons and more distinguished things that have obtained a nobler and more stable essence than others. Other things, which have achieved a weaker and more obscure essence, even if they are in truth loved, are not said to be "loved" but only "desired." For although I would never say that I love a thing not yet existing, I will love it so that it *may* exist; and if I have not yet attained it, I will certainly say that I love to attain it. For this is also the proper intention of one who seeks: that if the thing does not exist, he longs for and appetites its essence; and if it is not held, he desires its possession. 

Nevertheless, since "love" seems to be a most excellent name, it is chiefly applied to persons already existing and to more distinguished things that can make us perfect and are already possessed by us. The rest we shall say we appetite, wish for, or desire, rather than love, prize, or cherish; for those former things seem to be far more excellent and stable objects of love than these. Moreover, the common people are accustomed to adapt and attribute the name of "love" to the things themselves, but "desire" to their generation and acquisition, even if one and the same meaning exists entirely for both.

<margin>
Among brute animals, too, love and desire seem to converge entirely into one.
</margin>

**SO.** You have indeed abundantly satisfied the ambiguity I proposed, and I certainly confess that among humans, love and desire entirely converge and concur. But what do you think should be felt regarding the race of brute animals? They vehemently desire food, drink, sexual union, and freedom when they lack them; but they are seen to love only those present, such as their children, mothers, females or males, and their guardians and nurturers. 

**PH.** Indeed, whatever brutes desire, they love to have; and whatever...

->### LEO HEBRAEUS ON LOVE ###<-

<meta>catchword: happiness (from the Latin 'felicitatem')</meta>

...transfers and carries over these actions: for all these things seem to happen with love mediating between them.

<margin>According to Plato’s opinion, Love exists as beautiful not in actuality, but only in potential.</margin>
For this reason, the Philosopher <note>Referring to Plato</note> believed that love is not beautiful in act; for if it were, it would neither seek nor love beauty, since what is possessed in the present is never said to be sought. Instead, he thought that love exists as beautiful in <term>potentiality</term> <note>The capacity to become something, as opposed to 'actuality,' which is being that thing already</note>, and it is this potential that seeks and deeply loves present and actual beauty.

Therefore, according to Plato’s opinion, it seems we must say that love is either a medium between the beautiful and the ugly, or composed of both—just as potential is said to exist either as a medium between essence and deprivation, or as a composite of both.

**SO.** But why, Philo—you who are so devoted to Plato—do you not approve of the opinion and reasoning of such a great philosopher?

<margin>Socrates is a friend, Plato is a friend, but truth itself is a greater friend.</margin>
**PH.** I believe neither of those views should be followed because (as Aristotle affirms when attacking the teachings of his master) even if we are friends of Plato, we ought to be greater friends to the truth. <note>original: "Amicus Socrates, amicus Plato, amicior ueritas ipsa." A famous philosophical proverb about prioritizing truth over personal loyalty.</note>

**SO.** But why do you abandon and leave behind the opinion of such a great man?

<margin>Plato, who excluded love from the divine nature, seems to have both resisted the truth and contradicted himself.</margin>
**PH.** Because I find that he has spoken contradictory things. Elsewhere, he himself testifies that those who sharply contemplate divine beauty also attain divine friendship. Have you ever seen a friend, Sophia, who is not loved by their friend? Furthermore, Aristotle, in his books of *Ethics*, did not hesitate to declare that the studious and wise man exists as a happy being, becomes a friend of God, and is deeply loved by the divine power as something very similar to itself. Moreover, the Sacred Volumes <note>Referring to the Bible</note> confirm that God most greatly loves the just as His friends, and that the good are children of God, loved by God just as children are loved by a parent. How, then, do you think I could deny God’s love for the things He has created?

<margin>He demonstrates by reason that love is suitable to the divine nature, and confirms it with authorities as well.</margin>
**SO.** The authorities you have brought forward in favor of Divine love are indeed of no small weight; but unless they are supported by reasons, they seem likely to collapse soon. I did not ask you to list those who have introduced divine love, but rather to explain the *reasoning* that compelled them to attribute love to God—especially since a little while ago you confirmed, with the gravest authority and strong reasoning of the divine Plato, that love is foreign to the divine nature.

**PH.** Furthermore, the reasoning that persuades us to attribute love to the divine power can indeed be brought forward.

**SO.** I beg you, let it not seem troublesome or burdensome to explain it.

**PH.** God has already created all things.

**SO.** Most certainly.

**PH.** And He is always intent upon preserving their essences; so much so that if He were to desert them for the smallest moment of time, all things would immediately collapse and be reduced to nothing.

**SO.** Entirely so.

**PH.** You grant, then, that God is the true and common parent of all: He who first procreated those who were born, and then guards and preserves those already begotten with the highest care and diligence.

**SO.** I believe the name of "Parent" truly and properly fits God.

**PH.** Tell me, I pray, if a father did not desire offspring, would he ever procreate children? And if he did not follow his already-born sons with the greatest love, would he perhaps preserve them with such great diligence and anxiety?

**SO.** You have spoken rightly, Philo. I perceive that God’s love for the things He created—both their mutual love and their love for God—is to be placed far above the charity of parents for children, the mutual love of brothers, or the benevolence of children toward parents. But this doubt still remains for me: I see no love, and absolutely no desire, that does not assume some <term>defect</term> <note>A lack or missing perfection</note> conceived by the lover for the thing loved, just as you seemed to say a long time ago when speaking of divine love. Can you think of any example of "lower" loves where you assume a defect only in the thing loved, and not at all in the lover?

<margin>The love of God for the things He created seems to be very similar to the love of a parent for a child, a teacher for a student, and studious friends for each other.</margin>
**PH.** The love of God Himself for these lower things is certainly referred to and represented by the love of a father for a son, a teacher for a student, and the love of studious friends for one another.

**SO.** How? Will you perhaps contend that the similarity lies in the fact that a father desires to enjoy his son, and a friend his friend, perpetually? I should think you would hardly say this; for a desire of this kind for "perpetual enjoyment" assumes a defect on the part of the lover <note>The lack of the beloved's presence</note>, and such a defect does not fall upon God at all.

**PH.** Although the recently mentioned similarity is not found in that kind of love or desire, it nevertheless seems to be located in this: that parental love addresses every deficiency in the children...

...consists in seeking happiness. This love assumes a deficiency in the children who are loved, but by no means in the father who loves them. Similarly, a teacher desires virtue and wisdom for his students; these qualities are seen to be lacking only in the students, not at all in the <term>preceptor</term> <note>A teacher or instructor.</note>. In the same way, one friend desires for another friend the happiness they lack, so that the friend may obtain it and always enjoy it. However, this distinction exists between divine love and fleeting love: <margin>In what way divine love differs from human and mortal love.</margin> because the three types of lovers mentioned above, being mortal, only acquire a certain joy joined with pleasure when their desires are fulfilled and completed. This, however, never happens with God. He does not experience or acquire any new joy, pleasure, or any other <term>agitation of the soul</term> <note>original: "perturbationem." In Renaissance philosophy, this refers to emotional changes that disturb the mind's equilibrium.</note>, nor any new change whatsoever from the recent perfection of those things He has created and follows with the greatest love. For God is understood to be free and released from all agitation or <term>passion</term> <note>original: "perfeſsione." Likely a printer's error or variant for "passione." In this context, "passion" means the state of being acted upon by an outside force.</note>, subject to no change at all, and is believed to perpetually and abundantly enjoy immense gladness, joy, and pleasure. Only this difference is usually attributed to the Divine: His most splendid and glowing joy is seen to shine far more in His perfect children and friends than in those who are imperfect.

<margin>Which species of love, according to the mind of Plato and Aristotle, can be attributed to the best and greatest God, and which cannot.</margin>

**PH.** The philosopher most truly pronounced that only that species of love about which Plato disputed in the *Symposium* <note>Plato’s famous dialogue on the nature of love and desire.</note>—which contains and encompasses love granted to humans alone—is foreign to the nature of God. But that common and generic love, of which we now speak, can by no means be excluded or separated from God.

**SO.** I would like you to interpret this difference for me more distinctly and clearly. 

**PH.** In the *Symposium*, Plato seems to have discussed that species of love which is found among humans to <term>terminate</term> <note>To have its final goal or object.</note> in the lover alone, and by no means in the beloved; for this type is seen to have claimed the primary name of "love" for itself. But the other species, which terminates in the beloved thing, is more rightly called friendship and benevolence than love. The philosopher rightly defined the former love as the "desire for beauty," and he deservedly separated it from the Divine nature; for whoever seeks beauty certainly lacks it, and cannot in any way be called beautiful. 

But God, since He is the most beautiful of all—or rather, is the Supreme Beauty itself—needs no portion of beauty, however small, and cannot desire it. Therefore, this kind of love should not be placed in God. But we, who are speaking of love in a broad and universal sense, must embrace both: that which terminates in the lover (and assumes a deficiency in the lover himself), and that which ends in the beloved thing (designating the imperfection of the beloved only, and not the lover). 

Therefore, we have defined love not as the "desire for the beautiful," as Plato did, but simply as the desire for some thing or for the good. Either of these can be lacking to the lover or the beloved indifferently—just as the love of a father for a son, a teacher for a student, or a friend for a friend (mentioned above) have more than sufficiently demonstrated. In this kind of love, God is said to love those things which He once created, desiring only their good and not His own. Plato and Aristotle both harmoniously indicated this same species of love when they said that the best and wisest men attain divine friendship and are wonderfully loved by God. For God seems to love and desire their most happy perfection perpetually and without any change in Himself. Furthermore, Plato showed that the name of love commonly encompasses every desire of any thing and of any seeker; however, he added that properly it signifies only the desire for the beautiful.
