### LEO THE HEBREW ON LOVE ###

The Philosopher <note>Referring to Plato.</note> does not seem to have excluded every kind and category of love from the divine nature, but only that specific type which is defined as the desire for beauty. **SO.** I am very glad to hear that Plato neither lied nor contradicted himself. However, the definition of love he provided does not seem to exclude divine love at all, even though the Philosopher labored greatly to keep them separate. In fact, I would think his definition includes it no less than the one you provided. **PH.** Why is that? **SO.** Because just as you defined love as the desire for the good—thereby including in that very brief statement a lack of good in either the lover or the beloved person indiscriminately—likewise, when I follow Plato's authority and define love as the desire for beauty, I would certainly say that I am including a lack of beauty residing either in the lover or in the beloved person within that same concise description. From this, it follows that the Platonic definition of love undoubtedly includes divine love as well.

<margin>The difference between the good and the beautiful. Beauty belongs only to the lover, while the good is something common to both the lover and the beloved.</margin>
**PH.** If you persuade yourself that the beautiful and the good are one and the same thing, you are completely mistaken. **SO.** Do you then believe that the beautiful and the good are different? **PH.** Greatly. **SO.** Why? **PH.** Because the good is usually sought by the one who desires it both for their own sake and for the sake of the beloved person; however, the beautiful is usually sought for its own sake alone. **SO.** For what reason? **PH.** Because beauty is particular to the lover. What seems beautiful to one is often judged as ugly by another; thus, what I see as beautiful, you often see as not beautiful. But the good is a kind of universal thing; it does not relate to the lover more than the beloved, or to this one rather than that one, but it is referred back to the highest nature. For this reason, what is good for one often seems good to many. Therefore, one who desires the beautiful always desires it for themselves, for they lack it. But one who wishes for the good can desire it indiscriminately both for themselves and for a friend who lacks that good. **SO.** This difference you have devised between the beautiful and the good does not entirely convince me. Just as you claim that the same thing can seem beautiful to one and ugly to another, I would say that the same thing is judged good by one and evil by another. Here is a very clear example: wicked men believe that evil things are good, and so they pursue them; they think good things are evil, and so they flee from them. <term>Virtuous men</term> <note>original: "studiosi." In this context, people of high character and intellectual discipline.</note>, on the other hand, are seen to judge the opposite. Therefore, we see that what happens with the beautiful happens similarly with the good.

<margin>Good things are always good, and evil things are always evil, in the judgment of all who have sound minds and a right, well-disposed will.</margin>
**PH.** All people who have sound judgment and a right, well-disposed will perceive that good things are indeed good and evil things are evil; just as a well-tempered sense of taste seeks out sweet flavors and rejects bitter ones. But those who have earned the hostility of the divine and have been fated with a weak and corrupted mind and a depraved will, call the good "evil" and the evil "good" by inverting the names of things—just as a diseased sense of taste rejects the sweet and seeks the bitter flavor. Therefore, just as the sweet is truly sweet and is called so even if it seems bitter to a sick man, likewise the good remains a true and universal good even if it is judged as evil by a weak and vicious mind; it suffers no actual change because of that judgment. **SO.** Should we not feel the same way about the beautiful?

<margin>Beauty is not seen as one and the same thing among all those who have sound judgment and talent.</margin>
**PH.** Not at all. For beauty is not seen as one and the same thing among all virtuous and talented men. For even if all these men confess that the beautiful is good, a thing might seem so beautiful to one virtuous man that it entices him to love it, while another virtuous man will judge it to be good but not beautiful at all, and it will never be able to turn his will toward loving it. And just as good and evil, when related to the soul, imitate sweet and bitter when presented to the sense of taste, so too can the beautiful and the non-beautiful, when impressed upon the soul, be compared to the savory—which fills the taste with pleasure—and the tasteless.

...can be compared. However, that which is shameful and deformed to the soul truly seems to be compared to a most hateful, horrible, and execrable flavor, both being the sharpest enemies to the sense of taste. Hence, just as we often experience that one and the same thing is sweet to all healthy people, yet to one it is savory and pleasant while to another it is not at all: so we often see that one and the same thing or person is judged as good by all diligent observers, but is judged as beautiful by only one—so much so that he, captured by its excellent form and beauty, is inflamed to love it—while by another it is not so judged at all.

<margin>
Plato defined illustrious love as the desire for the beautiful; he deservedly separated it from the divine nature, as he seems to have placed it as a certain "great daemon" <note>original: "magnum quendam dæmonem"; in Greek philosophy, a daemon is a spirit acting as an intermediary between gods and humans, not necessarily an evil being.</note>—a middle ground between divine and human things.
</margin>

Therefore, you will see that frenzied lovers, who are driven by the sharpest stings of love, always seek the beautiful. Looking to this, Plato defined love as the desire for the beautiful: that is, the desire for joining with some person, or, to speak more generally, for attaining union with or acquiring the possession of some beautiful and shapely thing. Examples include a very large and magnificent city, a highly cultivated garden, a noble horse, a multi-colored bird, a purple garment, or a transparent gemstone. All these and similar things we desire either to have, or, having them, to enjoy perpetually; and each of them supposes either a present or future lack on the part of the lover. 

Plato deservedly separated this species of love from the divine nature, not because God is said to love nothing at all, but because potentiality <note>original: "potestas"; refers to the state of being able to become something, as opposed to being "actualized" or complete.</note>, possession, and privation <note>Being without something.</note> always accompany this kind of love; these three things are entirely foreign to the divine power. Furthermore, the Philosopher [Plato] added that love of this kind is a certain "great daemon," because, according to Plato’s opinion, the daemonic nature intervenes as a middle ground between the spiritual and perfect, and the corporeal and imperfect.

<margin>
The daemonic nature is midway between the spiritual and the corporeal.
</margin>

In this way, the powers and passions of our souls reside and are placed in the middle between corporeal or moral actions and intelligible or divine actions, as well as between the beautiful and the ugly. This is because potentiality has claimed for itself a middle place between privation and actual essence. 

<margin>
Potentiality is intermediate between privation and actual essence.
</margin>

Since, however, love seems to be greater and more vehement than all other affections or disturbances of the soul, for that reason Plato called it a "great daemon." 

But then love, taken generally and generically, embraces indiscriminately not only things both good and beautiful, but also things that are good even if they are not at all beautiful. It always follows whatever is good, whether it be called beautiful, useful, honorable <note>original: "honestum"; the moral good pursued for its own sake.</note>, pleasant, or of any other kind. Hence, it happens that there is a love for good things which are lacking sometimes to the lover, sometimes to the beloved, or to a friend of the lover. 

<margin>
God is thought to pursue whatever He has created not with a specific or properly defined love, but with a certain common and generic love.
</margin>

And in this wide and diffused kind of love, God is thought to love whatever He has created: namely, by abundantly bestowing upon them the goods they lack and need, so that He may lead them to a perfection suited to the capacity of each. 

**SO.** Was this wide and most common definition of love, which follows the universal good, devised by any of the ancient sages? 

**PH.** I find that no one has defined it better or more absolutely than Aristotle in his books of the *Politics* <note>Philo likely refers here to the *Rhetoric* or *Ethics*, as this specific definition is famous there.</note>, who determined that to love is nothing other than to wish good for someone: that is, either for oneself or for others. 

<margin>
Aristotle defined love, taken generally and generically, as that by which one desires good for someone.
</margin>

Consider, I pray, the great and almost divine skill of Aristotle, who, in order to embrace every species of love generally, thought it should be defined not by the "beautiful," but rather by the "good." By this elegant and brief description, he wonderfully encompassed all species of love. For if the lover desires good for himself, the good is clearly seen to be lacking in the lover; but if the lover desires the good of the beloved thing, then the good will be thought to be lacking only to the beloved or the friend, and not at all to the lover. Divine love is of this very kind. 

<margin>
Aristotle defined love in its most general sense through the "good"; Plato, however, defined love properly understood through the "beautiful."
</margin>

Therefore, Aristotle, who defined love generally through the good, also included divine love. Plato, however, who defined it properly by the name of the beautiful, seems to have excluded God's love toward lower things; for the "beautiful" designates a lack only on the part of the lover to whom it appears beautiful.

# THE DIALOGUES OF LOVE BY LEONE EBREO #

...always, and never looking to another's good, as Aristotle felt, I would judge: for the proper end, and the last of both human and any other actions, consists in pursuing one's own good, one's own pleasure, and one's own perfection: and to this end indeed all actions of all things are referred. But if someone wishes well to another, this is ultimately referred to one's own delight, which is perceived from that benefit. How then shall we defend the idea that the lover’s pleasure and goal in loving is occupied with the goods of another, as Aristotle felt?

<margin>The proper and ultimate end of the actions of any agent ultimately consists in its own perfection, pleasure, good, and happiness.</margin>

PHILO. You have doubted rightly and subtly indeed: for the proper and ultimate end of the actions of any agent ultimately consists in its own perfection, pleasure, good, and happiness. Nor is the good that a lover desires for a friend or beloved referred only to the proper pleasure which he himself perceives from those advantages; rather, the lover is thought to receive the very same good that is bestowed on the friend or beloved. For the lover seems to exist not only as the friend of a friend, but as "another self" <note>original: "alter existere"; refers to the Aristotelian concept of a friend being an *alter ego* or second self.</note>. Wherefore his goods should be judged not as foreign, but as his own: and the lover, wishing for the friend's good, augurs it for himself.

<margin>The lover is seen to be transferred into the person of the beloved.</margin>

For we have already said many times that the lover is converted and transfigured into the person of the beloved. Whence the advantages of the beloved are said to pertain more to the lover than his own, and they seem to be called the goods of the lover rather than the beloved, whenever the beloved person follows the lover with an equal and mutual love. For then the proper good of each of them, leaving its owner, immediately hastens to the other, and there finds its desired rest.

<margin>Two friends who follow each other with equal and mutual love should be considered either as only one, or as four.</margin>

Therefore, two friends who love each other mutually are by no means to be considered two. SOPHIA. How many then will they be? PHILO. Either only one, or four. SOPHIA. That two true friends are reduced to unity, I understand very well: because that wonderful power of joining both lovers into one, and collecting a pair into unity, is innate to love. But in what way can they be called four? PHILO. Since each of them is transformed into the other: by right each one, obtaining the status of both lover and beloved, is doubled: but a pair returning into itself produces the number four <note>Philo is using a mathematical metaphor: if each person in a couple acts as both themselves and the other, then 2 people x 2 roles = 4 identities.</note>. Therefore, it must finally be concluded that each of the lovers is two, and both lovers together are one—or exist as four. SOPHIA. I am wonderfully glad to have learned the unity and plurality of two lovers.

<margin>He defends that one species of love arises from the desire for another's good. A friend is another self.</margin>

But Aristotle’s saying seems all the more absurd to me—namely, that he pronounced that seeking another's good exists as one species of love. PHILO. We must understand that the Philosopher <note>original: "Philosophum"; referring to Aristotle.</note> supposed the end of love to be placed and located in the proper good of the lover himself. But this good is referred to the lover himself either immediately, with no medium intervening, or with the help and aid of the friend and the beloved thing interposed: and already the Peripatetic <note>original: "Peripateticus"; a term for a follower of Aristotle, or Aristotle himself, derived from his habit of walking while teaching.</note> has declared a friend to be "another self." SOPHIA. Even if this interpretation of the Aristotelian definition were perhaps granted to you, it still does not encompass divine love, as you labor to prove. PHILO. Why not? SOPHIA. Because if you wish God to love the good of those things which He Himself has procreated: by loving that, you must confess He also loves His own proper good. But this appetite for good would certainly imply a defect not only in the created things, but even in God the Creator <note>Sophia argues that if God "desires" or "needs" the good of creation for His own perfection, it implies He was previously lacking something, which contradicts divine perfection.</note>: which indeed anyone will very easily judge how absurd and foreign to the truth that is.

<margin>God is thought to attain perfection from the due and convenient perfection of the things procreated by Himself—not indeed His own, nor internal, but only external and relative.</margin>

PHILO. I remember having already said above that the imperfection of a work obscurely and latently signifies some defect of the craftsman, on account of a certain habit and relation of the craftsman to his own works. By this reasoning, when God loves the perfection of the things procreated by Himself, He is undoubtedly to be thought to love the perfection of His own actions related to His own works. These divine actions might perhaps be contaminated by some suspicion of defect arising from the defect of the procreated things: but from the completion of those things, the actions are confirmed in their highest relative perfection. Wherefore the ancients said that a just man renders the divine splendor perfect and conspicuous, but an unjust man obscures it...

# DIALOGUE III. #

...and they said to contaminate. I believe it must be granted, therefore, that since God loves the completion of His works, He also seeks the perfection of His own divine action. This kind of love and desire does not introduce a defect into the <term>divine essence</term> <note>The fundamental nature of God, which is traditionally considered perfect and unchanging.</note>, but only introduces a slight and subtle relationship from the Creator toward created things. For God, lest He should at some point conceive within Himself even a tiny stain from the defect of created things, desires His own purity without the slightest blemish together with the perfection of the things He has created.

**SOPHIA:** This response you have devised seems indeed learned and subtle. But I remember that in the first dispute we held, you said that love is the desire to achieve union. This definition certainly encompasses the divine love that provides for the goods of created things; however, it cannot be inferred from this that God desires a "coupling" with them. For no one desires a union with another unless that other thing is more perfect than oneself.

**PHILO:** We never see anything desire union with another, except for that with which, when joined, it becomes far more perfect than if it were not joined. And I also grant you that God's outward-facing action acquires a greater perfection for itself from the union of created things with their Creator than it would without such a union. 

<margin>God does not strive or desire to couple Himself with created things, but rather to join them to Himself.</margin>

Yet God does not seek to couple Himself with created things in the way that the common crowd of lovers desires to be joined with the persons they love. On the contrary, He strives most greatly that created things be coupled with His divinity—specifically so that, through such a wonderful union, they may enjoy absolute and stable happiness, and so that the divine action of the Creator itself, which relates to created things, may remain pure and perfect.

**SOPHIA:** You have indeed handled yourself excellently in untying this knot. But one ambiguity still remains for you to clear up: you seem to think that the "Beautiful," by which Plato defined love, and the "Good," by which Aristotle described it, differ greatly from each other; but I believe both are exactly one and the same.

**PHILO:** You do not judge correctly.

**SOPHIA:** Will you perhaps deny that everything beautiful is good?

**PHILO:** Not at all; but the common people would boldly deny it.

**SOPHIA:** Why?

**PHILO:** They say not everything beautiful is good; for some things that are judged beautiful are found to be evil within, while some things that seem deformed are known to be good in reality.

**SOPHIA:** In my judgment, the reasoning of those people can easily be dismissed. For whoever judges a thing to be beautiful will also judge it to be good insofar as it is beautiful; and if it is truly good, it will certainly be truly beautiful. Likewise, whatever is ugly will seem evil insofar as it is ugly; and if it is good in reality, it will happen to be not at all ugly in reality.

**PHILO:** You have spoken rightly; even if, as we have already cautioned above, the "Beautiful" seems more suited to signifying <term>appearance</term> <note>original: "speciem"; referring to the outward form or "species" of a thing.</note> than the "Good," and the "Good" more adapted to expressing <term>essence</term> than the "Beautiful." 

<margin>The "Beautiful" seems more suited to signifying appearance than the "Good," and the "Good" more adapted to expressing essence than the "Beautiful."</margin>

<margin>Every "Beautiful" thing is indeed "Good," yet not every "Good" thing is "Beautiful." Many things are found which are neither beautiful nor ugly.</margin>

But to come now to defining the ambiguity proposed: although every beautiful thing is good, either in reality or in appearance, I will not grant you in turn that every good thing is beautiful.

**SOPHIA:** Which things are called "Good" but by no means "Beautiful"?

**PHILO:** Food, drink, health, sweet smells, delicious flavors, and the most healthy regions, and other similar things—I think you will surely never deny that these ought to be called "Good." But you would by no means say they are "Beautiful."

**SOPHIA:** Even if men are not accustomed to calling these things beautiful, I believe they are indeed beautiful. For unless these were beautiful, they would certainly be deformed; but it seems quite absurd and contradictory for the same thing to be both "Good" and "Deformed."

**PHILO:** I would truly wish for you to speak more accurately. "Good" and "Ugly" <note>original: "turpe"; can mean foul, base, or morally ugly.</note> cannot dwell in the same subject, or in the same part of a subject. However, I do not think that whatever is "not beautiful" must immediately be called "ugly."

**SOPHIA:** By what name then will you signify it?

### OF LEONE EBREO ON LOVE ###

<margin>
Those things which are customarily called neither beautiful nor ugly are found to be of two kinds.
</margin>
...to which we are accustomed to apply both of the proposed names—"beautiful" and "good"—certain things are frequently seen to exist that are neither beautiful nor ugly. We see this happen much more often in the many forms of "goods" to which neither the praise of beauty nor the vice of deformity can be attributed. These are the types of things we just mentioned, which are said to be neither beautiful nor ugly in the proper sense. However, there is a difference between these things and human beings: we say humans are neither beautiful nor ugly when they are partly handsome and partly deformed, so that they cannot be called entirely beautiful nor completely ugly. But the "goods" just described cannot be called beautiful or deformed either entirely or in part. 

**SOPHIA:** I believe no one would deny this mixture of form and deformity seen in people of ambiguous appearance. However, I would like you to reveal the doubtful or twofold nature of those goods that exist as neither beautiful nor ugly through some similar and clear example. 

**PHILO:** Have you not noticed that many people are neither knowledgeable nor ignorant? 

**SOPHIA:** By what name, then, shall such people be called? 

**PHILO:** They might appropriately be called "believers of truth" or "those who hold correct opinions." For those who have correct and true opinions do not at all deserve the name of "the knowing" or "the wise," because they do not understand the causes of things or the <term>sciences</term> <note>In this context, 'science' refers to formal, demonstrative knowledge of causes, rather than modern laboratory science.</note>. Yet, they are far less likely to be called ignorant, since they are seen to believe what is true and hold correct opinions. The same judgment must be made regarding the many goods that are neither beautiful nor ugly. 

**SOPHIA:** Should "the beautiful," then, be called not simply "the good," but "the good" with something else added or attached to it? 

**PHILO:** Exactly. 

**SOPHIA:** And what...

<margin>
The "beautiful" is defined not as the "good" simply, but as the "good" endowed with beauty.
</margin>
...will that addition be? 

**PHILO:** Namely, beauty itself. For the "beautiful" is defined as the "good" endowed with beauty; however, a "good" will never turn out to be "beautiful" if beauty is not added to it. 

**SOPHIA:** But how is beauty defined? Is anything else besides goodness required to constitute it? 

**PHILO:** To explain or define the <term>essence</term> <note>The fundamental nature or 'what-ness' of a thing.</note> of beauty would certainly demand a long and detailed discourse. For many see it every day and frequently mention it, yet they do not truly know it. 

**SOPHIA:** Who is found with such a dull mind that they cannot recognize the beautiful and distinguish it from the ugly? 

**PHILO:** The recognition of a beautiful thing is indeed easy and common. But very few have been able to reach that highest and universal 

<margin>
The knowledge of beauty itself is indeed difficult.
</margin>
<margin>
Beauty is defined as a certain grace or loveliness recognized and perceived by our soul, which impels it to love.
</margin>
beauty, by virtue of which all beautiful things are rightly said to be beautiful. 

**SOPHIA:** I pray you, do not let it seem heavy or troublesome to define it for my sake. 

**PHILO:** Many different definitions of beauty were devised by the ancients. To review them all at present and distinguish the true from the false would be superfluous and foreign to our purpose—all the more so because a little later we shall speak about beauty quite extensively and abundantly. For now, it will suffice merely to explain a true, brief, and very common definition of it: **Beauty is a certain grace or loveliness recognized and perceived by our soul, which impels it to love.** <note>original: "Pulchritudo est gratia seu uenustas quædā animo nostro cognita & perspecta, quæ eum ad amandū impellit."</note> Hence, that thing or person which has loveliness joined to goodness is rightly called beautiful. But any good that lacks this kind of <term>grace</term> <note>Here, 'grace' (gratia) refers to a pleasing quality or 'charm' that goes beyond mere utility.</note> is neither beautiful nor ugly: not 

<margin>
An intermediate is found between the beautiful and the ugly; but between good and evil, no intermediate lies at all.
</margin>
beautiful, because it lacks loveliness; nor ugly, because it is marked by goodness. But that thing which lacks both—namely, grace and goodness—must be called not only "not beautiful," but also "evil" and "deformed." For an intermediate is found between the beautiful and the ugly, but between good and evil, no intermediate can be found at all. And not without reason, since "good" is said to signify <term>essence</term> and "evil" to signify <term>privation</term> <note>In medieval philosophy, evil was often defined not as a 'thing' in itself, but as the 'privation' or absence of a good that ought to be present.</note>. 

**SOPHIA:** Did you not just now wish for <term>potency</term> <note>The state of being 'potential' rather than 'actual.'</note> to stand between essence and privation? 

**PHILO:** Potency is indeed placed between actual and perfect essence and pure, sheer privation. For if it is compared with privation, it seems to have the character of essence; but if it is compared with actual essence, it seems to have the character of privation. Therefore, potency...

<margin>
Potency is placed as a middle ground between actual and perfect essence, and pure and sheer privation.
</margin>

<summary>Philo defines beauty as "grace" or "loveliness" added to goodness that moves the soul to love, distinguishing it from things that are merely "good" but not beautiful. He also argues that while there is a middle ground between beauty and ugliness, there is no middle ground between good (existence) and evil (the absence of existence).</summary>

### DIALOGUE III.

<margin>Nothing at all runs between essence and its privation.</margin>
...a certain proportional middle composed of actual essence and <term>privation</term> <note>In philosophy, privation is the lack of a quality that should naturally be present, such as blindness being the privation of sight.</note> exists, just as love is also said to reside as a middle between the beautiful and the ugly. Between essence and its privation, however, no middle lies at all, since between a <term>habit</term> <note>original: "habitum"; in this context, a "habit" refers to the possession of a quality or state of being, the opposite of privation.</note> and its privation nothing ever at all can come between. For these two terms seem to be contradictory to each other, since potency related to the pure privation of a habit is called privation, but when compared with an actual habit, it is most rightly called by that name. Between potency and mere privation, or between potency and the most absolute act, who would be so foolish as to contend that a middle is found? Since, therefore, nothing at all is seen to run between essence and the privation of essence, we have rightly said that between good and evil, simply speaking, nothing at all intervenes; yet we have already demonstrated more than enough that a middle is admitted between the beautiful and the deformed.

**SOPHIA:** You seem to have explained and determined this doubtful and involved matter excellently; but I would like to understand the reason why every good thing is not also graceful or beautiful.

<margin>The things that are presented to all five exterior senses are, according to the wise, truly good in reality, and are usually called good truly and properly. Of the five exterior senses, only sight and hearing claim some knowledge of beauty for themselves; the others, however, do not at all.</margin>
**PHILO:** Objects presented to all five external senses are customarily called truly and properly good, useful, temperate, and pleasant. But those which are presented to the coarser and more imperfect senses—namely taste, smell, and touch—are seen to be endowed with no grace or beauty at all that might compel the soul, through an intervening ineffable pleasure, or rather allure it to its love. But those things which are presented only to the two spiritual senses—namely sight and hearing—seem to have participated in grace quite liberally and copiously; this grace binds the souls of men to itself and renders them most studious and loving of it. Therefore, sweet foods, healthful drinks, most pleasant odors, most healthy regions, moderate and most delightful sexual unions, and other things similar to these: although they are good, sweet, pleasant, useful, and necessary for preserving the life of men and animals, they will nevertheless never be called beautiful. This is because such coarse and crude objects are entirely destitute of grace and beauty; nor can those three senses, so thick and solid, provide or exhibit an entry suitable enough to our soul for beauty or loveliness to drench it with pleasure and induce the love of the beautiful within it. 

But that elegance and handsomeness of which we speak is seen abundantly in things subject to sight: as can be perceived by anyone through the sense of the eyes in skillfully crafted statues and paintings; in the correct and suitable proportion of parts both among themselves and to the whole; in the many and different organs of living beings arranged harmoniously and breathing together into one; in soft colors; in pure and clearest light; in the golden Sun; in the silvery Moon; in the twinkling stars; and finally in the vastest heaven. The reason for this effect is said to be that things subject to sight, because of their spiritual nature, are marked by grace and loveliness, which, having entered through the spiritual sense of the shining eyes, immediately strive toward the soul to refresh and recreate it, and gradually compel and move it toward the love of beauty. 

Grace and beauty were also granted to those things which are submitted to hearing: as gentle speech, a moving oration, a resonant voice, the singing of strings and musical instruments, sweet melody, and harmonic proportion can testify. For all these things, since they are spiritual, have a certain grace joined to them, which, having insinuated itself into our soul through the spiritual sense of hearing, then affects it with internal pleasure and internal love.

<margin>Beauty participates in a spiritual nature, and offers itself to be tasted only by the spiritual senses.</margin>
Therefore, good things which are said to be endowed with a spiritual nature and presented to the spiritual senses, certainly participate in grace and beauty. But good things which are seen to be both coarser in nature and presented to coarser senses, seem to have been entirely destitute of beauty and loveliness; from which it happens that although they are good, they are nevertheless not beautiful or lovely.

**SOPHIA:** Besides sight and hearing, has nature bestowed upon us any other power that might perceive and know beauty?

**PHILO:** Those cognitive faculties, which...

<summary>Philo argues that while everything is either "good" or "evil" with no middle ground, beauty is a specific category of "good" that requires "spiritual" senses—sight and hearing—to be perceived. Coarser senses like touch and taste can identify what is useful or pleasant, but they cannot access the grace and harmony that constitute true beauty.</summary>

# LEO HEBRAEUS ON LOVE

<margin>
Beauty is seen to be known and discerned more and more, as if through certain steps, beyond sight and hearing: first by the phantasy, then by the intellect, and finally by the separate mind.
</margin>
...the two aforementioned senses <note>Referring to sight and hearing, previously discussed as the most "spiritual" of the five senses.</note> are more spiritual in nature; they know the beautiful even more perfectly than the senses themselves do. **SOPHIA:** What are those faculties said to be? **PHILO:** **Imagination** or **phantasy**, which composes, divides, and revolves those things already perceived by the senses. It further recognizes many acts, events, and individual concepts which, by the merit of the grace and beauty inherent in them, allure the soul toward a certain amorous pleasure. For this reason, men have often been accustomed to speak of a "beautiful phantasy," a "beautiful thought," or a "beautiful invention." Truly, however, the **reason** proceeding from the **intellect** is seen to have claimed for itself a much broader and more fertile knowledge of beauty. It grasps universal, incorporeal, and eternal graces and beauties distributed among individual and fleeting bodies. Indeed, these are accustomed to drench our souls in the sweetest pleasure and the most delightful love. In confirmation of this matter, pursuits, laws, virtues, and human sciences can be brought forward; for all these are very frequently called "beautiful," such as a "beautiful pursuit," a "more beautiful law," and "the most beautiful science." 

But the highest knowledge of the beautiful of all, which human powers can reach, is seen to have fallen to the **abstract mind** <term>abstract mind</term> <note>The "separate" or "abstract" mind refers to the highest level of human intellect, which functions independently of material constraints to contemplate divine truths.</note>. Raised to the loftiest knowledge of God and of things entirely devoid of matter, and seized by a certain ineffable and extraordinary pleasure, it burns most vehemently with the love of that highest grace and beauty which is seen in the parent and founder of all things; there it obtains its greatest and final happiness. Therefore, our soul is wonderfully moved to love and embrace beauty itself, which—passing through sight, hearing, thought, reason, and finally the mind—reaches the soul by a certain spiritual reckoning. This happens because those things presented to the aforementioned faculties of our soul participate in a certain loveliness because of their spiritual nature, which pours into the soul a massive pleasure and a vehement love of itself. However, those things which are subject to the remaining powers of the soul <note>Referring to the "lower" senses of touch, taste, and smell.</note> were least able to attain this kind of grace or loveliness because of their thick nature, which approaches too closely to matter.

<margin>
He concludes that spiritual beauty is a certain grace joined with goodness, exposed only to the spiritual faculties of our soul.
</margin>
Therefore, in order for a good thing—even a corporeal one—to also exist as "beautiful," it must have obtained some appearance of spiritual grace joined with goodness. This grace, reaching the soul through the spiritual faculties, can finally delight it and compel it to love the beautiful.

<margin>
Love, properly taken, is defined as the desire for the beautiful; but considered commonly, it is the appetite for the good.
</margin>
Let our discourse now return to the place from which it began: **human love**, which we have primarily proposed to treat. If it is taken properly, it is the **desire for the beautiful**, as **Plato** would have it; but if it is considered commonly, it will undoubtedly exist as the **appetite for the good**, as **Aristotle** felt. **SOPHIA:** This interpretation of the essence of love is so copious and widespread that I may more easily and conveniently understand those things which you are about to hand down concerning its origin in the future; in my judgment, it is more than enough. Now I wish for you to approach the solving of those five postulates concerning the origin of love which were set forth by me above. **PHILO:** First, you asked whether love has arisen: that is, whether it drew its origin from someone producing it, or whether it exists as the first of all things, eternal, and procreated by no one.

<margin>
Love is seen to be deduced from the lover and the beloved as if from two principles and two superior causes.
</margin>
To this I respond that love emanated from elsewhere, and the first place of eternity is by no means to be attributed to it; rather, it is undoubtedly preceded by certain superior causes. **SOPHIA:** For what reason? **PHILO:** Certainly for several reasons. First, because the lover precedes the love, just as the agent precedes the act. Whence it seems necessary to say that the first lover preceded the first love and brought it into the light. **SOPHIA:** You have rightly said that the lover, who produces love by loving, precedes it. Thus, that which loves can be found without love, yet love can never be found without that which loves. Please, proceed to the explanation of the second cause. **PHILO:** Just like the lover, so also the **beloved** must precede the love; for unless a lovable person or thing were supposed to exist first, we could never love, nor would any love truly [exist]...

<summary>Philo explains that beauty is perceived through a hierarchy of spiritual faculties—imagination, reason, and the abstract mind—and defines love as either the desire for beauty (Platonic) or the appetite for good (Aristotelian), originating from both the lover and the beloved.</summary>

### DIALOGUE III

...certainly would be found. **SOPHIA:** I perceive this second reason to be no less true than the first; for the same judgment must be made concerning the beloved as is made of the lover. You will never find love existing without a thing or a person that is lovable; yet a lovable thing can certainly be found without love, and might not be loved at all. From this, it seems one must deduce that the lover and the beloved are the principles and causes of love. **PHILO:** What distinction of causes would you think exists between the lover and the beloved? And which of them would you judge to be the more powerful cause of love? **SOPHIA:** The lover seems to me to hold the role of the active cause <term>causa agens; the primary force that initiates an action</term>, like a father; the beloved, however, seems to hold the role of the recipient, like a mother. Following the common use of these words, I would think the lover acts and the beloved is acted upon <note>In Latin grammar, *amans* (lover) is a present active participle, while *amatum* (beloved) is a past passive participle.</note>. I would therefore judge the lover to be the primary cause and the beloved to be the secondary cause of love. **PHILO:** You seem to have played the part of the doubter far better than that of the solver; for the truth is seen to be quite the opposite. The beloved is actually the active cause, which inspires the hidden love into the soul of the lover. 

<margin>The beloved is as the agent, form, and father; the lover, however, is as the matter, much like a mother, and concurs only for the procreation of love itself.</margin> The lover should rather be thought of as the one receiving love from the beloved. Hence, it should be said that the beloved is the true and legitimate parent of the love which he infuses into the lover; the lover, no differently than a mother, then brings to light the love already conceived from the beloved—a love as similar to its father as possible. For love is seen to terminate at last in the beloved, from whom it drew its initial origin. For this reason, the beloved is the principal cause of love itself, performing the duty of agent, form, and end <note>Philo uses Aristotelian terminology: the beloved is the 'Efficient Cause' (agent), the 'Formal Cause' (the essence/shape of the love), and the 'Final Cause' (the purpose or goal).</note>, and thus rightly claims the title of father. The lover, who holds only the role of the matter, should undoubtedly be likened to the pregnant and laboring mother. 

<margin>Love, according to the opinion of Plato, is defined as birth in beauty.</margin> And this is surely what Plato meant to understand when he defined love as "a birth in beauty" <note>This refers to a famous passage in Plato’s *Symposium* (206b) where Diotima explains that love is not just the desire for beauty, but the desire to procreate and give birth in the presence of beauty.</note>. For the "beautiful" is the very thing beloved, by which the lover—now filled and made pregnant—afterwards bears and pours forth a love most similar to its beautiful and cherished parent; to whom, finally, he refers and directs the newborn love as its ultimate end. **SOPHIA:** I was in error, and I am greatly glad to have recognized my error and learned the truth. But what do you think should be said about the meaning of the words, which entangled me in such great error? For "lover" certainly sounds like an active cause, and "beloved" like a passive one. **PHILO:** These two names were indeed rightly devised by the ancients. 

<margin>The lover as the active and the beloved as the passive cause must be considered not in relation to love itself, but rather in relation to amorous servitude.</margin> For the lover is seen to serve the beloved, and in that way certainly "acts," yet he does not procreate the love. The beloved is said to receive the servitude of the lover with a grateful and willing mind, yet does not receive the love itself <note>The beloved receives the *actions* of the lover, but the beloved *gives* the love (as a father gives life) to the lover's soul.</note>. If I were to ask you which is more worthy and excellent: the servant, or the one who receives the service? The obedient one, or the one to whom obedience is offered? The one who honors, or the one who is honored? Without a doubt, you would answer that these active roles are inferior to those who receive them. The lover holds the same condition in relation to the beloved; for the lover is seen to serve and obey the beloved, and furthermore to cherish and honor him. **SOPHIA:** This is certainly found to be true in lovers who are inferior to the things they love. But when the lover excels the beloved thing in dignity and nobility, I would judge that the opposite should rather be asserted: namely, that in the procreation of love, the lover plays the paternal and primary part, while the beloved plays the maternal and secondary part. 

<margin>Every lover, insofar as he is a lover, leans toward the beloved by an inclination of the will, and seems to adhere to it as an accessory to the principal.</margin> **PHILO:** Even though many lovers are seen to be more excellent than their beloveds by the merit of their own natures—as a man to the woman he loves, a father to his son, a teacher to his disciple, a benefactor to the one receiving the benefit, and, to speak more generally, the celestial world to the terrestrial, the spiritual to the corporeal world (which it loves vehemently), and even God to those things which He has procreated and follows with the greatest love—nevertheless, every lover, *insofar as he is a lover*, leans toward the beloved by an inclination of the will, and seems to adhere to it as an accessory to the principal. For the beloved begets and induces the love, while the lover is only moved by the beloved. **SOPHIA:** But how can it be that the superior is ever said to incline toward the inferior, and to draw near to the inferior? **PHILO:** We have already pointed out before that all the actions of a lover are referred back to his own perfection, joy, and pleasure; and although the beloved is not as perfect as the lover...

### LEONE EBREO ON LOVE

...it often happens; yet the lover, by joining the beloved thing to himself, either attains a greater perfection than before, or at least perceives a greater joy and pleasure from it. This newly arriving perfection, joy, and pleasure, which the lover acquires for himself from the union <term>copulatio; the spiritual or physical joining of two things</term> with the beloved thing—whether that thing be more noble than the lover himself or more ignoble—seems to be the most powerful reason why the lover inclines with his will toward the beloved. Nor, however, is anything taken away from the dignity and perfection of the lover because of this, nor is any defect or imperfection thereby introduced into him; rather, he even seems to gain the union and perfection of the beloved thing. Hence, it is seen that not only does one who is held by love for some person retain an inclination toward them because of the perfection and joy he gains from their union, but even one who has directed his love not toward a person but toward something else, so that he might finally come into possession of that thing, inclines his mind and will toward it; for he seems to have gained no small thing once the object itself is acquired. 

**SOPHIA:** This I understand perfectly; but when two love each other mutually, and each of them loves the other equally, and is likewise loved by the other, what do you think should be said? It is certainly necessary, if you wish to be consistent with yourself, that you must grant that each of them, when compared with the other, is both inferior and superior at the same time; and perhaps no greater contradiction than this can be imagined. 

<margin>Every lover, insofar as he loves, is in reality inferior to the beloved, insofar as they are loved; even if someone were held by the greatest love of himself.</margin> 

**PHILO:** I tell you that not only does this not contradict itself, but rather it is most true: namely, that each person, in relation to the beloved thing, is considered inferior insofar as they love, and superior insofar as they are loved. 

**SOPHIA:** Could the same thing perhaps be said to be superior to itself? 

**PHILO:** This also is undoubtedly true: that the beloved must be placed above the lover, as the superior is to the inferior. And if it should happen that someone loves himself, he would certainly surpass himself in the role of the beloved, while being surpassed in the role of the lover. And when we spoke previously about the commonality of love, we already noted that Aristotle—and his most famous commentator Averroes <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd) was a medieval Andalusian philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to Renaissance thought.</note>—held the opinion that God leads the first of all the spheres (which is called the *Primum Mobile* <term>the "first moved" sphere; in ancient astronomy, the outermost shell of the heavens that moves all others</term>) by the love of a certain more excellent thing. This same manner of love the other Intelligences <note>In this context, "Intelligences" refers to the angelic or divine beings that Renaissance philosophers believed moved the celestial planets.</note> are seen to observe in the turning of the other lower spheres. 

<margin>God, insofar as He is loved by Himself, is considered far greater and more sublime than insofar as He loves Himself.</margin> 

Since nothing at all can be imagined more worthy or more excellent than God—indeed, all other things are subject to His command—it seems necessary to say that God turns the *Primum Mobile* because of the love of Himself, and that God as the beloved is superior to God as the lover. This remains true even though the divine essence is proclaimed by all philosophers to consist in the purest unity, as you have learned from me before when I treated this matter more extensively. Therefore, since God, although He is one and most simple, is said to be greater and far more sublime insofar as He is loved by Himself than insofar as He loves Himself, it is not at all surprising that this same thing happens in the case of two other lovers who love each other with an equal and mutual love: namely, that each of them, insofar as they are loved, should be placed above not only the other person, but even above themselves as the lover. 

**SOPHIA:** I would certainly acquiesce to the reasons you have brought forward, unless I found that Plato was entirely opposed to them. 

**PHILO:** What then have you found that such a great philosopher has uttered contrary to our arguments? 

<margin>The Gods deemed the more liberal rewards of Achilles for his friend Patroclus to be worthier than the supreme zeal and benevolence of Alcestis for her husband Admetus.</margin> 

**SOPHIA:** I remember that in the *Symposium* <note>original: "conuiuio"; referring to Plato's famous dialogue on the nature of love.</note>, Plato taught that the lover is more divine than the beloved, because the lover is driven to love the beloved while seized by a divine frenzy <note>Plato’s "divine madness" (theia mania) suggests the lover is inspired by a god.</note>. For this reason, the philosopher then added that the beloved ones, who perform noble deeds for the sake of their lovers, find the Gods more favorable and kind than the lovers do, even though the lovers refuse to undergo no kind of danger or risk for the sake of the beloved. To confirm this matter, he brought forward the example of Alcestis, who, when she did not hesitate to meet death for the sake of her most beloved husband, obtained the greatest honors from the Gods and was soon returned to the breath of life; yet she did not pass over to the Isles of the Blessed, whereas Achilles, who for the sake of Patroclus (by whom he was greatly loved), seeking vengeance...

<summary>Philo explains that the beloved is ontologically "superior" to the lover because the beloved acts as the goal and perfection of the lover's desire, even in the case of God's self-love. Sophia challenges this by citing Plato's Symposium, where the lover is considered more divine due to being inspired by a "divine frenzy."</summary>

### DIALOGUE III.

...[he] was willing to be brought into the most certain danger of his life, as it is said to have happened. 

**PHILO:** This speech was attributed by Plato in his *Symposium* to Phaedrus, a young man of excellent character and a disciple of Socrates, who believed Love to be a certain great and most beautiful God, and therefore a lover of the beautiful. Since Phaedrus saw that love resides in the lover—or rather in the lover's heart as its proper home, no differently than an infant residing in the mother's womb—the youth persuaded himself that the lover, because of the heavenly power of Love dwelling within him, participates in divinity far more abundantly than the beloved. Indeed, it seems that the beloved only induces love in the lover, but does not possess it within himself. For this reason, Cupid <note>original: "Cupido," the Roman name for Eros, the god of love</note> is said to instill a certain divine frenzy <note>original: "furorem," referring to the "divine madness" of lovers described by Plato</note> into the lover alone, and by no means into the beloved. And therefore, the Gods are thought to favor the beloveds (who look to the benefit and utility of their lovers) much more than the lovers (who serve the gain and convenience of the beloveds), just as they favored Achilles. 

**SOPHIA:** Does this opinion and reasoning of Phaedrus seem true or sufficient to you? 

**PHILO:** Not at all; for both were challenged by Socrates, his teacher. 

**SOPHIA:** Why? 

**PHILO:** Socrates there attacked the orator Agathon, who, along with Phaedrus, worshipped Love as a great and most beautiful God. Socrates demonstrated that Love is by no means a God because he is not beautiful—since all Gods are seen to be endowed with grace and loveliness. He confirms that Love is by no means beautiful primarily by this argument: because Love is defined as the desire for the beautiful. Whatever is usually desired is clearly seen to be lacking in the one who desires it; for the firm and stable possession of a thing and the desire for it cannot be found together at the same time. <margin>The opinion of Socrates and Plato, who said that Love is not a God, but a certain great demon <term>daemon; in the Platonic sense, an intermediary spirit or force that bridges the gap between the divine and the human</term> midway between the celestial Gods and earthly men.</margin> Therefore, Socrates considers Love not to be a God, but a certain great demon situated in the middle between the celestial Gods and earthly men, placed at the boundary of both. Hence, he is neither beautiful like a divine power, nor deformed like a mortal man or anything else inferior, but exists as a medium between beauty and ugliness. For although the one who seeks something does not seem to be, in actuality, what the sought-after thing is, he is nevertheless said to be so in potentiality. Likewise, since Love is always seen to desire the beautiful, even if he is not beautiful in actuality like a divine power, he seems at least to be beautiful in potentiality. 

**SOPHIA:** What, finally, Philo, do you intend to signify by such a speech?

<margin>The beloved is seen to be a participant in divinity itself far more abundantly than the lover.</margin> **PHILO:** I wish to conclude from this that divinity consists in the beloved, and by no means in the lover: since I have already proved that the beloved is beautiful in actuality, like a God, while the lover—who longs for the beloved thing—is beautiful only in potentiality. Although the lover, lifted up by this desire, becomes divine, he nevertheless does not deserve to be called a God as the beloved does. Hence, you will see the beloved honored, worshipped, and observed by the lover as a certain celestial power, and his beauty regarded by the lover as something divine—so much so that, in the lover's judgment, this beauty surpasses all other beauties by a wide interval. Does it not therefore seem to you also, Sophia, that the beloved excels the lover in dignity, and plays the prior and more important part in the origin of love? 

**SOPHIA:** Most certainly. <margin>A most elegant reason why the Gods were more generous toward Achilles, who chose to die for his lover, than toward Alcestis, who calmly met death for her beloved.</margin> But how will you respond to the example of Achilles and Alcestis? 

**PHILO:** Alcestis, who endured death with a calm and constant mind for the sake of her beloved husband, was not held worthy of the same honors as Achilles, who was killed for the sake of Patroclus, his most devoted lover. This is because a lover is bound to serve the beloved thing as a certain divine power, and to expose himself to a most certain and doubtless death for the sake of the beloved's safety and benefit. Nor, if he loves from the soul, could he ever do otherwise, because he has already migrated into the beloved, and has placed and located his own happiness and his own good only in the beloved, and no longer in himself. But the beloved is seen to be free and released from every kind of servitude, nor is he compelled by love to meet death for the lover. If, therefore, he should wish to die for him—as Achilles did for Patroclus—he will be rightly judged to have committed a most noble and generous deed. Wherefore, for such a great deed, the greatest and most ample...

This explains why the sacrifice of a beloved (like Achilles) is more highly honored by the gods than the sacrifice of a lover (like Alcestis).</summary>

**PHILO:** The love of those things which have already been born and created always presupposes a defect. Divine love supposes a deficiency not in God who loves, but rather in the things loved by God.

<margin>Aristotle, and with him all the Peripatetics, judge the World to be eternal, emanating from God no differently than an eternal effect from an eternal cause.</margin>
Since all men agree and concede that the supreme maker and father of the World is eternal, and entirely devoid of all time, beginning, and origin: whether the World afterward came forth from eternity, or at some moment of time, they have been accustomed to doubt most greatly. Many of the Philosophers have thought the World emanated from God as eternal, nor did it ever experience any beginning of time, no differently than God himself. To this opinion, the great Aristotle seems first to have adhered, and the entire school of the Peripatetics <note>original: "Peripateticorū schola"; the followers of Aristotle, named for his habit of walking while teaching</note> followed it soon after.

**SOPHIA:** What difference, therefore, could we assign between God and the World, if both existed equally eternal?

**PHILO:** Their distinction would certainly be very great: for from all eternity God would have produced, and the World would have been produced: and one of them indeed would be called the eternal cause: the other truly would be named the eternal effect. <margin>Plato thought the World had a temporal beginning from eternal matter by God.</margin> But those who follow piety and religion, and who cultivate and observe the Mosaic Law, and its most holy precepts and institutes, judge the World by no means to have been produced from eternity, but to have been procreated by God from nothing <note>original: "ex nihilo"; a central theological concept that God created the universe without pre-existing materials</note> at some beginning of time: to which true and most pious opinion some philosophers also have assented: but first of all that divine Plato, who in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s famous dialogue concerning the nature of the physical world</note> testifies that the World was made and begotten by God, and then brought into the light out of a certain confused and tangled matter, from which all things seem to have drawn their origin as from a subject. And although Plotinus, his most famous interpreter, labored vehemently to pull Plato’s mind toward the opinion of the world's eternity—since he often repeated and insisted that the Philosopher understood nothing else by the 'generation' or 'making' of the World than its eternal emanation from God—nevertheless, Plato's words seem most clearly to signify a temporal beginning of the World, and were certainly so understood and explained by many other most distinguished men professing Platonic dogmas. However, it is this: that Plato pronounced Chaos, the common subject of all things, to be eternal: that is, produced by God from eternity, which opinion is indeed disapproved of by pious and religious men; for they think that only the almighty God existed before the first moment of creation, accompanied by neither World nor Chaos: and that He thereafter produced all things from nothing at the beginning of time: and Moses certainly does not seem to have introduced matter co-eternal with God.

The third is assigned to faith, which pronounced that all things were created from nothing at the beginning of time. <meta>This page continues the dialogue between Philo and Sophia. Previously, they established that many philosophers, following Aristotle, consider the world to be eternal, emanating from God as an eternal effect from an eternal cause. Here, Philo elaborates on why Aristotle believes the physical world—specifically matter, the heavens, motion, and time—cannot have a beginning.</meta>

### DIALOGUE III.

T 2

...it is contradictory that the natures of the five things mentioned by you ever had a beginning.

**SOPHIA:** And why could the **primary subject** <note>original: "primum subiectum"; also known as "prime matter," the most basic substance of the universe before it takes on any specific form or shape</note> not have been brought into the light at some point along with the birth and death of things? And what stands in the way of saying that the Heavens, circular motion, and the time proceeding from it once had an origin? 

**PHILO:** I will most gladly explain the reasoning for this matter, which I gather you strongly desire to know, even if we deviate slightly from our main purpose. <margin>Nothing comes from nothing.</margin> Primary matter, according to Aristotle, could never have been made at any moment of time: for whatever is produced must necessarily be produced from something; indeed, everyone admits that **nothing comes from nothing** <note>Latin: "Ex nihilo nihil fit." This was a fundamental axiom of ancient physics, suggesting that creation requires pre-existing material.</note>. Hence, if primary matter had once been made, it would surely have been produced from something else—and then that, rather than the matter itself, would more truly deserve the name of "primary matter." Since this sort of ascent (or rather, descent) into infinity cannot go on forever, one must eventually arrive at a truly primary and unbegotten matter. Therefore, it is rightly concluded that the first subject is eternal. 

It follows, then, that the **generation and corruption** <note>the natural cycle of birth/coming-into-being and decay/passing-away</note> of things—which are brought about from this eternal subject—must also exist perpetually. For since the essence of primary matter is said to be something most imperfect, it must always exist under some **substantial form**. <margin>Every birth is preceded by some decay, and every decay in turn is preceded by some birth.</margin> Hence, since the birth of a present thing always presupposes the decay of a previous one, it is necessary that **every birth be preceded by some decay, and every decay in turn be preceded by some birth**, just as we frequently see young chicks arise from the destruction of eggs. Let us conclude, therefore, that the birth and death of things are eternal, with no beginning ever repeated from on high; for example, any chicken egg always takes its origin from a hen, and every chick from an egg; nor can it be said or known which of the two came first.

<margin>Decay always proceeds from the dominance of one of two opposites. Birth is defined as a certain progression from one opposite to another.</margin> Furthermore, who will deny that the Heavens are eternal by the merit of their own nature? For if the celestial body had ever been born, it would also eventually decay. But it cannot decay at all, since nothing exists that is opposite or contrary to it. **Decay always proceeds from the dominance of one of two opposites**, and **birth is defined as a certain progression from one opposite to another**. The Heavens are judged to be entirely lacking in any opposite primarily because they seem neither to suffer nor to undergo any change of substance or quality; above all, their round shape—which alone of all shapes is rightly considered to lack any opposition—provides clear and ample proof of this.

Moreover, no beginning can be assigned to circular motion. Just as the circular shape of the celestial body appears to have no certain or determined beginning—rather, any point chosen on it is indifferently called both beginning and end—likewise, you may appropriately call circular motion something without a fixed or defined beginning or end. Furthermore, the perpetuity of **primary motion** <note>the original movement that drives all other movements in the universe</note>, considered simply and generally, is usually proved by this reason: if it were generated (since every generation is said to be a kind of motion), then the "first" motion would have another motion prior and superior to itself, which is impossible. Since an infinite progression in the generation of motions must be strictly avoided, we must finally stop at a first and perpetual motion.

<margin>Time is defined as nothing other than the number or measure of two parts of motion: namely, the "before" and the "after."</margin> Exactly the same judgment must be made regarding the time that follows that first motion. Since **time is defined as nothing other than the number or measure of two parts of motion—namely, the "before" and the "after"**—it follows that time exists as eternally as motion. <margin>Every moment, according to Aristotle's opinion, exists as a certain common bond between past and future time.</margin> This is rightly so, since **every moment** is seen to terminate past time and begin future time. Thus, no instant of time can be indicated or taken as its first and fixed beginning. Therefore, we must finally conclude that time is eternal and never had a beginning of its origin. 

**SOPHIA:** The arguments,

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Philo and Sophia. Philo is moving from a discussion of Aristotle’s "natural" (physical) arguments for an eternal universe to "theological" arguments used by Aristotle's followers. He then presents the counter-argument from the perspective of the "Law of Moses"—the belief in creation from nothing (ex nihilo).</meta>

->LEONIS HEBR. DE AMORE,<-

...I understand very well the reasons that drove Aristotle to ascribe eternity to **primary matter** <note>The most basic substance of the universe which has the potential to take on any form</note>, the nature of the heavens, the generation of lower things, circular motion, and the continuous succession of time. But can any other reasons besides these be brought forward to demonstrate the perpetuity of the World?

*PH.* Those which have been mentioned so far are indeed natural ones, and they acknowledge Aristotle as their author.

<margin>Two arguments of the Peripatetics <note>The "Peripatetics" were the followers of Aristotle, named for the covered walkways (peripatos) where they walked while discussing philosophy</note> drawn from the sources of theology and added to the previous ones to demonstrate the perpetuity of the World.</margin>
Truly, the Peripatetics then added two more reasons beyond the aforementioned ones, drawn from the sources of Theology, to confirm and strengthen the eternity of the World: one is taken and derived from the nature of the **supreme architect** <note>original: "summi opificis"; referring to God</note>; the other is taken from the purpose of divine works.

*SO.* I also greatly desire to learn those.

*PH.* They say that since God is called an eternal and immutable craftsman, and since the work of an artist always seems to reflect his own character, the World—as God’s most excellent work—must likewise be eternal and always remain similar to itself. This is all the more true because the Creator, while producing the World, intended nothing other than to do good. Why then did God perform this greatest good only then, and not before, or rather, eternally? What obstacle could have delayed or hindered an omnipotent and most perfect God from also gifting such a great good with perpetuity?

*SO.* The arguments of the Peripatetics seem by no means slight to me; especially the theological ones, which were taken from the immortal nature of the divine architect and from the purpose set by the divine will in the creation of the World. In what way, then, will the Platonists and all of us who profess the **Law of Moses** <note>A reference to the Judeo-Christian tradition of biblical creation</note>—asserting that all things were created from nothing at the beginning of time—defend our opinion against the arguments of the Peripatetics?

*PH.* We, too, bring forward many things in defense of the truth.

<margin>The reasons of the faithful, who affirm that the World came forth from nothing into light, and their responses to the arguments of the Peripatetics.</margin>
First, we concede that nothing can be made from nothing by nature. But we contend that by an omnipotent God, through a certain unusual and miraculous example, something can be produced from nothing: not that "nothing" is ever called the "matter" of things, as wood is for a statue; but rather that God can create or bring things into the light for the first time without the help of any pre-existing matter. By the same reasoning, even if the heavenly bodies and the **primary subject** <note>prime matter</note> are not subject to birth or decay by the merit of their own natures, they were nevertheless created from nothing during the first beginnings of the World because of the immense and admirable power of God. Likewise, even if it is contrary to the natures of mutual generation, circular motion, and time to have had a beginning, we must nonetheless confess that those three certainly began during the divine creation of the World; for they follow partly from the essence of primary matter and partly from the essence of the heavenly body, both of which we have already said had a beginning.

<margin>Divine actions proceed not from necessity, but from the free will and absolute power of God.</margin>
However, as for what concerns the nature of the supreme architect: we respond that divine actions proceed not from necessity, but from free will and absolute power. Just as God seems to have been entirely free and unrestrained in establishing the World—in defining the size of the lands, in determining the number, measure, and qualities of the stars, and in assigning individual things to the heavenly and elementary spheres—so too, using that same freedom of will, He judged that a temporal beginning should be assigned to the creation of things, even though He could have shared His own eternity with them.

Regarding what concerns the "end" or purpose of divine works, we respond in this way: even if the purpose of the worldly structure is said to consist in doing good, and even though men are accustomed to always prefer an eternal good over a temporary one, it is no wonder if we can never track down or know the specific purpose of divine works, since we are in no way capable of reaching a knowledge of God’s hidden wisdom. Indeed, in God's eyes, a temporary good perhaps precedes an eternal one in the creation of the World; for the absolute power of God and His free will are better known and perceived from the fact that He created all things from nothing, than if He had produced the entire universe eternally.

<summary>This page weighs the Aristotelian (Peripatetic) view of an eternal universe against the Mosaic doctrine of creation from nothing. Philo argues that God's creation of the world in time is an expression of His absolute free will and omnipotence rather than a lack of goodness.</summary>

**SO.** Why? **PH.** Because the unformed must always have preceded the formed. ### DIALOGUE III.

...he would assert that it <note>Referring to the "unformed" state of matter.</note> has been found. For a thing entirely formless and without any form whatsoever cannot be found at all; indeed, "form" is said to be that by which the unformed is seen to subsist. Therefore, we must say either that both—namely, form and matter, and from this the World itself—have always existed eternally, as Aristotle felt; or that both, and all things likewise, were created at some point in time, as the faithful profess. By this brief and compendious reasoning, the Theologians already mentioned by us have explained the Mosaic creation of the World. From this, they believed they had demonstrated, according to the Prophet’s meaning, that the unformed and confused Chaos preceded the creation, and by merit of that creation was afterwards divided and dispersed into the universe.

<meta>This page continues Philo’s explanation of how Platonic and Cabalistic philosophy reconciles the creation of the world with Aristotelian logic. Philo is explaining that while individual worlds are created and destroyed in cycles, the underlying components—the Divine Intellect and Prime Matter—are eternal.</meta>

### DIALOGUE III. 505
V

<margin>
Platonists and **Cabalists** <note>mystics of the Jewish tradition</note>, who proposed a succession of infinite worlds and the eternity of **Chaos** <note>the primordial state of formless matter</note>, seem to agree with Aristotle—who thought the world was single and eternal—much more than the faithful do. The faithful believe the world was created long ago by God out of nothing.
</margin>
...Indeed, which of them can more easily and swiftly dismantle the arguments of Aristotle that you mentioned earlier: Plato, following the opinion of the ancient theologians and the Cabalists, or the faithful, who believe that the world was created only once in the past? *PHILO:* Aristotle himself thought that those who said a previous world existed before this one, and another would follow after it in an eternal and perpetual series, were more correct than those who claimed the world had its first beginnings without any preceding material. For the former group seemed at least to observe an eternal and perfectly coherent succession in the birth of the world, never conceding that something could be made from nothing—two principles which the latter group clearly disregarded. Therefore, the opinion of the Platonists is not troubled or burdened at all by the stronger arguments of the **Peripatetics** <note>the followers of Aristotle</note>. Even if we say that nothing comes from nothing, or that **prime matter** <note>the fundamental substance of the universe</note> could never have been produced or born in time, they will not be concerned; for Plato also seems to have held these propositions as true and used them as his foundation. Furthermore, those two theological arguments—one stating that a divine work must be eternal like its eternal maker, and the other concluding that the goal of divine works should be eternal rather than temporary—

<margin>
The reasoning by which the Platonists and Cabalists defend themselves against the arguments of the Peripatetics, who assert the eternity of a single world.
</margin>
will by no means disturb the Platonists and Cabalists. For Plato concedes that both propositions are true regarding the divine "efficient cause" <note>the agent that brings something into being</note>.

<margin>
In Plato’s view, God grants His eternity only to those things that are capable of receiving and enjoying it, such as the **First Intellect** <note>the divine mind</note> and prime matter.
</margin>
But he adds that God grants His eternity only to those things that are capable of receiving and enjoying it: namely, to the First Intellect, in which all the **Ideas** <note>the eternal patterns of all things</note> are stored, and to prime matter, which is called Chaos. For the former is pure act and form, while the latter is pure potential and a completely formless subject. One is called the most universal father of all, and the other the most universal mother of all. These two alone could become participants in divine eternity because they seem to have drawn their origin from God not in time, but eternally. However, whatever was born later through the union of these two parents—such as the whole universe and every part required to build it—is not at all capable of eternity, as they are said to have been "made" and "formed" by God. For whatever is an "effect" and is "formed" is understood to be necessarily composed of matter supplied by Chaos and form granted by an intelligible Idea. All such things, as we have already said, must have a beginning and an end to their life. Therefore, the work and the goal of divine production achieve eternity in those first two parents of the world, but not in any single world once it is formed. Nevertheless, through the succession of many—indeed, infinite—worlds, created things also seem to participate in eternity in a certain way. Aristotle himself testifies that this occurs in the lower world; he clearly affirms that none of these individual things can achieve perpetuity, but that their continuous generation and prime matter alone have been gifted with eternity. *SOPHIA:* Plato seems to have most excellently dismantled both Peripatetic arguments drawn from the fountains of theology, as well as one of the natural arguments. But how will he refute the four remaining natural arguments of Aristotle? *PHILO:* Plato did not believe, as Aristotle supposes, that Chaos is ever found without form. On the contrary, he said that when Chaos has "sprouted" for a long time, it eventually collects all things back into itself and seems, as it were, to absorb them. It then rests for a certain fixed interval of time, while the Idea conceives new seeds, until it returns once more to sprouting and bringing forth the universe. Furthermore, Plato conceded that generation occurs perpetually within many worlds succeeding one another, but not within a single world. As for the conflict which will eventually cause the heavens to dissolve, he believed it was this: because they too are "formed," "made," and were once composed of matter and form, they are said—
