### LEONE EBREO’S ON LOVE
### 506

...are said of themselves; for all such things are seen to be dissolved either sooner or later at last. If indeed the celestial bodies <note>the sun, moon, and stars</note> are eventually destroyed, their circular motions will also be ended. Yet he judged that motion, taken absolutely and generally, exists eternally because of the perpetual and coherent birth of **Chaos** <note>the formless "prime matter" from which the world is made</note> itself, which proceeds by the help of succession. Finally, he granted eternity to time, not because of the motion of the heavens, but because of that everlasting motion of generating which we said is always found in Chaos at appointed times.

**SOPHIA:** These solutions you have brought forward to defend Plato's opinion against the Aristotelian arguments have indeed pleased me greatly. 

<margin>He briefly touches upon three notable opinions regarding the production of the World.</margin>

And regarding the production of the World, I think you have spoken enough so far: both concerning the view of **Aristotle** <note>the Greek philosopher who argued the world was eternal and never had a beginning</note>, who says there is only one World and it is eternal; then concerning **Plato’s** view, which posits an eternal succession of several Worlds following one after another; and finally, regarding the opinion of the **faithful** <note>believers in the Abrahamic traditions</note>, who assert the procreation of only one World and all things. Now the time certainly seems to demand that you approach the solution to the question of love proposed earlier: and that you devise a fitting answer to the second inquiry—namely, when love first arose, and who is said to have been the first of all loves.

<margin>The first love appears to be everlasting.</margin>

**PHILO:** That must certainly be considered the first love by which the first lover pursues the first beloved. But since neither of them is said to have had any beginning of birth or generation, but both exist equally eternal, it follows that their first and chief love of all never began, but exists everlasting together with them, and has drawn an everlasting origin from both.

**SOPHIA:** Tell me, I pray, whom do you call the first lover and the first beloved? For as soon as I know who both are, I shall immediately understand which love holds the first place among all loves.

**PHILO:** By the "first lover," I mean God as He who knows and wills; and by the "first beloved," I mean the same God as the **Supreme Beauty**.

<margin>The first love of God exists within Himself.</margin>

**SOPHIA:** Therefore, the first love is the love of God for Himself.

**PHILO:** Precisely.

**SOPHIA:** Many absurd and contradictory things would surely follow from this opinion. First, that the **divine essence** <note>the fundamental nature of God</note>, which is preached as the simplest of all things, would be divided into two different and distinct parts: namely, the "beloved who does not love" and the "lover who is not beloved." Next, that God as lover would certainly be inferior to Himself as beloved; for as you have already very well declared, every lover, insofar as he loves, seems to be inferior and less noble than the beloved. Since love is defined as a certain desire for attaining union, as you yourself taught above, God's love toward Himself would imply he desires a union he lacks. Since God is one and the same for Himself always, by this reasoning we would undoubtedly conclude that God "lacks" Himself. Thus, divine love would introduce a defect into that divine and most perfect essence—a defect which is entirely foreign to His absolute nature. Furthermore, many other absurd and impious things would follow this opinion, which my mind shrinks from recounting at present; I will leave them in silence, because they must be very well known both to you and to anyone who understands the nature of love discussed earlier.

**PHILO:** It is not at all fitting, Sophia, that we speak of the internal love of God as lover and beloved in the same way as we speak of the other common loves of the World. For God is not rendered diverse or manifold because He is said to possess the character of lover and beloved; on the contrary, He Himself, from this internal relationship, achieves a more perfect and certainly a simpler unity. For how could we ever say that His divine essence enjoys the supreme and most blessed life, unless the most wise lover, and beauty and wisdom themselves as the beloved, as well as the most excellent love of both, were reflected upon themselves? 

<margin>Just as in God the knower, the thing known, and knowledge itself are one and the same.</margin>

Whence, just as in God the knower, the thing known, and knowledge itself exist as one and the same—even if we frequently say that the knower becomes more perfect by the benefit of the thing known to him, and that knowledge is derived from both—so the lover, the beloved, and love itself, being divinely received, are within themselves entirely...

### DIALOGUE III.

<margin>
Similarly, the lover, the beloved, and love itself, when understood divinely, seem to agree deeply among themselves.
</margin>
...seem to agree deeply; which indeed, although they exist as three distinct and different things entirely to us—being counted by us separately, and with the lover being said to be perfected and shaped by the beloved, and love commonly said to arise from both as if from parents—yet all things considered divinely signify a certain most simple essence and unity, or an entirely indivisible nature, which cannot be multiplied by any logic.

**SOPHIA:** If you grant that God is nothing other than pure and most simple unity, from where does this triple reflection seen in Him proceed? 

**PHILO:** When His most pure light is impressed upon an intelligent mirror <note>The "intelligent mirror" refers to the human intellect, which reflects divine truth according to its own capacity.</note>, it is accustomed to produce this triple reflection of which we speak. 

**SOPHIA:** Therefore, the knowledge of God held by us would be entirely false and deceptive, since it seems to multiply pure unity into the number three. 

**PHILO:** We should by no means consider it false; for our intellect cannot perfectly comprehend the divinity, whose intelligible and most excellent nature surpasses us by an immense distance. Indeed, just because neither the eye nor a mirror can fully grasp the brightness and magnitude of the Sun, or the vastness and burning nature of fire, I would never claim that either of them errs or lies. For we consider it enough that the eye and the mirror receive these things according to their own capacity and nature; and this is judged to be abundantly sufficient to prove the reception of both, even if neither is able to perfectly attain the entire nature of the thing received. Likewise, the human

<margin>
The human intellect comprehends God according to the capacity and condition of its own intellectual nature, but not according to the pre-eminence of the divine essence.
</margin>
intellect—which we properly call an intellectual mirror—more than fulfills its duty if it receives and represents that divine essence (however immense) at least according to the capacity of its own intellectual nature, even if it stands at a great distance from the nature of that object and is far surpassed by it. 

**SOPHIA:** This happens, then, because our intellect is unable to perceive the object presented to it in an integrated and absolute way—not because it intentionally claims that pure unity is tripled. 

**PHILO:** On the contrary, since

<margin>
He gives a most elegant reason why our intellect cannot perceive the pure and most absolute unity of God himself except by using a triple reflection.
</margin>
it cannot grasp the most simple unity of God, it seems to distribute that unity into three by employing a certain relation and reflection. For a simple and most bright thing cannot be impressed upon something darker and more complex <note>original: "ad compositionem accedente" — approaching a state of being composed of different parts.</note> unless it first distributes its single and purest light into several darker lights. Consider how obscurely we view the Sun when it is impressed upon the clouds to form that **heavenly arc** <note>The rainbow.</note>, or when it is represented by other shining and bright bodies: see with what a variety of colors it appears to be poured into those receiving clouds, or into water, or into some mirror. Yet the light itself is seen to exist with no distinct color at all, but rather exceeding and encompassing all colors. In the same way, that divine form, although one and most simple, could never be perceived by others unless through the reflection of its light and the multiplication of its form. 

**SOPHIA:** But why does our intellect reduce unity to the number three <note>The "ternary" number.</note> rather than to some other number?

<margin>
The reason why our intellect, in perceiving that divine and simplest unity, reduces it to the number three rather than to some other number.
</margin>
**PHILO:** Because unity is the principle of numbers: for **one** is said to signify the first form, **two** the first matter, and **three** that first thing which is composed of both. Since our intellect, by the merit of its own nature, is "triple" and the first of composed things, it can in no way grasp unity without a triple relationship. Yet, it does not for that reason confuse or mix unity with the **Trinity**; rather, it understands unity only under the logic of a triple form. It persuades itself that the purest unity of that divine object exists, which encompasses the nature of the beloved, the lover, and love with a supreme simplicity, without any multiplication or division hindering it—just as the light of the Sun encompasses the essences of all individual lights and colors in a single, simple, and most excellent brightness. Thus the human intellect knows that it divides that supreme unity into the triple form of beloved, lover, and love only because of the humble and weak nature of the recipient itself. In this way, all the difficulties that might occur to you regarding the internal love of God as lover and beloved [can be resolved]...

<margin>

**PHILO:** On the contrary, I tell you that it is not only fitting but necessary that the divine unity be imprinted in us under a certain relation of production. Otherwise, the divine nature would seem not only unique but rather three-headed, representing three divided and distinct natures; and our intellect would moreover be rightly judged to lie and be deceived. For it cannot conceive of a multiplied unity unless that multiplication retains unity through a certain joining and uniting production. The lover, if we wish to speak correctly and precisely, should be said to be produced rather than born.
</margin>

<margin>
Love is truly and properly said to have been born from the lover and the beloved as if from parents.

...drawn, the World <note>original: "Mundus"; referring to the entire created universe</note> is distinguished by the tightest bond of the greatest love: it is thought to have emerged, procreated from the Intellect as father and from Chaos as mother. <margin>
The Lover, the beloved, and love itself—no differently than the one who understands, the thing understood, and the understanding itself—are seen to be divided insofar as they exist in potentiality; and for that reason they are seen to be joined because they exist together in act.
</margin>
For example, a man understands, and the nature of fire is understood by him. If both exist in potentiality <note>potentiality refers to the capacity for something to happen, while "act" or "actuality" is the thing currently happening</note>, two separate things are seen: the man and the fire. Understanding, too, if taken only in potentiality, seems to be a third thing distinct from both. But when the human intellect obtains the actual understanding of fire, it is joined with the essence of fire so that it is rendered entirely the same as the "intelligible fire" <term>intelligible fire: the mental concept or essence of fire as grasped by the mind, rather than the physical flames</term>. Similarly, actual understanding becomes the same as the understanding intellect and the intelligible fire, with no division coming between them. In no other way does a lover in potentiality exist as something undoubtedly different from the beloved in potentiality; indeed, both are said to be two distinct and different persons. Furthermore, love in potentiality seems to be a third thing most greatly separated from both the lover and the beloved. But when the lover in potentiality then exercises actual love, then the lover is thought to become entirely the same as the beloved and the love. Therefore, if three diverse and different natures are seen to be joined into one when "act" <note>original: "actu"; the state of being fully realized or in motion</note> arrives, how much more do you think this will happen in that supreme divine act, which is rightly considered a most pure and simple nature, free from any division? **SOPHIA:**

He finally gathers and concludes that God's internal love for Himself is eternal.

<margin>
Setting aside God's internal love for Himself, the first of all God's other loves is for the World itself.
</margin>

### LEO THE HEBREW ON LOVE

<margin>
From the external love of God for the World, both the two parents of the World and the World itself are said to have drawn their origin.
</margin>
...of those loves, namely the love of God toward the World, it is rightly thought that a produced love emerged. When this first and external love began, it is considered to have first given birth both to the first parents of the World and to the World itself. **SOPHIA:** Whom else besides these do you call the parents of the World? **PHILO:** Those whom God begat as the first and closest beings during the creation <note>original: "procreationem"</note> of the World: that is, the **First Intellect** <term>First Intellect: In Neoplatonic thought, the first thing created by God, containing the "blueprints" or Ideas of all things</term>, in which all the **Ideas** of that supreme Architect are seen to shine most clearly, and who is thought to have played the fatherly role in forming and generating the World; and **Chaos**, which, enveloped in the shadows of all those forms and containing all their essences, is rightly called the **Mother of the World**. Through these two instruments—which hold the first and most important parts in the procreation of things—God, by a most powerful love and desire, procreated, formed, and painted the entire World, expressed in the likeness of His beauty, His wisdom, and His divine essence. 
<margin>
Besides God, two additional parents of the World exist: the First Intellect and the First Matter <note>original: "prima materia"</note>. If these two are compared with God, they seem to have performed the roles of primary instruments rather than primary parents in the procreation of the World itself.
</margin>
Furthermore, in that procreation, another love besides the divine and external one seems to have been inserted: the love of Chaos for the Intellect, like that of a wife for her husband, and also the love of the Intellect for Chaos, like that of a husband for his wife. By the help of this mutual love, the World is judged to have come forth into the light. Finally, a third kind of love was necessarily required to establish the essence of the World: namely, the wonderful love of all the parts both for one another and for the whole itself—just as we discussed at length earlier when we spoke of the unity of love. 

<margin>
Three loves necessarily flowed together for the constitution of the World itself.
</margin>
All these three kinds of love arose either with the World or from the two first parents of the World. Therefore, if we say the World is eternal, as **Aristotle** <note>The ancient Greek philosopher who argued the universe had no beginning or end in time</note> believed, we would assert that these three loves arose from eternity together with that inward love that is in no way distinct from God. 
<margin>
The various opinions of philosophers and theologians regarding the origin of the World have brought into controversy whether the three loves required for the World's constitution were eternal or whether they emerged into light at some beginning of time.
</margin>
But if the World and its two parents were created at a specific beginning of time—as those devoted to piety and divine worship believe—then these three mentioned loves also began at some time when the World first started, following a certain order. For the divine love and divine desire preceded as the beginning, so that He might form the World expressed in the image of His beauty and His wisdom. Then, once the two first parents were procreated, their mutual love followed, holding the second place. Finally, when the entire World and its individual parts had newly emerged, the third species of mundane and most closely-bound love showed itself to be seen. 

If, however, we feel that the World had a temporal beginning while its two parents were granted eternity—as **Plato** <note>Plato’s "Timaeus" suggests the materials of the world might be eternal even if the world's current form had a beginning</note> thought—then that first love of God (by whose merit the first instruments required for the generation of the World, namely the Intellect and Chaos, came into the light) will be said to have arisen from eternity along with them. The other two remaining loves, proceeding from this first one, will be thought to have had a temporal origin along with the World itself. But they will be distinguished by this reasoning: the reciprocal love of both parents arose as the World began, but the mutual benevolence of the parts, both for each other and for the whole, will be said to have arisen once it was already perfected and complete. And as often as the construction of the World was repeated, so often must we consider the mentioned loves to have emerged. Therefore, various and different opinions about the temporal or eternal origin of love follow the diverse and dissimilar views on the procreation of the world. 

It is fitting for you, **Sophia**, who have set yourself to cultivate faith and piety, to believe that both the divine and external love, as well as the mundane and internal love—both of which took the first places after that inward love of God—began when the divine power once procreated the World out of nothing. **SOPHIA:** You have most excellently settled the second of the ambiguities I proposed: namely, when love first arose. For you have not only [presented] the various [opinions] of the wise...

He contrasts the views of Aristotle, Plato, and religious tradition regarding whether these loves are eternal or had a temporal beginning.</summary>

### DIALOGUE III

...you have recounted the opinions of the wise; furthermore, you have revealed the pure and faithful view which we ought to follow as the truest of all. Or perhaps in the celestial World, from its continuous motion? Or rather in the spiritual World, arising from its pure and intellectual vision?

<margin>The first love appears to have begun with God long ago, at the very beginning of the world's creation.</margin>
**PHILO:** Since we have already said that God’s external love—through which He once created the World—was born before all others, it should already be clear to you that love first arose within God.

**SOPHIA:** I remember this very well. However, since my mind cannot reach either the internal or external love of God due to the immense height of both, I would prefer you to speak only of worldly love, leaving the divine aside.

<margin>Putting aside the supreme love of God for the World, the first love is considered to have arisen between the first intellect and the first matter.</margin>
**PHILO:** Regarding these worldly loves, I remember saying a while ago that the first of them took its origin from that remarkable marriage of the **First Intellect** and **Chaos**. Therefore, after the divine love, these two first principles are rightly said to have first received love.

**SOPHIA:** I am not ignorant of this either. However, that kind of love seems to belong to the progenitors and parents of the World rather than to any of its individual parts. I am most uncertain about the love found *within* the World that was created by God (the Greatest and Best) through the labor of those two primary instruments. Where is it said to have first arisen? In the mortal part, the celestial part, or rather the Angelic part?

<margin>Love, as observed in the parts of the World itself, seems to have begun first in the Angelic region.</margin>
**PHILO:** The more distinctly and clearly you explain your question, the clearer and easier the solution will become. I say, therefore, that the Angelic World provided the first home for love, and from there it was soon shared with the celestial realm, and finally with the mortal realm.

**SOPHIA:** I pray, what reasons drove you to this opinion?

**PHILO:** Since beauty, as I have already said, precedes love, we will undoubtedly assert that love was first born where we see a greater, older, and more eternal beauty.

**SOPHIA:** You seem to be dealing with me in a deceitful and crafty way.

**PHILO:** Why?

**SOPHIA:** Because you now claim that love follows beauty; yet a moment ago, you showed that love always accompanies a *lack* of beauty.

<margin>Love proceeds from beauty as if from an efficient cause, but it certainly does not reside in beauty itself as its subject.</margin>
**PHILO:** It is not I, but you who seem to be deceiving yourself. I do not believe that love resides *in* beauty, but rather that it merely flows *from* it. Love is found alongside beauty, which acts as its cause, but I contend that love is not placed in beauty itself. Instead, it resides in the one who is lacking and desiring beauty, as its subject.

**SOPHIA:** If that is so, then we should say love is found primarily where we see the greatest lack of beauty, and that it was born there first. Since we see that the lower World lacks and misses beauty far more than the celestial and Angelic Worlds do, we should surely assert that it abounds in love more than either of them, and was the first to receive love.

<margin>Not only a lack of beauty, but also a prior knowledge of it, induces love and the desire for it.</margin>
**PHILO:** You seem to me more clever than wise, Sophia. I would prefer you to use your memory of higher things to discover the truth rather than to attack it. Are you unaware that it is not only a lack of beauty that induces love and desire? For love to strongly seek the enjoyment of beauty, that beauty must first be recognized by the lover who lacks it; it must be judged as good, excellent, desirable, and beautiful.

<margin>The love seen in the Angelic World is to be preferred over the love of the lower world because of its greater knowledge of beauty.</margin>
Therefore, the greater and more magnificent the knowledge of the beautiful held by the lover, the more intense the desire and the more fervent the love it will excite. Tell me then, Sophia, who do you think knows beauty more perfectly and absolutely: the Angelic World or the corruptible World?

**SOPHIA:** The Angelic, without a doubt.

**PHILO:** Therefore, Angelic love must be more perfect than the others and must precede them.

**SOPHIA:** If a lover’s love depends primarily on the knowledge they have of beauty, then the first place of love rightly belongs to the intelligible World...

### DIALOGUE III.

...indeed they ought to attain and equal [them]. Therefore, although you, Sophia, in your sharp intelligence, interpret these things in a different and opposing sense, and your reasons seem unassailable, you nevertheless deduce a certain conclusion which both overturns that most elegant proportion between a lack and the knowledge and desire of the missing thing, and also clearly contradicts the truth itself.

**Philo:** Although in the Angelic world—since it exists as far more beautiful than the mortal world—we have admitted that a smaller lack of beauty is found (for a smaller privation and smaller lack of beauty ought surely to follow from greater perfection), nevertheless, if you compare the degrees of the lack of beauty in relation to love and desire (of which both are said to be the principal causes), you will find that the Angelic world does not only equal the inferior world in its lack of beauty, but even exceeds it; and you will undoubtedly admit that the lack in the Intelligences <note>In the philosophy of this period, "Intelligences" refers to angels or purely spiritual beings that move the celestial spheres.</note> is greater than in mortals, leading them to a more intense desire and a more vehement love than the latter. 

**Sophia:** This certainly seems more novel and incredible. But first, set out to explain the reason why the lack in both of the proposed Worlds is said to be equal. Afterward, if you can, you shall assign the reason why the angelic lack is greater than the lack in the corruptible World.

<margin>Divine beauty is the common measure of all other beauties.</margin>
**Philo:** Since the beauty of the Creator himself excels as much as possible over all created beauties, and alone can deservedly be called perfect and absolute, you must grant that it is necessary for all other beauties to be commonly measured by it, and for each lack in the remaining beauties to be commonly referred back to it. 

**Sophia:** This surely cannot be denied in the least; for indeed, divine beauty is truly said to exist as the cause, the end, and the common measure of all created beauties; but continue.

<margin>Divine beauty exists as immense and infinite.</margin>
**Philo:** Furthermore, I think you will also confess that divine beauty is immense and infinite, and that it has no fixed or explainable proportion even to the most excellent of all created forms. 

**Sophia:** I judge this also must be admitted as most true and not to be doubted: namely, that between the creator and the things created by him, no proportion or correspondence of beauty can fall at all.

<margin>All perfections that are commonly attributed to God and to created things cannot be compared among themselves.</margin>
Wherefore the beauty, wisdom, and all other perfections of God and of created things can in no way be conferred or compared among themselves. But this brings me some suspicion: I seem hardly able to understand this name "infinite" <note>original: "infiniti"</note> which you have devised to extol and celebrate divine beauty; for among philosophers, "infinity" is accustomed to signify an unbounded and imperfect dimension. For perfect quantities have rightly claimed for themselves the name of "perfect" from the boundaries that complete them. Since, therefore, divine beauty exists as most perfect and most absolute, it seems it should be called complete and bounded rather than infinite. Moreover, this especially increases my suspicion: because "finite" and "infinite" are said to be conditions of extended or numbered quantity, which is found in bodies alone. Since, therefore, divine beauty is incorporeal and entirely foreign to every affection of bodies, I can think of no reason why it should be called infinite. 

**Philo:** Take care, Sophia, again and again, lest you be deceived by the condition of this word "infinite" <note>original: "infiniti"</note> which signifies an unbounded and imperfect quantity—a concept furthest removed from that divine beauty. For we are unable to express divine and incorporeal things except through terms or names that relate to corporeal nature, especially since language itself and the manner of speaking seem to savor of something bodily; of which thing, behold a clear example.

<margin>What the name of perfection itself, when attributed to God, is said to signify.</margin>
This word, "perfect" <note>original: "perfectum"</note>, is seen to be very little suited to the divinity; for "perfect" properly signifies something already made and worked out. However, we can by no means say that the divinity has been "made" or "worked out" <note>Philo is pointing out that "perfect" comes from the Latin "per-factum," meaning "thoroughly made." Since God is uncreated, the term is technically a metaphor.</note>. Yet we call God perfect for this reason: because he is entirely lacking in any defect, and his essence embraces all kinds of perfections in a certain most excellent manner.

### LEO HEBRAEUS ON LOVE,

<margin>In what sense all perfections attributed to God are said to be infinite.</margin>
In the same way, we call the divinity infinite because the perfection, wisdom, and beauty of the supreme creator cannot be compared at all with any created beauty, wisdom, or perfection; nor is it thought to possess any proportion to any of them. For he who is said to have created all things from nothing <note>This refers to the doctrine of "creatio ex nihilo," a central tenet in Jewish and Christian theology distinguishing the Creator from the creation.</note> must excel created things in perfection as much as the supreme essence stands above pure nothingness. Since this excellence is indeed entirely immense, it seems to utterly reject every kind of proportion and comparison. Therefore, it is called infinite, even though, when considered in its own most complete and perfect nature, it is seen to be entirely whole. Similarly, beauty, wisdom, essence, and all other virtues belonging to God are called infinite because they are not constrained to any specific essence or to any determined subject. On the contrary, all divine perfections are rightly called abstract, transcendent, and infinite because they are not limited by any specific subject or essence, just as the beauties and other perfections of all created things are seen to be bounded by their own essences.

**SOPHIA:** I am wonderfully glad to have learned the reason why infinity is usually attributed to divine perfections. However, it remains for you to explain why the lack of beauty seen in the angelic and the corruptible World <note>The "corruptible world" refers to the physical realm of change and decay, as opposed to the eternal, unchanging celestial realm.</note>

<margin>He first demonstrates that the lack of Divine beauty in the angelic and the lower world is equal and the same.</margin>
should be called equal or the same. 

**PHILO:** The infinite is always equally distant from any finite thing, whether it is the largest or the smallest. For the infinite can never be compared with either of them, no matter how many times they are multiplied, nor can it ever be bounded by the same common measure.

**SOPHIA:** This certainly seems consistent with reason. Yet, the imagination can hardly grasp that a large thing does not possess a greater proportion to the infinite than a small one, or that it does not approach it more closely or exist as a more suitable measure for it. I would certainly desire a clearer and more abundant explanation of this matter from you.

<margin>False imagination should bring no hindrance at all to right and true reason.</margin>
**PHILO:** In noble and excellent minds, we see that false imagination never brings any hindrance to right and true reason. You see very clearly, Sophia, that the infinite cannot be bounded by any kind of measure, whether the largest or the smallest. Otherwise, it would eventually be limited by some measure repeated many times, and then it would have falsely claimed the name of "infinite." Hence, we can 

<margin>The infinite can least of all be bounded by the largest or smallest of finite things, however often repeated; rather, it seems to be equally distant from both.</margin>
never apply to the infinite a half, a third, a fourth, or any other part; for that part, if taken many times, would finally measure and bound the infinite. Therefore, it must necessarily be said to be impartible <term>impartible: something that cannot be divided into parts</term>, indivisible, and immense, and closed off by no boundary or end. Nor can anything finite be found, however large or ample, that can be compared with it by any kind of proportion.

**SOPHIA:** I would like you to bring forward some example to confirm this, so that my imagination might also agree with my reason.

<margin>According to the opinion of philosophers, time is infinite.</margin>
**PHILO:** According to the opinion of philosophers, time is infinite, for they believed that it never began and will never end—even though we who cherish piety <note>Philo refers here to the religious conflict between the Aristotelian view of an eternal universe and the biblical view of a world created at a specific point in time.</note> curse this opinion as impious and profane. But since the philosophers thought that time was infinite, they said it could not be filled or consumed by any quantity of finite time, whether the largest or the smallest. For this reason, it escapes the proportion of a thousand years just as it does that of a single hour; and by the same logic, you will never see it exhausted by the latter, no matter how much it is doubled, nor by the former, no matter how often it is repeated. Thus, infinite time encompasses and exceeds a number of hours no less than a number of centuries, since neither of these can measure its infinity by any logic. Therefore, Sophia, I do not think you will ever deny that infinite time exceeds and surpasses a space of a thousand years no less than a space of only a single hour. 

**SOPHIA:** Indeed, I think it cannot be denied that the infinite exceeds the finite, whether large or small, in the same way, and that it surpasses both of them by an infinite interval.

**PHILO:** It is not at all appropriate, then, for you to wonder if divine beauty, which is proclaimed to be infinite, is equally distant from the most beautiful of all the Intelligences <note>The "Intelligences" are the angels or spiritual beings that govern the movements of the stars and planets.</note> (which are entirely free from matter) as it is from the ugliest of all mortal bodies.

### DIALOGUE III

Indeed, you yourself asserted long ago that the world represents the divine craftsman as a kind of image and statue. Furthermore, who will ever deny that the angelic world exists as more similar to the divinity than the rest? An image is always seen to correspond by a certain proportion to the model it represents, and a statue to the truth in whose likeness it was constructed. Therefore, since created things are said to be images of the creator, they will surely retain some fitting and similar proportion to him.

**PHILO.** The difficulties you propose certainly show the sharpness of your mind; yet their solution should not be considered difficult or arduous. It must be noted, <margin>Divine beauty, though infinite by its own nature, was nonetheless distributed in a certain finite manner to created things—more generously to some, more sparingly to others.</margin> therefore, that although divine beauty is said to be immense and infinite by the merit of its own nature, nevertheless that part which God, the best and greatest, saw fit to communicate with the university of created things, is undoubtedly finite. This part was distributed through various and defined ratios—more generously to some, but more sparingly to others. For all created beauties are attached to their own essences and limited subjects, and for that reason, they were made finite by them. The greatest part of that defined and participated beauty is handed down to the angelic world, a smaller part to the celestial, and the smallest of all to the corruptible world; these three portions of beauty retain some proportion to that imparted beauty. Hence, since the angels have obtained the greatest part of it from the divine power, they are rightly said to participate in divinity the most and to approach closer to it than the others. This is not because they obtained a greater proportion to God’s infinity than the rest—for what proportion can we find between the finite and the infinite? <margin>How it is to be understood that one created thing approaches closer to the creator than another.</margin> —but because they are seen to have attained more degrees of the beauty imparted by the creator to created things, and because the species or forms of the angels are seen to be less limited, less attached, and less defined by their own essences than the others. Therefore, when we say that one of the created things approaches closer to the creator than another, we by no means signify that this one holds a greater ratio to him than that one (as the first of your proposed ambiguities seemed to understand); but because the former is thought to enjoy the liberality of divine gifts more abundantly than the latter, we are accustomed to use this manner of speaking. <margin>The image and likeness of the divine form, however infinite, is seen to have been expressed in a certain finite way in created things.</margin> We shall also apply this same solution to settle the second difficulty: for the image and likeness of God is judged to shine most brightly in created things because of that finite beauty which His immense goodness decided to impart to the universe.

# LEONE EBREO ON LOVE
## PAGE 58

For it is necessary that the image of some finite thing also be finite; otherwise, it would have falsely claimed the name of "image." But in that case, which is represented by that image—for example, the Creator—He is best able to depict and express His own immense beauty in created things in a certain finite way. We often see this when we observe a large and most excellent figure reflected in a small and impure mirror. Yet, we do not say on that account that the image is equal to the divine exemplar; rather, we call it only a likeness, a representation, or an image of that highest exemplar. Therefore, it should be considered less absurd if man, the entirety of created things, and especially the pure assembly of angels, are called images and likenesses of God, even though none of these three can measure His immense beauty.

<margin>
He demonstrates through the authorities of the prophets that God, as an infinite being, cannot be compared with any finite thing among created beings.
</margin>

From this, we find the Prophet to have said: *To whom do you think God is like? And what likeness can you compare with Him?* <note>original: "Cuinam Deum similem esse arbitramini? & quod nam cum eo simulachrũ conferre potestis?" — referencing Isaiah 40:18.</note> Elsewhere we also read: *To whom do you think I am like, and with whom do I have a proportion? Says the Holy One: Lift up your eyes and see who created these things, who brings out their host by number and calls them all by name. Because of the greatness of His might and the strength of His power, not one is seen to be missing.* <note>referencing Isaiah 40:25-26.</note> How quickly this most wise Prophet shows the immense excess and inexplicable superiority of the Creator over all created things, even if we include the heavens and the angels themselves! He testifies that God produced all things, even those beyond number, and gave to each their own essences and names; and that because of His supreme power and infinite virtue, all things—which by their own lowly condition would be reduced to nothing—have maintained their essence as a certain divine gift, and have not been enveloped and obscured by eternal deprivation. What comparison or proportion, therefore, can be found between "nothing" and that most bountiful source of essences, who grants form and life to nothingness, and raises and extols pure deprivation to the sublime levels of perfection? For this reason, Hannah seems to have spoken rightly in her prayers: *None is holy as the Lord, for there is none beside thee.* <note>original: "Nullus sanctorum sit cum maximè Deus potest cōferri..." — referencing 1 Samuel 2:2. Hannah’s prayer emphasizes God’s unique holiness.</note> By these words, it is certainly signified that he who receives essence can in no way be compared with Him who bestows essence.

**SOPHIA.** You have now more than sufficiently shown that beauty is equally lacking in both the angelic and the corruptible <term>corruptible: referring to the physical world subject to change and decay</term> world. 

<margin>
He demonstrates that the lack of divine beauty is even greater in the angelic world than in the corruptible world because of the angelic world's fuller knowledge of that beauty.
</margin>

But it remains for you to explain by what reasoning the "lack" in the angelic world is said to be greater than the imperfection of the corruptible world. For this not only seems to be a new and absurd idea, but it actually seems to contradict what you said before: if you have already asserted that these types of lacks are paired and equal, why do you now affirm that one is greater than the other?

**PHILO.** You have already understood the reasoning for their equality. But I consider a greater lack of beauty to be found in the angelic world than in the corruptible world for this reason: because the angels know the beauty they lack more than mortals do. For a single and identical lack existing in two persons is judged to become greater in the one who recognizes that lack more, and it brings about in them a more vehement desire for the thing that is missing. 

For example, if you see that a scepter, a diadem, and other royal ornaments are equally lacking to both a Satrap <term>Satrap: a high-ranking official or provincial governor</term> and a peasant; in which of them do you think this will induce a greater sense of lack and a more intense desire? In the Satrap, who knows very well the things he lacks, or in the peasant, who scarcely understands their names? In the Satrap, without a doubt. For he who is ignorant of his lack cannot properly be said to lack the thing he misses, nor to desire it. 

**PHILO.** In the same way, even if an equal portion of divine beauty—which is to say, an infinite portion—is missing from both the angelic and the corruptible world, the lack nevertheless becomes greater in the angelic world. This is because the angelic world has obtained a fuller and more perfect knowledge of the immense beauty it lacks. From this, a more intense desire and a more vehement love is excited in it than in the mortal world. Hence, although all deficiencies are equal when compared to divine beauty...

<margin>
By what reason the defects of divine beauty seen in the angelic and the corruptible world are said to be equal, and by what reason unequal.

...or they seem to be equal; however, the ignorance of the defect itself is thought to diminish the lack, and consequently to weaken love and desire. Therefore, the defects of both worlds—the angelic and the material—are declared to be equal and even on account of the equal and infinite distance of the thing lacking in each of them <note>Philo argues that because God is infinite, the "distance" between Him and an angel is just as infinite as the distance between Him and a rock.</note>. **SOPHIA:** How the angelic world exists as not only equal and even to the sublunary <note>The "sublunary" world refers to the Earthly realm below the moon, subject to change and decay.</note> world in its defect of beauty, but even superior to it, I have understood very well. From this it follows that a certain more intense and burning desire, and also a more excellent kind of love, is found there rather than here; and that love certainly arose among the angels before it did among us. But this disturbs my mind not a little: that by this reasoning we seem to take away something from the excellence and dignity of the angels. For since a defect of beauty is said to signify imperfection, where a greater defect exists, it follows that a greater imperfection is also found there. From this, it would follow that the angelic world—which you judge to lack more beauty than the corruptible world—undoubtedly suffers from a greater imperfection and defect than the mortal one. Who could be found with such a crude and dull wit that they could not see the falsehood of this?

<margin>
A defect of beauty that simply induces privation signifies imperfection; but one that only kindles love and desire seems rather to signify perfection.
</margin>

**PHILO:** This absurdity would certainly follow if the "defect of beauty"—which we have already said is greater in the angelic world than in the corruptible one—signified simple privation. For this kind of defect, the greater it was, the more imperfect it would make the thing suffering from such a lack. But I never said the angelic world exceeded the corruptible one in *such* a defect; rather, I understood that it surpassed the other in a certain defect that only excites desire and infuses love. Since this kind of defect shows the perfection rather than the imperfection of created things, it ought rightly to be seen in the angels more than in mortals.

**SOPHIA:** I barely grasp this distinction of terms. First, declare to me both kinds of defect—both "simple privation" and that which "signifies the origin of love"—and then explain what difference lies between the two.

<margin>
The defect of perfection is twofold: for either it is deprived of the act only, while the power is retained; or it is deprived of both act and power at once. This first type of defect is properly called "defect," but the other is called "absolute privation."
</margin>

**PHILO:** The defect of perfection either shows only its absence in act <note>original: "actualem absentia" — "Act" here refers to the current state of a thing, while "power" (potentia) refers to its potential to become something else.</note>, while the power to attain it is still retained (and this first type is properly called "defect"); or it signifies that both act and power are simultaneously missing (and this second type is called "absolute privation").

**SOPHIA:** This division seems to demand some light from examples.

**PHILO:** Let us seek examples from you. A certain rough and unpolished piece of wood, even if it lacks the shape and beauty of a statue of Apollo, can nevertheless be marked with it. But if we take water, we see that it undoubtedly lacks not only the actual shape of a statue, but even the *power* to attain such a shape; for a statue cannot be made from water as it can from wood. That first type of defect, which is excluded from the act but at least retains the power within itself, is properly called "defect." But the second, which is entirely alien to both act and power at once, is called "absolute privation." Likewise, to bring an example from nature, prime matter <term>materia prima: The most basic, formless substance that underlies all physical things in Aristotelian physics.</term>, when joined with the form of fire or water, even if it then lacks the present form or essence of air, it carries with it a certain aptitude and power to acquire it; for air can be made from fire or water very easily. But the first celestial substance <note>original: "primum subiectum sydereum" — referring to the "aether" or the unchanging matter of the stars.</note> neither possesses solar, lunar, or celestial form in act, nor can it ever receive any of them; since prime matter is said to retain no power or aptitude at all toward the Heaven or the stars.

# DIALOGUE III.

<margin>By what reasoning the equal and unequal deficiencies of divine beauty are said to be seen in the angelic and corruptible World.</margin>
...or seem to be equal; however, ignorance of the deficiency itself is thought to diminish it, and to slacken love and desire. Therefore, the deficiencies of both Worlds are proclaimed to be equal and even, due to the equal and infinite "excess" <note>original: *excessum*, meaning the infinite degree to which God's beauty surpasses the creature</note> of the thing lacking in both of them. **SO.** I have understood very well how the angelic World is not only equal and even to the sublunary World in the deficiency of beauty, but even superior to it. From which it follows that a certain more intense and burning desire, as well as a more excellent kind of love, is found there rather than here; and that love certainly arose among the angels before it did among us. From which it would follow that the angelic World—which you judge to lack more beauty than the corruptible one—undoubtedly suffers from a greater imperfection and lack than the mortal one. Who could be found with so dull and blunt a mind that they could not see the falsity of this?

**PH.** A deficiency of perfection either shows only its "actual" absence, while retaining the "power" <note>original: *potestate*, referring to the Aristotelian concept of potentiality</note> of attaining it—and this first kind is properly called "deficiency"—or it signifies that it is missing in both "act" and "power" simultaneously—and this second kind is called "absolute privation."

<meta>This page continues the third dialogue between Philo and Sophia. Philo is explaining that while both the Angelic and Corruptible worlds lack God's infinite beauty, the Angelic world experiences this lack as a "deficiency" that inspires intense love, whereas the Corruptible world suffers from a more total "privation."</meta>

# LEONE EBREO ON LOVE,

...to your knowledge, which can be compared quite elegantly to the potential of **prime matter** <note>original: *primæ materiæ*. In Aristotelian philosophy, "prime matter" is the most basic substance of the universe, which has no form of its own but a "desire" or potential to receive any form.</note>.

<margin>☞ Love and desire kindled: greater [in the angelic world]; but in the sublunary world it is more remiss, while the former is seen to be more intense.</margin>
For just as the absence of an **act** <note>In this context, "act" or "actuality" refers to the fulfillment or completion of a thing's potential.</note> grants prime matter a certain inclination to receive whatever form it regards within its power, and infuses it with a no small desire to acquire that form; in the same way, the angels' knowledge and their innate leaning toward that supreme beauty—which they themselves lack—seems to bring upon them a most vehement love and an extremely ardent desire. This deficiency in the angels should by no means be called **absolute privation** <note>total lack or absence</note>; for whoever knows and seeks the thing they lack is not considered to be entirely deprived of it: for knowledge, love, and desire seem to represent the missing thing to us, at least in some state of potential. 

But the **lower World** <note>the physical, sublunary world of Earth</note> is defrauded of both that supreme form and the noble knowledge and desire for that highest beauty; it lacks both the act and the potential at the same time. This kind of deficiency shows an absolute privation and, clearly, the greatest imperfection. For it does not seem to provide knowledge, nor induce desire, nor kindle love as the higher world does; if it did, it would signify the perfection of created things rather than their imperfection. Therefore, in the angels, there is found a greater deficiency that induces knowledge and love, but a smaller deficiency in terms of total privation than is found among mortals. In the sublunary world, the opposite is true: they fall short in the deficiency that drives one to know and love, but they abound in the deficiency that deprives. Therefore, it is not at all surprising if they are spoken of poorly under the name of "imperfection."

<margin>The knowledge of Divine beauty held by mortals is neither clear nor lucid, as is that held by the angels. Actual intellect is not found in the lower world, but only in the angelic World. The knowledge of divine things and of God himself held by the human and angelic intellect differs as much as possible.</margin>
**SO.** I seem to have very well perceived the distinction between the deficiency of beauty that leads us to knowledge and love (the greatest part of which is said to have fallen to the **Intelligible World** <note>the realm of pure thought and angels</note>) and that privation which is utterly devoid of knowledge and love (the greatest portion of which was left to the **corruptible World**). I clearly see that the former shows the perfection of things, while the latter shows their imperfection. 

However, three additional difficulties remain to be examined. First, the deficiency of the sublunary world does not seem to deserve the name of "absolute privation" at all: for the human race, which is proclaimed to be its noblest part, is seen to know supreme beauty most of all and to desire it vehemently. Second, that kind of deficiency which infuses knowledge and desire for the supreme beauty of all things does not seem able to exist at the same time as the power to actually obtain the absent thing, as you just said: for power can be reduced to an "act," but no finite beauty is ever able to acquire that immense beauty for itself, even if it knows and desires it most greatly. Lastly, it seems truly absurd and alien to reason that God would confer upon a creature he made the knowledge and desire for an absent thing that could never be acquired by it—as you said happens in the angelic World. Philo, I greatly desire to hear your solutions to these three ambiguities, so that I may perfectly and most absolutely understand where love first arose in the past, as we began to discuss earlier. 

**PH.** As God loves me, I divined that you—being so ingenious and sharp-sighted—would propose such subtle difficulties. These will be all the more conducive to our discussion because, from their solutions, you will understand more perfectly that love originally arose in the angelic World. 

To solve the first of these, I answer you that the knowledge of divine beauty held by mortals is by no means clear and lucid. For knowledge of this kind can only be held through the benefit of **actual intellect** <note>pure, active intellect, completely realized</note> which is entirely separated from matter, and which represents the image of divine beauty like a most capable mirror. But this "actual intellect" of which we speak is not found in this lower World at all: for the inanimate mixed elements, plants, and animals are entirely destitute of intellect. <margin>

It is not without reason thought to reside as a middle between the human and the angelic, just as the angelic resides between the joined and the divine intellect. 

However, because the divine intellect is infinite, it exceeds the angelic by far more than a "middle" portion; it is placed at such a sublime height of beauty that it cannot be compared with any beauty whatsoever. And thus the division is completed by the number five. 

From these things, one may certainly know that, according to the opinion of the Philosophers, neither the human nor the joined intellect can ever directly perceive, know, or gaze upon divine beauty.

# DIALOGUE III. 523

<margin>Angels and the souls of the blessed, although they cannot acquire God’s boundless form for themselves, can nonetheless be joined and coupled with it as perfectly as possible.</margin>
...ever becomes infinite, just as it is completely impossible for any created thing to be converted into the nature of its creator. For this reason, the souls of the blessed possess no power to acquire such great happiness for themselves <note>The author argues that creatures cannot "earn" or "become" God, as the gap between finite and infinite is bridgeable only by God's grace or the act of union.</note>. However, even though they exist as finite beings, they can at least be joined and coupled with the infinite beauty of God. And this, indeed, is what the knowledge of God’s boundless beauty held by the angels provides for them; it seems that their love and desire hasten toward this goal alone. **SOPHIA.** How do you think the infinite can be known by the finite, and how can a boundless beauty be imprinted upon a limited mind?

<margin>A thing known is imprinted in the knower only according to the strength of the one knowing, not according to the dignity of the thing known; and thus it is usually received by the knower.</margin>
<margin>The boundless beauty of God is imprinted into the angelic or most blessed mind not according to its own infinity, but according to the capacity and finite nature of the intellect knowing it.</margin>
**PHILO.** I believe this is by no means absurd or incredible; for a thing known is usually imprinted in the one knowing, and received by them, only according to the capacity and strength of the knower, and not according to the nature or power of the thing known. Do you not perceive that the entire hemisphere of the sky is grasped by the eye? And that the pupil—the smallest and almost indivisible part of all our body—receives it, not indeed according to the celestial magnitude and nature, but only according to the capacity or power of the pupil? In the same way, that infinite beauty is imprinted into the angelic or most blessed mind, not according to the measure of its own infinity, but according to the capacity and finite nature of the intellect knowing it; just as the most abundant and ample light of the Sun is usually received by the Eagle <note>In classical and medieval bestiaries, the eagle was uniquely believed to be able to look directly at the sun without being blinded.</note>, not according to the most excellent and admirable nature of this planet, but immediately according to the condition and capacity of the Eagle. Furthermore, there is another angelic knowledge of divine, infinite beauty, which is most similar and equal to the thing known itself: by its merit, the highest creator of all knows his own beauty. This is exactly as if the Sun, by that same light which makes it visible, were also to see itself. This certainly claims for itself the name of a perfect and absolute vision, because the knowledge and the thing known are entirely equal and paired.

<margin>The knowledge or vision of God is threefold: the first and lowest of all is held by the human intellect; the second and middle by the angelic; and the third and highest by the divine intellect itself.</margin>
There are, therefore, three visions of God, just as there are three visions of the Sun. The first and lowest of all is ascribed to the human intellect, which gazes upon the divine beauty wrapped in the darkness and enigma <note>original: *aenigmate*. This refers to the theological concept of seeing "through a glass darkly," where physical reality acts as a distorted mirror for divine truth.</note> of the bodies of the universe that represent it—not unlike what happens to the human eye, which, being unable to look directly at the purest light of the Sun, gazes upon it either reflected from water or impressed upon any other transparent body. To this first type, a second species of vision succeeds, which is said to be proper to the angels. For the angelic intellect seems to look directly at the divine beauty; yet this kind of vision by no means equals the divine object, but grasps it only according to its own defined and limited capacity—just as the Eagle is said to gaze upon the most clear light of the Sun with the sharpness of its eyes. But the third species of vision belongs only to the divine intellect contemplating its own infinite beauty; this divine knowledge is undoubtedly equal and level with the thing known, just as if the Sun had an innate faculty for perceiving itself.

**SOPHIA.** You seem to have resolved the second ambiguity excellently. But one doubt and obscurity remains for me: how can angels—since they are said never to change and to always remain in the same degree of happiness—possess the power to pursue and bring to realization any further perfection, as you just said regarding their divine coupling? Indeed, if they are found to be always coupled with divinity, they ought not to be touched in the slightest by love or desire for that which they perpetually enjoy; for as you said elsewhere, desire is usually referred to the absence of a thing, not to its present and everlasting possession.

<margin>What kind of love, desire, and power seems able to be accommodated to the angelic nature.</margin>
**PHILO.** Since the divinity known is so much more excellent and superior to the angel who knows it, it should not be considered new or incredible if the knowledge which a finite mind has of infinite beauty—and simultaneously its coupling with that beauty—were said to perhaps receive continuous increase because of the appetite and love, both of which arise in a finite mind from the "absence" of the highest beauty relative to its own knowledge. By the merit of this increase, those heavenly intellects would more and more assiduously enjoy divine coupling and contemplation.

Therefore, since the acquisition of such wonders is despaired of, we rightly lack a desire for them; for the hope of attaining something pleasant, which is known to us and which we lack, seems to excite love and the desire to obtain it. Hence, if hope is slow and cold, it will never induce a stirred-up love or a vehement desire. But if hope itself is non-existent, and the acquisition of the thing is entirely despaired of, it will not impel the one who knows it toward either loving or desiring it.

<margin>They seem to desire immortality as a thing which, although most difficult, might nevertheless reach them in some way.</margin>
<margin>The desire for the immortality of bodies, although it seems vain, is nevertheless rooted in a certain stable foundation.</margin>

Hence, because of this divine power and authority, a certain lingering hope seems to creep secretly into their minds, followed by a kind of slow and relaxed desire. This is all the more so because everyone dreads death as much as possible, and corruption is exceedingly troublesome and hateful to every individual thing. A desire of this kind, however, does not propose to acquire some new thing for itself, but only wishes for the preservation of the present life. Since life is already possessed, it is not at all surprising if it persuades a man to desire his own perpetual safety through a certain deceptive reasoning, even if this cannot be achieved by the powers of nature. Therefore, such a slow and relaxed desire for so great a thing seems to indicate that it cannot be acquired at all, but exists only in thought. I will add further that the desire for bodily immortality is rooted in a certain stable foundation, even if it is seen to wander and slip into error afterward, being somewhat deceived by it. For the human desire to attain immortality does not propose to itself a thing that cannot be had. For the essence of man, as <term>Plato</term> rightly thought, is placed and located only in his <term>intelligent soul</term>: which attains blessedness and immortality through virtues, wisdom, and contemplation, as well as through the love of the supreme Creator of all things. For those who are afflicted with perpetual punishments and torments cannot properly or truly be called immortal: because the punishments of our souls are said to consist chiefly in the deprivation of the <term>Divine Vision</term>, which in a certain way renders the soul mortal, even if it does not seem to have been entirely destroyed.

But we, falsely thinking that the proper essence of man consists in this bodily frame, twist the natural desire for immortality toward our bodies; this desire, as we have already said, must undoubtedly be referred only to spiritual essences.

<margin>He confirms the immortality of our souls by a most certain sign.</margin>
From this, **Sophia**, a most certain sign can indeed be gathered that our souls are immortal; for unless man were immortal by reason of the intelligent soul (which truly and properly claims the name of "man" for itself), men would by no means seek immortality. For the <term>brutes</term> <note>Animals or non-rational creatures.</note>, just as they were allotted an entirely mortal nature, likewise seem neither to think of, nor know, nor desire, nor hope for immortality; indeed, even if they are seen to dread torments and death most greatly, and strive to avoid them with all their might, they perhaps do not know mortality itself distinctly or perfectly.

<margin>The knowledge of contraries is indeed one and the same.</margin>
The knowledge of <term>contraries</term> <note>A philosophical principle stating that to understand one concept, such as darkness, one must also understand its opposite, such as light.</note> is also said to be one and the same: just as humans, because they know death, therefore perceive and strive to attain their own immortality—that is, the immortality of the soul, as we have already said. They would certainly not seek it unless they hoped it could be acquired in at least some way, as we have already advised. From this right and true desire for perpetuity proceeds that other kind of false and perverse desire, which deflects the proper immortality of souls toward these mortal bodies, with several other causes, which we have reviewed above, flowing into this desire.

<margin>Plato thought love was not a God, but a certain great daemon.</margin>

Therefore, according to Plato's opinion, I would certainly think that Love began not in the angelic, but in the demonic world; the force and efficacy of which reasoning would then lead to the conclusion that angels are entirely devoid of love. For it is undoubtedly absurd and most foreign to the truth that a daemon would influence the higher angels with love, just as it does the lower humans.

<margin>
Love, depicted by Plato in the form and habit of a great spirit <note>original: "dæmonis"; in the Platonic sense, a *daimon* is a mediating spirit between gods and mortals, not an evil being.</note>, seems to be the principle only of human love, and not at all of angelic love.

...seems to be foreign. **PHILO.** We have now discussed love much more broadly and generally than Plato did in his *Symposium*. For we have sought the beginning or origin of the love of all created things from on high, whereas he investigated only the principle of human love. Indeed, since some people had placed love in the number of the Gods or Goddesses, and had falsely persuaded themselves that love continually pours and descends into the minds of men from the ethereal regions, Plato—attacking their opinion—demonstrates that love is by no means a God, primarily by this argument: that the Gods are accustomed to bestow a state of perfection and beauty upon those whose natures are said to be perfect and beautiful in *act* <note>In Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy, "act" or "actuality" refers to something being fully realized, whereas "potentiality" refers to a capacity not yet fulfilled.</note>. But love, as seen in the human race, is defined not as a state of beauty or perfection, but rather as a desire for a beauty that is lacking. Therefore, love of this kind seems to be beautiful not in act, nor in state—as is the case with angelic love—but only in *potentiality*. And this is not without merit, since love is seen to hold the first place among the affections of our soul, the essence of which certainly consists in this: that the lover may finally be able to cling to the beauty of the beloved. For this reason, Plato pronounced the principle of love to be below the Gods and, therefore, to be a certain spirit <note>original: "dæmonem"</note>, whose beauty holds the same proportion to angelic beauty as potentiality does to act. ...[perfection] it contemplates, by whose virtue and intervening love it also produces a second intelligence. To this sphere it is related: indeed, it is thought to move this sphere perpetually by reason of its own loving purpose. A second intelligence then follows this first one, which contemplates divine beauty—not directly like the superior one, but through the mediation of the first, just as if someone were looking at sunlight through a very pure intervening crystal. This intelligence also, like the superior one, enjoys two contemplations: first, of the beauty of the superior cause, by whose virtue and love it produces a third intelligence in turn; and also of its own beauty, by merit of which it produces a second sphere assigned to it, so that it may move it constantly. 

By this reasoning, those most excellent philosophers interpreted the contemplation of all intelligences, as well as the simultaneous origin of those and the celestial spheres, by carefully observing the succession and connection of both. They say the number of intelligences—under the principle of their goals—and the number of souls—under the principle of the "efficient causes" <note>An "efficient cause" is the primary source of change or rest; here, the souls are the agents that actually move the physical heavens.</note> assigned to move the heavens—is multiplied according to the number of celestial spheres. But because of the contemplation of the beauty of the superior cause, it is thought to produce the Agent Intellect <note>original: "intellectum agentem"; in medieval philosophy, this is the "active" power of the mind that allows humans to grasp universal truths.</note>, which is considered by these excellent men to be the intelligence of the lower world and, as it were, its very soul. This human intellect is led back from that lowly state of "potentiality" <note>The state of having the capacity for knowledge but not yet possessing it.</note> to the actual state and habit of wisdom by the benefit of a certain spiritual light. From the contemplation of this ultimate and most excellent end of all created things, the intellect is thought to acquire for itself the highest happiness joined with perpetual pleasure.

Now, however, I do not wish to argue whether this opinion is true or false; I judge it to be ingenious, plausible, and handled with great splendor. But please, proceed to interpret the different opinion of other Arabs in this discussion.

<margin>The opinion of Averroes, who thought that the immense beauty of God is imprinted immediately upon any parts of both the corporeal and angelic world, without the need for any intermediary at all. He believed this imprint exists as more illustrious or more obscure depending on whether the created things approach closer to the Creator himself or recede further from him; and that from this clearer or thinner imprint of the divine form in created things, there arises a more vehement or sluggish love, as well as a more intense or relaxed desire for divine beauty in their sight.</margin>
**PHILO.** Unless my mind deceives me, we have said elsewhere that **Averroes**, as the most faithful interpreter of **Aristotle**, strove as much as possible to oppose and confound those views that are not found stated by this most excellent philosopher. This was either because not all of Aristotle’s writings—especially those regarding metaphysics and theology—fell into his hands, or because these kinds of sentiments and opinions did not meet his approval. Therefore, since he had nowhere read in the Philosopher’s works about this entire connection celebrated with such praise by the previous thinkers, he judged for this reason that the aforementioned opinion of the Arabs should be rejected as being least consistent with Aristotelian doctrine. For he did not think it repugnant to truth that the multitude of all essences should proceed from the one and most simple God immediately, with no intermediary required; especially because all essences concurring in the composition of the universe, or the whole, seem to cling together and be joined into one, like the limbs of an individual human being. Thus, because of the unity of the whole, all its parts can certainly flow together from that most simple and divine unity; in whose mind the whole or the universe is thought to be figured and expressed in the same way as a certain form, skillfully crafted, exists in the mind of the craftsman. This kind of form placed in God does not introduce a multitude of many different essences into that most simple mind; rather, considered divinely, it exists as only one. But when it is thereafter imprinted on external things, because they degenerate so greatly from the perfection of the highest craftsman, it is rendered varied and manifold. For this reason, those **Divine Ideas**, if compared with the essences created in their likeness, are indeed said to be many; but because they are preserved pure and unsullied in the divine mind, they are therefore reduced to a supreme and entirely indivisible unity. Averroes, therefore, judged divine beauty to be greatest in all the intelligences moving the celestial bodies; and he believed that not only all of them together with their spheres, but also first matter, the individual species, and the human intellect—which three alone among all inferior things claim eternity for themselves—derive directly from God. Nevertheless, he then added this: that although divine beauty is imprinted in all things directly and without the intervention of any middle stage, this imprint nonetheless proceeds as if by degrees, being now greater or smaller, now more intense or more relaxed...

<margin>He turns to determine the fourth question proposed above. He reviews various opinions about Love itself.</margin>
**PH.** We find that the Greek and Latin poets, who worshiped Love as a certain divine power, differed in their accounts of his parts. Some called this god Cupid, while others called him Love; and we find that some of them even posited multiple Cupids. Yet almost all seem to have understood Cupid as that blind, naked, winged child, equipped with a bow and arrows. Many testify that he was the offspring of Mars and Venus, although some have said that Venus gave birth to him alone, without a man’s help.

<margin>What the poets seem to have understood by Cupid.</margin>
**SO.** What did the poets wish to signify by such "coverings"? <note>original: *involucris* — this refers to allegorical veils or metaphorical shells that hide a deeper philosophical truth.</note>

<margin>The allegory of the parents whom the poets attributed to pleasurable and lustful love, which they call Cupid.</margin>
**PH.** That Cupid, who is placed over love and ranked among the gods by the common people, is thought to represent a pleasurable, delightful, and especially lustful love. Hence, not without reason, the poets imagined that Pleasure was born from Love. Men are seen to abound and burn with this immoderate and glowing affection most of all when Mars and Venus dominate their births—either when they are in conjunction or when they gaze upon each other with a favorable and kind aspect. This is not without cause: for Venus is thought to provide an abundance of natural moisture, perfectly refined and most suited for exercising lust; Mars, however, is thought to bring heat and burning desire, as well as sharp provocations. Thus, the former seems to suggest the strength, while the latter induces the greatest inclination and propensity toward sexual union. Rightly, then, did the poets call Mars the father, as he is thought to confer the active quality (heat), and Venus the mother, since she supplies the moisture, which is the passive quality and plays the part of matter. Those who said that love was destitute of a father intended to signify that burning lust entirely lacks intellectual **reason**, which, no differently than an excellent parent, tempers and moderates the voluntary affections of our soul. Therefore, they reported that he was born from the mother Venus alone, because this goddess—or to speak more naturally, this kind of planet—is thought to preside over obscene and lustful pleasures.

<margin>The allegory of the parents whom the poets assigned to the love of riches and useful goods, which is also called Cupid by them.</margin>
Furthermore, the poets imagined that another certain Cupid drew his origin from Mercury and Diana, and that he also bears wings no differently than the one mentioned above. Through him, they very elegantly signified the immoderate desire for riches and possessions. They understood this to be the pursuit of "useful goods," toward which men are accustomed to run—and almost fly—to obtain. Indeed, those people are most affected by this pursuit in whose births Mercury and the Moon <note>The Roman goddess Diana was often identified with the Moon.</note> are seen to play the leading roles, with these two planets either in conjunction or looking upon each other favorably and fortunately, and being strongly placed. For Mercury makes men diligent and skillful in their dealings, while Diana (that is, the Moon) grants them an abundance of riches and possessions. Hence, not without reason, the poets called Mercury the father of useful goods, because he holds the role of the agent, and Diana the mother, as if she were the passive part and most similar to matter...
