# LEONE EBREO ON LOVE #

<margin>The conjunction of Jupiter and Venus, or their favorable aspect, is considered by Astrologers to portend the very best outcomes.</margin>
...uniting with Jupiter, the best of parents, for the procreation of honorable love, Venus is thought to desire intensely the enjoyment of the beauty of Jupiter, her husband. Astrologers also concur in almost the same opinion: when Jupiter and Venus rise together, or join in conjunction, or gaze upon one another with mild and favorable lights, they are seen to be exceedingly powerful and influential. For this reason, both of the aforementioned planets have claimed the name of "Fortunes" <note>original: "fortunarū nomina," referring to the "Benefics" in astrology—planets that bring good luck and harmony</note> due to their great and remarkable goodness. They prophesy that an infant born under such a benign and fortunate alignment will be, above all, a seeker of all good things and virtues, and will emerge as one most distinguished in noble and spiritual loves. Nor is this without reason: for in matters pertaining to the body, Venus is thought to bring the desire, while Jupiter is thought to adorn that desire with honorability <term>honorability: "honestas," implying moral integrity and social grace</term>. In spiritual or intelligible matters, however, Jupiter is seen to provide the desired object, and Venus to provide the desire for it. Thus, not without merit, in the procreation of honorable love, the former is said to play the part of the father and the latter the part of the mother. For just as Venus, when joined with Mars and strengthened by the powers of that planet, adds immoderate and raging appetites to our nature; so, on the contrary, she affects the union and marriage of Jupiter, restraining those appetites within the boundaries of honor and virtue.

**SO.** I have understood perfectly why the Poets wished for honorable love to be born of Jupiter and Venus. Now, I would like to understand the reason why they said he was a twin.

**PH.** We read a certain saying of Pausanias in Plato's *Symposium*, who thought that love was a twin for this reason: because just as there are two Venuses, so two loves are found to exist.

<margin>Two very dissimilar loves born from two various and diverse Venuses.</margin>
For indeed, each Venus is said to have given birth to a love. Since two Venuses are commonly spoken of everywhere, it follows that two loves must also be found. Because one Venus is described as great, celestial, and divine, honorable love is thought to have proceeded from her as from a mother. But foul and dishonorable love is said to be born not from this one, but from the other Venus—the one who is set over lower seats and lusts. Thus, the Poets handed down the tradition that love exists as a twin: namely, the honorable and the base.

**SO.** Therefore, it seems that honorable love is not "twin" in itself, as you said, but only one half of a pair.

**PH.** That "twin" love of which we have spoken so far is considered to consist of Cupid (the son of the lower Venus and Mars) and that Love born of Jupiter and the Great Venus. But now, leaving that kind of love aside, let us move to the opinion of those who considered "twin love" to be distinct from Cupid, and to be born solely from Jupiter and the Great Venus, desiring only honorability.

**SO.** I pray you, in what way is honorable love found to be twofold?

<margin>The reason why the Poets fashioned honorable love to be a twin.</margin>
**PH.** Some very famous Poets taught that love is a twin for this reason: because, as you have understood elsewhere, honorable love is accustomed to refer both to bodily things and to spiritual things—tending toward fewness in the former case, but consisting primarily in the greatest increase in the latter. Those who behave honorably in the one are seen to do so in both; for as Aristotle affirms, all wise men are good, and conversely, all good men are wise. Therefore, not without merit, since honorable love embraces both bodily and spiritual things at once, the ancients said it was a twin. Furthermore, this kind of doubling can be very well applied to the love of two friends and to honorable friendship: for true friends are seen to love each other mutually. As Cicero testifies, true friendship is usually contracted only between good men and solely for the sake of virtue; hence, it is not by chance that friends are said to pursue each other with mutual love through the mediation of virtue. This twin love is found most frequently both in friends and in lovers.

<margin>The beloved exists as the soul of the lover’s own soul.</margin>
For each of them bears the persona both of himself and of his friend or beloved; and rightly so, since the soul of the lover is said to be the beloved himself.

**SO.** I have understood perfectly which parents the Poets asserted gave birth to love. But now, I wish to know what the Philosophers thought on this matter.

## DIALOGUE III ##

Y 3

...I would certainly like to understand. **PHILO:** Plato, treating this subject through myth as he often does, pointed out quite elegantly that love draws its origin from certain other principles. For we see that in the *Symposium* <note>original: "conuiuio," referring to Plato's famous dialogue on the nature of love</note>, under the persona of Aristophanes, he assigned an origin to this kind of love. 

<margin>The myth of the Androgyne itself, through which Plato seems most skillfully to have described the origin of human love and its parents.</margin>

They say that in the beginning of the human race, a third type of human existed, which deserved the name of neither man nor woman alone. Instead, embracing both sexes—the male and the female together—it was called the **Androgyne** <term>Androgyne: from the Greek *andros* (man) and *gyne* (woman), a being combining both male and female characteristics</term>. Just as man is believed to have drawn his origin from the Sun, and woman from the Earth, so this Androgyne of whom we speak recognized the Moon (which partakes of the nature of both the Sun and the Earth) as the author of its origin, and worshipped it above all. 

<margin>The form of the Androgyne.</margin>

Now, the form of this monster is said to have been thus: it first had two human bodies meeting at the breast, and two heads connected at the neck with their faces turned away from each other. It possessed four eyes, four ears, two tongues, two sets of genitals, four arms with as many hands, and four legs with as many feet, such that it represented a certain spherical shape. Nor did it only walk upright in whichever direction it wished, as we do now; but with an incredible force and great speed, leaning on its four feet and four hands, it frequently spun in a circle. 

<margin>The rashness and arrogance of the Androgyne.</margin>

Since the Androgyne was extremely robust and quite terrible to look upon, it became puffed up with physical strength and greatness of spirit, attempting to fight against the Gods and becoming hostile and troublesome to them. Jupiter <note>original: "Iupiter," the king of the Roman gods, equivalent to the Greek Zeus</note>, moved by this indignity, called a council of all the Gods. After a long debate, he decreed that the humans should by no means be destroyed—for if the human race were extinguished, the worship of the Gods would be completely abolished. Yet, he did not think it right for them to persist in such arrogance, lest the assembly of the Gods suffer a stain of shame or infamy for leaving such a great crime unpunished. 

<margin>The punishment of the Androgyne.</margin>

Finally, he determined that the humans should be cut apart. He commanded Apollo to split them into two equal parts, keeping the length exactly the same, and by this means double the number of mortals. Thus, they would be able to walk upright on only two legs, and the worshippers of the Gods would be far more numerous. However, he threatened them that if they sinned against the Gods again, he would divide them in half once more, so that they would be forced to hop about as if lame, having only one eye, one ear, half a head, half a face, one hand, and one foot; they would resemble those half-images of men often seen painted on tablets. 

<margin>The cutting and division of the Androgyne into two equal parts.</margin>

Apollo is said to have fulfilled the task enjoined upon him by Jupiter in this way: after these monsters were dissected through the chest and belly, he turned their faces toward the site of the incision, so that by seeing and perceiving it, they would constantly remember the crime already committed. To help them better recognize the wounded and severed part, he stretched the skin over the bone of the chest; and having gathered and contracted all the parts of the belly that had been cut, he pulled them to the center of the stomach, where he bound and tied them all very firmly. This bond or ligament we are accustomed to calling the **navel** <note>original: "umbilicū"</note>. 

Marks and wrinkles arise from these scars, and God is thought to have left them there in plain sight so that humans, often looking upon those wrinkles, might frequently remember both the crime once committed and the punishments they endured. Now, once the division was complete, when each of the two divided parts saw that it lacked its other half, each was so intent on regaining its former perfection that it became entangled with the other, so that both were bound and joined together in the tightest of mutual embraces. Thus, completely losing all concern for eating and drinking, while they occupied themselves day and night only with reuniting their bodies, they exchanged life for death in a very short span of time. Their genitals indeed [turned] toward the parts, which...

### LEO HEBREW ON LOVE ###

...since they had previously been on the outer side, they later turned out to be on the front. Before this, they used to conceive and give birth like cicadas <note>The ancients believed cicadas reproduced by dropping seed onto the ground rather than through internal mating.</note>, with the seed falling upon the earth. Therefore, Jupiter, pitying the destruction and the lot of the human race, is said to have commanded Apollo to restore their genitals to the front parts, which are closest to the belly. This was done so that humans, through the benefit of union and intercourse, could beget offspring like themselves; being content with this, they might apply themselves more diligently to acquiring the things necessary for protecting and preserving life. 

<margin>The origin of human love according to Plato's opinion.</margin>
It is considered that Plato believed love then first began among humans, striving as much as possible to repair or restore their perfect and ancient nature. For he indeed seems to have devised and brought a remedy for that ancient sin—by which merit the human race was once distributed from one into two—by joining two into one in whatever way possible. Therefore, love is found to be double or twin in individual humans: namely, both that of the male for the female, and that of the female for the male. For individual humans now exist not as whole, but as halved; and each half strives as much as possible to be joined and coupled with the other half, so that it may attain its ancient perfection. Thus, that Platonic fable seems to have signified that human love sprang from the division of man, and was procreated by two separated parts—the male and the female—as if by parents, and that it vehemently desires the union and reintegration of both as its proposed goal. **SOPHIA:** By Hercules, a beautiful and ingenious story! I can hardly believe but that some philosophical mystery lies hidden and enclosed within it—especially since it was invented and devised by Plato, the prince of all philosophers without any controversy, while playing the persona of Aristophanes in his *Symposium* <note>original: "conuiuio"</note>. I beg you, Philo, uncover and reveal its meaning.

<margin>He demonstrates that the fable of the Androgyne was accepted by Plato from the Mosaic account of the procreation of the human race.</margin>
**PHILO:** The fable just recited by Plato seems to have taken its origin from an author more ancient and venerable than any Greek who ever existed; for it is found to have been derived from the procreation of our first parents, namely Adam and Eve, as treated by Moses at the beginning of Genesis. **SOPHIA:** I never understood that Moses treated this fable. **PHILO:** Moses, indeed, seems to have handed it down not quite as clearly or distinctly as Plato, but he touched upon the subject of the fable at least briefly and concisely. From him, Plato afterwards received it, and treated it ornately and copiously in the Greek manner, surely by this method confusing and mixing Hebrew truth with the inventions of the poets.

**SOPHIA:** How so? 
<margin>He recounts the sequence and context of the human procreation treated by Moses.</margin>
**PHILO:** On the sixth day of the procreation of the universe, God is said to have procreated man as the end of all divine works; Moses expressed and signified this beginning of the human race with an oration of this kind:

> God created man in his own image, in the image of God he formed him, male and female he created them, and God blessed them, and said: Increase and multiply, and fill the earth, and subject it to yourselves. <note>original: "Creauit Deus hominem ad imaginem suam..." - a translation of Genesis 1:27-28.</note>

Then the Prophet <note>Meaning Moses, the traditionally attributed author of Genesis.</note> added that on the sixth day the universe was perfected, and finally on the seventh, which the Hebrews call the **Sabbath** <term>Sabbatum: the day of rest, from the Hebrew *Shabbat*</term>, the divine craftsman rested from all work and blessed it. Furthermore, he revealed how, because of the vapors rising up from subterranean places, plants began to sprout and rains fell from heaven. Moreover, he discussed the manner in which God formed man from the dust and infused a vital spirit into him, by whose merit man was placed in the ranks of living souls. Afterwards, he described that famous history: how when God had prepared a most pleasant garden, filled with all kinds of trees that were beautiful and brought pleasure to the taste, and had planted among the others the **tree of life** as well as the **tree of knowledge of good and evil**, he placed man in this garden to cultivate and guard it. And he permitted him to eat of the fruits of all the trees; however, he forbade him from touching the tree of knowledge of good and evil, if ever [he would follow] the divine precept...

Therefore, God, having cast a peaceful sleep into his limbs, took a certain part from his body, in place of which He supplied flesh; and from that part taken from the human body, He procreated a woman, whom He soon placed before the man. Wherefore, the man, having looked upon the woman, is said to have burst forth into this speech: "This indeed is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called *virago* <note>original: "virago." In the Latin Vulgate, this term is used to show the linguistic connection to *vir* (man), mirroring the Hebrew *ish* (man) and *ishshah* (woman).</note>, because she was procreated from man." For this reason, a man shall leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall be joined into one flesh.

The Prophet <note>The author refers to Moses, the traditional author of the Pentateuch, as "The Prophet."</note> thereafter pursues with easy and clear discourse the fallacies of the serpent: the crime perpetrated by Adam and Eve, who, unmindful of the divine precepts, at the serpent's persuasion tasted the tree of the knowledge of good and evil forbidden to them; and the punishments that they both received. Afterwards, it is added that Adam embraced Eve his spouse, and from her procreated Cain and Abel. He relates moreover that Cain killed Abel, and, being hated by God, spent his life as an exile; he also recounts the posterity of Cain. Finally, the Prophet concludes his discourse with these words: "This is the book of the offspring of Adam, repeating the beginning from that day when God procreated man, and constructed him in His own likeness: He formed them male and female, and blessed them, and called them both by the name of Adam, which signifies 'man.' These things happened on that day when they were both procreated."

<margin>He shows more clearly than light that the Mosaic account of the procreation of the human race is inconsistent with itself and disagrees with itself.</margin>

SO. I am waiting to see what you finally wish to infer from this sacred narrative of human procreation. 

PH. I believe you have clearly seen that this most holy History is inconsistent with itself. For first it confesses that God procreated Adam on the sixth day as male and female; afterwards, correcting itself, it introduces Him speaking thus: "It is not right for Adam to lead a solitary life; let us place a helper before him," and therefore adds that God procreated the woman from the side of Adam as he slept. Therefore, it does not seem that the woman was formed at the beginning, as was said above. Finally, moreover, when the Prophet proceeds to recount the posterity of Adam, as if confirming the earlier points, he concludes that God, as you have already heard, procreated man in His image as male and female, and called them both Adam. It seems, therefore, that Moses most clearly signified in this last discourse that the first-formed man existed as both male and female at once; and that the woman was not later produced from the removal of a side or rib, as he said before. 

Furthermore, the context of the Mosaic discourse seems to fight with itself even more because first it testifies that God procreated Adam as male and female together in His image and blessed them. However, since the first male is said to have obtained the name Adam, and the first female the name Eve; and since God at first procreated only Adam, but not Eve, it seems it should be understood that He then procreated him as male only, and by no means as male and female together. Yet the words of the Prophet just cited manifestly cry out against this opinion. But that which is thought to have rendered the discourse of the divine interpreter [Moses] especially perplexed and ambiguous is that he himself concluded his speech with these words: "This is narrated to have been the posterity of Adam, repeating the beginning from that day when God procreated man and shaped him to his own likeness; He formed them male and female; and He imposed the name Adam on both on that day when they were procreated." Notice, I pray, Sophia, that the Prophet in this place most clearly affirms that God procreated Adam, and made them male and female, and called them both by the name Adam when they were first formed. But of Eve, which is the proper name of the woman, he made no mention at all, although he had said a little earlier that to Adam already...

### LEO HEBRAEUS ON LOVE ###

...procreated, and living a solitary life, God produced a woman from his side or rib, and called her Eve by her proper name. Doesn't the context of the Mosaic <note>Referring to Moses, the traditional author of the first five books of the Bible.</note> discourse seem to you, Sophia, to greatly contradict and oppose itself?

**SOPHIA:** Very much so; nor do I believe that the most holy Moses contradicted himself rashly, since the Prophet <note>Moses</note> seems to have spoken this conflict as if deliberately and with forethought. Therefore, I am persuaded that some very deep mystery lies hidden beneath this manifest and open disagreement of words.

**PHILO:** You think rightly: for the Prophet disagrees with himself for no other reason than that we, having perceived this disagreement, might investigate its reason and the true intention of the Author.

**SOPHIA:** What then do you think he meant?

<margin>
A certain ridiculous reconciliation of the Mosaic words thought up by some interpreters.
</margin>
**PHILO:** Some ordinary and common interpreters of the divine volumes, having only considered the words, have judged that this disagreement of the Mosaic passages should be reconciled in this way: that the Prophet first treats the procreation of both summarily and briefly, and then treats it in detail and specifically, adding the reason besides, explaining how God is said to have made woman from the human side. But this kind of reconciliation is not at all satisfying to me, for the Prophet seems to study to contradict himself on purpose: for he does not say God first procreated Adam and Eve, but only Adam, and made him male and female at the same time. This he also confirms at the end when he says: "And on the first day of human procreation, He called both by the name of Adam." But regarding Eve in this common procreation of man, he does not speak a single word; he mentions her only in the separation of the ribs. Therefore, the ambiguity already proposed persists in that same difficulty.

**SOPHIA:** What then do you think the Prophet meant by that opposition of terms?

<margin>
He reconciles and accords the apparent disagreement of the Mosaic words by reducing them to the Platonic fiction of the Androgyne.
</margin>
**PHILO:** In my judgment, this is the meaning of the Mosaic speech: that Adam, namely the first man, whom God formed on that sixth day of creation, existed as a certain joined human being, who embraced male and female at the same time with no division coming between them. Therefore the Prophet uses this context of words: *God created Adam in His image: male and female He created them.* <note>Original: "Creauit Deus Adamum ad imaginem suam: masculum & fœminam creauit illos."</note> Note where he first calls him "Adam" in the singular number—one man—then when he adds "male and female He created them," he seems to designate the same person in the plural number. I think it seemed good to the most holy Prophet to use this diversity of numbers to signify that since Adam, as we just said, was a certain joined human, he embraced both sexes, both masculine and feminine, at the same time. 

This exposition is also confirmed by the very heavy testimony of the Hebrews and the most ancient interpreters who followed the divine volumes in the Chaldean language <note>original: "Chaldaica dictione." This refers to the Aramaic Targums, which are ancient paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible.</note>: for these most learned men said that Adam seems to have consisted of two persons, namely male and female. But why do I seek external help? Moses himself at the end of the passage, as we have seen, concludes that God procreated Adam male and female at the same time, and called both by the name of Adam. This sufficiently shows that Adam embraced both sexes, and first, as a certain composite and joined being of both, obtained the name of Adam: for we never find a woman designated by the name of Eve until after she was separated from the male Adam. From this, Plato afterwards and many Greeks derived their view of that most ancient <term>Androgyne</term> <note>From the Greek 'aner' (man) and 'gyne' (woman); a being possessing both male and female characteristics.</note>, being part male and part female. 

But let us return to the Sacred History. God said afterward: "It is not right for man to lead a solitary life; let us place some helper for him from himself." I think these words should be interpreted thus: It does not seem fit that Adam, being at once male and female in this arrangement of joined bodies—with backs connected and faces turned in opposite directions—should live as if in perpetual solitude; rather, it is better if the woman, torn away from him, stands before him.

**SOPHIA:** In what way?

<margin>
The history calls for an interpreter. Both saying sin follows division, and division follows sin, are true.
</margin>
**PHILO:** That is certainly said to be sin which holds the power of dividing and separating man, just as, conversely, the rectitude of justice makes a man one and preserves his unity. But vice versa, we could also truly say that the division of man impels him to sin; for so long as he persists in his unity, he thinks himself to have no propensity at all toward sinning, nor can he ever fall away from right reason and that nature which is indivisible in itself. Hence, since the sin and the division of man seem either to be the very same thing, or never to be separated from each other, and always to be mutually converted: both can be very well defended—both that division arises from sin, as the Prophet narrated, and that sin [arises] from division.

...lest it should proceed from there, just as Plato believed. **SO.** I would certainly wish to understand the agreement of these two most excellent men better and more distinctly. **PH.** I will first explain the Mosaic History; then I will interpret Plato’s fable. Since, at the very beginning of human procreation, the male and female were found joined together (as we have already said), there was surely no place for sin. For the serpent, although cunning, hardly hoped that the woman could be deceived while she was with the man; indeed, the deceitful tricks of the serpent did not seem at all sufficient to mock them both while they were coupled together. 

<margin>He declares that a different order was observed by Moses and by Plato in explaining the crime of the human race and in recounting the punishment.</margin>

But as soon as they were torn away and separated from each other—with God himself being the author of this division as a good thing—so that both, standing face to face, might offer mutual help to each other and, by the benefit of sexual union, propagate the human race in a way most acceptable to God, a certain propensity for sinning is judged to have arisen immediately from this division. For then the serpent cunningly approached and deceived the woman, already separated from the man, so that she might taste the thing forbidden to her by God: the knowledge of good and evil. And the man likewise, by the persuasion of the woman and following her example, despised the divine commands. Therefore, both sinned, and both paid the penalty for their crime. 

This order is most strongly confirmed by the continuation of the Sacred History. For first, the Prophet <note>Moses, traditionally considered the author of the first five books of the Bible.</note> commemorates the construction of the earthly paradise; then he recounts how Adam, composed of male and female joined together, was placed there to cultivate and guard it. Furthermore, he records how God forbade Adam—who participated in both sexes—from eating from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. But soon after, he explains the division of Adam into male and female. Once this division was performed, he immediately follows with the deceits of the serpent, the sin of Adam and Eve, and the punishment further enjoined upon both for their sin. 

Therefore, by carefully looking into and considering the context of the Mosaic History, the division must have preceded the sin. But the Platonic fiction, although it was derived from the Sacred History and seems to agree with it entirely, nevertheless proposed a different order to be observed. For Plato demonstrates that the sin of the double or joined human drew its origin from the fact that he prepared to wage war against the Gods; he then adds that, because of this arrogance, the human was punished with the penalty of incision and division. Finally, he devised the transposition of the genitals as a kind of healing remedy, lest the whole human race be destroyed, as we have seen. 

But if, O Sophia, you were to penetrate with your mind into the allegorical sense of both narratives, you would certainly understand that the Prophet and the Philosopher, though speaking in different ways, proposed the same goal for themselves and wished to signify exactly the same thing. **SO.** Not only does the Platonic invention seem to include some most wise hidden sense, but I also believe that the Mosaic History—with that first unity of the joined human, and then the separation of the same after division—surely signified something deeper regarding human nature beyond the literal and historical sense. For I do not think that man and woman once stood in a different relation than they do now, but rather that they were always divided and separate. 

<margin>The allegorical sense, explaining something prior in the history of the human race as traced by Moses.</margin>

If you love me, Philo, uncover and reveal the meaning of both. **PH.** The Mosaic History seems to have designated this most of all: that when the human was already created and placed in the earthly paradise (that is, in the greatest state of bliss), even though he was endowed with both sexes—for the human species is not completed or filled by one of them, but by both together, namely male and female, and both joined together are thought to form one individual human who embraces the whole human species and essence—nevertheless, those two persons, who are said to be parts of the whole human, while dwelling in that highest bliss, looked toward opposite directions with their shoulders joined <note>original: "scapulis colligatis". This refers to the idea that the original humans were joined back-to-back.</note>. By this, it signifies that then neither of the two mentioned persons retained any propensity at all for sexual union or the mixing of the sexes, nor did they look at each other as those who demand the embraces of Venus <note>A classical reference to sexual desire or lust.</note> are seen to do; but rather, being entirely foreign to this foul propensity, they looked toward opposite things.

<summary>Philo explains the discrepancy between the biblical account (where division precedes sin) and Plato's myth (where sin precedes division), ultimately arguing that both stories allegorically describe the loss of a primal, spiritual state where sexual desire did not exist.</summary>

### DIALOGUE III.

...sides were said to have been joined: which union truly seems to designate a coupling of the human essence and of minds rather than of bodies. For both of them, being entirely intent upon the most blessed contemplation of divine things, were not touched by even the slightest concern for Venusian <note>Latin: "Venerearum"; refers to sexual desires or activities associated with the goddess Venus.</note> pleasures or the mingling of the sexes. But then, so that they might bring mutual help to each other and propagate the human race, they were divided and separated by God, the Best and Greatest. Then, for the first time, the woman, deceived by the serpent, sinned herself and led the man to sin; and both, unmindful of the divine precepts, tasted of the tree that grants the knowledge of discerning good and evil. 

This truly seems to signify that the pleasure of the flesh exists at first only as a semblance of good; but in the end, and in reality, it is evil. For it leads man from an immortal life to a state of mortality. Whence the Prophet <note>Referring to Moses, the traditional author of the Book of Genesis.</note> added, not without reason, that the first parents, having now committed the crime, soon realized they were naked; and having plucked leaves, they strove to hide the members required for generation as if they were shameful. For Venusian pleasures are believed to have drawn both away from that spiritual inclination which had previously rendered them most blessed. 

In order to pay the penalty for the crimes they committed, they were cast down from the earthly paradise—that most abundant fountain of spiritual delights—and began to practice agriculture, a most laborious way of life; for all bodily pleasures seem to bring us the greatest labors. Moreover, the care of posterity and the procreation of children was enjoined upon them as a fitting and healthy remedy for mortality. Therefore, the Prophet judged that the posterity of Adam and Eve should not be recounted until after both had been expelled from paradise; rather, after their expulsion, he immediately added those words: *Adam knew his wife*, who, having been embraced by the man, is said to have given birth to Cain. 

This first allegory can be brought forward regarding the human union and separation, as well as the crime committed by the first parents and the punishment enjoined on both. Because of the divinely made separation of male and female—so that both, with their faces turned toward each other, might more easily embrace and mingle—

<margin>The proper end of the human race consists in the most blessed contemplation of divine things. Immortality seems to have no need for the help of procreation.</margin>

it shows us that man was led from the contemplation of spiritual things to the pursuit of bodily things. 

**SO.** This allegory is quite approved by me, except that I would judge it somewhat absurd that God is said to have created man and woman not for the sake of generation but for some other end, and that generation—which is required above all for the conservation and perpetuation of the human species—took its origin from a preceding sin. 

**PH.** God indeed created man and woman fit and disposed for begetting; however, the proper end <term>end: "finis," the ultimate purpose or goal of a thing</term> of man does not seem to be placed in begetting, but in the most blessed contemplation of divine things and in inhabiting the divine realms. This beatitude, if continued and uninterrupted, would surely have rendered the first parents immortal and not in need of posterity; for in both of them, the human species and human essence would have been perpetually preserved. Immortal beings, however, value the succession of similar children and posterity as nothing; for we do not see angels, nor planets, nor stars, nor celestial bodies generate anything like themselves.

<margin>Generation is considered to be a certain timely remedy for mortality.</margin>

For generation, as Aristotle testifies, was devised by nature as a kind of remedy for mortality. Therefore, while man kept his immortality whole and uncorrupted, they are recorded to have fathered nothing at all; but as soon as he became mortal by the merit of his committed crimes, he is said to have relieved his miseries and inconveniences by the help of generation. However, the faculty of generating is thought to have been implanted in man by God from the beginning, so that in whatever way things might turn out, the human species might be perpetually preserved. 

**SO.** This first allegory of the Mosaic discourse which you have explained is most highly approved by me; and for that reason, you have instilled in me no small desire to learn the other. 

<margin>Another allegory most learnedly explaining the procreation of the first parents, their crime, the punishment for the crime committed enjoined on both, and also their posterity—all of which are treated more extensively by Moses.</margin>

**PH.** The first man—and indeed any other man we may take—as the Sacred Volumes <note>The Bible/Scriptures.</note> relate, bears the divine image and the likeness of God; and he exists as both male and female. 

**SO.** Why do you say that every man exists as both male and female at the same time? 

**PH.** Male, I say, and female.

# THE LOVE OF LEONE EBREO

...so that whether as male or female, [the human being] encompasses two so diverse and different sexes.
PHILO. Each of us understands within ourselves a masculine part, which is perfect and active: namely, the intellect; and a feminine part, which is imperfect and passive: namely, the body, which is seen to encompass matter. For this reason, every human being carries within themselves the divine image filled with matter; for the form, holding the rationale of the male, refers to the intellect, while the shaped matter, performing the female office, refers to the body. In the beginning, therefore, both proposed parts—the masculine and the feminine—were so joined and united in that most perfect human whom God created, that the body and the senses, acting as the female, always followed the intellect and reason, which played the part of the male, and most willingly obeyed its warnings and commands. Because of this, the human being, agitated by no internal rebellion or discord, enjoyed a certain intellectual and most happy kind of life. He is said to have been placed in an earthly paradise, which flourished with all kinds of trees pleasant to both sight and taste, and especially with that vital and most excellent tree; just as the intellect of Adam—or anyone else very similar to Adam—is thought to have shone with the knowledge of immortal and especially divine things, which is the most vital <note>Latin: "vitali"; here meaning "life-giving" or pertaining to the highest form of life.</note> form of cognition. God is then said to have commanded Adam to eat of the fruits of all the trees of paradise, and primarily of that vital tree which would grant him immortality; this is because the intellect, nourished by eternal and especially divine knowledge, becomes immortal and eternal, and acquires its own proper happiness. God is remembered to have forbidden Adam only the tree of discerning good and evil, threatening that if he should perhaps taste of it, mortality would follow. We may interpret this to mean that God warned Adam not to turn his intellect toward sensible or corporal actions; the pleasures of the senses and worldly affairs are of this kind, appearing good in form but found to be evil in reality. These are called the trees of "discerning good and evil" for this reason: because their cognition is by no means subject to truth or falsehood—as is the science of intelligible and eternal things—but only to "good" or "evil," insofar as these affect the human appetite in different ways. For if we say the Sun is larger than the Earth, we shall be judged to have spoken not of good or evil, but of truth or falsehood. But the acquisition of riches will be pronounced not as true or false, but as good or evil. Therefore, this kind of corporal knowledge, which turns the intellect away from other types of knowledge that elevate it to its highest and proper happiness, must surely be understood as the tree of discerning good and evil forbidden to Adam; for this alone could render him mortal and weigh him down. For just as the intellect acquires for itself a divinity, truth, and immortality similar to those things through the cognition of divine, true, and eternal things: so too, by revolving and turning itself around fluxible <note>Latin: "fluxibilia"; referring to things that are in a state of constant change or decay, unlike the eternal heavens.</note>, corporal, and mortal things, it approaches as closely as possible to the matter and mortality suited to their natures. Nevertheless, the Divinity perceived that this so close and tight a coupling of the two human parts—and the obedience of the corporal and feminine part to the intellectual and masculine part—although both parts raised the human to the highest peak of blessedness and immortality and rendered his true essence (that is, the intelligent soul) immortal: yet it threatened the corporal and feminine part with most certain destruction and

<margin>Intense and sustained contemplation seems to bring the greatest harm to the body and threatens it with imminent death.</margin>

imminent death. Nor did He consider only that the individual and particular human would perish for this reason—for the intellect, entirely intent upon the contemplation of eternal and divine things and seized by the greatest love for them, neglects the body itself and seems to bring about its premature death—but He also realized that the succession of the human species would soon cease. For those who have become accustomed to directing the sharpness of their genius toward the sustained contemplation of divine things, loathe amorous embraces as much as possible, and sexual intercourse...

they vehemently hate sexual union <note>Latin: "coitum ipsum"; the physical act of procreation.</note> itself as something most unworthy of human excellence. Since, therefore, the highest perfection of the intellect would have utterly done away with both the individual man and the human species, God judged it best that a suitable division be applied between the **feminine sense** and the **masculine intellect**. He decided it would be best for the sense and the intellect to descend together to desire and perform certain bodily actions which are most conducive to the preservation of both the individual and the specific human body. This indeed seems to be what those words attributed by the Prophet to the divine power signify: *It is not right for man to be in perpetual solitude; let us place a helper before him, or against him.* <note>Latin: "Haud æquum est hominem in perpetua solitudine versari, adiutorem aliquem coram eo, vel contra eum statuamus." This is a translation of Genesis 2:18. The "against him" reflects a common philosophical commentary on the Hebrew "ezer kenegdo."</note> This means: let us not allow the feminine sense to be so devoted to the masculine intellect that it does not resist it in the slightest; rather, let us grant the sense a certain faculty by whose help it may also draw the intellect down to bodies and corporal things, so that the human species may be preserved through the benefit of a succession of individuals and posterity. 

For this reason, when God placed all living creatures before the man, and when the man had perceived that a certain propensity for the preservation of bodies and the procreation of their own kind was implanted in each creature, he soon recognized his own defect. He understood that he himself retained no inclination or propensity toward the feminine or bodily part. Therefore, the man, proposing to imitate the example of the other living creatures in this matter (as the context of the **Mosaic discourse** <note>Meaning the Book of Genesis, traditionally attributed to Moses.</note> relates), fell asleep by God’s permission. While Adam was taking his sleep, God is said to have separated the feminine part from the masculine; Adam is then narrated to have pursued this part—as a wife divided from himself—with a certain perpetual benevolence for the future. 

Behold now, **Sophia**, the meaning of this narrative. When Adam was oppressed by a certain unusual sleep—that is, when he refreshed and recreated himself through leisure and the privation of that intellectual wakefulness and most sharp contemplation—the intellect began to incline toward the body as a husband toward a wife. He decided to have a moderate and tempered care for that part which was his own and committed to his faith, and to provide best for both his own well-being and for posterity and the preservation of the species. Thus, the separation of the male and female was ordained for a most excellent and conducive end; for once it was performed, the **feminine matter** obtained the power of resisting, and the **masculine intellect** is seen to have served the necessities and health of the body in a moderate and temperate way. 

But when reason later exceeded the limits set for it, contrary to the intent of the supreme Creator of all, and the intellect—utterly disregarding the proportion of that divine separation—began to turn toward matter and flatter the senses beyond what is just and good, human sin soon followed. This is what is signified by the History <note>The biblical narrative.</note> when it relates that the **serpent** deceived the woman and persuaded her to taste of the forbidden **tree of discerning good and evil**. It suggests a certain deceptive reason: that if the first parents should ever taste the fruit of that tree, their eyes would immediately be opened, and they would be like Gods, perfectly discerning good and evil. Thus the woman, moved by the persuasion of the serpent as well as by the appearance, beauty, pleasantness, and most excellent virtue of that tree, is said to have eaten the forbidden fruit and dragged the man into the same error. Therefore, both their eyes being immediately opened, they recognized that they were naked; and soon, having plucked and sewn together leaves from a fig tree, they are said to have made belts for themselves. 

The **serpent** primarily signifies the appetite of the **mischief-making flesh**. As soon as it finds the bodily and feminine part of man separated from the intellect (its husband) and resisting the most wholesome mandates of reason, it attacks that part first with cunning. It persuades it to fulfill the lusts of the flesh and to gape after the **acquisition of immoderate riches**—which, for the reasons already mentioned above, are rightly called "trees of discerning good and evil"—and thus lose its pristine purity. It adds that reason: that the eyes of both will be opened immediately; that is, that they...

He also promises that these men—that is, on account of a numerous posterity—will turn out to be like the immortal Gods. For just as the understanding God, through the celestial bodies which concur with Him, procreates and produces lower things, so too the man who is always intent on the knowledge of corporeal things, through the mediation of **sexual embraces** <note>original: "Venereis complexib."; referring to Venus, the goddess of love and physical union.</note>, provides most excellently for a numerous offspring and a copious posterity. And indeed, in this matter, our corporeal and feminine part not only refused to obey the warnings and precepts of its own intellect, but it even dragged the intellect headlong with it into a most vehement passion for corporeal things, with both of them tasting the fruits of the forbidden tree. 

Once this crime was committed, their eyes are said to have then first been opened—not indeed their intellectual eyes (for these then first lost their sharpness of vision), but those of the **corporeal imagination** <note>original: "corporeæ phantasiæ"</note>, which are primarily intent on beholding sexual gestures, hints, and embraces. From this, they are thought to have recognized their own nakedness—not by chance, but as the rebellion of the flesh against the intellect. Therefore, they deservedly sought to conceal those instruments required for procreation, namely the shameful parts, as they are rebellious to reason and wisdom. 

Next, the Prophet adds that, upon hearing the divine voice, they immediately hid themselves: that is, remembering the divine things which they had now abandoned, they were affected by a great sense of shame. We read that they immediately entered into the punishments for the crime they had committed. Hence, the sacred Historian narrated the many things inflicted separately upon the serpent, the woman, and the man. 

God first cursed the serpent with dire imprecations above all living creatures, and decreed that it should be dragged on its breast through the whole course of its life and eat the earth; He sowed the greatest enmity between the serpent and the woman, and not among the progeny of trees; and He predicted that the man would crush the serpent's head, and the serpent would bruise the man's heel. These things certainly seem to signify that **sensual appetite** <note>original: "sensibilis appetitus"</note> drives a man headlong far more than any other animal, and it is dragged by its breast along the ground: because it leads the human soul away from the contemplation of celestial things and drives it down to the pursuit of earthly ones. Furthermore, it is said to eat dust through the whole course of its life because it seems to be nourished by the lowest and most vile of all things. 

Truly, the reason for the hatred between the serpent and the woman can be brought forward: that the sensual appetite contaminates, weakens, and corrupts the body itself through the immoderate frequenting of **Ceres, Bacchus, and Venus** <note>original: "Cereris, Bacchi, Venerisq;"; an allegorical way of saying "food, wine, and sex."</note>. Indeed, immoderate and too-frequently repeated pleasures of the senses are seen to bring detriment and destruction not only to the body, but also to the sensual appetite itself; for when the body is weakened and sick, the appetite is very frequently seen to lose its strength, either partially or entirely. 

Then, for the crime committed, a punishment of this sort is narrated to have been enjoined upon the woman: that she should labor with the greatest anxieties and torments both in conceiving and in bringing forth children, and that she should be subject to the command of her beloved husband. Receive now the exposition of this matter: a luxurious and disordered way of living finally brings the greatest pains to the body, and all the delights of the senses ultimately fall back into inconveniences for those same senses. All the outcomes of pleasure, like a mother giving birth, are seen to be joined with the greatest labors and difficulties. Nevertheless, when the body follows the intellect with due love, as a wife follows her husband, its actions can again be ordered and tempered by the intellect. 

Finally, God is recorded to have spoken thus to the man, who had lent easy ears to the impious persuasion of the woman and had tasted the forbidden tree: "Because you have despised my warnings, therefore I will curse the earth. In tilling and cultivating it, as long as you draw breath, you shall feel the greatest labors and endure many hardships; you shall see it filled with briars and thorns, and you shall eat the herbs of the field everywhere. By watching and sweating you shall acquire your bread, until at last you are resolved into the earth from which you came; for from dust you emerged in the beginning, and to dust you shall at last return."

### DIALOGUE III

Let us also interpret this part of the sacred History. Terrestrial things are indeed poisonous and destructive to the intellect; and the scrutiny and investigation of them appears to be very inconvenient to the intellect, for it obscures its immortality and leads it down toward a mortal nature. Furthermore, the outcomes of terrestrial business or actions are found to be very thorny and prickly. The grasses suited only for feeding beasts are said to have been taken by Adam also for food, because he himself, no differently than a brute animal, had proposed to follow only his senses. But if he desired to taste bread, he would surely achieve this only through the greatest sweat—namely, by digging and laboring. This means that if he wished to take food suitable only for a man and not at all for a beast, and decided to carry himself as becomes a man, he would be seen as undertaking a burden of no light weight or small importance, because of the long habit he had contracted in that wild life <note>original: "vita ferina"</note> exposed to the pleasures of the senses alone. Lastly, we see that God predicted to Adam that all these inconveniences would happen to him because of sin, until he should return into the earth from which he had been taken; which I think should be understood in this way: Since, out of all the terrestrial and mortal works of God, immortality had fallen to man alone because of Divine munificence, he himself, having wallowed in the mud of base things and vices, seems to have entirely wished to become and turn out terrestrial. This is thought to have been the most powerful reason why Adam is predicted to return into the dust or earth, from which he was originally created, having shared the same condition of mortality with the other living creatures.

Immediately, however, the context of the Mosaic narrative adds that Adam called his wife Eve, as if we might say the mother of all living things, as if he wished to mark and designate by a name common to beasts that corporeal part from which all the wild and foul habits of men have proceeded, as if from a maternal womb. Furthermore, because the human intellect had descended to recognize and handle corporeal things—having abandoned the contemplation of divine matters—God soon began to instruct and educate him in the "base arts," <note>This refers to the mechanical arts or physical crafts needed for survival.</note> with garments made of skin to protect and preserve their bodies from the inclemency of the sky. Adam, however, is said to have been expelled by God from paradise to practice agriculture, since the intellect, deprived of the contemplation of heavenly things, immediately turns itself toward recognizing and handling terrestrial ones.

Yet, the ability to return, to taste that tree of life, and to acquire immortal life for himself again was not altogether denied to man. On the contrary, it is recorded that God placed two Cherubim at the eastern side of Paradise so that the tree of life might be more safely and securely guarded, and there He placed a flashing and turning sword. The Cherubim signify the two types of intellect granted to man: namely, the **potential** <note>original: "potestatis"</note> and the **active** <note>original: "agentem"; in Aristotelian philosophy, the "agent intellect" is the power that allows the human mind to grasp universal truths.</note> intellect. That turning sword, very similar to lightning, seems to signify the human **imagination** <note>original: "phantasiam"</note>, which is turned from corporeal things toward the spiritual and most flashing light of the intellect; so that it may discover whether, once its filth has been washed away and it is now clean and purged, it might again behold and pursue that vital tree, and once more attain an intellectual and immortal life.

Nevertheless, Adam, cast down from paradise and punished with mortality, seems to have provided excellently for the preservation of the species, or for a posterity of those like himself through procreation. But since he was then found to be stained and contaminated by recent sin, he is first said to have fathered Cain, a most wicked man infamous for the murder of his brother. Next, he is remembered to have had another son named Abel, whom you might call "nothing" <note>original: "nihil"; a play on the Hebrew name Hevel, which can mean breath, vapor, or vanity.</note>, because, having been killed by his brother shortly thereafter, he was considered as nothing when the logic of succession was considered. But as soon as the ancient sin lost its sharpness through the length of time, Adam, having completed one hundred and thirty years, returned somewhat into himself and into divinity, and fathered a third son, most like himself in intellect, named Seth—as if you were to say "foundation" <note>original: "positionem"</note>. This reason for the name was further adduced: because God [gave him] in place of the other son, Abel, who was killed by Cain...

Wicked and most evil men are seen to produce vicious actions similar to Cain, who signifies an evil disposition <term>habituum: a settled tendency or character trait</term>. Then, gradually letting go of these contracted vices, they produce actions that are useless and almost null, just as Abel <note>The name Abel was traditionally interpreted by scholars like Philo of Alexandria to mean "vanity" or "nothingness."</note> was produced. Finally, when they return to the intellectual life and the contemplation of the divine name, they are seen to bring forth a most happy offspring of virtues and sciences, very similar to Seth and his posterity.

<margin>
Epilogue of the allegorical wisdom which has demonstrated more broadly what can be deduced from the history of the human race as treated by Moses.
</margin>

Now therefore, O Sophia, we seem to have interpreted—learnedly and wisely, if I am not mistaken—the reason why the first man consisted of male and female joined together, and was placed in paradise, and what God commanded him; then how God divided him into two equal parts, and how both were deceived by the serpent, and what punishments all three together paid for the crimes they committed; and what remedy the first parents obtained from the celestial divinity for such great miseries and calamities; and what sort of wicked, useless, and laudable posterity they produced, and when. For all these things are said to have happened to the first man in a physical sense; but when reduced to an allegorical meaning, they demonstrate the lives and fortunes of individual men. They show us quite skillfully where their end and happiness consist, what things necessarily accompany the human condition and fortune, how far immoderate sins are accustomed to progress, what punishments follow our crimes, and how we can mitigate and lighten punishments of this kind. If you understand all these things correctly, Sophia, you will see most clearly—as if reflected in a mirror—the lives, advantages, and disadvantages of all men, what we ought to avoid and what we ought to pursue, so that we may finally attain that eternal happiness and immortality.

**SO.** For the labor you have undertaken on my behalf, I give you the greatest thanks; and I would certainly require a more abundant explanation of this sacred narrative from you, were it not that I vehemently desire to hear the allegory of the Platonic fiction. I have heard it takes its origin from the sacred fountain, and you have already undertaken to interpret it.

<margin>
The allegory of the Androgynous being devised by Plato is wonderfully consistent and in agreement with the allegory of the Mosaic history recently explained.
</margin>

**PH.** Having perceived the allegorical sense of the Mosaic narrative explaining the first procreation of man, it will not be a great matter to penetrate the hidden meaning of the Platonic fable as well. Plato relates that men were once said to have grown together into one body as twins and Hermaphrodites <note>Referring to the myth in Plato's *Symposium* where humans originally had two heads, four arms, and four legs before being split in half.</note>: for spiritual intellect and corporal sense were found so unanimous and harmonious in man from the first origin of procreation that the corporal part—having the nature of the female—most willingly obeyed the intellectual part—which held the dignity of the male—with no conflict or resistance intervening. Plato also adds this: that the masculine genius proceeds from the Sun, but the feminine from the Earth; while the whole Androgynous being, consisting of both, takes its origin from the Moon. For as we noted before, the Sun is the image of the intellect, the Earth of the body, and the Moon of the soul. Just as the soul bears the image of both the intellect and the body—which is why the soul is rightly called the "entire essence of man"—so also the Moon seems to embrace both the light given to it by the Sun and the solid matter, similar to Earth, according to the opinion of Aristotle. Therefore, when the Androgynous being was at its peak of strength and might, it prepared to wage war on the Gods. This means that when the soul was entirely turned toward the intellect and intent upon contemplation without any hindrance from the body, it strove to equal itself to those angels and separate minds. We find that David also confirmed this when speaking of the procreation of man: "You have placed him just below the Angels" <note>original: "Eum proximè sub Angelis constituisti." A quote from Psalm 8:5.</note>. Moses also brings in God speaking thus,

### DIALOGUE III

...introduces. Man was indeed most similar to us before, that is, before he had sinned against God. Therefore, so that Jupiter <note>Leone Ebreo uses the name of the Roman king of the gods to represent the Creator in the context of Plato's myth.</note> might restrain such great arrogance and boldness in man, he divided him into two equal parts, namely male and female. These two parts are seen to signify not an infused intellect and talent, as some have thought, but rather the intellect as the male and the body as the female, from which the entire and perfect essence of man is composed. 

For when man devoted himself to contemplation alone, he truly exceeded the human condition and worked his way into the order of angels and divine minds. This, however, was utterly contrary to the intention of the Creator, who had decreed that man should take care of both the intellect and the body in turn. Hence, when man altogether neglected the body and cared only for the intellect, being transferred into the class of angels, he seemed to have no concern for human composition, the preservation of individuals, or the perpetuity of the species. 

And I believe Plato <note>original: *Platonem*</note> meant this when he declared that the Androgynous <term>Androgynus: a being both male and female</term> challenged the gods to war. Therefore, lest this great evil spread or progress further, Jupiter is said to have divided man down the middle. He did this so that mortals might maintain a human life suitable to themselves rather than an alien and angelic one. He is thought to have granted a certain faculty to the body to resist the intellect, and to the intellect a certain propensity both for guarding and preserving the body and for retaining its own nature. 

From this principle, the philosopher <note>Referring to Plato</note> thought love had emerged: for separated and distinct parts always wonderfully love to be joined again and united together, and they desire it vehemently. And rightly so; for the intellect would take no care for the body at all unless it were driven to do so by love—the love by which it cherishes the body like a wife and a part entrusted to itself. Nor would the body allow itself to be ruled or governed by the intellect unless it loved the intellect as its husband and its own most noble part. 

Plato then added that when these two divided parts struggled greatly to be joined and grow back together because of their mutual love, they were dying most miserably, having utterly lost the care for acquiring the things necessarily required for the preservation of life. For this reason, Jupiter, moved by pity, saw to it that the genitals of both were moved to the front. From this, because of intercourse, the procreation of their own kind, and some kind of union of their divided bodies, they finally yielded to the divine will. 

In my judgment, these things are to be explained thus: that the intellect and body were divided and separated so that humans, limited by the pleasures of the senses, would have some care both for preserving individuals and for perpetuating the species through the procreation of their own kind. Finally, Jupiter is depicted as having warned mortals not to sin again, threatening that each of the two parts already divided would be cut once more, and then each of us would be seen remaining as a mere quarter of a man. 

I believe the philosopher meant by this that when our highest part, which we call the intellect, does not persist in its unity but is perhaps divided by tangled perceptions and uncertain counsels, it is reduced to the greatest imperfection and weakness. For just as it acquires strength and perfection for itself from unity, so on the contrary, because of division, it loses almost all its strength and splendor. Similarly, the other part, which we call the bodily part, when it seems united and gathered into itself only for the sake of acquiring necessities, is thought to retain the perfection suitable to it. But if it is seen as being distracted and divided in acquiring superfluities, and never places a limit on the desires for useful or pleasant things, it is rightly judged to suffer from the greatest imperfection and weakness. With this latest division of each part added to the former one, man...

### LEONIS HEBR. ON LOVE

...not only does he lose that prior and intellectual unity of the Androgynous, but he is also thought to lose that middle state or balanced condition <note>original: *mediocritatem*</note> which is necessarily required for the human way of life and which succeeded that original unity. Entangled in errors and vices, he seems to remain as if a medium of a medium. You have now, O Sophia, the allegorical interpretation of the Platonic fiction. As for the method of division prescribed by Jupiter and carried out by Apollo, as well as the council of the gods and other similar details—these were devised by the philosopher to adorn and polish the fable, and to maintain a sense of narrative realism.

**SO.** You have indeed set forth an ingenious allegory, Philo, and one most perfectly suited to the Platonic fable of the Androgynous. But I do not yet fully understand what benefit we may gain from it regarding the question of the origin of love proposed earlier.

<margin>Human loves and human desires seem to proceed from the harmonious division of our intellect and body, according to Plato's opinion.</margin>
**PH.** The mentioned allegory certainly seems to offer utility to us as we investigate the birth of love, for it signifies that all human loves and all desires proceed from the harmonious division of our intellect and our body. For the intellect—leaning toward the body committed to its care like a male toward a female—desires and loves those things which are said to look toward its convenience, use, and preservation. Hence, if it procures only those things that are necessary and moderate, honest loves and honest desires will immediately emerge because of the moderation and temperance applied. But if it is intent on acquiring superfluous things, then shameful loves, dishonest desires, unpraiseworthy inclinations, and soon vicious actions will sprout up. 

Likewise, if the intellect is raised up like a woman to love and embrace a man, it demonstrates that his perfection is most dear to it by these primary signs: it imposes upon and commands the eyes, the ears, the imagination, the memory, and all its faculties, that they should not refuse to undergo any labor, however arduous, for the sake of acquiring and gathering those things which primarily lead to adorning the intellect with right knowledge and habits of wisdom, so that the human intellect might finally attain its desired happiness. Now, who will deny that these devotions of the body toward the intellect and its desires are honest? Indeed, the more vehement they are, the more laudable and excellent they will be. 

Therefore, we seem to have said not without merit that Plato's aforementioned fable of the Androgynous demonstrated the origin of human loves alone: all of which the philosopher judged to be born of the intellect as if from a father, and the body as if from a mother. The first love, however, that is seen in the human race occurs between each part of any individual human being, no differently than between a man and a woman. From this first and internal love, as if from a root, and from the two primary parts of man as if from parents—

<margin>All human loves are included in three primary species.</margin>
—all the other kinds of human loves that refer to external things then sprout and come forth. These loves are indeed included in three primary species: for they either regard the intellect and immediately display honesty, representing the love of that unified and perfect man who once lived a most happy life placed in paradise; or they provide for the necessities of the body with a certain moderation, acquiring the name of "honest" only by their balanced temperament, imitating the life of man after the division but before sin; or finally they serve the luxury and lust of the body, which are indeed most dishonest, shameful, and depraved, and seem to reflect the life of man already contaminated by the knowledge of good and evil, and demonstrate that man is already confirmed and established in sin.

<margin>All human loves take their origin from the mutual and reciprocal love between the intellect and the body, acting as parents.</margin>
All the mentioned kinds of love take their origin, as we have already said, from that mutual and reciprocal love that exists between the intellect and the body.

**SO.** I understand well which parents Plato assigned to love as it is found in the human race, or in the "Little World" <note>original: *exiguo Mundo* — a common Renaissance term for the Microcosm, or the human being as a miniature version of the universe.</note>. Furthermore, I would wish to learn whether he made any mention at all of the first parents who procreated the love most common to the "Great World" <note>original: *maximō Mundo* — the Macrocosm, or the universe itself.</note> and the totality of all bodies. 

**PH.** Plato, after he, in the *Symposium* <note>original: *conuiuio*</note>...

### DIALOGUE III

...acting the part of Aristophanes, he recounted the parents of human love, as you have already heard. It seems he also handed down the first parents of the most common love of the bodies of the universe through the persona of a certain prophetic woman named Diotima—who instructed Socrates in the art of love <note>original: *amatoria facultate*</note>—reasoning in this manner:

<margin>The Platonic fiction that a love most common to the whole universe of bodies came into existence at the birth of the lower Venus, recounting that it arose from Penia as if from one of its parents.</margin>

As soon as Venus was born, all the Gods were received at a lavish and sumptuously prepared banquet, and with them, Metis's son <note>Metis is the personification of Wisdom or Counsel</note>, Poros—the God of Affluence—is said to have sat down to the meal. When they had dined, Penia (that is, Poverty), as if to beg for food in the manner of the needy and at least to collect the scraps of the divine feast, is said to have been present. Standing before the doors, she humbly prayed in the manner of the destitute that something to eat be given to her. Poros, indeed, drunk on the sweetest nectar (for the use of wine had not yet been introduced into the world), went into the most pleasant gardens of Jupiter to sleep. Penia, urged by her own want, devised by what craft or fraud she might conceive a son by Poros. Revolving many things in her mind, she finally lay down next to the God, and from him she immediately conceived Love. Therefore, from these as parents, Love is thought to have come forth: skilled in aiming his darts and most observant of Venus, since he was brought forth on her birthday. Since Venus is beautiful, he is seen to always desire the beautiful. And because he took his origin from Poros, the most affluent God, and from Penia, who was reduced to the highest want, he seems to reflect the nature and character of both parents.

<margin>The contrary oppositions of Love, reflecting the nature and character of both his parents.</margin>

For at first, he is dry and squalid, he walks with bare feet, he always flies near the ground; he lacks a home, a roof, bedding, and clothes. He is seen sleeping everywhere under the open sky <note>original: *sub diuo*</note>, and he imitates the nature of his mother, who is in want of everything. But as for what pertains to the father's side, he is always intent on acquiring the beautiful and the good; he is bold in strength, vehement, and a keen hunter, always scheming something new. He is a great seeker of <term>prudence</term>, eloquence, and philosophy; a deceiver, a sorcerer, an enchanter, and a <term>sophist</term>. Bearing a certain mixed nature, he is neither entirely immortal nor altogether mortal; but often, on the same day, he exchanges life for death and death for life, and now he seems to be reborn, now to fade away. Whence, because of the mixed and confused nature of his father and mother, he is seen to be subject to many changes; for he loses what he has brought forth, and acquires again what was lost. Therefore, he is never either a beggar or wealthy. Furthermore, he is placed in the middle between wisdom and ignorance. For none of the Gods <term>philosophizes</term> or strives to become wise, for they already are so; nor, moreover, does anyone who is wise philosophize. Neither do the ignorant apply themselves at all to the studies of philosophy, nor are they ever touched by any desire for acquiring wisdom. Whence, for this reason especially, the ignorant are considered most hateful to God: because they are neither wise nor do they strive to acquire wisdom; for those who do not know what they lack can never seek it out. A philosopher, therefore, truly seems to reside in the middle between the ignorant and the wise. For since he is not so beautiful as to be wise, he strives to acquire the rest of the wisdom he lacks; yet he is not like the entirely ignorant man, who, deprived of the light of wisdom and the desire for it, dwells in the deepest darkness and seems most foul. 

<margin>Love is placed in the middle between the beautiful and the foul. An allegory most skillfully explaining the Platonic fiction of the birth of love, its parents, and its conditions.</margin>

Love, therefore, is truly said to have obtained the middle place between the beautiful and the foul. 

**SO.** The fable indeed elegantly demonstrates that the diverse and opposite natures of both the most wealthy father and the poorest mother were expressed and blended in Love. But I vehemently desire to hear what the father Poros, the mother Penia, the time, the place, and the reason for the birth of love are intended to signify. 

**PH.** Diotima seems to have declared most wisely, by the recounting of the fable, both which parents begot Love, by what reason they brought him forth, and how Love was endowed with the natures of both, however dissimilar they might be. First, the prophetic woman relates that Love was born while all the Gods were celebrating the birth of Venus with a lavish and opulent banquet. Some, indeed, understand the birth of Venus to mean the influx of intelligence into the first angel...

-># LEONIS HEBREI ON LOVE<-

...first, and then they wished it to be understood as the Soul of the World; whereas previously, the essence of Saturn and that most ancient power of Uranus <note>original: *Celij*</note>—who are indeed three great Gods—far preceded the birth of Venus and the banquet held in her honor. [They thought that divine power] was infused into the angel, the worldly Venus, and the Soul of the World itself; however, this interpretation should be set aside as it is least consistent with the proposed fable. For Diotima herself, as you have just heard, most clearly showed that she understood the beautiful through Venus. She said that Love seeks the beautiful for this reason: because, with the most beautiful Venus having recently been born, he too was brought forth on her birthday. Therefore, this woman, who was foreseeing of the Fates, undoubtedly signified that Love began simultaneously with beauty. For any love strives toward the beloved; and every beloved thing is seen to be loved either because it actually is beautiful, or at least because it appears beautiful. Whence Love is not undeservedly defined as the desire for the beautiful.

The Prophetess <note>Referring to Diotima</note> therefore says that when the Gods celebrated the birthday of the newly arisen Venus with a joyful and cheerful banquet, the most impoverished <term>Penia</term> <note>The personification of Poverty or Need</note> stood by the doors, waiting for the scraps of the divine feast. A certain God, who was called <term>Porus</term> <note>The personification of Resource, Plenty, or Affluence</note> and was said to be the son of Counsel <note>original: *consilij filius*; referring to the Greek Metis</note>, having become drunk on divine nectar, withdrew from the gathering of the heaven-dwellers into the gardens of Jupiter to sleep. Seizing this opportunity, Penia, who was very eager to have illustrious children, embraced the sleeping God and immediately conceived Love from him.

To me, the following allegory of this fable seems very probable: when all the Gods—that is, the supreme God of all and the angels together—had decided to communicate their own beauty to the unity of created bodies, and this divine beauty was already being distributed largely and liberally into the corporeal World as if at a most splendid birthday banquet of beauty, Matter <note>original: *materia*</note> immediately ran toward them. Matter, by the very nature of the power it carries within itself, is deservedly reduced to the height of indigence <note>original: *summam egestatem*</note>. Thus, she was made a participant in those divine forms and angelic beauties.

<term>Porus</term>, the son of Counsel—namely, the overflowing Intellect <note>original: *affluens intellectus*</note>—being filled with heavenly nectar, that is, full of the divine Ideas and forms, decided to communicate his perfection to the lower World; even if, by descending to perfect lower things and accommodating himself to their capacity, he seemed to lose something of his own dignity. And this is precisely what is signified when it is said that Porus went to Jupiter’s gardens to sleep: that is, he lulled his mind, which was intent on constant contemplation, and transferred it to the corporeal World, which is occupied with motion and generation, and which is appropriately designated by "the gardens of Jupiter."

For the "dinner" of the intellect must be understood through the house and palace of Jupiter where the banquet was celebrated, and where that divine drink, which the Poets called "nectar," was taken. For **Nectar** signifies the everlasting contemplation of God himself, and the desire for divine beauty to communicate itself. Therefore, the celestial Intellect, considered the son of Counsel (that is, of the Supreme God), or perhaps being the Supreme God himself, decided to make the lower World a participant in his beauty and perfection. The most impoverished and needy Penia immediately ran to him; that is, Matter, which by the nature of its potentiality is established in the greatest beggary and is most eager to acquire perfection for itself, approached the Intellect. And from the Intellect—which was most desirous of perfecting corporeal things and was, as it were, "drunk"—she is said to have conceived and given birth to Love. This occurred because the Intellect was sleeping for a short time from its eternal, divine contemplation, calling back its mind from that sharpest contemplation to grant some part of its own perfection to the needy Matter. For **Love** is seen to signify perfection existing not in act, but in potentiality.

The same condition is seen to be undergone by the intellect when it is infused into a transitory and mortal body: for soon, degenerating from the excellence and dignity of the pure intellect, it is turned into a form joined with potentiality, and is called the "intellect of potentiality" <note>original: *intellectus potestatis*</note>. This intellect, by the benefit of its intellectual nature, discerns the beautiful...

<meta>This page continues Philo's interpretation of the Platonic myth of the birth of Love.
