-># DIALOGUE III<-

...but, disturbed by the disadvantage of its possession <note>original: *possessione exturbatus*; referring to the state of lacking form or beauty</note>, it seeks actual beauty. And this is precisely what Plato seems to have signified when he said that love intervenes as a medium between the beautiful and the ugly. For all the forms and powers of the intellect are entangled with matter: they occupy a middle place between matter—which is entirely formless and utterly crude—and the separate, actual, angelic, and intelligent forms, which are said to be as beautiful as possible. This is why Diotima, with great wisdom, seems to have gathered into Love—as if into the common offspring of them both—the poverty, mortality, changeability, and material density <note>original: *concretionem*</note> of the mother, Matter, along with the affluence, eternity, stability, and intelligence of the father, <term>Porus</term> <note>The personification of Resource or Abundance</note>. Furthermore, she presented the one who practices philosophy as being not yet truly wise; for the <term>intellect of potentiality</term> <note>The mind's capacity to learn, rather than the knowledge it already possesses</note> indeed desires wisdom and retains a certain inclination and power to acquire it for itself, yet it does not yet deserve to be called "wise in actuality" in the same way the angelic intellect does.

<margin>The Platonic fiction hides many deeper meanings.</margin>
Thus, under the veil of this fiction, Diotima seems to have hidden several wonderful meanings. First, she demonstrated that the intellect of potentiality exists as a certain part of the <term>agent intellect</term> <note>The "Active Intellect," a concept in medieval philosophy describing the power that makes thinking possible</note>, whether that be called angelic or divine. Next, she signified that this "potentiality" does not happen to the intellect because of its own intelligent nature—as some have falsely persuaded themselves—but because of its contagious association with the most impoverished matter, which is entirely devoid of all actual forms and reduced to pure potentiality. Furthermore, she showed that the first and most powerful reason for procreating love consists in an innate beauty itself. Finally, she seems to have hinted that the immediate and conjoined origin of love must be attributed to the knowledge of the beautiful as the father, and to the absence or defect of beauty as the mother. For whatever is loved and desired must surely first be known by us as beautiful, and we must also either lack it, or be capable of lacking it at some time, and thus we desire its perpetual preservation. Therefore, Sophia, I believe you have now perceived that the love common to the lower world was fathered by the knowledge of beauty and mothered by its absence.

**SOPHIA:** I have indeed. But it troubles me that the parents you mentioned are only suited and adapted to the corporeal world—or rather, only to the lower and mortal world. Yet you said earlier that love is found primarily and most importantly in the Angelic World; and you also attributed those same immediate causes—namely, the knowledge of beauty and its defect—to that world as well.

**PHILO:** We spoke truly when we said that not only the love of lower beings, but even more so angelic love, draws its origin from the knowledge of a beauty that it lacks. But in that case, we were looking toward that divine and immense beauty which all created intellects lack equally, and which they know most perfectly, love wondrously, and desire most vehemently. However, the beauty of the Angelic World is properly so-called: it knows no temporal origin whatsoever. For it persists as entirely eternal and immutable, and we cannot find a new origin for its love. But if we wished to assign some birth to it, 

<margin>The Love which Plato testifies was born to Porus and Penia when Venus had just arisen seems to be adaptable only to the corporeal and mortal world, and by no means to the angelic or divine World.</margin>
we would say that love was introduced into the Angelic World from all eternity. Nor does the defect of this beauty seen in that world happen because of a union between the most destitute <term>Penia</term> <note>Poverty or Need</note> and the most wealthy <term>Porus</term>—that is, from the association or mixing of matter with the intellect. For what matter could be imagined to exist in the angels? Rather, this defect is thought to occur because of the imperfection of any created thing precisely because it is "created," and its shortcoming compared to the supreme perfection of the Creator; or rather, because of the excess of divine beauty over all the beauties of created things. For this reason, the parents mentioned earlier by us—or rather by Diotima or Plato—gave birth to a "new" love at the birth of the lower Venus (which signifies the beauty imparted to mortal or falling bodies); this applies only to the lower world, and by no means...

<meta>catchword: ...to [the higher world]</meta>

<summary>Philo explains that while human love arises from a mix of potential intellect and physical matter (symbolized by Porus and Penia), angelic love is an eternal desire for the infinite beauty of God, born not from material lack but from the inherent limitation of being a created being.</summary>

# LEONE EBREO ON LOVE,

...which they have declared to be appropriate to the angelic state. For the Angelic <note>The "Angelic" refers to the higher, purely intellectual realm of existence</note> surpasses the drunken <term>Porus</term> <note>original: *Porum*; the personification of Resource/Abundance in Plato's myth</note>, resting in the garden of Jove, by an immense distance, and it seems to have had no commerce whatsoever with the most wretched <term>Penia</term> <note>original: *Penia*; the personification of Poverty/Need</note>. **SOPHIA.** I have well understood the myths devised both by the poets and the philosophers who, in seeking the origin of love, investigated its parents; I have also understood your hidden and most learned interpretations of them. I would further desire that you discuss, as clearly as you are accustomed to do, which of the first and most ancient fathers declared love to be not only human, but a universal principle common to all things. **PHILO.** I will most gladly comply with your wish. But first, I shall state whom I consider to be the parents of any kind of love in a general sense. Then, if it seems right to you, I will attempt to apply those parents to both human and worldly love. **SOPHIA.** You have chosen the best possible order to follow, for a general understanding must always precede specific knowledge. Tell me then, I pray, whom do you think can be designated as the parents of love, regardless of its type? **PHILO.** For my part, I do not call pure deprivation the mother, nor affluent knowledge the father of every love, as Diotima <note>The priestess in Plato's *Symposium* who teaches Socrates about Love</note> felt; nor do I confirm that the most beautiful Venus—at the birth of love, when neither its father nor mother were present—performed the duty of midwife, or of <term>Lucina</term> <note>The Roman goddess of childbirth</note>, or of the <term>Parcae</term> <note>The Fates</note>. This is what Plato seems to have intended in other places, contrary to the common opinion of almost everyone who thinks love is either joined with one of the gods or is the offspring of Venus alone. But, setting aside the fictions and myths of the poets,

<margin>
Love, taken most generally, takes its origin from the beautiful beloved as if from a father, and from the knowledge of the beautiful joined with its observed absence in the lover, as if from a mother.
</margin>

I tell you with certainty that all loves, however they are categorized, derive a common origin from the "beautiful" as a kind of father, and from the "knowledge of the beautiful" mixed with its "absence" as a kind of mother. Indeed, from both of these meeting and coming together into one—as if from legitimate parents—all loves and all desires truly arise. For the beautiful, when it is known to be lacking, is immediately loved and sought after. Thus, love is seen to come into the light soon after being conceived in the mind of the one who knows, who lacks, and who seeks the beautiful. Because of this, in the procreation of love, the beautiful beloved is seen to play the paternal part, and the mind of the lover, receiving the seeds of the beautiful, is seen to play the maternal part. Indeed, the "seeds of the beautiful" are said to be nothing other than certain impressed mental images <note>original: *exempla*; the formal patterns or species of the object perceived by the mind</note> of beauty itself in the mind of the one who knows. The mind, being "pregnant" with these, strives to achieve full knowledge of the beautiful, just as a mother strives to bring forth an offspring as similar as possible to the father. Above, we advised that the beloved reflects the nature of the father and the generator, while the lover reflects the nature of the mother who conceives from the beloved and—as Plato testifies—seeks to give birth in the presence of beauty. **SOPHIA.** This distribution of paternal and maternal roles in the procreation of love, which you have devised, is greatly approved by me. But before we move on to the rest, I would desire to reconcile certain things that seem to conflict. First, you called the "knowledge of the absent beautiful" the mother of love. Then, you added that the mind of the lover, having already conceived the "form" of the beautiful, seeks and loves that very thing. This makes me perplexed and uncertain; for if the mind of the one who knows is said to have already "conceived" the beautiful, since it carries it constantly within itself, it seems not to lack it at all. For we see that pregnant women carry the fetuses enclosed in their wombs with them, and by no means do they lack them.

<margin>
The lover is most strongly impelled to acquire and achieve union with the beloved by the mental image and form of the beautiful beloved being vehemently impressed upon the mind.
</margin>

**PHILO.** Unless the mental form <note>original: *species*; the intelligible form or appearance</note> of the beautiful had first insinuated itself into the mind of the lover under the guise of the "good" and the "pleasant," the lover would certainly never be induced to love the beautiful itself. For those who are entirely devoid of beauty neither are beautiful, nor are they seen to desire the beautiful. But those who desire the beautiful are not considered to be entirely deprived of it; for they at least *know* it, and their minds seem to have at least conceived the image of beauty. Yet, because they have not yet attained a perfect union with beauty itself, they therefore vehemently desire it as a matter of the greatest importance. They primarily seek to enjoy a most close union with the beautiful thing joined to them, whose form itself...

...impressed upon their minds, it greatly impels and inflames them to achieve this union; just as pregnant women desire to deliver their sons and bring the enclosed offspring into the light. Therefore the lover—whom we often call the "mother" of love—even if he has not yet acquired a perfect union with the beloved, nevertheless carries within an enclosed "species" <note>original: *speciem*; here meaning a mental image or essence</note> or image of the beloved beauty. This image wonderfully inflames him to love and seek a conjunction with the beauty he lacks. **SO.** You have spoken rightly. But there remains another ambiguity for you to explain. You seem to have inferred from your previous words that the lover—who, like a woman, is embraced by the beautiful beloved as if by a male—will give birth to the offspring's parent, no differently than a son. For you said that the common progeny of the lover and the beloved is nothing other than the very union and enjoyment <term>fruitio</term> <note>The state of "fruition" or "enjoyment" is the ultimate goal of love in Renaissance philosophy, representing the peaceful possession of the beloved</note> of the beloved, which the lover so vehemently desires.

<margin>The union and enjoyment of beauty acquired by the lover seems to differ somewhat from the beloved beauty itself.</margin>

**PH.** You argue most subtly, Sophia. But you should certainly realize that the intimate enjoyment of beauty should not be considered one and the same as the beauty itself, even if it is seen to be most similar to it, just as a son is to his father. For with the likeness of the father, a certain maternal impression of loving knowledge is joined; for the act of enjoyment reaches from the lover (the knower) toward the beauty (the known and loved). Thus, since it exists as the common son of both, it seems to consist of maternal knowledge as if of matter, and of paternal beauty as if of form. Rightly, therefore, did Plato define love as the desire to give birth to a beautiful offspring <note>original: *fœtus pulchri*; a reference to Diotima's speech in Plato's *Symposium*</note> that is most like its father. This definition can indeed be perfectly adapted to both intellectual and sensible <note>perceptible by the senses</note> love.

**SO.** For what reason, I pray, Philo, is each of these types of love called a desire to give birth to beauty? And why are these most beautiful "offspring" seen to be so vehemently desired by lovers?

<margin>Every love, both sensible and intellectual, is defined as a certain vehement desire to give birth to beautiful offspring.</margin>
<margin>The marvelous love of parents toward their children.</margin>

**PH.** Who is unaware how much not only humans, but indeed all living creatures, desire to recognize those similar to themselves? And who does not know how many labors, hardships, dangers, and finally death itself, parents—and mothers especially—expose themselves to for the sake of procreating, educating, and keeping their offspring safe?

<margin>The double intention of generation.</margin>

The first and most immediate intention of generation is to produce a beautiful offspring, very similar to the one from whom the mother conceived. But the last and somewhat more remote aim of that same generation is to obtain a hoped-for and desired immortality.

<margin>Generation strives toward the preservation of the species and immortality as its proposed goal.</margin>

For as Aristotle affirms, since individual living creatures can by no means preserve their own safety forever, they strive to achieve a specific immortality <note>original: *immortalitatem specificam*; meaning the immortality of the species through reproduction, since the individual must die</note> by generating things like themselves. Hence parents are often seen to love the lives of their children more than their own, and to provide more for their longevity. And not without reason: for they know they are hastening toward death; but from the safety of their children, who are rightly called "paternal limbs," they hope to attain a certain noble immortality through the benefit of continuous and frequently repeated procreation of like beings.

<margin>He declares the offspring and immortality of the human soul.</margin>

These two types of ends <note>goals or purposes</note> are also found to occur in the human soul. Since the soul is full of beauty, virtue, and intellectual wisdom—and is as if pregnant—it most greatly strives and desires to bring forth beautiful offspring: namely, virtuous actions and wise habits. By the benefit of such noble progeny, the soul achieves true immortality, which indeed seems to be far preferred to the perpetual succession of physical bodies. In this respect, however, the soul's immortality is very similar to the physical kind. For just as the limbs of parents are thought to flourish and be perpetually preserved in their progeny even if the parents themselves die, so the faculties of the soul, although they perish <note>as the individual dies</note>, are thought to acquire or attain perpetuity through virtuous actions and intelligible habits, which intervene as a kind of spiritual posterity. In this way, then, the roles of the father (the beautiful beloved) and the mother (the lover’s knowledge) have been assigned in the procreation of love. And thus the lover, conceiving as a woman from the beautiful beloved, strives and desires to bring forth an offspring most similar to the parent in beauty, so that through its intervention...

For the "father" is the very beloved beauty itself; the "pregnant mother" is the lover carrying and knowing the most beautiful <term>species</term> <note>original: *speciem*; here meaning a mental image, form, or essence</note> and image of the beloved impressed upon them; and the "offspring" so greatly desired is the return into that beauty itself through the benefit of a most intimate enjoyment. But I can hardly understand why beauty is valued so highly by you. For if it precedes every love and every lover, it would seem to precede not only this lower world and the human mind, but even the celestial and angelic world, since each of these is seen to be endowed with love and to engage in loving. Furthermore, since the Divinity himself—as you once said, and as the Sacred Volumes <note>A reference to the Bible, specifically the Hebrew Scriptures</note> also testify—pursues the things created by him with ineffable love, how, I ask, can any beauty be thought to precede the Divinity, who is the first and supreme of all things?

<margin>Beloved beauty, when the order of nature is carefully seen and considered, always precedes the lover and love itself.</margin>
**PH.** Let it not cause you any wonder, Sophia, that beauty is endowed with such a nature that by its merit every beloved is said to be loved and every lover to love. Thus it is the beginning, the middle, and the end of every love: it is called the "beginning" by reason of the beloved; the "middle" because it is reflected from the beloved to the lover; and the "end" by reason of the lover returning to the "beginning" to enjoy it and be joined to it. Since the Supreme Architect <note>original: *summus opifex*; God as the creator</note> of the world is said to be the First Beauty, the beauty of any created thing is judged, not rashly, to consist in the perfection of the work fashioned by that divine artisan. By merit of this perfection, the work represents its maker, and created things are seen to be most similar to the Creator himself. Since, therefore, the Divinity has shared his bounty with all parts of the universe, it should not be seen as strange, but rather as just, that he be considered to precede all parts of the universe. He makes the things to which he has communicated himself more largely than others to be lovable; likewise, he is seen to infuse the knowledge and love of them into the rest, joined with a vehement desire for their beauty first, and through that, for participating in the divine beauty itself. Indeed, this divine beauty not only precedes the love implanted in created things—whether corporeal and fading, celestial, or incorporeal, spiritual, and angelic—but it even precedes the love of God himself for the things he has created.

<margin>A very elegant definition of divine love.</margin>
For divine love is truly nothing other than a certain desire found in God that the beauty of created things should increase, and that they should finally be rendered most similar—according to the capacity of each—to the beauty of the Creator's form, after whose example they were created. Therefore, if you consider God alone, divine beauty precedes divine love, and God in the role of the beautiful and the beloved certainly precedes himself in the role of the lover.

<margin>He brings back to our memory the definition of beauty handed down earlier.</margin>
**SO.** Although you seem to have satisfied the difficulty I proposed with this response, I still cannot quite perceive the excellence or pre-eminence of that beauty you celebrate with such great praise; nor do I fully understand why it deserves to be called a most common principle of all sublime and perfect things. It would be very pleasing to me if you would treat the essence of this beauty more richly and copiously. I remember very well that you previously offered a definition of it, saying that beauty is nothing other than a certain "grace" <note>original: *gratiam*; a spiritual charm or divine influence</note> which allures the soul, when it is suffused with pleasurable knowledge, to love of itself. But as to the essence of this grace, or what that grace assumes for itself in the definition of beauty, or what help and importance it is thought to bring both to the Creator and to the universe of created things—to tell the truth, I am as ignorant of these as I was of the beauty you defined earlier.

<margin>Since beauty is something spiritual and entirely foreign to the filth of matter and bodily stain, it can be known and understood only by purified spirits, and not at all by bodily faculties.</margin>

### DIALOGUE III.

...of the three imperfect <term>senses</term> <note>Philo refers to the Aristotelian hierarchy of senses, where touch, taste, and smell are considered "lower" or more "material" than sight and hearing.</note>, it enters into our souls neither through touch, nor through taste, nor through smell. For you will never call temperate physical qualities, nor the most pleasant Venereal <note>original: *Venereos*; referring to sexual love or the goddess Venus</note> embraces "beautiful," nor will you ever commend sweet flavors or the most fragrant odors with the praise of beauty. Rather, beauty seems to fortify a path for itself to the soul through only two spiritual senses: first, through hearing, when we judge precise speech, elegant orations, subtle disputations, resonant songs, musical harmonies, proportional accords, and other similar things to be worthy of the honor of beauty; and then also through the faculty of sight itself, when we proclaim that artfully elaborated figures, perfectly tempered colors, praiseworthy compositions of bodies, shining lights, and many other things are beautiful. All of these things demonstrate more than enough that the name of "beauty" signifies something spiritual, removed from matter and the common impurity of bodies. Furthermore, we have declared above that even greater beauties are found in the more excellent faculties of our soul, which further transcend the corporeal condition: first, in the imagination, which is made most beautiful by sharp reasonings, prudent thoughts, and skillful inventions; then, much more illustriously in the intellect and in reason devoid of matter, which acquires the greatest beauty for itself when cultivated by noble studies, liberal arts, recondite disciplines, as well as by studious habits and actions; and finally, in the most perfect way, in the mind entirely separated from matter, which at last consists in Wisdom—a solid image expressed from divine beauty—attained at the final and supreme level of human happiness. From these things, Sophia, you can perceive how beauty ought to be considered foreign to matter and corporeal impurity, and how it rightly belongs to a spiritual nature.

<margin>The common people, no differently than with the praise of magnitude, are accustomed to attribute beauty truly and properly only to bodies, but to incorporeal things only through a certain similarity which they have with bodies.</margin>

**SO.** And yet we see the common run of men everywhere bestowing the praise of beauty only upon bodies, as if it were their own proper attribute—and perhaps not without merit, since beauty seems to belong to bodies first and foremost. For if incorporeal things are sometimes called beautiful, they are commended with this kind of praise because of a certain agreement and similarity which they have with bodies: just as we are also accustomed to call those same incorporeal things—such as the soul, talent, memory, art, and other similar things—"great" <note>original: *magna*; meaning large or great in size</note> at times, using a metaphor taken from bodies. For since incorporeal things are endowed with neither quantity nor dimension, they can by no means be properly called "large" or "small," except because of a certain similarity they have with measured bodies. By the same reasoning, the name of beauty seems to be applied properly to bodies, but to incorporeal things only improperly and metaphorically.

**PH.** Even if this is seen to occur in magnitude <note>size or greatness</note> as a proper affection of quantity and of the body, why do you feel the same about beauty?

**SO.** Setting aside the common manner of speaking, which attributes this name only to bodies, let us look at the reason. The common people (whom reason favors and many philosophers have agreed with) judge that true and proper beauty consists in the due proportion of the parts to the whole, and in a praiseworthy <term>symmetry</term> <note>original: *symmetria*; the proportional relationship between parts</note> of the whole with its parts. Therefore, beauty itself seems to be a certain property only of commensurable bodies, and of wholes that consist only of parts; thus, it properly presupposes a body endowed with quantity. If the name of beauty is sometimes transferred to the praise of incorporeal things, this happens because they also bear some similarity to bodies, and—no differently than bodies—they seem to consist of parts disposed and arranged in a right order, preserving a certain proportion: as we could demonstrate in a harmonic accord or an artful oration. Thus, not without merit, all such things are called beautiful because of the agreement they have obtained with bodies that are conspicuous for their praiseworthy composition and proportion of parts. Similarly, the thoughts and concepts of the imagination, reason, and the mind [are called beautiful] because of the parts composing the whole itself...

<summary>Philo argues that beauty is a spiritual quality perceived only by the "spiritual" senses (sight and hearing) and the higher intellect, while Sophia counters that beauty is properly defined by physical proportion and symmetry.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the third dialogue between Philo and Sophia. Philo is arguing that true beauty is spiritual and intellectual, while physical beauty is merely a faint reflection or "shadow" of that higher reality. He is countering the common view that beauty is simply the arrangement of physical parts.</meta>

...of things [the spiritual] are said to be very similar to the bodies themselves, which consist of parts endowed with dimension and truly exist as beautiful, and they are thus metaphorically called beautiful. Therefore, beauty—no differently than magnitude—seems to be properly placed and reside in bodies, as things which are properly subject to quantity and the composition of parts. 

**PH.** <note>Philo</note> The common people use this name "beautiful" according to a certain common and vulgar knowledge they have of beauty, as it is perceived; for unlearned men, unable to lift themselves up to perceive any other kind of beauty beyond what they receive through their eyes or ears, persuade themselves that no other beauty exists except the corporeal one—unless perhaps a fictional one, or one formed in the imagination seen during sleep.

<margin>Learned and wise men believe that beauty truly and properly belongs only to spiritual things, and from there it was distributed to bodies to adorn them and make them shapely.</margin>

But those who look with the edge and light of the mind far higher than those who look with corporeal eyes, claim for themselves a much greater knowledge of incorporeal <note>non-physical or spiritual</note> beauty than those people have of corporeal beauty. Indeed, they recognize that this beauty found in bodies, if compared with the true beauty of incorporeal things, is small, lowest, and wonderfully thin—existing as a shadow or a certain image of spiritual beauty derived from it. They think it is nothing else than a splendor imparted to the corporeal world from the spiritual world. 

Nor do they believe that the beauty inherent in bodies proceeds from their corporeal nature or from matter; otherwise, all bodies and everything consisting of matter would be seen to exist as beautiful in the same way, since matter and corporeal nature are equally distributed among all bodies. Or larger bodies would have received a larger portion of beauty, the opposite of which we often see happen: for beauty requires a moderation of the body, just as deformity, on the contrary, is said to "sin" <note>in the sense of an error or failing</note> in that very excess or defect. 

Rightly, therefore, these most distinguished men believe that beauty is derived into bodies from higher and incorporeal things; and indeed, the less beauty bodies have obtained from those sources, the more deformed they surely are. 

<margin>Corporeal deformity is proper to the body, but beauty truly and properly belongs to spiritual and incorporeal nature.</margin>

Therefore, deformity of bodies seems to be truly corporeal and proper to them, while beauty happens to them rather from the goodness and liberality of spiritual things. 

For this reason, you too, Sophia, do not look only at these corporeal beauties, but set beauty before yourself to be contemplated rather by the light of the mind and intellect, if you desire to know those true and most excellent beauties entirely unknown to the common people. For just as those who have lost the use of their eyes cannot perceive well-arranged figures and perfectly tempered colors, so those who labor under blindness of the mind can have no knowledge at all of the most excellent and spiritual beauties, nor can they take any pleasure from them. For what joy can beauty bring to a man who does not know it? Those who are without knowledge of the altogether lovely song <note>original: *carmine*; Philo uses the metaphor of a song to describe the harmony of spiritual beauty</note> of spiritual beauties are undoubtedly deprived of the sweetest joys. 

<margin>The beauty of bodies should be considered a shadow and a very thin image of spiritual beauty.</margin>

If, then, the beauty of bodies—which is considered a shadow and the thinnest image of spiritual beauty—brings such delight to those contemplating it that men, having lost their former liberty, direct all their actions and thoughts toward it, and study as much as possible to acquire it and finally turn themselves into it: what do you think that most splendid intellectual beauty will do, of which we have already said this corporeal form is only a shadow and a certain image? 

Beware, therefore, Sophia, lest you be so captured by the adulterated beauty of lower things that you neglect or leave behind that supreme beauty, the mistress and Queen of all others. 

**SO.** <note>Sophia</note> I promise you I will most carefully avoid the error of the common people. But that argument of the proportion of the whole and the parts brought up earlier remains to be dissolved—the one which, favoring the opinion of the masses, demonstrates that the name of beauty belongs properly to bodies, but to spiritual things only improperly and on account of a certain similarity they have with bodies. 

**PH.** That previous definition of beauty, which some more recent philosophers then confirmed, is neither...

<meta>This page continues the third dialogue between Philo and Sophia. Philo is arguing that beauty is not merely a matter of physical proportion or "symmetry" (the Stoic view), but something more spiritual and essential. He is demonstrating that simple, undivided things—like light, gold, and the divine—are beautiful despite having no "parts" to be in proportion to one another.</meta>

### DIALOGUE III.

...its own, nor ought it to be considered perfect; for otherwise no **simple body** <note>In Renaissance philosophy, a "simple body" refers to a substance not made of a mixture of parts, such as a pure element or a celestial body.</note>—since each of them lacks a composition of diverse and mutually corresponding parts—would deserve the name of beauty. Thus, the golden **Sun**, the silvery **Moon**, the twinkling **Stars**, most brilliant **Venus**, and noble **Jupiter** would unworthily claim the name of beauty for themselves.

<margin>He demonstrates with several arguments that beauty is by no means located in the "fitting proportion of parts"—either among themselves or to the whole—as the common people believe.</margin>

**SO.** <note>Sophia</note> Yet celestial bodies are also seen to be marked by a **circular figure**, the most beautiful of all figures, which, existing as a certain whole, encompasses its parts.

<margin>The circular shape is the most beautiful of all shapes.</margin>

**PH.** <note>Philo</note> The circular shape is indeed not undeservedly declared to be more beautiful than all other shapes. However, its beauty does not consist in a fitting proportion of parts either among themselves or to the whole; for since its parts are entirely similar and of the same nature, they cannot sustain any praiseworthy proportion <note>original: "proportionem"; here meaning a ratio between different things. Since every part of a circle's edge is identical, there is no "ratio" between different types of parts.</note>.

<margin>The beauty of the stars seems to be related to their light rather than to their circular shape.</margin>

Furthermore, the **Sun**, **Moon**, and other stars are not said to be beautiful because of the circular figure inherent to them; for then all orbicular bodies would equal the Sun in beauty. Rather, the stars are commended with the praise of beauty because of the **light** infused into them by the Creator, which has no dealings with shape, nor requires any proportion of parts. Likewise, glowing fire, gleaming gold, and conspicuous, precious little gems would falsely carry off the glory of beauty; for all things of this kind seem to possess the greatest simplicity, and the same nature entirely in both the parts and the whole, with not even the slightest proportion of diversity seen in them. 

What is more? If we follow the opinion of the common people, only the "whole" should be called beautiful; none of the parts could be named handsome, unless perhaps in relation to the whole. Moreover, the senses seem to more than sufficiently refute their opinion, since we see the same woman's face as beautiful at one time and deformed at another <note>Perhaps referring to changes in expression, health, or the light in which she is viewed.</note>, even while the proportion of the parts to the whole remains always the same. Therefore, it is now most clearly evident, I believe, that beauty does not consist in the proportion of parts. 

I also think it must by no means be overlooked that if the aforementioned opinion were true, neither pleasant colors nor **light** itself—which renders the entire corporeal world most beautiful—ought to be praised by the name of beauty. Similarly, if we take the sense of hearing, a most sweet voice would never be called beautiful. But if they themselves have judged that musical beauty is to be placed in the harmony and concord of diverse voices as if they were parts, in what will they think **intellectual beauty** resides? They will say, perhaps, that it is located in the order of reason. So be it. But what then, if we present to them the understanding of simple things, the purest divinity, and the supreme beauty of God? What do you think they will answer? Without doubt, they will fall silent. 

For this reason, if we weigh it correctly: even if beauty is found in things that are harmonious and retain a praiseworthy proportion, we will finally find that it is something other than the proportion of the parts and the whole. Whence not only composite things—in which the ratio of parts to the whole is most clearly seen—but also, much more so, simple things appear marked and conspicuous with beauty.

**SO.** And will things that are confused and have no proportion also be called beautiful?

**PH.** By no means. For things whose parts lack a praiseworthy proportion and a composite order are certainly imperfect and defective; and nothing defective is deemed worthy of the name of beauty. Nevertheless, we should not take proportion and beauty to be exactly one and the same thing. For the simplest things, entirely removed from any composition of parts, which seem neither to observe proportion nor to step outside it, are often seen to be most beautiful. Furthermore, those things that retain a harmonious proportion are not always said to be good or beautiful; which indeed happens for no other reason than because goodness and beauty by no means consist for long in the fitting proportion of parts.

<margin>The proportion and concord of evil things.</margin>

Tell me, I pray, Sophia: is not proportion and concord found also in evil things?

<margin>A proverb of merchants.</margin>

**SO.** Most certainly. Indeed—

He is responding to Sophia's request to define where physical beauty actually comes from if it is not found in the "symmetry" of parts.</meta>

# LEONE EBREO ON LOVE #

merchants themselves use this proverb most frequently: that fraud and <note>The Latin text here is slightly truncated; it likely refers to 'profit' or 'trade'.</note> truth agree best together. Fear also with tyranny, and extravagance with the unjust acquisition of riches, always seem to enter into partnership. Neither does beauty always follow or accompany proportion, nor proportion beauty, as those people falsely persuaded themselves. **SO.** <note>Sophia</note> If, therefore, beauty does not exist in proportion at all, in what aspect of bodies shall we say beauty consists? Or what reason will you chiefly bring forward as to why figures and bodies distinguished by the proportion of their parts are called beautiful?

<margin>
The deformity and foulness of bodies is to be referred to matter; their elegance and beauty to form, as to their nearest origin and proper cause.
</margin>

**PH.** <note>Philo</note> The **matter** <term>materia: the raw, chaotic physical substance of the universe</term> of all lower bodies, being properly the base and foundation, is by its very nature most foul; all the vices and foulness of bodies proceed from matter as if from a mother. But though matter is foul in itself, it is nevertheless adorned by the generosity of the **Spiritual World**, which distributes **forms** <term>forma: the spiritual "blueprint" or soul that gives a thing its identity and beauty</term> into the individual parts of matter, and thus it becomes beautiful. Hence, forms are said to flow from the Divine Intellect, or from the Soul of the World, or from the spiritual or celestial world into matter, like certain rays flowing from the Sun to the Earth; these are surely the things that remove foulness from matter and adorn it with beauty. Therefore, the beauty of the lower world derives its origin from the spiritual and celestial world, just as vices and foulness proceed from the deformed and imperfect matter from which all bodies consist. **SO.** All bodies, then, should be seen as endowed with equal beauty, since they all seem to have received their own forms equally from the higher world. **PH.** I think it must be granted that all bodies deserve to participate in some portion of beauty by virtue of the forms giving shape to their base and deformed matters; yet they ought not to be called equally beautiful for that reason. For forms are not thought to shape all lower bodies in the same way, nor to perfect them equally; for they are not said to remove the vices and deformities of matter equally in all bodies. 

<margin>
The grace and beauty of bodies seems to proceed from the triumph of form over matter; their deformity and foulness, however, comes from the dominance of matter over form.
</margin>

On the contrary, they seem to take away a small portion of imperfection and foulness from some, a larger portion from others, and a still larger portion from others yet again, ascending by degrees. Hence, the more a form is able to remove the deformity of matter, the more beautiful and shapely the body becomes; and the less it removes, the less beautiful and more deformed it turns out. This distinction is seen to occur not only between different species but also between individuals. Hence we often see one man more handsome than another, and one horse more beautiful than another. This happens chiefly for this reason: because the essential form of one is more powerful than the essential form of the other, and is able to remove more deformity from matter and bestow greater beauty upon the body. <margin>SO.</margin> But why, I pray, are bodies that maintain the best proportion judged by us to be beautiful? <margin>PH.</margin> Proportion 

<margin>
The excellent and fitting proportion of bodies takes its origin from the dominance and mastery of the form over the matter, as from its true and nearest cause.
</margin>

arises because a more powerful form—one that dominates the matter more—fashions the parts of the body to agree perfectly, both among themselves and with the whole. This maintains a right and intelligible order, with the parts aptly disposed to perform their proper duties and achieve their proper ends. Whether the parts are diverse or similar, homogeneous or heterogeneous, the form bestows the best possible fitness upon the whole and the parts together, so that the body becomes beautiful. But when matter, through its own imperfection and disobedience, fails to show the due obedience to the form to whose law of nature it is subject, then the form cannot unite and construct the parts of the matter as perfectly as reason requires to constitute the whole. <note>The original text contains a repetitive phrase here regarding matter's "quality," likely a printer's error; the translation maintains the intended meaning.</note> Hence it is no wonder if the whole, because of the failing of the matter to yield to the form that confers beauty, is rendered less beautiful and more deformed. <margin>SO.</margin> I am wonderfully glad to have learned what the beauty of lower bodies is said to be, where it comes from, and who confers it. But a certain doubt brought forward by you earlier—against those who thought beauty was located in proportion—seems to cause me some trouble.

# DIALOGUE III #

For charming colors, even if they are beautiful, are not said to consist of parts joined together by a form <note>Philo argues that if beauty required "proportional parts," a single beautiful color would be impossible, yet we clearly find colors beautiful.</note>. Likewise, everyone admits that light is most beautiful, yet no "formed parts"—nor parts flowing together into the unity of a composition—are found within it. Furthermore, the Sun, Moon, and other stars, although they are physical bodies, are not thought to consist of "deformed matter" or a "perfecting form" <note>In Aristotelian thought, the celestial bodies were considered to be made of a "fifth element" (ether) and were inherently perfect, unlike earthly objects made of changing matter and form.</note>. Why then are they called beautiful? Moreover, musical harmonies, the sweetest voices, composed speeches, resonant poems, and many other things—even if they do not possess deformed matter and perfecting form as "parts" concurring in their composition—are still called beautiful. Finally, as you yourself said, the most beautiful concepts of the human imagination, reason, and mind, even if they lack the composition of matter and form, surpass and excel all inferior bodies in beauty.

<margin>Forms, since by their own nature they are able to adorn their matter (which is by nature most foul) and perfect crude and uncomposed bodies, must be considered far more beautiful than all matter and the informed bodies themselves.</margin>

**PH.** <note>Philo</note> You have doubted rightly. And indeed, unless you had interrupted me, I was preparing to declare this very thing. All the beauties of lower bodies, as we have already shown, are accepted as being brought by **forms** <term>forma: the spiritual essence or "idea" that gives a physical thing its identity and beauty</term>. Since these forms are far superior to deformed matter, and they turn and handle its crude and undigested mass as they please, they naturally render those bodies most beautiful. But tell me, I pray: if forms give beauty both to shameful things and to shamefulness itself, will they not be far more beautiful than both matter and the bodies consisting of matter? Certainly. For unless we grant that forms are beautiful, we must say they are either foul or neutral—that is, neither beautiful nor deformed. If they were foul, how could things be rendered beautiful by their presence? The essence of a single nature never truly induces its opposite, but rather always brings about something similar to itself. If they are neutral, why do they bestow beauty rather than foulness? And why are they found always to do so? It is necessary, therefore, that we finally concede that forms are far more beautiful than the things perfected and informed by them.

<margin>The formal beauty of colors.</margin>

Therefore, colors are called beautiful by the common Law of forms, and not without reason: for if bodies that are excellently colored are judged beautiful by sight, so much more should colors themselves be considered either beautiful or rather worthy of the name of beauty. And much more so is light itself, which confers beauty on both colors and colored things; light is considered the form of abstract bodies, as we have said elsewhere, and is considered to be removed as far as possible from physical corruption.

<margin>Light is the most beautiful of all beauties by which bodies are seen to be distinguished, and exists as their Prince, so to speak.</margin>

Thus, since light seems to be the mother of lower beauties, it will surely carry away almost all the praise of beauty.

<margin>The extraordinary beauty of the stars consists chiefly in light.</margin>

The Sun, Moon, and stars are declared to be most beautiful because of their most abundant light, which is thought to have obtained the status of "form" in those divine bodies; indeed, in the opinion of **Themistius** <note>Themistius (c. 317–388 AD) was a philosopher and rhetorician known for his paraphrases of Aristotle; Philo uses him to support the idea that celestial bodies are "Pure Form."</note>, they seem to be called "Forms" rather than "informed bodies." Since the Sun is held by men to be the parent of the most beautiful light, the leadership and empire over all physical beauties is rightly deferred to it alone. To the Sun, the other stars immediately succeed, as they drink in the Solar light before other bodies.

Then follow all the lower bodies, both those that shine and those that are colored, which have received their own beauties from the Solar splendor: and especially **fire**, which is powerful by the virtue of its form, and because of its thinness and lightness, is less impure than any of the other elements and is more a partaker of Solar light.

<margin>The active and formal nature of Fire.</margin>

The active and, so to speak, formal nature of this element is recognized chiefly by the fact that none of the other elements can ever move or alter it from its state, unless perhaps by extinguishing it entirely. For fire, as long as it deserves the name of fire, cannot grow cold or wet by any other element acting upon it, nor can it receive any quality at all contrary to its nature. Yet fire itself is very frequently seen to exercise its power upon the other elements: since, even when the natures of the other elements are most resistant, it heats water, burns the earth, and dissolves the moisture of the air.

<margin>From light, as if from a most fertile fountain, all visible beauties seem then to emanate.</margin>

Therefore, light in the entire lower and sublunary World seems to have obtained the status of the most common form, which [adorns] the deformed and most obscure...

and drives away the foulness of matter and dissolves the darkness. Whence bodies that abound more in light are found to be truly more beautiful than others. And let these things said concerning visible beauty suffice.

<margin>Beauties perceived by hearing.</margin>
Now let us pass to beauty perceived by hearing. Harmony is called beautiful for this reason: because, like a certain spiritual form, it arranges and joins many different voices into one musical concord through intelligible reason. Moreover, the voices are marked by this kind of beauty either as parts or as the matter of the whole. Furthermore, the beauty of speech proceeds from an interior and spiritual beauty, which orders and binds together many very different words—acting as the matter—into a perfect and intelligible unity, while also maintaining harmonic proportion. For this reason, speech is deservedly judged to surpass other bodily beauties. The same principle is seen to apply to poems, which, besides their intelligible beauty, seem to participate in that harmonic proportion and melody even more than prose <note>The original "solutæ orationes" literally means "loosened speech," the standard Latin term for prose.</note>.

Finally, the beauties of cognition, of reason, and of the human mind surpass any physical beauty by a vast distance; for they themselves exist as true, formal, and spiritual beauties. They themselves order and join the many different concepts of the sensitive and rational soul; finally, they impart and pour the most beautiful teachings into ready and disposed minds.

<margin>Artificial beauty.</margin>
Lastly, in bodies constructed with skill, a certain artificial beauty is also found.

<margin>The beauty of the lower world descends from the spiritual World of Forms, which are distributed into bodies.</margin>
Therefore, the beauty of the lower world proceeds from the spiritual world, and soon passes into forms, and then into bodies by the benefit of those forms.

<margin>The foulness of matter reaches only to "informed" bodies, but not at all to the forms that give shape to such bodies.</margin>
However, forms of this kind—or "formal beauties"—seem to have no commerce at all with matter; for the beauty of the forms themselves is not diminished or hindered by any association with deformed matter. Whence virtues and wisdom are always found beautiful in the same way. But it is the "informed" bodies <note>In this philosophical context, "informed" means physical matter that has been given a specific shape or "form" by a higher principle.</note> that are indeed said to be sometimes beautiful and sometimes foul, according to whether the matter obeys or resists the beauty of the forms.

<margin>The beauty of natural things is always to be referred to natural forms, and likewise the elegance of artificial things to artificial forms.</margin>
**SO.** <note>Sophia</note> I have rightly understood how all the natural beauties of the physical world proceed from the forms that adorn matter and give shape to bodies. Now it remains for you to declare from where the beauties of artificial things arise, since we cannot assign to them a spiritual or celestial origin (which is proper to natural forms), with which artificial things seem to have no correspondence at all.

**PH.** <note>Philo</note> Just as the beauty of natural things derives its origin from natural forms, both essential and accidental, so too the beauty of artificial things proceeds from artificial forms. Therefore, the same definition is applied to both species of beauty.

**SO.** What, I pray, is this definition?

<margin>The most common definition of beauty.</margin>
**PH.** A certain formal grace which brings the greatest delight to the one who recognizes it, and allures them to the love of itself. Now this grace, which we call "formal," happens to artificial works by the benefit of artificial forms, just as it deservedly happens to natural bodies by the benefit of natural forms.

<margin>He explains through a fitting example that the beauty of artificial works proceeds from the form of art.</margin>
In order that you may better and more distinctly understand that the beauty of artificial bodies proceeds from the form of the art, place before your eyes two unformed logs of equal size: let one of them be fashioned into the image of the most beautiful Venus, while the other remains entirely rough and indistinct. You will conclude from this that the beauty of that sculpted Venus does not proceed from the wood, primarily because the other wood, equal to it, is seen to be not at all beautiful. It remains, therefore, that we must call its beauty the form or figure skillfully carved into it, from which the wood then acquires the name of "beautiful."

<margin>Beauty exists as threefold: artificial, natural, and Ideal.</margin>
Moreover, just as the natural forms of sensible bodies derive an incorporeal and spiritual origin both from the Soul of the World and from the first Divine Intellect—in which, as in the two first and most powerful causes, all forms [exist] in a far greater way than in divided bodies... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence, preparing to discuss the hierarchy of forms.</note>

### DIALOGUE III. ###

<margin>
He demonstrates that ideal beauty, reduced as if to a certain highest unity, far surpasses natural and artificial beauties which are scattered and diffused within the mass of bodies.
</margin>
...essences endowed with perfection and beauty reside and are preserved. Likewise, artificial forms proceed from the mind of the human craftsman, in which they are seen to exist in a far more absolute and beautiful state than they are later found to be in the physically constructed objects. And furthermore, just as if you were to mentally strip away the material mass from a beautiful work of art, nothing remains except the **Idea** <note>In this context, "Idea" refers to the perfect mental blueprint or Platonic form that exists before a physical object is made.</note> situated in the craftsman's mind; so too, once matter is removed from natural bodies, only the **Ideal forms** are seen to remain, pre-existing in the supreme Intellect of all and in the **World Soul** <note>The *Anima Mundi*, or World Soul, was a common philosophical concept representing an intrinsic spirit that connects all living things on Earth.</note>. I do not think you are at all ignorant, Sophia, of how much greater beauty the "Idea" of art possesses when it is joined and united in the craftsman’s mind than when it is diffused and scattered in a physical body. For every perfection and beauty is increased by union and diminished by division.

Whence the beauty of a statue—whether of Venus or any other thing—carved in wood, appears thin and weak when it is seen to be divided and distributed into many parts, if it is compared with the beauty stored within the mind of the craftsman. For in the craftsman, the **Idea** of the art is found at its most powerful; there, all its parts are enfolded and joined together, offering mutual help to one another to increase the beauty of each individual part. It is so integrated that the beauty of all the parts together resides in each one, and the beauty of each part resides in the whole, with no division or discrepancy standing in the way.

Therefore, if anyone were able to look upon both these proposed beauties with their own eyes, they would recognize that the internal art is far more beautiful than the external work of the craftsman. This is because the internal art is the cause from which the beauty of the constructed work proceeds. Indeed, the form loses as much perfection through its "partnership" with the body as the body gains in ornament by the form's arrival. For the more a crude and shapeless body is distinguished and refined by a form, the more beautiful and artistic it becomes; but the more a form is extended and dissipated by the mass of a body, the more it loses of its own luster and proper grace. Therefore, a **Form** <note>The "Form" is the spiritual or intellectual essence that gives a thing its identity and beauty.</note> released from the body must be considered most beautiful, just as, conversely, a body deprived of form must be considered most foul. Regarding our present purpose, we must feel exactly the same way about the works of art and the works of nature.

<margin>
Ideal beauties are thought to reside both in the First Intellect and in the World Soul, yet in a far nobler and simpler manner in the former than in the latter.
</margin>
<margin>
The dignity and excellence of the World Soul.
</margin>
For the forms that make natural bodies visible and beautiful are found to be marked by the highest beauty in the mind of the Supreme Craftsman—the most excellent architect of the World's fabric—that is, in the **Divine Intellect**. For there, all forms exist together, entirely free from matter, change, alteration, and any division or multitude. In each one of them, the beauty of all is included, and the loveliness of each one seems to be spread equally into all. Furthermore, the individual forms of things are said to reside in the **World Soul** as if in a "second craftsman," even if it is believed that they did not obtain as much beauty in the Soul as they did in the First Intellect and Supreme Architect. For in the Soul, which stands as a mediator between the Supreme Maker and natural bodies, the forms are by no means reduced to that purest unity, but are thought to retain a certain ordered multitude and diversity. Yet even there, they have obtained a far greater beauty than in natural things themselves; for there, they are seen to have achieved at least a unity of order, and to exist as far as possible from matter, alteration, and motion, while retaining a spiritual nature.

<margin>
The human soul is the noblest of all natural forms.
</margin>
<margin>
The greater or lesser beauty of natural forms takes its origin from their greater or lesser mixing and association with bodies.
</margin>
From this supreme and most excellent Soul, all souls and natural forms descend into this lower world, divided and distributed into diverse and distinct bodies. All of these are seen to be subject to alteration, motion, birth, and death—with the sole exception of the **human soul**, which is called "rational." The human soul remains entirely free from corruption, alteration, and physical motion; it seems to have reserved for itself only a spiritual motion for the purpose of reasoning and receiving "species" <note>In medieval philosophy, "species" are the mental images or spiritual imprints of objects that allow the mind to perceive and understand them.</note>. Nor is the human soul contaminated by any mixing with the body in the manner of other souls and natural forms, even though it takes its origin in no different a way.

# LEO HEBREO ON LOVE #

<margin>The greater or lesser beauty of natural bodies originates from their greater or lesser obedience and compliance with their natural forms.</margin>
...as we have said regarding artificial forms: the less they are mixed with physical bodies, the more they shine with greater beauty and render the bodies subject to them more beautiful. However, those forms that possess a poorly suited power and are granted a greater, excessive mixture with bodies are seen to be less beautiful and make the bodies handed over to them ugly and deformed. The opposite, however, seems to occur in natural bodies: for those that obey their forms more, and entrust themselves entirely to their faithfulness, are more beautiful; but those that resist their own forms and strive, as it were, to subject the forms to themselves, are always found to turn out more ugly. From these things, Sophia, you may now recognize that the beauty of inferior bodies—both natural ones and those crafted by the industry of art—is nothing other than a certain **grace** <note>original: *gratia*; a pleasing quality that transcends mere proportion</note> which deservedly belongs to each of them from their own form, whether substantial or externally added, whether natural or introduced by a craftsman.

<margin>An epilogue of the things declared thus far.</margin>
Moreover, you will also recognize that forms, in whatever way they are understood, always surpass the bodies they inform in beauty. Furthermore, these forms themselves, when considered in a spiritual manner, are seen to be far more excellent and beautiful than when they are joined with physical bodies. Nor should it disturb you that beauty infused into bodies exhibits itself to be seen by eyes and heard by ears, while spiritual beauty does not; for this spiritual beauty can also be seen by us with the inner eyes of the soul, which are remarkably illuminated by the light of the intellect.

**SOPHIA:** What agreement or similarity does our soul and our intellect have with spiritual forms?

<margin>The human soul is very similar to the World Soul.</margin>
**PHILO:** The human soul, which we call rational, since it was constructed in the image and likeness of the **World Soul** <note>original: *anima mundi*; the animating spirit of the entire universe</note>, was marked in a certain obscure way by all the forms existing in that same world soul. Therefore, with the help of reasoning, being very similar to that higher soul, it distinctly recognizes the forms impressed upon itself, perceives their beauty, and loves them.

<margin>The human intellect is the image of that first, divine intellect.</margin>
Similarly, our intellect represents that divine and most pure intellect, which is engraved with all the **Ideas** <note>original: *Idæis*; the eternal, perfect archetypes of all things</note> reduced to a supreme unity, acting as a kind of sacred image of it. When the rational soul has been filled and highly prepared by many excellent **habits** <note>intellectual dispositions or states of being</note> acquired through the work of reasoning, this intellect finally opens and pours into us a unique knowledge of the **Ideal essences** <note>original: *Idealium essentiarum*</note>—one that is far removed from common use and is, as it were, visible. Therefore, illustrated by the light of the intellect, we are able to gaze upon the supreme beauty of that first intellect and the divine Ideas with a single look; from this intellectual vision, we perceive the greatest delight joined with an immense love.

Likewise, when the eyes of the rational soul are opened and the praiseworthy sequence of thought is observed, we are finally permitted to behold the beauty of the World Soul and of all the forms residing within it in a wonderful order. This vision, although not as great as the first, nevertheless also brings us great pleasure and impels us toward a vehement love of it.

<margin>The two corporal or sensible beauties—namely those presented to sight and hearing—are seen to be most similar to those two spiritual forms: the first intellect and the World Soul.</margin>
Consider also, I pray, Sophia, how rightly those two physical beauties—sensed by sight and hearing—match and correspond as images and likenesses to those two spiritual beauties: the first intellect and the World Soul. **Visible beauty**, which consists entirely in light and glides into our eyes by the mediation of light, represents **intellectual beauty**. For we have already reminded you before that the Sun refers to the first intellect as the most abundant source of light. Thus, just as the first intellect illuminates and adorns our intellect with its light and spiritual beauty, so the Sun—the true image of the first intellect—illuminates our eyes with physical light (which is defined as a certain intellectual splendor converted into the form and essence of the Sun itself). Thus, by the gift of this most beneficent planet, the eyes perceive and recognize all physical beauties which, as we have said, participate in light. The other species of beauty, which is perceived by hearing, can be most excellently compared to the beauty of the Soul placed over the World, like an image to its archetype; for it consists in harmony, concord, and order, no differently than all natural forms consist in that harmonious and ordered union. # DIALOGUE III #

...the contemplation of these forms in the World Soul most greatly adorns our own soul, and is finally perceived by it with immense delight. Similarly, voices composed and constructed into a most sweet song, or into an elegant oration, or into an artful poem, are immediately discerned by the ears; and having entered through them to the rational soul, they affect it with incredible pleasure because of a certain internal concord and harmony delivered and instilled into it by the World Soul.

*SO.* I seem to have understood very well the reasoning by which bodily beauties—those perceived by sight and those by hearing—are said to be the primary understandings of spiritual beauties, and certain images and likenesses of the World Soul; and how, just as the eyes and the ears comprehend two kinds of bodily beauties, so our rational soul and our mind or intellect finally come to know two kinds of spiritual forms. Yet a certain ambiguity occurs to me from what has been said. For it is surely the rational soul and our intellectual mind, in my judgment, which—using the eyes and ears as intervening messengers—both judge the knowledge of bodily beauties for themselves and bring forth a judgment; they are seen to be greatly delighted by them and to love them vehemently. Therefore, the eyes and ears seem to perform no other duty than serving as certain bodily ways and paths that lead beauties to our soul and intellect. Whence someone might say, perhaps not without merit, that these senses are concerned with bodily beauties rather than spiritual ones.

<margin>
The knowledge, pleasure, and love of bodily forms are believed to belong to the inner power and faculty of our souls, rather than to the eyes or the ears.
</margin>

*PH.* Indeed, no one should doubt that the knowledge, judgment, sensation, delight, and love of bodily beauties belong principally to the soul, and not at all to the eyes or ears that convey them. For if the eyes and ears were said to truly and properly know and love the beauty of bodies, it would surely follow that everyone would have the same knowledge of bodily beauties, and perceive equal pleasure from them, and pursue them with equal love—since everyone is seen to be similarly endowed with eyes and ears. Yet the opposite happens: for you will see many truly beautiful things which are nevertheless not discerned at all by many very sharp eyes, nor do they bring any pleasure at all to those looking at them, nor do they instill any love for themselves. How many men could I find for you with excellent hearing who neither love nor approve of the beauty of music, but rather detest it as much as possible? Moreover, many are found who are entirely ignorant of the beauty of witty verses and highly ornate orations. Therefore, the knowledge, joy, and love of bodily forms do not reside in the eyes or ears—through which these two instruments they merely pass—but rather they seem to be placed and consist in the inner soul, toward which they strive.

*SO.* Although thus far you favor my side, I will not allow you to resolve the proposed ambiguity until you offer some reason why all the souls of men do not equally know, love, or pursue beauty itself, even though the eyes and ears of each person convey it to the soul in the same and similar manner.

<margin>
Our soul, according to the opinion of Plato and also Aristotle, exists full and shaped by spiritual forms impressed upon it by the World Soul in a certain obscure manner.
</margin>

*PH.* You are very well acquainted with the cause of this matter, along with the solution to the difficulty proposed. Moreover, we have already said that all forms separated from bodies and retaining the order of unity are found in a spiritual manner in the World Soul. Our rational soul is considered to be the image and likeness of this higher soul, because its essence is thought to consist in a latent and obscure figuration of all spiritual forms impressed upon it by the World Soul, as if from an exemplar <note>An "exemplar" is an original model or pattern from which copies are made; here, the World Soul is the blueprint for the human soul.</note> and its own origin. This latent and obscure figuration is clearly what Aristotle called "potentiality," and the most common preparation of the potential intellect <term>intellectus poteſtatis</term> <note>original: *intellectus potestatis*; refers to the "possible" or "potential" intellect, the capacity of the human mind to receive and understand universal concepts.</note> for receiving and understanding all forms. For unless all the essences of things were deservedly signed in our souls by potentiality or by latent reason, they could never actually receive them and understand them as if they were innate to themselves.

<margin>
Plato thought that human sciences were nothing other than certain reminiscences.
</margin>

Hence Plato thought that human thoughts and intelligences were nothing other than [reminiscences] of things in our souls...

<meta>catchword: noftris (in our [souls])</meta>

<summary>Philo explains that while eyes and ears are the channels for beauty, the soul is the true judge and lover of it. He reconciles Platonic and Aristotelian thought by suggesting that the human soul contains latent spiritual forms derived from the World Soul, which allows us to recognize beauty through "reminiscence" or "potentiality."</summary>

### LEO HEBRAEUS ON LOVE ###

<margin>
The senses do not seem to bring any new knowledge to our souls, but rather they appear to excite them to recover their ancient knowledge for themselves.
</margin>
...pre-existing in ours; but because of the oblivion that follows, they believe these are as if recoveries and certain reminiscences <note>original: "reminiscentias"</note> of what was possessed by them. Or truly, it is nothing other than that power introduced by Aristotle <note>A reference to Aristotle's "tabula rasa" and the transition from potentiality to act, which Philo here tries to reconcile with Plato.</note> to signify this very shaping we are now discussing. From what has been said, therefore, Sophia, you can certainly conclude that forms by no means leap from bodies into our souls; for it is quite impossible for things to migrate or be transferred from one subject to another. Instead, objects presented to the senses are only able to achieve this: that their native forms, which previously shone in our souls and poured out a most abundant light, might—once the shadows of oblivion are removed—finally regain their former splendor. This recovery of former splendor is called the "act of understanding" <note>original: "actus intelligendi"</note> by Aristotle, but is called "reminiscence" <note>original: "reminiscentia"</note> by Plato. Truly, these two most excellent philosophers, though using various and diverse terms, wished to signify exactly the same thing. Our souls, therefore, exist full of the beauties of forms; indeed, these are said to be their very own essences. But if these most excellent beauties lie hidden within them, this hiding occurs by no means because of the intellect, which grants the soul its essence, but rather happens to them from the association and connection with the human body and matter.

<margin>
The hiding of the forms imprinted on our souls certainly occurs because of the association with the human body and matter.
</margin>
For even if our rational souls are by no means mixed with bodies, nevertheless the union and binding which they have with bodies is considered the primary cause for the essences of the souls—that is, their formal beauties, which by their own nature are bright and most splendid—to be so shadowed and obscured. Consequently, the species and images of beauties diffused into bodies are necessarily required from sensible things, so that the interior, recondite, and hidden beauties of the soul may once again recover some purity of their ancient splendor.

<margin>
The reason why men are seen to behave in almost infinite and diverse ways in perceiving disciplines is quite elegantly attributed to the greater or lesser shadowing and obscurity of the forms imprinted within our souls.
</margin>
Since, however, this kind of shadowing and obscurity is seen to manifest in many and most dissimilar ways in the souls of individual men—depending on whether the bodies offer greater or lesser obedience to their souls—it happens that the soul of one man knows those hidden beauties more easily, while another does so with more difficulty. Indeed, the souls of some men, who perhaps carry a body made of matter hateful to God <note>A Neoplatonic way of describing matter that is coarse or unrefined, hindering spiritual clarity.</note>—being quite raw and uncomposed—are least able to gaze upon those forms implanted within them. For unrefined matter does not at all allow the darkness, which it has brought upon the soul, to be expelled or put to flight, nor the Sun <note>A metaphor for intellectual or divine light.</note> to be received. From this it also happens that some men perceive the beauties innate to them promptly and without the help of others; some, however, achieve this through the benefit of teachers and disciplines; and some, finally, are unable to acquire even the least bit of erudition. Furthermore, it is certain that the same man may know some beauties easily, but others with difficulty. This seems to happen chiefly because his matter has contracted a greater agreement and likeness with some forms rather than others. For this reason, recondite beauties do not lie hidden in all human souls in the same way; and therefore, for example, some of them are easily awakened in the soul of Socrates by sensible species, while others are known only with difficulty.

<margin>
Through bodily and lower forms, as if by certain steps, we ought to proceed and ascend to the contemplation of spiritual forms and the Ideal beauties hidden in the divine mind.
</margin>
Because of these many and most dissimilar dispositions of matter, so many obscurities dwell in human souls that they can scarcely be perceived. Now, therefore, Sophia, I judge it has become known to you that all the beauties anciently implanted in our souls, and then confirmed by the aid of the senses from external bodies, exist entirely with those forms which the World Soul <note>original: "anima Mundi"</note>—having received them from the Intellect—seems to have distributed through all bodies. It is with these that the World Soul informed and distinguished our rational soul, in order to make it as similar to itself as possible. Whence we may most easily ascend from the knowledge of bodily beauties to the contemplation of the beauty of our own interior soul, and then also to the beauty of the World Soul; and finally, supported by our pure and intellectual mind, we will be able to fly toward the intuition of the first and divine supreme beauty of the whole intellect.

He reconciles Plato and Aristotle's views on knowledge and describes the process of ascending from physical perception to the contemplation of the Divine Intellect.</summary>
