<margin>The difference between reason and the mind.</margin>
Whence, not without cause, we have already said above that we discern spiritual beauties by the light of our rational soul and mind or intellect, with only this distinction intervening: that **reason** <note>original: "ratio"</note> finally recognizes the beauties of the forms existing in the **Soul of the World** <note>original: "anima Mundi"; the Neoplatonic concept of a spiritual force that connects the physical universe to the divine intellect</note> after long revolving around the bodily forms that were previously constructed in their image. But the **pure mind** <note>original: "pura mens"</note> directly, and with a single glance, contemplates the singular beauty of all things in the **Ideas** of the supreme intellect and knows them most distinctly.

<margin>Human happiness.</margin>
Here, moreover, the final happiness <note>original: "beatitudo"</note> of man is said to consist.

<margin>The principal duty of our souls seems to be situated in separating spiritual forms from foul matter and recalling them from the impurity of bodies.</margin>
<margin>The praiseworthy love of our souls for spiritual beauties.</margin>
<margin>Summary of the things said thus far.</margin>
Furthermore, Sophia, you may gather from what has been said: that those souls who labor as much as possible to separate the spiritual portion of bodily beauties from vile matter and physical ugliness, will hardly ever attain the spiritual beauties of the soul itself—that is, the virtues, sciences, and wisdoms. Whence, just as although everyone endowed with the sense of sight looks upon bodily beauties, yet not everyone discerns their loveliness, nor perceives the appropriate pleasure from it, but only those who are more or less devoted to the beauty of things according to their worth; similarly, although all souls know spiritual beauties, yet not all reach a distinct understanding of their loveliness, nor do they all seem to desire their enjoyment equally: but only those who are seized with a greater or lesser natural inclination and love for such spiritual beauties. By this reasoning, I best understand how our souls know spiritual things first, then bodily things, and finally, with the help of these, the incorporeal beauties as well—which shine forth very clearly and conspicuously in the First Intellect and the Soul of the World, whereas in human reason they seem to lie hidden and wrapped in certain shadows. Moreover, I also understand that just as those who know bodily beauties in a more perfect way love them more intensely than those who happen to have an imperfect knowledge of them, so too those who more keenly contemplate beauties entirely separated from bodies follow them with a far greater love than others. You also added that those who easily and readily separate the spiritual part of bodily beauties from the impure, and claim for themselves the greatest knowledge of them, will certainly perceive the incorporeal beauties residing in the higher intellect and soul better and more promptly than others.

But a certain reasoning seems primarily to oppose these things. For if a vehement love of beauty proceeds from its perfect knowledge as if from a cause, it will surely follow that just as those who distinctly know bodily beauties also best perceive the incorporeal ones, so those who are most loving of bodily forms will also pursue incorporeal and intellectual beauties, such as wisdom and the virtues, with a most vehement love. Yet we see the opposite happens. For those who indulge too much in the love of bodily forms are almost always found to be devoid of the knowledge and love of intellectual beauties, and are very frequently found as if blind in them; whereas those ensnared by the greatest love of intellectual forms despise, abandon, flee from, and abhor bodily ones.

<margin>The soul is placed in the middle between the intellect and the body. Our souls possess two faces, of which the higher, turned toward the intellect, is called reason; while the lower, leaning toward the body, is called sense.</margin>
PHILO: I am not at all displeased that you have brought this difficulty forward; for from its solution, if I am not mistaken, you will receive the greatest benefit. For from our response you will surely learn by what reasoning you ought to love and pursue bodily beauties, and by what reasoning you ought to hate and flee them; what is perfect knowledge, what is true love, and what is called a false and counterfeit devotion to them. You understood above that not only the soul placed over the World, but also the human soul (constructed in its likeness) intervenes in the middle between the intellect and the body. This certainly seems to result in our souls possessing two faces—just as we said above regarding the Moon, which is turned partly toward the Sun and partly toward the Earth—of which one is turned toward the higher intellect, but the other toward the lower things...

He addresses the paradox of why those who love physical beauty often fail to appreciate higher, intellectual beauty.</summary>

...gazes at inferior bodies. These two faces of our souls seem to maintain contrary and opposite movements. For just as the

<margin>*The contrary and opposite movements of the two faces of the soul.*</margin>
superior face—which we call reason, or rational knowledge—transfers bodily things into incorporeal ones; so the inferior face—which we call sense, or sensible knowledge—approaching closer to bodies and delighted by their familiarity, leads the soul down to the bodies. Therefore, bodily beauties can be seen and perceived by us by both faces of the soul: namely, by sense and by reason, and through a double order of knowing, both bodily and intellectual. Moreover, from these

<margin>*Love exists as double, namely, sensible and spiritual.*</margin>
two so different ways of knowing bodily beauties, two very dissimilar loves also follow: for **sensible love** accompanies sensible knowledge, and the **spiritual pursuit** accompanies rational knowledge.

<margin>*He reviews several differences of the two faces of the soul in loving and pursuing bodily or spiritual forms.*</margin>
Furthermore, some are found who seem to have the bodily face of the soul endowed with abundant light, but the intellectual face obscured; this happens because their souls are too deeply submerged in bodies and adhere too closely to matter. Their bodies, in turn, obey their souls very little, and are seen to be conquered with difficulty by

<margin>*The most wretched kind of men.*</margin>
them. Men of this sort refer all their knowledge of bodily and sensible beauties, and all their pursuit and love for them, only to the senses. They neither recognize nor love spiritual beauties, nor do they perceive any delight from them, nor do they judge them worthy of any price or love. These are indeed the most wretched of all men and seem certainly to differ little from beasts; they are superior to them only in this name: that they carry rooted within themselves luxury, lust, concupiscence, greed, and other disturbances and sicknesses of the soul. Indeed, these vices not only depress a man and render him unworthy of the name of "man," but they even drag him headlong into a laborious, inexplicable, most turbulent, and never-consistent life; nor do they permit him to be refreshed by any stable rest or any perpetual joy of the soul. This happens because such appetites and delights, on account of their great imperfection, can bring no tranquility or stability at all to human life—especially since they take their origin from matter (which is perpetually agitated and never at rest) as if from the common mother of all sensible beauties.

Besides these, another kind of men is found, who are by far more worthy of the name of man than the ones above. These have obtained the face of the soul turned toward the

<margin>*The kind of most excellent and almost divine men.*</margin>
intellect filled with no less light than the other face verging toward the body. Some, moreover, are seen to have an intellectual face even more splendid than the bodily one. All these refer sensible knowledge primarily to the rational, as if to its proper end, and they love it accordingly. They seem to value and love the sensible beauties perceived by the inferior face only insofar as they can separate from them—by the benefit of the superior face—the **rational forms** <note>original: "rationales formas"; the underlying logic or design of a thing that reason identifies.</note> in which true beauty, as we have already said, consists. For although they are seen to move the spiritual soul toward bodies (using the inferior face as a mediator) so that they may know bodily beauty through sensible reason, nevertheless, using a contrary kind of prior motion, they lift the sensible appearances upward with the help of the superior and rational face. From these, they separate the intelligible forms and species, in which they judge the true knowledge of beauty to reside. They regard the bodily and sensible part as a kind of foulness and a garment—or rather, a shadow and image—of the incorporeal...

### DIALOGUE III. ###

They pursue sensible beauties with only as much love as they believe the perception of them will be useful for knowing and loving spiritual and insensible beauties. These [spiritual beauties] alone they love wonderfully as true forms and as the most excellent above all others; they strive and delight in enjoying them as much as possible. As for those bodily and sensible beauties, when separated from the incorporeal, they are so far from loving or pursuing them that they instead seem to hate them as if they were monsters, and they appear to flee from them as if from a most bitter enemy. 

Truly, the dross <note>The author uses the word "sordes," suggesting the waste or "filth" left over from a refining process.</note> of bodily things brings the greatest hindrance to our souls in attaining happiness, since the intelligible light is withdrawn from their superior face—in which human beatitude consists—and all its splendor is transferred to the inferior and sensible face. Hence, just as gold mixed with other more impure metals, and especially with earthy dregs, can exist as neither beautiful, nor perfect, nor pure (for its excellence is considered to be situated chiefly in this: that it be said to be entirely free of any impure mixture); so also the soul, entangled in the love of sensible beauties, will never return to its own beauty, purity, or beatitude, unless it has recovered its intellectual light and its original perfection by being entirely free and released from the pursuits of sensible forms. 

You seem to be ignorant, Sophia, of where the knowledge of sensible forms chiefly consists: for you think it is situated only in their sensible and, so to speak, material knowledge, even if no spiritual beauties are separated from them. And indeed you wander far from the truth: for this knowledge of bodily beauties exists as something quite imperfect. For he who persuades himself that an accidental thing <note>original: "rem accedentem" — in philosophy, an "accident" is a property that is not essential to the thing's core nature, like the color of a car.</note> holds the primary place does not judge rightly; and he who despises the light to follow shadows does not see clearly; and he who, neglecting the true forms and highest archetypes <note>original: "exemplaribus"</note> of things, loves only their likenesses and images, seems to hate himself. 

Hence the perfect knowledge of bodily forms requires first of all that, through their mediation, incorporeal beauties may be very easily distinguished from them. Then the inferior face of our soul, which looks toward the body entrusted to its care, will obtain a light suited to itself; since the superior face, serving the interests of the one turned toward the intellect, also strives as much as possible to fill it with the due light, and is seen to preserve the accidental, inferior, and servant nature. But if the superior face should perhaps yield to the inferior, then, both being destitute of their own light and turning in the thickest darkness, that soul must undoubtedly be considered most miserable and unhappy. 

<margin>The soul's greatest misery and calamity.</margin>

Then, therefore, the love of inferior beauties is judged right and praiseworthy when it strives to select and, as it were, extract from them the spiritual forms, which are said to be truly and properly lovable. 

<margin>The knowledge and pursuit of sensible and bodily forms ought only to be referred to the knowledge and love of spiritual and intelligible forms.</margin>

Hence love is situated chiefly in these [spiritual forms] and, because of them, even in bodies as certain accidental things. For just as glass eyes <note>original: "uitrei oculi" — this likely refers to spectacles or lenses, which were a common metaphor for mediating sight in this period.</note> are said to be fit, beautiful, and pleasing to us when their clarity is applied to our sight, and our eyes themselves are directed toward sight; but if they should perhaps be clearer [too strong] and do not retain the due proportion, they are found to be not only useless but even to bring some harm and hindrance to sight. Likewise, the knowledge of sensible forms then seems to be good and to procreate, as it were, true loves and honest pleasures, when it is related to the knowledge of intellectual beauties and pours into us their love and delight. But if it is by no means directed to this end, it is quite deservedly thought both to be harmful and to deny us spiritual beauties, intellectual splendor, and human happiness. Beware, therefore, Sophia, lest you be so [captured] by the love and pleasure of sensible forms...

He warns that focusing solely on material beauty leads to spiritual "darkness" and misery, comparing physical forms to shadows or lenses that should help, not hinder, the soul's vision.</summary>

But since this kind of beauty, if compared with incorporeal beauty and that which is entirely separated from matter, is said to be a certain shadow and image of it, I would first wish to understand what this incorporeal form is, from which all bodily beauties seem to flow as if from a most abundant fountain. Hence the true and most excellent forms of all things are stored in the Ideas, by whose benefit all bodies are then rendered beautiful and fair.

# DIALOGUE III #

<note>original: "DIALOGUS III."</note>

...[the essence of beau]ty is thought to lie hidden. Therefore, you wish to illustrate a more manifest thing by one that is more obscure: for beyond the fact that the essence of Ideas is far more unknown to us than that of beauty, it also exists as something much more uncertain and doubtful. For everyone concedes that a certain true beauty is found from which all others proceed. But many philosophers, and indeed the most distinguished among them, such as Aristotle and all the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, known for their focus on empirical observation rather than abstract "Ideas."</note> together, have undermined and overthrown those Platonic Ideas. In what way, then, can a certain thing be explained by a doubtful one, and a more manifest thing by one more obscure?

**PHILO**: Ideas are truly nothing else than certain notions of all 
<margin>
Ideas are defined as certain notions of all created things pre-existing in the divine mind.
</margin>
created things said to be pre-existing in the mind of the supreme maker and creator; which indeed I think no one of sound mind would ever deny. 

**SOPHIA**: Why can they not be denied in the least? 

**PHILO**: Because if the World was not brought forth into the light by chance, nor by random fortune—as the order of the whole and its parts seems most clearly to indicate—it must necessarily be conceded that it was procreated by a certain divine mind and a most wise intellect, which provided it with such an admirable order and such great harmony of its individual parts. 
<margin>
The wondrous partnership and providence of Ideas in the composition of the World and the creation of all things is demonstrated more than enough.
</margin>
A wise man, therefore, will most clearly behold the supreme perfection of the maker and the incomprehensible wisdom of the creator as if it were carved into such an admirable composition of the whole World, and into the order, proportion, and greatest craftsmanship of all its particles, however small. 

**SOPHIA**: This I would certainly never deny, nor would I think it could be denied by anyone; for I perceive the skill of the creator of this very universe and his wondrous providence both from myself and also from the ingenious structure of the individual parts of my body, which is surely so great that the talent of no man, however wise, can fully and completely perceive it. 

**PHILO**: You would certainly recognize the divine craftsmanship much more if you had ever seen an **anatomy** <note>The practice of medical dissection to study the structure of the body.</note> of the human body and each of its parts. For an admirable spectacle of this kind would have placed before your eyes the immense wisdom, providence, and art of God employed in the composition and structure of our body, so that, with awe as your guide, you would have most easily broken out into those words of **Job**: *From my flesh I contemplate God.* <note>original: "Ex carne mea Deum contemplor." A reference to Job 19:26.</note> 

**SOPHIA**: You think rightly indeed. But I pray you, do not leave the matter of the Ideas that you have already begun. 

**PHILO**: If the supreme maker of things seems to have had such a diligent and exquisite regard for the order, harmony, and perfection of each thing in the creation of the universe together with all its parts and the procreation of those parts, then the notions of things produced with such industry must necessarily have pre-existed in the most perfect mind of the divine maker by a certain reason—not otherwise than the notions of all artistic forms must first have lain hidden like certain seeds in the intellect of an artisan or an architect. These cognitions of the universe and its individual parts pre-existing in the divine intellect are surely those which are everywhere commonly called **Ideas**; that is, certain divine fore-knowings of all created things. You have now perceived, Sophia, if I am not mistaken, what they are and in what sense "Ideas" are properly understood. 

**SOPHIA**: Most excellently indeed. But tell me, I pray, why did Aristotle and the rest of the Peripatetics attack them?

**PHILO**: I will most gladly comply with your wish. Plato placed the entire essence and substance of things in the Ideas; so much so that he considered those things which were constructed in the corporeal world according to their likeness to be called shadows of essence and substance, rather than true essences or substances. For this reason, he himself looked down upon bodily forms: nor did he think they bring us any other utility than to raise and lead us to the knowledge of the Ideas, and he contended that their beauty was close to nothing. Aristotle, however, seems to have conducted himself more moderately in this business: for he judged that a most perfect craftsman undoubtedly constructed perfect works. For this reason, he himself considered that there exist true and proper essences and substances in the world and all its parts. He thought, however, that **ideal notions** <note>Aristotle's version of Ideas, often treated as categories or "universals" derived from observing the world.</note> should be called neither the essences nor the substances of things, but only the causes set over them for producing and ordering them. Therefore, he established that primary substances exist as individuals, and he wished the entire essence of the species to be preserved in each one of them: but he thought that species, accepted in a universal and common sense, were not indeed Ideas, nor causes existing in the reality of the thing, but only intellectual concepts which human reason draws out and extracts from the substances and essences of individuals existing in actuality. Hence, he called these sorts of common and universal concepts **secondary substances** <note>original: "ſecundas ſubſtantias"; in Aristotelian logic, individual things (like a specific dog) are primary substances, while the category (like "dog" in general) is a secondary substance.</note>, because they are extracted by our intellect from the primary and individual substances. He does not at all believe that the Ideas exist as primary substances, as Plato felt, nor even as secondary ones; but he testifies that they are the primary causes of all corporal substances, and certain principles of all essences consisting of **matter and form** <note>original: "ex materia formaq;"; the Aristotelian concept that every physical object is a compound of underlying "stuff" and a specific "shape" or "nature."</note>. For this most excellent philosopher affirms that matter and body concur to constitute the essence and substance of all corporal things: and in the definitions of all essences, which are composed of genus and difference, he teaches that the **genus** <note>The general category (e.g., "animal").</note> holds the first place as the matter or body, or the material and common form; while the **difference** <note>The specific trait that distinguishes a species (e.g., "rational" distinguishes humans from other animals).</note> follows as the proper and specific form. For he thought that the essence and substance of each thing consists of two parts, namely matter and form. Since, therefore, the Ideas lack both matter and body, the name of essence or substance can by no means be accommodated to them according to Aristotle's opinion: rather, they should be called divine principles from which all essences and substances are deduced—both the primary ones as their first and corporal effects, and the secondary ones as certain spiritual images and likenesses of the primary. Therefore, Aristotle—to conclude the matter at last in a few words—feels that the beauties of the corporal world are indeed true beauties, but they take their origin from those first and Ideal forms which reside in the first and divine intellect. From this greatest controversy of these two **Theologians** <note>Here used in the classical sense of "those who speak of the divine," referring to Plato and Aristotle.</note>, all other differences then proceed, both in this matter of Ideas and also in many other theological and natural disputations.

The controversy of Aristotle and Plato concerning Ideas consists more in names than in the things themselves.

### DIALOGUE III

<margin>
Aristotle seems preferable to Plato in his use of terminology. An elegant reason is given for why **Ideas** <note>original: "Idææ"; the eternal, non-physical templates or "Forms" of all things in Platonic philosophy.</note>, though celebrated with the highest praise by Plato, were seemingly held in contempt and rejected by Aristotle, using a metaphor drawn from the various and diverse methods of healing used by physicians.
</margin>

...you will recognize that you are dealing with the very same concepts. Therefore, if we look at their core meaning, since it is exactly one and the same, I believe both philosophers should be followed. But if we consider their use of vocabulary, I might perhaps prefer Aristotle to Plato. This is not surprising, since more recent thinkers often appear more diligent and skillful in polishing and elaborating their speech, as well as in devising specific terms that are perfectly suited to the natures of things. 

However, one might say in Plato’s defense that in his own time, he found that the most excellent Greek philosophers looked down upon any essences, substances, or forms other than physical ones; he sensed that they believed nothing existed beyond the body. Therefore, like a most skillful physician, he judged that they had to be restored to their former health by the application of a "contrary medicine." For this reason, he preached that bodies—by virtue of their own nature—were entirely devoid of all essence, substance, and beauty, and that they existed as nothing more than the thinnest shadows of that **incorporeal essence** <note>original: "incorporalis essentiæ"; a reality that does not have a physical body.</note> and **Ideal beauty** lurking in the mind of the Supreme Architect.

Aristotle, however, who succeeded Plato, perceived that philosophers—already persuaded by Plato—had essentially abandoned the physical world and transferred all beauty, essence, and substance into the Ideas. He saw that the corporeal world was being despised and treated as if it were nothing. Consequently, this most sharp-witted man realized that people imbued with these opinions would entirely desert and neglect the science of physical things, as well as the knowledge of actions, motions, natural alterations, and the causes of birth and decay. This ignorance and negligence is usually followed by an imperfect knowledge of spiritual and divine principles, since effects, when rightly known and understood, are what provide us with a perfect knowledge of their causes. 

Therefore, lest men should fall into most shameful errors by abusing Plato’s "salutary medicine," Aristotle behaved far more gently than his teacher. As we have already said, he showed that true essences and substances, flowing and emanating from the Ideas, are indeed found within the physical world. He demonstrated that true beauties also exist there, though they proceed from those most pure and perfect forms called Ideas. 

Thus, each of them seems to have performed the duty of an excellent physician, though in different ways: for Plato is thought to have been the first to heal the already-sick minds of men with a violent medicine, while Aristotle is thought to have preserved the health established by Plato by then applying a balanced temperament. 

**SOPHIA**: I understand well enough what the Ideas signify, why their use is said to be necessary, that Aristotle did not at all destroy them fundamentally, and how both of these most weighty philosophers understood and treated these Ideas differently. I shall require nothing further on these points, lest I perhaps hinder you from completing the previous discussion on beauty. I will bring forward only one difficulty, and one that is, in my judgment, quite suited to our purpose. You have placed true beauties in the **intelligible Ideas** <note>original: "Idæis intelligibilibus"; concepts that can only be grasped by the intellect, not the senses.</note>, or in the highest and first notions, or in the admirable order of the universe and all its parts residing in the mind of the Supreme Architect—that is, in the first and divine Intellect. Now, I concede that a prior and greater beauty is found in the Ideas as causes than in physical bodies; however, I do not believe that the true and first beauty itself, by whose merit all other things are called either beautiful or "beauties," is located within the Ideas. For since the Ideas are declared to be the first notions and, as it were, certain spiritual examples of the world and its almost innumerable parts, it seems necessary to say that they are many. Therefore, if each of those Ideas is called beautiful, or "beauty itself," there must surely exist something superior to them: a true and first beauty, through the communication of which the individual Ideas are subsequently called beautiful or beauties. For if one of those Ideas claimed the name of the true and first beauty for itself, then none of the others...

...considers to be a most precious image in which God has expressed His own likeness. **Sophia:** Truly, I desire to know one thing further concerning this divine beauty, which you described as the form, the pattern, and the <term>Idea</term> of the whole created world (both the bodily and the spiritual). Certainly, if the Idea of the universe were the first and true beauty of all, as you say, it would surely follow that the Ideal form of the world, since it holds the primary place, would surpass all other forms. <margin>The Idea of the universe and of its individual parts exists as one and the same thing with the Divine Intellect and Divine Wisdom; it is not distinguished from them by any reasoning whatsoever.</margin>

Because we have said that the Idea of the world resides *in* the Divine Intellect and Mind, you therefore think the Idea is something different from the Intellect or Mind where it is placed.

**Sophia:** Do we not truly pronounce that a thing which is placed in another exists as something different from that in which it is placed?

<margin>In any actual intellect, the thinker, the thing understood, and the act of understanding are found to exist as exactly the same thing.</margin>

Moreover, Divine Wisdom is seen to be in no way distinct from the Word, the Intellect, and the Divine Mind. For not only in God, but also in any of the <insert>created</insert> actual intellects, wisdom, the thing understood, and the understanding intellect itself exist as entirely one and the same; it is only by our reasoning that their most pure and simple unity is considered and perceived in this three-fold way. Now, if an intelligible unity of this kind belongs to any created intellect, it will without doubt be said to be far purer and more sincere in that supreme and Divine Intellect, which exists as one and the same with Ideal Wisdom, not distinct from it by any means at all. Therefore, the beauty of the Idea is the very beauty of the Divine Intellect itself. For form is not placed in Him as if in a subject; rather, the Intellect itself (or the Idea) is seen to possess the nature of the primary form, by merit of which all things afterwards became beautiful.

<margin>Ideal beauty is the very beauty of the Divine Intellect itself, since it is seen to be entirely one and the same with Divine Wisdom. **Philo:** Exactly.

# DIALOGUE III

<margin>
How Divinity far surpasses all types of sciences and knowledge within itself by a vast margin.

The understanding intellect, the act of understanding, and the thing understood exist as entirely one and the same. <note>Philo is citing a core principle of Aristotelian metaphysics: in the Divine Mind, the thinker, the thought, and the process of thinking are a single, indivisible unity.</note> Since, therefore, the divine essence is said to be one and most simple—with no appearance of multiplicity known to it, as such multiplicity would only hinder this unity—it is rightly judged that within this self-knowledge lies the most perfect cognition, both of the whole universe and of all created things simultaneously. This divine knowledge is far more eminent, perfect, accurate, and distinct than a divided or distributed knowledge of individual things. For that imperfect kind of science takes its origin from the things known, and is therefore seen to be divided, multiplied, and imperfect according to their nature and condition. But that divine knowledge, whether related to all things together or to each separately, is always judged to hold the status of a <term>First Cause</term>; thus, it is deemed to have no need of the help of effects to know them. On the contrary, because of the unity and simplicity of its own intellect, it retains a unified and most perfect knowledge of the entire World and of every individual created thing, even the smallest and lowest.

<margin>

</margin>

If, therefore, in scrutinizing the divine essence we wish to follow in the footsteps of the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle, so named because they reportedly walked about the "peripatos" or covered walkways of the Lyceum while debating.</note>, the solution to the difficulty you proposed appears quite clear and conspicuous. This beauty is rightly proclaimed as the first and truest of all forms, as we have already said. Because of its greater or lesser communication, other things are then rendered more or less beautiful. The universe itself, which encompasses all things as its parts, is seen to participate most strongly in that divine beauty, of which it is the true and proper image. Among the individual parts coming together in its composition, it is surely the intellectual nature <note>This refers to rational beings, such as angels and humans, who possess the capacity for thought.</note> in which the divine likeness is judged to have been expressed far more perfectly than in any other created thing, and which is thought to have claimed for itself the larger share of divine splendor.

They placed that First Cause above all intellects and all movers of the celestial bodies, just as we seem to have often said and declared when we discussed the commonality of love. Regarding their opinion, there is no need to speak further; for they, by combining the two views of the most excellent theologians (namely Aristotle and Plato) into one, constructed a new opinion that is lower than either of them and degenerates somewhat from the excellence of both.

This is because God is considered not as beauty itself, but as the *author* of His true and primary beauty, which exists as one and the same thing with His Supreme Wisdom and Ideal Intellect. Therefore, even if we concede that the wise and understanding God precedes His Supreme Wisdom and Intellect, we do not admit that His beauty precedes the beauty of that supreme and divine Wisdom. For God’s wisdom and His beauty are seen to be entirely one and the same,

Thus, divine beauty and the supreme wisdom of God are seen to coincide in every way as one thing. This divine form, communicated thereafter to others, adorns both the universe and all its parts with a fitting beauty. Therefore, in the series of "forms," three primary levels are said to be found: the origin of the form itself, the form itself, and the participant in the form. That is: the Beautiful one who bestows beauty, Beauty itself, and the beautiful thing that receives beauty. 

The "Beautiful" who bestows beauty, or the supreme parent of beauty, is God Himself. "Beauty itself" claims the title of Supreme Wisdom and the First, Ideal Intellect. Finally, the "beautiful" thing that receives beauty (or is shaped by beauty itself) is considered to be the entire universe of created things.

...and more abundant doctrine, I would also greatly desire to understand this: why you judged that God, the supreme good, should by no means be called by the name of beauty, but rather His first intellect; especially since no reason seems to compel us to assign an origin and principle to the first form—just as we do for the first wisdom and the first intellect.

PHILO: We seem to have been persuaded to do so for this reason: because it is thought that the name of true beauty can be better applied to wisdom than to the "wise one" <note>original: "sapientiæ potius quàm sapienti"</note> from whom that wisdom takes its origin. For beauty, by its very nature, exists such that it can be perceived and seen either by bodily eyes or by the light of the intellect; and because, by a certain grace infused within it, it seems to entice and, as it were, invite the soul of the beholder to love, benevolence, and the pursuit of itself: for this reason it has claimed the name of beauty for itself. 

However, as we have already said, no intellectual vision among those that were created is able to penetrate or discern anything higher than divine wisdom. Our intellect, it is true, rightly recognizes that there exists a principle of that wisdom—even through the wisdom it has perceived—yet it can observe or notice nothing worthy of the name of beauty in that principle. For this reason, it calls that highest "Beautiful" the principle and origin of beauty itself. 

But it rightly calls that supreme wisdom, which it knows from the series of divine works and the praiseworthy proportion of the parts of the universe, the "first and true beauty." For its unity, because it embraces all the essential and Ideal <note>Again, referring to the Platonic Ideas or archetypes.</note> stages of things, is judged to be most beautiful indeed by the intellects that can comprehend it. Moreover, this knowledge of beauty cannot be had at all from its most pure origin and principle, which is greatly hidden from us; for if we are ignorant of its proper name, how shall we ever be able to know its form? 

To confirm this matter, I would like to bring forward the Sun as a kind of bodily image and physical likeness of the incorporeal divinity. For the greater beauty of the Solar body, which bodily eyes can reach, is clearly the proper and exterior light diffused around the Sun. And although the eyes themselves are almost unable to look sharply into it to discern it, they nevertheless know it to be the first and highest light of the universe, from which all other lights scattered and sown throughout the bodily world proceed: just as we have already said that intellectual lights stand in relation to the supreme wisdom and first beauty. 

But as for what pertains to the innermost substance of the Sun, from which that exterior light is thought to come forth: the bodily eyes can discern neither light, nor beauty, nor anything else of it, except that they judge it to exist as a certain body or substance which procreates and produces that most beautiful light—always most closely joined to the Sun—which is the common origin of all lights and physical beauties. In the same way, intellectual lights can distinguish nothing besides the supreme beauty and wisdom, except that a certain "Highest Beautiful" and "Wise One" is found to be the first origin of the supreme beauty and wisdom. 

And just as that first solar light, proceeding from the first source of light, then makes other bodies (which are seen to be marked by beauty in the universe) beautiful and fair: so also that supreme wisdom and beauty, taking its origin from the Highest Beautiful (or the one bestowing beauty), and then being imparted to others, adorns with a fitting beauty all things whatsoever that were created and are commended by the praise of their form.

<margin>The author himself in this difficult discussion [asks] whether divine wisdom and Ideal beauty are nothing apart from God (as Aristotle held) or something else (as Plato held).</margin>
SOPHIA: This part being finished, nothing more seems to remain that could be desired or known in the proposed matter, except that you should reveal to which of the two mentioned opinions you grant the assent of your mind. 

PHILO: Since I wish to be considered a most observant follower of the Mosaic Laws <note>The Torah or the laws of Moses.</note>, I am compelled to assent to the second opinion, which is thought to have come forth from the Mosaic source, rather than the first. Indeed, Plato, who was far more studious of ancient wisdom than Aristotle, [followed] it...

# LEONIS HEBRAEUS ON LOVE #

<margin>
It seems he felt this way, distinguished by reason: he proposes that Plato’s opinion, being closer to the authority of the sacred volumes, should be followed rather than Aristotle’s opinion, which is more remote from them.
Plato was a disciple of the most wise Egyptian men.
</margin>
...we see that he also followed this path. Aristotle, however, who was quite unable to attain things that were too high and hidden, boldly denied them in his works on occult matters. Not striving toward anything higher, he asserted that this first and incorporeal principle of all things exists alone. But Plato, having been a student of the ancient Egyptians, was able to clearly intuit or discern a principle of first beauty or wisdom that was superior to Aristotle’s <term>First Mover</term> <note>Aristotle's "unmoved mover" is the primary cause of motion in the universe, which Philo argues is a lower concept than Plato's "Divine Wisdom."</note>. For this reason, that most serious Philosopher declared that first form and wisdom to be the second principle of the universe, because it draws its origin from God, the first and most universal principle of the order of things. Although Plato educated Aristotle in the liberal arts, since he himself had received knowledge of divine things passed down from the ancient Egyptians, he seems to have had much more excellent teachers in the genre of science than Aristotle.

<margin>
Plato is preferred to Aristotle in the contemplation of divine things and knowledge.
Aristotle's arrogance.
</margin>
Aristotle is said to have learned the doctrines later communicated to him by Plato; yet as the most recent disciple, he is hardly considered equal to his teacher’s master. Regarding Aristotle’s genius, I also suspect that although he is proclaimed to have been most acute, his mind was not as well-suited or adapted to the contemplation of things entirely separated from matter and body as Plato’s was. Furthermore, in the manner of other disciples, he could never bring himself to affirm as true—moved solely by the authority of his teacher—that which he was unable to demonstrate by the strength of his own natural talent.

SOPHIA: But I will set aside Aristotle’s arrogance and follow the rest of the Platonists. For, leaning upon your doctrine as if upon a stable foundation, I shall claim a certain and indubitable knowledge of whatever I am able to understand; as for the rest, I will yield full faith to you as to one far wiser than I. But I desire above all to know where Moses and the other holy Prophets seem to have signaled this Platonic opinion.

PHILO: Moses

<margin>
He demonstrates at length that the Platonic opinion of divine wisdom and divine beauty accords most especially with Moses and Solomon.
</margin>
is found to have taken the beginning of his narration from these words: *In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth* <note>original: "In principio creavit Deus caelum & terram"</note>. However, the most ancient context written in the Chaldean language <note>The "Chaldean language" refers to Aramaic, specifically the Targum, which is an ancient translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> says in place of that phrase, "In the beginning": *With wisdom God created the heaven and the earth* <note>original: "Cum sapientia creauit Deus Coelum & terram"</note>. Nor is this surprising: for "Beginning" among the Hebrews is called "Wisdom," which is confirmed especially by the testimony of Solomon, who says: *The beginning is wisdom* <note>original: "Principium est sapientia." Referring to the Hebrew word "Reshit."</note>. The word "In" <note>original: "In" / Hebrew: "Be-"</note> among the Hebrews is also frequently found to signify "With." Consider therefore, O Sophia, how elegantly he demonstrated at the very start of his Prophetic narration that the world was once procreated through the mediation of wisdom, and that wisdom once held the status of the second principle in the procreation of the world. It is as if he wished to imply that God, the supreme creator of all, brought the universe of created things into the light with the help of His highest wisdom and highest beauty, and adorned each thing with form and grace.

Therefore, the most wise Moses seems to have begun his narration from a triple beauty: namely, God, Wisdom, and the World. Then King Solomon, famous for the name of wisdom, performing the duty of an excellent disciple and interpreter, is found to have explained and clarified this sentiment of Moses in the Book of Proverbs thus: *The Lord by wisdom founded the earth, and by supreme knowledge he established the heavens: by his intellect the depths broke out, and the clouds drop down the dew.* <note>Proverbs 3:19–20</note> Wherefore he immediately adds these precepts: *My son, let these not flow away from your eyes; contemplate and guard the highest thoughts, which will minister life to your soul,* and the rest that follows. Who could have ever declared Moses’ meaning more clearly, or confirmed Plato’s opinion more strongly?

### DIALOGUE III ###

...[Aristot]le also, no differently than Plato, agrees that God perfected all things with wondrous wisdom. However, in this one respect he seems to differ from him: Aristotle considers wisdom to be one and the same, existing entirely as one with God; Plato, however, judges that it proceeds from God. You, who contend that Plato is a "Moses in Greek" <note>A common Renaissance idea that Plato’s philosophy was derived from the teachings of Moses.</note>, ought certainly to show that this disagreement of Plato with Aristotle was also expressed in the sacred volumes.

**PHILO:** Our most holy ancestors, when they speak of these kinds of mysteries, are accustomed to use their own proper expressions. For they do not say "a wise God created" or "He created wisely," but they preferred to say, "God created *with* wisdom." They did this, of course, to signify that God, existing as the supreme creator, used wisdom as a medium and instrument most perfectly suited for the procreation of things. We find this same point expressed even more clearly by David, the King most beloved of God himself, who says: *By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of the divine mouth all their host* <note>Original: "Verbo Domini cœli firmati fuerunt, & spiritu oris diuini totus exercitus eius." Psalm 33:6.</note>. This "Word" is the Wisdom that exists, which is rightly compared with the spirit coming forth from the mouth; for by that same reasoning, Wisdom is seen to emanate from the First Wise One, just as spirit emanates from the mouth. Nor are both said to be one and the same entirely, as Aristotle felt. 

But so that this matter may be understood more clearly, and as if placed before your very eyes, see, I pray, how clearly it is explained by King Solomon near the beginning of the Proverbs, who introduces Wisdom speaking in this way: "I am Wisdom." Afterward, he declares how she contains within herself all virtues and beauties in a unified way—sciences, prudences, arts, and the virtues that govern souls. Finally, he adds: *Counsel is mine, and reason; I am understanding, strength is mine. By me kings reign, and the founders of laws decree just things. By me princes rule, and the powerful know the truth. I love those who love me, and those who seek me diligently shall find me. I carry with me all riches, distinguished and just beauties, so that I may distribute them liberally and copiously to those close to me, and make their treasuries most full.* <note>A paraphrased translation of Proverbs 8:14-21.</note> 

After he explained, as it is read, in what way all kinds of wisdom, virtues, and beauties proceed in a general diffusion from Divine Wisdom—which she herself distributes lavishly and liberally to the men who love her and search for her—so that he might more expressively signify the clarity and loveliness of Divine Wisdom to us, he is found to have attributed this speech to her: *The Lord created me in the beginning of his ways: before he made anything from the beginning, I was ordained from eternity, and from of old, before the earth was made. The abysses did not yet exist, and I was already conceived; the fountains of waters had not yet erupted, nor had the mountains settled in their heavy mass. Before the hills I was brought forth; he had not yet made the earth, nor the breadths of the regions, nor the poles of the world. When he prepared the heavens, I was there; when he surrounded the abysses with a certain law and boundary; when he established the ether above and balanced the fountains of waters; when he assigned boundaries to the sea and imposed a law on the waters so they would not leap over the limits set for them; when he laid the foundations of the earth: then I was with him as a certain craftsmanship and art, composing all things, and exercising myself in building beautiful and skillful works. Daily I played before him, especially in the world of the earth: and my delights were with the children of men. Now therefore, children, hear me, and observe my precepts diligently,* and the rest that follows. <note>A translation of the famous passage in Proverbs 8:22-32, where Wisdom is personified as a co-creator with God.</note> 

Consider, I pray, O Sophia, how excellently the most wise King has demonstrated in this speech that the supreme Wisdom emanates from God and proceeds from Him, rather than being one and the same with God as Aristotle felt. He called the supreme Wisdom "the beginning of the divine ways," and not without reason: for the "divine ways" are seen to signify the creation of the world. Moreover, the supreme Wisdom is said to have existed as the "beginning" <term>principium</term> <note>Philo is playing on the Latin *principium* (beginning/principle), linking it to the first word of Genesis.</note> through whose mediation God is judged to have created the world. Therefore, the King, using the name of Wisdom, clarified that somewhat obscure saying of Moses: *In the beginning God created heaven and earth.* Solomon then showed that this supreme Wisdom first emanated from God and preceded the creation of the universe.

->LEO HEBRAEUS ON LOVE,<-

since through her <note>Wisdom is personified as female in both the Latin "Sapientia" and the Hebrew "Chokmah."</note> mediation both the totality of all things and the individual parts of the universe were procreated by God, the Best and Greatest. Moreover, by a certain [reasoning], he called her the art or craftsmanship of the supreme Craftsman; this is because supreme wisdom is said to be a most artistic exemplar placed in the divine mind, according to whose likeness God formed the universe, and thus she seems to claim for herself the name of art or craftsmanship. He added that she was "with God" <note>A reference to Proverbs 8:30: "Then I was beside him, like a master workman."</note> to demonstrate that supreme wisdom is by no means distant from its origin in reality or essence, but that both are forever most closely joined. He also declared that the most delightful forms and all delights are derived from her into the World, both the celestial and the terrestrial. He concluded that terrestrial beauties, if compared with the forms of men, are obscure and almost laughable. For, as I have already said, just as the beauty of Solar light is imprinted far more perfectly in subtle and transparent things than in solid and opaque bodies, so too the first form and supreme [beauty] leaves its footprint much more strongly imprinted in the procreated angelic and human intellects than in all the bodies of the universe. 

Nor did that most wise King only represent this Ideal outflowing—the principle of worldly procreation—under the name and character of supreme wisdom; he also designated the same in his *Canticles* <note>The *Cantica Canticorum*, or the Song of Songs.</note> under the name and appearance of beauty, where in its beginning he is found to have uttered those words: *You are all beautiful, my friend, and there is no flaw in you at all.* <note>Original: "Tota pulchra es amica mea, nec ulla in te macula prorsus existit." Song of Songs 4:7.</note> How clearly Solomon seems to have expressed the supreme and Ideal beauty of divine wisdom by granting her the purest form, obscured by no stain, however small. This praise is truly proper to her alone, and cannot be shared with any other things that are merely participants in form. For those things which participate in beauty are found to be by no means beautiful in themselves, but rather imperfect, insofar as they only receive it; and indeed, those things which claim some part of beauty for themselves cannot be entirely beautiful. 

Moreover, she is called the companion of God because she is found to have been associated with God in the procreation of the World, no differently than art is with a craftsman for the building of some artistic work. Elsewhere, we read that the most prudent King declared her unity and simplicity when he said: *There are seventy queens...* and so on. Also: *My dove is one, my perfect one.* <note>Original: "Septuaginta sunt Reginae... una est columba mea, perfecta mea." Solomon actually says sixty queens in Song of Songs 6:8; Leo's text here says "Septuaginta" (seventy).</note> Then he invokes her, saying: *You, my dove, hiding in the highest peak of dignity, let me discern your face and hear your voice; for your face is most beautiful and your voice is surely most sweet.* <note>A philosophical expansion of Song of Songs 2:14.</note> How lucidly in these words did the most wise Solomon declare the most simple unity of supreme beauty! And how elegantly he signaled that she can scarcely be known or seen by us, because she is placed in the highest rank and governs the totality of all created things. 

Therefore, the King finally offered humble prayers to her, so that she might deign to grant the presence of her beauty to bodies in a visible and apparent way, but to created intellects by voice and word alone—that is, to communicate through a certain wise reasoning. Furthermore, that King, captured by his great love for her, is found to have handed down many more things pertaining to supreme beauty in his *Canticles*; all of these I have decided to pass over in silence, lest I perhaps incur the mark of being wordy or talkative. I will add this one thing to the above: that just as he gave the name of supreme beauty to Ideal wisdom, so also he applied the title of "the Most Beautiful" to the supreme God of all, from whom supreme beauty is judged to emanate as if from a most fertile fountain. For he says: *Behold, you are beautiful to me, my beloved, and handsome; our bed is still flowering.* <note>Original: "Ecce tu pulcher es mihi dilecte atq; decorus: lectulus noster adhuc floridus existit." Song of Songs 1:16.</note> Indeed, the King seems to have signified by these words that God is by no means to be called "beautiful" like other things that participate in form, but rather that He, as the supreme one of all, produced beauty itself. Furthermore, he designated the bond and conjunction of the emanating supreme beauty with the "Most Beautiful One," from whom she is judged to emanate, by these words especially: *Our bed is still flowering.* For God, joined with supreme beauty, is [called] the true and proper cause...

### DIALOGUE III.

...it is said to be, so that the universe of created things may flourish and deserve to be called "beautiful." Solomon also, in the book of Ecclesiastes, touched upon the beauty imparted to the universe quite elegantly, saying: *God has made all things good, preserved in the opportunity of their time.* <note>Reference to Ecclesiastes 3:11: "He has made everything beautiful in its time." Philo is equating "good" with "beautiful."</note> Solomon seems to have taken this way of speaking from Moses, who said: *God saw everything that he had made, and they were very good.* <note>Genesis 1:31.</note> It is worth considering that the Prophet <note>Moses, traditionally regarded as the author of Genesis.</note>, describing the individual parts of the universe, says that God saw that each one of them was "good." But when the universe was already finished, he says God saw that "all things" he had made were "very good." That "good" indeed signifies "beautiful" is proven to us by the strongest argument: that he relates "good" to the sense of seeing. Indeed, no one should doubt that visible goodness signifies beauty. The Prophet says that this kind of "good" was seen by God, the Best and Greatest, in order to signify that divine vision and the supreme wisdom of God rendered the individual parts of the universe beautiful by imparting to them their own specific beauty; however, he made the universe itself the most beautiful and best of all by gathering all wisdom and beauty into it at once.

*SO.* I give you innumerable thanks for your singular devotion toward me, which you have shown so promptly and eagerly by solving all the difficulties I proposed—the more so because their solutions seem to have revealed a certain distinguished and hidden science of the theology of Moses. I require nothing further from you regarding the knowledge of true beauty; for I understand that it—along with that supreme divine wisdom which is seen shining in the whole universe and adorns its individual parts with a fitting beauty—exists as one and the same thing. Now, I would only desire from you an explanation of that love which King Solomon, in the *Song of Songs*, described as existing between the "Supreme Fair" and "Supreme Beauty." For since the "Supreme Fair" <note>Latin: *summum pulchrum*, referring to God as the source of beauty.</note> takes on the role of the lover, it would surely seem to be lower than the "beloved beauty"; for, as you have already shown above, the lover always seems to be less noble than the beloved. Yet you just said that the Supreme Fair is the origin and principle of Supreme Beauty. Behold, there is a clear and open contradiction in your words.

<margin>He carefully explains that love between the Supreme Fair and Supreme Beauty—like that between a man and a woman, treated so splendidly and copiously by Solomon in his Song of Songs—is the highest of all loves, from which the universe of created things is then considered to have flowed.</margin>

*PH.* I will attempt to give you the reason for this matter as well. Solomon, and the other theologians who profess the doctrine of Moses, think that the World was brought forth like a son from the Supreme Fair (as if from a father) and from Supreme Wisdom, which is true Beauty (as if from a mother). They add that Supreme Wisdom—being like a most perfect woman ensnared by the love of the man, with him also pursuing her with mutual benevolence—conceived from the great power of the Supreme Fair, and brought forth the universe as the common progeny of both, along with all its individual parts. And this is surely what that love signifies, by which Solomon in the *Song of Songs* testifies that his female friend loved her most beautiful beloved. Therefore, because he is superior and performs the duty of the producer far more than she, who is inferior and has obtained the condition of the produced, he deserves the title of "the beloved." For this reason, you will see her always addressing him—as an inferior to a superior—by the name of "Beloved" as a mark of honor. He, however, never calls her "Beloved," but—as a superior to an intimate—is most frequently accustomed to calling her "my companion," "my dove," "my perfect one," or "my sister." Nor is this surprising: for she, having obtained his love, acquires from him her greatest perfection; and like a fertile woman conceiving from her husband, she is seen to have brought the World, a most perfect work, into the light.

<margin>The Supreme Fair and Supreme Beauty are the parents of this first and most ancient World.</margin>

But that love, by which the Supreme Fair is said to love Supreme Beauty in return, bestows no additional perfection upon the Supreme Fair itself; for what, I ask, can be added to Him? Rather, He strives only to make the World, as their common son, most perfect. Even if some perfection—namely a relative one—might fall to Him from this: for the perfection of a son usually brings a certain perfection to the father as well, though it is not essential or real, in the way it is for Supreme Beauty herself. Similarly, we see an individual human being born from a perfect male and an imperfect female—whom the ancients called a <term>microcosm <note>original Greek: μικροκόσμον, meaning "little world"</note></term>. Likewise also in

->### LEO THE HEBREW ON LOVE<-

<margin>The love of the Sun and Moon.</margin>
...in the celestial region, the Sun and the Moon love each other with the mutual love of a man and a woman,
<margin>The love of spouses exists through the love of the Highest Beautiful and the Highest Beauty; she is said to be not only the wife of the Highest Beautiful, but also his daughter, the greatest of all children.</margin>
and they bear the image of marriage: from which, as we have already said above, all things in this lower world

through whose mediation the universe of procreated things is believed to have flowed out. In this Highest Beauty, however, a certain difference lies hidden,

<margin>The first love seen in the universe of all procreated things.</margin>
From these things we have said so far, I believe you understand well enough the reason why the first love seen in the universe
took its origin: from the First Beauty as if from a father, and from the knowledge of it
which is held by the first of all procreated intelligences—the "First Mover" <note>term: *primo mobili*; in ancient astronomy, this was the outermost sphere that imparted motion to all others</note>—which was chosen to move
the other bodies contained within its vast circuit, acting as a mother.
<margin>The origin of any love whatsoever.</margin>
This intelligence most vehemently desires that quality of the Highest Beauty which it recognizes is lacking in itself. By this same
reason, every individual love is thought to be born from the Highest Beauty communicated and imparted to things,
and from the knowledge of it held by the one who lacks it, and who aspires to and strives for union with it.
Hence, the greater the portion of the Highest Beauty that things obtain, or the more abundant knowledge they have of it,
the more fervently they will burn with love for it. Furthermore, the more excellent the form that lovers propose
for themselves to love, the more excellent they themselves will turn out to be and be called: for things that are excellent in form
are naturally accustomed to captivate their lovers with their beauty and render them more sublime. <margin>Bodily forms are either to be entirely left behind by us, or all study of them is to be directed only toward the knowledge of incorporeal forms.</margin> It seems right, therefore, Sophia, that we should leave behind
impure and imperfect beauties, such as all forms found associated with
matter and the body; and that we should love them only insofar as we can strive, by their help, toward knowing and loving
incorporeal and perfect beauties. But the rest of them, which are accustomed to lead our minds away from the noble loves
of spiritual forms, we should decline with all our strength and pursue with implacable and perpetual hatred. <margin>The chief study of man. In the knowledge and love of spiritual forms, we must progress step by step from the lower to the higher, until we finally reach the supreme and most excellent form of all.</margin> I think it is right
that the chief study of man should be occupied with those most excellent forms which are entirely separated from foul matter and
bodily stain: such as the virtues and sciences, which flourish with perpetual form and
seem to be entirely free from any foulness or imperfection. In these we must also have some

The end of any love seems to be placed chiefly in the pleasure of the lover himself.

For the end which men strive to acquire at the persuasion of Love is seen to be diametrically opposed to the end which they strive to avoid at the compulsion of Hatred. Whence it is not at all surprising if the means accommodated to such opposite ends are also said to be contrary. For the hope of Love and the pursuit of the delightful are considered very appropriate means; whereas for Hatred, fear and the flight from pain are the means. If, therefore, the alienation from pain (as if from an evil and ugly thing) is judged to be the end of Hatred, then the end of Love will surely be the approaching of pleasure (as if it were a good and beautiful thing).

Above all, consider those venereal embraces <note>original: *Venerei complexus*; sexual intercourse</note>, which are felt to be the greatest of sensible pleasures. All things of this kind seem to be entirely destitute of any beauty; they can be called neither beautiful nor ugly. Yet, if you wish to be consistent with yourself, they must certainly be called the "ends" of love, since all the things just mentioned are finally obtained by us through will and desire acting as intermediary means. Therefore, Love is not the desire for the beautiful, as you defined it before, but for the delightful...

<meta>This page continues the third dialogue between Philo and Sophia. ->### DIALOGUE III<-

...they are said to be both good and beautiful, which are indeed the goals of desire when it joins together with love into one. Some things, however, are perceived to be only good, and not at all beautiful, such as those things you listed a moment ago; and these seem to be the goals suited to desire when it is separated from love, which is properly called "sensible appetite" <note>The "sensible appetite" refers to the basic physical or sensory drives common to all animals, as opposed to the higher, intellectual love Philo is describing.</note>.
<margin>Pleasures that are both good and beautiful are the proper goals of love; those that are merely good, and not at all beautiful, are considered the proper goals of the sensible appetite.</margin>

**SO.** I have understood very well the difference you have placed between amorous desire and sensible appetite, and the reason why amorous desires define their own goals as pleasures that are both good and beautiful, while the appetites define their own goals as delights that are only good and not at all beautiful. But from this, I am struck by no small wonder: that you have conceded every pleasure to be "good" simply because it is sought after, and that everything sought after is considered to have the character of "the Good." For even if this is confirmed by the authority of Aristotle <note>A reference to the opening of the *Nicomachean Ethics*.</note>, who defined "the Good" as that which all things seek; and because of the Law of Conversion <note>In logic, a "convertible" definition is one where the subject and predicate can switch places and remain true (e.g., "Man is a rational animal" and "A rational animal is a man").</note>, which is especially required in a definition and the thing defined, just as every good is usually sought, so whatever is sought has the character of the good. Nevertheless, we often see the opposite happen in practice.
<margin>The definition and the thing defined are always interchangeable with one another.</margin>
For many pleasures are found to be not at all good, but rather evil and destructive; they are found to bring the greatest harm not only to the body and health, but also to the soul and its well-being. Yet, these are still sought by many people; otherwise, men would not labor so hard to acquire them. Therefore, it seems one should not concede that every desire is concerned with the good, nor that every desire is good, nor that every pleasure is good. On the contrary, many wicked desires and many terrible pleasures, which are most opposed to the human good, are found everywhere.

**PH.** I do not think we should agree that, according to Aristotle’s opinion, everything sought after is "the Good." For we do not find that the philosopher said the good is that which is *usually* sought; rather, he himself defined "the Good" as that which *all* things seek. Moreover, this definition of the good returns perfectly to the "Good" itself as the thing being defined: for that which all things seek is truly called the Good.
<margin>The Good is defined by Aristotle as that which all things seek.</margin>

**SO.** But what such "noble good" is found, I pray, that leads all men to desire it?

**PH.** Aristotle himself, as if explaining his own meaning, testifies that this kind of good is knowledge itself, or wisdom; for he is seen to have begun his *Metaphysics* from this principle: *All men by nature desire to know* <note>original: "Omnes homines naturaliter scire desiderant." This is the famous opening line of Aristotle's *Metaphysics*.</note>.
<margin>All men, with nature as their guide, desire to know.</margin>
This kind of desire, however, seems to be not only of the good, but also of the true and the beautiful. Therefore, I do not think it should be concluded from Aristotle’s opinion that everything sought after is "the Good."

**SO.** Why, then, did you just now concede it so easily, and moreover, assert it?

**PH.** Because I consider this to be so true that nothing truer can even be imagined. For the goal of the will and of desire consists entirely in the good, and whatever is sought is always sought under the aspect of being good and pleasant; and every pleasant thing, insofar as it is pleasant, happens also to be good and sought after.
<margin>All love and every appetite always strive toward the good.</margin>
But desires and the pleasures sought are seen to have the same diversity as those who seek them. For among those who seek, those who are seen to be of a well-ordered mind desire moderate pleasures; but those who possess a disordered mind are accustomed to seek immoderate pleasures.
<margin>Pleasures are rendered various and dissimilar according to the differing natures of the men who love and seek them.</margin>

**SO.** I [would have thought] that these latter pleasures were not at all good.

**PH.** Considered in the context of their own specific natures, they should indeed not be called good; rather, they are said to be good only to those who seek them. This is because those people consider these kinds of pleasures to be good, and they are accustomed to seek them as if they were good. Because of their wicked and corrupt nature, both in judging and in seeking, and also in the very pleasures they lust after, they are seen to commit many errors, taking evil for good.

**SO.** There are, therefore, some pleasures which, although they *seem* good, are not good at all. Likewise, some desires are not directed toward the good at all. These points certainly seem to contradict most strongly those things which you conceded and asserted above.

**PH.** Since...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Philo and Sophia regarding the nature of the "Good" and "Pleasure." On the previous page, Sophia questioned whether all things sought after are truly good, citing Aristotle's definition. Philo here begins to resolve her confusion by distinguishing between the inherent goodness of pleasure and the potential corruption of its source or context.</meta>

->### LEO HEBRAEUS: ON LOVE<-

<margin>
Pleasure is always good by its very nature.
</margin>
Since everything delightful seems to exist as a certain kind of good, it must participate in something beneficial, by merit of which humans desire, seek, and pursue it as a good. Indeed, let us grant that pleasure is good by its very nature, just as we grant that pain—the opposite of pleasure—is an evil by the very nature of pain. Therefore, we say it has happened not by chance, but by design, that just as the human mind rejects, dreads, and flees from every form of pain, it likewise desires, hopes for, and pursues every pleasure.

**SO.** Why then did you say that many pleasures are bad, and that many immoderate desires are found according to the depraved natures of those who seek them?

<margin>
Some pleasures are pure, some are impure; likewise, some are good in reality, while others are good only in outward appearance.
</margin>
**PH.** Good and evil can indeed dwell together harmoniously in the same subject—not as the same thing, but by virtue of different parts. For the same thing can be slightly good, and that only in appearance, while being mostly evil, and that internally or in its very essence. In this category, depraved and disordered pleasures must be placed; these are commended with the praise of "goodness" only insofar as they are seen to bring us delight. But if you carefully weigh their internal nature, you will surely find them to be depraved. For the good which they have received in their own proper form seems to be so entangled with the depravity of matter <note>In Renaissance Neo-Platonism, "matter" was often viewed as the lowest level of reality, which could "trap" or "obscure" the higher, divine forms or ideas.</note>, and so submerged in filthy matter, that such pleasures are in reality bad, and are to be called good only in their outward appearance because of a certain surrounding sweetness. Indeed, even that outward appearance is not simply good, nor is it entirely delightful; rather, it is found to bring delight only to those who desire such pleasures beyond what is fair and good. Such people are deceived by the smallest bit of goodness surrounding the exterior, and they rush headlong into desiring and pursuing them, having no consideration at all for the many evils lurking beneath that outward sweetness. But those who have reduced the immoderate desires of the soul to a healthy middle ground <note>original: "mediocritatem" — referring to the Aristotelian "Golden Mean," the virtuous balance between extremes.</note> are by no means deceived by that smallest and apparent good, for they recognize that a great deal of evil is mixed in with it. Therefore, they consider it neither delightful nor desirable; instead, they curse, fear, and flee from it as if it were some great evil. Moreover, these kinds of depraved and destructive pleasures are primarily sought by the imperfect senses, namely taste and touch—as anyone can recognize from the immoderate desire for food, drink, and sexual union <note>original: "venereorumque complexu," referring to the acts of Venus.</note>, as well as from the most hateful way of life led by those indulging in luxury, soft living, and idleness.

**SO.** Are not some sensory pleasures also called truly and properly good?

<margin>
Only those sensory pleasures that have been reduced to a laudable moderation are to be called truly good and honorable.
</margin>
**PH.** Most certainly: namely those which are called temperate and necessary for the preservation of human life and the propagation of the human species. For pleasures of this kind, though they are sensory, nevertheless have honor <note>term: "honesty" or "honor" (Latin: *honestas*), meaning moral excellence or virtue.</note> joined to them. For they have received a praiseworthy measure and an excellent balance from the intellect, which is the most outstanding author of all honor. Those who desire these moderate pleasures, and the desires themselves, are deservedly commended with the praise of virtue and honor.

**SO.** Come now, in the case of "beautiful" pleasures <note>These are pleasures derived from the "higher" senses like sight and hearing, which Philo distinguishes from the "lower" physical senses like touch.</note>, is the same difference found between the good and the bad as is found in those that are not beautiful?

<margin>
Both beautiful and non-beautiful pleasures undergo the same division: for both appear to be good either in truth or only in appearance.
</margin>
**PH.** Absolutely. For many things are loved by men as if they were beautiful—for which reason they are called "lovable"—yet they are so obscured by the deformity and baseness of their matter that they appear foul rather than beautiful, and should be cursed and avoided rather than loved or pursued. In this category we must place those "beautiful" things which are said to "smell of matter" <note>An idiom suggesting they are too tied to physical, corruptible existence rather than spiritual beauty.</note> and are considered superfluous and not at all necessary for the preservation of life. For the vehement pursuit of all these things is properly called "cupidity" and "greed." In this same category, we must place elegant speeches, elaborate orations, and resonant poems, which, even if they are sprinkled with wit and humor as if with flowers, nevertheless embrace dishonorable and foul meanings. The same is true regarding imaginations <unclear>s</unclear>

<summary>Philo explains to Sophia that while pleasure is inherently good, it can be corrupted when it is immoderate or tied to "filthy matter," leading to a distinction between true goods and those that only appear good on the surface. He argues that only sensory pleasures moderated by the intellect for survival and procreation are truly honorable, while excessive physical or even aesthetic pleasures (like clever but immoral poetry) are forms of greed.</summary>
