<meta>This page continues the third dialogue of Leo Hebraeus’s "Dialogues of Love" (Dialoghi d'amore), translated here from the Latin edition. Philo and Sophia are discussing how human desires are categorized based on whether the object of desire is truly good or merely appears to be so.</meta>

->### DIALOGUE III<-

<margin>A complete and absolute division of pleasures.</margin>
...imaginations and thoughts which seem beautiful in appearance alone, but are rejected by intellectual reason <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "intellectual reason" refers to the highest faculty of the soul, capable of perceiving divine truths beyond mere sensory data.</note> and convicted of baseness. I believe the same should be felt regarding glory and honor, as well as dominion and empire unjustly acquired; all of these, although they are most vehemently desired by men because of their apparent beauty, are nevertheless found in reality to be deformed and dishonorable. Therefore, we are accustomed to call an excessive pursuit of them **ambition**. To put the matter briefly: the vehement desire for all things that seem good in appearance, but are not good in reality, is commonly called **lust** <note>original: "libido"; here used in a broad philosophical sense for any disordered or irrational craving.</note>. **SO.** Four types of pleasures can therefore be gathered from what has been said: two of which are said to be both good and beautiful, while the other two are only good and not at all beautiful. Both categories are divided in two ways: for pleasures that are both good and beautiful are either real or apparent; similarly, pleasures

<margin>Desires do not admit of a fourfold division. The affections and the pleasures themselves that are sought are thought to be taken up. A very elegant division of seekers into temperate and intemperate, or honorable and dishonorable.</margin>
that are only good and not beautiful are thought to involve either a real good or an apparent good. Could this fourfold division perhaps be applied to desires and to those who seek them? **PH.** In desires, you will most clearly find the four differences of the pleasures sought. But as for the seekers themselves, only two types—and certainly no more—seem capable of being applied: namely, the **temperate** and the **intemperate**, or the **honorable** and the **dishonorable**. Those who behave temperately in pleasures—both those that are good and beautiful and those that are only good—seek those things which are such truly and in reality, and by no means in appearance alone. The intemperate, however, are seen to be occupied only in the pursuit of those pleasures which *seem* beautiful and good, but are not truly so. This

<margin>The difference between seekers arises from the true or merely apparent goodness and beauty of their own souls.</margin>
difference between seekers seems to proceed from the internal goodness and beauty of their own souls. For those who are truly good and beautiful within seek and love pleasures that are also truly good and beautiful. But those who have obtained an internal goodness and beauty that is neither true nor real, but only false and apparent, delight in similar pleasures. Between these two opposites, many middle states are found, composed of both extremes. For you will see some behave temperately and honorably in certain pleasures, but intemperately and dishonorably in others.

<margin>An epilogue of the things said so far.</margin>
Furthermore, some are seen to be temperate in most things and intemperate in a few, or vice versa. All of these take their name of honor or baseness from that part toward which they are said to be more inclined. **SO.** I have well understood the reason why all pleasures either truly exist as good, or at least appear to be good, and are sought for this reason. I also

<margin>The goal of love and of every desire consists in pleasure.</margin>
recognize that those pleasures which, besides goodness, also have beauty (either real or apparent) joined to them, are not only sought but are also loved. For this very reason, you placed the goal of love in the pleasure which the lover finally takes from the beloved thing; by a similar

<margin>In love, the union with the beloved so greatly sought by the lover, and the pleasure which the lover strives to obtain for himself from the beloved, are found to be one and the same thing.</margin>
analogy, I judge that the goal of desire should also be placed in the pleasure which the seeker finally perceives from the thing craved. For both seem to differ in nothing else, except that he who only desires but does not love is said to seek a thing that is not beautiful under the rationale of a good (either real or at least apparent). But he who desires and loves at the same time [seeks] the beautiful, whether real or only apparent to him. <note>The text here transitions to how this relates to the definition of love as union.</note> [How] will you reconcile the goal of love you have just devised with your previous definition of love, where you said that love is the desire for union? For union certainly seems to be something different from pleasure. **PH.** On the contrary, both are one and the same thing; for I believe that pleasure itself signifies nothing other than the union with the delightful. For the delightful, as we have already said, is either only good, or also beautiful; whether it is true, or at least appears so to the seeker...

Now, Sophia questions how this fits with Aristotle's traditional division of love into three distinct categories.</meta>

->### DIALOGUE III<-

...exists, is thought to be. Therefore, to conclude that the goal of love lies in the pleasure the lover receives from the beloved object is the same as saying that love is situated in the most intimate union with the beloved. **SO.** I understand this very well. But a doubt now occurs to me: since you seem to have placed the goal of love in pleasure—to the extent that anyone who loves would be led by this reasoning—did you not previously determine, according to Aristotle’s opinion <note>Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book VIII, defines three types of friendship/love: that based on utility, that based on pleasure, and that based on virtue.</note>, that love is threefold: namely, the pleasant, the useful, and the virtuous? Are you now retracting what was said, omitting the two primary types of love, and reducing them all to the "pleasant," affirming that the goal of every love consists solely in pleasure? **PH.** Although Aristotle, as we have said, divided love into three species and called only one of them by the name of "the pleasant" <note>original: "iucundi"</note>, you must realize, Sophia, that pleasure is the most common end for all three species of love combined.

<margin>The common end of all three types of love—the useful, the pleasant, and the virtuous—consists in pleasure.</margin>

For just as those held by the love of bodily pleasures strive to acquire pleasure for themselves from union with them, so too those who have proposed to love useful goods <note>Things that are "useful" (utilia) generally refer to wealth, status, or tools that help one achieve another goal.</note> and desire them vehemently are led to this kind of love and desire because they believe they will perceive pleasure from their acquisition and use. Indeed, many are found who take far more delight in the possession of useful goods than in food, drink, or sexual embraces. Hence, you will often see them neglect and despise the latter in order to obtain the former. Virtue <note>original: "Honestum"; in this context, it refers to moral and intellectual excellence or the "honorable" good.</note> is also seen to bring the greatest delight to men who are studious of it; they refuse to undergo no labor, however arduous, so that they may most joyfully enjoy virtuous pleasures. Therefore, because of the goal of each of the three mentioned species, love seems to be situated in the pleasure that the lover perceives from the union with the beloved thing—whether it be pleasant, useful, or virtuous. **SO.** Why then did Aristotle declare that only one species of love is concerned with "the pleasant" or pleasures, while the others are concerned with different things?

<margin>He gives several reasons why, although pleasure is said to be the common end of all loves, Aristotle nevertheless divided love into three species: the useful, the pleasurable, and the virtuous.</margin>

**PH.** Because the common crowd is accustomed to call and believe that sensory pleasures are the only "true and proper" pleasures, even though the reality is otherwise. For these sensory pleasures, being the lowest of all, are most closely tied to matter and are almost entirely destitute of beauty; they are only able to bring small and very thin delights. As we have already warned, they are more truly and properly said to be "desired" than "loved." Although they are thought to have some small portion of beauty, that beauty is so wrapped in darkness that their minimal form is obscured and seemingly corrupted by the great deformity of matter and their own meager goodness. Therefore, such things are judged by the most learned men not to be truly good or beautiful. But Aristotle, following popular opinion, labeled this species of love with the name "the pleasant." However, so that he might separate the pursuit of [useful] goods from this sensory species—even though men are seen to delight in them no less than the others—he called it the love of "the useful." He was also moved to do this for several reasons: partly because this kind of love participates more in utility than in immediate delight, and partly because its specific pleasures belong to the spiritual and thinking faculty of our soul, and do not seem exposed to the external senses in the same way as fleshly pleasures that reek of matter. Finally, to the pursuit of virtues and sciences—even though these are found to be by their nature far more pleasant than the enjoyment of sensory pleasures or the acquisition of useful goods—he assigned the name of "the virtuous" <note>original: "honesti"</note>. He did this both to express and signify them by their own distinct quality (namely, virtue/honor) and because the pleasures that accompany virtuous loves reach toward the mind—the most spiritual of all our soul's faculties—and thus can least be discerned by the imperfect senses in the way that sensory pleasures are.

<summary>Philo explains to Sophia that while Aristotle categorized love into three types (useful, pleasant, and virtuous), all three ultimately aim at "pleasure." He clarifies that intellectual and virtuous pleasures are superior to sensory ones, though the common people often fail to recognize them as pleasures.</summary>

### DIALOGUE III

Even if they seem to hold dominion over beasts and the common crowd of men, because they have been granted either nothing at all or very little of sincere goodness or beauty, they are rightly placed in the lowest seat of pleasures. **SO.** What are you saying, Philo? Are there not many sensory pleasures found that are necessarily required both for the safety of individual beings and for the perpetual preservation of the species? We see that men are frequently invited to the exercise of these—repeated often with a wonderful sweetness—by the very instruments of nature, which were fashioned with admirable craftsmanship and the greatest wisdom by the Supreme Architect <note>original: "summo Opifice," referring to God as the creator</note>. Why then do you think that pleasures of this kind, even though they are sensory, are not truly good, but only good in appearance? This certainly does not seem likely to me. **PH.** You will find that I never said pleasures of this kind were truly depraved or only good in appearance; rather, I confirm to you that they are truly and properly good. **SO.** And yet they are placed in the category of sensory pleasures and are reduced to the species of "pleasant love" <note>Aristotle’s category of love based on pleasure, *amor iucundi*</note>. **PH.** I grant that they are indeed sensory pleasures; however, I believe they should not be placed properly in the species of the "pleasant" alone, but rather in the species of "virtuous love" <note>original: "honesti amoris," meaning love of what is morally noble or virtuous</note>, provided that their moderate exercise is directed only toward the health of the individual and the conservation of the species. But if they should perhaps exceed this praiseworthy moderation, then they are called shameful and immoderate; and having been reduced to a pure pleasure entirely destitute of all virtue, they will participate only in an apparent good and beauty, but not a real one. **SO.** Why, Philo, do you move sensory pleasures out of their own category of the "pleasant" into the foreign category of the "virtuous" simply because of the moderation applied to them? I certainly do not know by what reason this is permitted. **PH.** I do not think they should be removed entirely from their own category. But I say this one thing: that they are by no means to be placed in the category of the "pleasant" alone, entirely separated from all virtue. For pleasures of this kind are clearly seen to be virtuous.

<margin>Sensory pleasures that achieve moderation and temperance are seen to participate in virtue as well as pleasure.</margin>

**SO.** Therefore, the same pleasure will be established under two diverse and different types of love: namely, the pleasant and the virtuous. **PH.** Precisely so, yet with some distinction coming between them. For these necessary pleasures seem to have received their "matter" from the pleasant and their "form" <note>Philo uses the Aristotelian concepts of matter (the raw substance) and form (the defining essence or purpose)</note> and excellent temperament from virtue. By merit of this, when they are directed toward necessary and praiseworthy uses, they are aimed only at the safety of individuals and the preservation of the species. The same is also seen to occur in the category of "useful love." For that love which proposes for itself the goal of mere utility—entirely devoid of any virtue, immoderate, neither providing for the necessities of life nor serving studious actions—is seen to be occupied chiefly with things that appear good and beautiful but are actually evil or deformed. Greed and avarice can provide us with most certain evidence of this. But whenever the love of the useful, having accepted a praiseworthy moderation, is ordered toward the two aforementioned ends—the individual and the specific—then it emerges as truly good and truly beautiful. It is then rightly placed in two categories of love: namely, the useful and the virtuous. For the useful seems to provide the matter, while the virtuous provides the form and the moderation. **SO.** Therefore, virtuous love is judged to incline sometimes toward the pleasant and sometimes toward the useful by reason of its matter. But could we perhaps find a love so excellent that it exists as entirely virtuous by reason of both its matter and its form, receiving nothing at all from the other two categories as if borrowed or shared?

<margin>The love of the pleasant, and likewise of the useful, when reduced to a praiseworthy middle ground, is seen to receive utility or pleasure from its matter, but virtue from its form.</margin>

<margin>The love of virtue is twofold: it refers either to moral or to intellectual virtues. Moral virtues do not embrace a pure or simple virtue, but one entwined with sensory pleasures, or joined with useful goods, or involved with such things pertaining to matter and the body.</margin>

**PH.** The love of virtue is thought to be occupied chiefly in pursuing moral and intellectual virtues with singular devotion. However, since moral virtues deal with human actions, their "matter" must also exist as varied and manifold, according to the multiple and diverse nature of the human actions subject to them. Whence continence or temperance in sensory pleasures [treats] those sensory pleasures as [its matter]...

<margin>
Moral virtues treat useful goods and sensible pleasures as their matter; they are perfected and made visible by virtue as their form.

...matter, and the moderation and temperament of these things is seen as their form. This brings a much greater and more excellent delight than their impure and corporeal matter usually brings, just as the soul excels the body itself. Similarly, generosity and restraint from superfluous and unjust possessions treat "useful goods" as their matter; however, through moderation of the mind and abstinence from both theft and the immoderate acquisition of goods, combined with their generous distribution, they are perfected by a most excellent form. This makes the possession of useful goods truly most pleasant to the noble lover <note>original: "honesto amanti," one who loves what is morally beautiful or virtuous</note>. In the same way, the other moral virtues exercised in human actions—such as Fortitude, Justice, Prudence, and many others—seek their own matter from nature; their form is considered to reside in the habits and temperament of virtue itself.

<margin>
Intellectual virtues, seized by a kind of divine love, pursue only pure virtue, as far removed as possible from the filth of matter and corporeal stain.
</margin>
But the intellectual virtues exist as entirely noble in themselves, nor do they seem to have any business or commerce with matter. For they are seen to be concerned neither with sensory actions nor with corporeal pleasures—from which matter might acquire some portion for itself—but with things utterly separated from the body and with intellectual matters. Indeed, all intellectual forms, being entirely separated from matter, are deservedly considered by the most learned men to be pure and noble by their own nature, rather than because of the sharing of some partaken thing, as is the case with the moral virtues.

<margin>
Plato called the love of intellectual virtues celestial and divine.
</margin>
Hence, Plato rightly called the love of these virtues celestial and divine.

**SO.** But by what names does such a great Philosopher <note>referring to Plato</note> designate the remaining species of love?

<margin>
He declares the Platonic division of love into beastly, human, and divine; he contends that this is exactly the same as the Aristotelian division into depraved, moral, and intellectual.
</margin>
**PH.** Plato indeed, no differently than Aristotle, seems to have distributed love into three kinds by a certain reasoning: namely, beastly, human, and divine love. By "beastly love," he understood that love which, in things regarding the body, is excessive and neither tempered by virtue nor restrained within the bounds of moderation by right reason. This is seen whether it fails through the luxury of sensory pleasures, through greed and avarice for useful goods, or through the immoderate desire for honors. For all these things, being without reason and lacking the balance provided by the human intellect, are soon turned into beastly habits. However, Plato called that love "human" by which we are accustomed to pursue the moral virtues that moderate all human actions—both those falling under the senses and those under thought—as well as the pleasures flowing from them. Since this love consists of corporeal matter and intellectual form (namely, virtue itself), much as a human being consists of a body and an intellect, it is therefore called "human" by that most excellent philosopher. Finally, Plato proclaimed the contemplative love of wisdom and the highest things to be "divine," as it is entirely intellectual, noble, and, so to speak, formal, appearing unpolluted by any association with matter or filth. For through this love alone, men become participants in divine beauty according to their strengths.

<margin>
According to Plato, pleasures, no differently than love itself, are divided into beastly, human, and divine.
</margin>
Moreover, by as much as human love exceeds the beastly, so much do the human pleasures following human love excel the blind, beastly, and sensory pleasures—even though the common crowd of men falsely persuades itself that those which are actually the lowest and thinnest of all pleasures hold the primary rank over the others. Similarly, by as much as divine love excels the human, so much must it be considered that divine pleasures are greater, more pleasant, stronger, and more vehemently sought after by those who know their excellence than those pleasures which accompany moral virtues and human loves.

<margin>
He concludes at last that pleasure is the end goal of love.
</margin>
Therefore, in dividing love, whether you follow the Peripatetics <note>term: Peripatetics; the followers of Aristotle, named for his habit of walking while teaching</note> or the Stoics along with Plato, you will find no love at all that does not seem to have proposed pleasure (which the lover finally takes from the beloved object) as the goal to be reached in the end, as we have already said. **SO.** Truly, the end of each...

### DIALOGUE III.

**SOPHIA.** I have well understood that pleasure consists in the union that a lover acquires from the beloved object. Now I would like you to come closer to defining the previous question, and specifically to declare why that most common "end" or purpose is said to be the reason why love was born and introduced into the universe in the first place. For it seems we can hardly assign pleasure—in the way we do for the loves of humans and other animals—as the universal purpose for all love.

<margin>The World exists as a kind of most beautiful birth and offspring of God, the Greatest Craftsman.</margin>
**PHILO.** I think it is now the right time to explain that as well. I do not think you are at all unaware, Sophia, that the World was once brought forth by the supreme Craftsman of all things through the mediation of love. Since the "Supreme Good" pursued its own immense beauty (which is perfectly known to itself) with a vehement love, and was also most vehemently loved by that beauty itself under the aspect of the "Supreme Beautiful," it followed that it generated and procreated the most beautiful universe according to the pattern of its own form. <margin>Plato thought the goal of love was birth in the presence of beauty.</margin> The goal of love, as Plato testifies, is said to be "birth in the beautiful" <note>original: "partus ad pulchrum." This refers to a famous concept in Plato's *Symposium* where love is described not just as a desire for beauty, but as the drive to create or "give birth" to something lasting and beautiful in its presence.</note>.

<margin>The nature of the love of God, Best and Greatest, toward the World He has already procreated.</margin>
<margin>The intention of divine love toward the procreated World.</margin>
As soon as the universe of things was constructed by the supreme Creator according to the image and likeness of His immense wisdom, the love of the Creator toward the universe is thought to have begun—not as the love of an imperfect thing toward something more perfect, but rather as the love of a most perfect craftsman toward his work (which is less perfect than himself), or like the love of a superior for an inferior, a father for a son, or a cause for its specific effect. Therefore, the intention of this divine love is seen to reside neither in acquiring beauty (which the lover lacks) nor in obtaining delight from a union with the beloved for his own sake. Rather, it exists so that the lover may consult and provide for the perfection of the beloved as much as possible—a perfection which the beloved could not obtain if the lover’s love were removed. Thus, the divine lover takes a most pleasant delight from the greatest beauty which the World (loved by Him) has attained through the mediation of divine love. This is the same way that causes are said to love their effects, superiors their inferiors, parents their children, teachers their students, and benefactors those they help.

<margin>The love of superiors for inferiors is most concerned with the perfection and adornment of those inferiors.</margin>
For the love of all these is truly nothing else than a certain desire that the inferior beings be raised to the highest degree of perfection and beauty suited to their purpose. When these qualities are acquired by the beloved and joined with it, the lover is affected by a certain incredible pleasure. This pleasure of the lover, which he takes from the perfection and beauty of the thing he loves, is considered a very fitting end for the lover's love itself.

<margin>The love both of superiors for inferiors and inferiors for superiors seems to have proposed pleasure as a most common goal, though in different ways.</margin>
**SOPHIA.** I remember that you treated this difference between the love of a superior for an inferior and an inferior for a superior excellently elsewhere. And although you have spoken differently here than there, you concluded with the same opinion. I understand, moreover, that although the goal of both types of love consists in the pleasure the lover perceives from the beauty of the beloved, they are distinguished in this way: the inferior is driven to love because of the beauty of the superior beloved (which the inferior previously lacked). Thus, the goal of this love is placed in the pleasure the inferior lover gains from the beauty of the superior once it is finally acquired. But the reason that leads the superior to love the inferior is beauty itself, which the beloved inferior (perhaps lacking it at the time) will finally obtain through union with the superior lover. Once this beauty is acquired by the beloved, the lover himself rejoices as if he had reached the goal of his love, no differently than the beloved; because he has finally joined and coupled with himself that which he previously most vehemently desired, he is filled with great pleasure.

<margin>The excellence and preeminence of divine love toward the World.</margin>
I perceive that the supreme Craftsman of things loves the universe He procreated with such a kind of love. The conditions of this most excellent love seem to apply more truly and properly to Him than to all other loves of superiors for inferiors, even if other superior lovers are seen to be very similar to that first lover of all in the name of this love. The excellence of this divine love is corroborated by this argument especially: that by its merit...

<meta>This page continues Dialogue III between Philo and Sophia. ### DIALOGUE III.

...we often see in elaborate works that their perfection consists chiefly in this: that the work be rendered as similar as possible to the very form and idea of the art existing in the mind of the craftsman. Indeed, this is judged to be the proper goal most intended by a craftsman undertaking any task. We must think in exactly the same way regarding the creation of the entire universe. **SOPHIA.** You have truly said that the first perfection of the universe brought into the light—and the first intention of the supreme Architect of the world when undertaking its creation—lies in the greatest possible similarity between the universe and the wisdom of the highest Creator. You have certainly declared this most elegantly using the examples of works of art. However, I do not think the ultimate goal of the divine Architect and the final perfection of the world consist solely in this.

<margin>There are seen to be two ends for all things constructed by art: one we correctly call the end of the operation, the other the end of the work.</margin>
For just as any work constructed by a craftsman—for example, a cup—is seen to have two perfections and two ends: first, that it approaches as closely as possible the proper and true likeness of the internal form existing in the craftsman’s mind; and finally, that it best serves its own use, for which it is directed and assigned (for example, that a cup be fit and suited for drinking). We shall not ineptly call the first of these two perfections the <term>end of the operation</term> <note>Latin: "finis operae"; the goal of the act of making itself</note>, and the latter the <term>end of the work</term> <note>Latin: "finis operis"; the goal or utility of the finished object</note>.

<margin>The double perfection of the world: one intended by the divine Architect in its creation, and the other once it was already created.</margin>
I believe we should think similarly regarding the whole of created things. For the first goal of the creator himself, and the first perfection of the created world, involves the completion of the divine work as a sort of proper image of divine wisdom. But the final goal of the creator, and the final perfection of the world, consists in the fact that the universe appears perfectly suited to perform its own duties and to achieve the proper use for which it was established.

<margin>The "end of the operation" exists as the proper goal of the one performing the work.</margin>
This is not unworthily called the "end of the work." For the essence of the work is the proper goal of the operation of the one working; then the work itself is ordered toward its proper use as its own proper goal.

<margin>Every work is ordered toward its own use as its own goal.</margin>
**SOPHIA.** What action, then, or what use, in which you have placed the goal and final perfection of the already created universe, do you think this is? **PHILO.** Many actions and perfections of the universe are found; but its final perfection certainly consists in the highest and most excellent of all remaining actions. The others, established beneath this one, should be regarded as lower steps seeking that highest and loftiest peak of perfection.

<margin>The final and most absolute perfection of the world consists in its return and reversion to the divinity from which it has already flowed out.</margin>
In this, however, all are said to agree: that just as the essence of the universe is judged to be situated in this—that divinity goes out and is diffused into the whole of created things—so the actions perfecting the world are believed to be placed in this—that the whole of things finally returns and recurs to that very divinity from which it flowed. Hence, just as divinity is said to have existed as the <term>efficient principle</term> <note>The "efficient cause" or the agent that brings something into being</note> of the world, so it is thought to be its final goal.

<margin>God is rightly considered to be the efficient cause, the form, and the goal of the world itself.</margin>
For God, the Best and Greatest, is preached to be not only the efficient cause of the world, but also its form and its goal: the efficient cause, because he produced the world; its form, because he protects and preserves it unharmed; and its goal, because he calls back and leads that same universe to himself through the proper actions that perfect it. **SOPHIA.** I well understand that God, the Best and Greatest, if compared with the universe, takes on the character of a triple cause: namely, efficient, form, and goal. Efficient because of the "going out" of divinity in creation; form because of his preserving power; and goal because of the reduction of all other things back to himself. But what, I pray, are those acts said to be which perfect the universe and lead it back to its creator? And which of all those acts is the ultimate and most absolute, in which its final perfection consists?

<margin>The return and reversion of the world to God consists in its acts, which are not corporal but rather intellectual.</margin>
**PHILO.** The acts of the universe are said to be partly corporal and partly incorporeal. It is most clearly evident that the world can by no means return to God, the highest of all, through the mediation of corporal acts; for these are by their own nature such that they separate the universe from the purest divinity rather than joining it with the same. Therefore, the recourse of the world to God must be established in incorporeal acts, which are performed by an intellect entirely devoid of matter...

These two names are said to differ there not in reality or essence, but only in <term>reason</term> <note>A scholastic distinction: "differing in reason" (ratione) means two things are the same in reality but are distinguished by the mind's way of thinking about them</note>. <margin>Love and desire belong to imperfect things, while knowledge that has been joined belongs to absolute union; thus, they are designated as that which leads back to the Creator himself.</margin>

...the knowledge was quite imperfect; for it did not yet possess any power of joining or uniting. Thus, because union was absent, a certain desire immediately followed that knowledge, by which it strives toward the most closely joined—and therefore most desired—perfection. Once this perfection is finally acquired, that initial, crude knowledge is seen to be taken away along with the defect that was removed. For this reason, the act through which a created thing approaches the Creator is the knowledge of divine Wisdom and divine beauty, which is first held by the intellect. When the intellect understands that it is as far as possible from attaining union with the First Cause, it is inflamed to love that Cause vehemently; it wonderfully desires to enjoy it and to be most perfectly coupled with it, turning toward it entirely, just as a lover turns toward a most beautiful beloved. Led by this intense love and desire for the divinity itself, the intellect reaches that last and most perfect end—namely, the union itself. In this union is found not only the blessedness of the intellect (which has been turned toward the divinity, coupled with it, and, to put it briefly, adopted into the order of divine things), but also the final perfection and supreme happiness of the entire universe of created things. The intellect is considered the most principal and worthy portion of this universe; through its mediation, the universe itself is able to be joined with the First Principle, rendered most perfect, and acquire supreme blessedness for itself from the enjoyment of divine union.

<margin>The coupling of the intellectual nature with the supreme Founder of all things leads the universe of created things back to the First Principle and finally joins it with him.</margin>

For I clearly discern that this last act of union or enjoyment, in which the perfection of the universe consists, pours a present love into the intellect and exists as a highly suitable end for another, higher love. Furthermore, I know well enough that the end of the preceding love, by which we see the whole universe affected, is located in its perfection—which seems to be the final act and the closest coupling of the World with the supreme Creator, mixed with the most pleasant enjoyment of divinity. <margin>The essences of the universe ascending by degrees from the first subject—the lowest of all things—all the way to God, the supreme of all.</margin>

This is indeed proclaimed to exist as the supreme being and the final end to which all things are directed; likewise also that act...

<margin>Loves, no differently than the essences of the universe, starting from prime matter and ascending by degrees, finally rest in the first efficient cause.</margin>
That love, belonging to both human and angelic intelligence—to which this most excellent and intelligible subject is seen to belong—seems to be the highest of all intellectual acts exercised by the human, celestial, or angelic mind. Indeed, all other inferior acts of the intellect are established for this one, as if toward their own goal and the most abundant perfection of all created things. Loves, distributed and spread throughout the universe, are also thought to maintain this same order: for they follow one another and always ascend step by step from the lower to the higher, until they finally rest in the supreme love of all things in the universe—namely, in the love for its Creator. Therefore, to finally put the finishing touches <note>Latin: *summam manum imponamus*, literally "to put the final hand," an idiom for completing a work.</note> on our subject, we must establish that the final and most consummate end of all loves found in the universe is that ultimate and supreme love of all created things for the Creator himself.

<margin>The very last and final of all loves ends at last in the divinity itself.</margin>
**SOPHIA:** I recognize this to be most true. For the most intimate enjoyment of the Creator, which the created intellect attains, is not only the end of the love of all intellects, but also the final and most universal goal of all loves found in the entirety of created things. However, you would do me a great favor if—just as you showed the series and degrees of the essences of the universe, starting from the lowest and ascending to the supreme—you would now recount the order of all loves from the first to the last.

**PHILO:** Tell me, Sophia, what do you require of me? Do you want only the semicircle of the universe's loves, just as we seemed to do recently when we spoke of the essences, or do you want their full and absolute circle?

<margin>One should choose the whole of what is good rather than just a part.</margin>
**SOPHIA:** Although I do not fully understand what a "half-circle" or a "full circle" of the universe's loves signifies, nor why the series of essences you just enumerated deserves the name of a semicircle rather than a circle, it seems to me that one should choose the whole of what is good rather than just a part. I would prefer you to complete that previous semicircle of essences and explain the full and absolute circle of loves.

<margin>The circle of all things, beginning from God and proceeding through all essences, finally returns to God.</margin>
**PHILO:** That which is called the "Circle of All Things" is the path that takes its origin from the first principle of things, and, touching all things step by step in its circuit, returns to that first principle as its final end. Like a geometric circle that eventually returns to the same point from which it began, it encompasses all the degrees of essences. 

<margin>The circle of all things is divided into two semicircles.</margin>
This circle is divided into two halves. The first runs from the starting point of all points down to its opposite, which is as remote from it as possible. The second half begins from this opposite and most remote point and strives back toward the first principle, returning to it.

**SOPHIA:** I see how this is true in a circular figure. But how do you think the same applies to the great circle of all things?

<margin>An elegant description and clear interpretation of the circle encompassing the universe of all things.</margin>
**PHILO:** Since the beginning and the end of this proposed circle is said to be the supreme Architect of things, its middle will be found by descending from the supreme Creator down to the lowest of all things, which is as remote as possible from divine perfection. From God, the angelic nature immediately proceeds; distributed into many classes, it always proceeds step by step from the more excellent to the less excellent. The celestial nature follows this, governed by a praiseworthy order, running from the Empyrean Heaven (the greatest of all) through the intermediate orbs down to the Lunar orb (the smallest of all). Finally, the sublunary globe follows this, along with prime matter—the most imperfect of all eternal substances and the most remote from the perfection of the supreme Creator himself.

<margin>God and prime matter are as opposed as possible.</margin>
For just as God is **pure act**, so the first subject <note>Prime matter, the underlying "stuff" of the physical world.</note> exists as **pure potentiality**. Here, the first half of the circle we mentioned comes to an end: that which begins from the Creator and, through intermediate essences arranged in the greatest order, reaches toward the lack... <note>Philo is describing Neoplatonic "Emanation" (the descent from God) and "Return" (the ascent back to God). **SOPHIA:** I have understood very well how the order and series of essences proceeds step by step in a circle. <margin>He describes the circle of all loves and demonstrates how it marvelously agrees with the circle of all essences.</margin>
**PHILO:** Just as the essences of things, shaped by the first half of the circle already mentioned, take their beginning from the first [cause] of all, and from there always descend step by step from greater to lesser until the lowest of all—which is called Chaos or prime matter—flowing down in the manner of a certain departure and procreation; and from here, as if guided by the other half of the same circle, they always ascend from lesser to greater, returning to the first [cause] of all as if to their common origin. In the same way, love, beginning from the supreme Parent of all, descends gradually with a kind of paternal affection from the greater to the lesser, and from the more perfect to the less perfect; or, to speak more properly, from the more beautiful to the less beautiful, so that the perfection and beauty of each, suited to their capacity, may be poured down from higher things into lower ones. In this way, it pervades the essences of both the angelic and the celestial universe, so that the superior essence seems to look after the inferior and succeeding procreation and salvation with a paternal zeal, and to impart its own essence and beauty to the inferior according to its capacity and condition. And thus the series of loves descends from the supreme God through intermediate essences down to the Chaos of all things. From there, love is then carried around by the other semicircle, ascending step by step from the lower to the higher, and from the imperfect to the more perfect, so that it may acquire its fitting perfection; and from the less beautiful to the more beautiful, so that it may be decorated with the beauty due to it. For the first subject <note>Prime matter.</note> is said to love and desire the elemental forms, the elemental forms the mixtures, the mixtures the vegetative forms, and the vegetative the sensitive forms, with a kind of natural zeal, as things more beautiful and perfect than themselves. The sensitive forms, moreover, pursue the intellectual form itself with a kind of sensible love. This intellectual soul, then kindled by intellectual love, ascends from one less beautiful intelligible object to another more beautiful one, until it finally achieves the understanding of the supreme and divine intelligible of all things, and at last enjoys the most excellent love of the highest beauty. This circle of loves finally rests and is perfected, having returned to the highest good and the final beloved—namely, God himself—whom we have already called the most common parent and creator of all, as well as the first lover.

The other, however, being opposite to this, strives conversely from the more base toward the more beautiful, and from the more imperfect toward the more perfect. But besides...

...than that it seems absurd for a beautiful thing to pursue a more shameful <note>Latin: *turpiori*, meaning baser or less perfect.</note> thing with love, since nothing usually desires something less perfect than itself. <margin>
The love of superiors for inferiors, and of the more excellent for the baser, seems to be far greater and more vehement than the devotion and benevolence of the latter for the former.
</margin>

PHILO: The love of a father for a son, a teacher for a disciple, and a cause for its effect is seen to be no less—indeed, even more vehement—than the love these have for them. For superior things, by producing inferior ones and perfecting them with goodness, seem to love them more than those inferior things—which only strive to approach their perfection—love the superior ones. This is true even if the inferior things are not endowed with the beauty that the superior ones lack (which might lead them toward a desire for it). Nevertheless, since superior things are held by a maximal love for their own [perfection], they also vehemently strive and desire to share that beauty with inferior things through their own power. Through this communication, once the inferior things have obtained a fitting beauty through the benefit of the superior, the form of the superior things is also rightly considered more excellent and distinguished. Furthermore, another cause of this matter could be brought forward: namely, that superior things are most intensely focused on the beauty of the universe and the whole, as we said above, and for that reason are primarily moved to love inferior things.

<margin>
The love of superiors for inferiors looks toward the procreation of things; but the love of inferiors for superiors is thought to be primarily concerned with the perfection of things and their return to their own principle.
</margin>

The first semicircle of loves, therefore, seems to descend from superior and more beautiful things to inferior and baser ones. Because this love consists in the "exit" or outcome of procreation, and the creator is always more beautiful than the thing created, it happens that superiors, through the persuasion of love, procreate inferiors. They grant them a portion of their own beauty, adapted to what that "captive" <note>The author uses *captiui* to suggest how divine beauty is "captured" or housed within the limitations of physical matter.</note> can receive. Truly, the order leads from the first Creator down to the "first matter" <note>Latin: *materiam primam*, the most basic, formless substance from which all things are made.</note>, the final extreme of all things. For the love of the superior for the inferior is considered the primary cause of procreation. But the other semicircle of loves—which begins from the first matter and strives toward the Supreme Good <note>Latin: *summum bonum*, referring to God as the ultimate goal of all desire.</note>—rightly leads inferior things back to superior things through the perfection of each perfecting agent. Thus it happens that love ascends step by step from the less beautiful to the more beautiful, so that the inferior may acquire for itself some part of the superior’s beauty and be joined with it as much as possible. This continues until it reaches the union with the supreme beauty itself, both of the intellectual nature and of all procreated nature, and finally the enjoyment <note>Latin: *fruitionem*, the state of blissful possession or "fruitful" union with the Divine.</note> of the Supreme Good through the human intellect, mediated by its final love. We have already more than sufficiently demonstrated that this act of union and enjoyment finally joins the universe with its Creator in its ultimate perfection.

<margin>
All the loves of the universe are led back to the closest union of the World with its Creator, as to the final act and most absolute end. God exists as the first principle and final end of all things.
</margin>

SOPHIA: I am truly overjoyed to have learned of this perfect and absolute circuit of all loves seen in the universe, which corresponds with a wonderful proportion to the circling of the essences themselves. Because of this, I recognize that all the loves of the universe are finally led back to that ultimate act—by whose merit the World is joined with its Creator—as if to their final end. For procreating loves are ordered toward returning loves, and returning loves, by ascending step by step to that final love, reach and are referred to that ultimate end—that which brings the universe together with the Supreme Good in a true act of enjoyment, as if with its final perfection. Hence all things seem to have flowed out from that pure, most beautiful, and divine unity so that they might finally return into it, being joined to it in the manner of a circle; there, the happiness <note>Latin: *beatitudo*, the state of ultimate blessedness.</note> of the whole and the universe is rightly judged to reside. But you, Philo, must remember that you previously established the end of every love to be in the pleasure <note>Latin: *uoluptate*</note> that the lover takes from the beloved thing, and you added that the love found in the universe of created things is an end of this kind. Now you, as if changing your previous opinion, have pronounced the end of this same love to be situated in the act joining the universe with the divine principle—which does not seem to differ from pleasure.

# DIALOGUE III.

<margin>Pleasure seems to either exist as one and the same with the act of union and enjoyment itself, or it always follows and accompanies it.</margin>

Indeed, just as that act—which is able to join the whole universe with the highest beauty—is declared more excellent than all other acts, so too is that pleasure which accompanies such an excellent act. This pleasure exists as the proper end of love, as we have already said. It is thought to exceed all other pleasures by a measure beyond any finite proportion; it alone deserves to be called the supreme and greatest of all pleasures by which created things are affected. <margin>The pleasure of lovers is defined as a certain union with the beloved beauty.</margin> For as we have already stated above, the pleasure of lovers seems in truth to be nothing other than their union with the beloved beauty. <margin>Pleasure is declared to be greater or lesser, maximal or minimal, finite or infinite, according to the proportion of the beauty that is beloved and joined.</margin> When this beauty is finite, the pleasure is also finite—sometimes greater, sometimes lesser—judged by the proportion of the beauty that is beloved and joined. But when that beauty is infinite (as we see happens in the highest good through the love of the intellectual part, which is the ultimate end of all created things), the end of this kind of love must also be placed in an immense and infinite pleasure. This is the most absolute end of all loves found in the created world; it is for its sake that love is thought to have descended into the whole universe. For unless things were touched by the love and desire to finally return to the highest beauty, they would certainly never have endured coming out into the light first, and receding further and further from the divinity. Without a certain paternal benevolence and a desire for procreating (representing divine love and zeal), a superior essence could never have produced or procreated a lower essence next to itself in gradual stages. Nor would the series of created things have reached such a distance from the divinity that they descended step-by-step, succeeding one another, all the way to ultimate matter. <margin>He concludes that the pleasure following the union and conjunction of all created things with God himself is the highest and most absolute end of all the loves seen in the universe.</margin> For paternal benevolence and the zeal for procreation seem to embrace the entire circuit of the first semicircle, from the highest essence of all down to the lowest, which is called Chaos <note>original: "Chaos"; here referring to the ancient concept of prime matter or the unformed state of the universe.</note>. Furthermore, it was quite impossible for already created essences ever to be joined with the divinity, or to taste that greatest pleasure in which the happiness and perfection of the universe consist—especially since they had been thrust down into prime matter as if into a kind of Tartarus <note>original: "Tartarum"; used here metaphorically as the deepest abyss, furthest from the light of God.</note> most remote from the divinity—unless they were finally led back by love and the desire to return to the divinity (as their ultimate perfection) to that final act in which the happiness of the universe is judged to reside. Therefore, since the love figured in the first semicircle (acting in the role of the procreator) is ordered toward the love designated in the second semicircle (acting as the part that leads back), and since this latter love refers to the ultimate perfection and blessedness of the universe, it must be concluded that the love seen in the universe of things arose so that it might finally bestow ultimate happiness upon the world itself. **SO.** I clearly see that love was introduced into the universe: first, so that it might enrich and expand the world through the help of procreation with a multitude of essences succeeding one another; and second, so that it might bless the world by finally leading it back to the highest good and joining it with the first principle, bathing it in the highest joy. You have indeed abundantly satisfied the fifth difficulty proposed earlier—namely, why the love embracing the universe of all created things arose. However, three things regarding the present proposal still remain for me to understand. First: although the pleasure of any natural or sensible love is considered a very fitting end (because such loves proceed either from the soul's contact with matter or from bodily powers), yet pleasure seems in no way able to be fitted to intellectual love as a suitable end. For pleasure is judged to be a certain affection <term>affection: "affectio"; in Renaissance philosophy, this refers to a state of being acted upon or a passion, which implies a change in the soul.</term>; but the intellect is said to be entirely devoid of matter, unable to be "affected" or to suffer <term>suffer: "perpeti"; here meaning 'to undergo' or 'to be passive,' as opposed to being active.</term>, and not subject to any kind of affection. If this is true for the human intellect, how much more must it apply to the angelic and divine intellect? Therefore, pleasure [cannot be] for any intellect exactly its own
->goal<-

# LEONE EBREO ON LOVE,

an end must be assigned. Therefore, it does not seem that pleasure itself exists as the most common end of all loves, as you just said. Second, even if I grant that all loves which you call "reductive" <note>original: *reduci*; refers to the Neoplatonic "return" of the soul to God</note> have proposed pleasure for themselves as their proper end, I would still not agree that the other kind of loves, called "productive," should be referred to the same end. For nothing can perceive any foulness from the approach of the beautiful. For this reason, the end of "productive" love seems to be placed in the distribution and sharing of beauty with those things that lack it, rather than in any pleasure. For what fruitfulness, I ask, can beautiful things perceive from those that are not beautiful? Third, you said above that the love of the Creator for the universe of created things leads the World back to its fitting perfection—just as you said that the love by which the supreme Architect is thought to pursue his own beauty brought the World into the light. But now you judge that the love which leads the universe back to its own perfection is that by which the universe of created things—through the mediation of the most excellent part of its intellect—is moved toward supreme and divine beauty. Therefore, the universe is led to its perfection not by God’s love for it, but rather by its own love for God. I vehemently desire to hear from you the solutions to these three proposed difficulties, as well as everything regarding the origin of love.

<margin>
*Sensible love and sensible pleasure exist as certain affections of the sensing soul.*
</margin>
**PH.** Since several small matters still remain for me to clear up, I think I should now eagerly set about their solution. Indeed, sensible pleasure exists as a certain <term>affection<gloss>A state of being influenced or moved; in this context, an emotion or "passion" of the soul.</gloss></term> of the sensing soul, just as sensible love is also judged to be an affection of the same soul. This difference alone stands between these two: that among these two disturbances of the sensing soul, love holds the first place, while pleasure claims the last place as the end of love. But intellectual pleasure should by no means be considered an affection of the lover's intellect itself. For if you agree that intellectual essences <note>Higher beings like angels or pure minds.</note> are endowed with a species of love that is not at all an "affection," you must also grant to them a certain pleasure entirely devoid of any "affection," which is judged to be the end of intellectual love, and thus more perfect and absolute.

<margin>
*Intellectual love and intellectual pleasure should by no means be called affections of the intellect itself.*
</margin>
**SO.** But I ask you, if neither love nor pleasure properly deserves the name of "affection" for intelligent essences, what then will they be?

<margin>
*The love and pleasure of intelligent essences are certain intellectual acts, entirely devoid of any natural affection.*
</margin>
**PH.** They exist as certain intellectual acts, as we have already said, entirely devoid of any natural affection; because of our poverty of vocabulary, we cannot signify them by a name of their own. However, as we have already warned above, the love implanted in any created intellect is defined as nothing other than a progression from this final, first, separate, and imperfect state toward the last, joining, and most perfect understanding of the most beautiful <term>intelligible<gloss>Something that can be perceived or known by the mind rather than the senses.</gloss></term>. Similarly, intellectual pleasure is determined to be nothing other than this last, joining, and most absolute understanding of the most beautiful intelligible itself, held by some created intellect.

<margin>
*What intellectual love is defined to be.*
*What intellectual pleasure is said to be.*
</margin>
**SO.** But what, then, will both be called when applied to the divine intellect?

<margin>
*What divine love is thought to be.*
*What divine pleasure is.*
*He demonstrates that pleasure also pertains to the divine nature, both by reasoning and by confirming it with sacred authorities.*
</margin>
**PH.** Divine love is a certain outflowing of the most beautiful Wisdom of God Himself into His most fair image—that is, into the universe of things created by Him—joined with a most ardent zeal so that the World may return to the supreme beauty of God Himself and finally be united with it. Likewise, divine pleasure is nothing other than the most absolute and narrowest union of the image with its exemplar—that is, of the universe with the immense beauty of God, and of the created World with its supreme Creator. Whence we find that David sang not without merit: *The Lord rejoices in his own works.* <note>original: "Dominus proprijs effectibus delectat." A reference to Psalm 104:31.</note> For from that union of created things with their supreme Architect, not only do the created things themselves perceive the greatest joy and attain the greatest...

### DIALOGUE III.

...we will be delighted by the principle of our salvation. Indeed, God himself is also thought to perceive a certain relative delight from that same union, specifically because of the happiness of his own effect <note>In this context, "effect" refers to the created world or the result of God's action</note>. Nor should it seem absurd to you that we attribute pleasure to God. For he himself is declared to be the supreme pleasure of the universe; and because of that eternal and immortal love by which God is thought to pursue his own form, it must certainly be felt that the highest pleasure resides in him, proceeds from him, and strives toward him.

<margin>
The Hebrews used a certain other reasoning, being accustomed to use these words to signify [this].
</margin>
Led by this very reason, the most ancient Hebrews were accustomed to signify a certain internal and hidden joy of theirs with a speech of this kind: *Blessed and great is he in whom pleasure is said to dwell* <note>original: "Felix quod ingens beatusq; sit ille, in quo uoluptas dicitur commorari"; this likely refers to Rabbinic or Kabbalistic interpretations of divine joy</note>, and one and the same pleasure is seen to exist both in the one bringing the sign of joy and in the one perceiving the pleasure. But why do we wonder so much that God perceives some pleasure from the perfection of the things established by him? Since the Sacred Volumes <note>The Bible</note> also describe the crimes of the entire human race—which in ancient times were purged and expiated by that memorable flood of waters—with a speech of this sort: *And God, seeing that the wickedness of men had grown beyond measure on the earth, and that all their thoughts fell daily into worse things, it repented him that he had made man, and he was affected by an internal grief. I will destroy, he said, man together with the other living creatures that were fated and procreated on the earth.* <note>A translation of Genesis 6:5-7 from the Latin Vulgate</note> If, therefore, the wickedness of man tortures God with a vehement and internal grief, how much more do you think the divine mind will rejoice in their perfection and blessedness? However, I would not want you to think that either grief or joy brings any "perturbation" <note>In classical philosophy, a "perturbation" is a disturbing passion or emotion that upsets the soul's balance; Philo argues God feels joy without losing his steady, divine nature</note> to God.

<margin>
What divine pleasure and divine sadness are believed to properly signify.
</margin>
Rather, divine pleasure seems to signify a certain pleasing harmony between God and his most perfect effect, just as, conversely, divine sadness signifies the lack of such harmony arising from the imperfection of the effect itself. **SO.** You have indeed satisfied the first difficulty excellently. For from what has already been said, I clearly discern that the delight of intellectual essences, which is entirely free of passion, deserves the name of pleasure more truly than the delight of corporal essences, which is joined with perturbation. Furthermore, I understand this very well: that intellectual love, because it is seen to be empty and free of all perturbation, is more vehement and truer than love joined with a certain corporal perturbation. Now that the first is settled, proceed to the solution of the second difficulty.

**PH.** From those things which we have said until now, it will not be a great task to derive the explanation of the second ambiguity as well. When dealing with the first semicircle <note>The Neoplatonic "semicircle" refers to the "procession" or descent of being from God down to the lowest matter</note>, which begins from God and extends all the way to the newest matter, we said that a higher essence loves the lower one entrusted to its faith.

<margin>
The pleasure of higher lovers consists in imparting their own beauty to inferiors, and in joining and coupling them to themselves.
</margin>
The pleasure which a higher essence proposes to itself as the end of love is by no means to be placed in achieving a union with a non-beautiful—or at least less beautiful—essence subject to it. Rather, it consists more in joining itself to the non-beautiful (or less beautiful), and in adorning and perfecting it by imparting its own beauty to it. This communicated beauty induces perfection and delight not only in the lower effect, but also in the higher cause, insofar as that cause is necessarily related to its own effect. For the perfection and beauty of the effect usually renders the cause more beautiful and perfect—and, as we have already said, makes it almost exultant by this relative and added perfection. Since we have demonstrated that God is delighted by the perfection of his effects and grieves at their defects, it will seem much more likely that this happens to individual created essences: namely, that each of them will be rightly said to rejoice in the good of the effect succeeding it, and to grieve at its evil. **SO.**

In solving the second difficulty, you have conducted yourself no less excellently than in the first. Moreover, you have clearly shown that all created things in [loves]...

### LEONE EBREO: ON LOVE

<margin>
The pleasure of higher and lower lovers, although existing for different reasons, stands as the most common end.
</margin>
In their own manners, they are accustomed to derive pleasure—perceived from the union with the beloved thing—as their goal, whether the lover is inferior or superior to the object. Only a third and final difficulty now remains for you to resolve. For if the love by which the universe of all created things follows God is said to be that through which the World attains its final natural perfection and is at last joined with the divine power, then why, I ask, did you recently suggest that the same effect—the union of the World with that supreme beauty—is caused by the love with which God loves the universe, like a parent loves a child?

<margin>
He demonstrates that love is not only of the World for its creator, but also of the creator himself for the World already created, to recall the universe of things to their first principle <note>The "first principle" is a philosophical term for the source of all existence—God</note>, and finally to join and unite them with divinity itself.
</margin>
**PH.** Indeed, just as the love by which the universe is drawn toward God leads the universe itself to divine union, final happiness, and supreme delight; so too it can by no means be denied that the love by which God follows the universe of things draws it toward divine union and final bliss, mixed with a certain supreme delight. For as we have already declared above, the parental love for *producing* children must not be considered one and the same as the parent’s love for children who have already come into the light of day. For the love for producing children is truly that by which the parent loves himself; in order to acquire his own perfection, he strives to become a parent in the true and proper sense by bringing forth a child similar to himself. And indeed, following that first love of the parent loving himself, another love of the same kind succeeds it toward the child already created. Moved by this, the father is seen to apply great diligence in nourishing and educating the child, leading him to the highest possible perfection. In the same way, the divine love of drawing the universe toward Himself should not be considered entirely one and the same as the divine love for the universe already produced; rather, the former precedes the latter without any controversy. For it is the love by which the divine power, in loving Himself, strives as much as possible to impart His immense beauty to a universe composed in His image and likeness.

<margin>
The love of God for the World not yet created, and his love for the World already created, seem to differ somewhat between themselves.
</margin>
For every perfection and beauty distributed among many seems to have taken unto itself strength and growth; just as we see everywhere that fruit-bearing trees are more beautiful than certain sterile ones, and flowing and emanating waters are more excellent than those standing enclosed in springs and vessels. However, once the World has been created, it is thought that God’s love for it—like a parent's love for a child already born—begins immediately alongside it. This love strives not only to preserve the World in the prior state acquired at its creation, but moreover, and much more so, to lead it to that final happiness and perfection, and to join the universe of created things with divine beauty.

<margin>
Perfection also becomes greater and more powerful when distributed among many.
</margin>
**SO.** Although, because of a certain clear similarity, the divine love for the universe already created is thought to be the same as that which leads it to its final end and ultimate perfection, this nevertheless seems to be the proper work of the love by which the universe follows the divine form. For through the mediation of *that* love, the World immediately attains divine union and finds its final and fitting happiness. God is also said to be the cause and reason for the effect; yet, I do not yet seem to have sufficiently perceived how this worldly effect is reduced to divine love as its proper cause. I would greatly desire you, Philo, to attempt an explanation of this matter.

<margin>
He explains, with an elegant and very appropriate example of the Sun, that the love of God for the World already created concurs most effectively toward this, so that the World itself may finally attain divine union.
</margin>
**PH.** Divine love concurs in the same way to bestow happiness upon the human race and the whole World as the Sun does so that we, by its clarity, might be able to see that most beautiful star. Truly, no one should doubt that we are led toward the light and toward gazing upon the solar body by the power of sight implanted in our eyes, joined with a certain desire to know light itself; and from the vision of that most splendid body, we are accustomed to take the greatest pleasure. But although the work of the eyes is required above all to perform this task, unless the eyes were first illuminated by the Sun and solar light, we could certainly never see that most radiant star. For without the Sun’s...

<meta>This page continues the third dialogue of Leone Ebreo’s "Dialogues on Love." Philo is explaining to Sophia how the love between God and the universe is a reciprocal process. He is transitioning from discussing God's love for the creation to how that divine love empowers the human intellect to return to its Creator, using the "Song of Songs" as a primary allegorical text.</meta>

### DIALOGUE III

The Sun itself can hardly be seen, even though it is by the Sun's benefit that we see anything at all. In the same way, even if the love of our soul and the love of the entire universe for divine beauty is said to be truly and properly the means by which we—and the world—attain a divine union mixed with final happiness and the highest joy; nevertheless, neither we, nor the universe, nor our own efforts could ever reach such a union. We could never be raised to such a sublime peak of perfection and joy unless that part of our soul called the **intellect** first received the necessary strength and the purest light from the supreme divine beauty itself, and from the divine love for the universe, in order to grasp such perfection.

<margin>
He confirms, using the authority of the Sacred Volumes, that God's love for the created universe (and especially for the human race) recalls the World—and specifically the intellect, as the most excellent part of the whole World—back to its own beginning, joining it with its Maker.
</margin>
For God’s love toward the totality of all created things is what raises and inflames the universe to love God—once the universe has been enlightened in its most excellent part, the intellect. This is done so that He may finally join the World with the divine form, gifting it with final happiness and bliss. For this reason, we find that David sang:

> Because of your light, we see light itself. <note>original: *Propter lucem tuam lucem ipsam videmus*, a reference to Psalm 36:9.</note>

Furthermore, we read in the Prophet:

> Turn us back to you, O God, and we shall immediately return. <note>original: *Revoca nos ad te Deus, & statim redibimus*, a reference to Lamentations 5:21.</note>

We find another who spoke to the same effect:

> Turn me back, and I shall return: for You are my Lord and my God. <note>original: *Revoca me, atq; redibo*, a reference to Jeremiah 31:18.</note>

And this is rightly so: for if we were destitute of divine help alone, we could truly never return to God. We find this same idea expressed far more clearly by Solomon in his *Canticles* <note>The "Canticles" refers to the *Song of Songs* or *Song of Solomon*.</note>, where he takes on the persona of the intelligent soul who deeply loves divine beauty, saying:

> Draw me, and we will run after you: If the King has introduced me into his chambers, we will exult and be glad in you, remembering your loves more than wine: the upright love you. <note>original: *Trahe me, & post te curremus...* a translation of Song of Songs 1:4.</note>

Consider, I pray, Sophia, how humbly the most wise Solomon prays to God to first draw and compel the intelligent soul toward the love of divinity. He predicts that once this happens, the soul—seized by a certain most ardent and almost "frenzied" love—will follow the divinity itself most swiftly, in the manner of those who run. He adds, moreover, that if the soul is introduced into the "Royal chambers"—that is, if it insinuates itself into the divine beauty of the Supreme King with divine help and is joined with it—it will attain the greatest pleasure as the most excellent end of its love for God. Finally, he promises that he will retain the memory of divine loves more than of wine; that is, he will perpetually keep the divine loves healthy, safe, and present in the mind, much more than worldly loves. Indeed, he rightly compared the pursuit of worldly things to wine, which frequently makes men drunk and induces an alienation of the most upright mind. Whence he concludes:

> The upright love you:

This means that men captured by the beauty of divine wisdom are by no means said to wander or go astray, as those who practice corporal loves do. Rather, such spiritual lovers, directed by the most certain rule of the intelligent soul in loving, are seen to always walk straight and never deviate from their intended journey, even by the smallest degree.

It is also worthy of great consideration, Sophia, that in the prayer of Solomon mentioned above, he begins in the singular number, saying:

> **Draw me:**

But immediately he switches to the plural, adding:

> **And after you we will run.**

Then, returning to the singular number:

> **If the King has introduced me into his chambers,**

And finally, he concludes his speech in the plural:

> **We will exult, and be glad in you, preserving the memory of your loves more than wine.**

The most wise King seems to have used this variety of numbers to demonstrate one primary thing: that when the intellect—the most excellent part of both man and the universe of all created things—is joined with divinity itself, not only does it become blessed itself, but all parts of the universe simultaneously acquire their final happiness along with it.
