<meta>This page concludes the third dialogue of Leone Ebreo’s "Dialogues on Love." Philo is wrapping up the philosophical discussion on the cosmic origin of love, shifting from the macrocosmic (God and the universe) back to the microcosmic (his own love for Sophia).</meta>

604 LEONE EBREO ON LOVE

<margin>
He explains by what reasoning the human race is led toward final beatitude—that is, the attainment of union with the Divine—and further declares this elegantly through the example of two lovers.
</margin>

...having assumed this, that wise leader of the Hebrews <note>Likely referring to King Solomon as the author of the Song of Songs.</note> says: "The upright love thee." <note>original: "Te rectitudines [diligunt]," from Song of Songs 1:4.</note> Truly, all the upright qualities of the intellectual faculty are rightly thought to strive toward divine love. For this reason, to resolve the question already proposed: a certain splendor of divine love is first spread through the human race, and soon we are stirred to embrace our own happiness and delight. Afterward, certain torches of the most burning divine love follow, which lead us at last to the highest union with divine beauty and to beatitude.

To understand this better and more easily, I would like to bring forward an example well-suited to our purpose: that of a man and a woman who love each other with a perfect love. Even if a loving man should waste away with the most burning love for his beloved, he would never enjoy that sweetest union in which the goal of the lovers' love usually consists, unless his lady-friend signaled that she responded to the lover's own love through her eyes, sweet words, amorous nods, favorable signs, and the most effective gestures. She would thus so ignite and confirm his faith in her that the lover, soothed by this hope, would boldly set out to attain the sweetest coupling with the beloved thing as the final goal of his love and the summit of its perfection. **SO.** To all...

<margin>
She collects and concludes this entire third discussion, together with the two previous disputes, in a very brief epilogue.
</margin>

...the difficulties I have posed, you have indeed satisfied me fully and abundantly. And as for what you undertook to interpret regarding the origin of love, you seem to have performed and perfected it with the best of faith. Just as you also acted excellently in the two previous disputes—treating first the essence of love and desire, and then the universality of that same love.

From this last and most recent discussion, I now know more than enough that love was truly and properly born: both the love of God for the universe and the love of the universe for God, as well as the mutual and reciprocal love of each of its parts, beginning together with the totality of created things. I even discern that love was born in the **Angelic World** <term>the realm of pure intellects or angels, existing between God and the physical world</term> before it was born in the other parts of the universe. I see that its most noble energy and its very being draw their origin from **Knowledge** and **Beauty**, as if from parents; and that **Lucina** <note>The Roman goddess of childbirth, used here as a metaphor for the "need" or "lack" that forces love into being.</note> played her part in its birth.

Furthermore, I understand perfectly well that the goal of love consists in the pleasure that the lover finally acquires from the union and enjoyment of the beauty of the beloved. Similarly, it seems certain that the aim of the entire universe must be placed in the supreme and divine beauty, as if in the final and most happy goal of all created things, just as you have said; may God, in His greatest liberality and highest kindness, deem us worthy to reach it. However, Philo, I was previously persuading myself that since lovers pursue their lady-friends with such vehement love, the illnesses, impatience, and tortures of the mind might also be called the "ends" or goals of love—explaining why love was introduced into the universe. **PH.** Although the love of lovers...

<margin>
The end of love itself is not to be found in the pains and torments of lovers, but rather in pleasure.
</margin>

...is frequently seen to bring about the greatest cares, illnesses, torments, and innumerable tortures, the proper end of love itself should certainly not be placed in these, but rather in the most delightful pleasure, which is the direct opposite of those pains. Yet, I do not think you were entirely wrong in what you said; for even if it is not true in every case, it is clearly seen to be true at least in my own devotion and love toward you. The end of my love is neither happy nor pleasant; on the contrary, I understand its beginning, its middle, and its end to consist rather in pains, hardships, and illnesses. **SO.** Why, I pray, does that which happens to everyone else conflict with you alone? And why is your love for me alone unable to reach the most common and happy end shared by almost all lovers? **PH.** You should ask this of yourself rather than me. For it is enough for me to seek you and love you uniquely with all the powers of my soul intent upon it. It is for you, thereafter, to perfect my love for you and lead it to its longed-for end.

Philo has argued that the goal of love is the union and pleasure found in the beloved, while Sophia is skeptical of his logic, given her own lack of response to his advances.</meta>

# DIALOGUE III.

...you neglect <note>original: "gligis," likely "negligis."</note>: why do you now seek from me an excuse for your error, Sophia? **SOPHIA.** On the contrary, Philo, you should rather bring a defense of your own fault into the open. For since your love for me is deprived of its proper goal—which you assigned to it a long time ago—it must be that either your love does not deserve the name of "true love" at all, or the goal you recently devised for it is false and certainly not true.

<margin>The goal of any love consists in pleasure. We are not always permitted to reach a proposed goal.</margin>
**PHILO.** The goal of any love undoubtedly consists in pleasure <note>The Latin "uoluptas" refers to both physical pleasure and intellectual delight.</note>. For this reason, since I love you truly and uniquely, I desire most wonderfully to enjoy you yourself in the most joined and pleasant way. This goal is indeed intended both by me as the lover and by my love for you. However, not everyone who strives toward a goal proposed for themselves always reaches it. On the contrary, many are frequently seen to wander from their intended target; this happens all the more easily when we require the help of others to acquire a goal, just as we see occurring in the pleasure of a lover, which we have established as the goal of love itself. For pleasure of this kind will certainly never happen to the lover unless the mutual love of the lady-friend has eventually led him to this longed-for end. Therefore, for no other reason is my devotion to you deprived of its proper goal, except that you respond not at all to the love and goodwill of my soul toward you. For while I clearly perceive that love has begun both in the whole universe of created things and in its individual parts, in you alone it seems to me that love has never arisen.

<margin>He most elegantly attributes the reason why Philo is unable to reach the goal of his love and devotion for Sophia to Sophia's own hardness and cruelty.</margin>
**SOPHIA.** Perhaps through the disadvantage of a faulty sowing, love has never produced any fruit in me. **PHILO.** Truly, I do not think that is the right reason: for it seems that the best field has utterly rejected the seed entrusted to it. **SOPHIA.** Then it labors under some defect or some imperfection. **PHILO.** Most certainly. **SOPHIA.** But since everything imperfect or deficient is also called "ugly," why I pray, Philo, do you think an ugly thing should be pursued with such great love? If you have perhaps fallen into this error because the ugly seems beautiful to you, then your devotion to me deserves the name of neither true nor right love, as you are often accustomed to boast.

<margin>Except for God Himself, nothing else deserves to be called absolutely or simply beautiful.</margin>
**PHILO.** Certainly nothing (the Highest Beauty alone excepted) is found so beautiful that it does not perhaps labor under some defect, however small. Thus you, Sophia, so excel in extraordinary form and excellent beauty that although that defect—which makes me most unhappy—accompanies it, nevertheless the charm and beauty infused in you from the divine has much greater power to win goodwill for itself than that tiny defect (the source of all my trials) seems to have for stirring up hatred toward itself. **SOPHIA.** I truly cannot see what this great beauty of mine could be that it drives your soul to love me so vehemently. For you have already taught above that true beauty resides in Wisdom <note>original: "Sapientia."</note>, of which I receive from you only that portion which you grant me because of the extraordinary generosity of your character. Therefore, the praise of true beauty seems to fit you rather than me. For this reason, I should burn with love for you, rather than you for me. **PHILO.** I consider it enough to have given the reason for my love for you alone. Truly, I am entirely ignorant of the cause why you do not respond to me in love: unless perhaps it can be argued that my devotion to you is such and so great that it leaves no empty seat or part of love for you to occupy. **SOPHIA.** I consider it more than enough for you to admit you are devoted to me, even if I am not beautiful: for you must concede either that beauty is something other than wisdom, or that your goodwill for me does not deserve the name of true and proper love.

<margin>Supreme beauty must undoubtedly be established and placed within divine Wisdom.</margin>
**PHILO.** You have indeed truly said that I placed supreme beauty in divine Wisdom: which is found in you both because of the extraordinary form and charm of your body, and also because of the praiseworthy and divine disposition of your soul,

# LEONE EBREO, ON LOVE

...although the final hand <note>original: "supremā... manus," a Latin idiom referring to the finishing touches on a work of art</note> of practice has not yet reached it, my mind shines so brightly with the most beautiful image of you impressed upon it that it is as if it worships and venerates some divine power. **SOPHIA.** I would never have believed those feigned words would flow from your mouth, nor would I have ever suspected you would act with me so cunningly and deceitfully in the manner of flatterers. Since I lack wisdom—even in your own judgment—I can by no means truly and properly be called "beautiful." But you call me not only beautiful,

<margin>The beauty of the intelligent soul consists in its disposition toward Wisdom.</margin>
but even divine. **PHILO.** That potential for wisdom is called the "native form," which God is thought to have distributed to intelligent souls in their creation through specific degrees. Hence a soul is judged to be so much more beautiful the greater the "disposition" <term>dispositio: the inherent potential or readiness to receive a quality</term> it received from the supreme Creator for attaining wisdom. Who would ever deny that your mind is highly disposed toward this? However, for it finally to emerge as wise in action, it happens by the help of divine instruction in the disciplines and by the help of practice, just as if an artist's hand were added to natural beauty. Do you think me so crude, Sophia, that I would consider an excellent and natural beauty inferior or leave it behind just because it lacked a bit of artifice and diligence?

<margin>Natural beauty is wonderfully to be preferred over artificial beauty.</margin>
I prefer to love a natural form entirely devoid of artifice, rather than an artificial beauty completely separated from the natural. Therefore, you seem to have falsely accused me of the crime of flattery. For unless the image of your beauty, which I carry around with me, were divine rather than human, my singular love for you could never have brought about the forgetting of all other things, and called back all the thoughts of my soul to contemplating and loving you alone. **SOPHIA.** Even if you perhaps escape the charge of flattery, you have fallen into this error: that you have received the image and likeness of a mortal and fleeting woman into your mind in such a way that you calmly allow it to be converted into a divine form.

<margin>The beloved, placed in the mind of the lover themselves, acquires divinity.</margin>
**PHILO.** Nor do I agree with you that I have committed any error because of that: for it is seen to be characteristic of the lover himself, and of lovers and beloved things, that the beloved, placed in the lover's own mind, acquires divinity, and is worshipped and observed by him as if it were some divine power. **SOPHIA.** We shall say then that this is a common error of all lovers. **PHILO.** Not all lovers can err commonly, unless love itself were perhaps said to be some kind of common error. **SOPHIA.** But how can it happen that the image of the beloved object, established in the lover's own mind, can undergo such a change as to be rendered from human to divine, without any error? **PHILO.** Since our soul is said to be a certain image or pattern of that highest beauty, and since, driven by natural desire, it strives to return at last to its own divinity: hence it happens that from

<margin>Our soul naturally loves and desires beauty.</margin>
that highest beauty—with natural desire also concurring—it is seen to be always most pleasing. From this, as soon as our soul beholds some beautiful person with the help of the eyes, it soon sees the divine form also impressed upon them, and contemplates it more clearly through them: for in that person, just as in an image, or rather in a mirror, the divine form shines. Moreover, the image of that beloved person, placed in the lover's own mind, by its own conspicuous beauty opens and brings out that divine and hidden beauty, which we have already said is the lover's soul itself; and it grants a certain similar perfection to it, as if the first and divine form were joined with the soul of the same lover. For this reason, it too acquires some divinity, and takes strength for itself, and emerges so much more beautiful

<margin>The vehemence of the life of love.</margin>
as divine beauty excels human beauty. From this it finally happens, as we see, that the lover's love for the beauty of the beloved is so intensified and inflamed that all his senses, and his whole imagination, and also all...

<summary>Philo explains to Sophia that the lover's mind transforms the image of the beloved into a divine form because the soul naturally seeks the highest beauty. He argues that human beauty acts as a mirror for a deeper, divine beauty that exists within the soul itself.</summary>

### DIALOGUE III.

<margin>Every beauty exists as a kind of ray of the highest beauty itself.</margin>
<margin>Divinity shines forth in the noble lover and in the beautiful beloved.</margin>
...so much so that it seems to occupy the mind entirely: just as divine beauty itself is accustomed to do, when it compels and leads the human soul back to itself, focused intently on its most sharp contemplation. Furthermore, the image of the beloved person, stored and placed within the mind of the lover, is worshipped by him as if it were a divine power <note>original: "numen"</note>, all the more so when the beloved person is seen to be more excellent—both due to the beauty of the soul and the grace of the body—and more similar to that divine beauty itself. Nor is this without merit, since the highest wisdom of God shines more brightly in such a person. To this end, the intellectual character <term>ingenium: the natural quality of a person's mind or spirit</term> of the lover, which is accustomed to receiving the form of the beloved thing, is thought to carry the greatest importance. For if that divine quality carries a beauty weighed down and enveloped by the darkness of matter and the mass of the body, even if the beloved happens to be very beautiful, the lover is able to acquire little of the divinity placed within them; this happens because of the scarcity of divinity existing in the mind of the lover himself. Added to this is the fact that the mind of a most ignoble lover can neither fully and abundantly perceive the beauty of the beloved thing (no matter how lovely it is), nor can it distinguish the order or condition of that beauty. For this reason, you will very rarely see vile souls, stained with the filth of matter, love distinguished and most excellent forms, nor will you ever see their loves strive toward arduous or sublime heights.

<margin>To establish a notable and praiseworthy love, two things are primarily required: a near-divine form [of the beloved] and the excellent and noble character of the lover.</margin>
But if it happens that the beloved person excels in form and is loved by an illustrious and noble character in whom divine beauty shines most greatly, then that beauty, having entered the most pure mind of the lover, soon acquires for itself the highest divinity. It is worshipped and observed by him with the greatest honor, no differently than a sacred power. Indeed, the study and intense love of such an excellent lover for the most excellent form of the beloved is rightly declared to be effective, as well as most vehement. Now, to finally return to where we digressed, I say to you again and again, Sophia, that your most excellent beauty of both body and soul is truly that which grants and bestows divinity upon me in my devotion to you. For even if my mind does not seem to be endowed with such brightness that it could make your form divine and immortal as it should be, nevertheless, I believe the splendor of your form has contributed a most pure light to my mind, even if it were perhaps dark by its own nature, chasing away all shadows.

<margin>He highly commends both the beauty of Sophia’s soul and her body.</margin>
**SOPHIA.** It seems, then, that the previous words you brought forth in my praise proceeded neither from error nor from any desire for flattery, but rather from love, and should be referred to the nature of the beautiful and of the soul. But I am not of such a rude or dull wit <note>original: "rudi aut hebeti... ingenio"</note> that I am entirely ignorant that the reason for this conversion of mine from a mortal into a goddess should be ascribed to the divinity and wisdom of your mind, rather than to my own fleeting and fragile form.

**PHILO.** I would rather your mind be led to love me from your heart—as would happen if you persuaded yourself that the praises I gave you were true—than that I should lead you only to celebrate my divinity and wisdom in words and appearance.

<margin>Our love for God seems to provoke and lead Him to love us back.</margin>
But even if you have spoken these things with a degree of pretense or feigning, as is your custom, you will by no means dare to deny this: that the supreme beauty of God, which surpasses all others by an infinite distance, is provoked (as it were) by the human mind that loves it. Although the human mind is lowest and finite when compared to Him, God is led to love it back, and to provide for its ultimate happiness, its highest delight, and its most blessed union <note>original: "copulationem"</note> with God Himself. You indeed, Sophia, who among humans seem so similar to that divine form, why do you not also strive to imitate it with such a grateful and reciprocal love?

**SOPHIA.** Truly, I do not believe I disagree with it in this regard. For just as that Divine Beauty strives to call back and lead the lover to no other union than a spiritual one, proper to the mind, and for that reason is thought to love in return; so I also love you, pursuing an honorable and noble love—

Here, Sophia responds by pivoting the conversation toward the distinction between spiritual and physical love, ultimately leading to the conclusion of their three-day dialogue.</meta>

### LEONE EBREO ON LOVE, DIALOGUE III

...indeed, I do not so much desire to join your mind with mine, but rather mine with yours, as if to be coupled as closely as possible with perfection. You can best infer this desire of mine from the fact that I am always anxious and focused—indeed, completely intent—on understanding the hidden concepts of your mind, and on embracing and enjoying your divine wisdom; from this, I am accustomed to feeling and perceiving the greatest delight. But as for the mingling of bodies, which lovers are usually so vehemently eager for, I would wish that absolutely no suspicion of this foul desire existed between us. For just as spiritual love is seen to be the best and most beautiful, and to overflow on all sides with delightful and healthy effects, so on the contrary, I believe corporal love to be depraved and shameful, and usually to produce sad and inconvenient effects. But so that I may understand this matter more distinctly and completely, I would desire you to review the effects following human love, as you already promised above. I would also like you to add which effects arising from love are good and praiseworthy, and which are depraved and worthy of blame—and whether the number of the latter is greater than the former. For when these matters are finished and added to what came before, you will be seen to have fulfilled everything you promised in the best of faith.

**PHILO**: I see, Sophia, that you are very shrewdly demanding that I fulfill my remaining promises so that you can escape my just accusations <note>Philo playfully suggests Sophia is using philosophy to avoid acknowledging his romantic feelings</note>. But I recall that I promised this to you earlier in a somewhat doubtful and ambiguous way. Now, however, neither the time nor the occasion seems to demand that these promises be fulfilled. For you see that we have spent a great deal of time in conducting this discussion on the origin of love. And now night itself almost seems to urge you to indulge in sleep and rest. Instead, you should set about fulfilling those things which you have long owed me, compelled by love, reason, and virtue. As for me, as soon as I find the leisure, I will strive to satisfy those things which I both promised of my own accord and am forced to fulfill by the unfair condition of lovers. Farewell.

->**Farewell.**<-

# GIOVANNI FRANCESCO PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA,
## TO THE AUGUST EMPEROR
### M A X I M I L I A N.

---

<image-desc>A large decorative historiated initial 'O' featuring symmetrical foliate scrollwork within a square frame.</image-desc>

> You seem to me to desire, Most Invincible Caesar, to excel not so much in wealth as in learning—a vow that was most vigorous in that great <note>original: "Macedone"; a reference to Alexander the Great, who was famously a student of Aristotle</note> Macedonian, and for which sake he was wonderfully praised by antiquity. For you command me to take care that certain monuments of the <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>The Jewish mystical tradition, which Christian scholars in the Renaissance sought to harmonize with Christianity</note>, once translated into the Latin tongue by the effort of my uncle Giovanni Pico, be transcribed and delivered to Your Majesty. Regarding this matter, I could hardly conceive in my mind, let alone explain in writing, how painful it is for me that I cannot obey your command (as is right). For among all human desires, my greatest is to gratify you, my Prince—indeed, the Prince of all. However, not a single page of the Kabbalistic faculty remains in my possession, just as the library of my deceased uncle no longer exists here, since my uncle Antonio—the testamentary heir of his movable goods—sold it to Cardinal <note>Domenico Grimani (1461–1523), a famous patron and collector of books and art</note> Grimani. I possess only some of his own inventions and meditations from the original manuscripts, transcribed with great labor and expense, which have nothing to do with the Kabbalah, part of which I have already published. But since this opportunity to comply with you has been offered to me, magnanimous Caesar, I entreat you with what faith and readiness of mind I can, that you do not cease to command whatever else you please, provided it can be accomplished by my strength. For in honoring you, I would certainly yield to many in talent and strength, but to none in loyalty and diligence. And although I know it is more fitting for a servant to act than to speak, and that these very things I promise are already yours—since nature itself delivered me to you and my will bound me—I could not restrain myself from offering these same things to you with a wonderful heat of goodwill. Farewell.

# CONRAD LEONTORIUS
## TO JAKOB WIMPFELING

->Sends Hearty Greetings.<- <note>original: "S. P. D." (Salutem Plurimam Dicit), a standard Latin epistolary greeting</note>

<image-desc>A decorative historiated initial 'Q' features a scholar seated at a desk or lectern with an open book, surrounded by his library, within a detailed square frame.</image-desc>
**A**S SOON AS I departed from you at Mainz, I immediately experienced within myself that proverb common among our French neighbors: *Nowhere is one enough with a friend, neither present nor absent.* For when I was present, I did not enjoy your company as much as our friendship deserves; this often happens to all lovers, who realize upon parting that they have omitted many things they had intended in their minds to do or say. But what I omitted, letters shall repair, through whose exchange I wish I could be with you more often. We were speaking of the *Book of Illustrious Men* from the house of **Sponheim** <note>Johannes Trithemius, the Abbot of Sponheim, was then compiling his "De scriptoribus ecclesiasticis," a catalog of famous authors</note>, which you said had been given to Basel for printing. I asked about **Doctor Johannes Reuchlin**, whether he had been included; when you hesitated and seemed to say no, I was utterly amazed. For whom could you consider more illustrious in every kind of learning in this age? If he were thoroughly familiar and known to you, you would find no one better. Therefore, you and your Abbot would pass him over only with great injury and loss to the German name. For he is a most skilled interpreter of three languages: Greek, Hebrew, and Latin. Add also, if you wish, French, which he learned thoroughly at **Orléans** <note>original: "Aurelianis"</note> while he was devoting himself to the study of law. As a youth, he translated several orations, some of which (unless I am mistaken) were composed by Xenophon in defense of Socrates. He has composed many pleasant poems and written many epistolary disputes, which he has filled with the opinions of both Greeks and Hebrews. Moreover, so that he might penetrate the secret doctrines of the Hebrews, he labored most strenuously for many years, and so unrolled their entire library that you will not easily find a Hebrew whom you could set against him. Led by this happiness and abundance of talent and learning, he applied himself to writing a Dialogue, which he titled **Capnion** <note>Reuchlin's Greek-style pseudonym, meaning "Little Smoke," a play on his German name Reuchlin (Rauch = smoke)</note>, or ***On the Mirific Word***, than which I have never seen anything more eloquent or more wonderful. It is divided into three books. The first explains all the secrets of philosophy under the name of **Sidonius**. The second introduces **Baruchias** the Jew, who unravels all those secret and portentous names and many other matters of the Hebrews. The third introduces **Capnion**, who approves and demonstrates the Christian faith from those two previous parts. There, he applies all the "mirific" <note>wonder-working or miraculous</note> words to the name of **JESUS**, so that he may demonstrate that the ineffable **Tetragrammaton** <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH, which was traditionally considered unpronounceable</note> has now been made effable <note>pronounceable or speakable</note>. If you read this Dialogue, you will affirm that no one—neither Philosopher, nor Jew, nor Christian—can rightly be preferred to Johannes Reuchlin. It would be a perpetual shame for us not to set such a man before all the Italians. Therefore, my Jakob, as I am about to seek **Augustinus** <note>Likely referring to a person or a specific monastery</note> and do not know at what time I shall reach Basel, I would like you to write with the greatest care and diligence to **Johannes Amerbach** the printer, so that he may assign Johannes Reuchlin of Pforzheim his proper place in the catalog. Farewell, my most delightful Jakob, joyful and happy. From Speyer, the eleventh day before the Kalends of May <note>April 21</note>,

->1493.<-

# TO THE MOST HOLY LEO THE TENTH
## SUPREME PONTIFF, JOHANNES REUCH-
->LIN HUMBLY COMMENDS HIMSELF.<-

**I**TALIAN Philosophy, Most Blessed Leo the Tenth, Supreme Pontiff of the Christian religion—originally brought down long ago to the greatest men endowed with excellent genius by **Pythagoras**, the first father of that name—had perished for very many years under the immense barking of the **Sophists** <note>Reuchlin uses "Sophists" as a derogatory term for the Scholastic theologians of the Middle Ages, whose complex logic-chopping he believed had obscured true ancient wisdom.</note>. It lay buried in darkness and dense night for so long, until **Lorenzo de' Medici**, your father—the most illustrious offspring of the Great Cosimo and prince of the city of Florence—arose through the favor of God for the sake of the best studies of the line of Solomon <note>original: "Solomonis generis"; a reference to the Medici family's reputation for Solomonic wisdom and patronage.</note>. If we knew him to be so capable in spirit and in the science of governing the Republic, and in conducting all things at home and at war with counsel and prudence, that no one in his age seemed more deserving of praise in civic practice, yet we must confess that he was born even more fitly for this—as if sent down from heaven—so that after the disciplines of eloquence and the arts of fine speaking had been handed down to the Florentine youth by the rhetoricians **Petrarch**, **Philelphus**, and **Aretino**, he might finally bring to his fatherland that wisdom which expels vices and the method of investigating secrets. These things had lain hidden in the books and monuments of the ancients until his own time, so that the citizens might be, without controversy, more polished than all foreign nations by a more elegant pen and more adorned by the purity of their language. For this task, he diligently summoned from everywhere the most learned men and those most skilled in ancient authors, who possessed sufficient eloquence along with knowledge of things: **Demetrius Chalcondyles**, **Marsilio Ficino**, **Giorgio Vespucci**, **Cristoforo Landino**, **Valori**, **Angelo Poliziano**, **Giovanni Pico**, the Count of Mirandola, and other most erudite men of the world, through whom the skill of the ancients and the secret antiquity, obliterated by the malice of chance, might return to the light. These great men competed to achieve this. For this one taught, another provided commentary; this one read, that one interpreted and translated languages into languages. Marsilio led Greece into Latium <note>That is, Ficino translated Greek philosophy into Latin.</note>. Poliziano brought the Romans back into Greece. Everyone pressed on with the work, each bringing the highest praise to the Medici. Upon these heroes, Most Blessed **LEO**, your birth-wand—a divine one, as they say—fell happily. By the grace of the Gods, it was certainly so that no kind of more elegant learning remained in which you did not turn out to be most skilled, having embraced the sweetness of the most polished Poliziano even as a boy. Why say more? Nothing was more flourishing than Florence in that age. In it, the best of the arts, all of which had previously fallen, were being reborn; nothing of languages and letters remained untouched in which the most noble Florentines were not exercised.

At that time, I was vehemently moved by that fame, touched by a desire for that place—and not only by the longing to see your ancestral home, which they called the house of the Great Cosimo (a building magnificent and unusual to us from the **Hercynian Forest** <note>original: "Hercynijs"; referring to the ancient name for the wooded mountain ranges of Southern Germany where Reuchlin lived.</note>), but also by the desire to see your father, from whom such great benefits had proceeded in our century. Therefore, having set out for Italy with the illustrious **Eberhard the Pious**, the first Duke of the Swabians in our time <note>Eberhard I, Duke of Württemberg (1445–1496), also known as "the Bearded."</note>, for whom I served as Secretary, I entered Florence around the 12th of the Calends of April, in the Year of Christ 1482. And when I had commended the remarkable nobility of the Medici family to that Duke, as indeed I truly ought to have done, he desired to have a conversation with that man. When Lorenzo had noticed this—revealed by I know not whom—he took the stranger's right hand most humanely and led us all to his home, showing us every single thing worthy of sight. # THE WORKS OF JOHANNES REUCHLIN

I will hasten to turn back, unless evening is already looming, when both you are weary from listening with distaste, and I myself am exhausted from speaking. For enough things have slipped from us in these brief hours, and what was either my rashness (if you wish) or, more truly, my singular love for you—because in such a great matter it ought not to have happened—yet I spoke extemporaneously when commanded. 

Then Philolaus said: "But we beseech you, complete the counting of the authors who both held and handed down the Kabbalah, so that we may not go to our lodging with this part of the discourse unfinished; then, let us go to dine." 

To which Simon replied: "Certainly there exist, in my judgment, innumerable Kabbalists (for I cannot encompass them in number), some of whom only listened, while others were both listeners and writers; nevertheless, since you urge it so, I will cursorily review some of those whose books on Kabbalistic contemplations come into daily use, as far as my memory serves me, although not all are intact in every part. Of some, only fragments have floated to the surface; the rest, alas, are so extinct that they are known to the records of most learned men only by the recollection of their names."

"For just as the fathers lost ancient volumes through the unfairness of the times and the long passage of years—with no small loss to posterity—so we, now living in the very sixth millennium of the world <note>Reuchlin refers to the Hebrew calendar; the year 1517 AD corresponds to the Hebrew year 5277, falling within the sixth millennium</note>, have lost the books of our predecessors. They have been lost either by old age (which consumes all things), or the malice of wars, or flood and devastation, or by the unforeseen accident of fire, or by that shameful and detestable hatred and envy which in our own time has incited inert and foolish book-burners." <note>This is a pointed reference to the contemporary "Battle of the Books" in which Reuchlin defended Jewish literature against those, like Johannes Pfefferkorn, who sought to burn them.</note> 

"Books of Enoch are cited by men of good character, and of our father Abraham; indeed, Moses even cites the *Book of the Wars of the Lord*, Joshua the *Book of the Just*, and the whole library of *Kiriath-sepher* <note>original: "Kiriath sepherim," meaning City of Books</note>, which Othniel captured under the leadership of Caleb. Ahasuerus cites the *Books of Memoirs*, and Jonathan in the Book of Maccabees mentions the 'Holy Books' sent to the Spartans. The Chronicles mention the *Books of Lamentations*, the *Books of Samuel the Seer*, *Nathan the Prophet*, *Gad the Seer*, *Shemaiah the Prophet*, *Iddo the Seer*, *Ahijah the Shilonite*, and the *Books of Jehu son of Hanani*, all of which are nowhere to be found. We also lament the library of Darius, as mentioned in the Book of Ezra; it was a precious one in Ecbatana. 

By a similar example, many authors in our own age have perished, although we do not doubt that many survive which we ourselves have not yet seen. Nor can I yet claim that glory for myself as Pico della Mirandola did—who once claimed that Ezra commanded seventy volumes of Kabbalistic secrets to be written down, which he sought out at the greatest expense. I lack the abundance of gold and silver <note>original: "fidem propè auri & argenti," literally "the credit of gold and silver"</note> to be able to buy those books, if they should remain and be offered."

"We use, however, though not having a vast library, the following to the best of our ability: 

The book of our father Abraham, titled **יצירה** (*Yetzirah*), 'On Creation,' which some learned men assign to Master Akiba; it is truly adorned with noble scholarly commentary, as it is otherwise hidden and obscure. 

The book **הבהיר** (*Bahir*), 'On Splendor,' which Simeon ben Jochai composed while he lay hidden in a vast and dark cave for twenty-four years. 

The book **המנורה** (*Ha-Menorah*), 'On the Candelabrum,' which is called the *Lucidarius* by your people. 

There are also the works published on Kabbalah by Abraham Abulafia, and the distinguished commentaries of Ramban <note>Rabbi Moses ben Nahman, also known as Nachmanides</note> on the secrets of the Law, whom the people of Gerona call their own. 

Also the commentaries of the most learned of all recipients, Rabbi Menahem Recanati, on the secrets of Ramban. 

The *Guide for the Perplexed* by Rambam <note>Rabbi Moses ben Maimon, or Maimonides</note>, whom they call Moses the Egyptian. 

The book **שערי צדק** (*Sha'arei Tzedek*), that is, 'The Gates of Justice,' written by Rabbi Joseph ben Carnitolis <note>Joseph Gikatilla</note>. 

The book **שער אורה** (*Sha'ar Orah*), that is, 'The Gate of Light,' by Master Joseph (as they say) of Castile in Spain. 

The book **האמונות** (*Ha-Emunot*), that is, 'On Beliefs,' whose author in Asia was Rabbi Saadia. 

The book **סוד התורה** (*Sod Ha-Torah*), 'On the Mystery of the Law,' which the wise Abraham Ibn Ezra composed. 

The book of Rabbi Hamai ben Hanina, who is called the head of the most eloquent in Kabbalah, and the book **עיון** (*Iyun*), that is, 'On Speculation,' by the same author. 

Finally, another book, **פירוש קדושה** (*Perush Kedushah*), that is, 'Commentary on Holiness,' which Rabbi Azriel wrote. 

And the book **שמות** (*Shemot*), that is, 'On Names'..."

# ON THE KABBALISTIC ART, BOOK I.

And there is the *Book of the Explanation of the Alphabet*, titled: <note>original: "סדר פירוש האלפאביתא" (Seder Perush Ha-Alef-Beit)</note> **The Order of the Explanation of the Alphabet**, attributed to Rabbi Akiva. There is also the book of Rabbi Amma, <note>original: "שער הרזים" (Sha'ar Ha-Razim)</note> **The Gate of Secrets**, regarding the hidden meanings of Psalm 19. Also the book <note>original: "יחוד" (Yichud)</note> **Unity**: that is, a singular work on union or collection, which Rabbi Abraham Ibn Ezra mentions in the first chapter of his *Mystery of the Law*. And the book <note>original: "סודות" (Sodot)</note> **Secrets**: that is, of mysteries. There is also the *Book of Abstruse Questions*. And the little book on Kabbalah published by Azariel, whom others call Oriel of Gerona. And the book titled: <note>original: "דרך האמונה ודרך המהרה" (Derekh Ha-Emunah Ve-Derekh Ha-Meherah)</note> **The Way of Faith and the Way of Expiation**. And the *Book of Roots* by Rabbi Joseph Albo, to which they likewise prefixed the title of "Kabbalah," even though he comments more on ethics than on spiritual ascents. Finally, there exists a most elegant book in Kabbalah directed against the "pseudo-philosophers," named **The Kuzari** <note>original: "Alkozer"</note> in the Arabic fashion, which Rabbi Judah Halevi composed; his words are these: <note>original: "כי אין קבלה טובה אלא עם הלב הטוב"</note> **"For there is no good Kabbalah except with a good heart."** In this, it seems to me he very wisely repelled the malicious Sophists from such holy contemplation—those who, like dying flies, spoil the sweetness of any ointment, no matter how precious. Finally, we use the commentaries on the *Book of Formation* <note>original: "יצירה" (Yetzirah)</note> by Master Jacob Ha-Kohen, and the composition on the same book by Rabbi Isaac, which he titled *The Explanation of the Holy Name*. There is also a book published by Rabbi Todros Halevi concerning the ten Kabbalistic enumerations <note>The ten Sefirot, or divine emanations</note>. I do not wish to include the book attributed to Solomon under the name of **Raziel**, for it is a magical fiction.

Up to this point, I have quite plainly revealed to you strangers the "paper-poverty" of my personal library <note>Simon is being modest about his collection</note>, which I am not usually wont to do with others; but in my opinion, no one has ever written on this art more skillfully, more distinctly, or more clearly until recently than **Rabbi Joseph ben Abraham Gikatilla**, a Castilian and citizen of Salerno. He industriously labored over three volumes of this discipline, through which he made the entire instruction of the Kabbalists clearer: the first regarding words, the second regarding letters, and the third volume regarding the vowel points. The title of his book is: <note>original: "גינת אגוז" (Ginnat Egoz)</note> **The Garden of the Nut**, following the Song of Solomon: *I went down into the garden of nuts, to see the fruits of the valley.* It appears that this "nut" is like a golden apple enclosed in a silver network, as we read in Proverbs: *A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver.* 

In this way, Kabbalah is that golden and divine apple, bound around with silver threads—that is, with ingenious instructions and human arts—just as is customary in the work of goldsmiths. These craftsmen, with subtle engravings, do not entirely hide or cover a golden, sweet-smelling apple with silver so that nothing of it can be seen; rather, through certain hollowed openings and silver lattices, they allow both the color of the apple to stand out and the scent of amber to waft through. 

<image-desc>A woodcut manicule pointing towards the text from the right margin.</image-desc> Nevertheless, to those looking from afar, the whole thing that is netted appears to be solid silver. But to those looking more closely, if they examine it studiously, they will simultaneously discover the gold as well. And just as gold differs greatly from silver, so too is "Kabbalah" proven to differ far more from the "Art of Kabbalah"—even though one single category of spiritual instinct embraces both species. But one precedes the other as a divine oracle precedes the priests; and just as one kind of gold is indeed "good," another is "the best." This is similar to the way it is told in the Five Books of Moses regarding Havilah: *that the gold of that land is good.* For it is not written there that it is "the best," as some read, but "good." And in Isaiah regarding Ophir: *I will make a man more precious than fine gold, even the gold of Ophir.* 

Thus, whatever lovers of the highest arts learn from Holy Scripture through natural science is equal to "good gold," and is called the **Work of the Beginning** <note>original: "Bresith" (Ma'aseh Bereshit), referring to physics/natural philosophy</note>. But that which we receive through spiritual science is called the **Work of the Chariot** <note>original: "Mercaua" (Ma'aseh Merkavah), referring to metaphysics/divine mysteries</note>, and is equated to the best and purest gold. For the Kabbalists write thus:

<margin>Tradition <note>original: "שמיעה" (Shemi'ah)</note></margin>

**"The Work of the Beginning is the wisdom of nature, and the Work of the Chariot is the wisdom of divinity."** <note>original: "בראשית חכמת הטבע ומעשה מרכבה היא חכמת האלהות"</note> And since both wisdoms deal in some way with the World and those things that exist in the World, the opinion of the Talmudists and Kabbalists is unanimous in this matter: that there are two Worlds. The first is the **Intellectual World**, which is called <note>original: "עולם הבא" (Olam Ha-Ba)</note> **The World to Come**—that is, as it pertains to us. And the second is the **Sensible World**, which is called <note>original: "עולם הזה" (Olam Ha-Zeh)</note> **This World**; this is clear from the words of the wise...

# OF JOHANNES REUCHLIN
### BOOK I

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page's discussion of the divine names.</note> ...we have received from our ancestors concerning the divine name of forty-two letters, where a diligent worshiper speaks thus: that such a person stands far off: **צלה ונהנחיל למטה ונוחל שני עולמים העולם הזה והעולם הבא** <note>original: "Tzelah ve-nohanchil l'mata ve-nochal sheni olamim ha-olam ha-zeh ve-ha-olam ha-ba"</note>—that is, **desired above and desired below, and inheriting two worlds: this world and the world to come.** Therefore, the Talmudists and the Kabbalists are divided into two faculties, even though both originate and emanate from the same credited traditions. For both give credit to the traditions of their ancestors, often without any reason being rendered. 

But they are distinguished by the order of their designation, because the successful Kabbalist directs all his study, all his effort, all his counsel, labor, and industry—indeed, the entire intention of his mind—to be finally transferred from the sensible world to the intellectual world <note>The "sensible world" is the physical world known through the senses; the "intellectual world" is the realm of divine ideas and pure spirit.</note>. The Talmudist, however, remains in the sensible world and does not transcend the soul of the universal world. If he occasionally proceeds toward God and the blessed spirits, he does not approach God Himself as immanent and absolute, but rather as the Architect and Cause of things, occupied with His creations. He views the angels as daily ministers carrying out the effects of the divine will, always drawing the contemplations of the highest things down to this lower world. 

Nevertheless, one of these faculties often borrows the insights of the other and draws them toward its own desire. Indeed, they sometimes share their studies back and forth, the Talmudists and the Kabbalists, like the active life and the contemplative life. Although they share one and the same context of Holy Scripture, the one usually invites the reader toward "servile fear" <note>Fear of punishment or legal consequence.</note> and the other toward "filial love" <note>The love a child has for a parent; a higher spiritual motivation.</note>, each in his own way with charming persuasion. 

For it will appear through sharp study that the Talmudist resides around the precepts and mandates of the Law; he explains them, distinguishes them, venerates them, and embraces them. Thus, we might correctly define "Talmud" as nothing other than the explanation of the Law according to the intention of its author. Hence they are called Talmudists, and also **פרשי** <note>original: "Perushim"</note>: that is, **Expositors** and Pharisees. They always insist on the work of the pulpit and the chair of Moses; they preach and exhort the common people with the Prophet, saying: "Serve the Lord in fear," and with Joshua: "Fear the Lord and serve Him." Furthermore, they say: "Do this in this way," and "Omit that in such-and-such a manner." From this, they have reduced the six hundred and thirteen precepts—contained in the single word **תריג** <note>original: "Taryag," a numerological shorthand for 613</note>—into two headings: **עשה לא תעשה** <note>original: "Aseh, Lo Ta'aseh"</note>: that is, **"Do" and "Do not do,"** which you are accustomed to calling affirmative and negative commandments. These are very convenient to know and extremely necessary in practice. 

The Kabbalists, however, although they are men who piously observe the Law (as truth bears witness), lean more toward contemplation. Therefore they are called **עיון מעלי התורה** <note>original: "Iyyun Ma'alei Ha-Torah"</note>: that is, **men of speculation from among the masters of the Law.** They leave the care of the republic and the management of rites and customs—both at home and at war, in judicial and moral matters—entirely to the Talmudists. They reserve for themselves only those things that pertain to the peace and tranquility of the soul and are referred to the love of God. For thus they say: **כלל התורה שני דברים והם תקון הנפש ותקון הגוף** <note>original: "Kelal ha-Torah sheni devarim ve-hem tikkun ha-nefesh ve-tikkun ha-guf"</note>: that is, **the intention of the entire Law consists of two things: the good disposition of the soul and the good disposition of the body.** 

For every Law tends chiefly toward the perfection of man, and according to it, we pursue two perfections: one of the mind and the other of the body. Far more worthy and of higher pre-eminence is that which aids the soul and perpetuates life, whereas a suitable habit of the body and its proper composition is prior only in terms of time <note>i.e., the body's needs must be met first in time, but the soul's needs are greater in importance.</note>. Therefore, the Kabbalists must be held in a higher place and a more dignified rank. They follow that exposition of the Law which, through certain symbols, elevates the mind to the heavens and propels it as much as possible toward Divine reality. Your theologians call this "anagogical instruction" <note>Interpretation that leads the mind upward from the literal to the spiritual.</note>, which is not only philosophy but is Wisdom itself. 

Hence they are deservedly called Sages, and **נגר החיים** <note>original: "Nachal Ha-Chayyim" or "Nochal Ha-Chayyim"</note> **Heirs of Life**, as the Preacher Solomon says, because they proceed to that place where life is. While still dwelling in their little bodies within the grasp of mortals, they ascend from time to eternity and from the lowest things to the highest. Make a trial of this if you wish, honored young men. "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." Truly, by "heaven," the Talmudists call all things of the visible world that are above the Moon, and that which is below they call "earth." Then, the Kabbalist also interprets heaven as "Form" and earth as "Matter"...

He argues that while both are necessary, the Kabbalist's pursuit of "Wisdom itself" is the higher calling.</summary>

# OF THE KABBALISTIC ART, BOOK I.

...constitute matter; wherefore in the beginning (they say) God created form and matter, whose composition He then skillfully fashioned in each individual thing through His creative oracle <note>Referring to the "Word" or "Logos" of God</note>, and He did not so much turn everything by hand as He shaped it nine times by the Word. For it is read: **וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹהִים** <note>original Hebrew: *Va-yomer Elohim*</note>: that is, **and God said**: "Let there be light," and God said: "Let there be a firmament," and God said: "Let the waters be gathered," and God said: "Let the earth bring forth," and God said: "Let there be lights," and God said: "Let the waters bring forth creeping things," and God said: "Let the earth bring forth," and God said: "Let us make man," and God said: "Behold, I have given you every herb." Therefore the heavens and the earth were finished with all their belongings and their entire furniture, such as the four elements, which are first named as darkness, the spirit of the Lord, the waters under the firmament, and the dry land. There follow likewise the other mixed things, which are commonly called elements, such as birds and flying things, beasts and creeping things, fish and great whales, and the master of them all, Man, to whom alone among all corporeal beings **Free Will** was granted. Lest he use it wrongly, Laws are established for him, constitutions are promulgated, and punishments for transgression are threatened.

Since likewise the inflowing fire is called heaven: that is, **שָׁמַיִם** <note>Hebrew: *Shamayim*</note>, as if it were **אֵשׁ-מַיִם** <note>a compound of *Esh* (fire) and *Mayim* (water)</note>, and it produces nothing from itself, but rather nourishes things already produced by the celestial sun—that is, by moist heat—then in a right order are recited the most powerful influences established in it: the Sun and the Moon, by whose leadership all the remaining armies are marked, the luminaries and stars, night and day, splendor and darkness, signs and seasons, days and years. These things, therefore, concern the corporeal globe and the mixed things enclosed within it. But two Worlds are accepted by the Kabbalists: the corporeal and the incorporeal, the visible and the invisible, the sensible and the mental, the material and the ideal.

The lower World and the superior World, when they read: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth," and thus they think that "heaven" symbolically designates the highest things, and "earth" the lowest things, interpreting in this way **בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא הַשֵּׁם הָעֶלְיוֹנִים וְהַתַּחְתּוֹנִים** <note>original: *Bereshit bara ha-Shem ha-elyonim ve-ha-tachtonim*</note>: that is, **In the beginning God created the highest and the lowest things.** By this they surely judge that the simple and immaterial World contains the highest things, while this compact and "cement-like" world contains the lowest. From this, the divine Law of *Bereshit* <note>the Hebrew name for the Book of Genesis, meaning "In the beginning"</note> concerning creation began with the letter **beth** <note>the second letter of the Hebrew alphabet: **ב**</note>, which in the art of Arithmetic <note>specifically Gematria, where letters have numerical values</note> signifies **two** among the numbers, as if it were notably insinuating that God principally created two things: the entire upper World with all those dwelling in it, and the entire lower World and everything belonging to it. 

For otherwise, it would have been enough for Moses to write **רֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים שָׁמַיִם וָאָרֶץ** <note>original: *Reshit bara Elohim shamayim ve-aretz*</note>, which would be read by the Latins in the same way: "In the beginning God created heaven and earth." For that summary of creation could have started without the letter *beth*. Just as Solomon says in Proverbs: "The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his ways," where the word "beginning" is placed without *beth* and without any other preposition. Moreover, beyond custom, he joined to these two created things the twice-two articles **אֶת** and **הַ** <note>the Hebrew particles *Et* and *Ha*</note>. One is of excellent demonstration, which is called *ha*, and the other is of all-encompassing comprehension, which is composed of **aleph** <note>the first letter</note>, the first element of the alphabet, and **thau** <note>the last letter</note>, the last; and it is what the Greeks call **α** and **ω** <note>Alpha and Omega</note>, and the Romans "prow and stern" <note>meaning from start to finish</note>. Wherein he seemed to embrace through "heaven" all things excellently simple and spiritual, from *aleph* to *thau*—that is, from the first to the last—and through "earth" similarly from head to heel <note>from top to bottom</note> all things excellently corporeal and contained within them; nevertheless, each individual thing is in that one "beginning" just like a single created thing. 

Just as Ezekiel’s wheel within a wheel, with all its various involvements, was seen to be one likeness of the glory of the Lord; and to use the very words of Rabbi Saadia in the book *Amunoth* <note>Saadia Gaon's *Book of Beliefs and Opinions*</note>: **כְּחֶלְמוֹן בְּתוֹךְ בֵּיצָה** <note>original: *ke-chelmon be-toch beitzah*</note>: that is, **Like the yolk in the middle of an egg**. Or as I myself am accustomed to say, like the white of a single egg, contained by the shell-like firmament, encompassing the yolk itself, so that first intelligible World enfolds the second, so that its entire power is governed from there. By which it happens that both are bound together by the chains of harmony, so much so that they often grant each other their own natures and names, as well as those of the things they contain, with mutual liberality. For in the second, that is the sensible World, nine spheres are moved by the immobile empyrean <note>the highest, fiery heaven</note>, over which **Metattron** <note>Metatron, a high-ranking archangel in Kabbalistic literature often called the "Prince of the Countenance"</note> continually presides; but in the first world, nine choirs of angels are moved by the immobile God. Just as in immobile silence the Creator of all things first [simultaneously...]

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "ninefold speech" (the nine times "God said" in Genesis) used to differentiate creation. It moves into the Kabbalistic doctrine of the "Two Worlds"—the superior spiritual realm and the inferior physical realm—and how every earthly thing has a heavenly archetype.</meta>

# JOHANNES REUCHLIN

...created all things at once, and later, by the ninefold speech, He moved each individual thing into its own specific distinctions by speaking. They are called in turn: fire, Seraphim and Cherubim; water, Tarshish <note>original: "Tharsis", often associated in celestial hierarchies with the "Virtues" or the sea</note>; Ariel, earth; and those things which are in the lower world are known by a much better mark in the higher ones. Wherefore these lower things may appropriately be called copies of the true things, and shadowed super-images, wood <note>original: "ligna", perhaps a reference to the "trees" of the Sephirotic tree</note>, marks, and symbols by which we are moved to think about the surviving and angelic substances, powers, and operations by a certain way of abstraction or assimilation, or by some other possible reason and mode not yet clothed in our understanding.

Hence they establish two Paradises as well, one celestial and the other terrestrial, in which the rewards of virtues are followed by both the earthly man and the heavenly man. Just as in the land of this world, so long as he is a guest in the body, man may gain a pleasurable honor, joy, gladness, and every desire for delight in a certain corruptible garden on account of some heroic or preeminent cause praised by the children of this age—though these are merely shadows and transitory things, similar to smoke.

But in that truly super-celestial land of the living, where the unfading paradise of pleasantness exists, the soul of a man who once acted rightly according to virtue in this mortal life is now stripped of the body. To such a soul, the most merciful, Greatest, and Best God shows every good thing, which it could not have even seen before when burdened by darkness and the thick corpse of the obscured body. That vision is named both in the **Kabbalah** and in the **Talmud** as **איספקלריא המאירה** <note>original Hebrew: *Aspaqlaria ha-me'irah*</note>, that is, **the Illuminating Vision**. This is a life-giving sight, which you call the "intuitive knowledge of God," as it befalls the separated soul through the light of glory and is proven a beatific vision only by those who have most maturely repented. For there is another vision through connatural species, which is not "blessed," and is called **א' ספקל' ריא שאינה המאירה** <note>original Hebrew: *Aspaqlaria she-einah ha-me'irah*</note>, that is, **Contemplation that is not illuminating**. 

Now, since the clear vision of God and the perpetual enjoyment of the highest divinity are granted as blessedness to the supreme part of man—the intellect and the will—by the best right, these things happen to no one except in the Highest World. Thus they say: **כי טרם שישיג לראיה תפרד נפשו מעליה** <note>original Hebrew: *Ki terem she-yashig le-re'iyah tipared nafsho me-aliyah*</note>: that is, **before he attains this vision, his soul is separated from him.** Wherefore, when God is said to be seen by a mortal man, it is thought to be done through an angel, **פי המלאכים** <note>original Hebrew: *pi ha-malakhim*, literally "by the mouth of angels"</note> as **Ramban of Girona** <note>Moses ben Nachman, or Nachmanides, a major medieval Jewish scholar</note> writes on the book of **Exodus**.

Therefore, for the double condition of man—spiritual and corporeal—and for the retribution of a double reward, they propose a double Paradise, as you have heard, saying: **גן ונהרותיו עם כל מים שתראה במעשה בראשית כלן בכנגד צורות השכליות ועליון נחת מן מי מרומים** <note>original Hebrew excerpt regarding the Garden and its rivers</note>: That is, **The garden and its rivers, along with every single thing placed in the Work of Creation <term>Bresith</term> <note>Genesis</note>, are all placed according to intellectual and supernal forms.** I feel the same even regarding the gold of Havilah, bdellium, and onyx, and other gems of infinite price.

In the same way and in the same form, the same **Kabalists** assert that a double **Gehenna**—that is, two Tartaruses <note>Hells</note>—has been designated, one of the Superior World and one of the Inferior World, for torturing harmful bodies in time, and souls in eternity. A common name is given to them: **ארקא** <note>original: "Arka"</note>, for it is the place of Tartarean punishment which, besides other things, contains seven monstrous receptacles of the harshest punishments, destined for those guilty of crimes by the just judgment of God. 

Wherefore that Kabbalist in the volume *The Nut Garden* <note>original: "Horto nucis", referring to Joseph Gikatilla's *Ginnat Egoz*</note>, in the second book, treats the seven habitations of the lower ones in these words: **שני גיהנם הן עליון ותחתון : אחר לגוף בעולם הזה לנפש בעולם הבא אחר זה : והמקום הכולל כל אלו הוא הגהנא כי בו הם גיהנם ושערי מות וצלמות ובאר שחת וטיט היון ואבדון ושאול** <note>Hebrew listing the seven levels of Hell</note>: That is, **There are two kinds of Gehenna, superior and inferior: one for the body in this world, and one for the soul in the world to come after this one; and the place encompassing all these is called Arka, because in it are Gehenna, the Gates of Death, the Shadow of Death, the Pit of Destruction, the Miry Clay, Perdition, and the Grave <note>Sheol</note>.** Thus far **Joseph of Castile** <note>Joseph Gikatilla</note>. Now these chains, this prison, these fetters, this servitude and captivity remain for the sins of the harmful, both for bodies in the present world and for souls in the future world, so that equal rewards of virtue may accompany the righteous, and the wicked may receive their due—

<summary>This page outlines the Kabbalistic doctrine of "as above, so below," explaining that the physical world is a shadow of the spiritual realm. Reuchlin describes the dual nature of Paradise and Gehenna (Hell), citing Nachmanides and Joseph Gikatilla to show how rewards and punishments apply to both the body and the soul.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the two Paradises—the earthly and the heavenly—and the rewards and punishments assigned to the soul. It moves into a contrast between the "Talmudic" (literal/physical) and "Kabbalistic" (spiritual/allegorical) interpretations of the Messiah and the liberation of humanity.</meta>

### ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH, BOOK 1

...the torments of vices are owed. What else is owed to the upright but life and honor; what else to the wicked but death and horror? Nor is this to be understood merely in a temporal sense, but as the Kabbalists wish, also intellectually <note>In this context, "intellectually" refers to the spiritual or higher cognitive realm, as opposed to the physical</note>. For they write: *The righteous, even in their death, are called living; and the wicked, even in their lives, are called dead.* <note>original Hebrew: צדיקים אפילו במיתתן קרואים חיים : ורשעים אפילו בחייהם קרואים מתים — a famous maxim from the Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 18b</note> To those skilled in the Kabbalah, God’s judgment will not be obscure: *In the day that you eat of it, you shall die the death* <note>Genesis 2:17</note>; namely, not a corporal death, but a spiritual one. For Adam lived more than nine hundred years after the forbidden eating, yet in that very moment, as soon as he had transgressed the Law, he died the death. He died, I say, in his sin—a sin far too poisonous and contagious for the whole human race and the propagation of future offspring, destined for the eternal dwellings of the lower regions.

This was to last until, by God’s good pleasure, that Messiah and redeemer should come, who would lead man back into paradise—not a terrestrial one, but a celestial one—and restore to his children the life which their parent had lost: an eternal life, not a temporal one; of the soul, not of the body. This is that very intimacy with God and the most joyful sight of divinity, filled with every delight. In this Messiah, all true Kabbalists (not the sophisticated ones <note>Reuchlin often distinguishes between "true" spiritual Kabbalists and those he considers mere hair-splitters or "sophists"</note>) fix and place all their trust. To him, they direct all the healing prophecies of the Holy Scriptures. 

Whether they speak of the Land of Promise, or of the city of Jerusalem (the participation of which is in that very thing), or of the mountain of God, or His holy place, His holy way, the sanctuary, the courts of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the house of the Lord, the gate of the Lord, and many other similar things—all these Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent Jewish philosopher</note> in his *Mishneh* <note>The *Mishneh Torah*, Maimonides' code of Jewish law. Reuchlin translates "Mishneh" here as "Deuteronomy," meaning "Second Law" or "Repetition"</note> also wished to be understood as referring to celestial beatitude. 

For this reason, we contend much and often with the Talmudists, and we frequently go our separate ways into two different opinions. They attempt to refer every liberation of the King Messiah to a physical captivity or to our true dispersion; they look toward tumults, the noise of arms, military expeditions, the storming of regions and the devastation of lands, and the victory of the Israelite army—just as we read happened to our ancestors under the savior Moses against the Canaanites and Palestinians. Or at least, they look toward some exquisite ingenuity of escape, which many use craftily (though I think it is used holily by some), seeing as they have been exiled and dispersed for so many centuries under so many kingdoms: under the Babylonian for seventy years, the Persian for fifty-four, the Greek for one hundred and thirty, and now under the Roman for one thousand four hundred years, and the end is not yet.

We, on the contrary, in my judgment, more rightly think in a Kabbalistic manner that the Messiah is to come to deliver the wretched mortals of the human race from the chains of unjust original guilt, to remit sins, and to save the souls of those piously serving God—souls excluded from eternal life in Adam our father—until the satisfaction of the Messiah. He, so that the justice of a merciful and clement God might be fulfilled, shall "put forth his hand and take from the tree of life and eat of it," so that through him we may live forever. 

That satisfaction ought not to have been made in royal pomp, nor in the boasting of honor and glory, because the original sin to be expiated by the Messiah sprouted from pride and elation. Rather, it should be in humility and endurance; not in chariots and horses, but in the name of the Lord our God. Not in victory, nor in human triumph, but in labor, fasting, vigils, fortitude of soul, contempt for vainglory, compassionate mercy, the chief love of God, the right love of men, and finally in that heroic, liberal, and spontaneous death. For against vice one fights with virtue alone; and no wise man ever highly esteemed the empires, princedoms, genealogies, or crowns of this world. Indeed, this is what it means to be wise: to despise the glory of this world, because when the glorious rich man dies, he shall take nothing with him (as the Psalmist says), nor shall his glory descend with him. 

Therefore, whatever is written about trophies and the subjection of peoples in the consecrated letters—even after accepting the history if any deeds are narrated—is nevertheless understood by Kabbalists as being about the intellectual world and the supernal powers. Thus, the future King Messiah will, by the best right, not only neglect but even despise these light and abject delusions of this age—magistracies, honors, and kingdoms—as vain and foolish things. He comes to abolish the guilt of the human species and to open the way for virtue...

<meta>This page continues Reuchlin’s argument that the Messiah’s role is spiritual and redemptive rather than merely political, focusing on the interpretation of Isaiah 53 as a Messianic prophecy rather than a metaphor for the suffering of the Jewish people.</meta>

# OF JOHANN REUCHLIN

...should come. From this, the true Messiah himself, if we are led by right reason, will be more clearly recognized from the fifty-third chapter of Isaiah alone, which begins thus: <margin>Isaiah 53</margin> "Behold, my servant shall act wisely" <note>original Hebrew: הנה ישכיל עבדי (*Hineh yaskil avdi*)</note>, and ends thus: "and he shall pray for the transgressors" <note>original Hebrew: ופגע לפשעים (*u-vifga la-posheim*)</note>. Regarding this, I marvel beyond what can be said—and not without a sense of shame for the rarity of such insight among other nations—and I shall speak confidently to you alone. 

I do not know by what faint-heartedness, or perhaps by what shame before the Gentiles, Solomon and David Kimhi <note>Solomon and David Kimhi (Radak) were highly influential medieval Jewish grammarians and biblical commentators</note>, and others of our sect who are not a little learned, interpret the entire context of Isaiah as referring only to the people of Israel who are now scattered everywhere. They do this quite harshly, when it is most plainly prophesied concerning the Messiah himself. Indeed, the Chaldaic translation <note>The *Targum*, an ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> expresses this by name, saying: "Behold, my servant the Messiah shall prosper" <note>original Aramaic: הא יצלח עבדי משיחא (*Ha yitzlach avdi Meshicha*)</note>. 

This is he who was described by Isaiah in the prophetic spirit in that place: a man of sorrows and experienced in infirmity, with his face hidden, a man of no honorable reputation, touched by a divine stroke, despised and avoided, led like a lamb, slaughtered like a sheep, cut off from the land of the living, and counted among the wicked, and inglorious among the sons of men. But truly, what of him among the sons of men? Was he not greatly exalted, and lifted up, and made very high? For who shall declare his generation? And the will of the Lord God is directed by his hand. 

Isaiah first abolished in him the iniquity of us all, because he struck him for the crime of the people. For he himself was wounded for our crimes, and crushed for our iniquities; he who certainly never committed iniquity, and there was no deceit in his mouth. But the Lord willed the bruising of that same wounded one. Therefore, since he is the righteous servant of God, he shall justify many by his knowledge; he himself shall bear their iniquity, and he takes away the sins of many, and shall intercede for sinners. Isaiah saw all these things concerning the true Messiah, and surely he did not lie. 

This is firmly that "Congregation of Israel," according to the opinion of the Kabbalists, and that salvation of our God so often promised, so that we may be justified "by his knowledge" <note>original Hebrew: ובידיעתו (*u-ve-da'ato*)</note>; not that we should be saved in tumult, nor in flight, but standing under one King and one army of faith, we may be liberated in death and by the knowledge of the Messiah. By this knowledge, sin is ended, and the obstacle to the clear vision of God is removed: that is, the original and contagious guilt of all mankind. Concerning this, we read thus in the book of the Kabbalah, regarding the expiation of the soul: 

"And this is the power of the Redeemer, which is the power of the created being that is guided by the seven [variations]" <note>original Hebrew: וזה כח הגאל שהוא כח הנברא המתנהג בשבע</note>; that is, "the thirteen orders of forgiveness by which the world is directed until sin is finished and the Messiah comes, who is the power of God. And in the power of grace, which is the angelic power, and in the power of grace diffused from it, which is the power of the prophet, the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him" <note>original Hebrew: ות שהם יג סדרי סליחה שהעולם מתנהג בהם עד שיבלה החטא המשיח שהוא כח אלהי ובכח האצילות שהוא כח המלאכות ובכח נמנד ממנו שהוא כח הנביא: הנח עליו רוח השם</note>: that is, the spirit of the Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter divine name, YHWH</note>, "the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and the fear of the Lord. Behold the seven variations which the Messiah uses to do good for the good, and to destroy the malignant, according to what is written: 'And with the breath of his lips he shall slay the wicked'" <note>original Hebrew: רוח חכמה ובינה עצה וגבורה רוח דעת ויראת יהוה הרי שבע תמורות שחמשית מי מתנהג בהן להטיב לטובים ולהחריב את הרשעים ברוח שפתיו ימית רשע</note>. 

This is the path demonstrating the grace-given power, or the island, which is the power led by seven variations, which are the thirteen orders of expiation by which the world is directed, until sin is finished and the Messiah comes, who is the power of God. And in the power of grace, which is the angelic power, and in the power of grace diffused from it, which is the power of the prophet, the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: that is, of the Tetragrammaton, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and the fear of the Lord. Behold the seven variations which the Messiah uses to do good for the good, and to destroy the wicked, according as it is written: "And by the breath of his lips he shall slay the ungodly." 

These are the words of the aforementioned Kabbalistic volume, by which we are warned that the King Messiah overcomes the adversaries of God's people not by hand, but by mouth; not by arms, but by the spirit. He grants God's sevenfold grace and slays the ungodly, all by the spirit of his mouth: that is, by his spiritual doctrine. By this, he shall scatter and sow just men and the chosen disciples of the Just One among all nations. Regarding this, the oracle of Isaiah relating to the time of the Messiah—"You shall draw waters from the wells of the savior"—Jonathan son of Uzziel interpreted in Chaldaic with these words: "And you shall receive a new doctrine with joy from the chosen of the righteous" <note>original Aramaic: לקבלון אולפן חדת בחדוה מבחירי צדיקיא (*u-tekablun ulpan chadat be-chedva mi-bechiri tzadikaya*)</note>. 

That truly is the new doctrine, that the true light may shine; and he who hates is in darkness, but he who loves dwells in the light. This, then, is the end of the commandments, that we may gather together in the doctrine of the Messiah: "The Lord : Pure : To the hearts : Of the nations" <note>original Hebrew: יהוה : ברור : לבנת : העמים</note>.

<summary>Reuchlin argues that Isaiah 53 refers specifically to the Messiah rather than the nation of Israel, citing both the Aramaic Targum and Kabbalistic texts to describe the Messiah's spiritual power and his "new doctrine" that justifies and saves through wisdom rather than force.</summary>

### ON THE KABBALISTIC ART, BOOK I.
