...that is, He who will teach the peoples to walk in the ways of the Tetragrammaton <note>original: *Tetragrammati*; the four-letter name of God, YHWH</note>, as Rabbi David Kimhi writes regarding the same Prophet in chapter 2, on the verse: "for the law shall go forth from me." Whoever follows this law shall be saved; whoever despises it shall perish. For the old things belong to fear, but the new things belong to love <note>original Hebrew: *shel ahavah ve-shalom melech shalem*, meaning "of love and peace, the King of Peace"</note>, which is of upright affection from a whole heart, according to our Masters. The Messiah will therefore be an example of life for all who are to be set free; upon him depends the universal salvation of the world, which is called eternal salvation. This is explained by our teachers as "throughout all the days of the ages," where one reads: "Israel is saved in the Lord <note>original: *Ihuh* (YHWH)</note> with an eternal salvation." Something regarding this is written in the book *Ancient Kabbalah* <note>original: *Cabala Hacadma*</note>:

"And this is the secret of King Messiah, who shall come quickly in our days; his entire operation begins in Y.H. and also Y.H., which is the mystery of the seventh day, and this name is his complete name, and every work shall be perfected by his hand." <note>original Hebrew: והוא סוד מלך המשיח שיבא במהרה בימינו שבל פעולתו החלה על יה וגם יה שהוא סוד יום השביעי והוא השם שמו ש ויה: ושלם והשלם כל המלאכה על ידו:</note>

Behold, it has been defined by the wise Kabbalists that all things are to be perfected through the Messiah, and his entire operation is carried out through the most sacred four letters Y.H.V.H. <note>original: *i. h. u. h.*</note> in the mystery of the seventh day. This is named so not from a number of days, but from the transition from the **active life** to the **contemplative life**: that is, in that very rest of the soul and peaceful tranquility, by withdrawing from the excessive anxiety of this world and from the "masonry works" <note>a metaphor for heavy, worldly labor</note> already performed. For it is written: *And he rested on the seventh day from all the work which he had done.*

Although the Talmudists <note>scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note> attribute many names to this King—as may be understood from the citations of many doctors in the book *Sanhedrin*, in the volume *Chelek* <note>original: *Helek*</note>, starting from the head where it is written: *And Rabbi Johanan said: What is the name of the Messiah?* up to the place where *Rabbi Eliezer took up the word, saying: The days of the Messiah.* And later in many of their writings, such as the commentaries on the Song of the Synagogue <note>possibly referring to the *Piyutim* or liturgical poems</note>: *He is the crown, the first and foremost.*

They explain the names of the Messiah as: **Shiloh, Yinnon, David, Hanina, the Branch, the Righteous, the Comforter**. Yet each of these is thought to be a surname or symbolic title, like the seven examples recounted there, which are: the ark, the mercy seat, the tablets, Aaron’s rod, the jar of Manna, and the spirit of God. But according to the Kabbalists, you have heard how this one ineffable name **YHWH** is proper to the Messiah, which will integrate and perfect his substantive name. For they teach that it must be believed that this is his complete name, which is piously and holily integrated in "compassions" <note>original: *miferationibus* / Hebrew: *rachamim*</note>. No Talmudist can secretly deny this, since that great Master in the mentioned place of the Talmud said that the name of the Messiah shall come to be called similarly **Hanina** <note>original: *Hannina*; meaning "Grace" or "Mercy"</note>, citing the verse from Jeremiah 16, which the Romans <note>referring to the Latin Vulgate</note> nonetheless read freely and improperly as: *who will not give you rest.*

But that is not an etymological interpretation. For in my judgment it is read more correctly as: *because I will show you no mercy.* Jonathan the Chaldean <note>the author of the Aramaic *Targum*</note> translated this as *rachamim*: that is, **compassions**. He meant to say, according to the Talmudists, that while you walk in the perversity of your heart so as not to hear God, there will be no Messiah (who is named "Compassions"). From this it clearly becomes known that through **compassions** <note>original Hebrew: *be-rachamim*</note> from the midst of Y.H.V.H., the name will be proper to the Savior Messiah. His dignity and office, though they may consist of rigor and severity—according to the prophecy of King David expressed about the Messiah without any controversy: *He shall judge your people in justice,* he says, *and your poor in judgment*—nevertheless, because **judgment** <note>original Hebrew: *mishpat*</note>, according to all Kabbalists, also admits clemency alongside justice.

For so it is read in the fourth chapter of the *Gates of Light* <note>original: *Portæ lucis* / Hebrew: *Sha’are Orah*</note>: *For judgment is half rigor and half mercy.* <note>original Hebrew: כי המשפט חציו דין וחציו חסד:</note> By these means, the reconciliation of the first fall shall come to pass through a repeated union and a certain new betrothal of the people with God, as Hosea predicted: *I will betroth you to me in justice and judgment, in mercy and in compassions* <note>Hosea 2:19</note>, where the word *be-rachamim* is placed. Lest anyone think that the coming of the Messiah itself is destined out of some legal necessity and not rather from pure grace and the most liberal gift of God, the illustrious name of **clemency** is rightly bestowed upon this Savior. This name, out of all its letters—both vowels and the consonant—will be composed of nothing other than "mercy." And this we conjecture will be...

<meta>This page continues Reuchlin’s exploration of the mystical name of the Messiah. He argues that the addition of the Hebrew letter "Shin" into the four-letter name of God (the Tetragrammaton) transforms it into a name of mercy and salvation—the name of Jesus (Yehoshua/IHSVH).</meta>

# OF JOHANN REUCHLIN

...through the four holy letters, which are depicted as marks and symbols, and through the consonant *Shin* [ש] by which the ineffable name is named. For it is a principle in Kabbalah <term>Kabbalah<gloss>A tradition of Jewish mysticism that seeks to understand the relationship between the eternal God and the mortal universe.</gloss></term> that this mark *Shin* is explained as *Shaddai* <note>original Hebrew: שדי (*Shaddai*), meaning "Almighty"</note> through the mark of "The name of the Tetragrammaton called" <note>original Hebrew: שם יהוה נקרא (*Shem YHVH nikra*)</note>, that is, for [the sake of the name]. Now, there are no other letters by which mercy alone is nakedly designated except these five: Y.H.V.H. and the consonant *Shin* <note>I.H.S.V.H. or Jesus</note>. Regarding the four vowels, one reads thus in the book *The Gate of Justice* <note>original: *Porta Iustitiae*; likely the *Sha'are Tzedek* by Joseph Gikatilla</note>: "For behold, Y.H.V.H. goes out from his place and goes out from the attribute [of justice] <note>original Hebrew: מדת הדין (*middat ha-din*), the attribute of divine judgment</note> to the attribute of mercy" <note>original Hebrew: רחמים (*rachamim*), meaning mercies or compassion</note>. And this is the mystery which our Masters (may their memory be in peace) spoke of: "Behold the four-letter name," says Micah, "Y.H.V.H. comes out of his place; he shall come out through the property of mercies." Concerning the consonant *Shin*, all Kabbalists who are not ignorant in Kabbalistic Gematria <term>Gematria<gloss>A system of Hebrew numerology where letters represent numbers, allowing for the discovery of hidden connections between words of equal value.</gloss></term> will not deny that *Shin* contains within itself the ratio of the entire four-letter name according to arithmetic proportion, and that the same property of clemency and mercy is possessed by it.

Therefore, the salvation of all men is to be expected from the mercy of God alone, which Habakkuk expressed openly when addressing God: "When you are angry, you will remember mercy." Regarding this, David Kimhi <note>A famous 12th-century Hebrew grammarian and biblical commentator from Narbonne</note> (whom our people call Kimhi, as others pronounce it Rabbi, and Germany says *Ribi* through a simple conversion of *a* into *i*, just as a similar judgment exists among the Greeks and Latins: they say *Grammatiki* and *Logiki*, we say *Grammatica* and *Logica*; they say *mitir*, we say *mater* <note>Reuchlin is discussing the "Reuchlinian" pronunciation of Greek, which favored the "i" sound for various vowels, similar to modern Greek</note>; so they say *Simson* [Samson], and *Kimhi* for *Camhi*, and many others). That Jewish Spaniard, David, teaches that in that place, through the name *Mercies* [Rachamim] placed there according to Kabbalistic arithmetic proportion, it must be understood symbolically as Abraham. It is as if Habakkuk were saying: "O God, when you are touched by the anger of our sin, remember the seed of Abraham, to whom you promised that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed." And again: "O God, you spoke to him, saying: in your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed."

But so that Habakkuk himself might indicate what that seed would be, he added: "You went forth for the salvation of your people, for salvation with your Messiah." Here the same David Kimhi writes: "This is the Messiah, the son of David" <note>original Hebrew: זה משיח בן דויד (*zeh mashiach ben david*)</note>. I say, therefore, with the wise Kabbalists, that our true salvation hangs upon the Messiah, as many of us as can reach him. It follows that, by stripping ourselves of all created things as much as we can, we should strive to ascend through all the degrees and migrate into him, so that if we do not fully grasp him, we may at least certainly attain him, according to each person's strength. For he is our master himself, to whose coming the whole law refers us (even intellectually), not only the scripture of Moses, but also the prophets and whatever is contained in the Hagiographa <note>The "Holy Writings," referring to the third section of the Hebrew Bible (Ketuvim)</note>. For we take the whole context of the *Esrim Varba* <note>original Hebrew: כ״ד עשרים וארבע (*Esrim ve-Arba*), "The Twenty-Four" books of the Hebrew Bible</note>—which you call the Bible—and we include it all under the name of the Law [*Torah*]. As it says in Daniel chapter 9: "Walking in the Law of the Lord our God, which he set before us by the hand of his servants the prophets."

We have determined that this scripture alone is so stable and firm that we can safely found all our thoughts upon it, and place the sublime contemplations of speculative men there without confusion. This is both because it was promulgated by the voice of the highest God, and because it is able to operate with such powers of energy in the minds of the most contemplative men, that through it we are able to ascend from any mixtures to simple things, from simple to the simplest, from effects to causes, and finally from the lower world to the higher, and from the higher to the Messiah—who is the supreme object of our mind and conceivable in the highest degree—as if to the King of the Ages. Through him, we may finally pass plainly into the incomprehensible God. At that time, through these sacred letters, as if through Jacob’s ladder touching the sky with its top, while God himself leans upon it, our angels ascend and descend, carrying gifts from here to there and back again, carrying petitions from here and bringing help from there, as one of your own authors says. And truly, I feel nothing else could bind our soul more closely to God than weaving into it that same Holy Scripture, which leads us first into the admiration of divine things, then into the knowledge of them according to human capacity, and finally...

### ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH, BOOK I.

...that most ardent love of the known divinity, bearing within itself the most certain effect of hope. Through this, with the living creatures and wheels of Ezekiel <note>A reference to the vision of the Chariot in Ezekiel 1:15-21, a foundational text for Jewish mysticism</note>, we are raised from the earth, so that we may go with those that go, and stand with those that stand. This is the only field of true contemplation, of which every single word is a sacrament, and every speech, syllable, letter, and point is full of hidden meanings—not only according to our own authors, but also according to the testimony of Christians. This is the Kabbalah <term>Kabbalah<gloss>A traditional system of Jewish mysticism that interprets the hidden meanings of the Hebrew Bible and the divine structure of the universe.</gloss></term>, which does not allow us to live on the ground, but lifts our mind to the highest goal of understanding; yet it cannot rationally transcend the soul of the Messiah, except through a certain incomprehensible intuition, by way of a momentary rapture. By this, we believe it is not impossible for us Kabbalists to be caught up in spirit near the Third World, where the Messiah flows into all lower things. For in the most general numbering, there are three worlds. The first is material, the second is formal, and the third is formless. Or, if you prefer it this way: I say the first is the lowest, which is also sensible <note>perceptible by the senses</note>; the second is the supreme and mental, which is also intelligible; and the third is "above the heavens" <note>original Greek: ὑπερουράνιος (*hyperouranios*)</note>, that is, the supersupreme—or if one might say, the most supreme, incomparable, and divine.

However, I have chosen to consider this corporeal world as the first world relative to us, as it stands beneath the others; though in a perhaps reversed order, it ought to have been last in the category of causes, acting as a receptacle for all things above. This world is composed, first, of the heavens and celestial beings; second, of the elements and things made of elements; and third, of human nature and individual men, who are called in Hebrew "The Small World" <note>original Hebrew: עולם הקטן (*Olam ha-Katan*)</note>, in Greek "Microcosm" <note>original Greek: μικρόκοσμος (*mikrokosmos*)</note>, and in Latin "The Little World." This entire body, as your Aristotle suggests in his book *On the Universe*, is a globe made up of heaven and earth and the natures contained within them, indeed with seven celestial dwellings and seven terrestrial dwellings. Rabbi Menahem Recanati <note>A 13th-century Italian Kabbalist and commentator on the Torah</note> enumerates these in his commentary on chapter 25 of Leviticus. Those belonging to the heavens are: *Shamayim* (The Heavens), *Raqiya* (The Expanse), *Shachaqim* (The Clouds), *Zebul* (The Dwelling), *Maon* (The Habitation), *Machon* (The Foundation), and *Araboth* (The Plains). Second, those belonging to the earth: *Eretz* (Earth), *Arqa* (Earth), *Ge* (Valley), *Yabashah* (Dry Land), *Charebah* (Waste), *Tebel* (The World), and *Cheled* (The Duration). Joseph of Salamanca <note>Referring to Joseph Gikatilla, a major Spanish Kabbalist</note> also recited the seven dwellings of the lower regions by name in his *Garden of the Nut*, as you heard a little while ago.

Concerning the Microcosm <note>the human being as a miniature universe</note>, it is not hidden from any of us that seven things pertain to the human condition, whichever way you look: the body, the soul, and the composite of these which we call *Nefesh* <note>original Hebrew: נפש (*Nefesh*), often meaning the "vital" or "living" soul</note>, as in the words of the King of Sodom: "Give me the soul" <note>original Hebrew: תן לי הנפש (*Ten li ha-nefesh*); from Genesis 14:21, usually translated as "Give me the persons"</note>, that is, "Give me the man," composed of the four powers of the soul and the four qualities of the Greater World. Since this world is truly animated, it is illuminated by its own mind, which is called Metattron <term>Metattron<gloss>A supreme archangel in Kabbalistic tradition, often viewed as the celestial mediator or the "Prince of the World."</gloss></term>. 

The second world is the supreme world of the "separate intelligences" <note>spiritual beings or angels that exist without physical bodies</note>, which the Kabbalists call *Sekhalim Nifradim* <note>original Hebrew: שכלים נפרדים</note> and the Hebrew philosophers call *Deot Nifradot* <note>original Hebrew: דעות נפרדות</note>. Indeed, the soul of the Messiah itself encompasses, surrounds, and rules that world, which is full of species, forms, and liberated minds and angels. In the Kabbalistic view, this soul is the "Ideal Idea" of all lives, to which all individual, specific, and generic vitality is referred. From there, as if from a nursery, all life is drawn, and it is called by the Kabbalists the "Land of the Living." Therefore, they interpret the verse: "Let the earth bring forth the living soul according to its kind" <note>Genesis 1:24</note>, as referring to the soul of the Messiah. These words are read thus in the second chapter of *The Gates of Light*: "Just as in the human world, which is called the Microcosm, the mind rules over the soul of man, so Metattron rules the celestial world, the soul of the Messiah rules the angelic world, and Adonai <note>The Lord</note> rules the incomparable world." Furthermore, just as the light of the mind is the active intellect, so the light of Metattron is *Sadai* <note>original Hebrew: שדי (*Shaddai*), "The Almighty"</note>, the light of the Messiah’s soul is *Elhai* <note>original Hebrew: אל חי (*El Chai*), "The Living God"</note>, and the light of Adonai is *En-soph* <term>En-soph<gloss>The Infinite; the divine reality of God prior to any self-manifestation.</gloss></term>. 

And since it easily seems to the most expert observers of natural things that the lowest part of a higher nature communicates with the highest part of a lower nature—to such an extent that one might often doubt whether closely connected things are merely touching or truly continuous—it is hard to say of what nature that point is where continuous things are united. It is much like the place where a horse's foot and its hoof meet: is it horn or is it flesh? This is due to the immediate connection of their existence. Therefore, I believe it can now be said without error that man, the Microcosm, and that great sensible world, comm-

### JOHANNES REUCHLIN

...they communicate in the mind. Likewise, the corporeal world and the intellectual world communicate in **Metattron** <note>In Kabbalah, Metatron is a high-ranking angel who serves as the celestial mediator between the divine and the human realms.</note>, who is the active intellect of the first moved sphere, being one with the celestial care as an inferior, and with the angelic nature as a superior—but he is supreme with the incomparable third world, and super-supremely communicates in the **soul of the Messiah**, which is, as it were, a certain essence continuous on both sides with the angelic and the divine world. For there is no gap between the soul of the Messiah and God. Rather, **Elhai** <note>original Hebrew: *El Chai*, meaning "The Living God"</note> is the fountain of living waters, and the soul of the Messiah is the stream.

The Third World belongs to the Deity, which is established by that which the **Seraphim** <note>Celestial beings often described as burning with love for God, who surround the divine throne.</note> thrice proclaimed: *Holy, Holy, Holy*, with the four-lettered name <note>The Tetragrammaton, YHWH, the sacred name of God.</note>. He is called Great, Mighty, and Terrible—or rather, Revered. Great before creation, Mighty in creation, and Revered after creation. And this is <term>אחד<gloss>Echad, meaning "One"</gloss></term>: that is, more properly, the principle of unity, because the letter *Aleph* <note>The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, numerically representing 1.</note> designates the beginning of unity, as if the principle of the one, containing all things in its simplicity of unity.

Its emanation, according to the Kabbalists, is this: <term>רוח דבר קול<gloss>Ruach, Davar, Kol: Spirit, Word, Voice</gloss></term>. For thus Rabbi Azariel, in his commentary on holiness, wrote these words concerning what I have just recited: <term>יצא הדבר והקול בלא פתיחה / שפתים ובלא דבור לשון ולא נשמת אדם<gloss>The Word and the Voice went forth without the opening of lips, without the speech of the tongue, and without the breath of man.</gloss></term> That is, from the Spirit are produced the Word and the Voice, not through the opening of lips, nor through the speech of the tongue, nor by the breath of a human being. And these three are one spirit, because God is one, as we read in the *Book of Formation* <note>original: *Sefer Yetzirah*, an ancient text exploring the creation of the world through Hebrew letters and numbers.</note> concerning creation: <term>אלהים חיים ברוך הוא ו / שמו של חי העולמים קול ורוח ודבר וזוהיא רוח הקרש ש / שתים רוח מרוח<gloss>The living God, blessed be He and blessed be His name, who lives forever; Voice, Spirit, and Word; and this is the Holy Spirit from which come two: Spirit from Spirit.</gloss></term> Thus spoke our father Abraham. And according to what the Rabbi wrote in the book <term>העיון<gloss>Ha-Iyun: On Speculation</gloss></term>: these three, which are one, have a relationship among themselves as: <term>אחד מייחד יחיד<gloss>Echad, Meyached, Yachid: One, Uniting, and United</gloss></term>. Indeed, he says the same above: <term>רחם ראש ואמצע וסוף<gloss>They are the Beginning, the Middle, and the End</gloss></term>; and these are a single point, and it is the <term>אדון הכל<gloss>Adon Ha-Kol: Lord of the Universe</gloss></term>. Thus in the place cited. Therefore, that incomparably highest third world, established from these things which are one, as if from the highest essence, power, and operation, extends into eternity and beyond; it is neither concave nor convex, neither square nor having a surface.

For as Azariel writes in the book previously cited <margin>concerning Divinity</margin>: <term>הוא ראשון בלי תחלה והוא אחרון בלי תכלה<gloss>He is the first without a beginning, and He is the last without an end</gloss></term>. Truly, not even our thoughts can reach this, and it is named **En Soph** <note>original Hebrew: *Ein Sof*, meaning "without end" or "the Infinite."</note>: that is, infinity, which is a certain supreme thing, incomprehensible and ineffable in itself. In the most remote withdrawal of its divinity, and in the inaccessible abyss of the fountain of light, it holds and covers itself, so that one understands nothing as proceeding from it, as if the absolute Deity remained in leisure through an all-encompassing closure of itself within itself, naked and simple, without any cloak of circumstances, neither poured out from itself nor concentrated in its splendor.

By its goodness, it is indiscriminately being and non-being, and all things which to our reason seem contrary and contradictory to each other, it enfolds in the simplicity of its free and segregated unity. For thus we read in the book *On Faith and Atonement*: <term>מרתי לך בי / א יש מאין אינו חסר ובי היש הוא באין בענין אין והאין הוא ב / ביש בענין יש ללמוד שהאין הוא היש והיש הוא האין<gloss>I have told you that he who produces being from non-being lacks nothing; and that being is in non-being in the manner of non-being, and non-being is in being in the manner of being. Learn, then, that non-being is being, and being is non-being.</gloss></term> Thus it is written there. This, however, transcends all our intellect, which cannot combine contradictions at their source by way of reason; for we walk through those things which are made manifest to us by nature, which fall far short of this infinite power, which can connect contradictions separated by infinity simultaneously—as that most philosophical German arch-priest of Jupiter <note>This refers to Nicholas of Cusa (Cusanus), a 15th-century German philosopher and Cardinal. Reuchlin uses the classical term *archisflamen dialis* to honor his rank. Cusanus was famous for the "coincidence of opposites."</note> left for posterity fifty-two years ago. Therefore, with the burden of worldly cares removed, and the sophistries of old wives' disputes despised, [we move] happily...

# ON THE KABBALISTIC ART, BOOK I.

...the Kabbalist through **KABBALAH** <note>original: CABALAM</note>: that is, through the received and trusted path, he breaks out of the darkness and leaps into the brilliance by which he reaches the light. Thus, he migrates from light into radiance, and through that radiance—as far as human nature can grasp—he comprehends that true luminary under the mode of "being," rather than "non-being," unless this happens through the abstraction of all things that are not the absolutely first principle. 

And frequently by this path, through ineffable joy and alacrity of spirit, the mind of the Kabbalist—leaving behind humble and earthly things within the secret of deep silence—is transferred to super-celestial and invisible things that transcend all human sense. Then, even if still dwelling in mortal skin, he becomes a companion of angels, just like an inhabitant of a super-celestial home whose frequent conversation is known to be in the heavens. At times he walks with them, as companions of his ways, to higher places and visits the **soul of the Messiah**. At other times, he descends to the lower celestial and other powers of nature under angelic guidance (yet not without his own reason), and he strives to understand their dignities and operations and to venerate them with singular honor.

From this arises the Kabbalist's intimate friendship with angels, through which—sometimes by rightly knowing the divine names—he performs wondrous things that the common folk call miracles. For instance, **Rabbi Meir** <note>A famous Jewish sage of the 2nd century, known for his wisdom and miracles.</note>, through a divine name (even when spoken by a Gentile), preserved his wife’s sister from the corruption of a brothel. Though she was forced into prostitution, no lecher, no matter how strong, was able to violate or defile her once the word was spoken. These things are recounted in the beginning of the **Gates of Light** <note>original: Portæ lucis, referring to the "Sha'are Orah," a fundamental Kabbalistic text by Joseph Gikatilla.</note> and many other such stories are cited along with their authors. 

Yet, in the memory of the fathers, this operation of miracles was so easy for Kabbalists that they were often ignorantly called "cunning Magicians" by the envious and profane—as if it were not **Michael** <note>The archangel of mercy and protector of Israel.</note> who performed those works, but rather, and most especially, **Samael** <note>The archangel of death and accuser; in this context, the source of dark magic.</note>, namely through Egyptian incantations and certain secrets. Nevertheless, the rod of the Kabbalists always devours the rods of the tricksters <note>A reference to Exodus 7:12, where Aaron’s rod swallows those of Pharaoh’s magicians.</note>, and anything divine acts more healthfully than anything demonic. For the art of Kabbalah always tends toward the salvation of men, whereas the poison of magical vanity always verges toward perdition—the latter through names of darkness and evil spirits, the former through names of light and blessed angels. 

Regarding these things—unless the **Sabbath** <note>The Jewish day of rest, beginning at sundown on Friday.</note> day of rest, according to our custom, were already encroaching this very hour in the evening—I would certainly treat more fully whatever I feel about the fruit of this art which you so desire. But the night is almost falling, excellent men, and we must withdraw—not only lest I be beaten for neglecting the commandment, but also lest I fail my Kabbalistic profession if, on this Sabbath, I were to dig out the supreme and hidden secrets with laborious toil beyond **Sabbathai** <note>The Hebrew name for the planet Saturn, which governs the Sabbath day.</note> (who is **Saturn**), rather than staying in silence and enjoying leisure for as long as the following day passes. We shall explain the rest of the Kabbalistic art here the day after tomorrow, or at whatever place you choose. 

Then **Philolaus** <note>One of the characters in Reuchlin's dialogue, representing a Pythagorean philosopher.</note> spoke: "You have taken up the most difficult parts of speaking for our sake; you who, after we began this afternoon, have brought forth so many wondrous things in such number in a continuous speech, though you seemed moved by no trouble at all." 

And he [Simon] then said: "My love for you, which I hope is mutual, has taken away all trouble. If the holidays were not at hand, I would not think it in my interest to let men such as you, who have traveled here for the sake of learning, go away so hungry and unsatisfied by the doctrine of Kabbalah. But the Law must be obeyed." 

To this, **Marranus** <note>Another character in the dialogue, representing a seeker of Jewish and Christian synthesis.</note> said: "I truly confess, **Simon**, that I have never departed more learned from anyone’s presence. For me—or for both of us, if you prefer—enough has been done, and more than enough, considering what was entrusted to the patience of the time." 

Then **Philolaus** said: "**Marranus**, I wish you would plead only your own cause; for myself, though these things are very great and most closely approach Pythagorean doctrine, I have an even greedier desire to drink them in more copiously. I will not think myself satisfied unless the adjourned day brings an end to the stars. For which reason, after that Sabbath of yours, **Simon**, when..."

# OF JOHANNES REUCHLIN OF PFORZHEIM, DOCTOR OF LAWS,
## BOOK TWO.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A' at the beginning of the text, featuring ornate foliage patterns within a square border.</image-desc>

As both the younger Philolaus and Marranus were departing from there toward home, their conversation along the way was varied and quite sophisticated—as one might expect from men so well-learned in philosophy—concerning this very Hebrew man <note>Referring to Simon, the Jewish scholar introduced in Book One</note>. They praised his supreme learning and his singular kindness toward travelers, as well as the dignity of his character which shone in all things and above all else. Everything about the man pleased them, except for this one coming Sabbath, which they judged with a sense of frustration, as it would tear them away from the most delightful conversation of so great a teacher. They felt cast aside until the third day <note>Sunday</note>, which was no small waste of time, especially since they were unaware if they would be able to set out the following morning. Thus, as they walked, they ruminated on the "juice" of his doctrine, mutually reviewing brief summaries of what had been said. In their fervor for learning, there suddenly returned to their minds the speech of that admirable Jewish man, the sharpness of his disputation, his grave manner of instruction, and the way he delighted them without causing weariness—a style neither feigned nor colored, but one that, where it bloomed most with the flowers of rhetoric, there it produced the most fruit. When they had finally retired from their journey into their lodgings, and before they had even caught their breath, Marranus began to speak:

"Of all the wise men I have heard since my tender years, there has never been one more subtle in speech or more sublime in thought than this one man, Simon. Even now, as I hold him in my memory, he has—though his style is plain, simple, unaffected, not sought from afar, and smelling not at all of Demosthenes' lamp <note>A classical idiom meaning 'not over-rehearsed' or 'not artificially polished'</note>—excited my soul to contemplate arduous things in such a way that I have conceived of nothing more pleasing. Good gods! A Jewish man, born of Jews, nourished, educated, and taught among them—a nation held everywhere among the gentiles to be barbarous, superstitious, vile, abject, and alienated from the splendor of all good arts! Believe me, I would have watched his face and heard his spoken words through this entire night with eager desire, had this wretched Sabbath not intervened."

Then Philolaus said: "Not even all the Greeks, to whom the discipline of many arts, the sharpness of wit, and the abundance of speech are attributed by universal consent, could have ascended into the high summits of secret things, had it not been for my Pythagoras, the father of philosophy. Yet even he received the excellence of his doctrine not from the Greeks, but rather from those very Jews. Therefore, by the best and most rightful title, he himself ought to have been called a **Kabalist** <note>original: Cabalista</note>; however, just as travelers returning from afar bring back something worthy of admiration to their homeland which the common people might more easily believe, he was the first to change that name of 'Kabbalah'—unknown to his own people—into the Greek name 'Philosophy.' We infer this from the following evidence: he left his disciples no faculty for inquiring by any sort of reason, but rather willed that the first principle of his dogma be this: that to those seeking a cause, they should answer *autos epha* <note>original Greek: αυτὸς ἔφα</note>, which is to say: 'He himself said it.' This follows the custom of the Kabbalists, who cite the reasons for things to be known in no other way than by saying *hachamim omrim* <note>original Hebrew: חכמים אומרים</note>, which is to say: 'The wise have said it.' So it was with our man and his *autos epha*: 'He himself said it.' For he is that same Pythagoras who is held to have bestowed the name of 'Philosophy' in this manner: since the greatest authors of the Hebrews were called *Hachamim* <note>Wise Men</note> and the most ancient of the Greeks were called *Sophi* <note>Sages</note>, he attempted to clothe the old discipline in the ornament of a new name. Nor should the things Simon the Jew brought forth seem to you less worthy of praise simply because they were taken from an ignoble author of the Hebrew race as if from barbarian authors, or related by a barbarian man; for our same Pythagoras, the greatest of all, began his first studies of the sciences together with a certain barbarian named Zora <note>Likely referring to Zoroaster, whom Renaissance thinkers often associated with ancient mystical wisdom</note>, and indeed that was outside of Con—"

<summary>Philolaus and Marranus reflect on the wisdom of the Jewish scholar Simon, arguing that Pythagoras himself derived his philosophy from the Hebrew Kabbalah and merely changed the terminology for a Greek audience.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Philolaus and Marranus. They are discussing the historical origins of philosophy, arguing that Pythagoras and Plato did not invent their wisdom but gathered it from older, "barbarian" (non-Greek) sources, specifically the Jews, Egyptians, and Chaldeans. This serves to validate the Kabbalistic teachings of Simon by placing them at the very root of Western thought.</meta>

### ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH, BOOK II.

...knowledge, at which time they philosophized among the Egyptians, who were then called Prophets; and the Chaldeans of the Assyrians; and the Druids of the Gauls; and the Samaneans from the Bactrians; and not a few among the Celts; and among the Persians, the Magi; and among the Indians, the Gymnosophists <note>literally "naked philosophers," a term used by Greeks for Indian ascetics</note>; and that Anacharsis among the Scythians; and in Thrace, Zamolxis, who was previously a slave to Pythagoras himself. All of this Alexander, surnamed Polyhistor <note>a 1st-century BCE Greek scholar known for his vast compilations</note>, left in writing in his book <term>περὶ πυθαγορικῶν συμβόλων</term> <note>original: "peri pythagorikōn symbolōn"</note>, that is, *On Pythagorean Symbols*; and finally, among the Indians, the Jews whom they called Brahmans, as Aristotle the Peripatetic mentions. Indeed, if one may speak the truth, Pythagoras is certainly never found to have learned anything of either divine or human matters from the Greeks or from the Romans. Rather, as Antiphon published in his book <term>περὶ τοῦ βίου τῶν ἐν ἀρετῇ πρωτευσάντων</term> <note>original: "peri tou biou tōn en aretē prōteusantōn"</note>, that is, *On the Lives of Those Who Excelled in Virtue*: Pythagoras went for the sake of learning to the Egyptians and Arabs, and to the Chaldeans, after he had obtained Pherecydes as his master and teacher from Syria, which is and is named Judea. Hence, he himself was also commonly called a Syrian at that time, whom others called a Tyrian, and others a Tyrrhenian; <term>ὥςτε βάρβαρον ἀλλ᾿ οὐχ᾿ ἕλληνα γεγονέναι τοῦτον ὁμολογεῖν τὸν πρῶτον φιλοσόφων</term> <note>original: "hōste barbaron all’ ouch’ hellēna gegonenai touton homologein ton prōton philosophōn"</note>, that is, so that they might proclaim this first of all philosophers to have been a barbarian <note>In this context, "barbarian" simply means non-Greek</note> and not a Greek.

These things, Marranus, my most learned guest, I know for certain you have read written in the works of Eusebius Pamphili, in the volume—if I recall correctly—*On the Gospel Preparation*, book eleven, who also published this: <term>μόνον ὅτε παρὰ τῷ σοφῷ ἑλλήνων ἔσχον ἐνδεῖν, πενίᾳ τῆς σοφίας καὶ ἀπορίᾳ συνοικοῦντων</term> <note>original: "monon hote para tō sophō hellēnōn eschon endein, penia tēs sophias kai aporia synoikountōn"</note>, that is: "He had nothing from the wise Greeks, dwelling as they did in a penury of wisdom and a lack of resources." Concerning these people, as it is written in Plato's *Timaeus*, a certain barbarian Egyptian, a very old man, seemed to have said most truly to Solon:

> O Solon, Solon, you Greeks are always children; you have no ancient opinion, no discipline gray with age.

Nor should we fail to highly praise Pythagoras, a man of outstanding wisdom and nobility, for the fact that on a foreign and distant soil, he scraped together—with immense labor, cold, and sweat, through much study and meditation over not a few years—those things from barbarian men. I will not say he made them better, but he brought them back to his homeland, and even to Italy (which was then called Great Greece <note>Magna Graecia, the Greek-settled areas of Southern Italy</note>), as if on his own shoulders, making them more splendid. This he did to the incredible admiration of all regarding himself and his followers, so much so that anyone who excelled in wisdom and learning was believed to have been a student of Pythagoras. From him, Italic philosophy primarily took its name. Numenius the Pythagorean supports this praise in his first volume *On the Good*, when he says that whatever the Brahmans, Magi, Egyptians, and Jews discovered, Plato and Pythagoras themselves set forth in Greek. 

We strongly suspect that what the most learned men and those skilled in various languages assert is true: that the things of the Jews, whether received by tradition or discovered, are set forth through the foreign thefts of the Greeks on one hand and the Latins on the other. Nothing is ours in philosophy that was not previously the Jews', however much in this century their deserved glory is taken from them, and all their works are now despised because the present age desires a more illustrious and polished explanation of all studies. Then you speak the truth most excellently, Philolaus, says Marranus, so that I may agree all the more with Euripides' *Hecuba*:

> <term>λόγος γὰρ ἔκ τ᾽ ἀδοξούντων ἰὼν κ᾽ ἀκλῶν δοκούντων αὐτὸς ὁ ταὐτὸς οὐ δύναι</term> <note>original: "logos gar ek t’ adoxountōn iōn k’ aklōn dokountōn autos ho tautos ou dynai"</note>.

That is: "For a word proceeding from the inglorious and from the glorious, though it be the same, does not have the same power." For if some Aristotle or some Theophrastus had brought forth those things which Simon taught us today, nothing in the opinion of all would be more worthy of hearing, nothing more memorable; he would have only added a more even style of speaking and some veneer of eloquence. Now, because it is a Jew who, after his own fashion, has approached and treated the whole matter somewhat more concisely, there is no doubt that these things will be filthy in the ears of those sophists of our age—who seem to themselves quite subtle—if any should hear or are about to hear them. Or rather, to all those who now philosophize either perversely or foolishly, these things may appear tangled, clamorous, gaping, meager, rough, and of a rustic harshness...

# JOHANN REUCHLIN

...and sounding of a foreign strangeness, even if, as is their custom, they have not been examined as thoroughly as they ought to be—just as we search for gold in the mud. But after we have now returned from this man to our inn by the straight path, with no one to guide us, and since dinner is perhaps not yet ready, I suggest that each of us recite amongst ourselves what we have heard, and especially fix those things in our memory so they do not slip away while they are fresh. And Philolaus, how prudently you spoke, Marranus: you have already thought ahead to those things so that we might approach the man better prepared the day after tomorrow, following this Sabbath <note>The Jewish day of rest, beginning Friday evening</note>—the "seventh day sacred to the man," as Ovid says <note>A reference to the Roman poet Ovid's mention of the Jewish Sabbath in his "Art of Love"</note>. Meanwhile, you take one chair, I will take the other, and sitting down together let us speak quickly about all that was given, until the things appropriate for dinner are prepared. However, lest we struggle in vain while we are alone—for that would be nothing other than wasting time—whatever comes to your mind, whether from remembering the past or the present, or for the sake of exploring a topic in whatever way it happens, speak it out.

Thus, then, Marranus began his discourse. "And although," he said, "this whole business we have been engaged in during the afternoon seems to me, when weighing each point exactly, to be deeper than we, who are cast down on the earth, can look up to, nevertheless, those things which appear difficult and impossible to men at first sight often become clear and easy through thin and tireless exercise and hard labor, according to that saying of Maro <note>The poet Virgil</note>: *Labor conquers all* <note>original: "Labor omnia vincit"</note>. Therefore, I will gladly bring into the open what I remember hearing from that man, and I will add to them what I myself think.

Indeed, our teacher, when he was about to treat the Kabbalah for us at our request, showed by that very name what ought to be understood. For 'Kabbalah' signifies 'reception' <note>From the Hebrew root QBL, meaning to receive</note>; at the same time, he brought up this point: that it is always implanted in our minds as we strive toward our natural best condition. For this reason, a desire for it is naturally generated within us, as the highest divine matters are more sublime and worthy than can be grasped or discerned by human reason. However, it is a trivial dogma for fit Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy</note>; for if I may cite the authorities with whom I have a usual familiarity, Al-Farabi <note>A major medieval Islamic philosopher (c. 872–950) who integrated Aristotelian and Platonic thought</note>, in the book he wrote *On the Sciences*, uses this sentiment: that divine and pious matters are of a higher order, since they are received by divine inspiration. In them are divine secrets, from the comprehension of which human reasons are weakened; nor do they attain them. 

This is what that Arab says, which our Simon also proved, who calls those orders 'regions,' and in the third part of our soul he established incorporeal things and substances that are free and immune from all weight of matter. These are not those fantastic and logical universals that Antisthenes <note>A Greek philosopher and pupil of Socrates who argued against the reality of universal concepts</note> thought of, but rather, I say, the real forms, species, ideas, and essences themselves, which are most certain. It is around these that the Kabbalists occupy themselves, as I hear, in contemplations of things that are nearly inexpressible. They trace each of these things, which we think we perceive or know, back to their origins, and finally reduce the universe into the One, which is the Good itself and the Principle, as if to the most healthy end of our mind. 

For this reason, Aristotle, in the 14th book of those things he wrote *After the Physics* <note>The *Metaphysics*</note>, said that which is <term>αὐτάρκης</term> <note>original: "autarkēs"; meaning self-sufficient</note>—that is, self-sufficient—is also 'salvation.' And Simon designated this in Hebrew as <term>תוּשִׁיָּה</term> <note>original: "Tushiyah"; meaning sound wisdom, resourcefulness, or success</note>. Just as the royal Psalmist says: 'Salvation belongs to the Lord.' And upon this human salvation, Simon laid the foundations of all Kabbalists, which must neither be investigated by reason, nor can they be investigated through reason, since the senses do not provide the starting point nor does the intellect provide the discipline. For they are the highest things, and for their sake no adequate cause can be found. From the knowledge of these things, even the most eloquent of the Peripatetic sect <note>The Aristotelians</note> took away the power of science; for he wrote thus in his *Supernaturals* <note>Referring again to the *Metaphysics*</note>:

> Up to a certain point we are able to contemplate through causes, taking our principles from the senses; but when we pass over to those very highest and first things, we are no longer able to do so, whether because of our own inadequacy...

<note>original Greek: "μὲν ἐν τῷ δυνάμεθα δι’ αἰτίω θεωρᾶιν, ἀρχὰς ἀπὸ τῶν αἰσθήσεων λαμβάν... επ’ αὐτὰ τὰ ἄκρα ϗ πρῶτα μεταβαίνωμεν, οὐκ ἔτι δυνάμεθα. εἴτε διὰ τὸ μη... ὥστε διὰ τὴν ἡμετέραν ἀδωγίαν"</note>

That is: Up to a point indeed we are able to speculate [about the cause], taking principles from the senses, but when either to those extremes...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Marranus and Philolaus. Marranus is arguing that human logic and the "syllogism" (formal deductive reasoning) are insufficient—and even dangerous—when applied to the study of the divine and the Kabbalah, which must be approached through faith and the "Divine Mind" rather than human "Reason."</meta>

### ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH, BOOK II.

...once we have crossed over, we can go no further, whether because we lack a cause or because of our own weakness. For concerning the supernal and divine things, prior to which nothing exists, from where, I ask you, could any "middle term" <note>In logic, a "middle term" is the link that connects two ideas in a proof.</note> for a demonstration be taken? For this reason, Plato says in the *Timaeus* that to explain such things is beyond our strength, and he commands us to believe those who have spoken before, even though they speak without the necessity of a demonstration. These very words of Plato, the commands of a truly wise man, I value so highly that I consider them to be held as an oracle. And if the Kabbalah has any fixed and established foundations, these are they. 

Therefore, I believe the logical **syllogism** <note>A form of reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two premises (e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal).</note> to be the sharpest enemy and waylayer of divine knowledge—which consists of pure and naked faith. Through the audacity and habit of the "Theosophists" <note>In this context, Reuchlin refers to those who attempt to apply scholastic philosophy to God, rather than the later 19th-century movement.</note>, the syllogism subjects God, the angels, the blessed and most simple minds beyond the powers of the mundane age, the entire host of eternity, and whatever accounts exist of supernatural things, to human mortality; it demands they be found, proven, and directed by the discourse of reason. It is as if one attempted to shut those illustrious substances into the **Tullianum** <note>The deepest and most notorious dungeon of the ancient Roman prison.</note>. This is surely like wanting to bind Jupiter, or tie him with a wicker branch or a sailor's rope.

Even Thetis, according to Homer, would not permit this, nor would the hundred-handed Briareus Aegaeon <note>In Greek mythology, Briareus was a giant who protected Zeus (Jupiter) from being bound by other gods.</note>. For this reason, I judge those contentious theologians and aggressive sophists—these conquerors of the celestial and super-celestial realms—to be no less than the twin **Aloadae** <note>Giant brothers who, in Virgil's *Aeneid*, attempted to storm heaven by piling mountains on top of each other.</note> of massive bodies, as Virgil says, who attempted to tear down the great sky with their hands. They are no different than the people of Shinar and the Babylonians of old, the sons of Adam: that is, those born of a human weakness they did not recognize in themselves, who built a very high tower <term>Babel</term> <note>original: "בבל"</note>: that is, the authors of confusion. From this comes Babel, which you call Babylon, where no one understood the language of the other. For through these talkative syllogists, all piety toward the university of divine things is lost in matters of belief, and brotherly hatred is stirred up by a passion for winning—like hunting dogs ready for sedition, a supreme poison of contemplation that ought to be expelled from the whole world. Let these devices of syllogisms triumph, if it be right, in nature and in human inventions and fictions.

But in the sacred oracles, let them hope for no place. For Parmenides, in Plato's writings, delivered this dogma to Socrates concerning separate substances, saying: <note>original Greek: "ἀλλ' ὁμοίως ἡμᾶς ἐκείνων οὐκ ἄρχομεν τῇ περὶ ἡμῶν ἀρχῇ, οὐδὲ γιγνώσκομεν τὰ θεῖα οὐδὲν, τῇ ἡμετέρᾳ ἐπιστήμῃ"</note> **"But similarly, we do not rule over them with our authority, nor do we know anything of the divine by our own science."** Even the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> agree with this speech, and Aristotle himself—both the craftsman and the "organ" (as they say) of knowing—affirms in the first volume of the *Posterior Analytics* that the knowledge of "immediates" <note>First principles that cannot be proven by something else because they are the starting point of all proof.</note> is indemonstrable.

A little later he says, "And we say that there is not only science, but also some principle of science, by which we know the terms." Themistius <note>A 4th-century commentator on Aristotle.</note> calls our "mind" the principle of science in that passage: and the "terms" are the subject and predicate from which the greatest axioms are composed.

But Philoponus (who is commonly called John the Grammarian) explained these things in a much more sublime and truer way, writing thus: <note>original Greek: "ὁ μὲν φιλόσοφος τὴν ἐξήγησιν τῶν προκειμένων ῥητῶν οὕτως ἀπέδωκεν. ἀρχὴν μὲν ἐπιστήμης, τὸν νοῦν εἴληφας, ὃ οὐχ ἡμέτερον, ἀλλὰ τὸν θεῖον καὶ ὑπὲρ ἡμᾶς. ὅρους δὲ τὰ νοητὰ καὶ θεῖα εἴδη. ὅρους δὲ αὐτὰ καλεῖσθαι οἷά τὰ πέρατα τῶν πάντων"</note> **"The philosopher indeed gave the explanation of the presented words thus: Taking the 'principle of science' to be Mind—not ours, but the divine Mind above us—and the 'terms' as the intellectual and divine forms themselves. These are called terms because they are the ends of all things."** Therefore, the knowledge of supernatural things that are believed depends on the **Mind** <note>The higher intuitive faculty (*mens*), rather than the logical reasoning faculty (*ratio*).</note>, not on reason, which can err through its calculations. For Aristotle writes the same: <note>original Greek: "ἐπιδέχεται τὸ ψεῦδος οἷον δόξα, & λογισμός"</note> **"It admits of falsehood, just as opinion does, so too does reasoning"**—which is why it is called a syllogism.

Finally, he concludes the *Posterior Analytics* thus: "All science," he says, "is with **reason**," <note>original: "λόγῳ" (logō)</note>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between the characters Philolaus and Marranus. In the preceding text, Marranus argued that human logic and the "syllogism" (formal deductive reasoning) are insufficient—and even dangerous—when applied to the study of the divine. He suggested that the Kabbalah must be approached through faith and the "Divine Mind" rather than human "Reason."</meta>

# JOHANNES REUCHLIN

is, it is with reason. Science, indeed, will certainly not pertain to First Principles. Since nothing happens to be truer than science except the Mind, it is the Mind that will certainly pertain to principles. Moreover, First Principles are called "the first things," and Hesiod and the ancient theologians made all the gods to be principles; therefore, this cognition is properly named "divine." And as that same Stagirite <note>A common nickname for Aristotle, who was born in Stagira.</note> wrote in his *Post-naturals* <note>The *Metaphysics*, so named because these books followed Aristotle's works on nature/physics.</note>, the possession of it is <note>original Greek: "δικαίως αν̓ οὐκ ἀνθρωπίνη"</note> "justly not human." This is because either God alone of all beings possesses it most greatly, or it would be unworthy for a man to seek no other science. For God alone holds this honor, according to Simonides.

But since nothing conducts us more toward happiness than the cognition of the highest divine things, by what path (I ask you, Philolaus) must a man proceed toward them, if not by science? Or by what modes is such highness to be comprehended? 

Then Philolaus said: By Castor! <note>An ancient Roman oath.</note> You yourself have shown a plain and open path. For although there are five "architects of cognition," as Ammonius <note>Ammonius Hermiae, a Greek philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note> testifies following Aristotle, he mentions only four of them in the first book *On the Soul*. These are <note>original Greek: "νοῦς, διάνοια, φαντασία, αἴσθησις"</note> **Mind, Reasoned Discourse, Imagination, and Sensation**. <note>Philolaus later adds "Opinion" to the list of five.</note> For indeed, even the senses do not create syllogisms; one is far above and the other far below reason. But neither does imagination, since it is a station for the senses and a reservoir of appearances migrating from there. Since the senses do not reason at all, it must not be thought that the appearances of the senses are able to reason. There will remain, therefore, **Opinion** and **Reasoned Discourse**. But Opinion is the conclusion of the discourse itself, for which reason it alone does not syllogize. Thus, the faculty of syllogizing is left to Reasoned Discourse alone, which is named <note>original Greek: "διάνοια"</note> **Dianoia**. This much is the sentiment of Ammonius in the commentaries he published on Aristotle's *Prior Analytics*. 

And since I have touched briefly in this list upon types of comprehension and the things comprehended, so that my speech does not wander too far, I am of the opinion that divine things are above the syllogism. They cannot be understood by human reason, as they do not derive their origin of being known from the senses, but depend upon pure **Faith**, received only because of the love of the one revealing them and believed for the sake of human happiness. There are, however, very many things which are so often mixed into divine speculation that—as the freedmen and tenants of a single family are sometimes accustomed to use a common name—they frequently allow themselves (I confess) to be treated by the Theological faculty. This is because they have obtained some order toward God, either through themselves or through reduction, or perhaps by some other reason such as creation, conservation, perfection, justification, happiness, salvation, and the like. Regarding those things, I am not thinking of them at present, since I know they become naturally known to us; a demonstration of "that they are" is brought forth in the *Post-naturals*, or a demonstration of "why they are" in the *Theological* works. 

I certainly permit **Reason** to handle those things which once arose from the senses and were deduced by human discourse. But for those things whose truth depends solely upon the authority of the one revealing, I do not think there is "science," nor would I wish the syllogism to dominate them. Instead, there is only that which will be more excellent than all: **Faith**. He who possesses it is called by Aristotle in the *Prior Analytics* <note>original Greek: "βέλτιον διακειμένος ἢ εἰ ἐτύγχανεν εἰδώς"</note> "better disposed than if he happened to know." Philoponus <note>John Philoponus, an Alexandrian philologist and commentator.</note> explained this to mean "knowing better than through a demonstration." 

To this Marranus said: I agree with you, Philolaus, and I also wish that those things which are of pure faith and are purely believable were not subjected to the "snares of logic," which are clearly more of a detriment than a benefit to those who contemplate. Our own writers, both Greek and Latin, assert the same. That famous Jerome of Dalmatia <note>St. Jerome, the translator of the Vulgate Bible.</note>, writing on Psalm 104, compares the art of the syllogism applied to Theology to the plagues of Egypt, saying: "The *cyniphes* <note>Referring to the gnats or lice from the third plague of Egypt (Exodus 8).</note> are understood as the sting of the dialectical art; although it seems to have in itself a small sting of deception, it nevertheless wounds human minds most severely." For this reason, that most learned man removed and rejected this trickery—which he calls the "vanity of the senses" and "obscurity of the mind"—entirely from **Hebrew studies**. He did this often, but most clearly when writing to Damasus regarding the questions proposed to him, where in the second part he uses these words: "It does not befit one disputing about Hebrew matters to [mention] Aristot-"

He uses Aristotelian and Neoplatonic classifications of the mind to show that "Reasoned Discourse" is limited, while Marranus quotes St. Jerome to warn that applying dialectics to Hebrew studies is as harmful as an Egyptian plague.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous discussion, where Marranus and Philolaus explore the limits of human reason. The previous page ended with a discussion on Aristotle's view of "First Principles" and the "Divine Mind" as being beyond mere human science.</meta>

### ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH, BOOK II.

...Aristotle, to seek out arguments. And in his commentary on Psalm 143, he writes concerning the divine seekers <note>The Latin *theosophistis* here refers to those who engage in the study of divine wisdom, often through philosophical or theological debate.</note> in this way: When they begin to dispute with you, their words are so brief and so enclosed in technical speech that it is difficult for you to escape. For when they have bound you with their syllogisms <note>A syllogism is a form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises (e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore, Socrates is mortal).</note> and shut you in—weaving and building a syllogism around you like a stone wall—it cannot fall, and you cannot pass through. You are held captive; there is no breach in the wall and no way out. And when they hold you there, as if enclosed in a circle, then you will not be on the narrow path that leads to life, but on the broad path that leads to death.

Since even the simplicity of faith is better than the persuasive reasoning of much labor <note>original Greek: "ἐπὲι καὶ ἡ ἁπλότης τῆς πίστεως, βελτίων ἐστὶ τῆς ἐκ πολυεργασίας πιθανολογίας"</note>; that is, because the faith of simplicity is better than the persuasive reasoning of curiosity. As Athanasius <note>A prominent 4th-century Bishop and theologian known for his defense of Christian orthodoxy.</note> said in his third book against the Arians, he confirms this same point in his work against the Greeks, which begins: "The knowledge of divine worship and the truth of all things does not so much require instruction from men as it possesses its own self-evidence" <note>original Greek: "ἡ μ’ πρὸς τὴν θεοσέβειαν καὶ τὴν τῶν ὅλων ἀλήθειας γνῶσις, ὁ τοσᾶτον θ’ πρὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων διδασκαλίας δᾶται, ὅσον ἀφ’ ἑαυτῆς ἔχει τὸ γνώριμον"</note>. 

So says Athanasius. Let each person decide for himself that nothing is truer than this. For what zeal for speaking, or what effort at persuasion, will be needed for that which I am prepared to believe of my own accord? I have already gladly received it solely through my love for the one revealing it and through singular veneration, not at all forced or led by the power of reason—especially the kind of reason that the dim dullness of the mind, sunk and bound in this body, can devise.

Justin <note>Justin Martyr (c. 100–165 AD), an early Christian philosopher who tried to reconcile Greek philosophy with Christian faith.</note>, that Christian philosopher, treats these matters much more fully in his book on the right confession, citing that ancient saying: "For nothing of divine things is clear to humans" <note>original Greek: "ὀδὲν γὰρ ἀνθρώποισι τῶν θείων σαφές"</note>, which also flowed from the mouth of Socrates. There is a letter from Xenophon, the follower of Socrates, to Aeschines, in which he says it is clear to everyone that divine matters cannot be grasped by human cognition. Therefore, it is enough to piously worship the Gods from the heart; what they are like is neither possible for us to find, nor is it right to seek. For it is not beneficial for servants, nor would I call it praiseworthy, if they should wish to scrutinize the plans of their masters beyond what pertains to their own service.

And as the same author wrote in the *Memorabilia* concerning Socrates and the followers of other philosophers: "He wondered, indeed, if it was not manifest to them that it is not possible for humans to find these things" <note>original Greek: "ἐθαύμαζε δ’ ἐι μὴ φανερὸν ἀὐτοῖς ἐστιν, ὅτι ταῦτα οὐ δυνατόν ἐστιν ἀνθρώποις εὑρεῖν"</note>. Such has always been the opinion of every age and nearly all religions: that the human intellect cannot grasp things that were not previously in human sensation. And what the intellect does not grasp, reason does not discuss; and what reason does not discuss, the discourse of reasoning—which they call <term>Dianoia</term> <note>Dianoia refers to discursive or "step-by-step" logical reasoning, such as mathematics or formal logic, which Reuchlin argues is distinct from direct spiritual intuition.</note>—will not judge. This fits perfectly with divinely revealed truth, even if we form for ourselves some imaginary concepts of the mind about them, so that whatever we have received religiously and piously, we do not subject it to the violence of argumentation or to any image placed before us.

Therefore, following that Gregory of Nazianzus—who stands out among all our people in every kind of theological skill, in all beauty and gravity of words and thoughts—he agrees with this doctrine in a similar way, affirming in the second book of *Theology*: "The divine is not graspable by human discursive thought, nor can it be imagined in its entirety" <note>original Greek: "τὸ, μὴ ληπτὸν εἶναι ἀνθρωπίνῃ διανοίᾳ τὸ θεῖον, μὴ δὲ ὅλον ὅσον δει φαντάζεσθαι"</note>.

Lest you suspect me, Marranus, of being entirely ignorant or negligent of the Christians, Philolaus replied: I remember that Athenagoras, the philosopher of Athens, acting as an envoy to the Emperors Marcus Aurelius Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus on behalf of the Christians, said this: "But since the very dogmas we hold are not human, but are divinely spoken and taught by God, we are able to persuade you all not to hold us as if we were atheists" <note>original Greek: "ἐπεὶ δ’ δι ἀὐτῶν τῶν δογμάτων, οἷς προσέχωμεν, ὀυκ ἀνθρώπικοι ὀι ἐσὶν, ἀλλὰ θεσφάτοις καὶ θεοδιδάκτοις, πᾶσαι ὑμᾶς, μὴ ὡς περὶ ἀθέων ἔχειν δυνάμεθα"</note>. Here he suggests that persuasion works one way regarding profane things, and another way regarding divine things. Although sometimes...

# OF JOHANNES REUCHLIN

...is, it is with reason. Of the first principles, there will certainly not be a science. Since nothing happens to be more true than science except for the mind, the mind must certainly belong to the first principles. Truly, the first things are called "principles," and Hesiod and all the ancient theologians made the Gods to be the principles; therefore, this knowledge is properly named "divine." And as that same Stagirite <note>A common nickname for Aristotle, who was born in the city of Stagira.</note> wrote in the first book of the *Metaphysics* <note>original: "postnaturalium," referring to the works following the "Physics."</note>, its position is **justly not human** <note>original Greek: "Δικαίως ἂν ὐκ ἀνθρωπίνη"</note>; that is, it is justly not human because perhaps God alone of all beings possesses it most fully, and man is unworthy to seek out such a science. For God alone holds this honor, according to Simonides.

But since nothing leads us more toward happiness than the knowledge of the highest divine things, by what way (I ask you, Philolaus) must a man proceed toward them, if not by science? Or by what modes is such height to be grasped?

Then Philolaus said: By Castor, you yourself have shown a plain and open path. For since there are five "makers" of cognition, according to the witness of Ammonius <note>Ammonius Hermiae, a 5th-century philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note> following Aristotle, he mentions only four of them in the first book *On the Soul*. They are **Mind, Discourse, Opinion, Imagination, and Sensation** <note>original Greek: "νόος, διάνοια, δόξα, φαντασία, αἴσθησις"</note>. Mind and sensation do not use syllogisms <note>Logical arguments consisting of two premises and a conclusion.</note>; the one is far above reason, the other is far below it. Nor does imagination use them, since it is a resting point of sensation and a reservation for the appearances migrating from there. Since the senses do not reason at all, one must think that the appearances of the senses can be reasoned upon. Therefore, opinion and discourse remain. But opinion is the conclusion of discourse itself, and for that reason, it does not itself use syllogisms. Therefore, the faculty of syllogizing is left to discourse alone, which is named *Dianoia* <note>A Greek term for "discursive reasoning" or the step-by-step process of thinking.</note>. Thus far is the opinion of Ammonius in the commentaries he published on Aristotle’s *Prior Analytics* <note>original: "prima resolutiva".</note>. 

And since I have briefly touched upon the types of understanding and the things understood, lest my speech wander too far, I am of the opinion that divine things are above the syllogism, and cannot be understood by human reason. They do not draw their origin of knowing from the senses, but depend on pure faith, received only on the authority of the one revealing them and believed for the happiness of men. There are, however, many things which often mingle themselves with divine speculation in such a way that they, like freedmen and tenants of a single family, sometimes usurp a common name for you. I confess that they allow themselves to be treated by the faculty of Theology because they have obtained some order toward God, either by themselves or by reduction, or perhaps by some reason such as creation, preservation, perfection, justification, happiness, salvation, and the like. 

I do not think of those things at present, for I know they become known to us naturally; their demonstration of *that* they are is opened in the *Metaphysics*, or *why* they are in the *Theological* works. I permit reason to those things which once arose from the senses and were given over to human discourse; but of those things whose truth depends solely on the authority of the revealer, I do not think there is a "science," nor would I wish the syllogism to dominate them. Instead, there is only that which will be more excellent than all: faith. He who possesses this is called by Aristotle in the *Prior Analytics* **disposed better than if he happened to know** <note>original Greek: "βέλτιον διακείμενος ἢ εἰ ἐτύγχανεν εἰδώς"</note>; that is, better disposed than if he were a man of science. Philoponus <note>John Philoponus, a 6th-century Christian philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note> explained this as meaning "to know better than through demonstration."

To this Marranus said: I agree with you, Philolaus, and I also agree that those very things which are purely of faith and purely believable are often subjected to logical snares, which are clearly more of a loss than a gain to those contemplating them. Our writers, both Greek and Latin, assert the same. That famous Jerome the Dalmatian <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into the Latin Vulgate.</note>, writing on Psalm 104, compares the art of the syllogism applied to Theology to the plagues of Egypt, and says: "The sting of the dialectic art is understood as the gnats <note>original: "Cyniphes," referring to the biting flies or lice from the third plague of Egypt in the Book of Exodus.</note>, which, though it seems to have a small sting of seduction in reality, nevertheless wounds human minds most severely." Wherefore, that most learned man removed and rejected this trickery—which he calls both the vanity of the senses and the obscurity of the mind—entirely from Hebrew studies. He did this often elsewhere, but most clearly to Damasus <note>Pope Damasus I, who was Jerome's patron.</note> concerning the questions proposed to him in the second [letter], where he uses these words: "When disputing about Hebrew matters, it does not befit Ari...

...to search for Aristotelian arguments. And regarding Psalm 143, he <note>Likely referring to a commentator or "theosophist" writing on the Psalms.</note> writes this about the <term>theosophists</term> <note>Those who seek knowledge of God through direct philosophical or mystical insight.</note>: "When they begin to dispute with you, their words are so brief and concluded with such artificial speech that it is difficult for you to escape. For once they have bound you with their syllogisms and shut you in—weaving and building a sort of stone wall of syllogisms around you—it cannot collapse, and you cannot pass through. You are held trapped; there is no breach in the wall, and no way across. And when they hold you there, as if enclosed in a circle, then you will not be on the narrow way that leads to life, but on the broad way that leads to death." For **simple faith is better than the laborious persuasion of words** <note>original Greek: ἐπεὶ καὶ ἡ ἀπλοϊκὴ πίσις, βελτίων ἐστὶ τῆς πολυεργασίας πιθανολογίας</note>; that is, since the faith of simplicity is better than the persuasive reasoning of curiosity. As **Athanasius** <note>St. Athanasius of Alexandria, a 4th-century bishop and theologian.</note> said in his third book *Against the Arians*, he confirms this same point in his work *Against the Greeks*, which begins thus: **The knowledge of divine worship and of the truth of the universe does not so much require instruction from men as it possesses its own clarity within itself** <note>original Greek: ἡ μὲν περὶ τῆς θεοσεβείας καὶ τῆς τῶν ὅλων ἀληθείας γνῶσις, οὐ τοσοῦτον τῆς παρὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων διδασκαλίας δεῖται, ὅσον ἀφ᾿ ἑαυτῆς ἔχει τὸ γινώσιμον</note>.

Athanasius concludes: Let everyone establish for themselves that nothing is truer than this. For what zeal of speaking, or what effort of persuasion, will be needed for that which I am prepared to believe of my own accord? I have already gladly received it through my love for the Revealer alone and through singular veneration, not compelled or led by even the slightest force of reason—at least not any reason that the dullness of a mind sunk and bound in this dark body could devise.

**Justin**, that Christian philosopher <note>Justin Martyr, a 2nd-century Christian apologist.</note>, treats these matters much more fully in his book *On the Right Confession*, citing an ancient iambic verse: **For nothing of divine things is clear to humans** <note>original Greek: οὐδὲν γὰρ ἀνθρώποισι τῶν θείων σαφές</note>, which also flowed from the mouth of **Socrates**. An epistle of Xenophon (the follower of Socrates) to Aeschines is cited, where he says: "It is obvious to everyone that divine things cannot be grasped by human cognition; therefore, it is enough to piously worship the Gods themselves from the soul. What they are, however, is neither possible for us to find, nor is it right to seek. For it does not benefit servants, nor would I call it praiseworthy, if they wished to scrutinize the counsels of their masters beyond what pertains to their own service." 

And as the same author wrote in the *Memorabilia* concerning Socrates and the followers of other philosophers: **He wondered, indeed, if it were not manifest to them that it is not possible for humans to find these things** <note>original Greek: ἐθαύμαζε δ᾿ εἰ μὴ φανερὸν αὐτοῖς ἐστὶν, ὅτι ταῦτα οὐ δυνατὸν ἐστὶν ἀνθρώποις εὑρεῖν</note>. Such has always been the opinion of all ages and almost all religions: that those things which were not previously in human sensation cannot be grasped by the human intellect. And what the intellect does not grasp, reason does not discuss; and what reason does not discuss, the discourse of reasoning—which they call <term>dianoia</term> <note>A Greek term for discursive or logical thought, moving from one premise to a conclusion.</note>—will not judge. This especially accords with divinely revealed truth, even if we form imaginary concepts of some of those things in our minds. Whatever we have received religiously and piously, we should not subject to the violence of argumentation or any proposed <term>phantasm</term> <note>A mental image or representation.</note>.

Thus, **Gregory of Nazianzus** <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople and one of the "Cappadocian Fathers."</note>—who stands out among all our people in every branch of theology for his beauty of words and thoughts as well as his gravity—imitated his ancestors and agreed with this doctrine in his second book of *Theology*, affirming: **That the divine is not graspable by human discourse, nor can the whole of what it is be imagined** <note>original Greek: τὸ, μὴ ληπτὸν εἶναι ἀνθρωπίνῃ διανοίᾳ τὸ θεῖον, μὴ δὲ ὅλῳ ὅσον ἐστὶ φαντάζεσθαι</note>. 

"Lest you suspect me, Marranus, to be entirely ignorant or negligent of our Christians," Philolaus replied, "I remember that **Athenagoras** <note>A 2nd-century Christian apologist and philosopher from Athens.</note>, the Athenian philosopher, acting as an envoy to the Emperors **Marcus Aurelius Antoninus** and **Lucius Aurelius Commodus** on behalf of the Christians, said this: **Since by the very doctrines we follow, we are led not by human things but by those spoken by God and taught by God, we can persuade you all not to hold us as if we were godless** <note>original Greek: ἐπεὶ δὲ δι᾿ αὐτῶν τῶν δογμάτων, οἷς προσέχομεν, οὐκ ἀνθρώπινοί ἐσμεν, ἀλλὰ θεοφάτοις καὶ θεοδιδάκτοις, πᾶσαι ὑμᾶς, μὴ ὡς περὶ ἀθέων ἔχειν δυνάμεσθαι</note>. Indeed, by the very doctrines on which we lean—not human ones, certainly, but sent from heaven and taught by God—we can persuade you (not holding us as if we were profane). Here he suggests that persuasion happens one way regarding profane things, and another way regarding divine things. Although some—
