<meta>This page continues the dialogue where Philolaus critiques the over-reliance on Aristotelian logic and syllogisms in matters of divine faith. It bridges the philosophical transition from human reason to divine revelation, specifically citing Dionysius the Areopagite to distinguish between causes and effects.</meta>

# THE WORKS OF JOHANNES REUCHLIN #

...since I have known many of you who base everything on logical inventions, and set up and confirm natural things by mathematical principles, and in turn, logic by natural things, topsy-turvy. But divine things are by no means equal to natural things, nor are natural things able to direct divine ones; much less can those things which stand by faith alone be demonstrated by any reason known to this world. Just as those things which are purely believed do not necessarily imply natural knowledge. For that most excellent **Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>A Christian theologian and philosopher of the late 5th to early 6th century, historically confused with the Dionysius converted by St. Paul. His works blended Neoplatonism with Christian theology.</note>, whom I would consider—not unwisely, I think—to be an outstanding remnant or image of the **Pythagoreans**, speaks thus in his book *On the Divine Names* regarding these theological cognitions: **"For there is,"** he says, **"no exact resemblance between effects and causes. But effects indeed possess the images they have received from the causes, while the causes themselves are removed from the effects and are established above them according to the principle of their own origin"** <note>original Greek: οὐδὲ γὰρ ἀκριβὴς ἐμφέρεια τοῖς αἰτιατοῖς καὶ αἰτίοις. ἀλλ’ ἔχει μὲν τὰ αἰτιατὰ τὰς τῶν αἰτίων δεχομένας εἰκόνας, αὐτὰ δὲ αἴτια τῶν αἰτιατῶν ἐξήρηται, καὶ ὑπερίδρυνται κατὰ τὸν τῆς οἰκείας ἀρχῆς λόγον</note>. 

How much more deceptive is the small net and false dogma of some of you, who trust in things revealed by faith alone, yet believe that not only must the properties of **syllogisms** <note>A form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note> be used, but also that whatever follows from the sacred oracles through the artifice of the syllogism, and is brought forth by good formal necessity and logical consequence, must be believed with equal dignity. For nothing is so far apart as being divinely revealed and humanly discovered. Whence, in the pure faith of things purely believable, believing and knowing are most disparate; there, the conclusion of a syllogism can never be more evident than the premises, and even if certain evidence is mixed with the premises, the conclusion still follows the "weaker part" <note>A rule in logic stating that a conclusion cannot be stronger or more certain than the weakest premise in an argument.</note> on its own. 

Therefore, we rightly affirm this: that in the same subject and with respect to the same truth, the habit of acquired faith and the habit of science generated through demonstration cannot stand together. He who contradicts the sacred oracles, therefore, contradict faith in an execrable manner. But truly, he who contradicts some conclusion collected and inferred from the revelations of the sacred oracles by human ingenuity, subtle little inventions, **Aristotelian** tricks, and the **Eleatic** discipline—whose author was **Zeno**, the **"leader of eristic philosophy"** <note>original Greek: τῆς ἐριστικῆς φιλοσοφίας ἀρχηγός. Eristic refers to argument for the sake of conflict rather than truth.</note> as **Galen** <note>An influential Roman physician and philosopher.</note> says—or by the snares of **Chrysippus** <note>A Greek Stoic philosopher famous for his contributions to logic.</note> or the syllogisms of the **Sophists**, he does not then contradict faith, but resists human science. He does not reject divine illumination, but mortal industry—not in an execrable way, but perhaps erringly, or sometimes perceptively, and certainly not basely. 

How, then, would anyone dare to affirm that what is divinely revealed and what is humanly discovered must be believed with equal dignity, unless he be one who, completely immersed, feeds upon the syllogism as an ox feeds on hay? Truly (I ask you), what parity of dignity exists between the former and the latter? The former is of faith, while the latter is of knowledge. The **Mind** is the seat of the former, while **Reason** is the seat of the latter; the former flows down from heavenly light, while the latter takes its origin from the senses. In the region of the Mind, some things are necessary which in Reason are only possible. In the Mind it is granted that contraries and contradictories **coincide** <note>A reference to the "coincidence of opposites," a mystical concept where logical contradictions are resolved in the divine mind.</note>, which in Reason are separated as far as possible. 

It is not, therefore, entirely true that if the premises are of faith, the conclusion will therefore be of faith. For this proposition is execrable: "no creator is to be worshiped." And even more execrable is this: "every carved image is to be worshiped." For in both of these, faith is blasphemed. And yet, this resulting conclusion is not "sacred" or "of faith": "no carved image is the creator." We can demonstrate this by natural reason; therefore, its truth does not depend on the authority of the one revealing it. Indeed, its evidence is far less than faith. By a similar persuasion, we are deceived in asserting that because a conclusion is of faith, one of the premises must necessarily be of faith. For who does not know that it is believed with the highest faith by the **Hebrews**, **Christians**, and **Hagarenes** <note>A term used in the Middle Ages and Renaissance to refer to Muslims.</note> that a carved image is not to be worshiped? Yet, to infer that assertion, I shall use natural premises: "no stone is to be worshiped; a carved image [is a stone]..."

<meta>catchword: you</meta>

<summary>Reuchlin argues that divine revelation and human logic operate on different levels of dignity, asserting that syllogisms cannot prove matters of pure faith. He distinguishes the higher faculty of the "Mind" (Mens), where divine truth resides, from "Reason" (Ratio), which relies on sensory data and human invention.</summary>

### ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH, BOOK II ###

...we see it to be a stone. Then **Marranus** said: You bring to my mind quite aptly, **Philolaus**, the sophistical refutations of certain of our contemporaries, when they say: "The conclusion is heretical, therefore so is one of the premises." In this matter, I marvel more than can be expressed that these people ever find anyone to believe such things from them. But why do I "try to wash an Ethiopian," <note>An ancient proverb (Latin: *Aethiopen lavare*) meaning to labor in vain, as no amount of washing can change a person's natural color.</note> who will never turn white no matter the effort? Furthermore, there are things which, although they are revealed, nevertheless also follow from things already revealed; if these are accepted by a believer, they will be a matter of faith because they are revealed, rather than a matter of science because they are inferred. Just as the things which my Church commands to be believed, even if composed by any degree of human wit, are presumed to be revealed by the **Holy Spirit** rather than discovered by human reason—no matter how much they are introduced with a certain syllogistic <term>syllogism: a form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</term> subtlety. 

Thus did the **Emperor Constantine** write to the Church of Alexandria concerning the **Council of Nicaea** <note>The First Council of Nicaea (325 AD), which established the foundational creed of Christianity.</note>, saying: **"For what pleased the three hundred bishops at once is nothing other than the judgment of God, especially since the Holy Spirit, dwelling in the minds of such great and numerous men, has brought the divine will to light"** <note>original Greek: ὁ γὰρ τοῖς τριακοσίοις ὁμοῦ ἤρεσεν ἐπισκόποις οὐδὲν ἔστιν ἕτερον ἢ τοῦ θεοῦ γνώμη, μάλιστά ὁπού γε τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα τοιούτων καὶ τηλικούτων ἀνδρῶν ταῖς διανοίαις ἐγκείμενον, τὴν θείαν βούλησιν ἐξεφώτισε</note>. He is speaking here of Bishops representing the universal Church moved by the divine spirit, not of the "headless" <note>likely referring to those acting without rational or spiritual guidance</note> and irregular minds of any "Polyphemuses" <note>A reference to the one-eyed giants of myth, suggesting a singular, distorted perspective.</note> you please. Therefore, let the mixtures of syllogisms about "being," "the necessary," and "the contingent"—or whatever other possibilities or impossibilities of logical curiosity there may be—withdraw to their own workshop. For there is no equal comparison between a speech faithfully believed and a necessary proposition, since a "necessary" thing can still be doubted, while nothing is more evident than what is revealed. Therefore, let such mixtures not occupy the **inner sanctuaries** <note>Latin: *adyta*, the most sacred, private parts of a temple.</note> of the holy rites, nor let them trouble the priests; instead, let them withdraw (if they wish to be capable of anything) to the manual arts, or the nature of masonry, or mathematical calculations. Let them not cross the limits, nor touch **"the untaught and hidden tradition of mystic symbols"** <note>original Greek: τὴν ἀδίδακτον & κρυφίαν μυστικῶν συμβόλων παράδοσιν</note>.

**Philolaus** said: You are walking straight, my friend, toward the dark hiding-places of **Pythagoras**—a man truly imbued with a more divine doctrine—which can be tracked down by no clever tricks of human wit. Such tricks strike us more with the fear of doubting than they generate the firmness of adhering. For such great splendor of divine things cannot be glimpsed by our "nocturnal eyes" through such thin and old-wifely cracks of sophisms. Rather, there will be a need for the greatest powers of thinking and believing, and especially (as **Terence** says) for **faith and silence**. 

Moved by this, Pythagoras—the first "believer" in philosophy after having drained all the disciplines of the whole world—taught his disciples nothing sooner than **to keep silent**, as **Apuleius** wrote. For this was the first rudiment of contemplative wisdom: to meditate, to learn together, to speak, and to unlearn. It was as if the Pythagorean sublimity of such august majesty were much more worthy than that which could be grasped by speaking and chattering with childishly boasted trifles. It is clear enough to us from what we have received from **Simon** <note>Simon is one of the interlocutors in the dialogue, representing the Jewish Kabbalistic tradition.</note> that Pythagoras, just like the rest of the **Kabbalists**, brought this kind of doctrine to Greece: namely, that a disciple, when questioned on a most profound matter, should remain silent. When questioned, he should only answer: **"He himself said it"** <note>Greek: αὐτὸς ἔφα (*Autos epha*). In Latin: *Ipse dixit*. This refers to the Pythagorean practice of accepting the master's word as final authority without further proof.</note>. In the same way, the Kabbalists answer: **"The wise have said"** <note>original Hebrew: אמרו חכמים (*Amru hakhamim*)</note>. And Christians also say to their own: **"Believe"** <note>original Greek: πίστευσον (*Pisteuson*)</note>.

Then **Marranus** said: Perhaps you are criticizing us, Philolaus, whom the **Emperor Julian** <note>Julian the Apostate (r. 361–363 AD), who sought to restore Roman paganism and critiqued Christian reliance on blind faith.</note> also reproached, saying: **"Your irrationality and rusticity, and nothing beyond 'believe,' belongs to your wisdom"** <note>original Greek: ὑμῶν ἡ ἀλογία καὶ ἡ ἀγροικία. καὶ οὐδὲν ὑπὲρ τὸ, πίστευσον, τῆι ὑμετέρας ἐστὶ σοφίας</note>. **Gregory Nazianzen** <note>A 4th-century Church Father known as "The Theologian."</note> wisely met this insult in his first invective, noting that for the Pythagoreans as well, the first and greatest foundation of discipline is to be silent, and then to offer no reason for their sayings except **"He himself said it."** Therefore, Julian wrongly rebukes us, seeing that **"this 'He himself said it' is heard as the same thing as the 'Believe' used among you, though in different syllables and words"** <note>original Greek: ὡς ταὐτὸν ἄκουσα τὸ αὐτὸς ἔφα, τῶι παρ’ ὑμῖν πίστευσον, καὶ ἄλλαις συλλαβαῖς τε καὶ ῥήμασι</note>.

<summary>In this passage, Reuchlin’s characters argue that divine truth relies on revelation and faith rather than human logic. They draw a direct parallel between the Pythagorean "He himself said it," the Kabbalistic "The wise have said," and the Christian command to "Believe."</summary>

### JOHANNES REUCHLIN ###

...believe it, even if in different syllables and words; so says Nazianzenus <note>Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390 AD), a Father of the Church known for his theological oratory.</note>. We now have the unanimous way of learning among those who, above all others, have handled sacred matters most diligently: namely, the **"They said"** <note>original Hebrew: *amru* (אמרו), a phrase used to introduce authoritative tradition</note> of the Kabbalists; the **"He said"** <term>original Greek: *epha* (ἔφα), referring to the Pythagorean *ipse dixit* or "the Master said it"</term> of the Pythagoreans; and the **"They believe"** <term>original Greek: *pisteuousi* (πιστεύουσι)</term> of the Christians. Indeed, whatever belongs to others is not divine. Truly, I thought long ago that all these things flowed from the Hebrews, as Philolaus says. 

Now, more certain than certainty itself, I know—for I see clearly—that whatever Simon showed us of the Italian philosophy <note>The "Italian philosophy" refers to the school founded by Pythagoras in southern Italy.</note> fits the Pythagoreans perfectly. Thus, I would not rashly judge if I said that all the doctrines of the Kabbalists and the Pythagoreans are one and the same. For both groups reduce all our studies to **Ideas** and refer back to them; and all beings that exist, or exist continuously, they refer back to the **Ideas**, which truly are, and to the **Idea of Ideas**. Whence both affirm that there are **three Worlds**, and that the third is infinite—or rather, not bounded—and that all things consist of three. **"For as the Pythagoreans say, the universe and all things are determined by three"** <note>original Greek: *legousi gar phasin hoi Pythagoreioi, to pan kai ta panta tois trisin hōristai*</note>: that is, just as the Pythagoreans say, the whole and all things are bounded by three, as Aristotle wrote in his books *On the Heavens*. For some things, he says, are bodies and magnitudes, while others inhabit and observe those bodies and magnitudes; and finally, there are the sovereignties and origins of those other inhabitants and guardians.

This I understand in this way: since the **Lower World** encompasses individual bodies and magnitudes with their own powers and the intelligences appropriated as movers of the spheres, as well as the caretakers and guardians of things that are born and die—who observe and rule bodies providently, as a province is assigned to each—antiquity sometimes called them "Powers," sometimes "Angels," then sometimes "Gods," and also "Demons" <note>In the classical sense, *daimones* were intermediary spirits, not necessarily evil.</note>. Or, because of the worry for the anxious affairs to which they are bound, antiquity frequently called them "Demons" and "Slanderers." Concerning these, Homer sings: **"Gods inhabiting Olympian dwellings"** <note>original Greek: *theoi olympia dōmat’ echontes*</note>: that is, the Gods inhabiting the Olympian roofs, namely, those who are put in charge of natural things and are often troubled by unfortunate affection; having been banished from the highest to the lowest, they speak of the causes of their labors: **"For many of us who possess Olympian homes suffer at the hands of men, bringing grievous pains upon one another"** <note>original Greek: *polloi gar pasin olympia dōmat’ echontes, ach anthrōp, chalep’ alge’ ep’ allēloisi tithentes*; a quote from Homer's *Iliad*, Book 5</note>. 

For the ancients understood "Olympus" to be the **fifth essence** or nature: that is, the heaven. Therefore, the "Olympian roofs" are the celestial spheres or the heavens, called "heavens" [*caelum*] from "concealing" [*celando*], just as "roofs" [*tecta*] are named from "covering" [*tegendo*]. They understood "Gods" to be the celestial virtues, elementary forces, and the properties of natural things. Hesiod, however, in his *Theogony*, says the Gods were born from Heaven and Earth; and Orpheus, the first theologian of the Greeks, writing to Musaeus, calls these same beings "Demons" in these words: **"Demons of the heavens, the air, the water, the earth, the underworld, and those following the fire"** <note>original Greek: *daimonas ouranious kai aerious kai enydrous kai chthonious kai hypochthonious kai aerophoitas*</note>. Also in his book *Works and Days*, Hesiod says: "Demons are the good terrestrial guardians of mortal men." Even **Apollo** himself once replied to the seeking Theophilus that he and those like him were **Angels**, according to the office of administration lying upon them, as is found in the oracles. For thus he sang, as he usually does all things heroically: **"A name not to be grasped by reason, dwelling in fire, this is God. But we, the Angels, are a small portion of God"** <note>original Greek: *onoma mēde logō chōroumenon en pyri naiōn esse-os, mikra de theou meris angeloi hēmeis*</note>. 

Let us raise our intellect to higher things, if it pleases, namely to the vital influences of this entire globe. For the **Higher World** encompasses the celestial beings, the incorporeal essences, the divine patterns and the seals of these orbs, in whose likeness the faces of all lower things were made. These Pythagoras called the **"First immortal gods"** <note>original Greek: *athanatous prōta theous*</note>: that is, the first immortal gods, like the principles of things—the **Ideas** produced from the divine mind—so that they are the essential **principles** <term>original Greek: *archai* (ἀpχαὶ)</term>, the sovereignties and origins of the bodies inhabiting them: that is, the species informing the composite things of this World. By which it is clearly understood that there are also other "second immortal Gods" there; for the first bring forth the second: incorporeal beings, singular and individual, not numbered by matter but formally differing among themselves by a formal difference. These, I think, are spirits free from all matter, simple and unmixed, which by their own nature are outside the heaven

# ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH, BOOK II. #

...dwelling [beyond] the sensible, and as Aristotle says, bound neither by time nor place; wherefore they neither grow old nor change. Much more so, affected by no variation, alteration, or finally any suffering, they lead for themselves a most sufficient and excellent life, and they inhabit eternity, which is called an "aeon," and in Greek *aion* <note>original Greek: αἰὼν</note>, as if it were *aei on* <note>original Greek: ἀεὶ ὤν</note>—that is, "always being." For this same eternity always was, is, and will be, outside of time, in the Divine Mind. Yet, through the energy of God, it was created "outward" and established outside the curves of our heavens as a most splendid home for the blessed spirits, whom the Pythagoreans consider true Gods. These are located at the sublime peak of the ether, looking both forward to what is before them and backward to their origin, endowed with a fivefold <note>likely referring to the five celestial zones or the quintessence</note> immortal and divine age. From this same eternity, existence and life are dispensed and granted to others—to some more clearly, to others more obscurely—as Aristotle likewise said. 

But what is it through which being is dispensed and granted from this divine and immortal eternity to other things (that is, to lower things)? It is not something that fell into them by chance, in passing, or superficially. Rather, it is the substantial likeness of every species. Certainly, the first of all, the Pythagoreans—Socrates and Plato following their teacher—taught the disciples of that family this: when they heard Pythagoras always speaking obscurely about divine matters, saying that the **Tetractys** <term>A mystical symbol of the number four (1+2+3+4=10), representing the harmony of the universe</term> handed down to our soul the "fountain of perennial nature," they clearly understood that the Tetractys was the **Idea** in the Divine Mind. The "fountain" is the **Exemplar Idea** handed down, and the "perennial nature" is the **Essential Idea** of things as it is received. 

Therefore, on the testimony of Alcinous <note>A Middle Platonist philosopher (2nd century AD) who summarized Platonic doctrine.</note>, they spoke in this way: "The Idea is, in relation to God, His thinking; in relation to us, an intelligible paradigm of the world; and when examined in relation to itself, it is essence" <note>original Greek: ἔστιν ἡ ἰδέα ὡς μὲν πρὸς θεὸν, νόησις αὐτοῦ, ὡς δὲ πρὸς ἡμᾶς νοητὸν κόσμου παράδειγμα. ὡς δὲ πρὸς αὑτὴν ἐξεταζομένη, οὐσία</note>. That is, a speaker’s voice—as it says in the works of the Areopagite <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist writer.</note>—is one and the same, yet it is perceived as one by many ears. For the voice is first in the speaker, second in the sounding of the voice, and third in each listener. 

Just as in the Sensible World a higher sphere always flows into all those following it, so in the Intellectual World we believe not only that each higher choir flows into all the lower choirs, but also that the whole Higher World flows into the whole Lower World. Thus, all things, according to their capacity, are led back—as far as possible for momentary things—to the eternal, and the lowest things are led back to the highest. However, nothing of mere creatures can be led back to the **Third World**, for nothing by its own nature is capable of such sublimity except God. And yet, I say, that Third World is the "Super-Supreme," containing all other worlds; it belongs to the Deity alone and consists of a single divine essence. It seems clearly to me to be rightly named the **Omnipotent Seat** <note>original Greek: παντοκρατορικὴ ἕδρα (*pantokratorike hedra*)</note>—that is, the almighty seat located, or rather existing, above every age and every century. For it is the "Age of Ages," the "pre-existing entity and unity of existence, substance, essence, and nature" <note>original Greek: ὑπάρξεως, ὑποστάσεως, οὐσίας, φύσεως, ὀντότης καὶ ἑνότης προοῦσα</note>.

This is what our Pythagoras called **$\psi$** <note>The Greek letter Psi, likely used here as a mystical symbol for the soul or a specific divine attribute</note>, and what the Pythagorean Parmenides called **Being** (*on*). Both, by a similar reasoning, called it "that which is not far from being, and being is one" <note>original Greek: οὐ πόρρω ὄν, καὶ τὸ ὄν, ἕν</note>—that is, the super-essential One and Being are one. But let no one be so hateful of antiquity or such a despiser of our ancestors as to think that the great and wise Pythagoras was corrupted by such "old-womanish madness" as to think that the numbers on a counting-board, or children’s dice with which they throw "four vultures," or the tokens of merchants and other things of that kind, were the principles of all things. Such things do not rule over reality; rather, they happen according to reality. 

On the contrary, he wanted to be understood as referring to the **Essentially and Simply One**, from whom, and out of whom, and through whom, and in whom, and toward whom all things are: they are ordered, they remain, they are contained, they are filled, and they are converted. This "First One" and "First Being" are the same, as Aristotle testifies in the second book of his *Metaphysics* <note>referred to here by the medieval title *Postnaturalia*</note> with these words: "For Plato and the Pythagoreans did not think that Being and The One were different things, but said that this was their nature: as being the same as the existing essence, The One and Being are the same" <note>original Greek: Πλάτων μὴ γὰρ οἱ πυθαγόρειοι ἑτέρον τι τὸν ὄν, οὐδὲ τὸ ἕν. ἀλλὰ ἔφη αὐτῶν τὴν φύσιν εἶναι, ὡς ὄνος τῆς οὐσίας ταυτό, τὸ ἕν εἶναι καὶ ὄν</note>.

...believe, though in other syllables and words; so says Nazianzen <note>Gregory of Nazianzus, a 4th-century theologian known for his eloquence</note>. We now have the unanimous way of learning among those who handled sacred matters more diligently than any others, namely: the "they said" <note>original Hebrew: אמרו (*amru*)</note> of the Kabbalists, the "he said" <note>original Greek: εφά (*epha*), referring to the authoritative 'Ipse dixit' of Pythagoras</note> of the Pythagoreans, and the "believe" <note>original Greek: πιστεύου (*pisteuou*)</note> of the Christians. For whatever belongs to others is not divine. As Philolaus says, I previously thought much the same—that all these things flowed from the Hebrews.

I now know this more certainly than certainty itself, for I see clearly that whatever Simon showed us regarding the Italian philosophy—that is, the Pythagorean—aligns perfectly, so that I would hardly judge otherwise than that all the doctrines of the Kabbalists and Pythagoreans are one and the same. For both groups reduce all our studies to the salvation of the human race; and all beings that exist, or exist continually, they refer back to the Ideas which truly are, and to the Idea of ideas. Whence both assert there are three Worlds: the first is the **Sensible**, the second the **Intellectual**, and the third the **Infinite**, or rather the **Unbounded**. They hold that all things consist of three, "for as the Pythagoreans say, the whole and all things are limited by three" <note>original Greek: καὶ γὰρ φασιν οἱ πυθαγόρειοι, τὸ πᾶν καὶ τὰ πάντα τοῖς τρισὶν ὥρισται</note>, as Aristotle wrote in his books *On the Heavens*. For some things, he says, are bodies and magnitudes, while others inhabit and observe bodies and magnitudes, and there are the sovereignties and origins of the inhabitants and guardians.

I interpret it thus: since the lower World encompasses bodies and magnitudes, each with its own powers and intelligences—the motors of the spheres appropriated to them—as well as the curators and guardians of things that are born and decay, who observe bodies providently as each is assigned a province. These, antiquity sometimes called powers, sometimes **Angels**, then sometimes **Gods**, and also **demons** <note>In the classical sense, 'daemons' were intermediary spirits or guiding geniuses, not necessarily evil spirits</note>, or frequently "demons" because of the anxiety and care for the things to which they are bound. About these, Homer sings: "Gods inhabiting Olympic dwellings" <note>original Greek: θεοὶ ὀλύμπια δώματ’ ἔχοντες</note>, namely, those who are often disturbed by a small affection for the natural things they oversee, and being relegated from the highest to the lowest, they complain of the causes of their labors. For they say: "For many of us who inhabit Olympic dwellings suffer at the hands of men, laying heavy pains upon one another" <note>original Greek: πολλοὶ γὰρ πλῆγὴν ὀλύμπια δώματ’ ἔχοντες... as found in the Iliad, Book 5</note>. For by "Olympus," the ancients understand the **fifth essence** <term>The 'quintessence' or ether, the pure material of the heavens</term> or nature—that is, the sky. Therefore, "Olympic dwellings" are the celestial spheres or heavens, named from "concealing" just as "dwellings" are named from "covering." From these come the celestial virtues, elementary forces, and the properties of natural things.

Hesiod says in his *Theogony* that the Gods were born from Heaven and Earth, and Orpheus, the first of the Greek theologians, writing to Musaeus, calls them "demons" in these words: "demons of the heavens, the air, the water, the earth, the underworld, and the fire-walkers" <note>original Greek: δαίμονας οὐρανίους καὶ ἀερίους καὶ ἐνύδρους καὶ χθονíους καὶ ὑποχθονíους καὶ πυριφοíτους</note>, that is, those assisting the fire. Also, in his book *Works and Days*, Hesiod says: "Good demons are the earthly guardians of mortal men." Indeed, Apollo himself once replied to Theophilus, who asked about him and those like him, that they were **Angels** according to the office of administration incumbent upon them, as is found in the oracles. For thus he sang, as he almost always does in heroic verse: "A name not even grasped by reason, dwelling in fire, this is God. But we Angels are a small portion of God" <note>original Greek: ὄνομα μηδὲ λόγῳ χωρούμενον... θεῦ μερὶς ἄγγελοι ἡμεῖς</note>.

Let us raise our minds, if you please, to higher things, namely to the vital influences of this entire globe. For the **Higher World** encompasses the celestial beings, incorporeal essences, divine patterns, and the seals of this globe, in whose likeness the faces of all lower things were made. These Pythagoras called the "first immortal gods" <note>original Greek: ἀθανάτους πρῶτα θεούς</note>, like the principles of things—the **Ideas** produced from the Divine Mind—so that they are the essential sovereignties and origins of those inhabiting bodies: that is, the species informing the composite things of this World. By this, he clearly understands that there are also other "immortal gods" there of the second rank; for first things imply second things: incorporeal beings, singular and individual, differing among themselves not by material number, but formally by form—I mean spirits free from all matter, simple and unmixed, by their own nature outside the heavens...

->### OF THE CABALISTIC ART, BOOK II<-

...dwelling in the sensible world, and as Aristotle says, unbound by either time or place, so that they neither grow old nor are changed; far more so, being affected by no variation or alteration—and finally by no passion—they lead a life most sufficient and best for themselves. They inhabit eternity, which is called the *aeon* <note>original Greek: αἰών</note> as if it were "always being" <note>original Greek: ἀεὶ ὤν (*aei on*)</note>. That is, "always existing," because that same age always was, is, and shall be, outside of time, in the divine mind. Yet, by the energy of God, it was created outwardly and established beyond the curves of our heavens as a most splendid dwelling for the blessed spirits. These spirits the Pythagoreans consider to be true gods, located at the high summit of the ether, four of them in front and four behind, endowed with a divine and immortal age. From this same age, being and life are distributed and granted to others—to some more clearly, to others more obscurely—as the same Aristotle said. 

But as to what that is through which being is distributed and granted to other (that is, lower) things from this divine and immortal age: it is not something that fell into them by chance, in passing, or superficially. Rather, it is the substantive reality of every species. Certainly, the first of all the Pythagoreans, Socrates and Plato, following their teacher, taught the disciples of that family this truth. When they heard Pythagoras—who always spoke obscurely about divine matters—habitually say that the **Tetractys** <note>The "four-fold" number 10, a sacred Pythagorean symbol</note> transmitted the fountain of perennial nature to our soul, they then clearly understood that the Tetractys was the **Idea** in the divine mind transmitting it; that the fountain was the exemplary Idea being transmitted; and that perennial nature was the essential Idea of things as received. 

Therefore, as Alcinous <note>A Middle Platonist philosopher</note> bears witness, they spoke in this way: "The Idea is, in relation to God, his own cognition; in relation to the sensible world, it is a model; but considered in relation to itself, it is essence" <note>original Greek: ἔστιν ἡ ἰδέα ὡς μὲν πρὸς θεὸν, νόησις αὐτοῦ, ὡς δὲ πρὸς τὸν αἰσθητὸν κόσμον παράδειγμα. ὡς δὲ πρὸς αὐτὴν ἐξεταζομένη, οὐσία</note>. This is like the voice of one speaking, as it is found in the Areopagite <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist</note>: though it is one and the same, it is perceived as one by many ears. For the voice is first in the speaker, second in the vocalization, and third in each listener. 

Just as in the Sensible World a prior sphere always flows into all those following it, so in the Intellectual World we believe not only that individual higher choirs flow into all lower choirs, but also that the entire Higher World flows into the entire Lower World. Thus, all things, according to their capacity, are led back—as far as possible—from the momentary to the eternal, and from the lowest to the highest. However, nothing that is merely a creature can be led back to the **Third World**. For nothing is capable of such sublimity by its own nature except God. Indeed, that third World, which is supreme above all and contains all other worlds, belongs to the Deity alone and consists of a single divine essence. It seems to me quite rightly named the "All-ruling Seat" <note>original Greek: παντοκρατορικὴ ἕδρα (*pantokratorikē hedra*)</note>: that is, the omnipotent seat located, or rather existing, above every age and every eon. For it is the "age of ages," a pre-existing entity and unity of existence, substance, essence, and nature <note>original Greek: ὑπάρξεως, ὑποστάσεως, οὐσίας, φύσεως, ὀντότης καὶ ἑνότης προοῦσα</note>. 

This is what our Pythagoras called *Psi* <note>The Greek letter Ψ, here used as a symbolic or mathematical shorthand for a divine principle</note> and the Pythagorean Parmenides called **The One**. Both did so by a not dissimilar reasoning: "the supra-essential One, and Being, is One" <note>original Greek: ὑπερούσιον, ψὺ καὶ τὸ ὂν, ἕν</note>. But surely no one could be so hateful of antiquity or such a despiser of our ancestors as to think that the great and wise Pythagoras was seized by such old-womanish madness that he thought the numbers on a counting-board, or the childish dice with which they throw "four vultures" <note>A high roll in ancient dice games</note>, or the pebbles of merchants and other things of that kind, were the principles of all things. Such things do not preside over reality but rather follow after it. 

Instead, he wished to be understood as referring to the **One** itself, essentially and simply, from which, and out of which, and through which, and in which, and toward which all things are, and are ordered, and remain, and are contained, and are filled, and are converted. He meant that the First One and First Being are the same, as Aristotle testifies in the second book of the *Metaphysics* in these words: "For Plato and the Pythagoreans held that Being and the One are not something different, but that this is their very nature: that the essence of Being and the One is the same" <note>original Greek: πλάτων μὲν γὰρ καὶ οἱ πυθαγόρειοι οὐχ ἕτερόν τι τὸ ὂν, οὐδὲ τὸ ἕν. ἀλλὰ τοῦτον αὐτῶν τὴν φύσιν εἶναι, ὡς οὔσης τῆς οὐσίας ταὐτὸ, τό τε ἓν καὶ τὸ ὄν</note>.

<meta>This page continues Reuchlin's exploration of the Pythagorean "One" and the "Infinite," linking these Greek philosophical concepts to the Christian understanding of the Trinity and the Divine Mind (the world of Ideas).</meta>

-># JOHANNES REUCHLIN<-

...and some being. Indeed, that Xenophanes, the teacher of Parmenides and a contemporary of Pythagoras—although it was the custom of those men to hide everything—nevertheless seems to us to have most truly explained what they understood that "One" itself to be, about which they spoke in their first principles. Now, I have said that this **One** is **God**, by which it is clear that the secrets of Pythagoras are revealed in us when he established that the infinite and the number one are the first principles of things. By "the infinite," he signifies nothing other than *Power* itself <note>original: "ipsum posse"</note>; for no one could ever even think that *being* comes before that which is most infinite in God—indeed, God himself is the infinite, in whom *being* and *power* are not separated. This Power contains the essences, virtues, and operations of all producible things and every individual thing, along with all the connecting differences and unions of properties and accidents. Furthermore, Anaxagoras also agrees with Pythagoras in this matter; Eusebius Pamphili <note>A 4th-century Christian historian</note> is the authority for the fact that before these men, no opinions of the Greeks held any knowledge of God. For Anaxagoras said, "all things were together." And Democritus said, "all things were together in potentiality" <note>original Greek: δυνάμει (*dynamei*)</note>, that is, in Power itself. This is also that "mixture" or "joining of things" spoken of by Empedocles and Anaximander—not at all confused by the "Chaos," "Night," and "Erebus" of Hesiod or Aristophanes, but rather distinct in the full divine light and ordered within the innermost sanctuary of that infinite light. However, if Hesiod is understood fairly, he certainly established that Chaos, Night, and Darkness are not the principles of things, but rather arose *from* the principles. For he brought this forth in his *Theogony*: "From the beginning and whenever the first of them was born, surely first of all Chaos came to be" <note>original Greek: ἐξ ἀρχῆς καὶ εἶπόθ’ ὅτι πρῶτον γένετ’ αὐτῶν. ἤτοι μὲν πρώτιστα χάος γ’</note>. Then follows: "From Chaos, both Erebus and black Night were born" <note>original Greek: ἐκ χάεος δ’ ἔρεβός τε μέλαινά τε νὺξ ἐγένοντο</note>. That is: From the principles, and if ever something was first made of them, certainly first Chaos was made.
<margin>x</margin>
Moreover, from Chaos, Erebus and black Night were born. But Aristophanes wrote differently in *The Birds*: "Chaos was, and Night, and black Erebus first" <note>original Greek: χάος ἦν καὶ νὺξ ἔρεβός τε μέλαν πρῶτον</note>. But he fashions this poetically in the manner of the Muses, alluding to his "birds," so that Love might hatch from an egg; at the same time, he acts as a parasite to Orpheus in the *Argonautica*, who holds a similar view. Therefore, by repeating this same point again and again, let me remember: all things and individual things exist in that very Power—not confusedly as in Chaos, nor in Erebus, nor in obscure Night, but distinctly and orderly in full light. That is, they exist in that same luminous and most splendid clarity of all the most shining rays, and in the gaze, notice, and knowledge of the illustrious and illuminating divine essence. This is rightly called **Idea** <note>The Platonic concept of the perfect form or blueprint of a thing</note> by the most ancient philosophers, from the Greek word "to see" <note>original Greek: ἴδω (*ido*)</note> comes "to know" <note>original Greek: γινώσκω (*ginosko*)</note>. This "Power to Be," since it embraces all things—mental, rational, intelligible, sensible, vital, substantial, inherent, and adhesive—pertains not only to those things that *are*, but even to those that *are not*. And truly Pythagoras was able to call that "the infinite," which was also called by the wisest men "**infinitely powerful**" <note>original Greek: ἀπειροδύναμον (*apeirodynamon*)</note>; that is, to be infinitely able, because he himself is infinite, and by one and the same infinite and essential **Idea**, he embraces infinite things. For nothing either was, is, or shall be in the super-celestial, celestial, earthly, corporeal, or incorporeal realms—in angels, in men, in beasts, in plants, in the whole universal nature—that is not "possible," or as we might say grammatically, "able to be." From this all things proceed, and this is the "infinitely powerful and almighty power-making power" <note>original Greek: ἀπειροδύναμον καὶ παντοδύναμον δυναμοποιός δύναμις (*apeirodynamon kai pantodynamon dynamopoios dynamis*)</note>. This is nothing other than the divine essence, within which, before all things, the **One** produces **Two**. 

Here, Marrano <note>Addressing Simon, the interlocutor in the dialogue; "Marrano" was a term for a Jewish convert to Christianity</note>, you have the whole of my Pythagoras. **Two** is the first number, but **One** is the principle of number. But if you believe Xenophanes, as you heard before, that "One" is God; and since the production of the "Two" remains within the divine essence (for number is constituted by itself, according to the Peripatetic author Boethius, and next to the one, only the dyad exists naturally), then necessarily those "Two" are also God, since outside of God, there is nothing but God. Therefore, since these **Three** things are the principle and the first, and do not exit the one essence of God, then they are clearly one God. For the essence is not split by the fact that two products are numbered from the one, just as in things...
<meta>catchword: bu- (continuation of "rebus" / "things")</meta>

...even in physical bodies, it often happens that unity, once moved into duality (if I may be forgiven the comparison), proceeds all the way to trinity while the substance of the thing remains the same—as with a tree trunk and its branches, or more accurately, as with a human body, an arm, and a finger. Therefore, from the One producing in divine matters, and two things being produced, a unity arises. If to these things we add an essence that is formally distinct from them, there will be a <term>formal quaternary</term> <note>The number four, viewed as a foundational structure of reality.</note>, which is infinite. One, two, three, and four, when added together in a collective progression, produce ten, and beyond ten, nothing exists.

For this very reason, **Pythagoras** understood that there is a certain principle of all things, which he named the **Tetractys**. For *tetras* in Greek means "quaternary" (the number four), and *actys* means a "solar form" or "ray." From such a formality—though it is now beyond mere substance—my own mind constitutes one illustrious name for the quaternary, as if it were composed of four things formally distinct from one another. And so that he might separate the sacred from the profane, he acted with the best reasoning by writing that holy name with an *ypsilon*, even though it was commonly written by the masses with an *iota*. Furthermore, he himself brought forth the **Tetractys** here as a masculine deity of excellent kind, in the same way the ancient Latins pronounced **Cupid** or **Venus** as masculine nouns, whereas at other times they spoke of the "tetractydinal" number itself—the instrumental quaternary—in the feminine gender. He wished to show that this was the God by whom he swore: "By the Tetractys" <note>original Greek: μὰ τὸν τετρακτύα (*ma ton tetraktya*)</note>, than which nothing should be held more worthy of veneration. For as **Aristotle** says, "An oath is the most honorable thing" <note>original Greek: ὅρκος τὸ τιμιώτατόν ἐστιν (*horkos to timiotaton estin*)</note>. 

In this matter, I certainly will not agree with **Hierocles** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist who commented on Pythagoras.</note>, as I believe that Pythagoras himself wrote the *Golden Verses*. Yet, I would equally hope, out of reverence for its wondrous holiness, that the **Tetractys** should not be called "quaternary" or "fourness" in the Roman tongue, but rather—with the word slightly changed—"quaternio" or "quaternitudo." You Christians observe this same practice, separating the sacred from the usage of the profane commoners: for while the words "ternary" or "threeness" should be read by the populace, you call the most holy <term>hypostasis</term> <note>The underlying substance or personhood of the Trinity.</note> by the altered name **Trinity**, as if it were a "unity of three," borrowing a letter from "One" itself because of the nature of the unity of each person.

But to sound the retreat: I say that there is one certain supreme thing over all things, the **Tetractys**, the Pythagorean principle. Then **Marranus** said: "I recall a most beautiful example from **Philolaus** regarding that sign of four letters, in which the salvation of the entire human race is present. **Simon** confirmed this to us with such a wealth of scripture that it truly seemed to me that Pythagoras did not do badly to change the Jewish **Tetragrammaton** <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH.</note>—or rather the four letters from which the name of the Savior is composed—into the Greek symbol of the **Tetractys**." 

Soon after, I said: "But **Philolaus**, I have certainly not yet departed satisfied regarding that **Tetragrammaton** and that salvation to which Simon has reduced almost the whole human race. Therefore, when I return to him, I will ask more about these things if he is willing—especially about that man who is to bring salvation to each of us, like an anointed king of all things, and is therefore called the **Messiah**. But I would like to see now whether he is **Aesculapius** <note>The Greek god of healing and medicine.</note> coming into this world again, perhaps through 'trans-animation' (reincarnation), as they say. Concerning him, the **Emperor Julian** writes in his second book *Against the Galileans*: 

> 'For Jupiter, from his own being among the intelligible gods, begat **Aesculapius**, and revealed him to the earth through the sun’s life-giving light. He, making his progression from heaven to earth, appeared in a uniform way in human form around **Epidaurus**. Having increased his reach from there, he extended his saving right hand over the entire earth, to restore souls that were poorly disposed and bodies that were weak.'"

If he had possessed a name composed of those four letters, even with any other reading character added, he would certainly have to be considered the Savior himself. Or surely, however great that **Hercules** had been...

### IOANNES REUCHLIN
### BOOK II. 654

The son of Alcmene, born of Jupiter, a divine seed, whom the people of Thasos named Sarem and inscribed on their public coins as: **Hercules, Savior of the Thasians** <note>original Greek: Ἡρακλέης σωτῆρ Θασίων</note>. I recently turned over such a silver coin, anciently struck, with these fingers of mine—reading and re-reading it, as is my habit, with incredible pleasure <note>original: "uoluptate"</note> for the most ancient things. From this, I not unreasonably conjectured that by the voice and consensus of all, Hercules was placed among the gods and proclaimed a savior. 

That there were, moreover, many others who brought salvation to mortals is indeed beyond doubt; among their number, I recall King Ptolemy of Egypt, who held the name **Soter**—that is, "Savior." Curtius himself restored the land to safety <note>referring to Marcus Curtius, a legendary Roman hero who sacrificed himself by leaping into a chasm to save Rome</note> by his own death, and the **Decii** <note>a Roman family known for "devotio," sacrificing their lives in battle for the state</note> bravely devoted their own heads to preserve their country, acting as wonderful authors of the common safety.

Then Marranus said: I would gladly remind you, by interrupting, to observe more clearly and interpret more fairly the things handed down by **Simon**. For after that man, skilled in every branch of his sect, had discussed many things regarding the **Cabala** <term>Cabala: Jewish mystical tradition</term>, showing what it was and what it was useful for—and that it was truly a revelation, opening a path for us to the height of bliss and supreme happiness—he was asked by us what the chief thing revealed to humanity was, to which all divine revelations might be reduced. He said it was that which is called the **universal restoration** after the primordial fall of the human race, which is named **salvation**. 

He said there would be given a just and peaceful man, a hero, whose name would contain four letters <note>A reference to the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God, or possibly the Hebrew name of the Messiah</note> in mercies, toward whom we ought to strive freely, releasing ourselves from all secular business, ascending through all suitable steps and migrating into him, each according to his strength. He taught that all our actions should be shaped toward this, all contemplation directed here, and all sacred scripture should tend here; it serves us as **Jacob’s ladder** <note>Genesis 28:10-19</note> placed upon the earth with its top touching the heavens. Through it, we can transcend this corporeal world into the other angelic world, even to the very soul of that **Messiah the Savior**, which is the rest and fullness of all souls to be saved, and our ultimate end. Beyond this we can progress nowhere, for it terminates the highest habitation of the supreme world and communicates with the world above—or, if the grammarians will allow, the "most supreme," or rather the incomparable world. This is the perpetual salvation of all people, completed by the gathering of all goods. 

If you remember these things as set out by Simon, though in a roundabout way, you will not, in my opinion, doubt that neither your saviors, nor even certain ones of the Jews (of whom the twenty-four books of the Bible often make honorable mention), were ever placed in such dignity that they could bring universal salvation to the human race, so that all humans in every corner of the earth might enjoy eternal life and return to grace with God after the Fall.

As for what many others thought of your **Aesculapius** <note>The Greek god of medicine</note>, you shall see; they assert he was born of a foul incest from **Coronis**, a pretty little woman of whom it is sung: "There was no one more beautiful in all Thessaly than Larissaean Coronis." They claim the priests of **Apollo** often subdued and compressed her in the temple, and then feigned that Aesculapius, born from their adulterous unions, was the son of a God worshipped in that place. 

However, an Egyptian, who first brought the art of medicine to Greece, was such a temple-dweller in that age that even after death he was worshipped as a god. Led by a similar favor toward the priests of Apollo, he took up the infant to be nourished and instructed, whom he then commended to his former disciple **Chiron the Centaur**, a most skilled physician, so that he might pour the art of healing and protecting the body into Aesculapius. Once this was done, Aesculapius emerged as a man great in both fame and wealth. But then, instigated by greed and a desire for honor, he traveled through various regions of the world to scrape together money through the medical art. And now, with much wealth...

->### ON THE ART OF THE CABALA. BOOK II.<-

...abundant, and endowed with great fame, he foolishly called himself a God, promising not only health to the sick, but even life renewed to the dead. For this, he paid the penalty for his pride to Jupiter: for he perished, struck by a lightning bolt. For so Pythagoras—or rather Pindar in his third *Pythian Ode*—sang concerning Asclepius <note>Asclepius was the Greek god of medicine, often depicted with a serpent-entwined staff</note>: *χρὴ σὲ δ’ ἄρα κερδίων ῥῖψας δι’ ἀμφοῖn, ἀμπνοὰν στέρνων καθεῖλεν ὠκέως, αἴθων δὲ κεραυνὸς ἐνέσκιψε μόρον* <note>original Greek from Pindar: "But even he was snared by gain... the lightning-bolt of Zeus took away his breath."</note>; that is: **Jupiter, casting forth with both hands, snatched away the breath from his chest; the burning lightning-bolt brought death.** In this same vein, Apollo is portrayed by Euripides as complaining over the death of his son Asclepius: *Ζεὺς γὰρ κατακτὰς παῖδα τὸν ἐμὸν αἴτιον Ἀσκληπιὸν στέρνοισιν ἐμβαλὼν φλόγα* <note>original Greek: "For Zeus killed my son Asclepius, the cause, by casting a flame into his breast."</note>. Therefore, unless we are utterly dull-witted <note>original: "plumbei" (leaden)</note> in divine matters, we will not think a man so far removed from dignity to be the Savior of the human race; nor indeed a healer of the whole world, when he brought help nowhere else but to Pergamum, Ionia, Taranto, Rome, Cos, Aegae, and the regions thereabouts. 

You are overcome by too much love for your own people, Marranus, Philolaus replied, and more by that than by the truth; you value all other men as less—indeed, you think them of the least possible worth—who are not "Galileans" <note>This term was often used by critics like Emperor Julian to refer to Christians</note>. It is a perverse habit, in my opinion (if you will pardon the word), not only to refuse praise to others, but even to revile them. Nor, as I see it, is it enough for you and those like you to contend that the best of men, famous for virtue in their own age—whom antiquity counted among the gods because of their extraordinary deeds—were not gods, unless you also make them out to be hellish devils. In this you imitate your friend Lactantius <note>Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325) was an early Christian author and advisor to Constantine who wrote against paganism</note>, who in the tenth chapter of his first book to the Emperor Constantine wrote thus: *Asclepius himself, born not without the disgrace of Apollo, what else did he do worthy of divine honors, except that he healed Hippolytus? He certainly had a more famous death, because he deserved to be struck by lightning by God.* So says he. 

But every tongue that is infected with gall lacks the taste for truth. Yet even he admits it is a thing worthy of divine honors to grant health—as all sick people would surely agree. But if Lactantius does not know what else Asclepius did, let him ask the wisest man, Socrates, who vowed that a cock should be offered to him, as is written in Plato’s *Phaedo*. This was not so that he might heal his body—for he had already been sentenced to death and had drunk the poison—but so that he might return his soul, as he was dying peacefully, with a shout of joy and a song of victory <term>pæan: a song of triumph or thanksgiving, often dedicated to Apollo</term> to the father, Apollo: that is, to the first and incorporeal Sun, the dispenser of eternal life. For the cock is sacred to Apollo Phoebus (who is called the Sun), being the watchful herald of the hours and the day. 

Furthermore, Asclepius was called by the ancients the "jubilation of Apollo’s victory and triumph," which is termed *pæan*, because they named it after the brief cessation and rest following liberation. For in that age, it was the custom for those about to enter battle to first offer a song to Mars, and after the battle, as victors, to offer a *pæan* to Apollo. How aptly, then, Socrates—being just on the verge of death—honored the Sun, the giver of life, in the person of Asclepius (who is the *pæan*). Let the right judgments of the most learned men see this: he judged it worthy and a duty for every good man, once the great serpent Python of this world had been conquered and trampled underfoot, and when the journey to true life is quickly taken through death, to offer something to Asclepius: that is, to celebrate the *pæan*. 

Thus Orpheus, the most ancient of poets and a contemporary of those gods (for he is said to have sailed with the sons of Tyndareus and Hercules), sang in his hymns: *ἰητὴρ πάντων ἀσκληπιὲ δέσποτα παιάν, ἐλθὲ μάκαρ σωτὴρ, βιοτῆς τέλος ἐσθλὸν ὀπάζων* <note>original Greek: "Healer of all, Lord Asclepius, the Paean, come, blessed Savior, granting a noble end to life."</note>; that is: **Healer of all, Lord Asclepius the Paean, come, blessed Savior, providing a good end to life.** The Emperor Julian asserts that he saw many people helped by Asclepius in the greatest dangers, and he confesses that he himself, when laboring in sickness, often escaped safely through his cures, citing Jupiter as a witness to this. 

But what does this matter to the whole world, Marranus responded, whose Savior the Messiah is proclaimed to be—not only of bodies, but of souls? 

And Philolaus replied: Indeed, Marranus, what about Hercules? Was he not the shaper of morals and the teacher of every noble discipline in all places of the world? Hence that image of Hercules among the Celts, which is very ancient and truly a landmark, where he himself, as an old man, draws countless men along wherever he wishes, each one bound by the neck with little golden chains that hang from his tongue. The Celts call him Ogmion <note>Ogmios was the Celtic god of eloquence, often equated with Hercules</note> in their native tongue...

->### JOHANNES REUCHLIN<-

<note>Philolaus continues:</note> Let his memory be found in Lucian, in the discourse on the *Celtic Hercules*, concerning whom they say: *We believe that Hercules, having become wise, accomplished all things through word and reason.* <note>original Greek: ἡμεῖς τὸν ἡρακλέα λόγον τὰ πάντα ἡγούμεθα ἐξεργάσασθαι σοφὸν γενόμενον</note>. For to tame vices through virtue and to remove ignorance through doctrine is nothing other than trampling upon monsters and killing snakes, striking the **Nemean lion** with a club, slaying the **Lernean hydra**, killing the **Erymanthian boar**, capturing the **hind** with golden horns in the Nalio grove, piercing the **Stymphalian birds** with arrows, strangling **Antaeus** in one's arms, fixing columns in the Ocean, conquering the triple-bodied **Geryon**, driving away the cattle, killing the bull, and overcoming **Achelous** in single combat. I omit the horses of Diomedes, Cerberus, and the apples of the Hesperides, and many other deeds of that kind; all of this belonged to virtue, all was the duty of right instruction and an example of living well.

**Marranus** replied: I would speak of the estimation others have of him, were it not that you would take offense at such a private opinion. I would briefly show that he was a man just as we are, perhaps a little more unworthy, though noble by the lineage of Proetus and Agenor. If Proetus was from Agenor, and Belus was the brother of Agenor, from whom was born Egyptus, from whom Lynceus, from whom Abas, from whom Danaë, whose son was Perseus, whose son was Alcaeus, whose son was Amphitryon, whose son Hercules was thought to be—though in truth they say he was the son of Jupiter, or rather the son of some adulterer. For from Alcmene, if the story is believed, Iphicles was born to Amphitryon and Hercules to Jupiter in a single birth. 

Indeed, the life of Hercules ended in sacred fire, because he avenged the attempted chastity of his wife Deianira against Nessus the Centaur with a dart; yet he himself showed the same lack of restraint toward the captive girl Iole, and was destroyed by the mere suspicion of the adultery he himself committed. Having been conceived in adultery, he likewise committed adultery himself; perhaps he was just toward others, but certainly most unjust toward himself. Do you say, Philolaus, that such a man could be the **Savior of the World**, as were Hercules or Asclepius? If for no other reason, then at least because both died under a shameful mark. For as Momus says of both in Lucian’s *Assembly of the Gods*: *They bear the marks of fire* <note>original Greek: ἐκ τῶν σημάτων ἔχουσι τοῦ πυρὸς</note>; that is, they were both burned up. 

Others praise Curtius and the Decii <note>Roman heroes who sacrificed themselves for the state</note> for their greatness of soul, but I accuse them of imprudence. What of those who, led by fawning flatteries or forced by the violence of tyrants, adorned with the name of "Savior" a man who not only did not heal or save them, but utterly devastated and destroyed them? For example, the Sicilians inscribed a public statue in Syracuse to **Verres** as *Soter* <note>Savior</note>, "he who gave health," according to Cicero’s testimony in the fourth speech against Verres. 

But these examples have no place here, where we treat the true salvation of men, which those figures never provided. For **true salvation** is eternal permanence, which is in God and is granted by God. As Aristotle wrote in the book *On the Universe* <note>De Mundo</note> to Alexander: *From God,* he says, *and through God, all things consist for us, and no nature is sufficient if it lacks that salvation which comes from Him.* Then he adds: *In His very essence, God is truly the Savior of all things.* <note>original Greek: τῇ γ᾿ οὐσίᾳ, ὁ σωτὴρ ὄντως ἁπάντων ἐστίν</note>. Wherefore, in the fourteenth book of the *Metaphysics* <note>original: postnaturalium</note>, Aristotle says: *It is a wonder if, to the first and eternal and most self-sufficient Being, this same primary quality does not belong as a good: namely, self-sufficiency and salvation.* 

By this we are warned that our true salvation stands in the first, eternal, and most sufficient Good, which is **God, the Best and Greatest**, and it is not to be sought elsewhere. For only that supreme Architect of the world, out of the most merciful will of His transcendent generosity, can give incorruption to corruptible things, eternity to those subject to time, and unshakable permanence to transitory things—whose own nature it is to fall as they decline and grow old as they increase. For so speaks the God in Plato's *Timaeus*: *The things made by me are indissoluble, provided I will it; otherwise, everything that is bound together is indeed dissoluble.* Behold, this is the view not only of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note>, but even of Plato himself.

<summary>Marranus critiques the pagan concept of "Saviors" like Hercules and Asclepius, arguing that true salvation is an ontological preservation of existence that comes only from God, as supported by Aristotle and Plato.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between the Pythagorean philosopher Philolaus and the Jewish scholar Marranus. Having discussed the symbolic labors of Hercules, they now turn to the philosophical and linguistic definition of "salvation" and the "Savior."</meta>

# ON THE CABALISTIC ART, BOOK II.

We receive it as a testimony from the Platonists that permanence is granted to all things, according to their capacity, by the sole will of God—and this is true salvation. For we say that to be "saved" is to be preserved from harm so that things may remain in tranquility. This was explained by the once magnificent and most adorned legates of the Greeks, with unanimous consent, in the year 1438 from the birth of **Jesus**, at the universal **Council of Basel** <note>A major ecumenical council of the Catholic Church held in the 15th century</note> in a certain illustrious and most eloquent oration. They spoke in these words: "For to be saved and salvation itself simply means nothing else among the Greeks and in our language than to remain and to exist" <note>original Greek: Τὸ γὰρ σωθῆναι καὶ σώζεσθαι καὶ ἡ σωτηρία ἁπλῶς οὐδὲν ἄλλο παρὰ τοῖς ἔλλησι καὶ τῇ ἡμετέρα βούλεται γλώττῃ ἢ τὸ συμμένειν καὶ εἶναι</note>. 

Therefore, men who are by their nature subject to death—so that they might cease to be—when they conform themselves to the will of God so that they may become immortal and enjoy a blessed state, are rightly said to have attained "salvation." And He who grants them that blessedness of immortality is rightly called the **Savior** (*Saluator*). This is a term that began to be used by the descendants of **Cicero**—having been unheard of before <note>Reuchlin notes that "Saluator" is a later Latin coinage, as classical authors like Cicero used "Servator"</note>—so that now "Savior" can be expressed in Latin. 

Indeed, every other form of "salvation" is named improperly and only by way of imagination. For what of it? If a doctor confers health upon a brute animal today, and the day after tomorrow it lapses back into plague and dies, never to return, shall that be called salvation? Or what of the gardener who aids a wilting flower, which is destined to fall the next day and be crushed into dust—is this three-day preservation of a thoroughly inconstant thing to be named salvation? In this way, **Hercules** once helped the Thasians, by which he is said to have given them "salvation," yet they often perished afterward, and today nothing of them remains but a name. In this way, **Ptolemy** preserved Egypt, which was afterwards devastated by so many wars and enemy incursions. In this way, the **Decii** <note>A Roman family famous for sacrificing themselves in battle to save the Republic</note> liberated Rome, which was nevertheless destroyed in a subsequent overthrow and fire. 

Believe me, every salvation that is broken by time is imperfect. Perfect salvation is that which makes the fleeting eternal, as **Apollo** taught concerning **Helen** after she was taken from death, in **Euripides'** *Orestes*, when he says: "She is here, whom you see in the folds of the air, both saved and not dead by your hand; for I saved her" <note>original Greek: ἡ δ' ἔσιν, ἣν ὁρᾶτ' ἐν αἰθέρ' πτυχαῖς, σεσωσμένη τε, κ' οὐ θανουσα πρὸς σέθεν. ἐγὼ γὰρ ἐξέσωσα</note>. And so that we might not be ignorant that this salvation proceeded not from Apollo, nor from other gods except as mediators, but more truly from the Supreme God to whom she dedicated herself by her singular virtue, he then adds: "For being the offspring of Jove, it was fitting for her to live incorruptibly" <note>original Greek: Διὸς γὰρ ἔσαν, ζῆν γὰρ ἄφθιτον χρεὼν</note>.

"By Castor, Helen’s brother, Marranus," said **Philolaus**, "you speak the truth, and you seem to have spoken wisely concerning true salvation. I agree that the **Savior**, about whom the sacred prophecies speak so magnificently and perpetually, must be one who is the preserver and restorer not so much of this Great World <note>The Macrocosm (the universe)</note>—not of regions and cities, nor of the lowest elements and stars, nor of wood and stones, nor of plants and trees, nor of fish, birds, or cattle (all of which follow nature as their guide and the instinct of their condition unerringly and properly, and remain what they are until their appointed end)—but rather of that **Lesser World** <note>The Microcosm (Man)</note>. That is, the savior of Man, who, often falling away from the rule of equity handed down to him and from the judgment of right reason, voluntarily plunges his noble nature through a heap of vices into the deep pools of evils and the pit of eternal corruption, from which he cannot turn back his step by his own strength or help. 

Here, Marranus, here I say, we have need of salvation; here we need a Savior. **Pythagoras** calls this class of creatures: 'Men who have self-chosen miseries' <note>original Greek: ἀνθρώπους αὐθαιρέτα πήματ' ἔχοντας</note>. Concerning whom he wrote thus in the *Golden Verses*: 'Wretched ones, who do not see nor hear the good things that are near; few understand the release from evils. Such a fate of mortals harms their minds, and they are carried from one place to another like rollers, having infinite miseries' <note>original Greek: πλήμονες, οἵτ' ἀγαθῶν πέλας ὄντων οὐκ ἐσορῶσιν, οὔτε κλύουσι: λύσιν δὲ κακῶν παῦροι συνίσασιν: τοίη μοῖρα βροτῶν βλάπτει φρένας, οἱ δὲ κυλίνδροις ἄλλοτ' ἐπ' ἄλλα φέρονται ἀπείρονα πήματ' ἔχοντες</note>. Indeed, our very prince of philosophers [Pythagoras] took this, without a doubt, from the **Hebrew Cabalists**...

# JOHANNES REUCHLIN

...accepted, as we can learn from Simon, he felt that the rational human is more noble than other things—namely, more divine—not merely content with a single operation or a uniform effect like other creatures that are always drawn by nature in a single way. Instead, the human is endowed with various gifts, like a **Pandora** <note>In Greek mythology, Pandora was the "all-gifted" woman; here it refers to the multifaceted nature of human talent</note>, which they may use in any event according to their free will. Because of this freedom, he says: **"A divine mind belongs to those mortals to whom sacred nature, bringing things forward, reveals each thing"** <note>original Greek: νοῦς θεῖος βροτοῖσιν οἷς ἱερὰ προφέρουσα φύσις δείκνυσιν ἕκαστα</note>. That is to say, the "sacred nature" is the intellectual soul. Therefore, I align the intellect with God, as the pure with the pure, whereas the soul recedes from God according to the lower senses, just as the impure recedes from the pure. From this it follows that reason—which, as he says, reveals things to us—makes us blessed when it turns itself toward the enjoyment of the mind. Conversely, it makes us miserable when it runs through the lust of the senses. Thus, the human seems to be placed in the middle between virtue and vice, like the substituted branching point in the **Pythagorean letter** <note>The letter 'Y' was used by Pythagoreans to symbolize the fork in the road of life: the narrow path of virtue and the broad path of vice</note> divided into two horns, where that famous **Hercules of Prodicus** <note>A reference to the "Choice of Hercules," a parable where the young hero must choose between a difficult life of virtue or an easy life of pleasure</note> sat down to deliberate in his tender youth.

Indeed, just as **Solon** (according to **Herodotus**) affirmed to **Croesus** <note>Solon was a Greek sage who warned the wealthy King Croesus that no one can be called truly happy until they have reached the end of their life well</note>, no one ought to be called blessed before their death and final funeral; likewise, no one should be thought truly miserable while living this life. But certainly, the final day is always to be awaited by the human, who, if they remain burdened by vices when the body is cast aside, begins to be truly miserable. As you heard in the previous discourse, **Pythagoras** divided that misery into two kinds. For after death, the miserable either lack the good things which are the gifts of blessedness (even though they neither see nor hear them, because they do not yet enjoy the vision of God)—these are among the number of those to be saved, not being so weighed down by misery that they might eventually escape their appointed punishments—or else the good things are most distantly removed from them, so that their evils shall never have any end. These latter are called those possessing "infinite loss."

Therefore, two dwellings of the lower world are described: the **Elysian Field**—that is, a transitory place for those to whom good things are promised so that they may return to the upper realms—and **Tartarus**, called so for its horrible sound ("tartar"), or perhaps named for its foulness (*teter*) or terror (*terror*). It is the place for those whose losses are infinite, who hang stretched upon the spokes and rays of wheels, where the unhappy **Theseus** sits and shall sit eternally, and others like him: **"From where they never emerge"** <note>original Greek: ὅθεν οὔποτε ἐκβαίνουσιν</note>, as is written by **Plato** imitating Pythagoras.

At this point, let the detractors approach me, those who do not cease to babbie against Pythagoras, a man of such great and outstanding character, whose teaching was trusted like an oracle of the gods. That seeker of truth was named by that age as "another Apollo," which the very name **Pythagoras** signifies <note>Reuchlin plays on the etymology: *Pythios* (Apollo) + *agoreuein* (to speak)</note>. However, a rumor has been spread everywhere that his opinion was that the human soul, after death, informs the bodies of certain brutes. This must seem incredible to men using reason, concerning such an excellent author of philosophy and such an abundant fountain of science, from whom the knowledge of divine and human things flowed to us. Rather, that suspicion of **metempsychosis** <note>The transmigration of souls from humans into animals</note> arose partly from ignorant men and partly from those hateful with envy. For the envious spite of his rivals—**Timon**, **Xenophanes**, **Cratinus**, **Aristophon**, **Hermippus**, and no small multitude of others—left nothing unpolluted concerning that man’s most outstanding virtue, his most innocent life, his distinguished learning, and his famous reputation. These men wrote many lies about Pythagoras in their books and published things that were never said or done by him. Or, if he did say such things, they twisted them into a worse sense so that it might easily be believed that such a great man taught inconsistently about the principles of things, about numbers, about not tasting beans, about abstaining from the flesh of animals, about the underworld, and about the transmigration of souls which we are now discussing. For how could he, who distinguished the patterns and species of things so clearly that they cannot be mutually transmuted or confused, communicate the human essence to a brute through its form? Since, by his own authority, not even a unity...

### ON THE CABALISTIC ART, BOOK II.

the substance of a certain number, according to its nature, is the unity of another number. For this reason he says: *The units in the <term>dyad</term> <note>The number two</note> itself are incomparable to those in the <term>triad</term> <note>The number three</note> itself.* <note>original Greek: αἱ δὲ μονάδες ἐν τῇ δυάδι αὐτῇ, πρὸς τὰς ἐν τριάδι αὐτῇ ἀσύμβλητοι</note> That is to say, the units in "twoness" are not the same as those in "threeness." This is how things consist in the physical world, though it is handled far differently in Mathematics, with which we have no business at present. Furthermore, the "one" of any thing is its participated essence, which will not occupy the essence of another thing. *For any substance participates in one species* <note>original Greek: ἑκάστη μὲν οὐσία ἑνὸς εἴδους μετέχει</note>. Therefore, life cannot pass into a different kind of living creature, nor into any beast whatsoever; rather, it remains in the Law of its own nature, holding its own duty. *Thus, species does not coincide with species* <note>original Greek: ὥς τε τὸ εἶδος εἴδει οὐ συνέχε-ται</note>. For although one seal impressed upon many bits of wax shapes them into many figures, the same piece of wax cannot bear the diverse forms of many different seals. Therefore, the seal of the human form, which is the **image of God**, is not permitted to seal a lower nature. 

Just as **Pythagoras** proposed all his teachings enigmatically, he designated the certain meaning of this opinion with his own specific mark, celebrating this as the most pleasing among his other symbols: *Do not carry the image of God in a ring* <note>original Greek: Ἐν δ’ δακτυλίῳ θεοῦ εἰκόνα μὴ περιφέρειν</note>. In my judgment, this is rightly understood in roughly this way: the image of God, which is the soul of man, cannot "seal" or give form to other natures round about it. For so says **Hermes Trismegistus**, the teacher of the Egyptians, in his book to **Asclepius**: "One part of man," he says, "is simple, which we call the form of divine likeness." And a little further down: "There are two images of God: namely, the World and Man." 

Therefore, those who are either envious or ignorant have explained him [Pythagoras] wrongly regarding the "passage of souls" after death, and also regarding their "descent" before the generation of a human. Surely there is no one endowed with any mind at all who would not now agree with me. For when many thought the soul of man was drawn out from the power of matter, our master himself determined it was more to be believed that the soul is infused into the body by God Himself. Because of this, he asserted that the soul exists "before" the body—which is not to be understood in terms of time, but in terms of purity and the dignity of its nature. 

Thus, he called this infusion the "descent" of the soul, which his followers later treated in various ways with many twists and turns, each in their own way, and not always according to the author's will. Pythagoras commanded that the descent of the human soul into the body should not be understood according to location, nor according to a movement from the Intellectual World through the individual spheres to the Elemental World (as **Proclus** and other supporters have claimed), but according to the series of natural forms, in which the final perfection of the human body is the rational soul. This soul so perfects the whole that man is called a "divine animal" by the best right. 

Pythagoras therefore intended that only those living beings whose "sacred nature"—that is, reason—demonstrates individual things, are of a divine race (namely, propagated by God, as he declared in the *Golden Verses*). Their species is neither changed nor converted; thus the forms of individual genera are permanent, even if they are dissimilar within that same form. 

After a man’s death, however, if he has died a just man, his soul transcends the pure <term>ether</term> <note>The clear, upper atmosphere of the gods</note> and spends eternity with the blessed, like a God among gods. For he says: *But setting the best driver, judgment, on high, when you leave the body and come into the free ether, you shall be an immortal God, incorruptible, and no longer mortal* <note>original Greek: ἀλλ’ ἡνίοχον γνώμην στήσας καθ’ ὕπερθεν ἀρίστην, ἡνίο’ ἀπολείψας σῶμα, ἐς αἰθέρ’ ἐλεύθε-ρον ἔλθῃς, ἔσσεαι ἀθάνατος θεός, ἄμβροτος οὐκ ἔτι θνητός</note>. 

But if a man dies unjust and wicked, in incurable and mortal sins, then he taught that his soul must wash away all its guilt through various punishments. These punishments, according to the magnitude and multitude of the crimes, would be more or less harsh and lasting. To these souls are assigned these lower places of nature and bodies—sometimes imaginary or figurative, sometimes real—not as an essential part that the soul informs, but which it inhabits like a **tenant** <note>original Latin: *inquilinus*</note> for the sake of enduring punishments. Or perhaps the soul assists these bodies through local proximity, like an internal mover to the thing moved, or is twisted with torture around them. Such is **Tityus** with the vultures, **Ixion** at the wheels of serpents, **Tantalus** in the river, **Sisyphus** at the stone, and **Prometheus** with the
