IOANNIS REUCHLINI

...eagles. <note>The previous page likely concluded a Pythagorean "symbol" or riddle involving eagles.</note> Since a hellish demon can seize even a body, why should a foul soul, condemned to the punishments of the lower world, not enter a body of true appearance by God’s dispensation? Or, it might clothe itself in air in whatever form it wishes for our sight, just as Dido, about to die, says to Aeneas: *I shall follow you, burning with black fires.* <note>original: "Sequar atris ignibus ardens" — from Virgil’s Aeneid IV, 384.</note> Pliny the Younger also writes of a believed occurrence regarding a house that the philosopher Athenodorus of Tarsus had purchased. It was infamous for its noise, because the phantom of a horrific old man was seen there. In our own age, similar terrifying sights occur, sometimes in thin forms and sometimes in thicker "skins." Then, the appearance and faces of wild beasts trick us in various ways: he becomes a terrifying and black tiger, a scaly dragon, and with a tawny neck he will give out a fierce sound of flame; he transforms himself into all sorts of miracles of things: both a horrible beast and a flowing river. <note>Reuchlin is quoting descriptions of the shape-shifter Proteus from Virgil's Georgics.</note> We certainly call these **apparent bodies**; that is, they are forms that can be taken up by the released souls of men. We know of this from the story of the <term>Lamia</term> <note>A mythological creature, often a female-faced spirit that preyed on young men.</note> of Menippus the Lycian, a philosopher, who took the form of a woman at Corinth. Apollonius of Tyana publicly revealed her to be a ghost. Finally, that ragged old beggar at Ephesus, who was the cause of a plague, is noted for this kind of metamorphosis; they say that when he was stoned, he appeared to be a dog, specifically a <term>Molossian</term> <note>A large, ancient breed of mastiff.</note>. Philostratus II wrote about both of these in the fourth book of his *Life of Apollonius*.

However, regarding what **Pythagoras** is said to have claimed—that he was once **Euphorbus** <note>A Trojan hero whose soul Pythagoras claimed to inhabit.</note>—there is another explanation. He did not first establish this as a literal belief, but rather it was a very old custom in popular speech. Because someone might be outstanding in a certain virtue or vice, they were likened to someone who had formerly been in that same condition to an eminent degree. For instance, if someone wanted to describe a man of most excellent strength, he would say he was **Hercules**. Thus Marcus Varro says: *A "Hercules" called Marcellus used to lift his own mule.* Numenius the Pythagorean also writes openly that *Plato is nothing other than Moses speaking Attic Greek.* <note>original: "nihil aliud esse Platone qua Moysen Attica loquente." Attic refers to the dialect of Athens.</note> Often, too, **Cicero** is called the "Latin Demosthenes." This happens because of an equality of virtues and works and a similarity of character, not because of a shared substance. Similarly, Litanus, the servant of Argyrippus in Plautus, said he was like Solon when he wrote laws; in the play *Asinaria*, he says: *For now I shall act as a man of influence here, clearly he is Solon, so that he may write the laws.* These lines from Plautus indicate a common ancient custom of speaking, where they said this man "is" that person because he was similar in nature, talent, character, love, cunning, or deed.

For this reason, the Romans used to add the little word "another" to this adage, as in: *You are another me,* and *I am another you,* even though they knew and saw that in reality I am not you, nor are you me. But because we perceive in both of us one talent, an equal pursuit, the same will, and the same effort, we look at the soul: *for the character of these men is being changed.* <note>original Greek: τὸ δὲ ἦθος αὐτῶν ἀνθρώπων μεταβαλλομένης</note> For the ancients called "souls" the movements and wills of men. Therefore, men of one character, care, and diligence, of similar purpose, equal motivation, and equal movement and sense, are called "unanimous" by affinity. Moreover, it is not at all foreign to the ancient philosophers to say that the soul is the "motive" and "sensitive" part in a human: *For the inanimate,* says **Aristotle**, *seems to differ [from the animate] in two ways especially: by motion and by sensation.* <note>original Greek: τὸ γὰρ ἄψυχον... δυοῖν μάλιστα διαφέρειν δοκεῖ, κινήσει τε καὶ τῷ αἰσθάνεσθαι</note> For the animate is seen to differ from the inanimate chiefly by these two: motion and sense. 

Therefore, whoever is affected and moved toward the same thing, and wants and seems to feel the same thing, is commonly said to be "of one soul" (<term>psyche</term>). From this comes the famous **metempsychosis** <note>Transmigration of souls.</note>; that is, "transanimation" is in reality nothing other to learned men than when an equal care, a similar movement, and a matching pursuit of some man of the past is found at a later time in another or the same living man. In such a context of common and practiced speech, Pythagoras—returning once from the **Persian Magi** (for that is what those wise men call their own)—could perhaps, for the sake of cheering the spirits of his friends, use the manner of the Magi and say that he was once **Euphorbus**, the soldier of the Trojans, and then Callicles, Hermotimus, Pyrrhus, Pyrandrus, Calidona, Alce, and then...

He also discusses the ability of spirits to assume physical forms, citing classical ghost stories and philosophical definitions of the soul.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that Pythagoras’s claim to have been the Trojan hero Euphorbus was not a literal statement of reincarnation, but a metaphorical or "ironic" expression of shared character and virtue. It transitions from discussing how spirits take on appearances to how historical figures can "live on" through shared traits.</meta>

->### ON THE CABALISTIC ART, BOOK II.<-

Pythagoras’s soul contained within itself an inclination toward certain noble things, specifically a disposition, devotion, and will situated in those particular individuals to whom he himself was most propensities moved during their lives. Most of all, since martial virtue had shone brightly in Euphorbus the Trojan, Pythagoras had obtained the soul of Euphorbus as if he now possessed Euphorbus's heart. Regarding this, he could indeed boast when athletes of military training praised him, seeing the strength of his sides, arms, and his whole body, and weighing his incredible love toward the strongest athletes. He demonstrated this to them with both costly equipment and magnificent expense; for previously, athletes were nourished on dried figs, soft cheese, and wheat, but he was found to be the first to nourish them with meat. Therefore, when they marveled that such a great love of fighting could exist in a philosopher devoted to letters, it is no wonder if he replied that "the soul of Euphorbus thrives in me." That is to say: the talent, the study, the movement, and the will of Euphorbus resided within him—who, although he was a teacher of peace and the author of quiet contemplation, nevertheless felt within himself a desire for war, as if for the Trojan War.

Upon hearing this, a rumor soon arose among the recklessly credulous, and the story spread far and wide—either through ignorance of the Pythagorean mysteries or through the malice of the envious, who always pervert the best things and repeat what they have heard much differently than it was said—that the soul of Euphorbus, slain in the Trojan war, had migrated into Pythagoras. This opinion was later supported by writers and poets. Hence Ovid, in the 15th book of his *Metamorphoses* <note>original: "Transfigurationis lib. 15"</note>, having borrowed these things among other trifles from the Greeks (who were accustomed to lying in the Cretan fashion), sang thus of Pythagoras:

> Souls lack death, and always, having left their former
> seat, they live in new homes and dwell there once received.
> I myself—for I remember it—in the time of the Trojan war,
> was Euphorbus, son of Panthous, in whose opposing breast
> once the heavy spear of the younger son of Atreus <note>Menelaus</note> was fixed.
> I recognized the shield, the burden of my left hand,
> recently in the temple of Juno in Abantian Argos.

But do not be amazed, excellent Marranus <note>Simon Marranus, a character in Reuchlin's dialogue representing a physician.</note>, for you will find none of these things written in the books of Pythagoras. For he himself published only three volumes: the first, *The Educational* <note>original Greek: παιδευτικὸν (Paideutikon)</note>; the second, *The Political* <note>original Greek: παλιτικὸν (Politikon)</note>; and the third, *The Physical* <note>original Greek: φυσικὸν (Physikon)</note>, which some attribute to Lysis. Therefore, let the third be for us the *Golden Verses*. Run through each of these, and nowhere in that man's work will you find anything regarding <term>transanimation</term> <note>The movement of a soul from one body to another; a synonym for transmigration or reincarnation.</note>. Thus, you may more easily believe that the rumor was falsely sown by the envious—whatever is fabricated concerning that <term>metempsychosis</term> <note>original Greek: μετεμψύχωσις (the migration of souls)</note>. This is clearly indicated by the diversity of the narrative: some affirm this shield was brought back to the temple of Juno at Argos, while others say it was dedicated to Pallas Athena in Athens, and that the inscription on the shield itself was: "To Athena, these things: Menelaus from Euphorbus" <note>original Greek: ᾶς τὰδ' ἀθηνᾶ, μενέλαως ὰς ἀθηνᾶς (As tade Athena, Menelaos as Athenas)</note>. This is recorded by Maximus of Tyre in his 16th Dissertation. 

How much faith one should place in testimony of this kind, let the legal experts decide. For my part, I cannot be led to believe that a man so excellent in every science and so grave taught Ovid’s fable about the passage of souls; and I should think it all the less believable the more that excellent authors have handed down a different tradition. For many claim that Pythagoras was the first among the Greeks to discover that souls are immortal, but they say what is manifestly false. For Homer, nearly the oldest of the Greeks and far earlier, brought forth this dogma; in his works, the souls of the deceased in the underworld discuss many things and prophesy many things. I ask you, does his admirable song suggest anything other than "images of the dead" <note>original Greek: ειδώλας τὲ νεκύας (eidolas te nekyas)</note>, meaning that our souls remain after death? Furthermore, in the companions of Ulysses, he clearly showed that the imprudent souls of men, when separated from the body, do not indeed take on the natures of beasts, but only put on the *habits* of brutes, and pay the penalties with such horror as Circe <note>The enchantress in the Odyssey who turned men into pigs.</note> commanded. However, whoever holds the root and the flower of <term>Moly</term> <note>A magical herb mentioned in the Odyssey used to protect against Circe's magic.</note>, their souls—on the authority of Mercury—will be secure, as it says in the tenth book of the *Odyssey*. 

But let us return to that irony concerning Euphorbus. Whenever suitable authors write about him, they confess that all the divine dogmas of Pythagoras were handed down as <term>enigmas</term> <note>original Greek: αινίγματα (ainigmata)</note>—that is, through obscure allegory. The famous Pythagorean, Apollonius of Tyana, in his treatise with Thespesion the chief philosopher...

<summary>Reuchlin argues that Pythagoras's claim to be the reincarnation of Euphorbus was a metaphorical expression of shared character, blaming poets like Ovid for misinterpreting it as literal transmigration. He asserts that the immortality of the soul was a Greek concept long before Pythagoras, appearing first in Homer's epics.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the "enigmatic" nature of Pythagoras’s claim to have been Euphorbus. Having established that the claim may have been a metaphor for shared virtues, Reuchlin now looks to the accounts of the Neopythagorean philosopher Apollonius of Tyana and other classical sources to argue that the "transmigration" described by Pythagoras was actually a lesson about the transformation of matter, not the literal movement of a soul between different species.</meta>

IOANNES REUCHLIN

speaking with a sage of the Gymnosophists <note>literally "naked philosophers," a group of ancient Indian or African ascetics</note> as recorded in the sixth volume of Philostratus: **"I touch upon enigmas; I grant these things to the wisdom of Pythagoras, having bypassed the enigma"** <note>original Greek: αἰνιγμάτων ἅπτομαι, σοφίᾳ πυθαγόρᾳ ξυγχωρῶ ταῦτα, παρελθὼν τὸ αἴνιγμα</note>. That is to say: if I touch upon riddles, it is because the wisdom of Pythagoras allows for this—namely, to speak in riddles. 

Furthermore, when he was disputing with the Brahmans of India in the third volume of that same work, inquiring about how they felt regarding the soul, he says: **"Just as Pythagoras taught you, we in turn have handed down to the Egyptians."** Apollonius then begins: **"Will you then say that you were one of the Trojans, as Pythagoras was Euphorbus?"** 

Hear now, Marranus, how cleverly Iarchas <note>The leader of the Indian Brahmans in Philostratus's account</note> responded, first asking which of those who led the Greek army to Troy he considered most worthy of reputation. To which Apollonius replied that Achilles held the first rank. Then Iarchas said: **"By the gods, Apollonius, consider him my ancestor—or rather, the ancestral body. For it was fitting for Pythagoras to say these things as well"** <note>original Greek: πρὸς θεῶν, ἔφη, ἀπολλώνιε· ὁ ἐμὸν πρόγονον ἐμὸν, μᾶλλον δὲ, τὸ πρόγονον σῶμα. ταῦτα γὰρ καὶ πυθαγόρας σύμφορον ἦν εἰπεῖν</note>. By this he meant: "Apollonius, consider that person even my progenitor, or more accurately, the 'pre-existing body' <note>term: <term>progignens corpus</term>, the physical matter that existed before and contributed to the current form</note>; for this is also what Pythagoras thought of Euphorbus." 

Next, he tells how King Ganges of the Indians, the son of the river Ganges, surpassed others in many virtues, and that he himself was that very "pre-generating body" which he now inhabited. These words speak not of the **transmigration of souls**, but of the **transmutation of bodies**, much like any material that is fit to take on the form of this or that thing. 

It is just as if a Comedy were to say, "I was previously a Tragedy," because a Comedy is born from the same letters and elements as a Tragedy, as Aristotle says in the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*. Or if a certain dog were to say, "Long ago I was a horse"—namely, that the body of a certain horse was eaten by the dog, and when that nourishment was converted into the substance of the thing nourished, that horse might be called, in common speech, the dog's **pre-existing body** <note>original Greek: πρόσωμα</note>; that is to say, the source from which it was generated. For no one would judge from such a statement that the soul of the horse had passed into the dog. 

Why then should we believe that Pythagoras taught that souls pass into other bodies solely because he said he was once Euphorbus? For here it is clearly confessed that this statement applies not to the soul, but that the body itself was judged to have been Euphorbus. Nevertheless, this saying of his was not plain, but a pure enigma, through which he wished to hint at a certain secret unknown to that age: namely, **prime matter** <note>term: <term>materia prima</term>, the fundamental "stuff" of the universe that has no form of its own but can become anything</note>, which is not only capable of receiving all forms, but is even "greedy" for them and is ultimately so restless that it is never satisfied by any single form. 

This was the view of the philosopher-Emperor Marcus Aurelius, when he wrote in the third book of his *Meditations*: **"Nothing is so dear to the nature of the whole as to change all things and make new things like them. For every thing is, in a way, the seed of that which shall come from it"** <note>original Greek: οὐδὲν οὕτω φίλον τῇ φύσει, ὡς τὸ τὰ πάντα μεταβάλλειν καὶ ποιεῖν νέα ὅμοια. σπέρμα γὰρ τρόπον τινὰ οὗ δὴ ἐξ αὐτῶν ἐσομένων</note>. 

And the same author says in the seventh book: **"The nature of the whole, out of the universal substance as if from wax, fashioned a little horse; then, dissolving this into the nature of a tree, it used that same matter for a little man, and then for something else"** <note>original Greek: ἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις, ἐκ τῆς ὅλης οὐσίας ὡς κηροῦ ἱππάριον ἔπλασε, συγχέασα δὲ τοῦτο εἰς δένδρου φύσιν, συνεχρήσατο τῇ ὕλῃ αὐτὰ εἰς ἀνθρωπάριον εἶτα εἰς ἀλό τι</note>. 

For this reason, nature is called by Orpheus by these epithets: **resourceful mother** <note>original Greek: πολυμήχανος μήτηρ</note> and **the decider of different forms of life** <note>original Greek: ἀλλοβιομορφοδίαιτος</note>. 

Whatever the case may be, I for my part will far more readily believe that when Pythagoras said he was Euphorbus or someone else, he introduced it as an enigma for the sake of an example. But if it is believed that he was weaving a literal history, then surely he must be thought to have done it for no other reason than to show that a soul, once separated from the body, can—by the authority of God—return to that **very same body** which it left and deserted long ago, and not into any other. For it would be one and the same body, though called by different names, in which Pythagoras lived again so many times. From this we could have learned long ago from Iarchas, the wisest of the Indians, that identity lies not in size or quantity, but in substance and being. Just as the sea, although it is of one kind and one body, we nevertheless say this part is the **Aegean**, that part the **Ionian**, and that other the **Myr-** <note>catchword: Myrtoan</note>

<summary>Reuchlin argues that Pythagoras’s claim of reincarnation was a philosophical "enigma" about the persistence of matter rather than the literal migration of souls. Using sources like Philostratus and Marcus Aurelius, he suggests that "being Euphorbus" refers to the shared physical substance or "prime matter" that undergoes constant transformation in nature.</summary>

# ON THE CABALISTIC ART, BOOK II.

...and another the Crisean. Thus, they named one man who was reborn several times: first Aethalides, then Euphorbus, afterwards Hermotimus, then Pyrrhus, and finally our famous Pythagoras. He, as a most speculative and divine philosopher, did not attribute so many regenerations to the forces of nature, but to God alone, whom he called Mercury (as Heraclides Ponticus reports in this *Palingenesia* <note>meaning "rebirth" or "regeneration"</note>), in order to show that no one lives again except by divine power. For as Justin relates—that Christian philosopher and martyr, in his *Exhortation to the Greeks*—God was especially honored by Pythagoras with this title: **"the animation of the universe"** <note>original Greek: ψύχωσις τῶν ὅλων</note>; that is, the Vitalization of all things, because He infuses the soul into all men, takes it away once infused, and restores it when taken away, as often and whenever He wills. Such a thing has often been seen in other men and is certain through experience, according to the accounts of the most noble writers.

For Aristeas of Proconnesus once died in the workshop of a certain fuller. Then, in the seventh year thereafter, he appeared alive to the citizens of that city, and he himself then composed poems about the hyperborean Arimaspians, which Herodotus mentions prominently in the fourth book of his *Histories*. Moreover, there lived in Armenia one Er, a Pamphylian by birth, who had fallen in battle. When the other corpses, already decaying, were picked up on the tenth day, he was found whole with an uncorrupted body. Having been carried home for the funeral rites, on the twelfth day after his death, while he was placed upon the pyre, he rose again and recounted what he had seen in the meantime. Plato wrote these things in the tenth volume of the *Republic*. 

To this also belongs what we read of a Roman girl who had died; as she was being carried to the grave, she was restored to life by Apollonius of Tyana, in the fourth book of Philostratus; and Alcestis is also told to have lived again for a long time after being resuscitated by Hercules. Then Marranus said: "How close you come to our views, Philolaus! For if Simon were standing here, he would recount to us from the Hebrew books how God once took from the spirit that was in Moses and gave it to the seventy men. After some time, when Elijah was taken from among men, his spirit settled upon Elisha, and likewise he himself made the son of the Shunammite woman live again after death. I add now the dead Samuel, whom a certain woman in Endor raised, and who spoke with King Saul after his resurrection. 

"Hear truly what that prophet Ezekiel saw: namely, a field full of the dry bones of the dead. And bone came to bone, each to its joint, and behold, sinews and flesh grew over them, and skin was stretched over them from above, and the spirit entered into them and they lived again, and they stood upon their feet. These things are contained in the sacred writings of the Hebrews, but many more are read in the described histories of the Christians. Indeed, for my part, I would dare to affirm this to you without parable, without enigma, and with all irony removed: that Jesus the Nazarene truly and plainly raised the brother of Martha, named Lazarus, who had been dead for four days. Furthermore, He restored to life the deceased son of a certain widow, and the daughter of Jairus, the leader of the synagogue, and others commemorated in Holy Scripture. God also raised this same Jesus, and at his death, many bodies of those who had died arose, and coming out of the tombs, they came into the holy city and appeared to many. Finally, Paul of Tarsus restored Eutychus, who had died by accident, alive to the light. Martin, not yet a bishop—indeed, not yet baptized—raised three dead men. 

"I could produce a catalog of men recalled from death to their former life, were you not aware that it is easily believed by us Christians that the souls of men return into bodies; for we plainly confess that a general resurrection of all human bodies will happen again for living. Concerning this, the most eloquent Athenian philosopher Athenagoras wrote an entire book for the Christians **"On the Resurrection"** <note>original Greek: περὶ ἀναστάσεως</note>, certainly worthy of learned ears. And to the Turks, Moors, and Hagarenes <note>descendants of Hagar; a common term for Muslims in Reuchlin's era</note>, Muhammad speaks thus in the Alcoran <note>The Quran</note>: To those who say, 'When you are bones, or reduced to nothing, how will you be made into new men?' respond: 'Even if you were made of stone or iron, or whatever is harder, He who created you the first time...'"

<summary>Reuchlin catalogs various accounts of resurrection and the return of souls from classical Greek, Hebrew, Christian, and Islamic traditions to argue for the soul's survival and divine power over life. He transitions from the Pythagorean idea of rebirth (palingenesia) to the Christian doctrine of the general resurrection of the dead.</summary>

...er, He will recall you to be resurrected again to life; even in the *Sura* <note>Original: *Azoara*. Reuchlin refers to the Quran, specifically Sura 45</note> again in 45, it says: "He who first formed us, will give us life a second time." Hence, I would wish that we follow Pythagoras with all the greater veneration, since he—more so than almost all other Greek philosophers—has come closer to our faith in nearly all matters. For we see how Aristotle handed down nothing that he could not touch with his hand, see with his eyes, or grasp with a syllogism. Therefore, at the end of his treatise *On Generation and Corruption*, he by no means admitted the return of a dead man, using a very weak argument; he agreed more with Alcmaeon than with his own teachers, contrary to the well-worn proverb: **"Human affairs are a circle"** <note>Original Greek: κύκλον εῖν τὰ ἀνθρώπινα</note>. Those others followed him, a crowd of philosophizers who are to be rebuked in this: that they presume to know everything and think others know nothing. They mock Pythagoras after all the rest, and cry out that famous line: **"Who is buying Pythagoras? Who wants to be more than human? Who wants to know the harmony of the universe and live again?"** <note>Original Greek: τίς ἀνώυεταε, τίς ὑπὲρ ἄνθρωπον εῖν βόλεταε, τίς ἀδέιναι ἡ τὸ ἁρμονίαν, καὶ ἀναβιώναι πάλιν;</note>. 

Ridiculously, they bid for him under the spear <note>A Roman custom for slave auctions</note> as if he were a piece of livestock to be despised, or a worthless slave. I will gladly allow those men to know many things, provided they also believe that others have learned something. This has so stirred my stomach now against those who are accustomed to easily disparage the most ancient teachers and the princes of philosophy, that I have flared up more extensively than was necessary, so that you may know that I love your Pythagoras no less than is right, and that I vehemently hate his calumniators—not as men, but as monsters of men. 

Then Philolaus said: "There are some," he says, "who must be forgiven for being ignorant of such hidden and divine mysteries, for we cannot all do everything. Therefore, they will return to favor if they have slandered things out of ignorance. However, those who were once trained in silence, but threw away the white Pythagorean toga and began to wound the majesty of his doctrine with insults and to diminish the status <note>Original: *caput minuere*, a legal term for losing civil rights or status</note> of such a great philosopher—those I shall judge not only arrogant, but the most ungrateful of men. Among their number is Xenophanes, who is said to have joked about him in his *Elegies* so that, when he saw Pythagoras once pitying a dog being beaten, he said: 'Stop this, for it is the soul of a dear friend which I recognized by its voice.' But that is a manifest taunt found in Diogenes Laërtius; as is the claim that Pythagoras's disciples feast with Pluto among the dead, and that he himself saw the soul of Hesiod bound to a bronze column, groaning and gnashing its teeth. Then also the soul of Homer hanging from a tree and surrounded by serpents. These and similar crimes of sycophancy are the defamations and calumnies of the most trivial sophists, who 'foul everything with their touch, pollute the feast with their mouths, and leave foul tracks behind' <note>A reference to the Harpies in Virgil’s *Aeneid*</note>. 

As for what they spread about the eating of meat and of all living things, which they claim Pythagoras prohibited, it disturbs me almost not at all, since there are very famous authors who refute those tales. For that distinguished writer Aristoxenus says that Pythagoras did not abstain from living things, but ate meat. Porphyry, in his book **On Abstinence from Animal Food** <note>Original Greek: περὶ ἀποχῆς ἐμψύχων</note>, proves this by the fact that while others were nourished by cheese or figs, he was the first of all to feed athletes with the food of meat, and said that meat has an incredible power for acquiring strength. So says Porphyry. And Apollodorus the arithmetician testifies that he sacrificed a hundred oxen when he discovered that **"in a right-angled triangle, the side subtending the right angle is equal in power to the sides containing it"** <note>Original Greek: ὃπ γώνε ὀρθογωνίε ἡ τὴν ὀρθὴν γωνίαν ὑποτέινεσα δύναται ταῖς περιεχόσαις. This is the first formal statement of the Pythagorean Theorem in the text</note>. 

Nevertheless, he was of a most modest life, of moderate nourishment, and very little drink, as Lycon of Iasus writes about Pythagoras. From this, perhaps his use of meat was rare; for often he fed only on thin honey, as Athenaeus says in his tenth book on the *Dinners of the Learned*. And for that reason, if he had diligently warned students of letters to avoid those things which would be heavy food, lest the brain...

<meta>This page continues the defense of Pythagoras against his critics, specifically addressing his dietary guidelines and his symbolic use of numbers as a method for spiritual and intellectual discipline.</meta>

### ON THE CABALISTIC ART, BOOK II.

...lest he be harmed by an imprudent burden on the stomach, whereby they might be able to apply themselves more vehemently to contemplation, who would not praise such a faithful teacher? For he had learned among the Hebrews that certain heavy foods were prohibited in their Law; he likewise knew that among the Indians certain things were to be avoided, such as sea fish, which are neither useful to the stomach nor accepted as offerings to the gods (for no one has ever heard of a fish being immolated in a sacrifice); and finally, he had received from the Egyptians the rule concerning the bean, that it is not a "clean" legume, as Herodotus noted in his *Euterpe* <note>The second book of Herodotus's *Histories*</note>. They clearly did not take these things as fodder, but perpetually sought tranquility of mind through the study of letters—although he did not wish such pious admonitions to be observed as exactly and "to the nail" as if they were the Law of the Twelve Tables <note>The foundational legislation of Roman law</note>. Indeed, it was reported by Xenophilus and Aristoxenus, and certain others of an older generation who were nearly his contemporaries, that he himself lived on small pigs and tender young goats; and you will find in the fourth book of the *Attic Nights* by Aulus Gellius that he used no legume more often than the bean, so that it might gently loosen the bowels. 

But concerning beans, it will be explained later among the other symbols. For now, let the earlier things I said come to your mind, as well as the later things I am about to say, so that you may recognize how impiously certain shameful buffoons of philosophy mock Pythagoras, the prince of philosophers, with a "rear-view sneer" <note>Original: *postica sanna*. A mocking gesture made behind someone's back</note> because he taught that **Number** is the principle of all things. Since number is truly a "discrete quantity," they argue it follows after things rather than preceding them, as if Pythagoras himself understood numbers to be like literal pebbles thrown about, from which all things originated. I marvel at such men, not without a laugh, because although they have heard from the testimony of the wisest men that almost all Pythagorean philosophy—especially that which concerns divine matters—is mystical and proposed through riddles, they nevertheless demand that this most divine part of wisdom regarding numbers be taken plainly and without any metaphor, thus imitating the stupidity of the Tyrrhenians. 

However, it was the custom of the ancients and the sages of the most remote age to hand down the deep investigation of wisdom through the allegories of secret letters and the mysteries of the senses. Thus, everything among the most ancient philosophers and poets is full of riddles, both because of the obscurity of the subject matter and because of a slight contempt for the common rabble. **"For of things not clearly seen by human weakness, a myth is a more distinct interpreter,"** <note>Original Greek: πραγμάτων γὰρ τὰ ἀνθρώπινα ἀσαφῶς ἢ καθορωμένων σαφῶς, εὐσημονέστερος ἑρμηνεὺς ὁ μῦθος</note> says **Maximus of Tyre** in his tenth dissertation. That is to say: for things not clearly perceived by human infirmity, a fable is a more suitable interpreter; indeed, it properly suits philosophers when it is enunciated under a pious veil of fictions, clothed in honest and upright matters and names, according to the authority of **Macrobius**. I believe this most carefully excites and introduces the minds of scholars to the notion of wonderful things. For that which is ready at the doorstep is sought with less diligence than that which is situated far off and hidden in the abyss of the deep. Thus, ease of apprehension (believe one who has experienced it) breeds negligence of study in students, and that which is very easily obtained is sought after coldly. 

It also happens sometimes that we cannot express abstruse matters with any proper choice of words, which we would be forced to enunciate with long circuits and variously composed speech, unless it had been conveniently found to use a brief riddle. Nor is this without practical use: for commanders in war are accustomed to issue certain signals to the opposing camps, which they call *tesserae* <note>Watchwords or passwords</note>, so that each leader can recognize his own soldiers, and they can recognize one another. Just as in Caesar's war the word was **"Venus the Mother,"** and for Sylla it was **"Delphic Apollo,"** and for Marius **"The God Lar,"** and for Jephthah it was **"Shibboleth."** <note>A reference to Judges 12:6, where the word was used as a password to identify enemies</note> Thus, it would not be at all unseemly to hand down the peculiar and secret symbols of doctrine to one’s associates, so that whichever disciples used them more frequently would become dearer to the teacher and love one another more than the rest. From this, the Pythagoreans fashioned for themselves a certain chain of indissoluble love and friendship through specific secret symbols. For Pythagoras was, above all, most studious in reconciling friendship, and if he learned that someone shared his symbols, he immediately took him as a companion and friend, as **Laërtius** <note>Diogenes Laertius, biographer of the Greek philosophers</note> records. And so it happened that all desired the Pythagorean symbols more ardently: that is, the knowledge of the mysteries...

# THE ART OF THE CABALA, BOOK II
## BY JOHANNES REUCHLIN

...to use signs, both so that they might be more pleasing to their teacher and so that it would be apparent to everyone that they were noble Pythagoreans. Moved by this, as Plutarch records in the eighth book of his *Table Talk* <note>Original: *vivualium*</note>, Philinus—alone among all the guests of Sulla the Carthaginian—abstained from animal flesh at feasts so that he might be recognized as a Pythagorean. For this reason, it is written that he followed the dogma more in its letter than its spirit, which was also a fault worthy of reproach in other Pythagoreans: those who were immodestly affected by strange and unique customs. For instance, they would not break bread at the dinners of companions and friends, or they sacrificed with bare feet, or when about to speak, they turned away from the sun. Leaving the public road, they departed through side paths; they never or rarely laughed with those who were laughing; or they entirely abstained from eating beans. They followed these family rituals more out of superstition than led by right reason. They were a mere imitation of the "shell" of the symbols, neglecting the intent, so that they might become known by such marks and be seen by the common people as Pythagoreans of that same order. These kinds of symbols are therefore merely the signs of a single group or "college."

But let us also add that, for those of us measuring the vast spaces of divine and human things and dealing with numbers, enigmatic symbols contribute very much to memory. These are marks fixed in the mind so that whenever one wishes to remember, they may quickly be offered to our faculties. Therefore, the most convenient symbol concerning the principles of things will be "one" and "two." For what occurs more quickly to those looking at individual things than "one" and "two," when we wish to scrutinize the causes and origin of the universe? Indeed, at first glance, the eye sees that which is "the same" and is "not another"—a concept we first grasp in the mind: that "the same" and "the other" are "one" and "two."

Alcmaeon of Croton, who lived in the age of Pythagoras, named many things in pairs, which he called "contrarieties"—perhaps like the "strife" of Empedocles <note>Empedocles was a Greek philosopher who proposed "Love" and "Strife" as the forces driving the universe</note>. Yet he set those down as wandering and diverse without limit, such as white and black, sweet and bitter, good and evil, small and large. Aristotle is a witness to this in his *Metaphysics* <note>Original: *postnaturalia* - literally "the things after the physics"</note>. But the Pythagoreans, because of their love for arithmetic, constrained those diverse things—which correspond to each other back and forth—into ten pairs, which the followers of Alcmaeon had called "contrarieties." They organized them into that famous and all-containing number ten:

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| Finite and Infinite | Odd and Even |
| One and Many | Right and Left |
| Masculine and Feminine | Resting and Moving |
| Straight and Curved | Light and Darkness |
| Good and Evil | Square and Oblong |

And they are each of these things because they are "two"; they are diverse precisely because they are two. For if they were "one," they would not be contraries. Indeed, they reduced all things into ten because that number is the most perfect of all. It is the number by which all nations and all people—except for the Thracians <note>Classical writers often claimed the Thracians were so primitive they only counted to four</note>—both Greeks and Barbarians, count individual things. They do not stop before it, nor do they proceed beyond it, as if following the natural "calculators" of the ten fingers. 

Surely this most adorned World shows its perfection, for we see it moved in only ten spheres according to the Pythagoreans. It is also so much more perfect than the rest as it contains more kinds of counting: even, odd, square, cube, long, plane, prime, uncompounded, and first compounded. Nothing is more absolute than this number, because within ten proportions, four cubic numbers are consumed, by which the Pythagoreans say the universe consists. 

Archytas also, that noble Pythagorean of Tarentum, encompasses everything that exists within the number ten. Aristotle the Stagirite, the leader of the Peripatetic school, imitates him and names the ten "genera of being" as the "Ten Categories." He chose to title his book with this name, showing philosophically—as Eustathius maintained—the ten <term>things</term> <note>Original Greek: *pragmata* - real entities or objects</note>; or as Alexander of Aphrodisias says, ten <term>voices</term> <note>Original Greek: *phonas* - words or spoken terms</note>; or as Porphyry says, ten <term>thoughts</term> <note>Original Greek: *noemata* - mental concepts</note>. Or, as Iamblichus perhaps more correctly says: ten simple words, not merely as sounds, but as signs for simple things themselves, mediated by ten simple concepts. Some...

# ON THE CABALISTIC ART, BOOK II

Alexander Aegaeus, Ammonius (son of Hermias), and Simplicius <note>These are famous ancient commentators on Aristotle, particularly active in the late antique period.</note>—all distinguished lovers of wisdom—agree on this point. They diligently judged that within those ten most general categories of being <note>Aristotle's "Categories" or "Genera," which classify every object of human apprehension.</note>, two primary types can be found into which everything is divided, even if they arise from a single essence: such as substance and accident, or the corporeal and the incorporeal, or the material and the immaterial, or the simple and the composite. For the number ten <note>The "denarius" or Decad.</note> loves duality in such a way that, progressing from the one, it is born through two, and through two it returns to the one.

For the first "uncomposed" <term>triad</term><note>The number three, regarded as the first "real" number by many ancients because it has a beginning, middle, and end.</note> does not consist of one and two as a "composite," but rather as a "constant." This is because "the one" <note>the Monad</note> has no "position" according to Iamblichus. Therefore, it does not create a composition if we wish to follow the proper meaning of the words: <note>original Greek: ὅτι γὰρ ἡ μονὰς μένουσα ἔτι μονὰς θέσιν προσλαμβάνει, ὅτι ἡ στιγμὴ μένουσα στιγμὴ τὴν θέσιν ἀπέβαλε</note> "For the unit, while remaining the unit, acquires position; for the point, while being a point, loses position," as Simplicius says in his commentaries on the category of quantity. From this, we can understand the difference that distinguishes the unit from the mathematical point. 

And since nothing exists before the one, we rightly say that the one is first. The <term>dyad</term><note>The number two.</note>, however, is not composed of numbers, because it is coordinated from only a single unit and another unit. Thus, it is the "first number," because it is the "first multitude," and it can be measured by no number except by the single unit, which is the common measure of all numbers. For "once two" is nothing other than two. For this reason, that multitude which is called the triad <note>three</note> is most truly called by the mathematicians the "first uncomposed number." The dyad that precedes it is not an "uncomposed number," but more properly a "non-composite." 

Therefore, the triad—desiring not to be idle, but rather that its goodness be multiplied among all creatures without envy—moves from power into action. It looks with its perpetual mind upon that "fruitful" part of itself which produces a great multitude (as numbers from numbers), and upon that "essential" part of itself which is the one, the source and origin of all production, the beginning of all procession, and the permanent stability of all immutable substance. And so, it turns back into itself, multiplying itself by way of unity and duality, saying: "once, twice, two are four."

Behold that <term>tetractys</term><note>The "Fourfold," which the Pythagoreans famously swore their oaths by; 1+2+3+4=10.</note> or "fourness" about which I spoke with you before. This is the "Idea" of all things that have been created because, as the mathematicians say, all progression is perfected in the number four. From this arises that <term>decad</term><note>The number ten.</note> which we call the ten most general categories of all things. For one, two, three, and four—coming out from omnipotent power into the act of energy—produce ten. 

The half of ten is five. Therefore, place five in the middle like a standard-bearer <note>Original: *signiferum*</note> in the midst of an army. On its right side, place the next higher number, which is six; on its left side, the next lower number, which is four. These two joined together also constitute ten. Again, place on its right side the next higher number, seven, and on the left, the next lower number, three; these two joined together similarly constitute ten. Place again on the right side the next higher number, eight, and on the left, the next lower, two; these two joined together also constitute ten. Finally, place on the right the remaining nine, and on the left, one. Now, reduce those nine back to one, and ten rises again. When these are referred back to twenty, they begin again to be a unit, and so on through all the cardinal numbers up to a hundred. For just as "twice one" makes two, and "thrice one" makes three, and "four times one" makes four, and so on, so "twice ten" makes twenty, and "thrice ten" thirty, and "four times ten" forty, and so on—no differently with a hundred, and no differently with a thousand and beyond.

This is the reason why we write "ten" in Greek using the letter *iota* <note>original: ι</note>, which is a straight stroke, or why we mark it in Hebrew with a single point <note>A reference to the letter *Yod* or the dot signifying the number 10.</note>. These signs represent a simple unit to both the "barbarians" <note>Non-Greeks/Non-Latins, often referring to Hebrews or Egyptians in this context.</note> and the Latins alike, since the number ten arises from the unit and ends in it. The Pythagorean symbol for this is "one, two," which Zaratas <note>A name often used in the Renaissance for Zoroaster, who was legendary as a teacher of Pythagoras.</note>, the teacher of Pythagoras, called the "names of propagation..."

# THE WRITINGS OF JOHANN REUCHLIN

...to use signs, both because they would be more pleasing to their teacher, and so that it would be apparent to all that they were noble Pythagoreans. Moved by this, in Plutarch's eighth book of *Table Talk*, Philinus—alone among all the guests of Sylla the Carthaginian—abstained from animal food so that he might be recognized as a Pythagorean. For this reason, he was rebuked by Naxius <note>original: "Nacio", likely referring to a specific follower or a person from Naxos</note>, a Tyrrhenian by birth and a disciple of Moderatus the Pythagorean <note>Moderatus of Gades was a first-century philosopher who revived Pythagorean teachings</note>, for following the written letter of the doctrine rather than its true meaning. 

This was a fault worthy of reproach in other followers of Pythagoras as well: those who, affected immodestly by separate and singular customs, would not break bread even at the dinners of associates and friends, or sacrificed with bare feet, or turned away from the sun when about to speak, or left the common road to travel through side-paths, or never (or rarely) laughed with those who were laughing, or completely abstained from eating beans—occupations of the household which they took up more out of superstition than led by right reason. By mere imitation of the "husk" <note>meaning the outer shell or surface-level appearance</note> of the symbols, neglecting the intent, they sought to be known by such signs and to be seen by the public as Pythagoreans of that same order. 

Therefore, symbols of this kind are the signs of a single fellowship. Furthermore, let us add that enigmatic symbols—that is, marks fixed in the mind—contribute greatly to memory as we measure out the vast spaces of divine and human affairs and handle innumerable subjects, so that whenever we wish to remember, they are quickly presented to our faculties. 

Therefore, the most convenient symbol concerning the principles of things would be **one** and **two**. For what occurs more quickly to those looking at individual things than **one** and **two**, when we wish to scrutinize the causes and origin of the universe? For at first sight, the eyes perceive that which is the "same," and that which is "not another," by which we first conceive in the mind that "the same" and "the other" are **one** and **two**. 

However, Alcmaeon of Croton, who lived in the age of Pythagoras, called "two" those many things which he said were "oppositions"—much like the "strife" of Empedocles <note>Empedocles proposed that the universe was governed by the forces of Love (attraction) and Strife (repulsion)</note>—yet he set them down as wandering and infinitely diverse, such as white and black, sweet and bitter, good and evil, small and large. Aristotle bears witness to this in the first book of his *Metaphysics* <note>original: "postnaturalia", a literal Latin translation of the Greek "Metaphysics," meaning the books following the "Physics"</note>. 

But the Pythagoreans, because of their love for arithmetic, compressed those diverse things (which are contrary to one another and which Alcmaeon called "oppositions") into the number ten—that famous and all-containing number. These include: 
1. Limited and unlimited 
2. Odd and even 
3. One and many 
4. Right and left 
5. Masculine and feminine 
6. Resting and moving 
7. Straight and curved 
8. Light and darkness 
9. Good and evil 
10. Square and oblong 

And so they are either one or the other; because they are two, they are diverse. For if they were one, they would not be contraries. Indeed, they reduced the universe to ten because it is the most perfect of all numbers, by which all nations and all peoples (both Greeks and Barbarians, except for the Thracians) count individual things, neither stopping before it nor proceeding beyond it, as if using the natural counters of the ten fingers. 

Surely this most adorned World which we behold shows its perfection, for it is moved by only ten spheres according to the Pythagoreans. It is also more perfect than the rest in as much as it contains more types of counting: even, odd, square, cube, long, plane, prime (uncomposite), and first composite. Nothing is more absolute than this, because in ten proportions, four cubic numbers are consumed, from which the Pythagoreans say the universe consists. 

Archytas, that noble Pythagorean of Tarentum, also encompasses everything that exists within the number ten. Aristotle the Stagirite, the leader of the Peripatetic school, imitates him, naming ten types of being as "ten categories." He chose to title his volume with this name, showing philosophically (as Eustathius wished) ten <term>pragmata</term> <note>original Greek: πράγματα; meaning real things or objects</note>: that is, real beings; or as Alexander of Aphrodisias had it, ten <term>phonas</term> <note>original Greek: φωνάς; meaning sounds or voices</note>: that is, words; or as Porphyry had it, ten <term>noemata</term> <note>original Greek: νοήματα; meaning thoughts or concepts</note>: that is, intellects or concepts. Or perhaps more correctly, as Iamblichus held, ten simple words—not merely as words, but as signifying the simple things themselves through the medium of ten simple concepts.

### ON THE CABALISTIC ART, BOOK II.

Alexander of Aegae, Ammonius son of Hermias, and Simplicius <note>Famous Neoplatonic commentators on Aristotle</note>—all distinguished lovers of wisdom—agree on this point. They diligently judged that within those ten "most general beings" <note>Referring to Aristotle’s ten Categories: substance, quantity, quality, etc.</note>, two primary divisions can be found into which all are divided, even though they arise from a single essence. These divisions are substance and accident, or the corporeal and the incorporeal, or the material and the immaterial, or the simple and the composite. In this way, the number ten loves the number two, so that having progressed from the One, it is born through the Two, and through the Two, it returns to the One. 

For the first "uncomposed" ternary <note>The number three</note> is not indeed *composed* of one and two, but rather *consists* of them. According to Iamblichus <note>A Neopythagorean philosopher</note>, the One does not have "position," and therefore it does not create a "composition," if we wish to follow the proper use of words. As Simplicius says in his commentaries on the category of quantity: <note>original Greek: "ὅτι γὰρ ἡ μονὰς μόνη ἔτι μονὰς θέσιν προσλαμβάνει, ὅτι ἡ σιγμὴ φύσει σιγμὴ τὴν θέσιν ἀπέβαλε"</note> "For neither the unit, while remaining a unit, assumes a position; nor does the point, while remaining a point, cast off its position." From this, we can recognize the difference by which a unit <note>a numerical one</note> differs from a point <note>a geometric one</note>. And since there is nothing before the One, we rightly say that the One is first. 

The binary <note>The number two</note>, however, is not composed of numbers, because it is coordinated from the unit alone—one and one. It is therefore the "first number" because it is the "first multitude," and it can be measured by no number except by the unit alone, which is the common measure of all numbers; for "once two" is nothing other than two. For this reason, that multitude which is called the ternary <note>three</note> is most truly called by mathematicians the "first uncomposed number." The binary which precedes it is not an uncomposed number, but more properly "not-composed." 

Now, the ternary, desiring not to be idle but rather to have its goodness multiplied among all creatures without envy, progresses from power into operation. It gazes upon and reflects with a perpetual mind on that fecundity within itself—which is highly productive of multitude, like number from number—and that essential quality which is the One, the source and origin of all production and the beginning of all progression, as well as the permanence of every immutable substance. Thus, it turns back into itself, multiplying itself by way of unity and duality, saying: "once twice two are four." 

Behold that **Tetractys** <note>The "four-fold" or "Quaternity," a sacred Pythagorean symbol</note>, that "fourness" of which I spoke with you before; this is the *Idea* of all things that have been created. For as the mathematicians say, every progression is perfected in the number four. From this arises that **Decad** <note>The number ten</note> which we call the ten most general genera of all things. For one, two, three, and four, exiting from omnipotent power into the act of energy, produce ten. 

The half of ten is five. Therefore, place five in the center, like a standard-bearer <note>original: "ligniferum," literally a wood-bearer or rank-leader</note> in the middle of an army. On its right side, place the next higher number, which is six; on its left side, the next lower number, which is four. These two joined together also constitute ten. Again, on the right side, place the next higher number, which is seven, and on the left, the next lower, which is three; these two joined together similarly constitute ten. Again, on the right, place the next higher, eight, and on the left, the next lower, two; these two joined together also constitute ten. Finally, place the remaining nine on the right and one on the left. Now reduce those nine to one, and ten rises again. When these are referred back to twenty, they begin to be a "unit" once more, and so on through all the cardinal numbers up to a hundred. For just as twice one makes two, and three times one makes three, and four times one makes four, and so on beyond, so twice ten makes twenty, and three times ten makes thirty, and four times ten makes forty, and so on beyond—not otherwise for a hundred, nor differently for a thousand and beyond. 

This is indeed the reason why we write "ten" in Greek with the letter **iota** <note>Written as "ι", which looks like a vertical stroke</note>, which is an upright little rod, or we note it in Hebrew with a single **point** <note>The letter "Yod", the smallest letter, often resembling a dot or point</note>. These signs, to foreigners as well as Latins, otherwise represent a simple unit, precisely because the number ten originates from the unit and ends in it. Of this, there exists a Pythagorean symbol, namely "one, two," which Zaratas <note>Another name for Zoroaster, whom Reuchlin identifies as a teacher of Pythagoras</note>, the teacher of Pythagoras, called the names of propagation...

### JOHANN REUCHLIN

...is accustomed to pronounce, calling the "one" father and the "two" mother, according to the testimony of Plutarch of Chaeronea <note>A Greek philosopher and biographer, c. 46–120 AD</note> in his *On the Generation of the Soul in the Timaeus*. For as was accepted before, the one and the two, together with the divine essence, produce that fourfold nature, the Tetractys <note>The Pythagorean "four," often represented as a triangle of ten dots, considered the root of all creation</note>, which is the Idea of all things completed in the number ten. Pythagoras affirms it to be the <note>original Greek: παγὰν ἀενάου φύσεως</note> "fountain of perpetual nature"—that is, the source of eternal nature, which is nothing other than the knowledge of things operating rationally in the divine mind. Indeed, Pythagoras allegorically called this Mind of God "Number," since he asserted that number is the principle of the universe. For so Plutarch writes in the fourth book of his *Opinions of the Philosophers*: <note>original Greek: τὸν δ᾽ ἀριθμὸν πυθαγόρας ἀντὶ τοῦ νοῦ λαβεῖ</note> "Pythagoras takes Number in place of Mind." This is a most fitting sign, because among incorporeal things nothing is more divine than the mind, and among separate things nothing is simpler than number. 

Furthermore, nothing can be thought of that is more similar to the mind; and from the fountain of perpetual nature, the Pythagorean number flows down through streams and channels. The one and the two—that which from eternity was, will be, and always is in the very fountain of the immense Ocean, gushing forth in abundance—are what men in the ancient age named "Zeus." This very "one" (as Aristotle wished, citing this line from Homer: <note>original Greek: εἷς κοίρανος</note> "let there be one ruler") they called *Zena* instead of *Zeua*, evidently from the word for "living" <note>Reuchlin is linking the name Zeus/Zena to the Greek verb 'zen', to live</note>. The Romans called him Jove, as if *Zeua*, and Cornutus <note>A Stoic philosopher of the 1st century AD</note> in his book on Greek theology asserts that he is the soul of the whole world. 

The "two," however, was named as the wife of that *Zenos*: that is, the sister and spouse of Jove, about whom Homer speaks in the fourteenth book of the *Iliad*: <note>original Greek: Ἥρη δ' εἰσεῖδε χρυσόθρονος ὀφθαλμοῖσιν αὐτίκα ἐγνωτὸν πρᾳ ζήνα δ' ἐπ' ἀκροτάτης κορυφῆς πολυπίδακος ἴδης ἥμενον</note> "Hera of the golden throne beheld with her eyes her own brother and brother-in-law Zena"—that is, Jove—"sitting on the highest peak of many-fountained Ida." 

By this, we can more easily understand the wisdom of the most learned poets regarding the origin of things. On many-fountained Ida—a mountain named for its "prospect" or "view," from <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ ἰδεῖν</note> "from seeing," or from the word <note>original Greek: ἐκ τοῦ ἴδω τὸ γινώσκω</note> "I see," meaning "I know"—Jupiter and Juno reside, just like the "one" and the "two" in that flowing Idea of the fourfold Tetractys. From there flow the principles of all things, which philosophers of a later age named "form" and "matter." The "form" and "primary matter" of the philosophers are the same as the "one" and "two" of the most ancient philosophers, and the "Jupiter" and "Juno" of the worthy and illustrious poets. They join together in the Cave of Mount Ida and meet in the Idea of the divine mind. Both are pulled by two-horse chariots, and both by four horses; but in descending, Jupiter remains on Olympus, while Juno tends toward lower things, as Homer testifies, saying: <note>original Greek: εἶμι γὰρ ὀψομένη πολυφόρβου πείρατα γαίης. νῦν δὲ σοῦ εἵνεκα δεῦρο κατ' ὀλύμπου τό δ' ἱκάνω</note> "For I go to see the ends of the fruitful earth; but now for your sake I come here down from Olympus." 

Yet, she does not entirely desert the other. In this way, the first beginning issues from the divine mind. For the Tetractys, looking back at that essence which is the first producer of all units, and simultaneously remembering its own origin from the first product (since it is a dyad or "two"), says: "once one, twice <unclear>two</unclear>." Soon the fourfold number is established, having the highest unity at the summit of its peak. Suddenly, it becomes a pyramid, whose base is the flat quaternary <note>The number four</note> which among mathematicians signifies a surface. Above this, the radiating light of the divine unity already mentioned creates the form and appearance of incorporeal fire. This is because of Juno's—that is, matter's—departure to the lower regions, from which immediately arises the nature of essential light; not a burning light, but an illuminating one. 

And this is the creation of the "Middle World," which Simon the Jew <note>Possibly referring to a specific Kabbalistic source or a literary persona in the dialogue</note> called the "Supreme World," because the World cannot endure comparison to the Deity; therefore, in its own judgment, it is called supreme and incomparable. But this world is rightly called the "Middle Olympus" because it is entirely bright and full of separate forms, <note>original Greek: ἐπ' ἀθάνατον</note> "on the immortal floor," as in the eighth book of the *Iliad*—that is, where the surface or pavement of the immortals stands. For it is nicknamed the "dwelling of the Gods," or as Virgil <note>Maro</note> more rightly says in the tenth book of the *Aeneid*, "the high house of the Gods," the peak of which is unity, the walls a trinity, and the surface a quaternary. And this is seen more clearly when number is already separated from the divine...

<meta>This page continues Reuchlin’s explanation of the "Tetractys" (the number four). Having established it as the "fountain of nature" on the previous page, he now transitions from numerical theory to geometry, explaining how the fourfold nature manifests as a pyramid—the symbol of divine fire and the structure of the intelligible world.</meta>

<page-num>669</page-num>
<header>ON THE ART OF THE CABALA, BOOK II.</header>

When the flow from its source has turned and diverted slightly toward the shape of created beings, let us then set down a square <note>original: "tetragonum"</note> to represent the Tetractys. In each of its corners, let us place a point like a unit, and for the unit at the summit—which now begins to have a fixed position—let us raise the highest peak as far as possible. Once this is done, the four sides raised upward will be four triangles constructed upon their quadrangular width and drawn together into a single high point. Behold, this is the very pyramid which is the form of fire, according to the testimony of Timaeus of Locri <note>A Pythagorean philosopher featured in Plato's dialogues</note>, who wrote in his book *On the Soul of the World* in the Doric dialect: <note>original Greek: ἐξ ὧ ἁ πυραμὶς τέσσαρας βάσιας καὶ τὰς ἴσας γωνίας ἔχοισα συντίθεται, ἀπὸ πυρὸς ὠκινάτοτατον καὶ λεπτομερέστατον</note> "from which the pyramid, having four bases and equal angles, is composed; the swiftest and most subtle form of fire." This is surely essential light, without matter, separate, closest to God, and eternal life—as we read in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics* <note>original: "postnaturalia," a literal translation of "Metaphysics" meaning "after the physics"</note> and in the second book of *On the Heavens*: "The work of the Mind is life, but the operation of God is immortality; and that is eternal life." Aristotle borrowed these ideas from the Pythagoreans.

And yet, God Himself is not a created light, but the luminous author of all light. Therefore, God—the Best and Greatest, incomparable in His divine Trinity—contains within Himself that most perfect and secluded pyramid, which similarly signifies fiery vigor, rising from a triangular base into the heights and encompassing the world. For this reason, both the Chaldeans and the Hebrews claim that God is fire. Indeed, the pyramid produced by the number four is the fiery light of the incorporeal and immaterial world of "separate intelligences" <note>Angelic or divine minds existing independently of matter</note>, beyond the visible sky. This realm is called *Aion* <note>original Greek: αἰών</note> by the Greeks, and by us it is called "age," "eternity," and "ether." From this, the ether is called the "splendor of eternity," where there is no body, no place, no vacuum, no time, no old age, and no change; rather, there are unchangeable and impassive beings possessing the best life, which they enjoy throughout the whole *Aion*—that is, eternity or the age. 

These are almost the very words of the Stagirite <note>A common nickname for Aristotle, born in Stagira</note>, which, like those of the Platonists and Socratics, flowed from Pythagoras. He wrote thus in his *Golden Verses*: "If, having left the body behind, you reach the free ether, you shall be an immortal god." Having overcome the trials of this life, you will recognize the cohabitation of the immortal gods and mortal men, which he elegantly calls *systasis* <note>original Greek: σύστασιν</note>, from "standing together." Through this, he shows us three properties of the "Middle World," which he names the "free ether," as it is segregated from the power of matter and preserved in freedom to be warmed by the glow of God, and to warm lower things by its imperceptible motion. For it is called "ether" from the Greek <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀεὶ θερμαίνεσθαι ἢ φαίνειν</note>, meaning "from always heating" or "shining." 

Its properties are these: condition, chorus, and order. The "condition" of that world is that everything within it is of the purest form. They assert its nature is "Jovial" <note>associated with the god Jupiter/Jove</note>, which gives form to both immortals and mortals, and through its specific nourishment preserves all things of both worlds in their being. Concerning this, the words of Maro <note>The Roman poet Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro)</note> survive: "O father, O eternal power of men and gods." For this reason, because of its nourishing heat, the spiritual Sun was called "Jupiter" by the ancients. Hence the priests of the "False Mars" <note>Mars Gradivus</note> called him *Lucecius* <note>Giver of Light</note>, and the Cretans called him *Phosphorus* <note>Light-bringer</note>. From him, Olympus is named, because it shines totally; there, the whole of Jupiter presides and rules—indeed, "he shook all of Olympus with his nod." Its "condition," I say, is to receive simple, immaterial, separate forms that exist by themselves, both universal and individual. For it contains all the "Ideated Ideas" <note>The archetypal blueprints of all things in the divine mind</note> of genera and species, acting as the very examples to be imitated by more limited copies. The "Signatory Exemplar" <note>The original seal or master-mold</note> of these consists in the divine mind. For we wish to name what is in the world of the Godhead as the "Absolute Exemplar"; in the Intelligible World as the "Abstract Example"; and in the Sensible World <note>The physical world we perceive with our senses</note> not as an example, but as that "limited copy"—just like a seal, the image on the seal, and the impressed wax.

To this is added, second, the "chorus," another property. It is so named from the Greek for "joy" <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ χαρᾶς</note>, referring to the infinite joy of the blessed spirits and the immutable pleasure of the gods, who are the inhabitants and citizens of that spring-like dwelling, triumphing with myrtle crowns of Olympian victory, feasting on ambrosia and...

<page-num>670</page-num>
<header>JOHANNES REUCHLIN</header>

...perpetually enjoys the nectar of the divine banquet, laughing with an inextinguishable laughter. Regarding this, that wisest of poets, Homer <note>original: "Homerus"</note>, wrote: <note>original Greek: ἄσβεστος γὰρ ἀρ' ἐνῶρτο γέλως μακάρεσσι θεοῖσιν</note> "For inextinguishable laughter was indeed raised among the blessed gods." This signifies that all their joy is everlasting, which the illustrious Melesigenes <note>A traditional epithet for Homer, meaning "born by the river Meles."</note> elegantly expressed in the first book of the *Iliad* as a continuous harmony of lyres and the beloved instruments of the Muses, with dancing, choral songs, banquets, and quiet chambers for sweet sleep. Why not, Marranus? <note>Marranus is one of the three interlocutors in this dialogue, representing a traveler and seeker of wisdom.</note> What greater pleasure can be imagined than to behold God's will, and after Him, the <term>Ideas</term> <note>In the Platonic sense: the perfect, original patterns of all created things.</note> and forms of all things, more purely and transparently than any secondary creature can? And then, to reveal this vision to those below—this is the unique and happy privilege of the gods. Therefore, in Latin they are sometimes called "Gods" <note>original: "Dei"</note>, and in Greek *theoi* <note>original: "θεοὶ"</note> from the word for "vision" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῆς θέας"</note>, which is to say, from speculation and seeing; for this reason, *theasthai* <note>original: "θεᾶσθαι"</note> means to gaze upon and to see. They are also sometimes called "angels" <note>From the Greek "angelos," meaning messenger.</note> when they announce what they have seen to others, as Orpheus says when invoking Mercury: <note>original Greek: κλῦθί με ἑρμεία διὸς ἄγγελε μαιάδος υἱέ. ἑρμενεῦ πάντων</note> "Hear me, Hermes, messenger of Zeus, son of Maia, interpreter of all things." For we use the word *angellein* <note>original: "ἀγγέλλειν"</note> to mean "to announce" and "to explain." 

Indeed, we frequently use one term for the other without considering their specific duties, so that in common speech we use "gods" and "angels" interchangeably. For when Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD).</note> wrote in his *Introduction* that both we and the angels are rational beings, Boethius <note>The Roman philosopher (c. 477–524 AD) who translated Porphyry into Latin.</note>, translating into Latin, said: "Both we and the 'gods' are rational." This usage is found in the books of many others. Therefore, let no one think that when we name these "gods," they are being made equal to the supreme and ineffable God who holds that name. For we call the supreme majesty "God" because He infinitely penetrates all beings and runs through every single thing—deriving the name from *theein* <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ θέειν"</note>, which means "to run." Truly, God is much more interior and intimate to every single thing than that thing is to itself; though He is nowhere, He is everywhere. But we do not call those others "Gods" in this way; they only carry out a limited province assigned to them and are sent for a specific task. 

As for <term>Demons</term> <note>In the ancient sense: spiritual beings that mediate between gods and men, not necessarily "evil" spirits.</note>, however good they may be, they are nonetheless not admitted into this choir of the Middle World by Pythagoras and his followers. For so says Plotinus <note>A major Greek-speaking philosopher (c. 204–270 AD), the founder of Neoplatonism.</note>—who, according to the testimony of Porphyry and Longinus, was seen to follow the mysteries of the Pythagoreans most perfectly—in his book *On Love*: "We say and believe that the race of Gods is free from passion. To the Demons, however, we attribute passions, though we also say they are eternal, occupying the rank immediately following the Gods." It is certainly better to call no one in the Intelligible World a "demon"; rather, even if a demon were placed there, he should be considered a God. Thus far Plotinus speaks, who is certainly brief in all his teaching and must be weighed with an attentive mind, especially in this difficult passage where the secrets of the ancient poets speaking of the gods can be read without trouble and without provoking many people. 

A third property of the Intelligible World was demonstrated by Pythagoras himself when he said: "If you live by right reason, grieving for misdeeds and rejoicing in good deeds, and pray to the Gods to perfect your work, then, having cast off the body and departed into the ether, you shall be an immortal God." Here we must consider the order Pythagoras observes in the pursuit of human happiness. For that incorporeal heaven of the Middle World and that invisible Olympus of the blessed admits nothing impure; therefore, vices must be fled, and virtues embraced. Secondly, the salvation of men lies in the mercy of God; therefore, the divinity must be worshipped, and the higher beings must be entreated to perfect our work. Only then is nothing of matter, nothing of the body, and nothing mixed received; thus, one must first die and cast off the holy body before being counted among the Gods. This is the "order of the ages," so that for pure and chosen men who have finished their lives, the super-celestial hall of the indigenous Gods is granted. Then, human nature shares a common life of perpetual existence with the sacred angelic spirits in the invisible, yet all-encompassing super-celestial heaven—a world of rest outside the sensible world, where the true Olympus exists. It is not imaginary or poetic, nor is it something that rolls or rotates and never rests. 

Then Marranus said: "How closely this approaches the sects of our own times..."

...Pythagoras comes closest of all. For in the Law of the Christians <note>The New Testament, specifically the Book of Revelation.</note> it is similarly read that dead men among the number of those rising again are like the angels of God in heaven, where the tabernacle of God is among men. Nothing defiled shall enter there, nor anything that works an abomination or a lie. You shall be like the voice of harpers harping upon their harps, and a new song; and the dead who are written in the book of life see a new heaven and a new earth. For the first heaven and the first earth had passed away from them. There too is the city of the blessed, possessing the glory of God, and its walls are constructed of jasper, and its foundations adorned with every precious stone. And the Lord Almighty is the temple of that city, and from His throne is brought forth a river of living water, as bright as crystal. Indeed, the foundation and surface of His city is a square: for the words of the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation 21:16.</note> from which these are taken, are these: <term>and the city lies square</term> <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἡ πόλις τετράγωνος κεῖται"</note>: that is, the city sits as a quadrangle, which Pope Hippolytus <note>Saint Hippolytus of Rome (c. 170–235 AD), an early Christian theologian.</note> explained to be so <term>on account of its stability and firmness</term> <note>original Greek: "διὰ τὸ ἑδραῖον καὶ πάγιον"</note>. You seem to me to lead this back to the number of your Pythagoras, and the figure of the pyramid, erected from a square base, which mathematicians are accustomed to count among the solids; clearly I would, by the best right, call him not only your Pythagoras but more truly *our* Pythagoras, and I shall indeed call him ours as long as I live, because he alone out of the whole crowd of ancient philosophers tasted our wisdom more aptly, more elegantly, and more properly. Nor does he stand very far in the foundation of his doctrine from the Persians and the Palestinians <note>A common Renaissance way of referring to the Jews/Hebrews.</note>, and in our age the Arabs, being himself the author of the Italian philosophy. For so we read in the first <term>Azoara</term> <note>From the Arabic "Sura," meaning a chapter of the Quran. Reuchlin is using a medieval Latin translation.</note> of the Law of Muhammad: that God will lead the good into paradise, where they will possess the sweetest waters, fruits of many kinds, various produce, and most becoming and pure women, and every good thing forever. And in the fifty-first Azoara: "But those who believe" (he says) "and do good shall possess the most beautiful places of paradise, they shall fulfill their every desire, and this is the greatest gain"; such a promise indeed announces to them the highest joy. Then, in the doctrine of Muhammad it is written: "If any kind of delight were lacking there, happiness would be least full. In vain, therefore, would delights be present if pleasure were absent." And a little earlier: "To its inhabitants" (he says) "whatever can be desired will be immediately present, and they will all be perfect in the stature of Adam, but in the form of Jesus Christ, never suffering any increase or decrease." And in the Quran, chapter 64: "There indeed the believers shall recline upon silk carpets and purple bedding, and they shall perpetually enjoy all things dear to them, and they shall marry the most beautiful girls, like hyacinth and pearls, never deflowered by men or devils, nor subject to menstruation. And there shall be trees shining with a color between green and yellow, and strongly flowing fountains, and palms and pomegranates." Do you not perceive here, Philolaus <note>One of the interlocutors in the dialogue, named after the famous Pythagorean philosopher.</note>, that the greatest part of these things is symbolic? And almost everything you have heard is narrated allegorically in the manner of the Pythagoreans, which Muhammad openly confesses in the book of doctrine when he says: "The other world after this world is one of which no likeness can be set forth: for its inhabitants are not mortal, nor are its days numbered." By which he declares himself to have written allegorically concerning divine matters, and not all things plainly and openly, even when he counted the days of blessedness as days of a thousand years, and years as forty thousand years. And he taught that paradise has a golden floor distinguished by emeralds and hyacinths frequently placed between, planted with every fruit-bearing tree, with streams running through pleasant fields, some of which pour forth milk, others white honey, and others the purest wine. These are in the book of the doctrine of Muhammad, where by a "sensible" <note>Meaning a paradise that can be perceived by the senses.</note> paradise he designates that garden of the Intelligible World which reason does not grasp. For Muhammad proposed two paradises to us in the Quran, when in the sixty-fourth Azoara he says: "He who shall fear while standing before God shall receive as an inheritance two paradises, fertile with manifold things and every kind of good." So also Abdias <note>Likely referring to Obadiah the Proselyte or a specific medieval polemical source.</note> shows two cities of Jerusalem when he asks in the book of doctrine...
