### JOHANN REUCHLIN

<margin>50</margin>

<warning>The right edge of the text is slightly cropped or obscured by the binding, resulting in the loss of final letters and punctuation on several lines.</warning>

Why Jerusalem is called the "blessed house." Muhammad <note>original: "Mahometh"</note> replied [concerning] where the celestial Jerusalem is directly situated. These things we have heard, our Simon the Kabbalist says, allude not a little to our own views—namely, concerning the two paradises, one [celestial] and the other terrestrial, signifying twin worlds: the visible and the invisible. You have explained [the invisible world] in few words; therefore, I pray you, Philolaus, that you proceed regarding our own world, which we inhabit. I shall do so diligently, Philolaus said, if I first warn you not to wander among those "philosophasters" <note>A dismissive term for fake or superficial philosophers.</note> who only understand those things which they perceive with their eyes. As Ammonius, the son of Hermias, wrote regarding Antisthenes, <note>Antisthenes (c. 445–365 BC) was a Greek philosopher and a pupil of Socrates.</note> when he had said: "I see a man, but I do not see 'humanity'." <note>This refers to the classic debate between Nominalism (only individuals exist) and Realism (universal concepts like "humanity" are real).</note> Hence he thought that humanity was nothing in the nature of things except a figment of thought: <note>original Greek: "ταῦτα ἐκείνων εἴδωλα, τῇ αἰσθήσει ζῶν καὶ μὴ δυναμένων τῷ λόγῳ εἰς μείζονα εὕρεσιν ἑαυτῶν ἀνηγμένων"</note> that is, **these things are but idols of those others, for one who lives by sensation alone and is unable, by use of reason, to lift himself up to a greater discovery of himself.** So says the son of Hermias in his *Isagoge* <note>An "Isagoge" is an introductory text; here it refers to a commentary on Porphyry’s introduction to logic.</note>. No different are those of such dull wit <note>original: "tufo ingenio"</note> who cannot contemplate anything more sharply than what the pupils of their eyes can grasp or their hands can touch. Whatever they hear concerning the heavenly life, the higher gods, souls in heaven, or the celestial beings, they immediately drag down to the visible heaven, the spheres of the stars, the moving firmament, and the orbits we perceive with our senses—as if the blessed life could consist in such a whirlwind of motions and unquiet tumult of changes!

But those who follow spiritual sense and subtle illumination understand that there is greater truth in those things which are not seen than in those which are seen. Toward this, the purpose of the Pythagoreans is inclined: so that they might believe that through this world, and whatever is placed within it, there is a **shadowed image** of that true world which exists outside the heavens, comprising only the <term>Intelligences</term> <note>Spiritual beings or "angels" in the philosophical sense.</note>, the forms, and the souls separated from bodies in substance, power, and operation. Hence, they firmly hold that the souls of men, purged of all foul filth and having cast off the bodily mass, live in the Olympus of eternity, far beyond all visible heavens and beyond any risk of misfortune, gifted with all liberty and subject to no necessity. For thus says the famous Pythagorean, Plotinus, in his fourth book *On One's Own Guardian Spirit*:
> Souls (he says) that have departed outside the sensible world must be understood to have transcended the demonic nature, and every lot of "becoming," and every necessity of this world, so long as they inhabit the intellectual world. Thus far Plotinus.

Whenever, therefore, mention is made of true gods, separate intelligences, pure forms, divine spirits, those above, angels, and the souls of the blessed, always remember and turn over in your mind that **Supreme World**: the intelligible, immaterial, simple, abstract, incorporeal heaven, the invisible Olympus, the mental paradise, the supernatural ether, perceivable neither by sense nor by [mere human] reason. Leaving that aside for now, let us descend to our corporeal and sensible world, the pattern of which is in the incomparable mind of the Deity, and the example of which is in the <term>Intelligible World</term> <note>The realm of ideas or spiritual realities.</note> of forms and archetypes, <term>the self-subsisting</term> <note>original Greek: "τὸ ἀνθυπόστατον"</note> in itself. And just as the **One** is the origin of the mental world, so the **Two** <note>The "dyad" in Pythagorean thought.</note> shall be for us the beginning of the corporeal world. For it would not be corporeal unless it consisted of these four: point, line, surface, and thickness <note>or depth</note>, according to the example of the cubic figure which one, two, three, and four constitute. For the One, fixed in position, creates a **point**. A **line** is drawn from one point to another and is made of two. A **surface** arises from three lines. **Thickness** is born from four: [extending] forward, backward, upward, and downward. Therefore, just as the binary number multiplied by itself—two times two—produces a **quaternion** [four]; so the binary, returning and twisting itself back into itself by saying "two times two, twice," makes the first **cube** [eight]. Therefore, after the five, which is the tetragonic <note>four-sided</note> pyramid—the principle of the Intelligible World—comes the cube of eight sides, which we set over the sensible world as its architect. For among the principles of things, no memory is held of the **seven** <note>septenary</note>: because...

He uses the progression of numbers (1 to 4) and geometric shapes (point to cube) to describe how the physical universe is structured as a shadow of a higher spiritual reality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discourse of Philolaus on Pythagorean cosmology. Having previously discussed the "square" as a symbol of the divine and the intelligible world, he now descends into the "sensible" world of physical matter, using the transition from a flat square to a solid cube as a metaphor for the creation of substance.</meta>

# ON THE KABBALISTIC ART, BOOK II.

...therefore it is "nothing-bearing," <note>original: "nihil pariens"</note> and for that reason it is named Pallas. <note>Pallas Athena was a virgin goddess; Pythagoreans associated the number one (the monad) with her because it is "motherless" and does not produce other numbers within the decad by multiplication.</note> We turn, therefore, first to the cube, a truly fertile number and the leader of multitude and variety, as it is constituted by two and by four. Wherefore, just as Pythagoras’s teacher, Zaratas, <note>Zaratas is a name often used by Renaissance authors to refer to Zoroaster.</note> named "two" as the mother, so we call the cube proceeding from it "matter," the floor of all natural things, and the foundation and seat of substantial forms. Concerning this, Timaeus of Locri, <note>A Pythagorean philosopher featured in Plato's dialogues.</note> that famous Pythagorean, writes in his book *On the Soul of the World*: "from the square is born the cube <note>original Greek: "λίθον" (lithon), literally "the stone"</note>, a body most similar and stable in every way; having six sides and eight angles." <note>original Greek: "ἐκ δὲ τοῦ τετραγώνου γεννᾶται τὸν λίθον, ὁμοιοτάτου καὶ στασίμου πάντη σῶμα. ἐξ μὲν πλευρᾶς, ὀκτὼ δὲ γωνίας ἔχον"</note> If any form, having been submerged, leans upon this floor—if it has slipped into this solid receptacle and been placed in this material seat—it is not received in a wandering or general way, but becomes stable, unique, individual, and incommunicable. It is as if it were assigned to a specific plot of land, subjected to time and place, and proscribed, as it were, from freedom into the slavery of matter.

Therefore, we see twin principles of temporal things flow from one source: the Pyramid and the cube—that is, form and matter. These are understood to have proceeded from the same square, whose Idea, as we have shown before, is the Tetractys, <note>The Tetractys is a triangular figure of ten points, a sacred symbol for Pythagoreans representing the organization of the universe.</note> the divine exemplar of Pythagoras. I have thus explained these primordial symbols as briefly as I could, which in truth designate nothing other than matter and form.

And since it is necessary to posit a third thing by which they may be united—for they do not flow together of their own accord, nor does a fortuitous clash of any forms into matter occur, nor does the matter of one thing happen to receive the form of another (for bronze or iron is not generated from a human body as soon as the soul has departed, nor does wool come from a stone)—since it is therefore necessary to posit some third thing by which they are united, it will be necessary, I think, to bring in a principle other than the Aristotelian "privation" <note>Aristotle argued that change requires matter, form, and "privation" (the absence of a form). Reuchlin finds this insufficient.</note> to move matter toward a desire for form, so that as this or that form ceases, another may be introduced in its turn. For privation and potentiality do nothing substantively, since they possess no real activity and thus the least amount of being; how much less can they join or unite a certain form to any matter?

Hence some were found who said that in place of privation, "motion" was the third principle. But since motion is an accident, <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that isn't essential to a thing's nature.</note> how shall it be a principle of substance? Or who shall be the mover of that motion? Therefore, both Athenians—Socrates, son of Sophroniscus, and Plato, son of Ariston—contemplated more wisely. In place of motion or privation, they placed God, the most active of all agents, saying that there are three principles of things: God, Idea, and Matter. Pythagoras had previously symbolized this secretly with these arcane notes, asserting that the principles of all things are: the Infinite, the One, and the Two. He designated God as the author of Infinitude, Form as the author of Unity, and Matter as the author of Alterity (Difference). He placed the Infinite in the super-supreme and incomparable World; the One (or Identity) in the Intellectual World; and the Two (or Alterity) in the Sensible World—for matter is indeed the mother of alteration.

Furthermore, God joins matter and form through a Law imposed upon nature itself. For this reason, long before the time of Pythagoras, that most ancient Orpheus, in his book of hymns, [placed a third principle] after Jupiter (that is, Form, who is named by him "the principle of all" <note>original Greek: "ἀρχὴ πάντων"</note>) and after Juno (that is, Matter, whom he calls "Jupiter’s bedfellow and mother of all" <note>original Greek: "διὸς σύνεκτροφον παντογενέθλον"</note>). For under the name of Juno, he addresses matter with these words: "For without you, nothing at all has known the nature of life, for you share in all things, solemnly mingled with the air." <note>original Greek: "χωρὶς γὰρ σέθεν οὐδὲν ὅλως ζωῆς φύσιν ἔγνω, κοινωνεῖς γὰρ ἅπασιν κεκραμένη ἠέρι σεμνῶς"</note> Therefore, after (I say) Jupiter as Form and Juno as Matter, the same Orpheus added "Law"—that is, distribution—so that there would be a third principle of nature, and he nicknamed it "the stabilizer of nature." <note>original Greek: "φύσεως τὸ βέβαιον"</note> For Law is called *Nomos* in Greek, as you know, from *nemo*, which means "I divide and distribute," <note>original Greek: "τὸ μερίζω"</note> since it distributes to all that which is their own, or that which pertains to them. This, he says, is the "righteous seal of celestial law." <note>original Greek: "οὐρανίου νόμου σφραγῖδα δικαίαν"</note> (Thus he sang in his hymns): that is, the celestial Law...

<summary>Philolaus explains the Pythagorean and Orphic view of the three principles of creation: Form (Jupiter/the One), Matter (Juno/the Two), and Law (the Divine sealer/God), using the transition from a square to a cube to represent physical reality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the transition from the metaphysical world to the physical world. The previous page ended with the description of how a universal "Idea" becomes a specific, individual thing when it is "proscribed" or limited by being placed into the "seat" of matter (the cube).</meta>

-># JOHN REUCHLIN<-

...a just seal: for the law of nature seals many materials with one form, just as the 
seal of a single ring’s image marks many pieces of wax. Now, however, any forms 
imprinted <note>original: "sigillatæ inriam" — likely a corruption of "infimae" (lowest) or "in materia" (in matter)</note> are no longer called "Idea"—that is, the archetype—but *eide*: that is, 
specific forms, <note>original Greek: "ὡς τὰ ἐν τοῖς ἀκροῖς ἐκτυπώματα ἀχώριστα τῆς ὕλης"</note> "like impressions in wax inseparable 
from the matter," as Ammonius <note>Ammonius Hermiae, a 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> wrote. For us, there now stands ready 
the origin of this sensible World, which the marriage of the pyramid and the cube, 
celebrated by the Law of Nature, has brought forth. The four-sided bases of 
those figures, when joined together, immediately produce the Pythagorean 
symbol <note>The OCR "symb-" is completed here as "symbolum."</note> which designates the universe itself, composed of matter and form. 
Alcinous <note>A Middle Platonist philosopher.</note> rightly remembers this regarding the dogma of Plato, saying thus: 
<note>original Greek: "τῷ δὲ δωδεκαέδρῳ τὸ πᾶν ὁ θεός κατεχρήσατο"</note> "God used the dodecahedron <note>A 12-faced solid.</note> for the universe"; 
certainly, when he was fabricating this World. For if you skillfully place a pyramid 
raised upon four triangles of equal sides upon an eight-angled cube, you will 
have constructed the edifice of the dodecahedron, where the cube (or die) 
submits as the mother, and the pyramid stands as the father. For so that noble 
Pythagorean, Timaeus of Locri, says in his book *On the Soul of the World*: 
<note>original Greek: "τὸ μὲν εἶδ’ ὁ λόγον ἔχει ἀῤῥενός τε καὶ πατρός, ἁ δ’ ὕλα, τε καὶ ματέρος. τρίτα δὲ τὰ τούτων ἔκγονα"</note> 
"The form, indeed," he says, "has the ratio of the male and the father. 
But matter has the ratio of the female and the mother; and the third are 
the offspring of these." We affirm, therefore, that all things of this World 
are made from these—not by chance, but by certain seeds and a secret 
faculty—truly with a marvelous variety, appearing different because of the 
varying measurement of forms to their materials, and of almost infinite 
accidents, which Epicurus <note>The Greek philosopher associated with atomism.</note> calls "symptoms": a mixture through 
abundance and defect, strife and friendship, motion and rest, tumult 
and tranquility, the rare and the dense. From these arise the spheres and stars, 
and likewise the four elements, from which evaporate the hot and the moist, 
the cold and the dry, and also every object of the senses. Thence, one thing 
befalls one person and another thing another, and it makes all things 
change their forms and alter their colors, according to the testimony of 
Lucretius. <note>Roman poet and author of *On the Nature of Things*.</note> Do you not sense how much we are now walking with the common 
crowd of philosophers, and treading the vulgar path, since we have slipped 
into these physics? Wherefore, since many have written much about nature, 
we should apply less effort to showing what Pythagoras felt regarding 
natural things, taking our beginning from the more noble and ancient things. 
There are "natural gods," and truly "supernatural gods" of the gods; the 
inferior World nourishes the former, while the superior World cherishes 
the latter, whence they are also called "supercelestial," concerning whom 
we have previously discussed not a few things. The "gods of gods" are 
most simple and most pure: because they are nowhere, they are therefore 
supercelestial; because they are everywhere, they are therefore with us—
natives there, but strangers here. For they are never in our world unless 
they are sent, wherefore they rejoice in the name of "angels" <note>From the Greek *angelos*, meaning "messenger."</note> when they 
reach these lowest depths, because they are messengers of the King of Kings; 
nevertheless, they appear to us in a habit and face of their choosing, 
according to the freedom of their will, always most full of benefits toward 
us. But the inferior gods never migrate to the supercelestial realms; 
nevertheless, they sometimes take up an embassy to us and our affairs, 
whence it is in a similar way that they are named "angels." But God, the 
Best and Greatest, inhabits the lowest and the highest and every single 
thing most inwardly, so that nothing of being exists without God. 
Furthermore, those who are ours <note>Likely referring to guardian spirits or souls.</note> are more excellent than we are. 
However, the souls in the human body are inferior; while the former are 
beside bodies, the latter are within bodies. In the middle of these, 
daemons and heroes maintain their place. Daemons are near the gods; 
heroes are near the souls. Pythagoras remembers these in his *Golden 
Verses*, and he attributed a specific worship to each. Yet he did not 
permit their altars to be defiled with blood, nor animals to be sacrificed, 
except for the sake of public utility; but he wished for divine and private 
sacrifices to be made more with incense and hymns. Whence that saying 
exists: "Appease God with incense, and let the little grain of corn grow 
without the plow." <note>A poetic sentiment suggesting spiritual devotion over material labor or sacrifice.</note> And since man is a certain image of this World, 
he is therefore called a "Microcosm": that is, he is named a "Little World."

### ON THE CABALISTIC ART, BOOK II.

nor is God named in the likeness of the supreme and primary mind, either by sharing the same name or by participation. And the rational soul, which through the mind inclines the will toward virtues and all the best things, is called a **good demon** or **genius**; but that which through the imagination and depraved affections drags the will toward vices and all the worst things, is named an **evil demon**. For this reason, Pythagoras prays to God to free men from evil and to show all people which demon they are using. If, upon finally stripping away the body, the soul remains fouled by vices, it becomes an **evil demon**, and its life is called *dysdaimonia* <note>original Greek: δυςδαιμονία; meaning ill-fatedness or misery</note>: that is, it is called unhappiness. If, however, it has cast off its vices, and yet a certain mark of worldly anxiety remains impressed upon it, and it has not yet entirely left behind all affection for human and mortal customs (however virtuous), it will be a **good demon** for a some time. It will dwell happily and fortunately in the pleasantness of this World with singular and constant joy—as one who has conducted affairs well, turning them over in a still-mindful spirit—and it retains a not-yet-extinguished will to perform those same deeds rightly. Its life is called by the Greeks *eudaimonia* <note>original Greek: εὐδαιμονία; meaning happiness or being "well-spirited"</note>: that is, happiness. From this arose that saying of Virgil: "The same pride in chariots and arms they had when alive, the same care to pasture sleek horses, follows them when they are laid in the earth." <note>A quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Book VI, lines 653-655, describing the spirits in the underworld.</note> I have learned that the ancients called such a soul a *lemur* <note>a wandering spirit of the dead</note>. If any of this kind is led by such benevolence toward us that they take up the care of us and our families, possessing the house as a peaceful and quiet divinity, they are called a **household lar** <note>a protective domestic spirit</note>. But if, because of the wicked merits of their life, they are punished with no good dwelling but rather by wandering—as if in a kind of exile—becoming an empty terror to good men but harmful to the wicked, they are named a **larva** <note>a malevolent ghost or specter</note>. When, however, it is uncertain which lot the soul enjoys—whether it be a *lar* or a *larva*—they call it by the name **Manes** <note>shades or spirits of the departed</note>, to which they added the title of "God" for the sake of honor, since they declare those to be gods who, having governed the course of life justly and prudently, have met a holy death. Furthermore, we indiscriminately call these "gods," "angels," and "demons," as well as "noble spirits," who are assigned as guardians to each individual human. Though they are least visible, they are always present, not only as witnesses of our actions, but even of our thoughts; they also follow us after death all the way to the power, judgment, and tribunal of the supreme demon <note>meaning the highest governing spirit or God</note>. All these things flowed to us from Pythagoras, which he himself learned partly from the Egyptians, partly from the Hebrews and Chaldeans, and among the most wise Magi of the Persians, and handed down to posterity. The most excellent authors have remembered these things: **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>literally "Mercurius Termaximus"</note>, the illustrious legislator and most contemplative writer of the Egyptians, in his *Perfect Discourse to Asclepius*; **Timaeus of Locri** in his book *On the Soul of the World*; **Hesiod** in *Works and Days*; **Plato** through Diotima in the *Symposium*, through Socrates in the *Phaedrus*, and likewise in the *Philebus*, and through the Athenian guest in the *Laws* and the *Epinomis*, and in other places in his books; **Porphyry** in *On Abstinence from Animal Food*; **Iamblichus** in *On the Mysteries*; **Proclus** in his commentary on the *Alcibiades*; **Plotinus** in his book *On Love* and in the book *On One's Own Proper Demon*; **Maximus of Tyre** in two disputations on the *Demon of Socrates*; and many other Greeks. Among the Latins, **Cicero** followed them in his volumes *On the Nature of the Gods*, *On Divination*, and in the sixth book of *On the Republic*; and also that **Apuleius of Madaura** in the book *On the God of Socrates*, and the rest followed after them. Nor are there lacking those among the Peripatetics <note>followers of Aristotle</note> who treated the movers of the orbs of the planets and stars, and the rulers of the elements—whether they assist those bodies from without, or exist within each as its soul, I forgo to mention. Now we shall enumerate in a few words only what remains concerning the sensible World. Pythagoras therefore said that this World, which is the imitator of eternity, is the containment of all wholes according to the order that is in it; and although it is corporeal, it possesses incorporeal primary principles. The Stoics did not agree with him on this, for they thought those principles were corporeal because they were spiritual. He himself asserted that the world was both generated and corruptible, but by the providence and indulgence of God, it would never be destroyed. He also said that the bodies of the elements are round, except for fire, which takes the shape of a cone. Color is the appearance of the body.

### ON THE CABALISTIC ART, BOOK II.

Time, the circle, the outermost limit of the World, motion, a certain difference or alterity in matter, and that matter is subject to generation and corruption. He taught that **necessity** weighs upon the World; some things happen by necessity, some by fate, some by choice, some by fortune, and some by chance; the cause of these is hidden from human reason, a view in which Anaxagoras also concurs. Our teacher [Pythagoras] also thought the World began from fire. Its right side is in the east, its left in the west. Then, following Thales, he divided the heaven into five zones, then into the equinoxes and solstices (two of each) and the Bear <note>Referring to the Arctic circle, associated with the Great Bear constellation</note>. He divided the globe of the lands likewise. Furthermore, he was the first of all to discover the **obliquity of the zodiac** <note>The tilt of the Earth's axis relative to its orbit, which creates the seasons</note> along the Sun's path. He said the Moon appeared to be an ignited terrestrial soil, containing fields, mountains, and valleys. Concerning the soul, he declared it in this way: it is a **self-moving number**, which he distributed through its powers thus: the vital part around the heart, the rational and mental part around the head. The whole soul cannot perish; for the rational part is the work of the eternal God, while the irrational part is corruptible. To the same author [Pythagoras] should be attributed a more true divination regarding sacrifices. He held that human seed is the foam of the most useful blood, belonging to corporeal matter but endowed with incorporeal power. Moreover, the female likewise emits seed. Furthermore, not only man but other living creatures have reason, though without a **mind** <term>Latin: *mens*; Reuchlin distinguishes between basic logic/instinct and the higher intellect</term>. That many of these do not seem to act rationally is surely blamed on a **dyscrasia** <note>original: "dycrasia"; a medical term for an imbalance of bodily fluids or "humors"</note> of their bodies: because they are not endowed with the proper instruments, they do not have words (whether they are tame or wild), but hold certain symbols and certain signs in place of words, by which signs they express their thoughts to one another. Thus, beasts speak but do not "discourse," which the Greeks say more significantly as *to babble indeed, but not to speak with structured meaning* <note>original Greek: λαλεῖν μὲν, οὐ φράζειν δὲ</note>. All those volumes of Plutarch on the opinions of the philosophers are very good witnesses of these things. Concerning the rest of this World, whether substances or accidents, there are almost innumerable writers in every sect of philosophers: some have spoken generally about the nature of the universe, such as Aristotle, Theophrastus, and almost all your Arabs and Moors; others spoke particularly about individual things, such as Julius Pollux, Dioscorides, Pliny, and those like them. Yet almost every later scholar has taken the heads of all disciplines from the treasury of Pythagoras’s philosophy like an heir, and cultivated that inheritance with literary study, and according to the peculiar quality of his own genius, adorned it as much as he was able and extended it with his full strength.

But what does it help to know or hold opinions on all things if they do not take away all sorrow and torment from us in this life, and in the next life—after the absence of evils—add the most abundant gathering of all the good things we have so diligently learned? What does it help, finally, if by knowing well we do evil, and by doing evil we cannot be entirely free from fear and so can enjoy no tranquil state of mind? Or again, if we always carry out orders like beasts of burden, being otherwise in all things foolish, stolid, fatuous, like mushrooms, slow-witted, and dullards, differing nothing from a brute? Therefore, it seemed appropriate to Pythagoras to direct all philosophy toward the peak of longed-for happiness and the ready security of eternal joy, which he placed in the **contemplation of the highest and divine things**. He thought that fruit, as if from a blessed tree, would undoubtedly follow our tireless studies of philosophizing, if we first—our soul having been purged—vehemently turn away from vices and diligently cultivate virtues. Thus, conscious of no evil within ourselves, we might apply ourselves with a joyful mind and cheerful zeal to **mathematical speculations**, which are observed by us as the middle ground between natural and divine things. For they are partly inseparable from matter like natural things, and partly separated like divine things. For a circle or harmony, although it does not exist without matter, is yet understood without matter; indeed, no concern for matter is involved when we handle any mathematical subject. Since, therefore, it was difficult—not to say impossible—for our intellect to leap suddenly from natural to supernatural things and from entirely material to purely immaterial things, Pythagoras therefore wished to provide his disciples with certain...

### ON THE CABALISTIC ART, BOOK II.

...to bring matters into the open that they could comprehend both by some sense and by the intellect. For this reason, he named the demonstrations of these things **mathematics** or **mathesis**—that is, "the disciplines." The book he composed on these subjects he titled *Of Instructions* or *Of Teachings*, as if suited for youths and children; it was for their sake he chose the name <note>original Greek: παιδευτικὴν (*paideutikēn*), meaning "the art of education"</note>, in which he explained everything that could be said about numbers, figures, and harmonies. From there, as if from one illustrious fountain, four most clear streams flowed forth, which we call the **four liberal arts**: Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, and—certainly counting Astronomy among natural things—he gathered the greater part of it into the book he called *Physics*, because it consists of the motion of bodies. 

But since there is such a wide array of literature on these subjects among the most skilled of our age, so that any one of these things constitutes a singular faculty, and each faculty leads its own class, I shall leave each to its own teachers. Because the night is now deep and the preparations for our dinner are at hand, I will make an end of speaking—I who have dared to beat upon your most tolerant ears with so many words until now.

Then Marranus said: "I swear by the gods above, you have filled me with such pleasure by your speaking that no Muse is more pleasing to me. Now, forgotten of dinner, I have turned all my hunger toward the desire for your teaching. Although I see the innkeeper is busy with the magnificence and expense of the feast, I would still wish you to explain the rest of Pythagoras's philosophy more intently—that which pertains to virtues, morals, and the diligence of the Republic—and do so as briefly as you can, while the servers lay the table for us and prepare the rest."

"Therefore listen, Marranus," Philolaus said. "Pythagoras wished all this part to be contained under the name of **urbanity** <note>In this context, *urbanitas* refers to civility or the conduct of a citizen</note>. Concerning this, he composed one volume among the rest, which he named *The Politic*—that is, 'civil,' or as the Latins have perhaps not quite properly translated it, *On the Republic*. This is because it explains not only what concerns the multitude, but also the individual concerns of each person regarding character and virtue. For he who is set over a city, unless he be worthy to rule his own house and himself as well, is clearly chosen under a bad omen. <note>original Greek: μέρος δ’ ἔστιν ἄρα ὡς ἔοικε καὶ ἀρχὴ τῆς πολιτικῆς τὰ ἤθη πραγματεία ἡ πολιτική</note>; that is: 'Therefore, as it seems, the study of character is both a part and a starting point of politics itself,' as Aristotle says in the book *The Great Ethics*. 

This civility indeed consists of the whole number of virtues, whose parts are men endowed with virtue admitted into one fellowship. For a conversation of evil men is no longer to be considered a city, but a meeting-place where vices are found, just as virtue is found among the good. As the famous Theognis of Megara says in his book to Cyrnus: *You will learn right things from right men; but if you mingle with the wicked, you will lose both yourself and your mind.* 

Therefore, setting aside **contemplative wisdom** (which Pythagoras referred to nature and enclosed in his book on *Physics* concerning principles and the modes of causes—how from the **Monad** <term>the indivisible unit or "the One"</term> comes the **indefinite dyad** <term>the principle of duality or "the Two"</term>, from these come numbers, from numbers points, from points lines, from lines plane figures, from planes solid figures, from which come solid bodies and that sensible globe of the World with its orbs and the elements of mixed things: fire, air, water, and earth—almost every detail being wrapped in allegory as is his custom), and likewise leaving behind the mathematical things which he showed through his book *The Educator* (that is, on instruction), I think I should review briefly what he taught concerning morals. He wrote of these more diffusely in the *Politic*, and more compactly, like a summary, in the *Golden Verses*. Since these are read publicly in our age, I will now pursue only those **symbols** <note>Pythagorean 'symbols' were short, cryptic maxims meant to be memorized</note> handed down without writing, so that disciples, relying on the strength of memory, might become accustomed to living according to the signs set forth for good morals, and daily confirm their professed order of philosophy among themselves with secret tokens. 

A great many of these the illustrious **Erasmus of Rotterdam**—a theologian by profession, easily the prince of the most eloquent in our century, and a 'sweet Siren' who by best right deserves great praise from all students of refined literature—has clearly expressed in his books of *Adages*, which are to be admired even by posterity. # THE WORKS OF JOHANNES REUCHLIN

Indeed, Pythagoras attributed no small amount of importance to habit in the cultivation of virtues, to the extent that it matters greatly what one becomes accustomed to from an early age. This is why morals are called *ēthē* <note>original Greek: ἤθη</note> as if they were *ethē* <note>original Greek: ἔθη</note>, which means "customs." This is a point that the Stagirite <note>Aristotle, who was born in Stagira</note> often confirms in his *Ethics*, and even our own Christ suggests choosing the best way of life, for habit will then make it pleasant. Therefore, he organized all of moral philosophy into three parts: first, the worship of God and divine things; second, the regard individuals have for their own souls; and finally, one’s duty toward others. Since divine matters are more excellent, he taught first that nothing is pleasing to the powers above that is not free from filth and entirely purified. For this reason, he passed down a proverb that should be "kept in the mouth" <note>constantly spoken or remembered</note>: *Do not pour libations to the gods from unpruned vines* <note>original Greek: μὴ σπένδειν θεοῖς ἐξ ἀμπέλων ἀτμήτων</note>. He also established that sacrifices should be made with the purest grain. From this comes his saying: *Do not sacrifice without meal.* This Pythagorean sacrifice is most ancient, being performed with wine and bread. Furthermore, he warned that things dedicated to God should no longer be transferred to human use, often saying: *Abstain from a white cock.* To his true worshippers, he commanded perseverance in honesty through this symbol: *Sit down when about to worship* <note>original Greek: καθῆσθαι προσκυνήσοντας</note>. For the fact that one ought to look all around during worship—from which arose the saying *Worship having turned around*—indicates prudence regarding divine matters, lest that rebuke be justly turned back on us: "You know not what you ask."

Furthermore, the standard for living rightly regarding ourselves consists in human decorum, which is the middle point between extremes—between abundance and deficiency. In either of those cases, a person is unbalanced, like someone missing a limb or having a hundred hands. Thus, the symbol *Do not step over the balance* commands that moderation be applied to all studies and actions. Elsewhere, he said more clearly: *Apply salt.* This directly pertains to our affections, which are called the "passions." For salt is a sign of modesty, since it is properly accepted in food neither in excess nor in too small a quantity; both are rejected—that which is unsalted and that which is overly salty. Therefore, *Do not overstep the salt* was an ancient proverb. 

Accordingly, all the affections and passions within us are moved by some appearance of good or evil. We rejoice at present goods and are saddened by present evils; conversely, we desire future goods and fear future evils. Therefore, joy and sorrow are the elements of the passions from which all the movements of our souls arise; their righteousness is called virtue, and their crookedness is called vice. Yet, things that are evil often appear to us as good, and conversely, things that are good seem not to be good. For as Seneca says, there is a great difference between the "true" and the "truth-like" <note>the plausible or probable</note>; thus, error easily befalls the unskilled crowd, of which there is a great abundance. For this reason, Pythagoras sought to turn his disciples away, symbolically warning: *Do not walk on the public road*—that is, do not follow the errors of the common people. Yet, because he also wished this to be seen: *Do not go outside the public road*, he had already insinuated that one should speak like the many; rather, do not attack what is agreed upon by everyone. From this comes the saying: *Do not speak against the sun*—that is, do not fall into dangers. This is also rightly advised by: *Avoid the sharp sword.* This is achieved if there is an honest shame in public, the mark of which is: *Do not urinate against the sun.* 

Now, therefore, regarding the error brought in concerning good and evil, he determined that pleasure and sorrow, desire and fear, must be tempered. Thus he said: *Hands should not be stretched out to laughter and sadness alike.* For he commanded us to enjoy joys and pleasure according to harmony—that is, with a certain honest temperance, which he called the **lyra** <note>the lyre, a stringed instrument</note>. Hence this symbol: *Use songs with the lyre* <note>original Greek: ὠδαῖς χρῆσθαι πρὸς λύραν</note>. This was not without a profound mystery, for he always used this before the beginning of sleep, so that he would not be troubled by disturbed dreams. When these dreams rushed in, he ordered those rising to turn and roll up the bed-covers; that is, to bundle the dreams together and cast them away, lest the memory of them weigh heavily. Regarding sorrow, he spoke thus: *Do not wear a tight ring*, by which he excluded all grief of the soul, except for a sin committed. For this reason, he himself sang in his verses: *If you have done evil, grieve.* In all other matters, Pythagoras commanded *The heart is not to be eaten*, which means: do not torture yourself, nor when you have boiled over in...

### ON THE CABALISTIC ART, BOOK II

**Scramble the mark of the pot in the ashes**, which signifies that one must let anger cool and that the memory of past evils should be erased. Regarding greed, he speaks in this way: **Do not nourish those with hooked talons**, which is a rule set against rapacious hands. Indeed, you should not be overly anxious even about your daily food, which is why he says: **Do not plot against the choenix** <note>original: "Chœnici ne insidias"; the choenix was a Greek measure of grain representing a daily ration. Pythagoras taught that one should not "sit upon" or plot over this measure, meaning one should not live in idleness or worry excessively about basic survival</note>. For the *choenix* is daily food, which some call a "prebend" and others call "doles." Likewise, so that you might show no sign of avarice hidden in your soul, he gave this warning: **Do not pick up what has fallen**, by which he forbade anyone from being an overly passionate lover of their own possessions.

Regarding fear, he says: **Do not turn back when you have reached the boundaries**. By this symbol, he not only forbids trembling at death, but also at whatever is destined by fate, however terrifying it may be. For these are the defined and determined boundaries that you will not be able to cross. Therefore, you fear in vain what you cannot turn back from or avoid; to never shrink from such an event is the mark of praised fortitude and distinguished greatness of soul. 

We have enumerated the Pythagorean marks in a cursory way—first those pertaining to divine matters, then those pertaining to each individual person. Now, listen briefly to those he used for how one person relates to another. Since nothing is more desirable than friendship, the greatest care after the gods is placed on gaining friends through virtue (as it says in the *Golden Verses*), yet not just any passing person. For this reason, he himself said: **Do not offer your right hand to just anyone**. And when you have found a friend worthy of your inner sanctum, you should make him a sharer in all your affairs. On this matter, Pythagoras himself used this proverb before all others: **All things are common among friends**, as Timaeus and Cicero attest. For a friend is another self, which is why friendship is *isotes* <note>original Greek: ἰσότης</note>—that is, equality and the same soul. 

However, one must by no means admit into friendship men who are otherwise "white" to the sight but who carry a "black tail" behind them (trust one who has experience!); the earth produces nothing more pestilential than these. They are like the "blue-white begging magpie" with a tail turning black between the shoulder blades—hypocrites who simulate and dissimulate everything. Therefore, Pythagoras said: **Do not be among the black-tails** <note>original Greek: μὴ γένεσθαι τῶν μελανούρων</note>, which is to say: *Do not taste of those who have a black tail.* These are the "false brothers" whom people call "those in mourning." As the grammarian Tryphon wrote: **For falsehood turns black at its extremities** <note>original Greek: τὸ γὰρ ψεῦδος ἐν τοῖς ἐσχάτοις μέρεσι μελαίνεται</note>. 

As for others who are less useful for deep friendship—whether relatives or friends—you should neither despise them nor accept them beyond measure. This is what this allegory teaches: **Neither urinate upon nor step upon the clippings of nails and hair.** Nor are we far from being commanded to cautiously avoid every ungrateful guest, every whisperer, and every talkative person among us; hence that saying: **We should not have swallows living with us.** Furthermore, a friend should be received deliberately, but once received, he should not be easily cast away. Indeed, it is inhumane to break a friendship, which is why he said: **Do not break the bread.** 

But you should wish to be a friend in such a way that you care for all your friend's affairs just as your own. You should please him not with flattering words and the "dye" of speeches, but with the pursuit of truth. For the seat of friendship is truth, not adulation; because of this, he himself said: **Do not wipe the seat with oil.** And just as the love of good men is to be won, so the wrath of evil men is not to be provoked; he warns of this very thing: **Do not poke the fire with a sword.** 

Furthermore, it is the duty of a good man to be of use to all and to harm no one. For if you are said to have aggravated even a small trouble, you appear to have given room to vice. You will deserve grace for your virtue when you help someone laying down a burden, so that he may be relieved of the weight more quickly; this is what he meant when he said: **To help lay down a load, not to help put it on** <note>original Greek: φορτίον συγκαθαίρειν μὴ συνεπιτιθέναι</note>. This is as if he were to say: help so that men may be relieved of trouble, not weighed down. 

A man who is unworthy and of perverse character, just as he should not be killed suddenly, should also by no means be cherished by you. For this reason, he forbade: **Do not put food into a chamber pot.** Finally, we must lay aside that ferocity so that absolutely no one acts cruelly against any innocent person. For Pythagoras also commanded this: **A gentle tree must not be violated or harmed.** From this comes the saying among the symbols: **Do not taste fish.** For surely a fish is...

...an animal of such a kind that nature itself does not harm humans. As far as it pertains to the Republic, there remains that which he himself said: **do not pluck**, meaning the Law must not be violated. And also this: **wood in the road**. By this we are warned that public property and those things which belong to the community are not to be seized. 

How truly ill-becoming pride, the inflation of majesty, and the swelling of honor are for a wise man, this secret symbol exhorts us: **Abstain from beans**. For magistrates were elected by beans according to the custom of the ancients <note>In ancient Greek democracy, beans were used as lots or ballots for electing officials; Pythagoras advised his followers to stay out of the messy business of politics</note>. They say it is an immeasurable evil for anyone to be anxiously occupied in taking up the affairs of the Republic. Therefore, Pythagoras, lest he should cause offense by openly discouraging the people, preferred to turn his disciples away from all ambition through a hidden mystery, like a faithful teacher, so that they would keep this in mind: **one must not engage in politics** <note>original Greek: *οὐ δεῖ πολιτεύεσθαι*</note>. 

There is no doubt that Hipparchus and Lysis, listeners of Pythagoras who held these precepts in their memory—which they, along with the other students, had preserved in their own minds instead of in books—brought them forth in the lecture hall at Thebes. However, I have not seen all of them, and in my haste, I did not wish to touch upon everything. I intended only this: lest you should commit me to oblivion, I wanted to show that almost all Pythagorean philosophy is full of "notes of words" and "coverings of things." It is a manner of teaching which, as I said before, is believed to have been first translated to the Greeks by Pythagoras from the Hebrews and Egyptians. For the Egyptians were accustomed to communicate certain things among the priests in fictitious letters, so that secrets would be kept from the common people, thereby ensuring they remained objects of wonder and were preserved for a longer time. 

For this reason, those Colossi, statues, altars, arches, and bronzes were prominent, with Egyptian sacred writings inscribed publicly to be seen by everyone, yet they were understood only by the expert and the initiated through hieroglyphs—as Chaeremon, Horapollo, and many others have written about them. Thus, my Pythagoras did not think it the mark of a man to explain the lyre to a donkey, or to offer mysteries to those who would receive them as a pig receives a trumpet, or a hearth receives perfumes, or a beetle receives ointments <note>These are traditional metaphors for offering wisdom to the ignorant or unworthy</note>. Therefore, he imposed silence upon his disciples, lest they reveal the secrets of divine things, which are grasped more easily by meditating than by speaking.

Then Marranus said: "I pray, my Philolaus, do not possess Pythagoras for yourself alone, but allow him to be ours, not yours only. Indeed, I have turned out to be neither deaf to your discourse nor unmindful of Pythagoras. So that I might commend to my memory all the mysteries, metaphors, enigmas, maxims, apophthegms, allegories, symbols, notes, signs, and sacraments of such a great man and of the other first philosophers—which you recounted in passing and cursorily, in the manner of a catalog—I have used the Ciceronian 'places' and the rhetorical art I heard from you <note>Marranus refers to the 'Art of Memory,' a technique involving the mental placement of images in specific locations or 'loci' to aid recall</note>. Shall I make a trial of it? 

For you asserted, if I remember correctly, that Pythagoras encompassed all parts of philosophy in three volumes: the Propaedeutic, the Political, and the Moral—that is, the natural, the disciplinary, and the moral. These he is said to have entrusted to his daughter in his will <note>original: "mori filiae"; likely referring to Damo, the daughter of Pythagoras, whom tradition says guarded his secret writings</note>, so that they would never be published outside the family, or indeed, at all. He himself, however, lived out everything contained therein only for the worthy and for the few in number; most especially, he demonstrated mathematical principles clearly, using no veil for his voice. To others, he spoke of other things in their own way. Therefore, speaking one way and thinking another—though always being the same wise man—he imparted his doctrine to his followers through certain symbols as reminders. Through the imitation of the ancients, one thing was said, but another understanding was conveyed. 

By him, to begin from the first principles:
*   **The Infinite and the One** are put for God.
*   **Numbers** for incorporeal things.
*   **Figures** for corporeal things.
*   **Harmony** for mixed things.
*   **Unpruned vines** for filth and sins.
*   **Purest flour** for that which is in the purest life.
*   **A white cock** is the mark of one dedicated to God.
*   **Sitting** designates humility.
*   **Turning around** designates prudence; and these pertain to divine things.

This next group looks toward private affairs and virtues:
*   **The Balance** (scales) is the symbol of justice.
*   **Salt** marks influence <note>original: "momen"; salt represents both wisdom and the preservation of character</note>.
*   **The public road** represents the errors of the common crowd.
*   **The Sun** is put in the place of things manifest and open.
*   **A drawn sword** signifies dangers.
*   **Urine** signifies shamelessness.
*   **Song** signifies the belly <note>Symbolizing gluttony or physical indulgence</note>.
*   **The Lyre** signifies harmony.
*   **Bed-coverings** signify dreams...
*   **A tight ring**...

# THE ART OF THE CABALA. BOOK II. 681

...matter: "Heart’s food" signifies torment, "A boiling pot" the eruption of anger, "Hooked nails" robbery, "A dry measure" <note>original: *choenix*, a Greek unit of volume</note> nourishment, "Falling things" fortune, "Boundaries" fate. These concern the man in relation to himself. Now follows that which concerns his behavior toward another: "The right hand" denotes friendship, "A black tail" false brothers, "Nails and hair" are symbols of kinsmen, "Swallows" represent talkative people and those whose ungratefulness exceeds bounds. "Bread" is the mystery of true friendship, "Oil" of flattery, "Wood" <note>possibly a slip in transcription or a specific symbolic reference to fuel</note>, "Fire" of wrath, "A sword" of provocation, "A burden" suggests trouble, "A chamber pot" figures the unworthy, "A mild tree" a useful man, and "A fish" an innocent man. So much for private life. 

Now for the Republic. "A crown" is the sign of the Law and of government, "Wood on the road" represents the property of the community, and "The bean" demonstrates ambition <note>referring to the use of beans as ballots in ancient elections</note>. All things are symbolic, all are figurative and allegorical. Unless you thought more could be found among the disciples of Pythagoras, I would indeed reduce all these things to that man’s mathematical proportions, since one and two, in the first progression, become three. 

Behold the Republic: and three times three are nine—behold divine matters! And three times four are twelve—behold private matters in relation to another! And four times four are sixteen—behold private matters in relation to one's self. Therefore, the Republic is a triangle <note>original: *trigonus*</note>, and the private matter is a square <note>original: *tetragonus*</note>. And just as sixteen is to twelve, so twelve is to nine, each in a "hemiolic" proportion <note>meaning a ratio of 3:2</note>; that is, a ratio of one and a half <note>original: *sesquialtera*</note>. 

See how teachable I am under your instruction and how excellently I "Pythagorize." But what do you make of me? 

Then Philolaus said: Clearly a Pythagorean! For now I permit you to break your silence; you have enough of the disciplines, if only you understand all formal things intellectually. 

To this Marranus replied: I certainly do not know what this is. 

I will tell you, he said: If you transfer all things that appear to you from the senses to the mind; that is, if you reject all bodily passions and enjoy the contemplation of the mind. For example, I would have you imagine seeing a man far off in a very wide space of a field. You, being ignorant of what it is, will think it is either a boundary stone or a tree trunk; for it has an upright figure and, in your opinion, unmoving matter. When you look closer, it will be thought to have grown into a small tree. Having thus rejected the idea of a heap of masonry, you think it lives with the life of a plant. Then, if you both approach one another with progressive motion, the form of the tree immediately vanishes and there occurs to you the image of some animal. In your ignorance and doubt, you wonder if it is a griffin or a stork or some other huge bird, for it is two-footed. Now, having come closer, you see that it has no tail or wings and walks with head erect; soon you leave behind all prior forms and think of the human form. 

Therefore, once you have met, you are the first to say "hello," and he responds, speaking rationally; then no suspicion of a faun or satyr or other phantom arises in you. Instead, you clearly recognize him to be a man, either a neighbor or a friend. When you ask him about his parents and kinsmen, as is usually done, he departs after satisfying your every question. 

As he leaves, you meditate alone on this man: that he was born of parents, and parents again from parents, and those likewise from human seed, and that seed from a certain man. Finally, since nature rejects an infinite series, it will perhaps seem not at all impossible to designate one certain man who was born without human seed. So Aristotle wrote in the 12th book of the *Metaphysics* <note>original: *postnaturalia*</note>, and he calls him <term>the perfect</term> <note>original Greek: *τὸ τέλειον* (to teleion)</note>. 

And when you accept from the philosophers that such a perfect man is given—whose body was not born like that of other men—then you will travel by reason to the soul of man, always moving from the perfect to the more perfect and noble. By the same possibility, you will consider concepts reaching toward a certain soul, not created like other souls, but perhaps one that co-created itself. This soul is not only perfect, or more perfect than others, but truly the most perfect of all that have been, are, will be, or could ever be. You will separate this soul, situated in the body of a mortal man, from the body, and you will place it above the rest of the separated souls (since it is the most noble) in the most noble habitation—not a place, but a dwelling. For the most noble mansion is that closest to God, which the Stagirite... <note>Aristotle is often called the Stagirite after his birthplace, Stagira</note>

# JOHANNES REUCHLIN
## BOOK II. 682

Aristotle pursues this at length in his book to Alexander, *On the Universe* <note>Original: *De Mundo*. Although traditionally attributed to Aristotle, modern scholars often view this as a later work of the Peripatetic school.</note>. We judge that this [form] dwells on the horizon of the highest world, which is called "incomparable," where the union of God and creature exists. Just as on the horizon of eternity we place the immobile mover of the first movable sphere, in whom the corporeal and incorporeal worlds meet. By this path, you have intellectually turned the human form into a "separate form" <note>A "separate form" is a philosophical term for an intellect that exists independently of matter, like an angel.</note>, and mentally led it to the highest mansion of eternity. From there, the highest bliss flows into all angels and gracious souls, and all soul-saving souls are regulated toward that same soul, as if toward a certain rule. 

Pythagorically, I would certainly not deny this regarding that most perfect body which we mentioned before. For he said that a man can become immortal like God, by which he clearly showed his opinion: that a single glory can glorify both parts of a man [body and soul] and make the whole man blessed. This happens when the greatest God himself either absorbs both into his own Deity, or grants it to the soul to flow brightness and glorification into the sublimated body: *as to a yoke-mate and fellow-traveler, registered together and having struggled together* <note>Original Greek: *ὡς ὁμοζύγῳ καὶ ὁμοπρούτῳ, συναπογραφέντι τε καὶ συναθλήσαντι*. This refers to the body being the soul's partner in the trials of life.</note>. This Pythagorean dogma sprouted again from Orpheus, as is found at the end of the *Hymn to Mercury*. 

Now you see hanging before your eyes Homer’s golden chain from the eighth book of the *Iliad*, let down from heaven by Jove to our frailty on earth; through this, by divine help, you may lift yourself into the heights both by acting and by contemplating. For it is necessary first to live according to the mind, and finally to contemplate with the mind, and while contemplating, to ascend ardently. Since power is prior to contemplation, and since both must be pure to attain that which nothing is purer than, certainly life must first be purged, and then contemplation must be illuminated. 

Therefore, what you saw in that abstraction of things from things which we brought forward, experience that within yourself: return to the mind through reason, and disentangle yourself from all external things, just as the Emperor Marcus Antoninus commands: *simplify yourself* <note>Original Greek: *ἀπόλυσον σεαυτόν*. Literally: "release yourself" or "untie yourself" from worldly distractions.</note>. For it is necessary for one migrating from this life to the next to have stripped off every garment and to depart naked—not only from all matter and corporeal appendages, but also as a fugitive and free man from the entire mass of disturbances, affections, and passions. Lucian of Samosata taught this very skillfully in the dialogue of Charon and Mercury, the most philosophical of all; if you have not read it, read it and imitate it. 

I ask you, what else are the three things Pythagoras divided, which place us in the tracks of divine virtue, if not <term>purgation</term> (purifying), <term>illumination</term> (enlightening), and <term>perfection</term> (completing)? For he says: *Work at these things, meditate on these things, these you must love; these will set you on the path of divine virtue* <note>Original Greek: *ταῦτα πόνει, ταῦτ' ἐκμελέτα τούτων χρὴ ἐρᾶν σε, ταῦτα σε τῆς θείης ἀρετῆς εἰς ἴχνια θήσει*.</note>. Hierocles wished this to be understood equally regarding the powers of our rational soul applied to divine ways, and "these things," he says, "will make us like God." 

Let us consider the words of Pythagoras. For he set down three things which, when joined, allow us to arrive at the highest bliss through an <term>anagoge</term> <note>A spiritual or upward interpretation.</note>: 
1. The **Labor** of virtue, which consists in action; 
2. **Meditation**, which is nourished by many studies of the disciplines; 
3. **Love**, which connects us to God as a necessary bond. 

The first is provided by moral philosophy; the second by natural philosophy along with mathematics; the third is offered in abundance to the studious by theology. None of these is sufficient by itself, but these three must come together. Porphyry, the greatest explorer of Pythagorean thought, treats this learnedly (as he does all things) in the first book of *On Abstinence from Animal Food*, in these words which I have chosen to bring forward because of the heavy authority of his testimony: *For us, blessed contemplation is not a collection of words and a multitude of teachings, as one might perhaps think, nor does it consist in quantity, nor does it receive its increase from the amount of arguments and speeches. For if that were so, nothing would prevent those who collect vast learning from being blessed...* <note>Original Greek: *οὐκ ἔστιν ἡ εὐδαιμονικὴ ἡμῖν θεωρία, λόγων ἄθροισις, & μαθημάτων πλῆθος...*</note>

### ON THE ART OF THE CABALA, BOOK II.
#### 683

For nothing would then prevent those who gathered all branches of learning from being blessed. And a little later, to omit the rest for the sake of brevity, he [Porphyry] says: 

*It is necessary for us to understand how we may return to our truly proper state, shedding all those things we assumed from our mortal nature, along with the very affection toward them through which our descent occurred. We must remember our blessed and eternal essence, and as we strive to ascend to the incorporeal and impassible, we must practice two meditations: one by which we strip off all that is material and mortal; the other, how we may return and prevail, ascending back to those things in a different way than we descended here.* <note>Original: Reuchlin provides this text first in Greek, then in a Latin translation. Porphyry was a 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on the soul's journey back to the Divine.</note>

And again, after a not very long discourse, Porphyry commands us there to thoroughly segregate the soul from the senses and things of that kind, as far as the necessity of nature permits. We should rightly arrange and articulately compose the things pertaining to the mind, preparing tranquility and peace from the war we have waged against irrationality <note>In this context, "irrationality" refers to the lower, impulsive parts of the soul or the passions.</note>. This is so that we might not only hear about the intellect and the intelligible things, but even, according to our strength, enjoy the contemplation of it—at one time translated into the incorporeal nature, at another living with the truth through the mind, and no longer falsely with the relatives of the body. 

We must therefore loosen many of our garments: both this visible fleshy garment, and those inner ones we are clothed in, which are closest to the garments of skin <note>A reference to the "coats of skins" in Genesis 3:21, interpreted by mystics as the physical body or the fallen state of humanity.</note>. Thus far Porphyry, who pursues these matters with much more discussion, all tending toward the idea that through sensible things we come to the enjoyment of the intelligible and mental good—by living honestly, by contemplating purely, and by loving divinely. All these things he drew from our Pythagoras as if from a certain vast river of all disciplines.

"I, for my part," Marranus said, "am clearly moved to the opinion by these things you have recounted in order that Pythagoras channeled that river of his from the infinite sea of the Cabalists (of which Simon promises us a happy voyage) into the fields of the Greeks, from which we may finally irrigate our own studies. Thus, the speeches and sentiments of Simon regarding the Cabalists and yours regarding the Pythagoreans seem to me to be equal to one another. For what else does either the Cabalist or the Pythagorean intend, except to return the souls of men to the Gods—that is, to promote them to perfect bliss? 

And what other way is there than the similar method of teaching in both, and an equal exercise for both through symbols and signs, adages and proverbs, through numbers and figures, and through letters, syllables, and words? Thus, the *ypsilon* <note>The Greek letter 'Y'. In Pythagorean symbolism, it represents the "fork in the road" of youth, where one must choose between the path of virtue or vice.</note> stands as the symbol of Pythagoras’s youth. Thus, the first syllable of the *Iliad* <note>The first letter of the *Iliad* is Mu (M), which in Greek numbering stands for 40, but Reuchlin is referring to the tradition of using the 24 letters of the Greek alphabet to number the 24 books of Homer’s epics.</note> is a sign and mark of how many books of Homer there are in each work. Thus, the word 'white' signifies good, and 'black' signifies evil. 

Not otherwise did our Simon transfer the first letter of the Pentateuch <note>The Hebrew letter *Beit*.</note>, and the middle of the five-letter name <note>Likely a reference to the Pentagrammaton (HSVH), the Christian Cabalistic name for Jesus.</note>, to other things; and he borrowed 'Raham,' according to the authority of David Kimhi <note>A famous medieval Hebrew grammarian and biblical commentator (c. 1160–1235).</note>, allegorically for Abraham; and the other things which we remember well enough from the conversation held with us. But listen with what a shout the innkeeper himself calls us to the dining room!"

## DOCTOR OF LAWS, ON THE ART OF THE CABALA
### BOOK THREE.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'P' featuring a foliage pattern within a square frame.</image-desc>After they had departed, and the dark moon in turn suppressed the light, and the falling stars brought sleep, both fell into slumber, having urged each other not to sleep beyond daybreak; and so they arranged to be awakened. 
In the morning, while they were dressing according to their custom, they recalled the long and varied words of that harsh Innkeeper. During yesterday’s feast, he had told his guests that on the previous day, certain propositions and conclusions had been sent from the Roman Curia to Frankfurt. These had been fabricated and cooked up by a certain individual against the Apostolic prohibition, directed against Johannes Reuchlin—who for more than five years now has suffered cruel persecutions with an innocent, yet brave and unbroken spirit. These documents had been posted at the gates of wisdom and the porches of the temples in Rome, but were soon thrown into the mud, dung, and filth, where they were trampled for just reasons. This was because such a deed had been attempted against the will of the Supreme Pontiff and without the knowledge of the most reverend judges, before whom that lawsuit had been pending in the Curia for three years following the Appeal. Furthermore, it became known to everyone that this piece of writing swarmed with the most blatant lies. For at the beginning, "Astaroth" <note>This is a derogatory reference to one of Reuchlin's inquisitorial opponents, likely Jacob van Hoogstraaten, named after a Phoenician deity often associated with demons in this period.</note> promised that those conclusions would be debated in the presence of the Pope; yet the Pope had refused and certainly prohibited it. This was because the matter had already been fully debated and discussed in many public sessions held in Rome the previous summer before the most learned lights of the world: prelates of the Catholic Church, archbishops, bishops, generals of the orders and their procurators, penitentiaries, and doctors—a great number of men highly skilled in both types of Theology <note>Likely referring to scholastic and mystical/biblical theology.</note>—who had decreed that Capnion <note>The Greek version of Reuchlin's name, meaning "Smoky," which he used as a literary pseudonym.</note> should be acquitted. 
Next, he had ignominiously called the *Eye Mirror* <note>Original: *Oculare Speculum*. This refers to Reuchlin’s 1511 book, *Augenspiegel*, written to defend Jewish books from being burned.</note> a work containing scandals and errors, even though that book has been definitively accepted by an Apostolic sentence. Then he also wrote of the same book that it had long ago been sentenced to the fire by five universities—which are certainly mere trifles and clear, bright lies. For there is not, nor has there ever been, any university in the whole world that condemned the *Eye Mirror*. Rather, only certain individual heads, with dizzy brains and crooked ways, deceived by a lazy error, met in a conspiratorial fashion against the form of law and justice; they wasted away with envy against the *Eye Mirror* and "concocted," as they say, their own private opinion. Finally, he rebuked those who rolled those corollaries in the mud and filth, affirming that in those same writings there was nothing contained from Alpha to Omega <note>Original: "$\alpha$ ad $\omega$"</note> that had not already been testified to, settled, and resolved in the public defense of Johannes Reuchlin against his Cologne calumniators—which would be clearly manifest to any reader. Thus, "Astaroth" always sings the same old song to cover the foulness of his tongue. 
Philolaus Junior and Marranus remarked that these were the Innkeeper's conversations with his guests and fellow-diners. They thought it much too grave a matter that people should fight so fiercely for so many years over such a small and childish thing. 
As soon as they were dressed, they hurried to Simon’s house as they had planned. When they had greeted each other most amiably, as was their custom, Marranus began: "It is quite incredible and can hardly be put into words, venerable Simon, how much your discussion yesterday delighted us. We were so impatient with the delay while you were away from us that, without any embarrassment, we have arrived before dawn now that the Sabbath has passed." 
And Simon said: "Welcome, best of friends. Does the holiday not also hold you today? The day you call the day of the Sun."

->### ON THE ART OF THE CABALA. BOOK III.<-

...we contemplate with the mind, nor do we think the Sabbath is anything other than leaving behind secular business to give effort so that we may adhere to divinity. For so Pythagoras commanded us, according to the author Laërtius: <note>original: "ξυνώναι δ' ἀεὶ τοῖς θεοῖς"</note> "one must always converse with the gods." Except that you venerate the number seven as most suited to leisure, which even among us Pythagoreans produces nothing, and is named Minerva. <note>In Pythagorean numerology, the number seven was called Minerva (Athena) because it is "virginal"—it is the only number in the first ten that is neither a factor of another nor produced by the multiplication of others within that group.</note> Then **Simon** said: The Law must be listened to, which distributes to each their own and is like a soul to nature itself; for it willed that those laws also serve the strengths of bodies, without which neither sound reason can exist nor the light of the mind be strongly preserved. For this reason, it established a meditation on the month of the Moon: <note>The lunar cycle was often used to represent the rhythm of time and rest.</note> that is, to rest for a seventh part of life, in which it is permitted to do nothing, unless it is something that, if omitted, would cause irreparable harm. These are called, if I remember correctly, the "fixed holidays" <note>original: "feriae stativae"</note> among the Romans, common to all the people and consecrated for performing divine rites. Just as that Neoptolemus in Ennius <note>Ennius was an early Roman poet; his character Neoptolemus famously argued that one should philosophize, but only in moderation.</note> does not allow one to always philosophize, so too it is not always, nor for everyone, nor should everything concerning God be meditated upon—even among your own writers there are those who teach this. Rather, there is a time, a person, and a limit, according to the author Nazianzenus <note>Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, a 4th-century Greek theologian known for his eloquence.</note> in his work *Against the Eunomians*, whom I once read in Greek—a most learned and eloquent man—when I was living in Achaia. Thus, that which is best and infinite will not become cheapened, but will be conceived finitely according to our measure. For six days, therefore, we work, and on every seventh day we rest corporally as much as the necessity of living permits, and mentally, after the purification of the will, we are intent on divine things; and festively, with all tranquility, we praise sacred matters, serving God alone at that time. To this points what our Cabalists say: <note>original: "שבת היא סוד אל חי"</note> **Sabbath is the mystery of the Living God**, as found in the second chapter of the *Gate of Light*. <note>The *Porta Lucis* refers to the *Sha'are Orah*, a fundamental Kabbalistic text by Joseph Gikatilla.</note> For there stands the symbol of the Upper World: that is, the Jubilee of eternity, where all labor ceases. For this reason, by a double usage of speech, it is enjoined in the laws in the fifth chapter of Deuteronomy: *Observe the Sabbath day*, which is intended to be understood concerning exterior actions according to the Lower World. And in Exodus 20: *Remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy*, namely by joining the powers of the soul to the mind for the progress of contemplation according to the Upper World. Do you recognize it now? That the Sabbath is a mark of divine enjoyment, by which the senses and reason are released from material occupations as much as human frailty permits, and the energy of the mind is bound to formal occupations for considering the things that are above. The Law wished to hint at this through these two words: <note>original: "שמור וזכור"</note> **Observe** and **Remember**. Regarding these, some of our masters understand the precept of the Sabbath to be both affirmative and negative, saying: "Observe," that is, "beware," which always signifies for them to avoid, insofar as it restrains us from everything that is contrary to holiness. Others explain "Observe" as "guard," so that they attribute guarding to the night and "remembering" to the day; and this fits quite directly the foundation of the Cabalists, who think this World is night, and the World to Come—that is, the upper and intellectual world—is day. In this world, servants dwell; in that one, the free live. To the former, one must say "beware," "guard," "observe"; to the latter, "reminisce," "recall," "remember." For this word <note>original: "זכור"</note> **Remember**, containing an affirmative precept, proceeds from love; but the word "beware," a negative precept, is fulfilled out of fear. Now, love belongs to the free, and fear to servants; in all precepts, we consider one more noble than the other. Moses Gerundensis <note>Also known as Nachmanides (Ramban), a major medieval Jewish scholar.</note> wrote at length on this sentiment in his commentary on Exodus, where we accept that there are two Sabbaths, led by the testimony of Scripture in Ezekiel 20: *I gave them my Sabbaths*. For the plural placement is contained in the number two—not only so that God might generally reproach us with a single word for each type of holiday numbered in the Law (as David Kimhi <note>A famous medieval biblical commentator and grammarian.</note> and the Talmudists think), but also so that by this peculiar name, we might always embrace with a mindful spirit the best gift and perfect boon granted to us by God, which we called the Jubilee above. Concerning which the *Gate of Light* says: <note>original: "זו היא שביעית עליונה שנקראת יובל"</note> **This is the supernal seventh [week] which is called Jubilee.** From whence all remission, propitiation, and infusion of grace descends, which no one is able to eloquently express...
