...composed a speculation from four non-magical, but solemn and common Sacred names; or rather, he received the composition from the fathers: <gloss>YHWH, Adonai, Yahu, Ehyeh</gloss> <note>These represent the Tetragrammaton, the name "Lord," a variant of the divine name, and "I Am."</note>. Moreover, <gloss>יהוה</gloss> <note>original: *YHWH*</note> is, according to the Kabbalah, the same as *El* <note>God</note>. Therefore, the practitioners of this science take the first character of the first name, the first of the second, the first of the third, and the first of the fourth, and the first seal is formed: <term>Y-A-Y-E</term> <note>Hebrew: יאיה</note>. Then they work in the same way with the second letters of the four most sacred names, and <term>H-D-V-H</term> <note>Hebrew: הדוה</note> arises. They fashion the third seal by joining each of the third letters, and <term>V-N-A-Y</term> <note>Hebrew: ונאי</note> is born. Finally, in the same manner, they couple the last letters, and the fourth seal emerges, which is <term>H-Y-V-H</term> <note>Hebrew: היוה</note>. The intention of these four seals is: 

->**The Lord our God, the Lord is one**<-
<note>Hebrew: *YHWH Eloheinu YHWH Echad*, the central declaration of Jewish faith known as the *Shema*.</note>

And this, they say, is the inscription of the four seals joined together. Finally, on the back of the parchment, they depict: <gloss>One, the head of His unity, the head of His singularity, His transformation, One.</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: אחד ראש אחדותו ראש אחותו ראש אחד</note>. And this "transformation" is understood as a literary permutation according to the third part of the Kabbalah. Thus, they stand with these seals and inscriptions before the Most High with a soul devoted to God; and whatever blessing they might ask from those eighteen benedictions, or contained in other just prayers, they hope to obtain it without fail. They trust they can often break any "honey" <note>likely referring to a flow of celestial influence or decree</note> threatening from heaven, or mitigate the <term>Adrastia</term>—that is, the inevitable power of divine laws—through the prayers of these crafted words.

For they think that a well-initiated Kabbalist can achieve anything through characters and figures, and even through words and songs, even those things that are considered wonders—which some of your own philosophers admit can be done. For **Plotinus**, in the second book of *On the Doubts of the Soul*, chapter 35, enumerates four things in which a marvelous power resides: namely, the hidden qualities of species, figures, harmonies, and vows. **Porphyry** and **Iamblichus** <note>Influential Neoplatonist philosophers who explored theurgy, or "god-working."</note> also say that through God specifically, and through good angels, we have authority over the lower spirits. Nor is there any race of men in the whole world who more easily agree with this opinion than the "diviner" Christians, as they are called, who cast out demons with names and figures, lay hands upon the sick and they recover, heal those who have taken deadly things, and perform similar miracles. But, to speak the truth as they assert it, they attribute all these things to faith rather than to the symbols, although they also believe there is some infinite power in prayers. For they say and believe that "the prayer of faith shall save the sick," and the worthy Kabbalists feel no differently, for they likewise affirm that miraculous operations depend on God alone and on the faith of the human being. Therefore, they pronounce those to be liars and fools who grant such great force and power for miracles to a figure alone, or to writing alone, or to mere lines, or to voices born from broken air. This is testified by **Rabbi Moses the Egyptian** <note>Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent Jewish philosopher.</note> in the first book of the *Guide for the Perplexed*, chapter 72. 

To these things **Philolaus** says: Not only the Kabbalists of the Hebrews, but also the most excellent of the Greeks have attributed much to the tokens and seals of faith. For **Antiochus**, surnamed **Soter** <note>Antiochus I (reigned 281–261 BCE), a Seleucid king.</note>, when he was on an expedition against the Galatians—brave men fortified by an innumerable gathering of soldiers—and was about to join a most difficult battle, when (as **Lucian** writes of him) <note>original Greek: πᾶσαν πονηρὰς εἶχε τὰς ἐλπίδας</note> **"he held all his hopes in a bad state,"** he saw in a dream at night **Alexander** standing by him. Alexander ordered him to announce a certain "seal of health" to his soldiers as their battle-token before the fight, through which he promised victory would befall him. It was the sort of sign that would be marked on their clothing, as the same man of Samosata <note>Lucian of Samosata</note> noted regarding the error in greeting: <note>original Greek: δι’ ἀλλήלων τὸ πεντάγραμμον</note> **"the pentagram [formed] through one another,"** that is, a triple triangle, five-lined within itself. 

<image-desc>A hexagram (six-pointed star) formed by two interlocking triangles. Small occult sigils or Hebrew letters are inscribed within the central hexagon and at each of the six outer points.</image-desc>
<image-desc>A complex vertical sigil or monogram resembling a staurogram or Chi-Rho. It consists of a vertical shaft topped with a loop (P), crossed by three horizontal bars of varying widths, with stylized decorative serifs at the ends of the bars and at the base.</image-desc>

And Antiochus, having raised that sign, obtained a marvelous victory against the Galatians. I myself have indeed often seen that symbol of the pentagon struck upon the silver coinage of Antiochus, which, when resolved into lines, shows the word <note>original Greek: ὑγίεια</note> **"Health."** 

"Will it not be relevant," says **Marranus**, "that which once appeared to **Constantine the Great**? It was a sign of God, as they then called the cross, which appeared at the very hour of noon before the whole army from above, inscribed with Latin letters thus: **'In this, conquer'** <note>original: *In hoc vince*</note>. And Constantine did indeed conquer by that same sign, and was then chosen and hailed as Emperor by the applause of the Roman people, and [became] of all Emperors the most unvanquished..."

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Simon the Jew and his companions, shifting from the technical construction of seals to their historical and spiritual efficacy. It specifically addresses the transition from Jewish Kabbalistic practice to the Christian understanding of the name of Jesus as the "perfected" form of the divine name.</meta>

-># JOHANNES REUCHLIN<-

...was surnamed the Great. For how much power these seals possessed, the greatest men will be witnesses: Maccabeus for the Jews, Antiochus for the Greeks, and Constantine for the Christians. Nor does it escape you, Simon, that concerning the Christians of a short time ago—for in this age, there is nothing more wonderful among that people in the crafting of signs, characters, and voices—those who, by the figure of the cross and the name of **Jesus**, stop rivers, soothe wild beasts, and repel lightning. 

Furthermore, there is nothing stronger than this character and effect, and in dangers, nothing more bringing of health, for no other reason—to speak freely—than that it is the symbol of the true Savior, just as the name **Tetragrammaton** <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH.</note> is the symbol of God for you. What the Kabbalists are able to do in the ineffable name with the seals and characters recently shown by you, faithful Christians can do in a much more powerful way through the ineffable name with its own signet of the cross. They consider themselves to pronounce the name **Tetragrammaton** far more correctly in the name **יהשוה** <gloss>Jesus / Yeheshua</gloss> <note>Christian Kabbalists added the letter 'Shin' to the middle of the Tetragrammaton (YHWH) to form the name of Jesus (YHSVH), arguing it made the name pronounceable.</note> of the true Messiah. 

They cite what your own writers have written in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>A rabbinic commentary on the Psalms.</note>: **"Why does Israel pray in this world and is not answered? Because they do not know the Explicit Name"** <note>original Hebrew: *Mipnei mah mitpallelin Yisrael ba-olam ha-zeh ve-eino ne’eneh? Bishvil she-eino yode’in ba-Shem ha-Mephorash.*</note>. This is what Rabbi Joshua ben Levi said, citing the master Pinhas, son of Yair: "Why do they pray in this world and are not heard? Because they have not known the *Mephorash*: that is, the name Tetragrammaton." So it is written there.

Then Simon said: This is well said by you, but what of the words? Certainly, the wiser Kabbalists wish to relate this figure of the cross to the **brazen serpent** <note>Referencing the serpent Moses raised in the desert to heal the Israelites (Numbers 21).</note> erected in the desert, though they speak of it very silently and occultly, and this through **Gematria** <term>Gematria: A Kabbalistic method where words with the same numerical value are seen as spiritually connected.</term>, that is, by the equality of numbers. For the characters of these names, **צלם** <gloss>Tzelem: Image/Cross</gloss> and **עץ** <gloss>Etz: Wood/Tree</gloss>, both symbolize one hundred and sixty <note>The Latin text here says "centum & quinque" (105), though the standard Kabbalistic calculation for these words is 160. Reuchlin may be following a specific manuscript variation.</note>; wherefore an easy transition is made from one to the other—from the cross to the wood, and from the wood to the cross. 

But I press my lip with my finger. The narrowness of time constrains us, best of friends, so that I have said less than I wished, and I am frustrated that my joy, which grows from the ornament and dignity of your speech, fails me in such dense night when it is time to retire. You have not disputed with me until now as common Kabbalists do with trifling and thin talk, nor with the combat of gladiators or the contention of opinions, but with a precise and sharp way of speaking, and with thoughts fit and accommodated to the matter at hand. I would wish that longer spaces of days were granted to us. For no one can say enough about the art of Kabbalah in a small moment; so great are the things, so deep, so innumerable and full of danger, that it is necessary for anyone eager and studious of it to strive with the greatest powers of his intellect. 

One must look around not only at the industry with which it is learned, but also the danger with which it must be moderated and exercised. For since that science concerns spiritual things and is practiced spiritually, and a man cannot easily bring judgment upon spirits—even one to whom power is granted to judge between angels and demons with discrete weighing or according to an even rule—assuredly, one should not apply himself to this faculty and exercise unless he has first purified his character and acts with great fear. We must not perhaps suffer the fate of the Prophet Balaam, nor be deleted from the land of the living, nor follow darkness under the guise of light. 

Fear for yourselves from those cast-down spirits and our most cruel enemies, and believe me, as there are angels among us mortals, so the devils each have their own banners. In the army of God there are four leaders: **Michael, Gabriel, Uriel, and Raphael** <note>original: *Michaël, Gabriël, Uriel, Raphaël*</note>, like the four elements, according to the four directions, or according to the four spiritual enumerations. Just as formerly the children of Israel set out under four banners (Numbers, chapter 2): Judah to the East, Reuben to the South, Ephraim to the West, and Dan to the North. 

Likewise, in the army of Satan, the vengeful standard-bearers spread their sails: **Samael, Azazel, Azael, and Mahazael** <note>original: *Samaël, Azazel, Azaël, Mahazael*</note>, concerning whom Menachem Recanati <note>A 13th-century Italian Kabbalist.</note> treats in Leviticus 16 and in the first book of the Pentateuch, in which place he handles the matter where Targum Jonathan <note>An Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> himself affirms it upon Genesis. Then, moreover, great crowds of demons and fugitive legions multiply, all having their portion in the "scapegoat" <note>Referencing the goat sent to Azazel in the wilderness (Leviticus 16).</note>, which I shall omit to recount here because of their filth and horror...

<summary>Simon discusses the protective power of the name of Jesus and the sign of the cross, using Gematria to link the cross to the biblical brazen serpent. He concludes with a warning about the dangers of Kabbalah and a description of the angelic and demonic hierarchies that govern the world.</summary>

-># ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH, BOOK III<-

...a great part is contained in the Holy Scripture. But I shall now make an end of speaking with the proverb of the Kabbalists: <gloss>the prudent will understand</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: *ha-maskil yavin*</note>, if I also add this: that just as Michael is <gloss>the high priest</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: *hu kohen ha-gadol*</note>, sacrificing in the upper world, presenting the unblemished souls of men to the blessed God, while sending the unclean and those burdened with vices to the Devil; so the high priest in the lower world, as it is written in Leviticus, is commanded to offer clean and innocent animals to God, but to deliver those burdened with crimes and the weight of guilt to Satan. The Kabbalists diligently approve of this, saying: <gloss>For all lower matters are representative, and as it is done below, so it is done above.</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: *Ki kol ha-inyanim ha-tachtonim hem menagedim u-k'fi ha-asot le-mata ki na'aseh le-ma'ala*</note> These things portend something both for the rewards due to virtues and the punishment for vices, so that each person must take care how they live and how they die. For this is the whole of our philosophy: that by living well, we may die well, lest by chance we become the portion of the underworld and the avenging Furies, with all hope frustrated, and thus it goes poorly for the wicked.

Now, though it pains me, I think we must depart, since I have been talking with you from morning until night more loquaciously than is proper. For just as I make a kind estimation of myself, I judge you not unworthy of rest, as sleep urges you to go. Then they said: "We are torn away with such regret, Simon," they said, "wishing to hear you forever; therefore, do not speak a word about loquacity. But as you command it, we comply and depart, intending to return to you tomorrow, unless it is inconvenient for you." To this Simon said: "I cannot hide from you, my friends, what I have decided. Tomorrow I shall migrate to a distant place, called away for a wedding, because my uncle has taken a wife at Regensburg <note>Latin: *Ratisponæ*</note>—may the matter turn out well."

Then Philolaus said: "I would urge you with all my strength to stay, were it not unfair, for I confess we are not born for ourselves alone; we grant a part of ourselves to our friends by their own right. Therefore, giving you thanks, we pray for favor upon your journey and your people." Here Marranus, touched with sadness, said: "Go then, with favorable omens, prosperously and happily, my dearest Simon, best of men. Meanwhile, we are forced to wait for the end of the Frankfurt Fair <note>The *nundinae Francofordienses* were major international book and trade fairs</note>, so that we may return more safely with our local merchants from this marketplace to our respective homelands." Then Simon, according to the custom of his people, said: <gloss>Peace be with you.</gloss> <note>Latin: *Pax vobis*</note> To which both of them replied: "Farewell, go, you our glory!"

***

You have here, most holy Leo the Tenth, from Capnio <note>Reuchlin's Greek-style pen name, meaning "Smoky," a pun on the German *Rauch*</note> your humble servant, the opinions and sentences of the ancients on the symbolic philosophy of Pythagoras and the wisdom of the Kabbalah, recited in a brief compendium. Though they are few in number, they may nevertheless provide students with a much broader handle for thinking and investigating. Concerning these matters, I—a man of mediocre talent and tiny prudence—would not dare to judge anything, nor shall I truly judge. But I subject this entire book to your authority, to whose judgment the censorship of the whole world has been committed, so that you may reject what displeases you, and I shall then rejoice that the rest has pleased. 

I trust that this effort of mine—which you may consider me to have undertaken for the sake of both our people and the Republic—will not seem entirely improper to you. This is partly because through my labor, foreign things are made open to our people, and partly because during this half-year of reading them, I have studied to alleviate that five-year war which my enemies carry out against me with your knowledge—if it could not be avoided altogether. Finally, I wish that there might be something of mine near you, so that your memory of us might be more benevolent whenever enemies strive to break and turn away your paternal mind toward me. For I know they do not cease daily to test your pious ears with whispers, now through hired agents, now through letters, such as those I recently read given to you on the 14th of October from Cologne <note>Latin: *Agrippina Colonia*</note>, in which the title lies about the author along with the false accusation. For it was not the venerable University of that worshipful Cologne, but a particularity and a certain foul collection of enemies—a very small part of the city and the more insane one—that did this deed, affirming things to your Holiness which are not true, and that against Apostolic Inhibitions and against the mandates of the Emperor's peace. You see also with what audacity in those same letters they presume to prescribe laws to you as if they were Solonian <note>Refers to Solon, the legendary Athenian lawmaker</note>, and to teach the source of law: by what path the judgment ought to proceed according to their nod and will, so that they might more easily overcome me with filth—as if my innocence were not already held as certain by almost the whole world. Whence I cannot be led to suspect that you would have faith in them—

<meta>This page continues Reuchlin’s formal dedication and defense to Pope Leo X. Reuchlin is responding to the "Reuchlin Affair," a major intellectual and legal conflict where theologians at Cologne sought to burn Jewish books and Reuchlin’s own writings. # JOHANNES REUCHLIN, ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH, BOOK III

...to have <note>This sentence continues from the previous page, where Reuchlin likely spoke of his enemies' audacity.</note> those who, having despised the Apostolic Inhibition and held your censures in contempt, burned my little book while the lawsuit was still pending, without following any legal path. I have, instead, placed my case before the more serious men of Upper Germany—men beyond all reproach—showing that I have caused no scandal and provided no occasion for ruin among any of the German people. These men are joined by the fellowship of the same language, in which language the Counsel of the Chamber is written—a language unknown to those Belgians <note>Reuchlin refers to his enemies at the Universities of Cologne and Louvain, then part of the Burgundian Netherlands or "Belgium."</note>. You can certainly, and indeed securely, believe that clear declaration in its single context, all the more firmly because you were informed of my innocence, piety, and faithfulness nearly three years ago through sealed letters and testimonies. These came from many illustrious rulers of the vast lands of our nation, from the German magistrates and people, and from the most holy towns and cities of our dioceses. 

There are held in your possession testimonies offered three and four times over for my sake by the invincible Roman Emperor-elect, Maximilian I, and by the Most Reverend Cardinal, my Lord of Gurk <note>Matthäus Lang von Wellenburg, a powerful advisor to the Emperor.</note>. After the bishops, testimonies were also given by illustrious presidents of provinces and dukes born of the noblest blood: the Electors of the Empire, Frederick of Saxony and Louis of Bavaria <note>Louis V, Count Palatine, who served as Imperial Vicar or "Interrex" during vacancies.</note>, the Duke of Württemberg, the Prince of Baden, and the most strenuous Master of the Teutonic Order. And their reverend and God-loving German prelates: the Bishop of Worms, the Bishop of Strasbourg, the Bishop of Constance (who, as my pastor, protects me as his sheep), and the Bishop of Speyer—the judge assigned to this case by Your Holiness. Acting with your authority and the counsel of experts, the Bishop of Speyer delivered a definitive sentence in favor of my innocence and that of my writings. 

Along with them, fifty-three towns—all most dutiful, brave, and upright men—likewise gave letters of commendation and testimonies of my correct faith, probity, and identity. To their testimony, the prelates of the Church add strength and weight with their distinguished learning and gravity. You joined these men as architectural supports <term>peristylia</term> <note>A Greek-derived term for a porch or row of columns surrounding a space, here used metaphorically for supporters.</note> to the columns of the orthodox faith, namely the most reverend judges of our cause, Cardinals Grimani and Accolti <note>Domenico Grimani and Pietro Accolti, the Cardinal of Ancona, were the high-ranking Roman judges overseeing Reuchlin's appeal.</note>. Archbishops, bishops, Generals of Orders and their procurators, Roman magistrates, Penitentiaries, and other most select theologians and jurists—to be named in the history of my times according to their individual dignities—were present in the public sessions held in Your Majesty's domestic sanctuary, which they call the Palatine Chapel. There, my advocate, who always acts faithfully as my orator, the most noble Johann von der Wyck <note>A prominent jurist who defended Reuchlin in Rome.</note>—a man of the knightly order and a most sharp debater in legal defenses—and my procurator, finally reached a conclusion. After the cause was fully known, they decreed through published written sentences that I should be freed and acquitted from this injurious prosecution. 

Nor would anyone have doubted that a definitive sentence from the oracle of the Most Reverend Judges would have been equal to this, as was right, had my accusers not then obtained from you a mandate to suspend the proceedings, as they claimed. If you recall the testimony of all those we have cited from every side, and if you care to have the acts of the courts read before you, you will find me entirely removed from every accusation of the informers. May the city of Rome and all the most learned of all nations be witnesses to this purity of mine; I receive grateful letters from them daily, even from the ends of the earth, confirming that I have never been a scandal to anyone in my writings, but rather that I build up the Church daily through various languages for the Holy Spirit, who gathered the nations in the unity of faith through the diversity of tongues. 

They certainly notice that I was the first of all to bring back Greek studies to Germany, and I was the first of all to grant and hand over to the Church this art and the study of the Hebrew language. Therefore, I hope that future generations of the Church will not be ungrateful for my merits; and I hope that the present Most Blessed Pope Leo, a judge of deeds rather than words, will justly return to me my peace and tranquility of mind as a reward for so many and such hard labors on behalf of the orthodox faith. But if you wish me to lie perpetually subject to the persecution of evil men, I would greatly rejoice...

->injuries for the sake of our Christ.<-

<meta>This page marks a transition in the compendium. While the previous pages contained the works of Johannes Reuchlin, we have now reached a new title page and dedicatory epistle. This section focuses on the "theses" or teachings of the famous Renaissance philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, as interpreted by the Franciscan friar Archangelo of Borgonovo. The dedication is written by the editor/publisher, Bernardino Aiano, addressed to the head of the Franciscan Order.</meta>

# OF THE KABBALISTS
## THE MORE SELECT AND OBSCURE
## TEACHINGS,
### Formerly excerpted by GIOVANNI PICO [della Mirandola] from their
### commentaries.
### And now for the first time illustrated with most brilliant
### interpretations by ARCHANGELO OF BORGONOVO,
### of the Order of Friars Minor.

> *In which you will find not a few things that contribute wonderfully to that most beautiful and hidden method of philosophizing through numbers and Mathematics.*

->BERNARDINO AIANO,<-
->TO THE REVEREND FATHER ALOISIO,<-
->most worthy General of the Order of Friars Minor,<-
->sends fondest greetings.<- <note>The original Latin abbreviation S.P.D. stands for Salutem Plurimam Dicit, a standard formal greeting meaning "sends many greetings."</note>

<image-desc>Ornamental initial N set within a square frame featuring a dense foliage and floral design.</image-desc>

I did not think it would be out of place, Reverend Father Aloisio, to signify to you in this letter what I think should be felt regarding this little book by your brother Archangelo. At the same time, I wish to show that I have not looked down upon the most honorable request of the deceased, nor do I seem to have poorly managed my own affairs; rather, I have carried out whatever was imposed upon me. Therefore, know that I have spared no expense (which I thought would be to the benefit of scholars) to comply with the will of your brother, a most learned man. I have seen to it that his most holy labors—which occasionally reveal the secrets <note>original: "arcana"</note> of the Kabbalists—be published with bronze types <note>A reference to the printing press.</note>. I have done this all the more gladly because I thought it would be most pleasing to you, a most erudite man and his own brother. I did this especially at the urging of most learned men, before whose faithful eyes I placed these writings before they were published. They only shuddered at the phrasing, which was not particularly Ciceronian <note>During the Renaissance, "Ciceronian" Latin—imitating the style of the Roman orator Cicero—was considered the gold standard. Medieval or technical Latin was often dismissed as "barbarous."</note> and contained many things closer to "barbarism" than to pure Latin. 

But I ask you, why should this be an obstacle to us? Have we not seen the Hagiographers <note>The "sacred writers" of the Bible.</note> everywhere despise the allurements of words? Do they not bring forth whatever "comes to the cheek" <note>An idiom meaning to speak plainly or whatever comes to mind.</note> in publishing their concepts? Therefore, since the style will not offend the ears of the pious, and the meanings will bring no small utility to all, it is only right that I bid you to hope well for this little book, and I consider myself and your brother to have been well-served. Therefore, let this book go forth happily; let it be received, reread, and loved. Meanwhile, fare thee well, and continue to love me, as you indeed do.

# TO THE MOST LEARNED, AND OF ALL
## KINDS OF RARE THINGS THE MOST ACCOMPLISHED
### MAN, LORD BERNARDINO OF
-> Aiano, a patrician of Parma, <- <note>original: "Ianno patritio Parmensi"</note>

# BROTHER ARCHANGELUS,
-> Franciscan, sends Greetings. <- <note>original: "Minorita, Salutem." The "Minorites" are the Order of Friars Minor, or Franciscans.</note>

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'D' containing a scene of a seated man, likely a scholar or saint, pointing toward an open book or document on a desk.</image-desc>

*Divine providence, reaching and disposing all things strongly, most illustrious Bernardino, established that religion [should be strengthened] not only by the sacred Prophets and firm Doctors, but also to adorn it in a certain elegant and more secret way of the <term>Mystical Theologians</term> <note>original: "secretiori The[ologorum]"</note>: so that Piety itself, the origin of all things, might more easily and safely reach that blessedness for which we were created, and toward which we labor with God. Therefore, Almighty God <note>original: "Deus omnipo[tens]"</note> sent down from on high in [these] times a divine Kabbalistic mind, destined to illuminate religion among all nations. But since until now the Sun of Kabbalistic light had not risen for the Latin or Greek peoples, that famous Pico della Mirandola <note>original: "Picus ille Mirandula"</note>, a man of outstanding piety in Italy, striving to propagate the Kabbalistic light (which is so very salutary for religion) among the Latins, designated many Kabbalistic conclusions as his own: (which I have most recently explained and given to the public for common use). Moreover, he inserted many noteworthy sayings of more secret theologians into his nine hundred conclusions, which he left untouched [unexplained]. But I, being a devotee of the goal of the name of Kabbalah <note>original: "Cabalae cul[tor]"</note>, have undertaken so serious a matter—not indeed by my own authority, but commenting on them in the hope that divine aid would not be lacking for so necessary and pious an office. But against those who bring forth new things, a thousand [dogs] immediately bark, a thousand <term>Charybdises</term> <note>In Greek mythology, Charybdis was a dangerous whirlpool; here it refers to overwhelming critics or obstacles.</note> appear: there is no lack of rivals who tear at such things with envious mouths, pour venom upon them, and spread blasphemous opinions throughout the world. They surely ought to have considered how much opportunity for mockery they provide to heretics and Jews <note>original: "Iudae[is]"</note>, when they see those whom they thought were defenders of Christian dogma now being refuted and rebuked—a sight in which their enemies rejoice, whom they themselves could not defeat in a hostile manner. What doctrine is more suited for overcoming <term>Chaldean</term> <note>The author uses "Chaldean" here to refer to Jewish or Aramaic traditions.</note> perfidy and for silencing the mouths of heretics than the science which is called Kabbalah? O, what a crime, which has never been sufficiently shuddered at (as is right)! I weep for such great glory of the secret theologians (as if for little flowers). For they, once moved by mercy, prepared noble garden springs and deep wells of water <note>original: "aquaru[m] puteos"</note> with tireless spirit for the sheep of Christ the Messiah. But to whom I should offer these, or who would care for these matters, I know not, unless you, most illustrious Bernardino, prove yourself [their protector]. And thus, they will be able to glory in enjoying the breeze of Parma <note>original: "aura Par[m]ēsi"</note> and the <unclear>secret teachings</unclear> <note>original: "secretior gi." - truncated</note>. Therefore, receive very kindly these sayings of the most expert Kabbalists, restored by our explanation and dedicated to you; use them frequently in your discourse, and may they always be most faithful companions to you. Though they have become like the poor of Saint Job, yet they are distinguished among the humble (like <term>Mordecai</term> <note>A hero from the biblical Book of Esther.</note>), and they carry in their pockets the innumerable jewels and furnishings of <term>Abraham</term>, with which your noble soul—like <term>Rebecca</term> <note>The biblical matriarch; the author suggests the soul is a bride to be adorned with spiritual wisdom.</note>—can be adorned. Therefore, what <term>Zacchaeus</term> was to Christ, do you pray for the secret theologians, so that through their sayings there may be salvation for your house in Christ Jesus.*

# ARCHANGELUS, A FRIAR MINOR
## OF
### BORGONOVO IN THE TERRITORY OF PIACENZA,
### ON THE EXPLANATIONS OF THE SAYINGS
->*of the principal, more secret Theologians: that is,*<-

->*AN APOLOGETIC*<-
### Preface to the Reader.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'I' depicting a figure in a study or library setting.</image-desc> AMONG so many varied and manifold gifts which we have received from God, the Best and Greatest giver of all good things, dearest Reader, no one who thinks rightly will believe that anything nobler or more salutary has happened to mortals than wisdom. For this governs the whole life of man. It teaches first how the mind is to be shaped toward God, and then how the whole of life is to be established. Indeed, it is the knowledge of divine and human things; the former [divine], which is concerned with divine matters, is received by the heart alone through "formed faith" <note>A theological term meaning faith animated by love or charity</note>; the latter [human], which regards internal and external human actions, is transmitted through the members of the body to posterity. This human knowledge arranges the exterior and civil life of man and distracts the soul toward the consideration of created things; but that divine wisdom is a most lively spirit, which cannot be expressed by the "killing letter" <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6: "the letter kills, but the spirit gives life."</note>, but is written by the finger of God in the hearts of the faithful, according to that testimony of Jeremiah: *I the Lord will put my Law in their inward parts, and write it upon their hearts; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people* <note>Jeremiah 31:33</note>. For the sake of obtaining this wisdom, among other things that are sought after, I observe nothing more desirable, nothing more useful, and likewise nothing holier than the fact that the monuments of the most ancient, orthodox, and more secret Theologians are now emerging into the light everywhere. For what could ever have been more necessary for the welfare of the Church, or for the convenience and progress of studies? Indeed, the Church will stand safer and firmer with works of this kind—even the smallest of safeguards—and the talents of students are always trained toward better fruit. For antiquity itself possesses I know not what peculiar gift in handling arduous matters and investigating divine business, which Marcus Cicero <note>The Roman orator and philosopher Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> also seems to have understood when, in his inquiries discussing serious causes, he says: Men who lived in those ancient ages, the closer they were to the birth of the world, were also more blessed in opinion and mind. If he seems to have said this aptly regarding the pagans, how much more rightly can we affirm it of our own? And even more so of the "more secret Theologians" <term>secretiores Theologi</term> <note>A term often used by Renaissance thinkers to refer to Kabbalists and mystical writers who sought hidden meanings in scripture.</note>, who do not delay the reader in the explanation of the sacred scriptures with various and clever questions, nor do they pursue useless battles of words and superfluous conflicts (from which envy, contention, and slander are accustomed to sprout). Rather, they are entirely occupied with this: that they may more diligently "shell out" the spirit hiding within the letter of the Law like a kind of husk, so that they may affect the mind, change the sense, lift the soul upward, and finally transform the whole man, however great he may be. And in performing this, they do not anxiously procure foreign aids, but following the maxim of the Apostle <note>St. Paul, specifically 1 Corinthians 2:13</note>, they "compare spiritual things with spiritual," and they blend together a vast force of scriptures preserved from the sacred letters as if from fountains (not without great judgment). For as far as the sense of the letter is concerned, it must be sought mostly from the Hebrews, since they are more dedicated to this business than those who are accustomed to darkness. For although we have procured what is worthy of knowledge from the Hebrews—just as those accustomed to the clearest light see less precisely (as Plato says) in dark places—so the eyes of our own Theologians, dwelling in the spiritual light of the mystical sense, sometimes see less clearly the dark difficulties when they observe them curiously. And because of this, Nicholas of Lyra <note>A 14th-century Franciscan exegete known for his focus on the literal sense and his use of Jewish sources.</note> almost always followed Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent Jewish commentator on the Bible and Talmud.</note>: so that we might test our eyes, and when they disagree with us, we might oppose them. Nevertheless, many things which are worthy of being known we shall note in our own places, as if taking them back from unjust possessors, imparting them to true Israelites: so that they [the Jews] may not boast that they have anything good which the Church does not also have. Jerome also did all these things (so Mirandola believes) in his introduction to the Psalms, unless he had been so occupied in translating that there was no leisure to interpret the Law of Moses; others did not touch Hebrew literature. The allegorical sense (as we have written elsewhere) relates to the literal just as matter relates to form, and it is a kind of species of it which properly and peculiarly suits the sacred letters: namely, that the things being discussed also signify something themselves. And just as the "form" is not seen by us, but only the "matter" clothed in accidental qualities (through the consideration of which we are granted the ability to contemplate forms), in no other way are we carried forward to the allegorical sense—which we do not behold with fleshly eyes—by the help of the literal. Therefore, allegory is established as the goal of understanding; for which reason it is not appropriate to seek it in all things: for not all things are the "end" of all things, but many things have arisen and been established both because of the end and because of necessity. The beginning of this true and heavenly wisdom is defined as the "fear of the Lord" <note>Psalm 111:10</note>: for this gift of God is not sent down into a malevolent soul, nor is that heavenly treasure committed to an earthen vessel, or thrown before swine. This spirit is handed over only to the children of God and citizens of the heavenly kingdom, who can cry from the heart: "Abba, Father." One receives it in this way, another in that; only Christ, in whom the fullness of divinity dwelt, received it without measure. The Philosophers lacked this wisdom, as did all those who were alienated from God. Therefore they vanished in their thoughts <note>original: "euanuerunt in cogitationibus"</note>...

<summary>In this preface, Archangelus of Borgonovo argues that divine wisdom is a spiritual gift written in the heart rather than just the literal text of the Law. He justifies the study of Kabbalah and ancient Jewish commentators like Rashi, claiming that Christians should reclaim this "secret" knowledge to better understand the allegorical and mystical depths of the Bible.</summary>

# TO THE READER.

...in their own reasonings, and their heart was darkened as they felt their way like blind men along a wall; they have nothing to grasp, stumbling at midday as if in the dark, to use the word of Isaiah <note>Isaiah 59:10: "We grope for the wall like the blind, and we grope as if we had no eyes: we stumble at noon day as in the night."</note>. These men were content with secular wisdom, which, although it is great and extremely necessary for this domestic and civil life, provides no help for the attainment of the future life unless heavenly wisdom is added. For "knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up" <note>1 Corinthians 8:1</note>. But if knowledge is joined with charity, then earthly wisdom migrates into the heavenly, and darkness is turned into light. Therefore, best Reader, from among those whom antiquity commends, I have brought forth the sayings of the principal Kabbalists <note>term: Kabbalists. Scholars of Jewish mysticism whose works Archangelus believed held hidden Christian truths.</note>, which are like divine utterances, illuminating a keen intellect and spreading the "good odor of Christ" <note>2 Corinthians 2:15</note>. 

I do not wish to boast here too arrogantly about my own labor or the genius of the authors; if you look a bit more closely, I believe you will not at all accuse our industry, and you will marvel at the dignity of the authors. All these things must be weighed so that we do not err, and also so that we do not provide our enemies with an opportunity to mock us as if we were ignorant. For this reason, it was most wisely decreed in the Council <note>The Council of Vienne, 1311–1312</note> (as Clement says in the unique decree *On Teachers* in the *Clementines* <note>term: Clementines. A collection of decretals or Church laws issued by Pope Clement V.</note>) that in the major universities—Bologna, Paris, Salamanca, and Oxford <note>original: "Exoniensi". Likely a transcription error for "Oxoniensi" (Oxford), as the decree *Inter sollicitudines* specified these four locations.</note>—and especially wherever the Roman Court happens to reside, there should be teachers of various languages: namely, Hebrew, Chaldean <note>term: Chaldean. In this period, this term usually referred to Aramaic or Syriac.</note>, Greek, and Arabic. 

The reasons he provides are these: so that the learned may know how to translate faithfully into Latin, and teach others, and so that men of these languages might be more easily and better instructed. For the meanings of sacred Scripture are gathered more clearly, and others are more easily persuaded, in one's own mother tongue (as they say) than in a foreign one. God, the Best and Greatest, has raised up so many and such great men in this our time studying Hebrew, so that those mysteries <note>original: "sacramenta". In this context, it refers to hidden spiritual truths or "mysteries" rather than just the seven sacraments.</note> which have been hidden until now may be brought out into the light. Therefore, we should not despise such things, lest we wish to appear ignorant, providing an occasion for scorn to those who wish to understand the true scriptures. 

Now, most upright Reader, it is time that we defend the truth itself rather than mere words. For your goodness knows very well that Jerome differs from Augustine in many things, Scotus from Thomas <note>Duns Scotus and Thomas Aquinas, leaders of the two main competing schools of medieval theology.</note>, and Henry <note>likely Henry of Ghent, another major scholastic theologian.</note>. Hence the oracles themselves must be diligently inspected and correctly explored, from which (as Plato correctly thinks) we ought to be taught about divine things. It must also be noted that in interpreting scriptures we should be devoted to no one, nor should we "swear by the words of any master" <note>A common Latin idiom from Horace, meaning to follow a leader blindly.</note>, except for the Church and the Sacred Scripture, whose passages (as is the custom of truly wise men) we must explain one by another—not through philosophy, or through the sayings of those devoted to philosophy. As Paul says: "See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit according to human traditions" <note>Colossians 2:8</note>.

->In these and in all my sayings and writings, I always submit myself to the censure of the<-
->Holy Roman Church and of learned men; and I believe nothing more or less than<-
->the Church itself, my mother, believes. Farewell, and pray to God for me.<-

### ON THE
## MORE SELECT DOGMAS OF THE KABBALISTS,
### EXCERPTED FROM THE COMMENTARIES OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA. <note>Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494) was a brilliant Renaissance philosopher who famously argued that Jewish Kabbalah could be used to prove Christian truths.</note>

> KABBALISTIC DOGMA. Just as the lower man and the Priest sacrifice the souls of irrational animals to God, so Michael, the superior Priest, sacrifices the souls of rational animals. <note>original: "Michaël Sacerdos superior sacrificat animalium animas rationalium." In this mystical context, "rational animals" refers to the souls of human beings being "sacrificed" or elevated to God.</note>

->BROTHER ARCHANGELUS<-

<image-desc>A large decorative initial letter 'S' featuring a woodcut illustration. It depicts two figures in a landscape with a tree: one appears to be a seated scholar or priest, while the other is a winged figure, likely an angel, suggesting the communication between the earthly and heavenly realms discussed in the text.</image-desc>The Priest of the Old Testament, wishing to offer a sacrifice to God, was bound by the Law to carry "doctrine and truth" upon his breast; or, as the truth of the literal text has it, *haurim veet hatumim* <gloss>the Urim and the Thummim</gloss>, which we say, if interpreting correctly, are "illuminations" and "purities," or "innocences," or "freedom from every stain." This is so we may be taught that a Priest must be enlightened, especially in the doctrine of the Law. Therefore it is said in Hosea: "Because you have rejected knowledge, I will reject you, so that you may not perform the office of Priesthood for me" <note>Hosea 4:6</note>. He must also display purity, innocence, and freedom from every stain. By God’s command, he was also required to wear a golden plate on his forehead, which the Hebrews call *tzitz zahab* <gloss>the golden crown or plate</gloss>, upon which was engraved the great four-lettered name of God, *YHWH* <gloss>the Tetragrammaton</gloss>. This was bound upon the linen cap common to all Priests. For the High Priest, however, that plate was fastened to his forehead with a violet ribbon; and this was so that he might enter to perform the sacred rites in the great name of God, from which comes all divine influence and atonement. He also wore a cloak with seventy-two pomegranates; for since he alone among the Priests of the entire world of the Law was the true and legitimate Priest, he alone could pray not only for the people of Israel, but for all the peoples of the world, which are seventy-two in number <note>In medieval tradition, it was believed there were 72 distinct nations and languages in the world.</note>. He also wore seventy-two bells alternating with those pomegranates, so that by them he might awaken the seventy-two princes who presided over the seventy-two languages. They were anointed with the anointing of the power of God’s name; this name of God is called "oil" or "chrism" <note>original: "oleum, uel chrisma"</note> because it makes men light <note>The author is likely making a play on words between "light" as in weightless/spiritualized and the lubricating nature of oil.</note>, just as is said of Jacob and David. It also signifies mercy and atonement, which are granted by the power of the Divine name. The priest, wishing to perform the rites for God, entered into the sanctuary, or into the Holy of Holies; and this occurred when he wished to obtain atonement for the people on the Day of Forgiveness, which the Hebrews call *iom hachepurim* <gloss>Yom Kippur</gloss>. This day was ordained in the seventh month—a number associated with release—and on the tenth day of the Moon of that same month, at which time a fast and "affliction of the soul" were proclaimed, so that the people might more easily obtain forgiveness. And the animals which were required to be offered had to be clean, whole, and without blemish, unless they were offered voluntarily, as is held in Leviticus. This is because unblemished things are owed to an unblemished God. It is commanded especially that they should not lack an ear or a tail; for whatever animal we offer signifies that our own "animal nature" is to be offered to God as an unblemished sacrifice, pleasing to God, just as Paul teaches the Romans <note>Romans 12:1</note>. Regarding this animal nature of ours, we must carefully ensure that it does not lack ears; for through no other sense can a man, while he is in this animal body, capture

# TO THE READER.

...in their own speculations, and their heart was darkened, groping like blind men for a wall, and like those who have no eyes, they stumble at noon as if in darkness, to use the word of *Isaiah*. <note>original: "ut Esaiæ utar uerbo." Referring to Isaiah 59:10.</note> These men alone were content with secular wisdom, which, although it may be great and especially necessary for this kind of domestic and peaceful life, nevertheless provides no aid toward the attainment of the future life unless heavenly wisdom is added. For knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up. <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 8:1.</note> But if knowledge is joined to charity, then earthly wisdom migrates into the heavenly, and darkness is converted into light.

And so, best Reader, from the number of those whom antiquity commends, the sayings of the principal Kabbalists are like divine utterances, illuminating a sharp intellect and giving off the good odor of Christ. I do not wish here to boast too arrogantly of either my own labor or the genius of the authors; if you yourself look inside a little more closely, I believe you will not in the least accuse our industry, and you will admire the dignity of the authors. All these things must be weighed so that we do not err; and also so that we do not provide our enemies an occasion for mocking us as if we were ignorant. 

Therefore, it was most wisely decreed in the Council of Vienne <note>Held in 1311–1312, this council dealt with church reform and the Crusades.</note> (*Clement* in the unique *Clementina* concerning Masters) <note>A reference to the "Clementines," a collection of canon law named after Pope Clement V.</note> that in many universities—those of *Bologna*, *Paris*, *Salamanca*, and *Oxford*—and especially wherever the Roman Curia happens to reside, chairs of various languages should be established: namely, *Hebrew*, *Chaldean* <gloss>Aramaic</gloss>, *Greek*, and *Arabic*. And assigning reasons, he said: "So that the learned may know how to translate faithfully into *Latin* <note>original: "Latinum"</note> and teach others, and so that men of those languages may be more easily and better instructed." For the meanings of sacred writings are gathered more clearly and others are more easily persuaded in their own mother tongue (as they say) than in a foreign one. 

Nor has the Best and Greatest God raised up so many and such great men in our time studying Hebrew without purpose; it is because, I believe, those mysteries which have lain hidden until now are being brought into the light. Whence we ought not to despise such things, unless perhaps we wish to seem ignorant, offering an occasion for contempt to those who wish to grasp the truth of scripture. Now, however, most fair Reader, it is time that we defend truth itself, and not the words of men. For your goodness knows very well that in many things *Jerome* differs from *Augustine*, or *Scotus* <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major High Scholastic theologian.</note> from *Thomas* <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274).</note> and *Henry* <note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293).</note>. Hence the oracles themselves must be diligently inspected and weighed with a right examination, from which (as *Plato* rightly feels) we ought to be taught concerning divine things. 

It must also be noted that in interpreting the scriptures we ought to be devoted to no one, nor swear by the words of any Master, except the Holy Church and the Sacred Scripture, whose passages (as is the method of truly wise men) we determine one through another; not, however, through philosophy, or through the sayings of those who are devoted to philosophy; for he says:

> *See to it that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit according to the tradition of men.* <note>Colossians 2:8.</note>

In these and in all my sayings and writings, I always submit myself to the judgment of the most holy Roman Church and of skilled men, and I believe nothing more or less than what she, my mother the Church, believes. Farewell, and pray to God for me.

# THE INTERPRETATIONS OF ARCHANGELUS THE MINORITE <note>Archangelus of Borgonovo (1512–1571) was a Franciscan friar and Kabbalist.</note> REGARDING THE MORE SELECT DOGMAS OF THE KABBALISTS, EXCERPTED FROM THE COMMENTARIES OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA.

->*KABBALISTIC DOGMA: Just as man, an inferior Priest, sacrifices the souls of irrational animals to God; so Michael, the superior Priest, sacrifices the souls of rational animals.*<-

->BROTHER ARCHANGELUS<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'S' depicting a figure (possibly a saint or scholar) seated in a landscape, surrounded by ornate foliate patterns.</image-desc>The Priest of the Old Testament, wishing to sacrifice to God, was bound by the Law to carry upon his breast Doctrine and Truth: or, as the truth of the letter has it, *The Lights and the Perfections* <note>original: "האורים ואת התומים *Haurim veet hatumim*," commonly known as the Urim and Thummim, objects used by the High Priest to determine God's will.</note>—which, by interpreting correctly, we call "illuminations" and "purities," or "innocence," or "freedom from every stain." This is so we may be taught that a Priest ought to be illuminated, especially in the doctrine of the Law. And for this reason it is said in Hosea: *Because you have rejected knowledge, I will reject you, so that you may not perform the office of Priesthood for me.* <note>Hosea 4:6.</note> He ought also to display purity, innocence, and freedom from every stain. 

By the command of God, he was also bound to carry on his forehead a golden plate, which the Hebrews call the *golden crown* <note>original: "ציץ זהב *tzitz zahab*."</note>; upon which was engraved the great name, the Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter divine name of God, YHWH.</note> יהוה. This was bound upon a linen cap common to all the Priests. However, for the High Priest, that plate was fastened to his forehead with a violet-blue ribbon. This was so that he might enter to perform the sacred rites in the great name of God, from which flows all influence and atonement. 

He also wore a cloak with seventy-two pomegranates; because, since he alone among the Priests of the entire world of the Law was the true and legitimate Priest, he alone was able to pray not only for the Israelite people, but for all the peoples of the world, of which there are seventy-two. <note>In traditional geography and biblical genealogy (the Table of Nations in Genesis 10), it was believed there were 72 distinct nations and languages in the world.</note> He also wore seventy-two bells alternating with those pomegranates, so that by them he might stir the seventy-two princes <note>Angelic governors believed to rule over the different nations.</note> who presided over the seventy-two languages. 

These were anointed with the anointing of the power of the name of God; which name of God is called "oil" or "chrism," because it makes men light—just as is said of Jacob and David. It also signifies mercy and atonement, which is granted by the power of the Divine name. And the Priest, wishing to perform the sacred rites for God, entered into the sanctuary, or the Holy of Holies. This took place when he wished to procure atonement for the people on the Day of Remissions, which the Hebrews call the *Day of Atonement* <note>original: "יום כפורים *iom hachepurim*," or Yom Kippur.</note>. This day was ordained in the seventh month (a number associated with release) and on the tenth day of the Moon of that month, at which time a fast and "affliction of the soul" was proclaimed, so that the people might more easily obtain remission. 

The animals that were required to be offered had to be clean, whole, and without blemish—unless they were offered voluntarily, as is held in Leviticus. This is because spotless things are owed to a spotless God. It is commanded especially that they should not lack an ear or a tail; for whatever animal we offer signifies that our own "animal" <note>The "animal soul" or the lower, instinctive part of human nature.</note> must be offered to God as a spotless sacrifice, pleasing to God, just as Paul teaches the Romans. <note>Romans 12:1.</note> For this animal, one must carefully see to it that ears are not lacking; for by no other sense can a man, while he is in the animal body, perceive—

### ARCHANGELUS’ COMMENTARY.

...[knowledge of] Divine things cannot be had, except through hearing: because faith, in which we are taught about divine things, comes from hearing: as Paul says <note>Romans 10:17: "Faith comes by hearing."</note>. For this reason, animals of this kind <note>Likely referring to the priests or those performing the sacrifice mentioned on the preceding page.</note> ought also to have [a golden plate], which signifies perseverance in good works. The Law also commands that two lambs be offered: one in the evening, and the other in the morning. The evening sacrifice was performed to appease the accusers who appear before the tribunal of justice; they accused the uncircumcised as if they were guilty of original sin not yet expiated. However, the morning sacrifice was performed to obtain the grace of mercy and piety from the tribunal located in the South. And the Law commanded that these two lambs be offered to God forever.

Many other sacrifices were also performed, for they possess a certain symbol or connection with the one to whom they are offered, and with those who are being expiated. This connection contains a hidden meaning <note>original: "nomen occultum"</note> so deep that the human intellect cannot fully grasp it, even though almost all nations confess that sacrifices are necessary. For sacrifice is a certain intermediate and supernatural act between God and man. To sacrifice to God (as Aristotle says in the fifth book of his *Ethics*, and Proclus in his book *On Prayers and Supplications*, as well as Plato, Plotinus, and Porphyry) is proper to man, just as lowing is to oxen or barking to dogs. Furthermore, they add that whoever neglects to perform this deserves to be cast out from human nature and denied the name of "man." For sacrificing is "proper" to man in the "fourth mode" <note>In Aristotelian logic, a "fourth mode" property is something that belongs to all members of a species, to them alone, and always (e.g., man’s ability to laugh).</note>: it belongs to every man, to man alone, and at all times.

However, the offering of this or that specific sacrifice for this or that expiation, although most fitting according to the natural order, was nevertheless instituted by God. Human inquiry is not sufficient to discover what God requires for our expiation in particular cases, according to the order of celestial things, so that the heavens may be rendered peaceful toward those being expiated through the expiating sacrifices, and may restrain themselves from executing the punishment that the committed sins deserve.

For the blood of animals is seen to purge away the sin committed in the flesh from the blood of our own animal nature, according to that saying of the Apostle: *Almost all things are cleansed in blood* <note>Hebrews 9:22.</note>. He says "almost" because earthenware and bronze vessels were cleansed with water. Therefore, not without reason, man—who is the bond of all things <note>original: "uinculum," a common Neoplatonic and Renaissance term for man as the 'bridge' or 'microcosm' connecting the material and spiritual worlds.</note>, contains all things, and holds his greatest power in his lower part, in which and through which the stain of sin is contracted—was purged through the blood of irrational animals offered by the priest of the Law.

Yet, even before this, there were certain sacrifices: for example, the fruits of the earth and the firstfruits, as seen in the practice of Abel’s father <note>Adam</note> and in the observation of the Law of Nature. Regarding these, God was satisfied for the expiation of sins, as Paul witnesses: *They are a law unto themselves, who show the work of the Law written in their hearts* <note>Romans 2:14–15.</note>, and so forth. And just as the Written Law stood as something more perfect than the Law of Nature, so God instituted within it more perfect sacrifices of animals; for animals are more perfect than the firstfruits of crops. 

And because the Gospel is more perfect than the Law, God has therefore instituted a nobler sacrifice: a sacrifice of love and filial fear, namely the sacrifice of the unblemished lamb, Christ, who fulfills all the things that were previously offered. For He offered and purged everything more perfectly, insofar as He Himself is the more exalted "bond" of all creatures—rational and irrational, insensate and celestial. Thus, the blood of animals was received into the holy place along with the sins of those for whom it was offered, until He should come, who through His own blood entered the holy place, having found eternal redemption.

To return to the matter from which we digressed: just as the priest of the Law offered the souls of irrational animals, so Michael is the priest and prince over the souls to be received, and he offers them to God. For Jude <note>original: "Thadeus," referring to the Epistle of Jude (often identified with Thaddeus).</note> mentions in his canonical epistle that Michael even contended with the Devil over the body of Moses. For the Devil (as the Hebrew teachers assert) and those unclean powers feed upon these thicker things composed of earthly matter. Just as it was declared by God to the ancient serpent in Genesis: *You shall eat the earth all the days of your life* <note>Genesis 3:14.</note>; and also through Isaiah, when the perfect rest of the elect is described, it is said: *and for the serpent, dust shall be its bread* <note>Isaiah 65:25.</note>.

...our animal nature, just as it is written: *God formed man from the dust of the earth* <note>Genesis 2:7</note>, for which we use the phrase "from the slime of the earth." This dust is the animal nature—not that which is changed for the better and rises spiritual, but that which is abandoned to corruption and cast off as earth, dust, and dregs. It is cast off to be food for the serpent, because, as Paul says: *Though we shall all rise, we shall not all be changed* <note>1 Corinthians 15:51 (Vulgate reading)</note>. This implies that some remain as food for the serpent, whom the adversaries strive to devour even in this life, as the Prophet sings: *The young lions roar after their prey, and seek their meat from God* <note>Psalm 104:21</note>. For the "young lions" are commonly interpreted by everyone as our adversaries <note>demons or spiritual enemies</note> who (as Peter says) *walk about seeking whom they may devour* <note>1 Peter 5:8</note>. They are said to "seek their meat from God" because they can take nothing for themselves unless God permits it. Therefore, carcasses are given to these serpents for food. This is the reason why such things strike terror into mortals; it happens because of their very presence.

For, as I have said, Michael also argued with the Devil over the body of Moses <note>Jude 1:9</note>. The Devil wanted to carry it away as something subject to sin, but Michael, on the contrary, wanted to present it to God as something purged by the Law and purified by divine fellowship. From this fellowship, Moses' face had been brought to such clarity that the children of Israel could not gaze upon it because of the brightness of his countenance. Thus Michael fought like a true priest—and his angels, that is, his ministers, fought with him—for the souls of all against the ancient serpent, who continually seeks to devour them. But Michael prevailed, and the dragon was cast out.

He is no less a help to the people of God now and continually, as we read in Daniel: *Michael the great prince, who stands for the children of thy people* <note>Daniel 12:1</note>; that is, for the elect. Michael therefore exercises a perpetual priesthood as the great priest of God. For this reason, the more secret theologians <note>the Kabbalists</note> call him the <term>High Priest</term> <note>original Hebrew: כהן גדול (*kohen gadol*)</note>. For just as that earthly high priest used to offer the souls of animals (as I said), so Michael the priest offers rational souls to God. He sacrifices as a vicar <note>a representative or deputy</note> in heaven, just as common priests, acting as vicars of Christ, sacrifice or offer the body of Christ, which has already been sacrificed and offered by Christ himself. In this, they perform that duty which Christ himself gave to them, saying: *Do this in memory of me.*

Michael himself is the prince of the host of Christ, appointed over all souls that are to be received. He weighs them, not indeed with physical scales or balances—for the soul has no weight—but he balances them with a scale that has a symbolic relationship with the measure of the heavenly city. He, the priest of heaven, equates the merits of each person with the reward to be given with the highest justice, so that no more or less is given than what those to be rewarded deserve. This is done not in an arithmetic proportion, but in a geometric one <note>Meaning the reward is proportional to the quality of the merit, rather than a simple one-to-one tally</note>. For all things are discussed with the utmost subtlety in the tribunal of divine justice. Michael holds the princedom of that place among the angels standing there.

Nevertheless, before souls are sacrificed by Michael, they have already been sacrificed first by Christ, the true and supreme priest according to the order of Melchizedek. For Melchizedek signifies "my just king." And Christ was a priest, not of the legal sort like Aaron, but a Royal one, like Melchizedek, who was the King of Salem. Hence Peter, addressing Christians who follow the priesthood of Christ, says: *You are a holy nation, a royal priesthood* <note>1 Peter 2:9</note>. And just as Melchizedek was the King of Salem—that is, of Jerusalem and of the lower peace—so Christ is the king of the heavenly Jerusalem and of the higher peace. 

Through the "southern and morning bread," every morning sacrifice is understood; and through the "northern and evening wine," every evening sacrifice is understood. One of these, the evening sacrifice, was performed (as I said) to appease the accusers; the other, the morning sacrifice, was for the obtaining of benefits, as the truly wise say. Christ encompassed all these things in a single sacrifice, just as Melchizedek had prefigured him; his priesthood remains forever. Hence Paul says: *Others indeed were made many priests, because by death they were not suffered to continue; but this man, Christ...* <note>Hebrews 7:23-24</note>

<header>ON THE TEACHINGS OF THE KABBALISTS</header>

Just as the matter of the heavens differs from the matter of things that are subject to birth and decay by a certain analogy, so too does the matter of angels differ from the matter of other things. This is why the ancient writers Basilius, Origen, and Gregory, as well as all the Academics <note>The "Academics" refers to the followers of the Platonic Academy, whose philosophy often blended with early Christian thought.</note>, said that angels possess bodies. For this reason, they can be called "living beings" <note>original: "animalia." In this context, it means a being possessed of an "anima" or soul, rather than a beast.</note> without error. Thus, Hermes Trismegistus, all the Academics, and many of our more ancient doctors assert that angels are corporeal and living beings. For Basilius says: "Angels have bodies, like certain thin spirits, airy and pure." We can learn this from David, who says: *He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire* <note>Psalm 104:4</note>. Indeed, an angel could not be moved from place to place unless it had a body, since local motion belongs only to a body. Hence Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, the primary source for Christian angelic hierarchy.</note> says that they are mixed with matter—specifically, I say, metaphysical matter. 

However, because there are degrees of perfection within them, and the angels of the first triad are closer to God than other creatures, they enjoy the expression of the image of the triune God and represent the diffusion of the highest essence in the Trinity. The Father, having the essence of all things as the object of His intellect, by understanding Himself, begets Wisdom, or the Word, or the knowledge of Himself: who is called the Son. Hence He takes for Himself the name of "Father." Therefore, when Wisdom is produced, since it is most like the producer and emanates from Him by a natural progression, it receives the name of "Son"; and the Love budding forth from both is called the Spirit, the bond of them both. 

With this Love connecting the Parent with the Offspring, the Seraphic and Cherubic orders correspond. For the one full of wisdom and beauty corresponds to the Son of the highest wisdom, who is called the "pleasure of the Father" and the splendor and beauty of all things. The Thrones, however, serve the Father; sitting upon them, He glories in the continual production of the Word and the Spirit, and through them they judge the world, as the Psalm testifies: *He has prepared his throne in judgment* <note>Psalm 9:7</note>. The Father grants this seat to the Son, attributing to him all-encompassing power of judging, as he himself testifies in the Apocalypse, saying: *I have overcome, and I sit on the throne of my Father* <note>Revelation 3:21</note>. 

Furthermore, since that Highest Good diffuses itself into others, it produced here another threefold order for the sake of producing and governing creatures. Through these orders and ministers, like a magnificent craftsman and prince, He decided to work and to rule. Because God the Father gives to all things that they might exist, He is rightly called the Lord of all. Of Him it is said in the sacred word: *You are the Lord of all things.* Hence the order of **Dominions** corresponds to Him. And because He presides with due order and Power, which He gave to the Son—who says: *All power is given to me in heaven and on earth*—they are called **Powers**, because they execute those things over which it was given to the Son to preside. And because He gives life, constancy, and holiness to all things rightly disposed, through the Spirit of holiness and life, another order is required: namely, the **Virtues**, through which all things are led to true life and holiness. And this is what the Psalmist says: *By the spirit of his mouth is all their virtue* <note>Psalm 33:6</note>. 

And since God Himself is triune, He communicates for a threefold reason; therefore, He decreed to care for Man, who is the "knot" of all things <note>The "knot of the world" (nodus mundi) is a classic Neoplatonic concept where man connects the spiritual and material realms.</note>, through a triple order. For He distinguished the human race by ranks—namely, superiors and inferiors—and He partitioned and distributed kingdoms and provinces, over which He commanded some to be preferred in spiritual governance and others in civil governance. Over these kingdoms and provinces, He placed the order of **Principalities**. Over princes and governors, He placed the order of **Archangels**. To every single human being, however, He distributed the order of **Angels**, as Christ testifies: *Their angels always see the face of my Father, who is in heaven* <note>Matthew 18:10</note>. 

The Hebrews, however, call the first order <term>חיות קדוס</term> <gloss>haioth kadosch</gloss>: that is, "holy living beings" or "lives." Through these angels, God, as the name <term>אהיה</term> <gloss>eheie</gloss> <note>Eheieh: "I AM," the name revealed to Moses at the bush.</note>, bestows the gift of being. Secondly, He bestows <term>אופנים</term> <gloss>ophanim</gloss>: that is, "forms" or "wheels," through whom God as <term>אלהים</term> <gloss>Aelohim</gloss> distinguishes chaos. In the third place are the <term>אראלים</term> <gloss>Arelim</gloss>, the "great, strong, and robust angels." Through these, the Tetragrammaton <term>יהוה</term> pronounced as <term>אלהים</term> <gloss>Aelohim</gloss>, or the Tetragrammaton <term>יהוה</term> with this conjunction <term>יהוה</term>, ministers the form of flowing matter. In the fourth place are the <term>חשמלים</term> <gloss>chaschmalim</gloss>, through whom the God *Elohe* fashions the shapes of bodies:

The matter of the heavens differs from the matter of things that can be born and decay by a certain analogy; in the same way, the matter of angels differs from the matter of other things. Hence the ancients—Basil, Origen, and Gregory—and all the Academics <note>The "Academics" refers to the followers of the Platonic school of philosophy.</note> said that angels have bodies. For this reason, they can be called "living beings" <note>original: "animalia." In this context, it refers to beings possessing an *anima* or soul, rather than "animals" in the modern sense.</note> without error. Whence Hermes Trismegistus, and all the Academics, and many of our older doctors assert that angels are corporeal and are living beings. For Basil says: "Angels have bodies, like certain thin, airy, and pure spirits." This we can learn from David, who says: *He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers flames of fire.* <note>Psalm 104:4</note> Nor could an angel be moved from place to place unless he had a body, since local motion belongs only to a body. Hence Dionysius says they are mixed with matter—I mean, with metaphysical matter.

However, because there are degrees of perfection within them, the angels of the first triad are closest to God and other created things. Because they enjoy the expression of the image of the Triune God, they represent the diffusion of the highest essence within the Trinity. The Father, having the essence of all things before His intellect, by understanding Himself, begets Wisdom, or the Word, or the knowledge of Himself, which is called the Son. From this, He acquires the name of Father. Thus, Wisdom having been produced—since it is most like the producer and emanates from Him by a natural progression—it receives the name of Son. But the Love blossoming from both is called the Spirit, the nexus of both. To this Love, which connects the parent with the offspring, the Seraphic and Cherubic orders correspond; for the one full of wisdom and beauty corresponds to the Son of the highest wisdom, who is called the "delight of the Father" and the decorum and beauty of all things.

The Thrones, however, serve the Father, in whom He sits and glories through the continuous production of the Word and the Spirit, and in them they judge the world, as the Psalm testifies: *He has prepared his throne in judgment.* This seat the Father grants to the Son, attributing to him every kind of power of judging, as he himself testifies in the Apocalypse, saying: *I have overcome, and I sit on the throne of my Father.* <note>Revelation 3:21</note> Furthermore, since that highest Good diffuses itself into others, He produced another triple order for the purpose of producing and governing creatures. In these orders and ministers, like a magnificent craftsman and prince, He decided to work and to rule. Therefore, because God the Father gives to all things that they may exist, He is rightly called the Lord of all. Of Him it is said in the sacred word: *You are the Lord of all things.* To Him, therefore, the order of **Dominations** corresponds. And because He presides with due order and Power, which He gave to the Son—who said: *All power is given to me in heaven and on earth*—they are called **Powers**, because they execute those things over which it was given to the Son to preside. And because He gives life, constancy, and holiness to all things rightly disposed, through the spirit of holiness and life, another order is required, namely the **Virtues**, through which all things are led to true life and holiness. And this is what the Psalmist says: *By the spirit of his mouth is all their virtue.* <note>Psalm 33:6</note>

And since God Himself is triune, He communicates for a threefold reason; therefore, He decreed to care for man—who is the knot of all things—through a triple order. For He distinguished the human race by degrees, namely the higher and the lower; and He partitioned and distributed kingdoms and provinces, over which He commanded some to be preferred in spiritual rule and others in civil government. Over these kingdoms and provinces, He placed the order of **Principalities**. Over princes and presidents, He placed the order of **Archangels**. But to every single human being, He distributed the order of **Angels**, as Christ testifies: *Their angels always see the face of my Father, who is in heaven.* <note>Matthew 18:10</note>

The Hebrews, however, call the first order <gloss>holy living creatures</gloss> <insert>original Hebrew: חיות קדוש *haioth kadosch*</insert>; that is, the animals of holiness, or lives; through which angels God bestows the gift of being, <term>Eheieh</term> <note>original: אהיה. A Hebrew name for God meaning "I AM."</note>. In the second place, He bestows <gloss>wheels</gloss> <insert>original Hebrew: אופנים *ophanim*</insert>; that is, forms or wheels, through which God, <term>Elohim</term> <note>original: אלהים. A common Hebrew name for God.</note>, distinguishes chaos. In the third place are the <gloss>strong ones</gloss> <insert>original Hebrew: אראלים *Aralim*</insert>, angels who are great, strong, and robust. Through these, the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter name of God, YHWH.</note> pronounced as *Elohim*, or the Tetragrammaton with this conjunction <term>Adonai</term> <note>original: אדני. Meaning "Lord."</note>, administers the form of fluid matter. In the fourth place are the <gloss>shining ones</gloss> <insert>original Hebrew: חשמלים *chaschmalim*</insert>, through whom the God *Elohe* shapes the images of bodies:
