# ARCHANGELUS’S COMMENTARY

images: in the fifth place are the **Seraphim** <note>original: *שרפים*; meaning 'the burning ones'</note>: through whom God as **the Mighty Lord** <note>original: *יהוה גבור* (YHWH Gibor)</note> brings forth the elements; in the sixth place are the **Messengers** <note>original: *מלאכים* (Malachim)</note>: through whom God as **the Divine One** <note>original: *אלה* (Eloha)</note> produces metals; in the seventh place are the **Godlike Powers** <note>original: *אלהים* (Elohim)</note>, that is, the Gods, through whom God as the **Four-Lettered Lord of Hosts** <note>original: *יהוה צבאות* (YHWH Zabaoth)</note> brings forth vegetation; in the eighth place are the **Sons of God** <note>original: *בני אלהים* (Bene Elohim)</note>: through whom God as the **Divine Power of Hosts** <note>original: *אלהים צבאות* (Elohim Zabaoth)</note> procreates animals; in the ninth are the **Cherubim** <note>original: *כרובים*</note>: through whom God as the **Almighty** <note>original: *sadai* (Shaddai)</note> cares for the human race. To these is added the order called the **Souls** <note>original: *אישים* (Issim); often interpreted as 'men' or 'individual souls'</note>: that is, heroes, strong and blessed men, through whom God as **the Lord** <note>original: *אדני* (Adonai)</note> bestows the gift of prophecy. 

Our own theologians, however, set out the distinctions of the angels differently, and divide each of these into three, making three primary groups that constitute nine orders and hierarchies, or choirs. In the **higher hierarchy**, they place the Seraphim, [Cherubim], and Thrones, as super-celestial spirits who contemplate Divine Providence: the first in God's goodness, the second in His essence, and the third in His wisdom. 

In the **middle hierarchy**, they place the Dominations, Virtues, and Powers, as worldly spirits cooperating in the governance of the Universe: the first command what the others execute; the second administer, never aspiring to perform miracles [on their own]; and the third ward off those things that seem able to disturb the divine law. 

In the **lower hierarchy**, they place the Principalities, Archangels, and Angels: these descend to care for lower things. The first of these care for public affairs, princes, magistrates, provinces, and each individual thing; the second are present at sacred rites: they direct Divine worship regarding individual matters, and they offer the prayers and sacrifices of men before God; they also distribute gifts, and each is present to an individual person: they even supply power to the smallest blades of grass and hairs. They have much in common with God and much in common with men, and they act as mediating ministers. 

However, if one wished to discuss the choirs of angels more fully, it would be a very long process. I will put forward a few things briefly. I say that the orders of <term>Intelligences</term> <note>In medieval philosophy, "Intelligences" refers to the non-physical minds that move the celestial spheres.</note>, as I have said, are nine according to everyone; and they assert this with good reason. Since God emanated in their production through the square of the three: which is nine. 

But the more secret and ancient theologians, although they do not differ in number, call these orders by other names: namely the **Brilliant Ones** <note>original: *שמלים* (Chasmalim)</note>, the **Cherubim**, the **Lion-like Ones** <note>original: *אראלים* (Arelim)</note>, the **Wheels** <note>original: *אופנים* (Ophanim)</note>, the **Souls** <note>original: *אישים* (Issim)</note>, and the **Divine Powers** <note>original: *אלהים* (Elohim)</note>. And they add the **Sons of God** <note>original: *בני אלהים* (Bene Elohim)</note>, who signify both the good and evil ministers of God's justice without distinction. Mention is made of all these in Holy Scripture. For Ezekiel mentions the *Chasmalim*. Mention is made of the Cherubim in Genesis and many other places. Ezekiel also mentions the *Tarsissim* [Chrysolites/Topaz-colored ones]. In the common edition [of the Bible], this is rendered as: "Angels or messengers." Ezekiel himself mentions the *Ophanim* [Wheels]. The *Issim* are named by Solomon. Mention of the *Elohim* is found in many places, especially in the first book of Kings: where the medium <note>original: *pythonissa*; referring to the Witch of Endor</note> said: *I saw gods [Elohim] ascending from the earth*; which the common translation renders as: "Gods indeed." The "Sons of God" (*Bene Elohim*) are mentioned as good ones by Job, and as evil ones by Moses and others. 

And although there are only nine orders of them, they nevertheless constitute many more divisions. Hence, the more secret theologians, trying to designate this number, distinguish their armies into **Constellations** <note>original: *מזלות* (Mizaloth); related to the Zodiac</note>, **El**, **Ligion** [Legion], **Rihaton**, **Kirton**, and **Giftera**. The *Mizaloth* are said to be twelve, according to the twelve signs of the Zodiac. They say *El* refers to thirty cohorts in each of those twelve. Whence there are three hundred and sixty soul-cohorts in number. *Ligion* [Legion], however, multiplies that number of three hundred and sixty by thirty. This results in the number ten thousand eight hundred. The Kabbalists themselves multiply this again by thirty: and it becomes *Rihaton*, consisting of three hundred and twenty-four thousand. And this number they still multiply by thirty...

Paul speaks of their natural disposition, but Daniel treats of those to whom duties have already been assigned. These offices of the angels are varied: some are standing at the Divine tribunal, continuously praising God; while others are ministering to Him, and to us. Those who minister correspond to these duties. Some of these are in charge of the four watches of the night, which Christ mentions, saying: "And if he comes in the second and third watch of the night," etc. Others are also placed over the four seasons of the year, through the four stations of the Sun, distinguished from one turning point to the next. Others are in charge of the planets. Others also preside over the twelve signs of the Zodiac, of which John <note>Referring to the author of the Book of Revelation</note> makes mention, saying that in the gates—that is, the signs, which (as Plato says) are the gates of heaven—there are twelve angels. And since some of these signs are Eastern, some Western, some Southern, and others Northern, John himself follows this by saying: "On the east three gates, on the north three gates, on the south three gates, and on the west three gates." Other angels are assigned to our protection and guardianship. Some preside over animals, others over plants, others over the stones which are called precious—as the more secret theologians and truly wise men affirm. Some are also in charge of war, others of peace, others of kings and prelates. Others are in charge of provinces and regions, which differ in their customs according to the difference of their guardians. Indeed, angels are placed over all things and operations, so that God works all things in this lower world through the ministry of angels. Therefore Paul, not being ignorant of these mysteries, says: "All are ministering spirits, sent forth to serve," as I have already stated.

-> KABBALISTIC DOGMA: *Although the ineffable name is the attribute of mercy, it must not be denied that it also contains the attribute of judgment.* <-

**BROTHER ARCHANGELUS.** Even if God is unique, and most truly one, He is nonetheless called by many names: not indeed so that multiple essences or deities might be expressed by them, but rather His attributes <note>original: *proprietates*; qualities or characteristics of God</note>. Although these emanate from the same fountain of the Deity, they are always rooted there as one. But they are called "many" by reason of their relation to us, upon whom many benefits and diverse gifts trickle down through various channels. For this reason, the most invincible God Himself receives diverse names (each of which I have declared individually in the *Gate of Light* <note>original: *Porta Lucis*; a reference to Joseph Gikatilla's *Sha'are Orah*, a fundamental Kabbalistic text</note>), yet in such a way that each of these names has an influence appropriated to itself. For example, this name **El** <note>original: *אל* (El)</note>, which we have translated as "God," cherishes all things and aids all with the highest piety and mercy, which is its proper nature; and therefore grace is attributed to it. To the name **Aelohim** <note>original: *אלהים* (Elohim)</note>, however, severe punishments, slaughters, and men of war are attributed; hence, God is also seen exercising His power as a strong warrior or a robust crusher. Therefore, He assigns judgment to this name. And the angels serving Him are rightly called *Aelohim*—that is, the sons of *Aelohim*. *Aelohim* therefore signifies terror and dread; hence the Northern region is assigned to it, from which all evil of guilt proceeds through the transgression of the Law, and the evil of punishment from the retribution for sin. If, therefore, we wish to ask for a thing of grace, we must invoke the name *El*, just as it is read concerning Moses (as is clear in the *Conclusions* of Pico <note>Referring to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, who wrote "900 Theses" including Kabbalistic conclusions</note>), who from

# THE COMMENTARY OF ARCHANGELUS

Regarding the gift of healing for his sister Miriam, who was suffering from leprosy, Moses sought it by praying: **"O God, please heal her now, I pray."** <note>original: "El, na, rapha, na, la" from Numbers 12:13</note>. **El** means the God of grace; **rapha** means "heal," as in "I beseech You, heal"; and **la** means "her." If anyone desires the influence of judgment and justice, they use the name **Elohim**, for that name is the minister of all punishments. Therefore, I conclude that we must request things from the appropriate spiritual locations, and the invocation of healing was appropriate to that place, as we said regarding Moses, who merited to pray for his sister's health. Therefore, for one who wishes to perform such spiritual work, a knowledge of the Names and their specific properties is necessary. Concerning this, see what I have arranged in my commentary on the *Gates of Light* <note>original: "Porta lucis," referring to the *Sha'are Orah* by Joseph Gikatilla, a foundational Kabbalistic text</note>. Regarding this matter, it is said in the assembly that the ineffable **Tetragrammaton** <term>Tetragrammaton: The four-letter name of God, YHWH, considered too sacred to pronounce</term> does not belong only to pure mercy, but also to judgment.

There are three principal Divine Names. The first is **Eheie** <note>original: "אהיה" meaning "I Am"</note>, the name of the simple and primary fountain of all mercy and the source of graces, sparing everyone, the Father of mercies, and the God of all consolation. Christ teaches us to pray to Him in times of need, saying: "When you pray, say: Our Father, who art in heaven," etc. And of the same Name, he adds: "The Father judges no one." The third name is **Adonai** <note>original: "Aedonai," written with Aleph, Nun, Yod, Daleth (אדני)</note>, which in itself belongs entirely to judgment, containing no grace except insofar as it receives favor from the first name, **Eheie**, through the intermediate emanations. This name **Adonai** is located in the last <term>sephirah: One of the ten attributes or "spheres" of divine emanation in Kabbalah</term>, just as **Eheie** is in the first.

The second name, mediating between these two extremes, is the ineffable **Tetragrammaton** (יהוה). It is located in **Tiphereth** <note>The Sephirah of "Beauty" or "Harmony"</note> on the central line—the line, I say, between the sephiroth on the right and the sephiroth on the left. Therefore, it participates in both sides, as if connecting the extremes. For this reason, it is called by the title "Beauty," and it proportionally contains all types of divine influences. Thus, although the Tetragrammaton is a name of mercy, it also takes on the flow from the sephiroth of the left side <note>The side of Gevurah or Strength/Judgment</note>, and thus it acquires the character of a name of judgment. 

In such cases, this name is marked with the vowel points of **Elohim**—namely *hataf-segol*, *holem*, and *hiriq*—and is thus pronounced as **Yehoi**, just like **Elohim**. However, by its own nature, it ought to be pronounced as **Jehovah**, with the vowel points *sheva*, *holem*, and *qametz*. Nevertheless, even if this ineffable name participates in both extremes (as we have seen), grace shines more brightly within it than judgment. For God uses total grace and mercy toward us more than judgment; He rewards us beyond what we deserve and punishes us less than our faults. Therefore, this ineffable name sometimes fulfills the role of a name of judgment, and sometimes a name of grace. When it is taken in judgment, it happens so that God may manifest that He brings judgment with great mercy, so that He feels sorrow for the one suffering, as the prophet says: "Alas, I will take comfort against my enemies," etc. <note>Isaiah 1:24</note>. And elsewhere: "The death of the sinner is not my will, but rather that he be converted and live" <note>Ezekiel 33:11</note>. Therefore, although the ineffable name is a name of grace, it cannot be denied that it is also one of judgment. 

The Name of God is the same as God Himself and the Divine Power, as the Hebrew doctors also feel when they interpret it this way: Just as the Lord testifies concerning the angel sent for the protection and guidance of Moses, saying: "Behold, I send my angel, who shall go before you; observe him and hear his voice, for my name is in him"—that is, the power of my name and my divinity, as the aforementioned scholars explain. In ancient times, wonders were performed through the name **El Shaddai** <note>original: שדי, meaning "God Almighty"</note> until the time of Moses; and from then until Christ, they were performed through the four-letter name **YHWH** (יהוה), that great name. 

Furthermore, all the letters of this most sacred name signify **circular numbers**. For *Yod* represents ten, *He* five, and *Vav* six. These are the only circular numbers <note>Circular numbers are those whose squares end in the same digit as the number itself (e.g., 5x5=25, 6x6=36)</note>, as was touched upon above in the conclusions of **Mirandula** <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, the famous Renaissance philosopher</note>. This hints that God is a true sphere and proceeds in all His progress in a spherical order, leading all things back into Himself just as they proceeded from Him. He testifies to this through Isaiah, saying: "I am the first and the last; my hands have founded all things." He establishes an order by bringing the same things back into Himself, so that He might follow a spherical order. For this mass of created things cannot tend toward anything else except toward Him, whose image it holds. Moreover, all the lines of a circle going out from the center to the circumference, and from the circumference back to the center, denote that all creatures emanate from the center...

# ON THE DOGMAS OF THE KABBALISTS.

The highest spheres tend toward the circumference of that same sphere, as if toward their end. Just as all **accidents** <term>accidents: in philosophy, qualities that depend on a substance to exist, like color or shape</term> lean upon **substance**, which is their subject and support, so all created things—which are like accidents in respect to the First Being, who exists of Himself—lean upon Him, upon whom they depend. They are contained in Him as if in a support, and they move within Him as if seeking to be unfolded into their own proper forms; they look toward Him and tend toward Him as if toward their own place and home. Hence, without Him, they cannot long persist, being like foreigners; instead, they strive to return to Him, especially **man**, who contains all things in his virtue and power, as **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic corpus</note> teaches. He, as he was dying (according to the report of **Chalcidius** <note>A 4th-century Platonic commentator</note>), said: "Hitherto, my son, I have lived as a traveler, driven from my fatherland as an exile; now, safe and sound, I seek my fatherland again. When, after a little while, I depart from you, released from these bodily chains, see that you do not mourn me as if I were dead; for I am returning to that most excellent and blessed city, to which all citizens must come by the condition of death. For there alone is God the supreme prince, who welcomes His citizens with wondrous sweetness; wherefore this, which many think to be life, should rather be called death than life."

**Didymus**, **Hiarchus**, **Porphyry**, **Proclus**, **Plotinus**, and **Iamblichus** <note>A list of Neoplatonic and late antique philosophers</note> arrive at this same opinion; all of them exhort us to pray to God with the hope of obtaining what they seek from His great goodness. Whence Proclus teaches, saying: "Those who wish to take up the divinity or the name of the supreme prince in their prayers ought to have knowledge of Him. For it is necessary that the one who invokes knows the one to be invoked, if he wishes to invoke Him rightly." Therefore the **Psalmist** sings: *I will protect him, because he has known my name* <note>Psalm 91:14</note>—not merely because he called upon it, but because he *knew* it. It is also necessary that he have knowledge and a **symbol** <term>symbol: here used in the Neoplatonic sense of a "token" or spiritual link between the human and divine</term> with the one invoked, according to that word of the **Apostle**: *No one can say "Lord Jesus" except in the Holy Spirit* <note>1 Corinthians 12:3</note>, that is, unless he tastes of the nature and lot of the heavenly and spiritual man. Finally, it requires that he be united with the one invoked, who is the head of the divine names, tending both toward **mercy** and toward **justice**.

And this is the reason why God indicated His name, the **Tetragrammaton** <note>original: "יהוה" (YHWH)</note>, to Moses through the **burning bush**: because He had chosen him to describe the fabric of the World and the Law. For both emanated from that very name. Hence, so that he might know the things he was about to write, He indicated that name to him. And this was done because he was going to strike down the one presiding over Egypt, **Ammomino** <note>likely a reference to Ammon or a specific spiritual principality attributed to Egypt</note>, who was to be crushed only by the power of His name. And also, so that he might perform the signs and wonders which God had decreed to send into Egypt, to be done by the virtue of His name. Existing in the **fire**, He wished to teach and indicate that God Himself is fire, and has a fiery name and fiery power; one must work with Him. The Tetragrammaton is good for the good, as is clear regarding Moses, whom He had filled with so much divinity that, full of God, he was called "the God of Pharaoh" <note>Exodus 7:1</note>; for he was to exercise the virtue of divinity against Pharaoh himself. Hence he was a true king, **anointed** with divinity, of which anointing John speaks, saying: *You have an anointing from the Holy One, and you know all things* <note>1 John 2:20</note>. Therefore, just as it is a name of clemency, so also it is one of justice, as is evident from the above.

->KABBALISTIC DOGMA: The sin of Adam was the cutting off of the Kingdom from the other plants.<- <note>original: "Peccatum Adæ fuit truncatio regni à cæteris plantis." This refers to the Kabbalistic concept of "cutting the shoots," or separating the Sephirah of Malkuth (Kingdom) from the higher divine emanations.</note>

**FRIAR ARCHANGELUS:** The method of teaching used by the Kabbalists is through **parables, figures, and similarities**. For a parable signifies, according to its definition, a comparison of dissimilar things; therefore, parabolic speech is good. First, because it is given regarding sensible things, from which both the ignorant and the learned can grasp the meaning—as is clear from that parable: *The sower went out to sow his seed*; for everyone perceives what seed is, what a field is, and so forth. Second, because narrated things leave an impression; for a parable takes the place of **artificial memory**. Third, because our knowledge takes its origin from the senses; therefore it has a symbol with sensible parables. Fourth, there is great spiritual consolation from the harmony of a parable with the spiritual reality figured through it. For **Paul**, conforming to this doctrine, says: *The invisible things of God are clearly seen, being understood from the creation of the world through the things that have been made* <note>Romans 1:20</note>. Here, therefore, the teacher, treating the sin of Adam parabolically and learnedly, does not observe the manner of our [scholastic] theologians. The sin of our first parents con-

### COMMENTARY OF ARCHANGELUS

...persists, because they did not obey the Divine precept, which was that they should not eat the fruit of that tree; and that tree is the Law. For when man was meant to be guided by the precepts of the Law, Adam—seeing himself established over all things (as the oracle had said: *Rule over the birds of the heaven, the fish of the sea, and the beasts of the earth*)—imagined that he did not need the Law. Instead, he believed he held absolute power <note>original: *merum imperium*</note> to dispose of all things at his pleasure, being persuaded especially by the woman—that is, the sensual and animal part of himself—who, having been seduced by an evil demon, easily rushed headlong into ruin. Here Adam despised the Law, devouring and trampling it. He sinned, therefore, through the woman, who represents the "left side," according to that saying of Jeremiah: *From the north all evil shall be spread* <note>Jeremiah 1:14; in mystical geography, the North is often associated with the "left" side or the source of judgment and shadow</note>. And this sin was voluntary; otherwise, it would not have been a sin. Hence Hosea says: *Your destruction, O Israel, is from yourself; but your help is in me.* This help, however, was foreseen from eternity for this sin, according to the words in John: *The Lamb was slain from the beginning of the world* <note>Revelation 13:8</note>, namely, as a remedy for sin.

In the same way, the sin itself was foreseen from eternity, and consequently, it was inevitable. This, Paul seems to confirm openly when he says: *God has enclosed all in unbelief and under sin, that He might have mercy on all* <note>Romans 11:32</note>. However, how those two things—divine foresight and human free will—can coexist has not yet been revealed to any mortal. Nevertheless, our theologians say that Adam’s sin can be considered in three ways: fundamentally, radically, and finally. For the "foundation" of his sin was disobedience; for sin, as **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, a central figure in Western theology</note> testifies, is a word, deed, or desire against God’s Law; or it is a transgression of the Law and a neglectful disobedience of the commands, according to **Ambrose** <note>St. Ambrose, the 4th-century Bishop of Milan</note>. The "root" of this was the pride <note>original: *superbia*</note> which arose in the barren land of disobedience. Its beginning was pride, which sprouted from the root of avarice; its end was gluttony. Therefore, Adam’s sin was built upon disobedience, rooted in avarice, begun in pride, and finally completed in gluttony.

Furthermore, the **Kabbalists** <term>Kabbalists: Jewish mystics whose traditions Pico and Archangelus adapted into a Christian framework</term>, considering that spiritual things are less known to our senses—and moreover, because our intellect is so bound to the senses that nothing is understood that was not first perceived by the senses—treat this matter using physical symbols. They say: The sin of Adam was the "cutting off of the kingdom" <note>original: *truncatio regni*; in Kabbalah, this refers to separating the final Sefirah (Malkhut/Kingdom) from the upper Divine emanations</note>, or the cutting of the last plant from the other plants. Thus we note that even a most balanced body sometimes feels the greatest dissonance. This happens for two reasons. One is the imbalance of the **humors** <term>humors: the four fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to control health and temperament</term>, arising from either excess or deficiency, or from an internal or external alteration. The other reason is because the body dissents from the celestial bodies, so that influences which are otherwise good become harmful to it. They indeed dissent when the mind turns away from that which the celestial influence requires. From this disorder many others follow, for the person is immediately subjected to the "dissipated demon" (as **Proclus** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> says) until he is purged by proper expiations. Leaving the imbalances of the humors to the physicians, we shall run through those things that belong to our field and concern the proper instruction of the "better man."

For the humors are imbalanced, and thus illnesses arise, not only from excessive, diminished, or altered matter, but more often because the body is poorly ruled by the soul. For if the body is fed with excessive food, from which excessive humors are generated, this is the fault of a soul that does not restrain its gluttony. And if harmful foods are eaten, that is the imprudence of the soul. And if a man commits something that gives rise to sadness, so that **black bile** <term>black bile: the humor associated with melancholy and depression</term> is increased and the humors are infected, or if he grieves and fears more than is proper in his circumstances so that **melancholy** takes hold: this comes from a soul in a bad state, absorbed by sadness, which corrupts physical power. But if the soul, acting as the leader of the entire human army and consenting with the Emperor and King [God], governs all lower appetites and powers well, fleeing all improper enemies—then even if some sadness attacks or labor encroaches, that sadness is "Evangelical." It is not harmful, but will soon be turned into joy. And just as for those who love God, all things work together for good, so for those who dissent from God, all things are harmful, and all things tend toward evil: because against such...

<meta>This page continues the discourse on the consequences of the Fall, shifting from the nature of the sin itself to the resulting physical and spiritual disorder in humanity, the necessity of the Incarnation, and the pre-existence of the Messiah’s soul in both Christian and Kabbalistic thought.</meta>

### ON THE DOGMAS OF THE KABBALISTS

Every creature arms itself for vengeance against the enemies of God, as it is written in the Book of Wisdom. Hence, Augustine says:
> The cause of all evils is sin: which is a disorder and imbalance of the soul and of the human guide. When this guide rules poorly, all things rebel and are thrown into disorder to the destruction of their master.

Then the animal spirits <note>In medieval physiology, "animal spirits" were subtle fluids that carried sensation and impulse through the nerves</note>, having lost their restraint, clash in battle; the bad humors rise up, and even the good ones become disordered, separated from one another by a certain turn of events, vexing and tormenting the body. Then the celestial influences become harmful. Then God's executioners <note>original: *lictores*</note>—the angels themselves—prepare to torment men, according to that word of the Prophet:
> And the sendings of evil angels. <note>Psalm 78:49</note>

Then (as Isaiah says) the Lord will strike you with corrupted air. Recognizing this, the Royal Prophet <note>King David</note> said:
> Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak: heal me, for all my bones are troubled: <note>Psalm 6:2</note> that is, my strengths and my virtues.

Nor should anyone say that infirmities arise only from those natural causes mentioned by Avicenna <note>A famous Persian physician and philosopher, 980–1037 AD</note>, namely: emptiness, an excess of food, infection of the air, sleep, wakefulness, or exercise; but they arise chiefly from the "accidents of the soul," specifically anger, sadness, joy, and the like. For these are governed by the mind, since all things (as I have said) are placed within its power. Nor should anyone blame their physical temperament <note>original: *complexionem*</note>; because, as Ecclesiastes says:
> God made man upright, and most balanced: <note>Ecclesiastes 7:29</note>

referring both to the body and the soul. Yet man himself involved himself in infinite questions, or as the Hebrew truth <note>original: *veritas Hebraica*; a common term for the original Hebrew text of the Bible</note> has it: *he sought out many schemes.* Hence, not content with the uprightness and perfect state in which the Creator had placed him, he wandered toward many things. From this followed the disturbance of soul and body, and a total fall from his state and his uprightness. This is most fully shown in the first-formed man <note>Adam</note>: who, not content with the upright Law that his Maker had established for him, began to seek his own "truth," from which that disturbance of the soul followed. And in this temptation Adam was not seduced, but the woman was seduced, as Paul says. And therefore the woman said:
> The serpent deceived me. <note>Genesis 3:13</note>

But Adam did not say this—that is, he did not say "someone deceived me." I say also that even if Adam was deceived, he was not deceived as much as Eve. The error lies in the animal part, which does not perceive the things of God, but not in the spiritual part, which (as the Apostle says) judges all things. Hence a sin committed through error or through frailty is easily forgiven. And because man did not sin while being deceived <note>suggesting a more deliberate choice</note>, forgiveness was most difficult, and had to be obtained from the Son of God alone. Whence some say that if Adam had not sinned, the Word of God would not have been incarnated. Hence Paul:
> God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the Law, to redeem those who were under the Law. <note>Galatians 4:4-5</note>

Since, therefore, Christ came as a redeemer, it seems that if there had been no sin to be redeemed, the Father would not have sent the Son. However, the Apostle says that he was predestined in power; and there is no "reason" for predestination: Christ would have been sent regardless of any reason or occasion, just as he had been destined. For just as all the members of this mystical body that are to be saved were predestined and pre-chosen from eternity—according to that word of the Apostle:
> The Father chose us in him (namely in Christ) before the foundation of the world: <note>Ephesians 1:4</note>

—so also, and much more so, was our head, Christ himself, in whose person the Prophet sings:
> In the head of the book it is written of me. <note>Psalm 40:7</note>

Whence even the Hebrews assert that the soul of the Messiah was from the beginning in the first Divine Mind, and was foremost over all creatures. In this sense Christ said:
> Before Abraham was, I am. <note>John 8:58</note>

To which Paul, in agreement, says:
> Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature. <note>Colossians 1:15</note>

The death of Christ was therefore necessary for the satisfaction of Adam's sin. Therefore the children, inspired by the Holy Spirit, sang:
> Hosanna to the son of David: that is, save us, son of David.

For while the sin of Adam remained, which was irreparable by human strength, no one could hope for salvation except from the God-man. And the reason is that the sequence of the divine arrangement required it. Also, the entire mass of the human race, being infected, could not be purified except by a heavenly man, coming from heaven. For God alone...

He explores the necessity of Christ's incarnation and redemption, noting that the soul of the Messiah was pre-existent in the Divine Mind according to both Christian and Hebrew traditions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the theological and mystical analysis of the Fall of Adam, specifically transitioning from the physical and spiritual symptoms of disorder mentioned on the previous page to a detailed Kabbalistic explanation of how sin disrupts the flow of divine grace through the Sephiroth.</meta>

-># ARCHANGEL'S COMMENTARY<-

...is to forgive sins. For this reason, the power to forgive sins was not given even to the Apostles except by the power of the Holy Spirit. Hence Christ first said: "Receive the Holy Spirit," and then added: "Whose sins you forgive," etc. Children moved by the Holy Spirit (as Christ himself hinted) begged for salvation from him as from God, who would forgive sins; and therefore it is said here: *The Child, Man, and God.* Consequently, the priest, who forgives sins in the place of God, was commanded to be anointed—specifically with the chrism of the Holy Spirit and Divinity—as is observed now.

Note also that men are called trees, as **Aristotle** says: *Man is an inverted tree.* For God gave man a face directed upward, but his root is attached to the Heavens; whereas for plants and trees, the root is at the lowest point. And since man was made in the image of God, it is the custom of the **Kabbalists** <note>Followers of Jewish mysticism</note> that God himself is called the *Ilan* <note>Hebrew: *ilan*, meaning "tree"</note>—that is, the archetypal tree, containing the trunk and the root within himself.

This coordination of divine attributes is called the **Sephiroth** <term>Sephiroth: The ten emanations or attributes in Kabbalah through which the Infinite (Ein Sof) reveals itself and creates the universe</term>. The trunk of this tree is *Tipheret* <note>meaning "Beauty" or "Balance"</note>, associated with the Tetragrammaton <note>The sacred four-letter name of God, YHWH</note>. The root is *Eheie* <note>meaning "I Am"</note>, which is *Keter* <note>meaning "Crown"</note>. There are eight remaining names, namely: *Yah* for *Chokmah* <note>Wisdom</note>, *Elohim* for *Binah* <note>Understanding</note>, *El* for *Gedulah* <note>Greatness/Mercy</note>, *Elohim* for *Gevurah* <note>Strength/Judgment</note>, the Tetragrammaton *Zevaot* for *Netzach* <note>Victory/Endurance</note>, *Elohim Zevaot* for *Hod* <note>Splendor/Majesty</note>, *Shaddai* <note>The Almighty, associated with the Sephirah Yesod or Foundation</note>, and *Adonai* for *Malchuth* <note>Kingdom</note>.

Therefore, from *Eheie* as the root, the outflow of divine goodness gushes down through all the Sephiroth according to a certain measure. And just as each Sephirah receives the influx, so it passes it on to the ones below, and finally into *Malchuth*. This dimension <note>Malchuth</note> enjoys as much of the influx as it receives from the higher ones. Just as when a root is cut out, the flowers, leaves, and fruits fall, so by the sin of **Adam**, *Malchuth* was cut off from the other "plants" <note>A common Kabbalistic metaphor for the Sephiroth</note>. Thus the Kabbalists say *Malchuth* was cut off from the root *Eheie* (*Keter*) and from the trunk *Tipheret* (the Tetragrammaton), and consequently from all the Sephiroth. So *Malchuth* remained empty of the good influx. It is called the "Kingdom," or the King's steward, providing divine mysteries <note>original: *sacramenta*</note> to created things.

While this dimension remains empty, no good can return to us. Before Adam sinned, *Malchuth* drew its influx from the highest level, *Keter*; and thus the whole **Sephirotic** order was fundamentally established alongside the lowest things. For the hierarchies of all creatures looked toward You according to the order of their ranks—higher things with higher things, and lower with lower, created things with created things. Therefore, just as there was peace with the things above, so it dwelt with the things below. The heavens and the elements shared a mutual embrace through a certain bond; one was mutually refreshed by the other. The "channels" <note>Hebrew: *tsinnorot*, the pathways connecting the Sephiroth</note> of the Sephiroth executed their work perfectly. The flow migrated most abundantly from above to below, so that both lower and higher things would reflect the name of the Most High, as **Rabbi Joseph** <note>Likely Rabbi Joseph Gikatilla, 1248–1305, a major Kabbalistic author</note> said.

But while the level of *Malchuth* cohabited with both earthly and heavenly things, Adam immediately became a sinner. Because of this, the orders were confused, and the channels became crooked; the flows of the pools were drawn away, and glory receded from *Malchuth*. That bond was entirely dissolved. When this happened, *Malchuth*, being cut off from the other plants, could not grant the gift of grace to us at all, and thus the tree remained sterile.

This can be shown by a social or political example: an Emperor has an inferior official (a constable) beneath him, and that official has a subordinate, who in turn has a steward. The inferior official obeys his immediate superior; however, if the Emperor commanded that lowest official directly—specifically the steward—not to distribute any funds <note>original: *fynam*, referring to resources or distributions</note> to anyone, then that steward would have to obey the Supreme Lord immediately. So God, the Tetragrammaton, as the Prince of Glory of the Sephiroth, commanded *Malchuth* (the lowest of all Sephiroth and the dispenser of holy anointings) during Adam's transgression not to flow the good influx into Adam. This is true even if *Malchuth* itself remained full of the good influx (which is always the case); if it is sometimes called "empty," it is only in respect to us, because it grants us no good, as if it were bare.

And this is the way of God according to the Kabbalists: when He seeks to respond to our merits, He commands His "Kingdom" or dispenser, *Malchuth*, not to flow into the person, as if it were cut off from the other plants. This is called "drying up the last plant." This cutting off did not only fall upon Adam, but also upon all his posterity, whom he infected; indeed, the whole world...

It uses an analogy of a royal hierarchy to explain how God restricts the flow of goodness based on human merit.</summary>

## ON THE DOGMAS OF THE KABBALISTS.

...did so. And if God is merciful, he nevertheless punishes even to the third and fourth generation, as Moses says in Exodus <note>original: "Exodo"; reference to Exodus 20:5</note>: because the malice of the parents passes down even to the fourth generation. Therefore, children are deprived of their paternal inheritance: just as it is also provided for in civil law that the goods of rebels, and of all who commit the **crime of treason** <note>original: "crimen læsæ maiestatis"</note>, are confiscated to the state treasury. Hence, the children remain deprived of these goods. Sometimes the son is also infected by the bad blood of the father: and sometimes from the goodness of the Father, the world becomes pure and full of blessing. From this, the children are more often infected by the youth of the parents; and from this, God has favored children for the sake of the parents. And because a son is infected by the bad blood of the parents, access to a menstruating woman is forbidden, lest the offspring be infected. 

But according to the more secret theologians, God punishes in the third: that is, in the **threefold soul** <note>original: "animam trifariam"; likely referring to the Platonic or Kabbalistic divisions of the soul: Nefesh, Ruach, and Neshamah</note>—and they speak in the Platonic and Kabbalistic manner—and in the fourth, namely the body, which is composed of a manifold **fourfold nature** <note>original: "quaternario"; referring to the four elements: earth, air, fire, and water</note>. And he spares in thousands: that is, the number one thousand because of that thousand-fold cube—specifically of the number ten—which is appropriate to God. For the number one thousand, in that it is the ultimate end of the final and perfected number, is attributed to God, who is the end of all things. 

Therefore, when Adam the first parent sinned, the entire mass of the human race, which was contained within him, sinned: for all the branches and fruits of any tree whatsoever follow the root. Hence, if the root was dispersed with some bitterness or color, the fruits are also bitter and colored with a similar color, as is evident in the blood-peach. Thus Adam, who was the root of the entire human race, having been infected, infected all the branches and leaves of the tree; as the Apostle says to the Romans: *A root of bitterness springing up hinders, and by it many are defiled.* <note>Reference to Hebrews 12:15, though the author attributes the sentiment to Romans</note> And concerning the good root, he says again: *And if the root is holy, so are the branches.* <note>Reference to Romans 11:16</note> Nevertheless, branch is not infected by branch, nor is it dried up; but that which is dried up, having been cut off, is delivered to the fire, while the others remain living in the trunk. 

And lest there remain in anyone a just complaint about the infection contracted from the first parent, the **Redeemer** <note>Christ</note> willed that all be reborn in him, in a better perfection and a more beautiful root than had been in the first parent—even though his own root had not been defiled. This is clear in the book of Genesis. **Rabbi Berachias**, commenting on that passage, *These are the generations of the heavens and the earth in their creation* <note>Genesis 2:4</note>, says: Although they were created according to their fullness and perfection, yet when Adam first sinned, they were diminished, corrupted, and shaken; and they shall not return further to their proper composition until the **Son of Peres** <note>original: "filius Peres"</note> comes. According to that passage in the last part of Ruth: *These are the generations of Peres.* <note>Ruth 4:18</note> This was clearly written as a sign that all things which had been diminished because of sin were to be perfected and completed through the Son of Peres (who is called **Phares** <note>original: "Phares"</note> by our people through a corrupted pronunciation). And this would occur at the coming of the **Messiah**, in whom the universe, which had almost collapsed because of Adam’s sin, was to be restored, and death itself destroyed—that is, the influence of **Samael** <note>In Kabbalistic tradition, the angel of death or severity</note>. 

And just as in the ancient Law they did not enjoy a good spiritual influence unless first purified by circumcision, or by an offering, or by some other way; so now we are not made worthy of the grace of the kingdom except by the merit of the blood of Christ, which prevails over all ancient bloods. And thus that innocent **Lamb** was worthy to open the gates of the kingdom: the first of which is **Malchuth** <term>Malchuth: The tenth Sephirah, representing "Kingdom" and the gateway through which divine energy enters the physical world</term>, which was taken away from the Jews and handed over to good Christians, as Christ said to the Jews: *The kingdom shall be taken from you and given to a nation* <note>Matthew 21:43</note>—that is, to the Gentile people. And thus he pours that influence into us abundantly through the seven channels of the **seven sacraments**. And when we offend God, this kingdom of spiritual gifts is taken away from us and is cut off from the other plants, as we have said.

**KABBALISTIC DOGMA:** God created the world with the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil, in which the first man sinned.

**BROTHER ARCHANGEL:** God created the world to show his goodness; for he did not establish it driven by external causes (as **Hierocles** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher</note> testifies), but out of his pure goodness. And although he created the world, God himself was not changed by this; since he says through the mouth of **Malachi**: *I am the Lord, and I do not...*

### ARCHANGELUS’S COMMENTARY.

...I am changed. And David says: *But you are the same,* <note>original: "Tu autem idem ipse es"; Psalm 102:27</note> namely, always. Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher; this quote is from his "Consolation of Philosophy."</note> wrote:

->Sower of the lands and the sky, who bids time to go<-
->forth from eternity: and remaining stable, you grant all things to be moved.<-

God was therefore stable in the wisdom by which he foresaw all things from eternity <unclear>...</unclear> in that state no change occurred; rather, mutability was in the thing itself, which received its being <unclear>...</unclear> just as it was in the Word and in Wisdom from eternity. Hence, the most wise Plato left us the teaching that in God there is providence and eternal wisdom; in <unclear>...</unclear> there is fate; but in particular things, there is contingency and novelty. The reason <unclear>...</unclear> which is most powerful, was this: that he might outwardly manifest his wisdom, which we have called the Son. Hence the Prophet sings: *You have made all things in wisdom:* <note>original: "Omnia in sapientia fecisti"; Psalm 104:24</note> because wisdom and the Word are the same thing, through which Word all things were made. <unclear>...</unclear> God by command alone, or by the Word. And this is because the Craftsman did not stand in need of any <unclear>...</unclear> tool to produce them; therefore the Word alone suffices. It was also done <unclear>...</unclear> in order: for since all things were produced by a certain ideal and intrinsic Word <unclear>...</unclear> what remained, except to unfold by the Word what had been conceived <unclear>...</unclear> all things were produced by the power of the divine name, by expressing those things which <unclear>...</unclear> were contained within the divine name, through the voice, or the command to produce all things <unclear>...</unclear> in that name, just as branches, flowers, leaves, and other things come forth from the trunk of a tree. Also by this Word, the heavens were made firm, and by the spirit of his mouth <unclear>...</unclear> their power, as the Psalm sings. The Word is the unique foundation according to that saying of the Apostle: *Upholding all things by the word of his power.* <note>original: "Portans omnia uerbo uirtutis suæ"; Hebrews 1:3</note> And this is because in <unclear>...</unclear> that is, in wisdom, God fashioned all things. Moreover, Wisdom <unclear>...</unclear> is the unique [attribute] of God by which he understands himself and the creature: for nothing can be produced by God acting through the intellect, except through the Word. Therefore [the Prophet] sings <unclear>...</unclear> *You have made all things in wisdom:* and although all things are said to be made through **Elohim** <term>Elohim: A Hebrew name for God associated in Kabbalah with the attribute of Justice and the "Left Side" of the divine emanations.</term>, which is the name of justice and severity, and from the **left side** (as the [Kabbalistic] masters relate), nevertheless they are said to be made in Wisdom, which is from the **right side** <term>Right Side: Associated with Mercy and the attribute of Wisdom (Chokhmah).</term>, and <unclear>...</unclear> in wisdom first: that is, all things were placed within the Word of God. <unclear>...</unclear> of John: *That which was made, in him was life.* <note>John 1:3-4</note> Whence in the **Jerusalem Targum** <term>Targum: An ancient Aramaic translation or paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</term>, where we have: *In the beginning he created:* it is written **Bechoema** <note>original Aramaic: "Be-chokhma"</note>, that is, *in wisdom* God created the heaven and the earth. About which **Elchanan** <note>Likely referring to a Jewish convert or scholar cited in Christian Kabbalistic circles.</note>, a Hebrew and a solemn authority, treats beautifully and at length, declaring that <unclear>...</unclear> the beginning of the building starts with the letter **Beth** ב, which signifies a **house**, and is the seal <unclear>...</unclear> we have spoken of in the **Conclusions of Mirandola** <note>referring to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's "900 Thesis."</note>. In which wisdom, as if in a <unclear>...</unclear>, all things existed before they were unfolded into their own proper forms through Elohim, or through the Holy Spirit: for the outward communication, which <unclear>...</unclear> was produced through the Holy Spirit, who is Love. The power of all <unclear>...</unclear> particular things, therefore, is from the Holy Spirit unfolding them. Just as the Word created the World, so it was the occasion for the transgression of **Adam**. # COMMENTARY OF ARCHANGELUS.

...his glory. Paul entered there: when he was caught up even to the third heaven, where he could not have arrived unless he had passed through the **Paradise of delight** <note>original: "Paradisus voluptatis"; the Latin Vulgate's term for the Garden of Eden.</note>. The wise know this. Moses also entered there, and all the prophets. It was there that they learned the things which he handed down, and where they learned the oracles they preached. However, this kind of error, when people succumb to it, is irreparable, as the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul in Hebrews 6:4-6.</note> teaches: because it is not removed through penance. Hence the Apostle adds: *Crucifying again the Son of God.* The truth of these words is that just as Adam’s sin received a remedy not through his own penance, but through the passion of Christ, so the sin of anyone introduced into that state is not deleted through penance; rather, the work of Christ’s passion is needed to delete it.

And those introduced there can be tempted and attacked. For the first parent was tempted and defeated there: for although the Paradise of delight is heavenly, Adam could still be tempted in that very place—even if "his place was not found in heaven," as John says <note>A reference to Revelation 12:8 regarding the fall of the dragon.</note>. Adam was in Paradise in his mind, just as Moses, the Prophets, and the Apostles were there; but his body and the **animal man** <term>animalis homo</term> <note>From the Latin "anima" (soul/breath); it refers to the physical or soulish nature of man as opposed to the "spiritual man."</note> were on earth. Hence, by a great mystery, it is written that the ancient serpent approached the woman: that is, the animal part of the soul, which was on the earth. Therefore Moses speaks cautiously, saying that God placed the **man** in the Paradise of delight, making no mention of the woman; she was certainly taken from the man who was already there. Thus, she was not placed there except by the company of the man who was placed there. Just as (by God's doing) the flesh and the animal man will be placed in the kingdom of blessedness by following the spirit that is capable of that kingdom. And this will happen if it is changed and rises as something spiritual, as the Apostle teaches.

The reason for this was that the Paradise of delight is an object perceptible in the intellect and in the higher, "masculine" portion of the soul. Hence the woman, who signifies the animal part, is not said to be introduced there except insofar as she is joined to the man and through his company, as has been said. And in that way, she was not introduced except through the man, and in the same way, she was cast out with the man. The "woman," or the womanly soul—that is, the animal part, which is a certain passive thing—is not capable of blessedness on its own. It is only capable through that which participates in the higher portion, which it receives from the man, whose image she is, as the Apostle says—just as man is nothing except through Christ, whose image he holds.

However, she was able to take from the **tree of the knowledge of good and evil** in the garden of delight, even though she had not been introduced there in her own right: because (as I said) she was there through her company with the man. And if the tree, as I said, is planted in the Paradise of delight, it nevertheless spreads its branches everywhere. For just as God, existing in himself, fills heaven and earth, so also the divine (which we have already said is the tree of the knowledge of good and evil), although it is in a heavenly place and planted in heaven, yet its power is spread everywhere, as John said: *Of his fullness we have all received.* And in his Apocalypse, John, speaking of it under the metaphor of a tree planted near the throne of God, says that its leaves were for the healing of the nations. For the nations in heaven do not need healing; rather, its power extends everywhere, even to those who are sick in their earthly and clay-like dwellings. Hence, in the same way, those living in these earthly dwellings can "devour" the tree itself by committing some offense against it.

In the same way, **Plato** in the *Phaedo* speaks of Paradise and the "true life." For he describes the "high earth" of the living: in comparison to which we, who inhabit this corruptible earth, are likened to those who live in the depths of the sea and see the Sun and the stars through the water, and who imagine that the sea itself contains the stars. But if anyone (just as fish emerging from the sea see the stars) were to see that true earth, and true light, and true heaven, he would confess that their beauty greatly exceeds our own. For these dwellings of ours are like caverns, or sand, or filthy mud. There, one would see trees with flowers and fruit far more precious than any found here. And truly sensing this, Plato says concerning the true Paradise: Those who live piously...

# ON THE DOGMAS OF THE KABBALISTS.

[...if they have lived purely] in these lands, they may ascend to higher things, released from these earthly places as if from a prison, and inhabit a pure region above the earth, obtaining dwellings more beautiful than these: the beauty of which is not easy to describe. For the reward is beautiful, and the hope is great, as he himself implies. This he had perhaps learned from Isaiah, who says: *Eye has not seen, O God, besides you* <note>original: "Oculus non uidit, Deus, absque te"; see Isaiah 64:4 and 1 Corinthians 2:9.</note>. The tree planted in the middle of the garden of delights, which is called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, was Christ, who is called the bread of life, the wood of life, and life itself. Moreover, it was planted in the middle so that everyone might more easily receive from the fullness of his life according to their own capacity.

And this tree of life—namely, the divine person grafted into human nature—is the tree of the knowledge of good and evil: because he alone, as I have said, existing as a <term>wayfarer</term> <note>From the Latin "viator," a theological term for a person on their journey through earthly life toward God, as opposed to a "comprehensor" who has reached heaven.</note>, experienced the good of beatitude and the evil of human passions. It is, furthermore, the tree of good and evil because he, above all others, knew how to discern good from evil, according to that saying of Isaiah: *Butter and honey he shall eat, that he may know how to refuse the evil and choose the good* <note>Isaiah 7:15.</note>. Finally, it is the tree of the knowledge of good and evil because to him has been given the judgment and the knowledge of discerning the good and the wicked in the universal judgment.

This tree, however, was forbidden from the beginning, so that it should not be touched, nor tested, nor eaten from: because no one ought to experience or test the Law and the judgment existing in him, but rather revere and fear it, and always have it before their eyes, so that we might direct all our actions toward its goal. In this sense it is said in the Law: *These words which I command you today shall be in your heart: and you shall tell them to your children, and meditate upon them sitting in your house, and walking on the journey, sleeping and rising: and you shall bind them as a sign on your hand, and they shall be before your eyes* <note>Deuteronomy 6:6-8.</note>. This is also said in the Psalms: *Blessed is the man who meditates on the Law of the Lord day and night.*

And how perfectly this tree of the Law, and the rule of the divine word, is said to be the knowledge of good and evil: because from it we can weigh what is straight and what is crooked, what is good and what is evil. For this teaches us when we ought to enjoy the supreme good, and when or how we are permitted to possess the lowest or the middle goods. And if that tree is kept, and the rule remains unhurt, then we can eat of all trees: that is, delight in all creatures and desire them with a desire that is not at all crooked.

Just as, therefore, all justice, all rightness, and finally all good things proceed from that tree when it is rightly and properly received; so we find that all evil has come upon the human race, and even upon the angels, from that tree being violated. For evil proceeds from good since it cannot proceed from elsewhere, as Augustine clearly defines in the *Enchiridion*; and before him Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist.</note> says: *The beginning and end of all evils is the good.* Assigning the reason, he says: *Nothing acts with its gaze on evil, but rather on a perceived good, which it either neglects or desires improperly.*

Therefore, this tree is the beginning of all goods and evils: because if anyone venerates and observes it, they perform good. If, however, anyone neglects it and presumes to devour or trample it, they perform evil; just as that most holy old man Simeon testified concerning that tree grafted into a human shoot, saying: *Behold, this child is set for the fall and the resurrection of many in Israel, and among all people, both angelic and human.*

For the angel sinned by refusing to receive him as the true Lord and true lawgiver, and by refusing to obey the rules described in him; and by being unwilling to revere him as the mediator through whom we might be made co-heirs according to the king's edict. This Paul made known to the Hebrews, saying: *And when he brought the firstborn into the world, he said: And let all his angels worship him.* But some of them, being insolent and proudly turning away from that supreme rule of truth, fell into error and lies. The very Fountain of Truth attests to this when he says: *That one was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth.* Indeed, he wished (as John says) to kill the Son of the Woman—namely Christ—by desiring equality with him in the manner mentioned above. Hence man also sinned, daring to extend a rebellious hand toward him...

### KABBALISTIC DOGMA: *The great North is the source of all souls—just as other days [are the sources] of certain ones, and not all.*

**FRIAR ARCHANGELUS.** The origin of souls is disputed by many, and [concerning] the [generation] of forms and where they proceed from. They generally agree... that corruptible and mortal souls emerge from the bosom [of matter], to use their words. However, concerning the intellectual soul, since it is still [debated] among them whether it is mortal or immortal, they have not determined where it comes from. [Aristotle], their prince, speaking with doubt, says: *If there is any form coming from outside, it is the intellectual soul.* But how can this be, unless the opinion ascribed to [Anaxagoras] is true—that "everything is in everything"? But they say that [the soul is] sometimes to be led into act: and they say that nature gave the [power] and the subject, so that a particular agent, by a seminal virtue, [brings it to] effect. What this nature is, however, they do not determine; but it can be nothing other than the first maker <term>first maker</term> <note>Latin: "primus opifex," referring to God as the ultimate Creator.</note> working all things in all, or the [secondary] agents at his command and by his virtue. He, therefore, is the first [cause], the first giver of forms, from whom all life, form, and order proceed. [Every] soul has its [being] from the supreme source of goods and the true giver of forms, through whom all things were made: as he himself testifies, saying: *My Father works even until now, and I work* <note>John 5:17.</note>, either by creating anew, as the [Theologians] say, or by infusing that which emanates from the source itself, as others assert. The heavenly Father and giver of all forms says: *All souls [are mine]*, namely, fathered by me and spread into bodies.

Hence the Hebrews, in their most secret mysteries, assert that the soul proceeds from the great four-lettered name of God, <term>Jehovah</term> <note>The Tetragrammaton, the sacred four-letter name of God in Hebrew (YHVH).</note>; but that the whole world proceeds from and is ruled by the ten numerations <term>Sephirot</term> <note>The ten emanations or attributes in Kabbalah through which the Infinite (Ein Sof) reveals itself and creates the universe.</note>. They are ruled by the three supreme ones by command, and by the remaining seven by [action]. For this reason, they call these seven numerations the "Seven of the Structure" <note>original: "septem annumerationes fabricae." These refer to the lower seven Sephirot associated with the seven days of creation.</note>. But since nothing [gives what it] does not have (as the Peripatetics teach), it is therefore necessary that every form [exist in the] maker from whom it proceeded. And the forms existing there are Ideas, according to which we have particular forms and being. And since that being is continually [flowing from] him who gave it, we have it from the Ideas according to which he grants it, from which we are sustained, [lest] we flow away into nothingness. Since our being continually flows, and [because it] flows, it is necessary that it be sustained in something permanent, which is the [Word] in whom all things were established; as Paul says: *Bearing all things by the word of his power* <note>Hebrews 1:3.</note>.

Pythagoras indeed (as Alexander and Laertius report) [maintained] something [similar], saying: *The soul is immortal, since that from which it [emanates] is immortal.* Christ truly instructs us clearly that we are fathered by God, so that with great confidence we may flee to God, calling him [Father] as he is; indeed, that we should know no other Father, while he says: *Call no one father to you upon the earth: for one is your Father, who is [in heaven]* <note>Matthew 23:9.</note>. And concerning himself he says: *I went out from the Father and came into the world.* [He...]

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the soul, moving from the Christological symbols of the previous page into a specific comparison between traditional Christian theology and Kabbalistic doctrine regarding the soul's origin and its status as the 'Image of God.'</meta>

# ON THE DOGMAS OF THE KABBALISTS.

...we are three <note>The Latin 'tres' (three) here likely refers to the three parts of the soul or the three powers mentioned later: memory, intellect, and will.</note> from the father rather than from the mother; and we undoubtedly came forth from him, though not with the same perfection and degree. Therefore Pythagoras speaks a blessing when he says: *A divine race is within men* <note>original: "Diuinum genus inest hominibus"</note>. This is because, as I have said elsewhere, the soul that is poured into us is in a certain sense the seed of God planted into the body. From this, a better man is generated, of whom Paul says: *The second man is from heaven, heavenly* <note>1 Corinthians 15:47; original: "Secundus homo de cœlo cœlestis"</note>. And for this reason, he is called the "image of God." Indeed, it is a commonplace that man was made with the image of God and led toward His likeness. 

However, we must investigate exactly what this image consists of. According to common doctrine, it is said that the three divine persons are represented in the three powers of the soul: memory, intellect, and will. Yet, this cannot truly be called an "image"—the purpose of which is to represent the whole and every aspect of the one depicted—as is most excellently determined by our more clear-sighted theologians. Rather, it is the nature of a "vestige" <term>vestige</term> <note>From the Latin 'vestigium' (footprint/trace). In theology, a 'vestige' is a faint trace of God found in all creation, whereas an 'image' is a more direct likeness found only in rational beings.</note> to represent not the full thing imagined, but some part or reason of it. And although the entire Trinity is contained in the three persons, and is represented in other parts besides the three aforementioned powers, God is thus full life, giving life to all members of the worldly body. The soul, too, is a certain fountain of life, yet one flowing from the supreme and divine sea, granting life to all the specific members of the body according to its condition. 

In Holy Scripture it is said: *And he breathed into his nostrils the breath, or soul, of lives* <note>Genesis 2:7; the author uses the plural "lives" (vitarum) to reflect the Hebrew 'Chayyim'.</note>, so that it might provide the body with vegetative, sensual, rational, intellectual, and even divine life. And God contains all things by His power; as the wise man says of man: *God made man from the dust of the earth, and gave him the power of containing all things.* God knew all things in a single act; man can also know all things, but successively <note>i.e., one after another, rather than all at once.</note>. Furthermore, God is a certain circle, drawing His origin from nowhere but Himself, and tending toward Himself; He leads all things there with Him. Man is also a circle proceeding from God and tending toward Him, leading all things there, since he contains all things. He emulates God in duration, at least through a certain succession. The soul is so similar to God that it cannot rest until it is united to Him, like a plant to its root.

The Kabbalists, treating this matter, say that the "Great North" is the source of souls. For there are ten divine fountains according to the number of the ten <term>Sephiroth</term> <note>The ten emanations or attributes in Kabbalah through which the Infinite (Ein Sof) reveals itself.</note>, or dimensions. Among these, one is given which is called *Ghebura* <note>original: "ghebura"; Hebrew: Gevurah, meaning "Strength" or "Severity."</note>, or the North. It is the fountain of all souls and lives; for (according to Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath (c. 980–1037) whose philosophical works deeply influenced Western scholasticism and Kabbalistic thought.</note>) all souls come from the "giver of forms"—that is, from *Ghebura*, the Northern property which favors the Egyptians. Because of this, the holy fathers of the Ancient Law descended into the northern Egypt, so that they might acquire the strength of life from there. 

And although all souls draw their origin from that fountain of Northern *Ghebura*, they nevertheless pass through other dimensions, or Sephiroth, before they are poured into the body, and they receive various properties from them. Each soul receives that portion of light according to the nature of the medium through which it is cast or with which it is connected. For if the soul emanates from that supreme light through the Seraphic <term>intelligences</term> <note>High-ranking celestial beings/angels characterized by fiery love.</note>, it becomes "Seraphic" and strives to reach the Seraphic dwellings (with God favoring and attracting it). But if it receives the splendor of knowledge through the Cherubic minds, the soul, having become familiar with that light, busies itself to reach the Cherubic seats—and so on for the others. Just as light passing through different colors spreads out colored rays—red through red glass, green through green, white through white, and so on—in the same way, the soul puts on the nature of the transparent medium through which it passes. The "transparent medium" for spiritual light is not air, but spirit and intelligence, which can receive and transmit that light. 

The Savior speaks of these when He says: *Their angels always see the face of the Father who is in heaven* <note>Matthew 18:10</note>. He speaks of assigned angels, who would not be rightly assigned unless they had some symbol or shared nature <note>original: "symbolum"</note> with those to whom they are destined. And just as angels are not of the same degree of perfection, neither are souls; for one is more perfect than another. They differ not only in accidental qualities, but even by certain intrinsic degrees...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of the soul, moving from the definition of the "image of God" to a debate on whether all souls are equal. It contrasts the views of Aristotle and the Parisian Scholastics with Kabbalistic and Platonic ideas about the soul's origin in the celestial spheres and the divine "dimensions."</meta>

### COMMENTARY OF ARCHANGELUS

...rooted in their very essence: by which every soul exists, one different from another through that which is its own property. **Aristotle** says that souls are like **numbers**; therefore, it is concluded that all souls are equal. However, the **Doctors of Paris** <note>Theologians from the University of Paris, the center of Scholastic thought.</note> say that the soul of Christ—and consequently the souls of many holy men—are more noble than the soul of Judas, or that of any wicked person.

We can also learn this from the **Gospel**, where it is said that "talents" <term>talents</term> <note>A 'talent' was a unit of currency, but here refers to the Parable of the Talents in Matthew 25, symbolizing spiritual gifts.</note> are distributed to each according to their own measure of gifts. For talents are free gifts corresponding to natural abilities, according to **Gregory** <note>St. Gregory the Great, a Doctor of the Church.</note>. In this sense, we must understand the words of the Savior regarding the ten minas given to ten servants, so that each might work according to the measure granted to him. He who works according to that power receives a reward based on the condition of the coin, or the gift provided. If, however, one neglects to use the gift, it is taken away and given to another who is working, so that he may fill the place prepared for that specific gift. 

Species are not determined by vocal numbers, which are indivisible; for when an offering or addition is made, the species of the number changes. Rather, they are determined by **natural numbers**, which are divisible—as is evident in music regarding the **semitone**, as I have said elsewhere. Through the proportions of numbers, the types of ratios are varied. These are the natural numbers by which species are determined. This is confirmed by the Wise Man <note>Referring to the author of the Book of Wisdom in the Bible.</note> saying: *I was a witty child and received a good soul* <note>Wisdom 8:19; original: "Puer eram ingeniosus, & sortitus sum animam bonam"</note>—meaning a soul better than the souls of many others. For so great is the distance of one soul from another in wisdom, goodness, strength, power, and disposition, that I do not see how souls could be assigned an equal rank. 

These ranks are the "talents": to one, two were granted; to another, three; and to a third, four. As Christ said: each was given according to his own virtue. By this, souls are determined in a certain rank, according to which they are capable of receiving the influx that sustains them. The reason for these distinct gifts or virtues is the varied way in which the **divine dimensions** <term>divine dimensions</term> <note>A reference to the Sephirot, the ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite interacts with the universe.</note> flow into them. For although all souls originate from one source—the northern **Ghebura** <note>original: "ghebura aquilonari." Gevurah is the Sephirot of Strength, Judgment, or Severity, often associated with the North in Kabbalistic geography.</note>—and are brought into execution by the remaining six dimensions (which they call the **seven generations of the structure** <note>original: "septem generationes fabricae." This refers to the seven lower Sephirot involved in the creation of the manifest world.</note>), they nevertheless proceed by the command of the three highest Sephirot, as I have said. According to the property of those seven dimensions through which they flow, souls drink in various influences. 

Indeed, our souls are placed in the **celestial spheres** in various ranks. Nor should anyone marvel if the **Pythagoreans** and the **Academics** <note>Followers of Plato's Academy.</note> say the spheres are filled with intelligences and souls located within them, since the same was said by **Moses** in his discourse: *The heavens were completed, and all their host* <note>Genesis 2:1; original: "Completi sunt cœli, & omnis exercitus eorum"</note>. In our translation, this is rendered as "their ornament." For the "host" and "armies of heaven" are the **intelligences** and **intellectual forms** which are the very beauty of the heavens. For through these forms—which **Plato** calls "armies" along with Moses—**Proclus** says the celestial spheres are adorned. For this reason, **Euripides** and many others said that the spheres are the dwellings and courts of the Gods (that is, of the celestial minds). 

However, exactly how many forms and intellects there are in the heavens, produced by the Most High, only He can know who *counts the multitude of the stars and calls them all by their names* <note>Psalm 147:4; original: "qui numerat multitudinem stellarum, & omnibus nomina uocat"</note>. He calls them by names not as physical bodies, but as **presiding intelligences**, as some wise men explain. For the entire school of wise men, and even the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note>, assigns at least one intelligence to each orb. But since every star has its own power which it pours into lower things, it is necessary that each has its own presiding intelligence to provide the power to act; for an operation cannot proceed from a purely physical body. Regarding our own souls, a difficulty remains; it is thought by many that souls themselves are placed in the spheres. This does not seem absurd to those with understanding. For even **Catholics** of no small intellect have sung that human souls are subject to various spheres...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nobility and origin of souls, shifting from the Scholastic debate of the previous page toward a synthesis of Platonic philosophy, Kabbalah, and Christian theology.
