# ON THE TEACHINGS OF THE KABBALISTS

...did you not agree with me for a denarius <note>A Roman silver coin; here used as an allegory for the number ten</note>, so that I might bless you with the ten divine influences, the ten <term>sephiroth</term> <note>The ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself</note>.

**KABBALISTIC DOGMA.** It is said that a river goes out from Eden, which is divided into four heads: this signifies that from the second numeration proceeds the third; which is then divided into the fourth, fifth, sixth, and tenth.

**FRIAR ARCHANGELUS.** We declare God to be the fountain, as he himself proclaims and laments in these words: **They have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, the Lord**, <note>original: "Me dereliquerunt fontem aquarum uiuentium Dominum"</note> as is said in Jeremiah. And David says: **with you is the fountain of life**; Isaiah also says: **You shall draw waters with joy from the fountains of the Savior**. These fountains are <term>Keter Elyon</term> <note>Hebrew: "Supreme Crown," the highest Sephirot</note> or the Supreme Crown called the Father, the first origin of all things; <term>Chokhmah</term> <note>Hebrew: "Wisdom"</note> itself, the Son of God; and also <term>Binah</term> <note>Hebrew: "Understanding"</note>, the Holy Spirit. Therefore, the first fountain and origin of all good things is the Father, of whom it is said in the Song of Songs: **A fountain of gardens and a well of living waters**. The Son is also a fountain, of whom Zechariah says: **In that day there shall be a fountain open to the house of David, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing of the sinner and the unclean woman**; which everyone interprets as referring to Christ, the Son of God. The Holy Spirit is also a fountain, of whom John says: **it shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life**; he said this regarding the Holy Spirit, whom those believing in him were to receive. However, he had first prefaced this by saying: **he who drinks of this water which I shall give**. This water of life, before the coming of Christ, irrigated only the Jews (because salvation is from the Jews); but when Christ arrived, then this water irrigated the entire earth. The Son was also the fountain of living water that Moses sought in the book of Numbers. Of this fountain it is said in the Song of Songs: **a fountain of gardens, a well of living waters**. Regarding this fountain John says: **He showed me a river of water of life, shining**; this unique water is Christ, or his wisdom, which is called the water of the Savior, since the Law that was given was present within him. Paul, revealing this mystery, said: **for they drank of the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ**. From this, he clearly wished to imply that the wisdom of the Law given to the Hebrews emanated from Christ, under the metaphor of a rock. And this is the reason why the Hebrews, though satisfied by the divine fountain of the Law they received, still seemed to thirst; for even if the Law had been given then, it was so shrouded in mystery that the people thirsted for its understanding. Hence ancient theologians commonly conclude that the Law was given twice: first in writing, and afterwards they assert it was declared orally; and they call this **Cabala** <note>Kabbalah</note>, that is, the revelation made to them by word of mouth. Of this fountain Zechariah says (as I mentioned): **there shall be a fountain open to the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem**. This fountain cried out in the temple, saying: **If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink**. Ezekiel speaks of this, saying: **I will pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your filthiness and from your idols, and I will give you a new heart and a new spirit**; that is, baptism. And these fountains, although they are always overflowing in themselves because they are infinite, are nevertheless said to be "dried up" in terms of our benefit; namely, when our sins require it, the channels flowing into us are blocked, according to the saying: **When you hide your face, they shall be troubled; you shall take away their spirit, and they shall fail, and return to their dust**. These three fountains constitute one fountain, just as the three divine persons are one God, and the outward works of God are undivided. Therefore, from that fountain—whether called a sea or the garden of Paradise—goes out a river of living waters, which is divided into four rivers, which are also called fountains according to Pythagoras <note>The author links Greek philosophy to scripture, suggesting a universal ancient wisdom</note>. This river went out from the place of pleasure to irrigate Paradise and all the blessed living there; for the Prophet sings: **They shall be inebriated by the abundance of your house, and you shall give them to drink from the torrent of your pleasure**. To irrigate the entire earth, however, it is divided into four heads. This is because the fourfold condition of earthly man requires it. For just as the number three is dedicated to divine things, so the number four is dedicated to corporeal and human things, because man is composed of the four elements. Furthermore, this river is divided four ways so that the river of all goodness may flow separately into the earthly man himself, who...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the divine "fountains" and "rivers" from the previous page, moving from the mystical nature of the Trinity and the Sephiroth to an exploration of how these divine waters flow into the created world, both allegorically and geographically.</meta>

# THE COMMENTARY OF ARCHANGELUS

...waters the blessed, who have been made one with God and joined to Him. For it waters you through grace from the South <note>In mystical geography, the South often represents the warmth of divine grace or "Midday" clarity</note> through knowledge and piety; from the North, it brings [purification] and expiation; and from the West, through a kind reception. From there, the rivers run in an everlasting flow to the sea from which they drew their origin, according to that passage in Ecclesiastes: **All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea is not full; unto the place from whence the rivers come, thither they return again.** <note>Ecclesiastes 1:7; original: "omnia flumina intrant in mare... unde exeunt flumina reuertuntur"</note> So also all creatures, [originating] from that great supramundane sea mentioned above, pass through [the world] in a most hidden way, as if through the pipes and veins of the World. Just as the seed of animals passes through most hidden channels all the way to the place where it [is formed] into a body. Once formed, it runs an unfailing course until it returns to the Archetypal <term>Archetype</term> <note>The original model or "blueprint" in the divine mind from which all things are copied</note> sea from which it came, unless it has been infected and weakened by sin. That sea is infinite; therefore, it does not overflow from the return of those creatures, just as it was not diminished when those waters went out. 

But as to what truth is contained in the literal sense regarding the description of those rivers, we must speak of where they arise, and to where and through which path they flow, according to the Geographers. **Pison**, therefore, or the **Ganges** (as Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate Bible</note> maintains), is in India, the most principal among the rivers that bring gold. Its source is in the [Caucasian] mountains, according to Artemidorus. And of this the text says: **and the gold of that land is the best.** **Gihon**, indeed, which is thought to be the **Nile**, passes through the entire land of Ethiopia, and flows from the furthest ends of the southern land toward the north in a [miraculous] course. Its origin is in the parts of Mauritania, not far from [a stagnant] lake there which they call Helis. It then hides itself for a journey [of several days], and breaks out again in another larger lake in Mauritania Caesariensis. Received [by the sands], it is carried through deserts for twenty days to the nearest Ethiopians, where it leaps forth into a spring which is called "Black." From there, dividing Africa from Ethiopia, it cuts through the middle of the Ethiopians under the name **Astapus**, and finally [enters] the Egyptian sea; this river arises in Africa. 

The **Tigris**, however, which goes toward the [Assyrians], arises in the region of Greater Armenia from a visible spring in a plain [where it] flows [slowly]. Up to the borders of the Medes, it is called **Diglitus**; then it begins to be called **Tigris**, because it seems to fly like an arrow—for the Medes call an arrow a "Tigris." It passes through Zeroada and Tesbite, [becoming] swifter as the Arsanias [joins it], and in [this] manner it merges into the **Euphrates**. The **Euphrates**, truly, is said to rise in Mount Parihedrus [in] Armenia, running through the same region of Greater Armenia, distinguishing it from Cappadocia, and [empties] into the Persian Gulf (which is called the Red Sea). 

Yet we can achieve no conjecture as to how those four rivers have [a single] origin, since they seem to arise from such distant places. Therefore, it remains that the Sea is the source of those four named [rivers]. But then there will not be any one particular place that can be called a garden or paradise by us that is inaccessible. From this, the [description] of the rivers seems entirely typical <note>Symbolic or allegorical rather than strictly literal</note>, through which are understood the four elements and principles [of things] produced; it also hints at that fourfold virtue of the fourfold man. 

Orpheus and Homer call the **Ocean** the origin of divine and human things, ever-existing: secondly, emanating into the generation of the Gods; thirdly, watering earthly things; fourthly, [pulsing] into all fluid [nature]. Its emanation is again seen through "Form" in the Angels; through "Participation and Image" in rational living beings; through "Instinct" in those lacking reason; and finally through "Shadow" in the figures of bodies. This fourfold emanation was also seen by Ezekiel in the four living creatures <note>The "Tetramorph" from the vision in Ezekiel 1:10</note>: of which the **Lion** is fiery; the **Eagle** is airy; the **Man** is chiefly in the soul, [and thus] watery; the **Calf** indeed is earthy, and always devoted to the cultivation of the earth. These [four] composed together show a single face and power; therefore it is said: **four faces to one, and four wings to one.** Thus is indicated that fourfold [power] of the four-letter name <note>The Tetragrammaton, the sacred four-letter name of God (YHVH)</note>, or the fourfold principal efflux from the Archetype.

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the "fountains" and "rivers" as allegories for divine emanation. It specifically links the biblical description of the four rivers of Eden to the Kabbalistic tree of life (the Sephiroth) and the Christian Trinity, explaining how divine life flows from the infinite source into the material world.</meta>

<page-num>769</page-num>
<header>ON THE KABBALISTS' DOGMAS.</header>
<page-type>text</page-type>

...all things are described through those four rivers: because they possess a likeness of those very things, just as higher sacraments <note>The author uses "sacraments" here in the older sense of "sacred mysteries" or "hidden signs."</note> are described through Trees, springs, a garden, and things of this sort. For since there is one fountain of double life, he who says in Jeremiah:

> They have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, <note>Jeremiah 2:13; original: "Me dereliquerunt fontem aquarū uiuentium"</note>

it is necessary that all things possessing both natural and spiritual life—and whatever else there may be—draw everything from that fountain, from which the river proceeds. Of this it is said in Genesis: *And a river went out of the place of pleasure*—which is God—*to water Paradise itself first*: that is, the whole archetype, through the various channels of things to be communicated to us. These are the "supramundane waters" which are said by Moses and David to be above the heavens. From that fountain of life, therefore, a water or river is said to emanate, which is immediately divided into four heads and waters the entire earth. These waters of life are first in the paternal source, *cheter Elion* <note>Hebrew: *Keter Elyon*, the "Supreme Crown," the highest Sephirah representing God's primal will.</note>: that is, the superior crown; afterwards in the son, *chocmah* <note>Hebrew: *Chokhmah*, "Wisdom," the second Sephirah, often associated in Christian Kabbalah with the Son or the Word.</note>: that is, wisdom. He himself is also a fountain (as I have said) existing with the Father, as it is said in the Psalm:

> For with thee is the fountain of life: <note>Psalm 36:9; original: "Quoniam apud te est fons uitæ"</note>

for the Son is with the Father; the Father, giving all things to him, also established him as a fountain, so that he might deservedly say:

> I am the life, <note>John 14:6; original: "Ego sum uita"</note>

bestowing, namely, both natural and spiritual life upon all. For when we say *all things that were made were life in him*, it is said concerning natural life: for from that divine fountain of life the water flows down—namely, the essence and the "being" of all things. This is divided by the first division into four elements, as if into the principles and primary material beginnings of things. This river of essence went out from "pleasure": that is, from the most happy Deity, to water and drench the entire earth: that is, matter, which, when first produced, was called "earth." It is rightly said to be divided at its first downward course into four heads: that is, into the four elements, with which the names of the rivers also agree (about which I speak elsewhere). But when he himself says:

> I am the resurrection and the life: <note>John 11:25; original: "Ego sum refurrectio, & uita"</note>

it is understood as spiritual life, which is made perpetual as eternal life, which we have from the Son of God himself, as he himself testifies in many places, saying:

> I give them eternal life: <note>John 10:28; original: "Ego uitam æternam do eis"</note>

and again:

> If anyone drinks of this water which I shall give, there shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life <note>John 4:14; original: "si quis biberit ex hac aqua... fiet in eo fons aquę salientis in uitam... æternā"</note> (as I have said).

There exists also another fountain of life in that most holy archetype: which is the Holy Spirit. This is sometimes called the "spirit of life," just as we read in Ezekiel:

> And the spirit of life was in the wheels: <note>Ezekiel 1:20; original: "Et spiritus uitæ erat in rotis"</note>

about which it is sung in the Psalm:

> Send forth your spirit, and they shall be created: <note>Psalm 104:30; original: "Emitte spiritū tuum, & creabuntur"</note>

namely, those things which had been dead and destroyed. And even if there are three fountains, they are nevertheless one in that fountain of life and Divine essence called *Enfoph* <note>Hebrew: *Ein Sof*, "The Infinite," God as He is in Himself before any manifestation.</note>: that is, infinity or infinitude, without which nothing lives and nothing exists; for all things proceed from the One. And because Paradise is in God, therefore "Eden"—that is, Paradise—is one. And just as all things proceed from God, so all things proceed from this Eden-Paradise, and in it all things find their rest. Concerning which the Psalm says:

> I shall be satisfied when your glory shall appear: <note>Psalm 17:15; original: "Satiabor cùm apparuerit gloria tua"</note>

for it is not in this dreg-filled earth, but in heaven. And because "pleasure" is called the support of the creator, the son *chocmah* sustains all things, as Paul witnesses:

> upholding all things by the word of his power. <note>Hebrews 1:3; original: "portans omnia uerbo uirtutis suæ"</note>

And thus all spiritual graces proceed immediately from the son *chocmah* himself, and are distributed by him through the Holy Spirit, *Binah* <note>Hebrew: *Binah*, "Understanding," the third Sephirah, associated here with the Holy Spirit and the "executor" of divine plans.</note> the executor. Concerning which Paul says:

> To one is given the word of wisdom; to another, etc. <note>1 Corinthians 12:8; original: "Alij datur sermo scientiæ: alij, &c."</note>

Moreover, the same spirit dividing to each as he wills—and these three first "numerations" <note>The *Sephiroth* are often called *Sefirot* or "Numerations" (countings), representing the ten attributes of God.</note> namely, *cheter Elion* the Father, *chocmah* the Son, and *binah* the Holy Spirit—are one and the same in essence and one in being. But when this one Divine being begins to communicate itself to the other lower *sephiroth* <note>The remaining seven attributes or dimensions of God's manifestation in the universe.</note>, then it is divided into four heads, just as there are four letters of the name "tetrag." <note>The Tetragrammaton, the holy four-letter name of God: YHWH.</note> through which all things were made. Thus, in the fabric of the World and of those things which belong to the Eden of the World: that is, the three first dimensions (which are called Paradise, as we have seen) are divided into four heads. For the perfect "being" of things and of the World required those four, which are *ghedulah*, *ghebura*, *tiphereth*, and *malchuth* <note>The Sephiroth of Mercy/Greatness, Power/Severity, Beauty, and Kingdom.</note>. Therefore the fountain which is divided into these four, *binah*, is total and whole there because it only looks inward; but when it flows into created things, it is divided into four heads.

Christ spoke of this fountain when he said: *It shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life.* <note>John 4:14</note> Afterward it is added: *But this he spoke of the Spirit, which those believing in him were to receive.* <note>John 7:39</note> The first of these heads <note>Referring to the four heads or "rivers" mentioned on the previous page.</note> is *gedulah* <note>Hebrew: *Gedulah*, "Greatness" or "Magnificence," another name for the Sephirah *Chesed* (Mercy/Kindness).</note>:
**Love and piety:** which concur in the production of things, as Zoroaster <note>The OCR "dic & leroëles" likely refers to Zoroaster, a figure frequently cited by Renaissance Neoplatonists regarding divine creation.</note> says: "God created all things by Love." The second is *ghebura* <note>Hebrew: *Gevurah*, "Power" or "Judgment."</note>: that is, the just distribution of graces, according to the capacity of things. For of all beings, each one has received as much in goodness, beauty, and perfection as was justly fitting. Therefore, Wisdom says: *You have made all things in number, weight, and measure.* <note>Wisdom of Solomon 11:20; original: "omnia in numero, pondere, & mensura fecisti"</note> The third concurring in creation is *tipheret* <note>Hebrew: *Tiferet*, "Beauty" or "Adornment."</note>: that is, the masculine virtue which flows in; the fourth is *malchuth* <note>Hebrew: *Malkhut*, "Kingdom," the final Sephirah.</note>: that is, the feminine virtue which receives. And do not be surprised that such sexes are found in the divine: for it is said in the last part of Isaiah: *I who make others to bring forth, shall I myself not bring forth?* <note>Isaiah 66:9; original: "Ego qui alios parere facio, ipse non pariam?"</note> For if He granted these sexes to created things, therefore He must have them within Himself; for He would by no means grant them to others if He lacked them: for "no one gives what he is denied to have." <note>A common scholastic legal and philosophical maxim: *nemo dat quod non habet*.</note> In creating, God used these four: first, goodness, because He created out of love; second, justice, by giving to each according to their capacity; and the dual sex, masculine and feminine. For just as a woman would not conceive unless a male poured seed into her, so too, unless *tipheret* filled and poured into *malchuth*, she herself could not give that good influx to things to allow them to exist. To conclude: from the second numeration, *chocmah* <note>Wisdom</note>, proceeds the third, *binah* <note>Understanding</note>; for the Son communicates to the Holy Spirit (which is the third), and the third into the fourth, *ghedulah* <note>Mercy</note>, then the fifth, *ghebura* <note>Judgment</note>, the sixth, *tipheret* <note>Beauty</note>, and the tenth, *malchuth* <note>Kingdom</note>.

*KABBALISTIC DOGMA: It will be true that all things depend on "fact," if by "supreme fact" we understand the word "fatum" [Fate].*

FRIAR ARCHANGELUS: *Factum* <note>The word for "deed" or "thing done."</note> written with a "c" is concrete, and signifies a thing already made. But *fatum* <note>The word for "Fate."</note> signifies a concurrence, or order, or connection of secondary causes foreseen by God. According to this concurrence, God defines the ends; and yet things are not so bound by this concurrence that they cannot happen otherwise—even though God knows them beforehand. This is because God's knowledge does not impose necessity. For any one of the future "contingent" <note>In philosophy, a "contingent" event is one that could happen or not happen, as opposed to a "necessary" event like 2+2=4.</note> contradictions is determined to a truth for any given moment just as much as the other. The power determining any one of the future contingents toward a specific outcome is also able to determine its opposite. And because God has infallible knowledge of future contingents, it is because He knew them no differently than they were going to be done. Just as He knows things already done infallibly and clearly, so He knows things yet to be done infallibly. However, although God has infallible and most certain knowledge of future contingents, they will nonetheless happen contingently and not necessarily. This is because the Divine Will determined the thing to be contingent: for He could have not determined it. Thus the knowledge of God does not impose necessity upon the things known by Him. Therefore, although He knows future contingents, He does not know them "necessarily," but "contingently," in the sense that He is able to not know them <note>This is a subtle scholastic distinction: God's knowledge is certain, but because the event itself is free, the knowledge is of a free event.</note>; for God knows future contingents just as the Divine Will does. Indeed, the Divine Will determines things merely contingently and freely. Therefore, God knows future things contingently and freely. It follows from this that everything that God knows will be, has the potential to have never been known as a future thing... <note>The author is navigating the "sensu composito" vs "sensu diuiso," a logical method used to explain how God can know a free choice without taking away the person's freedom to choose otherwise.</note> The difficulty lies in this: how the contingency of things and God's infallible knowledge (or Providence) can stand together. <meta>This page continues the commentary by Archangelus de Burgonovo on the Kabbalistic dogmas of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. The previous page discussed the flow of divine life through the Sephirot, specifically Gedulah (Mercy), Gevurah (Judgment), and Tipheret (Beauty). <header>ON THE DOGMAS OF THE KABBALISTS.</header>
<page-num>771</page-num>

Aristotle, in the twelfth book of his *Metaphysics*, places providence in God, asserting this of the Chaldean fathers—that is, the Hebrews. In his first book of *On Interpretation* and the second of the *Ethics*, he establishes the contingency of things, saying: "We are the masters of our own acts." <note>original: "nos sumus nostrorum actuum Domini"</note> Saint Augustine likewise says: "nothing is so much in the power of the will as the will itself." And the Psalm says: "My soul—that is, my will—is always in my hands." <note>Psalm 119:109; the author glosses "soul" as "will."</note> However, how these two things can coexist—namely, that an event is contingent <note>Meaning it could happen or not happen, depending on human choice.</note> while in God there is infallible providence, and in the heavens there is fate (as Plato believes)—is a matter of the greatest difficulty. William of Ockham says that this has not yet been revealed to any mortal.

The reason for this difficulty is that God is not measured by the same measure with which we measure. Some creatures are measured by **time** (those which have a beginning and an end); others by **aeon** <note>original: "æuo"; a philosophical term for duration that has a beginning but no end, often associated with angels and celestial bodies</note>, which have a beginning but lack an end, such as Angels, souls, and the celestial bodies. God, however, is measured by **eternity**, which lacks both beginning and end. And because this eternity is unknown to us, we do not know how to compare our own measure—that is, time—with eternity, nor how to understand their agreement or their difference from one another. For eternity is the "possession of the whole of life at once." <note>A classic definition of eternity from Boethius.</note>

And Solomon says: *He who reigns forever created all things at once* <note>Ecclesiasticus/Sirach 18:1; original: "Qui regnat in æternum creauit omnia simul"</note>—that is, eternally. Therefore, we err when we measure the works of God according to time, because we do not know how to reconcile time with eternity. Thus Paul sometimes speaks of eternity when he says: *Before the world's ages* <note>2 Timothy 1:9</note>—which is eternity—and sometimes of time when he says: *while we have time.* <note>Galatians 6:10</note>

Let us say, therefore, that all things come from the supreme fate: that is, from the entire coordination of the **Sephirot**, which are called the divine arrangement. For God acts toward us clothed in seven garments—the seven lower Sephirot <note>The Sephirot from Chesed to Malkhut, which deal with the created world.</note>—through whose mediation God provides for the World. For just as a particular soul gives life to the body it inhabits and all its members, and not only gives life but rules and moderates the whole and all its parts, so God—having formed this World—gives life to and rules this great machine through the mediation of the seven lower Sephirot.

This is confirmed by Plato, who says: "No place is unknown to the immortal God." And Orpheus: "The perfect eye of God and the mind of Jove <note>Jupiter/God</note> inspects all things that happen among us." And again in the *Hymn to Apollo*: "You hold the boundaries of the entire World: the beginning and the end are your concern; through you all things live: you temper the whole sphere with your resonant lyre"—that is, disposing all things most sweetly and harmonically. And David says: *Whither shall I go from thy spirit? And whither shall I flee from thy face? If I ascend into heaven, thou art there; if I descend into hell, thou art present.* <note>Psalm 139:7-8</note> And Christ says: *Consider the birds of the air, they sow not, neither do they reap, and your heavenly Father feeds them; consider the lilies of the field, how they grow,* etc. <note>Matthew 6:26-28</note>

The angelic minds that assist and minister to God are said to be two-parted. Truly, first there stand the **seven spirits** to whom is entrusted the administration of the whole celestial kingdom and of the hell which (as they say) is beneath the lunar orb. For these (as the more secret theologians say) rule all things through a certain succession of hours, days, and years, just as is said by astrologers regarding the planets over which they preside. And John speaks of these when he says: <margin>"</margin> *And seven lamps burning before the throne of God, which are the seven spirits of God* <note>Revelation 4:5</note>, through whom, as through chief ministers, He distributes all things—both the higher things, which rejoice in the number three (the supreme Crown, the Wisdom of God, and Intelligence), and the coarser things, which are in the number four and are composed of the four elements. From these three and four, that **sevenfold** number is completed.

John continues, teaching how they preside over the seven spheres and consequently over those things arranged by them, whence he says: *I saw in the midst of the Throne and in the midst of the elders and of the four animals, a Lamb standing, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth* <note>Revelation 5:6</note>—that is, extended everywhere by power so that they may see all things with their eyes and strike with their horns all things that must be struck. For they stand in the sight of God to hear and grasp all things that the Prince commands. They are sent out and go forth, or are extended by power, so that they may execute the commands entrusted to them.

<header>ARCHANGEL’S COMMENTARY</header>

by itself, or through the lower ministers of the heavenly host under their rule. 
As Mercury <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure associated with the *Hermetica*.</note> teaches, immediately after the Mind and the Spirit, there is a sacred power. 
> The Mind (he says), being God, most full of the fruitfulness of both sexes, being life and light, 
> by His own Word brought forth another Artisan Mind; which God, being of fire and 
> spirit, is a divine power. He thereafter fashioned seven governors, who encompass 
> the sensible world in their circles; their arrangement is called Fate. <note>original: "fatum". In this context, it refers to the celestial order governing the physical world.</note>

He calls the "other Artisan Mind" the Holy Spirit, which is understood not as a 
structure built from mortar and stones, but as one produced by the Father and the Word. 
This Spirit is himself an artisan and craftsman, possessing all power. 
Among spiritual beings, he says this Spirit fashioned those seven governors 
and disposers of earthly things as his most faithful ministers, together with 
multitudes of others, as we are taught by the prophecy of Daniel. Nor do those seven 
always stand before God without sometimes being sent forth: as we read of Gabriel being 
sent to Zechariah, Daniel, and Joseph to guard them, as the Hebrews assert; and 
likewise sent to Mary with that most happy embassy and the wondrous message he 
brought. Raphael was also sent to Tobit, and Michael as a support 
to the Israelites, as we read in Daniel. So too many others of those who stand 
before God are sent like legates from the side of a prince. <note>original: "legati de latere". A term used for high-ranking papal ambassadors with full delegated powers.</note> Those who stand 
there, as well as the ministers, are distributed into many offices. For they are 
divided into those nine orders which I have explained in the *Conclusions* 
of Pico della Mirandola and above. There are also seventy-two princes 
presiding over the seventy-two nations, about which each has 
his own station. Nor are there lacking those whose duty it is to care for us 
diligently, to defend and guard us, and even to undertake battles so that we 
may never strike our foot against a stone—except in accordance with what 
divine justice has decreed. There are also those who supply power to the 
most minute herbs, small stones, and all lower things. Indeed, they lead 
every kind of ministry toward the greatest gift of God. Their 
manifold duties transcend all human grasp, and their number is even 
greater. Therefore, no one presumes to assign a number to them, except he who 
utterly ignores what he discerns. And all these are subject to the command of the 
seven superior spirits, from whom Fate depends. Therefore, all things depend 
on the fate of the supreme Sephiroth <note>The ten attributes or emanations in Jewish Kabbalah through which the Infinite (Ein Sof) reveals itself.</note>, not on a "fate" from a lower order of created 
things, as those who argue that all things happen by necessity would have it. 

They argue that everything that will happen contingently <note>Events that might or might not happen, depending on choice or chance.</note> is 
known by God with determination. Therefore, whatever is to happen contingently 
is necessarily going to happen. For unless it were necessarily going to happen, 
it would follow that God could be deceived. For example: "God knows that Francis 
will run tomorrow." And yet, "Francis can choose not to run." If so, "God can 
be deceived." This first premise is a "necessary future" because it is a future 
being predicted of itself. Therefore, it is also a necessary consequence: 
every future event, therefore, necessarily must happen. 

To these objections, I respond and say that every contingent future remains 
contingently future. Because whatever can not-be a future event is not a 
necessary future; and that which is not a necessary future is contingent. 
And I say that a contingent future is contingent even when it exists; for when 
it does not exist, it *can* exist; and when it exists, it *can* not-exist. 
When I am actually writing, it is "contingent" that I am writing; for I am 
able not to write, and any contingent thing is of this sort. 

To the first reasoning, it is said that if a contingent future known by God is 
posited not to happen, then it will also be posited that God never knew it 
would happen; and consequently, unless it happens, God is not deceived. For 
if the thing happens, God knows it contingently (for it could have not happened 
had the will not determined it to be future), and He always knows it as a 
future thing. If indeed it never happens, He never knew it would happen. 
To the second point, I respond by denying the logical consequence; there is a 
fallacy of speech there, arguing from a "composed sense" to a false "divided 
sense." <note>A scholastic logical distinction. The "composed sense" looks at the whole proposition (It is impossible that [a man sits and runs at the same time]), while the "divided sense" incorrectly applies the necessity to the part (A man who is sitting is [by necessity] unable to run).</note> 
For this is true in the composed sense: "It is necessary that he who sits does 
not run." But it does not follow that it is "necessary for the one sitting not 
to run" in a way that deprives them of the power to get up.

The first proposition holds that for the same instant in which a sitting person sits, for that same instant they do not run; but the second holds that for another instant they necessarily cannot run, and this is false. This is because they can run [at another time]. Similarly, let it be said of the future: that which is future is future for that specific time and instant for which it is intended to be; however, it is not necessarily future for another instant, because it is possible for it not to come to pass.

## **ON THE DOGMAS OF THE KABBALISTS. Whoever knows in the Kabbalah the mystery of the gates of understanding will know the mystery of the great Jubilee.**

**FR. ARCHANGELUS.** What the gates of understanding are, and how many there are, I have explained elsewhere, and most notably in my commentary on Abraham’s *Sefer Yetzirah* <note>The "Book of Formation," one of the oldest and most fundamental books of Jewish mysticism.</note>. As far as the explanation of this conclusion is concerned, it must be known that the gates of <term>binah</term> <note>Hebrew for "Understanding," the third emanation (Sephirah) on the Tree of Life, often associated with the Divine Mother or the shaping of raw intuition into thought.</note>, or understanding, are fifty. We arrive at this number through the square of the number seven—namely, the seven lower <term>sephiroth</term> <note>The ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite (Ein Sof) reveals itself. The "seven lower" ones correspond to the days of creation and aspects of the emotional/physical world.</note>, by assigning a value of seven to each one. For seven times seven yields forty-nine, and when that number is reached, the process goes no further; then we enter into the fiftieth gate, which is the end of *binah* and the beginning of <term>chocmah</term> <note>Chokmah is "Wisdom," the second Sephirah, representing pure, undifferentiated intuition or the "point" of creation.</note>. 

This fiftieth gate was denied to Moses, because it would have been the entry into the gate of ultimate bliss, for it is through this gate and in it that we are made blessed. For this reason, Moses through his Law could make no one blessed; confirming this, Paul says: "No one is justified by the Law" <note>Galatians 3:11</note>—that is, so that they might become capable of the reward of bliss. Because of this, Moses in the Law promised the Jews nothing but temporal things, nor was it permitted for him to lead the people into the Promised Land. 

Christ, however, upon coming, entered this fiftieth gate by granting the remission of sins, just as he attributed to himself that saying of Isaiah: "The Spirit of the Holy Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach indulgence and remission to the captives, and the acceptable year" <note>Isaiah 61:1–2, quoted by Jesus in Luke 4:18–19. The "acceptable year" is traditionally linked to the Jubilee.</note>—that is, the year of the Jubilee, which was the fiftieth, in which the trumpets sounded as a sign of Christ’s coming in such a fiftieth year. That is, he was meant to enter this fiftieth gate by making us blessed. Therefore, he says: "I have come that they might have life, and have it more abundantly" <note>John 10:10</note>, which Moses was unable to do. Therefore, after the fiftieth day [Pentecost], Christ sent the Holy Spirit, who opened the gate of heaven for us. As a sign of this, in his resurrection, he led the holy Fathers out of Purgatory. 

In this way, Christ is the way and the ladder by which we ascend to God the Father; therefore, speaking of himself in the Gospel of John, he says: "I am the way; no one comes to the Father except through me" <note>John 14:6</note>. For this reason, he showed himself to the patriarch Jacob—in whose house he was to reign—in the figure of a ladder, by which the chosen descendants of that visionary might ascend to God; thus it was said to him: "In you shall all the tribes of the earth be blessed." 

Hence Christ, who not only showed the way but made himself the way, providing light and guidance to all, also provided protection, so that he might say: "No one shall snatch my sheep from my hand" <note>John 10:28</note>, whom I guard as a good shepherd. Confirming all this, Paul says: "Let us hold fast the firm confession of our hope, having a great High Priest (who has entered the heavens), Jesus the Son of God" <note>Hebrews 4:14</note>, so that he might also lead us there and present us to the Father. 

Let us say then, regarding the conclusion, that the number seven is the number of remission, because it belongs to the Holy Spirit (from whom all remission comes); and the square of seven is the number forty-nine; and in the fiftieth year, the remission of the Jubilee took place. This prefigured that the true remission ought to be performed by Christ in the manner mentioned above. The Jubilee and remission were given after the square of the sevenfold number. And this is because God willed it so, for God has instilled an order in things from which he never departs except by necessity. God follows this order, as the Church sings: "In the cycle of ten days, by which remission comes through the Law" <note>original: "Deno dierum circulo, quo Lege fit remissio." A liturgical reference to the timing of the Law or Pentecost.</note>. 

There was another reason: because the Jubilee will emerge from that dwelling of the Divine House which (as more secret theologians teach) has fifty gates. This number fifty is completed by the number five multiplied by ten, or vice versa. This ten is designated by the letter <term>Iod</term> <note>The Hebrew letter Yod (י) has a numerical value of 10 and represents the Father or the beginning of the divine name.</note>, the letter of Divinity attributed to the Father; while five is represented by the letter <term>he</term> <note>The Hebrew letter He (ה) has a numerical value of 5 and is the second and fourth letter of the divine name YHWH.</note>...

# **COMMENTARY OF ARCHANGELUS.**

...which is the character of the Holy Spirit. Whence the Father of mercies, and the Holy Spirit, through whom remission <note>The word *remissio* implies both the "forgiveness" of sins and the "release" of debts or captives.</note> is given, folded together make the "remissive number." But these letters, when joined together, compose **Iab** <note>original: "Iab יב". Note: While the text uses these characters, it is likely a reference to *Yah* (יה), the shortened name of God found in the word "Hallelujah," which the author connects to divine mercy.</note>, a name that is indeed most divine and most merciful, which we are commanded to praise whenever we say: *Hallelujah*. And although remission is obtained through the Son, it is not given by him except through the Holy Spirit, as he himself testifies, alleging that it was said of him by Isaiah:

> The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me and sent me to preach indulgence <note>or "release"</note> to the captives, and the acceptable year of the Lord.

Hence, also wishing to give the Apostles the authority to forgive sins, he breathed on them, saying:

> Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them.

**Jubilee** <term>Iobeleus</term> is said to come from the word **Iabal** <note>original: יבל (yabal), a Hebrew root meaning to lead, bring, or flow.</note>, which means "it flowed toward." From this, he implies that at that time every kind of divine influx <note>In Kabbalistic thought, "influx" refers to the flow of divine energy or light from the higher realms into the world.</note> occurred from heaven—not only of remission and restitution (as is held in the book of Leviticus) but of all spiritual gifts and goods. The institution of the sacraments of the Church is not a departure from the practice of the Jubilee, or the day of remission, or the oracle of Ezekiel; rather, it is the directing of those divine influxes toward a certain "pool." The keys to this pool are placed in the hands of the vicars of God and Christ—namely, the priests—so that they might open it at the will of the needy and those who ask. 

The cause of this institution of the Jubilee was this: just as the earth is renewed every year, and religious orders are renewed through their chapters and assemblies, and Republics through new rulers, so God willed that after a "square of seven" <note>Seven times seven years, totaling 49.</note> the Israelite Republic should be renewed. This was done especially with the favor of that fiftieth year, in which every heavenly influx was opened; hence that year was called the Jubilee, that is: "the influx." 

Since this renewal was accomplished with the greatest outpouring at the time of Christ, Christ himself was sent (as I said above) to preach the acceptable year of the Lord. And then John saw the holy city, the New Jerusalem, descending from heaven. This implies that renewals take place in heaven, for all things that are changed here below are preordained there. 

At the time of that Jubilee, the people were relieved of their burdens. For as the Supreme Truth <note>Referring to Christ.</note> says: *With the same measure you use for others, it will be measured back to you.* Thus, it was only fair that whoever desired remission and relief from God should relieve the people oppressed by them. Hence we are taught by Christ to say to the Father when praying:

> Forgive us our debts, as we forgive others.

For we are relieved through the remission of that burden of which the Prophet sings: 

> For my iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden, they are too heavy for me.

Therefore, possessions were restored to their former owners at the time of the Jubilee. This was so that if the loss of property had been permanent, the poor would not be consumed by sadness, having lost hope of recovering what was gone. But the most powerful reason was so that they might resume their own things at the very time when, having received remission from God and being cleansed of fault, they were considered worthy to recover their goods which they had lost due to their own evil merits. 

It was also intended to indicate that at the time of the Greatest Jubilee—when the course of seven thousand years is complete—all things must be restored to their original state, though in a better condition, according to that saying of Isaiah:

> For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth.

Also, in this Jubilee, slaves were manumitted <note>Set free from legal bondage.</note>. For just as they were to be liberated from the slavery of sin and the Devil, so it was fair that they themselves should free their own servants. Christ declared that this rule must be observed in the parable of the King who wished to settle accounts with his servants. For when the Lord had forgiven one servant ten thousand talents, because that servant was later unwilling to forgive his fellow servant a hundred pence, it was said to him:

> You wicked servant, I forgave you all that debt because you begged me; should you not also have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had mercy on you?

Wherefore the angry Lord delivered him to the torturers until he should pay the entire debt. Afterward, Christ himself added:

> So also my heavenly Father will do to you, unless each of you forgives his brother from your heart.

By the command of God, therefore, all Hebrew slaves were manumitted. For just as every servile work was forbidden on the seventh day, so on the seventh year <note>The Sabbatical year or the culmination in the Jubilee.</note> the servitude of the people of God was forbidden. For the seventh year...

From this we can learn that God wills that we exit from the servitude of this World in the same state in which we entered—and in a state so much better as the reward is greater, which is to be given to us as the wage for our service by God himself. In the seventh year, rest was also ordained, not only for men, but for the soil and all other things: because God wanted to conform us to himself and make us continuous; and not only us, but all things that have been granted for our use. Hence he commands us to rest, not only on the seventh day, but in the seventh year, and in the seventh millennium; about which John <note>A reference to the Apostle John and the Book of Revelation.</note> writes, since the unfolding of days, years, and millennia is the same, as is manifest to those who have skill in divine numbers.

Also, in the seventh month, the Day of Remission was ordained, which the Hebrews call **Yom Kippur** <note>original: "iom hachepurim יום הכפורים"</note>; because God, following the "remissive" number seven, chose that seventh month, beginning from March, which in the Law is called the first among the months of the year. In that month also (as many wise men believe) God fabricated the World, or at least man, whom He brought into the World when the fruits were already ripe and prepared for the overseer of that world, so that he might have things with which to be nourished. In that month, the influx of that goodness was ordained, with which God fed the man he had adorned with such great gifts. And thus that month will be the first "worldly" month; while the legal first month is March, and September is the seventh. And the remission was on the tenth day of that month, denoting the **Father**: to whom we attribute the letter **Yod** <note>The Hebrew letter י, which has the numerical value of 10.</note> and the number ten, because it is the end of all things, just as the number ten is the end of all numbers. 

The month, however, was the seventh, which is the number of the **Holy Spirit**: so that from the number of the month and the day joined together, they might be understood. The Father represents mercy, and the Spirit represents remission: as a most generous outpouring and influx in which, through the Father and the Holy Spirit, the **Son** (as we said recently) obtained for us, his brothers, a perfect and continuously lasting remission; according to that word of the Apostle: *He entered once into the holy place, having found eternal redemption.* <note>Hebrews 9:12.</note>

...of Abraham, God is said to have walked about, while he wished first to obey and to cover his sin: having fashioned a garment of skin from that [nature], He took away the sins of the World. For from that region all things are granted to us; for there He was born, there He taught, there He suffered, and in the same place He rose again: and from there He entered into that true South, and the supreme temple, from whence He gave gifts to men, and from whence comes all mercy, grace, and salvation. Therefore, he says (whoever knows the southern property) that he who understands this property of mercy will know why every departure of Abraham is always toward the South. In the Scripture, it is said that departing from Lot, Abraham walked toward the southern or austral part; and furthermore, that he pitched his tents toward the South. Abraham set out toward the South because he pitched his tents in Hebron, which is located to the south with respect to Jerusalem. And it is said in Genesis: Abraham going, and proceeding further toward the South. 

This is a mystery, suggesting (as the more secret Theologians <note>A reference to the Kabbalists.</note> explain) that the journey toward the South was toward the place of the Archetype—namely, the place of piety, clemency, and mercy. Indeed, Abraham’s excellence was in hosting strangers, in visiting the sick, and in other pious works. And he was of such great piety that he spared nothing for the sake of his neighbor; this is suggested in the Law where it is said that he yielded his own wife to the King, so that it might be well with him. Nor did he sin in this; rather, he deserved much by sharing his wisdom with him, whom he held as a wife (as Origen teaches, he sometimes held her as a wife, and sometimes, without sin, shared her as a sister), according to that saying of the wise man: *Say to wisdom: you are my sister.* <note>Proverbs 7:4.</note> Hence, on account of this shared wisdom, the Egyptians did favors for Abraham himself. 

Truly, Pharaoh was impure and subject to sins; he could not sustain that wisdom, and therefore he was scourged. For (as the Wise Man witnesses) wisdom does not dwell in a body subject to sins. This sin, therefore, was on the part of Pharaoh, not Abraham. Nor did he fail in imparting spiritual goods to him, nor toward any other in a distribution of this kind. Whence it is said of him in Genesis: That Abraham gave tithes of <term>kol כל</term> <note>Hebrew for "all."</note> (as the Hebrews say), that is, of all things possessed by him. Or (as the Kabbalists say) of that tenth measure, the tithe of all goods: for it contains the fifty degrees of understanding, according to the number of those things which he possessed in his inheritance (as the *Zohar* witnesses, and the *Porta Lucis* <note>The "Gate of Light," or *Sha'are Orah*, a fundamental Kabbalistic text by Joseph Gikatilla.</note>). 

As a sign of his piety, he spent only silver, as is said in the purchase of the double cave <note>The Cave of Machpelah in Hebron.</note>. For the Scripture studied to suggest the place from which Abraham came, and from which he continually drew. For from the South he drew influence, where silver is found; for they associate whiteness with the white clemency of mercy. Whence also he bought the double cave with silver, and did not wish to have it for free; because he did not want a common place (as the sons of Heth offered him), lest that place be profaned by the graves of the uncircumcised. He also wished to claim that place by right of purchase, lest anyone presume to move the bodies of the fathers from that place as if it were not his own. But the most powerful cause of that purchase with silver was this: because silver comes from <term>ghedulah</term> <note>The Sephirah of Gedulah, also known as Chesed, representing Lovingkindness or Mercy.</note>. Whence Abraham received every favor: so that with all things provided and arranged according to their proper symbols and convenience, he might receive that place, not only for their bodies, but for their very souls. 

His piety is shown in his praying for Sodom: whence we see him trying to appease that supramundane denarius <note>The "ten" (denarium) refers to the ten righteous men Abraham hoped to find in Sodom to save it from destruction.</note> against the vengeance prepared for them. Finally, Abraham himself returned to his home in Hebron. For in the text it says: Abraham returned to his place, namely, after the dialogue he had held was completed. Father Abraham had explored many places in the house of the Father. Hence he recurred now to one place, now to another: as the names he used indicate among the wise. And this was so that he might obtain mercy from one of those places (if it were possible). Just as, conversely, Balaam <note>Spelled "Belaham" in the text.</note> tried to obtain things contrary to them, offering a sacrifice in each of those places: so that from some one of them...

From there, so that they might better profit in that aforementioned southern place, he descended into Egypt, not only because of physical hunger, as some think, but because the presiding virtue over Abraham was not yet established in the land of Canaan. Hence there was a famine and a lack of divine things: because the celestial influence was then small there. Even if Egypt in Holy Scripture almost always implies something evil—because it was always hostile to the people of God—it nevertheless had some heavenly goodness in itself, according to that saying: *As the Paradise of the Lord, and like Egypt as you come to Zoar* <note>Genesis 13:10; the text uses "fegor," likely referring to Segor/Zoar</note>. For the river exiting from the right side enters and descends there: that is, from the South, whose name was Gihon, but now the Nile: therefore, so that Abraham might receive whatever goodness was found in Egypt, he proceeded there. Whence, because of the merit of that house, and dwelling, and piety, God promised that happy land to Abraham after his separation from Lot: for Lot was unworthy of that Divine inheritance. For just as he was a stranger to God, so he chose that region of the five cities <term>Pentapolis: the district of the five biblical "cities of the plain," including Sodom and Gomorrah</term> as a dwelling, not shrinking from those most wicked inhabitants: but clinging only to the fertility of temporal things, having entirely neglected divine and holy things. Nor was he rescued by the Angel from the burning of that region because of his own works or merits: but because of Abraham, as is clearly held in the text, where it is said: *When the Lord overthrew the cities of that region, he remembered Abraham, and delivered Lot from the destruction*. And that Lot was of such a character is indicated by the strife that occurred between the shepherds of Lot and those of Abraham: for they (as the Zohar <note>original: *Elzohar*; the foundational work of Jewish mysticism</note> asserts) wished to follow the worship of the nations of that region. Hence, it is not written without cause: *The Canaanite was then in that land*.

Truly, God commanded Abraham to go into the land of Canaan: because it was to be given to his seed: a land (I say) which ought to flow with milk and honey: namely, Gospel wisdom and prophetic vision, and where, as in a place peculiar to God, the temple was to be built. Yet it was first given into the hand of the wicked Canaan: because it was decreed (according to the Zohar) that Abraham himself, Israel, and all the people, as well as Moses, should descend into Egypt before the law was given: to which decree Christ also was subject, who spent his first years in Egypt. And this was by that Law of which Paul says: *God has concluded all in unbelief (or under sin), that he might have mercy on all* <note>Romans 11:32</note>. Just as he had chosen Abraham as the Father of faith, and of the family to be renewed, so he commanded him from there to go out from his land and his kindred: because all his relatives and fellow citizens were idolaters. Therefore he gave a lesson to posterity: especially to those who are of good minds, to whom it is said: *Hear, O daughter, and forget your people, and your father's house: and the King shall desire your beauty* <note>Psalm 45:10-11</note>. And the beauty of Abraham pleased God so much: who made him the father of that chosen family not only according to the flesh, but also according to the spirit. 

Whence after the blessing given to him, God said: *And you shall be blessed*, so that the blessing already given might be confirmed. Yet the truth of the letter has it: *And you shall be a blessing*: therefore another reason must be sought: which is: because God did not only give him a blessing, but the fountain (if it is right to say so) of blessing: from which, namely, the blessing to be communicated to others would proceed, since in him all the nations of the earth were to be blessed. Which (as Christian Doctors not ineptly say) was verified in Christ. Whence, not wandering from the truth, the Hebrews assert that a "pool of blessing" was given to Abraham. For a "pool" is some blessing to be communicated to others: we have this not only from the Hebrews—who gather it from many places of Scripture—but from the doctrine of Christ, who says: *Salvation is come to this house: because he also is a son of Abraham*. Hence he is called both the Father of faith and the Prince of this place of those to be saved: and as a sign of this, the Lord led Abraham outside: that is, outside the boundaries of the natural order, and outside the flesh: so that he might show him those stars, of which the Apostle says: *As star differs from star in clarity: so saint from saint in glory* <note>1 Corinthians 15:41</note>. ...to the lower spirits; thus there are guardian Angels for those over whom they preside. But there are also Angels of whom the Prophet speaks: *He who counts the multitude of the stars and calls them all by name* <note>Psalm 147:4</note>. God raised Abraham up so that he might see these Angels, clearly so that he might recognize from them the innumerable multitude of those they guard. For God said to him: *Count the stars if you can: for so shall your offspring be* <note>Genesis 15:5</note>. According to the Kabbalists, the sum of the Angels is 301,655,172, as is more clearly declared in the preceding conclusions. But this is mere imagination. Others, however, think they have calculated the number from the words of Daniel, who says: *thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten hundred thousand stood before him* <note>Daniel 7:10; the Latin text discusses various interpretations of "millia millium" and "decies centena millia"</note>, and thus in the computation already made there would be two thousand million. Although some of our own theologians have dared to assert that "ten hundred thousand" is more than "thousands of thousands," this proceeds from a lack of skill in arithmetic. Ultimately, we can obtain a true count of the Angels or the Blessed from none of these people. For the first group presupposes what they are bound to prove, while those who rely on Daniel would indeed have a completed count if the Prophet had declared that there are no more Angels than those two thousand million.

Hence Jerome says both beautifully and learnedly: the number of God’s servants is not defined by this saying of Daniel; rather, human speech has simply expressed the largest possible multitude. For these are the thousands, and these are the myriads of which it is said in the Psalms: *The chariot of God is ten thousandfold, thousands of those rejoicing, the Lord is among them* <note>Psalm 68:17; original: "currus Dei decem millibus multiplex millia lætantiũ"</note>. Therefore, the number of both Angels and saints is left unknown to us, but known to Him who recognizes every drop of rain and every grain of sand. If, therefore, the number of Angels is unknown to us, the number of the elect is also left unknown, since according to some Doctors the number of both will be equal, according to that saying of the Psalmist: *You have set the bounds* <note>that is, a determined number</note> *of the peoples* <note>that is, of all nations</note> *according to the number of the children of God* <note>that is, the Angels</note>. They are called "children of God" because secondary causes did not contribute to their existence, but God alone.

It remains, therefore, that Abraham was the fountain of the elect, or a source of blessing, for so many that their number is unknown. And Abraham did not only benefit the good and the elect, but even the reprobate; for when he prayed for Ishmael, it benefited him. Whence it is written: *And as for Ishmael, I have heard you* <note>Genesis 17:20</note>; and it profited him even though he had already been cast out with his mother. Therefore it is said in the text: *Behold, I will bless him, and I will increase and multiply him exceedingly; he shall beget twelve Princes, and I will make him grow into a great nation.* Thus Abraham was always delighted by a twofold family: the superior and the inferior, the spiritual and the carnal, the free and the servile—of which Paul openly treats with the Galatians. Hence there are twelve inferior princes corresponding to the twelve superior Princes, and a great inferior crowd against a great superior crowd. 

Many, however, grieve over this exceedingly effective prayer made by Abraham for the Ishmaelites or Hagarenes—who in our times are called Turks, and Arabs, or Mohammedans <note>original: "Turcæ, & Arabes, seu Mahumetici"</note>—because they prosper so much that they somehow prevail over the children of the free woman. This (I believe) was done by divine disposition, so that God might have in His house both a servile and a copious free family, as Paul seems to suggest. Many such things, and all good things, happened to Abraham because of the piety and mercy in which he excelled. As the conclusion says, every progression of Abraham was always toward the South—namely, to the clemency of *Gedulah* <note>original: "ghedulah"; Hebrew for "Greatness" or "Mercy," the fourth Sephirah</note>. Truly the heavens favor us so that we may know that, once impediments are removed, we should submit ourselves to our spirit as a leader. It will show us the way where the heaven, where the guiding spirit, and indeed where the supreme Moderator leads—which Porphyry, Firmicus <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonist, and Firmicus Maternus (4th century), an astrologer and later Christian apologist</note>, and many professors of this art were unable to do. And we see this if we attend to those things which the mind, distracted by no contagions, suggests to us from the beginning, or what we feel by the dictation of nature itself or the spirit when the mind is purged of all care and distorted affection; this we imitate and attempt more frequently, for nature and our spirit feel it.

->**KABBALISTIC DOGMA.** Unless the letter **H** <note>the Hebrew letter He (ה)</note> had been added to the name of Abram, **Abraham would not have fathered children.**<-

**FRATER ARCHANGELUS.** The changing of names effects much in men: for Jacob, who had been called the "supplanter," was made a Prince and an heir of God. In Genesis it is read that the angel said to Jacob: *Your name shall be called Israel.* The angel did not call him this then, but foretold what was to be: namely, that he was to be called Israel by God, as is found below in chapter 35. Whence **Israel** (according to Jerome) is interpreted as "seeing God"; it is also interpreted as "prince" or "heir of God" from *sharah* <note>שרה</note> which is "he inherited" or "strove," and *El* <note>אל</note> which is "God." For in the word "seeing," which is *roe* <note>ראה</note>, and in the word "God," which is *El*, the letter **Shin** <note>ש</note> is not found. The sense of this name, therefore, is that he was a prince and a soldier for God, and an heir of God. Hence Christ said: *I have not come except for the sheep that perished of the house of Israel;* that is, the House of those militating for God, according to that saying of the Apostle: *No one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully;* or the house of those who are appointed heirs of God. Of whom the same Apostle says: *Heirs indeed of God, and co-heirs with Christ.* For the Redeemer came for all those who fight for God, and who are appointed heirs of heaven. Not only do Catholics approve by custom that the changing of a name is of great benefit, but Astronomers and Platonists teach that there are twin **genii**: one of birth, and another of profession; and these are sometimes in concord, but sometimes lead to different things. If, therefore, someone has a concordant genius, he will feel a twin profit and increase—namely, of nature and of profession. But if they are disparate, he will sometimes perceive a better nurturing through his profession than through his birth. For in the change of profession, the force of nature changes; indeed, it is entirely overcome...

->### ARCHANGELUS’S COMMENTARY<-

The power of these sacraments is not seen, but this power is contained or signaled through external and sensible things, so that those who are only able to perceive through their senses and cannot yet approach the discernment of spiritual things might in some way grasp the mystery.

The Son of God and our Redeemer regenerates us as a Father; prophesying of Him, Isaiah addresses Him, saying: *You, however, are our light, our redeemer; your name is from eternity* <note>original: "Tu autem lumen nostrum redemptor noster, à seculo nomen tuum"; a variation of Isaiah 63:16</note>. Therefore, the letter **ה** <note>the Hebrew letter 'He'</note> was added to his [Abraham's] name so that it might be a sign that God had granted Abraham the power of generating and fathering a son. From him, the lineage would successively reach one individual, who is called *Berakhah* <note>Hebrew word for 'blessing'</note>, that is, the source of blessing and salvation, so that through him all could be blessed and saved. <margin>THE KABBALISTIC DOGMAS OF BROTHER ARCHANGELUS</margin>

For those who are addicted to bodily senses, the sacraments were given by nature under veils and sensible signs. Indeed, for those who are "exercised"—that is, the interior people who have their senses trained to the discernment of good and evil—solid food is given, and wisdom is communicated. This wisdom is perceived through the interior sense of those who have changed the use of their external senses for the better.

For there are two modes of understanding, distinct from natural ones. The first is the pure contemplation and contact of Divine things; the other is the alignment of truths explained by others with our own intellect. Regarding the first level, one proceeds through natural things, according to what the Lord had promised, saying: *You shall see my back* <note>original: "Videbis posteriora mea"; Exodus 33:23</note>, namely, the creatures, which are "afterward" or "behind" in respect to the Creator. These are His effects; therefore, Logicians, when arguing from effect to cause, are said to argue *a posteriori*. Concerning this way of knowing, Wisdom [the Book of Wisdom] says: *From the greatness of the form of the creature, their creator can be known* <note>original: "A' magnitudine enim speciei creaturæ, poterit cognoscere horum creatorem"; Wisdom of Solomon 13:5</note>. If Moses had not recognized this, he would have known how to arrange neither the Ark nor the Tabernacle, in which the image of the World—namely, the Archetypal, the Greater World [Macrocosm], and the Lesser World [Microcosm]—is perceived. Nor would he have correctly applied the sacrifices, etc. Divine things also spoke to him, saying: *I will show you all good.* And so Moses, dying the **death of a kiss** <note>original: "morte osculi"; a Hebrew mystical concept where the soul is drawn out of the body by a divine kiss, signifying a painless and ecstatic union with God</note>, saw that supreme and total Good. For by this death, all the saints and friends of God die when they enter into those secret depths of God.

Regarding the second mode of knowing—namely, through truth aligned with the intellect—Moses understood better than **Aristotle** and the other philosophers. For he clearly perceived the truth emanating from the marrow of the sacred letters; and with the veil removed, he looked face-to-face upon those things which are hidden from the common people and the "wise men" of the world. He saw them with such certitude that all perplexity was removed from him. Writing about this kind of wisdom, **Eupolemon** says: Moses was a contemporary of Inachus and Ogygis <note>mythical early kings of Argos and Boeotia</note>, a wise man who taught all his people wisdom. Returning to the proposal...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of Divine revelation and the spiritual hierarchy. It shifts from the regeneration through Christ mentioned on the previous page to the Kabbalistic understanding of how Divine light was perceived by the Patriarchs and Prophets before Moses, specifically through the Sephirah known as Malchut.</meta>

<page-num>783</page-num>
-># ON THE DOGMAS OF THE CABALISTS.<-

...that Divine light so far surpasses all intelligence that things are contained within it which remain hidden even to the highest Seraphim <note>The highest rank of angels in the celestial hierarchy</note>, as Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher</note> says. However, when this light is diffused into the angelic minds and received according to the nature of the receiving intelligence, it is divided into various ranks—all of which, nonetheless, are beyond the limits of reason. When it is sent down into man, it becomes rational; and this light is manifold according to the pleasure of the Giver, who distributes to each as He wills.

This Giver before Moses was **Malchut** <term>Malchut: The tenth and lowest Sephirah in the Kabbalistic Tree of Life, representing the "Kingdom" and the gateway through which Divine energy enters the physical world</term>; for the prophets who preceded Moses (such as the ancient Patriarchs) also prophesied within Malchut, as if they did not receive from the other higher **Sephiroth** <term>Sephiroth: The ten emanations or attributes in Jewish Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself</term>. Except from Malchut, they had almost no knowledge of the other Sephiroth. Others say that Abraham, who preceded Moses, had knowledge of all the dimensions; for he was the first who treated this matter of the Sephiroth or "dimensions" and left behind a book on the coordination of these dimensions—indeed, Enoch, who was even more ancient than he, left many things in writing concerning these matters. 

Regarding him, Berosus <note>A Babylonian priest and historian whose works were often cited in the Renaissance</note> says that not only the records of the Hebrews, but also those of the Chaldeans and Scythians, hand down that Noah existed full of Divine light. He predicted the future flood, built the ark, and preserved the seed of men and beasts. Afterward, he taught the Armenians, the Scythians, and then the Italians (whom Scripture calls **Chittim** <note>original: "chitimos"; a biblical term often associated with the peoples of the West or Mediterranean islands</note>) the secrets of nature, theology, sacred rites, the course of the stars, years according to the motion of the sun, and months according to the course of the moon. The former group resolves this objection by saying that these aforementioned Fathers obtained this privilege so that they might have such knowledge. However, according to the common Law, this was not granted to everyone.

The reason is that the Tabernacle, in which God took His rest before the coming of Christ, existed in a threefold distinction: the first was wandering—for God had no determined place in which men could gather to consult God and obtain grace, but they chose now this place, now that, for praying; indeed, sometimes particular men would build a temple to God. Hence it is said of Abraham that God rested upon him; for the text says: *Elohim rested upon the head of Abraham* <note>original: "Elohim quieuit super caput Abraham"</note>, as if (understand) upon his wandering tabernacle. Because God clings to the creature just as a stone sits upon the surface of the earth—movably, that is—therefore the place of God was indeterminate. In the time of Moses, however, the tabernacle was determined but mobile, portable from place to place like the Ark of the Covenant. In the time of Solomon, it was a determined and immobile tabernacle, or temple, that was built. Christ established the fourth tabernacle: which is our heart. *The temple of God is what you are*, says the Apostle <note>1 Corinthians 3:16</note>.

Therefore, the conclusion says: *All those before Moses prophesied through the one-horned hind*, that is, through Malchut. For just as the knowledge of a particular place for the adoration of God was not granted to them, so also the Sephiroth higher than Malchut were not known to the ancients; but only Malchut, the archetypal Moon, which is called the **one-horned hind**. We see hinds, fawns, gazelles, and goats celebrated all too often in Holy Scripture, not only in the Song of Songs, but in the Law and the Davidic hymns. For in the Law, He commands the Tabernacle to be covered with the tanned skins of goats. And while the kidneys and fat of every animal are forbidden, the stag and the gazelle are all granted to be eaten as clean, as we read in Deuteronomy where it is said: *But just as you eat the gazelle, so you shall eat the stag* <note>Deuteronomy 12:22</note>. And again: *They shall eat them, like the gazelle and the stag*—of which, clearly, all the intestines are eaten except the blood, because the soul is in it, which must not be eaten together with the flesh. For the soul of the animal does not become nourishment for man, but (as they say) leads to his depravity, pollution, and ruin.

In the title of Psalm 21 <note>Psalm 22 in modern Bibles: "To the Chief Musician. Set to 'The Deer of the Dawn'"</note>, where we have: *In the end, for the morning protection*, it is held in the truth of the letter: *To the Victor, for the hind of the dawn*. And in many other places, the Prophets here celebrate hinds so much that we clearly understand they refer to something better and hidden, just as Origen <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian</note> agrees when he says: *Stags or goats, animals indeed according to the nature which they bear corporally, refer to certain causes of incorporeal things*; so that to those invisible hinds there might seem to apply that which is written: *The voice of the Lord preparing...*
