# ARCHANGELUS’S COMMENTARY #

...perseverance, and consecrated by Divine assistance. Therefore, the higher powers fear them: they tremble; the Angels worship them; the Demons are terrified; and every creature reveres them, and every religion venerates them. They provide us with great virtue. They deify us through union, and even through a power of miraculous works and effects that are above nature. One must speak of these things "with salt" <note>original: "cum sale loquendum"; a Latin idiom meaning to speak with wisdom, discretion, or wit</note>; for these holy matters are to be scattered among the wise, but not made public to the common folk. If we wished to explain this doctrine beyond what has already been said, our weak strengths would not suffice, nor would time, nor would ink. But (to use the words of John) not even the whole world could contain the books that would have to be written if every single thing that Jesus did were set down in writing.

Nevertheless, with the help of Divine grace—and as much as the light of Jesus himself deigns to illuminate my eyes—we will, according to our strength and following in the footsteps of the Evangelists, suggest something of these wonders which are contained within the bark of the letter <note>The "bark of the letter" (cortice literae) refers to the literal or surface-level meaning of a text, as opposed to the "marrow" or spiritual core</note> of both pages [of the Bible], especially the ancient one. This Law was first given in its fullness to Moses; but by Christ, it was rolled up and led into a better state. It is just as if a potter were to take the same mass of clay that was under one shape and reform it into another, adding nothing except a new form, while the substance and material remain the same.

Thus Christ, our teacher, took that Law—which was previously subjected to the blood of animals for the sanctification of the "animal man" <term>animali homine: in the Pauline sense, the "natural" or "soulish" person focused on worldly life rather than the spirit</term>—and rolled that same mass in His own blood. He led it toward the sanctification of the "spiritual and better man," losing nothing and leaving nothing behind that pertains to the substance of the Law, but changing only its form and its effect into a better lot. And this is what he said: "One iota, or one apex <note>original: "unus apex"; often translated as "one tittle," referring to the smallest stroke or serif in a Hebrew letter</note> shall not pass away, until all things are done and fulfilled"—specifically through Christ, the Gospel, and the followers of the Gospel—which were spoken of in the Law.

Indeed, the *Iota* is the smallest letter of the alphabet, by which (as Jerome says) it is shown that even the things thought to be the smallest in the Law are full of spiritual sacraments, and that everything is recapitulated in the Gospel. There is also the *Apex*, the point and the accent. These, together with the letters, belong to the substance of the sacred speech (as the more secret theologians say). For the letters of the Law form the **body**; the points <gloss>vowel points</gloss> grant the **soul** and make that body live; and the accents provide the **spirit**, celestial life, and a consonance conforming to the harmony of the heavens. From these three, the Law is completed, making it in a certain sense "living."

According to that saying: "The word of God is living and effective." It lives, indeed, because it penetrates even to the divisions of the soul and spirit, looking into all the secret places of the heart. It is effective, moreover, because it divides the spirit from the soul—namely, uniting the "animal" part with the higher portion through a superior union—so that it may finally lead even the "animal soul," now joined to the spirit, into God. As it is sung in the Psalm: "The Law of the Lord is immaculate" <note>Psalm 19:7 (Vulgate 18:8)</note>; that is, perfect, converting souls to their Creator from whom they proceeded, and providing wisdom to "little ones" <note>the humble or simple-hearted</note> regarding human malice and cunning. Just as Christ our Lord, after he spoke of this wisdom hidden from the "prudent of the world," added: "And you have revealed them to little ones." Those who are immune to sin and pure of heart are admitted to this doctrine; it is denied to the "wise of the world," as if to unclean pigs and dogs.

Wishing to speak of this to the Hebrews, Paul said: "We have a great discourse." And it is discussed among the perfect, because it is a heavenly gift and a "hidden manna" which no one knows except he who receives it. Therefore, it should not be discussed except among the experienced, because others cannot grasp it. Furthermore, it concerns how a man becomes a participant in the spirit of God and "one spirit" with Him; how also the "good and better word of God" is tasted—that which sounds to the ears outside, and is scattered to the common people in parables. This is according to the saying of our Doctor to his more secret disciples: "To you it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God; but to the rest in parables." These are, moreover, the virtues of the world to come, and the happiness which we expect, which "no eye has seen, nor ear [heard]..."

nor has it entered into the heart of man, unless one has been subjected by the power of the Holy Spirit to recognize those things which man cannot investigate by his own strength. As Isaiah speaks, saying: "No eye has seen, O God, besides you, what you have prepared for those who love you." <note>original: "Non videbit Deus absq; te, quae praeparasti diligentibus te"; referring to Isaiah 64:4</note> These things were first demonstrated to the first parent [Adam] while he existed in the Paradise of delight—which the more secret theologians, along with Paul, call the "world to come": that is, the world to be restored to us who lost it. Upon these things depends a perfect knowledge of the origin and end of the soul; of the angelic spirits; of the condition and quality of that immense glory; and of the nature of that Paradise of delight described entirely through metaphors. All these things are included in the marrow and the kernel of the Gospel. ->*KABBALISTIC DOGMA: He who understands why it was said that Moses hid his face, and that Hezekiah turned his face to the wall, shall know what the attitude and disposition of one who prays ought to be.*<-

**FRIAR ARCHANGELUS.** Prayer is necessary for us, because through it we obtain those things which we do not have; for we are all in need, and therefore we have need of the Universe [God]: as Proclus <note>A Greek Neoplatonist philosopher (412–485 AD) whose works deeply influenced Christian mysticism.</note> teaches regarding the thought of Porphyry and other wise men. And since the salvation and preservation of every nature truly depends on its turning back toward its own totality, one who desires to possess virtue must persist in prayers. He must frequently supplicate so that He may pour it [virtue] in—He who contains all virtue in Himself and is the highest good and the cause of all goodness. He does not exist merely through a series or some succession, but produces all things immediately—even, if you will, matter itself. Nor is the Divinity removed or distant from anyone; rather, He is present equally to all, since everything exists by the gift of God. Nor is anything outside of God, since He Himself embraces and comprehends all things. And whatever we imagine to be outside of God is utterly nothing. Iamblichus <note>Another influential Neoplatonist (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote extensively on "theurgy" or divine rituals and prayer.</note> adds the necessity of prayers beyond all hope: because all things are produced and guarded by the Gods at the command of the Supreme. Therefore, he who desires to be saved must pray to those who save, by whom things cannot be overcome. For everything born that is torn away from its parents and its root immediately slides into non-being and ruin—especially those things which, although they have proceeded forth in themselves, nevertheless remain in the parent. Such are all created things, which begin from God and end in God Himself, according to the perfecting Trinity. By this Trinity, all created things effect a certain [motion] (as Proclus follows from the mind of Plato), beginning from God and ending in God, like the line of a circle which closes where it begins. However, so that they may return, they need the favor of those from whom they proceeded. Favor is obtained through prayers, the purpose of which is to persuade both the Angels and even God: that He might command, and they might guard with perpetual protection, and lead the soul back to that place from whence we came. And although prayer is necessary for everyone, it is especially so for upright men, since it is a certain application and joining of them to God. For like is born to be folded into and joined with like: and the upright and whole man is like God. Hence he must be joined with Him to obtain help, by which he may be drawn away from the blind prison and the bodily chains in which he exists as a wanderer from Him whom he resembles, and with whom he comes to be united. And just as children led away from their parents pray, driven by nature, until they return to them: so it is necessary for us, who are removed from the true Father of all, to pray and supplicate Him that we may be led back. Hence...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of spiritual ascent, moving from the internal interpretation of scripture to the specific practice and mechanics of prayer. It bridges Neoplatonic philosophy (specifically Proclus) with Christian theology to explain how the soul reaches God.</meta>

# ARCHANGELUS’S COMMENTARY #

Some Academics <note>Refers to followers of the Platonic Academy.</note> called those people "orphans" who, lacking both parents, neglected to turn toward the superior and Divine nature, having despised orations and prayers. Therefore, among various nations of men, whoever claimed a name for themselves under the guidance of virtue exercised themselves in the study of prayers and petitions: as among the Indians, the Brahmans; among the Persians, the Magi; among the Greeks, the Theologians; and among the Assyrians, the Chaldeans, who established the feasts of the Gods and hidden mysteries, venerating them with prayer. How much more must this be done by us, for whom the gate of heaven has been unlocked? However many well-composed minds there are, or uttered voices, or thoughts directed toward God for the tempering of needs or the obtaining of certain gifts, so many are the sweetest melodies offered to God—beyond the praises we frequently pay to His honor. 

For the most excellent composition of those melodies, *Proclus* <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher whose work deeply influenced Christian mysticism.</note> provides five most exact instruments. The first of these is the knowledge of the divine orders which the one who prays approaches; for one cannot properly and swiftly approach if they are ignorant of their properties. For this reason, the oracle—or Divine responses—commands that in the sacred worship of God, the "notion of fire" be kindled. This is accepted from the Mosaic institutions; for in Leviticus, by the command of the highest oracle, it is said: 
> The fire on my altar shall always burn. <note>original: "Ignis in altari meo semper ardebit"; referring to Leviticus 6:12-13.</note>

The second is kinship, or our affinity to God Himself, according to all the sincerity within us, from expectation and faithfulness in what has been committed to us. This is according to what the Supreme Doctor [Christ] said: 
> Whoever does the will of my Father, who is in heaven: he is my brother, sister, and mother. <note>original: "fecerit voluntatem Patris mei, qui in cœlis est: ille meus frater, soror, & mater est"; referring to Matthew 12:50.</note>

The third is contact, according to which we touch the divine essence with the supreme "head" of the soul <note>In Neoplatonism, the "head" or "flower" of the soul refers to its highest, most divine faculty.</note> and, leaning toward it, we find support. In this sense it is said: 
> What we have heard, and seen, and touched concerning the word of life. <note>original: "Quod audiuimus, & vidimus, & contrectavimus de verbo vitæ"; referring to 1 John 1:1.</note>

The fourth is adhesion. Whence *David* says: 
> But for me, it is good to adhere to God. <note>original: "Mihi autem adhærere Deo bonum est"; referring to Psalm 73:28.</note>

The fifth is union, which places that "one" which is in the soul into the unity of God, and renders us stable by reducing us into a single act; according to which we no longer live for ourselves, but for God, remaining in the divine light and being circled around by Him. This is the best end of true prayers: that it applies the conversion [of the soul] to its own procession <note>A philosophical concept where the soul "proceeds" from God into the world and must "convert" or turn back to its source.</note>, and that the "one" which proceeds from the one God may be placed back into the "one" and reconciled. 

This is the easy path to a happy and blessed life, while we are supported by prayers and ascend into God, who otherwise cannot be apprehended by us except through this medium of prayer. For we must direct our prayers to God the Father—I say the "Archetypal Father." Speaking of Him, *Proclus* says: all things pray except the first [the One] toward whom those who pray rightly direct their petitions. This is also what Christ taught, saying: 
> Our Father. <note>original: "Pater noster"</note> 

And this is so that you may recognize all things are to be given by Him, just as He himself recognized, saying: 
> All things have been handed over to me by my Father. <note>original: "Omnia mihi tradita sunt à Patre meo"; referring to Matthew 11:27.</note> 

And again: 
> My doctrine is not mine: but His who sent me. <note>original: "Mea doctrina non est mea: sed eius qui misit m[e]"; referring to John 7:16.</note> 

This is also because the Father is the primary source of mercy and piety. Hence the Apostle calls Him the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation. He Himself sent the Redeemer to us: *John 3*: 
> For God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son: so that everyone who believes in Him should not perish, but have eternal life. <note>original: "Sic Deus dilexit Mundum ut Filium suum unigenitum daret: ut omnis qui credit in illum non pereat, s[ed] habeat uitam æternam."</note> 

Therefore, we must pray to this Father continually; that is, the habit of prayer and charity must be continuous, even if it cannot be so in every single act. To this sense Christ said: 
> It is necessary to pray always, and never to faint. <note>original: "Oportet semper orare, & nunquam de[ficere]"; referring to Luke 18:1.</note> 

Because prayer ascends into the sight of God like incense, as *David* sings. For a man in fervent prayer directs his prayer into heaven like an arrow shot from a bow by a most robust arm. Sometimes it is of such efficacy that it can change the judgment of God, as regarding the Ninevites in *Jonah*, and regarding Ahab in the book of Kings. *Hezekiah*, moreover, by praying, earned an extension of life by fifteen years; in like manner, *Moses* by praying placated the Lord. Truly, when we ask in prayer, we do not yet have what we desire, but after being heard...

<meta>This page continues the technical and mystical discussion of prayer as a means of ascending to the divine. It transitions from the general necessity of prayer to the specific mechanics of how the soul interacts with the divine hierarchies, drawing heavily on Richard of Saint Victor, the Bible, Neoplatonic philosophy (Syrianus), and Kabbalistic concepts like Malchut and Tipheret.</meta>

### ON THE TEACHINGS OF THE KABBALISTS ###

Through prayer, and having now obtained the desired gift, we are introduced into the inner chambers <note>original: "penetralia"</note>, in which it is permitted to gaze upon those eternal spectacles with the full delight of the soul. And this is true contemplation, just as Richard <note>Richard of Saint Victor (died 1173), a prominent mystical theologian.</note> well defined in his work *On the Mystical Ark*, saying: "Contemplation is the free and clear insight of the mind into the spectacles of wisdom, suspended in wonder." For the Lord, having been struck by prayers, sometimes opens one of the many chambers; once entered, with eyes illuminated, the soul sees the spectacles of divine wisdom that are most hidden from the common crowd. And because these things extend into infinity, the mind of the viewer, unable to penetrate everything, remains suspended in wonder. For it is said in Ecclesiasticus: "Exalt the Lord as much as you can, for He is greater than all praise. For who shall magnify Him as He is?" Though the Blessed see Him as He is, they do not see Him in His full magnitude: for He is infinite, while they have determined grades of their own power.

Hence Isaiah, speaking familiarly with God Himself, says: *Truly you are a hidden God.* <note>original: "Verè tu es Deus absconditus." Isaiah 45:15.</note> Hidden, indeed, and yet revealed. For God is in all things; hence He is revealed to all. Yet He is in Himself, as if covered in the abyss of His own darkness, hidden from everyone, as it is said in the Davidic song: *He made darkness His hiding place, His pavilion round about Him, dark waters in the clouds of the air.* <note>Psalm 18:11.</note> For when dealing with an individual man, He sometimes hides His face from him, and says: *No man shall see me and live.* Yet man returns to God through prayer. And to do and achieve this, the one who prays must turn toward the "wall": for our whole mind and intention must be directed toward God, who is hidden from us behind a certain wall since He is invisible; therefore, God is accustomed to appear in a cloud.

For we read in Exodus that when Aaron spoke to the people, the glory of the Lord appeared in a cloud. And God said to Moses: *I will come to you in the thick darkness of a cloud,* just as He had previously filled the tabernacle. And in the Transfiguration of the Lord, Matthew says: *Behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them.* God does this so that the glory of His majesty is not seen by us who are unworthy, and so that those looking on are not struck down by His splendor. For if (as the Apostle says) the children of Israel could not look intently at the face of Moses because of the splendor of his countenance—and he was a corruptible man—how much less could they look upon the glory of the supreme and incorruptible God? 

The "wall," however, which is placed between us and God the Father, is *Malchut* <note>The Hebrew term for "Kingdom," the final Sephirot (divine attribute) in Kabbalah, often seen as the gateway between the divine and material worlds.</note>; without entering through this, we cannot possibly ascend to the inner chambers. To make this entry, it is necessary for us to have "commerce with the supernals"—that is, we must conform ourselves to them in righteousness, spirituality, and purity, and in all things according to our strength. Hence Syrianus <note>Syrianus (5th century AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher and the teacher of Proclus.</note> teaches in his *Theology* that the priests of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy and others who labor must be proportioned to the anagogic <note>Upward-leading or spiritualizing.</note> virtues of the Celestial Hierarchy. Indeed, it is necessary that we be conformed to the Supreme High Priest, if we wish to observe the words of Paul, who says: *Those whom He foreknew and predestined,* namely God, *to be made conformable to the image of His Son.* In this sense he said again: *No one can say "Lord Jesus" except in the Holy Spirit*—that is, unless he participates in the Holy Spirit, just as Christ Himself was full of it, from whose fullness (as John testifies) we have all received.

And because transition is easy among things that share a "symbol," we work through that symbolic force and conformity, and through the force of consonance <note>A Pythagorean and Neoplatonic concept where things in the same "chain of being" vibrate or respond to one another.</note>. For this is so effective that at the movement of one consonant thing, the movement of the other follows; just as is evident with true friends, where one is moved by the movement of the other, since for both (as it is said) there is "the same willing and the same nilling." Hence Orpheus <note>The legendary poet and mystic; the author refers to the "Orphic Hymns."</note> teaches in his singular operation that according to which the name is the same (though through analogy), of both natural and divine virtues, the hymn is the same and the work is the same—so that we might say: if I have the disposition to receive the light and favor of the Sun, while the Sun works in me, Raphael <note>The archangel traditionally associated with the Sun in various esoteric traditions.</note> also works, or whichever Intelligence presides over the Sun itself. And that divine power works as well, to which the Sun and that Intelligence correspond. This divine power is what David, Isaiah, and the more secret theologians call *Tiphe-* <note>The text cuts off here. It refers to "Tipheret," the Sephirot of Beauty and Harmony, which connects the higher and lower worlds.</note>

# ARCHANGELUS’S COMMENTARY #

[...it is] which is the heart of the Archetype <note>The "Archetype" refers to the original divine model or God's mind.</note>, just as the Sun is the heart of the heavens. And each corresponds to our own [heart] through illumination and fervent charity, for we are made to correspond to the divine and the higher beings, if we are willing to read the ancient theologians and carefully weigh the words of the Gospel. In all our members and operations, we can be conformed to God. This is proven at length [in other works], showing that all members of the human body find their mark in God through analogy. For this, Scripture is cited everywhere, attesting that God has eyes, eyelids, ears, a mouth, a tongue, and other such things, to which we are taught to be conformed in the Gospel.

First, we are warned to conform to the Divine heart, when it is said: *Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful.* <note>original: "Estote misericordes, sicut & Pater uester misericors est." Luke 6:36.</note> Christ urges us to conform to the hands of God: *Give, and it shall be given to you* <note>original: "Date & dabitur uobis." Luke 6:38.</note>—namely, from the hands of God. To the eyes also, when he says: *Blessed are those who mourn* <note>original: "Beati qui lugent." Matthew 5:4.</note>: that is, those who shed tears from the fountain of their eyes, for the divine fountain shall be opened to them, comforting them. And so it is with the other members: to hold this likeness, we ought to hide our face, just as Moses did, or turn to the wall, as Hezekiah did, as the conclusion states.

And we have lived in this world because we must pray toward the wall of *Malchut* <note>The tenth Sefirah in the Kabbalistic Tree of Life, representing the Kingdom or the physical manifestation of God’s presence.</note> by leaving behind these visible and sensible things, which are called "faces" because they are perceived by us. Whence Jeremiah says: *He shall sit solitary and lift himself above himself.* <note>original: "Eleuabit se supra se sedens solitarius." Lamentations 3:28.</note> We ought to pray in secret: that is, by abandoning temporal things and contemplating eternal ones. Therefore, while God spoke to Moses on Mount Sinai, Moses, being accustomed to the Divine light, hid his face, not yet having a fully purified sight. For (as the more secret theologians say), if anything foul or worldly defiles the eyes, they have a place in which they may be purged, until they come to that light which illuminates and perfects them, lest a filthy and weak eye be offended by its clarity. Thus, the eye must be accustomed before it fixes its gaze upon that most full light.

For (as Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) who wrote about the soul's ascent to "The One."</note> says): *An infected eye, not yet well-purged or weak, if it intends to look upon a most brilliant spectacle, will immediately grow dark. For it is necessary that the seer be made similar to the thing seen before he is admitted to the viewing. Never would the eye see the sun unless it were made solar; nor again would the soul see Beauty itself and God, unless it were made beautiful and divine.* It will only look upon the light once it has been made lucid and clear. Hence Solomon says in the Proverbs: *The path of the just is like light, shining as it goes, or proceeding even unto the perfect day.* <note>Proverbs 4:18.</note>

It is necessary, therefore, that he who wishes to contemplate God have a purged eye; otherwise, he would be struck by that light, like someone newly rising from sleep and looking into the light: for then his eyes are troubled, unless the eye gradually becomes "solar." So it happens to one unaccustomed to the Divine light. This same thing happened to the people of Israel, who could not look upon the face of Moses, which shone from his divine fellowship. In a similar way, it may be said of Hezekiah: to him appeared the Divine splendor, which he, being unable to bear (as he was unaccustomed to such light), turned his face to the wall. For that light is inaccessible.

Those speaking about it have wandered through many detours—indeed all those whose eyes He Himself had not illuminated. Therefore Pythagoras <note>Ancient Greek philosopher and mathematician whose teachings were often linked to mystical traditions.</note> commands that no one should presume to speak of divine things without light—without that light, I say, of which the Psalmist sings: *In your light we shall see light.* <note>original: "In lumine tuo uidebimus lumen." Psalm 36:9.</note> Drenched in this light, Adam saw God Himself walking at midday, recognized His voice, and truly perceived the natures of all things, so as to impose a fitting name on each. The same may be said of the Patriarchs, the Prophets, and the Apostles: all were drenched by that Divine light. Another reason Moses and Hezekiah acted thus was surely humility. Therefore, those who desire their prayers to be heard should hide their face following their example, deeming themselves unworthy, as [is said] of E...

# ON THE DOGMAS OF THE KABBALISTS #

it is read: "he who was justified by humility; but the Pharisee was condemned by pride." <note>A reference to the Parable of the Pharisee and the Tax Collector in Luke 18:9–14.</note> For the prayer of one who humbles himself penetrates the heavens: confirming this, the Psalm says: "Approaching the high <note>meaning: proud</note> heart, God shall be exalted" <note>meaning: shall be distanced from him</note>. <note>original: "Accedens ad cor altum (superbum) exaltabitur (elongabitur) Deus." A mystical interpretation of Psalm 64:6–7 (Vulgate 63:7–8).</note>

**KABBALISTIC DOGMA:** No spiritual thing, descending to a lower level, acts without a garment.

**FRIAR ARCHANGELUS:** This dogma holds as a firm foundation that man was formed in the image of God, and thus it is necessary that he enjoys a similar figure. For we attribute members to God in a human fashion—namely eyes, hands, and so on. He has a **right hand**, as the Psalm says: *The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand.* <note>Psalm 110:1.</note> Concerning the **left hand**, the Father says it is where the wicked shall be placed in the final examination <note>The Last Judgment</note>. Regarding His **sitting**, Isaiah says: *Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool.* <note>Isaiah 66:1.</note> Regarding His **walking**, it is said in Genesis that *He walked at midday* <note>Genesis 3:8, often translated as the "breeze of the day."</note>; and the Psalm says: *They have seen your steps, O God.* <note>Psalm 68:24.</note> Regarding **eyes and ears**, the Psalm says: *His eyelids test the children of men.* <note>Psalm 11:4.</note> Regarding the **nose**, Exodus says: *The Lord smelled a sweet odor.* <note>Exodus 8:21.</note> Regarding the **mouth**: Isaiah says: *The mouth of the Lord has spoken.* <note>Isaiah 1:20.</note> Regarding the **throat**, the Song of Songs says: *Your throat is like the best wine.* <note>Song of Solomon 7:9.</note> Regarding the **head**, the Song of Songs says: *Your head is like Carmel.* <note>Song of Solomon 7:5.</note> Regarding the **hands**, in the Psalms and Job: *Your hands have made me.* <note>Psalm 119:73; Job 10:8.</note> Regarding the **fingers**, the Psalm says: *I will see your heavens, the work of your fingers.* <note>Psalm 8:3.</note> Regarding the **teeth**, the Song of Songs says: *Wine is worthy for my beloved to drink, and food for his lips and teeth.* <note>Song of Solomon 7:9.</note> Regarding the **shoulders**, Isaiah says: *The government is placed upon his shoulder.* <note>Isaiah 9:6.</note> Regarding the **arms**, Isaiah says: *The arm of the Lord, to whom has it been revealed?* <note>Isaiah 53:1.</note> Regarding the **heart**, in the first book of Kings: *I have found a man after my own heart.* <note>1 Samuel 13:14.</note> Regarding the **back**, Jeremiah says: *I will show them my back, and not my face, in the day of their destruction.* <note>Jeremiah 18:17.</note> Regarding the **feet**, the Psalm says: *And darkness was under his feet.* <note>Psalm 18:9.</note>

God is even said at times to be **clothed** in a human manner; and this is when the Maker reveals Himself to us clothed in various garments. And these are the garments through which we are able to know God, whom we cannot grasp in His naked and pure essence. These "limbs" are the manifold powers within that one, most simple Being. And the "garments" are certain paths through which He pours Himself out into us. While acting through His limbs—that is, through His powers which are manifold to us—He remains in Himself a single, unified thing. 

The Kabbalists discuss these garments in the <term>Ilan</term> <note>Hebrew for "Tree," referring to the Tree of the Sephirot.</note>, or the Tree of the <term>Sephirot</term> <note>The ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals Himself.</note>. For through these garments, every virtue emanating from Him proceeds. Indeed, nothing flows from the "naked" God, who is entirely removed from every relation, for in Himself He contains all things as the fountain of all goodness. In that which He pours out, He takes on a certain relation, which they call a "garment." 

And there are ten garments. For God is said to be "naked" when He is considered in His naked and pure essence, entirely removed from every relation, whether coming from within or without—insofar as He is here, communicating Himself to no one. And He is called <term>Ensoph</term> <note>Hebrew *Ein Sof*, meaning "The Infinite" or "Without End."</note>, about which <insert>Pico della</insert> Mirandola wrote in his *Conclusions*. 

He, therefore, being supremely "here," before He acted with created things, begat the Son, with whom He simultaneously produces the Holy Spirit. <note>Archangelus is interpreting Kabbalah through a Christian lens, equating the first three Sephirot with the Trinity.</note> When, therefore, He begat the Son, He put on the first garment, which in Scholastic terms is called "Paternity"; and it is called <term>cheter Elion</term> <note>Hebrew *Keter Elyon*, the "Highest Crown."</note>, and it is called the "Father of Lights." Regarding this garment, the Psalm says: *Clothed in light as with a garment.* <note>Psalm 104:2.</note> This God the Father, looking upon the Son in His bosom whom He begat, puts on another garment, which is called <term>chocmah</term> <note>Hebrew *Chokmah*, "Wisdom."</note>, or Wisdom. And the Father, with the Son, breathing forth the Holy Spirit, puts on the garment <term>Binah</term> <note>Hebrew *Binah*, "Understanding."</note>, or Intelligence. 

Afterward, He clothed Himself in seven other garments. The first of these is called <term>chesed</term> <note>Hebrew *Chesed*, "Mercy" or "Loving-kindness."</note>, meaning mercy, piety, and clemency, by which He pours Himself out into others. He governs them most piously; He most mercifully goes before them, justifies them, and rewards them. And since clemency is tempered in the balance of the table of justice, He therefore assumes a garment for justice, which is called <term>ghebura</term> <note>Hebrew *Gevurah*, "Power" or "Severity."</note>, or justice: <term>midah adin</term> <note>Hebrew *Midat ha-Din*, the "Attribute of Judgment."</note>. Regarding this garment, the Angels wondered and said: *Why has your garment become red?* <note>Isaiah 63:2; the red color symbolizes the blood of judgment.</note> (namely, with the color of justice). And since He is supremely beautiful, making all things beautiful—especially human nature, to which He granted the total image of Himself—He henceforth puts on another garment, which in the [sacred] writings...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "garments" of God—the divine attributes or Sefirot through which the Infinite interacts with the world. Archangelus is mapping specific Hebrew terms from the Kabbalistic tradition onto Latin theological concepts and scriptural verses.</meta>

# ARCHANGELUS'S COMMENTARY #

In the holy [writings], especially in the Psalms, it is called **Tiferet** <term>Tiferet: Hebrew for "Beauty"; the central Sefirah that balances mercy and judgment</term>: which we translate sometimes as glory, sometimes as magnificence, and sometimes as beauty, but properly it is the name for Divine Beauty. Concerning these, David says: *The Lord has reigned, he is clothed, the Lord is clothed with strength,* etc. <note>Psalm 93:1.</note> After these two others, the supreme moderator is clothed: through which he shows himself more familiar to us, and through which he grants us many gifts. Concerning these, the Psalm says: *You have clothed yourself with praise and beauty* <note>Psalm 104:1; original: "Confessionem et decorem induisti."</note>: for through these, God makes men distinguished, and it is called **Hod** <term>Hod: Hebrew for "Majesty" or "Splendor"; the eighth Sefirah</term>. And, because God provides us with life and the stability of being, he wears that other garment, called **Yesod** <term>Yesod: Hebrew for "Foundation"; the ninth Sefirah, associated with the life-force and stability</term>. Finally, this Divine Majesty is clothed in the ultimate garment, by which he shows himself entirely domestic to us: and this the Kabbalists call **Malkhut** <term>Malkhut: Hebrew for "Kingdom"; the tenth Sefirah, representing God's sovereignty in the physical world</term>: that is, the kingdom: for he himself rules us familiarly, just as a King rules his people. It is also called **Shekhinah** <term>Shekhinah: The Divine Presence or "indwelling" of God within creation</term>: that is, the immediate indwelling of God in us. Concerning which it is said: *But you are in us, O Lord,* etc. <note>Jeremiah 14:9.</note> Lastly, God clothed himself in humanity so that he might clothe man in Divinity. Regarding the purpose of the conclusion (that no spiritual thing, etc.): for, if God wished to create the World, he clothed himself in the garment of creation: if he has mercy on us, he puts on the garment of mercy: if he punishes, he puts on [the garment of justice], etc. Because it implies that God stands within himself and creates something: for immediately a relationship arises between God and the creature, which (according to Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major Scholastic philosopher known for his complex theories on "relations."</note>) is of [the category of] relation: yet it would be better to say that it is real: for that kind of relationship are certain garments with which God is said to act with us. However, the relationship toward God is real according to everyone (no spiritual thing) that is, he who is absolute in himself (descending lower) by working, operates without a garment except in the manner of relationship just mentioned.

---

**KABBALISTIC DOGMA:** *The sin of Sodom was through the truncation of the last [plant].* <note>In Kabbalah, "cutting the shoots" or "truncating the last" (Malkhut) is a metaphor for separating the Divine Presence from the higher Sefirot, often used to describe heresy or sexual sin.</note>

**FRIAR ARCHANGELUS:** Sin, in both Angels and men, occurs when someone, departing from the highest good, wishes to take pleasure in a lesser one (according to Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential early Christian mystic.</note> and Hugh, his interpreter <note>Hugh of Saint Victor, a 12th-century theologian.</note>). Hence God himself encompasses the entire form of sin when he says through Jeremiah: *My people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the Lord, the fountain of living waters, and have hewn out for themselves broken cisterns, which cannot hold water.* <note>Jeremiah 2:13.</note> Nor is it only sin when a created good is preferred over the highest good, but also when, given two created goods, the lesser is preferred to the greater: such as when one puts their own advantage before the public good or the utility of the many. Turning away from this error, the Apostle said: *not seeking what is useful to me, but what is useful to the many.* <note>1 Corinthians 10:33.</note> In the same way, [it is sin] when bodily good and pleasure are preferred over spiritual delight. Therefore, sin and error exist when the proper order is abandoned: so that the saying of Augustine is true: *Evil is the privation of order and of due rectitude.* <note>Augustine of Hippo.</note> This error or perversion of order does not come from the power granted by God, but from our own weakness, or from the obscurity of our ignorance: which the Savior, and with him Dionysius and [John] Damascene, calls "night" and "darkness," saying: *He who is in darkness knows not where he goes.* <note>John 12:35.</note> And again: *He who follows me*—the supreme teacher and director—*does not walk in darkness*—meaning the darkness of sins. This darkness is followed by the eternal night of hell: regarding which he says again: *The night comes, when no man can work.* <note>John 9:4.</note> And just as night, or darkness, is the privation of light: so error is the privation of rectitude. From which it is concluded that the essential nature of sin is the privation of good, into which a man or an angel runs, either by confusing the order in their choice: or by presuming for themselves that which they ought to recognize as coming from the highest Good. Thus, the fault is not from God, but from the will choosing badly or presuming too much; but that which is badly chosen by the will is indeed from God: the will itself, by its own fault, errs in choosing. To the point: just as from the tree or the ultimate Archetypal plant, when received rightly and duly, all justice, every [perfect] act, and finally every good proceeds: so from that violated tree, all evil [comes].

### ON THE DOGMAS OF THE KABBALISTS ###

It is clear that [this] has come upon the human race and even upon the Angels: for evil does not arise except from good (according to Augustine and Dionysius). For these authors say that the beginning and end of all evils is good: for nothing acts with a view toward evil, but toward a good which it either neglects or improperly desires. For the Angel sinned by being unwilling to receive this "tree" <note>Referring back to the Sefirotic Tree as a manifestation of Divine Law and Christ.</note> as the true Lord and true lawgiver, and by refusing to obey the rules described within it: being unwilling to revere him as the Mediator, through whom we might be made co-heirs according to the King’s edict. This is what Paul revealed to the Hebrews, saying: *And when he introduced the firstborn into the world, he said: And let all the Angels of God adore him.* <note>Hebrews 1:6.</note> From this, Man also sinned, having dared to extend his rebellious hand toward that which is called by Moses the "Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil," placed in the middle of Paradise. Therefore, only that lack of order, that lack of harmony, or that absence of conformity with the rules existing in that tree is evil. From this it is most clearly inferred that evil comes from that tree—not indeed produced by it, but because the actor turns away from it, as the Apostle clearly proclaims, saying: *Where the Law is removed, sin is taken away.* <note>Romans 4:15; original: "sublata Lege, tollitur peccatum."</note> And again: *If the Law did not exist, sin would not be imputed.* <note>Romans 5:13.</note>

But the Law is truth itself and the rule of acting: which, in the Incarnate Word, is what is now called Jesus and the Redeemer. In ancient times, however, it was the Tree of Life and the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil: because from it we know good and evil, and from it we possess the means by which we work good or evil. Hence the sin of Adam and the sin of Sodom: both "pruned" <note>The "pruning of the plants" is a Kabbalistic metaphor for heresy or spiritual separation, specifically separating the Sefirah of Malkhut from the rest of the Divine structure.</note> this last plant and tree, **Malkhut** <term>Malkhut: The tenth and final Sefirah, representing the Kingdom of God and the physical manifestation of Divine presence</term>, from the other plants, the **Sefirot** <term>Sefirot: The ten attributes or emanations through which the Infinite God interacts with the universe</term>. And both [sins] were unpardonable by human remedy: for no man was a sufficient satisfier for an offense of this kind.

Yet they shared an unequal fate: for God provided a remedy for Adam's sin through the death of his only-begotten son. As a sign of this, God covered Adam with the skin of the lamb who takes away the sins of the world, forgiving his crime by granting him his own skin—that is, life. For Christ, by dying, brought Adam back to life. Because Adam's sin was against God, it could not be repaired except by God. For it was not a matter of ignorance (since ignorance was given as a punishment for the sin) nor mere fragility (since the senses had not yet rebelled), but pride was present, which caused both the Angels and man to apostatize from their Maker. This happened because both presumed to claim for themselves a more eminent rank than was appropriate for them, as I said in the conclusions of **Mirandula** <term>Mirandula: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), the famous Renaissance philosopher whose Kabbalistic theses Archangelus is commenting upon</term>. He did not sin out of ignorance or fragility, but rather, presuming too much from his most clear knowledge, he wished to take [the rank] by force. Hence it was a crime of treason.

These crimes could be expiated by no sacrifice, nor could they be purged by the Law, because the Law justified no one (according to Paul). Therefore, God was not content that man had covered his nakedness with an apron woven from fig leaves; He clothed him in a tunic of skin, fashioned indeed from the skin of that Lamb of whom the Baptist said: *Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world.* <note>John 1:29.</note> And here He vivified and brought back to life this plant, **Malkhut**, and joined it to the other plants of the dimensions. Confirming this, Christ said: *The Kingdom of God (**Malkhut**) is within you* <note>Luke 17:21.</note>—given to you, that is, by my merits. David greatly desired this, saying: *It is you who will restore my inheritance to me.* <note>Psalm 16:5.</note>

For God never entirely abandons sinners, except for the Sodomites: who pruned this plant of the Kingdom so severely that there was no hope of salvation for them. For neither a pure man nor a Divine one, like the Messiah, could satisfy [the debt], according to the Kabbalists. This is because they were not only in Sodom, but because they cut down and utterly uprooted the "last plant"—that is, the last measure, **Malkhut** (through which God acts immediately with mortals)—so that it would no longer produce in them the fruit of forgiveness or of good works. They did this by turning their faces entirely away from God, always thinking of evil. Those who were submerged in the waters of the Flood did the same: for never is any people utterly destroyed unless the sin of idolatry or rebellion intervenes...

For both have worked an abomination—namely, against the order of nature. Hence this crime is called a vice against nature. Just as Plato also, in a few words where he discusses a well-instituted republic, concludes saying: "do not sow seed where it cannot germinate or sprout." Similarly, one who has intercourse with beasts is commanded to undergo the same penalty: for he also perverts the order of nature by sowing where nothing can be born; or if something is born, a monster will be born, which is against the intent of nature, as the natural philosophers conclude. Also in this vice, man falls from his dignity, while he—the most noble—is mingled with a creature far inferior to himself. In detestation of this crime, the Law commands that he be killed along with the beast with which he coupled, and it threatens that the earth will vomit out those who perpetrate such crimes. Just as it vomited out the nations previously existing there who committed such outrages. Animals also are ordered to be killed, not only in detestation but as if polluted and stained, and because they intervened in the perversion of nature. In such a most filthy coupling, unclean spirits also intervene, polluting both parties. Therefore, such polluted and stained things are ordered to be removed from the earth, lest others be contaminated by them.

Time is divided by "twice fourteen" <note>original: "binarium quaterdenum"; referring to the twenty-eight "times" listed in Ecclesiastes 3:1–8 (e.g., "a time to be born, and a time to die").</note> according to Solomon, who said: "A time to be born, and a time to die," etc. And the wise man said this because of the periods of things, as some assert; but why he divided it by twice fourteen, they do not declare. He did so, therefore, because there are seven supramundane sources pertaining to the First Cause, and seven celestial ones—namely the planets—corresponding to the supramundane ones; by which God distributes all things that He grants. And these pertain to the secondary causes, from which the partitions of days and times flow. These sources joined together are fourteen: flowing with good things for those well-disposed, but with evil for those ill-disposed; just as it is apparent with the sun, which hardens mud but liquefies wax. Hence the wise man, skilled in these secrets, doubled the effects of these fourteen sources. 

Josippus <note>Likely referring to the *Josippon*, a 10th-century history of the Jews often attributed to Josephus.</note> wrote in the Greek language a description of Time: namely, that when he was asked what Time was, he replied: "The Occasion <note>original: "Occasio"; translating the Greek *Kairos*, the personification of the "opportune moment."</note> that gives all things," both good and bad. Hence Simonides praised Time, because all good things are produced by it. But Paron the Pythagorean condemned it, because all evils happen within it. And to the one asking why he always walks, he said: "Because I am unvocably following the motion of the heavens." ...answered to his face: because I am suitable for the one who meets me, having the back of my head bald, because no one can seize me from behind, since I am irrevocable <note>The author is describing the classical personification of Opportunity or Time (Kairos), who has a lock of hair in front to be grasped, but is bald behind, meaning once the moment passes, it cannot be caught.</note>. Therefore, time contributes to works: not indeed that time which is the measure of motion and rest (as the natural philosophers <note>Referring to the Aristotelian tradition of physics.</note> say), because that measure itself performs nothing; rather, things contribute which are more disposed to producing a certain effect at one time than at another. For we prove that our bodies are better disposed and stronger when the sun is in its cardinal points <note>The equinoxes and solstices.</note> than when it is in its "prisons" or its depressions <note>Astrological terms for when a planet is in a weak position in the zodiac.</note>. And since the Angelic guardians change every three months, and every three hours—indeed, in every single hour of the day there is some change (as the wise know)—hence we can have greater favor from them at one hour than at another. For they follow the disposition of the stars. 

Therefore the Angel said, while wrestling with Jacob: "Let me go, for it is dawn" <note>Genesis 32:26</note>: namely, the time in which I am compelled to praise God (as some say), or because I am weakened by the light; since my power belongs to the darkness. Because of this, at certain hours of the night, horror invades mortals: because in those hours the powers of darkness prevail, which are hostile to us. Hence the prophet sings: "You have appointed darkness and it has become night: in it all the beasts of the forest shall pass through: the young lions roaring as they seize their prey" <note>Psalm 104:20-21</note>. For the discourse concerns the powers of darkness which are hostile to us, as all [interpreters] explain. And these prevail in the night, but most especially before midnight. At which time harsh judgment (which the Hebrews call *din* <gloss>judgment</gloss> <note>original: "din" דין; the Sefirah of Gevurah/Din associated with strict justice and severity</note>) prevails. 

At other hours, however, we rejoice: because then good Angels, friends and supporters, meet us. Whence our heart is expanded, and they are inflamed to carry out their work. For no better observation can be had for beginning and pursuing a work than while the heart is inflamed, expanded, and eager to bring some work to completion: because then the heavens, the Angels, and all things are favorable. This difference of time proceeds from those above, who are not subject to time. For although they are not subject to this time proceeding from celestial motion, they nevertheless have their own spaces to which these spaces of time correspond. Otherwise God would not have said: "When the morning stars praised me" <note>Job 38:7</note>; that is, the Angels, who are assigned to perform morning praises. Whence it follows: "And all the sons of God shouted for joy"; and many things can be gathered from Scripture by which it clearly appears that even among the Angels there are certain distinct spaces: in some of which they are more at leisure for God, while in others they favor us more, with God concurring in this. 

And concerning this time, the prophet sings: "But as for me, my prayer is to you, O Lord, in the time of your good pleasure, O God" <note>Psalm 69:13</note>. Hence Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher influential in bridging Greek philosophy and mystical theology.</note>, among other things which he teaches must be known by one who prays well, commemorates "time." Christ taught us this observation of time in praying. Whence he himself said in John: "My hour has not yet come" <note>John 2:4</note>. David the prophet also chose, and taught us to choose, the hours of prayer, saying: "At evening, morning, and midday" <note>Psalm 55:17</note>. And again: "At midnight I rose to confess to you" <note>Psalm 119:62</note>. 

The Church, however, has prohibited the observation of days and hours, lest we should run into some superstition. But since Christ knew all things, he observed times without the danger of superstition. Indeed, if anyone were to observe these times with due reason, not only would he not sin, but he would receive favor. Hence the Eternal Father waited for the time of sending His Son. According to that [saying] of the Apostle: "But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son" <note>Galatians 4:4</note>. In the same manner He also ordained the Passover at the full moon; the Day of Atonement in the seventh month, namely September; the Jubilee in the fiftieth year; and many things of this sort, so that in these we might be conformed to the celestial beings and receive a more easy and abundant influx. 

Animals also observe time. Whence Jeremiah says that the swallow, the stork, the turtle-dove and such things know their time. They have this from nature, which Averroes <note>The 12th-century Andalusian philosopher (Ibn Rushd), famous for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> calls "non-erring intelligence." And this is true whether it be that "Universal Intelligence" which the Platonists call the *Anima Mundi* <gloss>Soul of the World</gloss>, or whether it be the particular spirits presiding over each individual, as the more secret Theologians <note>A common way Archangelus refers to Kabbalists.</note> teach. # THE COMMENTARY OF ARCHANGELUS.

All things must await the time decreed in heaven for their fulfillment, as it is said in the Psalms: *By your ordinance they continue*, <note>Original: "Ordinatione tua perseverat" (Psalm 119:91).</note> because all things serve You. Hence it is written: He marks the time for working. For this reason, God and Christ each awaited their own time, because "all things have their time," as Solomon says. Even if those Divine mansions do not contain time within themselves, they nevertheless act within time in relation to us, who are moved by time. Even those mansions themselves are moved according to a "supreme time," which is not the same as our time that is divisible into parts; rather, our time corresponds to it through a certain analogy. We are taught this by Moses and Peter, who say that a thousand years <note>term: millenarius (a period of one thousand years)</note> are as a single supreme day. The *Zohar* <note>The Zohar is the foundational work of Jewish Kabbalah.</note> reports this more clearly when explaining what is said in Genesis: namely, that Jacob served for Rachel, and those days seemed but a few to him. This was because he was looking toward the "Seven-fold" <note>term: septenarius (the number seven, representing a cycle or divine structure)</note> known as *Beersheba*—that is, the "Well of the Seven." In that well, the power of the supreme Seven-fold is gathered, from which the power of the lower realms and of all the planets proceeds. Hence, that span of time which here below is distinguished and prolonged into days and hours is, in the supernal realms, undivided. Just as we measure by days and years, God, in the progress of His eternity, sees the entire course of our lives at once. 

And Jacob served (according to the *Zohar*) the "Upper Seven" for Rachel because of the greatness of his love, but he served the "Lower Seven" for Leah. And because the higher number is not separated by voids but is entirely present at once, that seven-fold period seemed brief. However, the period in which he served for Leah was the "Lower Seven," which is small in comparison but moves in its own cycles. For Rachel designates the contemplative life, for which one serves in the spirit—which is free from time, except insofar as it is bound to the physical—and one serves with a mind so absorbed that the Savior says: "Indeed, one thing is necessary." <note>Luke 10:42, referring to Mary's choice of contemplation over Martha's busy action.</note> That state is entirely free from time. Thus, a mind fixed upon that "one thing" is liberated from time, as is evident in those experiencing a rapture; if they were to remain in that state for a year, it would seem to them as if they had not been there for even an hour. So it is with all the blessed who are elevated by the sight of God: they do not perceive the succession of time but rejoice in eternity or "aeuiternity" <note>A philosophical term for the state between time and eternity, often applied to angels.</note>. 

Leah, however, signifies the active life, which cannot operate without the distinction of that time by which all our works are measured. Therefore, not every time is suitable for gazing upon every favor; as the Wise Man shows when he says: "Everything has its time: a time for destroying, and a time for building; a time for acquiring, and a time for losing," and so on. Again, the Wise Man says: "Wait for the time," and elsewhere: "The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, nor riches to the wise, nor favor to the learned; but time and chance happen to them all." <note>Ecclesiastes 9:11.</note> 

Hence, the time for praying and working is praiseworthy, according to the verse: "For this [mercy] every saint shall pray in a seasonal time" (as I have said). This demonstrates that time can be favorable or unfavorable for praying or acting. To distinguish these times is very difficult and nearly impossible; however, there are some recent examples to the contrary. When harmful angels, or those assigned to the "army of *Gbeburah*" <note>note: Gevurah (Hebrew: גבורה) is the Kabbalistic Sephirah of Strength and Judgment; its "army" refers to angels of severity or punishment.</note>, are permitted to strike a certain place, that time is unfavorable, and one must flee from that place, just as Lot fled from the destruction of Sodom when warned by an Angel. At such a time, one must stay in one's place, as it was said to the Israelites when the firstborn of the Egyptians were being slain. One must abstain from work that can be deferred without loss. Concerning Joseph, the *Zohar* reports that he would not have sexual relations with his wife during the years of famine, for famine is a type of scourge; therefore it is written that he had his sons before the time of the famine. A favorable time, however, is...

...either at midnight, morning, noon, or evening (as I said above). Those who are accustomed to prayer can easily prove this, noticing how great a difference there is between one time and another. And, although the Angels are not subject to this earthly time that comes from the movement of the heavens, they nevertheless have their own spans of time to which our earthly spans correspond (as I have said). Furthermore, prayer offered in a low voice is more effective. Hence, to Moses, who was whispering and perhaps speaking only in his mind, God said: "Why do you cry out to me?" <note>Original: "Quid clamas ad me?" (Exodus 14:15). The implication is that God hears the "silent" cry of the heart as if it were a shout.</note> Wherefore the *Zohar* says: *Kol* <note>Original: "קול" (Voice/Sound)</note>—from which the letter *Vav* <note>The Hebrew letter Vav (ו) often represents a connection or the human element in Kabbalistic symbolism.</note> was heard in the house of Pharaoh, and is heard by God—which (as the Zohar itself says) signifies a voice made without noise, but with the affection of the heart. Such a voice is more effective than any other, according to Rabbi Eliazar, because it is performed with greater effect and attention than that which is done with shouting; for one can be heard without a voice. Hence the Apostle says: "I will sing with the spirit, I will also sing with the mind." <note>Original: "psallam spiritu, psallam & mente" (1 Corinthians 14:15).</note> Wherefore the Teacher of Truth says: "True worshippers will worship the Father in Spirit and Truth." <note>Original: "Veri adoratores adorabunt Patrem in Spiritu & Veritate" (John 4:23).</note> The *Zohar* asserts that three things are required for someone to obtain a blessing in prayer: namely, mind, intention, and word. I say the "mind," because prayer must not be uttered by chance, and the one praying ought to perceive what he says. Then "intention," because the petition must be directed toward God for the sake of some end. Finally, the "word," because the one praying ought to express what he wishes. This "word" can be two-fold: one is mental, and this suffices for God alone, because He alone is the knower of mental concepts. The other word is the expression of the concept, which is necessary for the Angels, whose duty it is to carry our prayers to God. For they cannot perceive the thoughts of the mind (or at least their purpose) except insofar as God reveals them, or a human manifests them by speaking in words. For prayers of this kind, two lambs were ordained in the Law <note>The Mosaic Law in the Old Testament.</note> to be offered and sacrificed: one in the morning hour and the other in the evening. These signified the two-fold prayer to be made at these two times. In the morning hour, we sacrifice to the good, benevolent, and favorable Angels assigned to the mystery of *Ghedulah* <term>Ghedulah: A Hebrew term meaning "Greatness," often synonymous with the divine attribute of Mercy (Chesed).</term> or mercy. And it is not enough to satisfy only these favorable Angels; one must also appease and honor the severe Angels assigned to the Divine justice of *Gheburah* <term>Gheburah: A Hebrew term meaning "Strength" or "Severity," representing the divine attribute of judgment and restraint.</term>. Therefore, in the evening hour, we ought to sacrifice to them so that they may become favorable to us. Because of this, God commanded these two times in the Law to be observed—namely morning and evening—and lambs to be offered and sacrificed in them, and God to be prayed to, so that these two dimensions, namely *Ghedulah* and *Gheburah*, might be rendered favorable to us. Therefore, the prayer before dawn, or the morning prayer, is offered to the tribunal of grace, *Ghedulah*, to attain some favor from *Ensoph* <term>Ensoph: From the Hebrew "Ein Sof," meaning "The Infinite" or "Without End," referring to God in His purest essence before manifestation.</term>, the Most High God. Let him pray at such an hour, then, who desires God to be propitious to him; and this is done while the good and peaceful Angels dedicated to *Ghedulah* are "eating" <note>A metaphorical way of saying the Angels receive the spiritual essence of the sacrifice/prayer.</note>. But he who desires to be guarded against some danger, and to be delivered from an evil already brought upon him, let him pray at the evening time; because then, the Angels of severe justice are appeased and rendered satisfied by such a prayer. The conclusion says, therefore: through the "secret of the pre-dawn prayer"—that is, prayer made before the light—we ought to understand the "property of piety"—that is, *Ghedulah*—which flourishes at such an hour. And thus the conclusion is clear.

->*KABBALISTIC TEACHING: Just as externally fear is lower than love, so internally it is superior to love.*<-

**FRIAR ARCHANGELUS.** The use of love and fear is necessary, as Augustine says most excellently: "Love and fear lead to every right action." <note>Original: "Ad omne rectè factum amor, & timor ducit."</note> Love for the kind promise and the thing promised, and fear of the punishing justice; these, like spurs, drive one toward every good work; or, like bread and wine, they refresh the mind of the worker. If, however, these two are disordered—and that which should not be loved is loved, and that which should not be feared is feared—they become spurs toward every evil, and a lethal food and drink. Hence Augustine adds a sentiment contrary to the first, saying: "Love and fear lead to every sin." <note>Original: "Ad omne peccatum amor, & timor ducit."</note> For just as the love and fear of God draws one to every good, so the love and fear of the World drives one to every evil.

### ARCHANGELO'S COMMENTARY

...drives out. From this, Augustine wishes to signify that there are two loves, and likewise two fears: namely, the filial and the servile. The first occurs when someone fears the commands of God, not out of a fear of punishment, but out of fear of a paternal offense—lest, specifically, His honor be diminished and God be rendered held in contempt—without regard for whatever punishment might befall them for such an offense. This is called "intrinsic fear," and it is more perfect because it presupposes love. For one does not fear because God is powerful, but because He is good. This is what is commonly said in the proverb: **The good fear [doing wrong] out of a love for virtue.** <note>Original: "Timent boni, uirtutis amore." A common medieval maxim derived from Horace.</note> The other is fear which is called "servile," when someone regards punishment as the end result, like a slave who fears to offend his master lest he be beaten. In this way, love is more perfect than fear.

But, because the author's purpose tends elsewhere, note that through these double fears and loves mentioned above, two dimensions or *Sephirot* <term>Sephirot: The ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite interacts with the universe.</term> are understood: *Gedulah* <note>Original: "ghedulah." The Sephirah representing Loving-kindness or Greatness.</note> of love, and *Gevurah* <note>Original: "ghebuhrah." The Sephirah representing Strength, Severity, or Judgment.</note> of fear. Two peoples are also understood: namely, the Hebrews and the Christians. For it was not fitting for the Jews to everywhere follow the mandate of loving Christ the Redeemer, who was not yet born in human form, nor was He fully known by them in all things. Instead, the servile fear of God was most suitable for them, the terrors of whose severity they saw in the plagues in Egypt. They also received the Law of the Decalogue in the desert with great terror, amid winds, thunders, lightning, portents of flames, the horrific sound of the trumpet, and the formidable voice of the Almighty. And whenever they committed some small transgression, they paid the penalty for their fault immediately, without any long-suffering, by the sword, by the earth swallowing them, by the burning of flames, by the bite of serpents, and by the punishment of the Father.

Therefore, the fear of the Jews, or of the Mosaic Law, was "extrinsic" and "servile," and consequently less perfect than love; it is the dimension of *Gevurah*, full of terror. But for the Apostle and the other followers of Christ—the Christians who saw Christ the Savior in the flesh—the mandate of love and all the ways of friendship were most fitting, as was "intrinsic" or "filial" fear, belonging to the *Gedulah* of love. Such fear is "Evangelical" <note>Referring to the Gospel (Evangelium).</note> because it is second to love, since it includes both love and fear. This signifies that the dimension of *Gedulah* (Mercy) is more perfect than *Gevurah* (Justice); for the mercy of *Gedulah* exalts itself above the justice of *Gevurah*. Because of this, the Evangelical Law is called the "Law of Love," while the Mosaic Law is called the "Law of Terror."

For Christ our author contains within Himself all the incitements and causes for us to be filled with friendship, and far more sublimely. Therefore, He is to be loved with the highest affection: because He is God, the propagator of the human race, to be loved as a parent. In the same way, He is also the firstborn Son of God, our neighbor and co-heir, and to be loved because through Him and in Him, eternal sweetness, glory, and the most pleasant joy of all are to be embraced. For as the Restorer of the blessed life, He is to be sought after. An immense love is urged by familiar companionship, and a love that is unheard of and known through clear experience—by which He did not shrink from so many inconveniences of life, from being spat upon, from lashes, and from the bitter punishments of death for us and our neighbors. 

Hence it is no wonder if the teachings of the Christian saints commemorate the mandates of love more frequently than those of fear. For this reason, Christ the Lord said to His own: **I will no longer call you servants, but friends.** <note>Original: "Iam non dicam uos seruos, sed amicos" (John 15:15).</note> To this is added that, since the Jewish people had formerly been driven into the vile and abject servitude of the Egyptians, and were defiled by their uncultivated and barbarian customs, there was a need for their education and for the preservation of the religion of true piety by a hard and rigid pedagogue, and a yoke of commandments proceeding from *Gevurah*. By this, their ignorance and untamed desire would be compelled rather by the dread of lashes than by a covenant of friendship. But the followers of Christ, already imbued with more refined manners and taught by Christ the best master through the spirit of wisdom and understanding, He taught to be educated and moderated not by any pedagogue, nor by any precept of servitude, but by the law of liberty and love proceeding from *Gedulah*. For...

...the spirit of slavery in fear, but the spirit of adoption as sons, in which we cry out "Abba, Father." <note>Original: "spiritum seruitutis in timore, sed spiritum adoptionis filiorum, in quo clamamus abba pater." A reference to Romans 8:15.</note> And Christ says: "Come to me all you who labor and are burdened," etc. <note>Matthew 11:28.</note> Therefore, the extrinsic fear belonging to the Mosaic Law is more imperfect than love—that is, more imperfect than the Law of the Gospel. However, the intrinsic fear, namely the filial fear of the Evangelical Law, is superior to love, because it presupposes love: for first, one loves; second, one fears. Another reason why fear is superior to love is because the Lord says in Isaiah: "To whom shall I look, if not to the one who is humble and meek and who trembles at my words?" <note>Isaiah 66:2.</note> For it is characteristic of all lords to seek reverence and fear from their subjects or subordinates. Fear also, according to the more "secret" theologians <note>A reference to practitioners of Kabbalah or mystical theology.</note>, belongs to the first measure of Divinity, which is the gate for entering the palace of the King. His name is placed before all others in the celebration of praises when it is said: "Lord, you will open my lips." <note>A standard opening for the Catholic Divine Office and Jewish prayer (Psalm 51:15).</note> In that place, the great four-letter name <term>Tetragrammaton: The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH (יהוה), considered too sacred to pronounce.</term>—יהוה—is not used, but rather this name of the "first measure" and the "gate." This name is pronounced as *Adonai* <note>original: "אדני"</note>, just like the other. Hence, the common translation confusedly uses one for the other. And because this measure, full of filial fear, is the entrance to God, it is said to be superior—not in dignity, but in service. In a Kabbalistic sense, it is also signified that *Gedulah* <term>Gedulah: The Sephirah of "Greatness" or "Mercy," often associated with Abraham.</term> (mercy) exceeds *Gevurah* <term>Gevurah: The Sephirah of "Strength" or "Judgment," associated with fear and rigor.</term> (justice), because the first includes intrinsic and filial fear, whereas the second includes only servile fear and love. And thus the conclusion is clear.

### BROTHER ARCHANGELO
Having heard these things which we said in the preceding conclusion, let us add a few points to the examination of fear. The wise man says: "Fear is a help to presumption, a betrayal of the aids of thought." <note>Wisdom of Solomon 17:11. In the context of the Bible, this refers to the psychological state of the wicked, but Archangelo is using it to pivot to the nature of fear itself.</note> Various names are attributed to fear by the Scriptures. Indeed, upon fear itself hangs the entire practice of piety and all the happiness of mortals. Therefore, note that a multifaceted condition precedes that affection which we call the "fear of God," which one may experience in any mortal. To this correspond the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: namely, **wisdom**, **understanding**, **counsel**, **fortitude**, **knowledge**, and **fear**. <note>The list follows Isaiah 11:2, standard in medieval theology.</note> For first, to every man—by a certain instinct of nature which we call **wisdom**—it becomes known that there is one thing in the scope of reality upon which all things depend. From this, the mind turns itself toward that which wisdom has conceived by the light of **understanding**; by this, it perceives that the Supreme Being is unbegotten, immortal, supremely good, wise, and omnipotent. Once this is known, the mind is immediately moved, and a certain desire for that very thing is raised up. By this, the mind is urged to revolve within itself (which we call **counsel**) whether by any Law it might be capable of attaining His pouring-forth goodness and the splendor of His wisdom. And when, by consulting, it gazes upon His immense bounty and the sweetness of His mercy, immediately a capacity to attain its wish arises (which we call **fortitude**), for it presumes that by no strength of its own can it become a partaker of its wish. But, when it subsequently turns its gaze downward through the cognition of moving and falling things (which we call **knowledge**) and considers its own unhappy lot—by which it is exiled in this blind and most foul prison, surrounded by the filth and stench of earthly things—the mind is soon tossed and fluctuates here and there into sloth and lethargy, destitute of all hope, presented with various arguments of distrust on one side and presumption on the other. This continues until the author of consolation and peace, the **fear of God**, arrives and places himself in the middle. Fear immediately settles every battle of thoughts and calms the turbulence of the mind; indeed, it beats back audacity by considering the immense greatness of that Supreme Good and its own despised, miserable smallness. It also eliminates the sluggishness and lethargy of distrust while it puts forward the unfailing bounty and mercy of the Supreme Good, and [provides] confidence...

...and he announces the confidence of aids against the insults of earthly things. While Moses, after he had led the flock of his senses to the interior of the desert, God rushed toward him: then he hid his face, for whatever had been thought out in him in a human way, he abandoned fear. <note>Original: "postquam sensuum gregem minasset ad interiora deserti ruit ei Deus." Referring to Genesis 15:12 regarding Abraham's vision.</note> And that saying of the most holy Job, who says: "Fear seized me, and trembling, and my bones were terrified: and when a spirit passed in my presence, the hair of my flesh stood up." <note>Job 4:14-15.</note> The splendor of Divine purity works all this: like a consuming fire, it allows nothing filthy, nothing defiled. Just as light does not allow darkness to be associated with it, so in that contact with Divinity, every profane thought of earthly things is immediately frightened away by fear and is consumed like straw in a whirlpool. From this (once the grain of earthly seed has been corrupted/destroyed), the soul is made more conformed to Divine purity: from the new and incorruptible seed of God, a new creature is brought forth.

When, therefore, Abraham was renewed like the [words] of God to him: "Walk before me, and be perfect": because God added the letter <term>He (ה): The fifth letter of the Hebrew alphabet, added to Abram's name to make him Abraham, signifying a new spiritual status.</term> to his name: and he was made a powerful man of generation. This renewal comes from the fear of God: because (as the Wise Man says) without fear no one can be justified. Therefore, the author's conclusion was brought forth deliberately and skillfully: that Abraham is praised in Genesis for fear—not an extrinsic fear from <term>Gheburah: The Kabbalistic attribute of Strength, Severity, or Judgment.</term>, but an intrinsic fear from <term>Ghedulah: The Kabbalistic attribute of Greatness or Mercy.</term>. Abraham, therefore, did all things through the property of piety, namely *Ghedulah*, including the offering of his son, etc. This love is the same as filial fear (as I have said). Saint Paul speaks of this to the Romans, saying: "For you have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear: but you have received the spirit of adoption of sons: in which we cry out: Abba, Father. For the spirit itself gives testimony to our spirit, that we are children of God. And if children, then heirs. Heirs indeed of God: but joint-heirs with Christ." <note>Romans 8:15-17.</note> And thus the conclusion is clear.

**BROTHER ARCHANGELUS:** Can a man accomplish anything through Music and song? Boethius and Cicero report that Pythagoras restrained a raging youth by changing the [musical] scales. And David drove the evil spirit from Saul with his lyre; for he who is entirely discordant cannot endure harmony. In his fall, the spirit of Saul lost all harmony which he ought to have had within himself, and with God, and with other creatures. Also, dances are led to the sound of some instrument because that delight of sound moves the mind and the strengths to dancing. So great is the power of proportionate harmony that it excites the minds and all senses to movements corresponding to the sound: just as soldiers and horses are excited by the clangor of trumpets. For nothing is moved toward the love or effect of anything except from the correspondence which it has with it: just as the strings of a lyre are moved by the touch of the string of another lyre proportioned to it. <note>A description of sympathetic resonance used as a metaphor for spiritual influence.</note> For motion is a certain act, from which local motion cannot proceed: it produces according to an alterative motion. Therefore, this consonance moves here, which is a certain natural power, feeling for a short time the nature of the substance: although it may work through some accident, just as fire burns, scorches, warms, and ignites by means of heat...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of "terror" or "fear" as it relates to God.
