# ON THE TEACHINGS OF THE KABBALISTS.

is a certain <term>accident</term><note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a property or quality (like color or heat) that exists within a "substance" (the thing itself) but is not the essence of that thing.</note>: yet its effect proceeds from the substance. And this happens by means of heat, which, even if it is proper to fire, is nevertheless an accident when it emanates outward. And just as terror in the Lord with respect to his subjects is something substantial implanted by God, yet as it emanates from the Lord into the subject, it is a certain accident. So also <term>consonance</term><note>Harmony or musical agreement.</note> in things is something innate in the nature and consubstantial to the thing; but in the fact that it reaches the perceiver through the air or a medium, it is a certain accident. Whence the effect proceeds from that substantial thing by means of the accident. For that consonance is so consubstantial to the thing that it is placed in its very definition. Just as Aristoxenus, defining the soul according to the mind of Plato, places "rational consonance" within it. For he says: *The soul is a number moving itself.* <note>Original Latin: "Anima est numerus seipsum mouens." This is a famous Pythagorean and Platonic definition of the soul often attributed to Xenocrates, here cited via Aristoxenus.</note> And such motion contributes to action: for every operation occurs through generative, corruptive, alterative, or local motion, as is said by the natural philosophers. Whence among other things contributing to health, Plato praises motion above all else. This we also prove in the earliest age of life: for to drive away crying, and to preserve or restore health, nurses are accustomed to move infants placed in cradles. This motion (as Plato says in the book he published *On the Laws*) drives away the dread that usually invades children, and restores proper tranquility. Whence motion contributes no small amount to every operation—unless the one operating is He who operates by will alone.

Those operating in just and lawful Magic use <term>characters</term><note>Sacred symbols, letters, or sigils believed to have spiritual efficacy.</note>; which can be done without any superstition. For Christ taught that works were to be done in his name. Which name cannot be expressed without letters, either spoken or written. These letters are certain characters. Paul also, in whose breast Christ resonated, says: *Whatever you do, whether in word or in work, do all in the name of Jesus.* The Cross is also a character with which we are accustomed to arm ourselves, as is in frequent use. The Priest in the ancient Law was also commanded to place the great name of God upon his forehead, written in its own characters thus: יהוה <note>The Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God (Yahweh), which the author notes was worn by the High Priest on a golden plate (Exodus 28:36).</note>, when he entered the holy places, as it says in Exodus. Therefore, not all characters are to be condemned: for there are holy characters, of which we have spoken. And these are like certain instruments in a Divine work, just as there are natural instruments in a natural work. There are also certain demonic characters invented by the Devil, so that, like an ape <note>A reference to the medieval idea of "Simia Dei"—the Devil as the "Ape of God" who mimics holy things to deceive.</note>, he might be worshipped through these characters. These truly are to be rejected, as the wise best know. 

And Hebrew characters are more excellent than others. Whence Orpheus, most skilled in operating, says: *Hebrew names are not to be changed in a work.* <note>Original: "non esse in opere immutāda Hebræa nomina." A common theme in Renaissance magic—that the specific sounds and shapes of Hebrew hold inherent power.</note> And he said this because their characters figure the images of the heavens. Which heavens are the instruments by which God acts with us. Also because they represent the seat of God and the properties of the super-mundane heavens, which are the primary fountains from which all things proceed. Described also in the Holy Law, they are in a certain way consecrated to God. Hence they are of greater efficacy, and are endowed with such virtue that in whatever way they are revolved <note>Permuted or rearranged, as in the Kabbalistic practice of *Temurah*.</note>, they always retain their meanings. To hint at these things by a marvelous order of nature or by God's command, some of them are impressed upon a certain herb when it is full of virtue, as the wisest men say. 

And now, he who wishes to operate must operate through the power or the Name which is above every name, and it is that at which every knee bows, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth. Which name Christ acquired for himself by the virtue of the cross, as Paul testifies. Just as Christ himself had protested, saying: *When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself*—namely, all powers and virtues of things, and of whatever names. Which Paul also affirms elsewhere, saying: *Because it pleased the Father that in him all fullness should dwell.* And again: *Spoiling principalities and powers, triumphing openly, he led them in himself.* And those who are to invoke a prince of this kind must be endowed with virtue. Whence Proclus teaches, saying: *Those who wish to take up prayer (in which, namely, the Divine name is invoked) must have knowledge, kinship, and union.* <note>The Neoplatonist Proclus argued that to reach the Divine, one needs "gnosis" (knowledge), "syngeneia" (affinity/kinship), and "henosis" (union).</note> For it is necessary that the invoker knows the one to be invoked, if he wishes to invoke him rightly. In which sense the Prophet sings: *I will protect him, because...*

...has known my name: for it is not said "because he invoked," but "he has known" [my name]. <note>This refers to Psalm 91:14: "I will deliver him, because he hath set his love upon me: I will set him on high, because he hath known my name."</note> Because of this, the Lord was angry against Moses and Aaron, and said: *You did not believe me, so as to sanctify me before the children of Israel: therefore you shall not lead this people into the land which I have given them.* <note>Numbers 20:12.</note> Seek a deeper origin for this matter: Moses did not lead the people into the promised land because, claiming for himself the miracle that he ought to have attributed to God, he said: *Can we bring forth water for you from this rock?* <note>Numbers 20:10. By saying "we," Moses was accused of taking credit for the divine act.</note> Also because He did not tell him to strike the rock, but to speak to it: yet he struck it. For there is a great difference between speaking and striking. For they were commanded to speak, so that they might obtain water through gentleness and piety, and by grace—water which proceeds from the <term>tribunal of grace</term><note>In Kabbalistic thought, God governs through different "tribunals" or Sephirot, such as Mercy/Grace (Chesed) or Justice/Judgment (Gevurah).</note>. But Moses struck the rock, as if extracting the water by force; for which reason God never works without some punishment. Hence the sentence was not passed against the people seeking water, but against Moses, who erred in his work. For those who err in their work commit an <term>unpardonable sin</term><note>Original Latin: *irremissibile*. In this context, it refers to a sin that must carry a physical penalty in this life (like not entering the Promised Land) even if the soul is forgiven.</note>—that is, one that cannot be released from its penalty.

Hence Moses, who was able to obtain all things from God for the sake of the people, was unable to obtain this: namely, that he should lead the people (as God had entrusted to him) into the promised land. Moses also erred because he struck the rock which (as the Apostle says) *was Christ* <note>1 Corinthians 10:4: "and the rock was Christ."</note>: for Christ offers water of His own accord and without being struck. Nor was that transgression small, considering the enduring nature of God’s work: for the striking hinted that God had intended to perform the miracle through piety, so that He might be more sanctified by the people, by commanding them to bring water out of the rock with a pious and sweet word, without striking. For the waters of mercy were not to be drawn through the harsh pipe of justice, as I have said. Therefore, after they wished to act with the people in an unjust manner (as they say), they deserved to feel the divine and iron justice mentioned above.

There are many secrets here concerning the rock, which in Hebrew is called <term>Eben</term> [אבנ]. In this word, two words are formed, namely *Ab* [אב] and *Ben* [בן]: the first of which signifies "Father," and the second "Son." <note>The Hebrew word for stone, *Eben* (Aleph-Bet-Nun), is seen by Christian Kabbalists as a combination of *Ab* (Aleph-Bet, Father) and *Ben* (Bet-Nun, Son).</note> To unravel all of these would be too long a discourse; therefore, etc. 

He who wishes to operate rightly, therefore, must possess knowledge of the powers [numina] assigned to the effects that are desired. It is necessary that he has a kinship and a <term>symbol</term><note>A "symbol" here acts as a spiritual resonance or link between the practitioner and the divine power.</note> with the one invoked, according to that saying of the Apostle: *No one can say "Lord Jesus," except in the Holy Spirit.* <note>1 Corinthians 12:3.</note> For this is required unless one tastes the nature and lot of the heavenly and spiritual man. Finally, it is required that he be united with the one invoked, who is the head—not only of some ecclesiastical body, but also of the world—since He is the bond of the whole world. For a member cannot act upon another member by the power of the head unless it is united with both. 

Therefore, from each of the holy names found in the Law—in which, wherever you find "waters," you will be able to draw the supernal waters of Divine gifts and wisdom—when you have drunk and known them, you will achieve the outcome of your virtue in every work. The foundation of the Law is to believe in His name: and if you walk in a straight path in your thoughts, your ways will be safe and your feet shall not stumble forever. For Ecclesiastes says: *Guard your foot as you enter the house of God* <note>Ecclesiastes 5:1.</note>; by which he taught that he who approaches to implore the Divine name should first examine himself, pay attention, and know the name and divine attributes suited to such a petition. 

Before all things, therefore, the meaning of the name must be known beforehand; for otherwise one would err in the work and be cheated of his desire. Not only would he fail to obtain what he hoped for, but he might fall into a contrary fate, just as happened to Moses at the <term>waters of contradiction</term><note>Also known as the Waters of Meribah.</note>. Moses, by invoking *Elohim* <note>A name of God associated with Justice and Judgment.</note> to a people who needed gentleness, perished (as I said above), because he ought to have invoked the name *El Shaddai* [שדי] <note>A name associated with Providence and sufficiency.</note> sent to them, by similar reasoning. The sons of Zebedee were justly rebuked by Christ when He said to them: *You do not know what you ask* <note>Matthew 20:22.</note>; because they did not know the end of their petition, whether it would be good or bad for them. Therefore, in those things which can be both good and bad, one must pray conditionally, because sometimes we pray for things in our prayers that result in our own prejudice. ### ON THE DOGMAS OF THE KABBALISTS.

...property, etc.) that is: (when we do not know the name appropriated to such an effect, or the <term>sephirah</term><note>A Sephirah (plural: Sephirot) is one of the ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite (Ein Sof) reveals itself and creates the universe.</note>: in such a case, one must have recourse to the house of the nose). The "House of the nose" is the spirit: regarding this we have in Genesis: *And he breathed into his nostrils the breath of life.* <note>Genesis 2:7.</note> And this spirit is called in Hebrew **neshamah** [נשמה]: that is, the "higher portion," according to **Augustine**: and it is a ray of the Divine spirit. For this reason, it is sometimes called the spirit of life, since it contains life within itself; it also strengthens, giving the power of working, according to that saying of the **Apostle**: *To be strengthened by his spirit.* <note>Ephesians 3:16.</note> And we read concerning **Samson** in the Book of Judges: *The spirit of the Lord rushed upon Samson, and he tore the lion to pieces.* <note>Judges 14:6.</note> For the spirit of man, which is called the rational soul, is a certain bond, binding the animal and coarser soul with the intellectual power, which is called the higher portion.

And this spirit is easily united with the higher mind and that Divine element which is in us. Hence, those who are made Divine are called "spiritual" in common and vulgar speech, because their study is to lead the body into the nature of the spirit as it presses toward the Divine; or because they study to be led back into God himself through the spirit of God. Therefore, when we do not know the dimension added to our petition, then we must have recourse to this spirit, the **neshamah**, which will obtain all things from God. And it is called "the nose," because it says in Genesis that He breathed it into the nostrils of Adam. And this spirit, which is called both the **neshamah** and the "higher portion," always prays for the best things, never sinning, but rather murmuring against sin and error. Without this spirit, we can neither understand God nor merit anything. And this is what **Paul** says: *it judges all things*: <note>1 Corinthians 2:15.</note> for it necessarily knows all things; therefore, one must have recourse to it. This **neshamah** is itself a certain power of the Holy Spirit illustrating all those who are purified, which **Plotinus** simply calls "the intellect." Concerning which **John** says: *You have an unction from the Holy One, and you know all things.* <note>1 John 2:20.</note> For the "unction" is the Holy Spirit, who also teaches. According to that word of **Christ**: *He will suggest all things to you, and will teach you all things.* <note>John 14:26.</note>

The Hebrews call this degree of the Holy Spirit familiar to us **hachma** [חכמה]: <note>original: "hachma". While the author likely means Chochmah (Wisdom), he defines it here as the "indwelling" or "inhabitation" of the Holy Spirit, which is more traditionally associated with the Shekhinah.</note> that is, the inhabitation of the Holy Spirit in us. **Paul**, being instructed in this manner of speaking, follows it, saying: *on account of the Holy Spirit indwelling in you.* <note>Romans 8:11.</note> Indeed, He is "holy" to the holy; but in others, He is the spirit of intelligence, carrying a ray of that light which illuminates everyone. Whence **Ambrose** wisely says: *Truth, by whomsoever it is spoken, is from the Holy Spirit.* Nor do I think this "universal agent intellect" that works in all things—by which our intellect, when illustrated, is called the "passible intellect" (that is, the light-receiving intellect)—is anything other than the **neshamah**, the higher portion, which descends from the Holy Spirit like a ray of Divinity from Him who illuminates us concerning all Divine things, to whom we must have recourse when we wish to act justly.

Whence the fathers of the primitive Church, by adhering to that spirit, performed so many wonders: so that **Peter** healed the sick by the mere shadow of his garments. On account of the lack of this, more recent followers of Christ, however distinguished by dignity, do not have the same power of performing wonders. Yet this gift can easily be recovered. Whence God says through **Ezekiel**: *In whatever hour a sinner shall have returned to me, I will no longer remember all his iniquities.* <note>Ezekiel 18:21–22.</note> It is true that the gift and grace of working well is restored to those truly converted in this way, though this is not a necessity for salvation; nor is it given immediately to the converted, but to those who are dead to themselves—that is, to the animal part—and live for Christ and God in the intellectual and rational part.

Hence there is a difference between the intellectual, the rational, and the animal man. For the **Theologians** and the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> say that there is a single soul in man, which is the principle of understanding, sensing, and moving according to place. But, if it is the same, how does one part perform a work to which the other does not pay attention? As **Plotinus** says, and as Holy Scripture testifies: namely, when **Lot** lay with his daughters; for then he generated according to the animal part, while his reason and intellect were not paying attention, as is held in the text. In the same way (as all confess), the animal portion of Christ...

...portion refused to drink the cup <note>A reference to Christ's agony in the garden, used here to illustrate the conflict between the lower soul and the rational will.</note>, but the rational portion willed it: just as [it is said], *He was offered, because he himself willed it.* <note>Isaiah 53:7 (Vulgate).</note> Indeed (as the Apostle says) there is an open [distinction] between the animal and spiritual man. ### KABBALISTIC DOGMA. Every good soul is a new soul, coming from...

FRIAR ARCHANGELUS. All philosophers have failed in defining what the soul is; nor is it a wonder, since knowledge of the soul (according to **Aristotle**) is profoundly difficult. As was written by **Plato** in the tenth book of the *Laws*, saying: What it is, and what power it has, almost everyone seems to have been ignorant of: therefore he refused to speak of it in common speech, following the more secret Theologians, who leave such arduous matters to their readers—whose footsteps he [Plato] undoubtedly followed. From him, therefore, this can be understood concerning the soul: that it is a certain divine substance emanating from divine fountains, according to number: not indeed that divine number by which the **Craftsman** <note>The Demiurge or Creator.</note> arranged all things, but a rational number: by which, having proportion with all things, it can [reach] all things. This was asserted by **Pythagoras**, the father of philosophers, saying in the *Golden Verses*: *Be confident, for a Divine race is in men.* <note>original: "Confide quia Diuinum genus hominibus inest."</note> And **Paul** in the Acts [of the Apostles] brings forward and approves the sentiment of **Aratus**, in which he says: *For we are his offspring.* <note>Acts 17:28; original: "Ipsius enim genus sumus."</note> See how clearly he concedes that the highest divine genus is in that part of the higher portion which the Platonists always venerated as divine. 

It is also a "number moving itself" (according to **Aristoxenus** and **Xenocrates**) because the soul itself is the principle of motion for the body (as **Aristotle** proves) and also for itself. From the doctrine of **Augustine**, the soul—meaning free will, or the will, which is the power of the soul itself—moves toward anything: for nothing is so much in the power of the will as the will itself. Which also, according to their opinion, can command the intellect to understand: and command itself not to will, carrying itself into anything. This motion, although it is not [local/physical] through a division into parts, is nevertheless a true change and motion; this is what they mean when they say the soul moves itself. And this motion also belongs to the Angels, according to **Job**: *Behold, those who serve him are not stable*—or *are not faithful in his angels; he placed change*—as the truth of the literal Hebrew has it; for which we read [in the Vulgate]: *he found wickedness.* <note>original: "reperit prauitatem." Archangelus is comparing the Latin Vulgate of Job 4:18 with a more literal reading of the Hebrew, suggesting the "wickedness" found in angels is actually their capacity for "change" or "instability" compared to God.</note> 

This change, although it does not happen through the division of part and part, is nonetheless a certain motion. It also moves the body, descending to the motion of the body: yet it is true motion, since it has the principle of motion in itself and is not moved by another. And the soul has "numbers" in itself, namely rational ones, that is: the species <note>The "species" or "forms" are the mental blueprints or archetypes of objects.</note> of things in itself, by which it understands them, and the numbers of things by which it counts them. These numbers and species are not merely adventitious and newly acquired, but are innate to the soul, existing in its being in a better way than they exist in the objects themselves. Just as all things agree in the "exemplars" or "ideas," they have a more perfect existence in the one producing and understanding them than in their own physical kind, as **John** says: *That which was made, in him was life.* <note>John 1:3-4. original: "Quod factum est, in ipso uita erat."</note> Life is both creative and divine, because nothing can be [true] life except the Divine. For the intellect could not perceive that it understands truth, unless it had something in itself to which that which it understands might conform. These things, however, are existing in act, but are hindered [by the body], as pleases **Plato** and the ancients; with whom [Augustine] agrees...

He reconciles Platonic and Aristotelian views with Christian scripture, specifically regarding the soul's distinction from the spirit and its divine origin.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary of Archangelus of Borgonovo. On the previous page, he began discussing the "Kabbalistic Dogma" that every good soul is a "new soul," contrasting philosophical views of the soul's nature with mystical interpretations of its origin and quality.</meta>

<page-num>847</page-num>
<header>ON KABBALISTIC DOGMAS. 847</header>

Aristotle says: *The soul is in a way all things* <note>original: "Anima est quodammodo omnia." A famous Aristotelian dictum from *De Anima*, meaning the soul can perceive and understand all things.</note>: because it contains all things in the order of understanding, or possesses a proportion with all things. And this is that rational harmony of which we speak, together with Pythagoras and the Platonists. Nevertheless, the soul falls far short of the first and supreme intellect, which understands all things simultaneously. Our soul does not understand all things in a single, actual act of intellection as the First Intellect does, but through many successive acts. The soul is therefore a certain intellectual thing, containing all things in a certain arrangement <note>original: "concinnio," a harmonious fitting together.</note>, so that it is able to understand all things that are to be understood by it. Therefore, all the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note> said that all souls were produced, and are produced, at equal levels. Their foundation for this is the saying of Aristotle: *Species are like numbers* <note>original: "Species se habent sicut numeri."</note>: in which, if one part is varied, the species is changed. For if a unit is added to the number three, the species changes and becomes the number four. 

However, more recent theologians say that souls differ not only in accidental qualities, but in intrinsic degrees rooted in their very essence. By these degrees, each individual thing is distinct from another through that which is proper to itself; for everything is distinguished first by its own nature—which is what it is—before it is distinguished by its principle of operation, or by its work, or by any accident. This is supported by that passage from the Book of Wisdom: *I was a witty child, and had received a good soul* <note>Wisdom of Solomon 8:19. The author argues this implies some souls are naturally "better" than others from the start.</note>—namely, a better one than many others. And this same point is confirmed by Christ in the distribution of the talents: to one he gave five, to another three, etc., to each according to his own proper virtue. This virtue is a certain natural power, determined by a specific degree, according to which a person is capable of their duty and receives it. 

The argument regarding numbers does not stand in the way, since the infallible Gospel and infallible Truth do not lie. For God created the entire mass of all souls at once from the beginning, as is evident in the first chapter of Genesis where it says: *that God created all things together for the making* <note>A Latin interpretation of Genesis 2:3, "creavit ut faceret."</note>; because, as the Kabbalists say, He creates nothing entirely new. God, therefore, creates no soul as a new creation <term>ex nihilo</term>, but He infuses it into a body anew. It is called "new" then because it informs the body for the first time; and it is called "good" because just as a mass of gold always contains some dross within it, so in that total mass of souls there is a similar dross and impurity, according to some Kabbalists. Therefore, the soul that is taken from the pure part of the total mass is good; but that which is mixed in part with the dross is bad. 

And if it is objected using that passage from Genesis: *God saw all that he had made, and they were very good*, we say that as a rule, absolutely everything God *made* is good, but not everything He *created*. For "making" pertains to the good, while "creating" pertains to the bad. Whence Isaiah says: *I am he making good, and creating evil; making light, and creating darkness* <note>Isaiah 45:7.</note>. This is understood as follows: since "to create" is to make from nothing and terminates in a subject or matter (which has the character of "evil" in the sense of lack or potentiality), it is therefore called "creating evil." And since "to make" terminates in a form (which has the character of "good"), it is therefore called "making good." Thus, whatever things decline toward matter have the character of evil, and those which approach more closely to the highest form have the character of good. Therefore, that soul which is created more from the thicker part [of the mass] is called bad, while that from the purer part is truly called good. 

And such a good soul comes from the East <note>In Kabbalah, the "East" is associated with the Sefirah of Chokmah (Wisdom).</note>. For as soon as it was created from **Chokmah** <term>Chokmah</term><note>Wisdom; the second Sefirah.</note>—the East—and placed in **Binah** <term>Binah</term><note>Understanding; the third Sefirah.</note> (intelligence), it entered into **Tipheret** <term>Tipheret</term><note>Beauty or Glory; the central Sefirah of the emotional attributes.</note>, not passing through **Gevurah** <term>Gevurah</term><note>Strength or Severity; the Sefirah of judgment and fire.</note>. This is because it contains no imperfection within itself that needs to be purged by Gevurah. Those who are "bad," however, make their journey through Gevurah, so that they may be made pure from that dross by its fire. And thus the conclusion is clear according to the Kabbalists.

Therefore Joseph was buried only in his bones, and not in his body: because his bones were the virtues and the armies of the higher tree, called **Zaddik** <term>Zaddik</term><note>The Righteous One; associated with the Sefirah Yesod (Foundation), which funnels divine influence to the world.</note>, flowing down to the higher land.*

<meta>This page continues the commentary of Archangelus of Borgonovo, moving from a general discussion of the soul's nature to a specific Kabbalistic analysis of the Patriarchs as "wheels" of the divine chariot, focusing specifically on Joseph as the archetype of the "Foundation."</meta>

<page-num>848</page-num>
<header>COMMENTARY OF ARCHANGELUS.</header>

...is. For before the building of the Temple and the giving of the Law, God had made His glory <note>original: "gloriam," often referring to the *Shekhinah* or Divine Presence.</note>—or rather His Holy Spirit—to dwell upon the four wheels that carried the chariot of glory. These wheels were certain "feet" sustaining God. These were the four principal fathers, namely: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph (about whom I speak in their own treatise). Leaving the first three aside, I shall speak only of the fourth, who claimed for himself a place in the archetype of <term>Yesod</term> <note>The ninth Sephirah in the Kabbalistic Tree of Life, meaning "Foundation." It is associated with the procreative force and the channeling of divine influx to the world.</note>, or the foundation of the entire divine influx. 

Therefore, when Scripture describes Jacob, it begins with Joseph, because he was the "Foundation of the World" <note>original: "fundamentum Mundi," a reference to the Hebrew concept *Zadik Yesod Olam*—the Righteous is the Foundation of the World.</note> and the shepherd of that family. He was a shepherd, I say, not only of physical nourishment in Egypt, but one providing living water and spiritual sustenance, of which his appointment in Egypt was a symbolic figure. For Joseph originated from that place where the "living water" is found.

And the *Zohar* <note>The foundational work of Jewish mysticism.</note> says: Joseph was the firstborn of Jacob, for he was the firstborn of Rachel, who was preferred above all other women. It was for her that Jacob served, and to her he had dedicated his heart even when he lay with Leah. Hence, according to Jacob's own intent, the firstborn of Rachel was his true firstborn. 

Furthermore (as the *Zohar* says), Joseph was the bond between the Sun and the supramundane Moon <note>In Kabbalah, the "Sun" often represents the Sephirah *Tiferet* (associated with Jacob) and the "Moon" represents *Malkhut* or the *Shekhinah*. Joseph (*Yesod*) acts as the bridge or "bond" between them.</note>, from which the lower generations proceed. For this reason, the image of Joseph (as the *Zohar* states) reflected the image of Jacob perfectly. Therefore, the text says: *Jacob loved Joseph*—specifically because of this likeness, for among those who share a likeness, the transition of affection is easy. He also possessed a character more closely aligned with his father than did the other sons. 

Just as Joseph drew nourishment for himself and his family, so too did he draw the nourishment of the spirit and of a better life. He also drew the power of generation and multiplication. For this reason, he himself possessed two tribes; the one called Ephraim, in particular, grew exceedingly. Thus, it was not without cause that his mother called him Joseph, which means "addition" or "increase." 

Wherefore in Genesis, he is called a *fruitful bough* <note>original: "filius crescens," referring to the Hebrew *Ben Porat* from Genesis 49:22.</note> and beautiful in appearance, because he was increased into two tribes: Manasseh and Ephraim (as I have said). One of these took the place of the Levite tribe, which was occupied with the performance of sacred rites and dispersed among all the tribes. He was also the "proof" of the Israelite family: in all things, he acquired success in the active life, because he grew quickly and greatly in dignity and honor in Egypt. 

He was "fair of appearance," bearing more than the others (as I said) the likeness of his father and his mother, the most beautiful Rachel. Indeed, he was endowed with such great beauty that if any women were to climb the roofs of houses or the walls (as one reads in Deuteronomy <note>This may refer to a traditional midrashic interpretation rather than a direct verse in Deuteronomy.</note>) to look down, they would see that most beautiful youth passing by. Regarding this, Jacob said: *The daughters run along the wall.* The literal truth of the text says <term>Ben Porat</term> <note>Hebrew: "A fruitful son."</note>, that is, a "beautiful son," because he was beautiful in body, but even more beautiful in mind. He is also called *porat*, meaning "one who increases," experiencing both types of growth: the temporal and the spiritual. 

All these things happened to him as a result of his imprisonment and his being sold—events he bore with equanimity—and his constancy as a man against the woman who tried to soothe and entice him. He triumphed over Egypt, which symbolizes the "lower vessel" <note>original: "craterem inferiorem." In Neoplatonic and Kabbalistic thought, this refers to the material world or the lower dimensions of the soul.</note>. Although Egypt is irrigated by a river proceeding from the garden of pleasure, it is suggested that Joseph himself triumphed over all lower things and whatever good that "vessel" received from on high. 

For the ring was his seal, by which he could authorize all his edicts. The linen robe was a royal garment; the gold chain was a sign of his presidency; the chariot denoted the tribunal of his empire; and the herald cried out that all should bow their knees to him as an execution of his lordship. 

Hence, Joseph himself was sold twice: first to the Ishmaelites, and second to Potiphar, the eunuch of Pharaoh. This occurred so that he might more fully experience the rule sung by David: *According to the multitude of my sorrows, your consolations have gladdened my soul.* <note>Psalm 94:19.</note> For God does not desert His friends in the night of tribulation. For of the Holy Spirit—or the Divine Presence, which the Hebrews call the <term>Shekhinah</term> <note>OCR: "fachinam." Archangelus uses this term to refer to the *Shekhinah*, the indwelling presence of God.</note>—it is written: *She rose in the night and gave prey to her household.* So it was for Joseph in the night and tribulation of Egypt.

<meta>This page continues the Kabbalistic interpretation of the life of Joseph, specifically examining how his experiences in Egypt and the blessings he received from Jacob serve as archetypes for both the Messiah and the structure of the divine emanations.</meta>

# ON THE DOGMAS OF THE KABBALISTS.

...to him: God marvelously came to his aid, snatching the prey from the hands of the Egyptians, even though the Egyptians were not even accustomed to eating with the Hebrews. Joseph’s double presidency also corresponds to his double sale: one over the Egyptians, because he was sold into Egypt; the other over his brothers, because he was sold by his brothers. In this same way, Christ was sold by the Jews and yet was called their King. Nor does it seem a marvel that the aforementioned things happened to Joseph, since even the Sun, Moon, and stars adored him. For the righteous are called stars, as Daniel says: *The righteous shall shine like the stars.* <note>Daniel 12:3</note> Paul supports this, saying: *As star differs from star in brightness, so does saint from saint in glory.* <note>1 Corinthians 15:41</note> For then that which was written was verified: the Sun (that is, Jacob, who has his tabernacle in the Sun, where Christ also dwells) was obscured (because he did not know of this) and the stars (that is, his sons) gave no light (because they did not understand a dream of this kind). 

Because of this, Jacob said: *Let these blessings be on the head of Joseph, and on the crown of the Nazirite <note>original: "Nazaræi." In the Latin Vulgate of Genesis 49:26, this refers to Joseph being "set apart" or "consecrated" from his brothers, though the author here likely alludes to the connection with Jesus the Nazarene.</note> among his brothers,* because the eleven stars had to adore Joseph (as I have said). And this was not only because of his presidency over Egypt (since Scripture always seeks higher meanings than the "killing letter" of the literal text presents), but because the <term>Keneset</term> <note>original: "chenezet," from the Hebrew *Keneset Yisrael*, the Assembly or Community of Israel, often identified in Kabbalah with the Shekhinah.</note>—that is, the Synagogue of Israel—was gathered out of the twelve tribes through a most high mystery. This was done by removing Levi, who was already dedicated to the priesthood and dispersed among his brothers, and also by removing Joseph, according to another most profound sacrament. In their place, Manasseh and Ephraim were substituted. 

Hence, while that whole family had its seat and root in the place which the Hebrews call the "Kingdom" <note>The Sephirah *Malkhut*.</note>—but which Christ calls the "Kingdom of Heaven"—and which is also called by another name, the "Sea" or the "Pool" where the super-mundane waters are gathered: Joseph had his root in a higher place, where the Fountain of Life is, from which waters of this kind flow. Concerning this fountain, the Prophet sings: *For with thee is the fountain of life.* <note>Psalm 36:9</note> Therefore, just as the waters of various streams are united in a fountain as if in a head, so Jacob commands the brothers to be united in Joseph as their fountain and head. 

For this reason, Joseph was endowed with many blessings in Genesis. The first is of the heavens above, with which his father Jacob was also blessed in the dew of heaven. The second is of the abyss—namely, of the earth or of lower things—so that nothing might prevail against him. The third is of the breasts and the womb—namely, carnal offspring. Or "of the breasts" about which it is sung in the Canticles: *I will give thee my breasts.* <note>Song of Solomon 7:12. The author links this to the milk of prophecy.</note> These breasts (as I have said elsewhere) provided milk to the Prophets. And <term>Rachem</term> <note>Hebrew: רחם</note>—that is, of "piety"—and not "of the womb." For *Rachem* signifies both; for there is no greater piety and love than a mother’s heart toward those who come forth from her womb. Hence, Zechariah swore by this, saying: *Through the bowels of mercy* <note>Luke 1:78</note>—that is, of the piety or love of our God, by which He shall visit us. 

The fourth blessing was that which Jacob received from Isaac. The fifth was because he was blessed with the blessings of his fathers, namely Isaac and Abraham, who (as was said above) became blessing itself. Hence Jacob said: *The blessings of your father have been strengthened by the blessings of his fathers.* And (to conclude with the *Zohar*) through that word *et* <note>The Hebrew particle את (*et*), consisting of the first and last letters of the alphabet, Aleph and Tav.</note> placed before *Shaddai* <note>Hebrew: שדי (Almighty)</note>—not out of any grammatical necessity—the entire influx of celestial things is hinted at, which Jacob prayed for upon Joseph; for there is the first and last letter of the alphabet. 

And Jacob, blessing Joseph, said: *Until the desire of the everlasting hills shall come.* The high mountains are those of which the Prophet sings: *The high mountains are for the deer.* <note>Psalm 104:18</note> These mountains, at the coming of the Messiah (as Joel witnesses), dripped sweetness, and milk and honey flowed; and (according to the oracle of Habakkuk) they were bowed down when (as John says) *the Word was made flesh.* By this bowing down (as David sings), the hills themselves were girded with exultation. The desire of such hills is to perfect man by uniting him with God. This will be in the Fatherland <note>Heaven.</note>. Therefore Jacob said: *May you be filled with these blessings until the desire of the hills comes*—that is, the virtues or the places of Him of whom the Apostle says: *God wills all men to be saved.* For it was for this purpose that God Himself created man. And as a sign of these things, his father Jacob made for Joseph a *tunica polymita*—that is, a multicolored coat—as a testimony of the many virtues with which Jacob had decorated him.

### COMMENTARY OF ARCHANGELUS.

[Joseph, whom Jacob] loved more than his other brothers. From this, he also gave him a portion beyond his brothers, [which] he took from the hand of the Amorite <note>original: "Amorrhęi"</note> with his sword and his bow. Also because he himself drew [water] from various fountains: just as his father did, namely for himself, for his brothers, and for the whole family. Therefore, primarily and principally: he did not leave him just any [field] (as it is said) which his father was accustomed to possess while he lived there; nor did Joseph, being the prefect of such a great kingdom, have need of such a small estate. Since he had already handed over the region and food to his brothers, the estate was therefore [given to Joseph] alone; next to which (not without a mystery) Jesus came with the Samaritan woman. Indeed, Jacob acquired this estate with the bow and sword of virtue, [with divine aid] provided. For the place is above-worldly <term>supramundanus: a philosophical term for the divine or celestial realm that exists beyond the physical world</term> with God: which [no] man [can take away]. According to that saying: *Store up for yourselves treasures in heaven.* <note>Matthew 6:20</note> [This] can be given to heirs. Just as Abraham gave all that he possessed to Isaac, Christ, however, acquired the fullness of estates: of which (as John testifies) we have all received. And in that same little field, or estate, Joseph was buried, which his father gave to him in Shechem <note>original: "Sichem"</note>: for just as his fathers had chosen for their burial that cave which was in Hebron, for reasons and mysteries assigned elsewhere, Joseph chose for his tomb that estate situated in the land of Shechem. For to those nations was given the covenant of circumcision: as we read in Genesis 34. For the [execution] of that covenant pertained most especially to him: whose origin (as the Theologians teach) is from the same place where the covenant itself comes. Hence, not without [great mystery], the Father, full of the Holy Spirit, handed over that place to Joseph with such [solemnity] as a peculiar gift, when he assigned to each of his sons their own heavenly [allotment]; just as those Fathers had chosen that cave [as] a place subject to that fountain: to which he intended to ascend (for which reason David chose the fortress of Zion as a place suitable and fit for himself), so [Joseph] chose that estate. For the suitability of place, sacrifice, and [prayer] contributes most greatly to the performing of sacred rites. Concerning the place, it is clearly evident [that God] has chosen certain locations: into which he pours particular influences: as not [only tradition] most constantly asserts, but as we also have clearly [proven] from the sacred utterances. For when Jacob had seen the Angels ascending and descending, waking from sleep, he said: *Truly the Lord is in this holy place: this is none other than the house of God and the gate of heaven.* <note>Genesis 28:16-17</note> Therefore, not without reason did Abraham buy from the sons [of Heth] the double cave (as I said), nor did David without cause buy the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite: where Isaac had previously been bound, and later the temple was built, according to [the direction given to] David himself, who was taught the mystery of the place by the Holy Spirit. Hence, if anyone were to know the correspondence of the lower places with the heavenly ones, he would know the influence of each tribe and family; for no place of that land is described [in the] distributions which does not represent some place of the [celestial] region, or [some] influence which it receives from there; nor is a boundary assigned here below which does not represent some boundary of the above-worldly house: concerning which [mysteries] much must be said in detail. Nevertheless, there are many places which God chose [as His] habitation: the first is Bethel, which was previously called Luz <note>original: "Luza"</note>; the second is Hebron, and most especially that double cave, bought by Abraham specifically for the burial of his wife, himself, and the chosen sons, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph. Another place is Jerusalem, which God chose to bring salvation to the human race. Some wish [to say] the fourth gate of heaven is in [this place]. From which it is clear that God chose certain peculiar places: thus also Michael [chose] Mount Gargano <note>Monte Sant'Angelo, a famous sanctuary in Italy dedicated to the Archangel Michael.</note>; and the Mother of Graces [chose] very many places, most especially Loreto <note>original: "Lauretum"; refers to the Basilica della Santa Casa, the "Holy House" of the Virgin Mary.</note>; [these] contribute to the prosecution of the work. Hence there is a maxim of the legal scholars: *place and time walk at the same pace.* Just as time contributes [to an action] (as I said above), so also does place contribute. Hence Christ cited that passage of Isaiah: *My house shall be called a house of prayer.* And if one place did not benefit more than another, God would not have commanded Abraham to go out from his land and kindred, and [go] to another...

# ON THE KABBALISTIC DOCTRINES. 851

[God commanded Abraham] to go to the place he would show him. Likewise, Isaac brought his wife Rebecca into the tent of his mother. It is not without reason that Plato praises the change of location for the benefit of both mind and body: because (as the wise know) different spirits dwell in different places. Some of these spirits favor certain people, while others do the opposite. Therefore, finding a suitable nation and place is most useful. Every detail mentioned in Scripture—such as the burial place of Moses and the bones of Joseph—shows that a great mystery <note>original: "sacramentum"</note> lies hidden within them.

Thus, when Joseph was dying, he made his brothers swear an oath: that when they were liberated from that Egyptian captivity, they would carry his bones with them and bury them in the tomb located in Shechem <note>original: "Sichen"</note>; this is recorded as having been done in the Book of Joshua. And so, a mystery is touched upon here, as I said above, regarding the favor of specific places. In confirmation of this, the Hebrews say that the gift of prophecy is granted only in Jerusalem and nowhere else. Even if Daniel prophesied in Babylon, this was because of the river Chebar <note>original: "chobar"</note> and the Euphrates, which flows out of the Paradise of Delight and carries such a spiritual influx with it. Therefore, it is said that the prophet stood by the river Chebar. 

By a similar logic, a spiritual influx matching Joseph’s nature flowed into Shechem from the celestial realms. In order for Joseph to reach that influx, he commanded his bones to be brought there, so that through that influx he might obtain greater grace with God. For the holy ones are not at their final destination (according to the Kabbalists) until the final day, as is clear from the fourth chapter of Proverbs: *The paths of the righteous grow until the perfect day.* 

Jacob therefore left this place to Joseph himself—that is, the influx of the "higher measure" corresponding to that place, which is called **Yesod** <term>Yesod: a Hebrew word meaning "Foundation," representing the ninth Sephirah or divine attribute in Kabbalah, often associated with the sexual organs and the flow of divine energy</term> and **Zaddik** <term>Zaddik: "The Righteous One," a title given to those who maintain spiritual purity, often identified with Joseph</term>. Therefore, Joseph had his roots in Yesod, the fountain of life.

And so, when Joseph was wandering, he was found by "a man"—that is (as the wise assert), by the Angel Gabriel. This same Angel is also called "a man" in the Book of Daniel, which is not without foundation or mystery. For of all the seven Angels standing before the divine tribunal, he is the closest to us and most familiar to mankind. Hence, he was sent to Zechariah and to Mary to report divine secrets. He was also sent to Daniel to reveal the visions and dreams of Nebuchadnezzar. For this reason, he was sent to Joseph—he whose name means "the strength of God"—to strengthen <note>Archangelus plays on the name Gabriel, derived from the Hebrew "Gebra" meaning strength</note> Joseph himself, who was destined to suffer and achieve so much. Gabriel taught him to interpret the dreams of Pharaoh and of those who were held in prison, as he saw fit. 

For the interpretation of dreams is the specific province of Gabriel, who presides over the Moon—under whose governance mortals dream. Because of this favor shown by Gabriel to Joseph, Joseph was raised to such great dignity that he was made prefect over all of Egypt. This was because God disposed it so, according to the words of the prophet: *I have exalted one chosen from my people.* <note>Psalm 89:19</note> There was another reason: because he kept the covenant <note>original: "pactum"</note> of the Lord, refusing to consent to the errors of his brothers (for he even accused them to his father); and when requested by the wife of Potiphar <note>original: "Phutipharis"</note>, he would by no means consent to adultery. 

Hence, it is not without a great mystery that he was named "the Righteous" <note>Zaddik</note>. For from the same source, both "the covenant" and "the righteous" proceed. For whatever belongs to justice is found written in the observation of the legal covenant in the heart of every person (as the Apostle says). From the observation of this legal covenant, one does not only obtain the name of "the righteous," but also peace, life, and perfect exaltation, as the Prophet sings: *How very precious are your friends to me, O God; how greatly their princedom is strengthened.* <note>Psalm 139:17</note> 

For while the whole family of Jacob had their faith and root in the place which the Hebrews call the Kingdom <note>original: "Regnum"</note>—but the Kabbalists call **Malchut** and Christ calls the **Kingdom of Heaven** (which is also called by another name, the "Sea" or the "Pool" where the super-mundane waters are gathered)—Joseph, however, had his root in the higher place called **Yesod**. There is the living fountain from which such waters first emanate. Just as the waters of different streams are united in a fountain as if in a head, so Jacob commanded the brothers to be united in Joseph, the fountain and head. Therefore, Joseph chose Shechem as a place of influxes, receiving from the fountain of Yesod itself.

The conclusion therefore says: Joseph was buried there only as bones, and not as a body—specifically in Shechem—because the form of the human body had been dissolved, with only the bones re-

# THE COMMENTARY OF ARCHANGELUS. 852

[...the tribes] remaining, when they carried him from Egypt into Shechem <note>original: "Sichen"</note> (because in him were virtues). For there are as many master and primary bones in the human body as there are affirmative precepts <note>Positive commandments, or things one "must do."</note>, namely two hundred and forty-eight. These represent so many virtues of the "better man" <note>The spiritual or perfected person.</note> to be perfected through those precepts; for every virtue is perfected through the precept corresponding to it, as is taught in sacred Theology. These precepts are also observed by the powers of the body. To Abraham—after a name was given to him by God containing, through numbers, two hundred and forty-eight <note>The Hebrew name Abraham (אברהם) sums to 248 in gematria, signifying his spiritual perfection.</note>—it was said: *Walk before me, and be perfect.* This means: "I have given you the powers by which you will be able to fulfill all the affirmative precepts," which indeed he did. Whence God said: *Abraham kept my precepts and my mandates, and my statutes, and he observed the whole Law.* God also handed down three hundred and sixty-five negative precepts <note>Prohibitions, or things one "must not do."</note>, which is the same number of nerves and ligaments in the human body, as has been proven by the most skilled anatomists. This was done so that, just as the bones of the human body are bound by ligaments, so too might the powers of the "better man" be bound together by these same ligaments, lest they leave their proper places and the whole man be disturbed, and the Spirit of God be impeded. For the Spirit does not enter except into a body in which the bones have come together, each one to its joint, just as we are taught by the oracle of Ezekiel. Therefore, so that God might perfect the whole man, both in his powers and his bindings, He gave the Law <note>original: "praeceptum"</note> in those equal numbers. Following this, the Savior said: *I have made the whole man whole.* For nothing was commanded in the Law or in the Gospel except for our benefit. All these things were granted to Joseph. And it is denoted that Joseph himself observed the aforementioned affirmative precepts and guarded himself from the transgression of the negative ones. Because of this, he was deservedly called "the Just" <note>original: "iustus"</note>, and <term>Yesod</term> <note>Foundation: the ninth Sephirah in the Kabbalistic Tree of Life, associated with Joseph.</note> (and of the higher "better man" called <term>Zadic</term> <note>Tzaddik: The Righteous One.</note>): that is, the power of influencing the aforementioned virtues signified by the bones and nerves of the human body, in the place called Yesod, or Zadic, or the Just. And that measure is called the "justifying just." And it is the "just" who is called the "foundation of the world," both of the archetypal world and the lower one. Since, therefore, Joseph was just and God-fearing, as is clear from what was said above—and just as Yesod flows into the higher land, that is, into the dimension of <term>Malchut</term> <note>Kingdom: the tenth Sephirah, representing the physical manifest world.</note> favoring all the other tribes—so Joseph favored all his brothers, providing them with the bread of life.

->KABBALISTIC DOGMA. *Therefore no one knows the tomb of Moses: because he was exalted in the higher jubilee, and above the jubilee he sent forth his roots.*<-

**FRIAR ARCHANGELUS.** In the last part of Exodus, it is held that God showed Moses the promised land. On Mount Nebo, in a prophetic spirit, God showed him the promised land; for *Nebo* <note>נבא</note> is interpreted as *Nebua* <note>נבואה</note>, meaning "prophecy." Therefore, he saw that land in spirit; he could not discern such a vast region with bodily vision, nor could he enter it physically, as the irrevocable sentence stood against him following the error committed in the striking of the rock. That error was an unpardonable sin, even against the Holy Spirit; yet Moses himself was not rejected because of it, even if his error was to be punished without any cleansing. Hence he could not obtain pardon in this matter, he who had appeased God for the crime of idolatry of the entire people. On account of that sin, he died on the summit of Mount Nebo. From this we understand that he died in body, but not in spirit; for his prophecy flourished even after death. He was buried, however, in the valley. Some of the Hebrews believe that Moses buried himself so that, having entered a narrow cave, he breathed out his spirit there. Others believe that God buried him, but by the hand of Angels, as is held in the apocryphal books. From these, Jude the Apostle seems to have spoken in his Epistle, where he writes that Michael the Archangel disputed with the Devil over the body of Moses. The Devil, no doubt, did not want the body to be hidden, lest the Hebrews be provoked to idolatry by worshipping him whom they knew to be nearly divine. Or perhaps his body was transmuted into a spiritual form; hence such a body cannot be seen by physical eyes, except at the will of those who enjoy it. Or perhaps his body was translated into heaven, just as the body of Enoch was.

# ON THE DOGMAS OF THE CABALISTS.

## THE COMMENTARY OF ARCHANGELUS. 853

...of Elijah <note>original: "Heliae"</note>. This was fitting, since it is written of Moses: *And there has not arisen a prophet since in Israel like Moses.* <note>Deuteronomy 34:10</note> Michael acted in this way for another reason: for just as Michael is appointed as the prince over the receiving of souls, so also the Devil—who in this context is called <term>Hazazel</term> <note>Azazel, often associated with the scapegoat and the demonic forces of the wilderness.</note>—has power over the flesh and corpses. Hence, just as a perpetual war is declared between the spirit and the flesh, so it is also between Michael and the Devil. Therefore, in a man's death, by common Law, Michael claims the soul for himself (as was shown above), but the Devil claims the body. For this reason, once the soul is separated from the body, the Devil surrounds it like an enemy, striking terror and horror into those standing by. 

However, since the body of Moses had been purified by God (so that the glory of God might be reflected back into his face and his flesh) and had been transformed into a spiritual lot, Michael, claiming the body itself along with the soul, was unwilling to yield it to the Devil. From this arose the dispute, but the victory belonged to Michael himself. There is another reason: for the "dragon" <note>The Devil</note> seeks to prioritize the sensitive part of man, which is domestic and friendly to him. Conversely, Michael intends to prioritize the spirit, so that the flesh and the "animal man" <note>The person driven by base instincts rather than spirit.</note> might be reduced to servitude. The Devil also seeks to subject the spirit to the flesh so that he may possess both. On the contrary, Michael strives to transmute the body into a spiritual nature, or into spirit itself, so that he may finally return it to God together with the soul. And this was the dispute between Michael and the Devil concerning the body of Moses, which Thaddeus <note>A reference to the Epistle of Jude 1:9 in the New Testament, where Michael disputes with the devil over Moses' body; the author attributes this to Thaddeus/Jude.</note> relates.

Moses was therefore buried not "in a valley" (as the common edition <note>The Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> has it) but in <term>gai</term> גיא. This word has two letters: one of which, <term>iod</term> י, yields ten; the other, <term>gimel</term> ג, yields three in number <note>The author is using Gematria, a Jewish system of assigning numerical values to letters. 10 + 3 = 13.</note>. From this it is hinted that his body was buried in the "thirteen-fold measures" of God's piety and mercy. Moses himself brought these forth when God showed him His glory while he stood in the hollow of the rock, showing him every good thing—namely, how He does all things well and with great mercy, although it very often seems the opposite to human judgment. That body was buried in those measures of piety by which it was transformed into a spiritual lot—the same lot which we ought to receive at the resurrection. 

Hence it is written that *no man has known his sepulcher unto this day* <note>Deuteronomy 34:6</note>; because no one was as pious as Moses, who had been influenced by those thirteen measures of mercy. For it is said of him that *he was the meekest of men above all others.* And no other could acquire the aforementioned thirteen measures of piety as he did; for he reached the forty-ninth gate of understanding, <term>Binah</term> <note>In Cabalistic thought, there are 50 Gates of Understanding; the 50th is generally considered inaccessible to mortals.</note>, which was granted to no one else. Joshua, however, investigated the Law through one gate less—namely through forty-eight. After the death of Moses, one gate was hidden from Joshua, and forty-eight gates remained. Even Solomon labored over that gate to bring it back, but he was not powerful enough.

Rabbi Akiba says, and the Cabalists say, that Solomon's wisdom was two degrees lower than the wisdom of Moses. Therefore, it is written in Deuteronomy 34: *There has not arisen a prophet since in Israel like Moses.* No one, therefore, could find his grave; that is, no one could reach as far as the forty-ninth gate of <term>Binah</term>. And this is what God said to Moses himself: *You shall not see my face, but my back.* For the "face" of God is manifold, and so is His "back." There is a "face of essence" which (as the ancient theologians assert) no one can see—according to the word of John: *No one has ever seen God*—even in the Fatherland <note>Heaven.</note>, since it is by its very nature infinite, and a finite power cannot reach it. His "back," however, are the garments which God puts on when acting with created things. And these the creatures can and do see. 

And in this way God is apprehended: when one approaches as closely as each person’s capacity allows—just as if someone were to grasp the hem of a garment, he would be said to have "grasped" the man clothed in it. But that "Good" which is named God cannot be fully reached by us because of the fragility of our condition, except by ascending steps and ladders. These indeed behave like a chain; but according to the divine words, they are stretched down to earth in the likeness of Jacob's ladder from the heavens above, like a garment, or a rope, or something directed to us from heaven, like a visual line penetrating various natures. God, therefore, clothed in garments, was known by Moses, just as the Rabbi says...

Eliezer <note>Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus, a prominent 1st-century sage</note>: who, when he had proposed this question, from where the heaven was created, responded: "He took from the light of His garment." For God produced the World with light as if with a garment: so that there might be light from light. BROTHER ARCHANGELUS: All things are one according to Plato, in the *Sophist* and in the *Parmenides*. For in the *Sophist* he understands "one" in species, which is alone intelligible, and of which alone there is intelligence and science—as Aristotle feels. In this sense, perhaps he said: He who does not understand "one," in the way Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher</note> declares, saying that by participation in a species, many men are one man. And Moses had signaled this earlier, when making mention of the species of animals, he always called them by a singular number, saying: *God made the beast, the wild animal, the bird,* and such things. However, by "one" in the *Parmenides*, he understands the divine being in whom all things are rooted, just like branches in a trunk or root. Whence, although all other things are divided in themselves, they must nevertheless be a unique "one" in that first principle itself, just as solar rays have one source in their root (which is the Sun), streams in a fountain, and various powers in the soul. Hence all creatures have being, not from themselves, but from God—the fountain of all streams, the principle of all rays, the life of all living things. And although Aristotle says that the soul of man is the principle of understanding, sensing, and moving, and Aristoxenus <note>A Greek philosopher and music theorist</note> (drawing from the workshop of Plato) agrees when he says "the soul is a number moving itself," since the soul has the principle of motion from itself, it seems also to have the principle of being and life, so that it might seem not to need the help of another to live. Aristotle thinks poorly here; for our Paul <note>The Apostle Paul</note> praises the saying of Aratus <note>A Greek poet quoted by Paul in Acts 17:28</note>, who says: *It is God in whom we live, move, and are.* Or perhaps Aristotle intends to exclude every secondary cause, but not the primary one, by whose power every secondary cause acts, as Proclus <note>A late Neoplatonist</note> teaches. Or perhaps Aristotle did not see or did not want to admit that "one" celebrated in the aforementioned *Parmenides*. All souls, therefore, were created together from the beginning; and though distinct and individualized, they are still said to have been created together because that "mass" from which all are plucked and individualized was created from the beginning. This is the eternally ideated mass (according to the manner of the Cabalists). They are distinguished, however, through matter or through bodies; yet radically and originally, they are all one, though in an ideal mass. Before the deluge, the Fathers lived for a long time, as we read in Genesis; and this was from the foods which the earth produced at that time, as the common people assert. # ON THE DOCTRINES OF THE CABALISTS.

...it is read <note>The text likely refers to Rabbinic interpretations of Genesis</note> that the fruits of the earth were better after the flood than they had been before. For after the flood, God accepted—indeed, he sought out—the first fruits and gifts of the earth's produce, which he had previously rejected, as is evident from the offerings of Cain. Specifically, we do not read of such fruits being offered before the flood. 

By God’s decree, the span of human life was originally an "age" of a thousand years. However, no one actually reached this limit, as many defects occur in man because of which the period of life is commonly shortened. Thus, God cut short the life of man, reducing it to a limit of one hundred and twenty years. The reason is assigned in the text <note>Genesis 6:3</note> where it says: *My spirit shall not remain in man* <term>le-olam<gloss>forever, or for an age</gloss></term> <note>original: לעולם "leholam"</note>: that is, for an age. This "age" refers to the maximum span of a thousand years, though the common edition <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> translates this as "forever." 

The cause is added: *Because he is flesh.* But this reason does not seem sufficient on its own. Therefore, God intended to imply (as some say) that because man is surrounded by flesh, he is fragile. Thus, the longer he lived, the more he would be weighed down by sins. But because the same could be said of good men—namely, that the longer they lived, the more they would be enriched by merits—God shortened life for another mystery. 

Since whatever He does is, without doubt, for our benefit (if not manifest, then hidden), this remains among His concealed secrets. Yet some Cabalists say that when souls are infused into bodies, a certain amount of merit is established for them to acquire, and the time for acquiring it is determined, according to that passage in Job: *You have appointed his bounds (namely, for earning merit) which cannot be passed.* <note>Job 14:5</note> If anyone acquires the merits prefixed for them in a shorter time, so that they anticipate that prefixed time, then such people are overtaken by death early; they do not "live out half their days." This is what Ecclesiastes <note>Actually Wisdom of Solomon 4:13</note> says: *Being perfected in a short space* (namely, by fulfilling the command to acquire merit) *he fulfilled a long time.* 

This is evident in Saint Louis <note>King Louis IX of France</note>, of whom the Church sings those words of the Prophet: *Being perfected in a short space, he fulfilled a long time*; and in Saint Francis, and in many others who, anticipating the time for acquiring merit commanded to them by God, were overtaken by death in their youth. 

To some, therefore, a long life is given; to others a longer one, and to some the longest, because they are <term>Saturnine<gloss>influenced by the slow-moving planet Saturn</gloss></term> or <term>Jovial<gloss>influenced by the planet Jupiter</gloss></term>. This is also because their <term>Hyleg<gloss>the "Giver of Life" in an astrological chart</gloss></term> and <term>Alcocoden<gloss>the "Giver of Years" that determines the length of life</gloss></term> decree it so, as the Astronomers say. Furthermore, it is defined by Him in whose power are all times and moments, as Christ maintains. Sometimes the span of life is even prolonged for some so that they might perform penance. But alas, unhappy are those who (as the Prophet sings) have "dissipated the Law of the Lord" during the time they should have been acting. 

To others, a short life is given, or even the shortest. This is because (as I said) they have been allotted an astrological influence such that they cannot draw out life to a great length—such as those who are pure <term>Mercurials<gloss>influenced by the fast-moving planet Mercury</gloss></term>, whose span of life the Astronomers decree to be thirty years at most. Also, because He who disposes all things—just as He had established a span of a thousand years before the flood and one hundred and twenty after the flood—decreed a proper span for each individual's life. Those who are allotted a shorter life cannot complain; for those who lead a long life are not necessarily happier, since they remain longer in a worse state within this "body of death." 

Hence the Apostle <note>St. Paul in Philippians 1:23</note> desired to be dissolved from this body and be with Christ, for he said that to die was gain for him. Therefore the Wise Man, in Wisdom chapter 4, said of one taken away early: *Being perfected in a short space,* etc. For God does not count works, but weighs them; nor does He look only at the works themselves, but at the will and the affection of the doer. We are taught this by the example of the poor woman putting two small coins into the Treasury, of whom Christ said: *This poor widow has put in more than all of them*—namely, those who were putting in great gifts. 

The conclusion therefore says: *when the soul has grasped whatever it can grasp*—that is, has acquired its assigned merit—*it will be joined to the higher soul*: that is, to that "mass" already mentioned, namely the World of Ideas. It was never entirely separated from that source, but was sent down into the body to purge the "rust of sin." In harmony with this, Plato says in the *Phaedrus*: unless the soul of man had known the things that are true, it would not have come into this body; because he believed that souls returned...

### ARCHANGELO'S COMMENTARY

...into the body, and that choice and option were given to them <note>The souls</note>, as to which body they would prefer to enter: and so that they might claim for themselves that state which they judged more suitable for expiation <note>Atonement or spiritual cleansing</note> and for their own progress. From this he concludes that it was never Plato's opinion or thought that the soul enters the body of brute animals (as some assert and feel), since there it could achieve neither expiation nor progress. And let these things be said according to the Platonic view. The soul, therefore, in its creation, chose a body so that it might be purged within it, as if in a melting pot <note>original: "vase fusorio," a crucible used for refining metals</note>, and be exercised in the war declared against the flesh: so that from there it might bring back glory and a better lot. It was also located and placed there so that, like gold in a furnace, it might be tested and might contain all the various grades of things. Also, by divine edict, a body is assigned—though it is given the choice to assume this or that one, as Plato himself thought. 

However, speaking in a Catholic and Christian manner, it must be said that the soul is placed in a body that opposes and contradicts it for a specific reason: so that by warring and conquering, it may follow the crown and obtain glory, which is not given except to those who strive and fight lawfully <note>A reference to 2 Timothy 2:5</note>, so that it may be granted a seat on the throne of God, as Christ our head proclaims, saying: 
> "To him who overcomes, I will grant to sit with me on my throne, just as I also overcame and sat down with my Father on His throne." <note>Revelation 3:21</note> 

And the body serves as such a purification for the soul that it may be able to obtain its appointed end, being restored to that original purity <note>original: "iustitiae," literally justice or righteousness</note> with which it first entered the body. And through the body, it arrives at such a transformation. 

And although the Wise Man says: "The corruptible body defiles"—or as it is held in the literal text—"weighs down the soul" <note>Wisdom of Solomon 9:15</note>, even if a garment seems to be defiled when the bitterness of a stain is smeared upon it, nevertheless, when water is applied, it cleanses what seemed to defile it. In the same way, even if the soul seems to be stained by the body, yet through the intervening water of wisdom and divine grace, the soul is better purified than if such a defilement of the body had been absent. Indeed, by subduing the body, the soul becomes the Mistress of all bodily things, since the power of all bodily things is found in the human body—just as the powers of all spirits are found in the rational soul. Hence, Man is rightly called a <term>Microcosm<gloss>a "little world" that mirrors the universe</gloss></term> <note>original: "Mundus"</note>, since he contains all things that are in the World. This is the meaning of the Wise Man's words: "He gave him the power of containing all things." 

Therefore, once purified, the soul leaves this material body and ascends upward together with the spiritual body, which is called the <term>quintessence<gloss>the "fifth element," a celestial and incorruptible substance</gloss></term>, in which the entire power and perfection of the material body consists. This is clearly seen in a sown grain: its material and imperfect part decays and returns to the earth, while the other material part, destined for rebirth, constitutes the plant. So it happens in our material body, that it takes on another form. And this is what Paul says: "When this mortal puts on incorruption, then" (one may add) "it shall ascend upward to unite itself with God," becoming one with God, as Christ says in John: 
> "I pray, Father, that as you and I are one, so these may be one in you." <note>John 17:21</note> 

And this is what is called <term>deification<gloss>the process of being made divine or united with God's nature</gloss></term>, namely, that it will be joined with Divinity. It follows then that the "earthly garment" (that is, the impure material part of the body) is "stripped away from its place" (that is, the more perfect part of the body will be separated from the impure part), following the teaching of Paul: "When this mortal, etc." And then the soul rejoices and exults, because God is the object suited to it and for which it was born, according to that saying of Augustine: 
> "You have made my heart for yourself, O Lord, and it is restless until it rests in you." <note>Confessions 1.1.1</note> 

This is also through the harmonious friendship that exists between God and man, who bears His image. For it is common to all those whose companionship is so delightful that, conversely, a man is saddened by the mere presence of an enemy—just as a sheep is at the presence of a wolf. This is also because God is the object of the mind, proportioned above all things; specifically, in the manner in which He communicates to each, as power and virtue, as much as they are able to receive.

It reconciles Platonic thought with Christian doctrine, describing man as a microcosm containing the essence of all creation.</summary>
