# ON THE DOGMAS OF THE CABALISTS.

**CABALISTIC DOGMA: The wise men of Israel, after the cessation of prophecy through the spirit, prophesied through the "daughter of the voice."** <note>original: *filia vocis*, known in Hebrew as *Bat Kol*, a divine echo or heavenly voice that provided guidance after the era of the great biblical prophets ended.</note>

**BROTHER ARCHANGELO:** The visions of the prophets are more certain than natural reasons, because natural reasons have their principles proven from visible and sensory things; for their [ultimate] principles are not known. Truly, vision is most certain, especially that of the prophets, who gazed upon an object that is least deceptive. Therefore, prophetic vision is at the highest rank of height, while at the lowest is reasoning deduced from the senses. The middle rank, however, is the correspondence of revealed light to a well-initiated intellect.

On this point, Eusebius, in his *Preparation for the Gospel*, rightly prefers seers to philosophers, saying: "When I compare philosophers among themselves, or with others, I would not easily deny that they were famous men. But when I compare them to the Hebrew theologians—who received their knowledge from the seers—and compare doctrine to doctrine, everything the philosophers devised seems falling away and frivolous to me. And no wonder: those things were published divinely, while these were produced humanly."

Thus, the proof of truth is not found in the bodily senses, as the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy</note> like; for spiritual senses are preferred over bodily ones and discern better. Whence the Apostle says:

> The spiritual man judges all things. <note>1 Corinthians 2:15</note>

But error arises here because the spiritual senses are not known, especially the visual sense. Regarding this, Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher</note> says: "An eye which all indeed possess, but very few use." These are specifically those who have the "acquired intellect" (as the Peripatetics call it) or who have acquired the "mind" (as Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary figure to whom various mystical and philosophical texts were attributed</note> likes) or those who are transformed into that same image—namely of God—and are united with Him, as Paul and Plotinus agree.

In this way were the prophets. And then they died while seeing those mysteries; for to the life of the one follows the death of the other. Such a death is called "precious in the sight of the Lord," because it is pleasing to God. For a man is then half-blessed when he comes to the "mind," with his intellect united with the divine, so much so that the seer and the seen become one—if Plotinus thinks rightly where he treats of the happiness of the One. 

But since that death is considered the same thing as rapture <note>A state of being "caught up" or spiritual ecstasy</note>, and rapture is the end-point of a violent motion, it would seem that there cannot be happiness in what is "violent." It must be said that this is not "violent against nature"—as if a stone were to fly upward—but "beyond nature," as if fire were impelled to ascend before being released from a burning brand. For it goes to its proper place, but before the appointed time. Thus the mind caught up into God goes to its place, but before its time: because as long as we are in this body (as the Apostle says) we are wandering away from the Lord. 

Therefore, prophets are to be held in great honor; for they are like gods hidden in a human body. Of them the Prophet sings:

> The mighty gods of the earth are greatly exalted. <note>Psalm 47:9</note>

And they are to be honored more or less according to the rank of the spirit and of prophecy with which they are filled. Having been made partakers of God, they must guard against every staining filth and error; lest, if they fall, they feel (according to the Apostle) the impossibility of being raised up again. They must also hide (as the Prophet teaches) the words of God in their hearts, lest they sin by revealing them, except where and when it is necessary. Therefore, they took care to speak enigmatically <note>Through riddles or metaphors</note>, hiding what they said so that secrets would not be publicized to the unworthy. 

Also, because these things are Divine, they cannot be explained in human words; nor do we have the vocabulary with which we could explain them. In this sense Paul said that it is not lawful for a man to speak the secrets of God. Furthermore, by speaking through riddles, they demonstrate the harmonic agreement that exists between visible things (through which they speak) and divine things (of which they intended to speak). 

Hence, oracles are to be interpreted not according to one’s whim, but with great skill regarding the harmony of lower things with the sublime. For true seers must proceed not by human thought, but with a purged mind and a clean heart; they must wait for what God suggests. For (as Baruch says) there is no one who can know the way of God, nor anyone who can devise His paths, but He who knows all things knows it. Peter supports this, saying:

> For prophecy was not brought at any time by human will, but holy men of God spoke inspired by the Holy Spirit. <note>2 Peter 1:21</note>

Isaiah also agrees when he says:

> Announce the things that are to come, and we will say: you are gods. <note>Isaiah 41:23</note>

Nor does Ptolemy <note>Likely referring to the *Centiloquium* attributed to the astronomer/astrologer Ptolemy</note> disagree, who says: "Only those inspired by a deity predict the future."

### THE COMMENTARY OF ARCHANGELO

...particular things: for the monuments of the prophets are called "visions," because they saw with an intuitive gaze in the **eternal mirrors** <note>original: *speculis æternis*, referring to divine reflections of truth</note> that represent the realities of things. These are usually seen by those who are "caught up to the third heaven," where those lofty breasts reside that provide the milk of wisdom; they are called **Nezach** and **Hod** <note>The Sephirot of 'Victory' and 'Splendor,' often associated with the sources of prophecy in Cabalistic thought</note>. All the prophets drew milk from these, as do all those who enter the garden of delights. Hence it is written: *I have come into my garden, and I will give you my breasts* <note>A paraphrase of Song of Solomon 4:10-11 and 5:1</note>, from which the manifold degrees of **Prophecy** are drawn.

The **first degree** is the **dream**; in the cases of Moses and Job, it is called *tardemah* <note>Hebrew: תרדמה, a deep, divinely induced sleep or trance</note>. For this, our translation uses the term *tardemah*, which is a middle state between sleep and wakefulness. In this way, Joseph was admonished by an Angel to go into Egypt and to return. Jacob also saw the ladder this way, and another saw a dream that he recounted to his brothers. God acts in this manner with those who are not yet fully initiated. However, we approve of a "good dream" when a result follows, as Jacob expected in the verification of his true dream—as is said in Genesis and also taught by God in Deuteronomy. A "fallacious dream," however, is impressed by the ancient enemy to deceive. Other dreams that come either from a strong imagination, from mere illusion, from excessive drinking, or from the play of a wandering fantasy, are to be despised as mere flesh.

The **second degree** is **vision in the spirit**, which occurs when the external senses are lulled to rest, and the person belongs to God alone, by whom their spirit is illuminated and instructed. Then the person’s spirit is joined with the Divine Spirit, by which they are taught. This happens when (as the Apostle teaches) the sword—the power of the Divine Word—separates the soul from the spirit, to the point that it desires nothing but God. It removes anger or the baser parts of the soul; strengthened by perfect charity, it fears nothing and has performed the other "purifications" taught by Plotinus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who emphasized the soul's ascent through purification</note>. Then indeed, a man has his spirit joined to the Divine, by which he is taught. According to the scripture: *He who adheres to God is made one spirit with Him.* Then he is said to be filled with the Holy Spirit and speaks in the spirit.

The **third degree** is **imaginary vision**, which is also called the **daughter of the voice** <note>original: *filia vocis*, or *Bat Kol* in Hebrew</note>. This is vision through images, such as those of Zechariah, John, and others who saw celestial beings, the buildings of the Temple, or a city. Beneath these images and imaginations lie hidden sacred mysteries to be discussed there, which is easy through the method of the **Cabala** <note>term: Cabala (The Jewish mystical tradition of scriptural interpretation)</note>. This oracle is called an "Echo" or "Daughter of the Voice" because, just as an echo is the reverberation of a voice uttered by a man, so these images are certain reflections of things produced by God from creatures—like a word uttered by a man, according to the text: *He spoke, and they were made.* This also occurs when someone knows how to understand the invisible things of God through those created things that have been made, since every creature carries some image, or at least the "footprint" of its Creator.

The **fourth degree** is called **intuitive vision**, not in a created mirror, but in the mirror of the Creator, in which all things shine back. This gaze Augustine calls the "morning vision." The Hebrews, however, call it *be-ispaklaria* <note>original: *bespecala*, from the Hebrew *b’ispaklaria*, meaning 'through a lens' or 'mirror'</note>, through mirrors, because they see through **Nezach** and **Hod**. These are two mirrors; or they are **Tipheret** <note>The Sephirah of Beauty, associated with the Sun</note> the Sun, and **Malchut** <note>The Sephirah of Kingdom, associated with the Moon</note> the Moon. In the light of *Tipheret* the Sun, Moses gave the Law, which is called "Zion" by Isaiah where he says: *Out of Zion shall go forth the Law,* even though in a material sense it was given on Mount Sinai.

The **fifth degree** is that of the **full voice**. This is when God speaks to someone with a distinct voice; then the voice is always doubled. Thus He spoke to Abraham, saying "Abraham, Abraham"; likewise to Moses, Samuel, and Paul. It is doubled in mystery to judge the degree to which one is assumed, and in which one was dear. Thus He called Moses on Sinai, and from a shepherd made him King and leader of His people. From a Levite <note>original: *Lẽ*, shorthand for *Levitam*</note> and a minister, He made him the High Priest. In the same way with Paul: from a persecutor, He made him an Apostle. Therefore, wishing to lead Abraham to a higher degree, He doubled the voice. And this degree of oracles is judged by the wise to be above [ordinary] prophecy. Hence, concerning John [the Baptist], who said he was a "voice," Christ testified that he was "more than a prophet."

The **sixth degree** is called **face-to-face vision**, of which the Apostle says: *Then we shall see face to face, even as He is.* David sought to see this, saying: *Show your face and we shall be saved.* Moses reached this: *I speak to him mouth to mouth,* as is clear in...

# ON THE DOGMAS OF THE CABALISTS

...nor is it a wonder, since he had an Angel assigned to him by God: who (as the more secret theologians teach) is called <insert>Metatron, Prince of the Faces</insert> <note>original Hebrew: *Metatron Sar Ha-Panim*; in Cabalistic tradition, the highest archangel who stands before the divine presence</note>. For his duty is to introduce before the face of God those whom God Himself commands. 

The **seventh degree** is **imaginary vision**, which is also called an oracle through a **mirror in an enigma** <note>original: *speculum in ænigmate*; a reference to St. Paul’s phrase in 1 Corinthians 13:12, "through a glass darkly," signifying indirect or obscured divine truth</note>. For this is, as it were, a vision of the imagination, which we discussed above. For this reason, some do not distinguish this degree of prophecy from the previous one. However, if they are distinguished, it is like when a person is given such light that they know how (according to the Apostle) to "understand the invisible things of God through those things that have been made," namely, through the creatures. Since every creature bears some image, or at least a "footprint" of its Maker, this is true not only in its being or its primary acts (as they say), but also in its operation. Such was the case with **Elijah**, when he recognized the Lord: not in the wind that shattered the rocks, nor in the earthquake, nor in the fire, but in the "whisper of a thin breeze." Or similarly, when his servant, on the seventh look, saw a "small cloud ascending from the sea," from which Elijah foretold the coming rain to King Ahab. 

The **eighth degree** is called **Echo**, or the **Daughter of the Voice** <note>Hebrew: *Bath Kol*; a secondary form of divine inspiration that remained with the Jewish people after the era of the great prophets had ended</note>. This is distinct from the higher degrees because it is caused by creatures and their images. This includes the forms of knowledge called **Geomancy** <term>divination using patterns of earth or dots</term>, **Hydromancy** <term>divination by water</term>, **Aeromancy** <term>divination by air</term>, **Pyromancy** <term>divination by fire</term>, and **Chiromancy** <term>palm reading</term>. Certainly, Hydromancy—which consists of washing animal entrails and inspecting the fibers—and Pyromancy—which looks at the shape of the fire consuming a burnt offering—undoubtedly do not exclude the appearance of idolatry. 

In **Geomancy**, however, no such thing is found; rather, it relies on Saturn and the "Lord of the Hour," which are placed as its root. These practitioners enjoy being supported by the logic of numbers, and many bear witness to its validity. This is not the case with Aeromancy, which is frivolous, even if it presumes to boast of numerical logic. Regarding Chiromancy, **Albertus Magnus** <note>a famous 13th-century philosopher and scientist</note> was unwilling to make a hasty judgment, because (as he said) it is perhaps a part of **physiognomy** <term>the practice of judging character from outward appearance</term>. This knowledge seems gathered from the signs of the "mastery of the stars" over both body and soul; the character of the mind is seen in the exterior shape of the body, not because one is the cause of the other, but because both are found to be caused by the same source. 

The Jews of our own time, after they lost the aforementioned modes of prophesying through the Holy Spirit and divine revelation, announce future things through these acquired human arts. However, those who follow the **true Cabala** perceive many divine secrets woven into the text of the Law. Confirming this, Paul says: "The invisible things of God are understood and seen through those things that have been made." This knowledge is called the "Daughter of the Voice"; for, just as the voice called an Echo is caused by a voice, so this knowledge of the Cabala is caused by the written Law. Similarly, for those following the arts mentioned above, their knowledge is caused by the image or the lineaments of the body, and so forth. 

From here, it remains to see for what cause dreams occur, what their purpose is, which part of the soul they belong to, and how difficult it is to pass down anything certain about divination. Regarding the distinction between vision, prophecy, and dreams; the causes of dreams; and dreams that possess the power of divination—I have written about all these things in my commentary on the **Apocalypse**, following the opinions of **Aristotle, Plato, Socrates, Avicenna, Averroes, Al-Farabi, Isaac**, the secret Theologians, and the moderns; therefore, look for them there.

They are set over irrational creatures, and even more so over rational ones. Indeed, many of them have been familiar companions to many men; they instruct, rule, and impel us, and always favor us—even while disagreeing among themselves to protect us. For there is indeed a kind of "envy" or emulation among the blessed and among the Angels. We have an example from the Gospel, where the son who was always obedient to his father felt envy and was saddened by the things the Father of Mercy had bestowed upon the son returning from a distant region <note>A reference to the Parable of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15), used here to explain how divine beings can have conflicting roles or "arguments" while still serving God's will</note>. There are also altercations in heaven, as Moses said: "The hand is upon the throne of **Jah** <insert>God</insert>" <note>Hebrew: *Yah*; a shortened form of the name of God</note>, fighting for the Lord against **Amalek** from generation to generation. # THE ARCHANGELS

...the more secret theologians teach that whatever happens on earth does not occur without it first happening in the heavens. As it was said: **the prince of the kingdom of the Persians** <note>original: *princeps regni Persarum*; a reference to Daniel 10:13, where an angelic "Prince" resists the messenger of God</note> resisted me for twenty-one days. For each of the blessed spirits immediately yields or moves (as was just said of **Gabriel**) so that they may be led by peace. Otherwise, that kingdom would not be one of unity and rest. In the same way, concerning a brother or an adversary, or those complaining that the righteous are rewarded with the same prize, the same must be said. 

Thus, if two men contend, one can by no means overcome the other unless he first overcomes the **guardian angel** of his enemy. It is clear that we have a twofold, principal enemy, and therefore we must struggle according to a twofold rule. This is the most constant opinion of theologians: that an enemy is conquered only after his protector has first been defeated in battle. 

When **Jacob** was returning from **Mesopotamia** and had a most bitter struggle with his brother **Esau**, he first engaged in a contest with Esau's **Intelligence** <term>Intelligence: a technical term for a celestial or angelic being that governs a person or a nation</term>, which was **Samael**. Regarding this Intelligence, although it was a fierce contest, **Samael** himself said: "If one prevails against Angels, how much more against man." But if the enemy is the Devil, one wins in the power of Him of whom the **Apostle** <note>St. Paul</note> says: "victory through Jesus Christ our Lord." 

The one most skilled in this kind of conflict teaches that we should take up the **shield of faith** against the prince of darkness and the **spiritual sword** of the word of God. This Word was later clothed in flesh to conquer the enemy, as He most truly said: "without me you can do nothing." For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, as **Paul** says. 

To the point at hand: Jacob overcame him. For it would be ridiculous to assert that the name "Angel" signifies nothing more than a man, as it must be interpreted here. Esau was wishing to snatch the **birthright** and the **blessing** away from Jacob, as if Esau believed they belonged to him. But when this birthright and blessing had rightfully come to Jacob, he triumphed in the contest. He asked that the angel would not take away those things already justly granted to him. Jacob also fought with the Angel—not just Jacob fighting an Angel with material limbs, but with his **intellect and will** (as I said), while preferring the spiritual part of the soul over the bodily part by holding the impulses of the flesh in check. 

And if it was a spiritual fight, why does the **Scripture** say he was struck in the thigh? This indicates he was struck in the thigh symbolically; for he was struck in the thigh so that he might not rely on the hands with which he worked. This means the wound Jacob received from **Samael** affected those who came from his thigh—his descendants—who "limped" from their paths. Thus, Jacob first fought against the **Angel of Esau**; and once that Angel was overcome, he prevailed over the man whom the Angel protected, according to the teaching elicited from various parts of Scripture.

It frames human struggle as a spiritual battle requiring the "shield of faith" and divine assistance.</summary>

# ON THE DOGMAS OF THE KABBALISTS

...the Intelligence <term>Intelligence: a celestial or angelic being that governs a person, city, or nation</term> having been defeated and removed. For this reason, it is held in Ezekiel that God, wishing to destroy Tyre, a most opulent city, first removed its guardian Angel by withdrawing power from him. Therefore, God, addressing the city, said: "I will draw the Cherub from within you, and I will cast you down from your seat." <note>original: *Cherub inde traham à te, & ponam te de sede*; a reference to Ezekiel 28:16-17</note>. For if God had not first removed the Cherub from it, the angel would have attempted to resist God’s judgment.

Likewise, Moses struck down **Ammomino** <note>A name used in Kabbalistic tradition for the angelic prince of Egypt</note>, the Intelligence of Egypt, before he overthrew the Egyptians. And David, before he conquered Goliath, removed his guardian through the power of the Divine Name; for this reason he said:
> I come to you in the name of the Lord.

In this same way, Christ, wishing to subjugate the World, first cast out its prince. Therefore, the conclusion states (that the King of the earth is not established), that is, he does not emerge as victor (unless he is first humbled), meaning he must be overcome (by the host in heaven), which refers to the guardian Angel. Hence, concerning the Angels guarding Babylon—or any city, or even a confused mind—it is said in Jeremiah:
> We would have healed Babylon, but she is not healed; let us forsake her.

And concerning Bozrah and Edom, it is said:
> All their host shall fade away, as the leaf fades from the fig tree and from the vine; for my sword is drunk in heaven. <note>original: *inebriatus est in cœlo gladius meus*; see Isaiah 34:4-5</note>

Such guardians will fade away either because they are removed from their guardianship or because they are punished for poor guardianship, as some prefer to believe.

<margin>KABBALISTIC DOGMA</margin> Through the word **et** <note>original: את; a Hebrew grammatical particle</note>, which is placed twice in that text: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth" [Genesis 1:1]: I believe Moses signifies the creation of the **intellectual nature** and the **animal nature**, which by natural order preceded the creation of the physical heaven and earth.

<margin>]</margin> **FRATER ARCHANGELUS.** <note>likely referring to the author or a specific commentator, Francesco Zorzi/Georgius</note> Two Worlds are accepted by the Kabbalists: the corporeal and the incorporeal, the visible and the invisible, the sensible and the mortal, the material and the ideal. These are the Lower World and the Upper World. When they read: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth," they believe that **heaven** symbolically designates the highest things and **earth** the lowest. 

Interpreting it in this way: "In the beginning God created the highest and the lowest," they judge that the simple and immaterial World contains the highest things, while this compact and secondary world contains the lowest. From this, they argue that the Divine Law (the Torah) began the account of creation with the letter **Beth** [ב], which in the art of arithmetic signifies the number **two**. It is suggested that this marks how God principally created two things: the entire supreme World with all who dwell in it, and the entire inferior World with everything pertaining to it. 

Otherwise, it would have been enough for Moses to write: *Resit bara Elohim samaim vearez* <note>original: *Resit bara Elohim samaim vearez*; Hebrew: "Beginning created God heaven and earth"</note>; that is, "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." For that summary of creation could have started without the letter **Beth** [ב] (which signifies "In"), and the word for "beginning" could have been placed without any preposition. 

Furthermore, contrary to custom, he added two articles to these two created things: that is, the word **et** [את] appears twice. These are signs of all-encompassing comprehension, because **Et** [את] is formed from **Aleph** [א], the first element of the alphabet, and **Thau** [ת], the last. It is what the Greeks call **Alpha** [α] and **Omega** [ω], and the Latins call the **prow and the stern** (the beginning and the end). 

In this view, "heaven" embraces all things excellently simple and spiritual, from Aleph to Thau (from first to last); and "earth" similarly embraces all things excellently corporeal from head to heel. Nevertheless, each individual thing was created in that one single "beginning" as a single creation. Just as Ezekiel’s "wheel within a wheel" [Ezekiel 1:16], with all its involvements, was seen as one likeness of the glory of the Lord. 

As **Rabbi Saadia** <note>Saadia Gaon (882–942), a prominent Jewish philosopher</note> says in the book *Amunot* (that is, *The Book of Beliefs*): just as the yolk is in the middle of the egg, or like the white of a single egg contained within the shell-like firmament, surrounding the yolk itself; so that first **Intelligible World** enfolds the second, so that its entire power may be governed from there. They are bound together by the chains of harmony, so much so that they often share their natures and names with one another in mutual freedom. 

For in the second, that is, the **sensible World**, nine spheres are moved by the immobile **Empyrean** <term>Empyrean: the highest part of heaven, thought to be composed of pure fire or light</term>, over which **Mettraton** <note>Metatron: a high-ranking angel in Jewish mystical tradition</note> presides continually; but in the first world, nine choirs of Angels are moved by the immobile God. Just as in the immobile silence the Creator of all things first created everything at once, and afterwards, through a ninefold speech (that is, nine times "Let it be"), He set each thing in motion toward its own distinction by speaking. They also establish two Paradises, one celestial...

### COMMENTARY OF ARCHANGELUS

...and the other is earthly (which are signified by those two instances of the word "And") <note>The author refers to the Hebrew particle 'et' (את) in Genesis 1:1, which Kabbalists often interpret as having deep structural meaning beyond a simple conjunction.</note> in which both might attain virtues—the earthly man as much as the heavenly man. As long as he is a guest in the body of this earthly world, as if in another corruptible garden of pleasure, he may gain glory, honor, joy, and gladness—the desire of his own love—from some heroic or preeminent cause of virtue praised by this age; yet these are but fleeting shadows, similar to smoke. 

But in the celestial "land of the living," the super-celestial realm where the unfading Paradise of eternal eternity exists, the soul of man—having lived rightly according to virtue in this mortal life and now being stripped of the body—is shown every good by that most merciful and best God. This is a good that the soul could not even see before, while it was burdened by the heavy and dense corpse of the dark body. That lower vision is called a "non-illuminating lens," while in the Talmud it is called "illuminating speculation" <note>original: *speculatio illuminans*; referring to the Hebrew term *Aspaklaria ha-me’irah*, a prophetic or mystical vision of clarity</note>: that is, a life-giving vision. Among our own theologians, this is called the "intuitive knowledge of God," <term>cognitio Dei intuitiua: the direct, immediate sight of God's essence</term> which the separated soul reaches through the "light of glory"; and this alone is beatific <note>Bringing supreme blessedness or happiness.</note>. For other visions are merely natural reflections which are not beatific; therefore, it is called a non-illuminating contemplation. 

However, the clear vision of God and the perpetual enjoyment of the supreme Divinity are granted to the blessed in the highest part of man—the intellect and the will. Therefore, no one attains these things except in the Supreme World. For this reason, whenever God is said to be "seen" by a mortal man, it is understood to be done through an Angel, as **Gerundensis** <note>Moses ben Nahman, also known as Nachmanides (1194–1270), a leading medieval Jewish scholar</note> writes regarding Exodus. 

Therefore, for the twofold condition of man, both spiritual and corporal, and for the retribution of a twofold reward, the Kabbalists establish a twofold creation, as I have said. Regarding the proposition of the conclusion, I say (concerning the word "And" being placed twice in that text) <note>Again, referring to the Hebrew particle 'et' in Genesis 1:1: *Bereshit bara Elohim **et** ha-shamayim ve-**et** ha-aretz*.</note> specifically in the first chapter of Genesis: *In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth*. So the Hebrew text remains. (I believe Moses signifies the production of the intellectual nature) namely, in its "ideal" state of being: because by "heaven," as I said, simple spiritual beings are understood; (and the animal nature) also in its ideal state, which is signified by "earth": that is, the compact and foundational part of this world. These two creations (preceded the creation and composition in the natural order), namely in the physical and material state of being. 

Through those two "And" particles, therefore, two linking propositions are understood: namely, the "ideal" heaven and earth, and the "physical" and material heaven and earth. Otherwise, there was no need for two conjunctive "Ands" if Moses had only intended to speak of a single creation—namely, the ideal only, or the physical only. Therefore, through the first "And," the ideal production is signified; through the second, however, the real and material production in physical existence is signified. The Kabbalists consider the first description in the aforementioned way; the Talmudists, however, consider the second, saying: *In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.* By "heaven" they understand all the visible things of the world which are above the Moon, and those things which are beneath it they call "earth." They also interpret "heaven" as form and "earth" as matter, the composition of which the Craftsman fashioned in each thing by his oracular word; he turned them with his hand, so to speak, and carved them nine times with his word. For it is read: 
> He said: Let there be light. 
> And God said: Let there be a firmament. 
> And God said: Let the waters be gathered. 
> And God said: Let the earth bring forth. 
> And God said: Let there be lights. 
> And God said: Let us make man. 
> And God said: Behold, I have given to you every herb. 

Therefore, the heavens and the earth were perfected with all their belongings: the spirit of the Lord, the waters under the firmament, and the dry land. Likewise follow the "mixed things," which are commonly called "elementals," such as birds and winged creatures, beasts, fish, and great whales; and the ruler of them all is man. To man alone among all corporeal substances is granted "free will" <term>liberum arbitrium: the power of making choices unconstrained by external necessity</term>, and because he might use it poorly, laws are established for him, constitutions are promulgated, and the punishments of hell are threatened. Many other things are said by the Talmudists, which I omit for the sake of brevity.

# ON THE DOGMAS OF THE KABBALISTS.
<sig>EE 2</sig>

->**KABBALISTIC DOGMA.** What is said by the Kabbalists—that a **green line** encircles the universe—is most appropriately stated regarding the final conclusion which we have mentioned according to the mind of Porphyry. <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was a Neoplatonic philosopher whose works on the soul and the cosmos were often synthesized with mystical traditions. The "green line" (Hebrew: *Kav ha-Yarok*) is a concept from the Zohar and other Kabbalistic texts describing a primordial line of light that encompasses the world.</note><-

FRIAR ARCHANGELUS: This position is very difficult to understand, and therefore requires a long discourse. For some say that this **green line** signifies the **Soul of the World** <note>original: *Mundi anima*; the idea that the entire universe is a single living organism with a spiritual essence</note>; for these thinkers propose that the World is animate, as are the celestial bodies. And this matters nothing to our orthodox faith. Hence Augustine in the *Enchiridion* <note>A "handbook" or manual on Christian doctrine</note>, chapter 43, says: "Neither do I hold it as certain whether the Sun, the Moon, and the animate stars belong to the heavenly city; although some appear to be shining bodies, they do not, however, seem to be intelligent ones. If the celestial bodies are animate, then the souls of those bodies belong to the fellowship of the Angels." The same author says in *On Genesis*, book 2. Again, in his *Retractions*, book 1: "But that this World is a living being (*animal*), as Plato feels and many other philosophers, I have neither been able to investigate by certain reason, nor have I known it could be persuaded by the authority of the Divine Scriptures. Hence, I have noted that something I said elsewhere, which might be taken that way, was said rashly in the book *On the Immortality of the Soul*; not because I confirm this to be false, but because I do not comprehend it to be true—that the World is a living being." Thus he says. 

So also Saint Thomas [Aquinas] says in *Against the Gentiles*: "But this which has been said concerning the soul of heaven: we have not said as if asserting it according to the doctrine of faith, to which it matters nothing whether it is said one way or another." Similarly, [Duns] Scotus—easily the prince of Theologians—says in his second book of *Sentences*: "As to the animation of the celestial body, it seems to be in doubt: if the heavens are animated, this is a matter of belief and not concluded by reason, because there is no condition in that body appearing so perfectly and clearly to be repugnant to the animation of the body." Thus he says. Saint Bernard, in his *Sermons on the Canticles*, says: "Furthermore, as to whether Angelic bodies are truly natural to the spirits themselves, as humans have their own, and whether they are living beings (*animalia*) like humans, yet immortal—I do not want you to ask me. For the Fathers seem to feel differently, and it is not clear to me what either side teaches, and I confess I do not know. But I do not think the knowledge of these things contributes much to our progress." Thus he says. 

It is clear, therefore, that he considers it no inconvenience for Angels to be naturally united to bodies and to reside in them. If, then, an intellectual substance is naturally inclined to seek the company of a body, it will be more prone to a sublime and eternal body than to an earthly one subject to corruption; for like clings to like more than to the unsuitable. From these things we clearly understand that in no part is it repugnant to reason or belief to admit an **animated heaven**.

Furthermore, I say that if the celestial body were inanimate, the Prophet would have passed over the cause of idolatry in silence; for the absence of a sailor is the cause of a ship's sinking, just as his presence is the cause of safety. So in this proposal: by keeping silent about such a lack of a soul, the Prophet would have given cause for the aforementioned error, and such a defect of explanation should by no means be attributed to him. However, that the Prophet was silent on this is clear to anyone examining the passages of Scripture that require expression of this matter—namely, where he might more vigorously speak the reason for rebuking the stars: that the celestial stars do not see, do not hear, nor do they understand; just as he rebukes the worship of statues. As in Deuteronomy 4: "You shall serve gods made by the hands of men, of wood and stone, which neither see, nor hear, nor eat, nor smell." And that passage of the Psalm: "They have a mouth and do not speak," etc. We read that the Prophet cried out these and many things of this kind in the reproach of idols and statues. But regarding the Sun and Moon and other stars of heaven, he did so not at all. 

Instead, when the Prophet rebukes the worship of the stars, he assigns a different cause (not that they do not hear, etc.), but that the people of Israel were not assigned to them as the rest of the nations were, since Israel is a people chosen as the inheritance of the Most High. Hence in Deuteronomy 4 it is said: "Lest perhaps, lifting up your eyes to heaven, you see the Sun and the Moon and all the stars of heaven, and being turned away you adore and worship them, to which all the peoples who are under the whole heaven have been assigned; but you the Lord took and brought out of the iron furnace of Egypt, that He might have..."

<summary>This page explores the Kabbalistic concept of a "green line" encircling the universe, identifying it with the philosophical "World Soul." The author compiles views from major Christian theologians like Augustine, Aquinas, and Scotus to argue that while not a requirement of faith, the idea that celestial bodies (like the sun and moon) possess souls is a reasonable and historically debated possibility.</summary>

### COMMENTARY OF ARCHANGELUS.

<margin>The Hebrew Truth</margin> ...would have a hereditary people. So much for that. And regarding those to whom these things are attributed, reason holds that He created them for ministry: however, the **Hebrew Truth** <note>original: *Hebraica veritas*; a term used by scholars like Jerome to refer to the authentic Hebrew text of the Bible</note> which I have interpreted, declares this. Therefore, the Prophet rebukes Israel concerning the worship of the stars: namely, because the chosen people of God are not subject (as other nations are in any way) to any celestial ruler, but only to the King of Ages, the invisible and immortal God. For if the prophet had then spoken of all the stars, it would have been a more effective argument for calling them back from this worship. His silence on this point would have given a reason for persisting in it—and it is absurd to attribute such a thing to the Prophet. 

Therefore, it is plain, or at least likely, that they declare the celestial bodies. The "garments" explain the nature of the soul: "Wandering," it says, "through all things in circuits" <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 1:6, often interpreted by Neoplatonists to describe the motion of the world-soul</note>: where he could have called nothing else "spirit" except either heaven itself or that power by which the celestial body is diligently turned around. Here Solomon does not speak of the local motion of a body, but of the spiritual course of the soul, by which the soul surveys all the "exemplars" <note>The divine patterns or ideas</note> that exist in the Divine Mind. From this spiritual circulation of the soul with the celestial body, a physical movement follows: just as in us, from the very bond of our soul with the organic body, the passions produce a noticeable effect in the body. Sadness, exercising a heavy anxiety of the soul, makes the body sluggish and almost immobile; while joy fits its body to be agile and most ready for movement. In the same way, the concepts of the [world] soul perpetually overflow into the celestial body itself. 

It wanders, therefore, by its spiritual motion. Thus, through the present conclusion: it is called the **line** that surrounds the whole building: therefore, the heaven is animate <note>This "line" refers back to the "green line" mentioned on the previous page, identifying it with the Soul of the World that encompasses the universe</note>. This is clearer by way of logical sequence: for the prophet posits that celestial bodies are more noble, therefore they must be animate. 

Hence Job 25 says: "Can a man be justified when compared to God, or can one born of a woman appear pure? Behold, even the moon does not shine, and the stars are not clean in his sight: how much more is man but decay, and the son of man a worm?" Likewise, David, the messenger of salvation, says: "I see your heavens, the work of your hands, the moon and the stars which you have established. What is man that you are mindful of him, and the son of man that you visit him?" Therefore, since the heaven is more excellent than man, nothing truly could be more excellent than man except for an animate heaven. Thus, the heaven firmly appears to be animate.

That a soul is given to the heaven is openly hinted at in Chapter 7 [of Jeremiah], saying: "The children gather wood, and the fathers kindle the fire, and the women knead the dough to make cakes for the **Queen of Heaven**." <note>original: *Regina coeli*</note>. And the same prophet repeats this title more often in Chapter 44. For if these words of Jeremiah are looked at in the Hebrew manuscript, all will see that the word **Queen** <note>original: *Malkat* <term>מלכת</term></note> is written one way in the context of the letter, and read another way in the marginal note (which they call the **Massara**) <note>The *Masorah* are traditional notes on the Hebrew biblical text ensuring its correct transmission</note>. For it is written as *Malkat*, which sounds like "Queen." But in the margin it is read as *Melachah* <note>original: <term>מלאכה</term></note> which indicates "work" or "office." 

Whenever a dissonance of this kind is found in the margin of the sacred canon, it is certain (according to the Hebrews) that some secret lies hidden. Just as in the Prophet Zechariah, hinting at the mystery of a great vision: "And they shall look at me," he says, "whom they have pierced." For in the manuscript context it is written as **To me** <note>original: *Elai* <term>אli</term></note>, but in the margin it is read as **To him** <note>original: *Elau* <term>אליו</term></note>. By this, the Prophet wished to insinuate that God, who speaks through the mouth of the Prophet, declares Himself pierced; yet He did not wish to be seen as God in that moment, but insofar as He was man. Therefore, the margin reads "To him," namely to the man as a man. 

The same rule must be judged here: although men worship celestial works and crafts, they do so not according to their physical nature, but insofar as the soul and the nourishing "Queen of Heaven" inhere in them. Nor is the worship of this queen called **dulia**, but only **latria** <note>Theologians distinguish between *Latria* (worship due to God alone) and *Dulia* (veneration given to saints or angels)</note>. Yet even the adoration of *dulia* must be avoided, lest through the progress of the body, *dulia* passes over into *latria*. Moreover, many testimonies of other holy Fathers exist, primarily those of the Divine Jerome...

<meta>This page continues Friar Archangelus’s defense of the animate nature of the heavens and the universe, transitioning from the interpretation of Solomon’s words in Ecclesiastes to the authoritative support of Scholastic theologians like Thomas Aquinas and Church Fathers like Origen and Augustine.</meta>

# ON THE DOGMAS OF THE KABBALISTS.

First, he says: *The spirit goes circling about, and returns into its circuits* <note>original: "Girans girando uadit spiritus, & in circulos suos reuertit"; a reference to Ecclesiastes 1:6</note>, whether he named the sun itself "spirit" because it is a living thing that breathes, flourishes, and completes its annual orbits in its course; this clearly indicates that the celestial stars are animate beings. Just as **Albertus** <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a polymath and teacher of Aquinas</note>, **Thomas**, and the rest of their followers do not doubt that this opinion should be attributed to **Jerome**. 

**Thomas**, speaking of spiritual creatures, affirms that the "Soul of Heaven" is joined to the orb, and is in fact distinct from the "unjoined" Intelligences which move the spheres toward a final goal. For he says: "Thus there will be a twofold order of spiritual substances: some united to celestial bodies as movers, and some which will be the ends [goals] of these motions, entirely abstract [separate]." So he says. Nor does he, because he said souls are joined to the orb as movers, deny that they give some inherent perfection to the heaven by way of "form," as he explains himself in that passage. 

However, celestial bodies are not animate in the same way that plants and animals are, but "equivocally"—that is, with the same kind of distinction by which the word "body" is used for both celestial and earthly things. For the condition by which the celestial soul provides "form" to its body is as far removed from the condition of the soul of decaying things as the supernal soul and the heaven itself are distant from the earthly soul and earthly bodies. **Petrus Aureolus**, a most learned theologian, confirms the same. 

The Church also seems to favor this opinion when it chants: *Through whom the Angels praise your majesty, the Dominations adore it, the Powers tremble, as do the heavens and the virtues of the heavens, etc.* <note>original: "per quem maiestatem tuam laudant Angeli, adorant dominationes, tremunt potestates, coeli coelorumq; uirtutes"; from the Preface of the Roman Mass</note>. In this passage, by "virtues of the heavens," it seems he meant "souls," as **Thomas** testifies in his *Quodlibetal Questions*. 

This same point could be proven by many other reasons. First: Heaven performs an act, or operation of life; therefore it is simply animate. Second: The soul is the first principle of living for the celestial body; therefore the soul is the "form" or "act" of the celestial body. Third: Heaven is a more perfect body; therefore its form is also more perfect, namely, a soul. Fourth: "Animate" is a descriptive naming; such naming comes from something inherent by way of form; therefore the soul inheres in the celestial body as its form. Fifth: There must be a "middle" that links the extremes, namely the intellect and the body. That which participates in both extremes is called the "middle," and such is the Soul of Heaven. 

Therefore, it is said in that conclusion that the soul is a **green line** <note>original: "anima linea uiridis"; a Kabbalistic term (the *Kav*) often associated with the life-force or the horizon that encircles the world</note>, especially the soul of the *primum mobile* <note>The "first moved" sphere in Aristotelian astronomy, which carries all other spheres</note>, whose ecliptic encircles the universe. Since, according to the philosophers, it is the ultimate heaven encompassing all things, I have chosen not to explain the five arguments mentioned above to avoid excessive length. 

Just as they admit celestial bodies are animate, so it can be admitted that the **World** is animate, or a "living animal." For one thing can be multiple or many. For the sun is single in itself, but multiple in its rays; single in essence, yet all-encompassing in its power. The soul is also single in itself, but multiple in its operation: for it hears in the ears, sees in the eyes, etc. From these things, it will be easily discerned how that single life would be multiple in its members, if it were admitted that the World is an animal, as many wise men agree. 

Such include **Augustine** and **Origen**, who strives to prove this opinion by the testimony of Holy Scripture in his work *On First Principles*, especially through that passage of **Jeremiah**: *Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord.* And through **Isaiah**: *Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool.* Which the Savior confirms when He says: *Do not swear, neither by heaven, because it is the throne of God, nor by the earth, because it is His footstool.* But there is also that which the Apostle [Paul] said when preaching to the Athenians, approving the sentiment of **Aratus**: *For in Him we live, move, and have our being.* 

And how is this so, unless because God, by His power, binds together, contains, and gives life to the entire World? How also is heaven the throne of God, and the earth His footstool, unless because He fills all things in heaven and on earth? Thus far **Origen**. **Eusebius Pamphilus** confirms the same in his *Theological Solutions*. Also, Cardinal **Cusanus** <note>Nicholas of Cusa (1401–1464), a philosopher who wrote on the "soul of the world"</note> says: "That Life of the World, which moves itself and all things, is perpetual; because circular and round motion contains all motion, just as a circle enfolds every shape within itself." Toward which soul the entire corporeal...

<meta>This page continues Archangelus’s discourse on the animate nature of the cosmos, moving from the specific theological views of Aquinas and Albert the Great to a broader philosophical synthesis. He draws on "Prisca Theologia" (Ancient Theology), linking the World Soul to Hermetic, Platonic, and Aristotelian traditions to show that God’s life sustains every part of the universe.</meta>

# ARCHANGELUS’S COMMENTARY.

The World stands in relation to its own soul just as the body of a man relates to its own. The Soul is in the World like a King in a kingdom, by whose rule the inhabitants are governed: various princes and leaders are assigned, by whose guidance the different parts of the people are ruled, yet they are never separated from the King of the entire domain. In this way, every single creature pre-existed first in that universal life, with a specific "leadership" <note>original: "ducatu"; referring to the guiding principle or form of a species</note> assigned to it—namely the species by which it lives, whether as an **Angel**, **Man**, **Lion**, **Eagle**, or **plant**. Yet, they are not separated from that one-of-a-kind Life; rather, when that particular life passes away, or that specific leadership is removed, the body returns to the more universal kingdom—namely, the element of **earth**—while the soul returns to the kingdom of the life of the universe. The spirit returns, says the Wise One <note>Solomon, in Ecclesiastes 12:7</note>, to God, who made it; though those who are cast down are violently bound in **Tartarean prisons** <note>The deep abyss of torment in Greek mythology, used here as a metaphor for Hell</note>. **Aristotle** confirms this same idea, along with his pupil **Theophrastus** and **Averroes** <note>The influential 12th-century Andalusian philosopher known as "The Commentator" on Aristotle</note>. **Democritus** says that the Soul of the World is God, and (according to **Eusebius** and **Plutarch**) they say that God is a spirit penetrating the entire World, called by different names according to the diversity of the things through which he passes.

The **Indians** <note>Referring to the gymnosophists or ancient sages of India, often cited in Renaissance philosophy</note> said the World is a living animal, and this is perpetual: because it fulfills the roles of both father and mother in the generation, nutrition, and love of all living things. **Zoroaster** <note>The text says "Zona," likely a shorthand or OCR error for Zoroaster, the legendary Persian sage</note> proves the World is animated, receiving life from God, who generates living beings from Himself. And **Hermes Trismegistus**, in the book *That God is both Manifest and Hidden*, says: *there is nothing even in bodies which is not He himself: for He alone exists as all things, bringing to light those things which are, and concealing those things which are not within Himself. He is the eye, the most manifest of all things; He is visible to the mind, and present to the eyes. He is incorporeal, yet (so to speak) multi-corporeal.* <note>Trismegistus is the legendary father of Hermeticism; this passage emphasizes "panentheism," where God is both the creator and the substance of the creation.</note> And in the book *On the Common*, he says: *nor is there anything in the All which is not God Himself. He is the life of all things.* And **John** says: *What was made, in Him was life, and the life was the light; all things were made through Him, and without Him was nothing made.* <note>John 1:3-4</note>. This can be understood in a double sense: either that nothing was made without Him, or that whatever was made without Him—without Him preserving, filling, and vivifying it—is nothing at all. And of these things **Orpheus**, in his *Theology*, sings at great length that it is God who is to be seen in all the members of the world; and all the **Platonists** affirm this same thing with one voice. For this is their specific dogma.

And if the World is an animal, it is nevertheless not altered, nor does it become sick or fail, like other animals. Hence **Chalcidius** <note>A 4th-century commentator on Plato's Timaeus</note> says in his commentary on the *Timaeus*: *That which is instituted by God is immune to the passage of time, to disease, old age, and death,* as all the **Academics** <note>The followers of Plato’s Academy</note> agree. And this is proven if one carefully weighs those things which are said to be produced immediately by God, and those produced through "secondary causes," as narrated by the most wise philosopher **Moses**. The World is a "total body," such that nothing exists outside of itself that could flow out, be diminished, or suffer loss, which usually happens from the destruction of parts while they are being resolved into something else. For all things that flow or do not flow as parts dwell within the World; since nothing of it exists outside its own boundaries, its parts—which sometimes flow when exhausted—return to that same nature of the universe, having been refreshed.

Therefore, the Soul of this World is called a **"line of power"** <note>original: "linea uirtutis"</note> which surrounds the universe, because the soul is in the whole and in every part. This is most fittingly stated in the final conclusion from the mind of **Porphyry** <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher and student of Plotinus</note>, which holds: *God is everywhere, because He is nowhere; Intellect is everywhere, because it is nowhere; Soul is everywhere, because it is nowhere.* But God is everywhere and nowhere in respect to all things that come after Him. The Soul is in the Intellect and in God, but everywhere and nowhere in respect to the body. So it is said. God, therefore, is everywhere, because all things receive life from the **Author of Life** according to their capacity; He is called now the **Fountain**, now the **River of Life**. This river spreads itself into the whole body of the world, just as the soul divides itself into all the members of its own body, so that all operations performed through any member of that body proceed from the vivifying and moving soul. Therefore, it is said that the soul is everywhere: thus God, as the Life of the World, shines in the **sun**, flows with different influences in the various **stars**, rains in the **clouds**, breathes in the **air**, and germinates in the **earth**.

Archangelus harmonizes Christian scripture with Hermetic, Platonic, and Peripatetic traditions to describe God as the "River of Life" present in all elements.</summary>

# ON THE DOGMAS OF THE CABALISTS. 867

He works in all things in such a way, as **Paul** says. For God is, indeed, the common nature at work, who, being diffused into all things, gives to all the power to act. And thus God is everywhere and nowhere. Because of this, "place" can be considered in two ways according to the **Theologians**: in one way, insofar as it is a certain created thing; and in this sense, God is in all places, just as He is in all things. In another way, it can be considered insofar as it is the container of that which is placed. And in this sense, God, according to Himself, is nowhere, because He is contained by nothing, but rather He contains and preserves all things. However, according to His effects, He is everywhere, because He fills every place with His effects. According to this specific mode, it is proper to God to be everywhere; for nothing fills every place with its goodness and effects except God. Yet He is "nowhere"—namely, in a "containing" <note>original: "contentiuè"; referring to being held within a physical boundary</note> or "circumscribing" sense—because those apply only to bodies; nor is He there in a "defining" sense <note>original: "diffinitiuè"; referring to the way a created spirit is limited to one location at a time</note>, because that belongs to created spirits. The reason is that both these modes imply limitation: the first implies the limitation of physical quantity, while the second proves a limitation of essence and power. According to neither of these two modes can anything be in several places at once, and much less everywhere.

To be in a place "repletively" <note>original: "repletiuè"; to fill a space entirely without being limited by it</note> belongs to God—not according to His own essence, but according to His effects (as I have said)—and thus it is proper to God to be everywhere. For only the Divine power extends itself to the production of all things that exist, or could possibly exist in a place, and this is what it means to fill a place with His effects. Thus, being "everywhere" belongs to Him not from eternity, but within time, just as does the production of the things with which every place is filled. 

And so the **World Soul**, which is God giving life to the World, is called the **green line**: because it flows every kind of influence into all created things, just as the color green is capable of receiving any other color <note>In medieval color theory, green was often seen as a middle point or a "bridge" between light and dark, or a base that could harmonize with others</note>. And this line surrounds the universe, because God, giving life to the World, is everywhere. The **Cabalists**, however, call this "green line" the last *midah* <term>midah: a Hebrew word meaning "measure" or "attribute," used by Cabalists to refer to the Sefirot, the ten emanations of God</term> or property, which includes all the influences of the entire Sephirotic order. This order is called the **Archetypal World**, which encloses within itself the many kinds of influences of **mercy** and **justice**. Other Cabalists call this line *cheter Elion* <note>original: "cheter Elion," Hebrew: Keter Elyon (כתר עליון)</note>: that is, the **Supreme Crown**, from which all Divine influences first fall, both to the right and to the left. Still others feel differently, saying this line is the name **Tetragrammaton** <note>The four-letter name of God, YHWH (יהוה)</note>, from which descend twelve "revolutions," which are called the twelve **archetypal signs**, and they preside over the twelve signs of the heavens. The ecliptic line of this Tetragrammaton is the very Name which presides over the first archetypal heaven, which surrounds all other divine things and flows into them.

->**CABALISTIC DOGMA.** Through the word "Amen," a specific order is maintained expressing how the influence of the numerations <note>the Sefirot</note> proceeds.<-

**BROTHER ARCHANGELUS.** "Amen" in Latin is said as *Amīn* <note>αμην</note> in Greek, and *Amen* <note>אמן</note> in Hebrew. In Latin, according to **Aquila** <note>A 2nd-century translator of the Hebrew Bible into Greek</note>, it signifies "faithfully," being an adverb derived from the word for faith, which in Hebrew is called *Emunah* <note>אמונה</note>; from this comes *Beemuna* <note>באמונה</note>, which means "faithfully," and "Amen" is the same. However, according to the **Septuagint** <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> interpreters, it is the same as if we were to say, "so be it" <note>original: "fiat"</note>. Hence, at the end of books (since the Psalter among the Hebrews is divided into five parts), it says "so be it, so be it," which they translated from the Hebrew reading "Amen, Amen." For this reason, the **Apostle** <note>Paul, in 1 Corinthians 14:16</note> asserts that no one can answer "Amen" to what has been said unless he understands what came before. 

Some wish (such as **Lyra** <note>Nicolaus de Lyra, a famous 14th-century Franciscan biblical commentator</note>) that just as "ay" <note>original: "ly etiam"</note> is an adverb of affirmation in Latin, so too is "Amen" in Hebrew. And through this double affirmation, it is hinted that it is an unretractable truth; and then the "Amen" is the same as "truly," as it is derived from the word *Emet* <note>אמת</note>, which signifies **Truth**. In this word, the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet is included, the middle, and the last <note>This refers specifically to the word Emet (Truth), spelled Aleph (1st), Mem (middle), and Tav (last), though the text links it to the structure of Amen as well</note>. By these letters, the texture of things is judged: namely, the going out from the beginning into the thing itself, and the return at the end. This is properly Truth and the rectitude that belongs to truth and firmness. Hence in **Geometry** or **Arithmetic**, those letters signify the solid number four <note>the "quaternary"</note> and the essence of all numbers. For **Aleph** signifies "one" and "a thousand." of all numbers. One thousand is also the cube of the complete number ten; while <term>Mem</term> <note>original: "m tem"; the Hebrew letter מ</note> signifies forty, which is the number derived through the simple complete ten and through the radical number four, the foundation of all numbers. That is to say, from the number ten, which is the ultimate simple number (as I have said), beyond which no process can occur. This ten is contained within the number four itself, in this manner: 1, 2, 3, 4. All of these added together constitute 10. <term>Thau</term> <note>original: "ת"</note> indeed signifies four hundred (400), a number derived through ten and forty, or through four and one hundred, which is the square of ten. For ten times forty, or four times one hundred, constitute the number 400. Thus are the numbers explained which are contained in the word <term>Truth</term> <note>Hebrew: אמת (Emet)</note>. Furthermore, the shapes of the letters themselves are solid and firm; these letters are "twice-squared." For the shape of those letters is such that they have feet and bases upon which each of them may stand separately, and more strongly together. 

By contrast, the word signifying <term>Lie</term> <note>Hebrew: שקר (Sheker)</note> is written with letters that have no firmness; they cannot stand alone, nor joined together. From this comes that proverb: *A lie has short feet*; indeed, they are "limping" <note>An ancient metaphor suggesting that while truth stands on a firm foundation, a lie is unstable and quickly trips itself up</note>. In Hebrew, "lie" is noted thus: *secher* <note>שקר</note>. In number, all these letters signify hundreds; they apply these numbers to lower and "thicker" <note>material or less spiritual</note> things where lies and falsehood flourish. For the letter *koph* <note>ק</note> gives one hundred; *resh* <note>ר</note> two hundred; *shin* <note>ש</note> three hundred. But the letters of **Truth** reach toward divine things: <term>Aleph</term> <note>א</note> signifies unity and one thousand; <term>Mem</term> <note>מ</note> signifies the tens <note>specifically 40</note>; and <term>Thau</term> <note>ת</note> signifies four hundreds. These things are evident to those who know the <term>mathematical science</term> <note>Referring here to Gematria, the practice of assigning numerical values to Hebrew letters to find deeper meanings</note>. 

**Amen**, therefore, is the same as "it is true." The Lord uses this word in the Gospel; and we also, when we wish to affirm something, are accustomed to respond "even so" or "Amen." There is this difference, however: God uses it at the beginning, while we use this word at the end of a prayer. This shows that He is the author of truth, while we are the disciples of truth, provided we show ourselves to believe in Him and toward Him. Just as <term>Emet</term> <note>אמת; Truth</note> includes the first letter of the alphabet, the middle, and the last (as noted above), so it demonstrates the expressed order of the flow of the <term>Sephirot</term> <note>The ten attributes or emanations in Cabala through which the Infinite reveals itself</note>. 

Wherefore **Aleph** <note>א</note> is ascribed to the Supreme <note>Keter, the highest Sephirah</note>, as if to the principle of all divine gifts. To **Mem** <note>מ</note> indeed is given <term>Tipheret</term> <note>The Sephirah of Beauty or Harmony</note>, as if to the heart of the divine dimensions, numbering within itself all divine "liquid" <note>spiritual influence or grace</note>. This place is called **Jacob the Archetype**, in whom **Messiah Christ** reigns; and He is signified by the letter **Mem** <note>מ</note>, because He is the beginning, middle, and end of all creatures. Consequently, He is the beginning, middle, and end of the Divine influences communicated to created things; for "from His fullness we have all received," as **John** says. For this reason He says of Himself: "I am the Beginning, who speaks"; and He showed Himself to be the middle in His life—born among animals, dying between thieves, and standing resurrected among His disciples. He also showed Himself to be the end, saying: "I am the Alpha and the Omega." This is shown through the last letter of *Emet*, called **Thau** <note>ת</note>, which in its full spelling <note>תאב</note> signifies "he has detested," namely, all evil things—which He will show most greatly on the Day of Judgment. See in the other conclusions for a fuller explanation of what **Amen** intends.

## CHAPTER ONE.

THIRTY-two paths of wisdom, most wonderful and hidden, <term>Yahweh</term> <note>original Hebrew: יהוה; the Tetragrammaton or four-letter name of God</note> God of <term>Hosts</term> <note>original Hebrew: צבאות (Tzevaot); a divine title implying Lord of the heavenly armies</note> engraved His name. There are ten <term>Sephiroth</term> <note>ten divine emanations or attributes through which the infinite God interacts with the universe</note>: that is, ten properties, beyond that which is <term>ineffable</term> <note>meaning "too sacred or great to be expressed in words," referring here to the Ein Sof or Infinite Godhead</note>, and twenty-two letters. These are the foundations: Three "mothers," seven "doubles," and twelve "simples." There are ten Sephiroth, beyond the ineffable. This is the number of the ten fingers, namely, five against five, and a covenant, uniquely intended for the One, in the middle. In the interpretation of the tongue and of circumcision <note>referring to the two "covenants" of speech and the flesh</note>: Ten Sephiroth without the ineffable. Ten and not nine. Ten and not eleven. Understand through Knowledge and be wise with Understanding: test them, investigate them, note them, reflect upon them, and imagine them; establish the matter in its integrity and cause the Creator to be seated on His throne. Ten Sephiroth beyond the ineffable, their ten properties are infinite. The depth of the first: the depth of the last: the depth of good: the depth of evil: the depth of height: the depth of depth: the depth of the east: the depth of the west: the depth of the north: the depth of the south: and the Lord, uniquely One, a faithful King, rules over all from His throne forever and ever. Ten Sephiroth beyond the ineffable. Fix their end in their beginning like a flame joined to a coal, because the Lord is uniquely One: and there is no second to Him. And before One, what can you count? Ten Sephiroth beyond the ineffable. Restrain your lips from speaking and your heart from meditation: and if your heart falters, return to the place. For it is written: "Go forth and return," and for this reason the covenant was cut: Ten Sephiroth beyond the ineffable.

# ABRAHAM’S TREATISE ON CREATION,

there are ten ineffable things: the Spirit of the living God, Air, Water, Fire, Up, Down, East, West, North, and South.

## CHAPTER TWO.

<margin>
The twenty-two combinations of the Alphabet, which are found above in Reuchlin on pages 718 and 719, pertain to this place. <note>original: "in Reuchlino"; referring to Johannes Reuchlin’s *De Arte Cabalistica*, a famous 16th-century work on the Kabbalah.</note>
</margin>

Twenty-two Letters are the Foundations: Three "mothers," seven "doubles," and twelve "simples." The three mothers are <term>Emes</term> <note>original Hebrew: אמש (Aleph, Mem, Shin); these letters represent the three primary elements</note>: that is, air, water, and fire. Water is quiet, fire is hissing, and air is the spirit, the <term>balance</term> <note>original Hebrew: משק (Mshq); representing the point of equilibrium</note> that mediates between them. He sculpted the twenty-two letters, weighed them, permuted them, composed them, and with them created every soul that has been created or is yet to be created. These twenty-two letters are sculpted in the voice, incised in the spirit, and placed in the speech in five locations: in the throat, in the palate, in the tongue, in the teeth, and in the lips. The twenty-two letters, the Foundations, are arranged upon a sphere with two hundred and thirty-one <term>gates</term> <note>the total number of possible pairs that can be made from the 22 letters</note>. When the sphere is rotated forward, it signifies good. When rotated backward, it signifies the opposite. Indeed, He weighed the letter <term>Aleph</term> <note>the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet</note> against all others, and all others against Aleph, and so on with each individual letter. By thus rotating each one through all the others, two hundred and thirty-one gates result. From these, all languages and every creature have emerged; He made something from the void, and from nothingness He brought forth existence. He hewed out great columns in the hollow of the orb and in the incomprehensible air. The sign of this thing is: twenty-two small marks <note>original: "iotalia"; literally "iota-like things," referring to the Hebrew letters</note> and one body.

---

## CHAPTER THREE.

<margin>
Three mothers: אמש <note>Aleph, Mem, Shin</note>
</margin>

The three Mothers, Emes (אמש), are their foundations. There is a scale of merit and a scale of guilt <note>original: "contradictionis"</note>, and the tongue of <term>the law</term> <note>original Hebrew: חק (Chok); often translated as "decree" or "statute"</note> of examination stands as the mediator between them. The three mothers are Emes. This is a great secret, most wonderful and most hidden, sealed with six rings; from them come forth fire, water, and air, which are divided into male and female. There are three mothers, Emes, and from them come three fathers, and with these all things are created. The three mothers, Emes, in the World are air, water, and fire. In the beginning, the Heavens were created from fire, the Earth from water, and the Air was created from the Spirit, which stands as the mediator. The three mothers, Emes, in the Year are heat, cold, and the temperate season. Heat was created from fire, cold from water, and the temperate season from the spirit, which mediates between them. The three mothers, Emes, in Man are the head, the belly, and the body <note>original: "corpus"; here referring to the chest or torso</note>. The head was created from fire, the belly from water, and the body, the mediator between them, from the spirit. Regarding the three mothers, Emes: He sculpted, incised, and composed them, and thus the three mothers were created in the World, the three mothers in the Year, and the three mothers in Man—both male and female. He caused Aleph to rule over the spirit, bound it with a knot, composed one with another, and with them He sealed the air in the World, the temperate season in the Year, and the body in Man, both male and female. The "males" are in the order of *Emes*—that is, in air, water, and fire. The "females" are in the order of *Asam*—that is, in air, fire, and water. He caused <term>Mem</term> <note>the letter representing water</note> to rule over water, bound it with a knot, composed one with another, and with them He sealed the earth in the World, the cold in the Year, and the fruit of the womb in Man, both male and female. He caused <term>Shin</term> <note>the letter representing fire</note> to rule over fire, bound it with a knot, composed one with another, and sealed with them the heavens in the World, the heat in the Year, and the head in Man, both male and female.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring the "Three Hares" motif: three running hares arranged in a circle, their ears interlocking to form a triangle in the center.</image-desc> AS soon as I departed from you at Mainz, I immediately experienced within myself that proverb common among our French neighbors: a friend is never enough, whether present or absent. For while I was present, I did not enjoy your company as much as our friendship deserves; this usually happens to all lovers, who feel upon departing that they have omitted many things they had intended in their minds to do or say. But what I omitted, my letters will repair; I wish I could be with you more often through their exchange. We were speaking of the little book on famous men by the Lord of Sponheim <note>Referring to Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), the Abbot of Sponheim, a famous chronicler and cryptographer.</note>, which you said had been given for printing at Basel. I asked about Doctor John Reuchlin, wondering whether he had been included; when you seemed to doubt it or denied it, I was amazed. For if you were thoroughly familiar with and knew the man, you would find no one whom you could consider more distinguished in every branch of learning in this day and age. Therefore, both you and your Abbot would pass him over only at a great insult and loss to the German name. For he is a most skillful interpreter of the three languages: Greek, Hebrew, and Latin. Add also, if you wish, French, which he learned thoroughly at Orléans while he was devoting his efforts to the study of law. As a young man, he translated several orations, some of which, if I am not mistaken, were composed by Xenophon in defense of Socrates. He has composed many pleasant poems and written several epistolary disputes, which he has filled with the teachings of the Greeks and even the Hebrews. Furthermore, in order to penetrate the secret dogmas of the Hebrews, he has labored most tirelessly for many years; and he has unrolled their entire library to such an extent that you will not easily find any Hebrew whom you could set against him. Led by this happiness and abundance of talent and learning, he applied himself to writing a dialogue, which he entitled *CAPNION* <note>original: "CAPNION"; This is a Greek translation of Reuchlin's German name, *Räuchlein*, which means "little smoke."</note>, or *ON THE WONDER-WORKING WORD*. I have never seen anything more eloquent or more wonderful than this work. <margin>The arrangement of the books.</margin> It is divided into three books: the first [contains] all things se- <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page.</note>

*CERTAIN curious explorers of secret matters, most sacred Bishop of Worms <note>Addressed to Johann von Dalberg (1455–1503), the Bishop of Worms and a key patron of German humanism.</note>, who are troubled by hidden powers, the abstruse energy of words, and the divine characters of secret names, are found in our age (so far as I can see) to depart not a little from the most ancient teachings of the leading Philosophers, and to wander often and much concerning the most full mystical reasons of miraculous effects. This is primarily because either the clarity of the sources has been obliterated by obscurity, or because those symbols of that sacred Philosophy and the venerable bonds of supernatural powers have been corrupted by the perversity of scribes, so that they can neither be understood nor even read. Therefore, many, affected by weariness and lazy fatigue, are abandoning this most laudable kind of contemplation—which they had long ago begun—either through fear or neglect. Hence, led by an incredible desire for teaching, and indeed by a singular love toward that pillar of every good art, John Lapidanus <note>Johannes Heynlin (c. 1430–1496), also known as Lapidanus, was a rector of the University of Paris and Reuchlin’s teacher.</note>, doctor of Theology, distinguished both by his Carthusian monastic life and his publication of books—and the first under whose rod my hands were to be trained in the exercises of the humanities—I will add further, my old friend Sebastian Brant of Strasbourg <note>Author of the famous "Ship of Fools" and a legal scholar.</note>, a man most expert in both laws and most adorned with polished letters, and likewise John Amorbach, excellent in talent, noble in the art of characters <note>A reference to Amorbach's skill as a master printer and typographer.</note> and learned in various disciplines, both most famous in the literary republic of learned men. Whether they are more illustrious for their human deeds or their city, they are citizens of Basel of no small praise. Moved therefore by the bond of the great friendship of such men, I have dared to enter the darkness and the so-obscured sacred—indeed secret—words, and to set forth for our age, as much as our memory allows, almost everything about the hidden oracles and the most ancient part of Philosophy, which in a former age wise men used in sacred matters and miraculous operations, whether they were the traditions of Pythagoras and the older philosophers, or the foreign memories of the Hebrews and Chaldeans, or Christian*
