<header>PREFACE.</header>

*...offerings, which may be seen brought forth from their books and languages in this work. For this reason, we have dedicated it to your name, since sacred things are due to sacred people, and especially priestly matters to the princes of priests, a dignity in which you stand above others: not only because of the greatness of your dominion and power, in which you are most abundantly wealthy, but also because of your inexpressible skill in various literatures. Witness to this is that library of yours, filled with Latin, Greek, and Hebrew volumes: the one treasure of our Germany, which I have always been accustomed to use according to the desires of my soul. Receive, therefore, the discussion of three Philosophers concerning the wonder-working Word, whom I have portrayed as arguing among themselves (as the controversy of their sects compelled): so that the hidden property of all sacred things might shine forth more clearly. From these, and from so many and such great ones, a easier opportunity may be provided for us to choose the one wonder-working and beatific name of sacred names. And so that you may know the whole matter by a brief summary: Sidonius, first thought to be of the School of Epicurus <note>A school of philosophy that emphasized seeking modest pleasure and freedom from fear and pain through knowledge.</note>, but later found to have sworn allegiance to no man's words—a philosopher of every kind—sets out on a journey abroad out of a desire for learning. After many travels, having entered Swabia <note>original: "Sueuiam", a historical region in southwestern Germany.</note>, he meets two philosophers in the town of Pforzheim <note>original: "Phorce".</note>: Baruchia the Hebrew and Capnion the Christian. With them, he discusses various disciplines, and soon the very knowledge of divine and human things; concerning opinion, faith, miracles, the virtues of words and figures, and the secret operations and mysteries of seals. In this way, the sacred names and consecrated characters of all nations which excel in some excellent Philosophy or non-secular ceremonies come into question. An enumeration of symbols is made, diligently by each according to the rite of his sect, until at last in the third book, Capnion, with great effort, gathers from all sacred things the one name "ihsuh" <note>The "Pentagrammaton" (IHShVH), a Christian Kabbalistic version of the Hebrew name of Jesus, formed by inserting the letter 'Shin' into the four-letter name of God (YHWH).</note>, into which the virtue and power of all sacred things is referred, which is blessed always and above all. But now, let us hear Sidonius himself.*

# SIDONIUS DISCUSSES HIS OWN BACKGROUND, THEN
# THE LINEAGE AND ORIGIN OF THE PEOPLE OF PFORZHEIM,
### and how an excellent character can be produced
### in rough and mountainous places. CHAPTER I.

->SIDONIUS.<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'S' depicting a stylized plant or leafy design within a square frame.</image-desc>
If there is anything at all in human nature anywhere, my friend Baruchia and you Capnion—both of you the goal and end <note>original: "Gades atq; meta", referring to the Pillars of Hercules/Cadiz as the ends of the known world.</note> of my unbelievable longing, and the refuge of my admiration which has followed me from afar (for it pleases me to speak fearlessly only when you alone are commanding and listening)—that produces perpetual pleasure for us, this one thing, as I think, is agreed upon by all: it is almost nothing else than to perceive new things daily, things foreign to our senses, or things perceived at another time or in another way than they were felt long ago. This is what usually entices our soul, which is greedy for beauty, to a desire for experience by some most recent and wonderful marvel, and propels it into a work however arduous. By this, I could easily believe that not only my ancestral lineage (which clearly has been famous for many centuries, and now stands out for its skill in all things) but also the whole of Sidon <note>An ancient Phoenician port city in modern-day Lebanon.</note>, from which I have both my name and origin, and even the whole fatherland, has been incited to labors—however sweet, yet hard—either by pleasant novelty or stupendous antiquity. For from ancient times, the Phoenicians have been accustomed to indulge, more than can be said, in the exploration of various regions and the study of new things: they who, by their own diligence, first invented letters, the benefit of which they bestowed upon the Greeks (who were perhaps not ungrateful men). And after an exquisite reckoning of numbers, they measured the lands and the heavens. They were likewise most expert in natural and martial arts. Finally, that nation always saw both the customs and the cities of many men; a fact which has brought glory to them in the greatest part of the lands...

yielded, and a great proclamation above the others. By your leave, I perhaps praise my own people too much; but love of country wins out, and nonetheless, so does the truth itself. For even that ancient dogma concerning atoms first belonged to a certain countryman of mine from Sidon, a man named Mochus, and that was even before the Trojan War. This is so you may recognize how much the Phoenicians <note>The Phoenicians were an ancient maritime civilization based in the Levant, credited in antiquity with inventing the alphabet and several philosophical concepts.</note> excelled through their industry and the investigations of many geniuses—a fact that was no more hidden from the historian than from the poet, who sang thus:

> *The Phoenicians were the first, if the story is believed, who dared*
> *To mark the enduring voice with simple shapes;*
> *Not yet did Memphis by the river know how to weave papyrus* <note>original: "biblos," referring to the papyrus plant used for paper in Egypt.</note>
> *And only birds and wild beasts, sculpted animals,*
> *Preserved magical languages on stones.* <note>These verses are from the Roman poet Lucan's "Pharsalia," describing the Phoenician invention of the alphabet before the Egyptian use of papyrus and hieroglyphs.</note>

Desirous of their names of praise and of following their footsteps, to which (as usually happens) the flow of my paternal blood finally led me, I have already been occupied for a long time among many things by sea and land, seeking out all the best craftsmen of people and things: so that I might hear what was said from one place, and learn what must be done from another. For I was not content with only my fatherland or the whole neighborhood of Tripoli <note>A major city in Phoenicia, modern-day Lebanon.</note>, where the mistress of diverse and rather universal arts truly began to be twisted by barbaric ritual; but I went away, I departed, I escaped, I broke out. After Lebanon and Syria, I traveled further than that famous Menelaus <note>A legendary King of Sparta in Greek mythology; Sidonius is comparing his own travels to the long journey of Menelaus after the Trojan War.</note>, who informed his guests Telemachus and Pisistratus about his wanderings with these verses:

> *I have indeed suffered not a few things, and in many dangers*
> *In which I arrived after eight years of toil,*
> *Even to Cyprus, then Phoenicia and the Egyptian fields,*
> *Then through the Ethiopians and Sidonians and Erembi,*
> *And Libya, where the horned lambs graze.* <note>A translation of lines from Homer's "Odyssey" (Book 4), where Menelaus describes his eight-year journey home.</note>

Thus, in so long a trial of those same paths, labor was not lacking for me, until, having first left Britain, then Gaul, and then with the Rhine as my guide, a journey into Germany was granted, so that I might see and test both of you wise men as much with my eyes as with my ears. For I would translate that saying of Plautus <note>A Roman playwright.</note> thus: one witness who has heard is worth ten who have seen, especially in getting to know those philosophers whom I have heard you are by your fame, most celebrated everywhere. 

So that I may first be permitted to speak of you, Capnion <note>original: "Capnion," the Greek translation of Reuchlin's name (Rauch means 'smoke' in German, kapnos in Greek). Reuchlin frequently used this Hellenized name.</note>, whom I had heard was from Pforzheim <note>original: "Phorcensem." Pforzheim is a city in southwestern Germany, Reuchlin's birthplace.</note> based on the inscriptions of your books and tablets; I wondered more often than about any other thing, why the wooded Swabia <note>original: "sylvestris Suevia," likely referring to the Black Forest region of the Swabian territory.</note> would produce philosophy. Then, there were certain companions of my journey, experts with me in the abstruse arts, who responded that it would not be difficult to believe, for a harsh environment can produce a certain outstanding natural talent. They commemorated a certain Bishop of Regensburg <note>original: "Ratisponanum... Antistitem."</note> called "Polyphemus" in the Greek language, but in the vernacular named Albert the Great <note>original: "Albrecht... Magnum." Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280) was a Dominican friar and bishop who was a teacher of Thomas Aquinas and a major figure in medieval science and philosophy.</note>, who seemed to surpass not only Aristotle, but also other primary followers of the Peripatetic <note>The school of philosophy founded by Aristotle.</note> philosophy, yet he was nourished in Swabia and of its stock. I myself knew this to have been so. For I had already read some of his books, written in Latin by that man, which by their singular excellence were translated—contrary to the usual custom—into the Greek language. 

Finally, they brought forward reasons for migrating that were neither vain nor fragile: that your people easily migrate elsewhere because of the thinness of their sustenance, because of the trouble of cultivating the fields, and because of the lack of money. I will add for my part that the region is not accustomed to merchants with abundance. Therefore, I thought that among the migrating Swabians there would always be a plenty of the best teachers, since those who flee sterile lands must travel toward all the best things. And so, the fact that you are powerful in learning, eloquence, and counsel is not because you were born from a forest—which they once called the Bacenic or the Hyrcanian, and now call the Black Forest <note>original: "Nigram."</note>—but as I hear from your people, it is because you have visited not only ancient Paris <note>original: "Lutetiam." Lutetia was the Roman name for Paris, a major center of medieval and Renaissance learning.</note>, but indeed almost the whole of Gaul and Germany...

# ON THE WONDER-WORKING WORD, BOOK I.

You have likely traveled through the schools of Italy and surveyed Rome, the very capital of studies. However, I seem to see that the suitability of the **Phorcensian** territory <note>Sidonius refers here to Pforzheim, Reuchlin’s birthplace, Latinized as *Phorca* or *Phorce*.</note> contributes not a little to the talents of its natives; and the vast number of learned men born there makes this evident. For one’s fatherland possesses a power of generative condition hardly less than that of one's father himself, if we believe Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) who wrote on the influence of environment and ancestry.</note>. You are hearing a rather long speech from a newcomer and a traveler who dares to discourse upon your own region. But, so that you do not think me a sluggish investigator of that place—which is a source of ancestry for one of you and a place of refuge for the other—I have discovered its history from the most learned authors of ancient monuments. For it is well established that long ago, during the Trojan conflict—less a war than a single great battle—**Phorcys** the younger was a leader of the Phrygian army, according to the testimony of Homer, who says in his catalog of ships:

> *That Phorcys was the leader of the Phrygians, along with Ascanius.* <note>original: "Phorcys ille Phrygum ductor fuit Aſcaniuſqꝫ," quoting Homer's Iliad 2.862.</note>

Thus, when Troy fell to adverse fortune, those few survivors from the countless many who had saved their lives were forced to seek other homes and hope for other kingdoms. Therefore, **Aeneas**, along with **Ascanius** and his companion in dangers, **Phorcys**, and many others besides, headed for Italy. But while Ascanius was founding a town beneath the Alban Mount, and while each of the others was designating a place for himself to stay here and there, this Phorcys the younger—the grandson of the elder Phorcys (who was King of Sardinia and Corsica, said to have been defeated by Atlas and submerged in the sea) by his mother Euryale—entered Germany by way of Italy and the Insubres <note>A Celtic people of Cisalpine Gaul, centered around Milan.</note>. Having crossed the vast lake between the sources of the Danube <note>The Latin *Ister* refers to the lower Danube, but here denotes the general source region in the Black Forest.</note> and the Rhine, he traveled through easier mountain passes and plains toward the setting sun. There he came upon a most crystal-clear river, rich with fish, and on its bank, a humble hut. An old man, weighed down by years and leaning entirely upon a staff, dragged his weary footsteps toward it; when he saw Phorcys approaching in such a deserted forest with so great a company of his household, he was terrified, thinking he was about to give up the ghost. When Phorcys asked him what this river was called, the old man replied that its name was **Aeneas**. <note>Reuchlin is engaging in a creative "folk etymology," identifying the local river Enz with the hero Aeneas.</note> Then Phorcys, stunned by that name and turning his face toward the river, immediately added:

> *Are you that Aeneas, whom to Dardanian Anchises,*
> *Gracious Venus bore by the wave of Phrygian Simois?* <note>original: "Tu' ne ille Aeneas quem Dardanio Anchiſę..." Sidonius quotes Virgil’s Aeneid 1.617.</note>

Virgil later transferred these verses into his *Aeneid*, delighted by their ancient, foreign character. Here, therefore, the newcomer took the omen and his lot—that this would be his place to stay. He began to exhort his multitude not to despise the divine oracle he had discovered in the name of the Trojan priest. For to those whom the original Aeneas had long since left behind across no small distance, another Aeneas now clearly revealed itself to them. The Phrygian leader, with both a royal mind and royal custom, commanded everyone to strive as much as they could to uproot the oaks on all sides and turn the deserted field into a plain for cultivation. In that place, he built a small town and a citadel, which he called **Phorce** after his own name and that of his grandfather. So great was his love for that most grave, holy, and honorable man Aeneas, that at the mere sound of the river being called *Aeneas*, he chose to settle there as if at a perpetual monument to the Trojan Aeneas. 

In the course of time, as the modest family grew into a populous people, and the narrowness of their initial settlement forced them to fell the neighboring forests, cultivate the fields, build villages, and raise up cities, they say he founded many other towns there besides the rural and urban ones. Each of these he marked with individual names—after his mother or after the building materials—for the eternal memory of his lineage. Some of these names devouring antiquity strives to abolish, while the immodesty of barbarians tries to change others. For what was once **Euryale** is now called **Aurelium**; what was formerly **Stheno** is now **Stein**; what was **Scylla** is called **Schöll**; and what was once **Medusa** was changed in a later age into a new citadel. <note>Reuchlin is linking the names of the Gorgons (Euryale, Stheno, and Medusa), who were the daughters of the mythical Phorcys, to local German place names near Pforzheim to give his home a classical pedigree.</note> Thus the Gorgon daughters of Phorcys (whose fame is widespread and whose remembrance is most ancient) are preserved in this fertile soil, this pleasant site of the town of **Capnion**—that is, in the furrow of your own birth—in the everlasting memory of men that shall endure through every age. And lest there should also be lacking to posterity the story of Ascanius, the companion who returned...

and a long-lasting monument to his colleague, he even began to build something similar in the world, taking the surnames of that city which he was furrowing under Mount Albanus, which by an equal name he called **Alba Longa** <note>original: "Longam Albam," the ancient mother-city of Rome, here used to create a parallel with Reuchlin's homeland.</note>. ## He explains the cause of his arrival; he opens his opinion on virtue, on law, and on metaphysics, and something regarding miracles. CHAPTER II.

After the arts of speaking, talking, and thinking <note>The Trivium: Grammar, Rhetoric, and Logic.</note>, in which I was instructed under the rod, and then after the disciplines of counting and measuring <note>The Quadrivium: specifically Arithmetic and Geometry</note>, drawn in by an inner spirit, I was led by an admiration of things both on earth and in the heavens toward natural teachings, in which I had determined to spend the whole course of my life; because concerning morals (which branch some call Philosophy), I thought little effort should be given. For I do not judge it worthy of too deep an occupation, because moral practice itself consists of common observation and the social interaction of common life; which threats, flatteries, fear, and vengeance teach to our elders, and also certain natural goods granted to the virtues themselves, which can neither be taught nor studied: but rather, they grow strong as the customs of each region demand. Whence we see that what is called Virtue here is considered a vice elsewhere.

<margin>Law.</margin>
Therefore, it is my opinion that civility and jurisprudence are contained solely in the persuasion of the common people or the judges, whether you achieve this through oratorical eloquence or through gifts and revenues, provided that he who presides over the pronouncement of the law is soothed. For in my reading, a most learned man is found without controversy: a certain man called **Barbarius** <note>Barbarius Philippus, a famous legal case of a runaway slave who was elected to high office in Rome; his acts were later upheld as valid to prevent legal chaos.</note>, who, though a fugitive slave, sought the praetorship at Rome, was then designated praetor and finally performed the duties of the praetorship; and it was accepted that none of those things he had done under the cloak of such great dignity should be rejected. This same grave author left written for posterity whether this could happen: that even he about whom a sentence has been passed ought to be accepted as free-born, even if in reality he was a freedman, because a judged matter is accepted as the truth. And **Paulus** <note>Julius Paulus, a highly influential 3rd-century Roman jurist.</note>, most skilled in the law of the Romans, says: Today, by the custom of the Emperors, if a silver-plated candelabrum is reported as silver, it is also the law [that it is silver], but not household furniture, because "error makes the law" <note>original: "error ius faciat," a famous legal maxim meaning that a general public error can create a valid legal precedent.</note>. Indeed, what has pleased the people or the prince or the king—that is, the judge—then has the force of law both through custom and through legal constitutions. For as **Julian** <note>Salvius Julianus, a Roman jurist who organized the Edictum Perpetuum.</note> says: Since laws hold us for no other reason than that they have been received by the judgment of the people; and since the people, by a royal law, appear to confer all command and power upon the king, it is clear that all jurisprudence depends solely upon the will of men. If it is supportive [of the people], a subduer of good and evil, it is called a good thing, both public and private; but if otherwise, the contrary. For on account of the iniquities which occur while the people either disapprove or tolerate them, **Hesiod**, in his book of *Works and Days*, when he had written about bad kings and judges and justice, finally intended that the common people often suffer for the sins of kings—that is, the judges. Indeed, not only he himself, but also **Homer**, and all of antiquity, named all judges "kings," who carry the scepter as a sign of jurisdiction. A witness of this against **Agamemnon** was that noble oath of **Achilles**, explained in six or seven verses of the *Iliad*. I speak not before the unlearned, but, as I think and say to myself, I speak in the sight of the most learned and most refined of men, so that it may not escape you how that famous and common exercise of law, and by whom

is bid for at a huge price, and held as almost more than divine by the consultants of controversies <note>i.e., lawyers</note>, is to be more rightly judged as being of no or mediocre importance—like some sedentary or cobbler's craft—especially for a man who willingly directs himself toward high and most worthy things with the greatest praise, and does not instead admire those fragile, falling, flowing, and empty things, the mere mockeries of glory, beauty, riches, and age. A grave and holy witness and a very good author, **Cicero**, will be cited (if you wish) for this discourse; he dared to defend my opinion in that cause before the tribunals, even while **Servius** <note>Servius Sulpicius Rufus, a famous Roman jurist and contemporary of Cicero</note> listened unwillingly, who then thought himself someone learned in civil law. I beg you, **Capnion** <note>The Greek nickname for Johannes Reuchlin, meaning "Little Smoke."</note>, who are said to have even sweated in the workshop of that same profession all the way to the crown and laurel <note>A reference to Reuchlin’s doctoral degree in law.</note>: what ornament, what dignity, what grace, what admiration is located in that study? It depends on such a thin opinion of men,
<margin>The highest law is the highest injustice.</margin>occupied with individual letters and the punctuation of words; it is proclaimed by everyone—I do not say only commoners, but also nobles—to be the authority for all factions, the strength of injuries, the fire of quarrels, and the fuel of inequity. It sets as its goal only the empty names of magistrates, honors full of daily fear, mercenary gains, and riches that no wise man should desire. Because of this, it openly wins the enmity of many for its practitioners, before whose faces so many **Antonies** and so many **Catilines** <note>Historical figures used here as archetypes of political enemies and chaotic rebels.</note> toss about, and do not allow a mind seeking rest to be quiet. Furthermore, it is not difficult to know what is observed by everyone; but that which is not observed in every street, they say is not law. Why, then, shall I admire so much what any butchers, cooks, sausage-makers, fishermen, bird-catchers, and hunters might know along with me? Does it seem a great thing to you to know the name of every law and to apply it to every outcome? Why will you not value more highly the perfumer—whom they call an **apothecary** from his "storing" of things—who knows all the jars, boxes, pitchers, bowls, cups, vials, spices, pigments, and drugs in his shop? Or the cobbler who remembers to match any mold to any foot, and at the same time does not forget the awls, needles, shears, and thimbles? All these things are taught by use, practice, necessity, and urgent poverty; sometimes a brute hunger forces one to imitate and fashion things similar to these:

> Who made his "Greetings" <note>original Greek: "chaire" (χαιρε)</note> easy for the parrot,
> And taught the magpies to attempt our words?
> The belly, master of art and giver of wit,
> Denies that the artist follows voices.

As that Satirist <note>The Roman poet Persius, quoting the prologue to his *Satires*.</note> says. Therefore, since it is not learned for its own sake, but for the daily commerce of human living and for earthly desires foreign to the human mind, how should I join it to most sacred philosophy as if it were a limb, without which philosophy might seem crippled—just as one who lacks a foot is called lame, and one who lacks a tongue is called mute? I leave these things aside, for I do not know what storm or what wave has drifted me here. I return, therefore, to where I had digressed. For I have determined to complete the whole course of my life in the contemplation of natural things, from which alone arises that which we can truly call <term>science</term> <note>original: "scientia," meaning certain knowledge derived from nature and logic, rather than mere opinion.</note>. For all other things are either instruments of science, or disciplines of calculation, or the use of common estimation, or fictions of thoughts about things which they believe exist without body or matter, and are therefore called "simple." Since these abstract concepts are nowhere, yet there is a kind of men who do not admit that they take their science from the things offering themselves to our senses—which can neither be deceived nor deceive—but instead they burden the mind with the thought of certain very thin breaths and separated forms. Because these are not in nature, but are thought to be *above* nature, they therefore call them **Metaphysics**. I do not argue these things with the intent of refuting learned men, although they seem worthy of reproach if we were to weigh in a fair balance the rite of knowing—from what fountain it is drawn and by what path it proceeds. On which matter you may allow your **Aristotle** to speak, best **Capnion**, in whose wrestling-ground <note>original: "palæstra," a metaphor for a school or place of intellectual exercise.</note> they say you have exercised yourself most greatly, and from there, after the set time of the gymnastic contest, you carried away the distinguished tiara and golden rings <note>Academic regalia signifying his doctoral status.</note>.

For this Baruchias <note>A character in the dialogue representing a Jewish sage</note> is said to follow **Pythagoras** more closely (from what I hear), even if he lived as a more ancient Magus <note>A term for an ancient priest or wise man, often associated with Zoroastrianism or hidden wisdom</note>. Therefore, that **Stagirite** <note>Aristotle, who was born in the city of Stagira</note>, in the second book of his *Posterior Analytics* <note>original: "resolutoriorum posteriorum"; Aristotle's foundational work on logic and scientific demonstration</note>, near the end, explained roughly according to this opinion four points that are quite relevant here. Listen both of you, if perhaps I can explain it well enough in Latin. For Aristotle is (as you know) excessively thorny in Greek, and even in Latin he is rough; he wished to be understood only by his own followers. His words have this meaning: from **sensation** grows that which we call **memory**; then from memory, through frequent practice, **experience** is born. For many memories constitute a single experience. From experience—or rather from the universal concept coming to rest in its entirety within the soul—the principle of **art** and **science** arises. This universal is the "one" that exists within the many individuals, being the same in each of them. You have heard Aristotle, to whom the poet **Afranius** <note>A Roman comic poet of the 2nd century BCE</note> gave a similar, charming, wise, and no less true account of the source of knowledge in his book titled *The Chair* <note>original: "Sellæ"</note>, in this verse:

->*Practice begat me, and Memory, my mother, bore me.*<-

Therefore, since those who would acquire knowledge must use the arts and the instruments of the senses, without which it happens that we are ignorant of everything. (For the blind man does not know colors, nor the deaf man the measures of verses or the melody of the lyre.) It will now be necessary for us to be able to grasp corporeal things, since from a body that which is most subtle flows in a kind of perpetual stream toward the openings of our senses. Imagination itself, with tireless motion and rejecting all leisure, draws this into its chamber, where the forms of things shine back into human intelligence, like a ray bent back into the pupil from within. All these things are bodies and the flow of bodies; and **Empedocles** <note>A Greek philosopher who famously proposed that "like is known by like"</note> seemed to me to have spoken more correctly in saying that like is known by like.

->*Neither delay nor rest is granted to any of the flowing.*<-

Since we perceive perpetually, as **Lucretius** <note>The Roman poet and Epicurean philosopher</note> says:

> Indeed, various senses are present in living creatures,
> Each of which perceives its own proper object within itself.

Why "properly"? Because other things either deceive or are deceived, which a person might believe while unaided by any senses. But by Hercules, though I fear I may be suggesting it in a foreign voice, that wise interpreter of **Epicurus** <note>referring again to Lucretius</note> attempts to draw me back:

> Indeed, he says, the greatest part of these things deceives,
> Because of the opinions of the mind which we ourselves add,
> So that things not seen by the senses are taken as if they were seen.
> For nothing is more excellent than to discern clear facts.

Those who try to climb above nature do not consider this; they leap into the heights from which they cannot find a footing. Despite so many things being born in the vastness of this world’s universe, they nevertheless labor over <margin>Human labor.</margin> fictions; they sweat over "naked entities" and the "species of things," over "immovable divine things," "subsistences," "primary parts of reason," "principles," and "substances of the gods"—simple, incorporeal things dwelling outside the home of heaven and leading the best life there. All of these (on the authority of the poets) were discovered through a specific and showy art of fabrication, serving as delights for the ears and as solaces for our greed, which is always hungry for diverse business. Therefore, let all who meditate on such disconnected things be gone; let them go to bed and sleep the whole night through. **Homer** said that sleep does not touch Jove alone, as if none of the other celestial beings could be alone; yet we clearly know nothing of him, but only dream of him. This, it seems to me, the same poet wisely suggests when he describes the Dream sent to **Agamemnon** as being a messenger of Jove. Whatever we know of Jove is most similar to a dream. Yet, what should we think of "dignities" and "principles"? The not-unskilled **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle's school</note>—whom all of Germany now uses, and uses alone, despising all other most noble authors—contend that there is no "science" of these things, because science and demonstration come from prior and better-known things; since all science depends on these, and yet there is no [science] of a principle...

<summary>Sidonius uses Aristotelian and Epicurean philosophy to argue that all human knowledge begins with sensory experience, dismissing abstract metaphysics and scholastic "entities" as mere poetic fictions or "dreams." He critiques the contemporary German reliance on the Peripatetic school to the exclusion of other ancient wisdom.</summary>

# ON THE MIRACULOUS WORD, BOOK I.

881

[...] beginning, since it is itself before all things. Yet it will not be fitting for that to be unknown, by which all things shine forth, appear, and are known. From where, then, shall we know the principles? From the senses. Listen again to your **Aristotle**, **Capnion** <note>The Greek-derived name Johannes Reuchlin used for himself, meaning "smoky," a translation of his German name</note>, in the first volume of his *Topics* <note>original: "locorum primo volumine"</note>, when he says: "If any person wishes to doubt whether all snow is white or not, he has need of his senses." Therefore, the faith which we have in science from principles consists entirely in things subjected to nature and the senses; wherefore nothing of those things that have not been connected to body and matter is rightly enclosed within the limits of science. But if this is so, one single knowledge of things will suffice, 

<margin>Physics.</margin>
which the Greeks call **physics**, and you are accustomed to call **natural philosophy**. It investigates and searches out the conditions of those things which are true and are perceived by us without a veil, along with their causes, effects, times, places, modes, outcomes, entireties, and parts:

->*From whence comes the trembling of the earth; by what force the deep seas swell,*<-
->*Breaking their barriers and sinking back into themselves again;*<-
->*The various eclipses of the Sun and the labors of the Moon;*<-
->*From whence comes the race of men and of beasts, and likewise rain and fire;*<-
->*Arcturus, the Pleiades, the Hyades, and the twin Triones <note>The Great and Little Bear constellations</note>;*<-
->*Why the winter suns hasten so much to dip themselves in the ocean,*<-
->*Or what delay stands in the way of the slow nights.*<-

Physics, the observer of natures, embraces all these things, in which all the most learned men may delight themselves in a marvelous way throughout their whole lives. For the sake of this, as you have heard from me before, I have traveled through many places and through the dangers of places, so that I might see the wonders of nature, or at least grasp them by hearing.

<margin>India.</margin>
I even set out for **India** itself: to see if I could discern those things which are reported to be seen there—though rarely, yet sometimes—with my own eyes, monstrous things and like portents: **manticores**, golden water, the magnetic stone, the **pantarba** <note>A legendary magnetic stone said to attract gold</note>, pygmies, **sciapodes** <note>Mythical "shadow-foots" who used their single giant foot as a parasol</note>, the tiger, the phoenix bird, pearls, and likewise the **ichthyophagi** <note>Fish-eaters</note>. 

<margin>Africa.</margin>
Then through **Africa**, so that I might look upon the tribe that keeps a dog for a King, by whose movement they divine commands for themselves. I omit other things which I was able to look at but not fully perceive: one-eyed princes, **Anthropophagi** <note>Cannibals</note>, and **Cynocephali** <note>Dog-headed people</note>, the greatest part of all of which is fabulous. Regarding springs and rivers, some of the things said are true, and some are adorned with fictions. 

<margin>Miracles of Nature.</margin>
In **Asphaltis** <note>The Dead Sea</note> bitumen is truly produced, but as for the claim that nothing is said to sink in that lake of Judea, certainly the opposite is sometimes found. In **Dodona**, the spring of **Jupiter** both lights extinguished torches and extinguishes those that are lit. The spring of **Hammon** is cold by day and boils at night. An island situated opposite the **Timavus** river abounds in hot springs right in the sea itself, which rise and fall with the sea; I experienced this very thing with the men of **Trieste**. The water of the **Lyncestae** makes people intoxicated like wine; indeed, even among your own people of **Swabia**, above the river Fils <note>original: "Philifsium"</note> at the town of **Göppingen** <note>original: "Geppiniæ"</note>, a spring flows with almost the taste of wine. Not a day, but a year itself would fail me if I desired to recount the individual miracles of nature, which nonetheless are not hidden from you. For from what I have received from the most learned men, you so abound in various experiences of both letters and things, that there is nothing, whether so small or so great, that escapes you, whether seen in places or known from books. From this, I easily conclude that I proclaim many of these wonders in vain; for while I am stunned by the novelty of the place where I stay, you, by your frequent experience, consider it a common and daily matter. 

But without controversy, I seek out you yourselves as the one miracle in **Germany**—men of such virtue and such learning, how grave, how holy, and how exceeding all that can be said in the best judgments of you. This I found sufficiently explored at the very entrance, at the very doors and the beginning of our greeting: what divine form of faces, what charm in words, what humanity in receiving me, what speeches of exact wisdom often interspersed—your entire characters show you to be most perfect men. It is incredible how much I rejoice to enjoy your conversation and your speech, adorned with learned words and polished oratory, and your sentiments worthy of being known and heard. Thus, by your so liberal and so generous conversation, I am able to lighten and soothe, or rather entirely lift away, the many and great labors I have undertaken on so many journeys.

*After Sidonius’s praise, Baruchias immediately sets out to refute his words, having gained goodwill by praising others and downplaying his own person.*

->### CHAPTER III.<-

<image-desc>A large, ornate woodcut initial 'T' featuring a stylized floral design with scrolling acanthus leaves within a square border.</image-desc>
**T**HEN, stirred by the abundance of words, **BARUCHIAS** said: "Listen to what Sidon has brought forth. For you so easily believe him while he proclaims great things about the Phoenicians; let those people now merely appear to condemn the East for its ignorance and barbarity, so that they might say some Scythian or Sarmatian <note>Ancient nomadic tribes often used as symbols of "uncivilized" people</note>, enemies of human learning, has invaded and held that region, so that no one may cultivate the arts in the future. But you, Sidonius, into what great wonders do you force me to speak?" But he replied: "There is little in me, Baruchias, that you should value so highly; for you wear yourself out in vain over those very tiny things I have recognized in myself. And take great care lest you have, quite rightly, given the name of 'eloquence' to my words. For what have we expressed with this meager breath of ours, other than that the Punic <note>Carthaginian/Phoenician</note> people are most fit for education? This is something that all histories hand down, and the matter is almost [certain]. I also touched upon the praise of your **Swabia** <note>Reuchlin's home region in Germany</note>: of which you are both rich examples to the world, and no other spectacle besides you will be needed." Afterward, according to his habit of long-windedness, a certain frenzy fell from his lips, namely: that only a nature perceptible by the senses is worthy of art or discipline. And if not concerning all things (as he [seemed] to think), then at least concerning these very things which lie beneath nature and are open to the senses, is that which we call **science** <note>original: "scientia"; in this context, it refers to systematic, provable knowledge</note> most [firm]. "For concerning divine things," he said, "I believe true cognition is granted to no one." When Baruchias interrupted this speech, he said: "Most learned Sidonius, and, as I think, the best of all men, it is far more excellent—forgive me. For a certain innate rashness in speaking almost makes me forestall this **Capnion** <note>The Greek-derived name Johannes Reuchlin used for himself, meaning "smoky"</note>, a man of venerable integrity, a veritable sea of letters, and a divine mirror of our age. In this dispute, he should rightly be preferred to me; but it is an old custom that whoever stammers the most is the most eager to speak, and no field lies more open than to the ignorant. This is what happened to me: that while you were discoursing, I might break the silence before this man of world-renowned wisdom. But bear it with an equal mind." Then he [Sidonius] said: "Nay, proceed freely and weave together what you have begun." 

"Therefore, however diligently and eloquently you have spoken on many matters, Sidonius," Baruchias began, "much more so than our local philosophers are accustomed to do—who, like certain jackdaws <note>original: "graculi"; a common humanist insult for Scholastic philosophers who repeat jargon without understanding</note>, chatter all day long in their business with nothing but a single barbaric noise, with no ornaments of words, no flower of eloquence, nor any duty of an orator. You would not think they were dealing with the most graceful philosophy, but rather the profane haggling of the common folk, the bidding for [stolen] goods, the tumult of revelers, or the insults of the lightest [gossips]. From their company, I have contracted a similar contagion and a matching stain, so that you might not unjustly hurl at me that line of Tyndareus written in the *Orestes* of **Euripides**:

> Live as a barbarian, since you are an old man among barbarians. <note>original: "Vivas barbare cum sis vetulus inter barbaros"</note>

Nevertheless, however things stand, I shall perhaps deliberately set aside the praises concerning our fatherland, yourself, and ourselves; for the honesty of both of us forbids the first, your own fame the second, and the renown of the lands the third. To increase with speech those things which are [already] beyond praise is beyond our power—lest I 'bring owls to Athens,' as the Greek proverb goes <note>A phrase meaning to do something redundant or useless</note>. Furthermore, you have found such stability and truth in [physical] bodies—which are subject to so many and various [changes] at any moment, to the sea, the storm, and the whirlwind, and which cling to the very matter of corruption, daily motion, and inconstancy—that you believe science arises from nothing except what is **sensible** <note>perceptible by the five senses</note>. This makes me wonder: for I consider nothing to be so equally contrary to sincere and perfect knowledge as this very thing you call 'sensible.' I think, however, that which [is related] to the body..."

### ON THE WONDER-WORKING WORD, BOOK I.

...which, as you were saying, flows through the openings <note>Latin: *foramina*. The ancients believed sensory data entered the body through literal holes or pores in the sense organs.</note> of our senses in a kind of stream—not without certain very thin skins <note>Latin: *uelleribus*, literally "fleeces." Referring to the Epicurean theory of "idols" or films that peel off objects and travel through the air to the eye.</note> traveling through the air until they reach our bodies. For what ray of the mind could either stand still or be reflected without shaking upon such a mobile surface—as are all the things of nature that men perceive from the outside—so that such an illustrious work of divine humanity, or human divinity, might be fashioned from it within us? I do not deny that there is a certain doctrine, opinion, or judgment regarding such things. We distinguish ice from water, and we judge the latter to be fluid and the former more lasting; even though the ice arose just the other day from the water, and the water is ready to be dissolved back into it tomorrow. But that a constant and perpetual science <term>Scientia: in this period, "science" referred to certain, demonstrable knowledge, as opposed to "opinion."</term> of these things could exist, I utterly deny—and not only led by **Pythagoras**, whose follower you wanted me to be through fear (which I receive gladly as an honor, since I understand from that greatest of men and almost the God of philosophers, **Plato**, that the disciples of Pythagoras were so highly esteemed that he did not hesitate, though poor, to buy the small books of **Philolaus** <note>A Greek Pythagorean philosopher (c. 470 – c. 385 BC) whose works Plato supposedly used to write the *Timaeus*.</note> the Pythagorean for ten thousand denarii). 

But **Aristotle** also agrees with us in this matter, whose patronage we happily employ. For in the first volume of his *Posterior Analytics* <note>Latin: *posterioris resolutionis*. Reuchlin uses a more literal Latin translation of the Greek title *Analytica Posteriora*.</note>, after he had discussed at length what kind of cause we should choose for knowing, and who might appear to know properly and who to appear more learned, he added: "Therefore, that which is the object of knowledge in the absolute sense, it is impossible for it to be otherwise." <note>Aristotle, *Posterior Analytics* 1.2. Baruchias is arguing that since the physical world is always changing, it cannot be the object of "absolute knowledge."</note> This is not foreign even to **Plato**, who, after he had divided the world into the first, the *intelligible*, and the second, the *sensible*, added that the former is judged through the mind with reason, while the latter is judged through opinion, not without the senses. See which **Epicurus** you follow, who builds everything upon dust with a shadowy speech. I shall easily win with such great patrons. 

And if it ought not seem shameful to me to be conquered, refuted, and proven wrong by so great a man as you—who excel others in genius, learning, and dignity—I have often been forbidden by the decree of our ancestors to touch Philosophical matters (even at the very surface, as they say). And for that reason, **Germany** nourishes **Jews** who, though religious, are little learned, because they persuade students that they should rather shrink from philosophers than fall into errors through carelessness or, rather, curiosity—of which they believe those philosophers to be the primary authors. But I have done what greedy men usually do: the more I was deterred, the more fervently I drank, according to the opportunity of circumstances, the time, and my own capacity. Therefore, I confess that I have sometimes read **Aristotle**, and I have looked into **Plato**, from whom that which I cited to you before emerged. 

And even without them, I would have believed this same thing (as indeed I do) because of the great diversity among all the greatest men who write about natural things with some immortal praise for themselves—a diversity in which the truth cannot consist. First of all, to go from the streams to the fountain, I think that neither you nor our friend **Capnion** <note>The Greek nickname for Reuchlin himself, meaning "smoky."</note> will deny that a whole thing is known in the same way that it is established to exist. For if otherwise, opinion would be deceptive, reporting the thing to the mind’s gaze differently than it actually is. But the universe has, as it happens, its own principles, even on the authority of your **Epicurus** and **Lucretius**, who said:

> It is necessary that all things be separated from their principles.
> And that the World arose from principles of every kind.
---
-> — the discord of which <-
> Disturbed the intervals, paths, connections, weights, strikes,
> Collisions, and movements, mixing up the battles. <note>Quotes from Lucretius, *On the Nature of Things* (*De Rerum Natura*).</note>

Therefore, we know all things equally from the principles out of which they are made; the demonstration of the sciences depends upon their rule and measure, just as the inner chambers depend upon the doors. But when one wanders at the doors, by what means could I believe that one will withdraw correctly into the inner chambers? Those who are ignorant of the way go astray nonetheless. They are ignorant, those who rush here and there in crowds around the crossroads, walking by more than one path, so that as much as they are distant from one another, so much are they distant from the truth.

### CHAPTER IV.

<margin>Thales.</margin>
Shall I begin with those Phoenicians of yours, who were endowed with such great—and as you thought, first—investigation into the whole of nature? Or rather, shall I begin with **Thales** himself? Although he was a citizen of Miletus, he was nevertheless a most noble Phoenician <unclear>descendant</unclear> of Agenor <note>Agenor was the mythological King of Tyre in Phoenicia. This reflects the Renaissance habit of tracing Greek wisdom back to older, "Oriental" sources.</note>, and was said to have discussed the nature of things before all others. And, if Plato is to be believed, he was the first to be called a "Wise Man." What did he find, after his innumerable efforts and tireless studies, for the sake of which he cast aside the republic and the highest magistracies <unclear>of state</unclear>? What, I ask, did he find through his constant searching that was a worthy foundation for this illustrious machine <note>Latin: *machina*, a common Renaissance term for the structure of the cosmos.</note> that we see? 

<margin>Water.</margin>
How famous is his conclusion? **Water is the principle of all things.** For from it all things have come forth, and into water all things shall be resolved. No one can <unclear>doubt</unclear> that if we were to entrust the building of this massive globe to Thales’ judgment, we would always have to fear floods and surging stagnations, because (in his opinion) nature would be said to support these buildings of hers upon a liquid floor, which would collapse at any movement of the water. I say nothing <unclear>of the arguments</unclear> against those who would labor at the art of Architecture, but choose a swampy region for their domestic structure. Yet Thales may have intended some "river," or (as I <unclear>believe</unclear>) a certain "influence" from elsewhere which could have been the <unclear>source</unclear> of fertile causes—the one which **Homer** seems to me to name "Ocean," when he sang:

->**Ocean, the father of the gods, and Tethys their mother.**<-
<note>original Latin: "Oceanumq; deum patrem Tethynq; parentem." This is a quote from the Iliad (14.201).</note>

From him, however, his fellow countryman **Anaximander**—first a listener to his teaching, then his successor in the school—departed far in his focused work. 

<margin>The Infinite.</margin>

<margin>Air.</margin>
**Heraclitus of Ephesus**, a hater of the Philosophers and a mocker of Homer, belched out from his <unclear>exhaling</unclear> lungs and hot guts a thing unheard of in letters <unclear>and</unclear> left it written in no common <unclear>style</unclear>: that a certain sterile element, which 

<margin>Fire.</margin>
we call **Fire**, gives birth to the universe and that all things are referred back to it. In vain, therefore, did the Romans place **Vesta** <note>The Roman goddess of the hearth and sacred fire, whose priestesses (the Vestals) remained celibate.</note> in charge of celibacy. There succeeded Anaximenes the illustrious man **Anaxagoras**, for some time a citizen of Clazomenae, but thereafter a most distinguished Philosopher who, for the sake of Philosophy, spurned the <unclear>affairs</unclear> of the republic and all popular dignity. 

<margin>Participation.</margin>

<margin>Dense Air.</margin>
thought that **dense, infinite air** provided the cause for all things so that they might exist, and for that reason he is called "the Physicist." There followed also 

<margin>Numbers.</margin>
the sun of all secret Philosophy, from whom that craft first received its name: **Pythagoras of Samos**. I would truly say that he did not err, but simply disagreed with others. For he himself constructed the universe out of **Numbers**. I cease to praise 

<margin>Atoms.</margin>
this prince of Philosophers, who saw no predecessor and has no second, because no equal praise can be found by me. which everything is born: fire, air, water, and earth. He also taught two principal powers: **Strife** and **Friendship**, of which the latter joins things together, while the former

<margin>
Matter, form.
Privation.
</margin>
...forms and matter. From these, we perceive that shape results first, and the rest follow. **Aristotle**, more famous for the nobility of his art than even for his pupil **Alexander**, the King of the Macedonians, argued that all things grew together from matter that was stirred toward a "hunger" for form by means of **privation** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "privation" is the absence of a form that should naturally be present, which drives matter to change and take on new forms.</note>. Whoever tried to discover something based on these ideas established a certain "motion" in place of privation, believing it more effective for joining the two together. 

Do you really presume, **Sidonius**, that in such a great diversity and conflict among so many eminent men—and to use the names common back then, so many "Wise Men" and "Lovers of Wisdom"—that a certain and faithful truth can be established? This is especially true when they fight with such a marvelous struggle over the very first principles, so much so that you are forced to be ignorant of which one you should justly and piously award the palm of victory or the "clover of surrender" <note>original: "herbam dare" - an ancient Roman idiom meaning to acknowledge defeat.</note>. For as **Firmianus** <note>Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325), an early Christian author often called the "Christian Cicero."</note> says, no one has yet descended from heaven to pass judgment on the opinions of each individual. Surely you might find some who approve of the mind of **Epicurus** along with you, just as I find those who do not reject the dogmas of **Pythagoras** along with me. But the choice of our profession leads us away; suspicion removes the judges, and witnesses who can be refuted are not admitted.

->*Baruchias proves his own opinion concerning the First Being, showing that no certainty is to be sought in these fleeting things.*<-

### CHAPTER V.

<margin>
Causes and the principles of things.
</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial Q containing floral motifs and stylized foliage.</image-desc>
WHAT then? What shall we say are the principles of things? Certainly, there has always been a massive struggle among the most famous Philosophers, and the lawsuit is still before the judge. Therefore, since the beginnings are not yet certain, I ask you: what kind of true knowledge of things will you have, which are said to have arisen from such beginnings? For **Aristotle** believes we know something only when we recognize its principles, its causes, and its individual elements. And not only that, but we must also know *why* it is the cause of that thing, and not some other cause in some other way. 

It is foolish to seek stability in decaying things. Leave acorns to the pigs, hay to the oxen, and the physical foreboding of the weather to frogs and crows. Let the brutes and those subject to slaughter perceive mortal things; let us strive for higher things and embrace them with an eternal mind—not the things that are fluid and fragile beneath the sky, but those which are everlasting above the heavens. 

I will not attempt to force into the ears of our people things they haven't heard before, which even the most practiced minds can barely understand. For they would say I am separating knowledge from all universal things—and indeed, they would be right regarding things subject to the changeability of nature. For while we attend to the permanence of knowledge, we also see that torrent of nature, that unstable river, of which we touch nothing at any time except for a single point. 

Did our Preacher lose his mind—whoever he was who wrote **Ecclesiastes**, whether it was **Solomon**, or as many say, **Isaiah** himself? "What is it," he asks, "that has been? That which shall be." <note>Ecclesiastes 1:9</note> And a little before: "A generation passes away, and a generation arrives." <note>Ecclesiastes 1:4</note> 
<margin>
Ecclesiastes.
</margin>
Indeed, how will you be washed unless the wood is transformed? <note>Likely referring to the burning of wood to heat water for a bath.</note> How are you nourished, unless the vessel of your body distributes life-giving juices to each limb from cooked and transformed food and drink? Cattle become dung; dung becomes manure; manure becomes grass; grass becomes milk; and milk becomes cattle again. 

The **Age** <note>original: "saeculum" - the world-age or temporal world.</note> rotates all things, and for that reason it is named from "following" <note>original margin: "Etymon seculi" - Reuchlin suggests *saeculum* comes from *sequendo* (following/succeeding), because things follow one another.</note>, because it pushes forward things that are born so that one thing may follow another. Nature is always sculpting, so as not to be idle; just as if from wax, it makes now a horse, now a lion, and once that is destroyed, a man. 
<margin>
The Etymology of "Age" (*saeculum*).
</margin>
One survives the other, and the second always buries the first: **Lucilla** her husband, then Lucilla is buried; **Secunda** buries **Maximus**, then Secunda follows. **Antoninus** buried **Faustina**, then Antoninus followed. Everything happens this way. **Celer** buried **Hadrian**, then Celer followed. Indeed, the entire court of **Augustus**—his wife, daughter, descendants, ancestors, sister, **Agrippa**, kinsmen, servants, friends, **Arius**, **Maecenas**, priests, and doctors. Death is the mistress of the entire court. 

Here you would establish for me "perpetual knowledge," as if you could know if whoever wove the history of these people wrote it truly. **Hippocrates**, who cured innumerable diseases, is dead. **Heraclitus**, who filled the world with his theories on fire, is said to have been extinguished by "water under the skin" <note>original: "intercute aqua" - dropsy.</note>. Lice born from his own body killed **Democritus**.
<margin>
Death.
</margin>

### JOHANNES REUCHLIN ###

...gnats, nearly the tiniest crowd of animals. It is no different in other matters. For Ebony, among the types of trees, is at one time wood, at another <margin>The Quran.</margin> [something else]. And according to the book which is titled the *Alkorran* <note>The Quran</note> among your people, it is asked whether wood might soon become spirit; they say that the staff of Moses was at one time wood and at another [a serpent]. 

Therefore, I will deal briefly with you; for you are not the sort of person for whom I must put pre-chewed food into the mouth, as nurses are accustomed to doing for wailing infants. Nothing has been written, painted, or fashioned that [fully explains] why I hesitate when I consider that our natural talents do not have the strength to scrutinize nature; indeed, a thorn of doubt is always pricked into our minds. Nor is the thorn stuck in the heel ever radically pulled out. Shall we boast about every species that gives form to any matter without a false judgment, <margin>Our soul.</margin> we who do not yet perfectly know what or how our own soul is—that by which we live, breathe, feel, and understand? Regarding this matter, there will be no need for me [to argue] with you. You yourself know how many varieties of opinion exist on this subject, and how many are circulated. For <margin>Epicurus.</margin> **Epicurus**, whom you seem to imitate, says the soul is a mixture beyond mere appearance:

->From this comes heat, motion, and the hidden power of wind.<-
->From this air begins; from this all things are set in motion.<-
<note>Reuchlin is quoting the Roman poet Lucretius, who explained Epicurean philosophy.</note>

**Xenophanes** says it is from earth and water; **Parmenides** from earth and fire. **Empedocles** and **Critias** say it is blood; **Anaximenes** says air; **Hipparchus** fire. The **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> say it consists of a "fifth essence"; **Democritus**, a spirit inserted into the mobile; **Zeno**, a spirit joined to the body. **Heraclitus** [the physicist] says it is of stellar substance. **Heraclitus of Pontus** says it is light. **Hippocrates** <margin>Various opinions on the soul.</margin> says it is a thin [spirit] diffused through the whole body. **Posidonius** calls it an "idea"; **Pythagoras**, a harmony; **Xenocrates**, a self-moving number; **Plato**, a moving essence. **Aristotle**, seeking a new name, boastfully invented "entelechy" <note>Aristotle’s term for the "actualization" or "perfection" of a body.</note>: the perfection of the soul, as if it were the goal of the craftsman. 

That these mortal discourses on the soul ought to be refuted is argued by that man of the greatest integrity and most ample dignity, the famous **Gregory of Nazianzus**, in his book against **Eunomius**. Therefore, if we are ignorant of ourselves, how do we hope to grasp the knowledge of the rest? <margin>Know thyself <note>original: "Γνῶθι σαυτὸν"</note></margin> How great was the multitude of excellent writers up until the times of **Jerome** and **Augustine**, and yet nothing certain had been left that one could grasp regarding the soul—which (as I, a seeker of every sect, testify) you were perhaps able to know from the letters sent back and forth between them? For concerning you, **Capnion** <note>Reuchlin's own Greek-derived nickname, meaning "Smoke."</note>, there is no reason to doubt, for you follow the doctrine of the Nazarene, of whose light both of these men were most studious heralds. 

You possess my judgment concerning things that are either joined to the body or can fall under the senses in some way: because of the speed of the moment—by which that swift torrent of nature immediately seizes and alters what stands—and because of the ignorance of the senses, the hidden lurking-places of causes, the "eyes of bats" <note>A common metaphor for human intellect being blinded by the "light" of truth, just as bats are blinded by the sun.</note>, and the <margin>Human science.</margin> discovery of immediate conditions (which they call "human passions"), science regarding these things cannot be acquired so suddenly, nor sit firmly, nor be faithfully perceived. For (as is the opinion of **Heraclitus**) the thing changes before you can apply your thought to its circumstances. I see **Empedocles** making a leap into Etna, and I think I know that Empedocles is [at] Etna; but while this voice is still gripped between my teeth, Empedocles is no more, and just like something that does not exist, a story will be told. More credit is given to the one speaking than is shown to the one listening. 

Even if you wish to announce in a single moment what you desire to be known, **Lycophron** (the son of **Periander** and **Melissa**), lest he describe a man by a long stretch of time, took away the verb of substance <note>The verb "to be" (is/was).</note> and called him "white man" in a momentary naming. Truly, even so, you have not escaped the flux of the world and the rapid torrent of nature. For in every point of time we cast away the present, and just like birds, whatever things exist in this vast <margin>World <note>original: "κόσμ." [kosmos]</note></margin> world—which takes its Greek name from "ornament" or "order"—never remain in one state.

<meta>This page continues the speech of Baruchias the Jew. ### ON THE WONDER-WORKING WORD, BOOK I. ###

Since, therefore, everything is always in motion, things are always in a different state, and one property drives out another. Thus, the ray of our knowledge cannot be reflected steadily because of this turbulence, nor can the light of our mind be directed when it is so often intercepted by the force of such alteration. For this reason, we shall rightly approve of the opinion of **Ecclesiastes** when he says: *I understood that of all the works of God, man can find no reason for those things which are done under the sun. And the more he labors to seek, the less he finds; even if the wise man says he knows, he will not be able to find it.* <note>original: "Intellexi, quod omnium operum Dei nullam possit homo inuenire rationem eorum, quæ fiunt sub sole..." This is a translation of Ecclesiastes 8:17.</note>

<margin>Socrates.</margin>
This is what you said Socrates believed, although he did not wish for there to be *no* science of things—for he disputes about so many things in the works of Plato—but rather that there is no *natural* science, while there is a great deal of *divine* science.

<margin>Arts.</margin>
He believed, finally, that there are very famous arts in human life by which mortals are kept busy so they do not grow sluggish, and which are at the same time somewhat conducive to both public and private affairs: the crafts of the smith and the metalworker, domestic management, civil politics, military science, agriculture, and whatever else depends similarly on the prudent will of man. For indeed, those things which are done according to our own arrangement will be valid in the place where they were established; in these matters, a transgressor will wander into error if he does not obey the precepts devised by us—precepts which we perhaps commanded because we were compelled by many experiments, or sometimes by our own will alone. Socrates thought that all these things were "seen" rather than "known." <note>Socrates famously distinguished between "doxa" (opinion/appearance) and "episteme" (true knowledge).</note> However, whatever things were necessary, he judged that they should be sought from divinity alone. Therefore, he who is commonly reported to have said he knew nothing seems to me to have known everything, not by nature, but by divine gift; for which reason he was judged most wise by **Apollo**—not a man, but a God (as you followers of Sidonius <note>Likely referring to the Latin poet Sidonius Apollinaris</note> poetically persuade us). The history of the ancients would be available to us, unless you are already weary, and the annals of our ancestors concerning the most memorable deeds and things most worthy of reading, which would support this same opinion in a wonderful way, and which (if we remember correctly)

<margin>The Muses of Hesiod.</margin>
inform us about a certain **Hesiod**. When he was a shepherd of flocks in Boeotia, and had driven his herd near a certain Mount Helicon at sunrise, he heard the harmony of the Muses, with sweet melody (as was fitting) indeed for the Muses. Drawing closer, where he beheld those divine countenances and the most lovely dance of the goddesses, he began to imitate the song to which they were dancing in rhythm. Then the benevolent Muses, not scorning the simplicity of the rustic man, offered the shepherd of Ascra <note>Hesiod is often called "the Ascraean" after his birthplace.</note> little branches of laurel and some pipes; having accepted these, he suddenly acquired the poetic art, not by nature but by God.

<margin>The origin of the arts. Gifts of the arts come from God.</margin>
It was no different with that **Demodocus** in Homer; and with **Minos** among the Cretans, who they say learned everything from **Jove** <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>, since he had frequent conversation with the God on Mount Ida, and indeed in a cave of that very mountain. The Athenians are accustomed to say that **Melesagoras** <note>OCR: Meleagor am</note> of Eleusis was taught by the nymphs, and **Epimenides** the Cretan by a certain very long sleep sent by the gods. There was also in Proconnesus a philosopher of especially wonderful knowledge named **Aristeas**, of whom there was a rumor that his soul would sometimes leave his body, and in turn return to the body after seeing distant regions. Although he had known innumerable things, he was nevertheless believed to have had no teacher other than divinity. Thus our **Socrates**, a man especially perfect and, by the testimony of Apollo (as we mentioned before), exceedingly wise, although he shrank from the study, care, and anxiety of natural things, yet nothing in nature had escaped him. The **Stoics** affirm that this happened to him not through human investigation, but by a presiding God, whom he himself called a *daemonion* <note>In Greek philosophy, a 'daimonion' was a divine inner voice or spirit, not an evil demon.</note>: whether it was a voice that he heard, or a vision that he saw, or something else by which he sensed the divine in a human way. But indeed, let us proceed from your stories to ours, which in my judgment are more faithful. Antiquity itself, whose authority was always held in the highest honor, has handed down to memory both by fame and by letters that the Hebrew nation and my ancestors followed a certain God with venerable worship—

<margin>Conversation with God.</margin>
whose name they commonly concealed (lest it become cheapened by common use)—on a long journey, for more than forty years through desert places, through briery and thorny ways, through mountains, through valleys, and through waters: a God who accompanied them for so long with paternal affection and looked upon them with merciful eyes, as long as they holily...

<meta>This page continues the discourse of Baruchias the Jew, who is arguing to Capnion (the humanist scholar Johannes Reuchlin) that human reason is inherently limited when faced with the shifting nature of the physical world and the mysteries of the soul. He transitions from the instability of physical matter to the contradictory opinions of ancient philosophers.</meta>

### OF JOHANNES REUCHLIN ###

...[small gnats], a crowd of almost the most minute animals. It is no different in other things that appear to us. For Ebony, in the genus of trees, is at one moment wood, and at another [stone]. <note>Ebony was often thought in antiquity to be so dense it occupied a middle ground between wood and mineral.</note>
<margin>The Quran.</margin>
And within the book which is titled the *Alkorran* <note>The Quran</note> among your people, it is lamented that what was once wood soon becomes spirit; they say this because the rod of Moses was at one moment wood, and at another [a serpent]. Therefore, I shall deal with you briefly, for you are not the sort of person into whose mouth I must feed chewed-up bits, as nurses are accustomed to do for children. Nothing is written, painted, or fashioned that [can fully capture nature]. Why should I hesitate when I consider that our own talents are not sufficient to thoroughly scrutinize nature? Instead, a grain of doubt is always cast into our thoughts. A thorn fixed in the heel is not easily pulled out by the roots. Shall we boast about any subject, or how any form shapes a thing, without the risk of false judgment? 
<margin>Our soul.</margin>
We, who do not yet perfectly understand or know what and how our own soul is—that by which we live, breathe, and feel? Regarding this matter, there is no need to labor with you. You yourself know how many various opinions exist about it, and how many [theories] are circulated. For Epicurus, whom you seemed to imitate, says the soul is a form mixed from four things:

<margin>Epicurus.</margin>
> ->From this comes heat, motion, and the blind power of the wind.<-
> ->From this begins the air; from this, all things are set in motion.<-
<note>original: "Inde calor motus & venti caca potestas. Occipit inde aër inde omnia mobilitantur." This is a paraphrase of the Roman poet Lucretius, who explained Epicurean philosophy.</note>

<margin>Various opinions on the soul.</margin>
Xenophanes says it is made from earth and water; Parmenides from earth and fire; Empedocles [from the elements]; Critias from blood; Anaximenes from air; Hipparchus from fire; [others] from [the elements]. The Peripatetic <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> claims it consists of a "fifth essence"; Democritus calls it a mobile spirit inserted [into the body]; Zeno, a spirit condensed within the body. Heraclitus the physicist calls it a spark of stellar substance. Heraclitus of Pontus calls it light. Hippocrates calls it a thin spirit diffused through the whole body. Posidonius calls it an "Idea"; Pythagoras and Philolaus call it "Harmony"; Xenocrates calls it a "self-moving number"; Plato says it is a substance that moves itself. Aristotle, being boastful, invented a new name, *Entelechia* <term>Entelechy: the state of a thing whose essence is fully realized</term>, describing the perfection of the soul as if it were the goal of a craftsman. The noble Gregory of Nazianzus—a man of the greatest integrity, vast intelligence, and illustrious dignity—asserts in his book against Eunomius that these discourses on the soul by mortals ought to be refuted.

<margin>Know thyself.</margin>
Therefore, if we are ignorant of our own selves <note>original: "Γνῶθι σαὐτόν" (Gnothi sauton), the famous Greek maxim 'Know Thyself.'</note>, how can we hope to grasp the functions of everything else? How great was the multitude of excellent writers even up to the times of Jerome and Augustine, yet nothing certain about the soul could be gathered from what they left behind. As you are a curious examiner of every sect, you have perhaps been able to learn this from the letters they sent to one another. For regarding you, Capnion <note>Reuchlin’s Greek-derived nickname, meaning "Little Smoke."</note>, there is no reason for me to doubt, since you follow the teachings of the Nazarene <note>Jesus</note>, of whose light these two fathers were the most studious heralds.

Regarding things that are either joined to the body or can in some way fall under the senses, you have my opinion: because of the speed of the moment in which they exist—which the swift torrent of nature immediately seizes and alters—and because of our lack of skill, the hidden depths of causes, and our "eyes of bats" <note>A metaphor for human reason being blinded by the "light" of truth</note>, and the difficulty of discovering the immediate conditions (which they call "passions"), human science cannot be acquired so suddenly, nor sit firmly, nor be faithfully preserved. 

<margin>Human science.</margin>
For sooner (as is the opinion of Heraclitus) does the thing change than you can add the circumstances in your thought. I see Empedocles making an assault on Etna <note>According to legend, the philosopher Empedocles jumped into the volcano Mount Etna to prove his divinity</note>, and I think I know that Empedocles is entering Etna; yet even as this voice is pressed between my teeth, there is no Empedocles anymore. A story will be told of something that is not, and the one who tells it is believed more than the one who is shown the truth by hearing it. Even if you wish to pronounce in a single moment what you desire to know, consider [Lycophron], the son of Periander and Melissa; so as not to describe a man through a long duration, he took away the word for "substance" and called a "white man" a momentary appearance. Truly, not even in this way have you escaped the flux of the world and the rapid course of nature. For at every point in time, we cast away the present, and like a flying bird, whatever exists never remains in one state in this vast [universe].

<margin>The World.</margin>
The World <note>original: "Κόσμος" (Kosmos), meaning order or ornament</note>, from which it takes its name in Greek due to its "ornament," is indeed only [a shadow]...

<meta>This page continues the argument of Baruchias the Jew, who asserts that human reason and observation of the physical world are unreliable due to constant change.
