### ON THE WONDER-WORKING WORD, BOOK 1. ###

Since, therefore, it is always in motion, the state of a thing is always changing, and one property pushes another away. Thus, the ray of our knowledge cannot be reflected steadily because of this whirlwind, nor can the light of our mind be directed when it is so often intercepted by the force of change. For this reason, we rightly approve of the sentiment of the Preacher <note>original: "Ecclesiastis"; referring to the author of the biblical book Ecclesiastes.</note> when he says: *I understood that of all the works of God, no man can find the explanation of those things that happen under the sun. And the more he labors to seek it, the less he finds; even if the wise man says he knows it, he will not be able to find it.* <note>A translation of Ecclesiastes 8:17.</note>

<margin>Socrates.</margin>
This is what you said Socrates believed—though he did not wish for there to be *no* knowledge of things (for he disputes many things in the works of Plato), but rather that there is no *natural* knowledge, whereas there is a great deal of *divine* knowledge. <margin>The Arts.</margin> He held that there are certainly very famous arts in human life by which mortals are kept active so they do not grow sluggish, and which contribute significantly to both public and private affairs—such as carpentry, metalworking, domestic management, civil governance, military science, farming, and whatever else depends similarly on the prudent will of man. Indeed, those things that are done according to our own ordering will hold their place as established; in these, a transgressor will err if he does not obey the rules we have devised, which we perhaps prescribed because we were compelled by many experiences, or sometimes by our own will alone. Socrates thought all these things were "viewed" rather than truly "known." <note>Socrates distinguishes here between *doxa* (opinion/belief) and *episteme* (true, certain knowledge).</note> However, whatever was necessary, he judged should be sought from the divinity alone. Therefore, he who is commonly reported to have said he "knew nothing" seems to me to have known all things, not by nature, but by divine gift; for which reason he was judged the wisest, according to his merit, by Apollo—who is a God, not a man (as you Sidonians <note>Reuchlin often uses "Sidonian" or "pagan" to refer to the classical Greek/Roman tradition.</note> poetically persuade us).

History of the ancients would supply us with more examples, unless you are already weary, and the annals of our ancestors—written concerning the most memorable deeds and matters most worthy of reading—would support this same opinion in a wonderful way. These annals (if we remember correctly) inform us about a certain man named Hesiod. <margin>The Muse of Hesiod.</margin> When he was a shepherd of livestock in Boeotia, and had driven his flock near a certain Mount Helicon at sunrise, he heard the harmony of the Muses, with a sweet melody (as was fitting for Muses). Drawing closer to where he beheld those divine countenances and the most graceful dance of the goddesses, he began to imitate the song to which they were dancing in rhythm. Then the benevolent Muses, not scorning the simplicity of a rustic man, offered the shepherd of Ascra <note>Hesiod is often called the "Ascraean" after his birthplace, Ascra.</note> some laurel branches and several reeds; having accepted these, he suddenly acquired the poetic art, not by nature, but by God. <margin>The origin of the arts. The gifts of the arts come from God.</margin>

It was no different with that Demodocus in Homer; and with Minos among the Cretans, who they say learned all things from Jove, having had frequent conversation with the God on Mount Ida, and indeed in a cave of that very mountain. The Athenians are accustomed to say that Meleiagoras of Eleusis was taught by nymphs, and Epimenides the Cretan by a certain very long, divine sleep. There was also in Proconnesus a philosopher of especially marvelous knowledge named Aristeas, of whom there was a rumor that his soul would sometimes leave his body and, after seeing distant regions, return to the body in turn. Although he had known innumerable things, he was nevertheless believed to have had no teacher other than the divinity. So too our Socrates, a man supremely perfect and, by the testimony of Apollo (as we mentioned before), exceedingly wise; although he shrank from the study, care, and anxiety of natural things, yet nothing in nature had escaped him. The Stoics affirm that this happened to him not through human investigation, but with the assistance of God, whom he himself called a <term>daemonium</term> <note>A guardian spirit or "divine sign." In the Renaissance, this was often interpreted as a pre-Christian understanding of a guardian angel.</note>—whether that was a voice he heard, or a vision he saw, or something else by which he perceived the divine through human senses.

But truly, let us move from your traditions to ours, which in my judgment are more faithful. Antiquity itself, whose authority has always been held in the highest honor, has handed down to memory through both fame and letters, <margin>Conversation with God.</margin> that the Hebrew nation and my ancestors followed a certain God with venerable worship. His name (lest it become cheapened by common use) they generally concealed. They followed Him on a long journey for over forty years through desert places, through rough and thorny paths, through mountains, through valleys, and through waters; He accompanied them all the while with paternal affection and looked upon them with merciful eyes, as long as they holily...

...might love and observe. And so that God—whoever the religious name he is called by—descended to one man out of so great a multitude of people, and one from an immense wealth of men, I say, to Moses, in whom a frequent devotion of mind was pleasing. He descended so that he might join seventy men to him, who might both act as magistrates with diverse prudence and apply themselves to various arts for the things that needed to be done for the enlargement of causes. But because this could not be done by natural industry—for we contend that the human condition is not capable of understanding the things in this world that are rolling in every direction with constant change <note>original: "uolubilium"; referring to the ever-shifting nature of the physical world.</note>.

<margin>The Spirit of Moses.</margin>
Therefore, from the spirit that had flowed from Moses, He also dispensed to the seventy elders. And when the spirits had rested upon them, they prophesied, and they did not cease thereafter. Concerning the craftsmen <note>original: "sellularijs... artificibus"; literally those who sit at their work, like artisans.</note> as well, sacred history records the same manner. For He sent His spirit to men endowed with craftsmanship, Bezaleel and Ahaliab <note>Biblical figures tasked with building the Tabernacle and its furnishings; see Exodus 31.</note>, so that they might do all works wisely and intelligently and discover every new thing for the storehouses of the sanctuary. Again, I am drawn to your own writers. For what is read in Plato’s *Ion* regarding Tynnichus <note>A poet mentioned by Socrates in Plato's dialogue *Ion* as an example of someone who wrote a great poem through divine inspiration rather than skill.</note> that is worthy of memory? From this, it seems to me that this poem truly arose, when it says:

->*There is a God within us, and we have dealings with heaven,*<-
->*From ethereal seats that spirit comes.*<-
<note>original: "Est Deus in nobis sunt & commercia cæli, / Sedibus æthereis spiritus ille uenit." A quote from the Roman poet Ovid.</note>

Therefore, Sidonius, and you, Capnion <note>The Greek-style pseudonym of the author, Johann Reuchlin, meaning "smoky."</note>, I will grant to ingenious men in the management of action: circumspection and foresight; in studies: sagacity and skill; in the consideration of all things: docility, art, and intelligence. But truly, I shall deny to man any constant, pure, and ineffable knowledge <note>original: "ineffabilem scientiam"</note> concerning any sensible things, unless it has been received not through human discipline, but through divine tradition from one to another, which we Hebrews call Cabala—that is, "Reception."

<margin>Cabala.</margin>
In this, our ancestors, to whom the fame of wisdom had added weight, labored with prepared seeds; such as Abraham once was, such as Simon son of Yohai <note>Simeon bar Yochai, the traditional author of the *Zohar*, the foundational work of Jewish mysticism.</note>, such as the second Abraham surnamed Abulafia <note>A 13th-century Spanish Kabbalist known for "prophetic" Kabbalah.</note>, such as that Ramban <note>Nachmanides (Rabbi Moses ben Nahman), a major medieval Jewish scholar and mystic.</note>, such as Recanati <note>Menahem Recanati, an Italian Kabbalist.</note>, and the rest who were studious through the cycles of many years concerning religion, institutes, solemnities, rites, shrines, observations, and sacred mysteries.

**C**ome now, Baruchias, SIDONIUS says, how many not only muddy things, but even rocks are rolled in this great river of your speech! Those ancestors of yours were right who tried to prohibit you from philosophy, as you say, by some edict. For what would have become of you if it had been permitted to you to penetrate the books of the philosophers? For I have never heard anyone speak more copiously or even more pugnaciously than you, so that I am hardly master of my own counsel to break this wall with a battering ram, which you have opposed to my empty words. I shall be silent, therefore, if I may suggest this one thing: it will be a heavy burden for men to be ignorant of that which one sees, hears, and touches. Just like that Sosia in Plautus <note>A character from the play *Amphitryon* who is famously confused about his own identity when confronted by a god, but trusts his own senses.</note>, who only moves us to laughter because, by touching, seeing, and hearing himself, he doubts himself. For who, looking at snow, would ever say it is black? And who has not judged by sense that fire is hot? Therefore, if you listen to Epicurus, you will find that the knowledge of truth was created from the senses.

<margin>The most accurate knowledge is from the senses.</margin>
But that divine things can be known by men, that I will not easily grant you. For thus, while the divine is grasped by the one knowing, you will be confessing that the divine is joined with the human, which are things as opposite as can be. For Divinity is said to lack a beginning, but human things are all closed within boundaries. Moreover, of that which is finite to the infinite (as the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> attest), there is no proportion. ### CHAPTER VII.

But I, said Baruchias, suspect that this "Latin Sardanapalus" <note>Sardanapalus was a legendary Assyrian king known for extreme luxury and decadence; Baruchias uses this as a disparaging nickname for Lucretius to associate his Epicurean philosophy with mindless self-indulgence.</note> of yours, whom others call Lucretius, has served both Philosophy and the whole choir of divinity poorly. If you do not take it badly, he contradicts himself here as in many other places. But let us touch upon the heart of the matter. For when he was describing the sacred rites of the Great Mother Cybele <note>A Phrygian mother goddess; Lucretius uses her myth to explain natural phenomena while denying her actual divinity.</note>, and asserting that armed men follow her chariot because they believed the goddess was showing them the protection with which to defend their fatherland, he nevertheless added that these things are vain to believe, in these words:

> “Though these things are set forth well and excellently,
> They are nevertheless driven far from true reason.
> For the whole nature of the gods must, of itself,
> Enjoy an immortal life with the highest peace,
> Far removed and separated from our affairs.
> For free from all pain, free from dangers,
> Powerful in its own resources and needing nothing from us,
> It is neither won over by good deeds, nor touched by anger.”
> <note>original: "Omnis enim per se diuum natura necesse est..." This famous passage from Lucretius (Book II) argues that gods are indifferent to human life.</note>

From this, it appears that the gods above grant us nothing of their mercy, lest they perhaps be affected by the trouble of our business. But later, in the third book, he speaks thus:

> “It must be said he was a God—yes, a God, noble Memmius—
> Who first discovered that rule of life which
> Is now called Wisdom, and who through his art
> Placed life out of such great waves and such great darkness
> Into such tranquility and so clear a light.”
> <note>original: "Dicendum est Deus ille fuit..." Here Lucretius refers to his master, Epicurus, as a "God" for discovering the philosophy of atomism.</note>

This speech can show nothing except that Philosophy is the breath of God, and that Philosophy is a divine illumination. He finally confesses this, forced by the truth itself—a truth we have barely wrenched from his hands, and which we have squeezed out without the threat of the rack <note>original: "fidicularum"; instruments of torture. Baruchias is saying Lucretius accidentally admitted the truth without even being forced.</note>. I will pass over the fact that at one moment he asserts the soul is mortal, and at another that it returns to its heavenly source:

> “And when I go on to say, for the sake of the word,
> That the soul is mortal, teaching this, you may believe
> That I also mean the mind.”

In another poem he says:

> “Finally, we are all sprung from celestial seed;
> That same father is for all...”

And after a few lines he concludes:

> “Likewise, what was from the earth before goes back
> Into the earth, but what was sent from the shores of the upper air,
> The shining temples of heaven receive back again.”
> <note>original: "Cedit item retrò de terra..." Lucretius (Book II) arguing that atoms return to their source, but Baruchias interprets this as the soul's return to heaven.</note>

Does he not fear to be caught being so thoughtless and impudent? He hoped to deceive us with trappings of words, or at least leave us in doubt—and as he himself betrayed, he tried to "touch it with sweet honey-moss." <note>original: "quasi musco dulci contingere melle"; a reference to Lucretius’s own famous metaphor of coating bitter medicine (philosophy) with honey (poetry) to make it palatable for children.</note> But I beg you, let him sing among the poets; do not let him preside over the platform of the philosophers. But if he has moved you, or anyone else, with his decrees and his writings—or even with the faction of Epicurus, which is as latest as it is most impure—

...I would think it to be moved, I would cry out and denounce with all my strength this sect as the filthiest nurse of all vices, a fanatical thing <margin>Leucippus</margin> planted by the dream of Leucippus <note>Leucippus was a 5th-century BCE Greek philosopher and the earliest developer of atomism—the idea that everything is made of indivisible units.</note> and later watered by the authority of Democritus. For philosophers of every kind [have noted this], although to root out this sacrilegious thing, there is no need for so many words, nor for a particularly sagacious and clear intellect.
<margin>CAPNION.</margin> **CAPNION** said: "Enough of these insults; let us consider the matter itself."

->Capnion orders that the quarrels be put aside, and beginning with praises of them both, finally, at their urging, he enters into a disputation concerning knowledge. CHAPTER VIII.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial E featuring scrolling floral and leaf motifs.</image-desc>**I**NDEED, I seem to see that both of you—explorers of the highest things, endowed with the greatest talents, a singular abundance of speech, and eloquence—have contributed much splendidly, much magnificently, and very much to the matter at hand, offering, as it were, a most noble tasting from the variety of you both. But when I reflect within myself what I might bring to your forum worthy of such litigants, truly I am filled with misery and weariness. I would not hesitate to force something too rustic and unpolished upon the ears of the most learned, were it not for this one thing that holds me back: that I have deliberately and with effort mingled myself in your company so that, by comparison with my rudeness and ignorance, the light and glory of such highly literary men might shine much more brightly—just as white things are accustomed to become clearer among many black ones, and anything appears more distinct by the presence of its opposite.

"Come now," said Sidonius, "I beseech you; I know this Baruchias agrees with me. Do not waste time even on an inopportune thing. For what need is there for this abdication of praise, of which we judge you most worthy? We know your prudence even among [us]... proceed then, Capnion, and explain your opinion to us. For this solitary place of philosophy contains us, and we shall not be prohibited by any noise from hearing, nor you from speaking."

"I will do so easily," said **CAPNION**, "provided you bear my ineptitudes with a calm mind. If my memory does not fail me, by Hercules, I consider it among the number of all enemies—with their very camps—that <margin>Reasons why no solid knowledge is achieved.</margin> knowledge <term>scientia</term> <note>In this context, 'scientia' refers to certain, demonstrable knowledge, often contrasted with mere opinion or faith.</note> cannot be acquired by human means, whether regarding things above or things below. This is due partly to prevailing human weakness regarding divine things, and partly to the temporary mutability and continual alteration of natural things, which is thought to belong to the very foundation of certain knowledge. A second reason also stands in the way: that mortals may not know anything even by divine means, lest the Gods should affect the daily appetites of men eager for learning with an intolerable longing. Moreover, and chiefly, it is because it is impossible to join divine with human operation—which would necessarily happen in knowledge of this kind—any more than if you should strive to connect the most diverse things with a harmonious bond.

Let us explain all this very briefly according to our capacity, weighing the power of the words over which you have been dueling almost from dawn until this evening. The treatment, however, will be from hidden principles, nor will it lack clear reasons for believing. For what else do the orbs of the eyes, enclosed in concave hollows, <margin>Sight.</margin> desire but to see? This is their one and proper solace, without which fruit of the spectacle they would certainly be in vain and idle. If you wish, remember what sort of song that Phrygian in Euripides brought not unsuitably:

> "Whoever," he says, "is a man, even if he were a slave, yet looks upon the light."
> <note>original: "Quísqnis... uir est... lucem tamen [videt]." A reference to Euripides, likely from the play *Orestes* or *Hecuba*.</note>

<margin>Hearing.</margin> What of that cartilage, softer than bone and firmer than flesh, hanging and bending on a man—does it not desire to drink in voices? Whence also "ears" [*aures*], they think, are so called by Virgil <note>The text suggests an etymological link between the verb 'haurire' (to drink/draw) and 'auris' (ear).</note> when he says:

> ->—and with these ears I drank in the voice.<-
> <note>original: "—vocemq; his auribus hausi." From Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Book IV, line 359.</note>

Capnion is explaining the hierarchy of human perception, moving from basic sensory input to the higher faculty of Reason, using Baruchias's physical appearance as a practical example of how we process information.</meta>

# OF THE MIRIFIC WORD, BOOK I.

<margin>Smell. Hearing. Flavor. Touch.</margin> And, to encompass the other instruments for perceiving things, what else is the fragrant power of the nostrils but to smell? What does the tongue desire more than to taste? Therefore, that which feeds the eye is color. So too for the ears, it is sound; for the nose, sweet scents; for the tongue, flavor; and all soft things become food for the touch. I ask next: if the eye did not exist, nor the ear, nor the nose, nor finally any tongue or sense, what benefit do you think color, voice, scent, the bitter, the sweet, the rough, or the smooth would bring us? Would all these not be in vain in the world, considered empty and nothing? Surely, set this aside from your hands and grasp not the weapons of the senses, but their strengths and powers. For unless a sharp judgment is present in them, all things will become indistinct and confused; you would not match the proper object to the sense, and the eye would "see" a voice, and the ear would "hear" color. I ask you, therefore, Sidonius, alongside your Lucretius <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BCE), a Roman poet and Epicurean philosopher whose work *De Rerum Natura* is quoted here.</note>: *Can the ears correct the eyes? Or touch correct the ears? Or will the taste of the mouth further argue against this touch? Will the nostrils refute the eyes, or will they also overcome the sense of taste?* <note>original: "An poterunt oculos aures reprehendere? An aures tactus?..."</note> Not so, in my opinion. For a separate power is divided for each. Both Baruchias and all the Academic Peripatetics <note>A group of philosophers who followed the teachings of Aristotle (the Peripatetics) but were influenced by the skepticism of the later Platonic Academy.</note> will answer you in the same way. But what is the occasion for this division? Let Epicurus say that the eye, and similarly the other instruments, do not know the actual nature and condition of things. What then? Listen to the verse:

->The reason of the mind must finally discern this.<-
<note>original: "Hoc animi demum ratio discernere debet."</note>

It is done now. For as the empty picture feeds the vision with color, so the form of the true, reflecting in the soul, will undoubtedly be the food of reason, which distinguishes one from the other through the mediation of thought, which they call "estimation." <margin>Reason. Estimation.</margin> I will review the whole cause as briefly as I can. A sensible thing projects from itself a most thin and incorporeal "simulacrum" <note>A mental image or representation of an external object.</note> in every direction, which is easily apprehended by the sense because of the friendly hospitality of the sensitive power. When it dwells in that place, it soon acquires a more eminent dignity; casting off the present existence of the thing, it becomes an "idol" <note>Reuchlin uses *idolum* here in the philosophical sense of a mental image (*eidolon*), not a religious idol.</note>, while retaining the other circumstances. Then, therefore, a certain imagination receives the image of the absent simulacrum. Finally, "phantasia" <note>The faculty of imagination or the ability to form mental representations.</note> estimates and judges the conditions of the idol through certain appearances, <margin>Phantasia.</margin> sometimes truly, sometimes fallaciously. This is why horses are accustomed to hating masks by discerning them wrongly, and flee as if from future harm. Just like birds, which shudder at the scarecrows <note>original: "terricula," literally "little terrors."</note> placed in gardens and fields, suspecting the worst, and often dreading traps and foreseeing snares. Later, though these coverings are diligently refined, they are still sprinkled with base appendages; a worthier virtue, which is called reason, sifts and weighs them, running from one property to another. By this <margin>Discourse.</margin> clear discourse <note>The process of reasoning from one premise to another (*discursus*).</note> in physical things, it affirms that this is crystal, while that is ice; and among gems, it debates whether amber <note>original: "electrum"</note> is sometimes mixed with both; therefore, it notices that this is a chrysolite, that is called resin, and the other is named glass. In actions and affairs, however, it judges one thing to be shameful and another to be decent. Therefore, reason always probes, and with diligent and untiring investigation, it first scrutinizes sensible things stripped of matter and the presence of the object, adding various intentions not received by any of the senses, which nevertheless cannot become known without sensible things. For example, when I look at this Baruchias, a man of medium stature, with a long beard, a somewhat sad brow, an aquiline nose, cloaked, wearing a circle <note>The "yellow circle" (*croceus circulus*) refers to the badge Jews were often legally required to wear on their clothing in Reuchlin's time.</note>, and as the Satirist <note>The Roman satirist Persius (34–62 CE).</note> says:

> With head bowed and eyes fixed on the earth,
> While he gnaws at murmurs and rabid silences within himself,
> And weighs his words with a protruding lip.
<note>original: "Obstipo capite & figentem lumina terræ..." from Persius, Satire 3.</note>

From this I divine that he is a Hebrew, for whom the yellow circle is the badge; a philosopher, because he is covered by a cloak; and most likely a Pythagorean or of another more divine sect. Because Saturn, the author of secret contemplation, is said to produce images of such a surface. Hereafter, according to the custom of his nation and profession, he is not very friendly to me, except insofar as letters now reconcile us, likewise rejoicing in the roof...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Capnion (Reuchlin), Sidonius, and Baruchias. Having established how the senses process physical objects like color and sound, Capnion now argues that Reason has its own "hunger" for Truth, just as the eyes hunger for light.</meta>

[the tooth] and shadow, and many things of that kind which are added to a person or appear as signs to the gods. Nor does the scrutiny of reason ever cease, but rather there is an innate and diligent desire for seeking; it lasts as long as the keen appetite for knowledge is not at all frustrated by the truth of its own wish. Nature itself makes both craftsmen and those who have been deceived blush at it, whenever the judgment of right reason between truth and falsehood is missing. By nature, we hate deceivers as such, and all those who have one thing under their tongue and another in their heart. And people consider nothing so shameful as to err, at least those endowed with good character and who prevail by the virtue of their soul—those are the ones I say are truly human when we must discuss differences. Infants torn from the breast, concerning whatever thing they see or feel, inquire curiously 
<margin>The love of discovery.</margin>
so that it is not unreasonable to admit that there is an innate faculty of the soul for finding the truth. Nor are we drawn or led to such madness as to think that the nature of the universe—which, as even Sardanapalus <note>Sardanapalus was a legendary king of Assyria, often associated with decadence, but here perhaps used as a witness for the basic observation that nature sustains all life.</note> testifies, creates and nourishes all things—would have impressed upon us such an appetite for truth in vain, when it has never been seen to act wrongly elsewhere. 
For just as you would admit that eyes were created in vain if they were never granted to look upon the light, so we shall think concerning holy and skillful Nature: she would never have implanted reason in our minds, nor inserted such a vigilant force of inquiry within it, unless she had first found it certain that the human soul could grasp the truth, and that this noble faculty, virtue, and power of hers would eventually emerge into operation, produce an effect, propel itself into action, and strike its appropriate object. 
<margin>Truth.</margin>
Truth is most keenly desiring its own. For truth is the food of reason, just as light is for the eye, scent for the nostrils, and harmonious sound for the ears. Therefore, it is clear in this structure of the world we behold that some triumphant truth exists, which so often moves, agitates, entangles, and unfolds our reason; so often she solicits the restless and sleepless mind in wondrous ways—not by accidental or external means, but by her own proper and original lures of nature. These do not occur in vain, and so it happens that we embrace the truth of things that are at the appropriate time. Whoever, therefore, truly understands that which is, whether by nature or aided by divine assistance, how should I not consider him to have obtained its knowledge? For I call knowledge <note>original: *scientia*</note> the true apprehension of a thing. This is what I said at the beginning: the meaning of names must be weighed, over which you fight so much.

->*The name of "knowledge" is understood in various ways, both concerning the two natures, and that there is no knowledge of dual things, but only opinion; furthermore, the object of reason and mind, and primary and secondary causes are discussed.*<-

### CHAPTER IX.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' containing a figure (possibly a philosopher or saint) in a landscape with foliage.</image-desc>In this cause, it can certainly be easily understood that the word "knowledge" <note>original: *scientia*</note> signifies various things, just as the things which are said to be known are manifold. Many, especially the Platonists, have decreed that there are two natures from which they claim to gather knowledge. One is that which can be seen by the eyes and touched by the hand, almost toward an alterable ferment <note>original: *admentum alterabilem* — possibly a printer's error for "element." Reuchlin is discussing the unstable nature of physical matter.</note>. Let pardon be granted (as the man from Madaura <note>Apuleius of Madaura (c. 124–170 CE), a Roman philosopher and Platonist famous for his work *The Golden Ass* and his philosophical orations.</note> says) to novelty serving the obscurities of things. Though this nature remains one and the same, it is nonetheless received into the hospitality of the soul’s virtue according to the manner of the thing; it is no more that which it is than that which it is not, which is how a thing is in truth: that is, mutable. Wherefore, I call the power in us for receiving a mutable thing—which should be equally clear among the many—the faculty of opinion <note>original: *opinabilem rationem*</note>. From this, it follows that you contend that the knowledge of natural and sensible things is a gift. For I do not agree, since as the things known change, so too will the knowledge change.

<summary>Reuchlin argues that the human soul has an innate, God-given hunger for Truth, which serves as the "food" of Reason. He begins Chapter IX by distinguishing between certain knowledge and mere opinion based on the mutability of physical objects.</summary>
<keywords>Nature, Truth, Reason, Knowledge (Scientia), Opinion, Platonism, Apuleius of Madaura, Epistemology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Capnion (the scholar Reuchlin), Sidonius, and Baruchias. Having previously discussed how the human soul has an innate appetite for truth, Capnion now distinguishes between the limitations of human "opinion" regarding the physical world and the certainty of "knowledge" gained through divine revelation and faith.</meta>

# ON THE WONDER-WORKING WORD, BOOK I.

...it matters whether you call this "knowledge" or "opinion," since the reality of the matter is clear. Shall I say it in a single word? Of all things dwelling beneath the canopy of heaven, there is no such thing among humans as what we truly call *knowledge*, but rather *opinion*. For whenever we hear that knowledge of these things has been obtained, the term itself always designates an opinion. 

However, they asserted that the other nature of substances is incorruptible, immutable, constant, and always the same; this is perceived not only by penetrating thought, but is even seen by the sharp edge of the mind—things such as we call "divine." For many call the preceding [physical] things "demonic" <note>original: *dæmonica*. In the Platonic tradition, this refers to the intermediate realm of nature and spirits, rather than "demons" in the modern sense.</note>. Hence, most people have named Plato "divine" and Aristotle "demonic" <note>Aristotle was often called "daimonios" (extraordinary or spirit-like) because of his unmatched mastery over the natural world and logic.</note>, because of the excellence of both in writing about such matters. 

Therefore, since these things are super-celestial and nowhere meet any sense, who, best of men (for I call upon you, Sidonius and Baruchias), who, I say, of mortals, could obtain even the slightest knowledge, except by divine means and by no human power? No one, by Hercules, no one! Therefore, truth is the object, the food, the bait, and the highest pleasure of the lower reason and the higher mind, each according to its capacity. However, in the vast expanse of the earth, no knowledge is held to be constant, complete, and irrefutable—as defined by Aristotle—except by divine revelation, since divine things are not touched [by the senses], and worldly things escape the senses at every moment.

<margin>
Art is long,
Life is short,
Experience is
difficult.
</margin>

For on one hand, a sufficient knowledge of causes is lacking; on the other, the constancy of permanence is missing; and what hinders us most is our fragile industry, late-coming prudence, and swift death. Thus it happens that what we often think is wisdom or knowledge is actually an error, whether it rests on the observation of the heavens or relies on the lofty suspicion of natural causes and material things. 

This is what that most noble prophet Isaiah, writing to the city of Babylon, reproached the Chaldean philosophers for: *Your wisdom and your knowledge, it has deceived you.* May the "Astrologers of the heavens" save you (which we perhaps translate as "the soothsayers of heaven": for in Hebrew they are the astrologers who contemplate the stars and calculate the months) from whom whatever things are to come may reach you. *You have failed in the multitude of your counsels; they have each wandered in their own way.* <note>Isaiah 47:10–13. Reuchlin is using the biblical text to critique those who rely solely on human sciences like astrology.</note> He has therefore encompassed both: those who pry into the causes of lower things, and those who care for celestial influences; one errs by calculating, the other by gathering counsels, both ignorant of the adequate power of operations and the condition of all circumstances.

Therefore, whether we *taste* <term>sapimus (to taste or be wise): Reuchlin notes the etymological link between "sapientia" (wisdom) and "sapor" (taste)</term> eternal things—from which the name Wisdom comes—or *know* perpetual things where only a small dreg of matter exists, or *perceive* momentary, flowing, and falling things subject to time and the heavens, right faith is always superior to them. Through faith, the active intellect <term>intellectus agens: the "active intellect," a concept in medieval and Renaissance philosophy describing the power of the mind that makes knowledge possible</term>—placed at the peak and summit of the human soul, pure, lucid, and clear—looks upon the states of all things, both mortal and immortal, as if in a mirror of eternity. These states shine in divine and super-celestial minds and reflect back; they are far more certain and more effective for both contemplation and action than any logical ordering, discourse, investigation, opinion, or science—indeed, more than any intellect, whether potential, active, speculative, or acquired, insofar as it visits things lower than itself. 

For if it is permitted to compare lower things to higher: just as the soul becomes something identical in act with sensible things through the senses, and with intelligible things through the intellect, so too, and even more so, through faith our mind becomes identical in act with the heavenly intelligences and joined with God.

In Him, all the causes of things shine back much more eminently and much more nobly than they can exist in their effects. For the First Cause [God] is more intimate to things than second [natural] causes are. The First contains the second, as a spring contains the waters of the streams. Indeed, just as the immense sea draws in all the waves at once, so is His comprehension most ample. This is what Agamemnon proclaims in Homer; for He holds all things, which is why He is said to have "the greatest power." <note>original: *mégiston krátos* (Greek: μέγιστον κράτος)</note>

<summary>Capnion argues that human knowledge of the physical world is merely "opinion" and that true certainty is only found through faith and divine revelation. He critiques human sciences like astrology and concludes that faith unites the human mind with the divine First Cause.</summary>

<keywords>Aristotle vs. Plato, divine revelation, faith, active intellect, First Cause, Isaiah, Chaldean astrology, Homer, Agamemnon, wisdom vs. knowledge</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous section where Capnion (Reuchlin's persona) discussed the nature of truth and the human mind's capacity to receive it. Here, he begins to explain the hierarchy of being and refutes the Epicurean view that God is too detached or "busy" to govern the world.</meta>

# JOHANNES REUCHLIN

->*How the union of God and man occurs, wherein the opinion of Epicurus regarding the idleness of the highest good and the supposed burden of divine influence is rejected, proving that one God exists and that all things are governed by Him.*<-

### CHAPTER X.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'O' depicting a seated figure, likely a scholar or philosopher, at a desk within a rectangular frame adorned with ornate foliate and vine patterns.</image-desc>

According to the testimony of Orpheus, the origin of every thing and its primary power of subsisting consists of a beginning, a middle, and an end. Believe me, when I turn these things over in my mind, and when I gather and separate the natures of the universe, I see clearly how man relates to those things closest to him. For just as the heavens share matter with fire, fire with air, air with the moisture of water, water with the cold of earth, and earth again with fire <note>Reuchlin is describing the "Chain of Being," where all elements are linked by shared qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in a continuous circle.</note>. So too God connects with intelligence—which in the idiom of the word we judge to be a "daemon" <note>original: *daemona* / δαήμονα. In the Platonic sense used here, this refers to an "intermediary spirit" or "knowing being," rather than an evil demon.</note>, that is, one who "knows" by virtue of immortality. The daemon connects with man through affection, man with the beast through sense, and the beast with the plant through that kind of soul which provides growth.

<margin>Differences among men.</margin>
Yet I find, finally, that the brute animal differs from man by reason, and man from the daemon by innate wisdom. But man differs from man most of all by faith. 
<margin>Paradise.</margin>
Now you see for what reason God placed man in the middle of paradise. Paradise is a garden of heights. All its ornaments are delights. Indeed, the "world" took its name from ornament, since in Greek it is called *kosmos* <note>original: κόσμος; meaning both "order" and "ornament." Reuchlin is making a linguistic argument that the universe is fundamentally beautiful and ordered.</note>. In civil law, after all, "woman’s world" <note>original: *mundus muliebris*; a legal term for a woman's jewelry and finery.</note> refers to those things with which women are adorned. Therefore, God placed man in the middle of the universe, common to both the heavens and the regions below, so that he might bear faith toward the beings above and reason toward those below. Among mortals, he is like a God through faith; among the heavenly beings, he is like a man through reason. He excels both through wisdom; though he is surpassed slightly by divinity, he remains the victor of the places he holds. This we have learned from King David: when speaking to the most high God, the Best and Greatest, concerning man, he says: "You have made him a little lower than the *Elohim*" <note>original: אלהים; a Hebrew name for God, often translated here as "the angels" or "divine beings."</note>, that is, than God.

Thus, you can remember what I think about this dispute of ours: namely, that there is a certain truth in eternal things, of which the mind itself becomes the receptacle. In mutable things, truth is mutable, yet it makes use of the dividing power of reason. The knowledge of the former can be called "wisdom," and of the latter "right opinion," but all things are uncertain unless they are strengthened by divine faith. 

However, there is a wicked obstacle of a certain weak argument—if I may say so with everyone's permission—dreamed up by the popular philosopher Epicurus. I think it is better to recite it subtly than to affirm it, given his singular caution for dignity and learning, with which he was remarkably endowed above others. He makes us doubt whether God is touched by a sense of trouble if He grants benefits to mortals, or if He desires to be asked through vows and constant prayers? Epicurus alone, impatient of labor, loved idleness too much, so that he placed the "highest good" in leisure and thought the influence of divinity was a burden. As if we should believe the sun is exhausted by its light and soon fails entirely because it has shone so long, or that the heavens grow weary when they provide life-giving influences to the lower worlds! 

If this long-lasting duty does not trouble the bodies of the world, does not wear them down, and does not weigh them down, what must be felt concerning that highest author of spirits? If He, along with Epicurus, Lucretius, and the other philosophers of pleasure, had loved sloth, idleness, and laziness, He certainly would not have brought forth and poured out from His own bowels this great and admirable ornament which we behold, nor would He have constructed this machine which He governs through all ages. For if—since we have experienced that there are individual managers, deputies, guardians, and 
<margin>Prince of the universe.</margin>
presidents for any business you like—one always recurs to this one Prince of the universe, without whom it must be thought that managers cannot manage, nor tribunes vote, nor presidents suffice. It is no different than light without the sun, or any secondary cause without the first. For the order of the universe requires both a "something first" and a "one," which it is a shame for a philosopher not to know, when even common soldiers know it.

<summary>Reuchlin describes the hierarchical connection between God, spiritual beings (daemons), humans, and nature, arguing that man's unique position allows him to bridge the gap through faith and reason. He refutes Epicurus's idea that God is too idle or burdened to govern the world, asserting that divine providence is as tireless as the sun's light.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical dialogue where Capnion (Reuchlin’s spokesperson) argues for the unity of God and the necessity of divine providence, countering the Epicurean view that the divine is indifferent to human affairs.</meta>

# ON THE MIRIFIC WORD, BOOK I.

<margin>All is one.</margin>
For as Ulysses harangues the army in Homer: "Indeed, we cannot all be in command, O Achaeans. For the rule of many is not good; let there be one ruler, one king." <note>A famous quote from the *Iliad*, Book 2, often used by Renaissance thinkers to justify monarchy or monotheism.</note> Where are your many atoms now, Epicurus, governing so great a kingdom? Where are the innumerable architects of a single world? If these tiny little bodies rule by reason, they cannot be simple and indivisible, since they would consist of both reason and a body. If they rule without reason, then it is necessary that all things are conducted unwisely. This is something that not only nature abhors, but even the very name of the "world" (*mundus*) rejects; for in it, nothing ordered, nothing "clean" could stand if individual parts were thrown into confusion and one thing tended toward another. <note>original: "mundi... mundi". Reuchlin plays on the Latin word *mundus*, which means both "the world/universe" and "clean, neat, or elegant." He argues the universe is named for its inherent order.</note> Therefore, He who is supreme is One; He who is One is simple. For if He were otherwise composed, He would be two, not one; wherefore He never receives into Himself any sorrow, weariness, disturbance, or trouble. For He would become varied and manifold, and changeable for the worse, which does not befit unity and supreme goodness. Furthermore, when He is said to be "like Himself"—that is, clement, beneficent, merciful, and the other terms that explain, suit, and pray to His goodness—then He is one and the same; and thus He will be at once clement and God. He is God when He is invoked, and clement when He grants our prayers.

<margin>The dignity and tranquility of God.</margin>
But is anyone more insane than a madman who thinks it possible that the everlasting, busy rest and restful activity of the divinity could be troubled by the prayers of those seeking punishment? <note>original: "operosa quies & quieta operatio". A paradox describing God's nature: He is always active yet always at peace.</note> His highest dignity is that He acts; His highest tranquility is that He provides. He even invites men to ask, which the Son of God, who is also God, taught us. "No one," He said, "comes to me unless my Father has drawn him." <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 6:44.</note>

<margin>Great consolation in the Gods.</margin>
It is a pleasure for God to look upon the faces of men who gaze upon and admire Him; it is not a trouble, nor a restlessness.

->*Lucretius is noted, who said that God finds prayers bothersome; then why He invites us to pray, or what joins us with God, and instruction is given on unity.*<-

### CHAPTER II.

<margin>Friendship with God is our consolation.</margin>
But you, Sidonius, and Lucretius (for I do not name you alongside such a sacrilegious sect out of respect for you), and your Epicurus as well, dare to remark that in God which would be impious to even think about good men: that they would find the prayers of friends to be a nuisance. For what else moves mortals to prayer toward the divinity except the hope that one is a friend to God? What governs faith in supplications besides love alone? Homer, who is most full of all the divine philosophy of our tradition, showed this when he said: "Apollo himself heard Chryses as he prayed, because he was very much a friend to him." <note>Refers to the opening of the *Iliad*, where the priest Chryses prays to Apollo.</note> It appears, I believe, from these things I have briefly touched upon—according to the meager faculty of speaking that lies within me—how one should respond regarding the human conjunction with the divinity itself. For the question now is not whether God and man can be one and the same, whether born of God or sprung from men.

<margin>Aesculapius</margin>
Such is the account of Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of medicine and healing.</note> which that deserter Julian <note>Reuchlin refers to Emperor Julian "the Apostate" (r. 361–363 AD), who rejected Christianity to return to Roman paganism.</note> recorded in his book published *Against the Galileans* <note>Julian's polemic against Christians, whom he called "Galileans."</note>. These are almost his exact words, though translated by my hand: "Jupiter, in his intelligible realms, begot Aesculapius from himself, and sent him to the earth through the prolific life of the sun; he, having been granted a descent from the heavens to the earth, appeared in a uniform manner in human form around Epidaurus. Having grown there, he extended his life-giving right hand over the whole earth. He passed to Pergamum, then set out for Ionia to Tarentum, and later to Rome. From there he crossed to Cos, and finally to Aegae, and to other places by sea and land, so that he might restore poorly disposed souls and bodies that were not in good health."

<margin>Gods appearing in human form.</margin>
Julian wrote these things, if indeed he saw them truly; nor shall we strive in this place to explain the controversy concerning the immortal Gods, how they moved about on the earth and were seen by men—such as Apollo pursuing Daphne, or being established in Thessaly under Admetus, or being recognized in Phrygia before Laomedon, or as both the high Gods feasted in the hut of the poor Philemon and Baucis, as Ovid wrote:

> "Jupiter came here in mortal form, and with him
> Came the grandson of Atlas, the caduceus-bearer, his wings laid aside." <note>A quote from Ovid's *Metamorphoses*, Book 8. The "grandson of Atlas" is Mercury (Hermes).</note>

<summary>Reuchlin argues against the Epicurean view that God is indifferent to human prayer, asserting instead that divine unity implies a provident and caring creator. He references classical mythology and Julian the Apostate to discuss the historical belief in gods appearing in human form.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue of Capnion (Reuchlin's persona), moving from a defense of monotheism against Epicurean "atoms" to an exploration of how the infinite God can truly unite with finite humanity—a central theme of Reuchlin's Christian Kabbalah.</meta>

# 896 JOHANNES REUCHLIN

<margin>The foundation of the doctrine of the Ubiquitarians.</margin>
Indeed, almost that entire book of transformations <note>original: "transformationis liber"; a reference to Ovid's *Metamorphoses*.</note> is nothing other than a communion—or rather, what would be more ridiculous, an actual change—not only with men, but with beasts, metals, and other things lacking a soul. Even to the Epicureans it must seem quite a marvel that the poets sing of the supreme Jupiter being mixed with such lowly things. For they say he was transformed, now into a swan, then a bull, then into the stone called Abaddir <note>In mythology, Abaddir was the stone Rhea gave to Saturn to swallow in place of the infant Jupiter.</note>, always proving himself more versatile than [this...] <note>The right margin is cropped here; Reuchlin is likely critiquing the absurdity of pagan myths compared to philosophical truth.</note>

<margin>Love born from faith and another hope.</margin>
<margin>O wonderful exchange. Unity.</margin>
We, however, whether we call it the fellowship of man with God or the communication of God with man (insofar as it serves our discussion), consider love, which faith has birthed and hope nourishes and preserves. God is love; man [is the...] and the bond between them both is faith. Divinity is joined to the mind, just as the mind is joined to the intellect, the intellect to intention, intention to image, image to sensation, sensation to the senses, and the senses to external things. This occurs in such a way that the higher virtue flows through each inferior level, according to the capacity of the living being, down to the very last. For it often happens that I direct my eyes toward something, yet I do not remember seeing it; this is because I was imagining something elsewhere. What it is that I suspect I see, a mind trained in natural philosophy provides through the intention of the intellect combined with reason. Unless the intellect is illuminated by the mind, it is not immune from error. The mind does not provide light to the intellect unless God is shining within it. Since He possesses the freest will (otherwise He would be inferior to man), He pours down more or less light according to the measure of His will; by this light, the other powers of mortals are watered. Nevertheless, there is no [strict] proportion of man toward God. For God is infinite and man is finite. By your leave, Sidonius <note>Sidonius is one of the three interlocutors in this dialogue, representing a Christian perspective.</note>, these two are not so utterly diverse that one is not also the other. They can, however, be joined in an unutterable union, so that one and the same being may be considered both a human God and a divine man. I speak with you, most learned men, familiarly in the school of wrestling <note>original: "palæstra"; a metaphor for a place of rigorous intellectual debate.</note>—not of secret faith, but of natural philosophy. For thus Unity, which has neither beginning nor end and is therefore called an infinite essence in power and operation—though it is not itself a number (for a number is a heap of many)—nevertheless creates number and joins itself to number. Its various interactions in the fellowship of numbers also varies the nature of those numbers, and it governs the whole numerical kingdom like a king. It humbles one, and exalts another. And as Hesiod says:

->This one easily raises up, and easily brings down the proud.<-
<note>A quote from Hesiod's *Works and Days*, describing the power of Zeus.</note>

For it drips down from [that...] since its permanence is the infinity, measure, and boundary of all things, acting as a sort of corner-stone of the whole, producing the highest peaks, since it is mixed into the [definitions] of all things. Furthermore, it reaches in its second exit a state agreeable to its nature: the first odd, uncomposed [number] of the indivisible sphere, which displays a certain appearance of a composite nature, being constituted from the initial principles of things, both even and odd. Then, in its third stage, it casts its rays upon the solid, penetrating sensible things through the circular number of "otherness," unceasingly agitating the most perfect foundation of the [material] pyramid. For the divine unity inhabits the wonderful middle of every number, where a marvelous reflection of indivisible "oddness" strives to [behold] itself most closely. For this reason, it has marked that very thing with a distinction, connecting it to the superior "second exit" mentioned before. For the architecture of the universe disposed a single difference between the two, with the body of the world interceding in the middle, so that we might perceive that Unity does not shrink from communicating with individuals. From this we may observe that it freely keeps company with men; the most prominent proof of this conversation is that we ourselves are the effectors of works that are beyond human power. At the same time, though established in nature, we dominate nature, and we mortals [perform] monsters, portents, and miracles of divinity with a single Word—which I dared to explain to you long ago.

<margin>Accomplishing great things.</margin>
**T**HEN, O Capnion, proceed," **S I D O N I V S** said. "For how I long to know where you are heading! As God loves me, I have never heard anything more delightful: namely, that it is situated and hidden within us to accomplish—by words alone (which among all human inventions we consider the easiest to produce and the most fragile of arts)—so many things, so wonderful, so difficult, so sudden, and so daring, as our mind desires. It is just as we read concerning Medea <note>In Greek mythology, Medea was a powerful sorceress; Reuchlin uses her here to illustrate the ancient belief in the power of incantations.</note>:

> *And three times she spoke the words that bring peaceful sleep,*
> *Which stay the troubled sea and the rushing rivers.*

<margin>Great power in words, great power in herbs.</margin>
For what can songs <note>original: "carmina"; refers here to incantations or ritual verses.</note> not achieve? Regarding these, the Sorceress seemed to me to boast much in the works of Naso <note>original: "Nasonem"; the Roman poet Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso).</note> when she says:

---
> ——— *I stay the shaken [waters],*
> *I shake the standing seas with song; I drive away the clouds,*
> *And I bring the clouds in; I both drive away and summon the winds.*
> *I break the jaws of vipers with words and song.*
> *I move the living rocks and oaks uprooted from their earth,*
> *And the forests; I command the mountains to tremble,*
> *And the ground to roar, and the spirits to depart from their graves,*
> *And I draw down you too, O moon.*

"Therefore, we must entreat Baruchias, and even offer a sacrifice to our friend Capnion here, so that we may not remain ignorant of what this 'word' is by which he asserts such things are done."

"And I agree with you," **B A R V C H I A S** replied. "And certainly, it will be a matter worthy of philosophers to discuss such great secrets among themselves. Although our race of men, in certain hidden books, has been no small bit curious about that part of religion. Nevertheless, I will speak as I feel: there is no Hebrew in this age whom that power of words wishes to accompany. Instead, we mutter through the whole night in vain because we have no prophecy; just as the oracles ceased at Delphi, and the Pythia <note>The priestess of Apollo at Delphi who delivered oracles.</note> was accused by Demosthenes of 'Philippizing' <note>Demosthenes famously claimed the Oracle was bribed to give answers favoring Philip II of Macedon.</note>—unless some sacrilegious person is found who, for the sake of profit, promises a portent <margin>Charlatans.</margin> to those as foolish as they are easily deceived. I speak of other nations first, then I shall remember my own, and likewise others. For a Phrygian augur will give responses <margin>Profit.</margin> to the wealthy, and for a tiny coin, Jews sell whatever kind of dreams you wish. The accursed hunger for gold has always been held in such honor by wicked men that, out of greed and desire for gain, they do not hesitate to contaminate both divine and human things with their outrages.

"As for certain priests of your time, Capnion, who boast that they are the purest and, as if the grandsons of God, most full of divinity—I would not dare to cast any reproach, lest you believe that through a singular neglect of that sect I am weakening or diminishing our friendship, which refined literature has won for us. For there exists an excellent proverb by Terence <note>The Roman playwright Publius Terentius Afer.</note>, which should be embraced with a mindful heart, saying: *Truth breeds hatred.* If I did not fear that, I would have to bring into the open the manner in which they profane all sacred things for a price, from the highest to the lowest, so that now <margin>Everything for sale.</margin> all things are for sale for a fee. While they forbid the actual handing over of coins by legal action before a judge, the money does not truly vanish; as if it were not a requested fee simply because it is sought out of 'custom,' when that which is contrived against God ought not even be called a custom.

"But I remain silent about what portents and miracles they preach to the people, so that the treasuries may be burdened with gifts and their whole world may overflow with coins. Just as Actius <note>Lucius Accius, an early Roman tragic poet.</note> says: *They enrich the ears of others with words, so that they may enrich their own homes with gold.* Not otherwise does this man bring magic songs, and that one Thessalian love-potions, and the Jews sell dreams. Therefore, if greed were to cease, I believe there would be no one hereafter who would promise that he will perform miracles with words or signs, unless some insane witch..."

...tains. <note>original: "montes"; this concludes the sentence from the previous page describing the powers of a sorceress.</note> [A woman] who might dwell in the countryside, powerful in her potions, who wishes to be believed by every fool, even to the point of displacing heaven, suspending the earth, hardening springs, melting mountains, raising the sea, weakening the gods, extinguishing the stars, and illuminating the underworld—such madness, when caught in its own outrages, is punished by the ultimate penalty of life, not only by Roman laws but even by the older laws of our people (that is, the Hebrews).

->Capnion refutes Baruchias’s opinion, showing that the Philosophers sought the aid of Jewish doctrine. CHAPTER XIII.<-

Immediately following this, as if touched by a certain annoyance, **C A P N I O N** modestly interrupted the discourse. "My dearest Baruchias," he said, "where is your speech leading you? Do you dare to persuade us that, unless profit is involved, men do not often perform stupendous and admirable things? Things not born of time, but arising suddenly; not spread out, but present and insistent in a brief moment; things which no one could have grasped beforehand or hoped for, and which are therefore called miracles—whether you perform them by command or perhaps by prayer. For it is so far from the case that they perform these for the sake of riches, that even to those devoted to greed, that venerable liberality of divine gifts is denied. For although the gods are named the 'givers of wealth' in Hesiod <note>Hesiod was an 8th-century BCE Greek poet; Reuchlin refers here to Hesiod’s *Works and Days*.</note>, the heavenly beings do not wish to be petitioned to obtain them, and the lower beings ought not to be—the latter because of their most wicked fellowship, and the former because of the ultimate foulness of greed. There exists a sound doctrine of the ancient Philosophers on this matter, evidenced by Theognis <note>A 6th-century BCE Greek poet known for his ethical maxims.</note>, who says:

> I do not love riches, and I do not seek them; but for me
> Let it be enough to live on moderate means, and to have no evil.

<margin>Note this, and why.</margin>
Likewise your Solomon, endowed with no less wisdom and antiquity, expressed the same sentiment, speaking with divinity in these words. Indeed, I will say it in English as best I can—for interpreting it would more rightly be your task. He said: 'Give me neither poverty nor riches; let me take my allotted bread.' <note>original: "Egestatem... et diuitias ne des mihi"; Proverbs 30:8.</note> Which they commonly say thus: 'Give me neither beggary nor riches, grant only what is necessary for my sustenance.' But as for the fact that those miraculous works have ceased among your Jews (as you say), believe me, it must be for no small cause. For that art was once practiced among them above all others, so much so that our ancestors, out of a desire for that philosophy, were led away from the sweet conversation of friends and companions and from their ancestral hearths—not only by much wandering but even as if into perpetual exile. Although I hear that 

<margin>Disciples of Hebrew Philosophy.</margin>
some are unwilling to agree that Thales, Pythagoras, Plato, and the others reached the Jews, but only the Egyptian and Memphite priests. Among their number, Lactantius Firmianus <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325 AD) often called the "Christian Cicero."</note> revealed himself to be one, in the fourth volume of the book he titled *Divine Institutes*, perhaps following no one but himself. But I am easily forced to the opinion—by the traces of Mosaic reading which I find in their books and teachings—to say that they bypassed neither the Syrian, nor the Judean, nor even the Chaldean school. For in their time, the sacred scripture of the Hebrews began to be held in such great honor and frequent veneration among the Babylonians, that they took care to translate it from its own language into the Chaldean tongue, and this near the fifty-sixth Olympiad <note>Approximately 556–553 BCE, the era of the philosopher Thales of Miletus.</note>, that is, in the age of Thales. Therefore, who could be so out of his mind as to doubt that those who were inflamed with such a great desire for investigating the truth that they sought exile, leaving their homes so that the most ancient monuments would not remain hidden from them, would not have approached Judea at the same time they sought Egypt? Especially so that, having tasted the streams, they might also drink from the source, and so that they might look into the Nabataean rites and be imbued with a purer divinity. In the handing down of which, the Jews were more noble than all the nations of the world, by the testimony of the oracle itself, which wrote for them...

He cites the early translation of Hebrew scriptures into Chaldean as proof of the international reach of Jewish thought in antiquity.</summary>

<margin>Neighboring peoples.</margin>
Added to this is what might strengthen my opinion: since there is so little distance between the Egyptians and the Jews, you will often find mixed populations in the same place, consisting of Egyptians, Arabs, Hebrews, and Phoenicians—especially in Sebaste of Herod (which is also called Samaria), in Philadelphia, in Jericho, and likewise in Galilee. I speak of a matter by no means obscure to you, Sidonius, who are most skilled and most dear to us both, since you were born not far from there.

### CHAPTER XIV.

<margin>The Nations obtained the highest wisdom from the Hebrews.</margin>
"Indeed, you speak the truth," said **S I D O N I V S**. "For one sees a single contiguous border between Judea, Egypt, Arabia, and the Babylonians. Therefore, it does not seem probable to me that those Philosophers failed to reach Palestine and the wisdom of the Hebrews, since I have indeed discovered that they often transferred not only the ideas themselves, but almost the very words of that nation into their own books."

"But proceed, Capnion," he added. To which Capnion replied: "You judge quite rightly. For regarding Plato, it is certain—whom I myself am accustomed to read occasionally for the sake of breathing room after a thousand business affairs and courtly turmoils. And, O good God, how much I find he has fished out from that source! For the most part, it is word for word. If you wish to know this more extensively, read the philosopher Justin <note>Justin Martyr, a 2nd-century Christian apologist who argued that Plato followed Moses.</note>, whom I believe you have read; although he is a martyr of my religion and of no small integrity, he is perhaps suspected by you—unless you are forced to agree with me by the facts themselves, rather than by his assertion. 

I return to the cause. That salutary power of words which has deserted you [the Jews], has chosen us; it accompanies us, and is seen to obey our every nod. That virtue of perfect religion, given and offered not by human counsel but by divine decree, changed its location not by chance, but by its own diligence and industry.

<margin>Causes of the Jews' misery.</margin>
Because you changed the lawful sacred rites, you therefore murmur in vain and invoke God in vain. You do not worship Him as He Himself wills, but flattering your own inventions, you even hate us, the worshipers of God, with an immortal spite. The Divinity, who desires to dwell peacefully in human minds, rejects this above all else. Nor would I easily accept our friend Sidonius unless he could be turned toward a sincere kind of believing. As for you yourself [Baruchias], there is scarcely any hope in me, born of that lineage which has always stood forth as stiff-necked <note>original: "durae cervicis," a common biblical idiom for the Israelites' stubbornness</note>—unless the great learning of your noble intellect, your many studies, your innumerable doctrines, and even your immense love of knowing might achieve something."

---

->*Both demand that Capnion proceed, desiring to be instructed by him whom he is leading toward the knowledge of God.*<-

### CHAPTER XV.

<margin>How divine things are to be learned.</margin>
Then both said: "We beseech you, Capnion, do not despair, and do not desert us. For that alone is the power of words which surpasses the knowledge of all things. Therefore, we submit our hands to your rod <note>A metaphor for a student submitting to a teacher's discipline.</note>, by whatever kind of discipline we may finally be initiated. I know, and so does Baruchias here, that in learning sacred things one must walk a far different path than mathematicians and physicists are accustomed to. For they think it most convenient first to butt heads and contend among themselves, fighting on both sides of an issue. Then, through certain antecedents or axioms—or 'principles' as you might call them—which you cannot refute, they soon conclude by the artifice of a certain combination, by which you yourself are compelled to stand. But on the contrary, in divine matters, silence is required, contention is rejected, and the syllogism <note>A formal logical argument</note> is mocked."

For there is no beginning to the divinity; nothing precedes it. Therefore, whatever conclusion is reached concerning it must be accepted immediately, under a condition far more demanding than that of mere science. We have already heard from you what that condition is. Renew your discourse, best Capnion, and teach us with what words we may establish our faith. I, for my part, vouch for this companion of ours in whatever lies ahead. Is it not so, Baruchias? Then he replied: It is so, Sidonius. I know you both to be good and learned men, both he who asks the promise and he who gives it. Whereas I might fear a sacrilege from certain other dull-witted men, I have no such dread here. Nor do I fear that the supreme divinity will be wronged by some perverse form of worship. For you both know how <term>nefarious</term> <note>original: "nepharium," meaning something impious or unspeakable in a religious sense</note> that would be, even to Philosophers.

I, indeed, said CAPNION, take you at your word. But you must both observe these prescribed laws without rebellion. Let this be your path to transformation: You, Baruchias, must withdraw from your Talmudic studies; and you, Sidonius, must depart from the teachings of Epicurus and Lucretius <note>Epicurus and Lucretius were ancient philosophers often associated with atomism and the denial of divine intervention in human affairs.</note>. Be washed and be pure. Acknowledge one God as the maker of all things, and all other powers as His ministering servants. Let there be vows and prayers to the First, and hymns to the lower powers. But if any petition is made to those lower powers, let it not be intended except as a delegated form of administration from the First. Let there be reverence and trembling before the Angels who fly from us to God, and from Him back to us. Toward them, according to their proven character, let there be joyful obedience. Let these sacred rites, whose observations you have come to hear from me, be for the worthy, but kept secret from the profane. I have judged that these edicts and prohibitions should be written down for you, so that you may weigh them carefully in your minds to decide whether they are to be accepted or rejected. For under no other condition could I, as a teacher, admit you into the Academy of divine and sacred names, unless you first wish to assent to such laws. For when you have undertaken these requirements willingly, I hope you will most easily reach those things you desire.

### CHAPTER XVI.
### Sidonius repeats each of the precepts which Capnion had delivered in the previous chapter, and confirms them with the authorities and ceremonies of the ancients.

<margin>Criticism of the Talmud</margin>
Then **S I D O N I V S** said: Thus far I find nothing intolerable, unless perhaps Baruchias here wishes to see the law itself as harsh. I myself have long been persuaded—and it was not difficult to convince me—that those arrogant factions and conspiracies of madness, which I once read about, were false, especially whenever they pertain to the divinity. These factions seem more intent on twisting the hatred, slaughter, and plundering of foreign nations than on directing them toward the salvation of all men. Yet I think he will easily let go of them if he considers in his own mind that those who committed their inventions and meditations to writing were men just like us. <margin>The Scholastics.</margin> They did so for the sake of their own schools, much like the commentaries of certain Scholastics <note>The "Scholastics" refers to the medieval university theologians, whom Renaissance humanists like Reuchlin often criticized for being overly logical and dry.</note>. Surely anyone may abandon these without penalty, just as I am now doing regarding Lucretius and Epicurus; for I never swore an oath to their words, nor to any other decrees of my ancestral profession. Therefore, if he takes my advice, he will not resist.

As for me, to speak for myself, why should I not undergo what right Philosophy persuaded me of long ago? For Epicurus and Lucretius have already been exploded <note>In the classical sense, "exploded" means to be hissed off the stage or rejected by consensus.</note> for many centuries by good and most distinguished men. Why should I doubt your other laws, which I learned previously from many men of various kinds, <margin>The ceremony of baptism among the Indian Brahmans.</margin> but especially from those who teach the magic arts? For concerning the washing, I learned that custom from the most wise men of India, whom they call Brahmans. I have turned that custom into my own habit, having become well-acquainted with it through long daily use. I was accustomed to wash daily with them in a spring not unlike the one called Dirce <note>A famous spring in Thebes, Greece.</note>, having first stripped off my clothes and anointed my head with drops and scents suited for that purpose. Then, after they judged themselves sufficiently pure according to their rite, it was necessary to go, around midday, as quickly as possible to the sacred rites held there in the manner of a choir...

# ON THE MIRIFIC WORD, BOOK I.

...we [saw them], dressed in white linen and a white miter <note>A miter in this context refers to a traditional priestly head-covering or turban rather than a modern bishop’s hat.</note>, wearing rings on their fingers and carrying staffs in their hands. This cleanliness of the body and dress was believed, as they said, to assist not a little in the purity of the soul. These things were done under the leadership of Vardanes among the Indians, the fourth after Iarchas <note>Iarchas and Vardanes were legendary leaders of the Brahmans in India, known to the Renaissance through the writings of Philostratus.</note>. For after Iarchas came Sauchnes, after him Sesonchoris, then Bocchoris—so named after the ancient kings of the Egyptians.

<margin>Gymnosophists.</margin>
I saw a similar thing when I lived among the Gymnosophists <note>literally "naked philosophers," a term used by Greeks for Indian monastics or yogis</note> for the sake of learning; I was admitted even more readily because it was a sacred rule to be washed three times by day and twice by night in cold water, before I could enter the inner sanctum of the sacred rites at those same times. Likewise, there was a linen garment, freshly washed every day.

<margin>What wool is.</margin>
For they consider wool to be a profane clothing, inasmuch as it is shorn from sheep like the waste of a beast's filth. We also read in Hesiod that this kind of precept is especially suited to divine matters. For he says (as you know) in the book of *Works and Days* almost thus:

<margin>Washing of hands.</margin>
> Let no one at dawn dare to pour wine to Jove
> With unwashed hands, nor to the other immortals.
> For they do not wish to hear such prayers and they despise them.

And in another poem thus:

> When an evil man crosses a river without washing his hands,
> The gods are angry with him and send him sorrows thereafter.

Telemachus <note>The son of Odysseus in Homer's *Odyssey*.</note> carefully guarded himself against this; for when he was about to pray to Pallas Athena, he washed his hands in the sea. Do you see now that this custom was not first devised by you, but was commended many centuries ago? Our Homer—that blind man who saw all things—seems to me not to have been ignorant of this when he describes the mother of Achilles, about to petition Jove, rising from the waves of the sea <note>Thetis, a sea nymph and mother of Achilles.</note>. Although he may seem to have explained another mystery even greater than that one, it is not relevant to this discussion. But as for the third law you brought to us, the clearest dogmas of the most ancient authors prove it. Listen to what Sophocles brings forth in this Iambic distich—which, though perhaps not translated by me with great elegance, is, I think, not unsuitably rendered—when he says:

> In truth, there is only one God,
> who created this heaven and the spacious earth.

Whom Euripides commands should be named Jove. Orpheus sang that all things proceeded into the light through His head; Orpheus himself praises Him in his first hymn as the father of all, the beginning and the end, using a single name. But as for what follows—that the other powers are to be considered ministers—I would believe you learned that from the poems of Homer, in the eighth volume of the *Trojan Rhapsodies* <note>The *Iliad*, Book 8.</note>. There, in a splendid speech full of majesty, Jupiter addresses the assembly of the gods, declaring himself the supreme dispenser of all things and that these others are inferiors; nothing is to be attempted except by his nod, and those who do otherwise will be cast down into Tartarus. Thus it appears how much more powerful Jupiter is than both gods and men. The poem is well known to you; render it from Greek into Latin as you prefer. Indeed, from this, the fourth law is artfully derived, as if in the manner of the logicians. For if He is the first who dispenses each thing, it is in vain that one flees to the rest, whether by prayer or by vow—a point that Nausicaa, the daughter of Alcinous, once persuaded her guest of:

<margin>Let the worshippers of the saints note this.</margin>
> Jupiter himself dispenses all things to men from above,
> Whether to the upright or the perverse, as he favors each case.

<margin>Thetis, Achilles.</margin>
Therefore, Achilles by no means asked Thetis to bring him safety against the king by whom he had suffered unworthy violence, but with hands outstretched and weeping, he prayed in this manner:

> But you, if you are able, embrace the cause of your son,
> And implore Jove, ascending to the threshold of Olympus.

For this Master and Father of the universe—as Menander says in *Diphilus*—we shall deem worthy of this highest honor, He who alone is the discoverer and possessor of such great goods. For it is naturally implanted in us that when the clear vein of the spring can be reached, we should abstain from the little streams. What then? Should we, contrary to the institutions of our ancestors, [venerate] the gods... <note>original: "superos," referring to the celestial beings or gods.</note>
