# JOHANNES REUCHLIN

...will we avoid the Hesperians <note>original: "Hesperos"; likely referring to Westerners or those of the "evening" lands, contrasting with the Eastern sages mentioned previously.</note> and seek the aid of Jupiter alone? And not by the warning of Pegnis <note>Possibly a reference to a classical poet or a corruption of a name like Panyassis.</note>:

> *A man must be daring in difficult circumstances;*
> *Should they then ask the gods above to snatch them out?* <note>original: "Esse uirum audentem duris in rebus oportet, / Eripiant superos inde rogare deos?"</note>

But perhaps, just as we use the help of friends, we might use their efforts in mutual exchanges—as we do with relatives or wise men—insofar as they are able to benefit us with counsel and consolation. By their learning, and by a united and always faithful impulse, we can undoubtedly conform our minds to the divine in any matter.

<margin>Reasons why divine beings are to be invoked.</margin>
For the divine beings <note>original: "diui"; Reuchlin uses this term to bridge the gap between classical "gods" and the "angels" or "saints" of his own era.</note> are more skilled; they know us better than we know ourselves, and they understand all the circumstances of our affairs. They join our matters more certainly and much more aptly to the decrees of God the Prince, like certain rays subordinating earthly bodies, so that from this, the future may be such for you that evils are declined. That is, when they are well-disposed toward us who have turned to them, we either escape this fate or endure that one. Indeed, it has been within the memory of the fathers and ancestors that the Fates imposed that majesty upon 
<margin>Fates.</margin>
mortals. The unworthy women <note>The "unworthy women" or "little women" (mulierculæ) likely refers to the Fates as seen by the common people, or perhaps the suitors' maids in the Odyssey.</note> now overcome by sleep, who address Ulysses in the nineteenth book (if I remember correctly) with these words: "Whenever the immortals have established the fate for mortals inhabiting the grain-eating earth." Thus Socrates proclaimed himself warned by a God <note>A reference to the *daimonion*, the divine voice or inner sign that guided Socrates.</note>. Thus Egeria led <note>Egeria was a nymph who, according to legend, acted as a divine counselor to Numa Pompilius, the second king of Rome.</note>. Thus no one was ever truly a Pythagorean who did not owe reverence to those beings because they are good, as if they were portions of the First Good. For honor and praise are by their own nature good, as Aristotle’s *Ethics* testify. Since honor is granted to the 
<margin>Elders.</margin>
elders, it should be some retribution for virtue. Moreover, the Elders are the Gods, and they are so not only as ours, but as rulers, because by their own nature they have more life and intellect; for this reason, they are sometimes called "Intelligences." Your subsequent laws are proved by the custom of mathematicians through what precedes them. Sophocles also showed the last of these when he speaks thus in *Orestes*:

->One must obey those who are superior in every way.<- <note>original: "Prestantioribus omnino est obediendum."</note>

And in *Ajax* he uses these verses:

> *For he in whom fear and reverence flourish,*
> *believe that he shall soon find safety.* <note>original: "Nam cui timor uiget & simul reuerentia, illum salutem mox habere credito."</note>

Therefore, it will be very easy for me, Capnion <note>Capnion is the Greek translation of Reuchlin’s name, meaning "Little Smoke."</note>, to grant consent to your commands, for the same cause which I have known to be accepted by learned men many thousands of years ago.

### CHAPTER XVII.

<margin>Error follows all times.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial 'T' with foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>
THEN Baruchias spoke. "Sidonius," he said, "it is found that some of the ages of our ancestors have erred. Do not think that all things from superior times are granted to be learned or should even be followed, unless reason discusses whether they are true. I would not wish to be led by any rashness into wanting to resist these laws you have promulgated, nor would I insidiously distrust your other presentations, which you bring into the open so abundantly from your excellent skill and your experience in various matters. I myself will also undergo those things, even if compelled by no ready reason, unless perhaps by the authority of revelation. For I agree with you, as in Cicero, regarding the assertion of the High Priest which he confidently showed to Balbus: that in the religion of our ancestors, one must believe even if no reason is given. Plato thought these men were the parents of the gods and knew them best. Therefore, as if regarding their own household, whatever they affirmed, the highest faith must be granted. But the common people..."

# ON THE MIRIFIC WORD, BOOK I.

...often mixed certain falsehoods with truths, which even the Philosophers themselves could scarcely escape without danger to their lives. 
<margin>Seeking truth through opinion.</margin>
Just as they accused Diagoras—who wrote many things about the divine differently than the common people saw them—of a crime, presenting a warrant for his head; but he avoided imminent death by a swift flight. 
<margin>Philosophers killed.</margin>
Anaxagoras was sentenced to the ultimate punishment at Athens, and Socrates was killed by poison. Even our own wise men, whom we once called 
<margin>Prophetæ occiduntur.</margin>
seers but now call prophets, often underwent the indignation of kings, sometimes of the people, and occasionally death itself for the sake of religion and divine matters. You remember that Jeroboam lifted his hand against the man of God, which was immediately turned dry; Isaiah was cut into pieces; Jeremiah was overwhelmed by stones in Egypt; Ezekiel was slain in Assyria by the command of a leader; Daniel was condemned to the beasts; Amos was killed with a club; Micah was cast over a precipice; Zechariah was slaughtered at the altar—all for no other reason than that they felt more holily than the unlearned masses. 

Therefore, you had added quite justly: "to learned men, and good ones too." Nothing now presses upon me more heavily or more bothersomely, nothing from which I more shrink, than to lack—not only for a time, but even forever—the great glory, the great splendor, and the good reputation among our most literate men (whom they call <term>Thalmudim</term> <note>Talmudists; scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note> from their learning). 

But since you wish it so, Capnion <note>The Greek-style pseudonym of Johannes Reuchlin, meaning "Little Smoke."</note>, I shall comply with your custom. I will even cast aside the <term>Thalmudim</term>, in whom, from my tenderest years as soon as I began to be wise, the highest pleasure always resided, more pleasant than the rest of life. I hope likewise that it will be an act not ungrateful to the Divine if I repel for His sake what was most pleasing to my soul. For it happens now, perhaps as never before, that I may easily do without all other things, provided that I do not miss such a holy knowledge of the wonderful names as you seemed to promise us—or, if I remember correctly, so that I may not be accused of wickedly carping at your words. 

You said you remembered a certain Word—I know not what—by which we mortals, established in nature, might rule over nature, and perform the wonders, portents, and miracles which are the marks of divinity. Come, Capnion, let us not be ignorant of this word. For my tribesmen hide many words almost "under a bushel" <note>A biblical idiom referring to hiding a light or truth (Matthew 5:15).</note> and keep them in secret, which are judged by them to be "mirific" <note>Wonder-working or marvelous.</note>, and which I myself have also read many times, but I never felt their effect. And that is perhaps because I either did not observe the proper method, or I believed fictions instead of truths.

"Suddenly you have hit the nail on the head," <note>original: "tetigisti acu"; a Latin idiom for being exactly right.</note> said SIDONIUS. "For here a snake lies in the grass; <note>A warning that there is a hidden danger or deception in what follows.</note> this is what pertains to the matter, and not a little indeed. For I once had a similar passion for certain triflers writing about the magic art, who were hardly worthy of the paper and pen they used. Moved by the index of books, I thought I was going to find some wonderful arts there, such as the operations of Zoroaster, Oromasis, Zamolxis, Epimenides, 
<margin>Authors of magic.</margin>
Orpheus, Pythagoras, Hostanes, Empedocles, or even the more recent Thessalian factions of Charinondas, Damigeron, Apollonius, and John Dardanus. But listen while I read what it really is: By Pollux! <note>original: "Edepol"; an ancient Roman oath.</note> it is nothing other than 그 Horace says:

> The mountains are in labor, and a ridiculous mouse will be born. <note>A classic metaphor for something that promises much but delivers very little.</note>

The rascals hang splendid titles before the doors of their volumes; 
<margin>The Book of Enoch.</margin>
sometimes claiming this to be the *Book of Enoch*, which antiquity asserted was more divine than all others, and at other times they lie that a book belongs to Solomon. They easily creep into unlearned ears with this notable conjecture, which one might guess from the books of Josephus. For he says 
<margin>The forged book of Solomon.</margin>
in the eighth book of *Antiquities* that Solomon discovered an art against demons for the benefit and cure of men, and established incantations against illnesses, and even a method of conjurations. To this he adds an experiment which he himself saw. Nevertheless, from the sacred histories of the Hebrews, it is well known that Solomon in his age was accustomed to discourse on trees and herbs, from the cedar of Lebanon even to the hyssop; likewise on beasts, birds, reptiles, and fish, all of which...

# THE WRITINGS OF JOHANNES REUCHLIN

...might present themselves as natural or false magic. But to one looking closely, the deceptive trickery of these charlatans reveals itself openly; indeed, their very volumes profess themselves to be fabrications of our own age. If anyone considers the order of the words, the force of the sentences, and the very type of characters used, nothing will prevent them from seeing clearly that all such books have sprung recently from the hiding place of a single conspiracy in our era. Furthermore, they have attached to their volumes the actions of the ancients which pertain to the art; yet, because of the coarseness of the letters, they can achieve nothing—not the words themselves, nor the numbers, nor the figures. They are ignorant of the fact that the Egyptians use a double character <note>Reuchlin refers to the distinction between hieroglyphic and demotic scripts</note>, one for profane matters and the other for sacred. Finally, we write the language of the Chaldeans <note>Aramaic</note> and the Hebrews—which they attest is necessary for the work—with a similar image of character. Robert, Bacon, Abanus, Picatrix, and the *Conciliator* <note>Pietro d'Abano’s "Conciliator," a famous work of medical and magical philosophy</note> amount to nothing, primarily due to their ignorance of languages; they could not teach precisely as is required, nor could the hands of the copyists avoid erring from the dual examples, much less could the disciples learn or the practitioners work. I see, therefore, in order to agree with Baruchias, that although there is an abundance of secrets of this kind, I have not perceived their effects myself because a suitable master was absent, by whose labor and talent... Therefore, let it not weary you to recite it again.

## *Capnion defers the discourse until tomorrow, to which both agree.*
### CHAPTER XIX.

And CAPNION <note>The Greek pseudonym for Reuchlin himself, meaning "little smoke"</note> said: "It is now evening, and it is so late that such a great and serious business—truly a priestly task and a philosophy most worthy of the light for wise men—cannot be completed before night. For we should not imitate the Brahmins <note>Ancient Indian philosophers/priests</note> in their contemplations, whose skin is most dark because of the constant heat of the sun which blackens nearly everything they have. This setting is so unsuitable for secret ceremonies and so profane for a celestial gift—indeed, for these rites—that it ought to be changed for a small chapel (if you agree); we should withdraw as if the sacred mysteries were urging us. Therefore, it is judged better <note>original: "tò satius," a mix of the Greek article and Latin adjective</note> to put the whole matter off until tomorrow, when we shall have the opportunity to meet at my suburban house." Meanwhile, remember this tonight: we have decreed that what is to be postponed must, above all, be felt, established, and most openly proclaimed and praised.

<margin>Right faith.</margin>
For right faith alone is the hinge of miracles; if you neglect it, you cannot penetrate either the secret arts or the assemblies of the oracles. Then SIDONIUS said: "The time and place are rightly appointed. But take care; I have no doubt of our faith, being led by your integrity as well as your singular learning." BARVCHIAS replied: "Whatever your opinion is, I would not believe it unless I acted upon it, lest Sidonius cite to me the verses of the most ancient Linus <note>A legendary Greek poet</note>, which say that all things are to be believed. For nothing is incredible, and all things are easy; nothing is impossible. Those are Linus's verses word for word (as you know). But Pallas <note>Athena</note> in Homer, whom we remember on this occasion, consoles Achilles with such speech: 'I have come to quiet your fury, if you will believe.'"

<margin>Daniel among the lions.</margin>
"I myself would more gladly bring forward something of my own: the history of Daniel, although it was written not in Hebrew, but in Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note>. For this is what the truth of the speech holds: 'And no wound was found upon him, because he [believed] in his God.' <note>Daniel 6:23</note> Therefore, I too will believe, along with Sidonius, whatever CAPNION shortly brought forth, producing certain tablets, and the matters in..."

# THE SECOND BOOK OF CAPNION, OR, ON THE WONDER-WORKING WORD, BY JOHANNES REUCHLIN OF PFORZHEIM, DOCTOR OF LAWS
## BOOK TWO
### PREFACE.

Now that the previous day has been successfully spent, Holy Prelate of Dalberg <note>Johann von Dalberg (1455–1503), the Bishop of Worms and a patron of humanism</note>, I pray you to listen patiently to how the three philosophers, having awakened after sleep, meet before dawn and spend the entire day discussing the Wonder-Working Word. The more powerful Baruchias <note>The Jewish representative in the dialogue</note> presides over this day, just as Sidonius <note>The representative of pagan/Epicurean philosophy</note> did yesterday. For today, you will learn much more taken from the books of the Chaldeans <note>Aramaic</note> and the Hebrews; and to grasp their principles, Sidonius began thus.

### SIDONIUS BEGINS, ACCUMULATING MANY THINGS IN HIS SPEECH CONCERNING THE MAGICAL ART, WHICH HE CONCLUDES TO BE VAIN AND DANGEROUS. CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>A rectangular woodcut initial letter 'A' containing a scene of two men in academic or clerical robes engaged in a conversation within an interior room. One man on the left points with his index finger while the other on the right listens attentively. A window in the background shows a background building and a landscape.</image-desc>
WE ARE PRESENT, Capnion, and we have almost prematurely arrived before the dawn itself, like restless men. For I see this Baruchias here as well, not just walking, but hurrying, lest he neglect any of your business; indeed, if it pleases you, I would have applied the spurs, even though he was already running. "Hey there, Baruchias, into the chapel!" But he, with gasping breath, said: "I am here, and with you, Sidonius; although a little later than I wished, yet still early, I think:

> "Before the dawn has moved the dewy shadow from the sky." <note>original: "Cùm ne humentem aurora polo dimouerit umbram." A quote from Virgil’s Aeneid, 4.7</note>

Certainly, this place is worthy of a philosopher, and I marvel at it, Capnion, because—contrary to the custom of your people, or rather now ours, since you have made us your own—it contains no idols (which you call *signa* <note>original: "signa"</note> in Latin) nor any images, unless something lies hidden in the inner chambers or in these very shrines. <margin>Image.</margin> And behold, there is the cross itself. Then Sidonius said: "Let it go for now, Baruchias; do you not know what is in the records? Beware of causing us trouble by being the author of a longer delay. But come, Capnion, teach us about the Wonder-Working Word, or if it should be some name that is even plural. For we do not press the matter like grammarians, provided it is that by which we, being situated in nature, may be able to work miracles above nature, as you were saying—whether this happens through foreseeing, such as prophecies, or by effecting the things themselves, the natural cause of which is commonly unknown, and therefore to be wondered at even by the most skillful men. For there are certain things, so composed by nature, which we marvel at because they are seen rarely or never, such as the Hermaphrodites, formerly called Androgynes, or the <margin>Phoenix.</margin> Phoenix about which it is sung:

> "Egypt gathers to the wonders of such a sight,
> and the cheering crowd greets the rare bird." <note>original: "Conuenit Aegyptus tanti ad miracula uisus, / Et raram uolucrem turba salutat ouans." From Claudian’s poem "The Phoenix."</note>

Herodotus says that although he waited for it for a long time, he never saw it, except in a painting. Likewise, the birth of five boys at once, and other monstrous things. And if we ourselves manufacture wonders with the aid of nature, such as what is found in Democritus <note>The pre-Socratic "laughing philosopher," often associated in the Renaissance with secret natural properties</note> regarding the liver of a Chameleon on the highest rooftops, which he says <margin>Stirring up rain.</margin> stirs up rain and thunder; or like the wooden dove of Archytas of Tarentum <note>A Greek mathematician and philosopher (4th century BC) credited with building the first flying machine</note>, which he had designed to fly, the like of which we ourselves have both seen and know how to fashion. These and similar things we produce either through our natural senses or by the aid of nature; this is a physical principle often known to unlettered men, mechanics, and common...

<meta>This page continues Sidonius’s opening speech in Book II. Having established the necessity of faith in the previous book, he now transitions into a critique of the "mirific" or magical arts—specifically astrology and ritual magic—contrasting their inconsistency and danger with the stable truth of the "Wonder-Working Word" they are gathered to discuss.</meta>

# JOHANNES REUCHLIN

...easily proves to troubled consciences. I demand none of these things from you, for they are so common that they are read in the streets and at crossroads, and even in daily lecture halls. <margin>Miraculous mechanisms.</margin> Nor do those miraculous mechanisms <note>Original: *machinamenta mirifica*</note> which the praises of the art promise interest me—whether in composing images, or carving, or predicting events, or dispensing fortune and misfortune by the incomprehensible power of the heavens sealed into the natures of lower things. Since these turn out to be so fallacious and so diverse among themselves in practice, the authors of that school oppose each other; they are of such great, insurmountable, and infinite labor that they hardly fall under an art that is not lying. I would rather speak true things through quiet than, with the greatest labors, follow a profession that is a laughingstock, which works devotedly at lying.

<margin>Harmony <note>Greek: *symphonia*</note>.</margin> For the clearest argument of truth is harmony, while the mark of falsehood is discord. But what will you find that is constant, firm, or sincere in that art which they call astrology? I am not speaking of the measurement of the stars—where the mathematicians and experience itself show nothing is more certain—but of the judgment conceived from them, which is a fallacious path and a foolish opinion. This is especially true in those things which concern the elementary dispositions of bodies, the moments of the year, and the figures of time, as your Baruchias Moses <note>Likely referring to Maimonides (Moses ben Maimon), whom Reuchlin often cites regarding the limits of astrology</note> hints. 

See how varied they are among themselves. <margin>Abu Ma'shar.</margin> Abu Ma'shar <note>A famous 9th-century Persian astrologer and astronomer</note>, whom they adore as the president and master of that faculty, deals with judgments; he says some astrologers think the planets signify universal things, like the elements and the species of natural things, but regarding individuals and the parts and acts of individuals—namely, growing up and similar things—they demonstrate nothing at all. Others, however, think they show only what is necessary, such as fire being hot and water cold, but not things that are contingent, such as whether a person speaks or is silent. Finally, others think the planets portend only the change of seasons, and only insofar as it happens to bodies through them. 

The later practitioners indeed follow the ancients, yet with no intention of judging the words of the ancients, since they say it would be impossible even for wise astronomers to find out the science of judgments. Nevertheless, they dare to introduce a doctrine by which they strive to persuade us that they know even the smallest thoughts of a person's mind, and can subvert and change the whole nature of things. The warning of Ptolemy <note>The famous Greco-Egyptian astronomer</note> does not terrify them, who asserts that such a profession deceives us for the most part. Nothing of the slipperiness of their principles stays them, which are most like a vain fiction, and which the ancients take one way, Ptolemy another, Almansor <note>OCR "mon" likely refers to Almansor, a common astrological authority</note> another, and Hermes another. 

Nothing of the infinite collection of second causes that happen to one thing deters them. Nothing of the great distance of the stars from us through innumerable media. Nothing of their uncertain heap, such an inconsistent multitude of stars, to the point that there are those which have not yet been seen, and they first confess they have never looked upon them: by whose virtue it is believed they are admitted into governing substances about to be born, as when that star which some call the Dog and others Sirius adds so much heat to the ruling planets, though it has scarcely been seen. 

Nor do I demand much from you regarding the methods by which wonderful things happen through magical factions. For I have spent no small amount of time in that prestidigitation, though I do not yet repent of its name, since by the highest reasons I can more easily turn others away from such great ruin. <margin>Dangerous magic.</margin> For when you have consumed your whole life in that sacrilegious business, you will hardly extort from it anything that is real, but only what is seen, and that only with the expectation of the greatest danger to your soul. Thus I myself saw Robert the Englishman <note>Robertus Anglicus, a 13th-century astronomer/astrologer whose works were still studied</note> miserably dead among the Swiss, and another whose name I keep silent, miserably captured and changed by fame. I have heard from most faithful men that many others, who were most flourishing in that art, were led away most miserably in this way.

<summary>Sidonius critiques the vanity and inconsistency of astrology and magic, arguing that their practitioners contradict one another and that the art is both scientifically unreliable and spiritually dangerous.</summary>

# ON THE WONDER-WORKING WORD, BOOK II.

<margin>The Magic Books of Mercury.</margin>
<margin>The movement of the gods.</margin>
<margin>See in our own magicians how much they observe their Divinity.</margin>
<margin>We should rightly give thanks to the Gospel of Jesus Christ, which has freed us from such darkness and thorns.</margin>
<margin>Seek the One in spirit and truth.</margin>
Indeed, the powers of darkness bestow their own patronage with honor. But if there are those who think they practice magic not through the bindings or incantations of evil spirits, but through the quiet help of good spirits <note>Original: *daemonum*, here meaning guiding spirits or intermediaries, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense</note>—perhaps because it seemed so to them—nevertheless, they have everything so entangled that it is necessary first to observe and mix together all the universal theories of the astrologers (which we refuted a few pages back) alongside the prescribed rites of their own sacred ceremonies to the letter. This is truly too intolerable, not to say impossible, for the human mind. For an entire human lifetime is scarcely enough just to read the books of that faculty, of which Mercury <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage to whom thousands of "Hermetic" texts on magic and philosophy were attributed</note> alone is said to have written thirty-six thousand five hundred and twenty-five, covering the universal aspects of sacred rites. What do you think of the rest? 

Finally, I grant that at last, through long vigils, much effort, and diligent observation, you might have abundantly acquired the admirable secrets of hidden magic along with the inventions of the astrologers—secrets by which the spirits of the dead <note>Original: *manes*</note> obey, the stars are disturbed, the divine powers are compelled, and the elements serve. Even if you wish to perform a work free from all clumsiness using the invincible power of that discipline and the blind violence of compelled deities—or, if you prefer, with a helpful crowd of bright Gods—nevertheless, you will then be so stunned and terrified by such a throng of spirits (who precede like forerunners and a sort of procession for that deity whose favor you wish to use for the intended action) that you will shrink back in horror. You will leave the work unfinished, destined to be a loss to yourself and a laughingstock to others. 

For it is known to no one—on the authority of Iamblichus and Porphyry <note>Neoplatonist philosophers who wrote extensively on theurgy and the nature of spirits</note>—how great a multitude of powers is usually stirred up when the gods descend and are moved, except to those priests who have already become experienced through the labor itself. Indeed, he who does not follow each one with a specific honor, nor distributes to all what is fitting for each, nor conducts himself with thanks, offerings, and gifts most similar to their condition, does not attain the presence of the deities themselves or the desired effects; just as in a harmony, if one string is broken, the whole thing suddenly sounds discordant. These are the places, these are the foundations of the discipline and the very methods of the art. 

Therefore, Capnion <note>The Greek pseudonym for Johann Reuchlin, meaning "Little Smoke," a play on his German name "Rauch"</note>, you have relieved us of a heavy annoyance and an unbearable burden by your promise—you who have come to free our study from so many stars, so many spirits, so many precepts, so many rites and vain observations. For, to pass over the inhabitants of heaven—how many and how great they are, being innumerable according to the infinite thoughts or "ideas" of the Primary Mind, of whom they say the ancient Orpheus <note>The mythical poet and founder of the Orphic mysteries</note> introduced three hundred and fifty gods by name—we shall consider only the earthly deities closest to us. Of these, the most noble writer of equal antiquity, Hesiod <note>Early Greek poet, author of *Theogony*</note>, numbered thirty thousand in his book *Works and Days*. To offer sacrifices to each of these is beyond man and exceeds our strength. But now the sun is rising; begin, most distinguished Capnion.

### CHAPTER II.

<margin>Simple truth.</margin>
Then he said: If nature had produced me a little more abundant in speech and not so ill-tempered, then certainly, as I reflect upon it, no small gratitude would be owed to you, Sidonius, for showing such a forest of miracles from which a great abundance of felled wood might be available to us for amply and magnificently illustrating the structure of such a divine work. And if I were one from the school of Chrysippus <note>A Stoic philosopher known for his rigorous logic and prolific writing</note>, I would greatly rejoice that these riches of your most ornate eloquence were set before us, from which my own speech could be made more copious. But I was neither born nor trained for such elegancies, nor does the matter under discussion require it. On the contrary, that which is divine and sacred rejects an abundance of speech and opinions disguised with flowery words: especially...

...especially in a doctrine dedicated to God alone, where every blemish must be avoided. We are warned that in a multitude of words, sin will not be lacking; even the more elegant literature <note>original: *litiores quoque literae*, referring to classical Roman poetry</note> commands this through the words of Flaccus <note>The Roman poet Horace: *Quicquid praecipies esto brevis*</note>:
> Whatever you teach, let it be brief.

<margin>Consider the time, measure, and mode of all things.</margin> This is what I intend to do, both by choice and by necessity, so that as briefly as possible... Indeed, if the greatest familiarity had not already begun between us, I would have first looked deeply into each of you—your nature, your way of life, your studies, your temperament, and your age—and I would have required patience of the ears and silence. For as Nazianzenus <note>Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, a 4th-century Church Father known for his "Theological Orations"</note> says, it is not for everyone, nor at all times, nor in all matters to philosophize about God; rather, there are specific people, times, and limits. But you have already been prepared for this task by yesterday’s discussion <note>original: *hesterna tabula*, referring to the previous day's debate</note>, and you possess the necessary qualities at home within yourselves. What more do I require from you, other than what Simo in the play by Terence <note>A character from the Roman comedy *Andria*</note> sought from Sofia: silence. For you have reached the age of more than twenty-five years, a threshold among the Hebrews—as our friend Baruchias here would admit—beyond which it is lawful to touch upon the secrets of divine things. Between us, there shall be a silence that is not without praise. Furthermore, this most sacred function of ours must not be handed over to the profane multitude, but only to those who seek it, as Dionysius of Syracuse <note>The tyrant of Sicily, though here likely referencing a philosophical anecdote</note> was warned about the highest matters, and as Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A Christian Neoplatonist writer whose works on the "Celestial Hierarchy" were highly influential in the Renaissance</note> carefully and diligently admonished Timothy. Indeed, priests are beyond controversy, even if no bishop's hands have been laid upon us, provided we hold divine wisdom with a pure heart. For there is a true saying of Lactantius <note>A 4th-century Christian author called the "Christian Cicero"</note> in those volumes he wrote to the Emperor Constantine: they are the teachers of true wisdom who are also the priests of God. Therefore, let both the handling of true Philosophy and the reverence of the one God be esteemed by us.

<margin>Humility.
Hope.
Faith.
Charity.
The Art of Miracles.</margin> Only humility makes for suitable listeners of such a great matter; hope makes them attentive, and faith makes us capable. Most excellent of all, however, is fervent love <note>original: *charitas*</note>, which preserves everything in its operation and grants the desired effects to our prayers. Since, therefore, every art—if any can truly be called such, as our friend Sidonius has taught and reviewed—is divided into three parts, each of which is a faculty in itself: namely Physics, Astrology, and Magic (which includes both <term>Goetia</term> <note>Lower magic or sorcery, often associated with dark spirits</note> and <term>Theurgy</term> <note>Higher magic or "divine work," aimed at union with the divine</note>). These are all joined together and are related, so that he who promises Astrology without Physics would be a deceiver, and he who dares to profess Magic without Astrology and Physics would wander far from the truth. But you yourselves reject all of these because of the empty and vast efforts that lead to frustrated outcomes, and you demand that I enter upon a **fourth way** with you, which consists of sacred discourse <note>original: *soliloquia*, literally "speaking alone" but here implying direct communion with God</note>, through which every purpose might succeed according to the prayers of those seeking it. As far as it is permitted, and as much as lies within me, I will not refuse to do this most diligently.

<margin>From where divine things are to be expected.</margin> But know this first of all, which was also long ago decreed by the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, known for his mysticism regarding numbers and silence</note>: the perception of divine things cannot be achieved by any human art, but must be revealed from above. This is what Plato handed down, and Proclus confirmed, and it is attested not only by your own teachers but also by the most proven theologians.

<margin>Preparation for attaining divine wisdom.</margin> It will behoove us first to be purged of our duties and to offer ourselves to the Deifying light; and then, with our senses closed and minds quiet, to wait for that rain of super-heavenly water falling from the heights. Sometimes we must also adore that sea of goodness, from which flow the streams not only of signs and sacred words, but of all miracles; and from which the most divine rivers emanate. Therefore, as we begin, this hymn must be brought forth in the Ionic meter and with the most sacred accent required for the sake of chanting:
> Generator and craftsman of every thing,
> King of the heavens, light of the spirit, hope of men,

## CHAPTER III.

<image-desc>Ornamental initial letter H featuring a detailed landscape scene with trees and a building in the background.</image-desc>

After this hymn was recited according to custom, Capnion <note>Capnion is the Greek-style pen name used by Johann Reuchlin; it means "smoky," a pun on his German name *Rauch*.</note> began again: Every miracle of man whose substance is found to be true and not imaginary—whether it be grand, mediocre, or minimal—if the prescribed order of sacred rites <margin>The All and the Beginning is God. <note>original Greek: *to pan kai archē ho theos*</note></margin> is observed, must always be referred back to the glorious God, whose name be blessed for ever and ever. For He alone is the one who performs such things as we marvel at, whether by Himself, or through a delegate (though not without Himself), or through a substitute acting from Him. We cannot know the adequate cause of these things, either why they happen or why they happen in this particular way. This precept stands out, drawn from the storehouse of sacred things. For thus the divine hymn contains: "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, <margin>God alone performs wonders.</margin> who alone does wondrous things." <note>A reference to Psalm 72:18.</note> If He alone does them, then men do not; if He alone, then demons do not; if He alone, then angels do not. Therefore, God alone acts, either by Himself or through His creatures. For it is an established principle of law: "Whatever one does through another, one is considered to do by oneself in one's own name." And Aristophanes immediately says: "Jupiter rules through some of the gods"—not that minor gods rule in place of the Supreme God, for then God would be absent and they would merely fill His place. That philosopher-shepherd of Virgil <note>Referring to the character Damœtas in Virgil's *Eclogues* 3.60.</note> will not permit us to say that, who sang among the flocks: "All things are full of Jove." Rather, it is that the angels rule in the name of God, govern duties, and carry out the office delegated to them; it is right for them to take up His commands, for God dwells in them, is carried by them, and walks upon them. We mortals are no different, as my Paul says, we are "co-workers of God," <margin>Cooperation.</margin> whose offspring we are (as Aratus witnesses in his *Phaenomena*) <note>Aratus was a Greek poet; St. Paul quotes him in Acts 17:28 to bridge classical philosophy and Christian doctrine.</note> along with the angels, in whom and through whom He acts as He wills. It is not we, therefore, who perform miracles, but God, the Best and Greatest, to whom you give praise, "who alone does great wonders, for His mercy endures forever." <note>Psalm 136:4.</note> You have here who the worker is: the God of gods. <margin>The Worker.</margin> <margin>The cause of the operation.</margin> You have the cause of the work: for His mercy, piety, beneficence, and grace are forever—not law, nor rigor, nor debt, nor any obligation. <margin>The end of wonders.</margin> You have the purpose of these miraculous operations: for confession, magnificence, glory, honor, and worship, of which the God of gods and Lord of lords is worthy, to whom you give praise because He is good. Therefore, let some be ashamed—those who consider themselves to have served Philosophy best—who, while professing many other things that walk the path of madness and insanity, strive most of all to persuade us that there is a certain "art" whose rules bind the wills of the gods by necessity, through the constraints of words or the bonds of characters. <margin>You advise correctly.</margin> In truth, they do nothing unbidden, and He who commands is not accustomed to be ruled but to rule, since He is supreme and therefore not subject to inferior fictions. Furthermore, there may be a doctrine of illusions <note>original: *praestigiorum*, meaning sleight of hand or deceptive magic.</note>, but of true miracles there is none, except a fervent union with divinity. Through this union, it is not we ourselves acting through God, but God acting through us to grant the wishes of His friends, producing something that others may marvel at. <margin>The sin of Moses and his brother.</margin> Thus, it was not with impunity that Moses and his own brother [Aaron] in the desert of Zin persuaded the people that they could produce water from the hardest rock; they did not attribute the act to its Author, but presumed the credit for themselves to the extent that the fame of their names might grow among the common people—most foolishly indeed, as...

<summary>Capnion explains that true miracles are performed only by God, often using angels or humans as "co-workers," and rejects the idea that divine will can be forced by magical formulas or characters. He cites the biblical example of Moses being punished for taking personal credit for a miracle to illustrate that the human is merely an instrument.</summary>

Especially in doctrine dedicated to God alone, every stain of error must be avoided. We are warned that in much speaking, sin will not be lacking; indeed, even the more refined literary arts command this, as Flaccus <note>original: "Flacco"; referring to the Roman poet Horace</note> says: 
> Whatever you teach, be brief.

<margin>Consider the time, measure, and manner of all things.</margin>
This I shall do both by choice and by necessity, so that I may be as brief as possible. Indeed, if I had not already begun to hold a most intimate Pythagorean friendship with you, I would first have needed to look deeply into the nature, lifestyle, study, disposition, and age of each of you, and I would have required the patience of your ears and your silence. For as Nazianzen <note>Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, a 4th-century theologian known as "The Theologian" for his work on the Trinity</note> says, one should not philosophize about God always, nor to everyone, nor about everything; there is a limit to whom, and when, and how much. But you are well-prepared for this business, you whom yesterday’s tablets—which you keep at home—have made my colleagues. What more do I require of you than what Simo in Terence <note>A character from the Roman playwright Terence’s comedy *Andria*</note> sought from Sosia: your silence. 

For you have reached many more than twenty-five years, a limit set by the Hebrews—for here Baruchias <note>The Jewish scholar in Reuchlin’s dialogue</note> acknowledges the womb—at which point it is lawful to touch the series of divine secrets, and there shall be among us a certain praiseworthy silence. Furthermore, this most sacred function of ours is not to be handed over to the profane multitude, but to those who are initiates, as Dionysius the Syrian <note>Dionysius the Great</note> and Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A judge of the Athenian Areopagus who was converted to Christianity; Reuchlin views him as a primary authority on mystical hierarchy</note> have learnedly and diligently warned Theophilus. Truly, we are priests without controversy, even if no hands of Bishops have been laid upon us, provided that we hold divine wisdom with a pure heart and holy worship. For there is a true sentiment of Lactantius Firmianus <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325) often called the "Christian Cicero"</note> in those volumes which he wrote to the Emperor Constantine: "The teachers of true wisdom are the same as the priests of God." Therefore, let us be esteemed as such, and let the treatment of true Philosophy and the reverence of the one God be our guide.

<margin>
Humility.
Hope.
Faith.
Charity.
The Art of Miracles.
</margin>
Truly, humility alone makes us fit listeners for such a great matter; hope makes us attentive; and faith makes us believers. But the most excellent of all is fervent love <note>original: "charitas"</note>, which preserves us in our work and grants the effects of our prayers. Therefore, since every art (if any may truly be so named, as our friend Sidonius <note>The pagan philosopher character in the dialogue</note> here teaches) is divided into three parts—each of which has its own power, namely Physics, Astrology, and Magic (which contains within itself both Goetia <note>Low or "dark" magic involving the summoning of spirits</note> and Theurgy <note>High or "divine" magic aimed at union with the divine</note>)—they are joined in order and are kin. Thus, he who promises Astrology without Physics, or who dares to profess Magic without Astrology and Physics, wanders far from the truth. But you yourselves reject all of these because of the empty results and the immense, laborious studies that end in frustration. You demand from me that I enter upon a "fourth way" with you, which we call "soliloquies" <note>original: "soliloquia"; here referring to internal prayer or direct communion with God</note>, through which any purpose whatsoever may succeed according to the favorable prayers of those who ask. I will not deny this to you, as far as it is permitted and as much as it lies within my power, which I shall do most diligently. But know this above all: that even by the Pythagoreans,

### CHAPTER III.

<margin>God is the whole, all things, and the beginning <note>original Greek: "to pan panta kai archē ho theos"</note>.</margin>
Once this hymn had been recited according to custom, Capnion <term>Capnion</term> <note>The Greek nickname for the author, Johann Reuchlin; it is a translation of his German name "Rauch," meaning "smoke"</note> began again: Every human miracle whose substance is found to be true and not imaginary—whether it be grand, mediocre, or very small—must always be referred back to the glorious God (whose name be blessed forever and ever), provided that the prescribed sacred order is observed. For He alone is the one who performs the things we marvel at, whether by Himself, or through a delegate (not acting without Him), or through a substitute acting from Him. We cannot know the adequate cause of these wonders, neither why they happen nor why they happen in this specific way. This precept stands drawn from the storehouse of sacred things. For thus the divine hymn <note>referring to Psalm 72:18</note> declares: *Blessed be the Lord God of Israel,* <margin>God alone performs wonders.</margin> *who alone does wondrous things.* If He alone does them, then men do not; if He alone, then demons do not; if He alone, then angels do not. Therefore, God alone acts by Himself or through His creatures. For it is a principle of established law: what someone can do through themselves, they can also do through another in their own name. Even Aristophanes <note>An ancient Greek playwright</note> says immediately: "Jupiter rules through some of the Gods." This does not mean that lesser gods rule in the place of the supreme God—for then God would be absent, and they would merely fill His place. That shepherd from Virgil <note>The poet Virgil, specifically his "Eclogues"</note>, who sang among the cattle, "All things are full of Jove <note>Jupiter/God</note>," will not permit us to say that to the philosophers. Rather, it is that angels rule in the name of God, govern their duties, and execute the task delegated to them. It is right for them to carry out His orders; God dwells in them, is carried by them, and walks upon them. It is no different for us mortals, as <margin>Cooperation.</margin> my Paul <note>The Apostle Paul</note> says; we are "co-workers" with God. As Aratus <note>A Greek poet quoted by Paul in the New Testament</note> testifies in his *Phaenomena*, we are of God's "offspring," just like the angels, in whom and through whom He acts as He wills. Therefore, it is not we who perform miracles, but God, the Best and Greatest, whom you confess, who alone performs great wonders, for His mercy endures forever. You have here the identity of the worker: because He is the God of Gods. <margin>The Worker.</margin> You have the cause of the operation: because His mercy is eternal—along with His piety, <margin>Cause of the operation.</margin> beneficence, and grace; it is not by right, nor rigor, nor debt, nor any obligation. You have the goal of these wondrous operations: for it is confession, <margin>The goal of wonders.</margin> and magnificence, and glory, and honor, and worship, because the God of Gods and Lord of Lords is worthy. Confess to Him, for He is good. Therefore, some people should be ashamed—even those who think they have served Philosophy best—who, while professing many other things that walk the path of insanity and madness, strive most of all to persuade us that there is a certain "art" by which the wills of the Gods are bound by necessity, either by the constraints of words or the bonds of written characters. Yet the Gods do nothing without being commanded, and He who commands is accustomed to ruling, not being ruled, since He is the highest and therefore in no way subject to inferior <margin>You advise correctly.</margin> fabrications. Furthermore, there can be a "doctrine" of magic tricks, but of miracles there is none, except for a fervent union with the divine. For it is not we ourselves who act through God, but God who effects something through us to gratify the prayers of His friends, which others then admire. Thus, it was not without punishment that Moses and <margin>The sin of Moses and his brother.</margin> his biological brother <note>Aaron</note> persuaded the people in the desert of Zin that they themselves could produce water from the hardest rock. They did not attribute this to its Author, but presumed it for themselves so that the fame of their own names might grow among the common people. Indeed, they acted too foolishly, as...

### CHAPTER IV.

"Therefore," said Sidonius, "we neither perform miracles, nor will there be any way by which we can learn to perform them. Thus, we have waited in vain for you to finally tell us something wonderful. This desire to know has kept me almost sleepless tonight—a matter for which, as you proclaim, there is no art, and of which we would not be the authors ourselves, even if some art existed. But by Jove! <note>original Latin: "ædepol"; an ancient Roman oath originally referring to Pollux</note> this seems to me most wondrous of all, Capnion <term>Capnion</term> <note>Johann Reuchlin’s Greek-derived pen name</note>, that you now deny what you so excellently affirmed before. You said, if I remember correctly, that we ourselves are the effectors of wondrous works. Now you tell another story: that neither the gods nor we ourselves do them, but God alone. What is this great inconsistency of yours? One moment you say yes, the next you say no: although we can fight most fiercely against you using the deeds of our ancestors, and win in the battle. For let us set aside that mention of the little woman:

of which that noble writer Philostratus is witness. By this example, we hoped to be instructed by you with equal learning, so that, omitting the anxieties of magicians, the observations of astrologers, and the investigations of physicists, we might by our word alone perform sudden things worthy of admiration and report, which would prove that Philosophy <term>Philosophy</term> <note>Defined here in the classical sense as the "knowledge of divine and human things"</note> is in us. It is nothing even that we profess to solve or unravel so many and such perplexed scholastic questions. Therefore, the common folk judge us to be fools and confused rather than wise:

It ought to be valid, even among us—though speaking of divine matters in human terms—to say that men full of the Spirit of God perform miracles; nevertheless, God Himself performs them primarily through the man. I do not know if you wish to be numbered among them. For my part, in the fellowship of letters, I wish that individuals like me were even lavish in publishing those things we have conceived in the mind and accumulated for ourselves through learning. Let us therefore test this in Baruchias. Sidonius replied, whether he should speak, or whether he had decided to keep this discourse to himself—he who is forced into a narrow corner—"Come then, speak of the words which your fellow tribesmen hide in secret and almost 'under a bushel,' <note>Reference to Matthew 5:15: "Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel."</note> as you were saying; for you used to bless yourself much in the relating of them." "Now I truly agree with you studious men," Baruchias said, "that the Hebrews have contributed not a little of our own, whom we also imitate more rightly than other nations; it is well known that within the memory of the fathers they gave the greatest devotion to the divinity and worshipped God rightly. And I will do so unforced, provided I do not seem to seek glory by allowing myself to be asked by such great men, or to say anything other than what is fitting. For there are few things regarding the sacred names that I was taught by the Hebrews in my native land, and therefore I will explain them in few words. But bar the bolts, lest any of the servants overhear, and lest the sacred things become a laughingstock to the profane—pearls foully trampled by swine <note>Reference to Matthew 7:6</note>. I shall also deliberately attempt to act more obscurely, so that you yourselves, through the goodness of your intellect, may understand what I intend."

### *Of the fellowship of the divine mind with the human, and how much God delights in man, and that nothing happens except what He has decreed, who is also called the Word <note>original: "logos"</note>.*

## CHAPTER VI.

<margin>Man as God's instrument.</margin>
FELLOWSHIP with the divinity within the human mind causes God to use man as an instrument, not unlike what the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> teach regarding the sensitive and vegetative natures of the city [of the soul]. For in man, the vegetative is in the sensitive; there, the vegetative will be in the place of an instrument: the sensitive is like the principal mover, which, when it begins to act, does not move toward the instrument, but through means appropriate to both, so far as there can be proximity and agreement, and toward that with which it can be occupied. For the power of the nutritive faculty, as a foster-child and nurse, digests and transforms raw food by means of intermediate heat, which is nevertheless the messenger of a certain hidden innate property. When it is better, it does not transform this any further. For otherwise you might cook nutrients more quickly on a hearth, but in the stomach—against which a character <note>original: "character"</note>, like some natural image and peace-broker, intervenes to digest food—it does not remain as food but migrates into its own substance. Nature does not re-transform this into a herb or plant, for then it would become more like the vegetative; rather, it purposefully converts it into flesh, most fit for touching, so that the mover itself <margin>Two images in created things.</margin> might dwell in it through touch. Thus, therefore, the most excellent exemplar of all things, by the testimony of Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurio ter maximo"</note>, fashioned two images: this [world]...

# ON THE WONDER-WORKING WORD, BOOK II.

...man: in order that he might play in the orb of the earth, as it says in the Proverbs, and find his delights among the sons of men. <note>A reference to Proverbs 8:31, describing Divine Wisdom playing in the world.</note>

<margin>The World.</margin>
In the World, He plays through wondrous operations, not only by the power of the stars or the elements, but also sometimes through an **occult property** <term>occult property: a hidden quality in nature that produces effects not explained by the four primary qualities of heat, cold, moisture, or dryness</term>. Just as physicians prove concerning the wearing of coral or other things—not because this or that is hot or cold, but because it is of such a nature—so we have said regarding animal nutrition: the transformation of digested things occurs not by specific heat alone, but through such a hidden quality. And just as natural heat in the digestion of food is like a shadow, holding the place of an occult property; so in the effects arising from the secret disposition of things, by which one individual differs from another—not nature itself, as is commonly thought, but something more obscure that precedes nature is the cause. The very word "nature" carries the likeness and type of this cause in common speech.

<margin>Man.</margin>
You have heard now of the World; let us likewise look at man, who is called the **Microcosm** <note>original: Microcosmus; literally 'little world,' a concept that man reflects the structure of the entire universe</note> by the Greeks, in whose company God Himself takes more pleasure than in the World. He strives to transform man into Himself according to human capacity, just as sensory nutrition transforms food. And He does this, as far as we are concerned, through the heat of the love we have conceived;

<margin>Intuition.</margin>
but as far as He is concerned, He does it through an occult property which we do not know—whether you call it a covenant, or an unspeakable pull, or by any other name. Although God, as the only omnipotent one, could perform all these things without any intermediate causes and with fewer observed limits to His actions, nevertheless He willed many participants of His goodness to concur. Some are accustomed to call these secondary causes, others powers, and some gods, angels, or good spirits <note>original: dæmones; here used in the Platonic sense of guiding spirits or intermediaries, not evil demons</note>. Indeed, whatever mediates these effects has a natural affinity for the mover, and at the same time is not at an enormous distance from the thing moved.

<margin>God's Delights.</margin>
Therefore, the Lord of Eternity, rejoicing in our company, holds the holy mind of man among His delights as something close to His own nature and origin. When He perceives that mind following with diligent devotion and perpetual religion, He—acting like an abundant nutritional power—always attempts (as far as human weakness allows) to transform it into Himself, digesting it not only through the heat of love but also through an occult property,

<margin>Divine nutritional power.</margin>
so that man might pass into God, and God might dwell in man. 

<margin>John 3.</margin>
But truly, just as that property by which we are transmuted into God and exceed human nature is secret and hidden from us, so by the highest right God has also given it secret and hidden names. He has placed within them certain agreements, so that when these are observed and the names are duly pronounced, He may immediately draw near to fulfill our prayer. Furthermore, just as in natural digestion there is the power of heat (which we recognize) and yet also a hidden power of **transcorporation** <term>transcorporation: the mystical process of changing one substance or body into another</term> (which we do not know), so in this most divine passage into God, there are certain words which we know, and some which we do not know. 

<margin>God, Word, Man.</margin>
Truly, this bond of words is fitting for both parties: for God is spirit, the word is a breathing-forth, and man is the one breathing. God is called ***Logos*** <note>original: λόγος; Greek for Word, Reason, or Discourse</note>. The Word is called by that same name, and human reason is expressed by a similar term. God is perceived by our mind and is brought forth by the word. Therefore, just as He chose the insensible seat of the mind for Himself, so also He chose a sensible dwelling-place for words—not all words, nor those falling by chance, but those which divinity first established for us, rather than those which human invention devised.

<margin>The Thought of God.</margin>
For God knows the thoughts of men, how vain they are. But the thought of God is preserving and health-bringing, permanent, invincible, and certain; as He thinks, so it shall be; as He treats it in His mind, so it shall happen. The Lord of the universe has decreed it, and who shall be able to weaken it? 

<margin>Which words are divine.</margin>
Therefore, not all words possess **divine power** <term>numen: a Latin term for divine presence or power inhabiting an object, place, or word</term> (if you have listened attentively to me speaking), but only those which the supreme God of the World and of men, or the insightful angels, have composed in a certain way by the command and providence of God. These words resonate with the harmony of eternity, hold fast to divinity, and breathe through the structure of a beneficial dispensation—sensible monuments, as it were, of an insensible deification. They rely on the immovable stability of letters and the everlasting firmness of vocal members, while simultaneously admitting both an unshakable alternation of modulation and a natural agility of pronunciation that is neither forced nor...

OF JOHANNES REUCHLIN

...not a feigned image, but one that is native, simple, and venerable. With these internal qualities, God strikes a covenant with man—not just any man, but one who shines with holiness, religious devotion, and most especially with the trust of faith. To such a man, to whom he must then reconcile human mortality through the power of speaking, it will be fitting for those most holy names—or words, if you prefer—to be ancient; even though you sometimes call them "barbarous" <note>original: "barbara"; in this context, it refers to non-Greek or non-Latin foreign languages, which Renaissance scholars often considered to possess more primal, divine power.</note> because of that very simplicity.

<margin>Faith.</margin>
<margin>God the ruler of eternity. Dan. 7.</margin>
Indeed, an ancient age is close to eternity, and eternity is neighbor to God, who reigns over eternity. Hence He is called the "Ancient of Days" <note>Daniel 7:9</note> by the early theologians because He presides over the Kingdom of all ages. Therefore, "barbarous" things are more divine. Thus, not without reason did Zoroaster, the first of the ethnic theologians, forbid "barbarous words" to be changed. Truly, those things called "barbarous" are Hebrew, or derived directly from it. For the little flowers of speech and the beauty of elegances were thought up later, after the division of languages, by men who were more curious than sincere.

<margin>The seduction of words.</margin>
<margin>The Hebrew language is the language of God.</margin>
However, the simple speech—pure, uncorrupted, holy, and enduring—is that of the Hebrews. In this language, it is maintained that God spoke with man, and men with God, face to face and not through an interpreter; not through a delirium, nor the cave of Trophonius, nor the tree of Dodona, nor the Delphic tripod <note>These are all references to famous Greek oracles where divine messages were sought through trances or natural signs; Reuchlin argues Hebrew revelation is direct and superior.</note>, but as a friend is accustomed to speak with a friend. But if you think I have spoken true praise rather than merely my own opinion, you will find no language purer or more modest than this one.

---

->*Concerning the antiquity of the Hebrew language, and who first handed down the characters of letters; the account of Moses as the most ancient of all writers, and the translation of the Seventy Interpreters. CHAPTER VII.*<-

<margin>Moses the most ancient writer.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative drop cap initial letter "D" containing elaborate floral and foliage patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>
REGARDING age and order, if you trust our historians less, learn at least from your own; it appears that none of all writers is more ancient than Moses. Three hundred and ten years are counted from him until Inachus <note>A mythical king of Argos, used here as a chronological marker for early Greek history.</note>. At that time, Jason led our people, Agamemnon led the Argives, Vaphres the Egyptians, and Marathus the Assyrians. Meanwhile, let someone unroll for me any other volume published before the Trojan War that records letters, besides the books of the Hebrews. For one hundred and fifty years after Troy, finally the primary Greek poets Homer and Hesiod followed Troy (as Cicero testifies), and Orpheus and Musaeus were only a little before them. But they are nothing compared to our author [Moses], who gave laws a very long time before. For in past centuries Eupolemus <note>A Hellenistic Jewish historian who wrote in Greek.</note>, a Greek historian, left records in the most noble monuments of his works that Moses was the first wise man, and was the first to give the knowledge of grammar and letters; he then bestowed it upon the Phoenicians because of their proximity. The Phoenicians then distributed the system of characters to the children of the Greeks because of frequent trade. I think Pliny was moved by this to say that he always considered the "Assyrian letters" to have been [originally] Assyrian, although others wish them to have been discovered in Egypt by Mercury, and that Cadmus brought them into Greece from Phoenicia. 

<margin>Opinion deceives many.</margin>
The fact that the entire region borders each other creates this variety of opinions. And it is no obstacle that some not-very-diligent writers called Moses an Egyptian priest, as Strabo does in the sixteenth book of his *Cosmography*. This is false; Moses, whose writing has reached us, exists as more ancient; before him, no monuments of letters are read. All the Greeks confess that antiquity, though one says it one way and another another. Our Philo also, and likewise our Eusebius and Josephus, while noting "Antiquity" in a title, prove nothing more ancient than Moses. Palæmon also, in the first book of *Greek Histories*, places him as the leader of the Hebrew people in the times of Inachus; and Apion, that learned man of Posidonius from Alexandria, claims that while Egypt was reigning, he was the leader of the fugitives, both in his book against...

<summary>Reuchlin argues that the Hebrew language is the original, divine tongue used for direct communication between God and man, predating all Greek philosophy and myth. He asserts that Moses is the world's oldest writer and that the Greeks actually received their alphabet from the Hebrews via the Phoenicians.</summary>

# ON THE MIRIFIC WORD, BOOK II.

...as even he [Diodorus] mentions in his fourth book of histories, and as Ptolemy of Mendes records in his *Histories of the Egyptians*. Finally, those who are considered illustrious in recording the affairs of the Athenians—Hellanicus, Philochorus, Castor, Thalus, Alexander (nicknamed Polyhistor), and easily the prince of all historians, Diodorus—who himself diligently surveyed nearly all of Asia and Europe with his own eyes. All these have proclaimed the most ample marks of antiquity concerning that wondrous leader <note>Referring to Moses.</note> and most excellent author of divine matters. Through these testimonies, it becomes manifest that he stands before all others in the age of his time, the antiquity of his religion, and the admirable power and divine discipline of his secret operation. For you would seek in vain from the Greeks for names that are words flowing from heaven <note>original: "uerba caelitus demanantia"; the OCR "deamentia" is likely a typo for "demanantia."</note> and contained by the divine vote of syllables, because of their novelty of expression and the very recent variety of their speech.

<margin>The Greeks are vain talkers.</margin>
For the Greeks, as Iamblichus of Chalcis (the disciple of Porphyry) says, are by nature fond of new things and are carried headlong in every direction, like a ship lacking ballast, having no stability. They do not preserve what they have received from others; instead, they quickly let it go and are accustomed to transform everything because of their instability and their habit of inventing new ways of speaking. Therefore, a certain Egyptian priest is rightly praised for his response to Solon in Plato’s *Timaeus*, when he said: "O Solon, Solon, you Greeks are always children; there is no such thing as an old man in Greece, because your souls are always young, containing no ancient opinion derived from the remembrance of antiquity, and no discipline gray with time." 

<margin>The library of Philadelphus.</margin>
Perhaps led by this, that famous Ptolemy Philadelphus, in his most sharp zeal for collecting books of antiquity, nearly filled the Library at Alexandria with almost seven hundred thousand volumes. 
<margin>A huge abundance of books.</margin>
But since Moses, the pillar of antiquity and the first monument of the past, was missing, he is said to have sent royal legates to Jerusalem to pray that six men from each tribe, most learned in Greek and most fit for translating the Pentateuch—or rather that volume which we call by the composite name "The Twenty-Four" <note>A common term for the 24 books of the Hebrew Bible (the Tanakh).</note>—might migrate with them to Alexandria. 
<margin>Hebrew interpreters.</margin>
When they arrived, the king did not place them in the city itself, but at the Pharos, nearly seven stadia outside, so they would not be hindered by the noise. He built seventy-two small cells according to the number of interpreters. Jerome, writing to Desiderius, did not think these cells were fables once he had more accurately weighed the "Exhortation" of Justin Martyr, who asserted that he had seen the remains of the cells still standing. Therefore, the Hebrew scripture was translated into the Greek language for the Egyptian king, lest among so many volumes he should lack the first elements of this world, and lest he should one day be forced to confess with Solon (compelled by the truth) that neither he nor any other Greek possessed any knowledge of antiquity. 

This warns us with the highest reason that for secret operations, no ancient names akin to the divine are to be sought from the Greeks—nor even from the discipline of the Egyptians, however much older they may think it is. For as Socrates philosophizes with Hermogenes in Plato’s *Cratylus*, surely all divine names were delivered either first by the gods, or by antiquity (the beginning of which is not easily known), or by the Barbarians <note>In the Renaissance, "Barbarian" often referred specifically to non-Greek/Latin cultures like the Hebrews, Chaldeans, or Persians, who were thought to possess more primal wisdom.</note>. 

<margin>The fictional playthings of the gods.</margin>
But in truth, the Egyptians fashioned their own gods with their own hands—by the testimony of their father Hermes Trismegistus—wandering away from the reason of divinity and not paying attention to the true worship and religion of God.

<margin>Origin of the Jews.</margin>
In truth, most noble is the Damascene field near the Persians, from which the first origin of the Jews was led, according to Trogus and Justin <note>Roman historians who wrote accounts of Jewish history, often conflating them with other Near Eastern peoples.</note> and likewise many not-to-be-despised historians. I should also add this: that the Egyptians, because of their unrefined state, for many ages had not yet discovered letter characters among themselves,

<margin>The writing of images.</margin>

The letter, turned about, although everywhere a in b <note>original: "a in b Loës"; likely a cryptic reference to a linguistic shift or a specific cipher used in the period.</note> is explained as "barbarian." Therefore, let the Egyptians blush to be called barbarians and take offense. And how will they accept this decree of the priesthood from Zoroaster <margin>Zoroaster.</margin> <note>Zoroaster was the legendary founder of Persian Magi; Reuchlin refers to a famous rule attributed to him: "Never change the barbarous names" in sacred rites.</note>, the prince of sacred matters as they say, when he forbids "barbarous words" to be changed in sacred rites? Therefore, the barbarous words which we use in an immutable and uncontaminated way among sacred things will not be Egyptian, but rather Mosaical. For that Moses the Hebrew confessed himself to be a barbarian before God: that is, heavy-tongued <margin>Moses the Barbarian.</margin> and slow-of-speech, when he said: "My Lord, I am not a man of elegances, but of a heavier and weighted tongue." <note>A reference to Exodus 4:10, where Moses describes his speech impediment. Therefore, we are not tongueless or rustic, but the first of men, whom all investigators of the most ancient things have always asserted to be barbarians. Some of our own people, not considering this accurately, have dared to teach that "Barbarians" are those who do not speak the Holy Tongue, such as Solomon the Scholar in his exposition of the hymn, which we mentioned in the interpretation of this word <term>הלל</term> <note>Hebrew: "Hallel," meaning "Praise."</note>, and certain other elementary teachers. But it happens even to our people as it does to other writers of the arts: <margin>Writers of the Arts.</margin>

->Learned and unlearned alike, we scribble poems everywhere.<- <note>A quote from the Roman poet Horace (*Epistles* 2.1.117), suggesting that everyone thinks they are an expert.</note>

But I would readily believe that the more illustrious priests of Egypt mingled the names of the Hebrews into their own, which they might use more effectively when they wished to bring some secret into the light; and indeed, they learned these only through long-lived and hidden study, just as you yourselves are able to learn. Unless these words had once been foreign to their native language, they could not have hidden them as much as we have seen in the histories. For although Plato and Eudoxus lived with them in Heliopolis for thirteen years <margin>Heliopolis.</margin> <note>An ancient Egyptian city ("City of the Sun") famous for its priesthood and wisdom.</note>, they were nevertheless scarcely able to pluck a few things from their secret words through long and constant conversation, which they might scatter in their own monuments. Regarding the philosophers of the Indians, whom they call Brahmans, there is no need for much dispute <margin>Brahmans.</margin>, since both many other infinite things and especially the numerous idols there serve as our proof that they began first from the Greeks; for they are both Greek and are worshiped with Greek rites, such as those of Minerva, of Delian Apollo, of Dionysius Lemnaeus and Amyclaeus, and others, of which Philostratus diligently makes mention in the *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*. The Indians also agree with the Greeks in opinions and disciplines. For Iarchas <margin>Iarchas.</margin> <note>A legendary Indian sage mentioned by Philostratus.</note> used to tell Apollonius his opinion on the human soul, that it was the same for them as Pythagoras had delivered to the Greeks and to the Egyptians themselves—as if the Brahmans were the teachers of the Egyptians; yet that indicates not so much an order of antiquity as a renovation of opinions: especially since the same Iarchas tells that his grandfather lived at a time when there was no great philosopher in India, nor did any noble genius sprout there. But among the Druids of the Gauls, one need not seek many human centuries <margin>Druids.</margin>, for they all philosophized in Greek, and therefore they are known to have been later than the barbarians. I have dared to batter your ears with too many words, most learned and kind men, out of my singular vice of talkativeness, while I attempt to affirm for a little while that the most ancient words of the barbarians are to be selected for the performance of miraculous works—not those of the Phoenicians, nor the Greeks...

### *Sidonius confirms the above, as he discusses voice, word, reason, and concept. CHAPTER IX.*

<margin>† while we are hardly noticing</margin>
<margin>Epicurus.</margin>
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
<margin>Ammonius.</margin>
<margin>Iamblichus.</margin>
<margin>Barbarous speech.</margin>
Truly, you do not seem to me to speak obscurely, Sidonius, except for the fact that you have threatened us with Baruchia <note>Baruchia is the Jewish scholar in the dialogue; the speaker is teasing Sidonius about the complexity of the upcoming Hebrew mystical arguments.</note>, so that these things might fit our philosophy: that God joins Himself to us and rejoices in us when we are formed toward Him according to our capacity, and that He sometimes works through us, just as through instruments, and sometimes—intervening with no other causes—He works certain things directly. For He can do both; and if He acts through us by some medium, it is fitting that this medium be suitable to both God and man. Such are our words, which reach toward God through the indwelling spirit and the sensible air—a concept I think that famous Epicurus (following Democritus) designated in two words. I do not say this because I wish to follow them—I have already renounced that—but because what is absorbed in our tender years often offers itself to memory, and nevertheless, the harmony of opinions is a trace of the truth. For they say our voice is a "stream of reason" <note>original Greek: ῥῦμα λόγῳ (rhuma logō)</note>. For sometimes reason drips onto the tongue, the air is broken, and a word is formed. Reason is the fountain, and the word is the stream, which in the fountain is united with God, and in the river is united with man. And just as there is nothing in the stream that was not first in the fountain, so according to the Stagirite Aristotle <note>Aristotle was born in Stagira, hence "the Stagirite."</note>, there is nothing in the voice that does not first exist in a concept of the soul, just as letters are the signs of the voice. So also wrote Ammonius the Peripatetic. (Forgive me if I do not interpret these matters elegantly or worthily.) For he says that letters only enunciate <note>To "enunciate" here means to signal or manifest something else.</note>, while things are only enunciated. Voices and thoughts, however, both enunciate and are enunciated. For voices are enunciated once, but they enunciate in two ways: first thoughts, and second, things. Conversely, thoughts are enunciated in two ways, but they enunciate only once. They are enunciated by both voice and letters—by the former primarily, and by the latter secondarily. This variety, shown to us by both Aristotle and Ammonius, demonstrates the nature of our words, insofar as they communicate partly with the spirit and partly with the body. Thus, it seems most fitting to me that there is a certain use of words for reconciling man with God. But as to why you chose "barbarous" <note>In the Renaissance, "barbarous" often referred to non-Greek/Latin ancient languages, particularly Hebrew, which were believed to have more direct divine power.</note> words rather than others, as if they were more akin to divinity, I do not much disagree. For as Iamblichus says, the gods approved that speech of the barbarians as being most suitable for sacred rites, especially because that way of speaking is the oldest and the first. And since the first men received names from the divine, they mixed them into their own language, tempering them as if with a familiar and agreeable tongue. Thus they handed them down to be preserved by us forever, and we must thereafter rightly preserve the rule of that tradition. By these precepts, he leads me into your opinion—except that you strive to persuade us...
