# ON THE WONDER-WORKING WORD, BOOK II.

<margin>Zoroaster.</margin>
Zoroaster said that one should not change "barbaric words," <note>original: "barbara uerba ne cōmutes." In the context of ancient magic, "barbaric" referred to non-Greek languages like Hebrew or Egyptian, which were thought to lose their power if translated.</note> suggesting they ought to be Hebrew. Indeed, Baruchias, you have used such great talent, such abundance of speech, and so many historical testimonies that you easily move me toward agreement. Nothing would now stand in the way of my believing you entirely, were it not for the singular experience of the ancients. They are said to have performed marvelous feats of the Magi using not only Egyptian and Assyrian words, but even Greek ones,
<margin>Egyptian, Assyrian, and Greek Magi.</margin>
and to have greatly excelled both in warding off dangers and in hastening beneficial things. For they report that the famous Orpheus—a follower of the Egyptian Mercury <note>The Egyptian god Thoth, often identified with Hermes/Mercury, the patron of writing and magic.</note>, a leader of the first priesthood, a theologian, and a prophet—averted a savage storm into which the Argonauts had wretchedly fallen by means of his sacred rites. He is also said to have been the first to demonstrate augury <note>The practice of divining the future.</note> not only from birds, but from other living creatures as well. Yet he used Greek invocations, as his hymns prove, which even now survive and are sung in Greek. Pythagoras and Plato also assert they were taught all their sacred mysteries by the Egyptians, and some by the Assyrians and Chaldeans, and others by various peoples; it is certainly incredible how many miraculous works they showed to men. Therefore, sacred names belong not only to the Hebrews, but also to other nations.

### What is Sacred, and in what various ways it is understood. CHAPTER X.

BARUCHIAS THEN SAID: <note>The original Latin begins with a decorative "T" for "TUM" (Then).</note> Sometimes we say "sacred" <term>sacrum: things set apart for divine use</term> is the same as "holy," namely that which is defended and fortified against the injury of men. Sometimes, as Martianus <note>A Roman legal authority.</note> replied in civil law, "sacred things" are those which have been consecrated publicly, not privately. Or, as Ulpian, most learned in the law, wrote: "the sacred is that which the sovereign has dedicated, or for which he has given the power of dedicating." In this way, whatever we consecrate to God and withdraw from common use is called sacred and holy, and sometimes "sacrosanct," regardless of which nation or people it belongs to. This is how that priest in the *Timaeus* <note>One of Plato's dialogues.</note> once told Solon that the deeds of many men worthy of memory are preserved in the temples of the Egyptians and contained in their sacred writings. Thus it is also customary to speak of the consecrated priests of every nation, saying they are devoted and hallowed to God, as Virgil sang of Helenus, the priest of Apollo:

> He entreats peace from the gods, and loosens the fillets
> of his hallowed head. — <note>original: "Exorat pacem diuum, vittasq; resoluit / Sacrati capitis." From Virgil's Aeneid, Book 3.</note>

And later in the eighth book of the *Aeneid*:

> But Caesar, entering the walls of Rome in triple triumph,
> was dedicating an immortal vow to the Italian gods. <note>original: "At Cæsar triplici inuectus Romana triumpho / Mænia dijs Italis votum immortale sacrabat."</note>

<margin>God is sacred both actively and passively.</margin>
In another way, and indeed more correctly, we call God—the author of all things—"sacred," as he is the principle and fountain of every sacred thing. Next, we call all things "sacred" after God through their participation in him, in which God himself dwells of his own accord with his presence and power. This differs from the previous definition. For in the former, we dedicate ourselves to God; in this latter, God dedicates himself to us, and illuminates our affairs with his assistance. Therefore, we most rightly name those things "sacred" in which God truly dwells. Not angels, nor demons, but God himself, the highest, best, and greatest. Because of this, we also call the angels themselves (or "gods") "sacred," since God dwells in them too, and they are often said to bear his name. Conversely, we call "profane" <term>prophanos: those outside the temple or the grace of God</term> those who are equally cursed,
<margin>The Profane.</margin>
from whom God is far removed, as Statius says:

> Fraternal battle-lines and alternating wars
> fought with profane hatreds — <note>original: "Fraternas acies alterna q; bella prophanis / Decertata odijs." From Statius's Thebaid.</note>

For according to the first way of using the word, just as "sacred" things are those dedicated by us to God, so we may interpret "profane" as being "far from the temple" <note>A pun on "procul a phano" (far from the shrine), the traditional etymology of "profane."</note> and religion—those things which exist outside of sacred matters. Indeed, that which is sacred arises so much from our own action that the title of "sacred" is given to the petty king who performs the rites <note>referring to the "rex sacrificulus," a Roman priestly office.</note>, the sacrifice itself which is performed by him, and the very act of making things sacred. As Ovid says in the twelfth book of the *Metamorphoses*:

# JOHANN REUCHLIN

> The festive day had arrived on which Achilles, victor over Cycnus, 
> Was appeasing Pallas by sacrificing a cow: 
> When he placed the cut portions upon the warm altars, 
> And the smell, accepted by the gods, rose into the air, 
> The sacred rites took their portion; the rest was given to the tables. 
<note>original: Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 12.150–154. Reuchlin uses this classical imagery to explain how a "portion" of a physical act becomes consecrated to the divine.</note>

For he intends to show that the sacred sacrifices consumed their own portion. Therefore, you should not doubt that images, characters, letters, and words—or names and voices dedicated by us to God—are sacred. This is true not only among the Hebrews, but also the Egyptians, the Greeks, and other nations, who consecrated and devoted such things as were worthy of the divine according to human prayer. Nor could I bring a more fitting example to this matter than what is sung in the hymn to the Lycian Venus by Orpheus—that ancient priest and prophet, follower of the Egyptian Mercury <note>The god Hermes/Thoth, legendary founder of writing and magic.</note>, and founder of the Pythagorean philosophy, whom you, Sidonius, introduced a little while ago—when he says:

-> For the leaders of our homeland, looking upon divine things, <-
-> Established a sacred Colossus near the little town. <-

Although some have thought this hymn belongs to Proclus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (5th century AD); Reuchlin is engaging in Renaissance literary criticism regarding the "Orphic" corpus.</note>, because he mentions his own homeland. But let us hear another poem, undeniably by Orpheus, concerning the stars:

-> Therefore, with sacred voices, I now invoke the pure spirits. <-
<note>original: "demones." In this context, these are 'daemons'—mediating spirits between gods and humans—rather than evil demons.</note>

<margin>What is truly sacred.</margin>
Therefore, that which is either God Himself, or finally that which God alone—the Best and Greatest—consecrated by His own presence and assistance (rather than humans doing so first), and into which He infused His own power: that alone, above all others, ought to be called and held as truly sacred. It is what God has sanctioned and reserved for His own honor, not by human allurements. From where else, then, do we say the "holy language" of the Jews comes, and the "sacred letters" written by the finger of God, and the "sacred names" not invented by men, but bestowed by God Himself?
<margin>Thrice dictated.</margin>
Indeed, while any nation may use its own voices in performing miracles, it is proven that there is something more excellent than a mere miracle; otherwise, it achieves its effect not through God’s assistance, but through the work of demons.
<margin>Note well.</margin>
How dangerous this may be was discussed by us at great length yesterday.
<margin>The distance between the miracles of the Hebrews and the idolaters.</margin>
In short, just as there is a distance between divine things and sorcery or witchcraft, so too is there a difference—to conclude in a few words—between the words of the Hebrews and the words of the idolaters in sacred rites. We were taught this through Moses, who turned a staff into a serpent by the word of God. The Egyptian sorcerers, however, called upon certain things; with incanted words similar to human learning, they poured out images before the eyes of the King, which the Mosaic fountain then swallowed up to reveal the deception. For this reason, it seems to me that a certain man named Joseph lately proposed in Rome, quite learnedly, that no names in licit magic work have as much power as the Hebrew names, or those derived closely from them, because these were formed first of all by the voice of God. For that in which all Magic is most powerful is the voice of God.

### Many Hebrew sentences and words contained in the New Testament, which are set down here according to the Hebrew truth, with examples compared from the Old Instrument. CHAPTER XI.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial "N" depicting two figures in classical dress, one seated and one standing, set against an architectural backdrop.</image-desc>
NOW, Sidonius, I will no longer allow you to hesitate in that which is manifest to me. For I believe many nations mixed Hebrew into their own hidden voices and secret operations for no other reason than to obtain their desires more surely. I think this is beyond doubt regarding Orpheus, Pythagoras, and Plato: that nothing of theirs was so greatly hidden or so secluded as the Hebrew names of divinity, which they wished to reveal to no one in writing—as Plato himself suggests regarding himself in his letter to the Syracusans.
<margin>The Hebrew voices of the Evangelists.</margin>

# ON THE WONDER-WORKING WORD, BOOK II.

...they permitted them to remain unchanged and untouched, and they inserted foreign words <note>original: *barbara uerba* — "barbarian" in the classical sense refers to non-Greek languages, here specifically Hebrew.</note> into the Greek, just as when the children cried out to Christ, **Hofchiana** <note>original: הושע-נא *Hofchiana*</note>: that is, "Save, Lord," though afterward it was corrupted by the ignorance of scribes and is now incorrectly said as "Hosanna." Luke, being more skilled in the Greek language and foresighted regarding what would happen, knew he was writing his Gospel for Greeks who would be unable to pronounce this expression according to the properties of the language; he judged it better to remain silent rather than offer the word to be mocked by those who would corrupt it. However, the other three Evangelists, fearing nothing regarding **Hofchiana**, decided by no means to omit it because of that notable particle **na** <note>original: נא</note>, <margin>Some think this is an adverb of entreaty <note>original: *Quidam putant esse blandiētis aduerbium.*</note></margin> which they say is one of the divine names. Likewise, Mark, in that excellent miracle which Christ performed in raising the daughter of Jairus, did not hesitate to write down the very Hebrew words of Christ by which the dead girl was restored to life and light. For taking the hand of the girl lying in the tomb, he said in two words: **Thabiti, Kumi** <note>original: טבתי, קומי *Thabiti, Kumi*</note>. The first of these pertains to life: that is, "Look up" <note>original: *Respice*</note>; the second pertains to the recovery of health: <margin>that is, Life, health. <note>original: *id Vita, sanitas.*</note></margin> that is, "Rise." In this passage, some later, insufficiently diligent transcriber dared to mix into the context of the speech what he had found in the margin of the history, so that now almost all books hold it as **Thalita, Kumi** <note>original: טליתא, קומי *Thalita, Kumi*</note>, which is interpreted as: "Little girl, I say to you, rise." Indeed, it is not to be believed that the Evangelist translated what is not present in the truth of the original. Therefore, "Little girl, I say to you"—this entire phrase—has no relevance here. 

Indeed, I greatly marvel at certain people of no small fame and reputation among you in the learning of all sciences, whom you also hold in high esteem, who say in this place that **Thalita** <note>original: טליתא *Thalita*</note> is the name of the maiden. As if it should be thought that Christ—whom I, however much I have been a Jew, have always esteemed greater than Apollonius of Tyana <note>A famous Neopythagorean philosopher and reputed miracle-worker from the 1st century AD.</note> or any of the philosophers—as if it should be thought that he (now taught by you, I affirm him to be more excellent than the angels and all gods, not just superior to men, and I believe he is and was God), as if it should be thought that he first wished to search for a name with which to chant a secret song <note>original: *carmen arcanum* — a magic incantation.</note>. This is what all the magicians agree about regarding Apollonius: when he had escaped the hands of Tigillinus (or more truly, Nero), he touched a girl encountered on the road who was thought to have died during her wedding, and at the start he diligently sought the name of the maiden. Having received it, he is said to have whispered something secretly by which <margin>The girl coming back to life. <note>original: *Puella reuixiscens.*</note></margin> the girl revived. 

And this was once observed as a custom among the Romans: whenever they besieged a city, they would accurately seek out the name of that city. Upon learning it, they were accustomed to use a certain song <note>An incantation or ritual known as *evocatio*.</note> to <margin>To call out the protective Gods through magic. <note>original: *Tutelares Deos euocare magicē.*</note></margin> call out all its protective gods, and thus finally conquer it. Because of this very fact, no one dared to betray the proper name of the city of Rome, lest they suffer the same from their enemies. From this we recognize that the proper names of things are of no use in incantations—which is far from him [Christ] who utterly abolished all worship of demons—nor would he desire to know the girl's name in this work, whom he had never seen before. Rather, **Thabiti Kumi** <note>original: טבתי קומי *Thabiti Kumi*</note> are the words of Christ, which are translated into Latin as "Look up, Rise": "Look up" so that you may live; "Rise" so that everyone may see you with their eyes as healthy, and confess that you have been delivered by my command not only from death but from every illness. 

But I preach to you in vain what you yourselves have often read among our people while investigating the scriptures. For instance, in the thirteenth Psalm, which begins: *How long, O Lord?* In the verse: "Look upon me, hear me, O Lord my God." And in the twenty-second, which begins: *My God, my God.* In the verse: "I will count all my bones, they themselves looked and saw me." And in the thirty-third Psalm: *Rejoice, O you righteous.* In the verse: "The Lord looked down from heaven." And in the following Psalm, in the verse: "Look to him and be enlightened." Where your translation <note>The Latin Vulgate.</note> has: "Come to him and be enlightened." And in the praises <note>The Morning Prayers or Lauds.</note> which you chant daily at the first hour: In the letter **Gimel** <note>Refers to the third section of the acrostic Psalm 119.</note>, "Open my eyes and I shall consider." Where it ought more truly to be placed: "I shall look upon the wonders of your law." For this is the same word **Thabiti** <note>original: טבתי *Thabita*</note> about which we must now discuss, since in the second person it becomes **Thabita** <note>original: תבתי *Thabita*</note>...

<margin>A shift in tense and person.</margin>
...**bita**, or **Thabiti** <note>original: תביטי *Thabiti*</note>: that is, "may you look" or "look." For, as the Muses <note>A classical metaphor for poets or inspired writers.</note> are accustomed to say "speak" when they mean "declare," so also among the Hebrews the same is frequently found in common usage, as here: "you shall look" for "look." But **Kumi** <note>original: קומי *Kumi*</note> is by itself an imperative of the feminine gender, as in the second chapter of the Song of Songs: "Behold, my beloved speaks to me: Arise <note>original: *surge*</note>, hasten, my friend." Where it is placed as **Kumi**: that is, "arise." You will find such places in the Holy Scriptures corrupted by the unlearned, while theologians are more accustomed to notice the dialectical sophisms of Aristotle than the words of divine inspiration and the Holy Spirit. Hence, by the pursuit of human education, the celestial tradition itself is neglected, and the talkativeness of men drives out the sacred word. For a similar error of the scribes is discovered in the Acts of the Apostles, which has begun to be common among you even for the learned and indeed for the teachers, regarding the raising of **Dorcas** <note>original: *Dorcadis*</note> from the family of the saints in Joppa, which is a district <note>term: *toparchia* — a small administrative district or province.</note> of Judea, as Pliny says, very close to Lydda. For there they do not correctly write the name of the little woman herself, as I have often found written in both Greek and Latin manuscripts. By this example, I would even say they failed in the previous Gospel: but the proper name of the faithful disciple was **Thabia** <note>original: תביא *Thabia*</note>, surely

<margin>Tabia.</margin>
with the same aspiration, and without the letter **T** <note>original: ת *tav*</note> in the final syllable, which its interpretation teaches us; for the name of the Assyrians <note>Reuchlin often uses "Assyrian" or "Chaldaic" to refer to Aramaic.</note> **Thabia** means a **Gazelle** <note>original: *Caprea*</note>, as we read in the Aramaic <note>original: *Chaldaico*</note> book called **Illen Pithgamai** <note>original: *Illen Pithgamai* — Aramaic for "These are the words," likely referring to a Targum or Aramaic translation of the Bible.</note>. For they brought to him a deaf and mute man, and they prayed that he would lay his hand upon him; taking him aside from the crowd, he put his fingers into his ears, and

<margin>Ephphatha.</margin>
spitting, he touched his tongue, and looking up to heaven he groaned and said: **Ethpathah** <note>original: אִתְפַּתַּח *Ethpathah*</note>, which is "be opened." This ought to be written at the beginning with the letter **P** <note>original: פ *pe*</note> but pronounced with a stronger aspiration <note>The "ph" sound.</note>. For it is the passive imperative of the verb **Pathah** <note>original: פתח *pathah*</note>, which is "he opened," and in the future **Ephathah**: that is, "I will open," as in the Psalm verse: "I will open my mouth in parables." And in the fiftieth Psalm <note>Psalm 51 in modern numbering.</note> in the verse: "Thou shalt open my lips," and so on for the rest. For you are not as thoroughly acquainted with or learned in Hebrew literature as you are in Greek; the singular masculine imperative **Hiphathah**—meaning "be opened" or "be thou opened"—is formed from the passive **Niphathah**. Just as Christ’s powerful word thundered: I shall come to his most enduring death, when hanging on the wooden cross and already dying, he spoke

Matthew recites it just as it is, although **Sabathani** is also said corruptly, through a defect in the first syllable which ought to be marked by the letter **Ayin** <note>original: ע *ayn*</note>. Your scholars observe that Mark is even less successfully corrected in this place, for he puts **Elohe** <note>original: אֱלֹהֵי *Elohe*</note> or, according to others, **Elohi** less appropriately. For **Elohe** is "God," but the possessive "my" <note>The suffix *-i*.</note> is not read there by the Hebrews. It could indeed designate "my God" through **Elohai** <note>original: אֱלֹהַי *Elohai*</note>, but the words of the prophet are not to be changed. They record that God was about to die, and that he began the Psalter from the beginning of the Passion until life was finished, reaching in his last breath of death the Psalm which is the thirtieth in order according to the Seventy translators <note>The Septuagint.</note>, so that both the beginning and the end of the Passion might be completed in one number. For just as the high priests gave thirty pieces of silver to the traitor Judas before Christ was taken, so he himself promised to God the Father

"And the Lord will save me; at evening, morning, and noon I will speak and declare." <note>original: "Dominus saluabit me, Vespere & mane & meridie loquar & adnunciabo." A reference to Psalm 55:17-18.</note> Thus, throughout the entire time of his passion, he spoke with God at evening, morning, and noon—most often in secret, as was prophesied through David: "My prayer shall return to my own bosom." <note>original: "Oratio mea in sinu meo conuertetur." From Psalm 35:13.</note> Nevertheless, he sometimes openly pronounced certain phrases from those same songs [the Psalms]; some of these his followers, listening nearby, committed to memory, while others perhaps went unheard by those further away. Among the words heard, we can consider that which he said: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" <note>original: "Eli Eli lamah asabathani." For after the death of Christ, whose final prayer was this thirtieth Psalm, we finally began to understand and see "him whom they have pierced" <note>original: "quem compunxerunt & in quem transfixerunt." Zechariah 12:10; John 19:37.</note>; for this reason he prayed with a special vow that the Father might forgive those crucifying him, since "they knew not what they did." But while I strive to explain the Hebrew words which the Evangelists, without external counsel, used in their writing, I have somehow slipped into the secret coverings of your religion. I say this so you may realize that I have arrived at your profession through previous meditation, and not so suddenly.

->CHAPTER XII.<-

**T**HEN SIDONIUS said: "My dear Capnion, how skilled this man is in the divine scriptures! What, then, shall I contribute to our conversation? But if I recall correctly, Baruchias has provided me much rest, so that I am not forced to discourse at length about sacred names. For he teaches us that only Hebrew words are numbered among those truly sacred; he attempts to affirm this based on their antiquity, their conversation with divinity, and a certain close covenant between God and the Jews, and because the language is more solid—by many arguments, in short. If these things are true, I, who have worn out my life in Greek and Latin more than others, shall be glad to have found time only for listening." And CAPNION said: "Indeed, I would wonder at his great knowledge of the Gospels, had he not confessed much earlier that he had spent no small labor upon them—as the facts show and the business indicates. But let us listen to him while the light lasts. For the day has already passed noon. Come again, Baruchias, do not shrink from publishing those things you have received concerning the secret words—hidden, as you said, 'under a bushel' <note>A biblical metaphor for hiding the truth, from Matthew 5:15.</note>. Finally, you have already become accustomed to conclude every prayer, whether public or private, with a single word, *Amen*, which is also found in Paul." To this CAPNION <margin>Amen <note>Hebrew: אמן</note></margin> said: "I will explain briefly so you do not get stuck. For he says in his book *Against Celsus*: 'In certain sacred names a wonderful power lies hidden; therefore, these names themselves are not to be translated from the Hebrew language into another, but are to be preserved in their very own characters.' You have what you have long wished to draw out: namely, that there is a wonder-working virtue in divine names and prayers; because of which, and..."

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous page, where Baruchias and his companions discuss the mystical properties of the Hebrew language. The speaker here (Capnion, Reuchlin's persona) transitions from discussing the necessity of keeping divine names in their original form to a broader theological discussion on the will of God as the source of all miraculous power. This leads into Chapter XIII, where Baruchias takes over to explain how divine mysteries are revealed.</meta>

<header>JOHN REUCHLIN</header>

...the forms of the characters and the words themselves must remain uncorrupted, lest the indwelling spirit and the entire power vanish—just as if the frame of a man were destroyed, the spirit enclosed in the body would likewise vanish. <margin>Iamblichus</margin> Furthermore, as Iamblichus replied to Porphyry <note>Iamblichus and Porphyry were influential Neoplatonist philosophers; Reuchlin often cites them to bridge Platonic thought with Kabbalah.</note>, if those names were established by human agreement and convention, it would not matter if some were exchanged for others. But as we understood long ago, Baruchia, and as we confess to be true: these names were received from the divine, not produced by humans. To this, that same noble Pythagorean, Iamblichus, adds: "For names translated into another language," he says, "do not preserve exactly the same meaning; rather, there are certain things proper to individual nations that cannot be expressed to other nations through speech." Added to this is the fact that even if we can interpret the properties of their meanings through another language, they do not preserve the same power (*potentia*) once changed. 

I would wish to respond to you using these authors, but I would have you think cautiously: I do not feel the same way as you do about all words—specifically, that they possess that majesty which you spread so widely by reputation. For who will doubt that God the Almighty—and as the Greeks say, the *Omnitenent* <note>original: "omnitenentem." A translation of the Greek *Pantokratōr*, meaning "All-Holding" or "Almighty."</note>—is able to adorn words with virtues? <margin>The will of God is the cause of things.</margin> Thus, the power of God is evident, but not yet His will, which alone is the cause of all things. For "Whatever the Lord pleased, He has done in heaven and in earth." <note>A reference to Psalm 135:6.</note> Therefore, unless you show that God willed this or that word to be endowed with such-and-such virtue, you will have achieved nothing.

### That no one knows God and His meaning, except His own Spirit, and those to whom it has been revealed; and then, in what manner miracles occur.

### CHAPTER XIII.

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'A' featuring floral and foliate motifs.</image-desc>

"BUT I promised," Baruchias said, "not to teach you, but to report what I once received from our college regarding the mysteries. If I perform this duty rightly, there will certainly be plenty for me to rejoice in, nor will I bind myself to any other post. Since yesterday evening it was agreed with one voice that in divine matters one must believe—though I know it will never be a matter of doubt among you that God can do all things. This is something our mind understands by its own nature: if God is over all things, and if all things depend on Him—both beings and non-beings, as even the most excellent theologians assert—then the highest power (indeed, a power superior to all power above the highest) resides with God regarding both what exists and what does not exist, and it is bounded by no limits. Otherwise, it would not be the highest, or above the highest. 

If He shows this power dwelling in a word or a thing, it matters not, as long as He desires His virtue to inhabit there. But we clearly recognize this decree and will of God either through the experience of deeds or through the speech of divine <margin>Inspiration.</margin> inspiration. To this end, it is necessary to apply both Holy Scripture and the doctrines of contemplative men (through whose mouths the Divinity speaks), as well as the heroic histories of the blessed. For who has known the mind of the Lord of eternity? No one, except the Spirit who is within Him, and finally he to whom He reveals Himself. Just as among creatures, nothing knows the thoughts within a man except his own spirit which is in him, or some friend to whom the spirit (through the man) or the man (through his spirit) has announced it or shown it by signs. 

Our ancestors, who were both learned and experienced, confirmed that God spoke in this way with Abraham, Moses, and Joshua, showing them the virtues of divine words and affirming them with miraculous effects. They committed these to memory through writing for us, the offspring of their lineage; and we, receiving them with a grateful heart, experience and feel them daily if we so wish. But to get to the matter: for those desiring to hear of wondrous things, let those things come to mind which were discussed by us abundantly above: that only the first and greatest God performs wonders, miracles, portents, and signs—at least those that are true and not deceptive illusions. Or, when He occasionally deigns to honor His angels with divine honor, He entrusts them with performing wonderful works: yet they do so in His name, lest He give His honor to others and His glory to another, and lest man turn to the worship of the creature, having abandoned the Creator."

<summary>Baruchias argues that divine names lose their mystical power when translated, citing Iamblichus. He explains that while God is omnipotent, miracles only occur through His specific will and revelation, as recorded in the history of the Hebrew patriarchs.</summary>

# ON THE MIRACULOUS WORD, BOOK II.

Because of His name, He places His authority in angels, so that we might not allow the worship of forms—which in Greek we call *idolatry* <note>original: "idololatriam"</note>—to take hold among us, a thing He has always hated most fiercely of all. Wherefore He says to His people: *Behold, I send my angel to go before you, to guard you on the way, and to bring you into the place I have prepared. Observe him and hear his voice; do not think him someone to be despised, for he will not forgive when you have sinned. For my name is in him.* <note>A reference to Exodus 23:20-21, emphasizing that the angel's power comes from the Divine Name residing within him.</note> Since, therefore, miraculous works are performed for our benefit first by God and secondly by angels, it seemed most appropriate to me to speak first of the divine name, which is known to pertain to God Himself (as far as my memory serves), and then of that which sometimes concerns an angel, according to the meager limits of our human frailty. In this matter, we shall maintain an order: first, we will review for you those names of God whose meaning has long been clear; after these, we will attempt to discuss those whose meaning is not yet manifest, or which we have received as being revealed only to a few.

### On the names of God, and first on their number. CHAPTER XIV.

<margin>The number of the names of God.</margin>
<margin>A cobbler should not go beyond his last.</margin>
<margin>Even the serpent.</margin>
<margin>Note Well</margin>
<margin>To touch.</margin>
<margin>Help, Counsel, Transgression.</margin>
<margin>One name of God.</margin>
THEREFORE, those who have dared to write about secret names are many; some from the memory of our fathers, and some of yours as well, are read even to this day. For this reason, my part in the discussion will be easier if I explain briefly those things which you have seen described at length among various authors. Jerome, in his letter to Marcella, mentions ten names of God. <note>St. Jerome (c. 342–420 AD) was a scholar who translated the Bible into Latin; his letter to Marcella is a foundational text for Christian study of Hebrew divine names.</note> Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A Christian theologian and philosopher of the late 5th to early 6th century, famous for his work "On the Divine Names."</note> lists nearly forty-five; others list seventy-two, some more, some fewer, each according to his own capacity. But truly, what definite number can there be for names of Him who is both unnamable and celebrated by every name? Therefore, let us neither push ourselves into a corner from which we cannot break free, nor act so slowly and half-heartedly in this cause that we are proved to hold no memory of divine honor. 

I desire that you agree with my words no more than I myself would agree, except as the sacred utterances permit. I do not wish to appear injurious to the Best and Greatest God—I who am but breathing mud and clay, a worm and not a man—nor do I wish to be like a second Uzzah <note>In the Bible (2 Samuel 6), Uzzah was struck dead for touching the Ark of the Covenant, even though he intended to steady it. Reuchlin uses this as a warning against human presumption in divine matters.</note>, touching the Ark and adding something beyond what God Himself has spoken. For I believe the first sin of the human race was that which Eve, the mother of all living, added to the words of God—more than God Himself had said—which was the beginning of subsequent crimes and the origin of divine vengeance. For before the woman had been created, God said to Adam: *From every tree of paradise you may eat, but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat.* Yet let us see how Eve, newly born, changed the words of the Creator when speaking to the serpent: *From the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of paradise,* she said, *God commanded us that we should not eat, and that we should not touch it, lest perhaps we die.* She added a plural pronoun to us, although He never commanded Eve not to eat (as she was not yet born). She also added: *And that we should not touch it,* which God had not said. Furthermore, as if she wished to make the Lord out to be a liar, she added a particle of doubt and unbelief, saying: *Lest perhaps we die,* whereas the Creator had threatened Adam alone, singularly and firmly: *For on whatever day you eat from it, you shall die the death.* 

From this, the serpent paid the penalty because of his counsel, Eve because of her help, and Adam because of his transgression. Therefore, lest I fall into the same fault or crime before the trembling Author of the universe, His supreme mercy must be prayed for: that He might notice our goodwill and piety rather than our ruin if, by chance, my foot should slip. In such an event, may He deign to help us from the most sacred inner chambers of His love toward us, for the glory and honor of His name, which is blessed forever. 

But as to what that illustrious word might be—so effective, so venerable, so health-giving, through which we may more easily obtain our prayers—we must consider the many names of the supreme God that are found. For when the prophet Zechariah exclaims: *In that day God shall be one, and his name one,* <note>Zechariah 14:9.</note> we are reminded by the meaning of this time that there are currently many names of God.

# THE WORKS OF JOHANNES REUCHLIN

...of God, because in the world to come there will be nothing but the One. Why do we drag [out the matter] and waste time in vain? Why do we wait so long, as if it were a great task [to explain] how that which lacks a name can be called by so many names? Or does some other name for divinity exist among those in heaven than among mortals? Will the usual naming of this world cease in the future [rest] of our souls? Does God, since He possesses a perpetual and permanent essence within Himself, have a name? Or is no name needed for Him then?

---

->On the name *Ehyeh* <note>original: אהיה</note>, where the story of Simonides is also told by Sidonius. CHAPTER XV.<-

Setting aside everything that pertains no more to the matter than to the slowness of our task, let us explain in a few words. Whatever the supreme divinity [is called] among the immortals, among the heavenly beings—and since it is likely the heavenly beings use some name according to their custom, though it be preeminent—we shall nevertheless speak more of those things which are relevant to our case, saying that according to human contemplation, from the [names] handed down to us...

<margin>The reasoning behind divine names. Essence.</margin>
...we attribute something of essence to the sacred names, something to power, [something] to operation, and the rest to our own affection toward God. Moreover, we [understand] essence [as] separation from things, and a total enclosure and [exclusion] within itself—as that noble philosopher of our age <note>Likely a reference to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</note> says—in the most remote [depths] of His divinity, [in] a profound and solitary retraction, hiding itself most inwardly in its own abyss of [shadows]. According to this, therefore, they affirm that [God] established for Himself an [ineffable] name among men, since He alone knows Himself and alone gives Himself a name. Now let us see by what argument they perceive this, and what that most sacred name of essence might be. [Moses] said to God: "Behold, I am going to the children of Israel and will say to them: The God of your fathers has sent me to you; and they will say to me: What is His name? What shall I say to them?"

<margin>1 <note>The letter Aleph, used here as a marker</note></margin>
God [said] to Moses: *Ehyeh* <note>original: אהיה; literally "I will be," often translated as "I am"</note>, and He said, "Thus you shall say to the children of Israel, [He who is] has sent me to you." Plato had learned this name during that long travels of his among the [peoples of the East], which finally [reached] the Greeks in two letters as *ōn* <note>original: ὤν; meaning "The Being" or "The One who is"</note>. For in the *Timaeus* he says: "It is therefore, in my opinion, first [necessary] to distinguish what *on* <note>Being</note> is: that is, the being which always is, and has no beginning, [from that] which has a beginning but never truly is. The former is always understood by the intellect as being through itself. The latter is perceived by opinion along with [the senses] as something subject to birth and decay, as that which never truly is." By this name, Plato distinguishes the World from the Creator, and a [multitude] of the most elegant [philosophers] followed him, except for the fact that some changed the neuter gender into [the masculine]. For Plato named the most excellent author of the universe "That which is" <note>original: τὸ ὤν</note> with a single word; but many of his followers call him "He who is" <note>original: ὤν</note>. This change [is avoided] by the Hebrews, because they [have a different grammar], only having two genders, masculine and [feminine]. Therefore, a neuter verb among the Latins or Greeks is easily included under their [masculine]. Wherefore, whether one says "He who is" or "That which is," it is pronounced in the essential name given to Moses as *Ehyeh* <note>original: אהיה</note>, which they derive from the verb *hayah* <note>original: היה; meaning "to be"</note> according to the laws of grammar, with a letter added at the beginning. I do not know if it is worthy of [pardon] that I speak so barbaricly in so elegant a cause before you most eloquent men. But though Demosthenes or Cicero might disagree, I would certainly believe them to be mute and tongue-tied in the face of God's secrets. For your Origen, not inferior to even the most splendid orators, in his twentieth homily (if I remember correctly) on Exodus, speaks in almost these words: "All men, in comparison to the divine word, are to be thought of not only as ineloquent but as mute." Therefore, if [you can endure] this constant barbarism without annoyance, I shall gladly proceed. "But do proceed," said SIDONIVS: "It is not..."

<meta>This page continues the dialogue in Book II of "The Mirific Word." # ON THE MIRIFIC WORD, BOOK II.

...for us, this task is the most difficult of all; and furthermore, I myself believe that divine matters can in no way be sufficiently expressed in a human manner, mindful of that 
<margin>Simonides.</margin> which histories relate concerning Simonides, a man of outstanding learning. For when the Tyrant Hiero asked him what God was, he requested a space of one day for deliberation. Returning the next day, when Hiero asked the same, Simonides requested two days. Then, as the Tyrant asked more frequently, Simonides always doubled the number of days. When finally asked by Hiero why he did so, he said: "Because the longer I consider it, the more obscure the matter seems to me." Therefore, I marvel that this business could be handled thus far even in our discourse and so clearly; wherefore, do not delay us further. To which, CAPNION also encourages him.

->*On the name Jehovah <note>original: יהוה</note> and Ehieh <note>original: אהיה</note>. CHAPTER XVI.*<-

<image-desc>A large ornamental initial T depicting a traveler with a walking stick journeying through a hilly landscape toward a distant town.</image-desc>THEN he said: You have the name of the highest God, which certain learned men have thought to be the first of all, since it seems to designate the very essence of God, nor is it shared with any other thing. For nothing outside of God is that which "is," since all things consist of a certain proportion of composition. God alone is most simple, and for that reason He "is who He is" <note>A reference to Exodus 3:14: "I am who I am."</note>; everything else, however, is indeed *by* that which it is, but is not the thing itself. However, other men, not to be looked down upon and most studious in the contemplation of the most secret things, enter much more closely into the very inner chambers of divinity; they most observantly weigh the magnitude of a certain other name, and set another name above this name <term>Ehieh</term> <note>original: אהיה, meaning "I will be" or "I am"</note> or <term>Jehovah</term> <note>original: יהוה, the Tetragrammaton</note>. For as that <term>Dionysius the Areopagite</term> <note>A 5th-6th century Christian theologian and philosopher whose works on "negative theology" were highly influential in the Renaissance.</note> explains to you, O <term>Capnion</term>: Jehovah himself—that is, "He who is"—is a certain "super-essential" [source] of the whole of being, the Founding cause and craftsman of being, of subsistence, of substance, of essence, and of nature; the principle and measure of eternities and of times; the entity and age of beings, and the time of those things which come to be, and the "being" for those things which exist in any way, and the generation for those things which are in any way produced. Here is perceived, not obscurely, the rushing together of the First Being with flowing things, to which He provides the power of persisting. And although it notifies us of the most simple essence of God, quite simply and quite freely—just as the whole is embraced in Himself, "being" itself having been preeminently received so that He is the super-essential [source] of the whole of being—nevertheless, it does not designate God as enclosed and resting, but as looking upon the things themselves, and insinuating Himself with things so that He may grant them subsistence: just as you easily understand from the words of the same Dionysius which you have just heard, after sharp meditation. 

Wherefore, considering the separate retreat into Himself of His ineffable pre-eminence, they especially venerate the most holy name <term>Hu</term> <note>original: הוא, meaning "He" or "The Same"</note> and place it before <term>Ehieh</term>. This name God Himself manifested to Isaiah, the most noble of prophets, saying: "I am the Lord, *Hu* is my name: I will not give my glory to another." <note>Isaiah 42:8. Reuchlin interprets "Hu" (He) here as a specific name of the hidden God.</note> You see that the said name contains a light within its midst, and indeed restrains the rays, and designates God dwelling solitarily in hidden retreats without any outflow of powers: but containing Himself in the most simple and most absolute consistency of Himself, not going out, governing nothing, but permitting all things; accepting those things which are done well, likewise not remembering those things which are done badly, as God speaks hereafter in the same prophet: "I am, I am *Hu*, blotting out your iniquities with myself, and I will not remember your sins." <note>Isaiah 43:25.</note> For because *Hu* does not give His glory to another, because He does not remember sins, because He blots out iniquities "with Himself" and not for the sake of another outside Himself, it declares the meaning of the name: since *Hu* denotes God so separated from things that He either acts, or permits, or rests, all within Himself. And often this name is placed before negative statements that follow, as God spoke a little above: "You may understand that I am *Hu*; before me no God was formed, and after me there shall be none." <note>Isaiah 43:10.</note> This so august and distinguished name was once called <term>tauton</term> <note>original Greek: ταυτὸν, meaning "the same"</note> by the Greek Philosophers, especially the Platonists, and "the very same" by the Latins. The Psalm—

<meta>This page continues the discourse of Book II, following the discussion of the name Ehieh. Here, the character Capnion explores the divine name "Hu" (He), linking it to the philosophical concept of absolute Identity and Sameness as found in both sacred scripture and classical literature.</meta>

# OF JOHANNES REUCHLIN
<meta>catchword: not</meta>

...for the hundred-and-first <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 102:27.</note> says of God: "And you are *Hu* <note>original: הוא, meaning 'He' or 'The Same'</note>, and your years shall not fail." You Latins sing in the assembly of the sacred rites: "But you are the same self." For this name "The Same," Virgil transferred to Jupiter with equal understanding when Jupiter was proclaiming an oracle, saying:

> Whatever fortune each has today, whatever hope each carves out,
> Whether he be Trojan or Rutulian, I shall hold them in no distinction,
> Whether the camp is held in siege by the fates of the Italians,
> Or by a wretched error and the grim warnings of Troy.
> Nor do I exempt the Rutulians; each shall find labor and
> Fortune from his own beginnings. King Jupiter is the **same** to all.

<margin>I myself am the same.</margin>
You see this name "The Same" attributed to King Jupiter. Therefore, this protective and helpful word <term>tauton</term> <note>original: ταυτὸν, meaning 'the same'</note>, which is *Hu*, is of such great majesty that it is eternal above all letters; it is unchangeable, remaining in itself, relating to the same things and toward the same things in the same way, similarly present to all things. It is placed firmly and inviolably according to itself and in itself within the most beautiful boundaries of substantive identity; it is untransmutable, inflexible, invariable, unmixed, immaterial, most simple, lacking nothing, incapable of increase or decrease. It is a whole—not as if not yet brought forth, or as if imperfect, or as if generated in this or that way, or as if it consists nowhere and in no manner—but it is through all things unbegotten and absolutely unbegotten. It always is, and is in itself, and is the same according to itself, pre-limited by itself uniformly and identically. I fear here that in translating these Greek concepts I might poorly offend learned ears. But perhaps I do not have to deliver a speech before a magistrate, nor do you, as I believe, sit as listeners in the benches of a courtroom, but in an Academy of the most secret Philosophy, where she desires bare facts more than adorned words—though if it were possible for me, I would follow the advice of Horace Flaccus:

> To say things that are both pleasant and suitable to the facts at the same time.

Whatever the case may be, I would fix the sublime dignity of that name at the very peak of all being, were it not that sometimes—indeed quite often—it flows down into these sublunary things so that it communicates itself to matters in such a way that it takes a surname from them. For this reason, we think nothing else exists but "the self-same," not only in substances, but as in the address to Aeneas:

-> —on account of you, that same one, my shame is lost. <-
But it also applies to those things following from substances, as Anna said to her sister Dido:
-> —you should have called me to the same fate, <-
-> The same grief and the same hour would have taken us both by the sword. <-
And likewise Virgil says of the companions of Aeneas:
> The same passion holds them all at once.

This participation of things with the same divinity seems to me to have been explained by Isaiah, through whom God speaks: *Hu*: I am the first, and I am the last. And a little later, in the fifty-first chapter: "I am, I am *Hu* who consoles you," by which he clearly suggests to us that *Hu* itself is occupied in the beginning, the end, and the middle of things.

<margin>The voice existing everywhere.</margin>
Whence, to demonstrate that your theologians agree with ours, hear again the Areopagite <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential mystical theologian.</note> concerning the word *Hu*, which he calls <term>tauton</term> <note>the Same</note>; he says: "The Same shines forth from itself upon all things that are, as it were, fit for a share of it, connecting some things to others by the abundance and origin of identity in itself, and containing opposites identically through the one and singular supereminent cause of all identity." From this, like a king, He rules all things by His nod: things celestial, worldly, and infernal. Nor is there any power in heaven or on earth or in the depths that is able to resist the power of this name; and therefore God is called *Hu*, because all power and might is subject to Him. Whence the prophet says in the twenty-third Psalm <note>Psalm 24:8-10 in modern numbering.</note>: "Who is *Hu*, that king of glory?" and the spirits respond in the prophet: "The Lord of hosts is *Hu*, He is that king of glory forever." Another thing occurs to my memory which the power of the aforementioned name alone...

Reuchlin draws parallels between Hebrew scripture, Greek Neoplatonism (Dionysius), and Roman poetry (Virgil and Horace) to show that God is the immutable source of all consistency in the universe.</summary>

# ON THE MIRACULOUS WORD, BOOK II.

I recall in memory: For among the seven names consecrated at once through Moses, along with *Hu* <note>original: הוא, meaning "He" or "The Same"</note>, there is also placed *Esh* <note>original: אש, meaning "Fire"</note>, in a single context of speech in the repetition of the Law, which you call Deuteronomy, which in Latin we call fire. And for that reason, He is more often heard in fire, as with Abraham, Elijah, David, and others of whom histories exist, <margin>Visions of God in fire.</margin> as if in a matter agreeable to the divinity. And Moses saw God in fire, and the angel in a flame of fire. And Ezekiel's divine vision was the splendor of fire, and lightning coming out of the fire. Likewise, Plato wished the supreme God to be in a fiery essence, whom his ungrateful disciple Aristotle—as often elsewhere, so now also—reproached, not without slander, in a certain booklet written to Alexander, King of the Macedonians. There he found, or rather did not find so much as learn from the Brahmans of India, that the "fifth essence" <note>Aristotle's *quintessence* or aether, which he distinguished from the four earthly elements.</note> is the dwelling place of divinity. "We," he says, "do not clearly say, as some wandering around the divine do, that God is in a fiery essence." Then he strives to cite a witness of the truth, namely a better Plato, when he adds: For so also says Homer:
<margin>The lot of Jove is heaven; he sits in the clouds of the wide ether.</margin>
Therefore, the prophet Zechariah spoke better, and certainly much better, because he heard God himself speaking from the mouth of an angel: "I will be to her," said God, "a wall of fire round about, and for the honor of *Ehieh* <note>original: אהיה, meaning "I Am"</note> in her midst." Regarding this, so that I may even flatter our Sidonius in bringing forward the Philosophers, that Plutarch, a man excellently learned in many arts, makes mention in his collection of physical dogmas. "They describe," he says, "the knowledge of God thus: an intellectual and fiery spirit, having no form, but transforming itself into whatever it wishes, and equaling itself to all things." Whence Zoroaster says: "All things are generated from one fire." You too, Capnion <note>Capnion is the Greek-style pseudonym for Johannes Reuchlin himself, derived from the German 'Rauch' meaning smoke.</note>, or rather we Christians (for I do not wish to desert the profession I have begun), commonly name God "fire" with Paul of Tarsus, who, writing to the Hebrews, says: "God is a consuming fire." <margin>God is a consuming fire.</margin> Although you venerate this name attributed to the Holy Spirit under a certain distinct property of divinity, which John the Baptist taught both in Mark and also in Luke, saying: <margin>The Holy Spirit. Luke 3:16 (noted as 9:11 in margin).</margin>
> I indeed baptize you in water unto repentance: but he who comes after me is stronger than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to carry: He shall baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire, through the figure of <term>pneuma</term> <note>original: πνεύματι, meaning "spirit" or "breath"</note> in the Holy Spirit: that is, fire, in whose appearance he appeared to the apostles after Christ was taken up.

### CHAPTER XVII.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'P' showing a floral or foliage pattern within a square frame.</image-desc>

THAT recitation of yours, says Capnion, pleases me greatly: since I think nothing is more consistent with our religion. First of all, there is nothing that I have ever received with greater pleasure than that you have ordered these divine names—not, I believe, by human instinct—so that, contrary to the opinion of many, even our own people whom we crown as Theologians, you have established not *Ehieh* (as they think), but *Hu* as the first, so that the order is *Hu, Ehieh, Esh* <note>original: הוא, אהיה, אש, representing "He", "I Am", and "Fire".</note>, as if one were speaking to the one ineffable Trinity and triune unity. Fire is the same, just as we say concerning the nature of visible things: substance, power, and operation, in the same one individual. And perhaps just as Orpheus arranged sacred hymns according to consecrated names, SIDONIUS says: <margin>The Sacrosanct and venerable Trinity.</margin>

->*Jupiter, darkening the clouds and reigning in the ether.*<-

# JOHANNES REUCHLIN’S

...of the Son, and the God of great counsel we call Him: whom you Hebrews name *Hochma* <note>original: חכמה, meaning "Wisdom"</note>. Concerning the third person:
> Thus having spoken, that father of men and gods laughed,
> and called shining Venus, to whom he said such things:

Concerning which ternary <note>A group of three; here referring to the Trinity.</note> that Virgilian—or rather Pythagorean—line is sung:
-> —God delights in an odd number. <-
For I seem to see that you have comprehended the whole majesty of the divine essence in a continuous triad. Hence perhaps, because He creates beings, He perfects the creature once begun. But why do I delay Baruchias? Come, if you have anything further, speak.

-> *Concerning* Hochma <note>Wisdom</note> *and* Sophia <note>Wisdom</note>, *and several other names of God.* <-
-> CHAPTER XVIII. <-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial 'T' inside a square frame featuring foliate scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>

THEN he said: I have indeed very few things which I once skillfully impressed upon my memory; however, they are nothing compared to these names which I have just now recounted. For I cannot think that of those things which I either read or learned by hearing, any name remains, besides those which were previously brought forth by me. For He alone is said <margin>In what way that fire is God.</margin> even in those three names we embrace, *Hu*, *Ehie*, *Jehovah* <note>original: הוא, אהיה, יהוה; meaning He, I Shall Be, and the Tetragrammaton</note>, which signify the essence of God, even if there were now no world, either spiritual or corporeal. For then God would be both the same Self, and His mere essence, and of a fiery nature. Not indeed as is elementary fire, nor as stellar celestial fire, but as an inexpressible splendor in Himself, in respect to which all other fires are shadow and darkness. This the monuments and poems of the Chaldeans among the works of Synesius <note>A 4th-century philosopher-bishop who blended Neoplatonism with Christianity.</note> indicate:
> Do not despise the black world without light,
> For which also a deep and dark shadow is spread beneath;
> It is filthy, likewise obscure, and likewise feeding idols.
For thus even that world, if any is the archetype <note>The original "blueprint" or ideal world in the mind of God.</note>, will be a shadow and an image in comparison to the divine light in itself; how much more this world of ours, a sharer in the dregs of the world, which is called both the shadow of the higher world and a certain likeness? But I know not what Sidonius whispered in my ear regarding *Hochma* <note>Wisdom</note>, as if it were a name among the names consecrated to the essence. I confess indeed that nothing "happens" to God <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that can change; the author argues God has no accidents, only essence.</note>, nor does anything extraneous cling to Him. For nothing is more one than Himself. Truly, every day with David <note>Referring to the Psalms of David.</note> we cry out to God: "You have made all things in wisdom." Therefore, before all things that were made, *Sophia* <note>Wisdom</note> was with God. If she were not as if outside of God—for otherwise she would by no means have been created before all things—she was therefore the essence of God. For we showed above that the word for "being" is the same, wherefore Sidonius, being now moved, as I myself surmise, feared lest I, through some lazy negligence, might omit those things which belong to *Sophia*: that is, *Hochma* or the essence. But when he meditates within his soul that *Sophia* is nothing other than His essence, it will not be difficult to know in what manner we distribute "insignificant" names <note>Names that do not fully capture the reality of the thing they label.</note>; for according to human custom, we acknowledge that we act improperly toward that supreme and most excellent nature of divinity; and therefore we also name it imperfectly. For <margin>God is the eye for mortal things.</margin> those names which are divinely handed down to us, we arrange according to the capacity of our understanding: so that some signify God according to Himself, stripped of all garments, naked, and free from individual applications which we see happening to other things. As when He is that supersubstantial fire; as when He is "Being" itself, encompassing uniquely and eternally the past, present, and future, bound together into one sea of eternity by a unifying bond; as when He is "The Same" itself, mixed with no proportion of otherness.

<summary>This page explores the divine essence through the names of Wisdom (Chokhmah and Sophia), arguing that God exists as an eternal, fiery "Being" or "Same" prior to and independent of the created world. It emphasizes that human language is inherently imperfect when attempting to name the "supersubstantial" and unified nature of the Creator.</summary>

### ON THE WONDER-WORKING WORD, BOOK II.
### 931

...they designate a certain pure nature of substance, even according to our mortal and weak knowledge of things. But Wisdom is of such a kind as we feel happens to men: for which reason we say one man is wiser than another. Similarly, we attribute that Wisdom to God, and its name is **Hochma** <note>original: חכמה (*Chokhmah*), the Sephirah of Wisdom</note>. Although it is judged to be of no small efficacy among the sacred names signifying God, yet it is permitted to name God not at all **according to Himself** <note>original: *κατ' αὐτὸ* (kat’ auto)</note>—that is, in His absolute essence—but **concerning Himself** <note>original: *πρὸς αὐτὸν* (pros auton)</note>—that is, in relation to His actions. Of this, the sacred utterances are a sign: *Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men.* From this it follows that Wisdom herself reveals this mystery about herself in the Proverbs, when she says: *The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his way, before he made anything from the beginning. I was poured out from eternity, from the head, before the earth was made. The abysses did not yet exist when I was conceived, nor were the heavy springs of water yet flowing. Before the mountains were settled, before the hills, I was conceived.* Later it follows: *And* **Ehieh** <note>original: אהיה (*Ehyeh*), meaning "I am" or "I will be"</note> *was the artisan according to himself, and* **Ehieh** *was the daily delight.* Which you read more elegantly as: *I was with him composing all things, and I was delighted day by day.* 

<margin>Wisdom.</margin>
Now, with the veil removed, you surely perceive that the wisdom of God is a certain emanation. Although produced before the constitution of the world, it nevertheless arose from the head of the Most High God through the contemplation of future things. Through this wisdom all things were made, and without it nothing was made—as if it were a companion habit and industry of **Ehieh** <note>The divine name "I Am"</note> itself—that is, of the first Being, whom he here calls the "artisan." I speak in a human manner because of our weakness. For in such a cause, we sometimes understand things that we are unable to express. 

<margin>Son of the living God.</margin>
Indeed, I believe that wisdom was a living substance and a working energy providing for the universe according to the will of the Maker. And although it is a holy opinion that God Himself was this, nevertheless my mind compels me to understand another property of God there, rather than His own naked immanence. Therefore, I believe **Hochma** is among those things which accompany God’s hidden seclusion within Himself—just as the power of God, which together with wisdom (mentioned a little before) contributed not a little to the machinery of the world. This is according to the testimony of Jeremiah concerning the creator, *who made the earth in his power, and prepared the world in his wisdom, and in* 

<margin>Providence.</margin>
**Binah** <note>original: בינה, meaning "Understanding"</note>—that is, in his understanding or providence—*he stretched out the heavens.* You have here again a religious name, which the Hebrews place after the "Crown" and "Wisdom" among the ten numerations <note>Reuchlin refers to the ten *Sephirot*, the stages of divine emanation in Kabbalah.</note> attributed to God—not as something uncommunicated, but as something radiating; not enclosed, but appearing; not abstract, but proceeding forth. 

The first of these is the inaccessible abyss of divinity, the sea of majesty, and the infinite power of all things, both those which are and those which are not. No contradiction shall escape this, no entanglement prohibits it, no dialectical reasoning of philosophy governs it—not the perplexities of the Sophists, nor logical phantasms. Finally, this 

<margin>The Crown.</margin>
<margin>The nine garments of God.</margin>
entire **Crown** <note>The first Sephirah, *Kether*</note>, hanging from the divinity, penetrates the kingdom once the barriers are broken. They call its name **Kether** <note>original: כתר</note>. There follow still nine "garments" of God; as often as the mind of the blessed touches their fringes, God responds: *Someone has touched me: for I also felt power go out from me.* For they are not so much the enjoyments of those nine beatitudes as they are the objects of enjoyment, which finally coincide in the nine 

<margin>9 Choirs.</margin>
hierarchies <note>The nine orders of angels</note> with the minds of the blessed, and allow a perpetual enjoyment of bliss to each. But if they take up the first numeration again to themselves, they will correspondingly fulfill the end of the "ten words" written by the finger of God. Concerning **Hochma** and **Binah**, Solomon says in his parables: *Blessed is the man who has attained wisdom, and who flows with understanding.* And in Job, Elihu the son of Barachel responded: *I said, days shall speak and a multitude of years shall know wisdom, but certainly it is the spirit in men, and the inspiration of the Almighty God gives them understanding.* Concerning **Nezach** <note>original: נצח (*Netzach*), the Sephirah of Victory or Eternity</note>, the prophet Samuel wrote in his book, which you call the First Book of Kings: 

<margin>The Triumphator.</margin>
*The Triumphator in Israel will not spare, and will not be bent by repentance. For he is not a man, that he should act with repentance.* After which divine name, King David, giving thanks to God...

Reuchlin links these Hebrew concepts to Christian scripture and the angelic hierarchies, viewing them as steps toward understanding the divine essence.</summary>

# THE WRITINGS OF JOHANNES REUCHLIN
### 932

<margin>3</margin> Regarding the expenses collected for the future temple, God placed another name near the end of the first book of the *Words of the Days* <note>original: *verborum dierum*, the Hebrew title for 1 Chronicles</note>, when He says: "To You, O Lord, is magnificence and power and glory and victory and **Hod** <note>original: הדו (*Hod*), usually meaning Splendor or Majesty</note>," which is translated in various ways as "praise" or "confession."
<margin>Pfal. 104.</margin> The one hundred and third Psalm <note>Psalm 104 in modern numbering</note> will manifest this very garment of divinity, in which God is extolled with these words: "You have put on **Hod** and beauty, clothed with light as with a garment." Following this confession of praise and glory is another holy and venerable name, an illustrious name full of heraldry, which is placed roughly in the
<margin>4</margin> middle among the ten **Sephiroth** <note>The ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals Himself</note>, just as the heart is in a living being: **Tiphereth** <note>original: תפארת (*Tiferet*), meaning Beauty or Ornament</note>. For so it is said in the previously cited book of the *Words of the Days* (which they call *Paralipomenon* <note>The traditional Latin name for the books of Chronicles</note>): "Now therefore, our God, we confess to You, and we praise Your illustrious name **Tiphereth**."
<margin>Pfal 96. Gloria.</margin> The ninety-fifth Psalm treats both: "**Hod** and beauty are in His sight, strength and **Tiphereth** are in His sanctuary." You may contemplate the power of this name in the eighty-eighth Psalm, when it is said:
<margin>Esa. 63.</margin> "Since You are the **Tiphereth** of his strength and valor, O God." And in the sixty-third chapter of Isaiah: "Thus You led Your people, to make for Yourself a **Tiphereth**
<margin>Gloriosum cingulum.</margin> name." But truly, after all these things, let us speak of the august belt of the High God, which He is said to have used together with other garments worthy of a prince in the ordering of the world. For "belt" is also a name for an ornament in civil law.
<margin>65.</margin> Concerning this, it is sung in the sixty-fourth Psalm: "Hear us, O God our savior, the hope of all the ends of the earth and far off in the sea; Preparing the mountains in
<margin>5 Fortitudo.</margin> Your virtue, girded with **Geburah** <note>original: גבורה (*Gevurah*), meaning Might, Strength, or Judgment</note>." Therefore, when such majesty comes forth from its hiding place, adorned with a diadem, wisdom, intelligence, victory, heraldry, and beauty—each of which He girds upon Himself by His own power—what else is this but a king proceeding into his kingdom? For God is our king before the ages; He is the Lord of virtues and the King of glory, a great King over all gods, King of all the earth; He shall reign forever and beyond. Wherefore arises that consecrated
<margin>6</margin> name **Malchuth** <note>original: מלכות (*Malkhut*), meaning Kingship or Kingdom</note>, which refers to such an illustrious kingdom and such a luminous empire, of which there shall be no end in the eternal course of the vast world. Concerning which it is written: "Your kingdom is a kingdom of all ages." Two royal insignias follow: the scepter and the sword—that is, mercy and fear. The name of the
<margin>7</margin> former is **Hesed** <note>original: חסד (*Chesed*), meaning Loving-kindness or Mercy</note>, which the royal Prophet mentions, saying: "Lord, Your mercy is in heaven." And not only this, but even above the heavens, as in the one hundred and seventh Psalm. And Moses, in that divine invocation of the highest Creator among the most sacred adjurations, did not hesitate to bring forth this name devoted to holiness, saying: "Lord **YHWH** <note>The four-letter name of God, the Tetragrammaton</note>, God, merciful and gracious, patient and of much mercy," which is **Hesed**. Finally, there is the principle of divine worship and perfect religion, which, if one rightly examines the individual properties of contemplations regarding the outflow of majesty itself, succeeds last toward us. But when we direct our gaze from ourselves to the clothing and
<margin>8</margin> ornament of the supreme divinity, it certainly—not without reason due to the reversal of the path—occupies the first seats and is called **Pahad** <note>original: פחד (*Pachad*), meaning Dread or Fear; associated with the Sephirah of Gevurah</note>: that is, fear. Whence that common trivial saying is sung not inelegantly: "Fear first made gods in the world." And there are some, even noble grammarians, who derived "gods" from "fear." For
<margin>Deus timendus.</margin> **Aidos** <note>original: Αἰδὼς (*Aidos*), the Greek personification of shame, modesty, or awe</note> in Greek is "fear" in Latin. However, this is not that fear by which the guilty dread torture; for that is worthy of the Furies and harmful demons and adverse spirits, about whom the inhabitants of the underworld complain in Virgil:
<margin>Quisque suos patimur manes.</margin>
"Each of us suffers his own ghost" <note>A famous line from Virgil’s *Aeneid*, suggesting that the soul endures its own specific purification or punishment</note>. It is not that divine and salvific fear, nor does it proceed from God, but it is a madness and a worm of a guilty conscience, which daily gnaws at and burns an evil mind and an evil soul. Concerning which Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his speech against Piso, discusses most excellently and copiously. "Do not," he says, "think, O Conscript Fathers, that you see men as on the stage..."

# ON THE WONDER-WORKING WORD, BOOK II. 933

<margin>Internal fear.</margin>
The wicked are terrified by the impulse of the gods; their own fraud, their own crime, their own wickedness, and their own audacity drive them from sanity and reason by the burning torches of the Furies. These are the Furies of the impious, these are the flames, these are the torches. There is, moreover, **Pahad** <note>original: פחד (*Pahad*), meaning "Fear" or "Dread," associated with the fifth Sephirah, Gevurah</note>, an internal fear, more excellent than love. Thus it is that a certain most noble philosopher of our age <note>Likely a reference to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, whom Reuchlin greatly admired</note> seemed to me to have rightly said that just as external fear is inferior to love, so internal fear is superior to love. You yourselves, surely, understand this to be true without anyone teaching you; how much better will you recognize that so holy, so worshipped, and so venerable a name was breathed into men by the divine spirit—not only as something consecrated, but as something divine, effective, and the strongest sacrament of religion. If you doubt this, read the monuments of the secrets, read the holy scriptures written concerning the patriarch Jacob. For Jacob swore by the **Pahad** of his father Isaac, which is interpreted as "Fear" <note>Genesis 31:53</note>. And he said to his father-in-law: "Unless the God of my father Abraham and the **Pahad** of Isaac had been with me, you would have sent me away empty-handed." You have heard briefly those names most worthy of observation regarding their inexpressible consistency; finally, the ten emanations <note>The Sephiroth</note> derived both within and without, and their praise, honors, glory, dignities, and sacred titles, signifying the mode of the arrangement of the divine essence, and chosen from the most sacred letters themselves. For us, therefore, the whole **Elohim** <note>original: אלהים (*Elohim*), a primary Hebrew name for God</note> has now gone out into the universe of things with such majesty, surrounded by so many ornaments and so many garments, and for that reason the one God is named by the plural word **Elohim**. But when we were treating the words of essence, it had to be briefly mentioned that, as truth holds, no name unfolded by us from those same three <note>Referring to the first three letters or perhaps the primary triad of the Sephiroth</note>, however much it designates the sole and proper essence of God himself, neglects created things; rather, by its own ornament, beauty, surname, and title, it clothes and names every creature depending on the Highest.

### CHAPTER IX. On the Four-Letter Name יהוה <note>original: *tetragrammato* (Greek: *tetragrammaton*), the four-letter name of God, YHWH</note>

<margin>Being.</margin>
<margin>Fire.</margin>
<margin>Individual vowels.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'E' with floral/foliate decorations.</image-desc>
And to begin from the Most High, which is the same itself: whatever is contained by itself and its own limits, whatever has obtained its own nature, an uncommunicated place, a peculiar dimension, whatever has obtained a distinguished mark of difference and a separate condition of status—that is said not to be something else, but the "same itself." Concerning that which "is," however, we see how great its communication is into individual created things. For not only that which rests upon its own substance, but even that which adheres to another, strives to use the title of "being," so that finally all things whatsoever that depend on the First are said to "be." But what shall we say of fire, since there is nothing anywhere that can be said to lack its spark, to such an extent that Heraclitus <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher known for his doctrine that fire is the fundamental substance of the universe</note> taught that all things were born from fire. Wherefore, to our intellect there also offers itself an excellent, adorable, and most distinguished name of the supersubstantial deity: the Unnamable, by which nothing else can be named except the one, only, first God. Among the Greeks it is called the **ineffable four-letter name** <note>original: τετραγράμματον ἀνεκφώνητον (*tetragrammaton anekphoneton*)</note>. Although it works all things, it names none of its works after itself, calls them nothing, and affects nothing with its own title. For the interpreters themselves, finding no word equal to it, called it "Lord" <note>original: *Dominum*, translating the Hebrew *Adonai*</note> at least on account of its supereminence. Not because the letters produce this sound—for they do not form any syllable—but, signifying the most simple thing, they refuse to be compounded. Existing as images of an incomprehensible voice, they are individual vowels: **YHWH** <note>original: יהוה (*Ihsuh*). Reuchlin here uses Latin characters to approximate the Hebrew letters Yud, He, Vav, He</note>. The Chaldeans <note>A term often used by Renaissance scholars to refer to Aramaic or ancient Near Eastern traditions</note> are accustomed to depict this with only four points arranged in order, lest such holy characters, written by the finger of God, should become common through the daily use of mortals. The Hebrews have now likewise assumed their custom, especially when they attempt to write it on paper. For then they bring in either incomplete versions of the four letters or the Chaldean figure. Furthermore, there are those who use only three points connected by a semicircle, and others in other ways. All this is out of reverence for such a great name...
