# OF JOHANNES REUCHLIN #
### ON THE WONDER-WORKING WORD, BOOK II. 934 ###

<meta>catchword: derat (was lacking/was missing)</meta>

The name was discovered, so that through frequent handling, a sacrament brought forth by the divine word should not be held in contempt. Now, even now, you have received, O <note>The text likely addresses Reuchlin's interlocutors in the dialogue, such as Philolaus and Marranus</note> melodic voices, the most secret seals: the Name—the Tetragrammaton <note>Greek for "four-lettered," referring to the Hebrew name of God, יהוה</note>—never found by man but handed down by God alone. It is a holy and formidable Name, the unique Name by which God alone is to be blessed with ancestral religion. It is most powerful: the beings above worship it, those below observe it, and nature itself kisses it. It is said that when this Name is absorbed by constant worshippers and consecrated by the mysteries of the priesthood, it grants miraculous commands to human faculty. It was bestowed upon the parents of our race alongside the inspiration of divine life. For regarding her firstborn, Eve <note>original: "Heua"</note> said: *I have possessed a man through יהוה* <note>Genesis 4:1. Reuchlin highlights that the Name was known even to the first woman</note>. These holy characters contain what no one before her is found to have uttered, and thereafter it was passed down into the good and fruitful generation of the first-created.

<margin>Seth, a worshipper of God.</margin>
For when a most delightful son was born to Seth himself, in the image and likeness of Adam, on that day the name יהוה began to be invoked. At that time, the previously hated race of men born from the lineage of Cain were wandering the earth, those with whom God did not have much conversation. Seth, therefore, because he was of the divine nature, rejoiced so greatly over his offspring that, together with his wife and family, he invoked the Name as taught by his parents. 

<margin>Enoch.</margin>
Yet there are those who teach in this place that Enos, the grandson of Adam, first began the invocation of the name יהוה. They are perhaps captured by an error, not fearing what the Stagirite Philosopher <note>Aristotle, born in Stagira</note> warns in his *Refutations*: that those unskilled in idioms are easily deceived. We see this happen to those who more willingly spend their whole lives on logical trifles and "spider webs" than a few years on divine literature. For while Jerome <note>The translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> translated it this way: *But to Seth also a son was born, whom he called Enos;*

<margin> "This one" instead of "then." </margin>
*this one began to call upon the name of the Lord.* <note>Genesis 4:26</note> Some judged that part of the speech to be a pronoun <note>Latin "hic" meaning "this man," referring to Enos</note>, when it is actually an adverb of time to be pronounced with a circumflex accent <note>Latin "hîc" meaning "at this time" or "then"</note>. It signifies the same as "then," just as in the works of Maro <note>The poet Virgil</note>:
->Here the almighty Father, thrice bright from high heaven<-
->Thundered: that is, **then** the almighty Father thundered from heaven.<-
And though it is a sign of place, by similar custom it sometimes signifies time, as in:
->Where the time itself shall be, I will wash all in the fountain.<-
Therefore, as soon as a son was born to Seth, **then** it began to be invoked; the name יהוה was called upon. Now indeed, this abuse has come about where, instead of the adverb "here/then," the pronoun "this one" is read, as if "this Enos" first began to invoke the name of the Lord. If that were true, you yourselves would understand it from the sacred letters and the Chaldean <note>Aramaic Targum</note> explanation. 

Next, this most holy and most worthy Name came down by a certain right of inheritance and perpetual succession—not through the rejected generation of Cain, but through the continued posterity of Seth himself—by zeal for religion, constant faith toward God, and integrity of virtue.

<margin>Abraham.</margin>
It reached all the way to Abraham, who, when he went into the land of Canaan, built an altar to God and there invoked the name יהוה. To him, God appeared a second time, saying: *I am יהוה, who led you out of Ur of the Chaldeans.* 

<margin>Isaac.</margin>
His son Isaac <note>original: "Ishac"</note>, near the well of the oath at Beersheba, imitating his father, also established an altar to God and likewise invoked the name יהוה. 

<margin>Jacob.</margin>
After him, when his son Jacob had lain down in Haran, God appeared to him leaning upon a ladder which, raised up, touched heaven. God said to him in a dream: *I am יהוה, the God of Abraham your father, and the God of Isaac.* When Jacob awoke, he said: *Surely יהוה is in this place.* Later, when he wrestled with God in the camp at night and asked for His name, God replied by rebuking him: *Why do you ask my name?* For He judged it superfluous for him to seek what he already possessed.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Capnion (Reuchlin's persona) and Baruchias (a Jewish scholar). In the previous page, Baruchias argued that the divine Name (the Tetragrammaton) was known from the very beginning of humanity, citing Eve's words in Genesis. Now, Capnion challenges this by citing the biblical passage where God tells Moses that He was not known to the Patriarchs by that specific Name.</meta>

# ON THE WONDER-WORKING WORD, BOOK II. #

->Capnion proposes a question regarding the God who was once unknown, to which Baruchias responds<-
->in the manner of the logicians; then he continues the established speech. CHAPTER XVIII.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'C' featuring a small landscape scene with a building inside a square frame.</image-desc>

With your permission, **CAPNION** <note>Capnion is the Greek-style pseudonym of Johannes Reuchlin himself, derived from the German "Reuch" meaning smoke.</note> says, I interrupt the discussion. For you seem to be led through pathless ways by the momentum of your own so-copious speech, and nearly thrown headlong. Do you not remember what God said to Moses concerning this name: *I am the Lord who appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty <note>original: "in Deo omnipotente," referring to the Hebrew title El Shaddai</note>, and my name the LORD <note>original: יהוה, the Tetragrammaton</note> I did not make known to them?* Yet you dare to teach us that they knew so hidden a name, as if it were an inheritance derived from the first mother of the human race? If that were so, the writers of the commentaries and the great, serious, and distinguished theologians would not have correctly handed down to us that it was first revealed to Moses alone, and was not known to the fathers before then; nor would it have been established by God, but rather devised by Eve and bequeathed to her descendants.

You recite true things indeed, **BARVCHIAS** says, but you conclude false ones. In turn, you must grant me pardon if, beyond my usual modesty, I employ the custom of the dialecticians <note>The "dialecticians" were scholars who used formal logic and debate techniques to reach the truth.</note> in speaking. Certainly, the sacred letters testify that Eve pronounced this name: but I will hardly agree with you that she first "devised" it, or "fashioned" it, or "established" it as if it were a human invention and a new beginning. And if you remember, I removed that possibility by saying—so far as my opinion goes—that it was breathed into the first parents along with the breath of life and known by divine means. This is a point that Isaiah, the most noble herald of divine secrets, is thought to greatly confirm when he says: *You are the LORD <note>original: יהוה</note> our Father, our redeemer; your name is from of old, or from eternity.* Therefore, before the time in which our earthly fathers were created, that name existed.

Furthermore, as for your assertion of the very words of God—who said He appeared to the forefathers of an earlier age as "God Almighty" but did not indicate the name the LORD <note>original: יהוה</note> to them—it is worthy of investigation so that I may untie this knot. Let us, therefore, make a trial of this matter. For who is there who, when hearing Ezekiel speaking of precious stones, does not remember having seen at least one of them? And what wealthy merchant is there to whom the Sard, Topaz, Jasper, Chrysolite, Onyx, Beryl, Sapphire, Carbuncle, Emerald <note>Baruchias lists the precious stones found in the High Priest's breastplate described in the Book of Exodus.</note>, or any of these, or several, or all, were never known—including those Moses added: the Ligure, Agate, and Amethyst? Who also is there who has not noted many and various species, with their names and shapes, from the lilies of the field, the flowers of the plain, and the herbs of the gardens?

> Here are greens, and here are the beets spreading their arms wide,
> As the poet <note>Likely a reference to the poet Columella or a similar Roman didactic poet writing on agriculture.</note> says:
> And the fertile sorrel, and mallows, and green violets,
> Here is the chickpea, and leeks that owe their name to the "head,"
> Here also is the poppy, cold and harmful to the brain,
> And lettuce, the grateful rest after noble meals,
> And the heavy gourd let down into its wide belly.

All these things we, even the ordinary members of the flock, know. But only the eminent and exceptional men know the virtues <note>In this context, "virtues" refers to the hidden medicinal or magical powers of plants and stones.</note> and powers of each individual thing in addition to their names—knowledge which either an educated physician <note>original: "physicus"</note> or a practiced empiric <note>An "empiric" was a medical practitioner whose knowledge was based on practical experience and observation rather than just theory.</note> has shown. Therefore, even a rustic man will not be lying if he says he knows Coral and Emerald, provided some merchant showed him the method of distinguishing them by color, shape, and price. For he knows that Coral is not Emerald, nor vice versa. But he who professes to know these stones without pretense must be thoroughly taught in their powers and operations: that such and such an Emerald is of such a size, and that an Emerald hung from the neck turns away the occasion of epilepsy, and Coral repels stomach pain; there is also a certain law for hanging the Coral, and other things consistent with that skill. If someone has not been taught such things, whoever he is, even if he has named and selected the gem, if I were the teacher, I would rightly say to him—

<summary>Baruchias argues that while the Patriarchs used the name of God, they did not truly "know" it because they did not understand its divine power and "virtues," comparing this to people who know the names of gems and plants without understanding their medicinal properties.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue where Baruchias explains the deeper mystery of the Tetragrammaton. He addresses the apparent contradiction in Scripture where God tells Moses that the Patriarchs did not know Him by His name "Yahweh," arguing that while they knew the word, they did not yet possess the delegated "miraculous power" or "covenant" associated with its pronunciation.</meta>

-># JOHANNES REUCHLIN #<-

I would say that I have not yet pointed out the gem itself, or the herb, or any other power. For I have not yet shown its property, its power, and its operations. Thus God also spoke to Moses about this name, since He appeared to the fathers as God Almighty <note>original: "in Deo omnipotente," referring to the title El Shaddai</note>. For in His omnipotence in previous years, God Himself performed miracles. But when the time for the Israelites' liberation came, He kindly wished to delegate His divine and miraculous power to men through the hidden virtue of this name יהוה <note>The Tetragrammaton, or four-letter name of God</note>, which was never before revealed to any mortal. For long ago, by a singular covenant, He enclosed within that word a majesty, an energy, and a miraculous power, which lay hidden from the patriarchs and our ancestors until the time of Moses. Therefore, there are three things: the name, the meaning, and the divine covenant or agreement.

<margin>1</margin>
The Name lifts the human mind. 
<margin>2</margin>
The Meaning of life adheres to the mind. Our ancestors knew these two: both the name and the meaning. Therefore, they called upon God by that same name, and in the course of their lives, He was favorable to them. 

<margin>3</margin>
But the third thing, which is much greater, in which is contained the surpassing power delegated to man by the highest God, was not known and was not indicated to the fathers. This is more clearly understood from the Hebrew language. For where we read "I made known," the Hebrew letter contains נודעתי <note>transliterated: Nodaëthi</note>: that is, "I caused to be known." For God did not cause His name יהוה to be known and understood by the previous age—those great wonders hidden deep within and entrusted to human fragility—but rather He caused it to be acknowledged, worshiped, and observed as a promise, like the other divine names. 

But now God has set this name forward, placing it at the summit above other names as wonderful, as great, and as terrible, specifically through the miracles performed by God through man. Therefore, Isaiah says: *O Lord, you are my God; I will exalt you, I will praise your name, for you have done wonderful things.* <note>Isaiah 25:1</note> This is what it means to know the name יהוה: when not only the characters and the word do not escape us, but also its pronunciation (which is hidden), its secret power, and the following signs of miracles.

<margin>Knowledge of the Name of God.</margin>
All of this will become clear both from the fourth chapter of Exodus and from the subsequent speech of God. The Lord says, "I will bring you out from the prison-house of the Egyptians, and I will deliver you from bondage, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and great judgments, and I will take you to myself for a people, and I will be to you a God; and you shall know that I am יהוה, your God." <note>Exodus 6:6-7</note> You shall know, for example, the Tetragrammaton <note>Greek for "four-letter word," referring to יהוה</note>. By what teaching? Because of the "outstretched arm." Behold, a miracle.

<margin>Faith.</margin>
This knowledge the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, who focused on empirical observation</note> call "posterior knowledge from a sign," from which arises **Faith**. 

<margin>Hope.</margin>
"You shall know," but by what capacity of our fragility? Because of the "great judgments." For the judgment is God's, the sentence of God, which the whole nation must obey without any prior preparation. Behold, **Hope**. 

<margin>Charity.</margin>
"You shall know," but what will be the manner of knowing? Surely it is the consideration of God with man: "Because I will take you to myself for a people, and I will be to you a God." Behold, on both sides, love and affection. This is **Charity** <note>In the sense of 'Caritas' or divine love</note>. For it is not just a matter of a common obligation and bond, but necessarily they will enter into a new covenant with God through the word יהוה, if we desire His power to work in us. 

For the Lord of the Universe spoke to Moses regarding this future bond of society from the Jewish people: "I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt." Thus they were already adopted into the people of God. And what else is it that He now says, "I will take you to myself for a people," except for this covenant, this new fellowship, which contemplative men now enter with God, and they most recently strike a covenant over יהוה? 

<margin>The Question of Manoah.</margin>
This is what the messenger of יהוה replied to Manoah <note>The father of the biblical hero Samson</note> when he asked about the name: "Why do you ask my name?" But it is "wonderful" <note>original: "mirificum"</note>; by which response he had known the name, and over it he sacrificed a kid, which among the ancients was a sign of a confederation, as you also read in Homer. Therefore it follows: *And he placed the offering upon the rock, offering to יהוה, who does wonders.* From this arose what Manoah said to his wife: 

<margin>Fear of the Lord.</margin>
"We shall surely die, for we have seen יהוה." They would not have feared to see angels, whose frequent conversation was in the memory of our ancestors' fathers. But he had understood the voice of God through Moses saying: "Man shall not see me and live."

<summary>Baruchias explains that "knowing" the Tetragrammaton involves more than the word itself; it requires the "pact" or "miraculous power" granted by God to perform wonders. He links the realization of this Name to the virtues of Faith, Hope, and Charity, using the story of Manoah to illustrate the Name's terrifying and wonderful nature.</summary>

# ON THE MIRIFIC WORD, BOOK II #

[He] <note>likely referring to Manoah from the Book of Judges</note> feared because he had seen God, until he was comforted. To the Patriarch Jacob, the name was not revealed even when he asked; instead, this alone was answered: "Why do you ask my name?" and the phrase "which is wonderful" was not added there. But to this man <note>Manoah</note>, because he had seen the miracle of the burnt offering, the answer regarding the name is that it is "mirific" <note>original: "mirificum"</note>, by which it could be known that it was יהוה <note>Yahweh, the Tetragrammaton</note>. Although you read in that passage of Judges: "My name, which is wonderful," it does not hold the same meaning here as it does in the eighth Psalm: "O Lord, our Lord, how admirable is your name in all the earth!" That is, "worthy of admiration and glorious," which the word אדיר <note>original: "Adir"</note> signifies. But here the word is פלאי <note>original: "peli"</note>, which refers to a worker of miracles <margin>Admirable, miraculous.</margin>. You now have the origin of so great a name, as well as its form, meaning, and power—which belongs to the best and greatest God alone, and which is called "great" by way of excellence among all names. Just as Joshua spoke to God: "What will you do for your great name?" which in Deuteronomy is called "Terrible." And in Isaiah, "Excellent, ancient, from eternity." And in Jeremiah: "Invoked over us." And in Ezekiel: "Gone out among the nations." And in Daniel, "Blessed." And in Amos, "יהוה <note>Yahweh</note> is his name." And in Malachi: "Great among the nations from the rising of the sun to its setting, and terrible among the peoples." 

I will intentionally omit, O most learned man, the childish little questions of the grammarians in such an outstanding cause and such a salutary business; the great theologians have involved themselves in these questions with such zeal in this passage that—it shames me to hear it—they have descended into vain contentions. Only that famous and most powerful pronunciation remains for me, which is said to be most secretly hidden in the abyss of mysteries. If this name possesses a pronunciation, it is not ineffable; if it does not, it is not a name. What then shall we do? Shall we deny it is a name, when we have brought forth such a number of witnesses against ourselves? Shall we deny it is ineffable, which both Greeks and Latins alike call it? Concerning which Solomon says in Proverbs: "Who has bound the waters as in a garment? Who has established all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is his son's name, if you know?" It is as if he were to say: "Speak the name itself if you know it, and utter that which is ineffable"—as if he considers it difficult for us to grasp the explanation of its pronunciation. 

I shall cite, Sidonius, your own Hermes Trismegistus <note>meaning "Thrice-Greatest Hermes," a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom and magic</note> in the dialogue of *Asclepius*. "For I do not hope," he says, "that the creator of all majesty and the father or Lord of all things can be called by a single name, even if composed of many." But the God of our fathers—not the God of the profane, the poets, the philosophers, or the heathens—but the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, imposed a proper name upon His own unknown and unnamable nature. He is likewise the institutor and teacher of that "impossible" pronunciation. He taught Moses to utter the unutterable name when Moses was complaining about the <term>ἀνεκφώνητον</term> <note>original Greek: "anekphoneton," meaning "unpronounceable" or "unutterable"</note> ineptitude of his tongue. The pronunciation is already known to you from that passage, which is contained in three clauses under a single period. I would not dare to step beyond the boundaries of these secrets, lest some unworthy person standing by the wall should overhear.

### CHAPTER IX.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'Q' featuring a figure in profile within a circular frame, surrounded by Renaissance-style floral scrolls and foliage.</image-desc>

**SINCE** indeed a name, as Plato says in the *Cratylus*, is an imitation of the essence itself; and it happens for us just as it does for painters or musicians through a manifold mixing and various distinctions, until we apprehend that which we wish to imitate. For if we desire to look into a noble structure with sharp investigation, we first resolve its individual parts; then, we rebuild it as it was formerly constructed, and finally, we preserve the framework itself in the mind. Moreover, that distinction or resolution of names is made into syllables, and of syllables into letters, and of letters into their properties and accidents. Then, when the letters are entwined again, the combination of the word expresses the thing. Therefore, our ancestors...

# 938 OF JOHANN REUCHLIN #

<margin>The Name explained.</margin> Our ancestors, relying on divine study and heavenly light, similarly attained a most pleasing explanation of this name and deigned to pass it down to us, their successors; this is what you call <term>Shem HaMephorash</term> <note>original: "Sem hammaphoras"; the "Explicit" or "Divided" Name of God in Kabbalah, often associated with 72 syllables or angels</note>. Indeed, upon the foundation of this name, I have known many men of great counsel to attempt things that nature alone would not have empowered them to do. But so that you may not be without this knowledge yourselves, I will explain it in a few words. The four-letter Name <note>The Tetragrammaton, YHWH</note> rests upon the summit of a ladder rising from the earth, whose top touches the heavens. Jacob lies on the ground, resting in sleep. The angels of God ascend first, and descend afterward. To Jacob himself, a promise is brought; he wakes, affirms that the Lord is in that place, trembles with fear, sacrifices at the altar, and makes a vow. Let us fill this ladder with steps: for in the Songs of the Sons of Korah it is said, "According to your name, O God, so is your praise." <margin>The steps of the ladder.</margin> The <term>Shem HaMephorash</term> <note>original: "Schem hammaphorash"</note> shall be the praise of God; therefore, the steps of the divine ladder are arranged according to His praises. In Hebrew, these praises are called <term>Tehillim</term> <note>original: "Thillim"</note>, which <margin>Mysteries.</margin> is the title given to the Book of Psalms. Therefore, the <term>Shem HaMephorash</term> will be the revealed explanation of the divine Name taken from the Book of Psalms. Each individual verse marks one step of the ladder, and each of these contains three formal characters. From these, by the suggestion of the Spirit of God, a single distinguished sign is forged—one to be worshipped and observed—formed of three letters. Within this sign, they say, is enclosed an angel of God, carrying with him the majesty of the divine Name. <margin>Angels ascending and descending.</margin> These are the 72 angels who ascend and descend. Into their mouths the majestic name of divinity is resolved, and by these same angelic mouths, it is eventually restored to us. It is not that the name ceases to exist when resolved, nor that it begins anew when restored, but it is like the sun's diffusion through the multiplication of its rays and light. For as the most contemplative of the Greek Philosophers <note>likely referring to Plato in the Republic</note> says: "What the Sun is to sensible things, God is to intelligible things." This is the psalmody of seventy-two verses; I shall pronounce these in English <note>original: "Latine"</note> according to the custom of your Church, and I will point out each holy sign with my finger; therefore, pay very close attention. Where the name of four letters, יהוה <note>YHWH</note>, is placed, I will follow the custom of the ancients and borrow the interpretation of אדני <note>Adonai, meaning "Lord"</note>.

<margin>The Compilation of the Psalms.</margin>
Do not let it disturb you, nor lead you into amazement, that this collection of venerable Psalms appears promiscuous and, as it seems, without order or chance—as if it consisted not by divine fate, but by human will and artistic ingenuity. For what Pisistratus and other students of poetry write concerning the poems of Homer—that they were not at first composed in the numbered order we see now, but were scattered and distracted, and finally reduced into order by the Grammarians who lived around Pisistratus and Aristarchus—our people do not say the same of the hymns of the Psalms. Even your men most learned in the Holy Scriptures, such as Hilary, the doctor and bishop, says clearly in his commentaries on this book: "It must not be ignored that among the Hebrews, the numbering of the Psalms is undistinguished, and they were written without any note of order. For no one there is noted as first, or second, or third, or fiftieth, or hundredth, but they are mixed together into one without any prescription of order." For they say, as ancient traditions tell us, that he collected them when they were uncomposed and dispersed throughout the volume according to the diversity of the authors' times. Since, therefore, there was once the tradition of the <term>Shem HaMephorash <note>original: "שם המפורש"; the Explicit or Explained Name of God, often associated with 72 parts or angels.</note></term> published before the seventy-two interpreters <note>The Septuagint translators.</note>, they are said to have established both the number and the order of the Psalms, and indeed far more justly. For surely you can judge that these verses, conceived by divine inspiration, do not serve human number and order, but rather a divine order, both fixed and proper, and truly infinite in nature yet finite to the infinite. From this, it finally proceeds that they can be subject to, and in turn refer back to, the numbers of the same adorable name <term>YHWH <note>original: "יהוה"; the Tetragrammaton, the four-lettered name of God.</note></term>, known in all ways.
<margin>The letters establish the number 27. <note>Refers to the 22 letters of the Hebrew alphabet plus 5 final forms.</note></margin>

<margin>Commendation of the quaternary number.</margin>
Then SIDONIUS said: You seem to me to have already pointed out most clearly that which you promised. They prefer this to all gods and the powers of the gods, and they ascribe it as being the fountain of perpetual nature flowing into our souls. A witness to this is the poem they call the "Golden Verses of Pythagoras," in which the <term>Tetraktys</term> is assumed in place of an oath, as if it were the highest thing upon which faith and religious belief might lean, with a perfect definition of its substance. ### ON THE WONDER-WORKING WORD, BOOK II. ###

...most excellent kind of contemplation, for those who have distinguished the chaos of the World into four elements; the Heavens into the four parts of the year; the Air into the four winds (East, West, South, and North); the Earth into four spaces according to the five zones; the Divinity into commoners, nobles, celestial beings, and the king's palaces; and Humanity into flesh, spirit, ghosts, and shadows. We read of these partly in the beginning of Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*, and partly they are shown in these verses which are often quoted:

> Twice two things make a man: ghosts, flesh, spirit, and shadow,
> These four places receive those twice two.
> The earth covers the flesh, the shadow flits around the tomb;
> The Underworld <note>original Latin: *Orcus*</note> holds the ghosts, the spirit seeks the stars.

The Stoics praise the splendor of our life based on the four virtues. <margin>A solid demonstration.</margin> Mathematicians find the first solid demonstration in the number four. Natural philosophers divide the judging powers of the mind into four: intellect, reason, opinion, and sense. <margin>The Square.</margin> Arithmeticians call "one" a Square <term>Tetragonus: a four-sided geometrical figure</term> in its potentiality. For when "one" bursts into action, it is a square number: the first to fulfill the entire difference of numbers, and perfectly completing the number ten <note>original Latin: *denarium*</note> within four terms. <margin>Parts of the number ten.</margin> For one, two, three, and four give birth to the substance of the number ten. Because of this, I might more easily believe those things which you, after the name of the Lord <note>original Hebrew: יהוה, the Tetragrammaton</note>, dared to introduce as the ten *Sephiroth* <term>Sephiroth: the ten divine emanations or attributes in Jewish Kabbalah</term>, even though it is a thing unfamiliar to the common people. Is it not also true that this same number, within those same four limits, contains the whole harmony of music? <margin>The number four contains all philosophy and the universe</margin> Indeed, it gathers together all of Mathematics: point, line, surface, and body. It encompasses all of Physics, in which we are taught first the seed-potential of nature; second, the natural sprouting; third, the maturing form; and fourth, the composite result. Finally, it introduces all of Metaphysics: essence, being, power, and action. This triplicity surely unfolds into a wondrous quaternary: so that in the beginning there is the point, the seed, the essence; second, the line, the sprouting, the being; third, the surface, the form, the power; and fourth, the body, the composite, the action. These seem to me to be the twelve stones which you, Baruchia, recited earlier by their names, and which your Moses reduced into a fourfold order.

Therefore, in the whole universe of the World and in its individual parts, that divine "four-ness" shines through. In the higher realms (as found in Orphic Theology), the Muse, Dionysus, Apollo, and Venus—those celestial deities—instill God-like attractions into our minds: the Muse brings poetry, Dionysus the mystery, Apollo prophecy, and Venus love. In the heavens, there are four triplicities. Beneath the heavens, there are four seasons. Within time, there are four qualities. Under those qualities, the four elements. Beneath the elements: substance, quality, quantity, and motion. Finally, under substance itself: the bodily, the vegetative, the sensitive, and the intelligent. Under quantity: the point, length, width, and depth (just as we say of numbers: one, two, three, four). Under quality: hot, cold, dry, and moist. Under motion: ascending, descending, proceeding, and circular. We have spoken of things above the heavens, things eternal, things temporal, and things mixed. <margin>The human soul.</margin> Let us see how the human soul has allied itself with the number four. Our soul indeed ascends through four steps to the final spirit within itself: through sense, imagination, fantasy, and intelligence. 

You hold, therefore, that the nature of the universe consists of a quaternary. The Maker of all things would not have made it in this way unless there were some Idea of a "four-fold" within Himself before He turned to the work of creation. <margin>The four ears of Jupiter.</margin> This is why the Spartans, it seems to me, rightly depicted the supreme Jupiter with four ears, because He Himself is the highest quaternary: that is, according to the Pythagoreans, the *Tetraktys* <term>Tetraktys: the sacred Pythagorean symbol of the number ten, represented as a triangle of four rows of dots</term>. Its emanation is found through "form" in the angels, through "true participation" in rational souls, through "imaginary participation" in those without reason, 

-> and it is found through a "shadowy participation" in the shapes of bodies, <-
-> and in the accustomed manner of a kind of eternal <-
-> rain, it flows down from on high to the lowest depths, <-
-> watering the whole universe. <-

### On the letters of the four-letter name יהוה <note>The Tetragrammaton: the four-letter Hebrew name of God, usually transliterated as YHWH.</note>, and on the Geometric shapes of the characters and the Arithmetic forms of the numbers. CHAPTER XXI. ###

<margin>A notable river.</margin>
<margin>The Ocean.</margin>
I listen very gladly, Sidonius, if you, Baruchias, apply yourself to our discipline. For, as I see, everything is arranged correctly according to the rule. For this river is thought by me to be that river which goes out from that famous and celebrated place of pleasure <note>original Latin: *loco uoluptatis*, referring to Eden</note> to water paradise with a fourfold head. This is what Orpheus and Homer call the Ocean, calling it the origin of human things: first, as always existing; second, as the leader in the generation of the gods; third, as watering earthly things; fourth, as distilling every fluid nature. This is that river Chebar <note>original: *Cobar*</note>, by which Ezekiel, touched by the hand of God, saw the likeness of four living creatures and four wheels. In the same river also, there were four cherubim on four wheels, and a wheel within a wheel. It is the same living creature that he had seen by the river Chebar. This is that great sea in which, according to the vision of Daniel, the four winds of heaven fought and four great beasts ascended from the sea. They wished to call its divinity "One," <note>original: *numen appellare unum*</note> who is said in the Orphic hymns to drive a four-horsed chariot. Therefore, the mystery of יהוה was known to the most ancient sages, and indeed to foreigners; although it was not used publicly, it was not unknown privately. Those sages, handing down the disciplines of the highest matters through riddles, established for themselves certain craftsmen gifted in the art of building: so that they might fittingly carve with a chisel the totality of all things and shape it into one image for the sight, lest there be frequent need to use this highest name, so that it might not be held in contempt through commonness. Indeed, they called this a "sacred image." 
<margin>Hieroglyphs.</margin>

By this gift, this very famous name is more pleasing to us philosophers, because it embraces Geometric secrets in the shapes of the characters, and Arithmetic sacraments in the forms of the numbers. So that I may perform the duty of a Mathematician generally, I might most rightly say: One, even, odd, whole, reduction. Nothing is prior to the infinite, nothing prior to the

<margin>Iod [is] ten.</margin>
letter of יהוה refers to the point, and is named *Iod*: that is, it is named the "beginning," and it designates the number ten <term>denarius: the number ten, which contains the sum of 1+2+3+4</term> as the end of number, and most simply penetrates every number, bearing the mark of unity. Unity, however, is the common mode of all numbers. And it, as the Arithmeticians write, holds the place of the point; although it is the beginning of interval and length, it is itself a participant in neither interval nor length. Just as a point placed upon a point becomes nothing but a point, just as if you join nothing to nothing. From which it happens that even unity multiplied by itself produces nothing other than itself. <header>ON THE MIRACLE-WORKING WORD, BOOK II.</header>

<margin>The persistence of unity.</margin>
Unity stands uniformly, and in itself it possesses every number uniquely; indeed, every number is joined together within the monad <note>The Monad refers to the number one as the ultimate source of all things.</note>. Truly, as much as something proceeds out of the monad, by that much is it distinguished and multiplied. We have spoken of persistence; let us now speak of <margin>The Binary process.</margin> process. Just as the motion of a point creates a line, and the motion of a line creates a surface, so the motion of unity creates the "other," and "otherness" creates the binary <note>The number two.</note>. For "otherness," according to Pythagoras and the heirs of his wisdom—as Boethius says—is ascribed to no other than the binary alone. Thus, on the authority of Servius the grammarian, "the other" <note>original: *Alter*</note> is spoken of only in reference to two, but the binary indicates a certain composition, for it is a heap of units. Composition is not understood without the suspicion of material proportion. Material proportion cannot exist without formal proportion, just as in truth matter cannot exist without form. Aristotle rightly judges that form is a certain divine thing. The odd number, and indeed the ternary <note>The number three.</note> especially, is asserted to be most proper to divine things. Not unlike this, Alphesiboeus sang in the *Pharmaceutria* of Maro <note>A reference to Virgil’s Eclogue 8. Alphesiboeus is a character in the poem.</note>:

->God delights in an odd number.<-

Therefore, everything that first flows outside of God, as soon as it is no longer God himself, becomes "other" than Him and equal to the first multitude <note>i.e., it becomes the number two, the first even number/plurality.</note>. Nevertheless, so that it may have being, it turns back again toward divinity, the sign of which is the odd number. For every process (as Abucaten <note>Likely referring to the philosopher Al-Battani or a similar medieval source</note> said) is effected through the likeness of the secondary things to the first. Thus, the angelic nature is to be signified by an odd number; by a number indeed, because it is a multitude proceeded from the One, but by an odd number because it is closest to God and relies upon participation in Him. For angels are, as it were, a small portion of God, just as the prophetic Apollo at Colophon once answered to a seeker through an oracle. Here, clearly, that which the Philosophers say they have experienced is not lacking: for where a superior nature touches an inferior one, there it reaches the highest point of the lower from the lowest degree of itself. But soon, when one arrives at the summit—that is, at unity—the opposite must be true: the highest point of the lower aspires to the whole condition of unity, since that which is one and most simple has no degrees. Now, the whole condition of unity is to be the same and always like itself, an agreeing immutability, in which only the odd number (as the Arithmeticians say) most greatly participates. Certainly, any number whose <margin>Arithmetic Axioms.</margin> middle is one, that number is odd. But a number whose middle is two receives "evenness" and can be separated into two equal parts. Therefore, you see that "oddness" is more related to God, while "evenness" is more dissimilar. Thus, the angelic nature—whether you call it ideal or the entire nature of the archetypal World—ought more rightly to be designated not by an even number, but by an odd one. And yet, since God alone admits no multitude within himself, while all other things, however simple, are as it were a certain "heaping up" and are constructed from act and potency, for that reason the first stream of deity ought not to be celebrated by some simple mark of oddness, but by one which consists of both the even and the odd number together. Even, so that it might be something; Odd, so that it might be "that much"—namely, that which had flowed out and that which would flow back. For "to be" is different from "that which is." Therefore, from the first binary and the first ternary, the quinary <note>The number five (2+3).</note> consists, which demonstrates the product from the <margin>The Quinary number.</margin> supreme light, the first ray of the intellectual World, by one sacred character: that is, the very letter ה *He*. Mathematicians have handed down this letter as the first "uncomposed" <note>A prime number.</note> of counting, and the Hebrew Grammarians describe it as the spirit of prolation <note>The "breath" required to speak.</note> and the substance of essence (functioning as the article). To my eyes, the most wise Solomon seemed to have painted this skillfully for the unrefined and unlearned. For he made two cherubim above the ark, in which the name of the Lord of Hosts might sit, so that one wing of the cherub was five cubits, and the other wing of the cherub was five cubits, as if a likeness of the super-celestial essence and nature just below God. I wish also to briefly explain the third character of this ineffable and miracle-working name, which they declare to be ו *Vau*. Although this is a copulative conjunction <note>The word "and" in Hebrew.</note>, yet in <margin>The Senary number.</margin> continuous speech it changes the tense of verbs, and in mathematics it signifies the senary <note>The number six.</note> number. Most aptly, therefore, let it be the mark of heaven and earth: that is, of all things joined from matter and form. For ו *Vau* couples and joins the parts of speech,

This number arises from many multiplications of the preceding numbers: whether you say once two times three, or conversely, three times two; indeed, it is a number most suitable for material things, because it is born from the alternating multiplication of the numbers preceding it. In multiplying things by one another, matter itself is the primary occasion. I pass over the fact that every perfect number obtains its sum from the unities of those preceding it. For from one, two, and three, the "senary" is collected <note>1+2+3=6</note>, so that you may recognize with the best reasoning that after Iod and He, the letter Vau itself ought to follow. 

Add to this that just as the nature of the corporeal universe—even by the authority of Aristotle—is perfect in every way, not abounding in superfluities nor lacking in necessities, so the number six, providing the seal of the whole corporeal world, is the only one in the whole sequence of numbers from one to ten that is so "perfect" <term>perfect number: a number that equals the sum of its divisors</term> that, by comparison to its parts, it is neither destitute through the poverty of want, nor superfluous through immoderate magnitude. For it has a half part: that is, three; and a third: that is, two; and a sixth: that is, one; which, when reduced into one sum, produce the body of the "senary." Other numbers lack this perfection. For in the case of eight, its half is four, its fourth is two, and its eighth is one, the combination of which reduces to a sum smaller than the whole body: that is, seven. Thus we find the sums of parts, when heaped together, either exceed or fall short of the root number; but the senary is perfect in this kind of totality. 

Wherefore, not without reason does this letter alone designate that which is whole and perfect. This opinion of ours regarding the Sacred Letters must be fortified, lest you suspect it to be a vain invention of my own thinking; and I will reveal to you, my companions, what few notice. ...lacking, and substances truly possessing matter, they follow after things which, while they are forms of bodies in matter, are at the same time separated from those bodies and materials. To this class belongs the rational soul <term>rational soul: the "animus rationalis," or the part of the human spirit capable of reason and divine contemplation</term>, for which, as Virgil says:
> *The soul has a fiery vigor and a celestial origin,*
> *so far as harmful bodies do not clog them,*
> *nor earthly limbs and dying members dull them.*
<note>original: "igneus est vigor, & caelestis origo, Seminibus quantum non noxia corpora tardant, Terreniq; hebetant artus moribundaq; membra." See Virgil, Aeneid 6.730-732.</note>

Although the soul, according to its more excellent essence, walks in equal company with the angelic nature, yet as far as its lower existence is concerned, it becomes secondary because it is immersed in corruptible things and joined to those that communicate with the body. Led by this very thought, the Royal Prophet <note>King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note> says: "You have made him a little lower than the angels." <note>Psalm 8:5.</note> I shall do you a great favor, my friends, who are now weary from listening as evening approaches, for I will conclude the cause as briefly as possible. <margin>Fire. Earth.</margin> In Plato’s book titled *Timaeus*, this dogma appears: that God in the beginning first created fire, then earth. But these two alone, being so opposite, could not fitly cohere without a certain third thing. Therefore, a middle ground between both remained, which would share partly with the higher and partly with the lower. Thus, since there are archetypes <term>archetypes: the original divine patterns or blueprints of all things</term> created first as fiery lights, and then the entire corporeal universe embracing the dregs of matter, it was fitting that some substance be made which would neither depend on matter nor exist without matter. This substance would dwell with the body regarding the operation of its powers, and dwell with the angels regarding the power of its essence, so that by one virtue or the other, it would not be absent from either World. <margin>The human soul.</margin> Therefore, the most direct middle point is the human soul, which, since it is neither one nor the other, participates in both. <margin>Praise of Mankind.</margin> <note>original Greek: "Ἐγκώμιον τοῦ ἀνθρώπου" (Enkomion tou anthropou).</note> Because of this, Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a syncretism of the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth, regarded as the author of sacred texts.</note> says: "O Asclepius, man is a great miracle, a living being to be adored and honored. For he passes into the nature of God as if he himself were a God. He knows the race of demons, knowing himself to be originated from the same source. He despises the earthly part of human nature within himself, trusting in the divinity of his other part." O, how much more happily tempered is the nature of man! Joined to the gods by a kindred divinity, he despises that part of himself by which he is earthly. All other things which he knows to be necessary to himself by celestial arrangement, he binds to himself with a bond of love, and thus he looks up to heaven. Thus he is placed in a happier position of "middleness," so that he may love those things that are within him, and be loved himself by those above him. You hear that the rational soul is the middle between the invisible World and the visible World, yet it is most closely related to the beings above. <margin>The middle of the number ten: ה (He).</margin> For both these reasons, it could not be designated by any other mark than the number five <term>quinarius: the number five</term>, which is the last letter called ה (He), undoubtedly the most just middle of the entire decimal counting system. For if you bind together the numbers on either side of five—the four above it and the six below—they come to ten, of which five is the middle. <note>Reuchlin’s math: 4 + 6 = 10; 3 + 7 = 10; 2 + 8 = 10; 1 + 9 = 10. In each pair, 5 is the mathematical center.</note> Again, three and seven, then two and eight, and finally one and nine; you will always find ten, and you will find that only the number five is the middle. If we inquire more accurately, the essence of the heavenly beings is indeed similar and should be shown by a similar character, and nothing but order makes the difference. For as the angelic World is more absolute, pure, and firm, it must be shown to our eyes by the first letter ה (He) and in a more eminent place. The human mind, however, is shown by the latter letter, though of the same character, because it is attached to the body and began to exist at the same time as the body. But because it will not cease with the death of the body—if it has followed its own nature and has not been weighed down by foreign allurements—it returns immediately and ascends, whether remaining in the body or flying outside the body, to its corresponding and supracelestial habitation, which I have called "the reduction" <term>reduction: the "reductio," or the process of the soul returning to its divine source</term>. <margin>The return of the soul to the heavens.</margin> Concerning this, Zoroaster says: "You must ascend to the light itself and to the rays of the Father, from whence the soul was sent to you, clothed in much mind." And Pythagoras handed down these words: "If you, leaving the body, pass into the free ether, you shall be an immortal God." This is the final ה (He), the "reduction" of man to divinity; this is the end, this is the limit, this is the goal, this is the boundary and perfection of this name, so sacred, so to be adored...

# JOHANN REUCHLIN, ON THE WONDER-WORKING WORD, BOOK III.

...so powerful, so wondrous, of whom God reminded Moses: "I will give you every good thing, and I will call out the name of יהוה <note>The Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God, often transliterated as Yahweh or Jehovah.</note> before you." <note>original: "E dam omne bonum tibi, & uocabo nomen יהוה coram te." See Exodus 33:19.</note> This is the [divine] thing, and as seen in Daniel, the appearance of the fourth is like the Son of God. <note>original: "species quarti similis Filio Dei." See Daniel 3:25.</note> For he gave to men the power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name.
<margin>The square letter ה (He).</margin>
The last ה (*He*) is like the fourth face of the eagle in the wheels which are seen continually in Ezekiel, and they did not turn back. <note>Ezekiel 1:10-12. The "wheels" refers to the Merkabah or divine chariot.</note> By the power and authority of this letter, Abraham, a centenarian, from Sarah, a ninety-year-old and barren woman, grew beyond the laws of nature into nations. 
<margin>The inserted ה (He).</margin>
And for that reason he was named אברהם *Abraham* [with the letter He inserted], whereas he was previously called *Abram*. Why say more? Our entire happiness is expressed by this sign of the number five <note>The letter He (ה) has the numerical value of 5.</note>, by which Alpha is united with Omega, and the waters under the heaven are joined with those that are above the heavens. By this we can do what we want, and want what is right.
<margin>The fifth part.</margin>
Wherefore Asher also received the fifth part, since happiness is most abundantly fulfilled in this letter. For we interpret *Asher* as "blessedness" or "happiness." <note>The Hebrew name Asher (אשר) means "happy" or "blessed."</note> Night falls too quickly, best of men; I have treated through a long discourse what the names seemed to signify concerning God. Learn the rest yourselves from Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist.</note>, Origen, and Jerome, whether they signify God’s power, his operation, or our affection toward him. Although there are some names not placed by those authors, nor by other Greek or Latin authorities, but only by us: such as this name איש *Isch* [Ish], which suggests both "man" and "God," with whom in the book of Genesis Jacob himself is said to have wrestled alone. <note>Genesis 32:24-30. Reuchlin plays on the word Ish (man) and its mystical connection to the divine.</note> And it follows: "Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but ישראל *Israel*, because you have prevailed with God and man." No less significant is the word נא *Na*, which we use in heavenly matters and in times of distress, just as Moses says in the book of Numbers: "Forgive now the sin of your people" <note>Numbers 14:19</note>; which you have translated as: "Forgive, I pray [obsecro]." And in Psalm 118: <margin>Psalm 118.</margin> אגא יהוה הצליחה נא [O LORD, save now; O LORD, send now prosperity].
Which you elegantly translate: "O Lord, save me; O Lord, let me prosper." For you also read יה *Iah* in הללו יה *Halleluiah* ["Praise Yah"], and צבאות *Zabaoth* [Sabaoth, "of Hosts"] in the prayers, and אדני *Adonai* ["Lord"] in Exodus, and אל *El* ["God"] in עמנו אל *Immanuel* ["God with us"], and the Greek *ischyros* [strong], which the Hebrews call שדי *Sadai* [Shaddai, "Almighty"]. And "before the sun ינון *Innon* is his name," <note>Psalm 72:17</note> which you say means "his name endures forever." There is also עליון *Elion* [Elyon, "Most High"] and many others not commonly used, such as מקום *Macom* ["The Place"] and כפו *Caphu*. There are also, certainly, general names for the angels, such as השמלים חיות אופנים תרשישים *Hasmalim, Haioth, Ophanim, Tarshishim* <note>These are different ranks of angels: the Glowing Ones, Living Creatures, Wheels, and "Chrysolites" or "Regal Ones."</note> 
<margin>General names of the angels.</margin>
and the rest. Then, individually, not a few: such as אוריאל *Uriel* ["Light of God"], רפאל *Raphael* ["Healing of God"], זוריאל *Zuriel* ["God is my Rock"], אביר *Abir* ["Mighty One"], מתתרון *Metattron* [Metatron, the Prince of the Presence], and those similar to these. I have finally committed to memory by hearing these sacred names, though what I have remembered is very brief and small. Although there are many other names of that kind that I could propose and explain—no matter how they were, whether larger than these or more moderate—it has already become dark and you are tired of listening. I will leave the remaining parts for Capnion <note>Capnion is Reuchlin's own Greek-style pseudonym.</note> to read tomorrow. Now let us go inside from here to dinner. You—

# THE WONDER-WORKING WORD BY JOHANN REUCHLIN OF PFORZHEIM, DOCTOR OF LAWS, ALSO CALLED CAPNION
## BOOK THREE

### PREFACE

Now the third day dawns, venerable Prelate <note>Addressing the work's dedicatee, likely Dalberg, the Bishop of Worms.</note>, in which, after the sacred names of the ancient Greek and Hebrew nations have been set forth, it is necessary that the continuous discourse of Capnion—a man of the Pforzheim nation and a Christian by profession—finally be heard. ### CHAPTER I

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap T containing a woodcut scene of two scholars in a study; one is seated at a table with an open book, while the other stands beside him, gesturing as they converse.</image-desc>THE WHOLE bedroom seemed to me to glow throughout the night, my Capnion <note>Reuchlin's pseudonym, derived from the Greek "Kapnion," a translation of the German "Rauch" (smoke).</note>, said Sidonius, and the very walls seemed to shake from those portents of words which Baruchias recited here yesterday in his speech to us; it was not only most delightful, but truly most admirable and learned. I believe that from such sharp and attentive thinking, the unheard-of novelty of such terms took hold of my mind as I drifted toward sleep, pulling it in different directions so that my imagination manufactured those movements of the walls. Or, if it is true as he thinks—and I do not strongly disagree—that a great chorus of heavenly beings could easily have followed those symbols of divinity. For no god would dare, as Homer's verses say, to remain in his seat when Jove is moved. <note>A reference to the Iliad, where Zeus shakes Olympus.</note> But come, Capnion, now is the time for the Wonder-Working Word; do not fail our hopes. At this, Capnion said: "Do you think anything was left by this preacher Baruchias yesterday for me to finish today? He is so full of a variety of names, it is a wonder if he did not pour out every incentive for miraculous actions." And Sidonius replied: "I certainly do think so. For he himself bore witness that until now, none of these words have prevailed by their force and power over the common course of nature, nor have any of his fellow countrymen ever been able to achieve this." Then BARUCHIAS said: "Sidonius speaks the truth. Therefore, Capnion, see whether you consider it a matter of your own honor to fulfill what you promised us: to explain that certain Word by which miracles are performed, along with its infallible ritual, and keep us in suspense no longer."

->*On the faith of the speaker, and the uttered word, God, the leader and cause of all things.*<-

If I name the Word itself and hand down the ritual for its use as you demand, I shall have rightfully fulfilled my duty. Although all these things may be ready and at hand, the matter itself seems to me to require seeking from a bit deeper. Think within yourselves and carefully recall the first day of our discussion, when it was agreed among us—and I do not know if anything else has sat more deeply or stuck more firmly in our minds and judgment..."

# ON THE WONDER-WORKING WORD, BOOK III.

<margin>Utterance.</margin>
If it is fitting to compare super-heavenly things to human ones, then at least the internal word of man—which you call our supreme reason—proceeding from the mind, should be considered; it is neither entirely the same as the mind, nor is it in every way different. For human reason, flowing forth from the mind, is not wrongly judged to be distinct from its source in the intellect; yet when it brings the mind out into the open, nothing else can be seen but the mind itself. Thus, the nature of the mental substance is judged to be different based on its underlying functions, even though it is the same. In the likeness of this faint image, one may perceive within the inner sanctum of the most majestic Deity the very Word of the Father’s mind, or His Reason. Because it is able to subsist through itself, it is therefore distinguished from the Father, from whom it simultaneously receives its existence. And yet, since it clearly reveals within itself all things that we contemplate being in God or concerning God, we affirm that it is the same as the substance of the Father’s mind—they are one. Nor is there anything else anywhere that indicates a distance between God the Speaker and God the Word, except for the nature of the utterance <note>original: "prolatio," a theological term for the "bringing forth" or "procession" of the Son from the Father</note> alone. In all other respects, they are equal—indeed, they are the same. Both are God, both are eternal, and therefore both exist before all time. The Father has always uttered, and the Word has always been uttered; the Word is equal in power to the one uttering it, and the Father is equal to the Word he utters. Even Plato himself, that tireless seeker of divine matters, suggests this in his religious writings in the *Letter to Hermias, Erastus, and Coriscus*, when he says toward the end: "It is fitting for all three of you to read this letter, but especially when you are gathered together. If that is not possible, then at least two should read it together as much as they are able; finally, as is just, they should use it as a covenant and a personal law, swearing an oath not without elegant zeal and that sister of zeal, discipline; calling to witness God, the leader of all things present and future, and the Lord and Father of that leader and cause, whom we shall know if we philosophize rightly." <note>Plato, *Epistle VI*. Reuchlin uses this Platonic passage to argue that even the Greeks glimpsed the relationship between the Father and the Son (the "leader and cause").</note> Do you not clearly see that the Word which Plato taught in the *Epinomis* <note>A dialogue traditionally attributed to Plato concerning astronomy and religion.</note> had arranged the order of the world, is in this place called God the cause and leader of all things, and is said to have a Father? Therefore, the Son is the Word, whose Father is named "Lord." Let us now recall the discourse which Baruchias <note>The Jewish interlocutor in Reuchlin's dialogue.</note> delivered so learnedly and extensively yesterday around noon. In teaching us, he wisely began with the Ineffable Name, which belongs most closely to the highest God alone; he explained that the translators placed "Lord" in the place of יהוה <note>The Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God, YHWH.</note> because they could find no equivalent word in any other language. Combine this, if you will, with the speech I myself gave three days ago. In it, I remember affirming to you that Thales, Pythagoras, and Plato traveled through Syria to be instructed in Hebrew disciplines, from which they contributed no small amount to their own writings; you see a trace of that here. Plato calls the Father of the leader and cause of all things "the Lord." Since that God is the leader and cause of all things present and future because he ordered the world, who will now doubt that he is that most divine Word according to Plato? And every person who is swept away into admiration, love, and perception of him shall be blessed. Therefore, the Word is the Son of the Lord; wherefore he is both God, and the leader, and the cause of the world. Thus he is named by many names, and in various ways by many people, and differently by others.

<meta>This page continues Reuchlin’s exploration of the second person of the Trinity, moving from the general concept of the "Word" to specific biblical titles and philosophical definitions. He is establishing the Son’s identity through both Hebrew prophecy and Greek philosophy.</meta>

# OF JOHANN REUCHLIN

<margin>The Only-begotten Son.</margin>
The Father called him *Pele* <note>Hebrew: פלא, meaning "Wonder" or "Miraculous"</note>: that is, Miraculous. For he is called by John the "only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father." <note>John 1:18</note> First of all: although the title of "Son" may be granted to other men, it nonetheless applies more properly—and in a way more closely related to mortals—to this most divine Word. For he is the same as the Father: and he is not only that, but he is *from* there. For the Father is he who provided the origin of being according to a nature like his own; the Son, however, is he who took the origin of being by birth from another. Therefore, he is called "only-begotten," which is most proper and peculiar to this Son; he is so called not only because he is the one born of the One, but also because he is born in a unique and incommunicable way, quite differently than in corporeal nature.

<margin>The Bosom of the Father.</margin>
Next, let it be determined what that "bosom of the Father" is intended to mean. It is rightly said first, "who is," so that we may recognize his union with the Father, who commanded Moses: "Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: 'He Who Is' has sent me," <note>Exodus 3:14</note> as if the Son is in him from eternity just as if in a bosom. For this reason, it is added: "who is in the bosom of the Father." By this speech, he declares the intimate nativity of the Son from the Father, and, so to speak, how familiar it is.

<margin>The Hand of God.</margin>
By another name, David calls him the "hand," when he speaks to the Father in this way:
> Why do you turn away your hand, even your right hand, from the midst of your bosom? <note>Psalm 74:11</note>
Therefore, the Son is the hand in the bosom of the Father, and in the bosom, the Son is the hand of the Father, through whom he made all things, and who says:
> I am he; I am the first, and I am the last. My hand also has laid the foundation of the earth, and my right hand has spanned the heavens. <note>Isaiah 48:12–13</note>
I show this to you so as to demonstrate the certainty of the cause.

<margin>Thence the Holy Spirit is the finger.</margin>
That this "hand" took its beginning from the Father is a truth drawn from the one hundred and eighth Psalm <note>Psalm 109 in modern numbering</note>, where the prophet prays thus:
> Help me, O Lord my God; save me according to your mercy: and they shall know that this is your hand, and you, Lord, have made it.
That the Father and the Hand are the same, of one substance, one God, and one Lord, will be easily seen in the forty-third Psalm <note>Psalm 44</note>, if one reads the verse in Hebrew characters. For it says:
> You are your hand, you have driven out the nations, and planted them. <note>original: "Tu es manus tua," a specific Hebraic reading Reuchlin uses to equate God with His "Hand" or Son</note>
As for what follows shortly thereafter regarding the "illumination of the countenance," that is a modest secret of the divine Trinity.

<margin>Logos <note>Greek: λόγος</note>.</margin>
Let us return again to the Son, whom the Greeks call *Logos* <note>Greek: λόγος</note>, a term much more significant and perhaps more correctly applied than "Word." For *Logos* signifies reason, definition, word, and speech. Therefore, after putting aside our unworthy lowliness, let us graft our fragile things onto divine ones. For just as human reason relates to the mind in which it subsists, so the Reason of God relates to the Father—not only because of the impulse of their generation, but also their cohesion. For there is no reason without a mind, nor any mind without reason.

<margin>The office of the Word.</margin>
Since the office of the Word is to enunciate the inner workings of the mind—as the Stagirite <note>Aristotle, born in Stagira</note> judges in his book *On Interpretation*—and to bring forth secrets from the innermost chambers of thoughts and to reveal the will of the speaker, for that reason this Son is most aptly judged to be the "Word of the Father":

<margin>Messenger.</margin>
"Since no one has ever seen God," says John, "the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has revealed him to us." <note>John 1:18</note> As a messenger of great counsel, he is for that reason surnamed *Angelos* <note>Greek: ἄγγελος, meaning messenger or angel</note>, as one who has revealed to mortals the super-celestial thoughts of God. Regarding the "definition" which is hidden from you, it must be of such a condition that it seems to eviscerate, in a way, the entire nature of the thing defined.

<margin>Reason.</margin>
Furthermore, "Reason"—which *Logos* signifies according to Aristotle's edition of the *Metaphysics*—is the definition itself. Consequently, in this manner, this most divine and substantive Word (indeed, it may rightly be called the "substantial reason" of the paternal nature) is a certain evident demonstration, whose total, adequate, and universal offspring is that silent description of generation, through which we might immediately know him with a clearer intuition whom we were ignorant of shortly before. "Therefore, he who sees me," he says, "sees also the Father," <note>John 14:9</note> calling the cognition of the intellect an "aspect" of this kind. For our eye is the mind itself.

<margin>Terminus <note>The End or Limit</note>.</margin>
The vision of him, therefore, will be the knowledge of things, which reaches its greatest perfection when the entire substance is opened in a brief speech, which the logicians call a "term" <note>original: "terminum"</note>. For if this is what it means to be begotten—namely, to be produced from the substance of the one generating as a whole similar according to nature—then truly the Father shall no longer be hidden, but reveals himself: he who is the perfect image of the Father, which Paul expressed in his letters.

# ON THE MIRIFIC WORD, BOOK III.

...exhorted the senses to give thanks to God and the Father, who has transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, who is the image of the invisible God. <margin>Image of God.</margin> But I ask you, wise men, in what way or how will any image of an invisible thing consist? By what outlines, what features, what likeness, what color will that thing—which no one has ever seen and which no one knows except the Son—imitate the pattern? But consider what follows: "No one knows the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son <margin>Matthew 11.</margin> wishes to reveal him." <note>Matthew 11:27</note> Therefore, the Son himself is a living and willing image, not made like colors by Apelles <note>A celebrated painter of ancient Greece.</note>, not carved by Pyrgoteles <note>A famous engraver of gems.</note>, not cast in bronze by Polyclitus <note>A renowned Greek sculptor.</note>, not poured by any craftsman’s bonding, nor sculpted with a chisel, painted with a needle, or molded from clay or wax. He is not like Dido's longed-for and imaginary "little Aeneas," who would represent his father only in his face <note>A reference to Virgil's *Aeneid*, where Dido wishes for a child to remind her of Aeneas.</note>, nor like Seth, born in the image of Adam, nor like the other sons of our own procreation, whom mothers desire to be as similar as possible in appearance to their husbands. For "Paternity" is said first and more truly of the divine generation; of us, it is said later and only in the manner of a certain shadow. For the Apostle writes to the Ephesians: "For this reason, I bow my knees to the Father of our Lord יהוה IHSVH <note>original: "IHSVH," Reuchlin's "Mirific Word" or Pentagrammaton, created by inserting the Hebrew letter Shin (ש) into the four-letter name of God (YHWH) to produce the name of Jesus.</note> Christ, from whom all paternity in heaven and on earth is named." <note>Ephesians 3:14–15</note> Indeed, in these mortal things, that which imitates its pattern is either not of one substance with it (though it may be of equal shape), or if by chance it is of one substance, it will not be entirely the same in other respects—not the same in power, similar in counsel, equal in effect, or equal in motion. But that divine likeness is as close to the Father as anything can possibly be; so much so that it should more rightly be called "the same" rather than an "image." But where the image is identity <note>original: ὁμοίος (homoios), meaning "similar" or "like."</note>, there the thing itself is seen as entirely of the same substance <note>original: ὁμοούסιος (homoousios), a key theological term meaning "of the same essence."</note> in the likeness, even though in its own nature it can be neither seen nor touched. They also sometimes call this very image, which is of the same substance as the highest Father, the "Seal," <margin>The Seal.</margin> following the same interpretation as above. For what a ring works into a seal in a linear form over time, this the Father expresses in his Word substantially throughout eternity, and in a far more excellent way. But concerning the "Character," <margin>Character</margin> <note>original: χαρακτήρ (charaktēr), meaning a mark, imprint, or distinctive feature.</note> since the Son is also honored by this name, I shall have another opinion, such as I will soon explain to you. My own boldness—or to speak more truly, perhaps my excessive confidence in your kindness toward me—has not only cast me into much-speaking or commended me to it, but has even surrendered me to it. Nevertheless, however it may be, I will gladly explain, if I first remind you of this: the names of the most divine and Mirific Word must be understood in a threefold way, according to the different conditions of the one to whom the names belong. For you have already learned clearly from the previous discourse—though it was brief, it was open, I think—that the Word is the cause of the universe, both God and the arranger of nature; and then that in the beginning he was with God, like a hand in the bosom of the Father.

### Three miracles in the sign of the conception, three states in the Word of God, and concerning a certain Trinity. CHAPTER IV.

<margin>Of the Word made flesh.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' depicting a scholar or religious figure seated in a high-backed chair within a vaulted room, gesturing toward an open book on a desk.</image-desc>
NOW also, it would be wrong to remain ignorant of what remains, which is of the greatest importance for our business of performing miracles: that this same God, the Word of God the Father, by his own Spirit proceeding from the Father, was at last incarnated from an incorrupt virgin in recent years, just as the prophecies of the prophets many centuries before had predicted it would be. Let us read the oracle of Jeremiah: "Because the Lord יהוה <note>The Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God.</note> has created a new thing on earth: a woman shall encompass a man." <margin>Jeremiah 31.</margin> <note>Jeremiah 31:22</note> This is the astonishing thing, this is the new thing, this is the admirable thing: that the female sex, without sexual intercourse, without the embraces of a man—but with God alone not only acting but also creating—bore in her womb and surrounded with her womb not an embryo, but a perfect man. Because of this, Isaiah says, "The Lord himself will give you a sign: Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a Son, and shall call his name <margin>Isaiah 7.</margin> 'God with us'." <note>Isaiah 7:14</note> For what else did the prophet wish to express by that word "Emmanuel" <note>original: עמנואל (Immanuel).</note> except this alone: namely, the Word made flesh? So that because he is the Word, he is God; and because he dwells among us, he appears incarnate. Otherwise, it would be a sign of no value to be so greatly sought from a king, or one in which it would be believed that God was tempted not in vain...

<margin>Three things to be weighed.</margin> It might be feared that he would not be believed if, according to the nature of his divinity alone, God fills the earth and had merely promised to dwell among us. No place is empty of God; but there were three things in that most excellent sign that must be weighed with great human wonder. First, that a virgin should conceive; second, that a virgin should give birth; and finally, that he should be both God and man at the same time. These individual points have been found to be signified even by the malice of the Hebrews. The universal Church of the martyrs will be witness, who were present for such a great matter and followed the <term>God-man <note>original: "θεανθρωπον" (theanthropon)</note></term> on foot. Therefore, John, his disciple,
<margin>The confirmation of Christ as the God-man.</margin> published it thus: *That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, of the Word of life; and the life was manifested, and we have seen, and bear witness, and announce to you eternal life, which was with the Father, and appeared to us.* For this so super-eminent gift was not given by God for this reason alone, nor is it so admirable because he appeared to us by bodily sight in a human body—as if angels had not also appeared in the past to the patriarchs, with whom they conversed and talked in a human manner, as did the Lord God on occasion. But it is because, by his arrival, he has steeped the whole of human substance, not unlike a superior leaven <note>Reuchlin uses the metaphor of yeast (leaven) to explain how Christ's divinity transforms the "dough" of human nature.</note> which is said to permeate the whole batch of dough and every circumstance. This is the miracle that excels, which we rightly value most highly, and which we pursue with our proclamation.
<margin>The Deity united with us in Christ.</margin> For the Deity of this divine man—that is, the Word incarnate—is like a leaven to the whole batch, which is our nature. By his permeating presence, once the obstacle of the condemnation of our forefathers and ancestors has been removed, he enables us to become divine and to be numbered among the gods. You have, therefore, three states: he is God, he is the Son, he is incarnate. For each of these we find most religious descriptions in the sacred scriptures, either denying or affirming. No one knows God more certainly than by either a privative particle <note>A "privative particle" refers to defining God by what He is not (e.g., infinite, meaning "not finite"). This is known as "negative theology."</note> or a negative word, although even that is not certain, since he himself, as far as his essence is concerned, is subject to no name. For whatever the affirmative symbols assert, all of that is neither his essence nor his nature, but what is believed to be from him.
<margin>Hermes.</margin> Whence that saying of Hermes <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many mystical and philosophical works were attributed.</note>: "Since his name cannot be spoken by a human mouth, because to utter it is beyond man." And likewise that which is in the revelations of our Theologian <note>Referring to John the Apostle in the Book of Revelation.</note>: *And on his head were many crowns, having a name that no one knows except himself; and he was clothed in a garment sprinkled with blood, and his name is called* 
<margin>The Word of God.</margin> *the Word of God.* In this place, that most sacred divination concerning this Son of God can clearly instruct us both when he has a name and when he has not. Here, I hope that speech comes to our memory which asserted the first emanation from God, which according to the Philosophy of the Hebrews is called <term>Kether <note>original: "כתר" (the first Sefirah in the Kabbalah, representing the Divine Will or "Crown").</note></term>: that is, the "Crown" and "Royal Majesty." And because it is the highest and most ample, it therefore contains in itself many 
<margin>The head of wisdom.</margin> crowns which are on the head: that is, in his multiform wisdom. Therefore, this first exit of divinity from the Father of Lights, since it is ineffable, cannot be measured by a specific name. For in spirit Isaiah exclaims: *Who shall declare his generation?* For if a prophet will not declare it, who will? Since nothing of the divine comes down to us from above except by the prophetic spirit—that is, through revelation.
<margin>The Arm of the Lord.</margin> Wherefore a little before he says: *To whom is the arm of the Lord revealed?* But since it is established from the above what "the hand" or "the arm" is in the sacred scriptures—namely, nothing other than a substance in God, whose nature is such that it always hangs with another and from another. For just as he is always the complete, perpetual Father, so he was never sterile, but always a parent; for without him he is a Parent beyond time, therefore the perpetual Father of a perpetual Son. Such a generation we conceive in the mind under the obscure cloud of thought. But when—
