# THE WONDER-WORKING WORD, BOOK III. 953

In a riddle, and in part we see; surely we can produce no name that is commensurate, clear, and complete. Therefore, wearing crowns upon his head, he has a name in the Apocalypse <note>original: *Apocalypsi*, referring to Revelation 19:12</note> which no one knows but himself: which was rightly said concerning a proper, adequate name that encompasses the entire definition of the thing. For no one knows this even regarding the whole Trinity—not even the angels—except in so far as divinity itself has freely produced it concerning itself, according to our measure; not as great as it is, but as great as we can grasp. Do you see clearly enough that the one wearing the crowns lacks an equal name among us? Yet you see him clothed in a blood-stained garment, so that he begins to be called the "Son of God" by men. For concerning the Son, nothing was stable, nothing firm, nothing known before the arrival of the incarnate Word, and before we held that same garment sprinkled with blood. Whatever we were taught by prophets, philosophers, or poets, we judged to be entirely full of smoke and darkness. The Lord said to my 
<margin>Psalm 109 <note>Psalm 110:1 in modern numbering</note></margin> 
Lord: *Sit at my right hand.* *You are my Son, today I have begotten you.* And *his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity.* And *the stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.* *This was made by the Lord*—or more truly, *this was from the Lord*—this is wonderful in our eyes. Indeed, these things are darkness in our eyes, these are riddles, these are doubtful oracles. For who in that age would then have shown me the Father and the Son in the "stone" which Holy Scripture 
<margin>Stone <note>original Hebrew: אבן (*Aben*)</note></margin> 
brought forth in Hebrew as *Aben*? It is well known, however, that *Ab* <note>original Hebrew: אב</note> signifies "Father" in that language, and *Ben* <note>original Hebrew: בן</note> signifies "Son." These three letters, joined into two syllables, make *Aben*: that is, they form "the stone." This is the mystery, this is the secret, which I believe I would not then have perceived; I would have been <term>Davus, not Oedipus <note>A Latin proverb meaning "a simpleton, not a riddle-solver." Reuchlin suggests that without Kabbalistic insight, he would be blind to these truths.</note></term>. Similarly, in the word *Bra* <note>original Hebrew: ברא (*bara*)</note> which is "he created," and 
<margin>Mysteries of the thrice-blessed Trinity.</margin> 
with which the book of Moses begins in the beginning, I would not have sought "a knot in this bulrush" <note>An idiom for looking for difficulty where there is none; here, Reuchlin uses it ironically to describe seeking deep meaning in plain words.</note> so as to have searched out those letters in which I might perceive **A** as the Father, **B** as the Son, and **R** as the Spirit. Nor would I have conjectured that the voice of *Bra* itself was the first syllable in the beginning, by which argument it would be clear either that the most Holy Trinity was the beginning of the world, or that the Father created heaven and earth in the Son—just as it is now. For if anyone joins the last of the three letters of *Bra* to the first, he will immediately 
<margin>In the Son <note>original Hebrew: בני (*Beni*)</note></margin> 
produce *Ab*, which we showed above to be the Father. Then, doubling the letter **B** for itself and adding the remaining **R**, it will sound as *Bebar ni*, "In the Son." For as you know, vowels among the Hebrews are not placed as such in the row of letters. Finally, if he takes the whole word, he will surely perceive that this entire meaning lies hidden in a single syllable: namely, *the Father created in the Son.* O wonderful thing, but one that requires a prophetic spirit or a divine inspiration! In this manner, there are infinite things encompassed in the most sacred characters—not only the fulfillment of past events, but also certain omens of the future, provided there is someone present who does not so much interpret them as prophesy them. For thus the spirits of the prophets of a past age become subject to future prophets, wherefore the Apostle says: *I wish that you all spoke with tongues, but even more that you prophesied. For he who prophesies is greater than he who speaks with tongues.* And some are seers, as Plato says in the *Timaeus*, while others are the interpreters of seers.

<header>ON THE MIRIFIC WORD, BOOK III.</header>

...dripping upon the earth, it is clear that he <note>Referring to the Word or the divine outflow</note> embraces the aether with his moist arms, with his shining river, and with that very outflow from the paternal remaining substance. This aether is that "spirit nourishing all things within" and the "fiery vigor," as Virgil says, <margin>The Holy Spirit.</margin> and it is of celestial origin—not from that heaven which we see with our bodily eyes, but from the invisible: that is, from the divine Son, and proceeding from himself, the heaven of heavens. On account of this embrace, the Hebrews name the heavens <term>Schamaim<note>Hebrew: שמים</note></term>, as if it were <term>Esch vmaim<note>Hebrew: אש ומים</note></term>: that is, fire and water. For <term>aether<note>Greek: αἰθήρ</note></term> is so called as if from the word <term>burning<note>Greek: αἰθῶν, from αἴθω</note></term>, and <term>air<note>Greek: ἀήρ</note></term>: that is, spirit; a name which, according to Greek grammar, signifies a "burning spirit." Therefore, according to Orpheus, heaven is born from night, and from heaven proceeds the aether. *And there was evening and there was morning, one day.* This matter is very like a miracle and scarcely credible—or rather, incredible—unless the Word of God had been incarnated to instruct us in such great mysteries. There was a "One" which was simultaneously evening, morning, and day, three days before the Sun, Moon, and stars were born. It was a single light, divided into morning, evening, and day, which existed with the same Disposer who said: *Let there be light.* Consider the words; release the mysteries. These are the words: *In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.* Behold the briefest summary of the entire creation. But what was it that was made, and what was there in the beginning before anything was made, and in what manner was that which was in the beginning, and who or of what condition was he who had already begotten the "beginning"? Then it follows: <margin>The condition of things during their creation.</margin> *Because the earth was a vast deformity.* Finally, the heaven was like a garment that surrounded and hid the earth, and like a nearby tunic, it wrapped it in a cloak. And it was called the "abyss," as in the 103rd Psalm: *You who founded the earth upon its stability, it shall not be bowed for age upon age. The abyss is like a garment of its clothing.* <note>Reference to Psalm 104:5-6 (Psalm 103 in the Vulgate numbering).</note> Above the heaven were shadows; after the shadows, water; and above the water, the Spirit of the Lord. Thus God, by speaking, made the Word flash forth, and there was light. And he divided the light from the darkness, and called the light Day, and the darkness Night; and there was evening and there was morning, one day. Indeed, the darkness and the evening represent the Orphic "Night," the Light and the Day represent "Heaven," and the Morning represents the "Aether." For the most ancient of the Latins used to say <term>manum</term> to mean "clear" or "bright," just as the Greeks say <term>aberon</term> <note>Original Greek: ἀβερὸν</note>; from this, the word *mane* <note>Latin for "morning"</note> is derived. Day indeed proceeds from night, and morning depends on both—but this occurred not only before the creation of heaven and earth, but even before all eternity. These things have perhaps fallen from our lips too rashly, yet for the sake of our discussion, they seem to me timely enough, so that you may not think there was any time in the memory of our fathers when our ancestors could have extricated these and many other such matters so accurately, so properly, and with such firmness of opinion before the Son was incarnated. But after that Word of God came into this flesh of ours to illuminate men, <margin>John 1.</margin> then the eyes of our mind were opened, so that many things promulgated by divine inspiration long ago are now understood almost more clearly by us than by their own authors—especially whatever pertains to the divinity of the Word. But let us return again to his names, from which it is necessary to select the one *Mirific* <note>Wonder-working</note> Name, in which alone we mortals, though situated in nature, may dominate above nature and above fate, and be able to perform portents, wonders, and the signs of divinity. And so that you may understand that various names have been attributed to that Word, <margin>Proposition of what follows.</margin> I have decided that I should recount first those which he holds in common with the Father and the Spirit; second, those which are thought proper to his own divine subsistence; third, those of the flesh; and lastly, those of the incarnate Word.

...power, and operation, and likeness, and whatever the supreme nature follows, or is connected to by significance, are predicated of the Son of God, whose name is wonderful, and simultaneously of the whole Trinity. We have decided to investigate these together in this way: some of them do not describe what the nature of divinity is (for this would be impossible according to human understanding), but rather what surrounds it. These indeed seem to signify essence, which you, my Baruchias, have completed abundantly and copiously as far as logic allows. Let us refer others, however, to the various management of the dispensation <note>The "dispensation" refers to the "Oeconomia," or God's plan and actions within human history, especially the Incarnation.</note>. This latest root springs up into two branches: the arrangement of things conducted without a body, and the manifestation of the flesh—that is, the human condition. The former are attributed generally, while the latter are attributed specifically to the Word. For all the essences <note>original: "οὐσίας" [ousias]</note> that were suited to names before the body was united to Him are common to the supersubstantial and one Trinity. Therefore, leaving behind those things which are essential—as we were sufficiently taught about them in yesterday’s discussion—let us now briefly attempt those things believed to indicate dignity and power.

For "He who is," and "I myself," and "consuming fire," and "YHWH" <note>original: "יהוה"</note>—which signifies the ineffable—seem to me to have been sufficiently explained by you, Baruchias, and with a sharper study of your people <note>Referring to the Hebrew scholars</note> than that with which I am endowed, which you [attribute] to the properties of substance. <margin>Epistle 11.</margin> Yet we cannot deny that "Lord," "King," and "God" signify imperial majesty, if we follow John of Damascus. Gregory Nazianzen, certainly, places these among the terms that are relative <note>Terms that define God in relation to something else, rather than in isolation.</note>. For we read: "Lord of lords," and "King of kings," and "Holy of holies," and "God of gods." Only "Being" <note>original: "ὄν" [on]</note>—that is, "He who is"—is thought to be God's name most primarily by itself. Although the grammarians report that the word "God" <note>original: "Deus"</note> is changed from the Greek word <note>original: "θεὸς" [theos]</note>, which is believed to have fallen from "to burn" <note>original: "θεῖν" [thein]</note> according to Plato—that is, because God is a "consuming fire," from which a mark of substance might seem to be seen—nevertheless, it is not of such a kind that it explains something existing according to itself without comparison to another. For the Lord said to Moses: "Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: The Lord God of our fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob has sent me to you; this is my name forever." That voice, therefore, will wait for certain others of whom He is God, just as a "Lord" is a Lord of subjects, and a "king" is set over inferiors; so He alone is "Most High" and "Exalted." I said, "You are gods, and all of you children of the Most High," who inhabit eternity in the heights. Cause, and prince, and leader, and first, and last, and Alpha and Omega <note>original: "Α & Ω"</note>, and beginning and end, and head, and the eye of man—each of these is understood as being relative to something. Truly, in His power, God is marvelous, powerful, great, terrible, living, seeing, eternal, the Ancient of Days, enduring, strong, eternal life, and the Lord of Virtues <note>Often translated as "Lord of Hosts" or "Sabaoth."</note>. Likewise, He is judged by some to exhibit "Energy" <note>Divine activity or operation.</note>, those who are accustomed to derive "God" <note>original: "θεὸς" [theos]</note> from "running through" <note>original: "θεῖν" [thein]</note>, that is, by running through, moving, and penetrating. Wherefore the Lord speaks in Exodus about not worshiping a strange god: "The Lord, Jealous is His name, He is a jealous God." But also from other works which Dionysius calls "caused" and Nazianzen calls "additional," God Himself possesses surnames. From the greatness and beauty of the things made, it happens that the Maker is reasonably estimated. For the supreme Creator is not easily made manifest to us from His own substance, which has no form, but from those things which are present, and from the very things effected. In this way He is called: "doer of wonders," "man of war," "crusher of battles," "protector," "life-giver," "Father of all," "Creator," "Redeemer," "Savior," and others of that kind.

...brought together into one origin, it might be called the "fount of life"; and from all brightnesses, splendors, and lights, with the entire light gathered into one clarity, it might be named the "Sun." For the divine philosopher <note>Reuchlin likely refers to Dionysius the Areopagite or Plato, who used the Sun as a primary metaphor for the Good/God.</note> wrote that what the Sun is to sensible things, God is to intellectual things. Another kind of similarity is taken from the comparison of one to another, and like to like; for instance, if I wished to compare the most divine Trinity to the clarity of the Sun, I would then compare any one of its lights to any one of the divine "subsistences."

<margin>Subsistence.</margin>
For I have become accustomed to calling the <term>hypostasis</term> <note>original Greek: ὑπόστασιν. In theology, this refers to a distinct person of the Trinity.</note> "subsistence," as you will hear more clearly hereafter—especially in divine matters. I do not call it "substance" as Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher who defined "person" in a way Reuchlin is refining here.</note> did, but, as it seemed more suitable to me, "subsistence," lest I stumble into the term <term>essence</term> <note>original Greek: οὐσίαν (ousia). This refers to the "whatness" or being of God shared by all three persons.</note>, which almost every translator routinely renders as "substance." For I have decided not to be a mere maker of words, but an imitator of established ways; nor will the matter be at great risk as long as the concept itself becomes clear through usage. You have certainly heard God called "the Sun" by the philosophers. Just as the Sun is a globe, a ray, and light, and all these are one Sun; so too is the "Sun" of God: Father, Son, and Spirit, and all are one God. The same may be judged concerning the soul.

<margin>The human soul is also a Soul.</margin>
For "God is a soul to us," as the poems say, which consists of mind, reason, and sense. The mind illuminates the reason, and the reason flows into the sense; all these are one soul.
<margin>The Center.</margin>
The center of nature, the middle of all things, the sequence of the universe, the face of all things, and the measure and bond of the world—by which it will be compared to God, even if under an obscure image, yet in whatever way possible. Furthermore, many things naturally accompany the divine, from which divinity has received its names, such as unity, and truth, and goodness. God is also said to be alone, always, and everywhere; understanding infinite things, understanding Himself first and then individual things; acting through His own being upon all things. He is named love and charity, immortal providence; He is proclaimed as wisdom, beauty, justice, peace, and perfection. Finally, there are a great number of things that describe God much more truly in a "privative" or negative way <note>This refers to "apophatic theology," which describes God by what He is NOT (e.g., infinite/not-finite) because God exceeds all human language.</note>, not because of any defect in Him, but because of His supreme excellence: for God exceeds all speech.

<margin>Names of God.</margin>
This entire list tends toward this point: that you should consider all these titles to belong not only to God the Father and the Spirit, but also to the Word, who is the most beloved Son of God—the best, the greatest, the eternal God, ineffable, incomprehensible, the immovable eternity, who is all things in one, and the source of all things that exist. For He Himself is the creator of all, and through Him the Father created all things; and He is also the "consuming fire," and the <term>wonder</term> <note>original Greek: τεράστιον (terastion), meaning a marvel or omen.</note>, the light, the day, the heavens, King of kings and Lord of lords, God of gods, Holy of holies, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob. He alone is the most high, the exalted, the sublime, inhabiting eternity, the prince, the leader, the first and the last, and the <term>Alpha and Omega</term> <note>original Greek: Α & Ω, the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet.</note>, the beginning, the middle, and the end. The head and eye of man, perfection, peace, justice, beauty, wisdom, immortal providence, charity and love; understanding infinite things, understanding Himself first and then individual things, acting through His own being upon all things, always and everywhere. Unity and truth and goodness, mind, reason, sun, ray, fount of life, sea of goodness, cause, Father of all, creator, protector, savior, redeemer, a man of war, doing wonders, crushing wars. The life-giving Lord, the zealous one, and the jealous God, God almighty, wonderful, great, terrible, living and seeing me, the Ancient of Days, the enduring one, the strong one, the Lord of powers, and eternal life.

<margin>The Praises of the Word.</margin>
With these and similar praises, the Word is celebrated in common with the other persons of the Trinity, but He is specifically celebrated by this: that He is the Son, begotten without a beginning. For He is said to have a Father but not a beginning, and to be begotten from the "Always-Father" always and without suffering; one from one and uniquely so, whom the Father reveals in His entirety, and whose nature He demonstrates adequately. Whatever words aspire to this, whatever words suggest such a distinction, will be of the sort that explain the most divine Word—which we investigate in the present discourse as worthy of highest praise—with a peculiar ornament: just as the "Only-Begotten in the bosom of the Father," of whom we spoke before, and the <term>express image of His person</term> <note>original Greek: χαρακτὴρ ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ (charaktēr hypostaseōs autou). A reference to Hebrews 1:3.</note>, of which we promised to speak.

Reuchlin (as the character Capnion) is refining the distinction between the "substance" (the shared divine essence) and the "hypostasis" (the distinct existence of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit), critiquing earlier translations by Boethius and others that he finds imprecise.</meta>

IOANNES REUCHLIN

...is read: "Who, being the splendor of glory and the figure of his substance" <note>Hebrews 1:3: 'Qui cùm ſit ſplendor gloriæ & figura ſubſtantiæ eius'</note>. This [distinction] is perhaps due to the way *hypostasis* <note>original: hypoſtaſis</note> is translated as "substance" from "standing under," rather than as "subsistence" from "standing by itself," by certain learned men. We are taught that this is sometimes the case in the book *On the Two Natures* attributed to Boethius. Yet he, when turning Aristotle’s volumes into Latin, calls *ousia* <note>original: οὐσίαν</note> "substance," thereby transgressing his own rules. This lack of precision casts a thick cloud over the eyes of many, such that no student of Latin theology can bear this inconsistency with a calm mind. It is tedious, or rather hateful, to interpret one word as having different meanings, especially in a matter not of oratorical display or flowery speech, but of the strength of truth and the firmness of teaching. Listen now, carefully and diligently, to the matter at hand.

## What must be believed concerning God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>Hypostasis. Seal. Splendor. Image.</margin>
THE council and the people of the Christian republic have DECREED that it must be so thought and so professed: that there is one sole true, eternal, immense, unchangeable, incomprehensible, omnipotent, and ineffable Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—three persons indeed, but one essence, substance, nature, and entirely simple. These are the very words of the decree; this is the right, this the edict, this the true Law of religion: by which we are taught that substance, essence, and nature are exactly one and the same. But *hypostasis* <note>original: ὑπόστασις; referring to a distinct individual existence or 'person' within the Trinity</note> in the supreme divinity is not used casually: for it belongs to the one and only essence, nature, and substance. There are three *hypostases* which the same Boethius translated into Latin as "persons," and in one single *hypostasis* two substances consist. Therefore, *hypostasis* and "substance" are not the same thing to say, nor are they used in the same way, just as "person" and "substance" are not. This is the Catholic faith: that we worship one God in Trinity, and Trinity in Unity, neither confounding the persons nor dividing the substance. We recognize that "substance" signifies one thing, and *hypostasis* another. For the Father, by eternally begetting the Son, gave Him His substance and yet retained it. The Son, by being born, received the Father's substance, but neither did the Father transfer His *hypostasis* (that is, His own person) to Him, nor did the Son take it from Him. For both are of two *hypostases* and two persons, yet truly of one and the same substance. Therefore, I would easily believe that in this passage Jerome <note>Hieronymus</note> translated "subsistence" rather than "substance" for *hypostasis*, especially in a matter of such weight, where no small difference is found to lurk between *hypostasis* and *ousia* <note>original: οὐσίαν; essence</note>. Which [ousia], in the light of the first volume and the fifteenth part of that book, is likewise and correctly found to be translated as "substance." For according to our custom, *ousia* is called "substance," but *hypostasis* must be named "subsistence"; so that when the Apostle says, "the character of the subsistence" <note>original: χαρακτὴρ ὑποστάσεως; Hebrews 1:3</note>, we may understand "the figure of the subsistence." For in this way the word "character" <note>original: χαρακτὴρ</note> becomes the seal or figure of the paternal substance, which is not merely similar but is truly that whole substance of the Father, besides which there is nothing else. Therefore, if the "character" is distinct from that whose form it expresses (as Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Church Father known for his eloquence</note> testifies), it was necessary for the Son to be called the "character" of the paternal *hypostasis*—that is, the seal of the subsistence—and not of the *ousia*—that is, the seal of the substance. For the Father, by begetting, sealed the person of the Son, just as the figure of a signet ring expresses the form of the seal, or as He Himself taught concerning Himself: "Work," He says, "not for the food that perishes but for that which remains unto eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you. For God the Father has sealed Him" <note>John 6:27</note>. He is further named "the splendor of clarity and glory," because He is Light of Light, as if indicating a communion of one essence, so that two subsistences might more truly become known to us. Moreover, the "Image" or *eikon* <note>original: εἰκὼν</note>, which is the complete showing forth of the Father, as we revealed a moment ago, is by no means...

<summary>Reuchlin defines the theological distinction between the Father and the Son, arguing that while they share one "substance" (essence), they are distinct "subsistences" (persons). He critiques existing Latin translations of Greek terms like hypostasis and ousia to clarify the relationship between the members of the Trinity.</summary>

<margin>The power of God.</margin>
The name must be understood not just as a label for the thing, but as being one with the thing itself; for it is not artificial, but natural, born outside of time, and the very cause of eternity. It follows that he is the "power of God and the wisdom of God," the titles by which our sun, Paul, writing to the Corinthians, names him. "We," he says, "preach to those called, both Jews and Greeks, CHRIST the power of God and the wisdom of God." <note>original: "CHRISTVM Dei uirtutem, & Dei sapientiam." quoting 1 Corinthians 1:24.</note> For he possesses all power within himself in the highest degree and beforehand, as the author of all power, bringing forth all things through a power that is most firm and unlimited. When the prophet contemplated this with the eyes of his mind, he exclaimed: "Be exalted, O Lord, in your power." <note>Psalm 21:13.</note> What shall we say 

<margin>Wisdom.</margin>
of his wisdom, whose "foolishness" is wiser than men? For he is full of all wisdom and understanding, and "of his wisdom there is no number." <note>Psalm 147:5.</note> But placed surpassingly above all reason, mind, and wisdom, he is the giver of all wisdom and the cause of all intelligence, having proceeded from the head of God. <note>An allusion to the birth of Athena from the head of Zeus, here applied to the Word (Logos) proceeding from the Father.</note> In him, truly, all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. Furthermore, 

<margin>John 14.</margin>
since the Son of God names himself "the way, the truth, and the life," it is surely fitting that we venerate these names with religious devotion, as they are the closest signs of the Almighty Creator, inviting us toward the highest blessedness of our souls. "Blessed," says the prophet, "are the undefiled in the way"; <note>Psalm 119:1.</note> for they attain the vision of God in a pure heart, which is the sole blessedness and happiness of men, granted to us through this one way. Let us hear it from his own mouth: "No one," he says, "comes to the Father except through me." The way, therefore, by which one goes to the Father is the Son. And he is the "life" because this door, this path, this gate is our science and knowledge of the Father; therefore, he is the "truth." Otherwise, it would be error, not science or knowledge. Moreover, he is the truth because he is one, whereas falsehood is many and not one—though perhaps these last two names are common to the whole Trinity. But "the Way" seems to be the Son’s own proper name. Many such forms of naming are contained in the Sacred Scriptures, differing in appearance but all praiseworthy in kind, which all harmonize at this goal: that the Word of God—that is, the Son—is alone begotten and the only-begotten from the substance of the Father without beginning. He is the <term>character</term> <note>original: χαρακτὴρ. Used here to mean the "exact impression" or "engraved mark" of God's essence.</note> and the figure of the Father’s subsistence, the splendor of glory, the filial hypostasis and person of the Word, the seal of the Father, light from light, the <term>image</term> <note>original: εἰκών (eikon). A representation that shares in the reality of the original.</note> or likeness, the power of God and the wisdom of God, the way, the gate, and the door. Now it remains to recount in a very brief speech those things which pertain to his human nature. Thus, although this Word is the eternal Son of God, begotten from the substance of the Fa-

### CHAPTER IX.

<margin>Gods of the nations.</margin>
Then SIDONIUS said: I very willingly escape this priestly duty and transfer it to you, who preside by rank over today’s discussion—or, if Baruchias here prefers, the platform should be granted to him. For I have been initiated into other sacred rites from my earliest childhood <note>original: "à teneris unguiculis," literally "from tender fingernails," a Latin idiom meaning from one's earliest years.</note>; I have known no majesty, no "Great One," no excellence, except for these brightest lights of the World which we see: the sun, the maker of the day, and the moon, the glory of the night, or perhaps those other little lights which you call the heavens and the stars. And afterwards, whenever I wished to be most deeply religious, those names of invisible powers occurred to me which Ennius correctly encompassed in these two verses:

->*Juno, Vesta, Minerva, Ceres, Diana, Venus, Mars,*<-
->*Mercury, Jove, Neptune, Vulcan, Apollo.*<-

Or those which the most ancient Orpheus, writing to Musaeus, enumerates at even greater length: Earth, Proserpina, Liber, the Foam-Born <note>original: "Spumigena," an epithet for Venus (Aphrodite), referring to her birth from sea foam.</note>, Hebe, Hercules, the Nymphs, Pan, Memory, the Muses, the Graces, the Seasons, the Year, Latona, Dione, the Curetes, the Corybantes <note>The Curetes and Corybantes were mythical groups of armed dancers who protected the infant Zeus/Dionysus.</note>, Castor, Pollux, Themis, Night, Day, Faith, Justice, Rhea, Saturn, Earth, Ocean, Eternity, Time, Styx, Providence <note>original: "Pronœa."</note>, celestial spirits, and those of the air, water, earth, underworld, and fire; Semele, Bacchus, Ino, Leucothea, Palaemon, Victory, Adrastia <note>A name for Nemesis or a goddess of inescapable destiny.</note>, Aesculapius, Pallas, the Winds, Thunders, the Month, Adonis, the Furies, Hecate, and others of whom that same grave author makes mention in his hymns. However, while reading at times when other matters were not pressing, I slipped lightly into foreign things and crept into alien camps as a scout. Thus I read the Gospels and the books of the Christians.

And I too, said BARUCHIAS. For those demons of yours, Sidonius—though with horror and trembling—I have nevertheless read of them occasionally; yet I always judged that they were not so much to be read as to be neglected, because they stood so far apart from our instruction. It did not agree with reason that something made by another should be called God. Thus, I more easily accepted that the Word of God is God, since 

<margin>Our virgin.</margin>
it is the same as God and exists without beginning together with the Father, and was born from the Father for all eternity and before all ages. For that which was born of the virgin was a matter as much of essence as of dispensation <note>The "dispensation" or "economy" refers to the way God manages human salvation, specifically the Incarnation.</note>. For so he willed it, and so it was; he could have taken another nature if he had willed. For the Lord did all things whatsoever he willed in heaven and on earth. 

But since you give me the choice of selecting among so many names, as to which might be effective for everyone in the performance of miracles, I myself previously professed that I know next to nothing about them. This is because the power of the sacred names seems to have followed my ancestors only up to this present age—just as in the memory of the fathers, great works, beyond nature and beyond all [human] works, are read to have been done in the name of Yahweh <note>original: "יהוה," the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God.</note>. Unless there be found—as elsewhere in the world, so also among the Hebrews—sacrilegious men, sorcerers, and superstitious exorcists, whose malignant spirits block the minds of every nation. Therefore we pray you, Capnion, proceed, so that from among all the most sacred names we may not be ignorant of what is more powerful for miracles, what is more ready, and what is most prepared. For so Sidonius also desires along with me.

I desire the same, and nothing else, said he; and I pray you again and again to proceed.

*That the omnipotence of God alone is the worker of miracles, and concerning certain figures: furthermore, concerning that miraculous name, in what manner it was known, and how it is to be used. CHAPTER X.*

ON THE WONDER-WORKING WORD, BOOK III.

<margin>A nobler power of operation.</margin>
...joined with a virtue of a nobler operation. For Aristotle, in the book he published *On the Soul*, left it sufficiently proved for the Peripatetics <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle's philosophy, named after the "peripatos" or covered walkways of the Lyceum in Athens where they taught.</note> that neither sound nor smell exerts any dominion over a body or produces any effect in substances, except through some accidental property <note>In Aristotelian logic, an "accident" is a property that does not affect the essential nature or "substance" of a thing—for example, the color of a stone vs. the fact that it is a stone.</note>. For we are composed of primary, not tertiary qualities. Therefore, the nobler virtue, by which words bring force to things beyond—or rather above—nature and the perpetual course of the world, is not some internal natural force, but is also above nature; this is because anything of this kind that acts under the guidance of nature operates either on something similar to itself or something inferior, but never above its own species. Therefore, since we agreed yesterday without controversy that the omnipotence of God alone is the creator of miracles—for, as the King <note>Referring to King David in the Psalms.</note> prophesied: *Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who alone does great wonders* <note>original: "Benedictus enim Dominus Deus Israël... q facit mirabilia magna solus." Referring to Psalm 72:18.</note>—we shall feel, not without reason, that God himself has bestowed a singular ray of his omnipotence upon every wonder-working word. This is the operative virtue of a miraculous effect, brought down even to us through the ministry of angels; just as we have discovered concerning certain figures or secret preparations, as the Holy Scripture <note>original: "sacro eloquio," literally "sacred eloquence."</note> bears witness.

<margin>The Serpent. Jealousy.</margin>
*Make a bronze serpent, and set it up as a sign; whoever is struck and looks upon it, shall live.* <note>Referencing Numbers 21:8.</note> Likewise: *If the spirit of jealousy <term>Zelotypia</term> <note>From the Greek word for jealousy; here referring to the ritual ordeal described in the Book of Numbers (chapter 5) for a wife suspected of adultery.</note> stirs you, after the offering is made, the priest shall take holy water in an earthen vessel, and put a little dust from the floor of the tabernacle into it. And when the woman stands in the sight of the Lord, he shall uncover her head, and put the sacrifice of remembrance and the offering of jealousy upon her hands. He himself shall hold the most bitter waters, in which he has gathered the cursed execrations, and he shall adjure her, and say: "If another man has not slept with you, and if you have not been polluted by deserting your husband’s bed, these most bitter waters, into which I have gathered curses, shall not harm you. But if you have turned away from your husband and are polluted, and have lain with another, you shall be subject to these curses: May the Lord set you as a curse and an example for all among his people; may he make your thigh rot, and may your swelling womb burst. Let the cursed waters enter into your belly, and as the womb swells, may the thigh rot." And the woman shall respond: "Amen, amen." And the priest shall write these curses in a book, and shall wash them out with the most bitter waters into which he gathered the curses, and shall give them to her to drink. When she has drained them, the priest shall take from her hand the sacrifice of jealousy, and shall lift it before the Lord, and place it upon the altar, and thus give the woman the most bitter waters to drink. If she is polluted and, having despised her husband, is guilty of adultery, when she has drunk them, the waters of the curse shall pass through her, and her belly being inflated, her thigh shall rot, and the woman shall be a curse and an example to all the people. But if she has not been polluted, she shall be unharmed, and shall bear children.*

<margin>The Blessing.</margin>
Let us hear also a third teaching of God: *Thus shall you bless the children of Israel, and you shall say to them: The Lord bless you and keep you. The Lord show his face to you, and have mercy on you. The Lord turn his countenance toward you, and give you peace. And they shall put my name upon the children of Israel, and I will bless them.* <note>The Priestly Blessing from Numbers 6:23–27.</note>

By using such words, by that power of figures, by the virtue of such preparations, and by these songs of curses or blessings and composed words, the thing itself is fashioned by a wondrous art—not by us, but through us. For if it is necessary for a divine virtue to be included in these names, and for an infallible divine power to hasten to them—a power that both surpasses and penetrates all laws of things and lies hidden—

<margin>Proposition of what follows.</margin>
it will be necessary not to be ignorant: First, of what that name is which is more excellent than the rest—indeed, the only one remaining out of all of them—by whose secret energy and hidden aids the whole business of wonder is accomplished. Second, how it is known that it is that very one, and no other besides it. Finally, by what path we may approach what we desire. And this is indeed a great matter, and I know not if it be the greatest; but yet, it is easy enough, step by step, for a prudent and mature investigation to thin out the cause of names, as if plucking wool, until you comprehend what lies hidden, and immediately prove that it is that which you desire. For from a huge heap of sacred words you have received certain things as unutterable <note>original: "ineffabilia."</note>, and certain things which are brought forth by the voice—

...[it seems] hard, if not impossible. But it is difficult for us to be moved by a voice from the ineffable <note>In this context, "the ineffable" refers to the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God (YHWH) which was considered too sacred to be spoken aloud.</note>, which we might use obediently, or which might be ready and at hand for us in any circumstance, any emotion, or any danger. Therefore, what remains is that, led by necessity, we turn with keen judgment to examine the named voices, if first we investigate as briefly as possible, with a somewhat deeper study, the cause of such great power and such virtue in names. For this reason, it seemed best to act more openly now. For just as the mercy of the sky, the rays of the stars, and the eternal fires of the heavenly bodies are believed to effect something in things below the moon by their downward flow:

> From this we can foretell the storms in the doubtful sky,
> From this the day of harvest and the time of sowing,
> And when it is fitting to lash the treacherous sea with oars,
> When to launch the armed fleets,
> Or to fell the pine tree in the woods at its season.
> Not in vain do we watch the settings and risings of the constellations,
> And the year made equal across four different seasons.

This is the work of nature, this the influence of rays, this descent of light, motion, and heat penetrating all things with subtle vivacity. Hence, as the same Mantuan poet <note>Virgil, who was born near Mantua.</note> says:

> The appearances of their minds are turned, and their breasts
> Conceive new movements—some now, others while the wind
> Drove the clouds; hence that chorus of birds in the fields,
> And the joyful cattle, and the ravens exulting with their throats.

And, to be brief, just as the nature of the universe acts naturally upon individual things according to its prescribed order, so the preeminent mistress of nature, the cause of all things—the divine will—acts supernaturally upon each and every thing through its limitless grace. And just as those natural things act through the medium of sensible qualities, so this divine will acts sometimes through the medium of intellectual names in a confederated way, without proportion, without similarity, and without measuring the cause against the effects. This is what God taught us through heavenly revelation via Isaiah. "For as the rain and snow come down from heaven," he says, "and do not return thither, but soak the earth and water it, making it sprout and giving seed to the sower and bread to the eater: so shall my word be that goes forth from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall do whatever I have willed, and shall prosper in those things for which I sent it." 

<margin>THE WORD OF GOD.</margin> Since therefore from the higher things, as I believe, the Word of God (which is called by another name "reason," since both are expressed by the Greeks with one word, <term>Logos <note>original: λόγος</note></term>) clearly appeared to us to be that by which God makes all things, and works all things in heaven, on earth, and in all the depths. Regarding this, I pray you, listen even to the mathematician Marcus Manilius in his *Astronomica* <note>A 1st-century AD Latin poem on astrology and astronomy.</note> addressed to Augustus, who says in his poem:

> This work, constructed of the body of the immense world,
> And the members of nature established in diverse forms—
> The force of the divine soul rules the air, the fire, the earth, and the lying sea;
> God conspires with a sacred path and governs with silent reason,
> And dispenses many covenants to every part.

And since that reason—and the same Word—has put on human flesh, so that we might better attain our advantage through its healing touch, when we see with these eyes and embrace with every sense that very thing which we can name no longer with an ineffable circumscription of letters as before, but with an enunciable voice and a comprehensible sound: it was now fitting that the individual pacts of God with our ancestors, every confederation based on the ineffable and <term>four-lettered <note>original: τετραγράμματω (tetragrammaton). And not only was it fitting to happen this way, but God so willed it, and foretold it long before, which I—if you bear it with an even mind—from...

### ON THE WONDER-WORKING WORD, BOOK III.

...most firmly, I shall confirm it as valid through the oracles. *Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not according to the pact that I made with your fathers on the day I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt, which they made void.* These things are read thus in Jeremiah. From this we clearly understand that the pacts entered into with God within the memory of the fathers have become empty and void in later years, and have been transferred into another covenant. Now, out of all the laws, edicts, and prohibitions—numbering six hundred and thirteen <margin>The 613 Laws.</margin>—this covenant regarding the ineffable name is the most prominent, which God entered into with the sons and daughters of Israel; this was the promise, this the alliance. *I*, He said, *am the ineffable יהוה <note>original: יהוה (YHWH). The Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God considered too holy to speak in Jewish tradition.</note>, your God, mighty and jealous.* And it follows: *You shall make an altar of earth for me, and offer upon it your burnt offerings and peace offerings, your sheep and your oxen; in every place where there is a memorial of my name, I will come to you and bless you.* These things are promised in the twentieth chapter of Exodus.

Yet, hear again in Isaiah how this covenant was broken. *Thus says the Lord: Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool; what is this house that you will build for me? And what is this place of my rest? My hand made all these things, and all these things were made, says the Lord. To whom shall I look, except to the poor man, the one contrite in spirit, and the one who trembles <margin>To whom God looks.</margin> at my words? He who sacrifices an ox is as if he slew a man; he who kills a sheep is as if he broke a dog’s neck; he who offers an oblation is as if he offered swine’s blood; he who burns incense is as if he blessed an idol.* Regarding the ineffable name, indeed, through Jeremiah: *Behold, I have sworn by my great name, says the Lord, that my name shall no longer be called out from the mouth of any man of Judah saying: "The Lord lives," in all the land of Egypt.*

->*On the other names of God, where nearly the entire collection of the works of Christ is found, and concerning the Messiah. CHAPTER II.*<-

<margin>Isaiah 56:b</margin>
Since we have shown that the agreed-upon covenant which God had with His sons and daughters of the people of Israel regarding the name יהוה has been reduced to nothing by God's own judgment, it will now be necessary to explain that this name has been changed into something else, which possesses either equal or greater power than the ineffable name. On this point, let us again observe the oracle of Isaiah, for *thus says the Lord to the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, and choose the things that please me, and hold fast to my covenant: I will give to them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name that shall not perish.* It is as if He says: "To my sons and daughters I gave a name that has ceased. But now, to the eunuchs who castrate themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven <note>A reference to Matthew 19:12, interpreted here as those who devote themselves spiritually rather than through physical lineage.</note>, I will give a better and more permanent name, which shall never cease."

Furthermore, because the translator correctly rendered "place" in this prophecy, you should know that in the Hebrew a great mystery is contained, which has been revealed to us Christians. For there, in Hebrew, it is written as יד (*Iad*) <margin>*Iad* (Hand): The Son of God, the Finger, the Holy Spirit.</margin>, which also signifies a "hand." From this, we judge it not without reason that the Son of God is promised to chaste men—the Son who is the "hand" of the Father—and that his name shall be given. Concerning this transfer of the name, the Lord speaks again to the Jews through Isaiah: *And you shall leave your name for a curse to my chosen ones, and the Lord God shall slay you, and He shall call His servants by another name. In which he who is blessed upon the earth shall be blessed in the God "Amen"*—that is, in the God who is not only the "hand" as mentioned above, but who is also the Truth, the Word of God incarnate, who said: *I am the way, the truth, and the life.*

Do you not see how this aligns with the oracle we brought forward at the beginning? *A child is born to us, and a Son is given to us, and the government was upon his shoulder, and he shall call his name פלא (Pele)* <note>original: פלא (Pele), meaning "Wonderful" or "Miraculous."</note>, *that is, Mirificum (the Wonder-Working).* This is that name which we seek. This is that wonderful name of the "Wonder-Working Word" which we expect, who before eternity and above eternity is God, and <margin>The Wonder-Working Word sought.</margin> was made man. A thing truly admirable at first: God and man, one person, two natures, or...

### JOHANN REUCHLIN

...of the earth, or, what is even greater, within one small body the nature of the Lord was enclosed; yet he was also begotten before all time. From the female sex, because he was born of a stainless virgin, which is divine. Hence he is without a father on earth, but of divine lineage from above. He was carried in the womb, yet while being carried in the womb he was prophesied by the one <note>A reference to John the Baptist leaping in Elizabeth's womb.</note> who rejoiced in the presence of the Word through whom he was being born. He was wrapped in swaddling clothes in the manger, yet he rose from death having unfolded himself from the linen cloths and the shroud. In the manger he was glorified by angels, pointed out by a star, and adored by the Magi. He fled into Egypt as a child, but he put to flight the idols of the Egyptians. Among the Jews he had no beauty of form <note>A reference to the "Suffering Servant" in Isaiah 53:2.</note>, yet he was more beautiful than the sons of men in the sight of God. On the mountain he shone transfigured like the Sun, revealing the majesty with which he will appear in judgment. He was baptized as a man, yet he forgave sins as God; he did not seek to be cleansed, but rather to cleanse the waters. He was tempted as a man, but he conquered as God, commanding us to have confidence because he has overcome the World. He was hungry, yet he fed thousands, and he himself descended as the living bread from heaven. He thirsted, but he also cried out: *If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink,* and *to whoever believes in him, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly.* He was weary, but 

<margin>See the wonderful works of Christ, the Lord <note>original: יהוה (YHWH)</note>.</margin>
he promised rest to those who are laboring. He was weighed down by sleep, but while waking he commanded the winds and the sea. He paid the tax, but from the mouth of a fish. He was called by names of reproach, but was left behind by the priests and Levites. He was said to have a demon, but he was recognized by the demoniac of Gadara, from whom he cast out a legion of demons, drowning them in the sea; he is the one who saw Satan, the leader of demons, fall like lightning from heaven. He was even to be overwhelmed with stones, yet he hid himself and passed through their midst. He prayed, but he also heard prayers. He wept, but he wiped away tears. He asked where Lazarus was, for he was a man; but he raised Lazarus, for he was God. He was sold for a small price, namely thirty pieces of silver, but he redeems the World at a great price. He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, but he rules as a King over Israel and the entire world. He was a silent lamb, but also the Word <note>original: Verbum (referring to the Logos/Divine Reason)</note> crying in the desert. He is struck and wounded, but he also heals every infirmity and sickness. He is killed while hanging on a tree <note>The cross.</note>, but by that wood he restores us to life, saves the thief, and brings darkness upon death. He is given vinegar to drink, but he turned water into wine. He gives up his spirit, but he also has the power to take it back; he hangs a veil over the temple, since the things that are above are revealed. The rocks are split, and the dead rise. He dies, but he gives life, and by his death he destroys death. He is buried, but he rises again. He descends to the lower regions, but he brings back souls, and ascends into heaven. He will come again to judge the living and the dead. Rightly, therefore, is his name "Wonder-Working," <note>original: Mirificum</note> for he is himself most full of marvelous wonders. And surely the Lord has made his holy one—who is the Holy of Holies—wonderful; let him hear us when we cry out to him. You have here that which is

wonder-working. But how is his name pronounced? And is it one of those already listed? Or do you seek something else besides? # ON THE WONDER-WORKING WORD, BOOK III.

...is interpreted as "Christ" <note>original Greek: χρισὸς</note>: whether that is the name, or perhaps something else that signifies the Son of God with a more immediate and specific sound. For "Christ" is not a proper name, but a common term and a designation of power and kingship. Individual kings and all priests, whoever was anointed, are "christs." For the word *chrio* <note>original Greek: χρίω</note> is interpreted as "I anoint" and *christos* as "anointed." Therefore, we must accept his more proper name, in which we may easily obtain everything we desire. We are commanded to search for this again within the sacred characters, not without careful diligence, at the urging of the very one whose name is being discussed. "Search the scriptures," he says, "for they are they which bear witness of me."

->On the name of Jesus, and the letters יהשוה <note>YHShVH</note> into which the letter ש <note>Shin</note> is inserted.<-

### CHAPTER XII.

**Q**UOTING what the holy books contain regarding our cause: I pray you, best of men, listen without weariness, lift up your minds. For now at last we have drawn near, and we stand almost at the very doors of finding the name. The history of the most holy Gospel is this: <margin>Luke 1</margin> In the sixth month, the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee, named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David, and the virgin’s name was Mary. And the angel came to her and said: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you, blessed are you among women." When she heard this, she was troubled by his words, and wondered what kind of greeting this might be. And the angel said to her: "Do not be afraid, Mary: for you have found favor with God. Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name יהשוה <note>IHSVH - Reuchlin’s spelling of Jesus, combining the four-letter name of God with the letter 'S'</note>; he will be great, and will be called the Son of the Most High." Truly, I will not recount the entire series of events, but I will start back where it concerns our business. And after eight days were completed, so that the boy might be circumcised, his name was called יהשוה <note>IHSVH</note>, which was called by the angel before he was conceived in the womb. <margin>A hymn of praise to the name of Christ</margin> O happy hour, O auspicious moment of this light, most distinguished men and most dear companions of studies, in which we have found so excellent, so powerful, so victorious a name, by whose nod and authority not only the vast circuit of the earth, but also this entire mechanism of the world and that renowned super-worldly region—the heavens and the underworld alike—are governed. The one of whom Moses wrote in the Law and the other prophets, we have found: יהשוה <note>IHSVH</note>, so often desired, long sought, deeply investigated, with the most pleasant fruit of delight and with a bond of charity between us that is infallible, as I judge, and destined to last for all time. The supreme and most surpassing name, a religious, holy, and honorable name, the name to which all sacred names are to be referred, which is above every name, which is named in heaven and on earth, even in the age to come. A miraculous and wonder-working name, pronounceable by the sound of the voice, no longer unutterable; not a *tetragrammaton* <note>a four-letter name</note> but a *pentagrammaton* <note>a five-letter name</note>. Nor is there any power in heaven or on earth that would dare to resist the name יהשוה <note>IHSVH</note>. Nor is there any other name that stands more holy or more religious, whose letters are God, whose syllables are Spirit, and whose speech is God and man. Why do you stand there astonished? Why do you look at me with fixed eyes? Why do you keep your mouths so intent? If you marvel, I will even add this: that which was previously unutterable for so long, indeed for so many centuries, has now—by the joining of one letter, not a vowel but a consonant—been made pronounceable. And if you still marvel, I will add further: when the Word descended into flesh, then the letters passed into voice. See how openly and how faithfully I reveal the whole secret to you. The grouping of letters is called a syllable, and the union of syllables is called a word. You lead me back at last to the elements of the grammarians, which, though small to the sight, are nevertheless greatest in power. <margin>The mysteries of letters.</margin> It is of no small weight, if we believe Plato, this business of letters; he himself proves their riches—indeed, their delights—with the greatest industry, sharp study, and wise genius in the book titled *Cratylus*.

# JOHANNES REUCHLIN

But let us return; for indeed, just as in this most excellent name of five letters <note>The Pentagrammaton, יהשוה (IHSVH)</note> a part carries the power of vowels and a part is a consonant, so too the power of the whole word lies in the syllables. The first of these arises from those letters acting as vowels, and the second arises from the assumed consonant *Shin* (ש). I ask you to remember from the records of the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible</note> that the Best and Greatest God wished to be signified by no likeness, no effigy, and no image, except by the voice alone. 
<margin>God is manifested by the voice.</margin> 
Therefore Moses addressed the people in this way: "The Lord," he said, "spoke to you from the midst of the fire; you heard the sound of words, and saw no form at all." And then he adds the reason, since the Lord himself is God, and no other besides the One: "From heaven he made you hear his voice, so that he might teach you, and on earth he showed you his greatest fire." 
<margin>Voice.</margin> 
Thus says Moses. Continue listening. The voice is spirit. For he makes the voice, like struck air; this is how Nicodemus is instructed in the Gospel of John: "The spirit blows where it wishes, and you hear its voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes." So it is; he himself is also spirit. Thus the Samaritan woman is instructed. Therefore, the most suitable sounds for God are the letters carrying the power of vowels, for indeed, without the voice they have remained lost until now. Now dismiss this, because the divinity is designated by those very letters. Now let us pass to the consonant, which we consider more corporeal because, without the boundary of the vocal spirit, it has no sound of the mouth, but only rests in silence. 

If indeed the consonant is a letter not chosen by chance, nor snatched up recklessly from lack of skill or ignorance, nor admitted unexpectedly or beyond hope, but selected from the providence of the highest God—who looks around at all things and dispenses all things—in this divine examination of his reason from among all characters, it is that which is named by our people *Shin* (ש) and by us *Esh* <note>original: "Es"; the Hebrew word אש (Esh) means "fire"</note>. For Baruch taught us, if you hold it in memory, that in divine speech the word *Esh* is considered a divine name, which is interpreted as "fire." This is that greatest fire of God, which he showed us on earth along with the divine voice, saying: "This is my beloved Son." And to them he said: "I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I wish but that it be kindled?" 

To help you understand and perceive more clearly (for I do not deal with you through ambiguities and obscure twists of words, but I shall act purposefully and openly), store this in your deepest senses: it will be a matter of no small account that *Esh*, which in Hebrew signifies fire, represents this body—not a celestial body, 
<margin>Against those denying the humanity of Christ.</margin> 
nor ethereal, nor deceptive, nor merely appearing—as the Manichaeans, Eutychians, Marcion, and Timothy Aelurus <note>A reference to various early Christian heresies that questioned the physical reality of Christ's human body</note> deliriously dreamed in their sleep—but a terrestrial body, such as the fire Moses names on earth, when we discuss it according to Pythagorean Cabala. 

O thing delightful to hear! Truly we shall find it consists of the same universal measure as our name of August Majesty, *IHSVH* (יהשוה), with equal harmony and balanced proportion. Furthermore, you will perhaps say: why do you say this *Esh*, which stands in the middle and makes the second syllable, should be pronounced not by common custom, but according to the usage of the Holy Language (for so they call the idiom of the Hebrew speech), 
<margin>Middle syllable.</margin> 
when we deal with sacred Scriptures and mysteries? O how I would not hesitate to introduce you more willingly into the inner shrines of mysteries, if I were to respond in the speech of Paul of Tarsus, when he says: "Thanks be to you, for this salvation has been sent to the heathens and the nations, and they themselves shall hear it." 

But I shall remain in the holy idiom, and thus I will explain the most sacred Hebrew name more easily and more clearly, in the manner and property of that same language. For Baruchias maintained in his dispute that the name *Esh* itself is more consistent with sacred things. Come now, you wish to explore precisely this consonant letter that is inserted; however, care must be taken that you do not forget the letters which precede and follow in the composition of this name. For there are only four, *IHVH* (יהוה), of which that ineffable Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter name of God, often rendered as Yahweh or Jehovah</note> consists, and which most properly demonstrate the divine nature—just as has been shown at great length and sometimes most memorably by this associate of ours. Since these cannot be spoken by human voice or faculty, it was certainly not fitting for God to be incarnated, besides these, another with the fiery...

# ON THE MIRACULOUS WORD, BOOK III.

...merely a character by which the unutterable sound and the then-invisible mark of the unnamable God might now, at last, resonate between human teeth and thus be called out speakably; so that what was previously uninvocable may now be felt as vocable. The Hebrews call this letter the consonant *Shin* (ש), which St. Jerome the priest <note>Jerome (c. 347–420 AD) was the primary translator of the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate) and a major authority for Renaissance scholars like Reuchlin.</note> interprets as "teeth." Writing to Paula of Rome, he says: "The seventh connection, which is the last, wherein there is a mystical understanding even in that number seven:

<margin>Dental letters.</margin>

*Qoph*, *Resh*, *Shin*, *Tav* (ק, ר, ש, ת): that is, 'calling,' 'of the head,' 'of the teeth,' 'signs.' Through the teeth, the articulated voice is brought forth, and one comes to the kingdom of heaven." I ask you, what is more sacred than this mystery? What is more pleasant than the delight of this sacrament? What foods, what honeys are sweeter than knowing the wisdom of God, entering into His secrets, beholding the mind of the Creator, and learning more fully through spiritual wisdom the words of the Lord your God, which are mocked by the "wise" of this world? These are not my words, but Jerome’s—a man of such authority that I might not seem to some to be trying to devise a fiction. 

Since teeth, then, are the most powerful instruments of speech—of which the letter *Shin* (ש) is said to be the most famous—is it any wonder if all the grammarians more noble than the rest (to say nothing of the theologians themselves) agree with me? Is it not clear that this element, and no other, was most conveniently summoned for the pronunciation of the ineffable Name? I truly do not know how it happened that the correct establishment of that venerable—or rather, adorable—Name has been probably noticed by no one until now, not even by one or two of the learned men and masters of divine philosophy. If we had used their discoveries for this discourse of ours, we could have been relieved of no small burden of meditation. Yet there are certain fitting aids and supports for this work found hidden in their volumes; we must lean on these diligently, not so much to discover the cause as to confirm what we have already found. Such is that excellent point which we recently fished out of Jerome’s letter.

->On the states of the world, and the arithmetical reasoning of the name of God.<-
->CHAPTER XIII.<-

I PERCEIVE <note>The Latin text reads "Serno," likely a printer's error for "Sentio" (I perceive).</note> that your minds have conceived no small delight in discussing this name IHSVH <note>The Pentagrammaton, יהשוה</note>. I shall add something of joy so that you may be more delighted and listen to me with a more cheerful countenance. It has been found through mathematical reasoning that a "body" must be sought in a composition of many parts, while "spirit" is sought in the simplicity of units. 

<margin>Most simple Divinity.</margin>

The closer any thing approaches unity, the more spiritual it is and the more cleansed from the attachments of matter. We have that most simple divinity of the Word of God, which is designated by unity itself. However, from Hebrew teachings, its mark is learned to contain those four characters of the Tetragrammaton name <note>The four-letter name of God, יהוה (IHVH)</note>. It remains for us to seek the "body" of the Incarnate One and its character. 

<margin>Composite body.</margin>

Let us therefore look to the "multitude" and to the time of the Incarnation, so that by the proportion of the sign to the thing signified, we may become more perceptive. First, at what age of the world did He who came for the world’s salvation assume a body? You will rightly answer me, with the Apostle's agreement: "In the final, or latest, days." For we are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come. 

<margin>Ages of the world, according to Elijah.</margin>

Concerning the ages of the world, different men have handed down different accounts. Ovid and the crowd of poets affirm there are four ages of the world; Hesiod says five, like the statue in Daniel's vision; others say six, according to the *Hexaemeron* <note>original: "ἑξαήμερον," the six days of creation</note> in which God created all things; others say seven, which is also my opinion. But they do not divide them according to my view, those who say the future age is the seventh age. For then God will create a new heaven and a new earth, and make all things new, as the sacred words suggest. Therefore, that will not be an age of *this* world, but a new world—not just a Sabbath, which the Hebrews consider the seventh, but a Sabbath of Sabbaths, and a duration of eternity...

<margin>State of the world.</margin>

I call an "age" a state of the world that exists between two significant and shared transitions, much like foreign movements of people. 

<margin>I. Age: Created <note>Hebrew: ברא (Bara)</note>.</margin>

Indeed, I judge the first to have been when the heavens and the earth, and all their adornment, were perfected. "And God saw all that He had made, and they were very good." This was done in the evening and the morning of the sixth day. Then followed a great movement 

<margin>II. [He was]</margin>

of the world after the seventh day, when God spoke to Adam: "Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree which I commanded you not to eat, cursed is the earth in your work." From the creation of the world, therefore, until the transgression of Adam, the first age of the world is established according to my meager judgment. 

<margin>III. [Generation/Torah]</margin>

From that point to the flood of Noah is the second age. The third, indeed, is from Noah to Abraham and circumcision, which is said to have occurred when the faithful people of God were separated from the idolaters at the Euphrates river. Hence Abraham was surnamed **The Hebrew** <note>Hebrew: העברי (Ha-Ivri)</note>, named after the language which the Hebrews, the sons of Shelah, had preserved intact for their own; "Hebrew" essentially means "from across the river," as if he were a "cross-over traveler" of the Euphrates. 

<margin>IV. [Completion]</margin>

From Abraham to the written law of Moses and the manifold ceremonies, we shall count the fourth age. 

<margin>V. [Foundation]</margin>

The fifth age comprises the kingdom of the Hebrews, beginning after the destruction of Troy, when they began to calculate time by **lustra** <note>A *lustrum* was a period of five years in the Roman calendar, used here by Reuchlin to sync Biblical and Classical history.</note>. 

<margin>VI. Authority.</margin>

The sixth age lasted until the city now called Rome, when individual matters were governed by the uncertain hand of a king, with no established law or legislation except for those minor decrees which Romulus later sanctified for the people, called the **Curiate Laws**. Regarding these, you may more accurately read the volumes of **Sextus Papirius** <note>A legendary Roman jurist said to have collected the laws of the kings.</note> on the history of power. That era began to count years by Olympiads, just as the preceding era did by *lustra*, until the age of the **Birth** <note>original: γένεσις (genesis)</note>, when the entire world was registered for annual censuses and tributes. 

<margin>Indiction.</margin>

This we call, up to our own times, the **Indiction** <note>A 15-year cycle used in Roman and Medieval administration for tax and dating purposes.</note>, containing three Olympiads <note>An Olympiad is four years; Reuchlin's math here reflects a specific medieval chronological tradition.</note>, which constitutes the seventh age. If you evaluate these things truly and fairly, and not with a sluggish mind, I shall rejoice that a moderate fruit of my studies is at hand. But if, as I fear, I offend someone with a far different view of my attempt, I will at least seem to have wished to please; nonetheless, according to my own talent and the reality of the matter, I shall place Christ in the number 

<margin>The Body is to be sought in the multitude.</margin>

of the ages—that is, that He assumed a body around the seventh age of this world. The "body," as we have said, must be sought in the "multitude" <note>In Reuchlin's Pythagorean/Kabbalistic logic, "multitude" refers to the expansion of numbers or letters.</note>. <margin>Mediator.</margin>

the letter **Shin** (ש) will appear in the seventh house and in the middle place of that connection, designating the **Mediator** of God and man, who is both God and man, one from both. Moreover, the connection of the seventh house is specifically held by the letters **Shin** (ש) and **Tav** (ת), which is interpreted in Latin as "of the Head." 

By the letter **Shin**, as if the alphabet were predicting and foretelling by prophecy, it is shown that this very letter would be the most fit character for figuring the name **IHSVH** (יהשוה), whom God 

<margin>The Body of the Church is the end of the law and the sign which is spoken against.</margin>

gave as the "head over the whole church, which is his body," as we read in the letter to the Ephesians. <margin>Holy <note>Hebrew: קדש (Kadosh)</note></margin>

Indeed, the heap of speech from these three—namely, the *Name*, the *Tetragrammaton*, and *Called*—collected together, is understood by the frequent use of the letter **Shin** (ש) according to the Kabbalah of the Hebrews. Thus, if the last things correspond to the first, this prophecy contains nothing else than: "If you hear the voice of **IHVH**"—that is, when the Tetragrammaton becomes audible and utterable—then the Tetragrammaton, "called" through the letter **Shin**, shall be upon you. It is just as if he were saying, *Shin*...

# ON THE MIRIFIC WORD, BOOK III. 969

If the unpronounceable **Tetragrammaton** <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH</note> is to become pronounceable, it must necessarily be called through the consonant named **Shin** (ש), so that it becomes **IHShVH** [יהשוה], who shall be above you, your head and your lord. Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord **IHShVH** [יהשוה] Christ, who from above drops into us the knowledge of the true name of His only-begotten Son and our Savior—or, according to the Greeks, our "healer." For Greek authors derive this name from "medicating" and "healing." <note>original: "à medendo & sanando"</note> The Hebrew grammarians, however, derive it from "saving," so that they think **IHShVH** [יהשוה] is the same as "Savior." Yet "savior" is a common noun, while **IHShVH** [יהשוה] is a most proper name, so much so that it fits no other except the incarnate Son of God. This is achieved by the variety of letters from which the word consists, the likes of which has never been heard in any other since the beginning of time.

---

### *Concerning other saviors to whom this name does not apply.*
### CHAPTER XIV.

<margin>Divinity in the names of mortals.</margin>
Within the memory of our fathers, there were many "saviors" called Jesus, but with different letters and different syllables. For no one ever dared to use these specific letters together for their own name, because the entirety of the Godhead is contained within them. But whoever was considered to be endowed with some holiness greatly desired to obtain some letter from those holy characters for his own name. For example, **Abram** [אברם] received the letter **He** (ה). For God said to him: "No longer shall your name be called Abram, but you shall be named **Abraham** [אברהם]." <margin>The added letter *Yod*.</margin> And **Hosea** [הושע] obtained the letter **Yod** (י). For when Moses decided to send men to explore the land of Canaan, he placed over them Hosea the son of Nun, of the tribe of Ephraim; so that he might have a more saving strength, Moses changed his name and added **Yod** (י), the first letter of the ineffable name, and called Hosea the son of Nun **Ihosua** [יהושע]—which our people have also translated as "Jesus." We also read of another from Beth-shemesh, whose memory is recited in the Book of Samuel. And a third with a similar name in the Book of Ezra, the son of Jozadak, who does not keep the **He** (ה), but is named **Jesue**. We also find in the prayer of the prophet Habakkuk, in the third-to-last verse, when he says: "But I will rejoice in the Lord, and I will exult in God my Jesus," that it is read again composed of fewer syllables as **Ishi** [ישעי]: <note>Hebrew: "my salvation"</note> that is, "salvation." It is as if the prophet said: "I will exult in God my salvation," which should by no means be considered the proper name of God, but rather His **Epithet** <note>A descriptive title</note> or an appositive construction. There is also a fourth, the high priest standing before the angel, from whom the angel took away his iniquity in the sight of Zechariah; he is likewise written with letters similar to the son of Nun, **Ihosua** [יהושע]. It is thought that Zechariah, in that place, saw a shadow of the true light that was to come. We read of a fifth, **Jesus son of Sirach**, who lived in the time of King Ptolemy of Egypt, surnamed Euergetes, and who is believed to have published the book titled <margin>Who was Sirach?</margin> **Ecclesiasticus**. However many there may be who are named "Jesus" in our common speech, none of them possesses those exact letters which this incarnate Word of God—our God, through whom the Creator also made the ages—possesses. His excellent name is full of wonderful majesty: a name renowned, fortunate, venerable, a name of the weightiest and greatest dignity, of most powerful authority in heaven and the highest office on earth; pleasant to angels, revered by men, and terrible to demons. It is composed of five letters: that is, from the four-letter name [the Tetragrammaton] and one inserted **Shin** (ש), by a wondrous craftsmanship of the Holy Spirit. Just as He to whom the name belongs is acknowledged to consist of divine and human essence. For as the rational soul and the flesh are one man, so God and man are one Christ. And thus the name **IHShVH** [יהשוה] is pronounced with the four-letter names and one consonant **Shin** (ש), so that it announces Him who is **Iah** [יה]: that is, God, and **Sauah** [שוע]: that is, "veiled." <note>Reuchlin is using a mystical etymology to suggest the name means "God Veiled" in human flesh.</note> To whom Isaiah speaks thus: "Truly you are a hidden God, the God of Israel, the Savior." This is difficult to believe, most excellent men, if my weak speech were not strengthened by the sacred monuments of the prophets. Therefore, I pray you, hear...
